en: The Vinaya of the Mūlasarvāstivāda School, Volume One.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Yijing by Imperial Command.
Introduction to the Vinaya. Introduction to the Vinaya.
I prostrate to the World-Honored One of Great Compassion, who is able to pity all beings;
whose face is full like the rising sun, and whose eyes are pure like blue lotuses.
The Buddha was born into a family of self-discipline, and his assembly of disciples is likewise disciplined.
Taming and eliminating all faults, I pay homage to the Honored One among the Dharma.
The Buddha taught the Three Piṭakas; the Vinaya is its foremost.
Within this teaching, I shall briefly set forth its praise.
Just as the root is supreme, from which branches and trunk arise;
so the Buddha taught that the Vinaya is the foundation, capable of giving birth to all wholesome dharmas.
It is like a great embankment, which a torrential flood cannot overstep.
The Dharma of the precepts is likewise: it can restrain the violation of prohibitions.
That the Buddhas realize Bodhi, that the Pratyekabuddhas possess tranquil body and mind, and that the Arhats attain their state—all are accomplished through the practice of the Vinaya.
The worthy sages of the three times, having distanced themselves from the bonds of the conditioned,
all take the Vinaya as their foundation and are thus able to reach the place of peace and security.
If this teaching of discipline remains established in the world, [the Dharma will endure].
These are the Tathāgatas themselves; the treasury of the True Dharma shall not perish.
Morality is that which can establish the lamp of the Tathāgata’s True Dharma;
apart from this, there would be no path to the peace of Nirvāṇa.
The Buddha wanders through the world, preaching the Dharma wherever he goes;
yet the teachings of the Vinaya are not like this, and thus one knows they are difficult to encounter.
Just as the earth supports all living beings and can cause all plants and trees to grow;
The Vinaya teachings are likewise; they can give rise to all merit and wisdom.
The Buddha taught that through the Vinaya teachings, one can produce manifold virtues;
by upholding them, one attains liberation, but by violating them, one is born into the evil realms.
If elephants and horses are not tamed, they are controlled with hooks and whips;
the precepts and teachings are likewise, bringing those who are untamed to goodness and compliance.
Just as a city has moats and ditches that can ward off all enemies, so too do the precepts protect the mind.
The Vinaya teachings are likewise able to prevent the breaking of precepts;
just as the waters of the great ocean can float away a corpse,
so too do the Vinaya teachings eliminate all violations of the precepts.
The Vinaya is the king among dharmas, the foremost guide of all Buddhas;
for bhikṣus it is like a merchant caravan, a priceless treasure.
Breaking the precepts exceeds the venom of a snake, while the Vinaya is like the agada medicine.
The vigor of youth is difficult to tame; take the precepts as its bridle and reins.
The precepts serve as a constant bridge over the path of virtue, and they can also act as a boat or raft across the ocean of evil destinies.
If one travels upon a perilous path, the precepts serve as a skillful guide;
if one ascends the city of fearlessness, the precepts serve as the ladder and steps.
The Great Teacher, the Most Victorious Honored One, personally proclaimed this teaching of the Vinaya.
These two are without distinction; all should pay homage and take refuge in them.
Both the Buddha and his noble disciples abide by the teachings of the Vinaya;
because they cultivate reverence for the precepts, I pay homage and take refuge in them.
I praise according to the Vinaya; this teaching should be revered.
By taking refuge at the very beginning, auspicious matters are accomplished.
The great ocean of the Vinaya is so vast its limits are difficult to know.
The characteristics of its distinctions are infinite; how could I possibly detail them all?
The Great Master’s ocean of Vinaya teachings is profoundly deep and difficult to fathom;
now, according to my own capacity, I shall briefly praise but a small portion thereof.
When the World-Honored One was about to enter parinirvāṇa, he addressed the great assembly:
"After my passing, you all should revere the precepts.
Therefore, I offer this eulogy, wishing to expound the Vinaya.
You virtuous ones, with sincere hearts, Should listen well to this teaching on discipline.
The Prātimokṣa Sūtra is difficult to hear Even throughout immeasurable koṭis of kalpas;
The same applies to its recitation, study, and upholding, But one who practices according to what is taught is even rarer to encounter.
The appearance of the Buddhas in the world is bliss; the proclamation of the subtle and sublime True Dharma is bliss.
The harmony of the Saṅgha in shared vision is bliss; their united practice with courageous diligence is bliss.
To see the noble ones is joy; to dwell together with them is also joy.
Not seeing those who are deluded is what is called constantly experiencing happiness.
To see one who is endowed with ethical discipline is happiness; to see one who is learned is also called happiness.
To see an Arhat is true happiness, because they are no longer subject to future rebirth.
There is joy in the delightful stairway at the river’s crossing; there is joy in conquering enemies through the Dharma.
When the fruit of right wisdom is realized, there is the joy of being able to eliminate the conceit of "I" entirely.
If one can form a resolute intention, well subduing the senses and desires while possessing great learning;
from youth until old age dwelling in the forest, one finds joy in the tranquility of living alone in an araṇya.
With palms joined in reverence, pay homage to the Lion of the Śākyas;
I shall speak of the Prātimokṣa Discipline—listen well, O virtuous ones.
Having heard it, you should practice correctly, just as the Great Sage has taught.
Regarding even minor transgressions, one should guard them with vigor and diligence.
The horse of the mind is difficult to restrain; it must be controlled with constant and resolute effort.
The Prātimokṣa is like a bit, possessing a hundred needles of extreme sharpness.
If a person violates the rules of conduct, they can stop as soon as they hear the teaching;
like a noble steed, such a Great Being shall emerge from the battle array of afflictions.
If a person lacks this bit, they will never experience joy.
They have perished in the battle against afflictions, Wandering deludedly through birth and death.
The summary verse for the four *pārājika* dharmas says:
If one commits impure conduct, Or takes what is not given, or kills a human;
To falsely claim the qualities of a superior person—these cases all entail non-cohabitation.
1. The Training Rule on Impure Conduct (Aśubha-caryā-śikṣāpada), Part One of the First: A Summary Verse says:
Suvarṇa was without offense; the bhikṣu was in the forest.
A weak waist, long roots, and the three offenses in the Land of Utmost Joy;
Sleeping in one’s chamber during the day, and those free from desire in the secluded forest;
Virtue and former causes and conditions—one should know that these verses encompass them all.
At that time, from his initial attainment of enlightenment until twelve years had passed, none of the Śrāvaka disciples had committed any transgression, nor had any sores yet arisen.
The World-Honored One, for the sake of his disciples, spoke this brief Prātimokṣa Sūtra:
"Commit no evil whatsoever; Cultivate all that is wholesome;
Thoroughly discipline your own mind— This is the teaching of all Buddhas."
To guard the body is excellent;
to guard speech is also good;
to guard the mind is excellent!
Complete restraint is most excellent.
A bhikṣu who guards everything can be liberated from all suffering;
he should well guard his speech and also well guard his mind.
"Do no evil with the body, Always purify the three types of action;
This is how one can follow The path traveled by the Great Sage.

In the thirteenth year, while [the Buddha] was in the country of Vṛji, at the time he was in the village of Kalandaka. There lived a son of Kalandaka named Sujāta, who was wealthy with abundant resources and many servants; his gold, silver, precious jewels, grain, and barley overflowed, and his stored wealth was like that of King Vaiśravaṇa.
He took a wife from a family of equal status and lived in happiness.
At another time, he conceived deep faith and reverence for the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha; he took refuge in the Triple Gem and received the five precepts:
namely, he completely abstained from killing, stealing, sexual misconduct, false speech, and the drinking of intoxicants.
Because his reverence and faith increased day by day, he abandoned the home life for the homeless state out of right conviction, shaving off his hair and beard and donning the dharma robes.
Having thus gone forth, he lived in association with his kinsmen, no different from when he was formerly at home.
At that time, the Venerable Sujāta thought to himself:

"How can I, having gone forth in this well-spoken Dharma and Vinaya, remain mingled with my kinsmen when there is yet to be realized what ought to be realized, and yet to be attained what ought to be attained?"
"I should now abandon my kinsmen and, taking up my robes and bowl, wander among the people.
Having formed this thought, he immediately left his relatives and traveled to another region.
During a time of famine, it was difficult to obtain alms; even parents would not provide for their own children, let alone other beggars.
Having had this thought, Sūciṇṇa reflected:
"Now my kinsmen possess abundant wealth and food; I ought to go to the village of Kalandaka and urge them to offer extensive almsgiving to the field of merit that is the Saṃgha."

Whether it be parched grain, rice gruel, regular alms-food, food offered upon invitation, or food provided on the eighth, fourteenth, or fifteenth day of the lunar month, he instructs his kinsmen to perform even small meritorious deeds for their own benefit.
Then Sūtraṇa, having left that region, took up his robes and bowl and traveled by stages until he reached the village of Karṇaṭaka; not far from there, he stayed in a small cell within an araṇya.
Then Sūciṇa went to his kinsmen and extensively praised the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha for them, causing the great assembly to provide various offerings and thereby bring about their benefit.

At that time, Soṇa was practicing the dhuta ascetic virtues in an araṇya; he possessed only the three robes made of discarded rags and always practiced alms-seeking by going from house to house in sequence.

On a certain day, after his kinsmen had daily offered excellent and delicious food to the community of monks, Soṇa took his robe and bowl and entered the village to beg in order. Upon arriving at his own home, he received nothing and departed.
Suḍaṇṇā’s mother had gone away on business; at that time, an old maidservant saw Suḍaṇṇa from afar, recognized his features, and knowing he had obtained nothing, she departed in haste.
Having seen this, the old maidservant went to the mother of Sujāta and said:
"Mistress, do you know?
Your eldest son Sujāta, who has been away from his native village for a long time, has now returned to his former home; having failed to obtain what he requested, he departed in haste."
At that time, Sujātā’s mother thought to herself:
"Could it be that my son has developed longing?
Has he become unhappy and wishes to return to the secular life? Does he no longer love the śramaṇa life and find it burdensome? Is he ashamed, weary of, and renouncing the practice of a śramaṇa?"
Having had this thought, he then departed from the village and arrived at the place where Soṇa resided, saying to him:
"Soṇa! Do you have any longing or attachment?"
"Is it because you have conceived a lack of joy and desire to return to the secular life?
Do you not love the state of a śramaṇa, but instead suffer under the burdens of being a śramaṇa, feeling ashamed and weary of the śramaṇa's practice? Sujaṇa!"

Listen now to my household goods and the dowry I received at my marriage: I have accumulated such a vast hoard of gold and silver that if people were to sit on both sides of it, they would not be able to see one another.

Furthermore, your father’s wealth—including official seals, gold, and silver—amounts to hundreds, thousands, tens of thousands, millions, and billions; what need is there to mention his other various kinds of goods? You may return home and enjoy pleasures as you wish, or perform meritorious acts of charity as you please.
When these words had been spoken, Sūṣeṇa said to his mother:

"I have no lingering attachment or affection that would cause me displeasure at returning to my former home; nor do I feel any lack of love for the śramaṇas, nor am I distressed by being a śramaṇa, nor do I feel shame, aversion, or renunciation."
When Sūṣeṇa’s mother heard these words, she thought to herself:
“It is not within my power to make him return to the lay life; I must devise another plan.”
Then the mother returned home and said to her daughter-in-law, "If your menses arrive, you must inform me.
The daughter-in-law respectfully agreed. Later, at another time, when her menses had indeed arrived, she spoke to her, saying:
"Everyone! My menstrual period has now arrived; what should I do?
Her mother-in-law said:

"When the time had passed, he bathed, donned a crown of various flower garlands, anointed himself with famous incenses, and put on all manner of necklaces and ornaments; every article for adorning the body was fully prepared, just as Suvarṇa used to do when he was formerly a householder, performing all the activities that his heart delighted in."
Having heard this, the wife completed her preparations and returned to her mother-in-law, saying:
"Madam! I have done for you exactly what Sūciṇḍa formerly loved; I have bathed and adorned my body and put on my garments. If there is anything to be done, now is the time."

Then Sujātā’s mother, together with her daughter-in-law, departed in the same carriage and went to the place where Sujātā resided; having arrived, she alighted from the carriage and proceeded on foot.
At that time, Soṇa was walking up and down for exercise outside a small hut. When his mother saw him, she said to him:
"Soṇa! As you have said, 'I have no longing or attachment,' and so forth, as described above."
"Now, my daughter-in-law, your body is pure; you should preserve the seed so that our property does not fall into the hands of the government.

At that time, Sūciṇḍa had not yet been subject to the formulated precepts and did not perceive the faults of desire. Seeing the young woman, his mind became stained with attachment; the fire of lust burned within him, and he said to his mother, "How could this be appropriate for me?"
The mother said, "To leave behind the seed of progeny, the method ought to be thus.
Then, Suvarṇa took hold of her two hands and led her to a secluded place; there he removed his dharma robes and immediately engaged in unchaste conduct three times.

At that time, there was a sentient being who sought the supreme practice; possessing the nature of liberation, he was oriented toward nirvāṇa and turned his back on birth-and-death within the three realms and five destinies, having no mind for attachment or delight therein. In his final body, he descended from a sublime and wondrous heaven to take conception in a womb.
If a woman of clear wisdom possesses five kinds of distinctive knowledge that differ from other women:
first, she knows when a man has a lustful mind;
second, she knows the proper seasons.
Third, she knows from whom she has conceived;
fourth, she knows it is a male;
fifth, she knows it is a female.
If it is a male, he remains by the right side; if it is a female, she dwells on the left side.
At that time, the wife’s heart was filled with joy, and she said to her mother-in-law:
"Do you know, my lady?"
"I am already pregnant, dwelling on my right side; it will certainly be a son who shall bring glory to our lineage.
Upon hearing this, her mother-in-law was filled with great joy and spoke these words:

"From of old, I have longed for a virtuous son to carry on our family line, hoping that as he grows up, he would always remember to repay my kindness and constantly cultivate merit and wisdom for our benefit."

Once her mother-in-law understood this matter, she placed the new bride in a high tower and provided for her needs at all times. Female physicians prepared her meals with such precision that no error occurred, and she was adorned with necklaces and ornaments, moving with a majestic deportment like a celestial maiden wandering in the Nandana Grove.

He always remained seated upon his couch with his feet never touching the ground; his eyes never beheld offensive sights, nor did his ears ever hear foul sounds; in sleeping, eating, or moving about, he was never subject to discomfort or contradiction.

After nine months had passed, she gave birth to a son whose countenance was so dignified and handsome that all people loved him; his forehead was broad, his eyebrows long, and his nose high and straight; his head was rounded like a parasol and his complexion as beautiful as gold; his hands reached below his knees, and everyone looked up to him with reverence.
After twenty-one days had passed, he held a gathering for his kinsmen. His paternal aunt addressed the relatives regarding the child, saying, "What name shall we give this boy?
The assembly deliberated and said:
"This child was obtained through the principle of seeds; he may be named 'Seed' (Bīja).
His paternal aunt then assigned him eight nurses:
two to provide milk and nourishment, two to carry him in swaddling clothes, two for bathing, and two to play with him joyfully.
He was nourished with milk, curd, clarified butter, refined honey, and other exquisite, sweet foods and drinks, whereby he grew rapidly, like a lotus emerging from a pond.

Having gradually reached the age of childhood, he studied various arts and skills—calculation, writing, and sealing—and he mastered the subtleties of taking and giving, as well as pledging and receiving collateral.
He was highly proficient in the eight types of divination and physiognomy:

namely, the examination of jewels, the examination of garments, the examination of dwellings, the examination of trees, the examination of elephants, the examination of horses, the examination of men, and the examination of women.
At another time, he developed deep and correct faith, took refuge in the Triple Gem, and received the five precepts; his faith grew moment by moment, just like that of his father.

He then abandoned the household life for the homeless state to seek the practice of liberation. Within the well-expounded Dharma and Vinaya, he shaved off his hair and beard and donned the dharma robes. Dwelling alone in seclusion, free from heedlessness, he applied himself with diligence and vigor, abiding in focused mindfulness, and purely cultivated the holy life.

In this very life, he realized full awakening; having shattered the shell of ignorance and severed the delusions of the three realms, he became an Arhat. Possessing the three knowledges and six supernormal powers, endowed with the eight liberations, he attained knowledge in accordance with reality: "Birth has been exhausted, the holy life has been established, what was to be done has been accomplished, and there is no further existence."

The mind is free from obstruction, like a hand waving through space; whether cut by a blade or anointed with fragrance, neither love nor hatred arises. Viewing gold and earth as equal and without distinction, one renounces all fame and profit; even Śakra, Brahmā, and the various devas all pay him reverence.
At that time, the Venerable Bījaka, having realized arhatship and experienced the bliss of liberation, spoke this verse:
"The noble practice is now perfected; I shall not fall from my father’s inheritance.
In this, my final body, All faults and afflictions are utterly eliminated."

At that time, after Soṇa had committed an act of unchastity, the Blessed One was teaching the Dharma amidst a great assembly of immeasurable hundreds of thousands of śrāvaka bhikṣus, namely: the liberation of mind and wisdom through detachment from greed, hatred, and delusion.

At that time, Sūḍañña was also among the assembly listening to the Buddha’s teaching of the Dharma. Having heard the Dharma, his heart was filled with sorrow and distress, and he felt deep remorse. With a downcast countenance and face bowed low, he remained silent and speechless; he then returned to his cell and dwelt there brooding over his grief.

Later, at another time, there were certain bhikṣus who, while touring the dwellings, arrived in succession at the room where Soḍaṇa resided; as they conversed together, they saw Soḍaṇa dwelling there filled with sorrow.
Then the bhikṣus said to Soṇa:
"In the past, when you saw a guest arrive, you would greet him with a joyful smile and first cry out 'Welcome!', while holding his robe, bowl, and various requisites for him."
Why is it that now, seeing us approach, you remain with a sorrowful heart, face bowed down, silent and speechless?
Sujaṇḍana, are you afflicted by physical illness?
"Are you suffering from heart pain?
Then Sūcarṇa said to them:
"Venerable ones!..."
"I do not have a physical illness, but my mind is burning with fever.
He asked, "For what reason is your mind burning with fever?"
Then Sūtraṇa related the matter in detail.

When the bhikṣus had heard his account, they neither rejoiced nor felt resentment; they rose from their seats and returned to the presence of the Buddha. Having arrived, they prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, sat to one side, and reported this incident in full to the World-Honored One.
At that time, the Blessed One addressed the bhikṣus, saying:
"This Sūciṇṇa previously committed unrighteous acts and impure conduct within the realm of outflows.

Then, for this reason, the Blessed One assembled the community of bhikṣus. The Buddha is the knower and the seer; he asks knowing the answer and does not ask without knowing it. He asks at the proper time and does not ask at the improper time. He asks when there is benefit and does not ask when there is no benefit. He asks to break through barriers and remove doubts, asking only when there is benefit. He then addressed Sūciṇṇa, saying:
“Did you truly commit such an unseemly act?
He replied to the Buddha,
“It is true, Blessed One.”
"Venerable One! the Buddha said to Sūjaṇḍa: "You are not a śramaṇa;
you do not practice in accordance [with the Dharma]; you are impure; you lack dignified deportment; this is not what one who has gone forth should do."
"Sonadanda!

Why have you now, having gone forth from the household life into this subtle Dharma taught by me—which is liberation of mind through wisdom and free from greed, hatred, and delusion—perpetrated such an unrighteous and loathsome act?"
"O fool! It would be better for you to place your male organ in the mouth of a fierce and venomous snake than to place it within a female organ.
Having thus rebuked Sūciṇḍa with various skillful means regarding the impurity of such matters, the Blessed One addressed the bhikṣus:
"For this reason and by these causes, I perceive ten benefits and establish a training rule for my śrāvaka disciples within the Vinaya.
What are these ten?
First, for the sake of maintaining the integrity of the Saṃgha."
2. To cause the Saṃgha to rejoice;
3. To cause the Saṃgha to dwell in happiness;
4. To subdue those who violate the precepts.
Fifth, because those with a sense of shame attain peace;
sixth, because it causes the faithless to gain faith;
seventh, because it increases the faith of those who already possess it.
8. Because it severs present outflows;
9. Because it severs future outflows;
10. Because it causes the holy life to endure for a long time.
To manifest and propagate the True Dharma for the great benefit of humans and devas,
I now establish a training rule (*śikṣāpada*) within the Vinaya for my śrāvaka disciples, which should be recited as follows: "If a bhikṣu,
having received the same training rules as the other bhikṣus, does not relinquish those rules nor confess his weakness in training, yet engages in impure conduct— the act of sexual intercourse."
"This bhikṣu also incurs a pārājika offense; he should not live in communal residence.
At that time, after the Blessed One had established this training rule for the bhikṣus, he was staying at the Bamboo Grove near the Kakrandaka Lake.
At that time, there was a bhikṣu living in a small hermitage cell not far from there.

In that forest, a female macaque, driven by a craving for food and drink, went to the bhikṣu’s location; the bhikṣu would regularly give her his leftover food, and they subsequently engaged in unchaste conduct together.

At that time, a great number of bhikṣus, traveling about for sightseeing, arrived at an araṇya and reached the dwelling place of the bhikṣus; they then conversed with one another and sat down to one side.

That female monkey, remembering her previous misdeeds, came to his location; looking at the bhikṣu, she drew close to him with her body. Upon seeing this, the bhikṣu was ashamed to be seen by others and immediately pushed her away, doing so a second and a third time.

At that time, the female monkey became greatly enraged; she immediately used her claws to tear and scratch the bhikṣu, so that his head, face, and robes were all ripped and torn, as she then moved to one side, crying out and leaping about.
When the bhikṣus saw this, they immediately asked: "Venerable one!

Why did this wild monkey, upon first arriving, look at your face and then press its body against you? As soon as you saw it, you repelled it; thus it did so a second and third time, whereupon it became enraged, clawed and tore at your robes until they were all rent, and then cried out and leaped about?"
Then that bhikṣu reported the matter in full.
When the other bhikṣus heard it, they said to him:
"Venerable one!..."
"Is it not the case that the Blessed One prohibited the bhikṣus from engaging in unchaste conduct?
He replied, "The Blessed One’s formulation of the precepts prohibits [this] only for those in the human realm, but does not prohibit it for animals."

When the bhikṣus heard these words, they neither censured nor rejoiced, but left him and went together with him to the place where the Buddha was. Having prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, they sat to one side and reported the aforementioned matter in detail to the World-Honored One.
The World-Honored One said:
"If even those in the human realm are to be restrained, how much more so those in the animal realm!
That foolish person has committed a *pārājika* offense."
At that time, the Blessed One, for this reason, assembled the community of bhikṣus and, though he already knew the matter,
asked them intentionally: "Bhikṣus,
is it true that you have committed such an unseemly act, an evil deed?"
He replied, "It is truly so.
The World-Honored One rebuked him in various ways, as extensively explained before.
At that time, the Blessed One addressed the bhikṣus:
"The former was the original enactment; this is the subsequent enactment. I now further establish a training rule for the bhikṣus within the Vinaya, which should be recited as follows:

'If a bhikṣu, having received the training rules together with other bhikṣus, does not relinquish those training rules and does not confess his weakness in training, yet commits an impure act through the method of sexual intercourse—even with an animal—this bhikṣu also incurs a pārājika offense and shall not live in community [with the others]. "
"Furthermore, regarding the term 'bhikṣu,' this refers to Sūciṇḍa and others.
There are five kinds of bhikṣus:
first, the bhikṣu by name;"
2. Bhikṣus by self-assertion;
3. Bhikṣus by begging;
4. Bhikṣus who have destroyed the afflictions.
Fifth, the bhikṣu who has received full ordination through the formal procedure of one motion and three proclamations (*jñapti-caturtha-karman*).

Regarding the "bhikṣu by name": this refers to one who has been given the designation "bhikṣu" as a personal name, or one who is so called because he is commonly recognized as such by the world, or because he belongs to a clan of bhikṣus; such a person is called a "bhikṣu by name."
What is one who claims to be a bhikṣu by his own word?

If a person is not actually a bhikṣu, yet says of himself, "I am a bhikṣu," or if he is a "thief-dweller" (cora-vāsin) who calls himself a bhikṣu—this is called claiming to be a bhikṣu by one's own word.
What is a mendicant bhikṣu?
If there are laypeople who constantly live their lives by begging for alms, they are called mendicant bhikṣus.
What is a bhikṣu who has destroyed the afflictions?

If a person can sever all the burning fevers of the outflows and afflictions, as well as the various sufferings of maturation—future birth, aging, and death—and can thoroughly understand how to eradicate their root forever, such that they realize the state of non-arising like the cutting off of the crown of a *tāla* tree, this one is called a bhikṣu who has destroyed the afflictions.
What is a bhikṣu who is fully ordained through the *jñapti-caturtha-karman*?
It refers to one who has no physical impediments or obstacles, whose ritual procedure is complete, and who is beyond reproach; such a person is called a bhikṣu fully ordained by *karman*.
Regarding the meaning of "bhikṣu" mentioned here, the intention is to take the fifth [category].
The word "furthermore" (punar) indicates that there are other similar types.
"Together with the bhikṣus" means together with all the other bhikṣus.

Regarding those who share the same training rules: even if one has previously received full ordination and has already lived for a hundred years, the matters that ought to be learned are no different from those of a newly ordained person.

If one has newly received full ordination, the matters one ought to study do not differ from those of one who has been fully ordained for a hundred years; that is to say, the precepts (*śīla*), the training rules (*śikṣāpada*), and the procedures for observance and transgression are all alike, and thus it is called "attaining the training rules in common."
Regarding the phrase "not relinquishing the training rules" (*śikṣāpada*): to what extent is one said to have not relinquished them?

It means that if one relinquishes the training rules in the presence of someone who is insane, mentally deranged, afflicted by intense pain, deaf, mute, or a fool, it is not considered a relinquishment at all.

If one perceives a solitary, quiet place as solitary and quiet, or perceives a solitary, quiet place as not solitary and quiet, or perceives a place that is not solitary and quiet as solitary and quiet, this does not constitute a violation of the training rules.

If a person from the central region speaks in the dialect of the central region to a person from a border region, the renunciation is not accomplished if [the listener] does not understand it; it is accomplished if they do understand it.

If a person from a border region speaks in the dialect of a border region to a person from the central region, or if a person from the central region speaks in the dialect of a border region to another person from the central region, the renunciation is not accomplished if [the listener] does not understand it; it is accomplished if they do understand it.
If a person from a border region speaks the language of the central regions to another person from a border region, it should be understood that the same principle applies as stated above.

Furthermore, if one addresses those who are asleep, in meditative absorption, non-humans, devas, or manifestations such as animals and various images; or if one is distracted by noise, or if one does not clearly inform those who remain in their natural state, the relinquishment of the precepts is not accomplished.
Regarding the statement "one who has declared weakness in training but does not speak [of it]," there should be four permutations:

(1) one who has relinquished the training rules but does not declare weakness in training; (2) one who declares weakness in training but has not relinquished the training rules; (3) one who has both relinquished the training rules and declared weakness in training; and (4) one who has neither relinquished the training rules nor declared weakness in training.
What is meant by "renouncing the training rules" rather than "confessing due to weakness in training"?

It is as follows: suppose there is a bhikṣu who harbors thoughts of longing and desires to return to lay life; he has no love for the path of the śramaṇa, and being distressed, ashamed, and weary of being a śramaṇa, he goes to another bhikṣu and speaks thus:
"Venerable one, please attend to me!..."
"I, [name], now relinquish the training rules.
This is called relinquishing the training rules.
Or one may say:
"I renounce the Buddha, the Dharma,
and the Saṅgha," or one says:
"I renounce the Sūtras, the Vinaya, and the Mātṛkās."
Some say: "I renounce my upādhyāya and ācārya. Others say:

"Knowing me to be a layperson; knowing me to be a śrāmaṇera, a śikṣamāṇā, a paṇḍaka, one who has defiled a bhikṣuṇī, one who has killed his father, harmed his mother, killed an arhat, caused a schism in the Saṃgha, or shed the blood of a Buddha with an evil mind; knowing me to be a follower of an external path, one who has gone to an external path, a thief-dweller, one living separately, or one who does not dwell in communion."
...and so on, until it says:
"Among you who are equal in the Dharma and fellow practitioners of the holy life (brahmacarya), I am not one of your companions.
This is called abandoning the training rules by stating that one's studies have become weak, rather than [abandoning them] while the studies are still vigorous.
What is it to be a trainee who, being weak, speaks [of his intention] but does not relinquish the precepts?

It is as when a bhikṣu, harboring attachment and longing for the life of a householder, lacks any love or joy for the path of the śramaṇa; distressed by being a śramaṇa and feeling ashamed, humiliated, and weary of it, he goes to other bhikṣus and says:
"Venerable sirs!..."
"Do you understand? The holy life is difficult to establish; dwelling in solitude is difficult; living alone is difficult; it is difficult to reside in the forest wilds and endure poor bedding.
I remember my parents, brothers, sisters, and teachers; I wish to learn various crafts and engage in agriculture, for my heart yearns to carry on the lineage of my family."
If a bhikṣu, despite making various such expressions of regret, does not say,
"I relinquish the training," this is called being weak in the training while speaking, rather than relinquishing the training.
What is meant by "declining in training" and "speaking while also relinquishing the training rules"?

For example, there may be a bhikṣu who, harboring feelings of attachment—as explained in detail previously—goes so far as to say, with words of regret: "I relinquish the training rules," as explained in detail previously, until it is said that he is no longer a companion to his fellow practitioners of the holy life. This is called "declining in training" and "speaking while also relinquishing the training rules."
What is meant by "not abandoning the precepts" and "not declaring one's weakness in training"?
This refers to cases other than those previously mentioned; this is what is meant by "weakness in training without declaration.
To speak of "engaging in impure conduct" refers specifically to sexual desire.
What is called "sexual desire" refers to the mutual union of two persons.
As for "dharma," this refers to what is contrary to the Dharma, yet is designated by the name "Dharma.
When the bodily karma performs what is improper, it is termed "action" (*kṛta*).
"Even with animals" refers to [animals such as] monkeys and the like.
"This person" refers to the individual in question.
"Bhikṣu" refers to one who has attained the nature of a bhikṣu.
What is the nature of a bhikṣu?
It is the reception of full ordination.
What is full ordination?
This refers to the formal procedure of the *jñapti-caturtha-karman*, wherein the matter to be performed is accomplished in accordance with the Dharma, reaching its ultimate fulfillment.

The candidate receiving ordination does so with a mind of perfection, aspiring for the full precepts; they vow to receive them with a heart free from resentment. Because this is manifested through verbal expression and the activity of speech, it is called "complete ordination" (*upasampadā*).
*Pārājika* refers to an extremely grave offense that is utterly loathsome; it is to be despised and not to be cherished.

Should a bhikṣu commit even one such act, he immediately ceases to be a śramaṇa and ceases to be a son of the Śākya. He loses his status as a bhikṣu and deviates from the nature of nirvāṇa; he falls, collapses, and is overcome by others, becoming beyond redemption.
Just as when the head of a *tāla* tree is cut off, it no longer grows, cannot flourish, increase, or expand, it is therefore called a *pārājika*.

Regarding the phrase "not living together" (*asaṃvāsa*): it means that this offender may not live in common with the bhikṣus. Whether in the *poṣadha*, the *pravāraṇā*, or in formal acts such as the *jñapti*, the *jñapti-dvitīya*, or the *jñapti-caturtha*; whether in matters concerning the Saṃgha where twelve types of persons should be appointed, he is ineligible for appointment; and whether in regard to the Dharma or material sustenance, they are not to be shared or used together. He should be expelled; for these reasons, it is called "one with whom one should not live together."
Regarding this, what are the characteristics of the offense?
The summary verse says:
"Engaging in sexual intercourse in three places; the three orifices, whether separated or not."
One should know whether an offense is committed or not in cases of: the deceased or the living;
the hermaphrodite, the female, or the male; engaging in sexual intercourse while seeing another asleep;
or when one is coerced by means of alcohol, drugs, and the like, whether there is pleasure or no pleasure.
If a bhikṣu performs the act of impurity—that is, engages in sexual intercourse—with respect to three locations, he incurs a pārājika offense.
What are the three locations?
They are the anus, the urinary tract, and the mouth; upon mere entry, he incurs a pārājika offense.
If a bhikṣu engages in unchaste conduct with three types of persons, he incurs a pārājika offense.
What are these three?
They are: a woman, a man, and a paṇḍaka.

If a bhikṣu, with the intention to engage in sexual intercourse, has intercourse with a living human woman at one of her three orifices that have not been damaged—whether he inserts what is obstructed into what is obstructed, what is obstructed into what is unobstructed, what is unobstructed into what is obstructed, or what is unobstructed into what is unobstructed—he incurs a pārājika offense at the moment of insertion.

If a bhikṣu commits sexual intercourse with a living woman by damaging her three orifices, provided the intervals and other conditions are as previously described, he incurs a sthūlātyaya offense upon entry.
If he does so with a dead woman whose three orifices are undamaged, provided the intervals and other conditions are as previously described, he incurs a pārājika offense upon entry.
If a bhikṣu damages the three orifices of a deceased woman, and the intervening distance is as previously described, he incurs a sthūlātyaya offense.
As it is with a human woman, whether living or dead, one should understand that the gravity of the offense is determined in this same manner.

Regarding female non-humans or female animals, whether living or dead, and whether their three orifices are damaged or undamaged, obstructed or unobstructed, the gravity of the offense incurred is the same as previously stated.

If, with respect to a human male, a non-human male, or an animal male—whether living or dead—and regarding the two orifices, whether they are damaged or undamaged, or obstructed by other factors, the offense incurred is the same as previously described.

If it concerns a male paṇḍaka, a non-human paṇḍaka, or an animal paṇḍaka—whether living or dead—and whether the two orifices are damaged, undamaged, or obstructed by a partition and so forth, the offense incurred is the same as before.

If a bhikṣu engages in unchaste conduct with a sleeping bhikṣu, there is no offense if the sleeping bhikṣu was unaware of it from beginning to middle to end; however, the one who committed the sexual act incurs the root offense.
If a sleeping bhikṣu is aware at the beginning but unaware during the middle and end, there is no offense; however, the one who commits the sexual act incurs the root offense.
If he is aware at both the beginning and the middle but unaware at the end, there is no offense; however, the one who commits the sexual act incurs the root offense.
If one knows [the act] at the beginning, middle, and end, yet has no mental experience of pleasure, there is no offense; however, the one who performs the sexual act incurs the root offense.
If one knows [the act] at the beginning, middle, and end and has a mental experience of pleasure, both incur the root offense.

Just as it is with regard to whether there is an offense or no offense when a bhikṣu approaches a sleeping bhikṣu, so too should one understand the gravity of the offense incurred when approaching a bhikṣuṇī, a śikṣamāṇā, a śrāmaṇera, or a śrāmaṇerikā, as described above.
If a bhikṣuṇī, a śikṣamāṇā, or a śrāmaṇerikā approaches a bhikṣu or a śrāmaṇera, whether there is an offense or no offense in each case should be explained according to the preceding rules.
If a śrāmaṇera approaches a bhikṣu, a bhikṣuṇī, a śikṣamāṇā, a śrāmaṇera, or a śrāmaṇerī, whether there is an offense or no offense is as explained above.
If a bhikṣu gives rice wine, flower wine, or wine made from roots and bark to another bhikṣu, causing him to become intoxicated and engage in unchaste conduct;

and if that intoxicated bhikṣu, throughout the beginning, middle, and end [of the act], whether he is conscious or unconscious, experiences pleasure or does not experience pleasure—then regarding the gravity of the offense, its lightness or severity, and whether there is a transgression or no transgression—even down to the case of giving wine to other groups of people to intoxicate them, it is as explained at length above concerning sleep.

Just as it is with those who are intoxicated, if one uses incantations or drugs to cause another to become deluded and engage in impure conduct with various objects, or even if members of the assembly engage with one another, the presence or absence of an offense is as described above.
If a bhikṣu forcibly compels another bhikṣu to engage in unchaste conduct, and the one being compelled experiences pleasure at the very moment of entry, both shall be expelled.
If one is displeased upon entering but pleased after having entered, both shall be expelled.
If one is displeased upon entering, displeased after having entered, but pleased upon exiting, both shall be expelled.
If one is coerced, there is no offense provided that one finds no pleasure in it during the three periods [of the day]; however, if one coerces another, they shall be expelled.
Just as with coercing a bhikṣu, one should understand that the same applies by analogy to coercing a bhikṣuṇī or other lower groups.
If bhikṣus and others mutually oppress one another, it is as previously described.
At that time, in the city of Śrāvastī, there was an elder who married a woman from a family of equal status; they lived together in mutual affection and joy.

Before long, he gave birth to a son whose waist and spine were as supple as those of a cat or a rabbit. After twenty-one days had passed and the relatives had gathered for a celebration, the father addressed the kin regarding the child, saying:
"What name shall we give this child?"
The crowd deliberated and said,
"This child’s waist is so supple that we should give him the name 'Weak-Waist' (Nandika).
As the boy gradually grew older, he sought to renounce the householder's life in order to practice the well-expounded Dharma and Vinaya.
Having gone forth, he went for alms in the village where he resided; maintaining his deportment and with his sense faculties undisturbed, he carefully guarded his mind and returned to his dwelling.

Having finished eating, he put away his robes and bowl, washed his feet, and entered his room; there, a lustful mind arose, and he inserted his organ into his own mouth to experience sensual pleasure.

Later, at another time, there were certain bhikṣus who, while inspecting the dwellings, entered a room and saw that weak-waisted woman performing such an act; filled with sorrow and sighing, they asked her:
"Venerable lady!..."
"What are you doing? He replied,
"I am enjoying sensual pleasures."
The bhikṣu replied,
"Is it not true that the Blessed One has prohibited the practice of sexual misconduct?
He answered:
"Venerable One!
The Buddha prohibits others, but does not restrain himself.

When the bhikṣus heard these words, they neither censured nor rejoiced, but departed from him. They went to the place where the Buddha was, and with their usual deportment, reported the matter to the Buddha.
The Buddha said:
"If one restrains oneself even toward others, how much more so toward one's own person!
This deluded person has committed a *pārājika* offense."

If a bhikṣu, with a mind intent on sexual intercourse and the intention to experience pleasure, inserts his own organ into his mouth or causes another's organ to enter his mouth, he incurs a *mūlāpatti* (a fundamental offense).

At that time, there was the son of a householder in Śrāvastī whose organ was exceedingly long; because of this, the people of the time called him Dīrghanakha (Long-Root), and he went forth in the Buddha’s Dharma and received full ordination.
Entering her own room, she inserted her own organ into the vaginal passage and took pleasure.
At that time, another bhikṣu, while walking through the quarters, saw her performing such an act with her long organ and asked: "What are you doing?"
...and so on, until he replied:
"The Buddha has prohibited this for others; what fault is there in doing it for oneself?
The bhikṣus reported this to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"If one restrains oneself even toward others, how much more so toward one's own person!
This deluded man has committed a *pārājika* offense. The Buddha was staying at Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park in Śrāvastī.

At that time, in the city of Uśīnara in Western India, there was a great merchant leader named Nanda. He was immensely wealthy with vast riches and abundant enjoyments; his assets were like those of King Vaiśravaṇa. He had taken a wife from a family of equal status and lived with her in happiness.

Although many years passed, she ultimately had no offspring; for the sake of seeking a child, she prayed and entreated at various celestial shrines and to all manner of deities everywhere, yet her wishes were not granted.
Now, as for those in the world who claim that one obtains a son simply by means of begging, this is truly false;
if it were real, everyone would have a thousand sons like a wheel-turning monarch.
However, it is only through three conditions that offspring are produced:
first, the union of the father and mother;
second, the mother’s body being pure and fit for conception; [and third, the presence of a gandharva].
Third, the manifestation of the scent of food.
At that time, through the convergence of karmic conditions, a certain deva came from the Exquisite Heaven (*Sudharmā*) and took conception in the womb of the merchant’s wife.
As for the five special knowledges of a wise woman, they are as explained at length above.
When she was pregnant and the fetus was in her right side, she joyfully informed her husband. He then placed her in a high tower, where she was attended at all times like a celestial maiden.
When the months were complete, she gave birth to a son endowed with all the auspicious marks. The father announced the child to his relatives, saying:
"What name shall we give this child?"
Now, according to the custom of the Middle Kingdom, a child born with such a handsome appearance that people delight in beholding him is named Sundarananda.
At that time, his relatives consulted together, saying:
"Since this child has such a handsome appearance that all people delight in beholding him, and he is the son of the merchant leader Nanda, we should give this boy the name Sundarananda."
He was entrusted to eight foster mothers, who raised him until he grew up as swiftly as a lotus in a pond; he mastered the four Vedas and perfected the eight arts.

At that time, his father constructed for him three palaces for the spring, summer, and winter seasons, as well as three gardens and three classes of courtesans—namely, superior, middling, and inferior—and he ascended a magnificent pavilion where various musical performances were played.
At that time, the merchant leader Nanda was constantly engaged in accounting; his taking and giving, his receipts and disbursements, never ceased for even a moment.
Then Sundarananda said to his father, "Why do you toil at these calculations without a moment's rest?"
Nanda replied, "How could you,
who spend your days in constant amusement atop a high tower, ever manage the affairs of a household?
I must certainly know how to conduct such business."
Having heard his father’s words, Sundarananda thought to himself,
“My father has uttered these words wishing to rouse me.
He knelt and requested:
"If this is the case, I wish to travel abroad to seek out means of livelihood; I pray you will grant me your permission.
His father said, "You should remain here for now. I possess precious wealth; why trouble yourself to seek it afar?"
Sundarananda replied,
"Though my father possesses wealth, I must certainly go.
His father then had this thought:
"I should now quench his craving.
He then took the keys and opened all seven treasuries, showing him gold and silver—both wrought and unwrought—which filled them completely.

He said to Sundarananda, "Since you possess such abundant wealth and treasures, you ought to sit with hands folded in ease and enjoy all manner of sensual pleasures; you may give as you wish and cultivate fields of merit. As for traveling to other regions, you should desist from this."
He replied, "My father used these objects to instruct me; if I were to have a son, with what would I instruct him?
At this, the father immediately had a thought:
“Excellent is this counsel!
After my passing, you must take charge of the family business; I shall now gradually instruct you in its affairs, and for the time being, let you take some goods and go abroad to test yourself.”
"First, I shall study the methods for seeking the sūtras; second, I shall visit my relatives and acquaintances.
By surveying the various districts, my mind will remain free from delusion.
Having thought this, he said to his wife:
"After my body has passed away, this Sundarananda shall take charge of the household affairs.
He informed her of all these previous matters, and his wife said, "This is a beneficial matter; you may proceed as you wish."
The father replied to his son:
"The resolve you have made is indeed excellent!
After my death, you shall take charge of the household affairs; all that was previously mentioned, I now urge you to undertake."
He ordered that his wealth and goods be taken to pursue trade in other lands.
Then the merchant leader Nanda immediately dispatched men to ring bells and blow conch shells, making a public announcement throughout the city to all residents and merchants from the four quarters:
"The merchant leader Sundarananda now wishes to take his merchandise to seek profit in other lands."
"If you, sirs, are able to go together with me, you shall not have to pay tolls at the passes, rivers, or ferries; all provisions for the journey must be prepared in advance.
At that time, there were five hundred merchants who, hearing this proclamation, each prepared their goods and waited for the date of departure.
At that time, his father Nanda prepared an extensive banquet and summoned all the practitioners. Once they had finished eating, he addressed them, saying:
"Gentlemen, you should know!
This Sundarananda is my son; I regard you all with no difference in heart."
"O merchants, those of you who wish to travel to other lands to seek wealth and profit face three afflictions:
namely, gambling, wine, and sensual desire.
If you see Sundarananda becoming defiled by these three delusions, you should restrain him; where there is a beneficial path, you should encourage him to practice it."
If you all can refrain from evil and exhort others toward good, and are able to follow these instructions, it shall be well.
If you do not heed these words, you should exchange the goods you have brought for merchandise and return home.
He also addressed Sundarananda, saying:
"You are my son; the remaining merchants are no different from you. You should accept their wholesome words and act accordingly."
The son respectfully agreed.

Having selected an auspicious day, he loaded various goods onto carts and horses and, accompanied by five hundred companions, traveled a long distance to the city of Śrāvastī, where he deposited his merchandise in a shop.

At that time, there was a courtesan in the city of Śrāvastī named Bhadrā, whose profession was the display of her beauty; she possessed an extraordinary and striking countenance that people delighted to behold, and she would only grant lodging to those who provided five hundred gold coins.

At that time, the courtesan heard that there was a merchant who had come from afar from the city of Uśīnara; his leader was named Nanda, and his son was Sundarananda, whose appearance was so handsome that all people delighted in beholding him. Accompanied by five hundred merchants, he had come from afar to this place and was staying, having deposited his goods upon her shop.
Even though he had thought,
"If I cannot seize all of that wealth, I shall no longer call myself 'Wise Head' (Bhadramukha)!
he then commanded a maidservant, saying:
"In a certain shop there is a merchant leader named Sundarananda, who possesses vast wealth and great riches.
Take these flower garlands, ointments, and fine garments, go to him, and say:
'Merchant Leader!'"
"This was sent by Mahāśreṣṭhin Śrīmat for me to bring, merely to extend a token of my faith.
He further addressed him, saying,
"For what reason does the merchant leader reside in this shop?"
"You should come for a moment.
The female messenger then took various flower garlands and went to the merchant leader’s place to inform him of everything in detail.
When Sundarananda heard this, he said to the messenger girl:
“You go on ahead; I shall follow behind, wearing these fragrant garlands.
Thereupon, the maidservant went forward to her home and reported to her mistress:
“I have come first; she will arrive shortly after.”

When Bhadramukha heard the messenger’s words, his heart was filled with joy; he immediately swept and sprinkled the courtyard, arranged various famous flowers, perfumed them with exquisite incense, prepared magnificent seats, and hung up curtains and canopies to await the merchants.

At that time, Sundarananda immediately bathed and washed himself, put on fresh, clean garments, and adorned himself with flower garlands; then, accompanied by chariots, horses, and attendants, he went to the house of Bhadrika.
At that time, Bhadrika saw him approaching from afar; his appearance and deportment were unlike those of ordinary men, so he asked a maidservant, "Is this Sthūlanandana, the caravan leader?"
The maidservant replied, "So be it.
Bhadradarśanā,
filled with joy, then spoke this verse:
"Without distinguishing between the wealthy and the poor, regardless of whether one is noble or lowly—
provided only that they possess beautiful features— they will surely disturb the hearts of women.

At that time, Sundarananda immediately dismounted from his vehicle, intending to enter the house.
Then, Bhadrika quickly descended from the high tower, went out the door to welcome him, bowed low to meet him, led him into the house, and settled him upon an exquisite couch.
Once he had been made to cease [his agitation], [the Buddha] asked his name, and he replied:
"My name is Sundarananda.
Śirīṣaka replied:
"Excellent! Your name is well-suited to your person. Had your parents not bestowed this name upon you, I would now have named you Sundarananda."
Then Sundarananda asked,
"What is your name? He replied:
“My name is Bhadramukha.
He replied, “Excellent!”
"The name and the reality correspond. Had your parents not established this name for you, I would have established the name 'Worthy Head' (Bhadramukha) for you myself.
Then Sudarśanānanda asked Bhadramukha, "If we were to stay together for one night, how much would the fee be?"
The woman said, "What is the meaning of this?
You speak like an ordinary person, with such vulgar and shallow words.
The attendant replied:
"One night's lodging requires five hundred gold coins.
Sundarananda replied to his attendants, saying,
"You may send five hundred gold coins every day."
Thereupon, he lived with her in pleasure and delight.

Generally, those possessed by lust find it difficult to reach satiety; though many days passed, he had no thought of abandoning her, and he constantly caused his family members to send money for her daily expenses.
The people deliberated, saying:
"Our merchant leader has been gone for a long time; where is he now that we no longer see him? Since he was entrusted with his father’s instructions, we ought to search for him."
He then asked the household members,
"Where is the merchant leader?
The household members replied:
“Gentlemen, do you remember the merchant leader today?
As soon as we first arrived, he went straight to the house of a courtesan.
The merchants said:
"How can we abandon this and fail to inquire?
Upon our return, we will surely be rebuked by our father.
Thus, they sent a messenger to summon him.
Having heard this, the merchant leader immediately desired to go out the door, whereupon Bhadramukha seized the hem of his garment and said:
"Do you not know, sir,
that there are two kinds of people in the world who may indulge in sensual pleasures?..."
First, your countenance is beautiful;
second, you are in the prime of youth.
Since you possess both these qualities and enjoy sensual pleasures, you should seek wealth and resources now while your years are not yet declined and your hair is not yet white.
Having been detained, he replied to the messenger, "You may go on ahead; I shall follow immediately.

The messenger reported these circumstances in detail to the merchants. The group gathered and waited for his return, but as he did not arrive despite their long wait, they all went together to where he was.
Having arrived at the gate, he addressed the gatekeeper, saying:

"You may enter the house and inform the merchant leader that his companions are all standing at the entrance; it would be well for him to come out briefly so that we may deliberate on certain matters."
After the messenger had delivered the message, the merchant leader wished to depart. At that time, Bhadramukha again grasped the hem of his garment and said:
"Wait! Those merchants desire me; they have come together to summon me and will not permit my lingering. For all who are greedy, their fetters increase day by day."
Then Sundarananda replied to the messengers, saying,
"Gentlemen, you may depart for now!
Wait until my desires are satisfied before returning."
The messenger delivered the message upon his return, and having heard it, the merchants said to one another, "Observing these circumstances, there is nothing that can be done.

They immediately engaged in trade and sold the goods they had brought; having acquired other items and readied their companions, they returned along the road, and from that point on, the delivery of goods was cut off.
Later, when Bhadrika encountered the messenger, he asked him,
"For what reason do you no longer send me goods?
The messenger replied:
"The merchants have already returned; where can one find such goods?
The woman asked again, "Could it be that Sundarananda’s goods were also taken back with them?"
He replied,
"I shall go as well.
When Bhadrika heard these words, he stayed with Sundarananda for two or three nights and then said to him:
"I possess no fields, nor do I engage in agriculture or commerce; I sustain my life solely by relying on others. You ought to calculate the days and provide me with the necessary funds.
If you do not do so, you had better depart quickly to make way for others."
Sundarananda said,
"You have never once looked back with a heart of longing.
He replied:
"Indeed! Have you not heard what people in the world say:
'A courtesan originally seeks wealth; when there is no wealth, she abandons him.'"
"Just as birds abandon a fruitless tree and do not linger there.
When Sundarī-Nandā heard these words, she replied to him:
"If you give me wealth, I shall follow your will; but when your goods are exhausted, I shall develop a mind to cast you aside."
The woman said:
"Have you not heard:
'If the heavens send down rain, the mountains and rivers flow together in a torrent;'"
"A man provides wealth and assets, yet a courtesan turns according to her own whims.
Sundarananda said, "A courtesan is a person who cannot be trusted."
The woman replied to him:
"A courtesan regards others as her own self until evening falls;
when night draws on and her heart grows cold, at daybreak she discards them like grass."
Sundarananda said, "O fair-faced one!
You are intimate with a man who possesses wealth, yet you suddenly cast aside a person who has nothing."
The woman said:
“If a person possesses wealth, courtesans all love him equally;
like an ox eating tender grass, who would look upon one with respect if he has no wealth?”
At that time, Sundarananda, perceiving her feelings had changed, was about to depart. The courtesan thought to herself:
"This Sundarananda’s countenance is peerless and difficult to find again; moreover, since no other men have yet brought me any gifts, I should detain him for now and not let him leave immediately."
He then hurriedly pulled at his robe to prevent him from leaving, saying:
"Could it be that within your household one may not speak in jest?
I spoke these words as a joke; for what reason do you find fault with me?"
He was by nature addicted to lust and remained fixed upon his words.
At that time, a man came to her house carrying five hundred gold coins; the woman, knowing his intent, immediately committed an unrighteous act with him right in front of Sundarananda.
Upon seeing this, Sundarananda thought to himself:
"Alas! How utterly heartless this courtesan is!"
He immediately treated me with contempt and rudeness, then abandoned me and departed;
not knowing the way, he stumbled through the streets and crossroads, losing his direction.
At that time, a bhikṣu was coming out from the city after begging for alms; having seen him, [the man] followed behind him.

When that bhikṣu had arrived at the monastery, he set down his alms-bowl and placed his water-strainer; he shook out his saṃghāṭī robe, washed his feet and hands, filtered water, inspected it for insects, and prepared a maṇḍala. Taking fallen leaves, he spread them upon the ground and ate.
At that time, Sundarananda was standing before him, and the bhikṣu asked,
"Would you be able to eat my leftover food?
He then thought to himself:
"If I do not eat, I shall die from hunger and exhaustion.
He replied,
"I wish to eat."
He then gave him the remainder from his own bowl to eat.
When he had finished eating, he asked:
"O worthy one!..."
"From where have you come?
He replied, "Noble One!"
"I am Sūdarśananda, son of the merchant leader Nanda from the city of Ujjayinī.

Having taken a great deal of wealth from my home, I traveled far with a caravan to seek my fortune here. Recently, driven by lust, I stayed at the house of a courtesan; there, all my goods and wealth were lost, and I alone now endure this hardship."
The bhikṣu replied, "If that is so,
why do you not go forth [into homelessness]?
At that time, Sundarananda thought to himself:
"If I were to return to my hometown and be ridiculed by others, it would be better than staying wherever I happen to be now.
He then informed the bhikṣu:
"I seek to go forth [into homelessness]."
Then that bhikṣu, in accordance with the Dharma and the Vinaya, granted him the going forth and the full ordination.
After instructing him in the practice of the rules for two or three days, he said:
"O noble one!..."
"Have you not heard that deer do not raise deer? The city of Śrāvastī is extremely vast; you should sustain yourself by begging for alms wherever it is appropriate to go.
Having received these instructions, he took up his robes and bowl during the first part of the day and entered the city to beg for food.
At that time, the courtesan felt remorse in her heart, thinking:
"What I have done is wrong; that Sundarananda is handsome and dignified in appearance, in the prime of his youth and vigor, and such a person is not easily found."
"I have been dismissed because of my wealth.
She replied to the maidservant,
"If you see Sundarananda again, you should invite him to come in."

At that time, Sundarananda, being unfamiliar with the places where alms were to be sought, wandered until he reached the house of that courtesan. Seeing him from afar, a maidservant hurried back inside and reported to her mistress, "Sundarananda is now standing outside the gate."
He replied, "Call her in.
The maidservant said:
"He has now already left the household life.
He replied,
"Even though he has left the household life, you should still summon him in."
He then led him forward; upon seeing him, Bhadrika beat his breast and said, "Noble One!
Why have you abandoned me to go forth?"
Sundarananda replied:
"You are shallow-hearted and full of greed, seeking only wealth; how could you act so improperly toward me?
Since I have been thus deceived and slighted, I shall certainly renounce the secular life."
She replied, "Noble One!

A woman's body is full of many faults; may you kindly forgive my one transgression. My person and my wealth both belong to you, Venerable Sir; I pray that you will once again enjoy our intimacy as before."
Sundarananda said: "You ignorant fellow!
You have already squandered my former wealth; do you now wish to break my precepts as well?"
The woman said,
"If one rubs the inside while discharging outside, or rubs the outside while discharging inside, it does not constitute a breach of the precepts.
Having heard this, Sundarananda gave rise to a thought:
"Is it not the case that when a bhikṣu goes on almsround, he performs such an act?
If it were not so, how could this be known?

At that time, Sundarananda was by nature fond of beauty; he then set aside his robe and bowl and followed her words to commit an improper act, satisfying his lustful desires before standing to one side.
Then that courtesan immediately filled a bowl with various kinds of exquisite food and drink and presented it to him, saying,
"Noble One! If you have any need, please come here frequently."
He then took his bowl and food and returned toward the monastery.
At that time, the World-Honored One was preaching the essentials of the Dharma for the great assembly, namely: liberation through wisdom of mind from greed, hatred, and delusion.

When Sundarananda heard the Dharma being preached, his heart was filled with distress and he felt profound regret. With a mind of remorse, he remained silent and speechless; with a downcast countenance and face bowed low, he sat immersed in sorrowful thought. His appearance was withered and lacked any luster, like a bundle of fresh reeds cut down and left to dry in the sun.
The bhikṣus asked,
"Venerable Sunda-ra-nanda!
Is this a physical ailment or a mental affliction?"
He, being thus ashamed, remained silent and gave no reply.
At that time, a physician happened to pass by their location, and the bhikṣus said to him:
"O worthy sir!"
"Observe for a moment: what ailment does this young bhikṣu have?
Having examined him, the physician reported to the people, "This venerable one has no physical suffering; his mind is merely scorched with fever."
The bhikṣu asked,
“What is meant by ‘feverishness of mind’?
He replied:
“Noble ones!
My physicians treat only physical ailments and do not treat the mind; may you, the Bhikṣus, cure this mental illness.
Having said this, he departed.
Then the bhikṣus asked him, "Venerable one!
You have no parents or kinsmen;
we, your fellow practitioners of the holy life, are your only relatives and acquaintances. You should speak the truth so that we may provide for you."
He then informed them of his lowly situation.
The bhikṣus said, "Who would have thought that the spring flowers would suddenly meet with frost and hail? You have only just completed your full ordination, and already this ulcer has broken out."

When the bhikṣus heard these words, they neither rejoiced nor became angry; they left him and went to where the Buddha was staying. Having prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, they sat to one side and reported everything in detail to the Buddha.
The Buddha said:
"This foolish person commits a *pārājika* offense.

If a bhikṣu, with a mind intent on sexual desire and the intention to experience pleasure, places his own male organ into the urinary passage, whether by rubbing internally and discharging externally or rubbing externally and discharging internally, he incurs a *pārājika* offense."
At that time, the Buddha was staying at the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park, in Śrāvastī.
At that time, there was an elder in this city whose wife died shortly after their first marriage; his second, third, and so on, up to the seventh wife all likewise passed away.
At that time, everyone called her "Husband-Obstructor," and she took this as her name.
From then on, whenever anyone wished to take a wife, people would refuse to give her away, saying:
"How could I possibly cause my daughter to die?"
"I cannot give her to you.
He then sought out a widow, wishing to marry her as his wife, but she replied to him:
"Would I not rather cast away my life than enter your house?"
At that time, the householder was unable to find a wife and had to manage the household affairs himself.
Later, on another occasion, a friend came to visit his residence and asked him,
"What are you doing, sir?"
He replied,
"I am attending to household affairs.
He was told:
"Why do you now manage the household affairs yourself?
He replied,
"I have already married seven wives, and all have passed away."
The friend asked,
"Why do you not seek something else?
He replied:
"Though I have sought her these past days, no one will give her to me, saying:
'How could I not cherish my daughter?
" [The King asked: "If this is the case, why do you not seek other widowed daughters instead?"
The householder answered in detail as before.
His friend said, "Not far from here there is an old courtesan; why do you not seek her?"
He replied,
"How could my household now become a brothel?
His friend said:
"She has long since abandoned unwholesome practices; let us go and seek her out.
He then went to her residence and asked, "Have you been well lately?"
He replied, "Welcome; what do you seek?
He answered:
"Therefore, we have come to seek you.
To whom do you belong? He replied:
"If you provide me with food and clothing,
I shall belong to you. He replied,
"Will you be able to reform the transgressions you committed in the past?"
He replied, "How could I not see that other men exist? Yet my original mind has long since been free from unwholesome dharmas.
He answered:
"If you can do so, you may live with me; I shall provide you with food and clothing, and you shall take over all the household duties.
She then followed him to his home.
He entrusted all his household affairs to her and said, "This is your home;
whatever you provide for me, I shall enjoy.
Knowing that the household affairs were well-managed and that food and clothing were abundant, before long her body became exceedingly plump and flourishing.
At the entrance stood several courtesans who were traveling together toward the Jeta Grove.
They asked the women,
"Where do you wish to go?"
He replied,
"Go to the Jeta Grove to behold the meritorious works.
He then said:
"Wait! Allow me to adorn myself, and then we shall go together.
Before she had finished adjusting her garments, the women passed by; having gone out the door and not seeing him, she hurried her steps in search of him.

The women all went ahead and entered the monastery; however, within that monastery there was a bhikṣu who was sleeping with his door open, his robes in disarray, and his male organ consequently erect.
At that time, the courtesans went round the rooms to inspect them; having seen this occurrence, they all laughed aloud and departed.
When the elderly courtesan saw the other women laughing as they left, she asked, "What are you laughing at?"
"Have you not heard that those who laugh within the monastery receive the retribution of decaying teeth?
At that, the women fell silent and departed.
The old woman thought to herself:
"Could it not be that while the women were walking about and looking around this monastery, they saw either fighting cocks or watched monkeys, and because of this, they laughed and chattered?

At that time, an old woman entered the monastery to look about; in one room, she saw a bhikṣu sleeping with the door open, his body exposed. Lust having arisen within her, she then committed an unrighteous act upon him, while the bhikṣu remained fast asleep and was unaware of it.
At that time, the woman thought to herself:
"We courtesans possess sixty-four skills, yet this renunciant possesses sixty-five; he is able to experience sensual pleasure without speaking a word."
When the old woman had thus satisfied her lustful desires, she then touched the bhikṣu with her hand and said, "Noble One!
My residence is in such-and-such a ward; if you have any need, you should come and visit me there."
The bhikṣu replied:
"You foolish person, you have defiled the dwelling place of the Saṃgha; now I have no intention to endure such an evil matter, so who would ever go to your home again?"
Upon hearing this, the woman departed in silence.
At that time, the bhikṣu felt remorse, thinking:
"Have I not perhaps committed a pārājika offense?"
He informed the bhikṣus, and the bhikṣus informed the Buddha.
The Buddha asked the bhikṣu:
"Did you have a mind that experienced pleasure?"
He replied, "At that time,
my sleep was so heavy that I had no mind to experience pleasure.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"This person has committed no offense, as he lacked the intention to do so.
Nevertheless, I shall establish a rule of conduct for those bhikṣus who dwell near village settlements.
Listen attentively!

If a monastery is situated near a village or town, those bhikṣus who sleep during the day should bolt the doors; or they should have another bhikṣu guard them, or else they should quickly bind their lower robes together in a tight knot.
"If one does not comply, one incurs an *dukkaṭa* offense when the side touches the bed.
The Buddha was staying at the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s Park, in Śrāvastī.
At that time, there was a bhikṣu in this city who had attained the four dhyānas while dwelling in an araṇya.
At that time, he frequently came to pay homage at the feet of the World-Honored One and the elder, venerable bhikṣus.
At that moment, an araṇya-bhikṣu was afflicted with scabies; a young bhikṣu who had previously been acquainted with him addressed him, saying:
"Venerable Elder!..."
"You have a skin ailment; why do you not consult a physician for treatment?
The Elder replied, "There is a future event that is certain to arrive."
That which all people of the world collectively do not love or delight in, that which all people collectively loathe and despise, and from which no one can escape—this is what is called death.
This ulcerous scab follows my own body wherever it goes; why then should it be treated?
The youth said:
“As the World-Honored One has taught:
‘If a person who upholds the precepts should live for a long time, their many meritorious deeds will increase; because their meritorious deeds increase, they will long enjoy celestial bliss.’”
"You should consult a physician.
Thereupon, that senior elder went to the physician's place.
The physician asked:
"Noble one, do you have sores or scabs on your body?
He replied:
"Yes," he replied. [The other] said,
"Why do you not treat it?"
He replied, "I have come for this very reason; please show me the remedy.
He was told:
“Venerable One!
Having eaten fine food, if you take mustard oil and smear it all over your body, and sit in the midday sun, you will surely suffer harm.
The bhikṣu said:
“Give me some pungent oil.
The physician said,
“Venerable One!”

"I have devised a method that does not involve giving medicine as alms; rather, whenever anyone comes to ask for it, I shall give them medicine. Consequently, my food and clothing will become increasingly scarce.
However, there is a certain elder who suffers from this scabies and skin disease; I shall prepare medicated oil for him and beg from him, for I am certain I shall obtain it."
The bhikṣu said,
"He is unwilling to give it.
He replied:
"Noble One! That person is faithful and respectful; he will surely grant it to you.
The bhikṣu said:
"O noble one! May you be free from illness; this itself is your gift.
Having said this, he departed and went directly to the house of that elder.
Having seen him, that person asked:
"Noble one! Your body is covered with many sores and scabs."
He replied, "It is so.
[The Buddha said,] "You may apply pungent oil to your body and sit in the sun."
The bhikṣu replied, "It is for this reason that I have come;
having heard that you possess oil, I hope you will grant me some, for it shall bring about the fruit of merit.
The householder said:
“We shall make a mutual agreement: if you accept my offerings today, I shall bestow them upon you.
He replied, “I will stay and eat.”
He immediately served him with excellent food; when he had finished eating, he filled a small bowl with pungent oil and presented it to the bhikṣu.
The bhikṣu replied, "May you be free from illness."

Having abandoned it and departed, he went to an araṇya and put on coarse, tattered robes. With oil smeared all over his body, he sat in the midday sun; when a pleasant sensation arose in his body, he leaned back and fell asleep. Inside his organ, there was a *uñchivika* insect that bit his penis, and because of this, he suddenly started up, his clothes thrown into disarray.

At that time, there was a stout woman who came to his side seeking cow dung; seeing his exposed form, she conceived a lustful desire and immediately committed an unrighteous act upon him. When the bhikṣu woke from his sleep, his body was so weak and frail that he was unable to resist.
The woman, her desires aroused, replied:
