"Noble one! I reside at such-and-such a place; you should go there whenever you have need of anything."
The bhikṣu replied, "You foolish person, you defile this araṇya!
I have no intention of accepting such an evil practice now; how much less could I ever again go beyond your house?"
The woman departed silently.
The bhikṣu felt remorse, thinking:
"Have I not committed a pārājika offense?"
He reported the matter in full to the bhikṣus, and the bhikṣus reported it to the Buddha.
The Buddha asked the bhikṣu:
"Did you have a mind that experienced pleasure?"
He addressed the Buddha, saying,
"I have already become free from desire and no longer possess a mind that experiences the pleasure of sensation.
The Buddha then told the bhikṣus:
"This person has committed no offense, for he was without lustful intent.
Nevertheless, I shall establish a code of conduct for those bhikṣus who dwell in forest hermitages (āraṇyaka).
You all should listen!

If one is in an araṇya (forest hermitage), one should construct a fence of thorny branches around the four sides of the dwelling. When wishing to sleep, one should have a bhikṣu guard it, or else quickly bind the hems of one's lower garment together.
"If one does not comply, one incurs an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*).
At that time, all the bhikṣus were filled with doubt and requested the World-Honored One, saying:
"If a forest-dwelling bhikṣu has attained the four dhyānas and is free from the defilement of desire, why does his male organ still arise?"
The Blessed One replied:
“There are five causes and conditions by which the male organ arises in a person who has not yet abandoned desire:

namely, the pressure of needing to urinate or defecate; being affected by the force of wind; being bitten by the *uṃcigga* insect; and the manifestation of sensual passion. These are called the five.”
There are four causes and conditions by which the male organ arises in one who has abandoned desire:
namely, the pressure of needing to urinate or defecate, being constrained by the force of wind, and being bitten by insects; these are called the four.
"At that time, that bhikṣu was bitten by a *uñchivika* insect, causing his penis to become erect; it was not due to defilement.
Then the bhikṣus again had doubts and questioned the World-Honored One:

"We pray that the Great Compassionate One will sever our doubts: for what reason did the bhikṣu Sūdena Kalandakaputra, when he was without fault and without blemish, first develop a blemish and engage in impure conduct?"
The Blessed One said: "O bhikṣus!
It is not only today that the first blister arose; in the distant past, even when there were no blisters, the first blister likewise arose."
"You all should listen!

When this world was about to be destroyed, many sentient beings were born in the Ābhāsvara Heaven. They possessed wondrous forms, were spontaneously formed with complete limbs and faculties, their bodies emitted light, they moved freely through the air, took joy as their food, and lived for a long time."
At that time, the great earth was a single body of ocean water. O bhikṣus!
This great ocean water, stirred and agitated by the wind, became blended into a single mass, like boiled milk.

Once it had cooled, a solid crust began to form upon it; this "earth-flavor" (pṛthivī-rasa) was fully endowed with color, fragrance, and exquisite taste, its color like fresh butter and its flavor as sweet as honey.

"O Bhikṣus! When this world-system was forming, a class of sentient beings whose merit and lifespan were both exhausted passed away from the Ābhāsvara Heaven and came into this human realm. They were spontaneously born with exquisite forms, possessed of all sense faculties, their bodies radiant, traveling through the air, subsisting on joy as food, and dwelling for a long time."

At that time, in this world-system there were no sun, moon, stars, or their reckonings; there was no day or night, no kṣaṇas, lava-s, muhūrtas, half-months, months, half-years, years, nor any distinction between male and female.
They merely called out to one another, saying:
"Sattva! Sattva!"

At that time, there was among the multitude a sentient being whose nature was prone to indulgence; suddenly, he tasted that "earth-flavor" with the tip of his finger. As he tasted it, a sense of attachment arose within him, and because of that attachment, solid food became his sustenance; it was at that moment that one may say he first partook of solid food.
When other sentient beings saw this eating, they immediately imitated them and began to eat that earth-flavor (*pṛthivī-rasa*).

Once those sentient beings had consumed the earth-flavor, their bodies gradually became solid and heavy, and their radiance vanished; at that time, the entire world was completely shrouded in darkness.
"O Bhikṣus!

When the world is in darkness, it is by the very nature of things that there exist the distinctions of sun, moon, stars, constellations, measures of time, day and night, kṣaṇas, lava-s, muhūrtas, months, years, and so forth."
Those sentient beings subsisted on the essence of this earth and lived for a long time; those who ate little possessed bodily radiance, while those who ate much lacked such luster.

Due to differences in the amount of food consumed, physical forms became superior or inferior; because of these differences in superiority and inferiority, they began to disparage one another, saying:
"My complexion is superior, while your countenance is inferior.
Because of this mutual arrogance, unwholesome states arose, and due to the arising of those unwholesome states, the flavor of the earth vanished.
"O Bhikṣus! Because the essence of the earth (pṛthivī-rasa) had vanished, those sentient beings gathered together in one place and dwelt in sorrow, all crying out:
'Oh, what a wonderful flavor!'"
"How wonderful is this delicious flavor!
It is just as when people of today, having once eaten fine food, later recall it and speak thus:
"How wonderful was that delicious flavor!"
"How wonderful is this delicious flavor!
When that savory earth-essence (pṛthivī-rasa) disappeared, all those sentient beings spoke thus:
"How wonderful is this delicious flavor!"
Yet they did not know what meaning was conveyed by these words.

O bhikṣus! After the *pṛthivī-rasa* (earth-essence) had vanished, through the power of their merit, *pṛthivī-parpaṭaka* (earth-cakes) appeared for those sentient beings, complete with color, fragrance, and flavor; their color was like that of the *kumuda* flower and their taste was like freshly ripened honey.
They lived for a long time subsisting on this earth-cake; those who ate little possessed a bodily radiance.
Because they disparaged one another as previously described at length, the earth-cake eventually vanished. Thereupon, all sentient beings gathered in one place and dwelt in sorrow, saying:
"Alas! What misery!"
"How bitter!
It is just as when someone has previously encountered a painful matter and, upon recollecting it again, speaks these words:
"How bitter!"
"Alas! In the past, I once encountered such a calamity.
When the earth-cakes disappear for these sentient beings, it is likewise so; yet they do not know what this statement signifies.

"O Bhikṣus! After the earth-cakes had vanished, by the power of their merit, forest creepers appeared for those sentient beings. They were endowed with color, fragrance, and flavor; their color was like that of the *uṃbara* flower and their taste was like freshly ripened honey. Consuming these forest creepers, they lived for a long time."

Those who ate little possessed a bodily radiance. Due to mutual contempt—as described at length previously—up until the disappearance of the forest-stalks (*vanalatā*), all sentient beings gathered in one place and dwelt in sorrow, saying:
"Depart from my presence!"
"Get away from my presence!
Just as when people harbor extreme resentment toward one another and refuse to allow each other to stand before them— as explained in detail above—
so it is with you, O bhikṣus!

Once the forest creepers had vanished, at that time, by the power of their merit, the sentient beings possessed a sublime fragrant rice that grew spontaneously without being sown; it was free from husks and chaff, stood four finger-widths high, and was harvested morning and evening, with the stalks regenerating immediately. By evening the morning's harvest would ripen, and though it was gathered repeatedly, it showed no sign of depletion; they sustained themselves on this food and lived for a long time.
At that time, because those sentient beings subsisted on solid food, impurities remained within their bodies; wishing to eliminate them, two orifices emerged.
Consequently, male and female sexual organs arose, leading to mutual passion and attachment.
Because they gave rise to defiled attachment, they subsequently drew near to one another and committed unrighteous acts.
When other sentient beings saw this, they vied with one another in throwing refuse, tiles, and stones at them, saying:
"You are detestable sentient beings who commit such unrighteousness!"
"Shame! Why do you now defile and insult sentient beings?

Thus, from the first night until the seventh night, they were not permitted to dwell together and were expelled from the community. This is just like the custom today at the beginning of a wedding, when people scatter various fragrant flowers and objects while wishing:
"May you always attain peace and happiness.

O bhikṣus! That which was non-Dharma in the past is now being treated as Dharma; that which was non-Vinaya in the past is now being treated as Vinaya; that which was formerly despised is now considered excellent.

Because those people of that time were driven out and expelled, they subsequently gathered together to practice unwholesome dharmas; they constructed dwellings and committed unlawful acts. This was the very first establishment of household life, and thus the name "householder" came into being.
"At that time, there was a sentient being who did not practice unwholesome dharmas and had subdued his sense faculties; he was called a 'Superior Person' (Jina).
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:

"Do not harbor other thoughts. He who, at the beginning of the kalpa in the past, created unrighteousness and caused sentient beings to become defiled and afflicted with sores, was none other than this Sūciṃśa."
"In my teaching, there was originally no wound; it is you who first committed evil, performing impure conduct and defiling the pure assembly.
Therefore, O bhikṣus, you should subdue the minds of passion, hatred, and delusion, and do not be negligent!"
2. The Training Rule on Taking What Is Not Given. The second [training rule] on taking what is not given, part one. The Buddha was staying at Rājagṛha in the Bamboo Grove, by the Kalandaka Pond.
At that time, there was a bhikṣu named Dhaniya, formerly the son of a potter, who lived in a grass hut in an araṇya.
Once, Dhaniya entered the city of Rājagṛha and went on his alms round from house to house in the proper manner.

At that time, the cowherds and shepherds, the wood-gatherers, and those who made their living by honest means as well as those who made their living by dishonest means, broke open the hut after the bhikṣu had departed and took away the grass and wood.
When Daṇḍakī returned and saw that his room had been destroyed and all its grass and wood taken away, he immediately rebuilt a new room.
This happened two or three times more, until his efforts were likewise broken by the people as before.
Then Dhanika thought to himself:
"Alas, what suffering! Alas, what extreme suffering!"
"As soon as I go out for alms, my hut is broken by people; this has happened three times now.
Since I myself am well-versed in the crafts inherited from my ancestors, why do I not construct a complete earthenware hut?"

Dhaniya then personally dug up the earth, mixed it with water free of insects to create a fine clay, first constructing the foundation of the hut and subsequently raising the walls. He installed an inner shelf, a roof covering, a clothes rack, poles, ivory pegs, a bed frame, and square stools.

Once the mud of the windows, doors, and pivots has dried, one should apply various pigments to paint them, then burn them with dry wood, cow dung, and grass; when thoroughly and perfectly matured, their color will be a deep red like that of the *dīpāṅkura* flower.
At that time, the bhikṣu Dhaniya thought to himself:
"My dwelling is well-constructed, its form and color are lovely; it would be fitting to celebrate this for myself.
Then, Dhaniya entrusted his nearby fellow bhikṣus to look after the dwelling, took up his robes and bowl, and set out to wander among the people.

It is the constant custom of the Blessed One that, until he has entered parinirvāṇa, he maintains his body in peace and security; yet, for the sake of transforming sentient beings, he occasionally goes to observe the hells, the animal realm, the realm of hungry ghosts, the celestial abodes, the human world, forest hermitages, charnel grounds, mountains, oceans, and other dwelling places.
At that time, the Blessed One, wishing to inspect his dwelling place, addressed the Venerable Ānanda, saying:
"Go and inform the bhikṣus: 'The Tathāgata now wishes to go and view the dwelling place; you bhikṣus who wish to follow him should take up your robes.'"

Then Ānanda, having received the instruction of the Blessed One, immediately went to the groves of trees, the monasteries, the outer quarters, and the walking paths, and addressed the bhikṣus, saying:
"The Blessed One now wishes to inspect his dwelling places; if any of you wish to accompany him, you should take up your robes."
When the bhikṣus had heard these words, they each took their robes and went to where the World-Honored One was.
At that time, the World-Honored One, together with the bhikṣus, proceeded by stages on his alms-round until he arrived at the dwelling place of Dhaniya.

When the Blessed One arrived, he saw that Dhanika’s cell was constructed entirely of tiles, its color a deep crimson like that of a *dīnāra* flower. Having seen this, he addressed the bhikṣus, saying:
"Whose cell is this?"
The bhikṣus said to the Buddha,
“This was built by the bhikṣu Dhānika, the son of a potter.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"You may break this chamber.
For this reason, the various non-Buddhists will slander me, saying:
'While the Śramaṇa Gautama currently dwells in the world, there are among his disciples those who commit such tainted acts; how much more so after he has passed into parinirvāṇa?'"
Then the bhikṣus, having received the instruction of the World-Honored One, broke open the chamber.
When the World-Honored One saw that the chamber had been broken open, he then left it and departed.
At that time, the bhikṣu Dhaniya came and saw that his cell had been broken open;
he immediately asked the nearby bhikṣus, "Who broke my cell? The bhikṣus replied:
"This is the Great Teacher’s instruction that the bhikṣus break it.
Dhanika said, "If the World-Honored One,
the Lord of Dharma, has commanded its destruction, then this is a righteous destruction."
At that time, there was a minister in charge of timber in the city of Rājagṛha who had previously been a close friend of the bhikṣu Dhaniya;
they were on such intimate terms that they shared mutual understanding in conversation. Then Dhaniya thought to himself:
"The minister in charge of timber is my dear friend; I shall seek wood from him to build another wooden hut."
Having had this thought, he went to the minister’s residence and said to him:
"Do you know, sir?
King Ajātaśatru, the son of Vaidehī from the kingdom of Magadha, previously gave me some wood. I wish to take it for use; please hand it over to me."
The minister replied, "Noble one!
If the Great King grants you the wood, it would be most excellent; you may take it as you please."

"However, all the timber within the city is under the custody and protection of King Ajātaśatru; it is stored with extreme care for the purpose of repairing the dilapidated sections of the great city of Rājagṛha, and as this is a task of great difficulty, he does not permit these logs to be given to others."
At that time, the bhikṣu Dhaniya took a piece of wood, cut it into sections, and carried it away.
Just then, a high minister who was patrolling the streets saw a large log being cut up and taken away; having witnessed this, he was struck with great alarm and thought to himself:
"Could it be that King Ajātaśatru of Magadha has enemies who intend to enter the city?"
"This wood is under the King's protection; it is not permitted to be given to others.
For what reason has someone taken it away so recklessly?
Having witnessed this, he immediately went to the minister in charge of the wood and said:
"Minister, do you know?
While I was recently walking through the streets, I saw a large piece of timber being cut and carried away.
Upon seeing this, I was struck with great terror and my hair stood on end; could it not be that King Ajātaśatru has enemies who intend to enter the city?"
"Or did the Forester’s Officer give this great timber to someone else?
The minister replied,
"I have never given this timber to anyone."
However, I once saw the bhikṣu Dhanika speaking thus:
"King Ajātaśatru gave this wood to me; you should give it to me as well.
At that time, I replied:
"Noble One! If the Great King has already given this wood to you, please take it and use it as you wish.
Is it not the case that he took this wood?
At that time, the city magistrate went at once to inform King Ajātaśatru:
"Does Your Majesty know?
While I was recently patrolling the streets, I saw a piece of wood required by Your Majesty for repairs and for difficult tasks, which has been cut up and taken away by another."
Having seen this, I was seized with great terror and my hair stood on end; could it be that the Great King has enemies or thieves who are about to enter the city?
I immediately asked the minister in charge of timber:
"Have you not given wood to others?"
He replied: "I have never given this wood to anyone.
However, I did hear the bhikṣu Dhaniya say:"
"The King has granted the wood.
At that time, the official in charge of timber reported,
"If the King grants it, you may take it as you please."
Then that bhikṣu immediately cut down a large tree and took it away.
"Great King, do you perhaps recall ever giving wood to anyone else?
The king said:
"I do not recall it.
He then commanded the Minister of Wood.

When the minister, having received the command, was about to go to the King's presence, at that time the Bhikṣu Dharmadinnaka entered the city of Rājagṛha on some minor business. Seeing the Bhikṣu Dharmadinnaka from afar, the Minister of Wood addressed him, saying:
“Does the Noble One know?
For your sake I have taken this wood, and the King now summons me.
The bhikṣu replied:
"You may proceed first; I shall follow.
Thereupon, the wood-warden set out ahead, while Butaṇika arrived later and, together with the messenger, went to the king's gate and stood there.
Then the messenger went to the king's presence and said: "Great King!
The official in charge of timber is now standing outside the gate."
"Even though that bhikṣu was not summoned, he has come to the gate.
The king said, "Do not let the wood-gatherer enter for now; you should summon the one who has left the household life."
The messenger went out and summoned the bhikṣu; upon entering, he extended his hand in greeting and said,
"May the Great King be free from illness and enjoy long life," and then stood to one side.
Then the King said to the bhikṣu Dhaniya,
"Noble one! If others did not give you wood,
was it appropriate for you to take it without permission?"
Dhanika said, "It is not permissible.
The King asked:
“If that is so, why did you take my wood and go? Dhanika replied,
“The king gave it to me first.”
The king said,
"I do not recall it; if you,
sir, remember it, please recall it for me."
Dhaniya said: "Does Your Majesty not recall that when you first received the consecration, you made a lion’s roar before the great assembly, declaring:

'In my kingdom, should there be any śramaṇas or brāhmaṇas who maintain their precepts, cultivate goodness, and do not commit theft, they may take at will all the grasses, woods, and water within my realm.'"
The king said:
"I spoke those words based on the assumption that the object was ownerless; yet this wood is an item under another's control—why did you take it so recklessly?"
Dhaniya said, "The King’s statement concerns those who have no owner; how does this concern the King's affairs?
Upon hearing these words, the King was seized with great rage; three furrows appeared on his forehead, his brows were knit and knitted together, and with eyes wide and hands brandished, he said:
“Śramaṇa! You deserve to die now, yet I cannot kill you; you should depart immediately. From this day forward, you must never act like this again.”
At that time, the great multitude raised their voices together and spoke these words:
"How extraordinary!
King Ajātaśatru of Magadha is by nature violent and acts with reckless haste."
"A śramaṇa deserves death, yet he was released merely because of a verbal reprimand.
At that time, Dhaniya returned to his residence and said to the bhikṣus,
"I have nearly been put to death by King Ajātaśatru."
The bhikṣus asked him the reason for this, and Dhaniya related the circumstances in full to them.
Then the bhikṣus went to inform the Blessed One of these matters. The Blessed One addressed the Venerable Ānanda, saying:

"Put on your saṃghāṭī robe, take a bhikṣu with you, and enter the streets and public gathering places of Rājagṛha. Whether they be brahmins or householders, or village heads, guild masters, or wealthy men—whether they have faith or not—you must question all such people as follows:"
"How much property must one steal to violate the laws of the kingdom and deserve the death penalty?
Having received the Buddha's instruction, Ānanda entered the city of Rājagṛha and questioned the people in detail, just as the Buddha had taught him:
"How much property must one steal for the royal law to prescribe the death penalty?"
The people replied, "Whether it be five māṣakas or more than five māṣakas, such a person deserves death.

Having finished his inquiry, Ānanda departed from Rājagṛha and went to where the Blessed One was; having prostrated at the Blessed One’s feet, he stood to one side and addressed the Blessed One as follows:
“Venerable One!
As the Buddha instructed, I went everywhere to ask people:
‘To what extent does one deserve death?’”
They all replied to me:
"If one steals five māsakas, or more than five māsakas, the royal law prescribes the death penalty.
At that time, the World-Honored One, for this reason, assembled the community of bhikṣus; he questioned them with full knowledge, not because he was ignorant.
He asked at the proper time and not at an improper time;
he asked for a beneficial purpose and not without benefit. To breach the dam of ignorance and sever his doubts, and for the sake of his welfare, he asked with a sense of timing:
"Upāli, son of a potter, did you truly perform such an unseemly act as taking wood belonging to the King?"
Dhaniya said, "It is indeed so,
Venerable Sir."
The World-Honored One rebuked him, saying:
"What you have done is not the way of a śramaṇa, not pure conduct, not a practice in accordance with the Dharma, and not an act befitting one who has left the household life."
After the Blessed One had rebuked them in various ways, he addressed the bhikṣus, saying:
"I, considering ten benefits, up to the long endurance of the True Dharma, shall establish a training rule for my śrāvaka disciples in the Vinaya, which should be recited as follows:
'If a bhikṣu, whether in a village or in a secluded place, should take with a thieving mind an object not given by another.'"
When one steals in this manner, whether a king or a high minister seizes them, kills them, binds them and banishes them, or rebukes them, saying:
“Man, you are a thief!
Foolish and ignorant, you have committed such a theft.
If a bhikṣu steals in this manner, he too incurs a pārājika offense and should not live in communal residence.
"Furthermore, 'if a bhikṣu' refers to Dhānika; the rest of the meaning is as explained above.
'If in a village' means within the walls or fences.
'In a secluded place' means outside the walls or fences."
"Another person" refers to a woman, a man, or a eunuch.
"Without having been given" means that no one has bestowed it upon him.
"Object" refers to gold and so forth.
"To take with a thieving mind" means to take an object not given by another with a robber's intent.
"At such a time of stealing" refers to when it is five *māṣakas* or more than five *māṣakas*.
As for "a king," this refers to whether one is a kṣatriya, a brāhmaṇa, a vaiśya, or a śūdra; anyone who has received the consecration of the kṣatriya royal rank is called a king.
If there is a woman who receives the position of consecration, she is also called a king.
As for a great minister, this refers to a royal counselor who deliberates on state affairs for the king and thereby sustains his livelihood.
"Seizing" means taking someone by force and bringing them forward.
"Killing" means severing their life-force.
"Binding" refers to three kinds of binding:
That is to say: iron, wood, and rope.
"Expulsion" means driving one out of the country.
One should issue such a reprimand:
"Hey! You man, you are a thief!
You are a fool who knows nothing!"—this is a statement of contemptuous disparagement.
"One who does this" refers to a person committing theft.
"Bhikṣu" means one who has attained the nature of a bhikṣu.
What is the nature of a bhikṣu?
This refers to receiving full ordination (*upasampadā*). What is meant by "full ordination"?

It refers to the formal procedure of a motion followed by three proclamations (*jñapti-caturtha-karman*), wherein the matter to be performed is accomplished in accordance with the Dharma, reaching its ultimate fulfillment and completion. The candidate for ordination, with a mind of perfection, aspires for the state of completeness; through earnest prayer and vows, they accept it without resentment or malice. Because this is made manifest through verbal expression and vocal action, it is called "full ordination."
*Pārājika* refers to an extremely grave offense that is utterly loathsome; it is something to be despised and not to be cherished.

When a person commits this offense, as soon as it is committed, they are no longer a śramaṇa and no longer a son of the Śākya. They lose their status as a bhikṣu and deviate from the nature of nirvāṇa. They fall and collapse, overcome by others beyond redemption, like a *tāla* tree whose head has been severed, unable to grow lush, increase, or expand; thus it is called *pārājika*.

Regarding "one who should not dwell together": such a person may not dwell together with other bhikṣus. Whether it be the *poṣadha*, the *pravāraṇā*, or the formal acts (*karmavācanā*) consisting of a single motion (*jñapti*), a motion and one proclamation (*jñapti-dvitīya*), or a motion and three proclamations (*jñapti-caturtha*), or even the formal acts involving the twelve types of persons, they should not be appointed for any of these. For this reason, they are called "those who should not dwell together."
Regarding this, what are the characteristics of the offense and its specific details?
A summary verse states:
"Taking for oneself from the ground, or falling [an object] from mid-air."
Carpets, vehicles, and cultivated fields, Taxes, and those who are never satisfied,
Caṇḍālas, and Śīla— These ten matters are all collected together.
The summary verse says:
Taking for oneself what is not given, with the intent to steal another's property,
and perceiving it as belonging to another— these constitute three sets of five distinct cases;
furthermore, there are four sets of four differences, along with two sets of five distinctions.
All these cases concern objects of significant value; one should understand that the application varies according to the circumstances.
There are three characteristics: if a bhikṣu takes another's property of significant value without it being given, he incurs a pārājika offense.
What are the three? They are:
taking it oneself, having it taken by looking on, or having it taken by sending a messenger.
What is "taking it oneself"?
This refers to taking by oneself, or inducing another to take and lift it from its original place.
What is meant by "taking while watching"?
It means taking by oneself while watching, or inducing another to take while watching and lifting it from its original place.
What is taking by means of a messenger?
It refers to taking it oneself by dispatching a messenger, or having a messenger lead it away from its original location.
If a bhikṣu, through these three conditions, takes another's property of significant value without it being given, he incurs a pārājika offense.
Furthermore, there are three conditions by which a bhikṣu incurs a *pārājika* offense for taking the heavy property of another that was not given to him.
What are these three? Namely:
the other has not given it; the substance is heavy property; and it is moved from its original place.
What is taking what is not given?
It refers to taking an object that has never been bestowed upon one by a man, a woman, or a eunuch; this is called taking what is not given.
What constitutes an object of significant value?
If it is five māṣakas or more than five māṣakas.
What is meant by "leaving its original place"?
It means moving from this location to another location.
If a bhikṣu, through these three conditions, takes the heavy property of another that was not given, he incurs a pārājika offense.
Furthermore, there are three other conditions by which a bhikṣu, taking the heavy property of another that was not given, incurs a pārājika offense.
What are the three? They are:
giving rise to the intent to steal, applying the means, and moving [the object] from its original place.
What is meant by "giving rise to the intent to steal"?
It refers to one who, with a thieving mind, desires to steal another's property.
How does he apply the means?
Whether by hand or by foot, he exerts himself to advance toward it.
The locations and other details should be understood as previously explained.
Furthermore, there are three conditions under which a bhikṣu incurs a pārājika offense by taking the valuable property of another that was not given.
What are the three? They are:
that which is under the control of another, the substance being of significant value, and its removal from its original location.
What is meant by "that which is under the control of another"?
That is to say, when heavy objects are taken possession of by women, men, or eunuchs, these are called "objects held by others.
Regarding heavy objects and their removal from their place, they should be understood as previously explained.
Furthermore, there are three conditions by which a bhikṣu incurs a pārājika offense for taking another’s valuable property when it has not been given:
what are these three?
Perceiving the object as being under another’s custody, the object being of substantial value, and its removal from its original place.
What is the perception of another’s possession?
It is when a bhikṣu thinks:
"This object is in the possession of another person, such as a woman or a man."
Perceiving it as another's property;
the rest is as explained above.
Furthermore, there are four conditions by which a bhikṣu incurs a *pārājika* offense for taking another's valuable property that was not given.
That is to say: if one takes an object belonging to another, perceiving it as such, and it is of significant value, by moving it from its original place, the bhikṣu incurs a pārājika offense.
Furthermore, there are four conditions under which a bhikṣu incurs a pārājika offense for taking another's property of significant value that was not given.
What are the four? They are:
having the intent to steal, employing the means, it being a valuable object, and moving it from its original place.
The rest is as explained above.
Furthermore, there are four conditions by which a bhikṣu incurs a pārājika offense for taking what has not been given from another.
What are these four?
It belongs to another; he perceives it as his own; it is an object of value; and he moves it from its place.
What is meant by "protected by others"?
It is like a person who places a valuable object in a vessel and either guards it himself or employs the fourfold army to protect it together.
What is the perception of ownership?
When a person places a valuable object within a chest, a vessel, or the like, they form the perception of ownership:
"This is my property."
The remainder is as stated above.
Furthermore, there are four conditions by which a bhikṣu incurs a *pārājika* offense for taking another’s valuable property that was not given:

namely, when it is guarded but he has no perception that it belongs to him; or when it is unguarded but he has the perception that it belongs to him; the object being of value; and its removal from its place.
What is meant by "having protection but no sense of ownership"?

It is like this: suppose thieves have plundered various cities and towns and fled into the forests and wilds; then, a road-guardian seizes their goods and keeps them gathered in one place for protection, yet does not claim them as his own.
What is meant by "taking what belongs to oneself when there is no protection"?

It is as when a valuable object is placed inside a chest or similar container, and although there are no guards such as men or horses to protect it, one takes it without it being given, thinking it belongs to oneself.
The gravity of the object, the removal from its place, and the nature of the offense are the same as previously described.
Furthermore, there are five conditions under which a bhikṣu incurs a *pārājika* offense by taking another's property that was not given to him.
What are the five?

Perceiving it as not one's own property, perceiving it as not belonging to a friend, perceiving it as not for temporary use, failing to inform others when taking it, and having a thieving intent—by these, one incurs a *pārājika* offense.
Furthermore, there are five circumstances under which a bhikṣu commits no offense. What are these five?

If one perceives the object as one's own, perceives it as belonging to a friend, perceives it as being borrowed for temporary use, informs another at the time of taking it, or lacks the intent to steal—there is no offense.
The Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya, Volume Two;
The Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya, Volume Three.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Yijing by Imperial Decree.
The second part of the second training rule on taking what is not given.
The summary verse says:
Whether it be on the ground, Or at times within a vessel.
Or again, [if they are] in a threshing floor or a granary, or various medicinal roots in a field.

If a bhikṣu knows that another’s valuable property has been placed on the ground—namely, necklaces, armlets, pearls, neck-ornaments, and other articles of adornment—and with the intent to steal, he rises from his seat, adjusts his robes, and departs; as long as he has not yet touched it, he incurs a *duṣkṛta* offense.
If he touches it but has not yet moved it from its place, he incurs a *sthūlātyaya*.
If one lifts and removes it from its place, this is called stealing.
According to the value at that time, if it amounts to five *māṣakas* or more, one incurs a *pārājika* offense;
if it is less than five *māṣakas*, one incurs a *sthūlātyaya*.
If the ground is a single expanse of fine, smooth surface, this is called one place.
If the ground’s surface rises up or cracks, or if there are large fissures, or if it is inscribed with letters or variously painted, this is called different places.
If a single section of a vessel or similar object is smooth and fine, this is called "one place.
If there are cracks, or even painted patterns, these are called "different places.

If a person’s valuable object, such as a necklace or even a jeweled ornament, is placed upon a floor and a bhikṣu, with the intent to steal, initiates the preparatory effort, he incurs the offense of *duṣkṛta* (wrongdoing) until he actually makes physical contact with it.
If he touches it but does not move it from its place, he incurs a sthūlātyaya;
if he lifts it and removes it from its place, this is called stealing.
According to the value at that time, if it reaches five [māṣakas], he incurs a pārājika offense.
If it is not full, one incurs a sthūlātyaya offense.
If the grains, wheat, and so forth on the threshing floor are leveled so as to form a single uniform mass, this is called "one place."
If grains such as rice and wheat are arranged in various heights and levels, forming diverse patterns, this is called "different locations.
If another person's heavy property is placed within a granary or a cellar—referring to various treasures or items such as necklaces and ornaments—[the same applies].
If a bhikṣu conceives the intent to steal and applies the means thereto, he incurs the offense of duṣkṛta (wrongdoing) until he has actually touched the object;
if he touches it but has not moved it from its place, he incurs a sthūlātyaya (grave offense);
if he lifts it and moves it from its place, and the value reaches five [māṣakas], he incurs the root offense (pārājika).
If it is not full, one incurs a sthūlātyaya offense.

If a person's valuable goods are placed inside a granary or a pit, and the grain, wheat, and so forth within that granary or pit reach the opening and are completely level, forming a single uniform mass, this is called "one place."

If grains, wheat, and so forth do not reach the level of the mouth, being uneven in height and appearing in various colors, or if there are obstructions such as wood, mats, or cushions separating them, this is called "being in a different place."

If there are various root-medicines in a person's field—namely, *kṛṣṇamūla* (雀頭香), yellow ginger, white ginger, and other types of root-medicines such as *vatsanābha* (烏頭)—and a bhikṣu employs a means and gives rise to a thieving mind, he incurs a *duṣkṛta* (惡作) offense until he has touched them;
if he touches them but has not moved them from their place, he incurs a *sthūlātyaya* (窣吐羅底也);
if he moves them from their original place and the value reaches five [māṣakas], he incurs the fundamental offense (*pārājika*).
If one is dissatisfied, one incurs a sthūlātyaya offense.
The summary verse says:
Regarding houses and such places there are three; regarding birds and objects there are likewise three kinds.
Regarding the taking of hidden treasures through incantations, there are three distinct cases.

If a person’s garment of various colors is placed upon the roof, and a bhikṣu, conceiving a thieving intent and employing the necessary means, sets up a ladder or steps and uses tools such as hooks or chisels to climb upon it, he incurs an *dukkaṭa* (offense of wrong-doing) for everything from the initial approach until he has not yet touched the garment;
if he touches the garment but has not yet moved it from its place, he incurs a *sthūlātyaya* (grave offense).
If one lifts it from its place, this is called stealing; one incurs an offense according to its value, the same as previously described.

If a washerman hangs clothes on his roof to dry and they are blown away by the wind, falling onto the walking path of a bhikṣu or near the door, if the bhikṣu conceives a thieving mind and employs the necessary means, he incurs a *duṣkṛta* (wrongdoing) until he has actually touched them;
once he touches them, he incurs a *sthūlātyaya* (grave offense).
If it is lifted from its place, the offense is the same as before.

If a person’s valuable property—such as various jewels or ornaments—is placed on an upper story, and a bhikṣu, conceiving a thieving intent and employing means, sets up a ladder or steps and uses hooks or chisels to climb upon it, he incurs an *duṣkṛta* (wrongdoing) for everything prior to touching the object;
if he touches it but has not yet moved it from its original location, he incurs a *sthūlātyaya*.
If one uproots [the trees] from their place, the offense is the same as before.

If a person plants flowering or fruit-bearing trees within a house or by the side of a garden pond, and on festival days adorns them with exquisite objects—namely, various precious necklaces and assorted silks and brocades.
At that time, there was a flying bird that, mistaking the jewel for meat, took it in its beak and flew away.
If a bhikṣu, conceiving a thieving mind and employing the necessary means, seizes that bird, he incurs a *duṣkṛta* offense as long as he has not yet touched the necklace;
if he touches it but has not yet moved it from its original place, and perceives it as the property of the bird, he incurs a *duṣkṛta* offense.
If one lifts and removes it from its place, this is called stealing.
One should calculate its value; if it reaches five [māṣakas], one incurs a sthūlātyaya offense;
if it does not reach that amount, one incurs a duṣkṛta offense.
If a bhikṣu thinks to himself, "This is human property;
how could it be appropriate for birds to possess such necklaces?
yet he touches them and has not yet lifted them from their place, he incurs a sthūlātyaya offense.
When lifting it from its place, if the value is five *māṣakas* or more, one incurs the root offense (*mūlāpatti*);
if it is less than that, one incurs a *sthūlātyaya*.
Suppose a person places various precious objects and jeweled ornaments inside a chest and leaves it on the roof; then, a flying bird seizes the items and carries them away.
If a bhikṣu, having conceived the intent to steal and having applied the necessary means, seizes that bird, he incurs a *duṣkṛta* offense as long as he has not yet touched the necklace;
if he touches the object but it has not yet been moved from its original place, and he perceives it as the property of the bird, he incurs a *duṣkṛta* offense;
if he lifts it and moves it from its place, this is termed "stealing."
One should determine its value; if it reaches five [māṣakas], one incurs a sthūlātyaya offense;
if it does not reach that amount, one incurs a duṣkṛta offense.
If a bhikṣu forms such a thought:
"This is a human being; how could a bird possibly possess necklaces?
Although he touched them, as long as they had not been lifted from their place, he incurred a *sthūlātyaya*;
at the moment they were lifted from their place, if the value reached five [units], he incurred the root offense (*mūlāpatti*).
If it is not completed, one incurs a sthūlātyaya offense.

If a person, within their house or inside a pond, for the sake of amusement, keeps various birds—such as parrots, śārikas, cuckoos, and kalaviṅkas—and adorns them with various kinds of necklaces and ornaments; [if one then takes them away, etc.]... [the preceding applies].

Having seen [the bird], the bhikṣu conceives a thieving mind and employs the necessary means, eventually seizing it. Up until the moment he touches the ornaments, he incurs an *duṣkṛta* (wrongdoing) offense;
if he touches the object but it has not yet been moved from its original place, and he perceives it as the property of a bird, he likewise incurs an *duṣkṛta* offense;
if he lifts it and moves it from its place, this is termed "stealing."
One should determine its value; if it amounts to five [māṣakas] or more, one incurs a *sthūlātyaya*;
if it is less than that, one incurs a *duṣkṛta* offense.
If one perceives this object as belonging to a person rather than as belonging to a bird, then even if one has touched it but not yet moved it from its original place, one incurs a *sthūlātyaya*.
If one lifts it from its place and the value is five [units] or more, one incurs a fundamental offense (*pārājika*);
if it is less than five, one incurs a grave offense (*sthūlātyaya*).
If there is a bhikṣu who, regarding two types of buried treasures:
One [treasure] has an owner, and one is ownerless.

When a bhikṣu intends to take that treasure with an owner, he rises from his seat, adjusts his belt and robes, prepares a maṇḍala, and drives *khadira* wood stakes into its four corners. He encircles it with five-colored threads and kindles various types of wood in a fire pit, reciting a prohibitive mantra while speaking these words:
"Treasure with an owner, you should come; treasure without an owner, do not come."
If, at that time, a treasure with an owner comes forth in accordance with one's words, as long as it has not yet been seen, one incurs a *sthūlātyaya* offense;
when it is seen with the eyes, this is termed "theft."
One should determine its value; if it reaches five [units], one incurs the root offense;
if it does not reach that amount, one incurs a grave offense (sthūlātyaya).
If one speaks as follows:
"One should say: 'May the treasure without an owner come; may the treasure with an owner not come.
If at that time the treasure without an owner comes according to these words, one incurs an offense of wrong-doing (*duṣkṛta*) from the moment it begins to appear until it has been fully seen."
If one sees it with the eye, this is termed "stealing.
One should calculate its value; if it amounts to five [māṣakas] or more, one incurs a sthūlātyaya offense;
if it does not amount to that, one incurs a duṣkṛta offense.

If one steals from hoards belonging either to an owner or to no owner by performing separate acts of theft at different times, one incurs an offense according to the gravity of the specific act, as described above.
The summary verse says:
If an object is upon a woolen rug or mat, or on a stone slab and the like,
or at a marvelous tree of flowers and fruit— one should understand that the matter applies according to each specific location.
If a person has placed valuable items upon a woolen rug, a mat, or a ground-covering— namely, various jewels and necklaces— and if a bhikṣu,
conceiving a thieving mind and employing the means thereto, has not yet touched them, he incurs the offense of *duṣkṛta*;
if he touches those objects but has not yet moved them from their original place, he incurs the offense of *sthūlātyaya*.
If one lifts [the object] from its place, this is called stealing; the offense incurred according to the value at that time is the same as previously stated.
If those grass mats are of a single color, they are considered to be in one place.
If various colors are distinct and different from one another, this is called "different locations.
If a person places a heavy object upon a stone, even if it does not reach the full measure, they incur a *sthūlātyaya* offense.
If a stone is fine, smooth, and forms a single continuous mass, it is called "one place.
If it is peeled, cracked, or split open, or if characters are inscribed upon it, or if it is painted with various colors, this is called "different places."

As it was with the stone slab, so it is for wooden boards, walls, mats, canopies, clothing bundles, wardrobe chests, clothes racks, ivory, pegs, beds, seats, four-legged scripture stands, doors, and door thresholds; the procedure for placing objects upon these is in every respect the same as before.
Regarding the three kinds of trees—
namely, flowering trees, fruit-bearing trees, and marvelous trees—
if a bhikṣu cuts down or steals flowering trees and the like, whether the value reaches the full amount or not, the offense incurred is the same as previously described.
The summary verse says:

Regarding objects on saddles and bridles, as well as elephants, horses, carts, and carriages—one should determine whether they are fat or lean according to their respective locations; there are also distinctions concerning the theft of boats.
Suppose a person has placed a valuable object on a saddle, such as various jewels or sets of necklaces and ornaments.
If a bhikṣu conceives the intent to steal and employs the necessary means, he incurs a *duṣkṛta* offense from the moment until he has not yet mounted [the saddle] or touched the object;
if he touches the object but has not yet moved it from its original place, he incurs a *sthūlātyaya*.
If it is moved to another location, and the value reaches five *māṣakas*, the offense is the same as before.
If a single-colored object covers [the horse] while on its saddle, this is called "one place."
If various colored objects are covered over, this is called a separate location.
If a person’s valuable possessions are placed upon an elephant—namely, various jewels and sets of necklaces—[this is also considered a separate location].
If a bhikṣu conceives the intent to steal and undertakes the preparatory effort, he incurs a *duṣkṛta* offense from the time until he has not yet ascended to or touched the object;
if he touches the object but has not moved it from its place, he incurs a *sthūlātyaya*;
if he moves it from its place and the value reaches five [māṣakas], the offense is the same as before.
If the skin, flesh, blood, and veins of this elephant are all fully developed, this is called "one place.
If its body is emaciated, or if one considers each individual part such as the tusks, ears, nose, belly, ribs, spine, or waist, these are called "distinct places."
If it is moved from its place, one incurs the full offense;
if it is not moved from its place, one incurs a sthūlātyaya.
If one decorates a canopy upon an elephant and places various precious objects and many types of necklaces and ornaments upon this canopy.
If a bhikṣu conceives the intent to steal and employs the means thereto, up until the point where he has not yet ascended or touched the object, he incurs the offense of *duṣkṛta*.
If he touches the object but has not yet moved it from its place, he incurs a *sthūlātyaya*.
If he moves it from its place and the value reaches five [māṣakas], the offense is the same as before.
If this canopy is covered with an object of a single color, it is called one place;
if it is covered with objects of different colors, it is called separate places.
As it is with the elephant, so it is with horse-carts, foot-carts, ox-carts, and even various litters—all are the same as described before.
If a bhikṣu sees a boat tied to a stake with a rope and intends to steal it away, he incurs a *duṣkṛta* offense at the moment he moves it;
if he unties it and it follows the current until it is still within his sight, he incurs a *sthūlātyaya*;
once it reaches a place out of sight, if the value reaches five [māṣakas], he incurs the root offense (*mūlāpatti*).
If it is not full, one incurs a sthūlātyaya.
If one travels upstream against the current, if the distance is equivalent to the width of the river, one incurs the root offense;
if one has not yet reached that point, one incurs a sthūlātyaya.
If one steals from this shore toward the other shore, the limit determined by visual perception remains no different than before.
If one drags a boat onto the bank and steals it away, this is likewise measured according to the limit of visual perception.
If [an object] is submerged in mud and later removed, at the moment it is covered by the mud, this constitutes theft; the offense incurred is the same as before.
If a bhikṣu, while stealing an object, hides it in mud, or burns it, or pierces it, or breaks it, he should form this thought:
"Let this object belong neither to you nor to me."
One who [does so] incurs a *sthūlātyaya*.
The summary verse says:
There are three kinds of cultivating fields; there are three distinct kinds of boats.
Geese and wild geese, as well as pond lotuses; hunting and fishing, along with stealing water;
and teaching disciples or acting as a guide for thieves—these three types of matters are distinct.
If a person engages in agricultural work during the autumn season, namely cultivating rice, sugarcane, or salt fields.
A bhikṣu, seeing that water might run short in his own field, blocked the water outlet of a shared irrigation channel and diverted the water into his own furrows, thinking to himself:
"May my field flourish, while his does not ripen."
If one benefits oneself while causing harm to another, and the value reaches five [māṣakas], one incurs the fundamental offense (pārājika);
if it does not reach that amount, one incurs a sthūlātyaya.
If one sees an abundance of water and, within a shared irrigation channel, diverts the flow of another’s water to block their own field plots, thinking thus:
"If my fields may flourish, but let his not ripen"—
if one benefits oneself while causing harm to another, and the value reaches five *māṣakas*,
one incurs the root offense (*mūlāpatti*); if it does not reach that amount, one incurs a *sthūlātyaya*.
There are four kinds of differences among objects:
first, those that are heavy in substance and heavy in value;
second, those that are light in substance but heavy in value;
Third, heavy substance and light value;
fourth, light substance and light value.
What is meant by heavy substance and high value?
That is to say: mani-jewels, pearls, lapis lazuli, conch shells, jade, coral, gold, silver, agate, mother-of-pearl, red pearls, and right-turning conch shells.
What is meant by "light in substance but heavy in value"?
It refers to fine silks, silk thread, saffron, and *suktimelā*.
What is meant by "heavy in substance but light in value"?
These refer to iron and tin.
What is meant by that which is light in substance and low in value?
These refer to wool, hemp, cotton, *karpāsa* (cotton cloth), and floss.
If these aforementioned items are placed within three kinds of boats—
namely, earthenware boats, wooden boats, and leather boats—

and if they are placed in whichever boat corresponds to their weight and value, whether heavy in substance and high in price, or light in substance and low in price, then should the boat break, the owner says:
"Whatever floats upon the water may be taken at will; whatever sinks belongs to me.

If a bhikṣu, conceiving a thieving intent and employing the necessary means, enters the water and causes it to sink, he incurs a *duṣkṛta* offense from the moment he has not yet touched the object until he does so;
if he touches it, he incurs a *sthūlātyaya*.
If one lifts it from its place and its value reaches five *māṣakas*, one incurs the root offense;
if it does not reach that amount, one incurs a *sthūlātyaya*.
If one sinks it into the mud with the intention of taking it back later, one incurs an offense according to the preceding rule.

If one acts with a mind that is neither for oneself nor for others, sinking [the object] into the mud so that the thing does not belong to him or to me, one incurs an offense according to the previous rule.
All subsequent precepts should be understood by analogy with this.
If one places items that are light in weight but high in value alongside items that are heavy in weight but low in value onto a single ship, and the ship breaks apart, the owner of the goods says:
"Whatever sinks in the water you may take; whatever floats upon the water belongs to me."
If a bhikṣu, having conceived a thieving intent and applied the necessary means, floats across water to take [an object], he incurs a *duṣkṛta* offense as soon as he has not yet touched the object;
if he touches it, he incurs a *sthūlātyaya*;
if he lifts it and removes it from its place, one should calculate its value, and the offense incurred is the same as before.
If one attempts to retrieve [a bird] that has sunk into the mud, one incurs an offense according to the previous rule.

If someone, for the sake of amusement within their home or at a spring or pond, keeps various kinds of birds—such as geese, wild geese, and mandarin ducks—and adorns them with many necklaces and ornaments.

A bhikṣu, having conceived a thieving mind and applied the necessary means, enters the water and seizes those birds; as long as he has not yet touched the necklace, he incurs a *duṣkṛta* (wrongdoing) offense.
If he touches it and forms the thought, "I am taking the bird's property," [he incurs a *thullaccaya* offense].
There is also an offense of wrongdoing (duṣkṛta);
if it is moved from its original place, one should calculate its value—if it reaches five [māṣakas], one incurs a thullaccaya;
if it does not reach that amount, one incurs an offense of wrongdoing.
If one thinks, "I am taking this person's property; how could birds possibly have such necklaces?
yet touches the object, one incurs a sthūlātyaya offense.
If [the plant] is moved from its original location, it should be valued according to its price;
if the value reaches five *māṣakas*, it constitutes a *pārājika* offense;

if it does not reach that amount, one incurs a *sthūlātyaya*. If there are aquatic flowers in a pond—namely, blue lotuses (*utpala*), white lotuses (*puṇḍarīka*), *kumuda*, *padma*, fragrant flowers, or seasonal flowers—which are beloved by the multitude.

If a bhikṣu conceives a thieving intent and employs the means to enter a pond to steal flowers, he incurs the offense of *duṣkṛta* (wrongdoing) from the moment he enters until he has not yet touched them;

if he touches the flowers, plucks and breaks them off, and carries them away, tying them into a bundle, he incurs the offense of *sthūlātyaya* (grave offense) from that point until he has not yet moved them from their original location;
if he lifts them and moves them from that place, he incurs the same offense as previously described.

On all four sides of the pond were various kinds of land-growing flowering trees, namely: the *aṭimuktaka*, *tagara*, *campaka*, *pāṭala*, *bālisika*, and *mallikā*; such were the various flowering trees.

If a bhikṣu employs means and gives rise to a thieving intent, desiring to steal those flowers, he incurs the offense of *duṣkṛta* (wrongdoing) from the time he first acts until he has not yet touched them;

if he climbs a tree to pluck and break off the flowers and place them within the hem of his robe, he incurs the same offense as previously described, whether the flowers have not yet been moved from their original location or have already been moved.
If there are hunters and their followers who, in forest or wilderness areas, set out various hunting implements—such as snares and the like—for the purpose of capturing or killing wild animals.
If a bhikṣu takes hunting gear with the intent to steal, he incurs an offense according to its value.
If, however, he destroys the hunting gear out of compassion, thinking:
"Let not this cause harm to the lives of many beings, nor let those hunters incur immeasurable demerit," [he incurs no offense].
...one incurs an *dukkaṭa* (offense of wrong-doing).
It should be understood that all subsequent precepts are the same in this regard.
If a bhikṣu, with the intent to steal, releases a deer caught in a snare, and the value [of the deer] reaches five [māṣakas], he incurs the root offense (*mūlāpatti*).
If it is not full [of fish], one incurs a *sthūlātyaya* offense.

If a fisherman or his accomplices block the main entrance of a river or pond and set traps and weirs to kill various kinds of fish, when a bhikṣu takes those traps with the intent to steal, he incurs an offense as previously described;
if he does so out of compassion, he likewise incurs an offense as previously described.
If one steals fish from a trap, one incurs the same offense as previously described, commensurate with their value.

If a large caravan carrying various goods passes through a dangerous path where water is scarce, and they travel with water in various vessels—whether jars, pots, flasks, or leather bags—the water is divided among humans and animals according to fixed portions. If a bhikṣu, conceiving a thieving intent and employing the necessary means, takes a portion of the human water, he incurs an offense commensurate with the previous cases, whether the water has been touched or not yet touched.
If it concerns animals, if the amount is five *māṣakas* or more, one incurs a *sthūlātyaya*;
if less than that, one incurs an *duṣkṛta*.

For example, suppose people of Jambudvīpa form a caravan, take various goods, and board a ship to go out to sea in search of treasures. Because they lack water, they store it in various vessels—namely, jars, pots, flasks, and bags. However, there is a distinction between the humans and the animals regarding the request for and the acceptance of these portions of water.
If a bhikṣu gives rise to a thieving mind and employs the necessary means, he incurs an offense according to the previous rules when stealing a portion belonging to a human;
he likewise incurs an offense according to the previous rules when taking a portion belonging to an animal.
At that time, there was a disciple traveling along a road with his two teachers; the teachers had some clothing and belongings which they entrusted to the disciple.

At that time, because the disciple had a thieving intent, he walked slowly and did not proceed; when he reached a place where [the object] could be seen with the eyes, he incurred a sthūlātyaya offense.
Upon reaching a place where it was no longer visible, if the value was five [māṣakas] or more, he incurred the root offense (mūlāpatti);
if it was less than five, he incurred a sthūlātyaya offense.
If a disciple abandons his teacher and departs hastily from before him, the offense is as previously determined once he reaches a place where he is no longer within eye-sight.

If the disciple has a thieving intent and wishes to take the teacher’s robe—whether proceeding from the room to the upper gallery, or from the upper gallery to the room, or descending from the gallery to the door-eaves and the foot of the steps, or going down from a three-story platform in the monastery to exit—the offense is the same as before, up until the point he reaches a place beyond eye-sight.
If there is a bhikṣu dwelling in an araṇya who is approached by bandits intent on plundering a village, and they ask him:
"Venerable sir,
do you perhaps know where such-and-such a village or such-and-such a house is located?"
The bhikṣu replied,
"I know its location.
The bandit asked again:

"Is that household one with many women and few men? Is there no vicious dog and no dense thickets of thorns? Is it easy to enter and easy to exit, such that I shall suffer no harm and be able to obtain the goods?"
"If you succeed as you intend, I shall share the goods with you, Venerable Sir.
If that bhikṣu replies, "Good sir, I know the house of so-and-so;
it has many women and few men, there are no vicious dogs or thorny thickets, and it is easy to enter and easy to exit. It will do you no harm, and you shall be able to obtain the goods."
Once the bhikṣu has given this instruction and the thief returns the object, [the bhikṣu] incurs a sthūlātyaya offense until the portion has been taken;
if he takes the thief’s portion, the gravity of the offense is the same as before.
If that bhikṣu, after having spoken thus with those thieves, subsequently feels regret once they have departed, and goes to the place where the thieves are and speaks as follows:
"Do you not know?..."

"I spoke these words in haste, without careful deliberation, like a foolish, ignorant, and deluded person who, being unskilled in the matter, offers a reckless response. However, that house has few women and many men; it contains many vicious dogs and dense thorns, making it difficult to enter or exit. I did not wish for you to retrieve the goods without injury."
Regardless of whether those bandits depart or not, the bhikṣu incurs a sthūlātyaya offense.
If this bhikṣu sees that the bandit gang intends to plunder a village or town and goes to their houses, saying these words:

"Sirs, remain alert and be most careful; tonight there will surely be thieves who enter; do not let your property all be carried off by the robbers, lest even your lives be subjected to injury or death."
Regardless of whether those thieves actually come or not, the bhikṣu incurs a sthūlātyaya.
If a bhikṣu acts as previously described, there are three types of matters constituting the preliminary effort for theft.
What are the three?
They are the matter of fields, the matter of houses, and the matter of shops.
Regarding the matter of fields, there are two kinds of acquisition:
First, taking through verbal dispute;
second, taking by surrounding.
What is meant by taking through verbal dispute?
If a bhikṣu, on account of a dispute over land with a layperson, goes before a judge, and if the bhikṣu is defeated while the layperson prevails, he commits a sthūlātyaya offense.
If a bhikṣu achieves victory, then as long as the mind of the layperson has not ceased [its intent], the bhikṣu incurs a sthūlātyaya offense.
If that layperson’s mind ceases, one should calculate the value according to the preceding rule to determine the offense incurred; this is called "taking through litigation."
What is meant by "enclosing"?

If a bhikṣu, regarding another's field, encloses it with tree branches, or with mats as a screen, or constructs a moat, or surrounds it with a wall—up until the enclosure is not yet complete—he incurs a sthūlātyaya offense.
If one encloses [the object] and thus commits the offense as previously described, this is called "stealing by surrounding.
As it is with the matter of fields, so too should the matters of houses and shops be understood as above.
The summary verse says:
Regarding goods subject to tax, carrying them for another;
Taking another's property and departing, Not having received it yet forcibly wearing it; Carrying things for the sake of one's parents.
Furthermore, for the sake of the Triple Gem, one shares the proceeds equally with those who follow;
the owner of the robes takes them for safekeeping; one causes others to dye clothes or not to dye them;
one carries taxes through a small gate; and one seizes all the goods of merchants.

At that time, when the World-Honored One had first realized unsurpassed wisdom and his teachings had not yet spread widely, it was difficult for the bhikṣus to pass through customs checkpoints while ordinary laypeople could pass easily.
On one occasion, a large number of bhikṣus were traveling with a great caravan of merchants to another country, and their route led through a customs checkpoint.
The bhikṣus said to the merchants, "Venerable sirs!

We currently possess a small amount of taxable goods; please carry them for us past the customs post before returning them to us, so that our share does not fall into the hands of those tax officials."
The merchant said, "So be it.
He then took the goods with him across the pass and returned them to that bhikṣu.
The bhikṣu gradually traveled until he reached a residence. The resident bhikṣus, seeing that the guest had first arrived, asked from a distance:
"Welcome, venerable one!
Was your journey peaceful?"
“Are the mountain passes and river crossings free from harassment by customs duties?
He replied,
“Most welcome, Venerable Sir!”
"As we travel back and forth, may we not be troubled by others. He asked,
"Is it that the venerable ones have no goods subject to taxation?"
He replied,
"I have a trusted merchant who, having passed through the customs, has just now handed it over to me.
The bhikṣus said to him:
"Did we thus cooperate in passing goods through the customs?
He replied,
"Even if it was improper, I have already passed them."
At that time, a bhikṣu traveling on the road felt remorse in his heart, thinking:
"Have I not committed a pārājika offense?
For this reason, he informed the other bhikṣus, and the bhikṣus informed the Buddha. The Buddha said:

"Monks, you have not committed an offense; however, monks must not carry goods across a customs post for private purposes. One who violates this shall incur an offense of transgression against the Dharma.

At that time, the Blessed One, having caused King Bimbisāra of Magadha to attain the vision of the Truths within the Śiṃśapā Grove, proceeded to Śrāvastī and taught the *Kumāraputra-sūtra* to King Prasenajit of Kośala, bringing him to subjugation.
At that time, those two kings each issued a proclamation:
"All bhikṣus within my kingdom shall be exempt from taxes, just like the crown prince; likewise, all bhikṣuṇīs shall be exempt from taxation, just like the women of the inner palace."
"Because of this, these bhikṣus and bhikṣuṇīs passed through the passes and rivers without having to pay customs duties.
At that time, the teaching of the World-Honored One was widespread; thus, while it was easy for the bhikṣus to pass through the customs, it was difficult for laypeople."
At that time, there was a bhikṣu who, traveling with a merchant caravan, went abroad on a journey and arrived at a customs checkpoint.
Then the merchants prostrated at the bhikṣu’s feet and spoke these words:
“Noble One!...”

For a long time, I have been oppressed by cold and heat, and harmed by wind, heat, poisonous insects, mosquitoes, gadflies, and the like; yet through diligent toil and hardship in seeking various wealth and goods, all that I have gained has been used to provide offerings for the Triple Gem.
"I now have goods for which tax must be paid; may you, sirs, carry them through the customs station for me and return them to me.
Then the bhikṣus carried them through for him and returned them to the merchants.
As the bhikṣu gradually traveled to Śrāvastī, the resident bhikṣus said to him,
"Welcome, Venerable One!
Was your journey peaceful?"
The details are as explained above.
He replied:
"Venerable Sir!"
"I also bestow benefit and grace upon others; how could I myself experience any toil or hardship!
The bhikṣus asked, "How was that?"
Then that bhikṣu reported the matter in full.
The bhikṣus asked, "Is it permissible to conceal goods in this manner when passing through a customs checkpoint?
He replied:
"Even though it was improper, I have already finished.
At that time, this bhikṣu felt remorse, thinking:
"Have I not committed a pārājika offense?"
He reported this matter to the bhikṣus, and the bhikṣus reported it to the Buddha. The Buddha said:
"This bhikṣu has committed no offense; however, bhikṣus should not carry goods across a customs post in private. One who violates this shall incur an offense of transgression against the Dharma."
At that time, there was a bhikṣu traveling with a caravan who arrived at a customs station. Then the merchants prostrated at the bhikṣu’s feet and spoke these words:
“Noble One!”
"For a long time I have been oppressed by cold, heat, hunger, and thirst," as described in detail above.

"Whatever profit I have gained has all been used to provide offerings for the Triple Gem. Now, regarding these goods of mine that are subject to tax, you should carry them through the customs post for me and return them to me."
The bhikṣu said:
"The Buddha has already established a precept that a bhikṣu should not pass through a customs station without paying the duty.
I do not dare to carry goods past the tax office now."
At that time, the merchants thought to themselves:
"The bhikṣu is unwilling to carry it across; we should employ a deceptive expedient.
They said to the bhikṣu:
"Noble ones!
Our minds are disturbed this morning and we are unable to prepare food; may you enter the village and seek alms as the occasion permits.
Thereupon, all the bhikṣus went into the village.
After the bhikṣu had departed, each of the people took the bhikṣu’s robe-bag, alms-bowl bag, and miscellaneous bags, and placed their own taxable goods inside them.
When the bhikṣu obtained food and returned to the caravan, and his meal was finished, he took up his own robes and bowl and passed through the customs checkpoint together with the others.
Then the merchants all came forward to open and unpack the bhikṣu’s belongings, whereupon the bhikṣu said,
"Why do you gentlemen touch my things without permission?
The men replied:
“Noble one!
I have placed these tax goods within your virtuous pouch; I now wish to take them.
The bhikṣu replied:
“O noble ones! You have intentionally caused me to commit an offense.
They then replied:
"Since you have not produced the three types of karma regarding this matter, how could there be any fault?
At that time, the bhikṣus felt remorse, thinking:
"Could it be that we have incurred a pārājika offense?"
At that time, as the bhikṣus gradually arrived at Śrāvastī, the resident bhikṣus saw them and said:
"Welcome, venerable ones!
Has your journey been peaceful?"
The full account was as related above.
He replied:

"I have suffered no hardship; however, while I was on the road entering a village for alms, my traveling companion opened my robe-pouch and privately placed various taxable goods inside it. We were unaware that we were carrying these past the customs checkpoint."
Later, upon seeing this, he felt regret and thought, "Have I not committed a *pārājika* offense?
Then the bhikṣus reported this matter in detail to the Blessed One. The Blessed One said, "The bhikṣu has not committed an offense.
However, bhikṣus, regarding one's robes and bowl, if there is no one to look after them, one should not abandon them and depart; rather, one should leave someone behind to guard them."
"If you do not keep watch, you shall incur an offense of transgressing the Dharma.
At that time, there was a bhikṣu traveling with a caravan who entered a village to beg for food, leaving one person behind to guard the goods.
The guardian then had to go to relieve himself or fetch water.

Then the merchants each placed their taxable goods inside the robes and alms-bowl bags of the bhikṣus; as before, they passed through the customs post and came to retrieve the taxable goods, eventually informing the bhikṣus.
The bhikṣus informed the Buddha, and the Buddha said: “Bhikṣus, there is no offense.
If one must guard goods, two bhikṣus should be left behind. At that time, a certain bhikṣu left two bhikṣus to guard his goods.

While one of them was away for the sake of relieving himself or fetching water, the merchants went together to the place where the single remaining bhikṣu was guarding. Some took hold of his hand, others grasped his feet, and they placed the taxable goods inside his robe-pouch. The bhikṣu thought to himself:
"I shall inform my fellow practitioners when they arrive.
When the bhikṣus returned from their almsround, the merchants devised a deceptive stratagem, manifesting a scene of great commotion so that those bhikṣus were unable to give him notice.
Having passed through the customs checkpoint, each of them came to take their belongings.
The bhikṣu said to them,
"Why have you gentlemen touched my things without permission?"
The merchant replied,
"I have placed these taxable goods inside this pouch.
Then the bhikṣus said:
"Now that you two have been ordered to guard the robes, how can you further cause us to commit an offense together?
At that time, the two bhikṣus related the matter in full.
At that time, the bhikṣus felt remorse, thinking:
"Could it be that I have committed a pārājika offense?
They reported the matter in its entirety to the other bhikṣus.
The bhikṣus informed the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"There is no offense. When the person watching the goods sees someone else place an item there, he should have a layperson or a śrāmaṇera remove that object."
"If there is no one of this sort, you should personally draw them out and hand each to that person.
Should you act otherwise, you shall incur an offense of transgression against the Dharma.

The Buddha was staying at the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park, in Śrāvastī. At that time, there was an elder in that city who had caused his son to go forth as a monk. Having traveled to another region, the son obtained two pieces of cotton cloth, whereupon he thought to himself:
“As the World-Honored One has said:
‘Even though one has gone forth, one must still provide for and support one’s parents.
These two pieces of cotton cloth—one is intended for my father and one for my mother.”
At that time, the bhikṣu abandoned his former residence and returned to his old home. On the road leading to Śrāvastī, he arrived at a customs checkpoint, where the tax collector asked him:
"Noble One!..."
"Is there anything subject to taxation?
He replied,
"Worthy sir!"
"I have no taxable goods.
He replied, "Stay for a moment; bring your goods here so that we may examine them."
As soon as he opened his robe-bag, he saw two pieces of cotton cloth and said, "Noble One!
You have gone forth into homelessness within this well-spoken Dharma and Vinaya; how could you possibly tell a deliberate lie for the sake of these two pieces of cloth?"
He said: "O worthy one! This is not my property."
He asked, "Whose property is this?
and she replied:
"One is a paternal object; the other is a maternal object.
He replied, "I do not recognize the father, nor do I recognize the mother; return the tax payment to me, and only then may you proceed."
He detained him for a long time to collect the tax, and only then released him to depart.
Once he had reached the city, remorse arose in his mind, and he informed the bhikṣus.
The bhikṣus reported this to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
“There is no offense.
One should not merely say, ‘These are my parents.
Rather, one should speak thus to the tax official:”
“O Worthy One! As the World-Honored One has said:

‘Parents undergo great toil and hardship for their children; they protect, nourish, and sustain them with breast milk. Among those who provide instruction in Jambudvīpa, even if a child were to carry his mother on one shoulder and his father on the other for a hundred years without ever growing weary, or were to fill this entire earth with mani-jewels, pearls, lapis lazuli, conch shells, coral, agate, gold, silver, jade, musāragalva, red pearls, and right-spiraling shells—offering all such treasures as worship to bring about wealth and happiness, or even ascending to a position of high honor—even by doing these things, one still could not repay the kindness of one’s parents.’”

If their parents lack faith, they cause them to abide in right faith; if they lack precepts, they cause them to abide in the prohibitive precepts; if they are by nature stingy, they cause them to practice generous giving; and if they lack wisdom, they cause them to give rise to wisdom.
If you, my son, can skillfully exhort and persuade your parents in this manner, causing them to abide in virtue, only then can it be called repaying their kindness.
Since your parents possess such profound and deep merit, I now wish to take these items to repay their benevolence.
"If, while praising and speaking thus of the parents' kindness, they let one go, that is well;
if they do not let one go, one may depart after paying the tax.
If they do not grant it, one incurs the offense of *sthūlātyaya*."
The Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya, Volume Three;
The Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya, Volume Four.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Yijing by Imperial Command.
The Second Chapter on the Training Precept Against Taking What Is Not Given, Part Three.
At that time, the Blessed One was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park, where he taught the Dharma-door of making offerings to the bhikṣus, speaking in verse:
“If a person does not perform meritorious deeds, They will constantly experience bitter retribution;”
"If one is able to cultivate merit, there will be happiness in this life and in future lives.

When the bhikṣus heard this teaching, they practiced extensive alms-gathering and made vast offerings to the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha; consequently, the Buddha’s teachings gradually increased and spread further.
