In this city there was an elder who, not long after marrying his wife, fathered a son. When the boy had gradually grown up, he went forth into homelessness. At that time, the bhikṣus thought to themselves:
"There are many bhikṣus in this city now, and it is difficult to obtain alms."
"I should now travel to other regions to offer worship to the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha.
He then went to various places to beg as he pleased, obtaining many kinds of silk fabrics and other items; he filled his robe-bag with them and returned to Śrāvastī.
As he was passing through a customs checkpoint, the tax collector asked him,
"Noble one! Do you have any goods subject to taxation?"
He replied, "O worthy one!
I have no goods subject to tax."
He said, "Wait! Bring the object here so that I may examine it."
As soon as he opened his robe-bag, he saw it was filled with various items.
The tax official said,
"If these things contained in this bag were exempt from taxation, why wait for them to be carried on a camel before paying duty?"
The bhikṣu said:
"O worthy one! This is not my property."
He asked, “Whose property is this?
He replied:
"The first is property belonging to the Buddha, the second is property belonging to the Dharma, and the third is property belonging to the Sangha.
He replied, "How could I possibly know the affairs of the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Sangha? I only require my tax payment before I may proceed as I please."
He detained him for a long time to collect the tax, and then released him and departed.
Upon arriving at Śrāvastī, he felt remorse and informed the bhikṣus.
The bhikṣu informed the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"This person has committed no offense. One should not merely say, 'These are the property of the Triple Gem.
Rather, one should speak thus to the tax official in praise of the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha."
How does one praise the Buddha?

That is to say: Bhagavān, Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Vidyācaraṇasaṃpanna, Sugata, Lokavid, Anuttara, Puruṣadamyasārathi, Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām, Buddha, Bhagavān—this is called praising the Buddha.
What is the praise of the Dharma?

It refers to the World-Honored One’s skillful exposition of the essential teachings of the Dharma, which brings about freedom from feverish affliction within the present life; it is taught according to the capacities of beings to lead them toward Nirvana, and through internal realization, the wisdom of the three knowledges is perfected—this is called the praise of the Dharma.

What is the praise of the Saṅgha? All the Śrāvaka disciples of the Blessed One abide in the correct principle, possessing a straightforward mind with reverence and compliance toward the supreme Dharma. Within the Saṅgha, there are those who have attained the stage of entering the stream and the fruit of stream-entry; those who have attained the stage of entering once-returning and the fruit of once-returning; those who have attained the stage of entering non-returning and the fruit of non-returning; and those who have attained the stage of entering arhatship and the fruit of arhatship. These eight types of great beings are all perfected in ethical discipline (*śīla*), perfected in meditative concentration (*samādhi*), perfected in wisdom (*prajñā*), perfected in liberation (*vimukti*), and perfected in the knowledge and vision of liberation (*vimukti-jñāna-darśana*). They are worthy of taking refuge in and should be revered; they are the most excellent field of merit for all the world. This is called the praise of the Saṅgha.
When praising the Triple Gem in this manner, it is well if the person allows one to pass;
if they do not allow passage, one should pay the toll and then depart.
If one does not pay it, one incurs a sthūlātyaya offense.
At that time, there was a bhikṣu who, for the sake of making offerings to the Triple Gem, carried various goods through a customs checkpoint.

Although he praised the Triple Gem in the presence of the tax official, the official refused to let him pass without charge and demanded the tax payment. Thereupon, the bhikṣu gave him a portion of what he was carrying.
The Buddha said, "It should be divided equally; it should not be given to one side.
When the bhikṣus divided the goods, the delay caused them to lose the merchant caravan, and they were subsequently harmed by thieves, tigers, and leopards.
The Buddha said:
"One should not make a division while on the road; rather, one should give a portion to the tax official as it is carried, and once arrived at the dwelling place, divide the goods equally."
"If one acts otherwise, one incurs an offense of transgressing the Dharma.

While the Buddha was staying at Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park in Śrāvastī, there was a bhikṣu in that city who was well-versed in the Tripiṭaka and widely recognized by the community; he was skilled in preaching the Dharma with unimpeded eloquence and traveled through the countryside until he reached Rājagṛha.
When the three-month rains retreat had concluded, a group of monks wished to seek out a caravan to travel to Śrāvastī in order to pay homage at the feet of the World-Honored One.

At that time, there was a merchant leader who intended to take his goods to Śrāvastī; having heard of this, the bhikṣus went to the merchant leader’s place and explained to him the three types of superior meritorious deeds: namely, giving, ethical discipline, and cultivation.

When he preached this Dharma, the merchant leader’s heart was filled with reverence and faith; he then invited the bhikṣu to his home for offerings and presented him with a fine cotton cloth. Prostrating at his feet, he spoke these words:
“Noble One, what may I do for you?”
The bhikṣu said, "O worthy one!
I now wish to go to Śrāvastī to pay homage at the feet of the World-Honored One; please give rise to a heart of compassion toward me and protect me with your mindfulness."
He replied, “Very well!
and then accompanied the merchant leader along the road.
The merchant leader said:

"You shall act as a beggar for alms and I shall cultivate merit; from Rājagṛha to Śrāvastī, regarding all necessities along the way—clothing, food and drink, bedding, and medicine—you need not worry at all."
The bhikṣu consented.
As they passed through a customs checkpoint on the road, the merchant chief paid all his goods as duty and then thought to himself:
"I have finished paying for my goods."
"The noble ones' white cotton cloth has not yet been taxed. If you demand tax, let the goods come from me; you should take that cloth and place it among my own goods.
He said to the bhikṣus, "Noble ones, please give me the white cotton cloth."
He replied,
"Does regret arise in your mind regarding the things you have given?
He answered:
“I have no regretful heart; however, my goods have already been taxed, whereas your bundles have not yet been taxed. If you seek to collect the tax, let the goods come from me.
He replied, “O worthy one!
"The World-Honored One has already established a training rule: if a bhikṣu carries goods through a customs checkpoint and does not pay the duty, he commits a root offense.
At that time, the merchant leader thought to himself:
"Observing his intention, he is unwilling to give me the cloth; I shall know the proper time myself."
He said, "Noble One!
My mind was disturbed this morning, so I did not have time to prepare food; you may enter the village and seek it according to your needs."
Having heard these words, the bhikṣu went to the village; the merchant took the cloth and placed it among his own goods.
Once they arrived at the customs post, the tax collector asked: "Noble one!"
"Venerable sir, are there any taxable goods within your robe-bag?
The bhikṣu replied,
"I have one bolt of cloth."
He replied, "Bring it here and let me examine it.

When the bhikṣu opened his bag and did not see the cloth, he immediately assumed a sorrowful expression and sighed with his hands behind his back. At that moment, the tax collector said to the bhikṣu:
"Why do you have such a sorrowful countenance, with your hands behind your back and sighing so deeply?
The bhikṣu replied,
"I had a single cotton quilt that was stolen by thieves."
The tax collector said, "Why do you say only that you, O virtuous one, have been robbed by thieves? I too have been robbed; because I lost this object, I have gained nothing.
At that time, after the bhikṣu had passed through the customs post, the merchant leader said to him:
"Why are you sorrowful and your heart so unhappy?
He replied,
"Your benevolence possesses the merit of giving, but lacks the merit of enjoyment."
He replied, "What is the meaning of this?
The bhikṣu said:
"The bolt of cloth you gave as a gift has been taken away by bandits.
He replied, "It was not taken by bandits;
fearing that they would demand the tax value at the customs station, I temporarily placed this item among my own goods. If it is indeed required, I shall now give it to you."
He replied,
“O worthy one!
It would be better to be robbed by bandits than for me to commit an offense because of this.”
He replied,
"Noble One! Since you did not give rise to the three types of karma regarding these objects, how could there be any offense?"
Having heard this, the bhikṣu felt regret in his heart and subsequently arrived at Śrāvastī.
The bhikṣus there said to him,
"Welcome, venerable one!"
"Are the traveling goods secure?
The bhikṣu reported the matter in full to the other bhikṣus.
The bhikṣus informed the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"That bhikṣu has committed no offense.
However, regarding the proper protocols for traveling on the road, I shall now explain them.
When a bhikṣu traveling on the road enters a village to beg for alms, he should mark his clothing and requisites with signs; upon his return, he should examine them carefully."
"If you do not comply, you shall incur an offense of transgressing the Dharma.
While the Buddha was at Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park, there were two bhikṣus—
one old and one young— who traveled together as companions through the human realm.
The elders possessed many garments and requisites for living, whereas the youths had few.
At that time, as the elders were about to reach the customs checkpoint and their goods required taxation, they thought to themselves:
"I have taxable items; if he questions me and I say there are none, I shall be guilty of intentional lying."
"If my path lies through here, they will certainly demand a toll.
What skillful means can I employ to avoid these two matters? He then had this thought:
"Take my belongings and give them to that young man; wait until we have passed through the customs checkpoint, and I shall take them myself.
He said to the young man, "Please lend me your arm for a moment to carry these things."
The youth then thought to himself,
"Could it not be that this old man’s body has grown weary and thus asks me to carry his belongings?
He then accepted them and went on ahead.
The tax collector asked,
"Venerable sir, do you have anything subject to taxation?
He replied:
"I have no goods subject to tax," he said;
the tax official let him pass.
The elder followed behind empty-handed, and the tax official did not question him.
Having passed through the customs station, he said:
"Venerable one!
Return my robes and bowl to me."
The youth asked,
"Venerable Sir!
Has your fatigue now been relieved?"
He replied:
"I did not cause you to carry this object out of weariness; rather, it was because I had goods subject to tax that I thought to myself:
'If those tax officials ask me whether I have goods subject to tax, [what shall I say?']"
If I say that I have received nothing, I would be speaking falsely; if I say that I have, I shall certainly pay the tax.
For this expedient reason, I am having you carry these goods past the customs post.
"Now that we have already passed through, you should return it to us.
"If it is so, the Elder himself will avoid the tax payment, but this will cause me to incur guilt."
He replied, "Since you were unaware of it, for what reason have you incurred this offense?
At that time, the young bhikṣu felt regret and remorse; he went to the city of Śrāvastī and arrived at the monastery (vihāra).
The bhikṣus saw him and said to him:
"Welcome, venerable one!
Was your journey pleasant?"
He replied,
"How could there be peace and happiness? He asked:
“What was the intention?
He related the preceding circumstances in detail to the bhikṣus.
The bhikṣus reported this to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"That bhikṣu is not at fault.
However, when bhikṣus are traveling on a journey, they should not carry items for others without first inquiring about them.
If one is to carry such items, one must ask thoroughly:"
"If there is nothing here subject to taxation?"—
it is proper for one to ask thus; if one does not ask,
one incurs an offense of transgression against the Dharma.

The Buddha said, "One should not pass through a customs checkpoint carrying goods subject to taxation; if one passes through with such goods, one incurs an offense of transgression against the Dharma.
At that time, there were sixty bhikṣus traveling among the people who arrived at a certain village.
There was a householder, immensely wealthy with abundant riches and many enjoyments, who possessed deep respect and faith; seeing the bhikṣus, he invited them to take a meal at his home.
After they had eaten, he gave each of them a pair of white cotton cloths, whereupon the bhikṣus said, "Householder!"
"The Buddha has prohibited us from carrying taxable goods past the customs post.
How, then, can we now take this property?
The elder remained silent and no longer gave it to them.
Then, after the bhikṣus had offered their blessings, they departed along the road.
Upon arriving at Śrāvastī, the bhikṣus said,
"Welcome, venerable one!"
"Was your journey pleasant? They replied, "Our journey was pleasant;
however, there was a donor who invited us to his house for a meal. At the conclusion of the meal, each person wished to give us a pair of white cotton cloths (*pāṭaka*), but we did not accept them."
"Because the Buddha has established the precepts and does not permit bhikṣus to carry taxable goods through customs, they have consequently lost this profit.
When the bhikṣus heard this, they informed the Buddha. The Buddha said, "You should accept them;
having accepted them, you should dye them."

At that time, there was a bhikṣu who obtained some goods and wished to dye them. In his pursuit of dyeing liquids, wooden basins, and cooking vessels, he was delayed; consequently, he missed the merchant caravan and was harmed by tigers, wolves, and other predators.
At that time, the bhikṣus reported the matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"One should sprinkle it with water and twist it until it breaks; then you may take it away as you please.
When they arrived at the customs post, they still could not avoid paying the tax, so the Buddha said:
"One should wash it with water or use cow dung juice to dye it a neutral color.
Still, the tax was not avoided. The Buddha said:
"One should even cut off the threads and fringes."

"If there are circumstances of difficulty, that which I have permitted for such times must not be used when no difficulties exist; if one uses it habitually under normal conditions, one incurs an offense of transgressing the Dharma.
This was spoken by the Buddha while he was staying at Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park in Śrāvastī.

At that time, there was a bhikṣu in Rājagṛha who, having completed the three-month summer retreat, had not yet received his share of the robes; he wished to go to Śrāvastī to pay homage at the feet of the World-Honored One.
Then the bhikṣus said to him,
"Why are you in such a hurry?
Wait until the distribution of the robe-merit has been completed before you travel."
At that time, that bhikṣu was not pleased with staying there. Another bhikṣu took a roll of cloth and presented it to him before departing.
Having received the cloth, he thought:
"If I were to dye it myself, I would have no leisure to bid farewell to my fellow practitioners of the holy life; I should give this to a bhikṣu who is a friend so that he may dye it."
He then took this cloth and gave it to him, saying, "Dye it for me and place it inside a robe-bag;
I shall go on a brief tour of the quarters to take my leave of the bhikṣus."
At that time, his acquaintance, harboring a lazy disposition, was unable to dye it and instead returned it to its original color, placing it inside a bag.
When the bhikṣu took the garment and departed, he arrived at a customs station. Then the tax collector asked the bhikṣu:
"Noble One!..."
"Is there perhaps some taxable goods here?
The bhikṣu replied,
"O worthy one!"
"I have no goods subject to tax.
The tax official said,
"Bring them here for a moment so that we may examine them."
He then brought it to show him; as soon as he opened the cloth bag, he saw a large bundle of cotton cloth and said, "Noble One!
Having gone forth out of faith within this well-spoken Dharma and Vinaya, how could you possibly tell a deliberate lie for the sake of a single roll of cloth?"
He replied, "O worthy one!
I truly did not know.
However, as I was setting out on my journey, another gave me this cloth; I took this cloth and had a friend dye it for me and place it within my robe-bag."
"I have taken my leave of those people; they, out of laziness, did not dye it a monastic color but placed it inside a bag.
The tax collector replied, "He is not your friend, but he is my friend. It is because of him that I obtained this object; you may now return the tax and proceed as you please."
Then that bhikṣu paid the price and departed, traveling along the road with a heart full of regret.
Upon reaching the residence of the bhikṣus in Śrāvastī, the bhikṣus saw him and said,
"Welcome, Venerable One!"
"Is your journey peaceful and pleasant?
He replied, "How could there be any peace or pleasure?"
The bhikṣus asked, "In what way are you unhappy?
He informed the bhikṣus of all that had occurred above. The bhikṣus reported this to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"This bhikṣu has committed no offense.
However, this bhikṣu should first question that bhikṣu before taking the item, and should ask him:
'Have you dyed it for me yet?'"
"If one takes [an object] without asking permission, one incurs an offense of transgression against the Dharma.
The Buddha was staying at the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s Park, in Śrāvastī.
At that time, the bhikṣu Nanda of the group of six said this to Upānanda:
“Those black-bowl monks all smear their feet with monkey fat.
When they wish to travel, they obtain great gains and offerings; when they return, they receive further hospitality and profit. All people hold them in affection and respect them all.”
"Our situation is like that of a frog in a well who has never ventured outside; how can we obtain offerings and support, or cause all people to hold us in mutual admiration?
We should now go forth together with the bhikṣus."
Upānanda asked, "Where do you wish to go? Nanda replied:
"I shall now go to seek out a caravan.
He then encountered a caravan intending to travel toward the north and asked them,
"Virtuous ones, where do you intend to go?"
He replied,
"We wish to go toward the north.
Nanda reported this, saying:
"I wish to go with you," [the monk] said.
The merchant replied, "The lands of the north are harsh and barren; there are many fierce dogs and the people are coarse and uncouth."
"You all have not yet found delight in that place. Nanda said,
"Though the land may be poor, my heart delights in looking toward it."
The merchants said,
"If you wish to go, you may travel together with us.
Nanda and Upananda then joined the caravan and proceeded northward.
Upon his initial arrival, his mind was not at ease; he therefore went out into the marketplace early in the morning. At that time, the merchants all came to pay homage at his feet and asked:
"Noble One!..."
"What is it like in the north?
Do you feel love and joy there?
He replied:
“O virtuous one!
When I first arrived, a feeling of unhappiness arose within me.
The merchant said:

"Did we not previously inform you of the circumstances? Their dwelling place in the north is a land of stony and barren soil; there are many fierce dogs, and the people are coarse and uncouth. You, O Benevolent Ones, could not have found joy there."
"Noble One, do you not now wish to return to the Middle Kingdom?
He replied to the merchants,
"I now wish to return."

The merchant said, "I have only recently arrived here and have not yet completed any trade; I shall return before long. However, there is a fellow traveler who has finished his business and wishes to return to the Middle Kingdom; you may go along with him."
"I shall now entrust you, my dear friend,
to a spiritual teacher. Nanda replied,
"Excellent."
They immediately entered the merchant camp and proceeded along the road.
The group of six [monks] were by nature averse to wind and dust, so they traveled sometimes ahead and sometimes behind.
As the merchants moved forward, they encountered other traders coming from the Central Kingdom (Madhyadeśa), and they exchanged greetings with one another:
"From where do you come, O benevolent one?
He replied,
"I come from the Middle Kingdom."
He asked again:
"How much profit do you gain from trading in the Middle Kingdom?
Do you not grow weary of the various customs duties?"

He replied, “Although one may gain much profit from trading in the Central Kingdom, the taxes levied at the frontier posts and garrisons are extremely heavy; they are like bandits. Even when one speaks the truth to them, they never show any leniency, but seize and carry away all of one’s goods.”
When the northern merchants heard these words, they each harbored grief and distress, resting their hands on their chins and brooding by the roadside. At that time,
the group of six monks arrived following behind them and asked the merchants,
"Gentlemen, why do you stand here with your hands on your chins, dwelling in sorrow?"
The merchants said, "O Noble Ones!

We are constantly oppressed by cold and heat, hunger and thirst, and harmed by mosquitoes, gadflies, wind, rain, and venomous snakes. Enduring toil and hardship without a moment's rest, we have come from afar to the Middle Kingdom in order to seek wealth and the enjoyment of peace and security."

Now, having heard the news concerning that place from traveling merchants, we learn that although those in the Middle Kingdom gain much profit through trade, they are everywhere deceived and robbed at the customs stations; the situation is like that of bandits, for all their goods and capital are plundered until nothing remains.
"How could we not be distressed upon hearing this?
The group of six replied, "You are our friends; why must you be distressed?"
The merchant said,
"Venerable One!
Could you not inform the King on my behalf so that he understands I have paid the tax without fraud?"
The group of six said, "We likewise cannot petition the king on your behalf; however, there is a royal decree in Śrāvastī stating that no tax shall be levied upon those who are unaware [of the law]."
"There are eighteen great gates and thirty-six small gates; through those small gates, we shall enter together.
Having heard this, the merchants departed with joy.

Not far from the city there was a village; they stayed there, and the group of six reported, "O people, you should let your camels and horses rest for now; we shall enter the city only when evening falls."

At that time, when the city tax collectors of Śrāvastī heard that merchants from the north intended to reach the city gate and were staying there to offer sacrifices to the yakṣa guarding the gate, the group of six monks said to them,
"Since it is now dusk, you may go through the small gate and enter the city together with us."
At that time, the merchants vied with one another to drive their pack animals laden with goods into the city; when daybreak arrived, they displayed the northern wares in the market stalls.
At that time, there was one person who could not keep pace with the preceding group and entered through the main gate;
when the tax official saw him, he asked, "Where have you come from? He replied:
"I have come from such-and-such a village.
He asked, "I have heard that there is a great caravan of merchants residing there; is this report true or false?"
He replied, "They were my traveling companions; I was left behind alone while they have already entered the city.
Upon hearing this, the tax official became incensed and spoke these words:
"I have been standing here waiting at the city gate, yet I have never seen him enter; through which way did he go?
The man replied, "If you do not believe me, come with me and witness the truth for yourself in the marketplace."
At that time, the tax collectors went with those men into the marketplace and saw various merchants displaying and trading in northern goods. Having seen this, the tax collectors asked:
"Who brought you all into this city?"
He replied, “I have enough.
The other said:
"I also know that you entered by walking on foot; I now wish to ask who led you inside and through which gate you entered?
He replied:
"I came through a private gate.
He asked, "I am now a close friend with you in virtue and righteousness; I would be grateful if you would tell me truthfully who guided you here?"
He replied,
"The six noble ones. Upon hearing this,
the tax official immediately gave rise to derision and reproached him, saying:
"This son of the Śākyas is a great and evil thief, not a true śramaṇa; he knows this is another's property and has used expedients to steal it.
When the bhikṣus heard this, they informed the Buddha. The Buddha said:
"A bhikṣu should not instruct others to evade the payment of taxes on private roads."
"If one instructs another [to do so], one incurs an offense of transgressing the Dharma.
At that time, the tax official thought to himself:
"These six groups of monks are all powerful and noble śramaṇas; I should form a bond of friendship with them to make their hearts rejoice."
During the first watch of the day, Upānanda took up his robes and bowl and entered the city to beg for alms. At that time, a tax official saw him and approached, saying:
"I pay homage to the Noble One!"
Upānanda replied, "O worthy one!
May you be free from illness and enjoy long life."
The tax official asked,
"Is there food in your bowl?
I wish to look at it for a moment."
He replied, "O worthy one!
Do you wish to seek out the taxed goods within my alms-bowl?"
“Noble One! I swear by my own oath that I truly have no such thought; if there is any delicious food, please grant me a small portion, for I wish to eat it.
He replied:
“Have you ever seen the waters of a river flow upstream?
You should give to me; it is not for me to give to you. “Noble One! [I have not.]”
"I was only joking!
Please come to my house.
Upānanda then went to his home, where he was given a bowl filled with the finest food. He prostrated at [the host's] feet and spoke thus:
“Noble One! I am the attendant to the Venerable One; if you have any business, please command me and I shall carry it out entirely.
He replied:
"O noble one! May you be free from illness and long-lived.
Having said this, he departed.

At that time, the six bhikṣus of the group generally stayed at the entrances of their dwellings, intending to proclaim the essentials of the Dharma to the śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas who came and went there, and to refute those who engaged in debate, thinking:
"The fame of us six bhikṣus will spread far and wide, and our gains and offerings will increase."

At that time, the room where Upānanda resided was close to the road. During the first and last watches of the night, while he was awake and reflecting from atop a high pavilion, he saw tax-evaders passing by at night not far from the monastery.
At that time, Upānanda was well-versed in the signs of sounds; having heard the sound of passing merchants, which was unlike any he had heard before, he asked from afar, "Who are these travelers?"
He remained silent.
He then quickly descended from the multi-storied pavilion and went to where the travelers were, asking them:
"Who are you that pass by traveling at night?"
He replied, "Noble One!
I am a merchant who evades taxes."
Upānanda replied, "Fool!
King Śreṇika Bimbisāra constantly makes offerings to the community of monks at this monastery, always ensuring they are fully provided for."

The Elder Kauṇḍinya personally offered a benedictory prayer for the king, saying: "May all the necessities of life, enjoyments, and precious playthings belonging to the Great King—those not yet possessed be obtained, and those already possessed always increase and expand."

"You were carrying goods that should have been brought into the city by way of the main road; now that you travel by night intending to evade the tax, how could I possibly remain silent? I shall cause you to suffer a loss."
Then that merchant, filled with fear, said:
"Noble One! You who harbor great compassion, I pray you grant me your forgiveness; I shall never forget your kindness toward me."
He replied, "What do you wish to do?
They answered:
“There is a small amount of food; I shall take it and offer it to you.
He replied, “If you can give it to me, go as you please.”
Having traveled some distance, they consulted among themselves, saying:
"We would not even pay the tax due to the Great King Śreṇika; how much less to this bald, hairless man, Upānanda!"
"Can I return the value of that food and drink?
He then entered the city of Śrāvastī that night and went to the marketplace at dawn to trade and depart.
At that time, Upānanda had finished eating quickly and was washing his bowl in front of the gate while looking around in all four directions.
At that time, there was a young bhikṣu who, seeing him looking about in all directions, asked:
"Venerable Elder, for what reason are you gazing toward the four quarters?
He replied:
“Venerable one!
I have a merchant acquaintance who is bringing various goods into Śrāvastī; I am now waiting for him.
The youth replied:
"When the Elder was eating, that person had already departed.
At that time, Upānanda became angry and thought to himself:
"I too have been deceived."
"Those ignorant people are like those who throw their fists at blades or pierce stone with needles;
as for what ought to be done toward such individuals, I shall know it myself.
Not long after, that merchant returned and was caught just as before, whereupon he said:
"I too have been deceived and deluded by you.
He replied, "Noble One!"

"At a previous time, I had some urgent business and did not have the leisure to pay my respects; I pray that you will again grant me your indulgence, and that I may repay both the former and subsequent kindnesses.
He replied, "O worthy one!"
"If you truly wish to give it, you may go as you please.
Once they had gone some distance, they resumed their previous discussion, saying:
"The Great King Śreṇika will not give us the tax; how could we possibly give it to a shaven-headed śramaṇa!"
Upananda thought to himself:
"Previously, he promised me that he would not come back to repay my kindness; it would be improper for him to deceive me once again.
Having had this thought, he rose early, took his alms-bowl, and went into the marketplace where he saw the merchant engaged in trade with wealth, displaying his usual demeanor.
The merchant replied, “O Noble One!
The goods have not yet been released; I wait until the transaction is complete. I dare not disobey your command, but I pray that you will grant me this indulgence for a short while.”
The merchants, having completed their trade, took their goods and departed without passing through the monastery gate.
Upānanda quickly returned to his residence; after finishing his meal and washing his bowl, he spoke at length as previously described, until the merchants had already left.
Having heard these words, Upānanda’s resentment increased all the more; rolling up his sleeves in a fit of rage, he said:
"This ignorant little man dares to mock me again! If I see him once more, I shall seize and bind him, ensuring that for the rest of his life he shall never again be a merchant."
Not long after, they returned once more. Upānanda caught them as before and said to them:
"You have repeatedly deceived me; now let me do something so that you may know my power."
He addressed them, saying:
"Virtuous ones!

Please grant us your forgiveness. We are merchants and our affairs are often tumultuous; although we have missed the appointed time, we dare not do so again. The value of the two previous favors, along with this present return, shall be sent all at once as soon as our trade is concluded."
Upananda then thought to himself,
"If I speak harshly, he will become aware of it.
Having had this thought, he said:
“O noble one! Can you truly do this?
He replied:
"I shall certainly give it. "If that is so, you all stay here for a while!
I will first scout the road for you, lest you incur blame and cause me to receive an ill reputation."
Not far from the monastery, some merchants were being plundered by bandits; those merchants stopped according to the instruction.
Upānanda went quickly to where the tax officials were and eavesdropped on their conversation.
At that time, the tax collectors sat up alert and deliberated among themselves, saying:
"How can we avoid being distressed?
Many merchants repeatedly steal the taxes, entering through side gates and failing to pay their dues."

"I have calculated that when the time arrives, the King’s nature is so violent and fierce that he will certainly not grant permission; my wife, children, and other relatives will surely die in prison.
Then Upānanda went to the group of people and said, "O worthy ones, why do you harbor such anxiety?"
He replied, "Noble ones! How could we not be anxious?
Many merchants frequently evade taxes by entering through side gates and failing to pay the dues. When the time for accounting arrives, the King’s nature is so violent that he allows no leniency."
He related everything as stated above. Upānanda said: "Fool!"

"Who appointed you as a tax collector? You ought to have been given many lashes and made to constantly carry earth or haul firewood; why then could you not seize the goods from those who evade taxes?"
He then said, "Venerable One!
King Śrāvastī has long had a decree that those who know [the goods] shall pay tax, while those who do not know shall not; there is no excessively heavy tax. Why then do you seize everything?"
Upānanda said, "You ignorant man!
In the city of Śrāvastī, there is a very heavy tax; one is taxed only after it has been known."
They then replied:

"We have long served as tax collectors, constantly collecting the due taxes; we have only ever heard of taking taxes according to what is known, but we have never heard of such an extremely heavy tax."
"How shall I now impose such an extremely heavy tax?
Upānanda said, "You should all stay here!"
"In the morning, I shall release the thieves who evade taxes; you must seize them and confiscate all their wealth.
If the merchants should say, 'In Śrāvastī, one only pays tax after being informed, and there is no excessively heavy tax,' [you should respond accordingly]."
To this, you should reply:
"There is a very heavy tax, which is collected only when it is known. If they say:
"We have long been merchants, yet we have never heard of such a heavy tax.
Now that this extreme tax has arisen, you all should come with us to the marketplace and go before the court of justice."
If anyone speaks such words, one must certainly not follow them; rather, they should be led before the king.
If the king should say:
"I have long been king, yet I have never heard of such an excessively heavy tax in Śrāvastī."
"Why has such an extremely heavy tax come into existence now?
One should say to the king:
"In ancient times, Great King Brahmadatta, together with the merchants and the people of the villages, established a regulation:..."
"If one enters the city from a certain garden, a certain shrine, or a place where people gather, they shall pay tax if it is known; if it is not known, there is no tax."

"If one enters the city without passing through this park, the temple grounds, or the assembly places of the multitude, they shall be subject to the maximum tax and their goods shall be confiscated in their entirety.
If it is asked:
"Where is this regulation located now?"
"You should reply to the king:
'It was placed in such-and-such a chest within such-and-such a storehouse, recorded clearly upon a sheet of red copper; the king should dispatch someone to retrieve it and examine it personally.'"
At that time, the tax officials, acting upon Upānanda’s words, immediately seized all the merchant's goods.
The merchant said,
"Why do you forcibly seize my property?"
“The merchants of Śrāvastī know this and only pay taxes; they do not impose excessively heavy taxes. You should take [your share] according to the proper proportion and then release me.
The tax official replied, “The merchants who steal from the road in Śrāvastī must pay an excessively heavy tax; I will not release you.”
The merchants replied,
"We have long been traveling merchants, and we have heard only that this city knows how to collect taxes but does not impose excessively heavy ones.
How is it that today such an excessively heavy tax has arisen?"
"You may now accompany me to the place of judgment.
The tax official replied, "I cannot go to an ordinary court; you must take yourselves directly to the King's presence."
Then the merchants raised their voices in a great cry and went to the place of legal adjudication, saying to the people:
"Gentlemen, do you know?
All our goods have been plundered; we pray for your assistance."
Then the judges went together to the king’s residence and addressed him, saying:

“There is now a merchant who has arrived in the city; all his wealth and goods have been confiscated and taken away by the tax officials. We pray that Your Majesty will grant relief according to the law.”
At that time, the Great King commanded his attendants, saying,
"Summon the tax official. Following the command,
they pursued him until they caught up with him.
The king asked,
"What was your intention in seizing all the goods from those merchants?
They all replied to the king:
"These people are tax evaders; Śrāvastī has extremely severe penalties for such offenses, and for this reason we tax-collectors have seized all their goods."
The king said:
"I have long been king, yet I did not know that this city imposed such extreme punishments; for what reason are there such extreme punishments now?
You should collect the tax dues according to the actual facts and release the merchants."
The tax official said:
"In ancient times, Great King Brahmadatta established a regulation together with the merchants and the people of the villages.
[He then] explained it in detail as previously described.
The king said to the tax collectors:
"If this is a command issued by my father, or a command from Śakra, or a command from Brahmā, let this be the final authority."
He then addressed the treasurer, saying, "Bring the copper plate with the royal decree.
Following these instructions, the treasurer brought it forth;
after the king had read it aloud before him, he was overcome with grief upon hearing his father’s command and spoke through his tears:
"If the commands issued by our former kings were decrees of Śakra or decrees of Brahmā, then it would be well for you to seize all these goods.
At that time, the merchants lost all hope and departed weeping, asking the tax officials:
"Who informed you that we were coming?"
He replied, "No one spoke to me;
I heard and knew it myself. However, though I have known of this since long ago, out of compassion I could not take everything away. Your current excess, however, I cannot endure."
The merchant replied:
"How can you gentlemen possess such compassion?
Now, my relationship with you is that of close friends; I would have been grateful if you had informed me who first spoke to you."
Upon seeing him speak these words of distress, he informed him, saying,
"The six noble ones have told me.
Then those merchants all joined in mocking and reviling him, uttering various harsh words:
"This son of Śākya is a great and evil thief, not a true śramaṇa; he has taught others in this way to seize my property.
When the bhikṣus heard this, they informed the Buddha.
The Buddha said, "A bhikṣu must not instruct another to seize the goods of a merchant; if one so instructs, one commits a *vyatikrama* offense."
The summary verse says:
Regarding those without feet, those with two feet, Those with four feet, and those with many feet—
If one steals such beings, One should know the gravity of the offense according to the corresponding rules.
Regarding those "without feet," this refers to snakes, leeches, and eels; these three types are kept by snake-charmers, royal physicians, and people of the mountains and forests.
What is meant by a snake-handler?
It refers to one who takes snakes and handles them for the sake of making a living.
What is meant by a royal physician?
This refers to those physicians who sustain their lives by treating illnesses with leeches.
What are those who dwell in the mountains and wilds?
They are like the people of the mountains who catch legless insects, administer medicine to make them vomit, and then roast them over hot tiles to provide for their drinking.
If a bhikṣu steals these insects, it should be assessed according to their value: if the value reaches five [māṣakas], he incurs the fundamental offense;
if it does not reach five, he incurs the preliminary offense.
Regarding "two-footed beings," this refers to humans and birds.
When stealing from a human, there are three means [of agreement]:
a designated place, a fixed time, and a signal.
What is the "appointed place"?
One informs that person, saying:
"If you see me in a certain garden, or at a gathering of people, or in a temple, at that moment you shall know that the matter has been accomplished."
This is called the appointed place.
What is the fixed time?
"If you see me from afar in the early morning, or at midday, or in the afternoon, know that the task has been accomplished."
This is called the fixed time.
What are the signs?

"If you see me with my hair and beard freshly shaved, wearing saffron-colored robes, holding an alms bowl and a mendicant's staff, and filled with ghee, oil, sugar, and rock honey—when you see these signs, know that the task is accomplished."
This is called "indicating signs.
When stealing in this manner, the offense should be determined according to the value of the object, as previously stated.
If one steals a bird, there are two preparatory methods:
This refers to lifting up from the ground or falling from the air.
What is meant by "lifting up"?
It means a bird lifts up [an object] on the ground and steals it away; whether it is full or not full is as explained above.
What is meant by "falling into emptiness"?

It is like a bird-catcher who sets fire to a vast marsh; being pursued by smoke and fire while seeking to capture birds, he happens to fall into the place where a bhikṣu practices walking meditation, or in front of a gateway house. If the bhikṣu takes it with a thieving mind, whether the value reaches the full measure or not is as explained above.
What are the four-footed animals?
They are elephants, horses, camels, donkeys, cattle, sheep, deer, wild boars, rabbits, and so forth.
When one intends to steal them, there are two methods:
That is to say, from a herd or from a place of confinement:
when a bhikṣu steals an elephant from among a herd of elephants, he incurs a sthūlātyaya offense as long as it remains within the range of sight;
once it reaches a place beyond sight, he incurs the fundamental offense.
What are the locations of confinement?
Whether it be an elephant tied to a pillar, a tree, or within a wall or enclosure—if a bhikṣu releases it, he incurs an offense as described above.
As it is with stealing an elephant, so it should be understood that for other animals such as horses, when a bhikṣu steals them, the rule is the same as before.
What are those with many legs?
They are the so-called grubs, locusts, moths, various bees, ants, scorpions, and so forth.
Among these, those required here refer to three types:
These are the judges, the city guards, and the maritime merchants.
What are the judges?

They are those who raise many-legged creatures, such as bees and scorpions, which they store inside jars. When they see a person being punished who does not submit, they cause that person to thrust their hands or feet into the jar; when they are stung by the pain, they quickly submit to the matter or else pay out much money and goods.
What is meant by a "city defender"?
It refers to one who manages the city and stores many bees within a clay jar;
should an enemy foe come to wage war against him, if they do not retreat, he may release the jar of bees from atop the city wall, and the thieves, stung by the bees, will scatter and flee.
What is meant by a maritime merchant?
It refers to a person who enters the sea to seek precious goods; he carries many bees within earthenware vessels to prevent emergencies, so that when pirates arrive, they may fight them together.
If they were victorious, it was well; but if they were not, they took a honey-jar and threw it from afar at the thieves' boat. Unable to fight any longer, the thieves dispersed in all directions.
The summary verse says:
"Caṇḍāla and Sūdayin; taking clothes and comparing them to one's own body, there is no thought of theft."
The Master Mūla did not speak to Vasudatta, who took a small bowl as his own portion.
Candra-gupta knew that the other intended to take the robe, while Durdhara took it away and incurred a *sthūlātyaya* offense;
in the Central Land of the Southern Kingdoms, such matters are not understood, so one must quickly return any found property to its owner.
The Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
There were two bhikṣus who were close friends, bound by mutual affection and living together in the same place:
one was named Caṇḍāla, and the other was named Sudinna.
He was well known among the *caṇḍāla* community; he possessed great merit yet was short in stature, and he had many robes, alms bowls, nets, and waist-bands.
Suddhipanthaka, however, had few acquaintances; he was tall and large-framed, possessed only the three robes, which were moreover old and tattered, leaving much of his body exposed.
The bhikṣus said to him:
"Venerable one!
Now that you have few desires yet your robes are torn and your body is exposed, is it for the sake of gain?"
"Is it because there is no gain or support? He replied,
"There is no gain."
He then replied,
"Why do you not beg for alms?
He answered:
“Who would abandon that field of merit consisting of the Buddha, Dharma, and Sangha to give to me?
He then replied, “That Caṇḍāla bhikṣu is your friend;
he has many acquaintances and possesses extra robes, alms bowls, nets, and waist-bands. Why do you not seek them from him?”
He replied,
"He was unwilling to give it.
He asked again:
"Have you already requested alms from him?
He replied, "I have not yet requested them."
He replied, "Have you ever heard that one should take off one's shoes merely upon hearing the sound of water?
You should beg for it; he will surely grant it to you."
Having been thus exhorted, he went to the cemetery; the man was not there, so he thought to himself: "This cemetery attendant is short and small of stature.

I shall take his saṃghāṭī robe and measure it out to see if it corresponds to my own body's proportions. If it fits me, I will seek it from him; if it does not match, what is the point of causing him offense?"
He then entered that room to examine the robes and clothing; seeing a *saṃghāṭī* on a clothes rack, he took it and immediately checked its length.
At that moment, a Caṇḍāla suddenly arrived from outside, saw him, and said:
"You have taken my robe with a thieving mind and put it on; you have committed a *pārājika* offense."
He replied:
"Venerable sir!
I had no intention of stealing these robes; I merely thought to myself:"

"The Caṇḍāla is short and small in stature; let me take that saṃghāṭī and measure it again. If its dimensions correspond to my own body, I shall seek it from him; if it does not fit, what use have I for such a cumbersome possession?"
He replied, "Venerable sir!
There is no need for you to feign denial and offer such evasions; you took my robe with a thief's intent and have thus committed a *pārājika* offense."
Having heard these words, he immediately felt remorse, thinking,
"Could it be that I have committed a grave offense?
and informed the bhikṣus.
The bhikṣus reported this to the Buddha, who asked,
"Bhikṣus, with what intention did you do this?
They then related the facts to the World-Honored One exactly as they had occurred.
The Buddha said:
"If this bhikṣu acts with the intention of measuring [the situation], there is no offense.
However, bhikṣus should not entertain the notion of friendship toward those who are not friends."
There are three kinds of friends:
namely, inferior, middling, and superior.
One entrusts matters with an inferior mind to an inferior friend; with a middling or inferior mind to a middling friend; and with a superior, middling, or inferior mind to a superior friend.
"If a bhikṣu entrusts his belongings to someone who is not a kinsman or friend, thinking of them as such,
he commits an offense of transgression against the Dharma. *Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya*, Fascicle Four [and] Fascicle Five.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Yijing by Imperial Decree.
The Second Chapter on the Training Rule Against Taking What Is Not Given, Part Four.
At that time, the Blessed One was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
There were two bhikṣus:
one named Sūśarmā and the other named Vasudatta, who were close friends and shared a harmonious bond of affection.
At that time, Sūśarmā possessed a fine large bowl, while Vasudatta possessed a fine small bowl.

At another time, after they had both finished eating together, they washed their bowls in one place. Then, Suśarmā took Vasudatta’s small bowl and placed it inside his own large bowl, saying these words:
"Venerable Vasudatta!"
"If a person possesses these two bowls, they will have sufficient means to reduce worldly entanglements and cultivate all categories of wholesome qualities.
Vasudatta said, "If you wish to obtain them, why do you not take them?"
At that time, Vasudatta had some minor business to attend to in a certain village, so he said to Susīma, "Venerable one!
I have some minor business in such-and-such a place; if there is anyone who can manage this task for me, I shall give them this small bowl."
He asked, "Is what you say true? He replied:
"I truly shall give it.
When Sūṣoma heard these words, he was about to go, but then a thought of regret arose within him:
"Let not this circumstance cause my fellow-practitioners of the holy life to speak thus of me."
Suśarmā worked for hire for others and consequently did not travel again.
At that time, Suśarmā had some business in that village and needed to go; he then thought to himself:
"It would be excellent if I could attend to my own affairs while simultaneously settling that business there!"
He immediately went there and completed those two matters, then returned and told Vasudatta:
"I have already attended to all your business in that village; you should now give me the small bowl."
Vasudatta said, "You may go as you please;
it is not for my sake. Who could possibly give a small bowl to you? Susīma said:
"If you do not give it to me, I shall take it myself.
Vasudatta said, "If it is rightfully yours to have, why do you not take it?"
At that time, Vasudatta had some business and went outside; while he was away, Suśīma took his small bowl and placed it inside his own.
When Vasudatta returned and did not see his bowl, he asked, "Venerable one!..."
"Who has taken my small bowl away?
Susīma replied, "The owner of the object has taken it."
Vasudatta asked, “Whose property is this?
He replied:
"This is my property.
Vasudatta said angrily, "You took it with a thief's mind; you have committed a *pārājika* offense."
Having heard this, Susīma felt remorse and immediately informed the bhikṣus of these circumstances; the bhikṣus then reported it to the Buddha.
The Buddha asked Susīma:
"With what intention did you take another's small bowl?"
He reported this in full to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"This bhikṣu took the bowl with the intention that it was his own property;
thus, there is no offense. However, bhikṣus should not accept wages to perform labor for others. If they engage in work through barter or do so seeking merit, there is no offense."
"A bhikṣu who accepts wages for performing labor incurs an offense of transgressing the Dharma.
The Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, there were two bhikṣus in this city:
One was named Duryodhana and the other was named Candrapāla; they became close friends and conversed with mutual delight.
Candrapāla was well-known to the public and possessed great merit, having an abundance of robes, alms bowls, bowl-covers, and waist-bands.
Duṣprasaha had few acquaintances; he kept only the three robes, which were moreover worn out and tattered.
Another bhikṣu said to him:
"Venerable one!..."
For what reason do you now have such few desires that you wear these tattered robes which cannot even cover your body?
Is it because you have [clothing] but choose not to wear it,
or is it because there is nothing to be obtained?
Duranjayin replied,
“I have no place of attainment. He said:
"Why do you not beg for alms?
He replied,
"Who would be willing to relinquish the Three Jewels and the Noble Assembly to give them to me, a mere ordinary person?"

He then said to him, "The bhikṣu Candrapāla is your close friend with whom you share a harmonious rapport; he possesses many robes, alms bowls, bowl-covers, and waist-bands—why do you not ask him for some?"
Durdharṣa said,
"He is unwilling to give it.
He was told:
"Have you previously begged from him?
Durdharṣa replied,
"I heard that he is stingy, so I did not beg from him."
He said, "Do not think that a ferryman will take off his boots simply because he hears the sound of water from afar; you should just go and beg, and perhaps he will give them to you.
Having heard this advice, he went to Candrapāla and said:
“Venerable one!
You should give me your bowl.
Candraprabha replied:
"I will not give it to you," he replied. Sudarśana said,
"If you will not give me the bowl, you may give me the saṃghāṭī."
Candrapāla said, "How could I possibly be your storekeeper?
You have searched for the bowl but not found it, and now you seek the great robe; I will not give you even a single thread, let alone the robe itself."
When Duṣprasāha heard this, anger arose in his heart and he said:
"I have always been the one who takes the lead in whatever tasks there were; why does he now beg from me and say that he will not give even a single thread?"
"If I am unable to seize those goods entirely, then I shall not be called 'Invincible' (Durjaya).
With this thought, he intended to take the goods.
He then saw Candrapāla himself dyeing his robes; Durjaya went to him and said:
"Venerable sir!
I also wish to assist you in dyeing the robe. He said:
"Excellent! I shall assist you in making it.
Durdharṣa then dyed the robe, rubbing and turning it over as he examined the cloth.
Having seen this, Candraprabha thought to himself: "Observe his intent;
he is turning my robe over and examining it closely. He must certainly intend to steal my robe."
Having thus conceived a doubt, he dyed the robe and, once it was dry, placed it in his robe-bag and lay down with it as a pillow.
These bhikṣus remained awake during the first and last watches of the night, dwelling in mindful reflection and mental application.
At that time, Durdharṣa said to Candrapāla,
"Let us go together and cultivate wholesome qualities.
Candrapāla replied:
"You go on ahead; my body is weary and I shall follow later.
Having heard this, he departed.
At that time, Candrapāla thought to himself:

"If I go, I will surely lose my robe; if I do not go, I will fail to cultivate the factors of virtue. What skillful means can I employ so that I neither lose my robe nor neglect the cultivation of wholesome deeds?"
He then placed his own cloth bag beside the other’s head and lay down with that cloth bag as a pillow.
When Duṣprasaha had finished his work and returned to rest, Candraprabha said to him:
“Venerable one!...”
"You should rise and practice wholesome qualities together.
He replied, "I have finished my work and am resting briefly from fatigue; you should be the one to rise and work."
Candrapāla then departed. Duṣprasaha thought to himself, "I shall wait and see whether the time is yet fit for me to go.
When it was nearly dawn, he took his cloth bag from beside the head [of the corpse] and went out the door.
He then thought to himself:
"I shall examine what kind of colored robe it is that causes me to commit a *pārājika* offense.
Upon opening his bag, he saw that it was indeed his own old, tattered garment; thereupon, he became distressed and thought as follows:
"I have committed a *pārājika* offense for the sake of my own clothing; this is not the conduct of one who has gone forth.
I shall rather swallow iron balls. He further thought:

"I shall now go to question the Blessed One, the World-Honored One. If I am fit to remain, I will cultivate the holy life (*brahmacarya*) in the presence of the World-Honored One; if I am unfit, I shall become a white-robed layman."
Having formed this thought, he went to where the Blessed One was.
At that time, the Blessed One was teaching the Dharma amidst an assembly of immeasurable hundreds of thousands of bhikṣus.
Then, seeing Duṣprasaha approaching from afar, the Blessed One addressed the bhikṣus, saying:
“Do you see that bhikṣu coming from outside?
They replied,
“We have seen him.”
The Buddha said, "This foolish person is difficult to overcome; by stealing his own robe, he has committed a *sthūlātyaya* offense.
He then addressed the bhikṣus:
"You should know this!
If one takes something with a thieving mind, such faults arise; therefore, even regarding one's own robes and bowl, a bhikṣu should not take them with a thieving mind."
"If one steals it, one incurs the offense of *sthūlātyaya*.
The Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, there were two bhikṣuṇīs:
One stayed in the east and one stayed in the south.
The bhikṣuṇī from the east went in front, while the bhikṣuṇī from the south followed behind.
These two bhikṣuṇīs together approached the place where the Buddha was; having prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, they sat to one side.
The Buddha preached the Dharma for them; having heard the Dharma, they paid homage to the Buddha and withdrew.
At that time, a nun from the east was walking ahead, carrying her saṃghāṭī robe over her shoulder.
As her robe was about to fall, a nun from the south saw it and said to her,
"Noble lady!
Your robe is about to fall."

At that time, the nun from the east was walking ahead, contemplating the Dharma; however, because their dialects differed and they could not understand one another, she did not notice her robe falling.
The nun from the south then picked up the robe and thought to herself:
"If I give this to her now, it will hinder her focused contemplation; I shall wait until we reach our dwelling place and then present it to her."
Having arrived at their residence, the nun from the east quickly washed her feet outside the room and then entered, sitting down in the half-lotus posture (*paryaṅka*).
At that time, the nun from the south thought to herself:

"If I were to give her the robe now, it would again result in the same abandonment of virtuous practice as before; I shall wait until she has emerged from meditative absorption and then entrust the robe to her."
She then placed it on a clothing rack in her own room.
At dawn, a nun from the east said to her disciple:
"Bring me my saṃghāṭī; I wish to go for alms."
The disciple entered the room and searched throughout the shelves, but not seeing the teacher’s robe, he returned and said,
"Venerable One,
I do not see the saṃghāṭī."
The teacher said,
"You may go to the nuns in the south and seek it there.
The disciple went to their quarters and, seeing the saṃghāṭī on the clothing rack, asked:
"Who brought this robe and placed it on this rack?
A nun from the south replied, "I brought it."
The disciple asked,
"For what reason did you bring this?
He answered in full detail regarding the matter.
At that time, that disciple had previously harbored resentment toward a nun from the south; out of anger, she said to her:
"You have stolen this robe with a thieving mind and placed it within your own room; you have committed a *pārājika* offense."
Then the nun from the south thought to herself,
"Could it be that I have actually committed a *pārājika* offense?
She related this entire matter to the other bhikṣuṇīs.
The bhikṣuṇī informed the community of bhikṣus, and the bhikṣus informed the Buddha.
The Buddha asked the bhikṣuṇī from the south:
"When you took the robe, did you not inform her?"
He addressed the Buddha, saying,
"Although I spoke to him, he did not understand.
The Buddha said:
"There is no offense if there is a difference in dialect such that one does not understand the other.
However, these faults all arise from picking up another's property and, after a long time, failing to return it to the owner while keeping it for oneself."

For this reason, if a bhikṣu or bhikṣuṇī picks up discarded clothing or belongings, they should not retain them for a long time; if they do so, they incur an offense of transgression against the Dharma.

At that time, a bhikṣu saw an item left behind by another and, knowing it was the property of a certain bhikṣu, went to that person's room, knocked on the door, and called out. The other bhikṣu emerged from meditative absorption and asked, "Who is it?"
He replied, "Venerable sir!
I found your robe at such-and-such a place; you may take it."
Then he said to him: "Venerable one!
It would be better for this robe of mine to be taken away by a thief; how could I, on account of this, allow you to knock on my door and disturb my supreme meditative concentration?"
At that time, the bhikṣu felt remorse and thought to himself:
"Could it be that I have now disturbed his meditative concentration and thereby incurred an offense?
For this reason, he informed the other bhikṣus.
The bhikṣus informed the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"That bhikṣu has committed no offense.
However, bhikṣus should not seek the attainment of another's supreme concentration for a minor reason."
If one finds a lost article, one should take it to its owner and hang it up with a rope so that it may be recovered later; do not disturb their meditative concentration.
Should one act otherwise, one incurs an offense of transgression against the Dharma.
At that time, there was a bhikṣu who saw an article left behind by another; recognizing it as belonging to a certain bhikṣu, he took the object and went to that bhikṣu, saying:
"Venerable one!..."
"This is your property; I found it and have brought it here, so you should take possession of it.
At that time, the owner of the goods had a prior grievance with this bhikṣu, and he said:
"You did not find this; you intentionally stole my property with a thieving mind. You should be dealt with according to the law for your offense."
At that time, the bhikṣu felt remorse in his heart, thinking:
"Have I not incurred an offense on account of this?
For this reason, he informed the other bhikṣus.
The bhikṣus reported this to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"This bhikṣu has committed no offense.
However, when bhikṣus obtain an object left behind by another, they should take it and hand it over to one who oversees the affairs of the Saṃgha."

Once the administrator has received these items, within a period of several days, he should announce them to the assembly two or three times. If the original owner comes forward to claim them, they should be returned immediately;
if there is no one who recognizes them, they shall be entered into the property of the Sangha of the four directions for communal use.
"If one acts otherwise, one incurs an offense of transgression against the Dharma.
The summary verse says:
"The disciple of Śailā tested another by begging for oil;"
Maudgalyāyana performed a supernatural feat to recover the son of the elder;
Pindola Bhāradvāja took back both the child and the protective object.
The details of his theft are extensively recounted; one should understand them according to what is said.
The Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, there was an arhat bhikṣuṇī named Śailā who had severed all afflictions.
At that time, a young incense-seller named Lokakṣema saw the nun Vimaladattā and conceived a deep sense of reverence for her. He went to her place, paid his respects with great earnestness, and said:
"Whatever items you require, O Noble Lady, please take them from my home as you please."
"I shall receive all your instructions with the highest reverence.
Then the bhikṣuṇī said, "Noble one, excellent!"
"May you be free from illness.
Later, at another time, the bhikṣuṇī Śailā was afflicted with a serious illness and was unable to go begging for alms, while other bhikṣuṇīs were traveling about to beg for food.
At that time, the incense-seller youth saw her and paid his respects, asking,
"Venerable Sela Bhikṣuṇī, for what reason has she not been seen?
She replied:
"O noble one! His body is afflicted by illness.
The youth replied:
"Noble One!
I previously said to you:
'If there is anything you require, please take and use it as you wish.'"
"I have never seen him come to seek anything from me; whatever he may require, I pray that you, Venerable One, will obtain it for him.
He then replied, "So be it, O worthy one!"
"May you be free from illness.
Having spoken these words, he left him and departed.
In this manner, he repeatedly and earnestly requested to give [the food] up to three times.
At that time, a young bhikṣuṇī had this thought:
"I have heard these words spoken by this youth many times; I should test whether they are false or true."
He then took a small bowl and handed it to the youth, saying,
"O noble youth! The Venerable Śaila now requires a little oil."
At that time, the boy had freshly pressed oil, which he filled a small bowl with and presented to the nun, saying:
"Noble Lady!
Should you require anything further, please come and take it as you wish."
The bhikṣuṇī accepted it and departed; she then applied this oil to Śailā’s body, extending it over her hands and feet until the oil was completely exhausted.
Śailā’s illness was cured, and she went forth to beg for alms.
Then that youth, upon seeing him, prostrated at his feet and said:
"Noble One! It has been a long time since we last met."
The nun then replied,
"I have recently been afflicted by illness. She said:
"Noble One!
You have already previously invited me, saying that whatever you may require from my home, you may take as you please; you have never sent a messenger to seek anything from me."
"I saw only one nun who said, 'The Noble One is ill; take oil from me. I filled a small bowl with fresh oil and brought it to that nun.
Śailā replied, "Excellent, young man!"
"I wish you freedom from illness.
Having spoken, she departed. After completing her almsround in due order, she returned to her residence and said to the junior nuns:
"Who was it that went to that young perfume-seller and brought back this oil bowl?"
A nun replied, "Venerable One!
While I was going for alms, I saw that boy tell me repeatedly: "The nun has stolen my food."'"

"Noble Śailā, I have already invited you and said that whatever you require may be taken at your pleasure; yet I have never seen you come to me to ask for anything. If Śailā has any need, I pray that you will take it for her."
I then thought to myself,
"I should test him to verify whether he is telling the truth or not.
I immediately took my small alms bowl and gave it to the youth, saying:
"The noble Śaila is currently ill and requires oil.

At that time, the youth filled a vessel with fresh oil and gave it to me. Having received the oil, I went into my cell and applied it to the body, hands, and feet of the noble one until it was all used up.
Then the elder nun said to the junior nun,
"Did I ever tell you to go to that boy and seek some oil?
The junior nun replied:
"I have never caused her to do so.
At that time, another bhikṣuṇī who had previously harbored a grudge against this young nun heard these words and said to Śailā:
"Noble Lady!..."

Now, because of your illness, this young nun has not merely taken oil from a single location; she has begged for it throughout the entire city of Śrāvastī, and the number of her *parājika* offenses is difficult to calculate.
When the young nun heard these words, she felt remorse, thinking:
"Could it be that I have actually committed a pārājika offense?
For this reason, she informed the bhikṣuṇīs.
The bhikṣuṇīs informed the community of bhikṣus, and the bhikṣus informed the Buddha.
The Buddha asked that young nun:
"With what intention did you beg for oil from her?"
He addressed the Buddha, saying,
"I conceived the thought of testing this youth.
The Buddha told the bhikṣu:
"If she acted with a mind merely to test [the situation], this bhikṣuṇī is not at fault.
However, no bhikṣu or bhikṣuṇī should go begging on behalf of a sick person without first inquiring after their condition."
When begging for it, one asks the patient:
"Are you seeking medicine from the infirmary of the Sangha,
or are you going to those who have faith or to your own relatives?"
"If there are many relatives, from whom should one seek [the requisites]?
One should seek them as directed.
If a bhikṣu or bhikṣuṇī seeks [requisites] without first inquiring of the patient, they incur an offense of transgression against the Dharma (dharmātikrama).
The Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.

At that time, the Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana, during the first part of the day, took up his robe and bowl and entered Śrāvastī for alms, proceeding in order until he reached the house of the householder Anāthapiṇḍada.
At that time, the elder was instructing his son in the study and recitation of non-Buddhist texts, grammar, and miscellaneous treatises.
When Mahāmaudgalyāyana saw the elder teaching his child to recite these non-Buddhist texts, he said to him: "Elder!..."
"What texts are these young boys studying?
The elder replied, "Ārya!"
"This is a non-Buddhist scripture," he said,
"O Householder!"
Now, non-Buddhist scriptures are like an iron pomegranate; though one may laboriously manage to produce it, it is ultimately unfit for consumption.

Studying non-Buddhist texts is likewise: one merely wastes effort and gains nothing in the end; it cannot, by itself, lead to liberation, entry into the assembly of those fixed in rightness, or the severance of all afflictions.

"However, that which the Buddha has taught is excellent in the beginning, middle, and end; if one understands it, one can proceed toward Nirvana. For what reason do you not teach us to study and recite the Buddha's Dharma?
The elder replied, "Noble One!"
"No one can teach him.
The Venerable One replied,
"I shall teach him to read."
The householder said:
"Excellent, Noble One!
I would be grateful for your instruction."
He then said to his son,
"You should now go to the Jeta Grove and approach the Venerable One to study the Buddha-dharma.
The youth replied, "So be it," and accepted the instruction.

At that time, every day, the elder would adorn his young son with jeweled ornaments and, accompanied by his attendants, go to the Jeta Grove to the presence of the Venerable Maudgalyāyana to receive instruction in the Buddha-dharma.
However, at the beginning of autumn in that country, there were always the Kṛttika bandits.
When the bhikṣus had completed their summer retreat, the autumn bandits deliberated among themselves, saying:
"What work shall we undertake so that, throughout this year, we may enjoy food, clothing, and comforts in abundance and ease without having to exert ourselves?"

"I have heard that the householder Anāthapiṇḍada regularly has his son adorned with ornaments every day to go to Jeta’s Grove and study the Buddha-dharma under the Venerable Maudgalyāyana; we should kidnap him together along the way."

The Noble One thinks the son is in the householder’s residence, while the householder thinks the child is with the Noble One; neither knows the other's whereabouts, so they have not yet sought him out.
If we can steal this boy, he shall serve us as our slave for as long as we live.
"If we cannot obtain [the boy], we shall take his necklaces and ornaments for adorning the body; by means of these, we shall enjoy peace and happiness without having to undergo any toil.
Having thus devised a plan, they waited for the boy on the road. Seeing him adorned with necklaces and intending to go to the park, they then proceeded to abduct the boy together.
At that time, the attendant saw the thief leading him away and ran back home to tell the elder:
"The boy who was receiving his lessons has been abducted by the autumn bandits.
Thereupon, the elder immediately went in haste to King Prasenajit and said:
“Great King!
My son has been abducted by the autumn bandits; I now beg this son from Your Majesty.
When the king heard this, he commanded Virūḍhaka, saying:
"You should go at once to apprehend the autumn bandits and seek out the son of the elder.
At that time, Vīradatta had a prior grievance with the householder Anāthapiṇḍada; thus, although he received the king's command, he did not act with urgency.
At that time, there was a deva who felt profound reverence for the noble Mahāmaudgalyāyana and addressed him, saying:
"Noble One, do you know?
Your disciple has been carried off by the autumn bandits; you should devise an urgent plan."
At that time, Mahāmaudgalyāyana thought to himself:

"If I do not save this child, both the parents and the son will suffer the pain of separation. Those who have no faith or respect will find pleasure in hearing this, while those who possess faith and respect may experience a decline in their resolve."
Those who come and go have been carried off by bandits; who else would now be willing to enter the Jeta Grove?
I should now quickly manifest my supernatural power to retrieve those children.
Having formed this thought, the noble Maudgalyāyana manifested great supernormal powers, conjuring an army of Vairūḍhaka deities who beat great war drums on all four sides.
At that time, when those autumn bandits suddenly saw themselves surrounded by the army, they were all struck with terror and spoke these words:
"Gentlemen, you should know!
Virūḍhaka has surrounded us on all sides with his soldiers; we must abandon this child so as to avoid being captured."
He immediately abandoned the boy and fled.
At that time, the Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana withdrew his supernormal powers and sat in meditative composure beneath a tree by the side of the road.
At that time, another boy came along the road and asked,
"Boy, where have you come from?
He replied:
"Noble One! I have been carried off by the autumn thieves.
"Who has abducted you?"
"This is Vairocanaketu. He replied, "Young man, you should return home at once;
your parents are deeply distressed. You may come back tomorrow as usual to continue your studies."
At that time, the youth accepted the instruction and returned home.
Then, Virūḍhaka arrayed his fourfold army—elephants, cavalry, chariots, and infantry—and emerged from the city of Śrāvastī. Seeing the youth, he asked him, "From where have you come?"
He replied,
"I was heading toward the Jeta Grove, but on the way, I was robbed by autumn bandits.
[The king asked,] "Who brought you here?"
He replied,
"This is General Vīradatta.
Then Vīradatta thought to himself:
"I was only just about to depart; why do you say that I brought this child?
Is it not rather that some other noble and holy being, endowed with great power, has taken this child away?"
He asked the youth,
"What person did you see there?
The youth replied:
"I saw the noble Mahāmaudgalyāyana by the side of the road.
Vīrūḍhaka thought to himself, "It must have been brought here by the supernatural power of that venerable one; no one else has such ability."
Having understood this, his heart was filled with joy, and he cried out in a loud voice:

"We have now gained a great and wholesome benefit! Within our kingdom we have obtained such a noble sage of great wisdom, endowed with all powers and majesty, whose taints are forever exhausted both in the present life and in future worlds."
Having offered this praise, he returned to the city of Śrāvastī.
At that time, the six bhikṣus of the group of six were leaving the city on some business when they encountered him on the road and asked him:
"Venerable sir, whom did you praise?"
He replied, “I praise the assembly of the benevolent and sages!
[They asked,] “For what reason do you praise us?”
He replied, "The son of the householder Anāthapiṇḍada was carried off by autumn bandits; the Noble One Mahāmaudgalyāyana used his supernormal powers to seize the boy and bring him back."
The group of six replied,
"You foolish person!
Although we possess such supernormal powers, people do not respect or believe in us."
Yet there is that foolish man who plucks out his hair, a naked ascetic toward whom one feels a heart of reverence and affection.
If that naked ascetic were to see this matter, he would point out the path to those autumn bandits.
Having heard this, Vimalakīrti remained silent.
At that time, the six bhikṣus—Nanda and Upananda—said to one another, "We have already answered the matter well;
however, those of few desires are now manifesting their transgressions. Let us go to them and cause them to repent."
Having returned to his dwelling and finished his meal, he went to the place where the Venerable Maudgalyāyana was; after first paying his respects, he said:
"Venerable Elder!
I pray that you will grant me leave, for I wish to pose some questions."
He replied, “As you wish.
[The other] said:
“Elder! The son of the householder Anāthapiṇḍika was carried off by autumn bandits; you have taken him back by force.
Is this matter true or false?”
He replied, "I brought it here. He said:

"I was already fully aware that the Elder had already entered meditative concentration and was experiencing the bliss of liberation; however, I truly did not know that although he possessed compassion, he was unable to extend it universally, showing concern for his disciples' future by causing terror among those autumn bandits."
Furthermore, you forcibly seized property belonging to others and brought it back; you have now committed an offense and should repent according to the Dharma.
He replied, “Venerable sir!...”
"I see no fault.
At that time, the group of six monks deliberated among themselves, saying:
"Virtuous ones, you should know that as the World-Honored One has said:"
"One who does not acknowledge their offense should be subjected to the *pratisāraṇīya-karman* (act of reconciliation).
