Thereupon, he went to the person in charge of affairs and said to him:
"Venerable sir!..."
"The *gandī* should be struck; we now wish to perform the *jñapti-caturtha-karman* of setting aside.
The *vaiyāvṛtyakara* asked: "For whom is this being done?"
He replied, "There is one who possesses few desires who has indeed committed an offense but does not repent; I am now performing the act of 'setting aside' (pratikṣepaṇīya-karman) against him.
At that time, Śāriputra, as the leader of the assembly, addressed the official in charge of affairs, saying:
“Do not allow anyone to cause harm or decline within this most excellent Dharma.
He asked again:
“Venerable sir!”
"With whom did he perform the *parivāsa* (probation), or the *mūlaparivāsa*, the *mānāpya*, and the *āvarhaṇa*?
He replied, "There was no other matter;

it was simply because the Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana committed an offense and failed to acknowledge it, that they intended to carry out the *pratisāraṇīya-karman* (act of reconciliation) against him."
Śāriputra replied,
"Venerable friend!
Do not trouble this elder with such a trivial matter."

However, the Bhagavat possesses all-knowing vision; having attained great mastery over the realm of unsurpassed wisdom, he is able to sever the doubts of others. You may inquire of him, and as the Buddha instructs you, so shall I uphold it.
Then the bhikṣus reported the matter to the Buddha. The Buddha, knowing the time was right, questioned them at length as described above.
At that time, the Buddha addressed Mahāmaudgalyāyana, saying:
"With what intention did you manifest supernatural powers to seize that boy?"
At that time, Maudgalyāyana reported the matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"There is no offense for the bhikṣu Maudgalyāyana when he manifests supernatural power with such an intention."
The Buddha was staying at the Bamboo Grove Monastery in Rājagṛha.
At that time, the venerable Pilindavatsa’s nephew was studying non-Buddhist scriptures in his own home.

At that time, during the first part of the day, Pilindavatsa took up his robe and bowl and entered the city of Rājagṛha. Proceeding in order for alms, he came to his sister’s husband’s house and, seeing the boy studying, asked his brother-in-law:
"What scripture or treatise is this child reading?"
He replied, “The non-Buddhist scriptures.

The Venerable One urged him to abandon the study of external doctrines and encouraged him to practice the Buddhist sūtras; he then became the teacher for his sister’s husband’s son, explaining at length as described above.
Eventually, fully adorned with various ornaments, he went to the Bamboo Grove. There, he was plundered by autumn bandits and placed upon a boat;
as they intended to depart downstream, his attendant saw the bandits taking him away and fled back home to inform his master, saying:
"The apprentice who received his training has been plundered and taken away by autumn bandits."
Then her brother-in-law immediately went in haste to King Bimbisāra and said:
"Great King!
My son has been abducted by the autumn bandits; I now beg the Great King for my son."
Then the king commanded Ajātaśatru, saying:
"You should go at once to arrest the autumn thief and seek out the brahmin’s son.
At that time, Ajātaśatru already harbored a grudge against the brahmin; thus, although he had received the king's command, he did not depart in haste.
At that time, there was a goddess who had conceived deep reverence for the Venerable Pilindavatsa and addressed him, saying:
"Venerable sir, do you know?
Your nephew has been carried off by the autumn bandits."
At that time, Pilindavatsa thought to himself:

"If I do not save this nephew, both the son and his parents will suffer the pain of separation; those who lack faith and devotion will find pleasure in hearing of this, while those who possess faith and devotion may feel regret."
"Those who come and go have been seized by the bandits; who else would now be willing to enter the bamboo grove?
I should now manifest my supernormal powers.
Having thought this, the Noble One used his supernormal power to reach the side of the ship and caused the bandits' vessel to be unable to depart.
At that time, the autumn bandit thought to himself,
"For what reason does my ship no longer move forward?
Then, he saw the Venerable Pilindavatsa standing upon the shore and gazing out.
Then the bandits said,
"Noble one!
For what reason do you distress us?"
He replied, "It is you who distress me with your evil ways; it is not I who distress you.
Had I not realized such noble Dharma, you, son of a brahmin, would have been carried away forever."
The bandits said, "Venerable One!
We release this child; you may take him as you please."
He immediately ordered him to go ashore.
At that time, the Noble One withdrew his supernormal power and said to his nephew:
"You may return quickly to see your parents; you shall receive your lessons tomorrow."
On the road, the youth encountered Ajātaśatru, who had set forth from Rājagṛha with his fourfold army arrayed in full battle order. Seeing the youth on the path, the king asked him:
"Where have you come from?"
He replied,
"I was on my way to the Bamboo Grove when I was robbed by bandits along the road.
[The king asked,] "Who brought you here?"
He replied,
"This is my maternal uncle, Pilindavatsa.
At that time, Ajātaśatru felt great joy and cried out in a loud voice:

"We have now gained a great and wholesome benefit, for within our kingdom there is such a holy one of great wisdom, endowed with all powers, whose outflows are forever exhausted in both the present life and future worlds."
Having offered this praise, he returned to the city of Rājagṛha.
At that time, the six bhikṣus were leaving the city on some business when they encountered him on the road and asked him:
"Venerable sir, whom did you praise?"
He replied,
“I praise the assembly of noble sages.
[They asked,] “For what reason do you now praise us, O Noble One?”
He replied, "The Brahmin's son was taken away by bandits while he was at the Bamboo Grove; the noble Pilindavatsa recovered his son through the power of his supernatural faculties."
The group of six replied,
"You foolish person!
Although we possess such supernormal powers, people do not respect or believe in us."
Yet there are foolish people who pluck out their hair and naked ascetics who follow external paths; instead, they even give rise to feelings of reverence and faith toward them.
If those naked ones were to see this matter, it would be as if those autumn thieves were being shown the way out.
At that time, Ajātaśatru remained silent and offered no reply.
Then the six bhikṣus—Nanda and Upananda—said to one another:
"We have already answered the matter well; however, this person of few desires has now committed an offense. Let us go to him and cause him to repent."
He then returned to his dwelling; having finished his meal and paid his respects to those in order according to seniority, he went to the place of the Venerable Pilindavatsa and said to him:
"Venerable Elder!..."
"I pray that you will grant me leave; I wish to pose some questions.
He replied, "Ask as you please."
“The son of a brahmin was taken away by autumn bandits; you, sir, snatched him back.
Is this matter true or false?
He replied:
"It is true; I shall take it and bring it here.
He replied, "I already knew beforehand that the Elder was dwelling in the sublime bliss of meditative concentration and liberation."
I truly did not know that my loving-kindness was not universal; while I felt compassion for my kinsmen, I harbored a lack of forbearance toward those autumn bandits.
Furthermore, I forcibly seized property belonging to others.
"Since you, O virtuous one, have committed an offense, you should repent according to the Dharma. He replied,
"Venerable sir!"
"I do not see any offense.
At that time, the group of six monks deliberated among themselves, saying,
"Venerable sirs, you should know what the World-Honored One has said:"
“Since he does not acknowledge his offense, you should perform the *pratisāraṇīya-karman* (act of suspension) against him.
“Who shall act as the administrator?
You should strike the *gandī* and perform the *pratisāraṇīya-karman* for this person.”
He then went to the person in charge of affairs and said,
"Venerable sir,
you should strike the ghaṇṭā."
The administrator asked,
"What business is being transacted?
They replied:
"One who is of few desires has indeed committed an offense but does not confess it; I wish to perform the formal act of suspension against him.
At that time, Śāriputra, being the senior elder of the assembly, observed whether the matter was appropriate or not and said to the official in charge:
"Venerable one!..."
"With whom did you undergo the *parivāsa* (probation), or with whom did you joyfully emerge from the offense after concealing the original *parivāsa*?
He replied, "There was no other matter;
it was simply because the Venerable Pilindavatsa committed an offense and did not acknowledge it, that they performed the *pratisāraṇīya-karman* (act of reconciliation) against him."
Śāriputra replied,
"Venerable one!
Do not disturb an elder of venerable standing with such a trivial matter."

However, the Bhagavān possesses all-knowing vision; having attained great mastery over the realm of unsurpassed wisdom, he is able to sever the doubts of others. You should consult him, and as the Buddha instructs you, so shall I carry it out.
Then the bhikṣus reported the matter to the Buddha.
The Buddha, knowing the proper time, questioned them, as described in detail above.
At that time, the Buddha addressed Pilindavatsa, saying:
"With what intention did you manifest supernatural power to take the son of the brahmin?
At that time, Pilindavatsa related the matter in detail to the Buddha.
The Buddha addressed the bhikṣus:
"If Pilindavatsa were to manifest supernatural power with such an intention, there would be no offense.
At that time, the Buddha was staying at the Bamboo Grove, the Squirrels' Feeding Ground, near the Kakrandaka Pond in Rājagṛha.
It was the established custom of King Bimbisāra to go daily to pay homage at the feet of the World-Honored One, as well as those of the virtuous and the senior bhikṣus.
On one occasion, having paid homage at the Buddha’s feet, he sat to one side to listen to the Buddha’s teaching of the Dharma.

Then the Buddha taught the essential points of the Dharma to King Bimbisāra, instructing, exhorting, benefiting, and gladdening him. Having heard the Dharma, the king paid homage to the Buddha and departed, proceeding to the dwelling place of the Venerable Pilindavatsa.

At that time, Pilindavatsa was personally repairing a damaged area in his dwelling. Seeing the king approaching from afar, he washed his hands and feet, went to his usual seat, adjusted his appearance, and sat down.
Having prostrated at the feet of the King, he sat to one side and said,
"Noble One, why do you trouble yourself with such labor?
He replied:
"Great King!
Those who have left the household life must all attend to their own duties.
Since I have already left the household life, whom do you wish to have perform them for me?"
The king said, "If that is so,
I shall serve as the attendant for the Noble One.
He replied:
"Great King! May Your Majesty be free from illness and enjoy long life.
Thus he spoke five times, each time reporting as above.
"I am the attendant for the Noble One.
At that time, the Venerable Pilindavatsa had a disciple who was upright by nature; he then addressed the King, saying:

"Since Your Majesty granted permission for the Preceptor to have an attendant, if my own teacher has ceased his repairs in accordance with Your Majesty's word, all of his dwellings have already fallen into ruin."
The king then replied,
"Venerable One!
How could it be that I have already granted permission for an attendant?"
He replied, "Great King! It was not only once;
it happened thus up to five times, but as the affairs of state were numerous, I forgot and could not remember."
It was the king’s established custom that whenever he spoke, his ministers would invariably record his words.
He asked the recorder, “Did I truly ever promise to grant this to the attendant?”
He replied, "It is indeed so.
It has already happened five times."
"If this is so, I ought to be punished; I shall now provide five hundred pure men to serve as attendants.
He then addressed the great minister, saying, "You should provide five hundred servants for the Noble One."
Then Pilindavatsa addressed the king, saying: "Great King!
Because I have gone forth into homelessness, I have completely renounced all service; what would you have me do now with this messenger?"
He said, "Noble One, you should accept this for the sake of the Saṃgha."
“If it be as Your Majesty says, I shall inform the Buddha.
The King said,
“Noble One!”
"You may go and inform the Buddha.
Then Pilindavatsa reported the matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said,
"If it is for the sake of the Saṃgha, you should accept it."
Then Pilindavatsa received the instruction as given.
At that time, although the attendants had been assigned to the Saṃgha, they were not yet exempted from royal service. These men said to the Noble One:
"When we first heard that we were to serve as attendants to the Saṃgha, our hearts were truly filled with joy; how could we have known that one person would be burdened with two types of service?"
He replied, "O virtuous ones!
Do not worry; I shall inform the Great King on your behalf."
Later, on another occasion, King Bimbisāra went to the place of the Noble One, prostrated at his feet, and sat to one side. At that time, the Venerable One said:
"Great King, regarding the attendants for the Saṃgha whom you previously bestowed as gifts—have you perhaps come to feel regret?"
The king said, “Noble one!
I truly have never had a thought of regret.”
Again, he addressed the king, saying,
"For what reason have these people not yet been exempted from royal service?
At that time, the king issued an edict to his great ministers, saying:
"I have given this attendant to the Noble One; since he has been relinquished to the Saṃgha, he may be exempted from royal service.
Following these instructions, the minister immediately released them all.

At a later time, when the state undertook a construction project requiring laborers, the minister summoned them, but none came. Even those who had not been given to the Saṃgha falsely claimed, "I am that very attendant."
At that time, the minister informed the king of the matter:
"Because they were summoned for labor service but did not come, they all claimed, 'I am a servant of the Sangha.
The king said:
"If this is the case, let all be restored as before to perform service for the king.
From that time forward, those who had previously been given away were all made to serve the king's commands.
Those who had been given away went to the Venerable One and said:
"We shall return to fulfill our duties for the state; please represent this earnestly to the Great King on our behalf.
The Noble One then made his representation:
"Do you now regret the attendants who were provided?"
The King asked,
"What do you mean? He replied:
"The attendant assigned to the Saṃgha has been conscripted back into the king's service.
The king said,
"Noble One!"
Whenever there were official duties or labor services, everyone claimed, "I am an attendant of the Sangha," which caused affairs to fall into neglect.
We only pray that Your Holiness will establish a separate quarters for lay attendants, distinguishing them from the others so that they do not become intermingled and confused.
The Noble One replied to the King,
"I shall inform the Buddha.
The King said:
"So be it. Then Pilindavatsa reported the matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said,
"I now authorize the construction of a lodging for laborers."
At that time, the bhikṣus did not know where they should build it.
The Buddha said:
"Between the royal city and the monastery, at the place where the sound of the call is heard, you should construct it."
Then the bhikṣus, having received the Buddha’s instruction, went to inform the minister:
"Now, at this location, we shall construct a residence for laborers in accordance with the World-Honored One’s teaching.
Thereupon, the minister informed the king, who said:
“As the Buddha has instructed,” the minister announced to all the attendants:
“The Sangha is now constructing separate dwellings for you; you should all go and reside there together.”

Having heard this, the attendant immediately went to that place; once they had constructed a dwelling and completed its arrangement, the attendant thereafter regularly went to the Bamboo Grove to serve as an attendant for the Saṃgha.
At that time, the assembly of bhikṣus said to the people:
"Pure deeds should be performed; impure matters should not be done at all.
Because one performs pure deeds, one is called a 'pure person' (śuddhakarman); if one guards the dwelling place, one is called a 'gardener' (ārāmika)."
Those pure persons and those who tend the monastery gardens went to the Bamboo Grove every day, creating a clamor that disturbed the bhikṣus and hindered their practice.
The bhikṣus informed the Buddha, and the Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"Do not allow them to assemble constantly; they should only be summoned when there is business. If there is no service to be performed, let them remain in their own quarters."
Then the bhikṣus again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"How should the clothing and food required by those lay attendants be provided?
The Buddha said:
"Those who act as messengers for the Sangha may be provided with food and clothing; those who do not drive [the cattle] shall not be given food or clothing.
To those who are aged or ill, food, clothing, and various medicines shall be provided."
Later, at another time, Upānanda was next in charge of the monastic affairs. He told the laborers:
"O worthy ones!
I am the one in charge of monastic affairs; you all should come to the monastery early tomorrow morning."
At that time, within the city of Rājagṛha, there was a bandit named Kāḷaka who frequented the area after the bhikṣus had completed their summer retreat.
These autumnal bandits deliberated among themselves, saying:
"What work should we undertake so that, without any toil, we may enjoy an abundance of food, clothing, and comforts throughout this year?"
Among those autumn bandits was one laborer who had previously been employed by a bhikṣu and was well-acquainted with monastic affairs;
he said to the bandits, "In the Bamboo Grove there is a lay-attendant’s quarters containing much wealth; let us go together to plunder it, and this year we shall have abundance and joy."
One thief said:

"Those bhikṣus are the masters of the lay attendants (śrāmaṇera); they do not even have enough to fill their own bellies from begging door to door, so how could these lay attendants possess any wealth?"
The thieves replied:

"You do not know that although these bhikṣus constantly beg for alms, there are many who give them gifts and they also seek wealth for themselves; were one to calculate their possessions, even the people of Rājagṛha could not match them, let alone the lay attendants—how could they have no clothing and goods?"
At that time, the bandits reached a consensus and, during that very night, went to the quarters of the *kappiya-kāraka* (the one who provides allowable goods) intending to plunder their property.
There was a deva who had conceived deep faith and reverence for the Venerable Pilindavatsa; he went to the Venerable and said to him:
"There are autumn bandits plundering those *kappiya-kārakas*; out of compassion, O Venerable One, please grant them protection."
At that time, Pilindavatsa thought to himself:
"If I do not save him, it will cause that person of pure mind to give rise to grief and suffering," as explained in detail above.
"I should now manifest my supernatural powers.
Having thought this, he manifested an iron wall surrounding the quarters of the attendants.

At that time, as the bandits were carrying their stolen goods and attempting to leave the quarters, they saw only the solid iron wall with no way out; struck with terror, they abandoned their loot, and in an instant, the iron wall vanished.
At that time, as the bandits returned carrying their stolen goods, the manifested iron wall suddenly reappeared; this occurred up to seven times.
The bandits said to one another, "Do you all know?"
"There must be a holy being endowed with great majestic power who has manifested this supernatural feat to protect these goods; we should abandon the items and flee together in haste.
Thereupon, the bandits gathered the goods in one place and all fled.
When the attendants (*karmadāna*) awoke, they clamored together in a loud voice, crying out, "We have been robbed!

Having lost their wealth, they were filled with grief and anxiety; they wandered all around the dwelling quarters searching for their belongings until they saw the clothes and goods piled in one place. They were immediately filled with joy and took the items, each returning to his own house to guard them as he lay down to sleep.
At that time, that deity spoke to the people within their dreams, saying:
"You have not been plundered by the autumn bandits; this is entirely due to the supernatural power of the Venerable Pilindavatsa."
When dawn broke, they said to one another:

"That we have escaped the loss of our wealth is entirely due to the power of this noble one's grace; no other person could have conceived such compassion. We ought to offer him a brief act of veneration."
They all bathed together, donned fresh white robes, adorned themselves with fragrant garlands, and took their offerings as they proceeded to the Bamboo Grove.

At that time, Upānanda rose early in the morning; taking the keys and locks, he intended to open the temple gates, extinguish the lamps, sweep and scrub the halls, and arrange the seats. He made offerings of incense and flowers at the stūpa, ascended the upper gallery, struck the gandi, and looked out in all directions. From afar, he saw the people dressed in fresh white robes and adorned with fragrant garlands.
Upānanda then had this thought:
"Who are these people coming here—householders, merchant lords, or wealthy men—who have arrived at dawn?
Upon approaching the gate, he recognized them as *karmadāna* (attendants), whereupon Upānanda became enraged and called out to them from afar:
"I did not tell you to come here so early in the morning; for what reason have you arrived?
The attendant replied, "Venerable One!"
"Last night, had it not been for the compassionate protection and mindfulness of the noble Pilindavatsa, our wealth would have been completely stolen by thieves.
Upānanda said to the attendant:
"You relied on his power to compete in such clamor; I shall impose a disciplinary measure upon him."
Having spoken these words, he summoned the group of six and went together to the place where the Venerable Pilindavatsa was, saying to him:
"Venerable Elder!
We pray that you will grant us leave; we wish to pose some questions."
He replied, “As you wish.
He then addressed him, saying:
"Regarding the property in the lay attendant's quarters that was stolen by bandits and then recovered through supernatural power—
was this incident real or false?
He replied:
"It is indeed so," he replied.

"I previously knew that the Elder was already dwelling in the sublime bliss of meditative concentration and liberation; however, I did not know that although he possessed compassion, it could not extend everywhere, such that he showed pity for and protected the pure person, yet surrounded the autumn bandits with an iron wall."
"Furthermore, you have forcibly retained property already taken by another; since you have committed an offense, you must repent according to the Dharma.
He spoke at length as above, until finally, the *gandī* was struck to propose the formal act of suspension (*pratisaṃharaṇīya-karman*).
The Elder Śāriputra caused him to investigate this thoroughly.
The bhikṣus informed the Buddha, who said to Pilindavatsa:
"With what intention did you manifest supernatural power to retain these pure objects belonging to others?"
Pilindavatsa reported the matter to the Buddha in full detail.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"If Pilindavatsa manifests supernatural power with such an intention, there is no offense."
Furthermore, there is no offense in the following cases: when the precept has not yet been established; when one is insane, mentally deranged, or overwhelmed by intense physical suffering.
This concludes the training rule on taking what is not given.
The Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya, Volume Five;
The Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya, Volume Six.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Yijing by Imperial Decree.
3. The Training Rule on Taking Human Life. The Third Training Rule on Taking Human Life.
A summary verse states:
First, the case of Dhaṣaka; Killing through one's own body and so forth.
[The Buddha spoke of] the poison, the harm, and the *vetāla* (reanimated corpse) spirits; subsequently, he discussed matters concerning the bathhouse.
A summary verse states:
*Dāsaka*, *Pavatta*, *Subhadda*, and *Sobhita*.
The bowl and robes, as well as the abortion, the elder, and the Mṛga-brāhmaṇa.
At that time, the Bhagavān was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, there were two bhikṣus in this city:
one named Dāsaka and the other named Palaga; they were close in spirit and lived as companions.
At another time, Pālaka fell ill, and Dāsaka served as his attendant.
Then, Pālaka suddenly wept loudly in the middle of the night, and Dāsaka asked him:
"Venerable one!..."
"For what reason are you weeping? He replied,
"I am afflicted by the torment of hunger and thirst."
Dāsaka replied, "Venerable sir!
One ought to restrain oneself regarding the dharma of renunciation; even if there were food, one would not give it to others, let alone when no food can be obtained at this time!"
He then wept until daybreak, saying,
"I am hungry and thirsty. Vatsaka said:
"Venerable one!
Please chew on a tooth-stick while I consult the physician.
Having gone to the physician's place, he reported:
“O Noble One! There is now a youth who has suddenly been stricken by an illness; you should provide a prescription for what is appropriate for him.
The physician replied:
"Noble one! That bhikṣu should be given such-and-such medicine.

After Vatsaka had departed for Dhānaka, Prāṇaka rose from his seat, adjusted his robes, put on his leather sandals, took up his water flask and tooth-stick, and went outside to rinse his mouth. Thereupon, another bhikṣu asked him:
"Venerable Pāṭaka!
For what reason have you been weeping in distress throughout the entire night?
He replied:
"I am extremely hungry and thirsty.
He asked, "I have rice gruel with water; why do you not eat it?"
He replied, "Excellent!
I must eat it now."
Having finished eating his fill, another bhikṣu asked him:
"Venerable one!
I now have milk-rice porridge, cakes, and meat soup; why do you not eat them?"
He replied, "I wish to have some.
He then went to the room and greedily devoured it; having become excessively full, he lay down on his side.
Then, having questioned the physician, Dāsaka returned with great haste, bringing with him the medicine prescribed by the physician, and said:
"Venerable Praloka!..."
"You should rise and chew a tooth-stick.
He replied,
"I have finished."
Dāsaka said, "Very well.
He then prepared the altar, wiped the copper vessels, and called out, "Come and eat. Out of consideration for the other's feelings, he immediately rose from his seat.
Then, Dāsaka had someone bring food and give it to him; [the monk] took two or three spoonfuls of food and then lay down.
Dāsaka said, "Venerable One!..."
"For what reason do you not eat?
He replied,
"It is that my heart has no desire."

He said: "Throughout the entire night you tormented me excessively with your crying and lamentations of hunger; now that I have given you food, you say you do not want it. It is certain that you will die this very day."
Then the other bhikṣus replied, "Venerable Dāsaka! There is no need to press us;
we have already eaten water, milk, curd-rice, thin cakes, and meat at our place, and are fully satiated."
Dāsaka asked Pālaka,
"Venerable one,
did you truly consume delicious food and drink?"
He then spoke slowly and softly with a sense of shame, saying,
“I have already finished eating.
Then, Dāsaka said to him:
"For your sake, I have exhausted my robes and bowl, abandoning the cultivation of wholesome deeds to serve you.
You yourself must take care of your own person; it would be better to consume poison than to eat such forbidden food."
When Pālaka heard these words, he was deeply filled with shame and thought to himself:
"How excellent are the words of my fellow practitioner in his reproach of me! It would be better for me to consume poison than to eat such forbidden food; indeed, I should now truly take poison."
He immediately rose from his seat, searched within his bag of various medicines, found a poisonous drug, and swallowed it.
The medicine took effect, causing him dizziness and distress until he was on the verge of death; his eyes rolled upward and he vomited froth from his mouth, weeping and crying out: "Dāsaka!"
"I am dying! I am dying!
When Daṣaka heard this, he arrived in a state of alarm and fear, and asked:
“Venerable Pāṭaka!
Why do you weep when you are not ill? Pāṭaka replied:
"I heard that you have undergone great hardship seeking medicine for me; rather than exercising self-restraint, you would sooner take poison than eat such forbidden food.
This led me to think:
'A fellow practitioner has labored so much for my sake, yet cannot exercise self-restraint; I should now take his poison.'"
Thereupon, he searched within his bag, found the poison, and immediately consumed it.
When Dāsaka heard these words, tears of sorrow filled his eyes, and he said to him:
“Venerable one!
"Why have you now committed such an unwholesome act?
He then ran quickly to question a physician.
The medicine was so virulent that its force could not be sustained, and he subsequently passed away.
At that time, the physician Dāsaka obtained medicine from his teacher and hurried back; seeing that Pālaka’s life had already come to an end, he was overcome with remorse and thought to himself:
"Could it be that I have now incited him to death?"
For this reason, he informed the bhikṣus, and the bhikṣus reported it to the Buddha.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"Because that Dāsaka had no intent to kill, there is no offense."
However, bhikṣus should not speak such words in the presence of a sick person as would cause that patient, upon hearing them, to seek death.
Should one speak such words, one incurs an offense of transgression against the Dharma (dharmātikrama).
This is the origin of the rule; however, the Blessed One had not yet established a training precept for his śrāvaka disciples within the Vinaya.
At that time, the Buddha was staying at Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park in Śrāvastī.
At that time, there were two bhikṣus in this city:
one named Kalyāṇavādin and the other named Śrī. They were close friends, bound by mutual affection and goodwill.
The bhikṣu Kalyāṇavādin had left behind hunting to go forth into homelessness, while the bhikṣu Śrī had left behind his status as a householder to go forth.
There were two youths who were the nephews of Suvāgīśvara; having lost both their parents, they wandered about in exile until they arrived and stood outside the gate of the Jeta Grove.
At that time, Suvāgīśvara came out and encountered them; observing their countenances, he recognized them as former kinsmen and immediately asked:
"Where are your parents now?"
The youth replied,
“Both have already passed away.
Upon hearing this, Shan-yu could not help but shed tears.
At that time, the bhikṣus saw them and asked,
"Who are these two boys?
They replied:
"He is my nephew. The bhikṣu said,
"Since he is a relative on your maternal side, why do you not take him in and support him?"
He replied, "When I go for alms, I do not even provide for myself; how much less could I sustain another?
The bhikṣu said:

"Let these two children provide the bhikṣus with tree leaves, flowers, fruits, and tooth-sticks; the bhikṣus, for their part, shall give them the remains of food from their alms-bowls so that they may be sustained."
When Suvādin heard this, he immediately took them in and raised them.

By nature, these two boys were respectful and diligent, serving [the monks] well; they would gather leaves, flowers, fruits, and tooth-sticks for the bhikṣus. In return, the bhikṣus gave them leftover food as well as clothing and provisions.
After a long time had passed, he gradually grew up until his physical form was fully developed. On one occasion, he was staying and playing before the gate of the monastery.
Other relatives, carrying bows and arrows, were passing by the Jetavana forest in pursuit of deer;
they asked the boy, "For what reason are you staying here?"
The youth replied, "My maternal uncle has gone forth among these sons of the Śākya; I dwell depending upon him.
The hunter said:
“Your maternal uncle, being unable to support himself, has gone forth among the sons of the Śākya to seek the homeless life; how is it that you yourselves cannot support yourselves?
You ought to resolve to follow in your father’s profession.”
The youth then replied to his relatives, "My maternal uncle has indeed shown us profound kindness; we should now go to him to consult him regarding this matter.
He then went to his uncle's place and said:
“Noble One!
I now take my leave, wishing to practice the father’s craft.
His maternal uncle then replied:
“I have supported you two with offerings given out of faith; why do you now return to practicing evil deeds?
The two sons replied, “Even if we were to wear a golden wreath upon our heads, we would still cast it aside; how could we possibly abandon the ancestral occupation of our forefathers?”
Consequently, they disregarded their uncle’s words and departed together, supporting themselves by engaging in hunting.
Later, on a certain occasion, Śrī became afflicted with a grave illness, and Kalyāṇavādin served as his nurse. At that time, Śrī, being tormented by the suffering of his disease, thought to himself:

"I have maintained my precepts and committed no evil; heaven and liberation are now separated from me only by a thin curtain. It is fitting now that I cast off this body, which is the basis of suffering, so that I may be reborn in a superior realm."
He further thought to himself:
"I am now oppressed by suffering; who will come to kill me and end my life?
He then recalled that his two nephews, Suvāga and Duḥsuvāga, were by nature coarse and violent.
"He can kill me; why rely on anyone else!
Having thought this, he said to Kalyāṇavādin:
"Venerable friend!..."
"Where is your nephew now? He replied, "I do not like to hear their names;

they were both sustained by my offerings of faith. Yet at this time, they have begun to practice evil deeds, joining their grandfather in the business of hunting, taking the lives of various creatures to sustain themselves."
Śrī said: "Do not harbor feelings of resentment toward those two;

however, since those two sons have been in the Jeta Grove, not even an insect has ever harmed them. Now that wicked men have enticed them into committing the act of killing, you should specifically exhort those evil associates to abandon their ways."
"Venerable sir, you have gone abroad while I remain here alone and ill; there is no one else capable of attending to me. If you see him, please summon him back to look after and serve me."

At that time, Kalyāṇavādin went out to beg for alms and saw his two sons at a butcher’s stall selling meat. When his nephews saw their uncle approaching, they both came forward to prostrate at his feet.
Kalyāṇavādin was then filled with resentment and said to them:
"What kinship do I have with you?"
He replied, “He is my maternal uncle.
“That venerable Śrī! [he said.]
"Furthermore, what kind of relative is he? He replied,
"He is also my maternal uncle."
He then said to him:
"Since you departed, that person has been afflicted with illness and has never returned even for a brief visit to see me.
He replied:
"I truly do not know; let us go at once to see what he intends to do.
He replied, "There is one who instructs him; you should perform the work for him."
Having spoken thus, he departed.
Then the two sons went to Śrīgupta; having prostrated at his feet, they sat down to one side.
Upon seeing them, Śrīgupta said to the two sons:
“What kinship do you have with the noble Suvāgīśvara?
He replied,
“He is my maternal uncle.”
“I am now your relative once again; what kind of relative am I?
He replied, “I am also your maternal uncle.”
Śrī replied, "I have recently been afflicted by illness, yet you never once came even for a moment to visit me.
He answered:
“Uncle, I truly did not know; it was only upon hearing you speak that we immediately arrived.
Śrī said, “Do you wish for me to be reborn in heaven?”
He replied,
"I wish to be born there.
[The Buddha] told him:

"If this is so, I shall go to another realm of abundance and joy; heaven and liberation are as close as a thin curtain. I wish to cast off this body, the basis of suffering, and be born in a place of bliss; you should now sever my life-faculty."
He replied, "How could such a thing be?
Even if another person were to come and harm my maternal uncle, I would kill them; how could we ever bear to join together in taking our uncle's life?"
He said, "Suvāca,
did I not already tell you that you should act as the instructor for him?
They replied:
“I have heard it said.
“If you have heard this, you should speak to one another and grant me my life-force, which is being severed by these afflictions.
At that time, the two sons deliberated together, saying:
"Could it not be that my uncle had previously planned this, which is why he summoned me to perform such a deed?
At that time, one of the two sons, who was extremely coarse and violent, immediately took a sharp blade and severed his uncle's throat, then covered the corpse entirely with a white cotton cloth.
Then Suvādin returned and said to them,
"How can you allow the patient to sleep while you are guarding him?
They replied:
“Uncle! This uncle is now asleep and there will be no time for him to rise again.
Hearing these words, Shan-yu was struck with extraordinary alarm and thought to himself:
"I ought now to inquire further with greater scrutiny.
At that time, the two sons related the circumstances of the matter in detail.
Then, as Śobhavācā became terrified, she went to see the white cotton cloth and saw that it had been killed; her heart was immediately filled with remorse.
"Is it not the case that I, seeking to hold a blade, have taken the life of another?
At that time, Suvāca, whose grief over the separation from his beloved had intensified, related this matter in detail to the bhikṣus, and the bhikṣus reported it to the Buddha.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"Since that bhikṣu had no intention to kill, he is not guilty of an offense.

However, bhikṣus should not appoint those who lack wisdom to act as caregivers. If there is a compelling reason for you to go outside yourself, you must instruct those who are unskilled in caregiving, saying:"

"One must ensure that the patient is not harmed through improper means; one should prevent them from falling into water or fire, consuming various poisons, wielding knives or axes, falling from cliffs or ditches, climbing high trees, or eating forbidden foods—all such things should be restrained so that no injury results therefrom."
"If a bhikṣu has an ignorant person attend to a sick monk and then departs after failing to give proper instructions, he incurs a *vyatikrama* offense.
This is the origin story (*nidāna*), before the training rule (*śikṣāpada*) was established.
The Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
In this city there was a bhikṣu whose almsbowl had lost its color and was cracked; another bhikṣu said to him, “Venerable one!...”
"Your almsbowl has holes and its color is faded; why do you not repair it by firing it?
He replied, "If one were to repair it by firing, many things would be required: a clay kiln, cow dung, and oil-cake, among other things."
The bhikṣu said:
"Venerable one!
If you have no bowl, how can you possibly survive?"
He replied,
"How could I possibly survive without a bowl?
However, there is a bhikṣu in a certain place who is afflicted by a grave illness and will not live much longer."
"He has a single alms bowl that is radiant, pure, perfect, and fit for use; should he die, I shall take it.
When the bhikṣus heard this, they said to him, "Venerable one!..."
"For the sake of an almsbowl, you have conceived such an extremely wicked and *caṇḍāla*-like thought.
Upon hearing this, he felt shame and remorse, and remained silent, thinking:
"Could it be that I have now committed an offense?"
He then informed the bhikṣus of these circumstances, and the bhikṣus reported it to the Buddha.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"Since that bhikṣu had no intention of wishing for death, he is not guilty of an offense."

Nevertheless, monks should not harbor such extremely wicked, *caṇḍāla*-like thoughts toward their alms bowls; whoever gives rise to such thoughts commits a transgression of the Dharma (*dharmātikrama*).
Monks should protect and maintain their bowls as they would their own eyes: those that require mending should be mended, and those that require fumigation should be fumigated.
"If a bhikṣu possesses a bowl that ought to be fumigated and mended, yet fails to do so, he incurs an offense of transgressing the Dharma.
This is the origin story; the training rule had not yet been established.
The Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
In this city there was a bhikṣu whose saṃghāṭī robe was tattered, worn out, and covered in dust and grime. Another bhikṣu said to him, “Venerable friend!...”
"Your saṃghāṭī is torn, worn out, and covered in dust and grime; why do you not wash, dye, and mend it?
He replied, "If I were to repair it, much would be required: firewood, dye, needles, thread, a basin, and so forth."
The bhikṣu asked,
"If you have no robes, can you still survive?
He replied:
"If I have no robes, how can I possibly survive?

However, at such-and-such a place there is a bhikṣu who is afflicted with a grave illness and will not live much longer; he possesses a saṃghāṭī robe that has been newly dyed red and is fit for use—I shall take it."
When the bhikṣus heard this, they said to him:
"Venerable one!
For the sake of a robe, you have conceived such an utterly wicked and *caṇḍāla*-like thought."
Upon hearing this, he felt shame and remorse, and remained silent, thinking to himself:
"Could it be that I have now committed an offense?
He then informed the bhikṣus of these circumstances, and the bhikṣus reported it to the Buddha.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"Since that bhikṣu had no intention of wishing for death, he is not guilty of an offense.
Nevertheless, bhikṣus should not give rise to such an extremely wicked, caṇḍāla-like mind regarding robes; whoever conceives such a mind commits a transgression of the Dharma."

However, all bhikṣus should cherish and protect their robes as they would their own skin; those that require washing, dyeing, or mending should be attended to accordingly. Should one fail to do so, one incurs an offense of transgressing the Dharma.
This is the origin story; at that time, the training rule had not yet been established.
The Buddha was staying in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park, in Śrāvastī.
In this city there was a householder named Jayasena, who was immensely wealthy, possessed of great riches, and lived in abundance. He took a wife from a family of equal status.
Before long, the wife became pregnant, and after nine months had passed, she gave birth to a son whose physical appearance was so handsome and dignified that all who saw him were delighted.
After twenty-one days had elapsed and the relatives had gathered for a celebration, the father addressed his kin regarding the child:
"What name shall we give this boy?"
The assembly deliberated and said, "This is the son of the elder Vijaya; he should be given the name Mahāsena.

Not long after, another son was born whose appearance was extraordinary and twice as superior to his elder brother’s. His physical marks were perfectly complete... [as described at length previously] ...after detailed deliberation, the younger brother of Mahāsena was named Candrasena.
Later, when Jayasena’s wife passed away, he escorted her to the forest and cremated her with fire.
As the days and months passed, his grief gradually subsided, and he thought to himself:
"If I were to take another wife, I fear it would distress my two sons."

Once Mahāsena was established, he took a wife for him. Before long, the elder fell ill; although medicine was administered, his debility increased day by day. He consoled his two sons and spoke these verses:
"All that is accumulated must dissipate; All that is lofty will surely fall. Those who meet must ultimately part; All who have life return to death."
Having spoken these words, he immediately passed away. His funeral rites were prepared and he was cremated in the outskirts of the city.
The Great Army (Mahāsena) performed extensive meritorious deeds for his father’s sake and thought to himself:

"When my compassionate father was alive, he provided me with clothing and resources. Now that he has passed away, I should seek my own livelihood so as not to let the family estate fall into ruin. I should now take my wealth and goods and travel to other lands to seek profit and sustain myself."
Having thought this, he said to Cūḍapanthaka, "Do you know, younger brother?
While our compassionate father was alive, we lacked for nothing in food and clothing; now that he has passed away, we must seek our own livelihood."
"You should remain at home and diligently oversee our affairs; I wish to go abroad for a time to seek profit, so that whatever I obtain may sustain our livelihood.
The younger brother replied to his elder brother, "Excellent!"
At that time, Mahāsena took a great deal of merchandise and traveled to other regions; whatever he sought along the way, all was successful. He sent a letter to his younger brother, saying:
"I am very well and have acquired much wealth and profit. You should be comforted and take good care of the family estate."
Driven by greed for profit, he traveled once more to distant lands; later, at another time, he sent a letter again to report his situation, as there is a verse that says:
"Out of greed one seeks profit, And upon gaining profit, greed increases further.
What should and should not be done— All is forgotten for the sake of greed."
Seeking profit by traveling in succession to distant borderlands, he was gone for many years without any news reaching them.
The wife of Mahāsena, provided with fine clothing and delicious food, conceived lustful thoughts and immediately manifested signs of sexual desire toward Kṣudrasena.
Cūḍapanthaka did not permit it, and his lustful thoughts increased further;
he said, "Venerable sir, why do you not consider this?
Hearing this, Cūḍapanthaka covered his ears and said:
"Do not speak such words; an elder sister is like a mother.

Regarding the deceptive nature of women, she knew it without being taught; she then put on tattered clothes and returned to her parents' house, manifesting an air of distress as she lay upon a coarse and wretched bed.
His mother and family members all asked him,
"What grief or suffering have you encountered that has brought you to such a state? He replied:
"The sufferings of women are not shared by others; I am being tormented and oppressed by lustful thoughts.
His mother then instructed and exhorted him with various skillful means.
However, he remained lying on his worn-out bed without rising, and spoke again to his mother, saying:
"I am oppressed by lustful thoughts; Mother, you should seek another husband for me."
His mother looked up and down at him and said to him, "Your younger brother-in-law has a handsome and upright appearance; why do you not seek him?
He replied:
"I have sought it with great hardship, yet he did not grant my request.
The mother then said to her:
"Do you not see how other women, when their husbands travel far away, maintain their chastity with single-minded devotion? Why do you alone now harbor such sorrow and distress?"
She replied, "As for her husband, he occasionally sends letters, so there was still hope; my husband’s letters have ceased, so he must certainly be dead.
Although her mother tried to entice and persuade her, she remained lying down and would not rise, and spoke to her mother again, saying:
"Set aside other matters for now; you ought to seek out a husband for me. If you do not comply with my wishes, I shall surely flee in secret, bringing great disgrace upon both our families."
At that time, her parents and kinsmen consulted together, saying:
"Observing this girl's intent, we see her base views will not change; it would be best to prepare various foods and drinks and summon Suvīra."
When Kṣullaka was summoned, he came to the banquet; having finished eating, [the king] said to him:
"I have now invited you for a private matter: your elder sister-in-law has been pressured by lust. You should take care to accept her with affection and prevent her from fleeing in secret."
Having heard this, Kṣullaka reflected to himself:

"This sister-in-law has entered my household since her youth; it would not be fitting to send her away abruptly to marry another man, nor do I wish for the ill repute of both families to become public."

Having formed this thought, she opened her mind and followed his lead; they returned home together to establish a household as husband and wife. Not long after they lived together, she became pregnant.
Her female companions, seeing this as strange, asked her:
"What is in your womb, and from where did you obtain it?"
She replied, "I have followed my husband away and resolved to remain a widow; for what reason do you all falsely defile me?
Furthermore, other intimate women said to one another in private:
"Though you wish to conceal it, your physical signs have already become manifest.
She then reported that she was pregnant.
He asked:
"Who permitted it?
He replied,
"It was Cūḍapanthaka."
The female companion said,
"If it is indeed the young master, what fault could there be in this?
As her belly gradually grew larger, her elder brother sent a letter to inform Xiaojun, saying:
"I have traveled far on business, and all my endeavors have been successful; do not be distressed, for I shall return before long.
Upon hearing this, Kṣulla had deep remorse and thought to himself: "I remember my elder brother as one longs for rain in a drought.

Having been cut off from his news for so long and having failed to return, I originally had no intention of committing such an evil deed; only now that my base conduct has been exposed do I speak of returning home."
There is a saying in the world:
"Among all enemies, none is more grievous than one who violates one's wife.
If my elder brother comes here and learns of this, he will surely harm me; we should now flee and hide our tracks in a distant land.
He further reflected:

"It is difficult to abandon one's homeland; now that King Prasenajit treats the son of the Śākyas as equal to his own crown prince, granting him complete freedom and unimpeded authority, I shall go to him and renounce the household life."
"Even if my elder brother were to return,
what would he do? He then went to the Jetavana Grove and addressed a bhikṣu, saying,
"Noble One!..."
"I wish to leave the household life; I pray that you will graciously grant me permission.
He replied, "Wealth and life do not last long; to be able to renounce them and leave the household life is most excellent!"
He then shaved his hair and had him don the dharma robes; having conferred full ordination and briefly instructed him in the ritual procedures, he said:
"Worthy one! Deer do not nourish deer, and it is extremely difficult for us to support one another. The city of Śrāvastī is vast and spacious; you should seek alms there to sustain yourself."
Cūḍapanthaka replied, "Upādhyāya!
I shall now follow your instructions."
At dawn, he took up his robes and bowl and entered the city to beg for food, eventually arriving at his own home.
Seeing him from afar, his wife beat her breast and cried out, "Kṣulla, why have you abandoned me to go forth?"
She replied, "Do not speak such words.

Do you not know that I remember my elder brother as one longs for rain in a drought? Since our correspondence has ceased and he has not come in person, I have committed this evil deed with you; should my brother arrive, he will surely kill me."
He replied, "If you wish to save yourself,
what can I do? Kṣullaka said:
"I was coerced by him and had no original intention; you, being bound by desire, should exert yourself for your own sake.
Having said this, he departed.
At that time, Sūkṣma had an old acquaintance who was previously learned in medical prescriptions; [Sūkṣma] went to his home and asked:
"Where is Kṣudraka?
His wife replied, "Having been humiliated by him,
he abandoned me and went forth into homelessness."
He asked, "Where is it? He replied:
"One may go to seek him at the residence of the śramaṇas in the Jeta Grove, as those who do not believe may do.
Following these words, he went to seek him and saw the assembly of bhikṣus; because their appearance and attire were similar, he did not know which one was Cūḍapanthaka.
He asked the bhikṣus, "Where is Cūḍapanthaka?
At that time, a bhikṣu pointed out his location; having seen him, he asked Cūḍapanthaka:
"Why did you not speak to us before coming here to leave the household life?

He replied, "You should not reproach me for leaving the household life so abruptly. I have related my elder brother's letter in full and recounted my own failings; having no other recourse, I became a śramaṇa."
The friend replied, "I am originally skilled in medicine and well-versed in prescriptions; for one who is pregnant, there is a medicine capable of inducing an abortion.
Upon hearing this, the young soldier remained silent.
Then that friend prepared a medicinal powder and sent it with the girl to the wife of Cūḍapanthaka, instructing her:
"This powdered medicine was sent by the bhikṣu Cūḍapanthaka; take it with warm water and you will surely recover."
The girl went to her and related the matter in detail.
Upon hearing this, the wife took the medicine and administered it according to the instructions; the fetus was then expelled, and she no longer showed signs of pregnancy.
When people became aware of this, the other women asked:
"Where is the fetus now?
He replied, "I have already said before:"
"Since her husband has gone away, she has lived as a widow, maintaining her resolve.
Do not bring anything defiling or improper to pollute her.
At that time, a close female confidante privately told her:
"As for what you previously said,
'This was permitted by Cūḍapanthaka,' for what reason do you say today:"
“I did not have it before. He replied,
“I came from there, and I shall return there.”
He asked again,
"How so? and was answered:
“Cūḍapanthaka gave me poison; having taken it, my fetus has been destroyed.
The women told one another and each raised their reproaches:
“The sons of the Śākyas are capable of such evil deeds; they are not true śramaṇas, for they give others poison to cause them to miscarry.”
This evil reputation spread throughout the city and countryside, with everyone saying:
"The bhikṣu Cūḍapanthaka has committed such a sinful deed.
When the other bhikṣus heard this, they went at once to inform the Buddha.
The Buddha asked Little Army,
"Did you truly do such a thing?
He replied:
"No, World-Honored One!
I merely rejoice in it."
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
"Because that Suddhananda lacked the intent to kill, there was no offense.
Nevertheless, bhikṣus, you should not give rise to a mind of rejoicing regarding such matters; if you do rejoice, you shall incur an offense of transgression against the Dharma."
Before long, the great army returned with spoils, joyful and triumphant; they halted for a short while not far from the city.
Generally, people of the world rejoice upon hearing of good fortune and feel sorrow upon seeing evil. Someone reported to the woman:
"The great army has arrived with abundant wealth and profit; you ought to feel joy."

The woman was naturally skilled in artifice, requiring no instruction; upon hearing these words, her heart was filled with great anxiety and fear. She donned coarse and tattered clothing and lay upon a wretched bed.
When the great army had entered the city and established their goods in the market stalls, she returned home and, seeing that her dwelling lacked auspicious signs, asked her servants:
"Where is the master of the house?"
He replied,
"I am lying down in my room.
Having heard this, [the other] went there and said to him:
“O noble one!
Upon hearing that I have come, do you not feel joy and celebration?
He replied:
"Now that I hear you have arrived, I am truly filled with joy; however, the small force you left behind to guard me has already caused me harm.
He asked, "In what way?"
He replied,
"Kṣudraka acted improperly, forcibly insulting and harassing me.
Mahāsena reported this, saying:
"He has not deceived you; he has deceived me.
You should rise at once, for I am able to cure him.
Where is Cūḍapanthaka now?"
He replied,
“Hearing that you were about to arrive, I secretly left home to become a renunciant.
He asked:
"Where is he? "He is at the Jeta Grove, with the Śākyaputrīyas.
He then informed his wife.
"Is that place not the City of Fearlessness? I shall surely punish him there according to the law.
At that time, another person went and informed him, saying, "Does Cūḍapanthaka know?"
"Your elder brother has arrived.
He asked, "What did your brother say?"
He replied, "Your elder brother spoke these words:
'Is that Jetavana Grove truly the City of Fearlessness? I shall now punish him with harsh laws.'"
When the younger brother heard this, he was seized with great anxiety and fear, and thought to himself:
"It was out of fear of him that I came forth to renounce the world; could it be that I shall meet his harm again in this very place?"
"Although I know that as a bhikṣu I am like a prince and face no obstacles, yet I have committed a transgression; if he comes to see me, he will surely harm me. I ought now to flee and escape."
At that time, having had this thought, Kṣudraka said to his preceptor: "Upādhyāya!
It was out of fear of him that I sought ordination; I have heard that he intends to come and inflict harm upon me."
The Teacher asked,
"Who is that person? He replied:
"He is my elder brother; having come from afar, he intends to slaughter me, saying:
'Is the Jeta Grove a city of fearlessness that you would seek to punish me with such harsh treatment?'"
"Although I know that according to the laws of the kingdom, I shall remain safe and unharmed like the Prince, yet because I have committed a transgression, they will surely harm me;
it is best that I flee now. His teacher asked him, "Where do you wish to go?"
Kṣudraka said,
"I now wish to go to the city of Rājagṛha.
The Master said:
“There is a bhikṣu who is my acquaintance in that place; you may take this letter of mine to him and stay there, for he will surely protect and care for you with kindness.
He replied, “Very well!”
Then his preceptor immediately wrote a letter to that bhikṣu, saying:
"This Śuddhodana is my disciple; he now wishes to go there."
"Having traveled from afar to seek refuge in you, may you extend your compassion; we pray that you will grant us your protection so that we may dwell in peace and happiness.

At that time, having received the letter, Kṣudraka paid homage to his teacher and departed. Looking left and right, he was filled with fear and apprehension as he proceeded by stages until he reached Rājagṛha, where he sought out the bhikṣu.
Having seen him, he prostrated at his feet and handed over the letter from his preceptor.
When that bhikṣu had read the letter, he said:
"Welcome, venerable one!"
"I am like your former teacher and you are like my disciple; it is fitting that you receive instruction in the Buddha-dharma from me.
Whatever you require—robes, alms bowls, bags, water filters, or waist-bands—I shall provide them all so that you lack for nothing."
However, the World-Honored One has said:
"Bhikṣus have two kinds of duties to perform:
namely, meditative reflection and recitation."
"What do you now delight in?
He replied,
"I delight in meditative concentration."
He replied, "Very well!
and instructed him according to the Dharma.

He then went to the Śītavana cemetery, where corpses were abandoned, and with diligent exertion he cultivated the path to sever all fetters and delusions. He realized the dharma of non-arising and attained the fruit of Arhatship, becoming free from the defilements of the three realms. He viewed gold and earth as equal and indistinguishable; whether his body was cut by a blade or smeared with fragrant ointment, he harbored no dualistic thoughts. Like a hand waving through empty space, his mind was free from obstruction. With great wisdom, he shattered the shell of ignorance, becoming fully endowed with the three knowledges, the six supernormal powers, and the four unhindered analytical knowledges. He renounced all craving for existence, gain, profit, and honor, and was praised by Śakra and the various devas.
Later, on another occasion, Mahāsena went to the Jeta Grove and asked the bhikṣus:
"Venerable sirs!
Is there not a son of a merchant in this city named Kṣudrasena who has gone forth here?"
He replied,
“There is one who is very close to you.
He asked:
“Where is this younger brother of mine now?
“He has already departed for Rājagṛha.
Then Mahāsena, having prostrated at his feet, departed and thought to himself:
"Even if I were to go there, that place is not a city of fearlessness; I shall go there and punish them according to the law.
Thereupon, the Great Army took a great quantity of provisions for the journey and arrived at Rājagṛha, proceeding to the Bamboo Grove where he asked the bhikṣus:
"Noble ones!..."
"Is there not a son of a householder from Śrāvastī named Cūḍapanthaka who has already gone forth and come here?
He replied,
"What kinship do you have with him?"
He replied,
"It is my younger brother.
He asked again:
"Where is he now? "He is at the Śītavana cemetery where corpses are abandoned. Having heard this, he went there immediately;

however, as that forest was filled with many bhikṣus practicing the holy life together, and as Mahāsena had been separated from his younger brother for so long that his appearance had faded, he could not recognize him at once among the crowd. Only after observing him closely for a long time did he finally recognize him.
Mahāsena thought to himself, "If he recognizes me, he will surely harbor a harmful intent; I should therefore remain hidden and devise another plan.
He then emerged from the forest, looked around in all directions, and saw a hunter holding a bow and arrows, seeking game. He approached him and asked:
“Virtuous one, what do you intend to do now that you hold this bow and arrow?
The hunter replied,
“I wish to go hunting.”
He asked, "How much profit have you obtained?
He replied:
"Sometimes one obtains profit, and sometimes one does not.
He asked: "If one does obtain profit, how much is its amount?"
He replied,
"I can get five or six gold coins.
He then informed [the other]:
"I will now give you five hundred gold coins; can you, for my sake, kill one of those bhikṣus who are my enemies?
At that time, the hunter, out of greed for profit, accepted the money. Having taken it, he thought to himself: "These bhikṣus have been granted favor by the king;
their status is like that of a prince, sovereign and unimpeded. I come and go here constantly, day and night; if I were to kill a bhikṣu, my wife and children would surely die in prison."
He further reflected:

"During the day, I once entered this forest and my heart was filled with terror such that the hair on my body stood on end; yet these venerable ones dwell here constantly, day and night, in peaceful security. Is it not because they have accomplished a sublime practice?"
"However, this man is like white pepper—his place of origin is unknown. Now that I have obtained my object, I shall turn back and kill him.
He then drew his bow into the shape of the letter *ṭha* and, with a poisoned arrow, pierced the man’s heart through and through. Having encountered such bitter agony, he conceived an evil thought:
"That this hunter should now turn against me and harm me must surely be because Little Army (Kṣudrasena) previously devised this plot."
"Though I die now, I vow to harm Little Army (Kṣudrasena) in my next birth.
Having made this evil vow, he immediately gave up his life and was reborn as a venomous snake beneath the door pivot of Little Army.
Even an Arhat, if he has not previously observed it, would not know of such a matter.

At that time, Sūkṣma opened the door-panel and crushed the snake to death; yet his poisonous intent did not cease, and he subsequently received the body of a snake upon the door pivot, where he was likewise crushed to death as before.
Beneath the feet of the bed, he again manifested as a venomous snake; in this manner, four times in succession, he was crushed to death beneath the bed.

Each time the snake died, it took rebirth again, its body becoming gradually smaller while its poisonous intent grew ever more intense. Later, at another time, it received the body of a venomous snake within the space of a clothes rack.
At that time, Cūḍapanthaka sat alone in silence within a quiet chamber; then, driven by resentment from a former enmity, a venomous snake cast itself upon his body and bit him with its poison.
At that time, Kṣudraka let out a great cry and addressed the bhikṣus:
"Venerable sirs!
A strange, venomous snake—fierce, blazing, and terrifying—small as an iron skewer and about four inches long, has fallen upon my body and bitten me with its venom."

"All of you come together and seize my body to carry it out of the room; do not let the flesh of this body disintegrate here like a handful of dust or sand that falls apart as soon as the hand is opened."
At that time, the Venerable Śāriputra was sitting in meditation under a tree not far from there. Hearing that cry, he immediately went to him and asked Cūḍapanthaka:
"I do not see any change in your facial expression; for what reason do you now say this:
'A strange, fierce, blazing, and terrifying venomous snake, as small as an iron chopstick and about four inches long, has fallen upon my body'?"

"All of you, come together and seize my body to carry it out of the room; do not let the flesh of this body disintegrate here like a handful of dust or sand that falls apart as soon as the hand is opened."
At that time, Cūḍapanthaka said to Śāriputra:
"Venerable Sir!

If there were a self or what belongs to a self in the eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind; if there were a self or what belongs to a self in forms, sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, and mental phenomena; if there were a self or what belongs to a self in earth, water, fire, wind, space, and consciousness; or if there were a self or what belongs to a self in form, feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness—then such a person might have their faculties and physical appearance undergo change."
"Venerable sir!

It is not so for me now; since I am without self or what belongs to a self regarding the faculties, objects, the six elements, and the five aggregates, how could my physical appearance undergo such a transformation?"
"Venerable Śāriputra!

Throughout the long night, all my attachments to 'I' and 'mine,' my conceit of 'I am,' and my latent afflictions have been known and abandoned; their roots have been forever uprooted. Like the head of a tāla tree cut off, they shall no longer grow, nor shall they arise again in future lives."
"How could it be that my complexion has changed so drastically?

Then the Venerable Śāriputra, together with a great many bhikṣus, carried Little Army (Cūḍapanthaka) out of the room. As soon as he was carried out, Little Army’s body fell apart into a hundred pieces, like a handful of sand or dust that scatters the moment one opens the hand.
At that time, the Venerable Śāriputra spoke these verses:
"The holy life has been established, The noble path has been well cultivated;
When my life comes to an end, I rejoice, Just as one is relieved when freed from many ailments."
The holy life has been established, the noble path has been well cultivated;
at the end of life one rejoices, as if casting off a vessel of poison.
The holy life has been established, the noble path has been well cultivated.
At the time of death, there is no fear, Like emerging from a house on fire.
The holy life has been established, And the noble path well-cultivated;
Observing the world with wisdom, It is like viewing grass and trees.
"Having accomplished what was to be done, he does not abide in saṃsāra;
within all future existences, his body shall no longer continue.

At that time, after Kṣudraka had entered parinirvāṇa, the Venerable Śāriputra, together with the bhikṣus, gathered his bones and flesh, cremated them as an offering, and went to where the World-Honored One was. Having prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, they stood to one side and said:
“World-Honored One!

The bhikṣu Cūḍapanthaka was bitten by a venomous snake that fell upon his body—fierce, blazing, and terrifying, as thin as an iron rod and about four inches long. Its venom was so lethal that his body burst open; it was like a handful of dust or sand that scatters as soon as one opens the hand. He has now entered parinirvāṇa.”
The Blessed One said: "Śāriputra!

If the bhikṣu Cūḍapanthaka had recited this verse and these protective mantras at that time, he would not have been harmed by the snake's venom, nor would his body have been shattered and scattered like fine dust."
Then Śāriputra requested of the World-Honored One, saying:
"What are the gāthās and the incantations?
We only pray that the World-Honored One will explain them for us; having heard them, we shall all together receive and uphold them."
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke these verses and incantations for the sake of the bhikṣus:
"I extend thoughts of loving-kindness To Dhṛtarāṣṭra,
As well as Virūḍhaka, Virūpākṣa, and Vaiśravaṇa."
May Gautama, Virūpākṣa, Nanda, and Upananda,
as well as those without feet and those with two feet, likewise give rise to thoughts of loving-kindness.
Toward all the nāgas who dwell depending upon the water, [may they likewise give rise to thoughts of loving-kindness].
Toward all classes of sentient beings, whether walking or staying, I arouse a heart of loving-kindness.
May all the multitudes of humans and devas, as well as spirits, ghosts, and animals,
all obtain benefit and peace, remaining free from illness and always joyful.
All that I see is virtuous and good; I encounter no enemies or evildoers.
Toward all, I arouse thoughts of loving-kindness: "May no harm or poison invade you.
Whether on cliffs, in valleys, or in perilous places, I travel everywhere.
May the venomous bite and the harmful poison never again afflict me.
By the true words of the World-Honored One, the Great Compassionate Father,
and because I speak these words of the Buddha, may no poisons invade me.
Lust, hatred, and delusion are the great poisons of the world;
by the Buddha’s words of truth, all poisons naturally vanish.
Lust, hatred, and delusion are the great poisons of the world.
By the true word of the Dharma, all poisons naturally perish.
Greed, hatred, and delusion are the great poisons of the world;
by the true word of the Saṅgha, all poisons naturally perish.
"May all poisons and harms be extinguished; may you be protected and sustained.
The Buddha eliminates all poisons; snake venom, you shall be destroyed!
Tadyathā | Aṇe | Dunbale Dunbale | Dunbe | Paridunbe | Nate Sunate | Kinate | Munaye Sumunaye | Dantine Narakise | Caruke Vi | Uviveyu-kule Svāhā. The Buddha said to Śāriputra:

"If at that time the bhikṣu Cūḍapanthaka had recited this gāthā and these divine mantras, whether by himself or through another, he would certainly have been spared from the harm of the venomous snake; his body would not have been made to rot and split apart, but would have scattered like a handful of dust or sand released from the hand."
At that time, all the bhikṣus were filled with doubt and addressed [the Buddha], saying:
“World-Honored One!
We pray only that you will sever our doubts.”
I now wish to ask:
what karma did the bhikṣu Cūḍapanthaka perform in the past?
By the power of that karma, he has been born in his present life into a family of great wealth, abounding in riches and treasures.
Furthermore, what karma did he perform?
By the power of that karma, he went forth as a renunciant under the World-Honored One, severed all afflictions, and attained the fruit of Arhatship.
Furthermore, what karma did he perform?
"By the power of that karma, although he had attained the fruit of an Arhat, he was bitten by a venomous snake; his body and mind were so tormented that he entered nirvāṇa.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus, saying:

"The karma previously committed by this bhikṣu Cūḍapanthaka must necessarily be experienced by him himself. Since the karma performed by Cūḍapanthaka has increased, matured, and its conditions have manifested before him—like a shadow following a form—he will certainly experience the retribution; there is no one else who can receive it on his behalf."
"O bhikṣus!

Whatever wholesome or unwholesome karma a person performs does not cause them to experience its retribution within the external elements of earth, water, fire, or wind; rather, it brings about its maturation entirely within one's own aggregates, elements, and sense bases."
He then spoke in verse:
"Though a hundred eons should pass, the karma one has created does not perish;
when the causes and conditions meet, its retribution is received by oneself."

“O Bhikṣus! In times past, when no Buddha had appeared in the world, there arose in the world a Pratyekabuddha Arhat who, out of compassion for the poor, always made use of coarse food and clothing himself; like a rhinoceros horn, he was the sole field of merit.”
At that time, there lived a hunter in a certain village. Not far from the village was a large forest pond, where many birds and beasts gathered and roosted along its banks.
At that time, the hunter had set many traps, snares, sticky glue, and nooses, by which he captured many birds and beasts every day.
On one occasion, a Pratyekabuddha arrived at that village and took up residence within a temple.
In the first part of the day, he took up his robe and bowl and entered the village for alms. Having received food, he thought to himself:
"This temple is crowded with many people; outside the village there is a quiet forest where I should go to stay after begging my meal."

Seeking gradually, he eventually reached the edge of a pond. Seeing a secluded grove suitable for dwelling, he set aside his robes and bowl, filtered water to examine it for insects, washed his hands and feet, gathered fallen leaves, spread them upon the ground, and sat down.

Having finished his meal, he washed his hands and bowl; having set the bowl aside, he then washed his feet and sat cross-legged beneath a tree. His majestic demeanor was tranquil and composed, like a dragon king coiled in its abode; because of the scent of his presence on that day, neither birds nor beasts came near.
Then that hunter rose early in the morning and went to the edge of the pond; he searched everywhere for his snares and traps but found nothing at all. He then thought to himself:
"In other days my snares and traps were never empty; why is it that today I have obtained nothing?"

He then looked around in all four directions from the edge of the pond and beheld human footprints; following the tracks, he arrived and saw a Pratyekabuddha sitting cross-legged, his demeanor serene and tranquil.
Having seen him, he thought:
"I observe this renunciant; his deportment is so tranquil that he seems to be fond of his dwelling.
If I do not take his life now, he will cause my supply of food and clothing to be cut off."
With a mind intent on harm and without regard for the future, he immediately bent his bow, drew the poisoned arrow, and struck him in a vital spot.
At that moment, the noble one thought to himself:
"How could I allow this ignorant hunter to suffer great torment in the evil realms for a long time? I should lend him a hand to rescue and deliver him."

"Just as a king of geese soars through the expanse of space, emitting water and fire from his body and manifesting great supernormal powers, those ordinary beings who witnessed these miracles quickly took refuge, bowing like the felling of a great tree; they prostrated from afar at his feet and said to him:
'O true field of merit, we pray that you descend swiftly!'"
"I only pray that you will descend quickly!
I am ignorant and deluded, sinking into the mire of desire; I pray that you will look upon me with compassion and pity, and rescue me.
At that time, out of pity for him, the Pratyekabuddha lowered his body and descended. The hunter, overcome with grief, knelt down, extracted the poisoned arrow, and bound it with a cloth, saying:
"Noble One!
Please come to my home so that I may prepare medicinal ointment for your wound; if you require gold leaf to apply to the wound, I shall also seek it out for you.
At that time, the Pratyekabuddha thought to himself:
"Now this body of mine is foul, putrid, and filled with pus and blood; that which was to be attained has now been attained, and I shall now enter the realm of the wondrous Nirvana without remainder."
He then ascended into the void, manifested various supernatural transformations, and entered *nirvāṇa*. At that time, the hunter was very wealthy and possessed great riches;

he burned the body of the noble one with various types of fragrant wood and extinguished the fire with cow’s milk. He then took the remaining bones and placed them in a golden jar, erecting a *śarīra* stūpa at a crossroads. Having offered various kinds of silk canopies, banners, flags, flowers, incense, and music as acts of worship, he prostrated before the stūpa with a sincere heart and made this vow:

"I am truly foolish and deluded, not knowing good from evil; I have thus committed an extremely grave offense against such a true field of merit. I pray that in future lives I may not suffer the retribution of evil."

By virtue of all roots of goodness from these offerings, in future lives they shall always dwell in wealth, happiness, and abundant enjoyments; their countenances shall be upright and handsome, bringing joy to all who behold them. Possessing such supreme merit and virtue, they shall serve the Most Excellent Great Teacher without ever becoming weary.
"O Bhikṣus! You should know that the hunter was none other than Cūḍapanthaka.
