Because in the past he shot a Pratyekabuddha in a vital spot with a poisoned arrow, by the power of this evil karma, he suffered the torment of burning for the full duration of a kalpa within the Avīci Great Hell."

There remained residual karma such that for five hundred lifetimes he was constantly subjected to poison; although in this present life he attained the fruit of Arhatship, he nevertheless encountered poison once more before entering nirvana.

Because he made that vow to be born into a family of wealth and happiness with a handsome countenance, from that time until now, there has been nothing he has not experienced, as described in detail above.

Furthermore, he went forth as a renunciant within my Dharma, severed all fetters and delusions, and realized the fruit of Arhatship. Among hundreds of thousands of koṭis of Pratyekabuddhas, I am the most supreme teacher, and he served me without ever becoming weary.
Therefore, bhikṣus! You should know this:

if one performs purely white karma, one will obtain a purely white maturation; if one performs purely black karma, one will obtain a purely black maturation; and if one performs mixed black-and-white karma, one will obtain a mixed maturation.
“O bhikṣus, you should abandon entirely black karma and mixed karma, and you should diligently train yourselves in entirely white karma.
This was the origin of the rule, yet at that time the training precept had not yet been established.

The Third Chapter on the Training Rule Regarding Taking Human Life, Part Two.
At that time, the Blessed One was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.

At that time, there was a householder in that city who took a wife from a family of equal status. Not long after they had enjoyed each other's company, a son was born to them. As the boy gradually grew up, his mother subsequently passed away.
Later, his father took a second wife. At that time, the elder addressed the junior wife, saying:
"Are you capable of providing for and raising a son who is not your own biological child, sharing both his sorrows and joys?"
She replied, "I can.
Not many months later, the woman became pregnant, and she then conceived an evil thought:
"If I bear a son, I shall employ that child as a servant and must not allow him to give rise to a mind of arrogance.
He then provided him with coarse clothing and poor food, further afflicting him with the hardship of whips and canes.
The son said to his father, "Father, do you know now?
My stepmother treated me with ill food and clothing, yet provided for my needs; she repeatedly applied the whip and staff, inflicting upon me extraordinary suffering."
The father replied to his son,
"I shall admonish your mother so that she does not act thus again," and he then addressed his wife, saying:
"O virtuous one! Previously, I already informed you:
'Would you be able to provide sustenance and nurture for a son born of one who is not your kinsman, sharing in his joys and sorrows?'"
"You replied, 'I can. Why then,
at this time, do you not follow your previous words, but instead provide this child with poor food and clothing, repeatedly subjecting him to lashes and whips of extraordinary cruelty?"
He replied, "I am instructing you so that you may advance; I fear that people of the world might mock me, but truly I have no other intention.
Her husband said:
"You need not instruct him; furthermore, you must not subject him to the suffering of hunger, cold, or physical torment to provoke resentment and pain.
He replied, "I shall certainly not do so."
Before long, he gave birth to a son; however, she conceived an even greater malice toward this child than she had for her firstborn, subjecting him to the same suffering as before.
The boy then thought to himself:
"My father cannot restrain my mother, so she continues to torment me just as she did previously. I should now leave home and go forth into the religious life."
He then went to his father and said:

"My stepmother shows me no compassion; although you, Father, have tried to restrain her, she still lacks kindness toward me. I now wish to leave the household life and pray that you will grant me permission. How could I endure suffering here until the end of my life?"
The elder then thought to himself:

"This wife of mine is by nature unkind; though I have repeatedly exhorted and admonished her, she still does not reform. I shall allow her to leave the household life so that her life may be preserved."
He then said to his son,
"I now grant you permission to leave the household life as you wish.
Having received his father's consent, he went to the Jetavana Grove and approached a bhikṣu to request ordination.
Then, having granted him the going forth and conferred full ordination, that bhikṣu said to him:
"Venerable one!
For all those who have gone forth, there are two kinds of duties:
"It is said there are meditation and recitation.
I have been practicing concentration lately; what practice do you prefer?
He replied:
“Upādhyāya! I wish to recite [the scriptures].
He replied:
"Excellent! You have studied the Tripiṭaka.
Thereupon, he thought to himself:
“The teachings of the Tripitaka are profound and vast in both letter and meaning; yet my own Master delights his mind in meditative concentration. Who, then, will instruct me in this?
It would be best for me now to go elsewhere.”
He said to his teacher,
"I wish to go to another region to study the Tripiṭaka.
The teacher replied:
"Excellent! Go as you wish.

At that time, the disciple took his leave and traveled to other regions, where he studied the Tripiṭaka extensively until he was thoroughly versed in both its words and meanings, becoming a great Dharma Master whose eloquence was clear and whose expositions were unimpeded.
He then reflected to himself:
"As the World-Honored One has said:

'Parents undergo great toil for their children; they protect, nurture, and sustain them with the nourishment of breast milk. Among those who have instructed me in Jambudvīpa, my parents are the foremost.'"

Even if a son were to carry his father on his left shoulder and his mother on his right shoulder for a hundred years without ever feeling weary, or were to fill the entire earth with mani-jewels, pearls, lapis lazuli, conch shells, jade, coral, gold, silver, agate, musāragalva gems, and red pearls turning to the right—offering all such treasures as an act of worship to bring them peace and happiness—even by doing these things, he would still be unable to repay the kindness of his parents.

If one's parents lack faith, one causes them to abide in right faith; if they lack precepts, one causes them to uphold the prohibitions; if they are by nature stingy, one causes them to practice generosity; and if they lack wisdom, one causes them to give rise to wisdom.
"If you can thus exhort and encourage your parents to cause them to abide securely in this way, only then may it be called repaying their kindness.
However, my father has not yet conceived faith or reverence toward the Triple Gem; I should now go and preach the essential Dharma for him.

He then took his robes and bowl and went to Śrāvastī; traveling by stages, he eventually arrived at his native land and stayed in the Jetavana Grove, where his fame spread far and wide and he was praised and revered by all.
Once that son of the householder had gone forth into homelessness, he traveled to other lands where he thoroughly mastered the Tripitaka and returned to the Jeta Grove.
When the householder heard this report, his heart was filled with joy and consolation:

"My son has gone forth, traveled far to other lands, and become fully versed in the Tripitaka; now that he has returned and is dwelling in the Jeta Grove, I should go there to share in this celebration."
He immediately went to the Jeta Grove and saw his son there, saying to him:
"Welcome, Bhikṣu!
Since you left me, you have become thoroughly proficient in the Buddha's teachings; that you have now returned to your former home brings me deep joy."
Having spoken these words, he sat to one side.
Then that bhikṣu expounded for him various subtle and profound meanings; upon hearing the Dharma, his father gave rise to deep faith and received the three refuges as well as the five precepts.
Then the elder invited the bhikṣu, saying, "Please come for a meal tomorrow," and the bhikṣu accepted by remaining silent.
After the father had paid his respects and departed, he thought to himself on the way:

"I was hasty and did not consider things well when I invited my son home and promised to provide a meal tomorrow. My wife is by nature negligent and haughty; she might lack respect and devotion toward my son. What shall I do now?"
He further reflected:
"I have already made this request; it would be improper to withdraw it now. I should instead use skillful words to entice and persuade him, so as not to cause him to become angry."
Upon arriving home, he said:
"O virtuous one!
There is the case of a son who has run away, one whose life has ended, and one who has gone forth into homelessness—do these three matters constitute one thing, or are they different?"
He replied,
"The three matters are no different.
He then said:
“O noble one!

Your former son left me to renounce the world and become a virtuous bhikṣu; he has traveled to other regions where he has become thoroughly proficient in the Tripiṭaka, and he has now arrived here in the Jeta Grove.”
His wife replied, "If that is so,
why do you not invite him to our home for a meal?
He answered:
“I have already extended the invitation; you should now prepare a fine meal.

At that time, the woman’s heart was filled with joy, and she prepared everything—both cold and hot dishes—in accordance with the season. In the morning, she sent a messenger to the Jetavana Monastery, saying:
“Venerable Sir!”
"The food and drink are prepared; you should know it is time.

Then, during the first part of the day, that bhikṣu took up his robe and bowl and went to his father’s house. Having arrived, he washed his feet, sat upon the seat that had been prepared for him, and washed his hands and rinsed his bowl.
The elder and his wife personally served him excellent food and drink with their own hands; once he had eaten his fill and rinsed his mouth, they filled his bowl.

Then his parents prostrated at his feet and sat down to listen to the essential points of the Dharma. Upon hearing the teaching, the stepmother developed deep faith and respect, requesting to receive the Three Refuges along with the five precepts.

At that time, once that household had received the transformation [of the Dharma], monks and nuns all gathered there like thirsty people rushing toward a spring or a pond; whatever they intended to give as alms or to have constructed was all directed toward the two divisions of the Saṃgha.
On another occasion, the elder fell gravely ill; when his son heard that his father was afflicted, he thought to himself:
"I shall preach the Dharma for my father, hoping that he may recover."
Thus, from time to time, he went to his father’s place and said:
"Father, do not worry any longer at this time. Why is that? Because—"

"Father, it is now because of me as a spiritual friend that you have taken refuge in the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Sangha, received the five precepts, and extensively cultivated various merits through generosity and ethical discipline. Having cast off this suffering body, you shall be reborn in a happy realm; heaven and liberation are now separated from you by no more than a thin curtain."
He replied, “It is indeed so!
Because of you, I have conceived a heart of faith and reverence; once I have cast off this body, I hope to be reborn in a superior realm.”
When the son, a bhikṣu, had finished preaching the Dharma for him, he departed. The father thought to himself:
"My son is well-versed in the Tripiṭaka and is a great Dharma teacher; he is wise and sagacious, possessing unimpeded eloquence, and everything he proclaims is entirely true."
"I am now gravely ill and my suffering is extreme; it would be appropriate to employ a skillful means to take my own life.
He further reflected:
"I am now gravely ill; who else could possibly take my life for me?"
In that household there was a maidservant named Pālikā, who was coarse, stout, and dull-witted.
She further thought to herself:
"This Pālikā will surely be able to kill me; no one else is capable of doing such a thing."
Not far from there, a householder’s son was engaged in wedding preparations; at that time, the elder’s wife was summoned to attend the ceremony and took Pālika with her as she departed.
When the marriage was concluded, the elder’s wife said to Paliya:
"You should return home and keep watch over the elder so that he does not sleep during the day; wait for me to take my leave, and I shall follow immediately after."
The maidservant, having received these instructions, returned home to the householder’s residence. The householder asked her, "Where have you come from?
Pālika related the matter to him in full detail.
He asked,
"Is your marriage happy?
She replied:
"Excellent," he said. "I have now arranged this marriage for you; are you pleased with it?"
He replied, "I am very glad.
He then spoke again, saying:
"If you perform everything according to my words, I shall know that your heart is joyful.
He replied, "I shall do everything according to your words."
The elder said, "Now a non-human being has entered my belly; you must expel it for me. He asked:
"In what place do you wish to cause the ghost to emerge?
He replied, "First press from the feet, then the calves and knees, up to the chest and neck; you should grip it firmly, and even if it struggles, do not let go."
Then that foolish maidservant obeyed his words and did as he said. As the elder was being strangled so tightly, he felt remorse and thought:
"If Pālika would release me from this heavy pressure, it would be most excellent."

At that time, Pālika recalled his previous instructions; although he saw [the other] struggling, he refused to let go. Because of this, the suffering became so intense that he immediately passed away.
Then a deva, having witnessed this event, spoke a verse from the midst of the sky, saying:
"If one is throttled by a fool, Or perhaps bitten by a tortoise,..."
"Pālika pressed down so urgently; how could he have survived?
Once he had passed away, she covered his entire body with folded bedding.
When the householder’s wife returned, she asked her maidservant:
"Why did you not wake the elder when he was sent here? Why do you leave him to sleep during the day?
At that moment, the wife shook the patient's hand to try to wake him, but her servant replied, "There is no need to wake him;
I have pressed out the evil spirit from within the elder’s belly for all of you, so he is able to sleep peacefully for a while."
Then the householder’s wife thought to herself:
"I shall observe what this evil spirit looks like.
She lifted the coverlet and looked; seeing that he had already passed away, she then thought:
"It was not my husband who took his own life; it must certainly have been the son of his former wife, the Tripitaka Master. It was because he preached such a teaching to him, saying:
'Father, do not worry.'"

Why is this? Because it is due to me acting as a virtuous friend (*kalyāṇamitra*) that my father has now taken refuge in the Buddha, Dharma, and Saṅgha, received the five precepts, and extensively cultivated various merits through generosity and ethical discipline. Having cast off this body of suffering, he shall be reborn in a happy realm; heaven and liberation are now separated from him by nothing more than a thin curtain.
"Since he has now died, he will surely be reborn in heaven.
When the bhikṣu returns, I shall live with him and entrust all household affairs to his management.

Having formed this thought, she was wracked with grief and distress; she prepared the funeral rites and escorted the body to the wilderness, and once the cremation was complete, she remained there in sorrow and resentment.
At that time, the son of the Tripitaka Master, hearing of his father’s death, thought to himself:
“All conditioned phenomena are impermanent; I should now go to offer the essentials of the Dharma for the sake of his surviving relatives.”
Having arrived at the house, his mother saw him from afar and immediately scolded him, saying:

"You, the son of my former wife, have now returned! It was because you understood the Tripiṭaka and preached the Dharma for rebirth in heaven that you caused your father’s death. Now you may return home to live with me; you shall take charge of all the household affairs."
When that bhikṣu heard these words, he felt shame and departed, giving rise to regret and thinking to himself:
"Could it be that I am now inciting someone to death?"
He then informed the bhikṣus of this matter, and the bhikṣus reported it to the Buddha.
The Buddha said: "Bhikṣus!..."
That bhikṣu is not guilty of an offense.
However, bhikṣus should not preach such a teaching in the presence of a gravely ill person—one that might cause the patient, upon hearing it, to take pleasure in death.
"If a bhikṣu speaks such a teaching as this, causing that sick person to desire death, he commits a *dharmātikrama* offense.
This was the origin of the rule; the training precept had not yet been established.

The Buddha was staying at the Śāla-śikhara forest on the banks of the Vipāśā River in Vaiśālī, where he taught the contemplation of impurity to the bhikṣus and praised the cultivation of this contemplation: "O bhikṣus!..."
"One should practice the meditation on impurity; through the repeated cultivation and frequent practice of this meditation, one attains great fruits and benefits.

When the Blessed One had thus taught the bhikṣus to practice the meditation on impurity so as to attain great fruits and benefits, the bhikṣus immediately began to practice it. Having practiced it, they developed a profound sense of revulsion toward the body of pus and blood. Some took up knives to commit suicide, some ingested poison, some hanged themselves with ropes, some threw themselves from high cliffs, and some killed one another.
There was a bhikṣu who felt a profound sense of revulsion toward this body of pus and blood; he went to where the brahmin-ascetic Mṛgāra was and spoke to him thus:
"Come, O worthy one!"
"I give you my robes and bowl; you must take my life.
At that moment, the brahmin took his life and, carrying the blood-stained knife, went to the banks of the Śubhavatī River to wash it in the water.
At that time, a celestial Māra emerged from the water and addressed the brahmin, saying:
"Excellent, O noble one!

What you have now accomplished will bring you great merit. Regarding this śramaṇa who is endowed with precepts and virtue—you who causes those not yet crossed to cross, those not yet liberated to be liberated, those not yet at peace to find peace, and those not yet in nirvāṇa to attain nirvāṇa—there is further benefit for you in obtaining his robes and bowl."
At that time, that brahmin’s evil views increased even further, and he thought to himself:

“I have indeed now acquired all manner of merit, for I am able to deliver, liberate, and bring peace and happiness to this śramaṇa who possesses the precepts and practices, leading him to the state of nirvāṇa; furthermore, I shall obtain the benefit of his robes and bowl.”
Then that brahmin, taking up a sharp sword, went to the monastery where the monks resided, as well as to other rooms, courtyards, and places for walking meditation, and addressed them, saying:
"If there is any bhikṣu who is fully endowed with the practice of the precepts, I shall deliver him, bring him peace and happiness, and lead him to nirvāṇa."
At that time, there was a bhikṣu who felt weary and ashamed of his own body; he went outside his cell and said to a brahmin, "O worthy one!
Since I have not yet attained liberation, peace, and nirvāṇa, you should cause me to reach the state of nirvāṇa."
Then that brahmin immediately went and killed him.
In this manner, he killed two, three, and even up to sixty bhikṣus,
until the entire assembly of bhikṣus had gradually diminished.
On the fifteenth day, during the time of the *poṣadha*, the Buddha, having sat down upon his usual seat, surveyed the assembly of bhikṣus and addressed the Venerable Ānanda, saying:
"For what reason has the number of bhikṣus gradually diminished until so few remain?"
Then Ānanda said to the Blessed One:

“At one time, the Buddha praised the cultivation of the meditation on impurity for the bhikṣus, saying that those who practice and cultivate this meditation extensively will attain great fruits and benefits.”

At that time, after the bhikṣus had practiced the meditation on impurity (aśubha-bhāvanā), they developed a profound sense of revulsion toward their bodies of pus and blood; some committed suicide, while others sought to have their lives taken by others. Māra came and exhorted them, leading to the slaughter of as many as sixty bhikṣus. Due to these circumstances, the Saṃgha was diminished.
The Buddha addressed the bhikṣus:
"Is it true that you instructed one another to kill?
They replied to the Buddha: [It is true.]
“World-Honored One,
it is truly so.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
"What you have done is wrong; it is not the way of a śramaṇa, it is not in accordance with the practice, it is impure, and it is not an act that one who has gone forth should perform.
Having rebuked him in various ways, he addressed the bhikṣus, saying:
"I consider ten benefits, from the gathering of the Saṃgha up to the long endurance of the True Dharma for the benefit of humans and devas."
I now, for the sake of my śrāvaka disciples, establish a training rule (śikṣāpada) within the Vinaya, which should be spoken as follows:

"If a bhikṣu should intentionally, with his own hand, take the life of a human being or a human fetus; or should provide a knife; or should himself take up a knife; or should seek out one who has taken up a knife; or should encourage death or praise death, saying: 'O man!'"
"What use is this sinful, burdensome, and impure evil life?
You would be better off dying now; death is superior to life.

If, following his own thoughts, he uses such words to exhort and praise [the other] so as to induce death, and that person dies because of it, this bhikṣu also incurs a *pārājika* offense and shall not live in communion.
The meaning of "bhikṣu" is as explained above.
Regarding the term "person" (puruṣa), it refers to one who has already possessed the six sense faculties within the mother's womb—namely, eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind.
A "human embryo" (puruṣagarbha) refers to that which has just entered the mother's womb and possesses only three faculties: body, life-force, and mind.
"Intentionally" means that it is done with deliberate intent, not by mistake or the like.
"With one's own hand" means performing the act of killing with one's own hand.
"Taking life" means causing the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*) of another to cease its continuity.

Regarding "or handing over a blade": if one knows that a person intends to commit suicide, one places a large sword, a razor, a dagger, or the like at their disposal with the intent that they may harm themselves.

"Or holding a knife oneself" means that because one's own strength is insufficient to carry out the killing, one merely holds the knife while causing another to grasp one's hand and take a human life.
"Or seeking someone to hold a knife" means looking for a man, a woman, or a *paṇḍaka* (eunuch) and commanding them to commit the killing.
Regarding the exhortation to death, one exhorts three types of persons to die:
namely, those who have broken the precepts, those who maintain the precepts, and those who are ill. How does one exhort a person who has broken the precepts?
Suppose there is a bhikṣu who seeks from a precept-breaking bhikṣu various requisites for a śramaṇa’s livelihood, such as robes, alms bowls, bags, water filters, belts, and other such items.
At that time, the bhikṣu thought to himself:
"If that person who has broken the precepts remains alive, there will be no way for me to obtain his robes, bowl, and other belongings; I should go to him and urge him to die."
He immediately went to him and spoke these words:
"Venerable sir!
Do you know?"
"You have now broken the precepts and committed various sinful deeds; through body, speech, and mind, you constantly create manifold evils.
Venerable one!
As long as your life remains, the evil karma you have created will only increase further. Because of this increase in evil, you shall suffer the torments of hell for a long duration."
If one who has broken the precepts hears these words, they will ask:
"Venerable sir! What should I do now?"
He replied, "One should abandon the body and take one's own life.
If that bhikṣu should then abandon his body or commit suicide, that bhikṣu incurs a pārājika offense.
If a precept-breaking bhikṣu does not accept the exhortation, that bhikṣu incurs a sthūlātyaya offense.

At that time, although the one who exhorted death had already spoken the words of exhortation as previously described, he felt remorse in his heart and went to where the precept-breaking bhikṣu was, speaking to him thus:
"Venerable One!..."
"You should know that what I previously said was like the speech of an ignorant child who lacks skillful discernment, fails to deliberate carefully, and speaks impulsively.
Venerable one!

If you can draw near to virtuous friends and confess the removal of your prior transgressions, the unwholesome karma of your three doors that you have committed will become purified through their power."
"Because of this purity, after casting off this body, you shall be reborn in the heavens.
If he is one who has broken the precepts, someone might ask him:
"Venerable sir!"
"What shall I do now?
He replied, "Do not abandon your body; do not take your own life."
If the person does not commit suicide, that bhikṣu incurs a sthūlātyaya offense.
Even if the person who has broken the precepts hears the aforementioned words but disregards them and commits suicide, the one who exhorted them to die also incurs a sthūlātyaya offense.
This is called a bhikṣu encouraging a person who has broken the precepts to die.
What is encouraging a person who upholds the precepts to die?

For example, there is a bhikṣu who seeks something from a bhikṣu who upholds the precepts—whether it be robes, a bowl, or other items—as described at length, and he even goes to that person and speaks as follows:
“Venerable one!
Do you know?

Since you uphold the precepts and cultivate all wholesome dharmas, you are further able to give with an outstretched hand, to give constantly, to give with joy, to give extensively, and to give distributively.”
"Venerable one!
Since you possess such merit, you will surely be reborn in the heavens.
When a person who maintains the precepts hears these words, they ask as follows:
"Venerable one!
What should I do now? He replied:
"One should abandon the body and take one's own life.
If that bhikṣu, having heard these words, then takes his own life, that bhikṣu incurs a pārājika offense.
If the precept-observing bhikṣu does not accept the exhortation, that [exhorting] bhikṣu incurs a sthūlātyaya offense.

At that time, although the one who exhorted death has already spoken such words of exhortation for death, he feels remorse in his heart and goes to where that precept-observing bhikṣu is, speaking to him thus:
"Venerable One!..."
"You should know that what I previously said was like the speech of a foolish child who does not discern well, does not deliberate carefully, and speaks impulsively.
Venerable sir!
Since you are able to uphold the precepts and cultivate all wholesome dharmas, you will certainly be reborn in the heavens."
If one who maintains the precepts should ask him,
"What should I do now? he replies:
“Venerable one!
Do not abandon your body; do not commit suicide.
If he does not commit suicide, that bhikṣu incurs a sthūlātyaya offense.
If, despite having heard these previous words, one disregards them and commits suicide, that bhikṣu also incurs a sthūlātyaya offense.
This is called a bhikṣu exhorting a person who upholds the precepts to death.
What is meant by encouraging a sick person to die?
It is as when a bhikṣu has certain expectations regarding a sick bhikṣu, such as his robes, bowl, or other requisites for life. At that time, the bhikṣu thinks:
"As long as this gravely ill person remains alive, there is no way I can obtain those robes, bowl, and so forth; I should go to him and encourage him to die."
He then went to him and spoke these words:
"Venerable one!
Do you know?"
"Since you are gravely ill and suffering extreme pain and distress, if you remain for long, your illness will only grow more severe and you will constantly endure hardship.
When the sick bhikṣu hears these words, he asks:
"What should I do now?"
He replied, "One should sacrifice the body by taking one's own life.
If the sick bhikṣu, having heard these words, takes his own life out of fear of further suffering, that bhikṣu incurs a pārājika offense.
If the sick bhikṣu does not accept the exhortation, that [exhorting] bhikṣu incurs a sthūlātyaya offense.
At that time, although that bhikṣu had already spoken of the aforementioned means for inducing death, he felt remorse in his heart and went to where the sick bhikṣu was, speaking to him thus:
"Venerable one!..."
"You should know that what I previously said was like the speech of a foolish child who lacks skillful discernment, fails to deliberate carefully, and speaks impulsively.
Venerable one!

You should now seek a spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitra) who can find for you the medicine appropriate to your illness, provide you with food and drink, and care for you according to the Dharma, following along without opposition."
"If you can do so, before long your illness will surely be cured and you will be at ease; your strength will be restored, and you may travel as you wish.
If the sick bhikṣu asks him:
"Venerable one!"
"What do you wish for me to do now?
He replied, "Do not abandon your body; do not take your own life."
If he does not commit suicide, that bhikṣu incurs a sthūlātyaya offense.
If the sick bhikṣu, despite having heard the aforementioned words, does not follow that advice and instead commits suicide, that bhikṣu likewise incurs a sthūlātyaya offense.
This is called a bhikṣu encouraging a sick person to die.
Regarding "praising death": if a bhikṣu utters words praising death in the presence of one who desires to die, saying "O man," this is a form of address.
"What use have you now for such sinful burdens, even to the point that death would be better than life?"—these are all words of disparagement.
"Following the thoughts of one's own mind" means that divergent thoughts arise in accordance with one's own mind.
"By other means of speech" refers to using numerous skillful methods to urge the person toward death.
"Praising" means speaking words of praise in the presence of the sick person, desiring that they will certainly die without any lingering concern.
"If he should die by this means" means that the bhikṣu brings about his death by the aforementioned means;
it is not due to any other matter, such as other virtuous states of mind or the like.
"Bhikṣu" refers to one who possesses the nature of a bhikṣu.
"The nature of a bhikṣu" refers to having received full ordination, as explained in detail above.
The meaning of *pārājika* is also as explained above.
Regarding this, what are the characteristics of the offense and the specific matters involved?
A summary verse states:
"Sometimes using one's own body, or employing external objects,"
Or when the internal and external [factors] combine, this is called the characteristic of killing.
What is internal killing?
It refers to if a bhikṣu, with a murderous intent, strikes a woman, a man, or a paṇḍaka with even a single finger, and by means of this expedient they die, that bhikṣu incurs a pārājika offense.
If one does not die at that time but dies later due to this as the causal condition, this bhikṣu also incurs a pārājika offense;
if one does not die at that time nor dies later, he incurs a sthūlātyaya offense.

If, using a single finger, or five fingers, a fist, a wrist, the head, the shoulder, or any other part of the body, even down to a toe, one strikes another with the intent to take their life, and that person dies, this bhikṣu incurs a pārājika offense.
If he does not die at that time but later dies as a result of it, the bhikṣu also incurs a pārājika offense.
If he does not die, he incurs a sthūlātyaya offense.
This is called killing by means of one's own body.
What is killing by means of external objects?

If a bhikṣu, with the intent to kill, shoots a woman, a man, or a paṇḍaka with arrows made of bamboo, iron, or other materials, and they die as a result of this means, that bhikṣu incurs a pārājika offense.
If one does not die immediately but dies later, one incurs a *pārājika* offense;
if one does not die at that time and does not die later either, one incurs a *sthūlātyaya*.

If, with the intent to kill and desiring his death, one hurls at another person spears, javelins, wheels, spikes, or other weapons—even as small as a jujube pit—from a distance, and that person dies by means of this expedient, this bhikṣu incurs a pārājika offense;
if he does not die immediately but dies later, he also incurs a pārājika offense;
if he neither dies at that time nor dies later, he incurs a sthūlātyaya offense.
This is called killing by external means.
What is killing by both internal and external means?

If a bhikṣu, with the intent to kill, takes up a great sword in his hand and kills a woman, a man, or a paṇḍaka, and that person dies as a result of this expedient means, this bhikṣu incurs a pārājika offense.
If one does not die immediately but dies later, one incurs a *pārājika*;
if one does not die at that time and does not die later either, one incurs a *sthūlātyaya*.

Just as it is with a great sword, so it is with all other weapons such as double-edged blades, single-edged blades, spears, and staffs, even down to a blade of grass or a stalk; if, with the intent to kill and the desire for them to die, one strikes or hacks at another by means of these instruments and they consequently meet their end, one incurs a *pārājika* offense, or a *sthūlātyaya*.
As explained in detail above,
this is called "killing through both internal and external means.
The summary verse says:
If one uses powdered poison, or [poison] located in two substrates,
or at times uses various liquors, or mechanical devices and the like to harm others—
how does one kill with poison?
If a bhikṣu, with the intent to kill, uses poison or food mixed with poison—such as cakes, rice, and so forth—to kill a woman, a man, or a paṇḍaka.
If one causes death through such means, one incurs a *pārājika* offense or a *sthūlātyaya*;
the detailed explanation is as above.
This is called killing by means of poison.
What is killing by means of poisonous powder?

If a bhikṣu, with the intent to kill, uses various types of poisonous powder—whether by rubbing it on the body, using it for bathing, mixing it with ointments, scattering it over fragrant garlands, or blending it into incense smoke—to kill a woman, a man, or a paṇḍaka, [he commits this offense].
If one brings about death by such means, this bhikṣu incurs a pārājika offense, or he incurs a sthūlātyaya offense.
The detailed explanation is as above.
This is called killing by poisoned powder.
What is killing by means of a location?
This has two types:
First, detention due to the ground; second, detention due to wood.
What is meant by detention due to the ground?

If a bhikṣu, with intent to kill, digs a pit in the earth and places a trap within it, binding the feet of a man, woman, or paṇḍaka in order to kill them, and they die as a result; [this constitutes detention due to the ground].
Or they release lions, tigers, leopards, eagles, vultures, and other such creatures to devour them;
or they cause their physical forms to be withered away by wind and sun; or they leave them hungry and thirsty until they become emaciated.
If one dies by means of such a stratagem, this bhikṣu incurs a pārājika offense;
if he does not die, he incurs a sthūlātyaya offense.
The rest is as described above.

Just as it was with the feet, so too if the calves, thighs, waist, chest, or even the neck are used as fetters, or if at times one wishes to have them devoured by lions and other beasts, until they become emaciated from hunger and thirst.
If one dies as a result of these means, one incurs a *pārājika* or a *sthūlātyaya* offense,
as explained in detail above.
This is called "killing by causing delay on account of the ground."
What is killing by means of obstructing with wood?
If a bhikṣu, with intentional malice, desires to kill a woman, a man, or a paṇḍaka, and binds their feet to a large log, a pillar, or a stake using a wet rope, and they die as a result;
or if he intends to have them devoured by lions and the like, until they are emaciated by hunger and thirst.
If one dies by means of this expedient, one incurs a *pārājika* or a *sthūlātyaya* offense,
as explained in detail above.
This is called "killing by causing delay through wood."
What is killing through intoxication with alcohol?
If a bhikṣu intentionally desires to kill a woman, a man, or a paṇḍaka, and gives them rice wine to drink, causing death as a result;
or causes a lion or other beast to devour them; or even causes them to become emaciated by hunger and thirst.
By means of this expedient, if one causes death to occur, one incurs a *pārājika* or a *sthūlātyaya* offense, as explained in detail above.

Just as it is with rice wine, so it is with wines made from roots, stalks, flowers, leaves, or fruits; or by enchanting the wine, or using medicinal wine, one causes another to drink it until their mind is deranged and they are rendered senseless and ignorant.
If one brings about death through such means, or if, out of intoxication, one causes a king, a thief, or an enemy to take one's life, one incurs a *pārājika* or a *sthūlātyaya*.
As explained in detail above,
this is called killing by means of alcohol.
What is killing by means of a mechanical bow?

If a bhikṣu intentionally desires to kill a woman, a man, or a paṇḍaka, he might set up a mechanical bow and provide it with an iron arrow, or place various blades and such along the side of a path; if that woman, man, or paṇḍaka passes by this way, he then severs their hands and feet, or cuts off their head and other body parts.
If, by means of such a contrivance, one brings about death, this bhikṣu incurs a pārājika or a sthūlātyaya offense.
As it is with a crossbow, so it is with a foot-trap, a catapult, or any other mechanical device intended for the purpose of taking a human life; the offense is the same as before.
The summary verse says:
If one raises a whole or half corpse, causes an abortion, or performs incantations;
pushes someone down, or [drowns them in] water or fire; or sends a messenger to kill by means of cold or heat.
What is the killing by means of a *vetāla* (reanimated corpse)?

If a bhikṣu, with a deliberate intent to kill a woman, a man, or a *paṇḍaka*, goes on the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight to a charnel ground and seeks a recently deceased corpse that has not yet been harmed even by ants; he then rubs it with yellow earth, washes the corpse with scented water, covers its body entirely with a pair of new cotton cloths, and anoints its feet with ghee while reciting incantations over them. At that time, the corpse stretches out and is about to rise; he places it upon a two-wheeled carriage, ties two copper bells beneath its neck, and places a double-edged sword in its hand.
The corpse immediately rose and asked the incantation master,
"Whom do you wish for me to kill?
The incantation master replied:
"Do you recognize that certain woman, man, or paṇḍaka?
He replied, "I recognize him."
He replied:
"You may go there and sever his life-force.
If the life-force is severed, the bhikṣu incurs a pārājika offense.
If in that house there are garlands and sashes made of various medicinal herbs hung crosswise upon the door, or a water jar placed there;
or if a cow is tied at the door together with a calf of the same color, or a ewe together with a lamb of the same color;
or if the house has a grinding stone for medicine along with its millstone axle; or if there is an Indra-post at the door.
Where there is a wooden stake, or where a fire is never extinguished, or where a household enshrines an image, or where there is the true body of a Buddha;
or where there is a Wheel-Turning King, or the mother of a Wheel-Turning King, or one who carries the fetus of a Wheel-Turning King;
or where there is a Bodhisattva, or the mother of a Bodhisattva, or one who carries the fetus of a Bodhisattva; or where one is about to recite the precepts.
Whether it be when reciting the precepts, or when about to recite the *Caturāgama*, or while actually reciting it; or again,
when wishing to recite or currently reciting a great sūtra— namely, the *Cūḷasuññata* and *Mahāsuññata Suttas*,
the *Pañcaka* and *Tika Nipātas*, the *Māyājāla Sūtra*, and the *Rājā Māgadha Ajātaśatru Sūtra*.
The *Sūtra on Welcoming the Buddha* and the *Sūtra on the Victorious Banner*.
If, while guarding against such occurrences as these, the vetāla that has arisen is unable to enter, this bhikṣu incurs a sthūlātyaya offense;
or, if he is not skilled in the methods for raising a vetāla and the vetāla instead returns to kill the mantra-practitioner, this bhikṣu also incurs a sthūlātyaya offense.
If a mantra-reciting bhikṣu kills that vetāla, he also incurs a sthūlātyaya offense.
What is the matter of the "half-vetāla"?

It is the same as before; the differences therein are that the chariot has only one wheel, a single bell is tied to its neck, and the sword has only a single blade. The details regarding the determination of the offense are as extensively explained above.
What constitutes killing by causing an abortion?
If a bhikṣu intends to kill a pregnant woman but not her fetus, he may trample upon her abdomen.
If the mother dies and not the fetus, the bhikṣu incurs a pārājika offense.
If the fetus dies but the mother does not, one incurs a *sthūlātyaya*;
if both die, one incurs a *pārājika* regarding the mother;
if neither dies, one incurs a *sthūlātyaya*.
If a bhikṣu intends to kill the fetus but not the mother, he then crushes her abdomen.
If the fetus dies and not the mother, the bhikṣu incurs a pārājika offense;
if the mother dies and not the fetus, he incurs a sthūlātyaya offense.
If both die, one incurs a *pārājika* offense;
if neither dies, one incurs a *sthūlātyaya*.
What constitutes killing by means of incantations?

If a bhikṣu, with the intent to kill, undertakes the means to slay a woman, a man, or a paṇḍaka, he constructs a maṇḍala and arranges a fire-pit; he kindles a fire, throws wood into it, and recites incantations while thinking:
"When this wood is completely consumed by the fire, may the life-force of that woman, man, or paṇḍaka be severed immediately."
If his life were to end when the wood in the fire had only just begun to burn halfway, this bhikṣu incurs a sthūlātyaya;
if his life ends once the wood is completely consumed by fire, he incurs a pārajika.

If a bhikṣu, with the intent to kill, undertakes the means to kill a woman, a man, or a paṇḍaka, and places one *śīrṣa* each of sesame seeds and mustard seeds into a mortar and pounds them while reciting incantations and forming this thought:
"If the substance in the mortar is pounded until it becomes powder, may that person's life end."
If the person dies before the [body] has been ground into powder, this bhikṣu incurs a sthūlātyaya;
if the person dies once it has been crushed into powder, the bhikṣu incurs a pārājika.

If a bhikṣu, with the intent to kill, employs a means by placing one *śroṇa* of yellow cow’s milk into a vessel, stirring the milk with his finger while reciting a prohibitive mantra, and forms this thought:
"If the milk in the vessel is entirely transformed into blood, may that person's life-faculty be severed."
If the woman dies while the milk has not yet been transformed into blood, one incurs a sthūlātyaya;
if she dies after the milk has been fully transformed into blood, one incurs a pārājika.
If a bhikṣu intends to kill a person, he employs a means by stitching a saṃghāṭī robe with five-colored thread while reciting incantations, thinking:
"Once this robe is finished, let his life come to an end."
If the person dies before the robe is finished, one incurs a *sthūlātyaya*;
if the person dies once the robe is finished, one incurs a *pārājika*.
If a bhikṣu intends to kill someone and employs a means such as drawing on the ground with his finger while reciting incantations and thinking thus:
"Draw [the figures] until the number seven is complete so that his life shall end.
If he dies before the seven are complete, one incurs a *sthūlātyaya*;
if he dies when the seven are complete, one incurs a *pārājika*.
This is called killing by means of incantations.
What is killing by pushing down?
If a bhikṣu, desiring to kill a person, pushes them over a precipice, a cliff, or some other dangerous place, and that person dies as a result, he incurs a pārājika offense.
If one does not die at that time but dies later because of it, one incurs a *pārājika* offense;
if one does not die at that time and does not die later either, one incurs a *sthūlātyaya* offense.

Just as it is with a precipice, if one causes someone to fall by pushing them against a wall or a tree, or onto an elephant, horse, carriage, bed, seat, or onto the head, shoulders, waist, back, thighs, knees, calves, feet, or any other part of the body, one incurs a *pārājika* offense if they die as a result;
if they do not die at that time but die later because of it, one also incurs a *pārājika*;
if they do not die at that time nor die later, one incurs a *sthūlātyaya*.
This is called killing by pushing down.
What is killing in water?
If a bhikṣu, wishing to kill a person, pushes them into water and that person dies because of it, he incurs a pārājika offense.
"Causing death" refers to the *sthūlātyaya* offense, as explained in detail above.
"Water" refers to rivers, oceans, ponds, wells, and springs; even if one causes death by throwing a single handful of water into another's mouth, this is called killing by means of water.
What constitutes killing by means of fire?
If a bhikṣu, desiring to kill a person, pushes them into a fire and they die as a result, the bhikṣu incurs a pārājika offense.
As explained in detail above:
"Fire" refers to such acts as burning villages, forests, or cities, or even placing glowing embers into one's mouth to cause death; this is called killing by fire.
What is meant by "causing death through instigation"?
If a bhikṣu desires to kill a person and dispatches that person toward a place of danger and difficulty, resulting in their death, he incurs a pārājika or a sthūlātyaya offense.

As explained in detail above, "perilous places" refers to locations where there are bandits, enemies, tigers, leopards, lions, and the like; to cause a person to pass through such places so as to bring about their death is called "killing by dispatching."
What is killing by freezing?

If a bhikṣu intends to kill a person and, during a time of extreme cold with fierce and severe winds, places the person in the shade during the day or leaves them sitting on wet grass in the open air at night, and the person dies as a result, the bhikṣu incurs a *pārājika* or a *sthūlātyaya*.
As explained extensively above,
this is called "killing by freezing.
What is "killing by heat"?

If a bhikṣu intends to kill a person and, during extreme heat, develops a feverish ulcer on his body, and whether by day he places it in the open air or by night he leaves it in a closed room, fumigating it with smoke and covering it with mats, straw, woolen blankets, or the like, and the person dies as a result, the bhikṣu incurs a pārājika or a sthūlātyaya offense.
As explained in detail above,
this is called "Killing by Intense Heat.
The summary verse says:
In the bathhouse and the warm hall, Kāla did not inspect the seats;
there are two distinctions in the offering of vinegar, and seventeen afflictions lead to ruin.
For an elder bhikṣu in an araṇya, one should recognize the gravity or lightness of matters according to the specific circumstances.
What is the matter concerning the bathhouse?

At that time, the Blessed One was staying in the Āṭavī forest. There was a certain bhikṣu who went from time to time to the home of a lay devotee with whom he was on friendly terms, preaching the sublime Dharma to him. He caused that lay devotee to give rise to a heart of reverent faith, whereby the layman received the three refuges as well as the five precepts.
At a later time, he went again and explained to him the seven types of meritorious actions involving material things (*sāmiṣa-puṇyakriyāvastu*).
The householder said: "Noble One!
I wish to perform a meritorious action involving material things for the sake of the Saṃgha."
The bhikṣu replied,
“Excellent! This matter should be done.”
He said, "Noble One! What do you wish to have done?"
He replied, "The Sangha currently has no bathhouse; it would be appropriate to have one built.
He then made this formal announcement:
"Noble One!
I possess wealth, but I have no one to look after it.
He replied:
"I am here to oversee the construction and cultivate meritorious deeds.
He replied, "Excellent!"
At that time, the householder provided him with abundant wealth for the construction, and the bhikṣu immediately began the work.
Now, there was a great festival in the Vana-vyūha forest, and none of the laborers came to join the work. The bhikṣu then summoned those laborers and said to them, "O worthy ones!..."
"Why have you all not come today?
They replied,
"O Noble One!"
"Today many people have gathered for a great festival; it is because of this that I did not come.
He replied, "O worthy one!"
"Those who possess merit may hold a celebratory feast; what kind of feast is this for you who live by manual labor?
Come here and work for me, and I shall pay you double wages.
He replied:
“Noble One!

That fortunate man always holds festive gatherings, whereas we laborers encounter such occasions but once in a long while; even if you were to pay me double my wages, I would still be unable to work for him.”
Having spoken thus, he departed. At that time, the householder thought to himself:
"I shall now go and see how much merit has been produced by these meritorious deeds.
In the early morning, he went to inspect them, but found that nothing had been undertaken. Upon reaching the place where the bhikṣus were, he paid his respects and said:
“Noble one! For what reason did the hired laborer not work today?
He replied:
“Householder!
He is unwilling to do it.
He replied:
“What does this mean? He replied,
“That hired laborer spoke these words:”
"Today the people of the world are all gathering for a festive assembly, yet I am unable to participate.
The householder said,
"Noble One!..."
"What joy or celebration could that hired laborer have?
Is it not because the Noble One did not pay him his wages that he was unwilling?
He replied:
“Householder!
I offered to pay you back one-and-a-half times [the value], yet you still refused to do it.
Then you said to me:”

"Those who possess merit always have joyful gatherings; as for me, a hired laborer, such occasions are encountered but once in a long while. Even if you were to pay me double, I still could not do it.
The householder said, "Noble One!"
"I cultivate this merit neither for myself nor for my relatives.
How excellent, O Noble One!
Please assist me in its fulfillment so that it may not be abandoned or left incomplete."
Then that bhikṣu reported the matter to the Buddha.
The Buddha said,
"As long as the task is not yet completed, you must have the bhikṣus assist him in the construction."

Then the bhikṣus, following the instruction of the Blessed One, assisted in the construction by passing bricks to one another; however, because they held the bricks too loosely, one fell and struck a bhikṣu on the head, resulting in his death.
At that time, the bhikṣus felt remorse and spoke thus:
"O venerable ones!
This alms-seeker has engaged in many activities and forced himself to toil so hard that he has brought about the untimely death of our beloved fellow-practitioner."
They were seized with doubt, thinking:
"Could it not be that because of this we have all together committed a *pārājika* offense?
Then the bhikṣus reported this matter in detail to the Blessed One.
The World-Honored One said:
"None of you bhikṣus have committed an offense.
However, bhikṣus should not pass bricks to one another by tossing them; they should hand them over with their hands."
"If there are cracks or fissures in the bricks, inform [the donor] before handing them over; otherwise, one incurs an offense of transgression against the Dharma.
The Buddha said:
"One should assist in the work."
At that time, the bhikṣus worked throughout the entire day, and the brahmins and householders all gave rise to derision, saying:
"How is it that these bhikṣus work all day long like hired laborers?"
At that time, the bhikṣus reported this matter in detail to the Blessed One.
The Blessed One told them:
"One should not work all day long; one should perform one's tasks for only half the day."
At that time, the bhikṣus performed manual labor in the afternoon during the hot summer season, and in the forenoon during the cold winter season. The Buddha said:
"You should not do so; you should perform labor in the afternoon during the cold winter season, and in the forenoon during the hot summer season."
Those bhikṣus ceased their work only when the time for the meal approached; with their bodies smeared with mud, they went out to beg for alms.
Those who lacked faith saw them and mocked, saying:
"Noble ones!..."
"Your Honors' labor exceeds that of hired hands; while those hired laborers know to rest even before the time for their meal, you only cease your work when the mealtime approaches."
Then the bhikṣus reported this matter in detail to the Blessed One.
The Blessed One said:

"You must cease your work early, taking into account the time of day. Those who go for alms should adjust their appearance and deportment before going out to beg. Those who eat at the monastery should also prepare in advance to attend the regular meal."
As the Blessed One said,
"One should adjust one's deportment before going on almsround or proceeding to a meal," the bhikṣus did not know what constituted this preliminary adjustment of deportment.
The Buddha said:
"From the time one has washed one's hands and feet and cleansed the alms-bowls until that point is called 'preparation.
Now I shall explain for all bhikṣus the rules of conduct to be observed when engaged in construction."

If there is a supervisor, he should know that those people who perform manual labor in the morning should be provided with a light meal, and if it is afternoon, he should seek non-timely beverages and oil for anointing the hands and feet.
"If the supervisor does not act according to the instructions, he shall incur an offense of transgressing the Dharma.
This is called the matter concerning the bathhouse.
*Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya*, Fascicle Seven.
The Vinaya of the Mūlasarvāstivāda School, Volume Eight.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Yijing by Imperial Decree.
The Third Part of the Third Training Rule on Taking Human Life.
What is the matter concerning the heated hall?
At that time, the Blessed One was staying in the Araṇya forest.
The monks constructed a heated hall similar to a bathhouse; the point of distinction therein is as the World-Honored One said:
"Regarding those tasks that are not yet completed, you should have the bhikṣus assist in the construction.
At that time, the bhikṣus assisted with the construction at the heated hall; together they carried the timber to install the beams and rafters, while the craftsmen below held them up from a distance.
While moving the timber, a bhikṣu’s hand slipped and a large log fell, striking a carpenter on the head and causing his death.
Thereupon, the bhikṣus felt remorse and spoke thus:
"O Venerable Ones!..."

"This alms-seeker has engaged in many activities and forced himself into strenuous labor; because of this labor, he struck and killed a craftsman. Is it not the case that we have committed a *pārājika* offense?"
They reported these circumstances in detail to the World-Honored One.
The World-Honored One told them:
"You are not at fault."

However, bhikṣus should not arbitrarily lift objects that they cannot control by their own strength. If there is a specific reason that necessitates moving such an object, they should have laypeople interspersed among them to assist in lifting it together; whether lifting or lowering, they must signal one another simultaneously. If a bhikṣu does not follow this instruction, he incurs an offense of transgression against the Dharma (dharmātikrama).
As the Blessed One said:
"A bhikṣu should not arbitrarily move heavy objects that he is unable to restrain.
The bhikṣus did not know up to what point an object was considered appropriate to lift.
The Buddha said:
"If a layperson carries a burden on one shoulder, a bhikṣu should divide it so that two people carry it; whoever violates this incurs an offense of transgression against the Dharma.
This is called the matter of the warm hall.
What is the story of Kāḷakalodāyin?
The Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the Venerable Kāḷakalodāyin converted a Caṇḍālī woman, causing her to give rise to reverent faith, and he received her into the Three Refuges and the five precepts.
Then that woman, having prostrated at his feet, requested: "Noble One!
Should you lack any medicinal herbs, food, or other necessities, I shall provide them all as offerings."
At that time, Kālodāyin was unwilling to accept it and said to the woman, "Sister!
The teaching of the World-Honored One is foremost in its universal benefit; my intention now is to bring profit to many people."
The woman said, “Noble One!

If you do not permit me to accept my invitation, I now wish to prepare an excellent seat for you, so that whenever you come for alms, you may always sit here and depart after you have finished eating.”
He replied, "So be it. Thereafter,
he would go daily to that place to eat, and having finished his meal, he would depart.
At that time, Kālodayin had a separate matter requiring him to go elsewhere, so he thought to himself:
"I should now go and inform my sister so that she may know."
He then went to her and said, "Sister!
I now wish to travel through the human world; you may keep this [child] for yourself."
He addressed him, saying:
"Noble One! It would be fortunate if you would return home early."
"Do not linger long elsewhere, lest I be filled with sorrowful longing for you.
Having spoken thus, he was about to return to the Jetavana Grove when the Blessed One,
wishing to travel through the human realm, addressed the Venerable Ānanda:
"You may inform the bhikṣus:
'I wish to travel through the human world,'" and so on,
as explained at length.
Then Ānanda addressed the bhikṣus, saying:
"Venerable sirs!
The Blessed One now intends to travel through the human realm."
"If any of you, Venerable Ones, wish to practice this, you should prepare your robes.
When Kālodāyin heard these words, he thought to himself:
"There are eighteen kinds of benefits for those who follow the Buddha."
First, fear of kings;
second, fear of thieves;
third, fear of water.
Fourth, no fear of fire;
fifth, no fear of hostile nations;
sixth, no fear of lions, tigers, wolves, and other predatory beasts.
7. No fear of frontier outposts;
8. No fear of ferry tolls;
9. No fear of lacking defensive support;
Tenth, no fear of humans;
eleventh, no fear of non-humans;
twelfth, from time to time obtaining visions of various devas.
Thirteen, they hear celestial sounds;
fourteen, they see great radiance;
fifteen, they hear the voice of the bestowal of prophecy.
Sixteenth, receiving the sublime Dharma together;
seventeenth, receiving food and drink together;
eighteenth, having no physical suffering or illness.
At that time, Kālodāyin thought to himself:
"The Buddha brings great benefit wherever he goes; it would be fitting for me now to follow the Buddha on his tour of conversion.
He then did not depart.
At that time, another woman in Caṇḍā’s household gave birth to a son.
Then Caṇḍā said to that woman, "You should bathe the child, adorn his body with a new white cotton cloth, and place him upon the seat of the ṛṣi so that the boy may have a long life."
He then followed the instructions and placed [the seat] within the hall.

At that time, after Kālodāyin had finished his alms-round, he went to Caṇḍa’s house; however, as it is not the practice of an Arhat to act without prior observation through noble wisdom, he simply sat down, letting his body fall onto the old seat.
At that time, the child’s mother, in a state of panic and fear, said:
"Venerable One!
There is a child on the seat."
He then rose in haste, but the child’s life had already departed; seeing this, the mother immediately broke into wailing.
At that time, Kāḷodāyin replied:
"Sister!..."
"Do not weep; your child planted the karma for a short lifespan, as the World-Honored One has said:
'All conditioned phenomena are impermanent; they are of the nature of arising and ceasing.
However, it is I who ought to weep now, for although I have attained the fruit of Arhatship, I failed to exercise proper discernment."
"O Great Teacher, World-Honored One!
On account of me as the occasion, you should establish a rule of training for all disciples.
For this reason, he informed the bhikṣus, and the bhikṣus reported it to the Buddha.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"Kālodāyin is not at fault.
However, when bhikṣus enter the homes of laypeople, they must not sit down hastily without first examining the seat; to sit down without having examined it constitutes a violation of the Dharma."
This is called the matter concerning Kālodāyin.
What is the matter concerning the two conditions for giving vinegar?
The Buddha was staying at the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s Park, in Śrāvastī.
In this city there were two householders, both immensely wealthy with abundant riches and many servants; at that time, the two became close friends who shared mutual affection and harmony.
Later, as they gradually became impoverished and worn out, the two of them deliberated, saying:
"In the past we were wealthy and happy, but now we are poor and suffering; what is the use of living on?"
"I think it would be fitting for us both to go forth together.
Thereupon, within the well-expounded Dharma and Vinaya, they shaved off their hair and beards and cultivated the practice of renunciation.
Later, at another time, one of them fell ill, and the other attended to him. As the patient grew increasingly emaciated and was unable to rise again, he asked the caregiver:
“Venerable one!
When you were still a layperson, did you ever suffer from illness?
He replied:
“There was. He asked, “What medicine serves as the antidote?”
He replied,
"I once drank salted vinegar.
[The other asked,] "If that is so, why do you not drink it now?"
He replied, "I will drink.
The other then sought out salt and vinegar and gave it to him to drink; having drunk it, he died immediately.
At that time, the bhikṣu felt remorse, thinking:
"Could it be that by giving him unsuitable medicine, I have caused his death and thus committed a pārājika offense?
For this reason, he informed the other bhikṣus, and the bhikṣus reported the matter to the Buddha.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"That bhikṣu has committed no offense.
However, bhikṣus should not casually provide medicine for a patient to take without first consulting a physician."
If there is no physician, one should ask a bhikṣu who was formerly a physician;
if there is none such, one should ask someone who has been a close friend of a physician;
if there is none such, one should ask someone who has previously suffered from illness.
If these are not present, one should consult an elder bhikṣu.

If a bhikṣu, without consulting a physician or even an elder, arbitrarily administers medicine to a patient according to his own judgment, he incurs an offense of transgression against the Dharma (vayadharmāpatti).
At that time, the bhikṣus were all filled with doubt and went together to inform the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!
By what causes and conditions did that sick bhikṣu die immediately upon taking vinegar, which was previously a medicine?"
The Buddha said:
"In the past, when he lived at home, his ailment was phlegm; now it is wind and heat.
For this reason, the medicine that was effective before is not so now."
The Buddha was staying at the Jetavana Monastery in Śrāvastī.

At that time, King Bimbisāra of Magadha, having attained the vision of the Truths, was accompanied by eighty thousand devas, as well as an immeasurable multitude of hundreds of thousands of brahmins and householders from the kingdom of Magadha.
At that time, King Bimbisāra beat the drum to proclaim a decree throughout the city of Rājagṛha and to all those arriving from outside, announcing:
"All people should know that those residing within my kingdom must not commit acts of theft."
"If anyone commits robbery, they shall be banished to a distant land, and the value of what was lost shall be reimbursed by me from my own treasury.

At that time, after the World-Honored One had preached the *Kumāra-sūtra* for King Prasenajit and inspired faith in him, King Prasenajit beat the drum and issued a proclamation throughout the kingdom of Kośala, announcing to all the cities and towns as well as travelers from the four quarters:
"All people should know: those currently residing within my realm must not commit robbery."
"If anyone commits robbery, their life shall be taken, and the value of what was stolen shall be reimbursed by me from the state treasury.

At that time, the bandits from both the realms of Magadha and Kośala, having heard this decree, all abandoned their respective countries and settled wherever they pleased in the territory between the two kingdoms.

At that time, the people of both countries all heard and knew that there were many bands of bandits dwelling in clusters within the borderlands between the two realms, ambushing traveling merchants to plunder their goods and kill them.

At that time, there were several merchants in Magadha who wished to travel to the kingdom of Kośala; having heard of this matter, they sought out many companions and, carrying various goods for trade, set out along the road, passing beyond the borders of Magadha and entering the territory of Kośala.
At that time, the merchant said to the men:

"Gentlemen, you should know that I have heard King Prasenajit of Kośala is fierce and violent; should I encounter bandits, I shall be able to compensate them with my own treasury goods. Therefore, these guards may be released to return home."
Then the reinforcements took their leave and returned.

At that time, the bandits stationed scouts at the strategic pass; when the scouts saw that all the reinforcements had departed, they reported to the bandit leader, saying, "The reinforcements have gone."
"You all should go among the traveling merchants and seize their wealth.

At that time, those bandits plundered the caravan in a perilous forest; some they took their lives, others they wounded in their limbs. Some fled and reached the city of Śrāvastī, where, with dust covering their bodies, they went before the king and said, "Great King!"
"We merchants have now arrived in Your Majesty’s kingdom, yet all our wealth has been lost.
The King asked,
"What do you mean?"
He addressed him, saying:
"Great King! Within the borders of Your Majesty's kingdom, we have been plundered by bandits."
At that time, King Prasenajit immediately issued a command to Prince Virūḍhaka, saying:
"You must go at once to capture those thieves along with the stolen goods."
Having received the command, the Prince arrayed the fourfold army—elephants, cavalry, chariots, and infantry—and sought out the bandits at a strategic location.
At that time, the bandits were unaware of the approaching troops and were dividing their loot together within a forest.
At that time, the Crown Prince took them by surprise; some were executed on the spot, some fled into the forests and wilds, and sixty others were captured alive.
Once the bandits had been defeated, the prince took the sixty bandits along with their plunder and delivered them to the king; having paid his respects, he addressed the Great King, saying:
"These are the bandits and the stolen goods."
The king asked the thief,
"Have you not heard my proclamation of edicts, which states that whoever commits theft shall have their life taken, and the value of what was lost shall be reimbursed by me from the royal treasury?"
The bandits replied,
"We have heard them all.
The king said:
"If you have heard this, for what reason did you become a thief and seize those merchants?
He replied, "Great King!"
"If we do not commit robbery, we will remain poor and unable to survive.
The King said, "If that is the case, simply take their property; for what reason should you kill them?"
He replied, "I wish to terrify him; therefore, he must be killed.
The king said:
"If that is so, I now possess a dharma that shall terrify you—
a thing never seen before, which you shall behold today. The king,
being of a violent and cruel nature, commanded his ministers, saying:
"Now you may take these bandits to that slaughterhouse and cut off their hands and feet; let the merchants who were robbed repay me with my own treasury goods.
Following these instructions, the minister led the bandits to the charnel ground and had their hands and feet severed, after which he returned the stolen goods to them according to the count.
As the Blessed One said, addressing the bhikṣus:
"You should know that you must skillfully examine what brings harm to oneself and others, as well as what brings happiness to oneself and others."
For what reason?
O bhikṣus! Both the affliction of oneself and others, and the happiness of oneself and others—all such things are states that should be reviled and abandoned.
At that time, the bhikṣus, remembering the Buddha’s words, went frequently to the charnel ground out of a sense of revulsion.
Then some bhikṣuṇīs also went to the charnel ground and saw a group of bandits with their hands and feet all severed.
At that time, there was another person also in the charnel ground who, observing the bandits together, spoke these words:
"If there is one with a kind heart who pities this suffering, they may give him salt and vinegar to drink; once he has died here, he shall be reborn and drink his mother’s fresh milk."
At that time, among the bhikṣuṇīs there was one named Pūrṇā, who was coarse, sturdy, and simple-minded. Having heard these words, she thought to herself:
"I have attained the opportunity to go forth within this well-spoken Dharma and Vinaya; how could I now abandon this mass of merit?"
"I should now seek out salt and vinegar to give as alms.

Thereupon, the bhikṣuṇīs all returned to their residence, while Pūrṇa went alone into the city. Having obtained salt and vinegar, he filled a large jar to the brim and acquired sixty earthen bowls; carrying these back, he arrived at the place where the robbers were.
At that time, those bandits were tormented by suffering and, oppressed by hunger and thirst, found no way to survive.
Upon seeing the bhikṣuṇī, they spoke these words:
"Excellent, Noble Lady!"
"I am tormented by thirst; I pray that you will relieve me with water from your jar.

At that time, the bhikṣuṇī, with the intention of seeking merit, first gave her a bowl of water, followed by salt and vinegar. Each person filled their vessel, and having received them, they drank and all passed away.
At that time, a bhikṣuṇī returned to the monastery late in the evening; finding the monastery gate already closed, she immediately knocked and called out.
A nun from the monastery asked, "Who is knocking at the door?"
He replied, "I am Pūrṇa. He asked:
"Why have you returned only now at such a late hour?
She replied,
"Sisters, rejoice!"
"Sisters, rejoice!
The bhikṣuṇīs asked, "What have you done?"
Is it for the sake of attaining the fruit of Arhatship?
Or for attaining the fruits of Non-returner, Once-returner, or Stream-enterer?
Or is it for the sake of constructing a dwelling place for the Saṃgha?
"Or have you sought out food, drink, or exquisite robes for the Saṃgha?
She replied, "Sisters!"
“Virtuous ones, you have nothing further to do; you seek only food, drink, clothing, and shelter?
The bhikṣuṇī asked, “If you have none of these, what work do you perform?”
Pūrṇa replied, "Gentlemen,
did you not see those sixty men in the charnel ground whose hands were severed and feet cut off?
They answered:
“I saw them. Pūrṇa said, “I was teaching and converting many people;
they each drank their fill of salt and vinegar and all passed away, only to drink their mothers’ fresh milk in their next place of birth.”
Upon hearing this, the bhikṣuṇīs said to her:
"Foolish woman!
You have filled your belly with a *pārājika* offense, yet you cause us all to rejoice together in it!"
At that time, having heard this, Pūrṇa felt remorse and thought to himself:
"Could it be that I have committed a pārājika offense?
For this reason, he informed the bhikṣus, and the bhikṣus reported it to the Buddha.
The Buddha said:
"This bhikṣuṇī is without offense.
However, if one intentionally causes another to die, one incurs a pārājika offense."
Nevertheless, bhikṣuṇīs should not give vinegar to a sick person at their bedside to drink until they die;
rather, they should maintain this thought:
"By means of this medicine, may this patient recover early."
There is no offense in such a case.
However, if a bhikṣu or bhikṣuṇī should form this thought:
"By means of this medicine, I shall cause [the person] to die."
"If one causes death through such means, one incurs the *pārājika* offense.
The Buddha was staying at the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park, in Śrāvastī.
At that time, the Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana took seventeen young boys and granted them the going-forth and full ordination, with Upāli as their leader.
If one among these seventeen persons serves as the administrator, the remaining sixteen shall all assist him.
At another time, when a religious duty arose that required reciting the scriptures throughout the night, those seventeen persons came together to oversee the proceedings.
On another day, when a matter concerning the bathhouse arose for the Saṃgha, he also came in detail to provide mutual assistance.
On yet another day, there was one person who was responsible for the affairs of the monastery; on that very day, he adorned the monastic buildings.
At that time, the steward was guarding with single-minded devotion. Among them, one person thought to himself:
"I am exhausted; let me sleep for a while. How could those sixteen people possibly fail to guard [him]?"
At that time, each of the sixteen men had this thought:
"I am weary; let me sleep.
All sixteen of them fell into a deep sleep.

There was only one administrative officer who remained on duty throughout the night without sleeping; when dawn arrived, he extinguished the lamps, opened the temple gates, swept and sprinkled the rooms and courtyards, and inspected whether the water was clean.

Observing the time of day, they prepared the seats and spread out the bedding; at the stūpa, they burned incense so that its fragrance pervaded everywhere, and then sounded the *gandī* on the upper terrace of the monastery.

At that moment, the sixteen men who had been sleeping were awakened by the sound of the *gandī*. Each emerged from his room carrying his alms bowl, only to see one man among them fleeing in a state of panic to attend to the affairs of the monastery.
Then the sixteen men said to one another:
"Venerable sirs!
Is there not even a single person among us who would assist in this construction?"
At that time, one person spoke these words:
"I had this thought: 'I am exhausted;
let me sleep for a while. How could the other sixteen not be able to look after things?'"
All the people spoke these words; having heard this clearly, they said to one another:
"This man has always been our leader in whatever we do. If we do not assist him, he will surely become angry. Let us finish our meal first, and then beg for his favor."

Having finished eating, they went together to that place to offer mutual apologies; those who were younger immediately prostrated at his feet, while those who were older or senior patted him on the shoulder and said, "Venerable One!"
"You should grant me your forgiveness.
At that time, he remained silent and did not respond; a friend nudged him with his finger, whereupon he smiled and said, "Sukha! (O Joy!)
"Give him joy!

Each person thought this was a clever stratagem; whether one or two, or even all the people together, they began to tickle him. At that moment, his vital breath surged upward and he immediately passed away.
When the people saw him dead, they wailed and wept bitterly.
At that time, the bhikṣus, finding it strange, asked them:
"Why are you all gathered here weeping and crying now?"
He replied, "Venerable Sir!
In the past we were a group of seventeen; now there are only sixteen. How could we not weep!"
"Furthermore, since my dear fellow-practitioner has died, I suffer the pain of separation from those I love, and I have also committed a defeat (pārājika).
How could I not be overcome by grief and distress?
When the bhikṣus heard this, they departed, while those sixteen men remained on one side, dwelling in sorrow.
Another bhikṣu, knowing that his companion had struck the wooden post and thereby caused death, saw him and rebuked him, saying:
"Venerable one!
You, the group of seventeen, are like a fire burning grass—quickly ignited and quickly extinguished; at times you are playful and joyful, and at other times you are filled with sorrow."
His heart was scorched by the fire of grief, and although he heard these words, he did not respond at all.
At that time, the bhikṣus reported the matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"Since those bhikṣus had no intent to kill, there is no offense."
"However, bhikṣus must not tickle one another; if they do so, they commit an offense of transgression against the Dharma.

While the Buddha was staying at Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park in Śrāvastī, there was a village not far from there. In it lived a householder who was immensely wealthy, possessing vast riches and many servants. He possessed pure faith and a virtuous disposition.
He constructed a monastery for the Saṃgha; it was lofty and grand, featuring a magnificent stone gate, with surrounding corridors and halls all exquisitely adorned, bringing joy to all who beheld it.
Having invited sixty bhikṣus to this residence for the summer retreat, and having completed the *pravāraṇā* ceremony, they departed as circumstances required.
