At that time, the donor, seeing the monastery empty, ordered people to guard it, fearing that thieves might steal the beds, mats, and other belongings.
Furthermore, sixty bhikṣus were traveling through the human realm when they arrived at this village seeking a place to stay.
At that time, a man addressed the bhikṣus, saying:
"Noble ones!..."
"Why do you not stay at the monastery? He replied,
"O worthy one!"
"Where is there a monastery? He replied,
"There is a fine place for dwelling in the forest outside the village."
The bhikṣu then went to see the guardian.
Having seen him from afar, the guardian said: "Welcome!"
He immediately provided him with a dwelling, bedding, blankets, pillows, as well as a small stool and three wooden chests, saying:
"Venerable One, please filter the water first; I shall now go briefly to inform the householder."
He said to the householder,
"Your merit shall now increase twofold, for sixty visiting bhikṣus have arrived at the monastery. Upon hearing this,
the householder was filled with a mixture of surprise and joy, and he informed his family members:

"You should take ghee, honey, granulated sugar, pomegranate, rock sugar, grapes, black pepper, ginger, and long pepper—substances suitable for making non-time gruel—and carry them to the monastery. When visiting members of the Saṃgha arrive at the residence, you should prepare this non-time gruel so that they may drink their fill."
Having heard this, the family members followed the instructions and escorted them all to the monastery.
Once the bhikṣus had filtered their water, each assumed his proper dignified demeanor and settled wherever he was assigned.

At that time, the elder went to the monastery; seeing from afar the bhikṣus filling the temple like a cluster of lotuses, his faith increased all the more and his devotion deepened. He spoke this verse:
“Whether in a village or a forest, whether on high ground or low, wherever the Saṃgha dwells, it causes the mind to give rise to love and joy.”
Having prepared the non-seasonal beverage and finished its seasoning, he personally handed it to them.

Once the assembly of bhikṣus had drunk their fill of the beverage, the elder prostrated at the feet of the Saṃgha, took up an incense burner himself, and led the monks out to circumambulate the caitya. Returning to his residence, he knelt before the presiding elder.
The Elder expounded the essentials of the Dharma for him, and the householder said:
"At noon tomorrow, I pray that the noble assembly will deign to accept a modest offering at my residence."
The bhikṣus consented; he prostrated at their feet and departed.
On the following day, he prepared various delicious foods to offer to the Saṃgha. After the Saṃgha had finished eating, they offered him words of blessing before returning to their residence.

Furthermore, after midday, non-time gruel was served; once they had washed and rinsed their mouths, the elder took a censer in his hand and addressed the great assembly before the senior monk, saying:
"O Noble Ones!..."
"This dwelling place was not built by me for my own sake, nor for the sake of my relatives;
rather, my original intention was solely to establish it for the Saṃgha of the four quarters. I pray that you will show compassion and spend the summer retreat here."
The bhikṣus said to the householder:
"The World-Honored One, the Lord of Dharma, currently resides in Śrāvastī. From time to time, he proclaims these predictions:

'Such-and-such a bhikṣu has realized arhatship; such-and-such a bhikṣu has perfected the contemplation of impurity. King Prasenajit, Queen Vaidehī, Rāṣṭrapāla, Mother Viśākhā, and other householders and brahmins all likewise revere and have faith in him."
“We shall go there; whether it be the Dharma or food, we shall enjoy them together, and we wish to go.

The elder replied, “The benefit of receiving the Dharma is known only to you, sirs; as for clothing and food to sustain the body, I am willing to provide these. I pray that you will remain here with a settled mind; I shall provide the four requisites of support so that you lack for nothing.”
The Elder addressed them, saying:
"Venerable ones!
As the Blessed One has said:
"If the donor possesses reverence and faith, one must increase that faith through compassion.
Having thus resolved to dwell here, he immediately observed the interior and exterior of the place;
he then saw fragrant flowers filling the trees and beautiful fruits abounding on the branches, with clear ponds and lush forests all most delightful.
The Elder said:
"Venerable ones!

Since this dwelling place is now abundant with flowers and fruits, and the fruits have not yet ripened for those who enter the earlier rains retreat, we should instead observe the later rains retreat."
Having thus deliberated, they proceeded to enter the later retreat (*paścimikā varṣā*).

At that time, that elder had constructed only a single monastery; all his meritorious deeds were concentrated therein, and as there was no other monastery in this village or in neighboring settlements, the meritorious deeds of all people likewise converged upon it.
At that time, the bhikṣus had received abundant offerings during their rains retreat; having completed their *pravāraṇā* ceremony, they remained there.
Then, there were some Kāṛṣṭika thieves who deliberated among themselves, saying:
"What work can we perform so that, for the duration of one year, our food and clothing will be abundant without the need for toil?"
Some among them said,
"We ought to steal the property of the bhikṣus.
The other thieves replied:
"He passes through a hundred doorways in a single day; though he begs with great hardship, he barely manages to fill his own belly.
What could he possibly possess? Among them was one thief who knew the bhikṣu intimately, and he said to the others, "You do not know that he possesses great wealth."

Thus we know that there is such a thing as "having": this elder who built the monastery possessed a pure and virtuous faith and constructed only a single temple; yet all his meritorious deeds were contained therein. In this village and other hamlets, there were no other temples, and consequently, the meritorious deeds of all people also converged within it.
"At this time, the bhikṣus have received abundant offerings during their summer retreat; those who do not believe may come together to witness it for themselves.
The people replied, "If that is so, you may go on ahead; we shall follow later."
He replied, “Very well.
He then adjusted his robes,
walked with slow and composed steps while reciting a verse (*gāthā*), circumambulated the stūpa, and entered the monastery.
At that time, there was an elderly monk (mahallaka bhikṣu) at the entrance of the gate; when the thief saw him, he prostrated at his feet and asked:
"Noble one! Whose monastery is this?"
"The chambers are magnificently adorned and inspire love and joy; for those wishing to be born in the heavens, they serve as a ladder.
The bhikṣu replied, "O worthy one!"
"This was established by a certain elder.
He asked, "Noble one!"
"Is this a vihāra, or is it a vigata?
the bhikṣu asked.
"What is meant by *vihāra*?
What is meant by *vighāta*?
He replied:
“If this monastery is fully supplied with requisites, it is a *vihāra*; if it lacks what is needed, it is a *vigaḍa*.
The bhikṣu replied, “Noble sir!”
"If it is so, this is a vihāra and not a vigata; in this dwelling place, resources are abundant and requisites are complete.
The thief then replied, "Noble one!"
"If one has sufficient rice, one should not eat earth; if one has sufficient clothing, one should not wear tree bark. How much clothing do you have, sir?
At that time, the mahallaka was by nature simple-minded and straightforward; he took the thief's hand and entered the room together, saying, "Look at how much clothing there is on the rack."
He asked, "Venerable sir!
Is this your own property or the property of the Saṃgha?"
He replied,
"O worthy one! This is my private property."
He asked, "Noble One!
Are you the Elder, or are you the Dharma Master?"
He replied, "Worthy one!
I am neither a senior elder nor a Dharma teacher; I am a śrāmaṇera, ranked below the monks."
He replied, "I am already aware of all that you possess; however, do you have any stores accumulated in your various treasuries?
He answered:
“O virtuous one! Even though I dwell at the very lowest level, my household goods are abundant; how much more so for those within the Sangha?
He replied:
"Noble One!
For the food cooked in the kitchen for the great assembly, do you use earthenware vessels or copper cauldrons?
The bhikṣu then led him to the storehouse and said:
"This storehouse is filled with copper vessels.
Having realized this, the thief was about to leave when he said,
"Noble One!..."
"In the past, my neglect of benevolence and goodness hindered my livelihood; now I shall take my leave for the time being and offer my respects again later.
He replied, "Very well."
The bandits then prostrated at his feet and departed; they went to their fellow bandits and said, "I have personally observed that monastery;
its wealth and provisions are as abundant as those of a wealthy merchant, so you should steal it."
Among them, one man said to the bandits:

"I have heard it said that sixty men who were highly skilled in archery have gone forth as monks here; you must not rashly commit robbery. Only when the assembly has gathered to listen to the sutras may you enter the monastery."
The people asked,
"We do not know on what day he intends to recite the sutra.
The man who was thoroughly familiar with the details informed the bandits, saying:
“Eight days have passed; since it is now the middle of the month, we should recite [the precepts].
Thus, they remained there counting the days on their fingers.

When the fifteenth day arrived, the Elder himself recited the *Pātimokkha* for the *poṣadha*. Having completed this, he had the reciter ascend the lion throne; as soon as the verse was recited, he said:
“The Buddha was staying in the Jeta Grove, Able to sever all delusions, with all faculties serene and settled. He addressed the assembly thus:
‘Among the hosts of humans and devas, I proclaim the subtle and wondrous Dharma.’”
"Having heard this, practice as taught, and you shall reach the end of suffering.
At that moment, the bandits knocked on the door and called out;
the bhikṣu asked, "Who are you?"
He replied, “Noble one!
I am a son of good family.”
At that time, the bhikṣus thought to themselves:
"Perhaps people from the village will come here to hear the Dharma; we shall open the gate for them.
Once the gate was opened, the bandits rushed in together to seize the property. The bhikṣus said to them:
"You previously reported that this good man, having now entered the monastery, has stolen my property.
The thief then replied:
"Noble One!"
"I have two names:
outside the monastery I am called 'Virtuous Son,' but once I enter the monastery, I am called 'Thief.
The bhikṣu said:
"The one who gave you this name is no good person.
Having stolen the goods, he immediately left the monastery.
When the bhikṣus had been robbed by the thief, they deliberated among themselves, saying:
“Venerable ones!
As the Blessed One has said:
‘Those who milk cows should not allow them to be completely exhausted.’”
"If this householder were to see that we have encountered bandits and, upon returning, were to provide goods for the monastery and give to us as well, he would surely be completely exhausted.
We should go to Śrāvastī, to the place where our fellow practitioners reside, to seek out robes."
They said, "Our bodies are exposed; how can we travel on the road?
One person told them:
"By day we shall enter the thickets, and by night we shall travel the roads.
Without informing the elder, he set out and gradually reached Śrāvastī.

There, during the first and last watches of the night, the bhikṣus remained awake, reflecting and diligently cultivating wholesome qualities. Seeing a naked ascetic arrive before their gate, looking about in alarm and distress, the bhikṣus called out from afar:
"You who go about naked and have plucked out your hair, for what reason have you come here?
This is a vihāra; it is not a place for you to dwell.
They replied:
"Venerable one! I am a bhikṣu, not a naked heretic.
He asked again:
"How could there be such a physical appearance?
The bhikṣu replied,
"I was plundered by bandits."
He asked, "What is your name? He replied:
“I am named Buddhagupta, Dharmagupta, Saṃghagupta, and so forth. He then replied:
“Welcome, welcome!”
"Venerable sir!

he said, and immediately opened the door. He then entered the monastery, and whether it was the three robes, the two lower garments, the *saṃkakṣikā*, the water filter, or the waist-belt for the bowl—whatever they possessed, they all shared and provided him with in full.
At that time, the bhikṣus reported the matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:

"Whenever one is not well acquainted with someone during the night, one should not rashly open the door for them; rather, one should ask their lineage and name, and only if they are known to you should you open the door."

However, while reciting the sūtras, one should have a bhikṣu act as a guardian. If he knows that thieves are approaching, he should manifest an appearance of alarm and shout out, but must not open the door.
He should speak these words: "Bring the ghaṇṭī!"
Along with these, a mallet and pestle, a Kālacakra, a saṃghāṭī, a seven-strip robe, a five-strip robe, a robe pouch, a shoulder-hook, a cord, and other such items were brought.
Upon hearing these words, the thieves were startled and departed.
Now, I shall establish the rules of conduct for the senior monks who serve as leaders of the assembly.
Whenever the community gathers to recite the scriptures, the senior monk (upādhyāya) should ask the administrator (vaiyāvṛtyakara):
"Are the gates already closed?
Have you searched throughout the monastery?
Have you appointed guards?"
"Has the reciter of the scriptures been requested?
Have the places for the great and small necessities been swept and wiped?
If the senior monks of the assembly do not act in accordance with these previously established regulations, they shall incur an offense of transgression against the Dharma.
At that time, the resident bhikṣus of the Anāthapiṇḍada Monastery said to the bhikṣu who had been robbed by bandits:
"Venerable ones!
We have distributed among ourselves whatever robes and bowls we possess, yet they are still not sufficient for all."

However, the elder who built the monastery at the site where he was robbed possesses a profound and sincere faith; it would be appropriate for you to go there to meet him again, for he will certainly provide you with clothing and other necessities.
Having heard these words, they deliberated together:
"Venerable friends!

What the fellow-practitioner of the holy life has said is excellent; however, we previously arrived in such haste that we did not inform the householder. We should go once more to inform him, for he might perhaps provide us with some clothing."
He then went to the householder’s residence.
Upon seeing him, the householder prostrated and asked:
“Noble One!
"Why did you depart for another place without informing me?
The bhikṣu replied,
"Householder, as the Blessed One has said:"
"When milking, one should leave a small amount remaining.
At that time, we thought to ourselves: "The monastery has now been robbed;

having seen this, the elder has provided goods for the monastery and also given them to us. We fear that if we were to exhaust his resources, it might cause him distress. Therefore, without informing him, we departed for Śrāvastī to seek robes from our fellow practitioners of the holy life."
The householder said:
"Venerable One!
If a thief has struck the monastery, could it be that my own home has also been robbed?"
"Excellent, O Noble One!
Out of compassion for me, please come again to see us.
Having thus redoubled their reverence, each person offered him thirteen sets of requisites.
Having heard this, the thieves returned once more; they knocked on the door during the night while the monks were reciting the sūtras.
At that time, the bhikṣus, knowing that the thieves had arrived, said to one another:
"Venerable ones!..."
"The deceitful thief of former times has come again; you should act with great alarm according to the Buddha’s teachings and not open the door for him.
He then cried out in a loud voice:
"Quickly bring the *ghanṭī*, mallets, staffs, *kālacakra*, *saṃghāṭī*, seven-strip robes, five-strip robes, robe-bags, shoulder-hooks, and cords!"
Upon hearing this, the bandits were greatly terrified and fled in all directions.
Then, certain devas spoke these verses:
“The Two-legged Muni is able to preach the teaching, Causing his disciples to strike fear into the bandits.”
"From his mouth he uttered cries of alarm to guard himself well, and the band of five hundred thieves all fled in dispersal.
At that time, the monk Ān-si (Anśī) said to his fellow thieves:
"Why did you suddenly startle yourselves?"
The bandits replied, "Have you not heard that there are sixty men who have gone forth as renunciants and are all skilled in archery? Why should we not flee?"
"However, we have never before heard of such things as the *gaṇḍī* or the staff;
these must surely be weapons for killing one another. He then replied, "None of these are actual weapons."
The bandits asked, "What is this? He replied:

"The *gandī* wood sounds to assemble the Saṃgha; the mallet is the instrument for striking the *gandī*; the time-wheel is used to observe the shadow of the sun; the *saṃghāṭī* and other items, as well as cords and ropes, are necessities for clothing; the bag is intended for storing the three robes; and the hook is the key for opening the door."
"We should not be afraid; let us go back and steal [the goods] together.
At that time, the bandits all returned to the monastery, and one of their ringleaders climbed up a ladder.
At that time, there was an elder *bhikṣu* (*mahallaka*) within the monastery acting as its guardian. Seeing him ascend the ladder, he thought to himself:
"This stubborn thief is plundering my robes and bowl, leaving me naked. If I now let him go, it will leave us all standing naked; I shall manifest a terrifying appearance to him."
He then walked slowly, took up a wooden *gaṇḍī*, and struck the thief on the head; struck by the wood, the thief fell from the ladder and died.
The mahallaka immediately cried out, "There is a thief!"
"There is a thief!
At that moment, the bhikṣus abandoned listening to the sutra and scrambled up to the upper gallery, asking,
"Where is the thief?"
The mahallaka replied, “I climbed up the ladder beside this monastery; I showed them signs of terror, and they all fled.
The people reported this, saying:
"It would be most excellent if we could cause the bandits to flee.
At dawn, they opened the gate and searched for the place where the bandits had ascended; there they saw the leader of the bandits, dead with blood flowing from his head.
Having seen this, the assembly was each filled with terror and said to one another:
"The previous incident was not an encounter with bandits; this present one is an encounter with bandits.
Because we struck and killed a person, we have consequently committed a *pārājika* offense.
At that time, the bhikṣus felt remorse and reported the matter to the Buddha.
The Buddha said:
"You have committed no offense.
However, bhikṣus should not harbor such an intention as to strike another's body with an object thrown from the side or from behind, intending to cause them terror and the sound of a startled cry."
"If a bhikṣu strikes another's body with such an intention, he incurs an offense of transgression against the Dharma.
What is an "old bhikṣu"?
When the Buddha was staying at Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park in Śrāvastī, there was a householder in that city who took a wife from a family of equal status.
Later, he fathered a son who gradually grew up; at that time, the elder’s wealth was depleted, his kinsmen had estranged themselves, and his wife had passed away. He then said to his son:
"I am now old and infirm, no longer able to manage the affairs of the household. I wish to part from you and hope to go forth into the religious life."
The son said to his father,
"If that is so, I too shall go forth.
The father replied to his son:
"This is also excellent.
Thereupon, father and son went together to the Jeta Grove and approached a bhikṣu; having prostrated at his feet, they said:
"Noble One!..."
"I wish to renounce the household life.
The bhikṣu asked,
"Does this boy also wish to renounce the household life?"
He replied, "I also wish to.
When asked whether there were any obstacles or impediments, it was granted that he might go forth together with him.

It is the constant custom of the Buddhist community that the elders receive the benefits while the juniors manage the affairs; at this time, the father and son were constantly subjected to forced labor.

The son said to his father, "I am being bullied by the assembly and am always made to perform menial tasks instead of pursuing my studies. We should now go together to another region to study the scriptures."
The father said,
"Excellent! I shall go with you."
"Wherever he went, because of his youth, he was made to perform menial tasks and serve as a steward.
The son said to his father:
'Although he is made to serve as a steward in Śrāvastī, the World-Honored One, the Master of the Dharma, is personally present there; from time to time, one hears him deliver prophecies.'"

Such-and-such a bhikṣu has realized arhatship; such-and-such a bhikṣu has perfected the contemplation of impurity; and King Prasenajit, Queen Śrīmālā, Rājaka-Śuddhodana, Mother Viśākhā, as well as other elders and brahmins, all likewise possess reverent faith.
"We shall go there and partake equally of whatever Dharma or food is available; we now wish to return thither.
Having thus abandoned the other regions, they arrived at Śrāvastī.
As the hour of noon drew near upon reaching their residence, they heard the sound of the *gaṇḍī* and reported to their father:
"The sound of the *ghanṭī* bell is urgent; we must go quickly.
The elder was weary and exhausted and could not walk fast, so his son pushed him forcefully to advance on the path.
The son thought to himself:
"It is beneficial to carry it out.
Yet he pushed him even more forcefully; at that moment, the old father’s face was pressed against the ground and his mouth filled with dust, whereupon he immediately passed away.
When the son saw his father die, he wailed loudly and placed him on the left side of the road; then, taking his robes and bowl, he went to the Jeta Grove.
When the bhikṣus saw him, they said to him, "Welcome, Mahallaka-putra!"
"Where is your aged father now?
He then began to weep, and the bhikṣu asked,
"Venerable one!"
"Why are you weeping? He replied,
"My father has died."
The bhikṣus said to him, "Venerable one! All conditioned phenomena are impermanent;

they are of the nature of arising and ceasing. Since you have left the home life for homelessness within this well-expounded Dharma and Vinaya, you should restrain yourself and not give way to sorrow or suffering."
He replied, "I pushed my father down to the ground, and he died immediately; therefore, I am one who has killed his father.
The bhikṣu said:
"What you have said is truly worthy of lamentation; you shall incur both an ānantarya offense and a pārājika offense, and shall suffer for a long time in the Avīci Hell."
At that time, the bhikṣus reported the matter to the Buddha.
The Buddha said,
"He has committed no offense."
However, bhikṣus should not, while on a journey, forcibly push aside those who are weary or exhausted.
I shall now establish the rules of conduct for bhikṣus traveling on the road.

If, while traveling on the road, you see someone who is utterly exhausted, you should massage them to relieve their fatigue and carry their robes, bowl, and other requisites; it would be well if they were able to proceed.
If they cannot go, you should walk ahead to the place of residence, wash the bowl, prepare leaves, and, having inspected them for insects, request food on their behalf.
If there are those who cannot come, you must take food to meet them so that they do not go without a meal; if it is not the proper time [for a meal], send them non-time-appropriate drinks.
For bhikṣus traveling on the road, if they do not act in accordance with my regulations, they shall incur an offense of transgressing the Dharma.
At that time, all the bhikṣus were filled with doubt and went together to address the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!
For what reason did that son of an elder (mahallaka) commit the taking of his father's life without it being an ānantarya offense, nor a pārājika offense?"
The Buddha said: "O bhikṣus!
It is not only today that this man has killed his father without incurring guilt; in the past as well, he already killed his father and did not receive a grave punishment."
"You all should listen.
In a certain village of the past, there was a washerman who had an only son who had gradually grown up.
At that time, there was a great festival in the village, and many people were washing their clothes together."
At that time, the father and son obtained many soiled garments. The father said to his son:
"Since we have washed so many clothes, we will not be able to return for our meal; you should take this rice and go to the edge of that pond."
Later, when the son took the food and departed, the father, having finished eating, said to his son:
"You should wash the clothes; I am weary and wish to sleep."
He then fell fast asleep.

However, because the father had no hair on his head, many mosquitoes and insects came to bite his crown. After the son finished washing the clothes, he went to his father's side; seeing that there were many mosquitoes and gnats upon his head, he immediately brushed them away for him.
A mosquito, greedy for blood, struck away and returned again.
The father, enraged, said, "While I am still alive, how can I allow such a pest to drink my father's blood?
He took a laundry-beating stick and struck at the insect; though the mosquito flew away in scattered flight, his father’s head was split open, and he died as a result.
At that time, a deva spoke these verses:
"Better to be at enmity with the wise than to form a friendship with a fool;
It is like a foolish child who, while brushing away a mosquito, Struck his father’s head with a stick until he passed away."
"O bhikṣus, do not harbor any other thoughts: the old man who was washing clothes at that time was none other than this Mahallaka;
the son at that time was none other than this bhikṣu who pushed his father."
Just as in the past, although one killed his father, it was not an ānantarya offense;
so too now, although one has severed his father’s life, it is not an ānantarya offense, and he does not commit a pārājika.
Furthermore, there is no offense in the following cases: when the precept has not yet been established; when one is insane, mentally deranged, or overwhelmed by intense physical pain.
Thus concludes the training rule regarding the taking of human life.
*Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya*, Fascicle Eight.
The Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya, Volume Nine.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Yijing by Imperial Order. 4.
The Training Rule on Falsely Claiming to Have Attained Superhuman Qualities (Pārājika 4). The Fourth Training Rule: Falsely Claiming to Have Attained Superhuman Qualities.
The summary verse says:
At the beginning, in Kapilavastu, there were five hundred fishermen;
a bhikṣu dwelling in an araṇya contradicted his own prognostication.
At that time, the Bhagavān was staying in the High Pavilion Hall beside the Monkey Pond in the city of Vaiśālī.
At that time, there were five hundred fishermen living together in a community on the banks of the Vipāśā River.
At that time, the fisherman had two large nets:
the first was named "Small Feet" and the second was named "Large Feet.

When there were few people buying fish, he used the Small Feet net; when there were many people buying fish, he used the Large Feet net; and during great festivals, he would set both nets simultaneously.

At another time, there was a great festival in the city of Vaiśālī; many people were buying fish, and two nets were cast together. Five hundred men were divided into two groups, each holding one net. Those with smaller feet caught many fish, turtles, soft-shelled turtles, and crocodiles, which were piled up on the shore like a great heap of grain.
At that time, there was a great makara fish sleeping in the ocean; carried along by the tide, it drifted into the Śatadru River, where Mahāpāda immediately caught it with his net.

Then the two hundred and fifty men pulled at the net together; as the net pressed against the fish's body, it immediately woke up and dragged the net along with the men downstream. Each of them cried out in great alarm, calling to the man named Little Feet:
"We and our net have both been dragged away by the fish; you must come quickly to help us!"
Having heard this, they all came together to pull [the net], but the five hundred men and the great net were carried away by the fish and could not be held back.
Then the five hundred men raised a great cry and called out to the people nearby, saying:
"All you people, you should know that we five hundred men and our great net have both been pulled by the fish and are being carried downstream; come together to rescue us!"

At that time, those dwelling nearby—whether they were cowherds and shepherds, woodcutters and grass-gatherers, those who made their living by honest means, those who made their living by dishonest means, or other various people—came in groups of hundreds, thousands, and tens of millions to pull at the net.
At that time, the bodies of those men were wounded and their nets torn asunder;

only with the greatest hardship did they manage to haul the creature onto the shore. That makara had eighteen heads and thirty-six eyes; some were the heads of humans, some the heads of elephants, some the heads of horses, camels, donkeys, oxen, monkeys, lions, tigers, leopards, bears, brown bears, cats, deer, water buffaloes, pigs, dogs, and fish. Then people from all directions spoke to one another:

"By the banks of the Vipāśā River, five hundred fishermen have cast a great trawling net and caught a fish which they have hauled onto the shore; its form is extraordinary and large, possessing eighteen heads and thirty-six eyes."

Upon hearing this, immeasurable hundreds of thousands of koṭis of nayutas of beings gathered at the river in competition; some beings went there out of a sense of joy and curiosity to behold it, while others were awakened by their roots of merit from previous lives and impelled to depart.

The six teachers of non-Buddhist paths within and outside Vaiśālī also felt joy and went together to the place where the fish were; the great multitude gathered like clouds, gazing intently and observing closely, and they said to one another:
"Virtuous sirs, do you all recognize this head?"
Giving rise to a sense of wonder, he pointed [toward them] and remained there.
It is the constant law of all Buddhas that they observe the world; there is nothing they do not see or hear, and nothing they do not know.
They constantly give rise to great compassion to benefit all beings, being the foremost among those who provide protection and the most heroic and valiant.

Free from duplicity of speech, abiding in concentration and wisdom, he manifests the three types of supernormal knowledge (*tisro vidyāḥ*), excellently cultivates the three trainings (*triśikṣā*), and skillfully disciplines the three modes of action (*trikarma*).

Having crossed the four torrents (*catasra oghāḥ*) and established himself in the four bases of power (*catvāra ṛddhipādāḥ*), he practices the four means of attraction (*catvāri saṃgrahavastūni*) throughout the long night.

He abandons the five hindrances (*pañca nīvaraṇāni*), remains far removed from the five factors [of the lower realms], transcends the five paths of rebirth, and [perfects] the six faculties (*ṣaḍindriya*).

Fully endowed with the six perfections, he has brought them to completion; he universally bestows the seven riches, opens the flowers of the seven factors of enlightenment, remains detached from the eight worldly dharmas, and reveals the eightfold noble path.
Having forever severed the nine fetters, he is clear and proficient in the nine meditative absorptions;
filled with the ten powers, his fame reaches the ten directions. Among all those who possess mastery, he is most preeminent, having attained the various fearlessnesses.

Having subdued the hosts of Māra and enemies, emitting the great sound of thunder and letting out the lion’s roar, he constantly observes the world with the Buddha-eye throughout the six periods of day and night: "Who is increasing?"
Who is declining?
Who is encountering suffering and calamity?
Who is heading toward the evil destinies?
Who is mired in the mud of desire?
Who is capable of receiving transformation?
By what skillful means may they be rescued and brought forth?

He causes those who lack the noble wealth to obtain it; with the *añjana* of wisdom, he breaks the film of ignorance. He causes those without roots of goodness to plant them, and causes those who possess roots of goodness to increase them. He places them upon the path of humans and devas, leading them securely and without hindrance toward the city of Nirvana.
As it is said:
"Even if the tide of the great ocean should miss its appointed time,
the Buddha never fails his appointed hour in delivering those he transforms."
Just as a mother who has but one child constantly protects that child’s life,
the Buddha’s compassionate concern for those he transforms exceeds even that.
The Buddha’s loving-kindness toward all sentient beings is never abandoned.
"I shall seek to rescue them from their suffering and hardship, just as a mother cow follows her calf.
At that time, the World-Honored One thought to himself:

"This makara fish has now encountered this calamity; it has already planted roots of goodness under previous Buddhas. For the sake of this fish, I shall cast the great net of the Teaching to transform and deliver sentient beings; I should go to the banks of the River of Supreme Wisdom."

It is the constant law of all Buddhas that, while they have not yet entered parinirvāṇa and remain in the world, they go out of compassion for the sentient beings to be converted to the various realms of hell-beings, animals, hungry ghosts, humans, and devas; they may go to charnel grounds or to riverbanks.

Now, because of this matter, the World-Honored One desired to go to the banks of the River of Supreme Wisdom (Vimala) and immediately smiled, emitting five-colored rays of light from his mouth. At times they shone downward, and at others they ascended. Those rays that shone downward reached the Avīci Hell and other hells; those suffering from heat all attained coolness, and those dwelling in cold ice obtained warmth.
Those sentient beings each found peace and happiness, and all thought to themselves: "Have you and I died from hell to be reborn in another place?"
At that time, after the World-Honored One had caused those sentient beings to give rise to faith, he further manifested other signs. Upon seeing these signs, they all thought:

"We have not died here to be reborn elsewhere; rather, it must be through the power of the majesty and virtue of the Unsurpassed Great Sage that our bodies and minds now experience such peace and happiness."

Having given rise to reverent faith, they are able to extinguish all sufferings and receive superior and wondrous bodies within the realms of humans and devas; they shall become vessels for the Dharma and perceive the principles of the True Truths.
Those who ascend reach the Akaniṣṭha Heaven, where, amidst the light, they proclaim the dharmas of suffering, emptiness, impermanence, and non-self, and further recite two gāthās:
"You should, within the Buddha's teaching, Diligently seek the path of liberation."
One can shatter the army of birth and death, Just as an elephant destroys a thatched hut.
Within the Dharma and Vinaya of the Buddha, One should train with courageous diligence;
Able to abandon birth and death, One shall attain the end of suffering.
Then that radiance, having illuminated the trichiliocosm, returned to the place where the Buddha was.

If the Buddha, the World-Honored One, speaks of past events, light enters through his back; if he speaks of future events, light enters through his chest; if he speaks of matters concerning hell-beings, light enters through the soles of his feet; if he speaks of matters concerning animals, light enters through his heels; if he speaks of matters concerning hungry ghosts, light enters through his toes; if he speaks of matters concerning humans, light enters through his knees; if he speaks of matters concerning a Cakravartin King of Power, light enters through the palm of his left hand; if he speaks of matters concerning a Universal Monarch (Cakravartin), light enters through the palm of his right hand; if he speaks of matters concerning devas, light enters through his navel; if he speaks of matters concerning Śrāvakas, light enters through his mouth; if he speaks of matters concerning Pratyekabuddhas, light enters between his eyebrows; and if he speaks of matters concerning Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, light enters through the crown of his head.
At that time, the light circled the Buddha three times and entered through his navel.
Then, the Venerable Ānanda joined his palms in reverence and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!”
“The Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, does not smile joyfully without cause or condition.
He then spoke these verses to request the Buddha, saying:
“From his mouth issue various wondrous rays of light, Flowing and filling the great trichiliocosm in manifold forms.”
Pervading all lands throughout the ten directions, like the sun’s light illuminating the entirety of space;
the Buddha is the most supreme cause for sentient beings, able to remove arrogance as well as grief and sorrow.
Without a specific cause, he does not open his golden mouth; when he smiles, he will surely proclaim something rare and wondrous.
The Muni, serene and discerning, who delights in speaking for those who wish to hear, utters a sublime roar like the lion king; may he resolve our doubts for us.
Like the King of Mountains within the great ocean, Which does not shake without cause or condition, You, with sovereign compassion, manifest a smile;
For those who look up with longing, please explain the causes and conditions.
At that time, the World-Honored One said to Ānanda: “So it is,
so it is, Ānanda!”
It is not without cause or condition that the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, suddenly manifests a smile.
You should now inform the bhikṣus:
"The Tathāgata wishes to go to the riverbank for a stroll."
"If any of you, venerable ones, wish to follow the Tathāgata, you should take up your robes.
Then, having received the Buddha's instruction, the Venerable Ānanda addressed the bhikṣus, saying:
"Venerable ones!"
"The Buddha now wishes to go and wander along the riverbank; if any of you venerable ones wish to follow, you should take up your robes.
When the bhikṣus had received these instructions, they all came to where the Buddha was.
At that time, the World-Honored One went to the River of Supreme Wisdom (*Jñānavatī*). Being himself disciplined, he was surrounded by those who were disciplined;
being himself tranquil, he was surrounded by those who were tranquil; liberated, he was surrounded by those who were liberated; secure, he was surrounded by those who were secure;
well-composed, he was surrounded by those who were well-composed; an Arhat, he was surrounded by Arhats; free from desire... [he was surrounded by those] free from desire.
Desiring to surround him, they surrounded him with exquisite beauty; like a sandalwood tree surrounded by sandalwood trees,
like a lordly elephant surrounded by a herd of elephants, like a lion king surrounded by lions,
like a great bull king surrounded by cattle, like a king of geese surrounded by geese, and like a garuḍa.
Surrounded by various birds, like a Brahmin surrounded by his disciples, like a great physician surrounded by patients,
like a great general surrounded by his troops, like a great guide surrounded by travelers,
like a merchant leader surrounded by his traders, like a great householder surrounded by a multitude of people...

Surrounded by the ministers of a great king, like a wheel-turning monarch surrounded by a thousand sons, like the bright moon surrounded by the multitude of stars, like the solar disc surrounded by a thousand rays of light, like the Heavenly King Dhṛtarāṣṭra surrounded by the hosts of gandharvas, like the Heavenly King Virūḍhaka surrounded by the hosts of kumbhāṇḍas... as if [surrounded by]... so it was.
The Heavenly King Virūpākṣa was surrounded by a host of nāgas, like the Heavenly King Vaiśravaṇa surrounded by a host of yakṣas,
like the King of the Pure and Wondrous (Sudharmarāja) surrounded by a host of asuras, like Śakra surrounded by the thirty-three gods,
and like the Brahmā King surrounded by the Brahma-host; he was like the great ocean, serene and tranquil.
Like a great cloud hanging low and spreading wide, like a king of elephants who has stilled his wild intoxication,
his faculties were subdued and his deportment was serene. Adorned with the thirty-two marks and graced by the eighty minor characteristics,
a halo of one fathom shone more brightly than a thousand suns as he advanced slowly with a steady gait, as if moving a mountain.
On Mount Ratnagiri, where the ten powers, the four fearlessnesses, great compassion, and the three foundations of mindfulness are fully perfected along with immeasurable virtues,

the great śrāvakas— Venerable Ājñātakauṇḍinya, Venerable Aśvajit, Venerable Bāṣpa, Venerable Mahānāman, Venerable Aniruddha, Venerable Śāriputra, Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana, Venerable Kāśyapa, Venerable Ānanda, and Venerable Khāṇu-putra— and such other great śrāvakas, together with the assembly of bhikṣus, proceeded to the riverbank.
At that time, the great assembly saw from afar the World-Honored One and his community of bhikṣus approaching from the distance. Those who lacked faith deliberated among themselves, saying:
"All you people should know: I have heard that the śramaṇa Gautama has severed all joy and pleasure; yet he too comes out of fondness for it to observe these fish."
Those who were full of reverence and faith then said:

"All you people should know: since the World-Honored Buddha has long since abandoned joy and pleasure, is it not because of this fish that he has today, for the sake of the great assembly, brought forth great compassion and intends to preach a rare and subtle Dharma?"
They spoke together in verse:
“The Muni has long since abandoned thoughts of joy and pleasure, yet those without faith give rise to slander.
The Most Victorious One now comes to this place; he will surely speak subtle words for the sake of the assembly.”

At that time, when the great assembly saw the World-Honored One arrive, they all rose in astonishment; for when the Buddha was a bodhisattva, he always maintained a spirit of reverence toward those worthy of respect, such as his teachers, preceptors, parents, and elders.
At that time, the World-Honored One entered the great assembly and sat down before the bhikṣus; he then addressed the five hundred fishermen, saying:
"O virtuous ones!
In your previous lives, you committed evil deeds; due to these conditions, you were born among lowly people who catch fish for their livelihood.
Now, you further hold knives and nets in your hands, sustaining yourselves by the act of killing.
"Dying now here, where will you be reborn?
The fisherman asked,
"I do not know what I should do now."
The World-Honored One said,
"You should now release these fish, turtles, and other aquatic creatures.
He addressed the Buddha, saying:
“As the Blessed One has instructed,” they replied, and immediately released it.

At that time, by means of his supernormal powers, the Blessed One caused the fish, turtles, and other creatures to enter the Vipāśā River as if swimming in water; however, the makara alone remained behind and did not go. Recalling events from its previous life, it was able to speak the language of humans and engaged in conversation with the Buddha.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the makara fish, saying:
"Are you Kappila? He replied:
“I am Kappila. The Blessed One asked again:
“Have you ever committed unwholesome actions of body, speech, or mind?”
He replied, "I have.
[The Buddha asked,] "Do you know that these three types of unwholesome conduct bring about an unpleasant ripening?"
He replied, “I know. [The Buddha asked:
“Do you know that you yourself must experience the fruit of this karma?”
He replied,
“I am experiencing it now.
[The Buddha asked,] “Who is your evil friend?”
He replied, "My mother. [The Buddha asked,] "Where was she reborn?"
He replied,
“I have been born in hell.
[The other asked,] “To which realm have you been born?”
He replied, “Among the animals. [The Buddha asked:
“Having died here, where will he be reborn?”
He replied,
"I shall die here and be reborn in hell.
Having spoken these words, the makara fish immediately wept.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke these verses:
"You have fallen into the realm of animals; I can do nothing for you now!
Dwelling in a state of no leisure, what benefit would there be in weeping?"
"I now feel compassion for you; you should give rise to a virtuous mind, weary of and renounce this animal body, and you shall surely ascend to the heavens.
When the makara fish heard these words, he conceived deep reverence and faith toward the World-Honored One.
The World-Honored One then taught him the Dharma in three verses, saying:
"O Noble One! 'All conditioned phenomena are impermanent; all dharmas are without self.'"
"Quiescence is itself Nirvana; these are called the Three Dharma Seals.
At that time, the great assembly was filled with wonder and deliberated among themselves, saying:
"For what reason did the World-Honored One question this fish, causing it to remember its past lives, and why did it speak as a human being to engage in dialogue with the Buddha?"
"Friends, you should know that the Great Sage, the Tathāgata, is of such majestic and venerable power that we, being humble and insignificant, did not dare to inquire about this.
We should go together to the Venerable Ānanda and ask him about its origin, so that we may receive and believe it as he explains."
At that time, those who were devoted and faithful immediately went together to Ānanda and said to him:
"Venerable One!
For what reason does this fish understand human speech so well, and engage in a discussion with the Blessed One regarding matters of past lives?"
Then Ānanda replied to the people, saying,
"You should now go and inquire of the World-Honored One.
The people answered:
“The Tathāgata, the World-Honored One, possesses such majestic and solemn authority that we, being mediocre and ignorant, do not dare to lightly approach him.
Ānanda said, “I too share your fear of the Buddha’s majesty; now, for your sake, I shall briefly inquire about this matter.”
Then the Venerable Ānanda rose from his seat, went to where the Blessed One was, prostrated at His feet, stood to one side, and said:
“Blessed One!”
"By what cause and condition is this fish able to understand human speech and discuss matters of past lives with the Blessed One?
At that time, the Blessed One said to Ānanda:
"Do you now wish to hear the karmic conditions of this Makara fish from his previous lives?"
Then Ānanda said to the World-Honored One:
"World-Honored One!
We wish to hear this; now is precisely the right time."

We only pray that you will explain the causes and conditions pertaining to this fish’s past lives, so that we bhikṣus and the great assembly, having heard the Dharma, may receive it with faith and uphold it.
The Buddha said to Ānanda:
“Listen attentively, apply your mind to the utmost, and reflect upon this well.

In a past age, during this Bhadrakalpa when the lifespan of humans was twenty thousand years, there appeared in the world a Buddha, a World-Honored One, named Kāśyapa Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Perfect in Knowledge and Conduct, Sugata, Knower of the World, Unsurpassed Leader, Tamer of Men, Teacher of Gods and Humans, Buddha, Bhagavān. He was dwelling at the Deer Park in the Abode of the Sages near the city of Vārāṇasī, together with a great assembly of twenty thousand bhikṣus.”

At that time, there was a king in that city named Kṛkī. The world was peaceful and happy, with abundant harvests; the population was vast and livestock flourished. There was no strife or conflict, and weapons were laid aside; there was neither the suffering of disease nor any bandits or thieves. He ruled the kingdom according to the True Dharma as a great Dharma King.

In that country there was a young brahmin who said he had traveled from his own land far to the south, where there lived a brahmin who was extensively learned in all arts and well-versed in the four Vedas; people from near and far came to him from every direction.
At that time, the youth went to his location; having arrived, he paid his respects and sat to one side.
That brahmin said: "Welcome, youth!"
"From where have you come?
What do you seek? He replied:
"I have come from China," he said, "and wish to personally receive the teachings of the Way at the feet of the Great Master.
The Master asked him,
"What texts do you wish to study?"
He replied,
"I am studying the *Caturvidyā-śāstra*.
The other said:
"Excellent! You should train in this way; this is the duty that a brāhmaṇa ought to perform.

At that time, the youth immediately began his studies. Whenever students reached their days of rest, they would either go to rivers or ponds to bathe, or go to the city markets to look about, or gather fragrant firewood to provide for their sacrifices.
At that time, when it was a holiday, the youth went out with his fellow students to gather firewood;
along the way, they asked one another, "You all belong to the Brahmin caste; from where have you come?"
One person replied,
"I have come from the east.
Another said:
"I have come from the western country," said one.
"I have come from the north," said another.
Then that youth said,
"I have come from the Middle Kingdom.
The people asked:
"I have heard briefly of the various other regions and kingdoms, but the protocols and customs of the Middle Kingdom have never been mentioned.
He then spoke in verse:
"Wisdom emerges from the East; Divisive speech prevails in the Western lands."
"Those who are respectful and compliant are born in the Southern Land; those who use harsh speech dwell in the Northern Land.
At that time, the disciples asked the youth, "What is the situation in your Middle Kingdom?"
The youth replied, "My central land is preeminent among all regions;

it is abundant with sugarcane, fragrant rice, and fruit, and its livestock are plentiful. It is a place of joy and security, where the population is vast and everyone values compassion and salvation. Its people are intelligent, virtuous, and possess skills that surpass others."
There is the auspicious and pure Gaṅgā River, its waters flowing level along both banks.
There are eighteen sites where ṛṣis dwell, each of whom, through great asceticism, has attained rebirth in heaven.
He asked him again, saying,
"In the land of the Middle Kingdom, are there any who are as wise, eloquent, and skilled in debate as my teacher?
He replied:
"There is currently a master of treatises in China who is as sovereign and unimpeded as a lion king; even my own teacher felt shame upon seeing him.
When the boy thus praised the Middle Kingdom, everyone who heard it desired to go there.
Then the young boys each took firewood and went to their teacher’s house; having set down the wood, they approached their teacher and each said to him:
"This boy has praised the Middle Kingdom so highly that he has made all of us desire to go there."
The teacher replied, "People everywhere speak highly of this land as being exquisite; however, it can only be heard of by the ear—it is not appropriate to go there immediately.
The disciples said:
"That youth said: 'Currently in the Middle Kingdom there is a master of treatises who is as sovereign and unimpeded as a lion king; if my teacher were to see him, he would surely feel shame.'"
The master replied:
"This land abounds in rare treasures and its people are many and eminent; how could I say of myself that within this realm I alone am superior and there is no one else who surpasses me?"
He spoke again to his teacher, saying:

"If it be so, I now wish to go for two reasons: first, to tour the various kingdoms; second, to bathe in the River of the Immortals, to submit to and receive instruction from great masters of treatises, to subdue all opposing doctrines, to discourse with vigor and eloquence, to establish a reputation, and to acquire much wealth."
At that time, the brahmin, being by nature free from worldly affairs and compassionate toward his disciples, replied to the people, saying:
"You should take my requisites—the deerskin, the coarse garment, the triple staff, the water jar, and the sacrificial implements—and I shall now go with you all to seek a teacher."
He then accepted the instruction and went together with him to the Middle Kingdom.
In every city and town they reached, they established great debating arenas; all who came to debate were defeated, their carriages destroyed, and they returned home filled with shame.
Some even struck them on the head with jars of ashes, just as when one shoots at a crow according to the instructions, the birds scatter and fly away.
Some came from far and near to welcome him with silk canopies, banners, and streamers, all declaring themselves his disciples as they followed behind him.
As the brahmin traveled by stages, he was honored as the preeminent leader in every city and town he passed through. Upon reaching the city of Vārāṇasī, he thought to himself:
"Why do I now abandon the root to grasp at the branches?"
"Since all those who are intelligent and skilled in debate, as well as other scholars, are gathered at the royal court, I should now go in person to the King's presence.
Having formed this thought, he immediately went to visit King Kṛkī.
Having arrived at the king’s location, he offered a blessing for the king, saying:
"May the King subdue all enemies and enjoy long life and freedom from illness.
Having spoken these words, he sat to one side and addressed the king, saying:

"Your Majesty, you should know that I have indeed sought out teachers in my own country and have studied various scriptures, treatises, and scripts to some extent. I wish to establish a point of debate in Your Majesty’s presence and venture to briefly engage in a spirited exchange of challenges with these people."
Having heard this, the king commanded his great ministers, saying:
"Is there anyone in my kingdom who can engage in debate and provide a fitting response to this man?"
He replied, “There is. He asked:

“Where is he? He replied, “In a certain village there is a brahmin named Kapphiṇa Śyāma, who is well-versed in the four Vedas and other treatises; he is able to establish his own doctrines and skillfully refute the positions of others. Possessing great wisdom and brilliance like a leaping flame, he is the foremost among the multitude.”
The King said,
"Summon him here. Following these instructions,
the great minister summoned the master of logic.
Having arrived at the king’s location, he offered blessings as before and sat to one side.
The minister announced:
"This is the great master of logic who was summoned."
The king said,
"Excellent, Great Master!
Would you be able to engage in a debate with me and the brahmin?"
He replied, "I can.
The king then commanded his minister, saying:
"Your Excellency should now prepare the debating arena with great splendor and ensure that both the proponent and the opponent are properly accommodated.
Following these instructions, the minister made elaborate preparations, and the King, having readied his carriage, proceeded in person to the site of the debate.
Once the king was seated, the minister addressed him, saying:
"Great King!
Whom do you wish to dispatch to represent our initial position?"
The king said, "Since this brahmin has come from afar from the southern kingdom, let the etiquette of host and guest grant him precedence.
That brahmin then established his thesis and delivered five hundred verses of skillful rhetoric; his eloquence was so swift and sharp that few among the listeners could comprehend it.
At that time, as soon as Kapphiṇa Śramaṇa heard the assembly’s realization, he immediately refuted their errors, saying:
"This is contradictory; this is inconclusive; this is unestablished."
When the brahmin had been thus defeated, he remained silent.
Generally, in debate, one who is unable to provide a response falls into the position of defeat.
Seeing that he had won, the king was greatly delighted and asked:
"Where does the Great Teacher reside?
He replied, "Great King!"
"In a certain village.
He replied, "The Great Master has spoken most eloquently; that village shall serve as the reward for his skillful discourse."
He then took his leave of the king and departed with joy.
Having attained great wealth, he subsequently took a new wife; not long after, he gave birth to a son.

On the day of his birth, the child’s head was covered in yellow hair. When the twenty-one days had passed, he summoned his kinsmen in great numbers, intending to bestow an auspicious name upon his son.
The father addressed his kinsmen, saying,
"Now, what name shall we give this son of mine?
The kinsmen replied:
"This is Kappila-Sama; furthermore, since his hair was the color of kappila when he was first born, this son should be named Kappila."

Having thus bestowed upon him a name and nurtured him with care, they fed him with milk and curd, interspersed with various kinds of butter, and provided him with excellent and wonderful articles for his enjoyment according to the season; he then grew rapidly, like a lotus emerging from a pond.

Once he had been established [in the household], he was instructed in the study of writing, seals, calculation, and arithmetic; he became thoroughly proficient in all worldly affairs of receiving and giving. Next, he was taught the ritual protocols of the Brahmins: handling ashes and earth, carrying vessels, the methods for bathing and purification, and the four Vedas—their various recitations known as the *Ṛgveda*, *Yajurveda*, *Sāmaveda*, and *Atharvaveda*.

He mastered the rituals himself and taught them to others; he mastered the recitation himself and taught it to others; he understood the rules for bestowing gifts and receiving wealth. Having clarified these six matters, he became a great Brahmin, widely versed in the various scriptures, elucidating his own school and refuting the doctrines of others, possessing sharp intelligence and wisdom like a great bright torch.
Later, at another time, Kapphiṇa Sāma was teaching five hundred brahmin youths to recite the Vedic scriptures.
At that time, his son Kapphiṇa also studied under him and asked his father,
"What is the meaning of the word 'Niraya'?"
The father told him:
"The meaning of the characters you have asked about is extremely profound; though passed down by successive masters, it is ultimately difficult to fully comprehend.
He then asked his father again:
"How could it be that the Great Teacher of old spoke without meaning? Nevertheless, as I reflect upon it, there seems to be some truth in it.
Upon hearing this, his father immediately thought to himself:
"All people in the world desire their sons to excel; now that Kāpilavastu’s son excels me in the arts and sciences, I shall entrust him with five hundred youths."
He then said to his son, "Your mastery of the Way and the arts now surpasses mine; you should instruct these five hundred men.
Thereupon, following his father's command, he taught the five hundred men.
The father abandoned his disciples and had no further concerns, wandering wherever his heart desired.
At another time, he went to the Deer Park and approached a bhikṣu, saying:
"Noble One!..."
"What is the meaning of these words?
The bhikṣu replied,
"O noble one!"
"You should not ask such a question now; if you were to ask this, the meaning would not be fully comprehensive. You should ask in this way instead, and only then will you obtain a complete answer.
When the brahmin had been thus admonished, he immediately thought to himself:
"If even the questions I have posed are not sufficient, how much less could I engage in debate as his equal?"
He conceived a heart of reverence and faith toward the bhikṣus and, from time to time, invited them to his home for a meal.
Later, the brahmin fell ill and said to his son:

"In all places traversed by the sun and moon, there is no one else equal to you; after my death, you shall have no cause for doubt or fear in any assembly of debate, with the sole exception of the śrāvaka disciples of the Buddha Kāśyapa."

Why is this? That school is vast and profound, difficult to fathom; it cannot be subdued by worldly discourse nor known by mundane wisdom. Its members are of one mind, seeking neither fame nor profit; therefore, you should not engage them in contentious debate.
The son replied, "Very well.
At that time, the illness of the brahmin gradually worsened; although he was treated with medicinal decoctions, he grew increasingly emaciated and exhausted, as it is said:
“Accumulations all disperse; what is lofty must fall;
those who meet end in separation; all who have life return to death.”
At that time, the brahmin passed away.
His son and his kinsmen placed him upon a bier adorned with five-colored silks and carried him to the charnel ground; having cremated him with fire, they remained there dwelling in grief.
When the other masters of the treatises heard that his father had died, they said to one another:
"Gentlemen, you should know that the Brahmin Suvādin has now passed away; we ought to go to King Kṛkī and request the opportunity to present our arguments."
They immediately went together.
Upon arriving at the king’s location and having offered blessings for his prosperity, they addressed the king, saying:
“We have studied a small amount of script under our teacher; we venture to establish the opening of a debate in the presence of Your Majesty.”
The king said to his minister,
"You should now go and summon that master of debate.
The great minister replied:
"The teacher has already died.
The King said,
"For this reason, just as the sparrows in a field now all come vying with one another."
"But does that Great Master have any sons or brothers?
The minister replied,
"He has a son named Kapila."
The king said,
"You should order him to come.
Following the command, he was summoned.
Having arrived at the king's location and offered prayers for his welfare, he sat to one side.
The minister addressed the king, saying,
"This is the son of our great teacher, named Kāpilavastu."
The King said: "Welcome!
Now, masters of various treatises from near and far have all gathered here, wishing to initiate a debate against me. Are you able to engage them in discussion?"
He then addressed the king, saying, "I venture to present my arguments.

Thereupon, a debating arena was established to facilitate the exchange of challenges; the king prepared his carriage to personally observe the victory or defeat, and he appointed all the visiting debaters as presiding masters, dispatching Kāpilavastu to serve as the opposing debater.
All interrogations were pursued to their ultimate conclusions, and all those who had put forward arguments fell silent; for in any formal debate, failure to respond constitutes a defeat.
When the King beheld such unimpeded eloquence, he was filled with the utmost wonder and marveled, saying:
"This child, though in his tender years, surpasses all the eminent scholars in virtue."

Filled with joy and uttering words of extraordinary wonder and praise, he granted him exceptional rewards, commanding that he be mounted upon a great elephant, consecrated, and enthroned as the "King of Debaters," an object of veneration for all.
From afar, the mother of Kapphiṇa felt a surge of anxious concern, thinking:
"Could it be that my young son, being by nature flighty and impulsive, has been stripped of his fiefdom and has no face to return?"
Having reflected thus, he remained there dwelling in sorrow.
At that time, having received the consecration as the Great King of Debaters, Kapphiṇa returned to his own residence accompanied by a multitude of eminent scholars.
His mother, in great haste, asked him:
"Have you already defeated all the masters of debate?
He then replied to his mother:
"Everything has been destroyed, with the sole exception of the śrāvaka disciples of Kāśyapa Buddha.
His mother immediately turned her face away and waved her hand.
Then Kapila said to his mother:
"Why did the Honored One Maitreya turn his face away and wave his hand?
His mother said,
"Do you know now?"
"Even the fiefs we possess have not yet been secured; they will ultimately be seized by the bhikṣus in common. You should now go and refute those śramaṇas.
He then said to his mother:
"On the day my compassionate father passed away, he left me this final instruction:"

“With the sun and moon shining upon you, there shall be no one else equal to you; after my parinirvāṇa, you will have no doubt or fear in any assemblies for debate, with the sole exception of the śrāvaka disciples of the Buddha Kāśyapa.”

Why is this? Their doctrine is vast, expansive, profound, and difficult to fathom; it cannot be subdued by worldly discourse nor understood by mundane wisdom. They are of one mind and seek neither fame nor profit; you must not debate with them.
The mother then replied:
"When your father was alive, he was a slave to a śramaṇa; how could you now become a slave in turn?
You should go at once to blunt his sharp edge."
Kapphiṇa was by nature benevolent and filial; he did not disobey his mother’s words and set out for the Deer Park.
On the way, he encountered a bhikṣu and immediately asked him, "Bhikṣu, from where have you come?"
He replied,
"From the Deer Park at Ṛṣipatana. He asked:
"How many bhikṣus are there at Ṛṣipatana?
He replied,
"There are more than twenty thousand."
He asked, "The assembly of bhikṣus is already numerous; how many sūtras do they possess?
He replied:
“The scriptures for bhikṣus consist, in total, of three piṭakas.
He asked: “What is the number of texts within each individual piṭaka?”
He replied,
"One collection of verses contains one hundred thousand. He asked:
"Have the lay followers at home heard it?
He replied,
"They have heard the two collections, namely the Abhidharma and the Sūtras."
"The Vinaya teachings are the ritual procedures for those who have left the household life;
it is not appropriate for laypeople to hear them. Kapila then thought to himself:
"The methods of this polemical debate are not permitted to be known by others."
Having formed this thought, he said to the bhikṣu,
"Venerable sir, please explain to me now some of the essential meanings of the Buddha's teaching.
The bhikṣu then reflected:
"This brahmin is a debater; does he ask this question to weigh my understanding, or does he inquire out of ignorance?
I shall now test him."
He recited a verse, saying:
"Where should the flow be brought to rest?
Where should the path be traversed?"
"Where can the matters of worldly suffering and happiness ever come to an end?
Having spoken this verse, he addressed him, saying: "Brahmin!"
"You should explain the meaning of this verse for me.
At that time, Kāpya thoroughly deliberated upon all branches of knowledge, yet to the full extent of his wisdom and understanding, he could not fathom its meaning.
"What is the cessation of the outflows?
What is the practice of the path?
He then looked around in all directions so that no one else might see or hear him, and then he thought thus:
"If there were anyone here capable of verifying the meaning, my person would surely be subjected to defeat.
He then practiced deception and said to the bhikṣu:

"I observe that the lineage of this verse is extensive and its meaning profound; you should go for now to Vārāṇasī. I have some minor business to attend to at the Deer Park (Mṛgadāva), so it is not possible to explain its meaning in haste. When we meet again later, it will not be difficult to resolve it."

Having spoken these words of parting, he went to the Deer Park. There he saw the bhikṣus reciting, meditating, and diligently seeking the path to liberation. Feeling deep reverence and faith, he thought to himself:
"Who could be so heedless of the next world and harbor such cruel malice as to seek out the faults of these wise ones and engage in such frantic, idle debate?"
Having formed this thought, he returned to his own dwelling.
When his mother saw him, she asked:
"Have you already defeated and broken the disciples of Kāśyapa?"
He then said to his mother,
"Judging by your intention, you wish for me to lose my current fiefdom.
His mother replied to her son:
"What is the meaning of what you have said?
The boy replied immediately, "Go and try;
you will encounter a bhikṣu on the road to the Deer Forest."
They reported everything to their mother exactly as before.
Having heard this, the mother replied:
"If that is the case, you should now study the Buddha-dharma."
He asked, "What do you wish to learn?
and he replied:
"That treatise on the Dharma does not instruct worldly travelers; you should go forth into homelessness and study under him.
He further said to his mother, "How could one from a noble family cast himself among the common folk for the sake of some minor cause and go forth?"
His mother replied to him, "Once you have finished your studies, you shall return to secular life; how could one grow overgrown weeds upon one's head?
Although his son was by nature kind and filial, he was driven by his mother’s pressure and desired to leave the household life.
He then proceeded to the Deer Forest and, arriving at the place where the bhikṣus were, addressed them, saying:
"Venerable Sirs!
I wish to go forth into homelessness."
Then that bhikṣu thought to himself:
"This brāhmaṇa is highly skilled in debate; if he were to go forth, he would cause the Buddha-dharma to flourish.
Having had this thought, he replied:
"Excellent!
It is according to your own inclination; for fame, honor, and great prosperity are all impermanent, and to renounce them and leave the household life is the most excellent course. Kapila said:
"I am well known here; it would be better for me to go to another land to truly leave the secular world.
The bhikṣu said, "Very well."

He was then taken to another region, where he was ordained and received full ordination (*upasampadā*). He was subsequently instructed in the study of the Tripiṭaka until he mastered them all, becoming a great Dharma Master whose eloquence and rhetoric were unimpeded.

If one expounds and recites the sutras and the Dharma, one shall surely ascend the lion throne made of various jewels; as the twin conch shells are blown and the great drums are struck, the king, the officials, and the commoners will all gather like clouds, and those who hear it will rejoice.
At that time, Kapphiṇa thought to himself:
"My diligent studies have now reached their fulfillment; I should go to the Blessed One Kāśyapa at Vārāṇasī to personally attend upon and make offerings to the Great Teacher."
Having arrived at the city, the mother heard that her son had come; she immediately went searching for him and reached the Deer Park. Seeing her son, she asked him:
"Have you already defeated the disciples of the Śramaṇa Kāśyapa Buddha?"

He then said to his mother, "Although I understand the teachings, I have not yet realized the fruits; those disciples possess clarity in both teaching and realization—how could I possibly presume to refute them?"
His mother replied,
"You must certainly destroy it.
Urged and pressed by his mother, he could not escape her demands, and so he said to her:
"If you hear the drum beaten and the conch blown for the adorned throne when the great assembly gathers, then the mother shall arrive.
The mother replied,
"Very well!"
"The time has come; I shall arrive.

Later, at another time, when Kapphiṇa ascended the Dharma seat in succession, the great assembly had all gathered. Hearing the drum roll, his mother went in alarm to the Deer Park and stood silently by the side of the high seat.
At that time, the Dharma master ascended the high seat; he first expounded the True Dharma, but subsequently uttered various heterodox words.
When the bhikṣus heard this, they said to him:
"Venerable One!..."
"Do not slander or disparage the Buddha's teaching.
By raising the banner of Māra and destroying the standard of the Dharma, once you have cast off this body, you shall be reborn in the evil realms.
He remained silent without offering a reply, then descended from his high seat and said to his mother:
"Do you see this? He replied,
"I see it."
Kappila said: "Have I not already stated that I am merely learned in the teachings, whereas he is proficient in both the teachings and their realization; how could I possibly be able to refute him?"
The mother said,
"I shall teach you the skillful means of polemical debate.
When you preach the Dharma again, first discuss the True Dharma and afterwards describe the heterodox schools."

When those bhikṣus offer words of admonition, citing matters of both good and evil, if you do not listen to their speech, you should speak with words like swords drawn from your mouth, uttering unrighteous speech; then those śramaṇas, fearing an ill reputation, will immediately fall silent, and the people of the world at that time will say they have been defeated.
He then replied to his mother, "This is an excellent stratagem; when you see me ascending the seat, you should come back again.
He spoke thus.
"Very well," she replied.
Later, he invited her as before; when the conch was blown and the drums beaten and the seven assemblies had gathered, his mother came and sat silently at the edge of the seat behind him.
Then Kapphiṇa ascended the high seat and, following the prescribed ritual, recited the scriptures; he first recited the orthodox sūtras and afterwards expounded heterodox doctrines.
At that time, the bhikṣus said to him:
"Venerable one!..."
"Do not destroy what is right and promote what is false, lest you be reborn in the evil realms.
He then recalled his mother's words, and from his mouth issued swords and blades as he replied to the bhikṣu:
"What do you know, you whose mouth is like that of an elephant?"

If you regard what is Dharma as non-Dharma and what is Vinaya as non-Vinaya—being like the mouth of a horse, a camel, a donkey, an ox, a monkey, a lion, a tiger, a leopard, a bear, a brown bear, a cat, a deer, a buffalo, a pig, a dog, a fish, or a fool—how could you possibly know what is Dharma and what is non-Dharma?
Then the bhikṣus said to one another:
"Since he has spoken these words like brandishing swords, we ought to depart.
Those who could not endure it all left; those who were patient remained in their seats to listen, thinking thus:
"If he expounds the True Dharma, I shall listen; if he proclaims a false doctrine, he shall suffer.

Then, Kapphiṇa, having uttered eighteen kinds of abusive insults against the noble bhikṣus—both those in training and those beyond training—descended from his high seat and said to his mother, "Mother, are you happy now?"
The mother said to her son:
"I am now greatly rejoiced; we should return home together. Kapila replied:
"I cannot return home; my heart is devoted to and cherishes the unsurpassed, perfect teaching of the Buddha Kāśyapa.
His mother said, "Have you not heard the Brahmanical scriptures, which state that the instructions of one's parents must never be transgressed?"
"You should now return home with me.
He then replied to his mother, "I cannot go;
if I must wander through the cycle of birth and death, I pray that I may never again encounter such a mother as you."

"Because of an evil friend, I have uttered coarse and harsh words toward the noble ones, both those in training and those beyond training; due to this evil karma, I will certainly experience the ripening of suffering in the future."
At that time, as her mother could not get him to come despite calling out, she spoke these words in the midst of the crowds at the streets, crossroads, and lanes of Vārāṇasī:
"O people, you should know! The disciples of Kāśyapa have forcibly seized my son; you must assist me."
Upon hearing this, those who were respectful and faithful comforted one another;
however, those who lacked faith began to mock them.
At that time, the old woman was so overcome with shame that she vomited warm blood and immediately passed away to be reborn in the Nāraka hell.

Because the bhikṣu Kapphiṇa committed eighteen kinds of harsh speech, reviling those who were in training (śaikṣa), those beyond training (aśaikṣa), and other bhikṣus, after his life ended he was reborn among the makara fish, his form being loathsome.
When the great assembly had heard what the Buddha had said, they said to one another:

"All you people should know that this bhikṣu Kapphiṇa is a great Dharma teacher, possessed of unimpeded eloquence and skilled in preaching the Dharma, causing hundreds of thousands of listeners to rejoice."
"Since it is solely due to harsh speech that one is born in the evil realms, where shall we be reborn when our lives come to an end?
Thinking thus, they remained there filled with anxiety.

At that time, the World-Honored One observed the differences in the inclinations, afflictions, and faculties of the great assembly, and preached the Dharma to them according to what was appropriate for each.

Having heard the Dharma, some attained the stages of Heat, Summits, Patience, and the Supreme Mundane Dharma; some attained the fruits of Stream-enterer, Once-returner, or Non-returner; some left the household life, exhausted all outflows, and realized Arhatship; some conceived the aspiration for the enlightenment of a Śrāvaka, some for the enlightenment of a Pratyekabuddha, and some for Unsurpassed Enlightenment; furthermore, they caused the great assembly to give rise to supreme faith in the Triple Gem.
At that time, the World-Honored One, having extensively tamed them for their great benefit, departed from them.
Then the great fish Makara thought to himself:
"Should I now eat again after having heard the Dharma of the three phrases from the World-Honored One?"

He immediately undertook a fast; however, as his rebirth in the animal realm was intensified by the power of his own karma and he was oppressed by hunger and thirst, his veneration for the Blessed One became even deeper, and he passed away to be reborn in the Heaven of the Four Great Kings.
Whenever any being, whether male or female, is born in the heavens, three thoughts immediately arise:
"From where did I die?
Where have I now been born?"
"By what karma was this brought about?
