He then recalled his previous life:
"I died in the realm of animals and have now been born among the Gods of the Four Great Kings, because I gave rise to respectful faith toward the Buddha."
Then that deva thought to himself:
"I should not remain here overnight before seeing the World-Honored One.
Having had this thought, the deva immediately adorned his body, putting on various necklaces of exquisite brilliance, and then filled the corner of his robe with wonderful celestial flowers.

The so-called utpala flowers, padma flowers, kumuda flowers, puṇḍarīka flowers, and māndārava flowers came to the place where the Buddha was after the first watch of the night; having scattered these celestial flowers as an offering to the Buddha, they prostrated at his feet and sat to one side.
The radiance of that devaputra was so brilliant and magnificent that it illuminated the high pavilion and hall on all sides.
At that time, the World-Honored One, in accordance with that devaputra’s inclinations and faculties, taught him the Dharma so that he might realize the principles of the Truths.
At that time, having heard the Dharma, the devaputra immediately attained the fruit of stream-entry while still on his seat. Having seen the Truths, he addressed the World-Honored One, saying:
"Venerable Sir!..."

It is by the Buddha, the World-Honored One, that I have been enabled to realize the fruit of liberation; this was not something that could be accomplished by my parents, kings of men, hosts of devas, śramaṇas, brāhmaṇas, friends, or kinsmen.

Because I have encountered the World-Honored One as a virtuous friend, he has rescued me from the realms of hell, animals, and hungry ghosts and established me in the superior and wondrous states of humans and devas. I shall bring an end to birth and death and attain the path to nirvāṇa; I shall dry up the ocean of blood, transcend the mountain of bones, and with the vajra-pestle of wisdom, shatter the view of a self-identity accumulated since beginningless time, thereby attaining the fruit of stream-entry.

I now take refuge in the Triple Gem of the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha. May the World-Honored One bear witness that I am an upāsaka; from this day forth until the end of my life, I shall observe the five precepts, from abstaining from taking life to abstaining from drinking intoxicants.
Thereupon, before the Buddha, he spoke in verse:
"By the power of the Buddha, The three evil realms are forever closed to me;
I have attained birth in a supreme and wondrous heaven, And shall long follow the path to Nirvāṇa."
Relying upon the World-Honored One, I have attained the pure eye;
having realized and seen the principle of the True Dharma, I shall reach the far shore of the ocean of suffering.
The Buddha transcends gods and humans, free from the afflictions of birth, old age, and death.
Difficult to encounter within the ocean of existence, I have met [the Buddha] and now attained the fruit.
With this adorned body and a pure mind, I prostrate at the Buddha’s feet;
having circumambulated the Dispeller of Enmity, I now depart for the celestial palace.

At that time, having expressed his aspirations, the Makhādeva Devaputra was like a merchant leader who had acquired great wealth and profit, like a farmer who had harvested a bountiful crop, like a valiant warrior who had subdued his enemies, or like a gravely ill person whose many ailments had been removed. Then, taking leave of the Buddha, the devaputra departed for his celestial palace.

At that time, the bhikṣus remained awake during the first and last watches of the night, dwelling with focused minds in contemplation; seeing a great radiance at the place where the World-Honored One was, they conceived a doubt.
When dawn had broken, he said to the World-Honored One:

"During the night, did any of the devas from the Brahma world, or Śakra, Lord of Devas, or the Four Great Kings, or any other host of devas possessing majestic power, come to pay homage to the World-Honored One?"
The Blessed One said:
"O bhikṣus! It was not Brahmā nor any other host of devas; did you bhikṣus not see that great fish Makara with eighteen heads, for whom I preached the sublime Dharma in three statements?"
The bhikṣus said to the Buddha,
“We all saw it.
The Buddha said:
"He came to me during the middle watch of the night; I taught him the Dharma, and having attained the vision of the Truths, he returned to his celestial palace.
Then the bhikṣus again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"What karma did this former-life son of a Mākaṭika fish perform to be born in the realm of the Four Great Kings?"
"Furthermore, by what karma did he personally realize the Four Noble Truths in the presence of the Buddha?
The World-Honored One replied, "O Bhikṣus!"

The karma created by that Fish Devaputra has increased, matured, and reached its fruition through conditions; like a torrential flood, it cannot be turned back. Its retribution is certain to be experienced, and there is no one else who can undergo it on his behalf.

"O bhikṣus! Whatever evil karma that the Devaputra Matsya himself has created, he does not undergo its retribution within the external elements of earth, water, fire, or wind; rather, he experiences its maturation within his own aggregates, elements, and sense-bases."
He then spoke in verse:
"Even if a hundred eons pass, the karma one has created does not perish;
when the causes and conditions meet, one must experience the retribution oneself."
“O bhikṣus! There is karma to be experienced in this life, and there is karma to be experienced in future lives.
What is karma to be experienced in this life?

In a previous life, he was a makara fish; because he conceived a mind of reverence and faith toward me, the maturation of that karma caused him to be reborn in the Heaven of the Four Great Kings. This is called "karma to be experienced upon rebirth."

What is karma to be experienced in a subsequent life? It is as follows: Kapphiṇa went forth in the teaching of the Perfectly Enlightened Buddha Kāśyapa; he recited, mastered, and upheld the teachings, expounding them for others. He became thoroughly skilled in the aggregates, elements, and sense bases, as well as in dependent origination and the possible and impossible. Through the power of the roots of virtue accumulated by that karma, he was reborn in the heavens, and now, in my presence, he has seen the Four Noble Truths. This is called karma to be experienced in a subsequent life.
"O bhikṣus, you should know this:

if one performs purely black karma, one will obtain a purely black ripening; if one performs purely white karma, one will obtain a purely white ripening; and if one performs mixed black-and-white karma, one will obtain a mixed ripening."
"Therefore, monks,
you should abandon purely black karma as well as mixed black-and-white karma, and should diligently cultivate and train in purely white karma.
When the monks had heard what the Buddha said, they rejoiced and accepted it with faith.
Then those five hundred fishermen said to one another:

"Gentlemen, you yourselves have heard that that Kāpilavastu was a great Dharma teacher who was well-versed in the Tripitaka, possessed unimpeded eloquence, and converted hundreds of thousands of people, causing all who heard him to give rise to joy; yet, solely because of harsh speech, he has fallen among the animals."
"We have constantly engaged in evil deeds and lacked compassion, sustaining our lives by killing many sentient beings.
Where shall we be reborn after death?

If we were not born into lowly families at this time, we would have gone forth into homelessness within the well-expounded Dharma and Vinaya of the Tathāgata, rousing a courageous mind to seek diligently without weariness, transcending the four yokes and crossing over the four torrents."
Having spoken these words, they each rested their cheeks in their hands and remained there filled with sorrow.

It is the constant law of all Buddhas that, while abiding in the world before entering parinirvāṇa, they constantly observe the worlds with the Buddha-eye throughout the six periods of day and night out of compassion for the sentient beings to be converted, as explained in detail above.
It was the same for all the great śrāvakas.

Then, the Venerable Śāriputra, observing the world with the wisdom-eye of a śrāvaka, saw that five hundred fishermen were dwelling in a state of weariness and sorrow. He immediately went to where those five hundred men were and addressed them, saying:
"O noble sirs!"
"For what reason, sirs, do you sit here supporting your cheeks with your hands, dwelling in sorrow?
At that time, the fishermen replied,
"Noble One!"
"How can we not be filled with grief and suffering?

We personally heard that Kappila was a great Dharma master who well understood the Tripitaka; he preached without impediment, transforming hundreds of thousands of people and causing all who heard him to give rise to joy. Yet, solely due to harsh speech, he has fallen among the animals."
"We have constantly engaged in evil deeds and lacked compassion, sustaining our lives by killing many sentient beings. Where will we be reborn after death?

If we were not born now into lowly families, we too would have gone forth into homelessness within the well-expounded Dharma and Vinaya of the Tathāgata, rousing a courageous mind to seek the goal with diligence and tirelessness, thereby transcending the four yokes and crossing over the four floods."
"This is not my lot; how could I not feel sorrow and distress?
At that time, Śāriputra said to him:
"O noble one!"
"Within the holy teachings of the Muni, the Lord of Dharma, victory is not determined by family lineage or clan; rather, right conduct alone is held foremost.
He then spoke this verse:
"In the teaching of the Tathāgata, Lineage and clan are not taken into account."
"Observe only the good and evil deeds performed in past lives.

If you have the aspiration in your hearts and desire to leave the household life within the Buddha’s Dharma, and further seek full ordination as bhikṣus, you should go to the World-Honored One and request ordination; the World-Honored One, knowing the proper time, will fulfill your wishes."
The people replied,
"Noble One! If it may be so,
we shall invite the Buddha and seek to go forth into homelessness."
Then Śāriputra, taking five hundred sons of good family, went to where the Buddha was, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, sat to one side, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

"Venerable Sir, these five hundred sons of good family have a deep-seated aspiration; they seek to go forth in this well-expounded Dharma and Vinaya, and wish to receive full ordination (*upasampadā*) to become bhikṣus. We only pray that the World-Honored One, out of compassion, will grant them the going forth and the full ordination."
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the five hundred men, saying:
"Welcome, bhikṣus!
You may practice the holy life."

As soon as the Buddha had spoken these words, his beard and hair fell away of their own accord; the dharma robes were donned upon his body and the alms bowl and water flask appeared in his hands. His majestic deportment was perfected, like that of a bhikṣu with a hundred years of seniority.
A verse says:
"The World-Honored One proclaimed, 'Welcome!'"
His hair fell away and his robes and bowl appeared;
all his faculties were perfectly tranquil and composed, and everything was accomplished according to his thought.
*Vinaya-vibhaṅga of the Mūlasarvāstivāda*, Fascicle Nine.
The Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya, Volume Thirteen,
translated by the Tripitaka Master Yijing by Imperial Decree;
the Fourth Section, Part Two, concerning the training rule on falsely claiming to have attained superhuman states (*uttaramanuṣyadharma*).

At that time, after the Blessed One had granted the full ordination to five hundred fishermen and allowed them to go forth from the household life, he traveled from Vaiśālī to the north of the Bamboo Grove village, where there was an Ambapālī grove, and took up residence there.
At that time, a famine occurred and alms were difficult to obtain; even parents did not provide for their own children, let alone other beggars!
Then the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus, saying:

"Now, during this famine, alms are difficult to obtain and even fathers and sons do not provide for one another. You should each go to a place where you have friends with whom you are on good terms, and observe the rains retreat in a village near Vaiśālī."
"I and Ānanda shall dwell in this forest.
Having heard this, the bhikṣus assented and accepted the instruction; each followed his own companions and friends to a nearby village of Vaiśālī to observe the rains retreat.
At that time, those five hundred *svāgata* bhikṣus, having witnessed this event, said to one another:
"Virtuous ones, you should know what the Blessed One has said:
'In these times of famine, alms-food is difficult to obtain; even fathers and sons do not provide for one another, let alone other beggars!'"
"You should each follow your own companions and observe the rains retreat in the villages near Vaiśālī.
Ānanda and I shall remain here in this grove."
"We have no relatives here upon whom we may rely to observe the rains retreat.

However, I have relatives in a village of fishermen; it would be appropriate to go there to inquire after them and to establish a temporary grass hut outside that village for the purpose of observing the rains retreat."
Then the five hundred bhikṣus went to the fishing village and asked for lodging; they were temporarily provided with small rooms outside the village.
At that time, the bhikṣus said to one another:
"We have heard little and possess no learning. If our kinsmen come to question us, how shall we preach the Dharma to them?"

"When they come, we should praise one another, saying: 'Your kinsmen have gained great merit and benefit, for such a superior and wondrous Saṃgha has been able to dwell here in retreat within your village.'"
This bhikṣu attains the perception of impermanence; the perception of suffering in what is impermanent; the perception of emptiness in suffering;
the perception of non-self in what is empty; the perception of revulsion toward food; the perception of lack of delight in all worldly things; the perception of danger; the perception of abandonment;
the perception of dispassion; the perception of cessation; the perception of death; and the perception of impurity.
The perception of bluish discoloration, the perception of bloating, the perception of oozing pus, the perception of being devoured by worms, the perception of blood-stained flesh,
the perception of dismemberment, the perception of white bones, and the perception of contemplating emptiness— by means of these, this bhikṣu attains the first dhyāna,
the second dhyāna, the third dhyāna, and the fourth dhyāna, and attains loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy, equanimity, and emptiness.
In the sphere of infinite space, the sphere of infinite consciousness, the sphere of nothingness, and the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception,
one attains the four fruits, the six supernormal powers, and the eight liberations.
Later, at another time, when those kinsmen came to visit and inquire after them, the bhikṣus, seeing the kinsmen arrive, immediately began to praise one another:
"Your kinsmen have gained great merit, for in your village there dwell such excellent and sublime Saṃgha members who are observing the rains retreat here."
"This bhikṣu has attained the perception of impermanence," and so on, up to "he has attained the eight liberations.
When his kinsmen had heard this teaching, they said,
"Noble One!"
"You, O virtuous ones, have realized such a supreme fruit.
They replied,
"We have all attained it."

At that time, when the people of the world heard that those who attained the fruits [of the path] were being so honored, they all conceived a sense of affection and joy; consequently, they failed to provide relief for their own parents, wives, children, and relatives, instead each supplying food and drink to the bhikṣus.
At that time, while the World-Honored One had not yet entered parinirvāṇa and remained in the world, he held two great assemblies with his disciples:
the first was on the fifteenth day of the fifth month when they were about to enter the rains retreat;
the second was on the fifteenth day of the eighth month when the period of *pravāraṇā* (the invitation to point out faults) was concluded.

Those who observe the earlier *varṣā* (rainy-season retreat), having received the instructions, go to cities, towns, villages, and settlements to perform the retreat. When the *pravāraṇā* ceremony is concluded, they all assemble; each reports whatever realization they have attained, and those who have not yet attained it request the Dharma for realization.

The bhikṣus who had recently completed their summer retreat near Vaiśālī, having finished making their robes at the end of the three months, were haggard in complexion and emaciated in appearance; carrying their robes and bowls, they proceeded toward the Bamboo Grove Village.

Having arrived at the village, the Venerable Ānanda saw the bhikṣus from afar; out of compassion for his fellow practitioners of the holy life, he called out "Welcome" from a distance and went forward to receive them, taking up their robes, bowls, staffs, water-pots, and other miscellaneous requisites and belongings of the śramaṇas.
He asked again:
"Venerable ones!
From where did you come after completing your summer retreat?"
He replied,
"I observed the three-month rains retreat in the village of Pāvā and have now come here. Ānanda said:
"Gentlemen, during those three months of the rainy season retreat, was it not laborious for you to beg for food and drink?
They replied,
"Although we dwelt there in peace and comfort, begging for food and drink was exceedingly difficult."
At that time, Ānanda replied:
"It is indeed so, venerable sir!
Judging by his evident physical decline and haggard appearance, it is certain that food and drink must be difficult for him to obtain."

At that time, five hundred bhikṣus from the village of fishermen, having completed their summer retreat, also arrived at this village carrying their robes and bowls, their complexions radiant and their countenances robust and flourishing.

At that time, Ānanda saw the bhikṣus from afar; feeling a sense of compassion and affection for his fellow practitioners of the holy life, he called out "Welcome" from a distance and went forward to receive them, taking up their robes, bowls, and other miscellaneous belongings.
As previously detailed, he asked all the questions up to:
"In the village of fishermen, is food and drink easily obtained, and is it a place where one can live in comfort?
The bhikṣu replied:
"I dwell there having truly attained peace and happiness; the food and drink I seek are easily obtained and not difficult to find.
Ānanda replied, "Venerable One!"
"Judging by your physical robustness and the radiant luster of your complexions, it is evident that food and drink must surely be easy for you to obtain.
At that time, Ānanda immediately asked:

"Since this present age is one of famine where food and drink are difficult to find—such that even parents and children cannot provide for one another—why is it that you, venerable sirs, find food so easily?"
He replied: "Regarding my own circle of followers, I have praised them, saying:
'This bhikṣu has attained the perception of impermanence, up to and including the eight liberations.'"
Ānanda asked: "Is the matter you have described true,
or is it false?"
He replied, "It is false. He asked:
"Venerable ones!
Is it appropriate for you to claim, for the sake of a mere bit of food and drink, that you have truly attained superhuman states?
They then replied:
"Whether it was appropriate or not, we have already done it.
At that time, those bhikṣus who delighted in few desires all together censured, disparaged, and rebuked them for their unrighteousness, saying:
"How can you, out of greed for food and drink, falsely claim to have attained the superhuman states when you have not actually attained them?"
Then the bhikṣus reported the matter to the Buddha.
The Buddha, on account of this, assembled the community of bhikṣus; knowing [the cause], he questioned them as previously described in detail.
The Buddha asked the bhikṣus by the banks of the Vipāśā River:
“Monks, did you truly claim to have attained the qualities of a superior person when you had not?
They replied to the Buddha,
“It is true, Blessed One.”
"Venerable Sir!
At that time, the World-Honored One rebuked the bhikṣus in various ways:

"You are not śramaṇas; you do not act in accordance with the practice. This is what should not be done; it is not proper conduct, nor is it something performed by those who have left the household life."
"O bhikṣus! You should know that there are three great thieves in the world.
What are these three?"
"O Bhikṣus!

Suppose there were a great bandit—whether a group of a hundred, a thousand, or a hundred thousand—who would go to a city or village, break through walls or pick locks to steal the property of others; who might sometimes block roads and commit murder, or sometimes set fire to villages, or plunder royal treasuries, or loot towns and districts. This is called the first kind of great bandit dwelling in the world."
"O Bhikṣus!

Suppose there is a great thief who does not have a band of a hundred, nor a thousand, nor a hundred thousand; he does not go to cities or villages to break through walls, pick locks, or steal the property of others, nor does he block roads, burn villages, or plunder the royal treasuries. Yet, he takes the firewood, grass, flowers, fruits, bamboo, timber, and so forth belonging to the Saṃgha, sells them for his own livelihood or gives them to others. This is called the second great thief dwelling in the world."
Furthermore, monks!

There is a great thief who does not have a band of a hundred, a thousand, or a hundred thousand followers; he does not go to cities or villages to break through walls, pick locks, or steal the property of others, nor does he even take grass belonging to the Saṃgha for his livelihood or give it to others. Yet, while having truly not realized the state of a superior person within himself, he falsely claims to have done so. This is called the third great thief dwelling in the world.
"O bhikṣus! Those who are the first and second great thieves are not called 'great thieves';
they are called 'minor thieves. O bhikṣus!"

If one falsely claims to have attained the supreme state of a person when, in truth, they have not, among humans, devas, Māras, Brahmās, śramaṇas, and brāhmaṇas, such a person is a most grievous thief.
He spoke in verse:
"One who is not truly an Arhat, yet claims, 'I am one';
among all gods and humans, such a person is called a great thief."
At that time, after the Blessed One had rebuked that bhikṣu in various ways, he addressed the bhikṣus, saying:
"Having considered ten benefits for the sake of my disciples, I shall establish a training rule (śikṣāpada) in the Vinaya, which should be recited as follows:

'If a bhikṣu, being actually without knowledge and without thorough understanding, knowing for himself that he has not attained the state of a superior person (uttarimanussa-dhamma), the tranquility of a noble one (ariya), the sublime realization, or the dwelling in bliss through wisdom and vision, yet says:'"
"I know; I see.
At a later time, whether questioned or unasked, desiring to purify himself, he speaks thus:
"Venerable sirs!..."
"I truly did not know or see, yet I said that I knew and saw.
Because of this false and deceptive speech, he incurs a *pārājika* offense and should not be lived with.

At that time, after the Blessed One had established the training rule (*śikṣāpada*) for the bhikṣus, there were many bhikṣus dwelling in forest hermitages (*āraṇya*). They made use of coarse bedding and applied themselves to diligent exertion; they attained a slight degree of tranquility through the skillful means of observing specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*), and by means of mundane mental attention (*manasikāra*), they subdued their afflictions so that sensual desire and malice no longer manifested.
Then they immediately said to one another:
"Venerable ones!
Do you know what is happening now?"
That which is to be attained in the araṇya, I have now attained.
Birth has been exhausted, the holy life is established, what was to be done has been accomplished, and there is no further existence.
"I should now abandon my dwelling in the forest hermitage and reside within a village.
He then left the tranquil grove and settled in a village.

There, he frequently encountered women, as well as lay attendants and novices with whom he lived in close association; consequently, his afflictions arose once more, and lustful desire and anger manifested again.
Then those people each had this thought:
“The World-Honored One has established a training rule for his disciples in the Vinaya:

‘If a bhikṣu, being truly without knowledge and without universal knowledge, knowing for himself that he has not attained the state of a superior person, the tranquility of a noble one, the sublime realization, or the dwelling in bliss through wisdom and vision, should nevertheless say:’”
"I know; I see.
At another time, whether questioned or unasked, desiring to purify himself, he makes this statement:
"Venerable sirs!..."
"I truly neither knew nor saw, yet I said that I knew and saw.
One who speaks such false and deceptive words commits a *pārājika* offense and should not be lived with.
Then the bhikṣus said to one another:

"We lived in araṇyas, using coarse bedding and applying ourselves with diligence; having attained a slight degree of tranquility through the skillful means of observing our own characteristics, we subdued our afflictions. Yet we have abandoned the forest hermitage and come to the village. Now that we observe various sensory objects and find our afflictions manifesting as before—as described at length—could it not be that we have committed a pārājika offense?"
"Let us go together to the Venerable Ānanda and inform him of this matter; we shall carry out whatever he instructs.
Having said this, they went to him and asked the Venerable Ānanda:
"Venerable One!..."
Do you understand?
Just as the Buddha, the World-Honored One, has prescribed the training rules for his disciples:
if a bhikṣu commits even a pārājika offense, he should not live in communal residence with them.
"While we were in the araṇya, afflictions did not arise; now that we have come to the village, afflictions have arisen again," as explained at length above.
"We all have doubts: could it be that we have committed a pārājika offense?"
"We shall ask the Venerable Ānanda and practice according to what he says.
For this reason, we have come now to the Venerable's presence to seek his detailed counsel and resolution; could it be that we have committed a *pārājika* offense?"
At that time, the Venerable Ānanda, having heard these matters spoken by the bhikṣus, led the group to the place where the Blessed One was, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and sat to one side.
Then the Venerable Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One, Great Virtuous One!
Thus, for the sake of the bhikṣus, you have established this training rule within the Vinaya:”
Furthermore, if a bhikṣu—expanding the description up to the point where he has committed a *pārājika* offense—is no longer to be lived with.

These bhikṣus dwell in an araṇya, utilizing marginal lodgings and applying themselves with diligence; having attained a slight degree of tranquility through the skillful means of observing specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*), they apply their attention to subdue the afflictions, so that sensual desire and malice no longer manifest.
Then they immediately spoke to one another:
"Venerable ones!
Do you know what is happening now?"

That which is to be attained in the araṇya, I have now attained: birth has been exhausted, the holy life has been established, what was to be done has been accomplished, and there is no further existence.
"I should now abandon my dwelling in the forest hermitage and go to live within a village.
He then abandoned his quiet retreat and took up residence in a village.
There, he frequently encountered women and saw attendants and novices living in close proximity with them; consequently, his afflictions arose once more, and sensual desire became manifest.
Those bhikṣus each gave rise to a doubt, thinking:
"Could it be that I have committed a pārājika offense?
For this reason they came to question me, yet I did not dare to resolve their uncertainty.
They have all come here.
O Virtuous World-Honored One!
Could it be that they have committed an extremely grave offense?
The Blessed One said:
"Ānanda, setting aside cases of overweening pride, he has committed no offense."

At that time, the World-Honored One, having used various skillful means to provide exhortations and instructions in accordance with the needs of those who delight in the precepts and those who revere the precepts, spoke to the bhikṣus, saying:
"O bhikṣus!..."
Thus it should be understood: the former was the original prohibition, while this is a subsequent allowance. I now declare to my śrāvaka disciples:

"If a bhikṣu, being truly without knowledge and without thorough understanding, knows for himself that he has not attained the state of a superior person—the noble, sublime realization, wisdom, vision, and dwelling in bliss—and yet says:
'I know; I see.'"
At another time, whether questioned or not, desiring to purify himself, he speaks thus:
"Venerable sirs!
It is true that I neither knew nor saw, yet I said that I knew and saw."
"False and deceptive speech—excepting overweening pride—this bhikṣu also incurs a pārājika offense and should not be lived with.
The meaning of "bhikṣu" is as explained above.
To say "there is no knowledge" means not knowing form, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness.
To say "there is no thorough knowledge" means not thoroughly knowing form, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness.
Regarding "the state of a superior person" (*uttarimanussa-dhamma*): "superior" (*uttari*) refers to the Form Realm being above the Desire Realm, and the Formless Realm being above the Form Realm.
"Person" (*manussa*) refers to an ordinary person.
"State" (*dhamma*) refers to the five hindrances (*nīvaraṇa*) and so forth; because one can eliminate these hindrances, it is called "superior."
"Quiescence" refers to nirvāṇa.
"Noble ones" refers to Buddhas and śrāvakas.
"Exalted realization" refers to the four fruits of the śramaṇa.
The stream-enterer, the once-returner, the non-returner, and the arhat.
The wise speak of four knowledges:
the knowledge of suffering, the knowledge of its origin, the knowledge of its cessation, and the knowledge of the path, as well as other various knowledges.
"Seeing" refers to the vision of the Four Noble Truths.
"Abiding in peace and happiness" refers to the four dhyānas; these are cultivated, not innate.
"I know" refers to knowing the dharmas of the Four Truths.

To speak of "viewing the self" (*ātma-dṛṣṭi*) means: seeing devas, seeing nāgas, seeing yakṣas, seeing garuḍas, gandharvas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, kumbhāṇḍas, kaṭapūtanas, and piśāca ghosts; hearing the voices of devas up to the voices of piśāca ghosts; going to the abodes of devas up to the abodes of piśācas; and those various devas, nāgas, up to the piśācas coming to my presence. [Thinking: "I am constantly familiar with and conversing with these devas and others," and "those devas and others also come to me, and we are constantly familiar with one another and converse together. Yet, although they have not actually realized it, they claim, "I have realized it," saying that they have attained the perception of impermanence (*anitya-saṃjñā*), and so on extensively up to attaining the eight liberations (*aṣṭa-vimokṣa*).
"At another time" means at a different occasion.
"If questioned" means being asked by another.
"If not questioned" means that one spontaneously gives rise to regret and harbors distress.
"One who desires self-purification" refers to one who aspires to emerge from the offense.
To say, "Venerable sir, I truly did not know," refers to the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*); to say, "I truly did not see," refers to the visual consciousness (*cakṣurvijñāna*).
"False and deceptive speech" is a synonym for this.

"Excepting those with overweening pride" means excluding those who, though they have not actually realized [the path], claim to have already attained it; because they lack a deceitful mind, they do not commit a fundamental offense.
"This" refers to that person.
"Bhikṣu" means one who abides in the nature of a bhikṣu, as explained in detail above.
Up to and including the point that one should not be appointed to perform the twelve types of duties; for this reason, it is called "one with whom one should not co-reside."
Regarding this, what are the characteristics of the offense and its specific details?
The summary verse says:
Seeing signs at an araṇya, Accepting an exquisite seat within a dwelling.
Being able to know their own characteristics, they manifest their bodies through skillful means.
If a bhikṣu, desiring thus and assenting thus, should speak these words:
"I see the devas, even down to the kaṭapūtanas."
If one says, "I saw a *pāramīṣika*," one incurs a *pārājika* offense; even down to saying,
"I saw a *pāṃśukūla-preta*," one incurs a *sthūlātyaya* offense.
If a bhikṣu, desiring it thus and approving it thus, speaks these words:
"I have heard that there are gods, even down to the kaṭapūtanas."
For one who [speaks thus], a *pārājika* offense is incurred;
even for one who is a *pāṃśukūla-piśāca*, a *sthūlātyaya* offense is incurred.
If a bhikṣu, with a deceptive mind, speaks these words:
If one says, "I shall go to the abodes of the devas,
even to the abodes of the kaṭapūtanas," one incurs a pārājika offense;
if one says, "even to the abodes of the pāmsupradhāvanas (scavenger spirits)," one incurs a sthūlātyaya offense.
If a bhikṣu, with a false mind, speaks these words:
"The devas have come to my place," or even, "The kaṭapūtanas have come to my place."
Regarding the phrase "one who says," if [the statement] is made with a deceptive mind, one incurs a *pārājika* offense;
this continues down to the case of a *pāṃśukūla-preta*, for which one incurs a *sthūlātyaya*.
If a bhikṣu, with a deceptive mind, speaks such words as these:
"If one says, 'I am constantly familiar with and converse with the various devas,
even down to the kaṭapūtanas,' one incurs a pārājika offense;
if one says 'scavenger spirits' (pāṃśukṛmi), one incurs a sthūlātyaya offense."
If a bhikṣu, with a deceitful mind, speaks thus:
"The devas come to me constantly to socialize and converse with me, even down to the kaṭapūtanas."
If [one says this], one incurs a *pārājika* offense;
if one says "a *piśāca* who eats excrement," one incurs a *sthūlātyaya*.
If a bhikṣu, with a deceitful mind, speaks these words:
If one has not actually attained the perception of impermanence yet says,
"I have attained it," they incur a *pārājika* offense;
this applies even up to falsely claiming to have attained both-fold liberation (*ubhayatobhāgavimukti*), for all such cases, one incurs a *pārājika* offense.
If a bhikṣu, with a deceitful mind, speaks these words:

"There are many bhikṣus dwelling in villages or in forest hermitages who are frequently harassed by non-human beings; among them, those who have attained the fruit of stream-entry, once-returning, non-returning, or arhatship will not be harassed by non-human beings."
"If one says, 'I was not harassed by non-human beings there,' one incurs a *pārājika* offense.
If a bhikṣu, with a deceitful mind, speaks these words:

"In a certain house, having accepted an invitation to a meal, a magnificent seat adorned with various colored fabrics was prepared; only one who has attained the four fruits of the path may approach that seat to receive food and drink."
If one says, "I too have obtained that excellent seat and food," that bhikṣu incurs a *pārājika* offense.

If there are many bhikṣus dwelling in a forest hermitage (*āraṇya*) within a village, who possess a small degree of self-mastery and have attained concentration of mind, and who, by means of the mundane path (*laukikamārga*), have suppressed and eliminated the afflictions (*kleśa*) such that desire, greed, hatred, and anger no longer manifest; [if among them...]
A bhikṣu, with a deceptive mind, speaks thus:

"I too dwell in that araṇya; I have attained a slight concentration on specific characteristics and, by means of the mundane path, have suppressed and eliminated the afflictions, so that sensual desire and ill-will no longer manifest."
If a bhikṣu, with a deceitful mind wishing to exalt himself, speaks these words:
"There is a bhikṣu who has personally seen the devas," he incurs a pārājika offense.
If one does not say, "This is me," regarding [these beings], one incurs a *sthūlātyaya* offense;
likewise, even down to seeing a *kaṭapūtana*, if one does not say, "This is me," one incurs a *sthūlātyaya* offense;
even down to a *pāmsu-śmāśānika* (scavenger ghost), one incurs a *duṣkṛta* offense.
If a bhikṣu, with a deceitful mind, speaks these words:
"There is a bhikṣu who has heard the voices of the devas," and does not say,
"It was I," he incurs a sthūlātyaya offense.
In this manner, up to hearing that it is a *kattapūtana* and not saying "it is me," one incurs a *sthūlātyaya*;
up to hearing that it is a *pāmsupreta*, one incurs a *duṣkṛta* offense.
If a bhikṣu, with a deceptive mind, speaks these words:
"A bhikṣu has gone to the realm of the devas," without saying "I am he," he commits a sthūlātyaya offense.
Up to the realm of the *kaṭapūtana* spirits, one incurs a *sthūlātyaya* offense;
up to the realm of the *vighasa-bhuj* (scavenger) spirits, one incurs a *duṣkṛta* offense.
If a bhikṣu, with a deceptive mind, speaks these words:
"If there is a bhikṣu to whom devas come to visit, or even kaṭapūtanas,
and he does not say, 'It is I,' he incurs a sthūlātyaya offense."
If it concerns a *pāmsu-śuṣka* (filth-eating) spirit, one incurs a *duṣkṛta* offense.
If a bhikṣu, with a deceptive mind, speaks thus:
"There is a bhikṣu who constantly goes to the celestial realms to converse and debate with the devas, even down to the *kaṭapūtanas*."
If one says, "This is not me," one incurs a *sthūlātyaya* offense.
If it is a *pāṃśukula* (scavenger) spirit, one incurs a *duṣkṛta* offense.
If a bhikṣu, with a deceptive mind, speaks these words:
"If there is a bhikṣu to whom devas come to converse and discuss matters, even down to the kaṭapūtanas,
and he does not say, 'It is I,' he incurs a sthūlātyaya offense."
The description of the refuse-rag robe is the same as before.
If a bhikṣu, with a deceptive mind, speaks these words:
"There is a bhikṣu who has attained the perception of impermanence," as extensively explained before, up to "he has attained the eight liberations."
If he does not say, "It was I," that bhikṣu incurs a sthūlātyaya offense.

Suppose there are many bhikṣus living in a forest hermitage village who are constantly harassed by non-human beings; among them, there is a bhikṣu who has attained the four fruits and is not harassed by non-human beings. If that bhikṣu, with a deceitful mind, speaks these words:
"There is a bhikṣu living in that village who is not harassed by non-human beings."
If one does not say, "This is mine," one incurs a *sthūlātyaya* offense.
If there are many bhikṣus sitting on excellent seats in a layperson's house and receiving food, they all obtain the four fruits [of the śramaṇa].
If a bhikṣu, with a deceitful mind, speaks these words:
"There is a bhikṣu who has accepted an excellent seat in that house," and does not say,
"It is I," he incurs a sthūlātyaya offense.

If any bhikṣus dwelling in an araṇya-village attain a minor concentration on specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa-samādhi*), and by means of the mundane path (*laukika-mārga*) suppress and eliminate the afflictions such that desire, greed, hatred, and ill-will no longer manifest, yet they do not claim "this is I," they incur a *sthūlātyaya*.
If a bhikṣu, with a deceptive mind, speaks these words:
"There is a bhikṣu residing in that village who has attained a slight concentration on specific characteristics (svalakṣaṇa-samādhi) such that even the afflictions do not manifest."
If one does not say, "This is mine," one incurs a *sthūlātyaya*.
The summary verse says:
"Predicting victory and speaking contrary to the truth; during a drought, there is little rain."
Through the power of karma, a man became a woman; at a hot spring, she heard the sound of elephants.
The Buddha was staying in the High-Storyed Hall by the Monkey Pond in Vaiśālī.
At that time, King Ajātaśatru of Magadha had previously been at odds with the Licchavis of Vaiśālī.
King Ajātaśatru then arrayed his fourfold army—elephants, cavalry, chariots, and infantry—and set out for the country of the Vṛji to engage them in battle.
At that time, the people of the Vṛji informed the Licchavis of Vaiśālī, saying:
"Ajātaśatru, King of Magadha, has arrayed his fourfold army and is coming here desiring to fight."
When he heard this, he also arrayed his fourfold army and went out of the city to resist them.
As the troops were setting forth,
the Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana took up his robe and bowl and entered the city of Vaiśālī during the first watch of the day, intending to go on almsround.
At that time, the Vṛji assembly within this city saw Mahāmaudgalyāyana from afar and said to one another: "Do you know?

We have heard of the Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana as being a third-order saint who has nothing—however small—that he does not see or know. We ought to ask that noble one which of the two kingdoms will emerge victorious in their battle."
He immediately went to inquire, saying:
"Noble One!
King Ajātaśatru of Magadha has come to destroy our kingdom; we have now gone out to meet him in battle. Which side shall prevail when the two armies clash?"
The Venerable One replied, "You have won.
Having heard this, they said to one another:
“Noble One! Maudgalyāyana has granted us this prophecy: ‘In battle, you shall be victorious.

Having heard this, the people were filled with joy and leaped for gladness; they deceived their enemies by attacking them unawares. They immediately engaged in combat and utterly defeated them; the enemy forces fell apart like a crumbling wall as they pursued the fleeing remnants toward the banks of the Gaṅgā River. Once the people of Vaiśālī had achieved victory, their courage and vigor redoubled.
At that time, King Ajātaśatru thought to himself:
"The people in this city harbor fierce and violent intentions; if they cross the river now to seize me, they will slaughter me all together, like fish caught in a net."
Having formed this thought, he addressed the entire army, saying:
"All of you must unite your minds and turn back your forces to fight together.
Upon hearing the King's command, each member of the assembly had this thought:
"We came from our own country to punish Vaiśālī; we must not now be defeated and allowed to live.
With one mind, they all turned their forces back to fight. At that time, the people of this city were subsequently defeated and retreated into the city, closing the gates to fortify themselves.
Once the King of Magadha had achieved victory, he withdrew his army and returned to Rājagṛha.
Subsequently, the Licchavis within the city gathered in the streets and alleys and began to mock him, saying:
"That Mahāmaudgalyāyana predicted our victory in battle; yet now this entire city has been utterly defeated and lost—how can that be called a victory?"
At that time, the six bhikṣus entered the city to beg for alms; hearing their disparagement, they asked them, "Whom are you now disparaging?"
The people replied,
"They are disparaging you!
The group of six reported this, saying:
"What offense have we committed that causes you to reproach us?
The people replied, "Noble One!"
"Mahāmaudgalyāyana prophesied that I would be victorious in battle, yet now this city of mine has been completely destroyed by them;
how can this be called victory? The group of six replied, "In your initial battle, which country did you defeat?"
The people replied,
"We were victorious at the beginning of the battle.
The group of six answered:
"Once you have won the battle, you should immediately return; who would further send you to pursue the enemy host?
Have you not heard that even a jackal, when driven by necessity, possesses strength equal to a fierce tiger?"
When those people heard these words, they realized they were without justification and remained silent, offering no reply.
At that time, the group of six bhikṣus said to one another:
"We should respond according to the occasion regarding the matter of victory in battle, so as not to cause great offense among these people."
"However, since Mahāmaudgalyāyana has committed an offense, I should now interrogate him so that he may confess his transgression.
At that time, the six bhikṣus returned to their residence; after eating, they went to where Mahāmaudgalyāyana was, joined their palms in reverence, prostrated at his feet, and said:
"We wish now to inquire about a minor matter; we pray only that you will grant us your compassionate attention and permission to speak."
Maudgalyāyana replied,
"You may bring forth any of the five classes of offenses as you wish.
The group of six addressed him, saying:
“Venerable sir, you prophesied that the Licchavis would be victorious in battle, yet Vaiśālī has been destroyed by others; how can this be called victory?

You wander for alms with your bowl, yet instead of sustaining yourself, you utter false prophecies regarding the affairs of others. Seeing no evidence of reality, you cause the masses to harbor contempt and suspicion, such that wherever we go, slander fills the roads and we are unable to obtain alms.”
"Since you, O virtuous one, have committed an offense, you should repent according to the Dharma.
Maudgalyāyana replied,
"O Venerable One!"
"I see no fault. At that time,
the group of six monks said to one another, "Do you all know?"
As the Blessed One has said:
"If one does not acknowledge their offense, one should perform the formal act of suspension for not acknowledging an offense (adarśana-pratiniḥsarga-sthāpana-karman) against them.
What constitutes "not acknowledging" an offense?
"This matter cannot be concealed.
Who is the official in charge?
Send someone to strike the *gandī*."
The administrator asked,
"What do you wish to do?
He replied:
“Since the one of few desires, Maudgalyāyana, has committed an offense but does not see it, we should now perform the *jñapti-karman* of setting him aside.
Then the official in charge went with the group of six toward the place of the senior monks; at that time, the Venerable Śāriputra was the senior of the assembly.
Then the official in charge said to the Elder,
"The gong must be struck.
The Elder asked:
"What do you wish to do?
Do not allow the True Dharma to suffer any impairment; for whom will you perform the *parivāsa* (probation) and even the *āvarhaṇa* (expiation of the offense)?
He replied:

"There are no such matters as you claim; it is merely that the Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana has falsely prophesied events concerning others, as described at length above, and refuses to acknowledge his fault.
We shall therefore perform the formal act of 'not acknowledging a fault' (*adarśanīya-karman*) against him in accordance with the Dharma."
Śāriputra said: "Venerable ones!
Do not commit what is contrary to the Dharma by harassing the elder bhikṣus of virtuous standing."
The Great Master, the World-Honored One, is endowed with all-encompassing wisdom and has attained great mastery over all matters.
You should now go and request the Buddha to resolve your doubts; you should then carry out whatever the Buddha instructs.
At that time, the bhikṣus went to inform the Blessed One of these circumstances. The Blessed One told them:
"Whenever there is combat, non-humans fight first, and only afterwards do humans; if the non-humans are victorious, the humans shall also be victorious."
When Maudgalyāyana prophesied that the Licchavis would be victorious, the non-human spirits of Vaiśālī were victorious and those of Rājagṛha were defeated.
Once they reached the riverbank, however, the non-human spirits of Rājagṛha were victorious and those of Vaiśālī were defeated.
I have recorded only the initial excellence, not what followed later.
If one were to ask about the matter from beginning to end in this manner, Maudgalyāyana would have answered all its details at that time.
You bhikṣus!
Mahāmaudgalyāyana was without offense.
If a bhikṣu records a matter with such an intention, he is without offense;
if it is otherwise, he incurs an offense of transgression against the Dharma (vayadharmika-āpatti).
The Buddha was staying in the High Hall by the side of the Monkey Pond in Vaiśālī.
At that time, the various non-Buddhist practitioners gave a prophecy to the laypeople, saying that for twelve years there would be no rain due to drought.
The Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana took up his robe and bowl and entered the city of Vaiśālī to go on his alms round.
At that time, the people of the city asked him,
"Noble One!..."
"When will it rain?
Maudgalyāyana replied,
"After seven days have passed, it shall rain."

When the people heard that the Sage had prophesied rain after seven days had passed, they all sowed the rice and wheat stored in their granaries within the fields. After seven days had elapsed, clouds rose and thunder rolled, but only a small amount of rain fell; it was just enough to settle the dust before it ceased.
At that time, the people in the markets and on the streets all began to mock and disparage them, saying:
"Do you people know?

It would be better to believe in the non-Buddhists than to believe in the śramaṇas, the sons of Śākya, who constantly cover their bodies with saffron robes like birch bark, yet are truly devoid of awareness."
At that time, as the group of six bhikṣus were entering for alms, they heard these words of disparagement and asked them,
"Whom do you all despise?
They replied:
"We detest you! they said.
He asked, "What fault have we committed that causes you to revile and detest us?"
The people replied, "Mahāmaudgalyāyana clearly prophesied that after seven days had passed, rain would surely fall.
Having heard this, we planted all the grain and wheat within our storehouses in the fields; yet the heavens did not send rain."
The group of six replied, "You always associate with non-Buddhists;
when you see them predict that clouds have risen and lightning has struck, and there is only a slight drizzle, you immediately proclaim that it will rain heavily."

"Even though Maudgalyāyana predicted that there would still be much rain from the heavens and flowing water on the earth, how could that noble one have made such a prediction for you all—that the crops you have sown would all ripen?"
He replied, "No.
The group of six monks said to him:
"If it is as you say, what fault is there in that for which you are seen to be censured?
At this, they remained silent and speechless.
The six bhikṣus then said to one another:
"Nanda and Upānanda! For now, I shall answer the assembly as the occasion requires;
however, since the one of few desires, Maudgalyāyana, has himself committed an offense, we shall go to him and cause him to confess and repent."
Having returned to the monastery, finished his meal, and put away his robes and bowl, he went to where Mahāmaudgalyāyana was and said to him:
"I pay homage to the Elder!
Maudgalyāyana replied:
“I am free from illness.
He spoke again with renewed earnestness:
“Venerable Elder, I pray that you will grant me leave; I wish to interrogate him regarding his offense.”
He replied:
"Among the five classes of offenses, you may interrogate me as you wish.
He then spoke:
“Does the Elder know?
The non-Buddhists have predicted that there will be no rain for twelve years, yet you, Venerable One, have predicted that it shall rain after seven days.”

"Venerable Elder, you ought to lift your robes so as not to let them be stained by mud; surely alms-food held in a bowl is enough to sustain one's body. Why do you falsely record matters concerning others with such empty intent, such that the path we travel is filled with slander and we are unable to obtain alms?"
"Since you have committed an offense, you should repent according to the Dharma.
Maudgalyāyana replied,
"Venerable friend!"
"I see no fault. At that time,
the group of six monks said to one another, "Do you all know?"
As the Blessed One has said:
"If one does not acknowledge their offense, a formal act of suspension for not acknowledging an offense (adarśana-pratiniḥsarga-sthāpana-karman) should be performed against them.
Who is the official who administers this?
"Sound the *ghanṭā*.
This was explained at length until it reached the point where Śāriputra, acting as the senior elder (*sthavira*), was sent to inform the Buddha.
The Buddha addressed the bhikṣus:
“There are five causes and conditions by which the heavens do not send down rain, yet those who practice astrology, failing to understand them well, declare that it will rain.
What are these five?
Bhikṣus, you should know!”

If one sees clouds rising, lightning striking, thunder rolling, and winds howling, the astrologers at that time record and say, "It will rain. Yet this great earth possesses a fire element which rises into the void and dries up the rain; this is the first cause and condition for no rain.
Furthermore, monks!

If one sees clouds rising and the wind stirring, and the astrologers predict that it will rain, yet a great wind arises in the sky and blows this rain into the Śara grove, or into the Kalinga forest, or into some woodland, causing the rain to fall only there, this is the second cause and condition for the lack of rain.
Furthermore, monks!

If clouds arise and the wind stirs, the astrologers may predict that it will rain; yet at that time, the rain-deities remain negligent and do not pour down sweet rain from time to time. This is the third cause and condition for the lack of rain.
Furthermore, monks!

Even when astrologers record that it shall rain, because sentient beings delight in unwholesome dharmas, give rise to improper greed, and abide in wrong views, due to these causes and conditions, the heavens do not send down rain from time to time; this is the fourth cause and condition for the lack of rain.
Furthermore, monks!

Even when astrologers record that it will rain, the asura king Rāhula emerges from the great ocean and, with both hands, scoops up the falling rain and casts it back into the great ocean. This is the fifth cause and condition for the lack of rain, yet the astrologers do not know this and still record that it will rain.
"O Bhikṣus, you should know!
When Maudgalyāyana predicted rain, the Asura King Rāhula cupped the rain in his hands and cast it into the great ocean; yet, it was not that there was no rain."
"Did he not at that time ask whether the crops had all ripened?
At that moment, Maudgalyāyana answered according to the facts.
Bhikṣus, you should know this!"
"Mahāmaudgalyāyana is without offense.
Should it be otherwise, one incurs an offense of transgression against the Dharma.
The World-Honored One was staying in the High-Roofed Hall beside the Monkey Pond in Vaiśālī.
At that time, there lived in this city a disciple of the Nirgrantha (Naked Ascetic) school whose wife was pregnant.

Then, the Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana entered the city to beg for alms and arrived at the house of the Nirgrantha disciple. When the head of the household saw the Venerable One, he thought to himself:

"This Mahāmaudgalyāyana is renowned by all as the third among the Noble Ones, who is without anything he does not know or see. I should now ask him whether the child my wife is carrying will be a boy."
"Are you a woman?
Having had this thought, he asked Maudgalyāyana:
"Noble One!..."
"Is my wife pregnant with a girl or a boy?
The Venerable One replied:
"O Noble One! A male child is within your womb.

When ordinary people hear such news of prosperity, they all rejoice; they immediately leap for joy and, filling their alms bowls with excellent, exquisite, fragrant, and delicious food, offer them to the Venerable One, and further entreat him, saying:
"Please come again on another day.
He replied,
"I am free from illness."
Having dismissed him, he departed.
Nearby, at the dwelling of a follower of a non-Buddhist sect, there was a naked ascetic who served as their leader. Seeing Mahāmaudgalyāyana departing with his alms-bowl full, he thought to himself:
"I have only one family that provides me with food, yet it has been snatched away from me by the conversion of a son of the Śākya śramaṇa; this is no good thing."
"I should now go to the householder and ask him the reason for this; what counsel shall we deliberate upon with that śramaṇa?
He then went quickly to his house and asked, "Householder!"
"Has the śramaṇa Maudgalyāyana come to our home?
The householder replied,
"He has come."
He asked, "What is it that you wish to inquire about? He replied:
I asked: "Is the child your wife now carries in her womb a boy or a girl?"
He replied, "It is a boy.
At that time, the naked ascetic was skilled in divination; having divined that it was a girl, he immediately turned his face away, flipped over his palms, and laughed.
Having seen this, the elder approached and asked,
"For what reason do you turn your face away, flip your palms,
and laugh? He replied:
"I observe this woman and do not see any man.
At that time, the face of the elder manifested an expression of anger, with three peaks rising upon his forehead, as he addressed her:
"What do you know or see, you who have plucked out your hair and bared your body?"
"How could the wisdom of Mahāmaudgalyāyana be inferior to yours?
The Noble One prophesied that a son would certainly be born; yet you, with your shallow understanding, insist that it will be a daughter.
Having been thus rebuked, he recalculated the matter and determined it was indeed a girl. He then changed his expression and said to the elder:
"Even if the śramaṇa Gautama has predicted that this will be a boy, it is not a boy; she will certainly give birth to a girl.
When her months were fulfilled, she indeed gave birth to a girl.

At that time, the elder and his entire family all gave rise to derision and extensively spread slanderous rumors, saying: "It would be better if those non-Buddhist practitioners were not mistaken in their predictions; they do not compare to these śramaṇas, whose words are all false. Maudgalyāyana predicted a son, yet instead a daughter was born."
At that time, rumors spread clamorously throughout the city and its suburbs; consequently, the people in the markets, shops, streets, and thoroughfares all began to mock and disparage him, saying:
"Do you people know?"
"It would be better to favor non-Buddhists than to place no trust in the Śramaṇas, the sons of Śākya.
At that time, the six bhikṣus were entering for alms; hearing these words of disparagement, they said to them, "Whom do you find so objectionable?"
He replied,
"I am dissatisfied with you.
They reported this, saying:
"What fault have I committed that causes you to revile and disparage me?
The people replied,
"O Noble One!"
“Maudgalyāyana predicted that this woman of the non-Buddhist sect would give birth to a son, yet now she has given birth to a daughter.
Having heard this, the group of six monks said to the people:

“All people in this world are adrift and submerged in an ocean of ignorance; only the Buddha, the World-Honored One, speaks without falsehood when granting predictions, whereas what others say may contain discrepancies.”
"However, as for those born among humans, they are either male or female; how could they possibly be born as dogs or monkeys?
When the people heard this, they remained silent and did not answer.
At that time, the group of six—Nanda and Upananda—said to one another:
"I shall answer the assembly as the occasion demands; however, the one of few desires, Maudgalyāyana, has committed an offense himself.
He spoke at length as previously described, concluding by saying:
"Among the five categories of offenses, you may interrogate him as you please."
He addressed him, saying:
"Venerable Elder, you should know: do you not remember that you predicted to the disciples of those outsiders that the pregnant woman would certainly give birth to a son?"
"Now that a son has been born, we should celebrate together; you may eat as much sugar and rock honey as you please.

However, by carrying your alms bowl to beg for food, you fail to alleviate our hunger; furthermore, by idly recording others' affairs with a distracted mind, you have caused us to be unable to obtain alms."
"Since you, Venerable One, have committed an offense, you ought to repent according to the Dharma.
Maudgalyāyana replied,
"Venerable One!"
"I do not see any offense.
At that time, the group of six called upon the official in charge of affairs and struck the *gandi* to assemble the Sangha, as previously described in detail.
Eventually, the World-Honored One said:
“O bhikṣus! There are four things that should not be contemplated.
If one forces oneself to contemplate them, the mind will become confused or driven to madness.”
What are the four?
First, the conceptualization of a self-soul;
second, the conceptualization of the world.
Third, he contemplates the karmic maturation of sentient beings;
fourth, he contemplates the realm of all Buddhas.
However, at the time of his prophecy, Mahāmaudgalyāyana was actually male; later, through the maturation of karma, he was transformed into a woman.
If that householder asks Mahāmaudgalyāyana:
"When my wife gave birth, was it a boy or a girl?"
Then Mahāmaudgalyāyana declared,
"It is a girl. O bhikṣus!
"Because Maudgalyāyana recorded the events based on what was actually present at that time, there is no offense.
The Buddha was staying at the Bamboo Grove, the Kalandaka Pond, in Rājagṛha.
Within this city there was an elder who heard it said:
"If one provides food and drink for the Saṃgha without prior announcement, their wealth and provisions will suddenly be replenished, and whatever they seek will increase."
At that time, the householder thought to himself:
"This is an excellent means for acquiring wealth; I should now suddenly provide a meal for the Sangha without giving prior notice."

He immediately went to the marketplace and purchased a great deal of pure meat; he then added ghee to it in a large cauldron to prepare a delicious porridge. Having completed the preparations, he went to the city gate and said to the gatekeeper:
"You should know this now!"
"If you see a bhikṣu begging for food or drink, please have him come to my home.
He replied, "Very well!"
"I shall send him away.
Seeing that the bhikṣu was about to go out for alms, he said to him,
"Noble one!"
"Today, before midday, the householder so-and-so will give food to those who beg.
When the mendicants heard this announcement, they all went to that householder’s residence.

"O bhikṣus! This Mahāmaudgalyāyana spoke with the perception of reality, and thus there is no offense.

The Training Rule on Intentional Emission of Semen. The First Training Rule on Intentional Emission of Semen. At that time, the Blessed One was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.

At that time, it was the habitual practice of the Venerable Udāyin that whenever he resided in a village, a town, or within a monastery, he would rise early in the morning to sweep the courtyards and dwellings, smearing them with fresh cow dung. Having washed his hands and feet outside the room and used a tooth-stick, he would take up his robes and bowl during the first part of the day and enter the village or town to go on almsround; however, he did not properly guard his sense faculties nor abide in right mindfulness.
Having obtained food, he returned to his original place; when he had finished eating, put away his robes and bowl, and washed his feet, he entered his cell to rest.
Whenever a sensual desire arose within him, he would grasp his penis with his hand to discharge semen and experience pleasure.
At that time, a great number of bhikṣus, while inspecting the dwellings, arrived at the place where Udāyin resided; they exchanged greetings with one another and sat down to one side.
Then the bhikṣus asked Udāyin: "Venerable one! Are you able to endure the various affairs of the community?
Are you free from illness and affliction, and do you dwell in comfort?"
"I do not consider begging for food to be a hardship.
He then addressed the bhikṣus, saying:
"I am now able to endure all matters without any illness or affliction; alms-food is easily obtained, and I dwell in peace and happiness."
The people asked, "For what reason,
Venerable One, are you able to endure all these matters and dwell in peace and happiness,
free from anxiety and distress? Udāyin replied:
"Venerable sir, do you not know?

It is my regular practice that whenever I am staying in a village, a town, or within a monastery, I rise early in the morning to sprinkle and sweep the courtyards and dwellings," and so forth, as described previously.

Even to the point of holding his organ with his hand to discharge semen for the sake of pleasure—by means of this cause and condition, he attains freedom from feverish distress and dwells in peace and happiness, not regarding the practice of begging for food as suffering.

When the bhikṣus heard these words, they were neither pleased nor displeased; they left him and went to the place where the World-Honored One was. Having prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, they sat to one side and reported the aforementioned matter in detail to the Buddha.
For these reasons, the Buddha, observing two matters, assembled the community of bhikṣus.
What are the two?
First, he wished to let my śrāvaka disciples know that the actions they have performed are contrary to the Dharma.
Secondly, because this served as the condition for my desire to establish a training rule (*śikṣāpada*) for the śrāvakas.
It is the constant law of the Buddhas to inquire knowingly; thus, it is said at length. Then, the Blessed One, knowing the proper time, asked Udāyin:
"Is it true that you have committed such an unseemly act?"
He replied, "It is indeed so.
The World-Honored One rebuked him with various words of censure:
"What you have done is not the way of a śramaṇa, it is not in accordance with the Dharma, it is not a pure practice, and it is not what one who has gone forth ought to do.

How is it that you, a deluded person, having gone forth within my well-expounded Dharma and Vinaya, and having heard the teaching on the subtle Dharma of liberation through wisdom of mind and insight—which is free from greed, hatred, and delusion—could commit such an unwholesome act?"
"O fool! It would be better for you to grasp a terrifying black snake with your hand than to grasp your own generative organ with a defiled mind and discharge impurity.
How can you, O fool, receive with both hands the food and drink offered by those faithful brahmins and householders?"
"How can one perform such an unrighteous act with one's hands while claiming it will bring peace and happiness?
After the Blessed One had rebuked them in these various ways, he addressed the bhikṣus, saying:
"Having considered ten benefits—as explained at length previously—I shall establish a training rule within the Vinaya for my śrāvaka disciples. It shall be stated as follows:"
"If a bhikṣu intentionally emits semen, it is a saṃghāvaśeṣa.

At that time, after the Blessed One had established this training rule for the bhikṣus, there were some bhikṣus who emitted semen during sleep in dreams; they each felt remorse and were uneasy, and said to one another:
"Do you know, sirs?"
The Blessed One established a training rule for the bhikṣus in the Vinaya:

"When we were sleeping, we emitted semen in our dreams; at that time, we had the perception of emission. Is it not the case that we have committed a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense?
We should go together to the Venerable Ānanda and report this matter in detail; we shall uphold whatever he says."
Then the bhikṣus went together to where Ānanda was, and having arrived, they said to him:
"Venerable Ānanda, do you know?
The Blessed One, the World-Honored One, has established training rules (śikṣāpada) within the Vinaya for the sake of the śrāvakas:..."
"If a bhikṣu intentionally emits semen, it is a saṃghāvaśeṣa offense.
When we emitted semen during dreams, we all had intentional thoughts and felt remorse, thinking:
'Have we not committed a saṃghāvaśeṣa offense?'"
"For this reason, I have come to inquire of the Venerable One!
Whatever you may explain, I shall uphold it.

When Ānanda had heard these words, he took the bhikṣus and went to the place where the World-Honored One was. Having prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, he sat to one side and addressed the Buddha, saying:

Those venerable ones all felt remorse, thinking:
"Could it be that we have committed a saṃghāvaśeṣa offense?
They did not know whether the bhikṣus had committed an offense or not.
The Blessed One said to Ānanda:
"I do not say that those bhikṣus have no mental activity of perception and cognition; however, what occurs within a dream is not a reality, and thus it should be excluded from the dream."

At that time, the Blessed One praised those who maintain the precepts and those who revere and honor the precepts. Having taught the monks the Dharma conducive to their welfare so that they might increase in wholesome qualities, he addressed the monks, saying:
"The former was the initial formulation; this is now a subsequent allowance. Therefore, I now re-establish a training rule within the Vinaya for the monks, which should be recited as follows:
'If a monk intentionally emits semen, except during a dream, it is a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*.'"
The meaning of "bhikṣu" is as explained above.
"Intentionally" means with deliberate volition.
"Emission" means that the semen actually flows out and is displaced from its original location.
There are five kinds of semen:
namely, blue, yellow, red, thick, and thin.
Among these, the "blue" refers to that of a Wheel-Turning King (*cakravartin*) and his eldest son who has received the consecration (*abhiṣeka*); their semen is both blue.
The remaining sons were all yellow in complexion.
The minister Lūhipa was red in complexion.
Those who had already reached adulthood possessed thick vital essence (*śukra*), while those who had not yet reached adulthood possessed thin vital essence.

If a person is wounded by female desire, or carries heavy loads, or travels long distances, or suffers injury to the male organ—among such categories as these, the emission of the five essences may occur.
"Except in a dream" means that if one is in a dream, there is no offense.

"The Saṃgha" means that if one commits this offense, one must rely upon the Saṃgha to perform the legal procedure and rely upon the Saṃgha to attain purification from the offense; one does not rely upon an individual.
The term *pāyattika* (or *pāyattika*) signifies "that which remains.
If a bhikṣu commits any one of the four *pārājika* offenses, there is no remainder; he may not live in community [with the others].
These thirteen dharmas, although committed by a bhikṣu, leave a remainder; because they are subject to treatment, they are called *saṃghāvaśeṣa*.
What are the characteristics of these offenses and what are their specific matters?
There are five distinct matters:
first, for the sake of pleasure;
second, for the sake of incantations.
Third, for the sake of seeds;
fourth, for the sake of medicine;
fifth, for the sake of self-testing.
What constitutes pleasure?

If a bhikṣu, for the sake of the pleasure of emitting semen, has a mind of lustful desire toward the internal sense-base of form, employs a means to stimulate the generative organ and emits semen to experience pleasure, he commits a saṃghāvaśeṣa offense.
Even if one employs skillful means, if the semen is not emitted, one incurs a *sthūlātyaya* offense.

Likewise, if one intentionally emits semen for the sake of the pleasure of moving the generative organ, or for the sake of the pleasure of rubbing, touching, or grasping it, or for the sake of the pleasure of the head of the generative organ, the gravity of the offense is as explained extensively above.

As it is for the sake of pleasure, so it is if one emits semen for the sake of incantations, for seeking seeds, for medicine, or to test one's strength; the gravity of the offense is as described above.

If a bhikṣu, for the sake of pleasure, desires to emit the vital essence (śukra), and with a mind of lustful desire toward the internal sense-base of form, employs the means to discharge that essence—whether seeking it to be yellow, red, thick, thin, or otherwise—he incurs an offense as described above.
As it is with internal forms, so it is with external forms.
The summary verse says:
"If there is dancing or [flying] in the air, and the semen moves and is discharged from within the body,"
The pleasure felt when rubbing and stroking, the degree of defilement in the mind, the physical parts produced,
whether one looks with a defiled mind, or whether it is against or with the current,
or against or with the wind— one should know the gravity of the offense accordingly.

if the semen is not emitted, he incurs a dukkaṭa offense.
If a bhikṣu intentionally wiggles his hips in mid-air and emits semen, he incurs a saṃghādisesa offense.
If the semen is not discharged, one incurs an *dukkaṭa* offense.
If a bhikṣu experiences trembling and agitation of the semen and then restrains his mind, yet the semen is nonetheless discharged, he incurs a *sthūlātyaya*;
if it is not discharged, he incurs an *dukkaṭa* offense.
If the semen has already been emitted but remains within the body, and one employs further means to cause it to be emitted, one incurs a *sthūlātyaya*;
if it is not emitted, one incurs a *duṣkṛta* offense.
If a bhikṣu has his body massaged by another and consequently emits semen, he incurs a sthūlātyaya offense;
if he has a defiled mind but does not emit it, he incurs a duṣkṛta offense.
If a bhikṣu measures his sexual organ with the intention of experiencing pleasure, and consequently discharges semen, he incurs a sthūlātyaya offense;
if he does not discharge it, he incurs a duṣkṛta offense.
If a bhikṣu views the male organ with a defiled mind, he incurs an offense of wrongdoing (duṣkṛta).
If a bhikṣu, with a mind of lustful desire, holds his own male organ against the current, he incurs a thullaccaya;
if he holds it with the current, he incurs an offense of wrongdoing.
If a bhikṣu, with a mind of lustful desire, holds his own penis against the wind, he incurs a sthūlātyaya;
if he holds it with the wind, he incurs a duṣkṛta offense.

There is no offense in the following cases: if one runs, jumps about in play, swims, leaps over ditches, moats, or railings; if one touches one's thigh or one's robe while walking; if one enters a bathhouse; if one recalls a former partner; or if semen is discharged upon seeing a pleasing form or scratching an itch—provided there is no intention to experience pleasure. These six bhikṣus were such that there was no lineage or clan among the great six cities, nor any distinction of craft or name, that they did not know; there was no person who was not known to them.

At that time, the Venerable Udāyin, having chewed his tooth-stick at dawn and donned his saṃghāṭī robe, paid homage to the stūpa and was walking to and fro for recreation outside the gate of Jetavana.

It was the established custom of this city that whenever Brahmins, householders, or housewives would go out from the capital to the Fragrant Grove (Pāricchattaka-vana) to wander about and inspect it, bringing with them various flowers and fruits, they would enter the Jeta Grove to pay homage at the feet of the World-Honored One and the great virtuous ones.
At that time, a great number of laymen and laywomen went to the Jeta Grove; seeing them, Udāyin spoke thus:

"It is just like the new moon, which appears for only a single moment.

"Although you have abandoned formal cultivation, you should still provide instruction.

"You should pay homage with a sincere heart at his venerable feet.

"Sisters!

If even a mad elephant, upon raising its eyes to gaze at him, immediately abandons its frenzy and intoxication, becoming one of few desires and contentment who practices the dhūta austerities—being foremost among the disciples of the Great Teacher in his majestic dignity and honor—you should with a sincere heart pay homage at his feet.
