fourth, birth in a central land is difficult;
fifth, the possession of all sense faculties is difficult.
"Sixth, it is difficult for faith to arise.
Sisters! This is a difficult thing that you have already attained."
"You should arouse faith; as if you were sitting in person before the Buddha to hear the essentials of the Dharma, I shall speak for you.
At that time, the women immediately prostrated at the feet of Udāyin and sat to one side, listening to the Dharma with single-minded devotion.

At that time, Udāyin preached the Dharma for her; as he spoke the Dharma, she immediately conceived a defiled mind. It was just like a sorcerer who, when performing an incantation with poor magical arts upon one afflicted by a ghostly illness, is struck by the ghost at the very moment of the incantation.

Udāyin was exactly like this: as he preached the Dharma, his mind was touched by defilement. Once the defiled mind had arisen, he rose from his seat and immediately used his hand to touch the woman’s body.
At that time, among the women, those who were in love with one another spoke lewd words and flirted, their bodies touching one another.
Those who did not love him immediately went outside the room, walking slowly along the eaves and corridors, collectively expressing contempt and disparagement, saying:
"Who would have thought that fire would erupt from within the water? In this place of refuge, we have instead given rise to terror."

In the past, we thought this monastic dwelling was secure, a state of nirvana, free from affliction and unimpeded; yet, it appears that within this very place there are further calamities, terrors, and anxieties.
When the bhikṣus heard those words of reproach and derision, they asked:
"Sisters! Whom do you reproach and revile?"
He replied,
"I reviled you, sirs.
They reported this, saying:
"What have I done to cause you such resentment?

She replied, "In the past, although we have encountered robbers and madmen, we have never heard such vulgar words as those spoken by Udāyin. Although my body has occasionally been touched by my husband, it was never subjected to such forceful violation as that by Udāyin."
If our parents, brothers, sisters, or husbands were to hear of this, they would not even permit us to hope for the Jetavana, let alone enter the park to pay our respects.
The bhikṣus replied, "Sisters!
That bhikṣu maintains the precepts perfectly; however, as the son of a high minister, he is by nature full of desire and has employed this expedient means to satisfy his lustful mind."
The woman replied,
"Noble one!
Though the horns of a cow may be sharp, how could they possibly turn back and break its own belly?"
"If one possesses a defiled mind, how could one possibly maintain the integrity of the holy life?
The bhikṣus said,
"Sisters, wait a moment!"
"I shall restrain him.
He replied, "Noble one!"
"It would be most excellent indeed if you were to prohibit this.
If you do not prohibit it, we shall never again come to visit and traverse the Jeta Grove with such heavy feet.
The bhikṣu replied:
"I shall join you in stopping this, so that it does not happen again.
Then the women, feeling resentment, departed together.
At that time, the Venerable Udāyin came out of his room laughing; when the bhikṣus saw him, they asked:
"Venerable Udāyin!
Having committed such vulgar and disgraceful acts that bring shame upon the śramaṇas, for what reason do you indulge your passions and break into laughter? Udāyin replied:
"What have I done? Have I perhaps drunk alcohol or eaten onions and garlic?
The bhikṣus said:
"You still perform such coarse and heavy deeds; why do you hesitate to drink alcohol and eat garlic?
He replied, "What kind of deed am I doing?"
The bhikṣus said, "This Brahmin and these women of the household have gone away after reviling us; is this not a transgression?
He replied:

"You merely understand how to carry the black alms bowl and wander from house to house begging; yet, your hearts are entangled by stinginess and envy, which increase day by day, such that you are unable to explain even a four-line verse of the Dharma to others, and when seeing others preach, you instead give rise to jealousy and disdain."
The bhikṣus said,
"We observe that although you, Venerable One, have spoken thus many times, not a single person has been able to realize the Truths.
He replied:
"First let their faculties ripen, so that they may gradually enter the gateway of the Truths.
Those bhikṣus who possessed few desires all joined in censuring and rebuking him, saying:
"How is it that a bhikṣu acts contrary to what is right? He ought to feel shame and remorse, yet instead he gives rise to arrogance?"
At that time, the bhikṣus reported this matter in detail to the Blessed One.
The Blessed One, because of this, assembled the bhikṣus and, though he already knew the truth, asked them:
"Udāyin, did you truly commit such a base and evil deed?"
He replied, "It is indeed so.
The Buddha said:
"What you have done is wrong; it is not the way of a śramaṇa, it is not in accordance with the Dharma, it is impure, and it is not what should be done.
After the World-Honored One had thus rebuked him in various ways, he addressed the bhikṣus:
"Having considered ten benefits... [omitted] ...I now establish this training rule for my śrāvaka disciples within the Vinaya, which should be recited as follows:"

"If again a bhikṣu, with a mind entangled by lust, makes physical contact with the body of a woman—whether grasping her hand, grasping her arm, grasping her hair, or touching any part of her body—with the intention of experiencing pleasure, it is a saṃghāvaśeṣa."
"Furthermore, regarding 'if a bhikṣu': this refers to Udāyin or others of a similar class.

Regarding 'with a mind bound by defilement' (*saṃkliṣṭacitta*): there are cases where there is a defiled mind but not a bound mind; cases where there is a bound mind but not a defiled one; cases where both are present; and cases where neither is present."
What is defilement that is not an entanglement?
It refers to when a defiled mind, but not an extremely defiled mind, is present before one.
What is an entanglement that is not defilement?
This refers to a mind that, while taking external objects as its object, has not yet given rise to a defiled state of mind but remains attached to them.
What is a mind associated with the fetters of defilement?
It refers to a defiled mind or an extremely defiled mind that greedily seeks after objects and possesses attachment.
What is neither defiled nor bound?
It refers to cases other than those previously described.
As for "a woman," it means either a wife or a young girl capable of engaging in sexual acts.
"Physical contact" refers to performing the act of touching by bringing one body against another.
"Grasping the hand" refers to the area from the wrist upward.
"Grasping the arm" refers to the area below the wrist.
"Seizing the hair" refers to the head hair and the tied *śikya* (ascetic's cord).
"Each individual limb" refers to the various joints and members of the body.
"Forming a mind that experiences pleasure" means the mind experiencing sensual desire.
Regarding the *saṃghāvaśeṣa*, the detailed explanation is as previously stated.
What are the characteristics of the offenses herein?
There are nine matters.
What are the nine? They are:
touching, intense touching, leaning against, grasping, pulling, dragging, lifting up, lowering down, and embracing all over.
What is "touching"?
If a bhikṣu, with a mind bound by defilement, makes physical contact with the head of a woman capable of sexual intercourse when there is no clothing intervening, he commits a saṃghāvaśeṣa offense;
if there is clothing intervening, he commits a sthūlātyaya offense.
As it is with the head, so it is when touching the shoulders, the back, the navel, the calves, or even the toes; whether clothed or unclothed, it is as described above.
As it is with touching, so it is likewise for pressing, leaning against, or grasping.
What constitutes "pulling"?

If a bhikṣu, with a mind bound by defilement, takes hold of a woman capable of sexual intercourse and pulls her from a distance to a nearby place, or pushes her from a nearby place to a distance, he incurs an offense identical to that previously described.
What is "dragging"?
It refers to a bhikṣu seizing a woman and dragging her from the right side toward the left, or from the left side toward the right, or from her feet to her head, or from her head toward her feet.
What constitutes the upper limit?
It refers to seizing a woman and lifting her from the ground so that she rises above the level of one's toes; if there is no intervening garment, one incurs the root offense (*mūlāpatti*);
if there is an intervening garment, one incurs the preparatory offense (*prayogāpatti*).
If it is thus with the toes, and likewise if one raises [the body] from above the calves, knees, or other parts of the body up to the crown of the head;

or if one is raised onto a bed or seat, or onto an elephant, horse, carriage, or palanquin, or up to a multi-storied pavilion—if a bhikṣu, with a mind ensnared by passion, experiences the pleasure of touch and forms the thought of gratification, then at the moment his body makes contact with those parts, if there is no intervening garment, he incurs the root offense;
if there is an intervening garment, he incurs the preparatory offense. This is called "raising up."
What is "lowering"?

If a bhikṣu takes hold of a woman capable of sexual intercourse and lifts her down from atop a multi-storied pavilion, or onto an elephant, horse, carriage, or bed, lowering her until her toes touch the ground, he incurs an offense identical to the one mentioned before; this is called "lowering."
What is "embracing all over"?

If a bhikṣu, with respect to a woman capable of sexual intercourse, grasps or squeezes her neck down to her toes—whichever part of the body he touches—he incurs an offense identical to that previously described.
Whenever one touches a woman’s body, if she is capable of engaging in sexual intercourse, one incurs the root offense when there is no intervening garment;
if there is a garment, one incurs an offense of preliminary preparation.
If she is incapable, one incurs a grave offense (*sthūlātyaya*) even without a garment.
If one possesses clothing, there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*).
If a bhikṣu, with a mind bound by passion, touches a male or a eunuch capable of sexual intercourse, if he is without clothing, it is a grave offense (*sthūlātyaya*);
if he has clothing, it is an offense of wrong-doing.
If the object is not capable [of sexual intercourse], one incurs an *dukkaṭa* (offense of wrong-doing) whether one has clothing on or not.
If one touches an animal, whether it is capable or incapable, one likewise incurs an *dukkaṭa*.
If there is no defiled mind, touching one's mother, daughter, or sister constitutes no offense whatsoever.
If one sees a woman being swept away by water, or at times committing suicide by hanging, or ingesting poison, etc., there is no offense in touching her for the purpose of providing rescue.
Furthermore, there is no offense for the very first offender, or for one who is insane, mentally deranged, or overwhelmed by intense physical pain.

3. The Training Rule on Speaking Vulgar and Evil Words. The third training rule concerning speaking vulgar and evil words was established when the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the origin of the story concerning the bhikṣu Udāyin was the same as before.

Furthermore, whatever teaching he encountered, it would defile his mind; once such a defiled mind had arisen, he would address women with coarse and vulgar speech—namely, talk associated with base and evil sexual desire—just like a husband and wife discussing worldly matters.
At that time, among the women, those who were fond of one another spoke flirtatiously and touched each other’s bodies.
Those who were not fond of them went outside the room and spoke words of derision:
"Who would have thought that fire would emerge from within the water? In this place of refuge, we have instead given rise to terror."
The full explanation is as previously stated.
Up to: "Having formulated this training rule, it should be spoken thus:
'If a bhikṣu, with a mind bound by defilement, engages in vulgar, evil, and improper speech concerning sexual desire with a woman, such as that between husband and wife, it is a saṃghāvaśeṣa.'"
"Furthermore, 'if a bhikṣu' refers to Udāyin or others of a similar class.
Regarding 'with a mind bound by defilement,' there are four permutations, as explained in detail previously."
Regarding the term "woman," it refers to a wife or a maiden who is capable of understanding the meaning of words, whether virtuous or non-virtuous.
As for base and evil speech, there are two types:
first, that which gives rise to a *pārājika* offense; second, that which gives rise to a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense.
Why is this called base and evil speech?
Answer:
Because it is base by its own nature, and because it arises from what is base.
"Evil" refers to transgressions; it refers to speaking words concerning sexual intercourse.
"Like husband and wife" means, for example, as when a husband and wife speak improper speech.
Regarding the *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offenses, they are explained in detail as stated above.
What are the characteristics of the transgressions herein,
and what are their nine specific instances?
These are: well-spoken, ill-spoken, direct begging, indirect begging, direct questioning, indirect questioning, citing examples, praising, and reviling.
What is well-spoken?
If a bhikṣu, with a mind bound by passion, addresses a capable woman with words that clarify good and evil, saying:
"Sister! Your three orifices are truly of excellent form and lovely."
If it is spoken in conjunction with the *yava*, one incurs a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*;
if it is not spoken in conjunction with the *yava*, one incurs a *sthūlātyaya*.
This is called well-spoken.
What is ill-spoken?
If a bhikṣu, with a mind bound by defilement, addresses a capable woman who understands good and evil speech and speaks as follows:
"Sister! Your three orifices are truly of an unattractive form and loathsome.
If she speaks thus in combination with the *yava* [analogy], she incurs a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense.
If one does not combine it with the word *yava*, one incurs a *sthūlātyaya* offense.
This is what is called "evil speech regarding *yava*"; it specifically refers to the improper talk concerning male-female sexual union prevalent in the West.
If one were to follow the local pronunciation of this region, the words would be largely vulgar and coarse.
Furthermore, as regional dialects vary from place to place, I have retained the original characters.
However, when Western teachers speak these words, they do not pronounce them in their entirety because they are considered vulgar; they simply say the syllables "ya" and "ba."
What is "direct begging"?
It refers to when a bhikṣu speaks as follows:
"Sisters, come!..."
"Perform such and such an act together with me.
If he speaks in conjunction with the *yava* (barley), he incurs a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*;
if he does not speak in conjunction, he incurs a *sthūlātyaya*.
This is called begging directly.
What is begging by means of skillful methods?
It is explained in detail as before, up until making such a statement:
"Sister! If a woman performs such acts with a man, that woman will certainly be held in high regard and loved by him.
If you perform such acts with me, I too shall now cherish and love you."
If one speaks in combination with a *yāva*, one incurs a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense;
if one does not speak in combination, one incurs a *sthūlātyaya*.
This is called "soliciting by means of stratagem."
What is direct questioning?
It is explained in detail as before, up until these words are spoken:
"Sisters!..."
"If a man performs such an act with a woman, that man will certainly be cherished by her.
Now that I have performed such an act with you, can you not give rise to affection and love for me?"
The rest is the same as before.
What is a "crooked question"?
It is explained at length as before, up until he speaks these words:
"Sister! If a woman performs such an act with a man, that woman will certainly be beloved by him.
I now love you; are you able to perform such an act for me?"
The rest is all the same as before.
What is the citation of the event?
It is explained in detail as before, up until these words were spoken:

"Sisters! Previously, at a certain park, a shrine, or a gathering place for the assembly, I would eat exquisite food and drink fine honey-liquor together with various women; we would arrange fragrant flowers and set out excellent couches and seats, and throughout the night we would line up bright lamps in the courtyard and speak these words to those women:
'If, sisters!'"
"At that time, those who came to the assembly, I too would have done such a thing together with you.
The rest is the same as before.
What is meant by "praising"?
The detailed explanation is as before, up until these words were spoken:
"Sister! If some man were to say this to you:..."
“Sister! If a man were to do such things for you, he would obtain present pleasure and receive celestial bliss.
I too shall do such and such things with you, and likewise obtain present pleasure and receive celestial bliss.”
The rest is the same as before.
What is "abusive speech through anger"?
It refers to when a bhikṣu, with a mind bound by defilement, addresses a capable woman who understands words of good and evil, and speaks to her in this manner:
"You should engage in sexual intercourse with snakes, donkeys, and other such animals.
If one utters such insults, and if they are spoken in conjunction with the word *yava* (barley), one incurs a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*;
if not so spoken, one incurs a *sthūlātyaya*.
This is called reviling with anger.

Just as previously, when a bhikṣu spoke of nine matters to a wife or a young girl, if that wife or young girl was capable—meaning she understood words of both good and evil—and came before the bhikṣu to speak thus:
"Noble One!..."
"The two 'wound-gates' of a virtuous man are truly of excellent form and lovely.

If a bhikṣu, having heard these words, with a mind bound by passion, forms the intention to experience pleasure and remains in approval, responding with speech as the statement was made—if he speaks in conjunction with the *yava* (barley), he incurs a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*;
if he does not speak in conjunction, he incurs a *sthūlātyaya*.
This is called "well-spoken.
What is "ill-spoken"?
As explained at length previously, it includes even when a woman approaches a bhikṣu and speaks to him in this manner:
"Noble one!
Your two orifices are truly of an unattractive and loathsome form.
The rest is as stated above.
What is "direct begging"?
It is explained in detail as before, up until the point where a woman approaches a bhikṣu and speaks these words:
"Noble One!..."
"Come and do such and such a thing for me.
The rest is as explained above.
What is "begging by means of expedient means"?
The detailed explanation is as before, up until a woman approaches a bhikṣu and speaks these words:
"If there is a man who performs such-and-such an act with a woman, that man will surely be held in high esteem by her."
"If you, O virtuous one, would perform such and such deeds with me, I too shall now cherish and love you most deeply.
The rest is as explained above.
What is "direct questioning"?
The detailed explanation is as previously stated, up until a woman approaches a bhikṣu and speaks these words:
"Venerable sir!
If a woman performs such-and-such an act with a man, that woman will certainly be loved and cherished by that man."
"I am now performing such an act together with you; are you able to feel affection and compassion for me?
The rest is as previously stated.
What is a "crooked question"?
The detailed explanation is as before, up until he spoke these words:
"Noble one! If a man performs such an act with a woman, that man will certainly be loved by her."
"I now love you; would you be able to do such a thing for me?
The rest is the same as before.
What is meant by "citing an example"?
The full account is as previously described, up to these words:
"Noble One!

Once, at a certain place in a park, at a shrine of the gods where a great assembly had gathered, I partook of exquisite food and fine honey-liquor with various men. Having arranged fragrant flowers and spread out excellent couches and seats, we then lit bright lamps in rows throughout the courtyard for the entire night and engaged in such activities together with those men."
"If the Noble One had come to the assembly at that time, I too would have performed such and such deeds together with you.
The rest is the same as before.
What is meant by "praising"?
He even spoke these words:
"Noble one! If there is a woman who performs such an act with you, she shall obtain present happiness as well as enjoy the pleasures of heaven."
"I shall also join you in performing such deeds, so that we may both obtain happiness in the present life as well as enjoy the pleasures of the heavens.
The rest is the same as before.
What is meant by "hating and reviling"?
That is to say, a woman capable of engaging in sexual intercourse and who understands both virtuous and non-virtuous speech comes before a bhikṣu and speaks these words:
"You should engage in sexual acts with donkeys and other such animals."
Thus he utters insults.

If a bhikṣu, with a mind of lustful attachment, intends to experience pleasure and consents while remaining present, responding with words at the time of such speech—if it is spoken in conjunction with a *yava*, he incurs a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*;
if not so spoken, he incurs a *sthūlātyaya*.
If it is a woman who lacks the capacity [to respond], one incurs a sthūlātyaya.
If it is a man or a paṇḍaka capable of engaging in sexual intercourse, one incurs a sthūlātyaya;
if they are incapable, one incurs a duṣkṛta.
Whether the animals are powerful or powerless,
[speaking thus] constitutes an offense of wrong-doing (*duṣkṛta*).
There is no offense if one says *yava* when meaning "barley," or if one says *yavani* when meaning "curtain."
If, within a particular region, one speaks vulgar or evil words that are not considered offensive there, it does not constitute an offense.
Furthermore, there is no offense for the very first person to commit such an act, or for one who is insane, mentally deranged, or overwhelmed by intense physical pain.
4. The Training Rule on Soliciting Offerings. The fourth training rule concerning soliciting offerings. At that time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, it was the constant practice of the six bhikṣus that every morning one of them would always remain stationed at the gate of the Jetavana to keep watch.

On one occasion, seeing a multitude of people entering the monastery, Udāyin immediately guided them, assigned them quarters, and led them to pay homage to the Buddha and the Saṅgha, as described in detail previously.
He even preached the Dharma to women while praising himself, saying: "Sisters!
This is the foremost among all offerings; those who maintain the precepts and cultivate goodness like me should offer worship by means of the dharma of sexual desire."
When these words were spoken, those among the women who felt mutual affection immediately laughed with joy.
Those who did not take pleasure in it uttered words of derision and reproach, as described in detail previously.
Having heard this, the bhikṣus rebuked him and went to inform the Buddha.
On account of this matter, the Buddha assembled the bhikṣus and, up to the point of establishing a training rule for them, said:
"If a bhikṣu, with a mind bound by passion, speaks in praise of his own person before a woman, saying: [text continues]"

"Sisters! If there were a bhikṣu similar to me—one who is fully endowed with ethical discipline (*śīla*), possesses superior wholesome qualities, and practices the holy life—you might offer this practice of sexual desire to him."
"If a bhikṣu speaks in such a manner, it is a saṃghāvaśeṣa.
"If a bhikṣu" refers to Udāyin, or others of a similar class.
Regarding those whose minds are entangled by defilement, there are four permutations, as explained in detail previously.
As for "women," this refers to wives and young girls who are able to understand the meaning of words—both good and bad—namely, when they praise themselves or seek offerings.
The statement,
"Sisters... this is the most excellent among offerings," refers to the foremost [offering].
"One who resembles me" refers to himself.
"One who is fully endowed with śīla" means one who possesses the aggregate of ethical discipline (śīlaskandha).
"One who possesses superior wholesome dharmas" means one who possesses the aggregate of meditative concentration (samādhiskandha).
To speak of "the holy life" (brahmacarya) means to be endowed with the aggregate of wisdom.

To speak of "this practice of sexual desire," the word "practice" (dharma) here refers to what is non-practice (adharma); it indicates that this practice of sexual desire is nothing other than such an act.
"Sexual desire" refers to impure conduct.
The rest is as explained above.
In this context, what are the characteristics of the offense and its specific details?
There are eighteen matters:

namely, supreme, excellent, distinguished, sublime, virtuous, good, worthy of offerings, lovely, vast, most supreme, most excellent, most distinguished, most sublime, most virtuous, most good, most worthy of offerings, most lovely, and most vast.
If a bhikṣu, with a mind bound by passion, speaks thus to a capable woman:
"Sister! Among all forms of offering, this is the most excellent."
If one says, "As I am endowed with the practice of the precepts,
you should honor me with the act of sexual intercourse," one incurs a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense.
Just as it has been stated for the term "most" (*parama*), so too should it be understood that this applies by analogy up to the term "extremely vast" (*paramodāra*).
Just as it is with being endowed with the precepts, so it is with being endowed with wholesome qualities (*kuśala-dharma*) and the holy life (*brahmacarya*); these are each explained individually.
Or one might say:
"I am one who is endowed with the precepts and wholesome qualities; I am one who is endowed with the precepts and the holy life."
"The wholesome qualities possess the precepts; the wholesome qualities are the holy life (brahmacarya).
The holy life possesses the precepts; the holy life consists of the wholesome qualities.
Thus they are explained in pairs.
Or they say:
"I am one who possesses the precepts and the holy life;
I possess the holy life and the precepts."
"The holy life is endowed with precepts and wholesome qualities.
Thus, three items are spoken of together.
If one says:
Regarding the statement, "We, like those of our kind, shall offer worship by means of the dharma of sexual desire," one incurs a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense.
If a bhikṣu, in the presence of a woman capable of engaging in sexual intercourse, with a mind bound by defilement, speaks in this manner:
"Sister! This offering is the most excellent; those like us who possess the precepts should receive such offerings.
To speak thus without associating it with the practice of sexual intercourse, one incurs a sthūlātyaya offense.
Just as it is with the "maximum," so too should it be understood that this applies by analogy up to the "extremely vast.
Likewise, whether explained individually one by one, combined two by two, or combined three by three, in all such cases, one incurs a *sthūlātyaya* offense.
If a bhikṣu, with a mind bound by defilement, speaks thus to a woman capable of sexual intercourse:
"Sister! This is the supreme among offerings; if there is a bhikṣu who is a person endowed with precepts, he should be offered support."
If one speaks in conjunction with the act of sexual intercourse but does not say "those such as we," one incurs a *sthūlātyaya*; the rest is as previously stated.
If a bhikṣu speaks at length as before but neither says "those such as we" nor speaks in conjunction with the act of sexual intercourse, he incurs a *duṣkṛta*.
Each individual case should be understood according to the principles established above.
For example, if one acts toward a woman capable of sexual intercourse, one incurs the root offense;
if one acts toward one who is incapable, one incurs the preparatory offense.
If one acts toward a man capable of sexual intercourse or a paṇḍaka, one incurs a sthūlātyaya;
if one acts toward one who is incapable, one incurs a duṣkṛta offense.
If [one acts] toward animals, whether one has the power or lacks the power [to prevent harm], it is in all cases merely *duṣkṛta* (wrongdoing).
Furthermore, there is no offense for the very first offender, or for one who is insane, mentally deranged, or overwhelmed by intense physical pain.
