The Training Rule on Brokering Marriages. The fifth training rule on brokering marriages: At that time, the Blessed One was staying in Śrāvastī at the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.

At that time, there was an elder in this city named Kṛṣṇasāra, who conceived deep faith and reverence for the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha. He took refuge in the Triple Gem and received the five precepts:
abstaining from taking life, abstaining from stealing, abstaining from sexual misconduct, abstaining from false speech, and abstaining from drinking intoxicants.

In this city, there were many acquaintances—brahmins and householders—who found favor with him; whenever there was a daughter in their families who had grown up and was marriageable, they would ask Kṛṣṇamṛgaputra:
"Do you know of a young man from such-and-such a family?"
He replied, "I know there is.
He asked again:

"Is that young man diligent and free from laziness, well-managing his household affairs, able to provide his wife and children with abundant food and clothing so they do not suffer, and ensuring they have little labor to perform?"

If Kṛṣṇaśāri replies, "Although he has sons, they are by nature indolent and do not attend to their household affairs; they are unable to provide their wives and children with peace and happiness or an abundance of food and clothing."
Upon hearing these words, she did not give him in marriage.
However, if he were to report:

"The youth of that family is diligent and free from laziness; he manages the household affairs well and is able to provide his wife and children with ample food and clothing, ensuring they do not suffer."
Upon hearing these words, he immediately gave her in marriage.
If anyone seeking a wife asked the Black Deer (Kṛṣṇasāra) about it, he would inquire:
"Do you know whether that family has a daughter to be given in marriage?"
He replied, "I know there is.
The other then asked:
"Is that young woman diligent and untiring in managing the household affairs?
If one says, "She cannot."
He then did not marry her.
If he says, "I can," [he may do so].
Thus, they arranged a marriage.
When a woman was sent by her family to her husband's home and it did not meet with her satisfaction, her kinsmen would then reproach and revile Kāḷakaṇṇi, saying:

"We were acquainted with Kāḷakaṇṇi as dear friends; we dispatched him to act as our matchmaker, yet instead he has caused our daughter to suffer such hardship that the food and clothing she seeks cannot suffice."
If a woman was well-provided with food and clothing at her husband’s home and did not have to labor, he would immediately praise her in the presence of Kṛṣṇa Mṛgāraputra.

Conversely, if a man had taken a wife who was not diligent in household duties and did not please her husband, he would likewise, as before, express extensive disdain and revile her in the presence of Kṛṣṇa Mṛgāraputra.

If there is a man who, having taken a wife, is filial, supportive, and diligent; who is capable of managing the household affairs; and who is harmonious with his wife—then, regarding Kāḷaka, he would immediately offer extensive praise as previously described.
At that time, in the city of Śrāvastī, the reputation of Kṛṣṇa Mṛgāraputra became manifest both for its excellence and its flaws.
On a later day, Kṛṣṇa Mṛgāraputra conceived even greater faith and devotion toward the Triple Gem; he subsequently went forth as a renunciant within the well-expounded Dharma and Vinaya.

Having gone forth, he returned once more to his former ways, extensively acting as a matchmaker among his relatives and friends; thus, the name "Kṛṣṇa Mṛgāraputra" again became the talk of both good and ill throughout the city.
This was merely a matter of dependent origination; however, the Blessed One had not yet established a training rule (*śikṣāpada*) within the Vinaya for the śrāvaka disciples.

At that time, the group of six bhikṣus also acted as go-betweens for marriages, conveying the intentions of men to women and the intentions of women to men, even arranging secret liaisons between men and women.
At that time, the non-Buddhists all voiced their derision and reproach:
"You should know, sirs!
These śramaṇas, sons of the Śākyas, do what ought not to be done; their practicing matchmaking—how is this any different from us?"
"Who else could take the food and drink from the royal court and offer it to these shaven-headed śramaṇas, the sons of the Śākyas?
At that time, the bhikṣus reported this matter in detail to the World-Honored One.
The Blessed One, on account of this incident, assembled the bhikṣus and, knowing the matter, asked the group of six intentionally:
"Is it true that you act as matchmakers, conveying a man's intentions to a woman, a woman's intentions to a man, and even facilitating secret liaisons?"
They replied,
“It is true. Thereupon,
the World-Honored One rebuked the six bhikṣus, saying:
"You are not a śramaṇa, you do not follow [the path], you do not practice pure conduct, you do not possess good deportment;
this is not what one who has gone forth should do. Having thus rebuked him in various ways, the Blessed One addressed the bhikṣus, saying:
"Having considered ten benefits, I shall establish a training rule for the bhikṣus; it should be spoken as follows:"

If a bhikṣu acts as a matchmaker, conveying a man’s intentions to a woman and a woman’s intentions to a man, whether for the purpose of formal marriage or for illicit sexual relations, even for as brief a moment as a snap of the fingers, it is a saṃghāvaśeṣa offense.
"Furthermore, regarding 'a bhikṣu': this refers to Kṛṣṇa Mṛgāraputra and the group of six bhikṣus; the remaining meanings are as explained above.
As for 'acting as a matchmaker,' it means acting as a messenger to go back and forth."
To speak with a man’s intent to a woman, or with a woman’s intent to a man, means to convey the respective intentions of each other to one another.
If for the purpose of establishing a wife or for illicit intercourse, there are seven kinds of wives and ten kinds of illicit partners.
What are the seven kinds of wives? They are:

the one given by pouring water, the one purchased with wealth, the one won by the royal banner, the one who marries for pleasure, the one supported by food and clothing, the one who lives together, and the one for a moment.
A summary verse says:

The seven types of wives are: those obtained through the water-rite (*udakadattā*), those obtained through wealth (*śulkadattā*), those obtained through the royal banner (*dhvajahṛtā*), those who live by their own pleasure (*svairiṇī*), those who live by food and clothing (*āhārasthāyinī*), those who live together (*saha-jīvā*), and those who are for a moment (*kṣaṇikā*).

Regarding the wife obtained through the water-rite: this refers to not taking any material wealth; the parents of the girl pour water into the hand of her husband and address him, saying: [as follows].
"I now give this daughter of mine to you as your wife; you must guard her well and ensure that no other person should ever wrong or violate her.
This is called the "water-given" wife (*udakadattā*).
Regarding the "betrothal by wealth": this refers to obtaining a girl by means of wealth and giving her to the man, as explained in detail above; such a woman is called a wife obtained through wealth.

Regarding the "wife by royal banner": for example, when a consecrated Great King of the Kṣatriya caste arrays his military banners and strikes down a rebellious state, having achieved victory in battle, he issues a proclamation saying:
"Any women captured at will shall serve as wives."
This refers to obtaining a woman as a wife or concubine through the power of the royal banner.
Furthermore, if someone acts as a bandit chief and captures a woman as his wife after plundering a village or city, she is called a "wife by the royal banner."
Regarding "one who desires [him] herself": if a woman or a maiden goes in person to the place of a man she has taken a liking to and says, "I now desire to be your wife."
If he then accepts her, she is called a "wife by mutual consent.
As for a "wife by provision of food and clothing," it is when a girl or young woman goes to a man's place and says:
"You should provide me with food and clothing, and I shall become your wife."
This is called a wife for food and clothing.
As for a wife who lives together, it is when a girl or young woman goes to a man's place and says:
"Whatever wealth I possess and whatever property you have, let us combine them in one place to live our lives together."
This is called a lifelong wife (*sahajīvinī*).
A momentary wife (*muhūrtikā*) refers to one who acts as a wife for only a brief period; this is called a momentary wife.
What are the ten kinds of illicit unions?
That is to say, they are protected by ten [groups]:

protection by the father, protection by the mother, protection by brothers, protection by sisters, protection by the paternal grandfather, protection by the maternal grandmother, protection by kinsmen, protection by caste, protection by clan, and protection by the royal law.
The summary verse says:
The ten protections refer to one's mother and father, Brothers and sisters,
the paternal grandfather and maternal grandmother, One's own kin, and the laws of the king.
What is protection by the father?
If a woman’s husband has died, or has been imprisoned, or has fled, and her father provides protection for her, this is called protection by the father.
Protection by the mother is likewise.
What is protection by brothers?

If a woman’s parents and husband have all passed away, or have at some time been lost, and she goes to live in the home of her brothers, where the brothers provide her protection—this is called protection by brothers.
It is the same for sisters.
What is meant by "protection by a paternal uncle"?

If a woman’s parents and kinsmen have all passed away, and her husband is ill, or has become insane, or has migrated and lost contact with her, she lives under the protection of a paternal uncle, who then declares: [text continues]
“Daughter-in-law, you may dwell by my side with a joyful heart; I cherish you as I do my own child.
The grandfather then protected her according to the Dharma; this is called protection by the grandfather.
The same applies to the protection of one's kin.
What is meant by "protection of kin"?
All those belonging to one’s lineage from the seventh ancestor back are called kin; beyond that, they are not kin.

If a woman’s parents, brothers, sisters, and husband have all passed away, or if she has become insane and so forth, or has wandered to another land, and she then dwells in dependence upon other relatives, this is called "protection by relatives."
What is protection by lineage?
It refers to women who abide according to their lineage—namely, those of the Brahmin, Kṣatriya, Vaiśya, and Śūdra castes—which is called protection by lineage.
What is protection by clan (*gotra-rakṣā*)?

It refers to the fact that among the Brahmins and others there are distinct lineages, such as the Bhāradvāja, Śāṇḍilya, Vātsya, and so forth; because a woman is protected by these, it is called protection by clan.
What is protection by royal law?
If a woman has no kinsmen and stands alone, yet because of the royal law no one dares to欺 (deceive or harm) her, this is called protection by royal law.

Furthermore, there is that which is called "Dharma-protection" (*dharmarakṣā*): if there is a woman who, being a widow, maintains her integrity, preserves her pure conduct, and keeps her heart chaste, such that no one deceives or violates her, this is termed Dharma-protection.
*Saṃghāvaśeṣa* means as explained above.
Regarding the characteristics of the offense herein, what are its specific instances?
There are seven types of circumstances concerning the separation of wives, as previously described.
The summary verse says:
Fighting and having fought, breaking off grass and throwing three tiles,
according to the Dharma and "she is not my wife," and the public announcement to many people.
What are the seven?
First, they separate while in the midst of a quarrel;
second, they separate after the quarrel has ended.
3. Separation by breaking the grass into three pieces;
4. Separation by throwing tiles in three directions;
5. Separation through formal procedure in the presence of relatives.
Sixth, the separation by saying, "She is not my wife";
seventh, the separation by publicly announcing it to the multitude.
If a bhikṣu sees a layperson separating from one of the first three wives due to quarrels and the like, and he reconciles them so that they are united, he incurs one *duṣkṛta* (wrongdoing).
If one performs the second act of mixing and blending, one incurs two *dukkaṭa* offenses;
if one performs the third act of mixing and blending, one incurs three *dukkaṭa* offenses;
if one performs the fourth, fifth, or sixth acts of mixing and blending, one incurs one, two, or three *sthūlātyaya* offenses respectively.
If one effects a seventh separation from a wife, one incurs a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense.

If a monk subsequently reunites any of the four other wives or those with whom he had illicit relations—regardless of which of the seven types of separations occurred—he incurs a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense in every case.
The summary verse says:
Receiving [the precepts] oneself or through an envoy; the two bhikṣus and the four modes of conduct;
walking one after the other; the causes regarding status and the matters [of the rule].
If a bhikṣu receives the message himself, goes to deliver it himself, and returns to report it himself, he commits a saṃghāvaśeṣa offense.
If a bhikṣu receives the message himself, goes to deliver it himself, and dispatches a messenger to report back, he commits a saṃghāvaśeṣa offense.
If a bhikṣu personally receives the message, sends a messenger to deliver it, and returns himself to report it, it is a saṃghāvaśeṣa offense.
If a bhikṣu personally receives the message, sends a messenger to deliver it, and the messenger returns to report it, it is a saṃghāvaśeṣa offense.
If a bhikṣu receives a message from a messenger and then goes himself to deliver it and returns himself to report it;
or if he receives a message from a messenger, goes himself to deliver it, and dispatches another messenger to report it;
or if he receives a message from a messenger, dispatches a messenger to deliver it, and returns himself to report it.
If one receives the message from the messenger, sends a messenger to deliver it, and sends a messenger to report back, one incurs a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense in each case.
If a bhikṣu receives the message from the messenger’s messenger, goes in person to deliver it, and returns in person to report;
or if he receives the message from the messenger’s messenger, goes in person to deliver it, and sends a messenger to report back; [in these cases, he likewise incurs the offense].
Whether one receives a message from a messenger, sends a messenger with a reply, and returns the report oneself;
or receives a message from a messenger, sends a messenger with a reply, and dispatches another messenger to report it back—in all such cases, one incurs a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense.
If two bhikṣus personally receive the message, both go to deliver it, and both return to report it, both incur a saṃghāvaśeṣa offense.
If two bhikṣus personally receive the message, both go to deliver it, but neither returns to report it, both incur two duṣkṛta offenses.
If two bhikṣus receive a message from one another, yet both fail to go and deliver it, and both fail to return with a reply, both commit one *sthūlātyaya* offense.
If two bhikṣus receive a message from one another, and one says:
"Convey my meaning; go and deliver it, and return with a reply," [the other commits an offense].
Regarding "acting according to the words," both commit a saṃghāvaśeṣa offense.
If two bhikṣus receive a message from someone, and one says:
"I shall only go to deliver the message; I will not return with a report."

If one returns to report it, the one who went to speak and the one who returned to report it both incur a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense; the one who did not return to report it incurs two *sthūlātyaya* offenses.
If two bhikṣus receive the message themselves, and one says:
"I will neither go to speak it nor return to report it," [the other] incurs a *sthūlātyaya* offense.

The one who goes to deliver the message and returns with a report incurs a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense; the one who does not go to deliver the message nor return with a report incurs one *sthūlatyaya* (grave) offense.
If a single bhikṣu travels along the same road with one man and one woman, and that man says to the bhikṣu:
"Noble One!..."
"Would you be able to speak to this woman, saying:
'Could you become the wife of this man, or dwell with him even for a short time?
Or perhaps a woman might say to a bhikṣu:
“Venerable One!
Could you please speak to this man and say:
‘Would you be able to become the husband of this woman, or dwell together with her for even a short time?’”
If this bhikṣu, having received these words, immediately speaks in reply on their behalf, he incurs a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense.
As it is with walking, so it should be understood that standing, sitting, and lying down are to be treated accordingly.
In this way, if two bhikṣus, two men, or two women; or three bhikṣus, three men, or three women, and so forth—as explained at length—one incurs the offense of *saṃghāvaśeṣa*.

If two bhikṣus travel together, one preceding and one following, and the one preceding receives the message himself, delivers it, and returns with the reply, the preceding one incurs a saṃghāvaśeṣa offense, while the following one is not guilty of an offense.

If the bhikṣu who is traveling ahead accepts the message himself and sends the bhikṣu following behind to deliver it, and once the truth has been ascertained, the bhikṣu traveling ahead returns to report it himself, the bhikṣu traveling ahead incurs two *sthūlātyaya* offenses, while the bhikṣu following behind incurs one *sthūlātyaya* offense.

If the bhikṣu who is traveling ahead accepts the message himself, and the bhikṣu who is traveling ahead goes in person to deliver it, while dispatching the bhikṣu following behind to return with a report, the bhikṣu traveling ahead incurs two grave offenses (sthūlātyaya), and the bhikṣu following behind incurs one grave offense.

If the bhikṣu who went ahead has already accepted the message himself, and then dispatches the bhikṣu following behind to deliver it and report back, the following bhikṣu incurs two *sthūlātyaya* offenses, while the bhikṣu who went ahead incurs one *sthūlātyaya* offense.
Just as it should be understood regarding the amount of offense incurred by the preceding bhikṣu based on the actions performed by the following bhikṣu,
so too should it be understood by analogy regarding the amount of offense incurred by the preceding bhikṣu when sent away by the following bhikṣu.
There are two types of householders:
one who has autonomy and one who lacks autonomy.

That which is called "autonomy" refers to the principle of ownership; regarding one's own sons and daughters, one may give or take them as one pleases. Even if one goes before the authorities or to a gathering of the public and speaks of false matters, people will still believe and accept it; this is called autonomy.

Lack of autonomy means being base and lowly; it refers to having no power over one's own sons or daughters in matters of giving or taking them away. Even when one goes before the authorities or to places where crowds gather and speaks the truth, others do not believe or accept it; this is called lack of autonomy.

If a bhikṣu receives a message from one who has authority, goes to deliver it to that person of authority, and returns to report it to that same person of authority, he incurs a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense.

If a bhikṣu receives a message from one who has authority, goes to deliver it to that person of authority, and returns to report it to someone who does not have authority, he incurs two *sthūlātyaya* offenses and one *duṣkṛta* offense.

If a bhikṣu receives a message from one who has authority and goes to deliver it to one who lacks authority, returning with a report to the one with authority, he incurs two *sthūlātyaya* offenses and one *duṣkṛta* offense.

If a bhikṣu receives a message from one who has authority and goes to deliver it to one who lacks authority, returning with a report to one who also lacks authority, he incurs one *sthūlātyaya* offense and two *duṣkṛta* offenses.

If a bhikṣu receives a message from one who lacks authority, goes to deliver it to one who lacks authority, and returns to report it to one who has authority, he incurs two *duṣkṛta* offenses and one *sthūlātyaya*.

If a bhikṣu receives a message from one who lacks authority, goes to deliver it to one who has authority, and returns to report it to one who lacks authority, he incurs two *duṣkṛta* offenses and one *sthūlātyaya*.

If a bhikṣu receives a message from one who lacks authority, delivers it to one who has authority, and returns to report it to that same person with authority, he incurs two *sthūlātyaya* offenses and one *duṣkṛta*.
If he receives a message from one who lacks authority, delivers it to one who lacks authority, and returns to report it to one who lacks authority, he incurs three *duṣkṛta* offenses.
Furthermore, there are three conditions by which a bhikṣu acts as a matchmaker; even if he receives a message but does not convey it back in words, he still commits the offense of matchmaking.
What are these three?
First, fixing a place; second, fixing a time; third, manifesting signs.
What is meant by "the appointed place"?
It means telling that person:
"If you see me in a certain garden, or at a certain shrine, or at a gathering of people, then you should know that the matter has been accomplished."
This is called the appointed place.
What is the fixed time?
"If you see me at the time of the morning meal, or at midday, or in the afternoon, then you should know that the matter has been accomplished."
This is called the fixed time.
What are the signs?

"If you see me with my hair newly shaven, or wearing a new outer robe (*saṃghāṭī*), or holding a mendicant’s staff (*khakkhara*), or at times carrying an alms bowl filled with ghee or oil, you should then know that the matter has been accomplished."
This is called "indicating signs" (liṅga-darśana); these constitute the three conditions by which one becomes a matchmaker even if, having received a message, one does not reply with words.
Furthermore, there are three other matters that constitute the act of matchmaking at the time of commissioning another.
What are the three?
First, speech; second, writing; third, hand gestures.
If a bhikṣu personally accepts a verbal mission and conveys it by speech, and reports back by speech, he incurs a saṃghāvaśeṣa offense.
If a bhikṣu himself accepts a verbal messenger and conveys the message verbally while reporting it in writing, he incurs a saṃghāvaśeṣa offense.
If a bhikṣu himself accepts a verbal messenger and conveys the message in writing while reporting it verbally, he incurs a saṃghāvaśeṣa offense.
If a bhikṣu personally accepts the message of a messenger, conveys it by means of a letter, and receives a reply by means of a letter, he incurs a saṃghāvaśeṣa offense.

If a bhikṣu personally accepts the message of a messenger, conveys it by means of a letter, but receives a reply by means of a sign, or by fixing upon a place, or by fixing upon a time, or by means of a visible gesture, he likewise incurs a saṃghāvaśeṣa offense.
This is called the fivefold distinction regarding verbal messengers and written messages.
If a bhikṣu personally accepts a verbal message, conveying it verbally and returning the report verbally, he incurs a saṃghāvaśeṣa offense.
If a bhikṣu personally accepts a verbal message and conveys it verbally while returning the report by means of a hand gesture, he incurs a saṃghāvaśeṣa offense.
If a bhikṣu personally accepts a verbal message and conveys it by means of a hand gesture while returning the report verbally, he incurs a saṃghāvaśeṣa offense.
If a bhikṣu personally receives a verbal message and conveys it by means of a hand gesture, and receives a reply by means of a hand gesture, he incurs a saṃghāvaśeṣa offense.

If a bhikṣu personally receives a verbal message and conveys it by means of a hand gesture, but receives a reply by means of a sign, or by fixing upon a time, or by manifesting a physical indication, he incurs a saṃghāvaśeṣa offense.
This refers to the fivefold distinctions among speech, manual gestures (*mudrā*), and seals (*mudrā*).
Just as there are two sets of five differences between speech combined with written seals,
so too should one explain in detail the mutual combinations of writing combined with speech and manual gestures, and of manual gestures combined with speech, writing, and both speech and writing.
If a monk who acts as a family preceptor goes to a donor’s house and speaks thus:
“This girl has grown up; why does she not go forth to marry?
This boy is already of age; why does he not take a wife?”
These [remarks] all constitute an offense of wrong-doing (*duṣkṛta*).
If one says:
"Why does this woman not go to her husband's house? [it is likewise an offense].
If one says,
"Why does this man not go to his wife's house?
one also incurs an *dukkaṭa* (offense of wrong-doing).
If a gatekeeper monk goes to a donor’s house and utters words of opposition, he incurs an *dukkaṭa* (offense of wrong-doing) in every case.
Those who are exempt from offense are: one who is a first-time offender, or one who is insane, mentally deranged, or overwhelmed by intense physical pain.
**The Sixth Training Rule on Building Small Dwellings** The Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, the Anāthapiṇḍada Park.

At that time, many bhikṣus were extensively constructing dwellings; some found them too long or too short, others found them too wide or too narrow, and still others found them dilapidated and unfit for repair, so they would all abandon them to build new houses instead.
By doing so oneself or employing others, one has many affairs to attend to; this leads to the neglect of recitation and hinders meditative reflection.
Furthermore, by repeatedly begging from elders and householders for grass, wood, vehicles, and laborers, one causes distress to those donors.

At that time, the Venerable Mahākāśyapa was dwelling in an araṇya near this city. Having heard that many bhikṣus were constructing many dwellings, even to the point of troubling their donors, he went to the place where the Blessed One was, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, sat to one side, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“Blessed One!”

I have heard that many bhikṣus are constructing numerous dwellings; some, dissatisfied with the dimensions of their current ones, are building new ones again, which hinders the cultivation of wholesome qualities and even causes distress to the donors. I have reported this matter in detail as before.
"I only pray that the Blessed One, out of compassion, will instruct the bhikṣus on the proper method for constructing dwellings.
When the World-Honored One heard these words spoken by the Venerable Kāśyapa, he granted his consent in silence.
At that time, having understood that the Buddha had granted his permission, Kāśyapa prostrated at his feet and departed.
When night had turned to dawn, Kāśyapa, wishing to protect his fellow practitioners of the holy life, took up his robes and bowl and set out to wander among the people.
At that time, the Blessed One, for this reason, assembled the bhikṣus and questioned them, saying: "Bhikṣus,
did you truly construct various dwellings,
or out of dissatisfaction with their width or narrowness, engage extensively in building activities, even to the point of troubling the donors?"
The bhikṣus said:
“It is indeed so,
World-Honored One!”

At that time, the World-Honored One rebuked him in various ways for having many desires, being insatiable, difficult to satisfy, and difficult to support; he praised those with few desires and contentment, who are easy to satisfy and easy to support, who obtain whatever is necessary to sustain the body, who practice the dhūta austerities, whose deportment is orderly, and who receive offerings with moderation.
The Buddha addressed the bhikṣus, saying:
"Having considered ten benefits, I shall establish a training rule within the Vinaya for the sake of the bhikṣus; it should be proclaimed as follows:
'If a bhikṣu should beg for materials himself to construct a small dwelling, and it is for his own use and has no owner, he must construct it according to the prescribed measurements.'"
Regarding the measurements herein: it shall be twelve spans of the Buddha’s hand in length and seven spans in width.

That bhikṣu should lead a community of bhikṣus to inspect the site; that community of bhikṣus should inspect the site to ensure it is a place that accords with the Dharma, is pure, free from dispute, and is a location conducive to spiritual progress.

If a bhikṣu, at an improper place, an impure place, a place of contention, or a place where there is no access, should personally beg for materials to build a hut for himself when there is no donor, and without having other bhikṣus go to inspect the site, should he construct it there in excess of the prescribed dimensions, it is a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*.
"Furthermore, 'if a bhikṣu' refers to one who belongs to this Dharma; the remaining meanings are as explained above.
'To beg for oneself' means to personally beg for grass or wood, or to seek out vehicles and manual labor."
A "small room" is one in which the four modes of deportment—namely, walking, standing, sitting, and reclining—can be accommodated.
"Constructing" it means either building it oneself or having another person build it.
"Without an owner" means that there is no donor for it, such as a man, a woman, or a *paṇḍaka*.
"Made for oneself" means that one should make it according to the proper measure for one's own sake.
Regarding the measurement herein, the length is twelve *hasta* of the Buddha.
"The Buddha" refers to the Great Teacher; one *hasta* of his is equivalent to three *hasta* of an ordinary person.
Twelve *hasta* in length is eighteen cubits for a person of medium height; seven *hasta* in width means ten and a half cubits for a person of medium height.
"This bhikṣu" refers to the person who constructs the dwelling.
Regarding the instruction that one should lead the community of bhikṣus to the place of observation: if one has not first observed it oneself, one should not immediately lead the bhikṣus there.

If, upon personally inspecting the site, one finds it contains snakes, scorpions, insects, ants, or similar creatures serving as their burrows, this is termed "impure," and one should not seek the Dharma there.

If it is pure, one should next examine the location upon which it relies. If it is near a royal palace, a temple, a householder’s residence, a non-Buddhist hermitage, or a bhikṣuṇī convent, or if there is a fine tree that must be cut down, this is called being subject to dispute and contention; in such a place, one should not seek the Dharma.

If there are no such dangers, one must still examine whether the area within a fathom on all four sides allows for coming and going; if there are rivers, wells, or precipices nearby, this is called "lack of access," and one should not seek the Dharma there.

If there is a place that is pure, free from contention, and where there is diligent progress, that bhikṣu should go to the monastery, arrange the seats, strike the gavel, and first announce it with these words.

Once the assembly had gathered, he removed his leather sandals within the great multitude, bared his right shoulder, and having paid respects according to their seniority, he crouched before the presiding elder and, with palms joined, spoke these words:
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!
I, the bhikṣu [Name], who am engaged in construction, have already inspected that the site for building the dwelling is pure.
I, the bhikṣu [Name], who am engaged in construction, wish to build a small dwelling on this pure site and request the Saṃgha’s permission.
"I only pray that the Venerable Saṃgha will listen as I, the bhikṣu so-and-so engaged in construction, am building a dwelling in a pure location; out of compassion for me.
Thus, [he should repeat this] up to three times.
At that time, the bhikṣus should not, out of faith in those bhikṣus' words, refrain from going to investigate.
The bhikṣus should go together to investigate; or alternatively, the Saṃgha may dispatch a large number of trustworthy bhikṣus to inspect the dwelling place.
If there is a place that is, as previously described, impure, subject to dispute, or lacking in conditions for progress, one should not permit the construction.
If the site is pure and free from all obstacles, that bhikṣu should return to his residence, assemble the Saṃgha according to the Dharma, and stand crouching before the Elder, speaking these words:
"Venerable Saṃgha, please listen!"

We have personally inspected the site where the bhikṣu so-and-so, who is undertaking the construction, intends to build a small dwelling; the location is pure and free from all obstacles. May the Saṃgha now deign to consider the time appropriate.
Next, one bhikṣu should perform the formal motion (*jñapti-karman*) as follows:
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!
This bhikṣu so-and-so, acting as the overseer of construction, has inspected and confirmed that the site for building the dwelling is pure."
This bhikṣu who is overseeing the construction has ensured that all matters regarding the site for the building are in accordance with the Dharma and pure; he now requests permission from the Saṃgha.

If it is the proper time for the Saṃgha, may the Saṃgha grant its consent, so that the Saṃgha may now authorize this bhikṣu [Name], who is overseeing the construction, to build a dwelling on a site that is in accordance with the Dharma and pure.
"The motion is thus announced.
Next, perform the *karmavācanā* (formal ritual act) according to the procedure for the announcement.
Once that bhikṣu has been granted permission by the assembly, he may act as he wishes; do not harbor any doubts.

Regarding the term *saṃghāvaśeṣa*: this offense is to be removed and extinguished by means of the Saṃgha; even the formal rehabilitation from the offense does not depend on any individual other than the Saṃgha. Whether it is "with remainder" (*sāvaśeṣa*) or "without remainder" (*anavaśeṣa*) has already been explained above.
In this regard, what are the characteristics of the offense and how does it occur?

If a bhikṣu, at an impure site, a site subject to dispute, or a site lacking access, builds a small hut himself or causes another to build it, should any one of these three faults be present, he incurs a sthūlātyaya offense.
If one constructs it without the Sangha’s permission, it is a sthūlātyaya.
If one constructs it in excess of the prescribed measurements, it is also a sthūlātyaya.
If one constructs a dwelling possessing all the aforementioned faults, one incurs a saṃghāvaśeṣa offense.
If a bhikṣu goes to another bhikṣu and speaks thus:
"Venerable sir, you should seek the community's permission for me regarding a place free from dispute and conducive to progress; do not allow me to construct a small hut of excessive size."
At that time, those bhikṣus constructed small dwellings in places subject to dispute, in places lacking access, without the consent of the Saṃgha, or in excess of the prescribed dimensions.
Those bhikṣus who act as supervisors shall each incur a sthūlātyaya;
if one constructs a dwelling while possessing all the aforementioned faults, he incurs a saṃghāvaśeṣa.
If that bhikṣu goes to the bhikṣu who is overseeing the construction and speaks thus:
"The house you are now building is excellent; it does not deviate from what I have instructed."
"If there is a slight deficiency in grass, wood, mud, or other materials, I shall provide them.

If [the dwelling] is in a place subject to dispute, or in a place where progress toward it is impossible, or if the Sangha has not granted permission, or if the time limit is exceeded, both individuals incur a sthūlātyaya offense.
If all the aforementioned faults are present, both individuals incur a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense.
If that bhikṣu goes to the bhikṣu who is overseeing the construction and speaks as follows:
"The house you are currently building is extremely improper; it contradicts everything I have said, and whatever is deficient or lacking, you do not provide."
If the laborers commit an offense as previously described, that bhikṣu is not at fault.
There is no offense if he obtains a pre-existing house or an already occupied dwelling, or if he repairs and maintains an old room.
Furthermore, there is no offense for one who is the very first offender, or for one who is insane, mentally deranged, or afflicted by intense pain.
The Seventh Training Rule on Building Large Monasteries. The Buddha was staying at the Ghoṣitārāma in Kauśāmbī.
At that time, while the six bhikṣus were residing in another monastery, they constantly harbored feelings of disdain. Then Nanda said to Upānanda:
"Look at this monastery; its rafters and beams are collapsing and its walls are crumbling, like an elephant stable unfit for habitation."
When the bhikṣus heard this, they said to them:
"Venerable ones!

You know only how to dwell in the old monasteries of others; you yourselves lack the power to lay even a single stone or build a small hut, yet you spread idle rumors and disparage the affairs of others."
At that time, the six groups of monks said to one another:
"Nanda and Upananda!
We are now being utterly despised by those with black bowls; we ought to build separate monasteries that those with black bowls have never seen before."
They further said to one another,
"If we all work together on this construction, those black-bowl men will find our vulnerability and say:
'The six bhikṣus are all working like hired laborers.'"
"Because of this, when we go out to beg for alms, people look down upon us with contempt.

We should now appoint from within our own community one person who is intelligent, sharp-witted, and skilled in discerning the proper occasion—one capable of inserting a fine needle into a coarse pestle, and who can obtain great wealth with little speech—and I shall request him to serve as our steward."
Upānanda replied, "Excellent! However,
within my assembly, who is wise, possessed of sharp intelligence, and skilled at discerning the appropriate timing?"
“The noble Ānanda is that very person; we should go together to his place.
Having arrived there, they said to him:
“Venerable Ānanda! [...]”
"Virtuous One, do you know now?
I shall relate the preceding events to you in their proper order.
Only one of great virtue, wisdom, and eloquence, who well understands the appropriate timing and circumstances, is fit to serve as the administrator."
Chanda replied,
"Excellent! Excellent!"
"This great field of merit brings benefit to both oneself and others; let us not oppose the will of the assembly, but together cultivate sympathetic joy.
At that time, the Venerable Chanda, having washed his feet outside the cell, entered the cell and sat cross-legged, thinking:
"By what means can I build a great monastery for the Saṃgha?"

He further reflected: "Now, among the multitudes of humans and devas in this world, all have conceived universal respect and faith toward the World-Honored One; yet, such-and-such a family has conceived respect and faith in the Venerable Ājñātakauṇḍinya; another family in the Venerable Aśvajit; another in Bhadrika; another in Vāṣpa; another in Mahānāman; another in Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra; another in Vimala; another in Gavāmpati; another in Śāriputra; and another in Mahāmaudgalyāyana—and likewise for other great bhikṣus—each has donors who have individually conceived respect and faith."
"Since I have no generous donor, upon whom can I rely to build this monastery?

At that time, there was a brahmin in this city who was immensely wealthy and possessed great riches; however, he was by nature so miserly that he would not even give away the water used for washing his vessels to others.
"If you can convert him and cause him to develop faith, you may build a great dwelling for the Saṃgha.

At that time, after dawn had broken, Chanda put on his robes, took up his bowl, and entered Kauśāmbī to beg for food. Having first obtained a small portion of parched grain from one or two houses, he proceeded to the house of that brahmin, intending to enter it.
Then the gatekeeper said:
"Dharma Master!
This is a Brahmin household; you should not enter here without due cause."
Chanda replied:
"As for the Blessed One, the World-Honored One, he prohibits alms-seekers from five types of households:
first, those who make proclamations;..."
2. The house of a courtesan;
3. The house of a liquor seller;
4. The house of a caṇḍāla.
"5. A royal family.
Could this house possibly be one of the five types mentioned before?
At that time, the gatekeeper replied:
“The Dharma Master is being greatly ridiculed; this is not a public proclamation nor even a royal residence, but rather the house of a certain Brahmin. You need not enter.”
At that time, Chanda thought to himself:
"If they will not even allow me to approach when I seek to grasp the hem of his robe, how could I possibly obtain anything else?
Just then, an elder passed by the gate with his newborn son; it was a great occasion of celebration, with drums and music being played and many dancing girls accompanying them.
The gatekeeper, distracted by his eager gaze at the music and performance, left his post; at that moment, Channa slipped inside.
His deportment was so composed and dignified, like that of one who has transcended desire, that when the Brahmin saw him approaching from afar, he addressed him, saying:
"Welcome, Venerable Channa!"
"It would be fitting to sit here for a moment to rest.
However, what Cunda had proposed lacked the proper expedient means;
he said to the brahmin, "I have already gone from door to door begging and obtained a portion of parched grain; you may roast it for me."
Then the brahmin said to his young maidservant,
"You may take a sieve and sift this flour.
The girl immediately followed her instructions and began to sift it.
At that time, Chanda examined the flour for sale;
a brahmin asked him, "What are you looking at, sir? Chanda replied:
"I wish to examine for insects; if there are any insects, I should not eat it.
The brāhmaṇa replied, "If one eats insects, what fault would there be?"
He replied: “As the World-Honored One has said:

‘If one who kills living beings practices this habitually, at the dissolution of the body after death, they will fall into hell and undergo various sufferings; even if they should obtain human birth, they will be short-lived and frequently ill.’”

However, the bhikṣu Cchanda was thoroughly versed in the Tripiṭaka and possessed unimpeded eloquence, being well able to preach the Dharma; he then proclaimed the essentials of the Dharma to the brahmin, extensively expounding upon the ten paths of unwholesome action.

When the brahmin had heard the Dharma, a heart of reverence and faith arose within him; he immediately entered his house and ordered various kinds of exquisite, fragrant, and delicious foods—both solid and soft—to be prepared as an offering for Chanda.
Upon seeing this, Chandaka immediately thought to himself:
"I have heard that wooden pots are used for cooking only once; if I were to accept this food, it would serve as both my morning meal and my evening meal."
He replied, "Donor!
I have already accepted the flour offered by another; how could I possibly discard it to eat fine food?"
The brahmin said, "According to the law of my clan,
if one first obtains coarse food and later encounters something exquisite, there is truly no fault in discarding the former inferior food."

Chanda replied, "The Brahmin caste does not observe the precepts and acts according to their own whims; however, I have received the collection of precepts—how could I dare to lightly discard the offerings of faith given by others?"
When the brahmin heard these words, his profound faith redoubled; Chandaka then took his leave and departed.
The brahmin said, "Venerable Sir!..."
"From time to time, please come to visit my house. Chanda replied,
"I truly wish to visit you frequently, yet the gatekeeper, like a fierce jailer, does not allow me to proceed."
Then the brāhmaṇa called to the gatekeeper and said,
"If you see the Dharma Master Khandaka, do not stop him.
The gatekeeper replied:
"So be it. At that time, Chandaka immediately thought to himself:
"If other black-bowl monks enter here, they may not recognize the proper occasion and cause the donor to lose faith. I should now prepare a skillful means in advance to prevent them from entering."
He replied to the gatekeeper,
saying, "O man!
Do you know now?"
“O Brahmin, I have caused you to give rise to respectful faith through a great cause.
The gatekeeper replied,
“I already know this.”
He told him:
"From this day forward, do not allow any other black-bowl monks to enter this gate; if you should allow one to enter, I shall give you a heavy flogging and replace you with another person."
He replied, "It was not my intention for you, sir, to enter this gate; how could I allow others to advance so abruptly?
Please do not worry."
At that time, Channa would visit their home from time to time and proclaim the sublime Dharma to the Brahmin couple, leading them to receive the three refuges and uphold the five precepts.

At that time, the brahmin emptied all his household possessions and offered them with a sincere heart; whatever was required, he gave without any stinginess, yet at that moment, Chandaka accepted nothing at all.

Later, at another time, he came to his house and, for the sake of the brahmin, praised and explained the seven types of meritorious actions involving material things. Upon hearing this explanation of the benefits, the brahmin felt profound joy and said to Canda:
"Noble One!..."
"I now wish to cultivate meritorious deeds involving material things.
He replied, "O noble one!"
"Now is precisely the right time; you may do as you please.
The brahmin asked, "What do you wish to do?"
Chanda replied,
"You may build a dwelling for the community of monks," and he immediately gave rise to this thought:
"I have previously offered my entire household wealth as alms many times, yet the Noble One has never accepted even a single thread.
Although he now permits it for the sake of the Sangha, seeing this [practice of] such few desires, I feel a most profound and deep reverence."
He addressed [the Buddha], saying:
“Venerable Sir!
I now truly possess abundant wealth and wish to build for the Saṃgha; however, all the land belongs to the King, and there is no place to construct a monastery.”
Chanda replied, "Worthy sir!
You need not worry; I shall go to the king and seek that land for you."
Chanda thought to himself:
"Whom should I approach first?
Shall I see the king?"
"Are you a minister?
When making a formal request for alms, one does not approach the king directly, but should do so through his messenger.
At that time, Channa went toward the minister's house to request alms, and the minister asked him:
"Noble Ācārya Cunda!
For what purpose have you come here?
He replied to the minister:

“Now there is a certain brāhmaṇa who wishes to construct a dwelling for the Saṃgha; however, since all the land belongs to the king, there is no place to build. I now venture to inform Your Majesty on his behalf, and pray that you will graciously grant your benevolence to assist him in its completion.”
The minister replied,
"Venerable sir!
If the king remains in leisure, I shall summon you."
At another time, when the king had no affairs of state and was attended only by his ministers, he commanded one man, saying:
"You should go and summon the venerable Channa.
That man, having received the command, went to summon him and arrived at the king's gate, where he addressed the gatekeeper, saying:
"You should now go and inform the Great King that the bhikṣu Chanda has arrived outside the gate and wishes to see the Great King.

At that time, the gatekeeper immediately reported this to the king. Upon hearing it, the king ordered him to enter, for who would dare to obstruct the Venerable Chanda? Having reached the king's presence, he then offered a blessing:
"May the King be free from illness and enjoy long life."
The king prepared a seat for him, and he immediately took his place. Then the minister addressed the king, saying:

"The Dharma Master Khandaka is a son of the Śākyas; having renounced worldly life to become a monk, he is well-versed in the Tripiṭaka, possesses unimpeded eloquence, and is endowed with great merit."
The king said,
"I knew this beforehand.
Welcome, O Noble One!"
"By what means did you arrive here?
Chandaka replied, "Great King!"
"There is a certain brāhmaṇa who wishes to construct a dwelling place for the Saṃgha.
However, as this land belongs to the King, I now inform the Great King on his behalf."
The king said, "Noble One! Do as you wish;
you may certainly take pleasure in this and establish it as a monastery. I shall depart for the outside, provided that you do not act otherwise."
"Except for the royal palace, you may establish gardens and fields elsewhere as you please.
Chandaka offered this prayer:
"May the King be free from illness and enjoy long life."
Having taken his leave, he departed.
At that time, Chanda returned to his dwelling and said to the group of six:
"Nanda and Upananda!..."
"May you all rejoice; the King has granted me this boon.
With the exception of the royal palace, I shall build monasteries according to my pleasure upon any other gardens or fields.
At that time, the group of six immediately went together to the brahmin’s house and said:
“O Noble One! You should know that the King has granted my wish; with the exception of the royal palace itself, you may build monasteries at your pleasure upon all other gardens and fields.
O Noble One, please provide me with the funds required for these expenditures.”
Thereupon, he immediately gave him a great deal of wealth.
Having received the goods, he took them and departed, and they said to one another:
"In what place shall we build a vihāra?"
One man deliberated, saying:
"From Kauśāmbī toward the Ghoṣitārāma, there is a large tree of lovely form along the way; beneath this tree, a brahmin is teaching five hundred youths and receiving them as his students."
Whenever a bhikṣu passed by this place, the students would constantly tease him, saying: "Hey!
Bhikṣu, here is the first alms-collector; here is the second alms-collector; his alms-bag is wide open and has room for much!"
"He has always mocked and ridiculed me.
Now that he has provoked my resentment, I shall cut down his trees to provide for the needs of the monastery.
Having deliberated thus, he immediately went among the laborers to hire five hundred workers, negotiated the wages with them, and brought them all to the monastery.
The servant said,
"Venerable sir!
Show me where I am to work."
He then said to him,
"Please have some light refreshment.
After he had eaten, he asked:
“Noble one! Where should it be made?
He replied:
“Furthermore, you should apply oil to your body for a short while.
Next, after providing him with the afternoon meal until the time of sunset, he said:
“Noble One!
"You must pay back the price. He replied, "Fool!"
"You all are making a great living today by demanding a price from me," the employer replied.
The laborers reported, "How could we,
who have been commanded by the Noble One to perform work, fail to do so?"
Chanda replied, "O noble one!
You may take a basket, hold a mattock, and carry an axe; I shall pay you back double the value of these, and you should follow me as I show you the place where they are to be made."
He then led the men to that great tree and said to them,
"You may cut down this tree.
The laborers replied:
"This is a magnificent great tree; I have but one head. Who dares to cut it down?
He replied, "Fool!"
"The King has granted us our wish; with the exception of the royal palace, everything else may be used as needed to construct the monastery.
For what reason, then, do you not fell [the trees]?
At that time, the laborers immediately deliberated together:
"I shall now cut it down; whatever punishment there may be for this, they themselves shall know.
He then felled the tree, hacking it to pieces, and dug up its roots to cast them into the river. Having leveled the ground and marked out the foundations with a cord, they said to one another:

"Nanda and Upananda shall build a monastery for the Saṃgha on this site; here we shall construct a fragrant hall for the Blessed One, here a gatehouse, here a warm room, here a kitchen, here a meditation hall, and here an infirmary."
Having thus made his arrangements, he departed.

It was the regular practice of those students that every day one of them would rise early in the morning to sweep and cleanse the area beneath that tree, and to smear it with fresh cow dung as an adornment.
On that very day, he went beneath that tree but did not see it; he immediately ran back to report to his teacher, saying, "I do not see the tree.
At that time, the other disciples saw him and said:
"There are no trees," he said, and then addressed him,
"Does the Master know this?"
"This man must certainly have eaten rice mixed with vinegar yesterday; the hot vapors have affected his eyes, so he cannot see the tree.
The Master then ordered a student in charge of affairs to go and look at the tree.
He went to that place but did not see the tree either, and returned to report to his teacher, saying:
"Just as he said, the tree truly does not exist.
Upon hearing this report, the master himself led five hundred students to the site of the former tree to examine the matter in detail.
One who possessed mindfulness replied to them, saying:
"This is the place where our teacher used to discourse; this is the place where we used to attend to the aggregates and karma.
Then those disciples, having reflected together, remained there filled with sorrow.
At that time, a traveler passed by that place and asked,
"Sir! Why are you so distressed?"
He replied, "Do you not know?
There was once a magnificent tree in this place; suddenly last night, we do not know who felled it?"
He replied, "Sir!
Yesterday at sunset, I saw the group of six monks leading laborers, all carrying axes and mattocks; could it not have been they who were cutting down the trees?"
Although he heard these words, his sorrowful thoughts did not cease.
At that time, the group of six monks came to that place and asked the teacher,
"Master, why do you appear to have a look of sorrow?"
He replied, "Venerable One!
Previously there was a magnificent great tree at this spot; I do not know for what reason it has vanished overnight?"
Upon hearing this, the group of six monks burst into loud laughter.
The brahmin asked,
"Could it be that these people are felling this tree?"
The group of six replied:
"Fool! We intended to vex and disturb you on purpose; do you not recall how you once spoke these words to mock us?"
"This is the first alms-seeker; this is the second alms-seeker. Their alms-bag is opened wide and has great capacity.

The Brahmin said, "The Śramaṇa sons of the Śākyas stubbornly harbor resentment and together revile one another. Beings such as these burn away the True Dharma and lose the conduct of a Śramaṇa; they are like a magnificent great tree being cut down for no reason."
When the bhikṣus heard this, they reported the matter to the Buddha.
On account of this, the Buddha assembled the bhikṣus and spoke at length as previously described, up to: “I shall establish a training rule for the bhikṣus, which should be recited as follows:

‘If a bhikṣu constructs a large dwelling with a patron for the sake of the Saṃgha, that bhikṣu must take a group of bhikṣus to inspect the site. That group of bhikṣus should inspect the site to ensure it is a suitable and pure location, free from disputes, and conducive to spiritual progress.’”

If a bhikṣu constructs a large dwelling in an unsuitable location, an impure location, a location subject to dispute, or a location lacking access—whether for himself or for the sake of the Saṃgha—and does so with a patron, yet fails to lead other bhikṣus to inspect the site before constructing the large dwelling in such a place, it is a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*.
"Furthermore, 'if a bhikṣu' refers to the group of six; the remaining meanings are as explained above.
Regarding 'building a large monastery,' there are two kinds of 'large':
first, the largeness of the donated materials."
2. Second, it is large in size and volume.
Here, "large" refers to the largeness of the object given as a gift.
Regarding the "dwelling place," it means that it must be capable of accommodating the four modes of deportment: walking, standing, sitting, and lying down.
"Having an owner" means having women, men, or *paṇḍakas* (hermaphrodites) and so forth acting as the donors.
"For the sake of the community" means for the sake of the Tathāgata and the community of *bhikṣu* monks.

Regarding the phrase "one should lead the assembly of bhikṣus": one should lead the bhikṣus to observe the site, ensuring it is pure, free from dispute, and conducive to spiritual progress; then, returning to the great assembly, one should request their permission.
The assembly, by means of a *jñapti-dvitīya-karman*, granted permission for the construction, with all details explained at length as previously stated.

Regarding the gravity of the offenses, whether committed individually, in pairs, or collectively, and even cases involving those who are insane, mentally deranged, or afflicted by intense pain, these matters are also explained in detail as in the case of the previous dwelling.

Volume Thirteen.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Yijing by Imperial Decree. 8.
The Training Rule on Groundless Slander. The Eighth Training Rule on Groundless Slander. At that time, the Blessed One was staying at Rājagṛha in the Bamboo Grove, by the Kalandaka Pond.

At that time, in the kingdom of Pāpā, there was a powerful minister named Jayasena. He was immensely wealthy with abundant resources and enjoyments; his assets were like those of King Vaiśravaṇa. Although he was not of royal lineage, the warriors of the time performed the consecration ceremony and established him as king. He took a woman from a noble family as his queen and lived in happiness.

Although many years passed, she still had no son or daughter; seeking a child, she prayed to the gods and spirits, visiting all the temples and shrines of the deities born together with her, yet her hope for a descendant was not fulfilled.
However, it is said in the world:
"To obtain a son by means of begging is truly a falsehood; if this were true, everyone would have a thousand sons like a Wheel-Turning King."
"However, it is through three conditions that a child is conceived.
What are these three?
First, the act of sexual union between the father and mother;"
Second, the mother’s body was pure and fit for conception;
third, the scent of food appeared before her.

Through the convergence of the king’s karmic conditions, a certain deva descended from the Sublime Heaven (*Sudharmā*) and took up residence in the queen’s womb. This was his final birth; he delighted in cultivating sublime practices, possessed the nature of liberation, and was oriented toward *nirvāṇa*. He felt aversion toward *saṃsāra* and found no pleasure in any of the realms of existence.
If a wise woman possesses five special knowledges—as explained in detail above—up until the point where the fetus is situated in her right flank, she joyfully says to the king:
"Great King, you should know!..."
"The child I carry shall surely bring glory to our clan; that it resides now in my right flank, it is undoubtedly a male.
When the King heard this, he was filled with great joy and spoke these words:

"For a long time I have constantly contemplated the succession of an heir to continue my great enterprise. Having raised him, he will ultimately repay my kindness by practicing extensive acts of charity for the benefit and welfare of his kinsmen, and after I have passed away, he shall proclaim my name and offer prayers of blessing on my behalf."
"May the places where my parents are born be adorned with merit.

At that time, the king placed his consort in a high tower to dwell as she pleased; he provided her with all necessities according to the season, constantly employing female physicians to prepare her food and drink so that the temperature was perfectly balanced and all flavors were complete. Adorned with exquisite pearl necklaces, she was like a celestial maiden wandering in the Garden of Joy (Nandana), always remaining on couches and seats with her feet never touching the ground, her eyes never beholding unwholesome sights, and her ears never hearing unwholesome sounds.

After nine months had passed, he gave birth to a son whose countenance was extraordinary and beloved by all people; his forehead was broad, his eyebrows long, his nose high and straight, his head perfectly round like a parasol, his complexion as beautiful as gold, and his hands reached down past his knees—a sight praised by the multitude.
After twenty-one days had passed, the kinsmen gathered together. The father showed his son to the relatives and asked, "What name should be given to this child?
Since birth, the child had been naturally pure and clean; even before leaving his bedding, he had not required the use of the toilet. The people deliberated and said:

"In the laws of China, that which is naturally pure and clean is called 'real' (*śrī*). Now, this boy’s innate consciousness is pure; he has not yet left his bed and does not yet defecate or urinate. His cleanliness surpasses that of others, thus he becomes a 'real thing. Furthermore, as he is the son of a powerful great king, he should be given a name: Śrīgupta."
On the very day Prince Śaktimān was born, five hundred warriors each gave birth to a son, who were named according to their respective clans.
Then King Jayasena entrusted the prince to eight nurses:

two to provide milk, two to carry him in swaddling clothes, two for bathing, and two for play; he provided him with milk, curd, clarified butter, and honey, so that he grew rapidly like a lotus emerging from a pond.
At that time, there was a physiognomist who, seeing the child within his mother’s womb, immediately formed this thought:
"This child is a field of merit for bipeds; if anyone offers even a small amount of worship to him, that person shall obtain supreme merit and benefit."
Having formed this thought, he said to the wet nurse, "Please, out of compassion, entrust me with your child;
I wish to offer him my service for a short while according to my own inclination.
The wet nurse replied:
"I have no authority over the child; if you wish to obtain him, you may inform the King.
At that time, the physiognomist went to the Great King and said to him:
"Your Majesty’s noble son is a supreme field of merit; if anyone offers even a small amount of worship to him, that person shall obtain the benefit of supreme merit."
"I am fortunate to have been granted this; I wish to extend a small offering.
The King replied, "You may do as you please."

Then that physiognomist took him back to his home; having first bathed him, he next anointed him with exquisite perfumes, covered his body with garments of the highest price, and placed ghee, honey, and milk porridge in precious vessels which he brought as offerings. Having completed these offerings, he sent him back to the king’s presence.
At that time, as the youth gradually grew older, he became fully proficient in writing, arithmetic, hand gestures, and technical arts.

Furthermore, regarding all the crafts and skills according to the dharma of the Kṣatriya royal lineage—namely, riding elephants and horses, driving chariots, and the use of weapons such as swords, spears, halberds, hooks, and lassos—as well as manual dexterity and the techniques of hacking and archery—he mastered them all without exception.

At that time, five hundred boys were born on the same day; like the former [prince], they all became proficient in the arts and crafts. His father then constructed for him three palaces and three gardens for the spring, summer, and winter seasons, as well as three classes of female attendants—namely, superior, middling, and inferior.
Later, on one occasion, Bālaputra ascended to a high tower and amused himself with various female entertainers.

Every day at the three times of the day, five hundred youths would regularly come to visit him. On another day, those five hundred men went out hunting; they galloped about all day long but returned empty-handed, having caught nothing at all.
They then stayed in the forest and wilds; the next day they went out on a journey and, having gained much, did not return until evening. They then consulted one another, saying:
"Since the sun is already setting, there is no way for us to attend the assembly; we shall see the Prince only when morning comes."
On the third day, the crowd finally saw him; at that time, the Prince said to the people, "You and I were born together and have always played together; for what reason have you not come until now?"
They replied,
"We have gone out on a hunt. He said:
"What is meant by 'hunting'?
He replied:
"It is the widespread killing of various deer."
The Prince asked,
"What do they eat and drink?
He replied:
"They drink water and eat grass.
[The other asked: "If that is so, they do no harm to humans; for what reason, then, do you injure and kill them?
He replied:
"When seeing [a victim] being killed, you feel joy in your hearts.
The Prince said,
"Gentlemen, you should not take pleasure in seeing others suffer."
The people deliberated, saying:
"Because this Prince does not go hunting himself, he treats us with contempt; we must cause him to join us in the hunt as well."
Then those people went to the Great King and said, "Great King!

Your Majesty’s crown prince has been born and raised within the deep seclusion of the palace; if an enemy state should come, he will surely feel fear and trepidation. For what reason do you not allow the prince to go hunting?"
"If he goes out hunting frequently, his mind will become courageous and robust, and when fighting the enemy kingdom, his spirit will be free from retreat or cowardice.
When King Jayasena heard this proposal, he told Sthāvaraka:
"You should now go out and try practicing the hunt."
He replied, "I do not wish for it.
The king said:
"You are of the Kṣatriya caste; you ought to practice the arts of war.
At that time, the Prince did not dare disobey the command and went out with the crowd. The people deliberated, saying:
"If our father passes away, this Prince shall surely become king. If we now serve him with all our hearts, we will be able to increase his wealth and status in the future."
He said to the Prince:
"You may stay here; I shall drive the herd of deer to this place and settle them within the enclosure."
At that time, those men were driving a great herd of deer. Seeing them from afar, the Prince observed that the herd was fleeing in terror; one deer, struck by an arrow, arrived with its mouth agape.

Thereupon, he thought: "Even if there were someone who lacked compassion and feared nothing of the future life, they would still not give rise to such a poisonous and evil intent toward this creature, much less inflict slaughter."

Not far from there were some hunters guarding the enclosure; out of consideration for their feelings, the Prince discharged three arrows from afar at the herd of deer, so that they either passed between their thighs or pierced the joints of their antlers, yet the arrows fell to the ground without causing them any injury.
Whenever deer arrived at the place where the enclosures were set, he would release them all so they might flee as they pleased.
At that time, the attendants all thought to themselves:
"The Prince has long been well-versed in the art of archery; today he must surely kill many deer."
When they arrived and searched thoroughly, not a single one was to be found. They all thought to themselves:
"Perhaps the Prince has already had the carriage carry them back first.
Then those people asked the Prince:
"Where is the deer you caught now?
The Prince replied, "The fierce beast bolted in terror; it nearly killed me!"
The guards reported to the people, saying:
"For what reason have you appointed those who do not harm others to guard this place? If you wish to kill him, you will not succeed; simply watch him as he goes straight ahead and escapes."
Having heard this, the people were all filled with resentment and anger, saying:
"We have gathered these deer with extreme hardship, our bodies wounded and exhausted; yet he has released them all. We ought to kill him together."
Again they deliberated, saying:
"If we harm this man, the King of the country of Pāpā will surely kill us; it would be best to abandon him and return.
At that time, the Prince had this thought:
"These ones played with me while stroking my dust; yet, failing to catch the deer, they have abandoned me in the wilderness. If I were to become king, these people would not be benefited."
Having had this thought, he slowly returned to his native city; once arrived at the palace, he sat with his cheek propped in his hand, dwelling in sorrowful contemplation.
At that time, a woman of the inner apartments came to where he was, but the Prince did not look upon her. Seeing this, the woman went in and informed the King, saying:
"Great King, you should know!"
"The Crown Prince saw me and did not look at me directly; he sat with his hand supporting his cheek, looking distressed and dejected.
The King asked him personally, "What is the reason for your current state? Why do you harbor such grief and find no joy?"
He replied, "My father the King has commanded me to engage in the work of butchery and hunting; how could I not be distressed?
The King said:
"Do you not take pleasure in the business of hunting?
He replied, "Truly,
it is not what I find pleasing."
The king said,
"From this day forward, do not go out hunting again.
At that time, Srigupta (Śrīgupta) had this thought:

“Worldly folk encounter many hardships and are oppressed by manifold sufferings; they are constantly bound by the fetters of afflictions (*kleśa*). To leave the household life for a state of seclusion, and to maintain a pure, unadulterated, and perfect holy life (*brahmacarya*) until the end of one’s existence—this is what I should now do with right faith: departing from home for the homeless life, I shall distance myself from the secular world.”

At that time, there lived nearby in the kingdom of Pāpā six non-Buddhist teachers, namely: Pūraṇa Kāśyapa, Maskarī Gośālīputra, Sañjayī Vairaṭīputra, Ajita Keśakambalīputra, Kakuda Kātyāyanīputra, and Nirgrantha Jñātiputra. Though they were not omniscient, they harbored the conceit of omniscience, causing the masses of people to look up to them with longing and to take refuge in their sincerity.
At that time, the son of Gṛhapati went to where those six teachers were and said to Pūraṇa Kāśyapa:
"What is the principle of the Dharma upon which you, Venerable Sir, rely?"
"With what instruction do you guide your disciples?
What fruit shall they obtain by diligently practicing the holy life?
The teacher replied:

“Prince! That which I follow is held as such a view and taught as such a doctrine: there is no giving, no receiving, and no sacrificial offerings; there are no virtuous or non-virtuous deeds, no causes and conditions of karma, and no ripening fruits; there is no present world and no future world; there is no father and no mother, nor are there any beings born by transformation.”

In this world, there are no arhats who have rightly entered and rightly practiced, who have attained self-awakening in this very life regarding this world and the next, and who have fully realized and understood all things, knowing: "Birth has been exhausted, the holy life has been established, what was to be done has been accomplished, and there will be no further existence. Such things do not exist at all.
The presence of life within this body is called birth.
Once this body has passed away, the five great elements separate and there is no further possibility of life; this is called death.

Earth returns to earth, water returns to water, fire returns to fire, wind returns to wind, and the sense faculties return to emptiness. Carried by four men to the place of cremation, once consumed by fire, there remain only the residual bones and nothing more can be known; thus it is the same for both the foolish and the wise.
"The giver is called 'the donor,' and the taker is called 'the recipient'; all those who claim these things exist speak falsely.
When Śrīgupta heard these words, he thought to himself:
"This Great Teacher has turned his back on the right path and walks upon a wrong way; like a perilous road, it is terrifying and should be abandoned by the wise—it ought not to be practiced."
He spoke a verse, saying:
"One of evil wisdom who preaches evil dharma, though truly a fool, calls himself a Great Teacher;
if this dharma is what is considered right, then what could be called non-dharma?"
Having understood this, he realized it was like striking an empty vessel that produces nothing but a hollow sound; he abandoned them and departed.
Then, the venerable Sthavira went again to where Māṣa-kaḷyāṇa Gauśālīputra was and said to him:
"What is the principle of the Dharma upon which you rely?"
"With what instruction do you guide your disciples?
What fruit shall they obtain by diligently practicing the holy life?
The teacher replied:

“Prince! The doctrine I follow maintains this view and makes this proclamation: all sentient beings possess afflictions without cause or condition; all sentient beings are oppressed by afflictions without cause or condition; all sentient beings attain purity without cause or condition; all sentient beings achieve purification without cause or condition; all sentient beings possess ignorance without cause or condition; all sentient beings comprehend the objects of ignorance without cause or condition; all sentient beings are without power, without diligence, without valor, without progress, without self, and without other; all sentient beings who possess life lack any sovereign authority, constantly experiencing suffering and pleasure within the six realms of birth, and beyond these, there is nothing more.”
When Sthavira Śrīgupta heard these words, he thought to himself:
"This Great Teacher has turned his back on the right path and follows a wrong way; like a perilous road, it is terrifying and should be abandoned by the wise and not practiced."
He spoke in verse:
"One of evil wisdom who preaches evil doctrines, though truly a fool, calls himself a Great Teacher;
if this dharma is what is considered right, what then can be called non-dharma?"
Having understood this, he realized it was like striking an empty vessel that produces nothing but a hollow sound; he abandoned him and departed.
Then, the venerable Sthavira went again to the presence of Sañjayin Vairaṭīputra and said to him:
"What is the principle of the Dharma upon which you rely?"
"With what instruction do you guide your disciples?
What fruit shall they obtain by diligently practicing the holy life?
The teacher replied:

“Prince! The doctrine I follow holds such a view and makes such a teaching: whether one kills oneself or causes another to kill; whether one cuts oneself or causes another to cut; whether one cooks oneself or causes another to cook; or whether one commits theft, sexual misconduct, lying, or drinking alcohol—and furthermore, because one teaches others to commit killing and so forth; or because one breaks walls, picks locks, ambushes on dangerous paths, or wields swords and wheels to slaughter multitudes of beings, hacking down every sentient being upon the great earth until their lives are severed and their bodies form a great heap of flesh—whether one performs such evil deeds south of the Ganges River or establishes a great assembly of merit north of the Ganges River—it is not by virtue of these that the causes of sin or merit give rise to the retributions of sin or merit.”
"Furthermore, one does not obtain the fruit of the future through generosity, observance of precepts, few desires, or contentment.
When the Venerable Sthavira Śrīgupta heard these words, he thought to himself:
"This Great Teacher has turned his back on the true path and walks upon a deviant path; like a perilous road filled with many terrors, it is abandoned by the wise and should not be practiced."
He spoke in verse:
"One of evil wisdom who preaches evil doctrines, though truly a fool, calls himself a Great Teacher;
if this dharma is considered right, what then can be called non-dharma?"
Having understood this, he realized it was like striking an empty vessel that produces nothing but a hollow sound; he abandoned it and departed.
Then, the venerable Sthavira went again to where Aśvajit Kāśyapa was and said to him: "Master!..."
"What is the principle of the Dharma upon which you, O Venerable One, rely?
With what do you instruct your disciples?
And what fruit shall they obtain by diligently practicing the holy life?"
The teacher replied: "Prince!

As for our tradition, we hold such a view and maintain such a teaching: these seven constituent elements of the body are incapable of acting and have no agent; they are incapable of transforming and have no transformer; they cannot be harmed, and their substance exists eternally."

What are these seven? They are the earth-body, the water-body, the fire-body, the wind-body, the body of suffering, the body of pleasure, and the life-body. These gather together in one place like a bundle of reeds; they move and transform without disturbing one another, and their transgressions, merits, sufferings, and pleasures do not interfere with each other. Even if someone were to cut off another’s head, there would be no pain; within the cavities of the body, swords and blades pass through them as if through empty space without harming the life-force. In this regard, there is truly neither a killer nor a slain, neither an interrogator nor an interrogated, neither a rememberer nor a remembered.
In its four directions, there are fourteen thousand doors of dependent origination;
furthermore, there are sixty-six thousand, down to fifty-three, two, one and a half, types of karmic differentiation;
additionally, there are sixty-two modes of conduct, sixty-two intermediate kalpas, two thousand hells, three thousand faculties, and thirty-six vital essences.
There were forty-nine thousand families of nāgas, forty-nine thousand families of garuḍas,
forty-nine thousand families of heretics who subsist on human skull-bones, forty-nine thousand families of naked ascetics,
and forty-nine thousand families of heretics who live by wrong livelihood; there were seven kinds of perceptions and seven kinds of *ārūpya* [attainments].
There are seven kinds of asuras, seven kinds of piśācas, seven kinds of devas, and seven kinds of humans; there are seven hundred and seven ponds,
