seven hundred and seven dreams, seven hundred and seven banks, seven hundred and seven peaks,
seven kinds of superior births, ten kinds of increases, and the eight stages of the great person.
In this manner, throughout eighty-four thousand great eons, all who are both foolish and wise reach the end of suffering.

It is like a person who takes a fine thread, casts it into the air, and it falls back to the ground; in the same way, the foolish and the wise, after eighty-four thousand great eons of wandering through saṃsāra, reach the limit of the end of suffering. In this world, there is truly no śramaṇa or brāhmaṇa capable of making such a claim as:

"I have established precepts and prohibitions so that my disciples may always be diligent, austere, and firm in their cultivation of the holy life (brahmacarya), such that even unripened karma can be brought to maturity."
"Once karma has ripened, one is able to abandon all evils and reach the end of suffering; one will certainly be able to sever the suffering and pleasure of all realms of existence.
He said that during the increase and decrease of kalpas, these matters do not exist at all, yet one must nonetheless undergo the cycle of birth and death.
At that time, having heard these words, the Venerable Ghoṣila thought to himself:
"This Great Teacher has turned his back on the right path and is traveling along a wrong path; it is like a perilous road full of terrors, which the wise abandon and should not cultivate."
He spoke in verse:
"One of evil wisdom who teaches evil doctrines, though truly a fool, calls himself a Great Teacher;
if this dharma is what is considered right, then what could possibly be called non-dharma?"
Having understood this, he realized it was like striking an empty vessel that produces nothing but a hollow sound; he abandoned it and departed.
Then, the venerable Sthavira went again to where Kakuda Kātyāyana was and said to him:
"Master!..."
"What is the principle of the Dharma upon which you, O Benevolent One, rely?
With what do you instruct your disciples?
By diligently practicing the holy life, what fruit do they obtain?"
The teacher replied: "Prince! This is the doctrine I follow;
such is my view and such is my teaching. If someone were to come to me and ask this: [he would answer thus]."
"Is there a future world?
I replied, "There is."
“Is there not? I replied, “There is not.”
"Is it both existent and non-existent?
I replied, "It is both existent and non-existent."
"Is it neither existent nor non-existent?
I replied: "It is neither existent nor non-existent."
"If someone were to ask me, 'Is this so?
I would reply:"
"Is it so? "Or is it not? I replied:
"No. "Is it then that this is not so? I replied:
"It is neither right nor wrong.
"Is it not that it is neither right nor wrong? I replied:
"It is neither 'is' nor 'is not.
"If one asks whether [the self] is identical to or different from the next world, the answer is likewise.
When Śrīgupta heard these words, he thought to himself:
"This Great Teacher has turned his back on the right path and walks upon a wrong way; he is like a perilous road full of terrors, which the wise abandon and should not practice."
He spoke in verse:
"One of evil wisdom who preaches evil doctrines, though truly a fool, calls himself a Great Teacher;
if this dharma is what he considers right, what then can be called non-dharma?"
Having understood this, he realized it was like striking an empty vessel that produces nothing but a hollow sound; he abandoned him and departed.
Then, the venerable Srigupta went again to where Nigaṇṭha Sañjayī Vairaṭīputra was and said to him:
"Great Master!..."
What is the principle of the Dharma upon which you, O Benevolent One, rely?
With what do you instruct your disciples?
By diligently practicing the holy life, what fruit do they obtain?
The teacher replied: "Prince!

The doctrine I follow holds such a view and makes such a teaching: if people perceive any experience of suffering or pleasure, it is entirely due to the causal karma created in previous lives. By the power of ascetic practice, one can eliminate past karma and refrain from creating new karma; thus, the dam of birth and death is broken, the state of outflow-free dharma is realized, and all karma comes to an end. Because all karma is exhausted, all suffering is likewise exhausted."
When the Venerable Sthavira Śrīgupta heard these words, he thought to himself:
"This Great Teacher has turned his back on the right path and follows a wrong way; he is like a perilous road full of terrors, which the wise would abandon and should not cultivate."
He spoke in verse:
"One of evil wisdom who preaches an evil doctrine, though truly a fool, calls himself a Great Teacher;
if this dharma is what he considers right, what then can be called non-dharma?"
Having understood this, he thought it was like striking an empty vessel that produces nothing but a hollow sound; thus he abandoned it and departed.
Returning to his own home, he ascended to the upper story of a high tower and, resting his cheek in his hand, reflected thus:

"In this world—among humans, gods, Māras, Brahmās, śramaṇas, and brāhmaṇas—is there perhaps even one person who possesses a single, two, three, or four-line efficacious mantra, spell, or method for medicinal clarity, which would allow me to escape from the prison of ignorance within birth and death without requiring great effort?"
It is the constant law of all Buddhas to observe the world; there is nothing they do not see or hear, and nothing they do not know.
They constantly give rise to great compassion to benefit all beings as their great protectors;

they are foremost in heroic prowess, their word is never twofold, they abide in meditative concentration and wisdom, they manifest the three types of supernormal knowledge, they have well-cultivated the three trainings, and they have skillfully disciplined the three modes of action.
Having crossed the four torrents and established the four bases of spiritual power, you have cultivated the four means of attraction throughout the long night;
having abandoned the five hindrances, distanced yourself from the five factors, and transcended the five paths; with the six faculties complete and the six perfections fulfilled;
bestowing the seven riches universally and opening the flowers of the seven factors of enlightenment; free from the eight worldly dharmas, you demonstrate the eightfold noble path.
Having eternally severed the nine fetters and being clear and proficient in the nine meditative absorptions, he is replete with the ten powers and his fame resounds throughout the ten directions.
Among the thousand masters of sovereignty, he is the most preeminent; having attained the four fearlessnesses, he utters a great sound, performing the lion’s roar.
Six times throughout the day and night, he constantly surveys all worlds with the Buddha-eye: who is increasing? Who is declining?
Who has encountered grave suffering and perilous calamities?
Who is heading toward the evil realms?

I shall now, by means of supreme skillful methods, rescue those in the three evil realms and deliver them, establishing them in the realms of humans and devas and causing them to abide in nirvana. For those mired in the mud of desire, I shall constantly contemplate their salvation; for those who lack the noble wealth, I shall cause them to obtain the noble wealth.
When a Buddha appears in the world, who is it that shall obtain benefit?
Who has the cataract of ignorance covering their eyes, such that he may use the medicine of great wisdom to cause their vision to open and become clear?

Who lacks roots of goodness, such that he may cause them to plant roots of goodness? Who has planted roots of goodness, such that he may cause them to reach maturity? And who has reached maturity, such that he may cause them to attain liberation?
As it is said:
"Even if the tide of the great ocean should ever miss its appointed time,
the Buddha never fails his appointed hour in delivering those he transforms."
Just as a mother has an only son and constantly protects his life,
the Buddha’s compassionate concern for those he transforms exceeds even that.
The Buddha’s loving-kindness toward all sentient beings is never abandoned.
“I shall strive to rescue him from his suffering and hardship, just as a mother cow follows her calf.
At that time, the World-Honored One thought to himself:

“This Śrīgupta has previously planted various roots of goodness in the presence of the Buddha; he is like a ripe abscess waiting only for the lancet’s incision. Now is precisely the right time for him to be capable of being transformed through my teaching.”
He further observed whether this person was to be transformed by the Buddha, by a disciple, by supernatural power, or by dignified deportment;
he perceived that they could only be delivered through the dignified deportment of a disciple.
At that time, among gods and humans, the bhikṣu Aśvajit was foremost in his dignified deportment; the World-Honored One then addressed the bhikṣu Aśvajit, saying:
"You should know the proper time; you ought to observe Prince Śrīmat in the kingdom of Pāpā."

Then the bhikṣu Aśvajit silently accepted the instruction. When the following day arrived, during the first watch of the morning, he took up his robe and bowl and entered the city of Rājagṛha to beg for food in sequence. Having finished his meal, at the time after eating, he put away his bedding and seat, took up his robe and bowl, and traveling by stages, arrived at the country of Pāpā and stayed in the Śiśumāra Grove.

Returning at the first watch of the day, he took up his robes and alms bowl and entered the city of Pāpā for alms in regular order; whether lifting or lowering his feet, looking or stretching, or holding his robes and bowl, his dignified deportment and every movement were entirely deliberate and composed.

At that time, Sthavira Dravyamāla saw him from atop a high tower; his gait was composed and serene, such as had never been seen before, and his deportment and movements were flawless. Having seen him from afar, he thought to himself:
"Among all those who have gone forth in this kingdom, I have truly never seen such an air of deportment."
"However, those who have gone forth maintain a dignified and composed demeanor within a village, yet do not do so in the forest hermitage (araṇya).
Now, I should have someone observe whether those dwelling in the wilderness can indeed act in such a manner."
Having formed this thought, he immediately dispatched a messenger with these instructions:
"Follow wherever this bhikṣu goes; whether he dwells in an araṇya secluded from human company, observe whether there is any difference in the deportment of either of you."
The messenger, having received these instructions, followed behind Aśvajit to observe him in private.

At that time, after the bhikṣu Aśvajit had obtained food within the city, he went to the Śiśumāra Grove; having set aside his robes, bowl, and water filter in one place, he shook the dust from his robes, filtered the water through the strainer, washed his hands and feet, took some fallen yellow leaves and spread them upon the ground, and sat down to eat.

Having finished his meal, he gathered up and discarded the leftover leaves, set out his robes and bowl, washed his hands and feet, and sat cross-legged; like a coiled dragon, he remained with a tranquil demeanor, his body upright and steady.
Then, having completed his observation, the messenger returned and reported to the prince:
"I observed that bhikṣu within the city with dignified and orderly deportment; once he reached the forest and fields, he was a hundred times more excellent than before."
Then, the son of Śroṇa said to the charioteer, "You should now quickly prepare the carriage; I wish to go to the grove to see that bhikṣu.

Following these orders, the charioteer readied the team of horses. The prince mounted the chariot and proceeded with his retinue, but upon reaching the grove, he alighted and walked on foot. He went to the dwelling of Aśvajit and, seeing from afar the Venerable Aśvajit sitting cross-legged in meditative absorption, he thought to himself:
"I should not disturb that bhikṣu’s sublime concentration; I shall wait until he emerges from meditative absorption and then pay my respects.

Having formed this thought, he remained where he was. When the Venerable Aśvajit finally emerged from absorption late in the afternoon, Sāriputra gradually approached, prostrated at his feet, stood to one side, and said:
"Venerable Sir!"
"Is this the Great Teacher,
or is it a disciple? Aśvajit replied:
"I am a disciple, not the Great Master.
He asked him again,
"How do you compare in quality and excellence with the Master?"
Aśvajit replied, "There is an extreme difference in quality.

Prince, you should know that Mount Sumeru, the king of mountains, compared to a mustard seed, and the waters of the great ocean compared to a cow's footprint, are like the sun compared to the light of a firefly."
Then the Venerable Aśvajit spoke these verses:
"The Sumeru compared to a mustard seed, The great ocean like a cow’s footprint;
The expanse of space like a hole in a lotus fiber, The bright sun compared to the glow of a firefly."
"Whatever things exist in the world cannot serve as a metaphor;
the disciple’s expectation of the teacher is likewise so.
When Śrīgupta heard this teaching, he thought to himself:
"Since the Bhikṣu has thus described the distinctions of merit, is it not the case that there is further a World-Honored One of Sublime Awakening and a particularly excellent Dharma?
Having realized this, he asked Aśvajit:
"Venerable Sir!..."
“May I now, in this well-expounded Dharma and Vinaya, go forth, receive full ordination, become a bhikṣu, and practice the holy life under the Venerable One?
Aśvajit replied, “Prince! [It is possible.]”
"Have your parents given you their permission?
Śrīgupta replied,
"Venerable Sir!"
"I have never heard it permitted.
Aśvajit replied,
"If the Tathāgata or his disciples grant someone the going forth, they should not abruptly ordain them if their parents do not permit it."
The Venerable Sthavira said: "Virtuous One!
By means of skillful methods, I shall certainly cause him to grant his permission."
Aśvajit replied, “This is most excellent!
Having heard these words, Srigupta paid his respects with joy, took his leave, and departed. He returned to his own palace and said to his parents:
"Parents, you should know that I have attained right faith and now wish to go forth into homelessness.
His parents replied,
"Do you not realize this now?"
This is my only son, whom I have always cherished and gazed upon without weariness; even if his life were to end, I would not wish to be parted from him, much less while he still lives in this body!
The Prince said, "It would be well if you grant me leave; if you do not permit it, from this day forth I shall no longer eat or drink.
Although he spoke these words, he was still not granted permission.
At that time, the son of Śrīgupta fasted for one day; likewise for two, three, and even up to six days, neither drinking nor eating.
Then his parents went to where their son was and said to him:

"From your childhood you have always enjoyed comfort and ease, never having experienced any hardships. The holy life (*brahmacarya*) is difficult to practice, living alone is difficult, and dwelling in a forest hermitage (*araṇya*) with suitable bedding is difficult. You must live out your entire life in the company of fierce beasts; you must live out your entire life begging for food from others; you must live out your entire life abandoning all sensual pleasures; and you must live out your entire life forever severing all play and amusement."
"Prince! You should remain here and enjoy all manner of sensual pleasures, bestowing gifts as you wish and cultivating various meritorious deeds.
Although the Prince heard these words, he remained silent and offered no reply.
Then his parents had their kinsmen urge Srigupta; the kinsmen came together to exhort him, repeating everything exactly as their parents had said, yet Srigupta remained silent and gave no answer.

Then his parents had his close friends and acquaintances likewise offer him exhortations; they repeated all the words previously spoken by his parents, yet Srigupta remained silent as before, and for a second and third time, he gave no verbal reply.

At that time, his friends observed his steadfastness; though they spoke a second and a third time, he gave no verbal reply. Then, those kinsmen, knowing that Rāhula’s resolve was firm, went to the king and the queen and fully explained the situation:
"We entreated him with great earnestness, yet his will remains unshakable; observing his countenance, it is certain that he will not turn back."
I fear it may harm the Crown Prince; I pray that you will grant me permission to leave the household life and renounce worldly affairs, for this is what the wise collectively praise.
If you permit me to abandon my home so that my life may be preserved, I shall have no desire to return to my original palace later on;
for if one is separated from the conditions of birth, where else could one go?
The parents replied, "If this must be so,
we shall permit you to leave the household life to fulfill your aspirations.
Following their instructions, the relatives informed the Prince:
"My parents have shown me such compassion as to permit my entry into the religious life.

Having heard this, Śrīgupta’s joy increased even further; he partook of some food and drink, gradually regaining his strength. He took leave of his parents and went to that forest grove. There he paid homage to the bhikṣu Aśvajit and sat to one side, saying:
"Venerable Sir!"

"My venerable parents have already granted their permission; I pray that you will compassionately grant me the dharma of renunciation, allow me to receive full ordination, and instruct me in the rules of decorum, so that I may cultivate the holy life under your guidance, O Virtuous One."
Then the Venerable Aśvajit replied,
"In this very way, you shall receive both the going-forth and full ordination.
He then said to him:
"Do you know now?
There are two kinds of activities for a bhikṣu:
namely, recitation and the cultivation of meditative concentration."
"Are you engaged in recitation and study,
or are you practicing meditative concentration?
He then replied to his teacher, saying:
"Upādhyāya! I shall do both.

Thereupon, during the day he devoted himself single-mindedly to recitation, and at quiet nights he focused his mindfulness on meditative reflection. In this way, before long, he became thoroughly proficient in the Tripiṭaka. Through diligent exertion without ceasing for even a moment, he severed the afflictions and realized the fruit of Arhatship.

At that time, all the disciples and followers of the bhikṣu Aśvajit, having been instructed according to their respective inclinations and the specific branches of study they pursued, departed for other villages, cities, and market towns to observe the rains retreat.

When the summer retreat was completed on the fifteenth day of the eighth month, having finished making his robes, he took up his bowl and outer robe and went to the Grāhakūṭa Forest near the city of Pāvā. There, he set down his bowl and robe, washed his feet and hands, approached his teacher, prostrated at his feet, and sat to one side.
Then those people each reported in detail to their preceptors according to what they had realized. They further inquired about other essential points of the Tripiṭaka and said to their preceptors:
"Since we have seen our Upādhyāyas and received their personal instruction and resolution, we wish to go and pay homage to the Blessed One."
He replied:
"Venerable one,
go as you please."
Then the Venerable Bahula said to the Bhikṣu Aśvajit, "Upādhyāya!
I have already beheld the Tathāgata’s Dharma-body, but I have not yet seen his form-body."
"I now wish to go and behold the physical body of the Buddha.
He replied, "As you wish."

You should now know that the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, is a great treasure appearing in the world; he is truly difficult to encounter, appearing only once in a while, like the udumbara flower.
When the venerable Sthavira had received permission to depart, on the following day, during the first watch of the day, he took up his robe and bowl and entered the city of Pāpā to wander for alms.

Having returned to his original location and finished his meal, he took up his robes and bowl and proceeded toward Rājagṛha; with the same dignified deportment as before, he washed his hands and feet and went to where the Buddha was.

At that time, the World-Honored One was preaching the Dharma amidst an assembly of immeasurable hundreds of thousands of bhikṣus. Seeing from afar that Śrīgupta was approaching, the World-Honored One addressed him, saying: "Welcome!"
"Now is precisely the right time; sit as you please.
Then, having prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, the Venerable Sthavira sat to one side.
At that time, the community of bhikṣus in Rājagṛha was not distributing monastic bedding according to their respective categories—namely, the Dharma-preachers and the Vinaya-experts.
Sūtra masters with Abhidharma masters; Sūtra masters with Dharma masters; Sūtra masters with meditation masters;
Vinaya masters with Abhidharma masters; Vinaya masters with Dharma masters; Vinaya masters with meditation masters; Vinaya masters with Sūtra masters;
Abhidharma masters with Dharma masters; Abhidharma masters with meditation masters; Abhidharma masters with Sūtra masters.
...the Abhidharma master with the Vinaya master; the Dharma master with the Meditation master; the Dharma master with the Sūtra master; the Dharma master with the Vinaya master;
the Dharma master with the Abhidharma master; the Meditation master with the Sūtra master; the Meditation master with the Vinaya master;
the Meditation master with the Abhidharma master; the Meditation master with the Dharma master; [and] regarding the Sūtra master, the Vinaya...
When assigning rooms and bedding, one should not group together those of the same class— such as teachers, masters of treatises,
dharma-preachers, or meditation masters— in this way, one does not rely on commonality when distributing dwellings and bedding.

At that time, the bhikṣus, out of mutual consideration for one another, neglected their assigned duties; consequently, each of them failed to increase their wholesome qualities, like a lotus flower that withers daily in the sun for lack of water.
At that time, the World-Honored One had this thought:
"This Śrīgupta has long held a true vow before previous Buddhas.
Having formed this thought, he said:
"How shall I become one who distributes bedding for the Saṃgha?
At that time, the Blessed One addressed the bhikṣus, saying: "O bhikṣus!..."
One should appoint Śrīgupta as the distributor of bedding for the Saṃgha.
If there are others of a similar class who possess the five qualities, they should also be appointed as distributors of bedding;
if they lack the five qualities, they should not be appointed, and if they have been appointed, they should be dismissed.
What are the five? They are:
having attachment, having aversion, having delusion, having fear, and not knowing what is appropriate and inappropriate to assign.
One who possesses these five qualities should be appointed; once appointed, one should not be dismissed.
What are the five? They are:
being without attachment, without hatred, without delusion, without fear, and knowing what is appropriate and inappropriate. One should be appointed in this manner.

As is customary, the *gandi* should be struck, seats should be prepared, and after first making the formal announcement (*jñapti*), the Sangha is assembled as a whole. One should then question the candidate before the assembly and offer exhortation, saying:
"Can you, [Name], act as the person who distributes bedding for the Saṃgha? He replies, "I can."
“The formal procedure (*jñapti-karman*) for this bhikṣu shall be carried out in detail as set forth in the *Ekottarakarman*.
At that time, after Śrīgupta had been appointed by the assembly to distribute the bedding, he assigned all the monastic dwellings and bedding according to their respective types.

Sūtra masters gather with sūtra masters; Vinaya masters gather with Vinaya masters; Śāstra masters gather with Śāstra masters; Dharma masters gather with Dharma masters; and meditation masters gather with meditation masters.

Having obtained permission to dwell together as he pleased, his deliberations were free from conflict; the wholesome qualities he cultivated increased day and night, like a lotus in a pond that flourishes when filled with water and exposed to the sun.
At that time, some bhikṣus arrived only at the half-watch; then, by means of his supernormal powers, the powerful son (Śrīgupta) emitted light from a single finger to distribute the bedding.

Furthermore, there were other groups of bhikṣus who, desiring to see the rare and superior human dharmas and supernormal powers of the powerful son, arrived at the first watch to seek lodging. Then, the powerful son emitted light from two fingers to distribute the bedding;
when they arrived at the one-and-a-half watches, he emitted light from three fingers.
If he arrives during the second watch of the night, light will emanate from his four fingers;
if he arrives at midnight, light will emanate from his five fingers, and they shall share their bedding with him.
When the bhikṣus had witnessed these extraordinary feats of supernatural power, each of them thought to themselves:

"We should not allow a great śrāvaka endowed with majestic power to distribute bedding, yet instead lie on our sides upon the beds and sleep as we please; this is something that ought not to be done."

Each of them, during the first and last watches of the night, diminished their sleep and dwelt with focused attention; through such diligent exertion, they realized what was not yet realized and did not fall away from what had already been realized.
At that time, the Blessed One addressed the bhikṣus, saying: "Bhikṣus!
Among my disciples, this Śrīgupta is the foremost in distributing bedding and furniture for the Saṃgha."

Once the holy teaching of the Blessed One had become widespread, the brahmins and householders prepared various foods and drinks for the community of bhikṣus. At that time, the group of six bhikṣus, knowing that there was excellent and exquisite food and drink, went there immediately to eat it.
At that time, the faithful brahmins and others spoke these words:
"Venerable One! Noble sir, for what reason do you not come?"
The group of six replied,
"How could he possibly come to eat such coarse food?
The donor then said:
“The World-Honored One has declared me the foremost among those who receive offerings; how could those elders possibly fail to eat?

Noble sir, you have abandoned the secular life for the well-spoken Dharma and Vinaya, yet you do not guard your speech and utter words devoid of shame. You should depart at once and never return again.”
When the bhikṣus heard of this matter, they went to inform the Buddha. The Buddha said:
"You should appoint Sthavira Śrīgupta as the distributor of food; if there are others of a similar kind, they too should be appointed as distributors of food."
One who does not possess these five qualities should not be appointed; if already appointed, they should be dismissed.
What are the five? They are:
having attachment, hatred, delusion, fear, and ignorance regarding what is a proper distribution and what is not.
The procedure for this should be reversed.
Following the previous method, one should appoint [the official] in this manner, having a single bhikṣu perform the formal motion (jñapti-karman) as detailed in the *Ekottarakarma*.
At that time, after Sthavira Bāḍhila had been appointed by the community as the distributor of food, he divided the Sangha’s food into three grades:
namely, superior, middling, and inferior.

At that time, there was a guest bhikṣu to whom the host provided superior food on the first day, middling food on the second day, and inferior food on the third day; on the fourth day, he was made to go out for alms.

At that time, Sthavira Sthūlanandika assigned rooms, bedding, food, drink, and other necessities to the bhikṣus—whether guests or residents—distributing them according to their current status from the eldest to the youngest, never failing in his duties.

At that time, the powerful son (Ghaṭīkāra) was accompanied by two bhikṣus—one named Kalyāṇamitra and the other Mahāpṛthivī—who had been his constant enemies throughout successive lifetimes; they came from the southern country to the city of Rājagṛha.
At that time, two bhikṣus asked other bhikṣus,
"Who is the monk designated by the saṃgha as the distributor of food?
The next one replied:
"It is the Venerable Sthavira Śrīgupta. Thereupon,
those two went to Śrīgupta's place and informed him, saying,
"The two of us have been served our food in due order."
Then, on his first day of arrival, Sthavira Śrīgupta was served excellent food by two people.
At that time, the donor asked:
"Who will come to my house for a meal tomorrow?"
He replied, “This is my friend; this is my land.
Having heard this, the donor thought to himself:
"Upon hearing of those two bhikṣus' misconduct, we shall provide whatever is appropriate when they come to receive food.
On the second day, it was their turn for the midday meal; however, the donor had business to attend to and there was no fine food. On the third day, it was their turn for coarse food.
Then those two men spoke these words:
"We are now in extreme suffering.
Why has the Venerable Sthavira Śrīgupta intentionally given us coarse and unwholesome food for three days, tormenting us and causing us to undergo such great pain?"
"I shall do them harm.
Those two had a younger sister, a bhikṣuṇī named Mitrā, who resided at the Rājaka-vihāra.
At that time, Mitrā went to her two brothers; having arrived, she prostrated at each of their feet and sat to one side.
At that time, although the two brothers saw their sister arrive, they did not look at one another nor speak together.
Then the sister asked her two elder brothers:
"For what reason, O noble ones, do you see me come and yet neither look upon me nor speak with me?"
The two of them replied, "Sister!
After the Venerable Srigupta had given us food for three mornings in succession, he gave us nothing but the most coarse and foul food for us to eat."
"Why do you now not assist me, but instead remain dwelling in your own peace?
The female friend replied,
"Noble One!"
"What should I do now? She replied,
"Sister!..."
"You should now go to the World-Honored One and speak thus:
'Venerable Sir!
That noble Śrīgupta has committed an improper act by engaging in unchaste conduct with me; he has violated a *pārājika* offense.'"
"I too shall go and speak these words:
'What my sister has said is indeed true; we knew it beforehand.
The female friend replied:
"How can I now know for certain that he is truly a pure bhikṣu who has never committed an offense? How could I have so hastily slandered him with groundless charges of a pārājika transgression?"
The two of them replied,
"As long as you do not speak to us in such a manner, we will never look upon you or engage in conversation with you."
At that time, having heard these words, the maiden Mitra looked up and down for a moment and said to her two elder brothers,
"I shall perform this task.
Her brothers said:
“Sister! You stay here for now;
we shall first go to the place where the Blessed One is, and you may follow later.
Then the two bhikṣus went to the place where the Blessed One was, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and sat down to one side.
Then, when her brother arrived, the female friend went to where the Buddha was, prostrated, and stood before him. She addressed the World-Honored One, saying:
"Venerable Sir!
That noble Śrīgupta has committed an improper act by engaging in unchaste conduct with me; he has violated a *pārājika* offense."
Then the bhikṣu Mitramati immediately addressed the Buddha:
“It is indeed so, Blessed One!”
"It is truly so, Sūgata!
As our sister has said, we already knew this."
At that time, the Venerable Sthavira Śāriputra was also present, staying within this great assembly.
*Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya*, Fascicle Thirteen. *Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya*, Fascicle [Thirteen].
The Fourteenth:
The Training Rule on Groundless Slander, Part Two.
Translated by the Tripitaka Master Yijing by Imperial Command. At that time, the Blessed One addressed Śrīgupta, saying:
“Did you hear these words?
He replied to the Buddha,
“I heard them.”
"Bhagavan, I have heard it. Sugata!"
The Buddha said,
“Srigupta! What is the matter?”
The Venerable Sthavira Śrīgupta addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
Whether I am truthful or false, only the Buddha knows.”
The Buddha said, "Sthavira Śrīgupta!
At such a time, do not speak in this manner; you should speak thus: if it is real, say it is real; if it is false, say it is false."
The Venerable Sthavira Śāriputra said:
"I do not recall it, Blessed One!"
“I do not recall it, Sugata!
At that time, the Venerable Rāhula was fanning the Buddha from behind with a fan; then Rāhula addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
Why trouble yourself to ask about that Śrīgupta?
We see with our own eyes that the bhikṣuṇī Sakhī herself is present before the Buddha, saying:”
"Śrīgupta and I committed an evil deed together and incurred a *pārājika* offense.
The two brothers testified with their own faces, saying,
"It is true."
The Buddha said to Rāhula:
"I shall now question you; answer as you see fit. Rāhula!"
If a bhikṣuṇī comes to me and speaks thus:
"Venerable Sir!
The noble Rāhula has committed an improper act; he has engaged in unchaste conduct with me and has thus incurred a pārājika offense."
Then the bhikṣu Mitabhāṣin immediately testified, saying:
"It is truly so,
Blessed One!"
"It is truly so, Sugata!
As our sister has said, we already knew this."
"Rāhula! Upon hearing these words, I immediately asked you:
'Is this matter true or false?'"
“How would you answer?
Rāhula addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One, Great Virtuous One!”
"If you remember it, say you remember; if you do not remember it, say you do not remember. The World-Honored One replied, "You are but a fool that you can say, 'I do not remember.
Why then should one be surprised that the pure bhikṣu Śrīgupta says he does not remember when he is truly without fault?"
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
“As for the bhikṣu Śrīgupta, he is truly without fault.
You should know that the bhikṣuṇī Mitrā falsely claimed to have committed an offense; she ought to be expelled.”
His two fellow bhikṣus should carefully examine and skillfully inquire about this matter: "How did you see it?
Where did you see it?
By what causes and conditions did you go to see that event?"
When the Blessed One had spoken these words, he immediately entered his room and remained in meditative absorption (*samādhi*).

At that time, seeing the Buddha in meditative absorption, the bhikṣus collectively recalled that Śrīgupta was a person of pure conduct, and thus they, together with the bhikṣuṇī Sundarī, carried out his formal expulsion based on her own confession.
Friends, the two bhikṣus from the earth questioned him about the matter:
"How did you see it? Where did you see it?"
"For what reason did you go to witness that event?
Then the bhikṣus questioned them in detail,
and those two bhikṣus spoke as follows:
"Venerable sirs!

As for that Śrīgupta, I do not see that he has committed an offense of unchaste conduct (*abrahmacarya*) constituting a *pārājika* offense; however, because Venerable Śrīgupta provided me with coarse food for as many as three days, my physical strength has declined and I have been greatly distressed."
It was out of desire, hatred, delusion, and fear that I spoke thus.
That venerable Śrīgupta is truly pure and without fault; he did not engage in impure conduct, nor did he commit an offense involving expulsion (*pārājika*).
At that time, in the late afternoon, the Blessed One rose from his secluded dwelling and took his seat among the assembly of bhikṣus.
Then the bhikṣus addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"

"O Venerable Ones, while we bhikṣus were observing the Blessed One as he entered his chamber for meditative seclusion, we collectively recalled that the son of Śrī was a pure person; thus, by her own admission, the bhikṣuṇī Mitrā has been subjected to the formal act of expulsion."
Friends, the two bhikṣus of the Earth thoroughly questioned him about the matter:
"How did you see it? Where did you see it?"
"By what causes and conditions did you witness that event?
We questioned them fully,
and at that time, those two bhikṣus spoke as follows:
"Venerable ones!
As for that Śrīgupta, I do not see him as having committed an act of unchaste conduct that constitutes a *pārājika* offense.
However, because that venerable Śrīgupta provided me with inferior food for as many as three days, my physical strength has been weakened and I have been greatly distressed."
It was out of desire, hatred, delusion, and fear that I spoke thus.
That venerable Sthavira Śrīgupta is truly pure and without fault; he did not engage in impure conduct and has not committed a *pārājika* offense.
When the World-Honored One had heard these words, he addressed the bhikṣus, saying:
"How can those two foolish men,
for the sake of a mere trifle of food and drink, commit intentional falsehood and slander a pure bhikṣu?"
At that time, the Blessed One spoke these verses:
"If a person intentionally speaks falsehood,
Transgressing the true Dharma and fearing nothing of the next world, There is no evil they will not commit."
"Rather swallow a red-hot iron ball, with fierce flames burning all over the body,
than with a mouth broken by precepts, eat the food offered out of faith.
At that moment, a host of devas in the sky spoke this verse:
“Even one whose power surpasses the three realms of existence still incurs slander;
therefore, the wise person should not delight in birth and death.
Edible food is truly loathsome, the most extreme of all sufferings.”
"It is just like eating the flesh of one's own son; it increases all manner of afflictions.
"How is it that you now know a pure bhikṣu has truly not committed an offense, yet you slander him with groundless charges of a *pārājika* offense?"
At that time, the Blessed One explained the matter in detail as previously described, and finally addressed the bhikṣu Māṭhara:
"You two foolish men, knowing that a pure bhikṣu has not actually committed an offense, do you indeed defame him by charging him with a groundless *pārājika* offense?"
The two of them said to the Buddha,
“It is indeed so,
World-Honored One!”
The Buddha rebuked him in various ways:
"What you have done is wrong; it is not a pure practice, nor is it a compliant practice; it is something that should not have been done.
He then addressed the bhikṣus, saying:
"It should be known that there are three types of persons who are certain to fall into the niraya hells.
What are the three?
If a person breaks the precepts themselves and encourages others to break the precepts, this is called the first person who is certain to fall into the niraya hells."
If a person practices impure conduct themselves and then slanders a pure bhikṣu with a groundless charge of a pārājika offense, this is the second person who is certain to fall into the niraya hell.
If a person holds such a view and speaks thus:
"Sensual desire is pure; sensual desire is sublime; sensual desire may be enjoyed; sensual desire is without fault."
"Being excessively attached to objects of evil desire—this is the third person destined to fall into the hells.
At that time, the Blessed One spoke these verses:
"If a person is born into this world, Their mouth constantly produces swords and blades; If they speak harsh words, They will surely go to hell."
Because of these evil words, one constantly cuts one's own body.
If one praises the wicked and slanders the virtuous,
many transgressions arise from the mouth, and one will certainly not attain peace and happiness.
Just as a gambler loses his wealth, which is but a minor fault,
so too, to slander one who is pure is a grave transgression.
For hundreds of thousands of years, one shall fall into the womb-of-flesh hell.
Furthermore, within this very hell, one shall undergo suffering for another forty thousand years.
If, with an evil mind, one speaks words that slander and revile virtuous people;
by reason of such karmic conditions, one shall fall into hell.
At that time, having finished his reprimand, the Blessed One addressed the bhikṣus, saying:
“I consider ten benefits... [as extensively explained before] ...even unto this: within the Vinaya, I establish this training rule for the śrāvakas, which should be recited as follows:
‘If a bhikṣu, harboring anger and refusing to let it go, intentionally slanders a pure bhikṣu with a groundless *pārājika* offense, desiring to ruin that person’s pure conduct.’”
At a later time, whether questioned or not, if it is known that this matter is groundless slander,
and that monk spoke these words out of malice, it is a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*.
"Furthermore, 'if a bhikṣu' refers to the bhikṣus Mitra and Bhūmi, or anyone else of a similar class.
'Harboring anger' means that resentment has arisen in one's mind."
"Does not relinquish" means that anger does not cease.
"Pure bhikṣu" refers to Śrīgupta.
"Without offense" means that he has not committed the act.
"Without grounds" means lacking the three grounds:
the ground of having seen, the ground of having heard, and the ground of doubt.
Regarding the *pārājika* dharma, it refers to any one of the four matters being spoken of.
The Dharma has already been explained as before.
To "slander" means to speak what is untrue.
To "wish to destroy that practitioner" means to wish to damage that person's pure training rules (*śikṣāpada*).
"At another time" means at a different occasion.

"Whether asked or unasked" means that after having spoken the slander, one feels remorse and regret of one's own accord, rather than due to being questioned by another; thus it is known that this matter was groundless slander.
"Slander" means contention.
There are four kinds of contention:
namely, contention through strife, contention through what is not spoken, contention through offenses, and contention through legal matters.
Regarding the phrase "speaking these words out of anger," this specifically refers to the words of slander.
As for the *saṃghāvaśeṣa*, it has already been explained as before.
In this context, what are the characteristics of the offense and how does it occur?
If one slanders a pure bhikṣu, there is an offense in ten instances and no offense in five instances.
What are the ten? That is to say:

not having seen the matter, nor heard it, nor suspected it, yet forming such a false and deceptive notion, and while actually lacking any seeing or the like, falsely claiming, "I have seen, heard, or suspected it. When one makes such a statement, one incurs a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense.

If one has forgotten what was heard, or forgotten due to doubt, yet forms such an understanding or such a conception, saying, "I have not forgotten what I heard or doubted," at the time of making such a statement, one incurs a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense.
Whether one hears and believes, or hears and does not believe, yet claims "I have seen it";
or whether one hears and doubts, or hears and does not doubt, or merely doubts oneself, yet says "I have seen it"—when one makes such a statement, one incurs a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense.
These are called the ten matters that constitute an offense.
What are the five matters that do not constitute an offense?

They are when one has not seen, heard, or suspected, yet possesses the conviction that one has seen and so forth, and possesses the perception that one has seen and so forth, and speaks these words accordingly:
Regarding the statement, "I have seen, heard,
or suspected," there is no offense.

Or, if one has heard but forgotten, or suspected but forgotten, and speaks of having "heard" and so forth while maintaining the perception that one had heard or suspected, there is likewise no offense.
Just as when one slanders a pure person, ten matters constitute an offense and five matters do not;
it is the same when one slanders a pure person who merely appears to be impure.
If one slanders a person who is not impure, there are eleven matters that constitute an offense and six matters that do not.
What are the eleven? They are:

when one has neither seen, nor heard, nor suspected [an offense], yet forms such an understanding, forms such a conception, and being truly without any seeing or the like, falsely says: [“I have seen,” etc.]... [and so forth].
If one says, "I have seen, heard,
or suspected," when speaking thus, one incurs a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense.
Or, having seen but forgotten, or having heard but forgotten, or having suspected but forgotten, yet forming such an understanding and such a conception, one says:
"Never forgetting what has been seen, heard, or suspected.
When one makes such a statement, one incurs a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense.
This applies whether one has heard it and believes it, or heard it and does not believe it, yet says, "I have seen it."
Whether one hears [the claim] and doubts it, or hears it and does not doubt it, or merely doubts it oneself and says,
"I saw it"— when one speaks in this manner, one incurs a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense.
These are called the eleven cases that constitute an offense.
What are the six cases where there is no offense?

They are: when one has not seen, heard, or suspected, yet possesses the conviction that one has seen and so forth, and possesses the perception that one has seen, heard, and so forth, and speaks accordingly.
Regarding the statement, "I have seen, heard, or suspected," there is no offense.

Whether one has forgotten what was seen, forgotten what was heard, or forgotten what was suspected; or whether one has a cognition of having seen and so forth, or a perception of having seen and so forth, yet says "I have seen, heard, etc.," in all such cases there is likewise no offense.
These are called the six matters that constitute no offense.
If one slanders a person who resembles one who is pure, there are eleven matters that constitute an offense and six matters that constitute no offense; it is likewise so in this case.
At that time, all the bhikṣus were filled with doubt; to dispel their doubts, they addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One, Great Virtuous One!
What karma did the Venerable Sthiramati previously commit?"

Due to that karma, he drew forth the ripening fruit of being born into a wealthy and noble family, possessing abundant riches and enjoying ample sustenance. He renounced the secular life to rely upon the Buddha and become a monk; having severed all afflictions, he realized arhatship and was declared foremost among those who distribute rooms and dwellings. Although he had attained such a supreme fruit, he was nonetheless subjected to slander and vilification.
The Buddha addressed the bhikṣus:
"Listen well! I shall explain to you the causes and conditions of that matter."

O monks, if one performs an action oneself, its retribution will certainly not ripen in the external elements of earth, water, fire, or wind; rather, the retribution for wholesome and unwholesome karma ripens only within one's own aggregates, elements, and sense-bases.
He then spoke in verse:
"Though a hundred eons may pass, the karma one has created does not perish;
when the causes and conditions meet, one must experience the retribution oneself."
"O Bhikṣus! In a past age, there was a great caravan leader in a certain village named Matsyabandhu (The Fisherman).
At that time, the caravan leader took his merchandise and, together with other merchants, set out for the great ocean, desiring to seek precious jewels."

At that time, as no Buddha had appeared in the world, there was a Pratyekabuddha who manifested in the world to provide relief to the poor and lowly; he constantly partook of coarse and simple food, drink, and bedding, and at that time, he alone was the supreme field of merit.

At that time, a certain Pratyekabuddha, having joined this caravan leader, was traveling through the human realm; during the night, he entered the meditative absorption of the "blazing fire. When the night-watchman saw his light, he informed the caravan leader, saying:
"Do you know, sir, what this is?"
"This bhikṣu has accomplished the holy practices; I saw him in the night like a mass of fire emitting great radiance.
Upon hearing this, the merchant leader felt profound reverence. He went to the bhikṣu's location, prostrated at his feet, and addressed him thus:
"O Noble One, you seek food, while I seek merit. I pray that you will accept my humble offering from the caravan; after you have eaten, please depart with us."
At that time, he silently accepted the invitation to eat.
Following him, they gradually reached the shore of the great ocean, where the merchant leader asked:
"Noble One!..."
"I am now leading a caravan intending to enter the ocean; will you, virtuous one, go along with us?
The Pratyekabuddha replied, "Virtuous sir!"
"You have entered the great ocean for the sake of your wife and children to seek various precious goods; for what purpose would I enter it with you?
At that time, the merchant leader, having provided him with food, presented him with new and exquisite cotton cloth.

At that time, that Great Virtuous One manifested only supernatural powers but did not preach the Dharma; out of compassion for the caravan leader, he soared through the expanse of space like a king of geese, emitting water and fire from his body and displaying great supernormal powers.
When ordinary beings witness such a divine transformation, their minds immediately turn toward it like a great tree collapsing; they prostrate from afar at his feet and make this vow:

"By the ripening fruit of this karma resulting from the offerings I have made to such a true field of merit, may I be born into a wealthy and noble family, may I attain such supreme majesty and power, and may I serve a Great Master even more sublime than this one."
"You all should know!
That fisherman at that time was none other than Śrīgupta.

Because he made a great vow while formerly making offerings to a Pratyekabuddha, he has now been born into a family of supreme wealth and nobility with abundant enjoyments; he has gone forth from the world within my Dharma, severed all afflictions, and realized arhatship."
"I am the Great Teacher, surpassing hundreds of thousands of koṭis of Pratyekabuddhas; you should serve me without ever giving rise to weariness or aversion.
Furthermore, monks, although this Śrīgupta has attained the fruit of Arhatship, he still encounters malicious words and slander.
I shall now speak; listen well!
O bhikṣus, in times past, there was a great householder in a certain village who took a wife from a family of equal status. They lived together in mutual affection and joy.
Although many years had passed, he still had no son or daughter; he thus rested his cheek upon his hand and sighed with sorrow, thinking:
"Within my household there is much precious wealth, yet I have no heir to succeed me. After my death, it will surely be confiscated by the government."
When his wife saw this, she immediately asked him:
"Noble son! For what reason do you rest your cheek upon your hand, lost in long contemplation with an expression that seems to bear the hue of sorrow?"
He replied: "O worthy one!

My house now contains much wealth, yet I have no offspring; should I pass away, it will all be confiscated by the authorities. Given these circumstances, how could I not be filled with sorrow and anxiety?"
His wife replied,
"If it is due to my own fault that we have no son or daughter, you should now take another wife so that we may have offspring.
He replied:
"O Worthy One!
If there are two wives in a person's household, they shall not even drink flour-water or thin gruel; they will constantly cause turmoil and quarreling within the house."
The wife replied to her husband, "You may seek him out;
if his appearance is like my younger sister's, I shall act as my sister and look upon him.
If he resembles our daughter, I shall act with the mind of our daughter and gaze upon him."
At that time, in another village, there was an elder who had recently married and soon fathered two sons and a daughter. Later, at another time, both the elder and his wife passed away.
At that time, the elder brother went to his two elder brothers to seek their younger sister in marriage for the sake of obtaining a wife; they then gave her to him.

It is the nature of worldly affairs to discard the old upon obtaining the new. Consequently, the elder brother’s heart became attached to his junior wife. When the former wife saw this intimacy, jealousy arose in her mind.
Not long after, the senior wife became pregnant and said to her husband, "Your junior wife harbors improper thoughts."
Her husband said to her:
"O virtuous lady!
You have conceived an evil thought."

The wife remained silent, and subsequently gave birth to a son. When he reached the age of five, his wisdom was clear and discerning; all his speech was entirely truthful, so people of the time named him Satyavādin (the Truth-Teller).
His mother then thought:
"Although I have borne this son, my husband still loves his later wife; what skillful means can I now employ to cause them to be separated?"
She said to her husband,
"Although you cherish your junior wife exceedingly, she possesses no heart of integrity or purity toward you.
Her husband replied:
"O Worthy One!
You have again conceived an evil thought.
The wife remained silent, but devised another stratagem and said to her son:
"Do you not know the sufferings of a woman?
The son said to his mother,
"I have never known them."
She then said to her son:
"It is because of jealousy.
The son replied to his mother:
"This is not a good thing," he said, and then spoke to his son:
"I wish to expose the ill repute of your stepmother; you must serve as my witness."
The son said to his mother,
"Is this true?
Or is it false?"
The mother said,
"This is false.
The son said:
"The people of the world all know me to be a speaker of truth; how could I utter a falsehood from my mouth merely to follow what my mother says?

His mother said, "I carried you in my womb for nine months. If you do not comply with this small matter, there is no need for me to labor over verbal testimony; if your father asks you, you need only nod your head."
The son was filial and did not oppose his mother's wishes, so she finally gave her permission.
On another occasion, the mother said to her husband:
"Your beloved wife has committed an evil act with another man."
The husband said:
"Worthy lady!
You have again conceived an evil intention."
The wife said,
"If you do not believe me, you should ask one who speaks the truth.
The father thought to himself:
"This boy of mine is universally recognized by the world as one who speaks the truth; how could he speak a falsehood to me?
Such a thing is certainly impossible.
At that time, the boy was playing not far from his father. His father called him over, placed him upon his lap, and asked him:
"Do you know that your stepmother has committed an evil act with another man?
Since a woman’s disposition is deceptive and not known through learning, she immediately covered her son's mouth with her hand and said to him, "She is your mother;
there is no need to speak. If the matter is true, you may simply nod your head."
He nodded his head.

At that moment, a foul odor issued from his mouth, and immediately a bad reputation spread far and wide: "He is not a speaker of truth, but a liar who testified to a false matter on behalf of his stepmother. Thus, his reputation for speaking the truth vanished.
At that time, everyone called him a liar.
When his father saw this, he said to his second wife, "You have committed evil deeds; you should not remain here."
She was then driven out; having been expelled, she went to her two elder brothers. Her brothers asked her, "For what purpose have you come?
The sister replied to her brothers:
"I have been cast out by my husband.
"What fault have you committed?
"He falsely accused me of misconduct."
"If you have acted privately, you should not remain here.
"I am truly without private motives; it is by the testimony of my own truthful speech that I know he is a speaker of falsehoods and not one of truth."
The elder brother said,
"How can this be known?
[The younger brother replied,] "If you do not believe me, you should go and ask the neighbors living nearby."
Then those two elder brothers privately questioned their neighbors, and everyone said, "He has committed no evil deeds.

When the brothers realized he was innocent, they harbored resentment and vexation. Later, on another occasion, a Pratyekabuddha suddenly came to their house while wandering for alms, and they immediately invited him to eat.
Having finished eating, the woman recalled the matter of the slander she had suffered and made this evil vow:
"Just as I have been slandered by you today, even if you should attain the fruit of Arhatship in a future life, I shall likewise slander you and never let you go."
At that time, his two elder brothers saw him and asked,
"What vow have you made?
He answered his two elder brothers in detail regarding the matter.
The elder brother said,
"At that time, I was your brother and witnessed this matter together with you.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"What do you think? Do not harbor any other thought:
at that time, the one of truthful speech was none other than Śāriputra; the woman of different lineage was the bhikṣuṇī Mitrā; and those two elder brothers were the bhikṣus Mitra and Kṣema."

Because of his past malicious slander of his mother, Śrīgupta’s son suffered the torments of burning and boiling in the hells for many thousands of years; due to the remaining residue of that karma, he was constantly subjected to malicious slander throughout five hundred lifetimes, and even today, though he has attained arhatship, he is still slandered.
"O bhikṣus! By this you should know:
purely black karma yields purely black retribution; purely white karma yields purely white retribution; and mixed black-and-white karma yields mixed black-and-white retribution."
"You all should abandon purely black and mixed karma, and diligently cultivate the white category.
You bhikṣus! You should train yourselves in this way."
“O bhikṣus! What karma did Bālaputra previously perform,
such that he became the foremost among those who distribute robes?”
"You all should listen!
In the distant past, during this present Bhadrakalpa when the human lifespan was twenty thousand years, the Buddha Kāśyapa appeared in the world, fully endowed with the ten titles."

At that time, Dravyamāṇava left the household life for homelessness within that Buddha’s teaching; he diligently practiced the holy life (brahmacarya) for as long as he lived, yet ultimately attained no superior fruit. At the moment of his death, he made this vow:
"I have left the household life for homelessness within the teaching of Kāśyapa Buddha, the supreme field of merit, yet I have attained no superior fruit whatsoever."
"As the Buddha has prophesied, when the lifespan of humans in the future reaches one hundred years, there will be a Māṇavaka who shall certainly attain Buddhahood.

I shall go forth in his teaching, sever all afflictions, and realize arhatship, just as my upādhyāya today is foremost among the disciples of Kāśyapa Buddha for distributing the bedding and requisites of the Saṃgha."
"In a future age, among the disciples of the Unsurpassed Perfectly Awakened One Śākyamuni, I shall also be foremost in distributing the bedding and requisites of the Saṃgha.
By the power of that vow, within my own Dharma, he is likewise the very first in distributing the bedding and requisites of the Saṃgha.
"O Bhikṣus! You should train yourselves in this way.
The Ninth Chapter on the Training Rule Regarding False Accusations Based on Fabricated Grounds. At that time, the Buddha was staying at the Bamboo Grove near the Kakrandaka Pond in Rājagṛha.
At that time, the Venerable Sthavira was on Vulture Peak Mountain. Not far from there was a stone-paved pool, and its bank was the place where Sthavira spent his days.

At that time, the bhikṣuṇī Utpalavarṇā, through the spiritual friendship of the venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana, was able to go forth within the well-spoken Dharma and Vinaya; she severed all afflictions and attained arhatship.
He frequently went to the presence of the Blessed One to pay respectful homage, as well as to other senior and virtuous bhikṣus.

He felt a particular sense of reverence for the Venerable Sthavira Śāriputra; because Śāriputra did not shrink from toil and hardship, he abandoned the sublime bliss of tranquil meditative concentration to serve as the *vaiyāvṛtyakara* (steward) for the Saṃgha, distributing rooms and bedding according to the Dharma.
On another day later, the bhikṣuṇī Utpalavarṇā, having paid homage to the World-Honored One, proceeded to visit the assembly of great virtuous monks.
Upon arriving at the place of Sthavira Śrīgupta, she prostrated herself before him and sat to one side in order to listen to the Dharma.

At that time, the two bhikṣus, Mitra and Bhūmi, harbored a karmic enmity from a previous life with Śrīgupta. Having obtained a great quantity of discarded robes (*pāṃśukūla*), the two of them thought to themselves:
"Where shall we wash these robes?"

He then went at once to the edge of a stone-paved pond intending to wash his clothes; having arrived there, he saw two deer who, after drinking the water of the pond, were performing impure acts of sexual intercourse.
At that time, the elder brother said to his younger brother: "Brother!
We have now seen this Śrīgupta committing impure conduct and practicing sexual intercourse with the bhikṣuṇī Utpalavarṇā; we should go and inform the bhikṣus."
The younger brother replied to his elder brother, saying, "Our sister-nun was previously expelled by the community for our sake; how could we now wish to suffer expulsion together?
The elder brother replied to his younger brother:
"What you said before was false; what I say now is the truth. Do you not see that Śrīgupta has committed impure acts and engaged in sexual intercourse with the nun Utpalavarṇā?"
The younger brother remained silent, and the brothers together went to inform the bhikṣus, saying:
"Who among the people of this world is truly trustworthy?
We, your brothers, have just witnessed the son of Śrīgupta engaging in sexual misconduct with the nun Utpalavarṇā."
When the bhikṣus heard these words, they said to Mitrabhūmi, "Venerable one!

You have now utterly abandoned the path of humans and devas, and your mind is intent solely on entering the three evil realms. This Śrīgupta has realized arhatship, dwells in the eight liberations, has attained the qualities of a superior person, and manifests great supernormal powers."
"How can you now slander him with a *pārājika* offense based on matters that are entirely different?
The two replied, "This was truly not our fault;
it was the fault of our eyes. We ought to have our two eyes plucked out."
The bhikṣus said:
“As the Blessed One has taught, one must investigate thoroughly and inquire well about the matter: ‘What was seen?
What kind of appearance was seen?’”
"Where did you see him?
For what purpose did you two go there that you were able to see him?
When the bhikṣus had finished their inquiry, the two men then related all the aforementioned matters to the bhikṣus in detail.
At that time, some bhikṣus who possessed few desires collectively censured and rebuked this matter, saying:
"How is it that you, knowing that a pure bhikṣu is truly without offense, nevertheless slander and defame him with a groundless *pārājika* charge?"
At that time, the bhikṣus reported this matter in detail to the Blessed One.

Thereupon, the Blessed One, for this reason, assembled the community of bhikṣus, as described at length previously, up until: "I shall establish a training rule (śikṣāpada) for the bhikṣus, which should be recited as follows:
'If a bhikṣu, harboring anger and refusing to let it go, intentionally slanders a pure bhikṣu with a groundless *pārājika* offense, desiring to ruin his pure conduct.'"

At a later time, whether questioned or not, if one knows that this is a matter of a different nature and not a legitimate part [of the case], yet brings about a groundless accusation by means of some slight similarity of dharma;
and if that bhikṣu utters such words out of malice, it is a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*.
"Furthermore, 'if a bhikṣu' refers to the two, Mitra and Bhūmi, as well as others of a similar kind.
'Harboring anger' means that one previously held resentment and did not let it go."
"Hence" means that the mind of anger does not cease.
"Regarding that pure and unoffending bhikṣu" refers to one who has never committed a pārājika offense.
"A matter other than what is appropriate": "other" refers to nirvāṇa, as it is contrary to saṃsāra; this means that the four pārājika dharmas are not his lot.
Regarding the *pārājika* offenses: among these four, one brings a charge against another by means of any one of them.
To "bring a charge" means to falsely allege those matters.
To "corrupt a practitioner of pure conduct" means to intend to cause that person to fall away from their pure conduct.
...up to the point of committing a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense, as explained in detail previously.
In this context, what are the characteristics of the offense and the specific circumstances?

If a bhikṣu sees another bhikṣu commit one of the four *pārājika* offenses, yet conceives the notion that it was not an offense, understands it to be no offense, and accepts it as no offense, he then speaks these words:
"If one says, 'I saw that bhikṣu commit a pārājika offense,' one incurs a saṃghāvaśeṣa when making such a statement.
Furthermore, if a bhikṣu, upon seeing that bhikṣu commit a pārājika offense, perceives it as a saṃghāvaśeṣa, understands it as such, and assents to it as such, and then speaks these words:"
"I see that bhikṣu committing a pārājika offense.
When one speaks these words, one incurs a saṃghāvaśeṣa offense.
If a bhikṣu, upon seeing that bhikṣu commit a pārājika offense, perceives it as a pāyattika, understands it as such, and assents to it as such, yet then speaks these words:
"If one says, 'I saw that bhikṣu commit a pārājika offense,' when making such a statement, one incurs a saṃghāvaśeṣa offense. If a bhikṣu,
upon seeing that bhikṣu commit a pārājika offense, conceives the notion that it is a pāyantikā, understands it as such, and assents to it as such, and then speaks these words:"
"If one says, 'I saw that bhikṣu commit a *pārājika* offense,' one incurs a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense.
If a bhikṣu, when seeing that bhikṣu commit a *pārājika* offense, conceives the notion of a *duṣkṛta*, forms such an understanding, and accepts it as such, yet then speaks these words:"
"If one says, 'I saw that bhikṣu commit a pārājika offense,' one incurs a saṃghāvaśeṣa offense when making such a statement.

If a bhikṣu sees that another bhikṣu has committed a saṃghāvaśeṣa offense, yet conceives the notion that there is no offense, forms the understanding that there is no offense, and maintains the conviction that there is no offense, he may then speak as follows:"
"If one says, 'I see that bhikṣu commit a pārājika offense,' when these words are spoken, one incurs a saṃghāvaśeṣa.
In this manner, up to seeing him commit a duṣkṛta, there are five versions for each; they should be explained in detail as above."
There is no offense in the following cases: speaking according to the facts regarding the first commission of an offense; being insane, mentally deranged, or overwhelmed by intense physical pain.
The Tenth Training Rule on Obstructing the Sangha’s Reconciliation through Admonition. At that time, the Blessed One was staying at the Bamboo Grove near the Kakrandaka Pond in Rājagṛha.

At that time, as it was a year of famine, alms were difficult to obtain. Those bhikṣus who possessed supernatural powers went to the Jambūvana forest—after which the continent of Jambudvīpa is named—and having reached that forest, they took jambu fruits endowed with perfect color, fragrance, and flavor, filling their bowls to the brim. Carrying these back, they satisfied themselves and distributed the remainder to the other bhikṣus.

Alternatively, there were other bhikṣus who, not far from this forest, found piṇḍa fruits, kapittha fruits, and āmalaka fruits; they likewise brought them back and shared them with the others for eating.

Or there were bhikṣus who went to Pūrvavideha, or to Aparagoyānī, or to Uttarakuru, where they gathered naturally grown fragrant rice and, as before, brought it back to share with the rest for eating.
Sometimes they go to the Heaven of the Four Great Kings or to the Heaven of the Thirty-three, take celestial delicacies, and as before, bring them back to share with others;
or they go to other regions of abundance and joy, take fine food from there, and as before, share it among themselves.
At that time, Devadatta thought to himself:

"Now that we have encountered a year of famine, almsfood is difficult to obtain. At such times, those bhikṣus who possess supernormal powers go to the Jambūvana grove—as described at length previously—and take excellent food to share together as before."
"If I were to obtain the power of supernatural faculties (*ṛddhi*), I too could take [the food] back as before and eat it together.
He then reflected:
"Who has the power to teach me these supernatural faculties?"
"I should now go to the World-Honored One to inquire about this matter; whatever he may say, I shall receive and uphold.

Then, in the late afternoon, Devadatta rose from his place of seclusion and went to where the World-Honored One was. Having prostrated at the Buddha's feet, he stood to one side and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
"I only wish that you would explain for me the matters of supernormal powers (ṛddhi).
At that time, the World-Honored One, knowing that Devadatta had conceived an evil and perverse thought, told him:
"You should first purify your ethical discipline (śīla) and diligently cultivate meditative concentration (samādhi) and wisdom (prajñā); only then may you practice the matters of supernormal powers."
At that time, Devadatta thought to himself:
"The World-Honored One is unwilling to explain the matter of supernormal powers to me.
He then paid his respects, took leave of the Buddha, and departed. He went to where Ājñātakauṇḍinya was, and after conversing with him, he said to him:
“I only pray that the Elder will explain for me the matter of supernatural powers.
Then the Venerable Ājñātakauṇḍinya observed the Buddha’s mind and saw that the Buddha knew Devadatta intended to give rise to evil thoughts; he then said to Devadatta:
“You must observe form according to reality before you can attain supernatural powers and other superior virtues.”
"Feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are also thus.
At that time, Devadatta thought to himself:
"Even the Elder Ājñātakauṇḍinya did not explain the matter of supernatural powers to me."

He then left them and went to visit the bhikṣu Aśvajit, Bhadrika, Vāṣpa, Mahāyaśas, Pūrṇa, Vimala, Gavāmpati, Subāhu, and so on, up to the five hundred elders; he visited each of their abodes and requested the dharma of supernatural powers.

At that time, the five hundred senior bhikṣus all observed the Buddha’s mind and saw that the Buddha knew Devadatta was about to give rise to an evil thought. They also each observed the minds of the other senior bhikṣus and knew that Devadatta was about to give rise to an evil thought. Thereupon, they said to Devadatta:
"You should observe form according to reality, and only then will you attain supernormal powers as well as other superior virtues;
it is the same for feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness."
At that time, Devadatta thought to himself:
"These five hundred senior bhikṣus have not taught the dharma of supernatural powers to me."
"Is it not the case that all these people previously made verbal agreements, yet not one of them ever taught me the methods of supernatural powers?
At that time, Devadatta again thought to himself:
"Who is able to teach me the dharma of supernatural powers?"
At that time, the Venerable Daśabala-Kāśyapa was residing in the Vulture’s Peak Cave at Rājagṛha. Then Devadatta had this thought:

“Daśabala-Kāśyapa is by nature free from guile and deceit, and his words are truthful; he is my younger brother Ānanda’s upādhyāya, and he will be able to teach me the methods for supernatural powers.”
Having formed this thought, he immediately went to the place where Daśabala Kāśyapa was, prostrated at his feet, stood to one side, and said:
"Venerable Elder!..."
“I pray that you will explain to me the methods for attaining the supernormal powers.

At that time, the Venerable Daśabalakāśyapa, without examining the Buddha’s mind or those of the other elders, and unaware that Devadatta intended to give rise to evil and heterodox thoughts, proceeded to teach the methods for supernormal powers to Devadatta.

At that time, Devadatta, through diligent practice and self-exhortation during both the first and last watches of the night, attained the first dhyāna by means of the mundane path during the final watch. He immediately manifested supernatural powers: he could transform one into many and many into one, appearing and disappearing at will;
he passed unimpeded through mountains, rocks, and walls as if they were empty space;
and he entered the earth as if it were water and walked upon water as if it were solid ground.
He sat cross-legged in mid-air like a soaring bird;
at times, he even stroked the sun and moon with his hand.
Having acquired such powers, Devadatta then thought to himself:
"Since it is now difficult for the bhikṣus to obtain almsfood, I shall go first to the Jambūvana grove, take some fragrant and delicious fruits for myself, and share the remainder with others.

[He thought: "Shall I go to the eastern, western, or northern continents, to the Cāturmahārājakāyika gods, the Trāyastriṃśa heaven, or other places, take [fruits] from them as before, and distribute them to the rest?"
"Should I first convert the Lord of Magadha? Once he has been converted, many others will be subdued without the need for toil or hardship.
Then this thought arose again:

"After his father’s death, this Prince Ajātaśatru shall become the sovereign king with great power; it would be fitting for me now to convert him first, so that many others may be subdued without toil or hardship."
Then Devadatta immediately manifested himself as a magnificent elephant and entered quietly through the rear gate of the prince’s residence, exiting through the front gate;
he entered through the front gate and exited through the rear gate.

At other times, he manifested as a noble horse and entered and exited as before; or he manifested as a bhikṣu with his hair and beard shaven, wearing a saṃghāṭī robe and holding an alms bowl in his hands, entering and exiting as before.
At that time, Prince Ajātaśatru thought to himself,
"This is a display of supernatural powers by Devadatta. Thereupon,
Devadatta transformed his body into the form of a young boy, adorned with various necklaces and ornaments, and began to roll about within the prince's lap.
At that time, the prince seized the boy, cradled him, and kissed him, then placed his own snot and saliva into the boy's mouth.
Because Devadatta’s mind was entangled by greed for gain and offerings, he swallowed the saliva.
At that time, the Prince, on account of this, gave rise to an evil and heterodox mind, thinking to himself:
"How extraordinary is Devadatta!
Compared to the Great Teacher, the Buddha, his virtue is superior."

His faith and reverence increased further as he desired to offer his worship; at that time, during both the morning and evening, the Prince would regularly follow with five hundred precious chariots to visit Devadatta to pay his respects, and at every mealtime, he would present five hundred cauldrons of exquisite food and drink.
At that time, Devadatta was the leader, and five hundred bhikṣus received these offerings.

Then, a great number of bhikṣus entered the city of Rājagṛha at dawn to go on their almsround, and they heard that Devadatta was receiving such excellent and sublime offerings: Prince Ajātaśatru, during both the morning and evening, constantly followed him with five hundred precious chariots to pay his respects, and at every mealtime, he provided him with offerings of five hundred cauldrons of exquisite food and drink.
With Devadatta as their leader, five hundred bhikṣus received this offering.

When the bhikṣus heard of these events, they returned to their own quarters; having finished their meal, they put away their robes and bowls after the meal, washed their feet, and went to the place where the World-Honored One was. They prostrated at the Buddha’s feet and sat to one side.
Then the bhikṣus said to the Buddha:
"World-Honored One!
This morning, while we bhikṣus were entering the city to beg for alms, we heard that Devadatta had received such offerings along with five hundred bhikṣus."
He related the matter in full.
The World-Honored One said: "O bhikṣus!"
Do not take delight in Devadatta’s receiving of such offerings. Why is this?
Devadatta is now being destroyed by the very offerings he receives, just as the plantain tree is killed by bearing fruit, or as the bamboo and reed are destroyed by producing seed.
Just as a mule that conceives inevitably destroys its own body, so it is with Devadatta;
by accepting the offerings of others, he will surely bring about his own destruction. You bhikṣus!
When Devadatta obtains gain and offerings, this deluded person will undergo matters of disadvantage and suffering for a long night.
Therefore, you bhikṣus!
"Do not seek fame, reputation, gain, or offerings; even if you obtain them, let your mind have no attachment to them.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke these verses:
"When the plantain bears fruit, When the bamboo or reed produces its seed; [They perish. "
Just as when a mule becomes pregnant, it brings about its own destruction;
so too do gain, offerings, and fame— things cherished by the foolish—
which destroy all wholesome qualities, like a sword cutting off one's head.
When the bhikṣus had heard what the Buddha had spoken, they received it with reverence and departed.
At that time, having obtained such honor and offerings, Devadatta immediately gave rise to an evil thought:
"The World-Honored One is now old, aged, and decrepit; he serves the fourfold assembly:..."
"Bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, and upāsikās are weary from being instructed.
You may now entrust the great assembly to me; let me instruct them, and I shall take charge of them."
“World-Honored One, you should indeed diminish your contemplations and dwell in the tranquility of experiencing the bliss of the present life.
