As soon as Devadatta gave rise to this thought, his supernormal powers were lost; yet, although his powers were lost, he was not aware of it himself.

At that time, there was a Kakuṭa bhikṣu who was a disciple of the Buddha. Having formerly cultivated pure conduct in the presence of the Buddha and trained in the four Brahmavihāras, and having extensively practiced the removal of desire for sensual pleasures, he was reborn in a Brahma palace after his death.

At that time, the Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana was dwelling on Mount Paṇḍava in the Bhīṣaṇa Forest. Then, Kakuṭṭha, observing with his divine eye, saw that Devadatta had fallen away from his supernormal powers.

Having understood this, like a strong man extending or contracting his arm, he vanished from the Brahma palace and went to the Forest of Fear, arriving at the place where the Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana was. Having prostrated at his feet, he said to him:
"Venerable Sir, do you know?"
Because Devadatta’s mind was bound by the fetters of greed for gain and offerings, he gave rise to such an evil thought and came to address the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One, you are now advanced in years, aged and decrepit;
you are weary from instructing the fourfold assembly: bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, and upāsikās.”

"Now you may entrust the great assembly to me; let me instruct them and I shall uphold [the teaching]. World-Honored One, you should now reflect little and dwell in the tranquility of experiencing the bliss of the present dharma."
At that moment, as soon as Devadatta conceived this thought, his supernatural powers were immediately lost.
"Excellent, Venerable Maudgalyāyana!
You should go to the Buddha's presence and report these matters in detail."
Then Mahāmaudgalyāyana silently consented to his proposal.
Knowing that he had consented, the Brahmā Kakuda vanished from sight.

After the Brahmā had departed, Mahāmaudgalyāyana immediately entered a state of superior meditative concentration (*samādhi*) regarding that matter; then, in the time it takes a strong man to bend and extend his arm, he disappeared from the Forest of Fear and appeared in the Bamboo Grove.
He went to where the World-Honored One was, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and sat to one side.
Then, Mahāmaudgalyāyana reported in full to the World-Honored One the words spoken by that Brahmā.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Mahāmaudgalyāyana, saying:
"Did you not already know beforehand that Devadatta harbored an evil mind, only for Brahmā to come later and inform you?"
“Venerable One!
I already knew this beforehand; it was only later that Brahmā informed me.
At that time, the World-Honored One and Mahāmaudgalyāyana discussed other matters in the interim.
At that time, Devadatta, together with four companions—first, Kokālika;
second, Khaṇḍadravya; third, Kaṭamorakatiṣya; and fourth, Samudradatta—approached the place where the Buddha was.
At that time, the World-Honored One saw Devadatta approaching from afar and addressed Mahāmaudgalyāyana, saying:
"You must carefully guard your words; Devadatta is about to arrive."
"This foolish man has personally come before me and confessed his own great [transgression].

At that time, Mahāmaudgalyāyana prostrated at the Buddha’s feet and immediately entered meditative concentration; in the time it takes a strong man to bend and extend his arm, he vanished from the Bamboo Grove and went to the Bhairava Forest.
At that time, Devadatta, having arrived at the place where the Buddha was, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet and stood to one side, addressing the Buddha:
“World-Honored One, you are now advanced in years, aged and decrepit;
you are weary from instructing the fourfold assembly: bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, and upāsikās.”
"Now you may entrust the great assembly to me; I shall instruct them and I shall uphold their guidance.
World-Honored One, you should consider this briefly and dwell in the tranquility of experiencing the bliss of the present dharma."
The Blessed One said:
"You foolish man!
Even to Śāriputra and Mahāmaudgalyāyana, I did not entrust the community of bhikṣus; how much less, then, to you, a fool who eats the snot and spittle of others!"
At that time, Devadatta thought to himself:
"The World-Honored One has praised Śāriputra and Mahāmaudgalyāyana, yet he calls me a fool, a corpse, and a witless man who eats saliva."
This was the first time Devadatta conceived the intent to kill the Buddha and harbored a mind of resentment,
saying, "I am Devadatta," as he shook his head three times and departed from the Buddha's presence.
At that time, the Venerable Ānanda was standing behind the Blessed One, fanning him with a fan.
Then the Blessed One, knowing that Devadatta had departed, said to Ānanda:
"You should now go to the vicinity of the Bamboo Grove near Lake Kalandaka and have all the bhikṣus assemble in the regular dining hall."

Having received the Buddha’s instruction, Ānanda immediately went to the Bamboo Grove; once he had gathered all the bhikṣus in the vicinity into the regular dining hall, he went to the World-Honored One and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!”
"May all the bhikṣus residing in the vicinity of the Bamboo Grove assemble; may the Buddha know that the time has come.

At that time, the Blessed One went to the Hall of Constant Assembly, took his seat among the great multitude, and addressed the bhikṣus, saying:
“In this world, there are five kinds of teachers. What are the five?

Suppose there is a teacher whose precepts are actually impure, yet he claims his precepts are pure. However, because they live together with him, his disciples come to know that he is not pure, and they say to one another:”
"Our Great Teacher’s precepts are truly impure, yet he claims his precepts are pure.
If we were to speak of this to others and our teacher heard it, he would become displeased; how then could we continue to rely upon him?"
"We should remain silent; he will know for himself.
Furthermore, our teacher has always provided us with food, drink, clothing, bedding, and medicinal requisites for our illnesses; we ought to protect him together."
However, that teacher thinks to himself:
"My disciples are concealing my faults.
This is the first kind of Great Teacher who dwells in the world.
Furthermore, there was another teacher whose livelihood was actually impure, yet he claimed his livelihood was pure.
His disciples, through living together with him, came to know that it was not pure, and so they said to one another:
"Our great teacher's livelihood is actually impure, yet he claims his livelihood is pure."
"If we were to speak of this to others, they would feel displeasure upon hearing it.
How then could we rely on one another?
We should remain silent; they will understand for themselves."
Furthermore, our teacher has always provided us with food, drink, clothing, bedding, and medicinal requisites for our illnesses; we ought to protect and support one another accordingly.
Yet that teacher thinks to himself:
"My disciples are concealing my faults.
This is the second type of great teacher who dwells in the world.
Furthermore, there is another teacher whose wisdom and vision are impure, yet he himself claims that his wisdom and vision are pure.
His disciples, through living together with him, come to know that his wisdom and vision are impure; the details are as explained previously. This is the third great teacher dwelling in the world.
Furthermore, there is another teacher who is unskilled in the art of prophecy, yet claims, "I am skilled in the art of prophecy and understand it as it truly is.
His disciples, through living together with him, come to know that he is unskilled in prophecy; the details are as explained previously. This is the fourth great teacher dwelling in the world.

Furthermore, there is another teacher who relies upon and associates with a poorly taught doctrine and discipline (*durākhyāta-dharmavinaya*), yet claims that the doctrine he relies upon is a well-taught doctrine and discipline (*svākhyāta-dharmavinaya*).
His disciples, through living together with him, come to know that it is a poorly taught doctrine and discipline, as explained in detail above; this is the fifth great teacher dwelling in the world.

“O bhikṣus, my observance of the precepts is pure and without fault; I now declare myself to be one whose observance of the precepts is pure and free from transgression. You, my disciples, need not protect me, nor do I have any intention for you to conceal anything on my behalf. This is the first way in which I abide in the world.”

Furthermore, O Bhikṣus, I abide in pure livelihood; I now declare for myself that my way of life is pure and free from fault. You, my disciples, need not protect me, nor do I have any intention to have you cover for me. This is the second instance of my abiding in the world.
Furthermore, monks, my knowledge and vision are purified—explained at length as before; this is the third way in which I dwell in the world.
Furthermore, monks, I am well-versed in prophecy and understand it as it truly is—explained at length as before; this is the fourth way in which I dwell in the world.

Furthermore, monks, regarding that well-expounded Dharma and Vinaya which is my refuge—I myself now declare this well-expounded Dharma and Vinaya, as explained at length previously—this is the fifth way in which I abide in the world.

“O Bhikṣus! I now address you with earnest and piteous words; you should practice them with sincere hearts. It is just as when a potter fires his earthenware vessels: they are all scorched by the same firewood, yet those that are good are perfected, while those that are flawed are destroyed.”
"You all should properly follow my words so as not to bring regret later.
At that time, Devadatta addressed his four companions, saying:

"You four should now join me in breaking the Saṃgha of that śramaṇa Gautama and destroying the Wheel of Dharma, so that after my death, I may obtain a good reputation whose fame fills the ten directions."
He spoke thus:

"The śramaṇa Gautama currently exists in the world; however, Devadatta possesses great power and influence, and together with Kokālika, Khaṇḍadravya, Kaṭamorakatiṣya, and Samudradatta, he has split the harmonious Saṅgha and broken the Wheel of Dharma."
Then Kokālika said to Devadatta,
"I will not assist you in this matter now. Why is that?..."

However, the Blessed One’s śrāvaka disciples possess great power; their divine eye is clear and penetrating, and they discern the minds of others. Though things may be far away, they can see them from a distance; though their own bodies are nearby, people do not perceive them, yet they already understand in advance all that we do.
At that time, Devadatta said to his companions,
"Gentlemen, you should all devise a stratagem together.
His friends replied:
"What is the skillful means?
Devadatta replied,
"I shall now go to where those elders of long-standing virtue and senior monks reside, and provide them with all manner of excellent requisites and necessities so that they lack for nothing."

He also provided for the young bhikṣu, causing him joy, and gave him robes, alms bowls, bowl bags, and waist-bands; he further instructed him in recitation and in the application of mental attention (*manasikāra*).
The friend replied,
"This is a good expedient.
At that time, Devadatta extensively employed such deceptions, desiring to cause a schism in the Saṃgha.
The great bhikṣus, perceiving that Devadatta was proceeding with the intent to destroy the wheel of the Saṃgha, reported this matter in full to the World-Honored One:
"Devadatta has the intention to destroy the wheel of the Saṃgha."
At that time, the Blessed One addressed the bhikṣus, saying:
"You should each separately admonish Devadatta; if there are others of a similar kind, you should likewise admonish them, saying:
'Devadatta!'"
Do not, Devadatta, cause a schism in the Saṃgha by persisting in acts of strife and contention. Devadatta, you should live in harmony with the Saṃgha,
rejoicing and free from dispute, with a single mind and one voice, like water mixed with milk, so that the Master’s teaching may be made radiant and the community may dwell in peace and happiness.
“Devadatta!
You should now desist from performing acts that cause a schism in the Saṃgha.
When the bhikṣus had received the Buddha’s instruction, they immediately went separately to admonish Devadatta, saying:
“Devadatta! Do not cause a schism in the Saṃgha; do not engage in contentious matters and dwell in what is contrary to the Dharma.
Devadatta!”

One should dwell in harmony with the Saṃgha, joyful and without dispute, with a single mind and a single voice like water and milk blending together, so that the Teacher’s instruction may be made radiant and one may abide in peace and happiness.
“Devadatta!
You should now abandon this act of causing a schism in the Saṃgha.
When the bhikṣus were thus admonishing him individually, Devadatta remained obstinate in his position and had no intention of relinquishing it, saying:
"This alone is true; all else is false.
Then the bhikṣus reported this entire matter to the Blessed One, saying:
"Venerable Sir!..."
"I have already offered a private admonition to Devadatta; while we were offering that private admonition, Devadatta remained obstinate and refused to relinquish his position, saying:
'This alone is true; all else is false.'"
At that time, the Buddha addressed the bhikṣus:
"You should perform the *jñapti-caturtha-karman* against Devadatta to admonish him before the assembly; if there are others of a similar kind, they should be admonished in this same manner."

When the sitting mats have been spread and the *ghanṭī* has been struck, one should first announce the matter and subsequently assemble the Saṃgha. Once the Saṃgha has assembled, he should instruct a single Bhikṣu to perform the formal motion (*jñapti-karman*), which should be done as follows:
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!
This Devadatta desires to cause a schism in the harmonious Saṃgha and persists in unlawful conduct by engaging in strife.
At that time, the bhikṣus have already offered him individual admonition.
During this individual admonition, he stubbornly clings to his position and refuses to relinquish it, saying:
"This matter is true; all else is false.

If the Sangha deems the time has come and grants its permission, the Sangha shall now perform the formal motion followed by three proclamations (*jñapti-caturtha-karman*) to admonish Devadatta regarding this matter: "You, Devadatta!..."
"Do not wish to cause a schism in the harmonious Saṃgha by engaging in quarrelsome matters and persisting in them. Devadatta!

You should live in harmony with the Saṃgha, joyful and without dispute, with a single mind and one voice, like water mixed with milk, so that the Great Teacher’s instruction may be made radiant and you may dwell in peace and happiness."
"You, Devadatta! You should abandon the act of schisming the Saṃgha.
Thus it is announced.
Next, the *karmavācanā* is performed:
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!
This Devadatta desires to cause a schism in the harmonious Saṃgha, engaging in and persisting in acts of contention."
The bhikṣus have already administered a formal admonition to him.
During this formal admonition, he stubbornly clings to his position and refuses to relinquish it, saying:
"This matter is true; all else is false."
The Saṃgha now performs the formal motion and threefold proclamation (*jñapti-caturtha-karman*) to admonish Devadatta regarding this matter: "You, Devadatta!
Do not seek to cause a schism in the harmonious Saṃgha by persisting in and adhering to matters of contention."

Devadatta! You should live in harmony with the Saṃgha, joyful and without dispute, with a single mind and one voice, like water mixed with milk, so that the Teacher’s instruction may be made radiant and you may dwell in peace and happiness.
"You, Devadatta! You should desist from this act of schism.
If the venerable ones consent to perform the formal rite of *jñapti-caturtha-karman* (a motion followed by three proclamations) to admonish Devadatta regarding this matter:
“Devadatta! Do not seek to cause a schism in the harmonious Saṃgha by taking up and persisting in matters of contention. Devadatta!”

One should dwell in harmony with the Saṃgha, joyful and without dispute, with a single mind and one voice, like water mixed with milk, so that the teachings of the Great Master may be made radiant and the community may abide in peace and happiness.
"You, Devadatta! Since you should abandon such an act of schism, remain silent.
If you do not consent, speak.
"This is the first *karmavācanā*.
The second and third [recitations] are also spoken in this manner.
'The Saṃgha has now completed the *jñapti-caturtha-karman* to admonish Devadatta; the Saṃgha has granted its consent, as indicated by their silence. Thus do I now uphold it.'"
When the bhikṣus had thus received the Buddha’s instruction, they immediately exhorted Devadatta by means of a *jñapti-caturtha-karman*.
At that time, Devadatta remained obstinate and refused to relinquish his position, saying:
"This alone is true; all else is false."
At that time, Devadatta had four companions who followed him in harmony as he spoke of the matter of schism; they addressed the bhikṣus, saying:
"Venerable sirs!..."
Do not engage in any discussion with that bhikṣu, whether it be good or bad. Why is this?

For that bhikṣu is one who speaks according to the Dharma and speaks according to the Vinaya; he speaks only by relying upon the Dharma and the Vinaya. He speaks knowing [the truth] and does not speak out of ignorance. What he delights in, I too delight in.
Then the bhikṣus reported this matter in detail to the Blessed One, as described above, concluding with: "I, too, delight in it.
The Blessed One said: "O bhikṣus!..."
You should perform the formal admonition with the four companions; if there are others of a similar kind, they too should be reprimanded and admonished.
It should be done as follows:
"You, Kokālika, Khaṇḍadravya, Kaṭamorakatiṣya, and Samudradatta, you know that those bhikṣus desire to cause a schism in the harmonious Saṅgha and persist in engaging in contentious disputes."
"You all should act as companions to one another; do not follow along in speaking of matters that cause a schism in the Saṃgha, and do not speak to the bhikṣus in this way:
'Venerable sirs!'"
Do not engage in any conversation with that bhikṣu, whether it be favorable or unfavorable. Why is this?

Because that bhikṣu is one who speaks according to the Dharma and speaks according to the Vinaya; he speaks only by relying on the Dharma and the Vinaya. He speaks knowing [the truth] and does not speak out of ignorance. What he delights in, I also delight in.
Why is this? Venerable sir!

That bhikṣu speaks words that are not in accordance with the Dharma and Vinaya; he does not rely upon the Dharma and Vinaya in his speech; he speaks without knowing, rather than speaking from knowledge, and remains obstinately attached to his position.

Do not take delight in causing a schism in the Saṃgha; you should instead delight in the harmony of the Saṃgha. You ought to be in concord with the Saṃgha, joyful and without dispute, being of one mind and one voice like water mixed with milk, so that the Teacher’s instruction may be made manifest and may abide in peace and happiness.
"Venerable ones!
You should now relinquish these actions that accord with causing a schism in the Saṃgha and leading to discord.
Then the bhikṣus, having received this instruction, proceeded to admonish those four men with a formal separate admonition, speaking to them as follows:

“You four, Kokālika and the others, know that those bhikṣus desire to cause a schism in the harmonious Saṃgha and persist in acts of contention; do not associate with them, nor follow what is false and oppose what is right.”
"Venerable friends!
Do not speak thus to the bhikṣus:
'O Venerable Ones!'"
Do not engage in discussions with that bhikṣu regarding what is good or what is bad. Why is this?

That bhikṣu speaks in accordance with the Dharma and the Vinaya; he relies upon the Dharma and the Vinaya in his discourse. He speaks knowing [the truth] and does not speak out of ignorance. What he delights in, I also delight in.
Why is this? Venerable one!

For that bhikṣu speaks words that are not in accordance with the Dharma and Vinaya; he does not rely upon the Dharma and Vinaya in his speech; he speaks without knowing, rather than speaking from knowledge.
"Venerable one!

Do not take delight in the schism of the Saṃgha; you should instead delight in the harmony of the Saṃgha. You ought to live in concord with the harmonious Saṃgha, joyful and without dispute, with a single mind and a single voice, like water mixed with milk, so that the Teacher’s instruction may be made radiant and may abide in peace and happiness."
"Venerable one!
You should now abandon these actions that accord with causing a schism in the Saṃgha and promoting discord.
When the bhikṣus were thus admonishing him individually, his companions refused to accept their words, stubbornly persisting and refusing to relinquish their position, saying:
"This alone is true; all else is false.
Then the bhikṣus reported this matter in detail to the Blessed One:
"Venerable Sir!..."

"We have already given private admonition to Kokālika and the others. While we were giving them private admonition, Kokālika and the others stubbornly clung to their position and had no intention of relinquishing it, saying:

The Buddha addressed the bhikṣus:
"You should perform the *jñapti-caturtha-karman* against Kokālika and the others to admonish them before the assembly.
If there are others of a similar kind, you should likewise assemble the community as before and perform the *jñapti-karman* in this manner."
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!

These individuals—Kokālika, Khaṇḍadravya, Kaṭamorakatiṣya, and Samudradatta—know that this bhikṣu intends to cause a schism in the harmonious Saṃgha; they persistently engage in acts of contention and adhere to those discordant matters."
When the bhikṣus offer such admonition, you must not speak to those bhikṣus in this way:
"Venerable sirs!
Do not join with that bhikṣu in discussing his words, whether they be good or bad."

Why is this? Because that bhikṣu is one who speaks according to the Dharma and speaks according to the Vinaya; he speaks in reliance upon the Dharma and Vinaya, speaking what he knows rather than speaking out of ignorance. What he delights in, I too delight in.
At that time, the bhikṣus gave him a formal admonition.
During this formal admonition, he remained obstinate regarding that matter and spoke these words:
"This matter is truly so; all else is false."

"If the time is ripe for the Saṃgha and the Saṃgha permits, let the Saṃgha now exhort the four individuals, Kokālika and the others, by means of a formal motion followed by three proclamations (*jñapti-caturtha-karman*):

'You, Kokālika and the others, know that those bhikṣus desire to cause a schism in the harmonious Saṃgha, engaging in acts of contention and persisting therein, and you follow them in their discordant conduct.'"
When the bhikṣus offer such admonition, you must not speak to those bhikṣus as follows:
"Venerable sirs!
Whether the speech of that bhikṣu be good or bad..."

Venerable ones!

“Venerable Sir!

"This alone is true; all else is false.

He then addressed Kokālika and the others:
"You should know that the śramaṇa Gautama has prophesied concerning me:

At that time, Devadatta became even more resolute in his efforts to split the Saṃgha. When the bhikṣus heard of this, they reported it in full to the Blessed One.
Thereupon, the Blessed One, for this reason, assembled the community of bhikṣus and spoke at length as previously described, until the Blessed One questioned the bhikṣu Devadatta, saying:

Devadatta replied,
"Venerable Sir,
it is indeed so."
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Devadatta, saying:
"You are not a śramaṇa; you do not follow the path; you are impure; this is improper and should not be done; it is not the conduct of one who has left the household life."
After the Blessed One had thus rebuked him in various ways, he addressed the bhikṣus, saying:
“Having considered ten benefits, I shall establish a training rule for the bhikṣus, which should be spoken as follows:
‘If a bhikṣu, having devised a means, seeks to cause a schism in a harmonious Saṃgha, and persists in his intent to cause such a schism without relinquishing it.’”
The bhikṣus should say to that bhikṣu:
"Venerable one!
Do not desire to cause a schism in the Saṃgha by persisting in your obstinacy."
"Venerable one!

You should live in harmony with the Saṃgha, dwelling together in joy and without dispute, speaking with a single mind like water and milk blending, so that the Teacher’s instruction may be made radiant and endure for a long time in peace and happiness."
"Venerable one!
You should relinquish this act of schism.
When the bhikṣus have admonished him in this manner, it is well if he relinquishes it.
If he does not relinquish it, one should admonish him earnestly and correctly two or three times; following the instruction, one should interrogate him so that he may relinquish this matter.
If he relinquishes it, it is well; if he does not relinquish it, it is a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*.
"Furthermore, regarding 'if a bhikṣu': this refers to Devadatta, or anyone else of a similar kind.
As for 'in harmony,' it means being of one flavor."
The "Saṃgha" refers to the community of the Tathāgata’s śrāvakas.
"Wishing to break" means wishing to divide it into two parts.

"If he relinquishes it, that is well; if he does not relinquish it, he should be admonished three times," and so forth, as explained at length.
Regarding the *saṃghāvaśeṣa*, the matter is as previously explained.
What are the characteristics of the offense herein?
If a bhikṣu employs means with the intent to cause a schism in the Saṃgha, he incurs an *duṣkṛta* (wrongdoing) offense in every instance.
If, when admonished individually regarding the matter, one does not relinquish it, one incurs a *sthūlātyaya* offense in each case.

If one performs the formal procedure of a *jñapti-caturtha-karman*, and during the time of such admonition—conducted in accordance with the Dharma, the Vinaya, and the Buddha’s instructions—one relinquishes it, that is well.

If one does not relinquish it, one incurs a *sthūlātyaya* offense at the conclusion of the *jñapti*; one also incurs a *sthūlātyaya* offense at the conclusion of the first proclamation; and one also incurs a *sthūlātyaya* offense at the conclusion of the second proclamation. If, at the conclusion of the third proclamation and the finalization of the *karman*, one still does not relinquish it, one incurs a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense.

If one performs what is contrary to the Dharma yet the assembly is in harmony; or if one performs what is in accordance with the Dharma yet the assembly is not in harmony; or if one performs what resembles the Dharma yet the assembly is in harmony; or if one performs what resembles the Dharma yet the assembly is not in harmony; or if one conducts a legal procedure in a manner that is neither in accordance with the Dharma, nor the Vinaya, nor the Buddha’s teaching—in all such cases, there is no offense.
Then that bhikṣu, while seated upon the mat, addressed the great assembly, saying:
"Venerable sirs!
I, the bhikṣu [Name], have committed a saṃghāvaśeṣa offense."
If he does so, it is well.

If he does not speak, then until his offense has been confessed and atoned for according to the Dharma, if he should again perform a *jñapti-karman* or even a *jñapti-caturtha-karman* together with other bhikṣus, for each instance he incurs an *duṣkṛta* (wrongdoing).
Furthermore, there is no offense for one who is a first-time offender, or for one who is insane, mentally deranged, or overwhelmed by intense pain.

The Eleventh Training Rule: On Following Those Who Seek to Cause a Schism in the Saṃgha Despite Being Admonished. "Furthermore, you need not rise; the Saṃgha has a minor matter to attend to.

Because that bhikṣu speaks according to the Dharma and the Vinaya, and he bases his speech upon the Dharma and the Vinaya; he speaks only what he knows and does not speak out of ignorance. What he delights in, I also delight in.
"Is this not so?

“World-Honored One!

“As explained at length previously, up until: ‘I, considering ten benefits, shall establish a training rule for my śrāvaka disciples, which should be recited as follows:

Then that bhikṣu said to the other bhikṣus:
"Venerable sirs,
do not engage in any discussion with that bhikṣu, whether regarding his good qualities or his faults."
Why is this? Because that bhikṣu accords with the Dharma and the Vinaya; his speech, being based on the Dharma and the Vinaya, is free from falsehood. What he delights in, I too delight in.
The bhikṣus should say to that bhikṣu:
"Venerable one!
Do not speak in this way."
"That bhikṣu conforms to the Dharma and the Vinaya; his speech regarding the Dharma and the Vinaya is without falsehood. What he delights in, I too delight in. Why is this?

That bhikṣu does not conform to the Dharma and Vinaya, nor does he rely upon the Dharma and Vinaya; his words are entirely false. You must not delight in causing a schism in the Saṃgha; you should instead delight in harmony with the Saṃgha. You should be in accord with the Saṃgha, joyful and without dispute, speaking with one mind like water and milk blending together, so that the Great Teacher’s teachings may be made radiant and endure in peace for a long time.
"Venerable one!
You should abandon this evil view of causing a schism in the Saṃgha; you must cease from following what is wrong and opposing what is right by persisting in inciting strife and remaining obstinate.
When the bhikṣus have admonished him in this manner, it is well if he abandons it.
