One should understand that there are cases where a single household has one *śakti-bhāga* (sphere of influence) and cases where it has many *śakti-bhāgas*.

Likewise, for musical performance halls, non-Buddhist hermitages, shops, stores, multi-storied buildings, courtyards, vehicles, boats, groves, and trees, there are four distinct types of *śakti-bhāgas*, whether they consist of one or many.
What is a single-dwelling village?
It refers to mountain dwellers who reside together in one house.
To what extent does its boundary (sīmā) extend?
This refers to the entire interior of the house, extending one fathom outward;
furthermore, the area encompassing the places where pounding, roasting, grinding, eating, drinking, and social gatherings take place is also called the "sphere of influence" (sīmā).

If a bhikṣu’s robe is inside a dwelling while his person is within the boundary, or if the robe is within the boundary while his person is inside the dwelling, there is no offense when the dawn appears.

If the robe is placed inside a robe-storage shed or within its precincts, and one remains in a different location, one incurs a *dukkaṭa* offense until the appearance of the dawn light; when the dawn light appears, one incurs a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika*.
If one dwelling is thus, two dwellings are likewise.
What is a "village of many dwellings"?
It refers to a village where the houses of the families have no orderly sequence and are situated in a disordered manner.
To what extent is this called the "sphere of influence" (pradeśa)?
Is it distinct or identical?
Answer:
This village has no common boundary; there is difference and not sameness.
The limit for being apart from one's robe is determined according to the house.
What is meant by a "walled-in village"?
This refers to a village surrounded on all four sides by walls.
To what extent is this called its "boundary" (*sīmā*)?
It extends throughout the interior of the walls, with an additional *vyāma* (a fathom) outside.
Furthermore, it extends as far as the place where a rooster can fly and land;
it also extends as far as the place where a person feeling shame performs their bodily functions—this constitutes its boundary, while the rest is as previously described.
What is a village surrounded by a fence?
It refers to a village whose four sides are enclosed by a fence.
To what extent is this defined as its "boundary" (sīmā)?
This refers to the area inside the fence, extending one *vyāma* (fathom) beyond it;
furthermore, it includes the area reachable by a twelve-cubit ladder;
and it also includes the space where a bamboo cart drawn by six oxen can turn around—this constitutes its boundary.
What is a village surrounded by a moat?
It refers to a village whose four sides are encircled by a moat.
To what extent does this constitute its "boundary zone" (sīmā)?
This refers to the area within the moat itself, extending one fathom outward;
furthermore, it includes the area reached by the dust raised by the hooves of cattle and sheep;
and it also includes the area reached by large bricks and stones when refuse and sweepings are discarded—this constitutes its boundary.
What is meant by one village having one *sīmā* (territorial boundary)?
It means that within this village there is a single grove, a single shrine, and a place where the community gathers; this is called one village having one *sīmā*.
To what extent is this defined as the "sphere of influence" (*pradeśa*)?
It extends throughout the gardens and groves, reaching one *vyāma* beyond;

furthermore, it includes the areas where mortars, pestles, frying pans, and grinding stones are kept, as well as places for eating, drinking, and social gatherings—this constitutes its sphere of influence.
What is meant by a single village having many spheres of influence?
It refers to a case where this village contains many groves, many shrines, and many places for public assembly; this is called a single village having many spheres of influence.
To what extent is this called the "sphere of influence" (pradeśa)?
Is it distinct or identical?
Answer:
This has no common boundary; it refers only to what is defined within the confines of a single dwelling.
What constitutes many villages having one common boundary?
It means that these many villages share a single grove, a single shrine, or a place where the community gathers; this is called many villages having one common boundary.
To what extent is this defined as the "sphere of influence" (*sīmā*)?
Within the village, it extends throughout; outside, it is one *vyāma* (fathom) on each side.
Furthermore, the area where pounding, grinding, roasting, milling, eating, drinking, and social gatherings take place is also called the sphere of influence.
What is meant by many villages having many *sīmā* (territorial boundaries)?
It refers to when these many villages have many groves, many shrines, and many places of assembly; this is called many villages having many *sīmā*.
To what extent is this called the "sphere of influence" (pradeśa)?
Is it distinct or identical?

This [monastery] has no shared boundary (*sīmā*).

What constitutes one family having a single shared boundary?

That is to say, in a household where there is only a single head of the family and the brothers have not divided their property, this is called "one family having one area of influence" (*sīmā*); the details are all the same as what was explained regarding a village of single-roofed houses.
What is meant by one household having multiple spheres of influence (*sīmā*)?
It refers to a case where there are many heads of the household or brothers living separately within that same house; this is called one household having multiple spheres of influence.
To what extent is this called a "sphere of influence" (*sīmā*)?
It means that from the gate onward, there is no further sphere of influence.
How can there be a single sphere of influence for many households?

This refers to cases where, within various households, there is only a single head of the family and the brothers do not divide their property; this is called "many households having one area of influence" (*ekasīmā*).
What is meant by "many households having many areas of influence"?
Regarding these households where there are multiple heads of family or distinctions among brothers:
to what extent is this defined as the "sphere of influence" (*sīmā*);
what is common and what is distinct?
Answer:
This has no *sīmā* (boundary).
How could there be a single *sīmā* for a house of musicians?
This refers to a case where there is a householder in this family whose brothers have not divided the property; this is called "one family having one area of influence" (*sīmā*).
To what extent does this "area of influence" extend?
The entire interior of the residence constitutes the boundary, extending outward for one *xun*;

furthermore, the area including the space where poles, drums, lutes, flutes, and pipes are set up, as well as the place where offerings are prepared and food and drink are gathered, also constitutes the functional domain.
What is meant by a single musical household having multiple spheres of influence (*sīmā*)?
It refers to a case where there are many heads of household within this family, such as brothers living separately; this is called a single household having multiple spheres of influence.
To what extent is this called the "sphere of influence" (*sīmā*)?
What is common and what is distinct?
The distinct refers to the boundaries according to where the brothers reside; the common refers to the area extending from where the flagpole is set up.
What is meant by "many households of musicians sharing a single jurisdiction"?
It refers to these various households having only one head of the family whose brothers have not divided their property; this is called many households sharing a single jurisdiction.
To what extent is this called the "sphere of influence" (*pradeśa*)?
It encompasses the entire interior of the dwelling and extends one *vyāma* (fathom) outside;
furthermore, it also includes the area where poles and such are erected, all of which are termed the sphere of influence.
What constitutes a house with many musical instruments having a large *sīmā* (boundary)?
It refers to those houses where there are many heads of households and distinctions among brothers.
To what extent is this defined as a *sīmā*?
What is common and what is distinct?
Answer:
This has no shared functional sphere (avasthāna).
What is meant by "one household having one common domain" among the followers of non-Buddhist paths?
It refers to a household where there is a single shared view and no divergent intentions.
This common domain extends throughout the entire house and reaches one fathom beyond it.

Furthermore, they come from places where cow dung is leveled and dried in the sun, where firewood and *kamaṇḍalu* water vessels are kept, where sacrificial rites are performed with strainers, ladles, and hearths, and where food is pounded and gathered for communal feasts.
How is it that a single non-Buddhist sect possesses many domains of influence (*śakti-vibhāga*)?
It means that within this sect, there are many views and intentions that differ from one another.
Regarding these domains of influence, what is common and what is distinct?
This refers to those who share a common altar.
What is meant by "many members of non-Buddhist sects having a single shared domain"?
It means that within various households, they possess the same views and have no differing intentions.
This area of influence encompasses the entire dwelling, extending one fathom outward;
it also includes areas such as where cow dung is dried and exposed.
Why, then, do those outside the Buddhist fold have many such areas of influence?
This means that these various schools possess many different views and intentions;
regarding this sphere of influence (*pradeśa*), what is shared and what is distinct?
Answer:
This [area] has no *sīmā* (boundary).
How can a single shop have one *sīmā*?
It means that within this shop there is a householder who is the head of the family, whose brothers have not divided the estate.
This area consists of the space between them, totaling one fathom on the outside;
furthermore, it includes the space for placing goods evenly, as well as the place for weighing, measuring, and conducting transactions.
How can a single shop have multiple spheres of influence (*sīmā*)?
This refers to a case where there are many heads of households and brothers within this shop, each with separate divisions.
Regarding these spheres of influence, what is shared and what is distinct?
This refers to the exchange of seating areas.
What constitutes many shops having a single shared boundary?
It means that all these shops have only one head of the household, with brothers who do not divide their property.
This area of influence consists of the entire interior space with an additional one *vyāma* (fathom) on the exterior;
it also includes places where goods and such are stored.
How can there be multiple areas of influence for many shops?
That is to say, when these various shops have many owners or are divided among brothers,
to what extent does their "influence zone" (sīmā) extend?
What is shared and what is distinct?
Answer:
This has no shared domain (sīmā).
How could there be a single shared domain for one shop?
This refers to a shop where a patriarch and his brothers live together without having divided their inheritance.
Regarding its boundaries: the interior space is entirely included, while the exterior extends one *vyāma* (fathom);

furthermore, it includes the area where small wheat, large wheat, sesame, mung beans, millet, non-glutinous rice, cotton, silk floss, garments, and other such items are placed side by side for weighing, measuring, and trading.
How can a single shop have multiple spheres of influence (*sīmā*)?
This refers to a case where there are multiple shop owners within this shop, or where brothers have divided their interests.
To what extent does this sphere of influence extend?
What is shared and what is distinct?
It refers to the area where objects, boards, and beds are kept.
How can there be a single functional boundary (*sīmā*) for many shops?
This refers to those shops where the sole owner’s brothers do not divide the business.
The extent of this area is the entire interior space plus one *vyāma* (fathom) on the outside;
furthermore, it includes the space occupied by grain, beans, and other goods stored therein.
What constitutes multiple shops having multiple spheres of influence (*sīmā*)?
This refers to cases where these various shops have multiple owners, or where brothers have divided them.
To what extent does this sphere of influence extend?
What is common and what is distinct?
Answer:
This has no shared sphere of influence (*avibhāga*).
What is meant by a single building having one common boundary (*sīmā*)?
It refers to a case where there is a single owner of this building who is a brother with whom the property has not been divided.
This common boundary extends throughout the interior and for one *vyāma* (fathom) on the exterior.
Furthermore, it comes from places where people gather for meals.
How can there be multiple spheres of influence (*śakti-vibhāga*) within a single building?
It is said that within this building there are multiple owners, or brothers who have divided their property.
To what extent does this constitute its boundary?
What is common and what is distinct?
It refers to the place where the ladder is set.
What is meant by multiple stories having a single common boundary (*sīmā*)?
It refers to these various stories having a single owner who is a brother with whom the property has not been divided.
This boundary consists of the entire interior space and extends one *vyāma* (fathom) outward, where they gather for food and drink.
What is meant by multiple stories having multiple spheres of influence (*sīmā*)?
It refers to cases where these various stories have multiple owners, or where brothers have divided them separately.
To what extent does this sphere of influence extend?
What is common and what is distinct?
Answer:
This has no shared sphere of influence (*avasthāna*).
What is meant by a single enclosure having one boundary (sīmā)?
It refers to a case where there is a single master of the enclosure who is a brother whose property has not been divided.
This boundary consists of the entire interior space, plus an area of one fathom (vyāma) on the outside, which is the space for placing baskets and measures for storing grain and barley.
How can a single enclosure have multiple spheres of influence (*sīmā*)?
This refers to a case where there are many owners of the enclosure, or brothers who have divided it.
To what extent does this sphere of influence extend?
What is common and what is distinct?
It refers to the boundaries of the precincts.
How can there be a single *sīmā* (territorial sphere) for many precincts?
This means that among these various fields, there is one field whose owners are brothers who have not divided their property.
Within this boundary, the entire central area and an additional span (vyāma) on the outside is designated for the storage of grain and barley.
What is meant by "many enclosures having many spheres of influence"?
This refers to cases where these various enclosures have multiple owners, or where brothers have divided them separately.
To what extent does this sphere of influence extend?
What is common and what is distinct?
Answer:
This has no shared sphere of influence (*avibhāga*).
What is meant by a single dwelling having one shared boundary?
It refers to a case where there is a single master of the hall who is a brother with whom the property has not been divided.

This shared boundary consists of the entire interior space, plus an area of one *vyāma* (fathom) on the exterior—meaning the area reached by where oxen and horses are tethered, where grass is cut, and where dung is discarded.
How can a single hall have multiple spheres of influence (*sīmā*)?
This refers to a case where there are many hall-owners within this hall, or where brothers have divided [the property].
To what extent does this sphere of influence extend?
This refers to arriving within the gate.
What is meant by "many halls having a single boundary"?
It means that these various halls have a single master, whose brothers do not divide the property.

Regarding this area of influence (*śakti-bhāga*), it encompasses the entire interior space and extends one fathom (*vyāma*) outward; this refers to the distance reached by where one might tether oxen or horses, cut grass, or discard dung.
How can there be multiple areas of influence for many halls?
It is said that these various halls have many hall-owners, or brothers who are separate.
To what extent does their respective sphere of influence extend?
What is shared and what is distinct?
Answer:
This [space] has no *pradeśa* (circumferential extent).
How can a single chariot have one *pradeśa*?
This refers to a single chariot belonging to brothers who are co-owners and have not divided their property.

Its "sphere of influence" (sīmā) includes the entire area where the chariot is driven or parked, extending one fathom (vyāma) beyond that; it further includes the space used for eating and drinking, tethering oxen, cutting grass, and discarding dung.
How can a single chariot have multiple spheres of influence (*pradeśa*)?
It means that this one chariot has many owners, or is divided among brothers.
To what extent does its sphere of influence extend?
This refers to the level of the carriage yoke.
What is common and what is distinct?
The common part is the location of the front crossbar (the *śīrṣaka*).
What is meant by many chariots sharing a single *sīmā* (boundary)?
It refers to these various chariots having a single owner who is a brother with whom they have not divided their property.
This *sīmā* refers to the area traversed while the chariot is being driven.
What constitutes many vehicles having multiple spheres of influence (*sīmā*)?
It means that these various vehicles have multiple owners, or are divided among brothers.
To what extent does this sphere of influence extend?
What is common and what is distinct?
Answer:
This has no shared sphere of influence (*avasthāna*).
What is meant by "one boat having one common boundary"?
It refers to a single boat where there is one boat-owner whose brothers do not divide the property.

This common boundary includes everything within the space between the boat’s movement and its mooring, extending outward for one *vyāma* (fathom) on all sides—namely, the area where the boat is tied up and where food and drink are consumed.
How can a single boat have multiple spheres of influence (*sīmā*)?
It is said that this single boat has many owners, or is divided among brothers.
To what extent does its sphere of influence extend?
This refers to the boundary level with the edge of the boat.
How can many boats have a single sphere of influence (*sīmā*)?
It is when these various boats have a single owner whose brothers do not divide their property.
This "sphere of influence" refers to the movement and stationing of ships.
How can many ships have multiple spheres of influence?
It is because these various ships have multiple owners, or are divided among brothers.
To what extent does this constitute its sphere of influence?
What is shared and what is distinct?
Answer:
This [area] has no common boundary (*sīmā*).
How can a single grove have one common boundary?
It is said that within this grove there is a single owner, brothers who have not divided their property.
This area of influence refers to the entire interior of this grove, extending one fathom outward;
furthermore, it includes the place where they gather flowers and where they eat and drink.
How can a single grove have multiple spheres of influence (*sīmā*)?
It is said that this single grove has many owners, or is divided among brothers.
To what extent does its sphere of influence extend?
This refers to the extent of a well.
What is meant by a grove of many trees having a single boundary (sīmā)?
It means that these various groves have a single owner who is a brother whose property has not been partitioned.
This area of influence consists of the interior space in its entirety, extending one fathom outward, which is the range for gathering flowers.
How can many groves have multiple areas of influence?
It is because these various groves have multiple owners, or are divided among brothers.
To what extent does this constitute its sphere of influence?
What is shared and what is distinct?
This has no sphere of influence.
What is meant by "a single tree having one sphere of influence"?
It refers to the area reached where the branches and leaves overlap and are dense;
this includes the entire interior space, extending outward for one *vyāma* (fathom).

Furthermore, it is at the spot where the shadow of a tree falls at solar noon on the fifteenth day of the fifth month; or where flowers, leaves, and fruits fall when there is no wind; or where drops of water fall during rainfall.
How can a single tree have multiple spheres of influence (*sīmā*)?
This refers to a case where the branches and leaves are sparse and do not interlace.
To what extent does this sphere of influence extend?
What is shared and what is distinct?
It refers to that which is level with the roots of the trees.
How can many trees have a single *sīmā* (boundary zone)?
This refers to the entire area covered by the interlacing branches and leaves of these trees.
How can there be multiple *sīmā* (territorial boundaries) for many trees?
This refers to cases where these trees stand at some distance from one another so that their branches and leaves do not interlace.
To what extent does this constitute its boundary?
What is shared and what is distinct?

At that time, the Venerable Upāli addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One, Great Virtuous One!
When a bhikṣu is walking, standing, sitting, or lying down, to what extent does he remain within the sphere of influence of his robe?"
The Buddha said:

If one is standing, sitting, or lying down, it is within a single fathom;
if one is lying down between two boundaries, the range of influence (*sīmā*) extends as far as the corner of the robe does not leave the body.

The Training Rule on the One-Month Robe (Māsa-cīvara-śikṣāpada). The third [training rule]: The Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the bhikṣus accumulated many robes; some obtained blue cloth but did not immediately make it into a robe, instead merely keeping it in storage while hoping for more, thinking:
"If I obtain similar material like this, I shall then make a robe."
Just as it was with the blue robes, so too did they store yellow, red, and white ones, as well as those that were thick or thin.
At that time, the bhikṣus of few desires collectively felt disdain and reproached them, saying:
"How can a bhikṣu possess so many clothing materials, accumulating and storing them away rather than making robes?"
Then the bhikṣus reported this matter in detail to the Blessed One.
The Buddha questioned the bhikṣus about these circumstances in detail, and the bhikṣus replied,
“It is indeed so.”
The Blessed One rebuked them, and spoke at length as before:
"Observing ten benefits, I establish this training rule for my śrāvaka disciples within the Vinaya, as previously stated:

'If a bhikṣu has finished making his robes and the kaṭhina cloth has been removed, and he obtains an out-of-season robe, he may accept it if he needs it; having accepted it, he must quickly have it made into a robe.'"
If there is a source from which one expects [cloth] and seeks to fulfill that expectation, yet it remains insufficient, one may keep it for up to one month.
If this period is exceeded, it constitutes a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* offense.
Furthermore, if a bhikṣu’s robes are finished and the kaṭhina cloth has been removed, there are four cases, as explained in detail previously.
Regarding the phrase "obtaining out-of-season robes," what constitutes the season?
What is the improper time?
If the *kaṭhina* robe has not been spread at a residence, it is one month, namely from the sixteenth day of the eighth month to the fifteenth day of the ninth month;

if the *kaṭhina* robe has been spread at a residence, it is five months, namely from the sixteenth day of the eighth month to the fifteenth day of the first month. These are called the proper times; all others are called the improper times.
"Having a source of expectation" means that one has acquired only a small amount of clothing and seeks to obtain more.
"Keeping it for one month" refers to having such an expectation, thinking: "My parents, brothers, sisters, teachers, or preceptors will give me clothing."
If there is a five-year assembly, a six-year assembly, a *uṣṇīṣa* assembly, or a youth assembly, I shall obtain robes.
If they are sufficient, it is well; if even one of the three robes is insufficient, one may possess them for up to one month.
If one keeps [the item] beyond this limit, it is a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika*, as explained in detail previously.
Regarding the characteristics of the offense herein, what are its specific instances?
A summary verse says:
Regarding the expectation and non-expectation of obtaining cloth: when the expectation is severed, one does not wear the same garment;
the distinction between new and old *pāṃśukūla* (rag-robe) lies in the number of strips and the measurement in cubits.

Suppose a bhikṣu obtains a small piece of blue-colored cloth on the first day of the month and keeps it without yet having made a robe, while still maintaining the expectation that he might obtain more. If he then obtains cloth of the same color, [he thinks: "I shall make a robe."
If on that very day he obtains cloth of the same color,
that bhikṣu must, within ten days, either make it into a robe, keep it, relinquish it, or perform the formal ritual (karmavācanā).
If he does not keep it, relinquish it, or perform the ritual, when the dawn of the eleventh day appears, it constitutes a naiḥsargika-pāyattika offense.
If a bhikṣu does not obtain another robe on the first day, but obtains one on the second, third, or even up to the tenth day,
that bhikṣu must, within ten days, either have the robe made up, keep it, relinquish it, or perform the formal ritual (karmavācanā) regarding it.
If one neither retains, nor relinquishes, nor performs the formal ritual (karmavācanā) until the dawn of the eleventh day, it constitutes a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika*.

If a bhikṣu does not obtain another robe on the tenth day, nor on the eleventh, nor on the twelfth, and so on until he does not obtain a robe on the nineteenth day, but only obtains another robe on the twentieth day, he should perform the ritual as previously described; if he does not perform the ritual, he commits an offense of forfeiture and transgression (*naiḥsargika-pāyattika*).

If a bhikṣu does not obtain an extra robe until the twenty-first day, and subsequently obtains an extra robe on the twenty-ninth day, he must make the robe within the thirtieth day; it should be kept, or relinquished, or processed through the formal procedure of distribution.

If one neither retains, nor discards, nor makes a distinction [regarding the robe], and the dawn of the thirty-first day appears, it constitutes a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* offense, because the prior acquisition of the robe has continued through its stained continuity.
Just as it is with obtaining a blue garment, the same applies to obtaining garments of other colors.
Suppose a bhikṣu obtains a blue garment on a certain day; he does not make it into a robe but keeps it, having no expectation of obtaining another, and then thinks:
"If I obtain a garment of this same color, I shall make it into a robe."

If, on that very day, he obtains cloth of a similar kind, the bhikṣu should, within ten days, make it into a robe; he should either keep it, relinquish it, or perform the formal ritual of distribution (*vibhāga*).
If one does not perform the formal act, then when the dawn of the eleventh day appears, it constitutes a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika*.
If no other robe is obtained on the first day, but a robe is obtained on the second day, or even up until the thirtieth day a robe is obtained, the details are as extensively explained before.
Just as it is with obtaining a blue-colored robe, the same applies to obtaining robes of other colors and so forth.

If a bhikṣu obtains a blue-colored robe on a certain day and keeps it without making it into a garment because he has expectations of obtaining more, yet those expectations involve a long period of time, do not match his requirements, or he lacks the power to obtain them; or if he obtains a blue-colored robe on that day, he should make it into a garment within ten days.
Thus it is explained at length, up until the point where on the thirtieth day one finally obtains a robe of a different color; the circumstances are as previously described.

If a bhikṣu obtains a blue-colored robe on a certain day and keeps it without making it into a formal robe, yet there is a place from which he expects to obtain more, and although he has not yet received the expected robe, his intention to do so has not ceased; or if on that very day he obtains a blue-colored robe—the details are as extensively explained before.
If a bhikṣu obtains a blue-colored robe on a certain day and keeps it without processing it, yet harbors the expectation of obtaining more,
and if all sources of his hope are cut off, that bhikṣu must, within ten days, either keep the robe he has obtained or relinquish it, as explained in detail previously.
At that time, the Venerable Upāli addressed the Buddha, saying: "Bhadanta,
how many kinds of robes are there?"
The Buddha said:
"There are two kinds:
first, new; second, old."
"New" refers to what has been newly woven; "old" refers to that which has already been worn for four months.
Upāli! Furthermore, there are five kinds of robes:
1. Robes with a donor;
2. Robes without a donor;
3. Robes obtained through travel.
Fourth, the garment of the deceased;
fifth, the refuse-rag garment.
What is the "donor's garment"?
This refers to cases where women, men, or *paṇḍakas* act as their donors.
What is "robe without a donor"?
It refers to cases where there are no women, men, or *paṇḍakas* acting as their donors.
What is the "robe for going and returning"?
It is when, upon the death of someone, their relatives, out of grief and remembrance, present a robe as an offering, placing it upon the corpse and accompanying it to the cremation site.
Once the cremation and burial have been completed, one returns to offer these robes to the community of monks.
What are "clothes of the dead"?
They are the remaining garments of those who have died in the charnel grounds, which are not claimed or possessed by anyone.
What are the refuse-rag robes?
There are five kinds. What are the five?
1. Garments discarded on the road;
2. Garments from a refuse heap;
3. Garments discarded by a riverbank.
4. Robes worn by ants; 5. Tattered robes.
Furthermore, there are five other kinds:
1. Garments burnt by fire;
2. Garments soaked by water;
3. Garments gnawed by rats.
4. Cow-chewed robes;
5. Discarded robes by nurses.
"If a bhikṣu obtains a new robe and wishes to make a garment from it, he should wash, dye, cut, and sew it; [he may make] two layers for the saṃghāṭī and two layers for the niṣīdana."
One layer is for the *uttarāsaṅga* (upper robe), and one layer is for the *antarvāsa* (inner robe).
If a bhikṣu makes a *saṃghāṭī* (outer robe) of two layers and wishes to add a third layer, he incurs a *duṣkṛta* offense at the time of patching it;
when the dawn light appears on the eleventh day, he commits the *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* offense.
If a bhikṣu removes the old lining from a new saṃghāṭī with the intention of using it for another purpose, he incurs a duṣkṛta offense at the time of removal;
when the dawn of the eleventh day appears, he commits a naiḥsargika-pāyattika offense.
If a bhikṣu removes the lining of a new saṃghāṭī, washes, dyes, and sews it, and then wishes to reattach it, there is no offense;
however, if by the time the dawn of the eleventh day appears he has not finished reattaching it, he incurs a naiḥsargika-pāyattika.
Just as it is with the *saṃghāṭī*, the same applies to the *niṣīdana*.
If a bhikṣu has a new *uttarāsaṅga* with a second patch, at the time of patching he incurs a *duṣkṛta*; when the dawn of the eleventh day appears, he commits the offense of *naiḥsargika-pāyattika*.
The *antarvāsa* is also treated in the same manner.

If a bhikṣu obtains an old garment and wishes to make it into a robe, he should wash, dye, and sew it; four layers are made for the *saṃghāṭī*, four layers for the *niṣīdana*, and two layers for the *uttarāsaṅga* and the *antarvāsa*.
If a bhikṣu possesses two layers of an uttarāsaṅga and an antarvāsaka, and wishes to add a third layer, he incurs a duṣkṛta offense at the time of patching them;
when the dawn light appears on the eleventh day, he commits a naiḥsargika-pāyattika offense.

If a bhikṣu, regarding these heavy robes, wishes to remove a patch or to apply one—whether it be properly or improperly applied—the details concerning whether there is an offense or no offense are as explained extensively above.

If a bhikṣu obtains robes with an owner, robes without an owner, robes received through exchange, or the robes of a deceased person, he should understand that they are to be treated according to their newness or oldness and their number of layers.
"If it is a *pāṃśukūla* (rag-robe), one may, at will, stitch it together in layers as many times as desired, without limit.
At that time, the Venerable Upāli addressed the Buddha, saying: "Bhadanta!"
“How many types of saṃghāṭī robes are there,
and what is their number of strips?
The Buddha told Upāli:
“There are nine distinctions.
What are the nine? They are:
those with nine strips, eleven strips, thirteen strips, fifteen strips, seventeen strips, nineteen strips, twenty-one strips, twenty-three strips, and twenty-five strips.”
Upāli? Regarding the first three types of robes, there are two long pieces and one short piece.
Regarding the next three types of robes, there are three long pieces and one short piece.
"Next, regarding the three kinds of robes, they should have four lengths and one shortness.
They should be made and worn; beyond this measure, they become 'tattered rags' (pāṃśukūla).
Upāli addressed the Buddha, saying:
“Venerable Sir!
How many differences are there in the size of robes?
The Buddha said:
"There are three types of saṃghāṭī:
namely, superior, middling, and inferior.
The superior is three cubits in height and five cubits in width."
The smallest [robe] is two and a half cubits in length and four and a half cubits in width;
those within these two dimensions are called the medium.
As for the *uttarāsaṅga* and the *antarvāsaka*, they likewise have three types:
That is to say, there are superior, middling, and inferior [sizes], with measurements as explained for the saṃghāṭī.
Upāli, furthermore, there are two kinds of antarvāsas:
Two vertical and five horizontal;
two vertical and four horizontal.
If the *antarvāsa* is placed at the very bottom and covers only the three wheels, this is the smallest among the types of robes for wearing.
If the *naiḥsargika* robe is of the smallest size, it shall measure exactly one cubit in both length and width.
If a bhikṣu commits an offense involving forfeiture (*niḥsargika-pāyattika*), he should perform the three procedures as extensively described above.
Furthermore, there is no offense for the very first offender, or for one who is insane, mentally deranged, or overwhelmed by intense physical pain.

The Fourth Training Rule: On Causing a Non-Relative Nun to Wash Old Clothes. At that time, the Bodhisattva descended from Tuṣita Heaven and took birth in the house of King Śuddhodana in the city of Kapilavastu. At that moment, a great reputation spread in the four directions, saying: "A prince has been born into the Śākya clan."

On the slopes of the Snowy Mountains, by the side of the Salt River, at the dwelling place of the seer Kapila, there lived not far away a brahmin seer named Asita, who was skilled in the interpretation of signs and physiognomy.
The King summoned the observer, who reported two kinds of auspicious omens regarding the prophecy:

"If he remains a householder, he will become a Wheel-Turning King (*cakravartin*) who transforms the four continents, serving as a great and holy sovereign endowed with the seven treasures—namely, the wheel-treasure, the elephant-treasure, the horse-treasure, the jewel-treasure, the woman-treasure, the minister-treasure of the treasury, and the minister-treasure of the military. He will have a full thousand sons of great majesty, peerless in valor and strength, capable of subduing all enemies. Throughout this entire earth to the very limits of the four oceans, there will be no thieves nor cruel punishments; he shall govern the people according to the Dharma, and they shall dwell in peace and security."

If one leaves the household life, shaving off hair and beard with right faith, going forth from home to homelessness, one shall attain the state of a Buddha, an Arhat, a Samyaksaṃbuddha, whose fame shall spread throughout the ten directions as he extensively delivers all classes of beings.

At that time, the great kings of all nations heard that the Śākya Prince had been born in the Snowy Mountains and that his fame had spread throughout the ten directions as he extensively saved all beings; each of them thought:
"I should now go to serve the Prince, so that in the future I may receive his blessings and prosperity."
He further thought to himself:
"At present, I have no opportunity to see the Prince; however, if I serve King Śuddhodana, it will be as if I am serving the Prince's person."
At that time, all the kings dispatched envoys bearing state credentials to King Śuddhodana.

Later, while the Bodhisattva was being raised in the inner palace, he gradually grew older; having witnessed old age, sickness, and death, his heart became filled with distress, and he consequently departed for the forest to withdraw from worldly affairs.
When the various kings heard of these matters, they all thought to themselves:
"The reason we now serve King Śuddhodana is that we intend to serve the Crown Prince.
Now that the Prince has gone to the forest seeking liberation, what purpose is there for us to continue this service and merely waste our resources?"
Consequently, all communications from messengers and envoys from various kingdoms were completely severed.

At that time, King Prasenajit of Kośala and King Śuddhodana shared a border; although the exchange of official correspondence had ceased, messengers still traveled back and forth, and from time to time they dispatched envoys to inquire after one another. The envoy sent by [King Prasenajit] was a high minister of the state named Guptaka.
At that time, Guhyapāla went to King Śuddhodana; after discussing matters of state, he took up residence in the house of the minister Udāyin.
Whenever King Śuddhodana sent a messenger to inquire after King Prasenajit, he would dispatch the minister Udāyin to go.
At that time, Udāyin arrived at the city of Śrāvastī; having discussed matters of state with King Prasenajit, he took up residence in the house of Guptaka.
At that time, Guptaka had a wife named Gopā, who was of such exquisite beauty that all who beheld her were delighted. Then Udāyin committed an unrighteous act with Gopā.
At that time, having heard that his wife had entered into a secret intimacy with Udāyin, Guptaka thought to himself:
"I shall take the lives of these two wicked people."
Later, he reflected further:
"If I were to kill him, it would throw the royal city into turmoil and cause great alarm; how could I, for the sake of such a sinful woman, kill a brahmin?"
He then set it aside and did not inquire further.
Later, at another time, Guptika died; because King Prasenajit had no son, all of his wealth and property were collected into the royal treasury.
When Udāyin heard of this matter, he thought to himself:
"While I am still alive, how can I allow Guptā to be left without anyone to rely upon?"
He then contemplated matters of benefit and harm throughout the night, and at dawn went to King Śuddhodana and addressed him thus:

"Your Majesty, as the kingdoms of King Prasenajit and Your Majesty are adjacent, seeing such unstable circumstances, you ought to dispatch an envoy there to deliberate upon them; if you do not inquire, it will bring about disaster and ruin."
The King replied, "If that is the case,
you shall act as the envoy and go there to deliberate.
Thereupon, Udāyin immediately set out for Śrāvastī, thinking to himself:
"Should I see the Great King first,
or should I see the minister first?
Having formed this thought, he reflected once more:
"The principle for seeking what one desires begins from below.
He then went to the prime minister of the kingdom and presented his original intention, saying:
"I wish to inform my lord that I intend to take Guptā; I pray that you, out of benevolence, will assist me with your word."
Having heard this, the minister agreed to the proposal.
Thereupon, Udāyin went to King Prasenajit to discuss matters of state and addressed the king, saying:
"I pray that Your Majesty will grant me a place to stay."
The king asked,
"Where have you been staying since you last came?
He replied:
"I previously stayed at the house of Guhyaka.
The king said,
"Now you should likewise stay there."
He then addressed the king,
saying, "Gupta has died.
The king said:
"Householder, though he has died, does the house die as well? Udāyin replied,
"Though the house does not die, all its property and wealth are gone."
The king commanded his ministers, saying,
"Find a place where Udāyin may stay.
After Udāyin had departed, the ministers addressed the king, saying:
"How could it be that Udāyin has no other place to stay?

However, he previously had an illicit liaison with Gopā; his original intention was to report this matter. If Your Majesty can now take this man under your protection, you will effectively be taking King Śuddhodana under your protection as well."
At that time, King Prasenajit immediately dispatched a messenger to summon Udāyin, and addressed him, saying: "Udāyin!
I truly did not know of your prior intimate relationship with Gupta. I now grant Gupta to you as a wife, and I shall provide you with both her residence and her wealth."
Then Udāyin bowed in thanks and departed. At that time, when Gopā heard that Udāyin had come to her house, she immediately went out to the door and wept aloud.
When Udāyin arrived at the door, he asked Gopā,
"For what reason are you weeping? Gopā replied:
"My beloved husband has passed away; would you, O Benevolent One, now likewise abandon me?
Udāyin replied, "I came here originally for your sake and have already informed the King."
"I shall give you everything, including my family and possessions;
will you stay here for this reason, or will you go toward the city of Kapilavastu?
Guptā thought to herself:
"If I were to go to Kapilavastu now, the Brahmin’s wife would not spare my life; it is therefore fitting that I remain here in my own home."
At that time, Udāyin came to possess two residences:
one in Kapilavastu and one in Śrāvastī.

Then, after the Bodhisattva had practiced asceticism for six years without possessing anything, he subsequently desired to enjoy excellent food and drink according to his wish; he immediately smeared his body all over with rice, food, and various ghee and oils, bathed with warm water, and then proceeded to the two cowherd girls in the village of Saṃjaya.

One was named Nandika and the other was named Nandibala; having partaken of sixteen times the usual amount of milk-rice until they were fully satiated, they went again to the man Sudhāna to take the auspicious kusa grass.

At that time, the Naga King Kāla praised the Bodhisattva; he then spread grass with his own hands beneath the Bodhi tree so that it was not disordered, sat down cross-legged, straightened his body and composed his mind, and said with his mouth what he intended in his heart:
"If my various outflows are not yet completely exhausted, I shall never break this cross-legged posture."
At that time, while the Bodhisattva had not yet broken his cross-legged posture, all delusions were utterly exhausted.

Then, having subdued an army of thirty-six billion māras and realized all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*), the World-Honored One accepted the invitation of the Brahma King and proceeded to Vārāṇasī, where he turned the Wheel of Dharma with its twelve aspects in three cycles and delivered the five bhikṣus.
Having followed the five bhikṣus, he then proceeded to the Śāṇa Forest, where he delivered the sixty members of the Bhadravarga and established them in the vision of the Truths (satyadarśana).
He further went to the village of Aṭṭhakanāgara, where he delivered two cowherd girls and likewise established them in the vision of the Truths.
Furthermore, he went to the vicinity of the Uruvilvā forest, where he ordained a thousand non-Buddhist practitioners as monks and conferred full ordination upon them.
He then proceeded to the summit of Mount Gayā, where he manifested the three miraculous transformations to teach and transform them, leading them to abide in the peace and security of nirvana.

Furthermore, arriving at the Śāla Grove, he caused King Bimbisāra, the ruler of Magadha, to abide in the vision of the Truths, and he delivered eighty hundred thousand devas who had gathered there, as well as immeasurable hundreds of thousands of brahmins from the kingdom of Magadha.
Next, he arrived at Rājagṛha and accepted the Bamboo Grove Monastery; there, he also ordained Śāriputra and Maudgalyāyana, granting them full ordination.

Next, he went to Śrāvastī and accepted the Jeta Grove and Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park. Then, having traveled to Kośala and preached the *Kumāraputra-sūtra*, he caused King Prasenajit to attain the vision of the Truths, after which he resided in the Jeta Grove.
At that time, King Prasenajit dispatched a messenger bearing a letter to King Śuddhodana, saying:
"Great King! You should now rejoice;
the Prince has already realized unsurpassed perfect enlightenment and is causing sentient beings to partake together in the nectar of immortality. He currently resides within the Jeta Grove."
When King Śuddhodana heard this message, he rested his cheek in his hand and sighed in sorrow:
"In the past, when Prince Sarvārthasiddha was practicing austerities, I constantly sent messengers to inquire after his well-being."
The messenger returned shortly after to report my location;
yet, despite my sending messengers to inquire, not a single one has ever returned.
Now you say he has come within the Jeta Grove—what is the matter?
Then the minister Udāyin approached the king and said to him:
"Great King, for what reason do you sit with your cheek propped in your hand, dwelling in sorrow?"
The king said,
"How could I not harbor sorrow now? In the past,
when Prince Sarvārthasiddha was practicing austerities, I constantly dispatched messengers to inquire after his well-being."
The messenger has now returned to report my dwelling place;
yet while I was sending messengers to inquire after you, not a single one has returned.
Now there is news that says:
"Prince Sarvārthasiddha has realized unsurpassed perfect enlightenment and is bringing all sentient beings to partake of the nectar of immortality; he is coming to the Jeta Grove.
How could you not be filled with anxiety?
Then Udāyin said to the king:
"If it is so, I shall go as an envoy, carry the message, and return.
The king said:
"Since you are now departing, will you stay there and not return? Udāyin replied,
"Having received the Great King’s command, your servant shall certainly return."
At that time, King Śuddhodana composed a letter himself, saying:
"From the very moment of conception, I have nurtured the World-Honored One;
The fire of afflictions has constantly burned me, And I have always longed for the most excellent tree."
"Now that he has reached full maturity, his followers are beyond counting;
while others enjoy peace and happiness, I alone endure hardship.
Having finished writing and sealing this letter, he gave it to Udāyin.
Then Udāyin, carrying the king’s letter, went to Śrāvastī and arrived at the place where the World-Honored One was, presenting the letter to him.
The World-Honored One accepted the letter and read it himself. At that time, Udāyin addressed the World-Honored One, saying:
“World-Honored One!”
"Can you go toward the city of Kapilavastu?
The Buddha said to Udāyin,
"I shall go with you."

At that time, Udāyin recalled how in the past the Prince had left the city to renounce the world, and despite his father the King’s repeated summons, he ultimately did not return to the kingdom. He addressed the Buddha again, saying:
"If the World-Honored One is truly unwilling to return, I now possess the power to take him back by force."
At that time, having heard these words, the World-Honored One immediately spoke a verse in reply to Udāyin:
“If the net of craving for birth and death were entirely removed, There would truly be no one left to lead;
The power of the World-Honored One has no fixed location— By what means could you possibly carry him away?”
If the net of craving for birth and death were entirely removed, there would truly be no one to lead;
the realm of the World-Honored One is without location—by what means could you possibly carry it away?
The Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya, Volume Seventeen; The Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya,
Volume Eighteen.

The Fourth Section, Part Two of the Training Rule on Having a Non-Relative Nun Wash One’s Used Clothes, translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Yijing by Imperial Decree. At that time, having heard the verses spoken by the Buddha, the World-Honored One, Udāyin prostrated at the Buddha’s feet and said to the Buddha:
“World-Honored One!”
"I wish to return to the palace to inform my father, the King.
The Buddha told Udāyin:
"For one who acts as a messenger for the Buddha, such conduct is not appropriate."
Udāyin said to the Buddha,
"What are the duties of one who acts as the Buddha’s messenger?
The Buddha told Udāyin:
"Only those who have left the household life are truly the messengers of the Buddha.
Udāyin said, "I wish to leave the household life;
however, as there is a matter of a solemn agreement that must be reported back to King Śuddhodana, I shall depart for now."
The Buddha said,
"Once he has gone forth into homelessness,
you shall then fulfill your previous promise. Udāyin said:
"Excellent! I shall now go forth into homelessness.

However, when the World-Honored One was a bodhisattva, in every lifetime he never disobeyed the lawful instructions and commands of his two teachers, his parents, or those worthy of respect; for this reason, it is said that he was one who never opposed.
Then Udāyin said to the Buddha,
“I shall now go forth.
The Buddha addressed Śāriputra:
"You should grant Udāyin the going forth, so that he may obtain lasting benefit for a long night.
Śāriputra said, "So be it."
The Blessed One then granted him the going forth and the full ordination, briefly informing him of all the rules of conduct.
Having received these instructions, Udāyin paid homage to Śāriputra and then went to the place where the Blessed One was; prostrating at the Buddha’s feet, he addressed the Buddha, saying:
“Blessed One!”
"I have already left the household life.
The Buddha said, "You may go now; however, do not enter the royal palace in haste. You should go to its gate, stand there, and announce:”
"Śākyabhikṣu has now arrived outside the door.
If he is summoned to enter, one should follow him inside. If he asks:
"Are there any other Śākya bhikṣus besides these?
He replied, "There are more."
If asked, "Does Prince Sarvārthasiddha also have such a physical appearance?
one should answer:
"Make it in this shape as well.
You also must not stay overnight within the royal palace.
If you are asked:
"Did Prince Sarvārthasiddha spend the night in the royal palace?
He replied, "He did not."
He asked, "Where do you stay?
He replied:
"Whether it be an araṇya or a vihāra," if one asks,
"Will Prince Sarvārthasiddha come here?"
He replied,
"I wish to come.
If [the other] says:
"When do you wish to come?
He replied,
"I shall arrive here only after seven days have passed."
Then Udāyin prostrated before the Buddha and departed.

At that time, the World-Honored One bestowed his supernatural power upon him, so that in the time it takes to stretch out one’s arm, Udāyin arrived at the city of Kapilavastu and stood outside the royal gate, saying to the gatekeeper:
"Announce me to the King."
"Śākyabhikṣu is now outside the gate.
The gatekeeper asked,
"Are there any other Śākyabhikṣus besides him?"
He replied, "There is more.
The gatekeeper immediately entered and informed the king, saying:
“Great King!
Śākyabhikṣu has arrived outside the gate; may he be permitted to enter?
The king said:
"Call him in!
Let me observe what the Śākya bhikṣu looks like.
The gatekeeper led him in, and once he had reached the king's presence, the king recognized his features and asked:
“Udāyin! Have you now gone forth?
He replied:
“I have already left the household life.
The king then asked,
“Does Prince Sarvārthasiddha also have such an appearance?”
He replied, “Great King,
it is exactly like this.”

At that time, King Śuddhodana, whose affection had been heavy with weight since beginningless kalpas, fainted upon hearing these words and threw himself prostrate on the ground. After being sprinkled with cold water for a long while, he regained consciousness;
rising from the ground, he asked Udāyin, "Does Prince Sarvārthasiddha wish to come here?"
He replied,
"I wish to come.
[The other asked,] "When do you wish to come?"
“Only after seven days have passed will he come here.
At that time, the king immediately commanded his ministers, saying:

“The Crown Prince Sarvārthasiddha intends to return to his former residence after seven days have passed. You should all repair the city walls and moats and adorn the roads; you must also command the women of the inner palace to sweep and clean. The Crown Prince wishes to come.”
Udāyin said, “The World-Honored One does not dwell in royal palaces or within the inner quarters.
The King asked:
"Where do you reside?
He replied,
"Either in an araṇya or in a vihāra."
The King said to his ministers:
"Go to the Aranyaka region, to the Kuruṭa Grove, and together with those at the Jeta Grove, construct a residence consisting of sixteen large courtyards, each courtyard containing sixty rooms."

At that time, having received the king’s command, the ministers went to the Kuruḍa Grove in the araṇya and constructed sixteen great courtyards, each containing sixty chambers, just like those at the Jetavana.

However, by the King’s command, everything was accomplished as soon as the word was spoken; through the focused minds and deeds of the most excellent devas and humans, and by the power of meditative concentration and intentionality, all things were realized. Within this city, the streets, lanes, and alleys were cleared of all impurities and sprinkled everywhere with sandalwood-scented water. In every place there were exquisite fragrant offerings, with various silken banners and streamers suspended and victory standards erected. The arrangement of incense and flowers was so truly delightful that it resembled the Nandana Garden of Śakra.
At that time, the great assembly, each harboring deep longing and veneration, gazed toward the World-Honored One and remained there with expectant thoughts.
Then, while the World-Honored One was at Jetavana, he addressed Mahāmaudgalyāyana, saying:
"You should now go and inform the bhikṣus:"
"The Tathāgata wishes to go toward the city of Kapilavastu.
If any of you, Venerable Ones, desire to see the meeting of father and son, you should take up your robes and bowls.
Then, having received the Buddha's instruction, Mahāmaudgalyāyana addressed the bhikṣus:
"Venerable friends!
The Blessed One intends to go toward the city of Kapilavastu.
Venerable friends!"
"Those who desire to see their fathers and sons meet shall take up their robes and bowls and follow the World-Honored One.
When the bhikṣus had received this instruction, they all came to follow the Buddha.
At that time, the World-Honored One—being himself tamed, was surrounded by those who were tamed; being himself serene, was surrounded by those who were serene;
liberated, was surrounded by those who were liberated; secure, was surrounded by those who were secure; well-disciplined, was surrounded by those who were well-disciplined;
free from desire, was surrounded by those who were free from desire; an Arhat, was surrounded by Arhats; and upright...
He was surrounded by a majestic and dignified retinue, like a sandalwood tree surrounded by sandalwood trees;
like a king of elephants surrounded by elephant calves; like a lion king surrounded by lions; like a great bull king surrounded by cattle;
like a king of geese surrounded by geese; and like a king of garuḍas surrounded by garuḍas.
Like a Brahmin surrounded by his disciples, like a great physician surrounded by patients,
like a great general surrounded by his army, like a guide surrounded by travelers,
like a merchant leader surrounded by merchants and traders, like a great householder surrounded by a multitude of people, like a king of nations...
He was surrounded by his ministers, like the bright moon surrounded by the multitude of stars; like the solar disc surrounded by a thousand rays of light;
like the Heavenly King Dhṛtarāṣṭra surrounded by gandharvas; like the Heavenly King Virūḍhaka surrounded by kumbhāṇḍas;
like the Heavenly King Virūpākṣa surrounded by hosts of nāgas; and like the Heavenly King Vaiśravaṇa surrounded by yakṣas.
He was surrounded by a host of yakṣas, like King Vemacitrin surrounded by his asura hosts,
like Śakra surrounded by the gods of the Thirty-three Heavens, like Brahmā the Great King surrounded by the Brahma-hosts;
he stood as serene as the great ocean, like a massive cloud hanging low and spreading forth, and like a lordly elephant with its breath stilled.
Free from intoxication and madness, his faculties were subdued and his deportment was serene; he was adorned with the thirty-two marks and embellished by the eighty minor characteristics.

A halo one fathom wide shone more brightly than a thousand suns, and he proceeded with a steady gait like a moving mountain of jewels, endowed with the ten powers, the four fearlessnesses, great compassion, and the three mindfulnesses.
Dwelling there, they had all fully perfected immeasurable merits.
The great śrāvakas— Venerable Ājñātakauṇḍinya,

Venerable Mahānāman, Venerable Vāṣpa, Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana, Venerable Aniruddha, Venerable Śāriputra, Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana, Venerable Kāśyapa, Venerable Yaśas, Venerable Pūrṇa, and others— along with the other great śrāvakas and the rest of the assembly, proceeded toward Kapilavastu, traveling by stages until they reached the Rohiṇī River.
At that time, some of the bhikṣus were washing their hands and feet, some were chewing tooth-sticks, some were filtering pure water, and others were bathing.

At that moment, all the people of the city of Kapilavastu, hearing that Prince Sarvārthasiddha was now about to arrive, were filled with great joy and rushed together in competition toward the Nyagrodha Grove.

At that time, King Śuddhodana prepared seats upon a spacious area to await the Prince. Then, an immeasurable multitude of hundreds of thousands gathered like clouds; some were mutually awakened by their roots of virtue from previous lives, while others gave rise to joy and happiness, thinking thus:
"Should the father pay homage to the son?"
"Is he bowing to his father?
At that time, the Buddha, the World-Honored One, thought to himself:
"If I were to enter the city on foot, the Śākyas would each give rise to arrogance and collectively harbor disbelief, making such remarks as:"

"The Prince Sarvārthasiddha has suffered a great loss; when he departed in the past, hundreds of thousands of celestial beings followed him through the air as he circumambulated the city of Kapilavastu on his way out."
"Having now attained the unsurpassed, wondrous wisdom, I shall instead return on foot.
Desiring to cause all people to cease their attitude of contempt, I should now enter the city of Kapilavastu by means of a supernatural transformation.

At that time, the World-Honored One entered *samādhi* according to his mental intention; having entered meditative absorption, he vanished from his seat and, together with the bhikṣus, leaped into the air. Like the full moon surrounded by its retinue, or like a king of geese spreading its wings, he extensively manifested miraculous transformations throughout the four modes of deportment: walking, standing, sitting, and reclining.

At that time, the World-Honored One first entered the fire-light samādhi in the eastern direction, manifesting various flames of blue, yellow, red, white, crimson, and crystal colors; or he manifested supernatural powers, with water flowing from his upper body and fire from his lower body, or fire flowing from his upper body and water from his lower body.
Just as it was in the eastern direction, so it was likewise in the southern, western, and northern directions.
Next, he withdrew his supernormal powers and stood in mid-air at a height of seven *tāla* trees.

At that time, the bhikṣus were six *śākhā* trees in height; the World-Honored One was six, and the bhikṣus were five. When the Buddha was five, the assembly of five was four; when the Buddha was four, the assembly of four was three; when the Buddha was three, the assembly of three was two; and when the Buddha was two, the assembly of two was one.

When the Buddha’s retinue consists of one person, it is equal to six persons; when the Buddha’s retinue consists of six persons, it is equal to five; when the Buddha’s retinue consists of five persons, it is equal to four; when the Buddha’s retinue consists of four persons, it is equal to three; when the Buddha’s retinue consists of three persons, it is equal to two; when the Buddha’s retinue consists of two persons, it is equal to one; and when the Buddha’s retinue consists of only one person, he stands alone upon the ground.

The World-Honored One rose above the ground by the height of one man and traveled through the air, surrounded by a vast assembly of hundreds of thousands of koṭis of humans and devas, until he reached the city of Kapilavastu.
When King Śuddhodana had seen the Buddha, he prostrated with his head at the Buddha’s feet and spoke this verse:
“When the Buddha was first born, the great earth shook, And the shadow of the Jambu tree did not leave his body;
Now for the third time I pay homage to the One of Perfect Wisdom, Who has subdued the hosts of Māra and attained Perfect Enlightenment.”
At that time, the Śākyas and the rest of the great assembly, seeing King Śuddhodana prostrate at the Buddha’s feet, were overcome with indignation and cried out together:
"How can a venerable father prostrate at the feet of his son?"
Then King Śuddhodana addressed the Śākyas, saying:

"You should not speak such words. On the day the Bodhisattva was first born, the great earth shook and a great radiance was emitted, illuminating the world everywhere with a brilliance surpassing that of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven—even reaching those dark regions between worlds where the majestic light of the sun and moon does not reach."
At that time, they were all bathed in radiance; having been illuminated, the sentient beings who had long resided there were able to see one another and spoke these words together:
"Venerable beings, you too dwell in this place."
At that time, having witnessed this rare occurrence, I prostrated at the Buddha’s feet.

Furthermore, when the Bodhisattva once went to the fields to inspect his agricultural holdings, he sat cross-legged in the shade of a Jambu tree; free from sensual desires and unwholesome states, with directed thought and sustained evaluation, he attained the concentration of joy and bliss, entering the first dhyāna.

The sun had already passed the meridian, and while the shadows of all the other trees hung entirely toward the east, only the shadow of the Jambū tree remained stationary, shading the Bodhisattva’s body.
At that time, having witnessed this rare occurrence, I again prostrated at the Buddha’s feet.
"This is the third time he prostrates at the feet of the World-Honored One.
At that time, the World-Honored One sat down upon his seat amidst the assembly of bhikṣus and the great multitude.
Then King Śuddhodana again prostrated at the Buddha’s feet and sat to one side; this was the fourth time he prostrated at the feet of the World-Honored One.
At that time, the Śākyas prepared excellent seats and superior offerings in a most exquisite location within the Kuluṭa Grove to await the World-Honored One and the assembly of bhikṣus.
At that time, the World-Honored One proceeded to that grove and took his seat among the great assembly.

Then King Śuddhodana, having presented various kinds of exquisite and supreme offerings, the finest in the world, to the Buddha and the Saṃgha, sat to one side together with King Śuklodana, King Droṇodana, King Amṛtodana, and the rest of the hundreds of thousands of people who had gathered. Some individuals merely joined their palms in reverence; others sat silently, gazing afar at the World-Honored One.
Then King Śuddhodana addressed the Buddha with these verses:
"When the Buddha was formerly in the royal palace, He went out riding upon elephants, horses, and carriages;
How is it that now, with his two feet alone, He wanders amidst thorns and brambles?"
The World-Honored One replied:
"By means of my supernormal power of psychic travel, I move freely through the air;
I traverse the entire great earth, yet the thorns of affliction cannot wound me."
The King asked again:
"In the past, you wore garments of the finest quality, and your countenance was full of radiance;
now you wear coarse and tattered clothes—how can you endure this?"
The World-Honored One replied:
"Shame and modesty are the supreme garments; wearing them, one is most dignified and majestic.
Those who see one give rise to joy, as one dwells in tranquility within the forest wilds."
The King asked again:
"In the past, you ate fragrant rice served in exquisite golden plates;
now you beg for coarse and sparse food—how do you manage to sustain yourself?"
The World-Honored One replied:
"I partake of the subtle and wondrous Dharma; its flavor accords with meditative concentration.
Having eliminated craving for food and drink, I accept this out of compassion for sentient beings."
The King asked again:
"In the past, you ascended the sublime palace towers and dwelt in peace according to the seasons;
now that you are among the mountain forests, why are you not struck with fear?"
The World-Honored One replied:
“I have severed the root of fear; all afflictions have been completely eliminated.
Though dwelling in the midst of forests and wilds, I am forever free from all anxiety and dread.”
The King asked again:
"Formerly, while within the royal palace, you bathed with fragrant waters;
now that you dwell amidst the forests and wilds, O Muni, with what do you bathe?"
The World-Honored One replied:
“The Dharma-pool is a ford of merit, pure and praised by those who know;
the wise bathe therein, removing defilement without being stained.”
The King asked again:
"Formerly, when you were in the royal palace, you bathed with water poured from golden jars;
now that you are by the rivers and ponds, what vessel do you use to pour water over your body?"
The World-Honored One replied:
"I bathe in the water of pure precepts, Poured forth by the vessel of the sublime Dharma;
Wise ones together admire and praise it, For it can cleanse the defilements of body and mind."

At that time, having answered King Śuddhodana with these sublime verses, the World-Honored One then observed the inclinations, latent tendencies, and the distinctions of the elements within the great assembly, and preached the Dharma in accordance with their respective faculties.

Those who heard the Dharma were King Śuklodana, King Droṇodana, King Amṛtodana, and the rest of the hundreds of thousands of the great assembly who had gathered; together they heard the sublime Dharma and attained the fruit of stream-entry (*srotāpanna*), or the fruit of once-returning (*sakṛdāgāmin*), or the fruit of non-returning (*anāgāmin*). Some left the household life, severed all afflictions, and realized the fruit of arhatship; some gave rise to the mind of solitary enlightenment (*pratyekabuddha-bodhicitta*); and some generated the mind of unsurpassed enlightenment (*anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi-citta*). Furthermore, all the remaining members of the assembly were led to take refuge in the Triple Gem and abide in right faith.

At that time, because King Śuddhodana was so overcome with extreme joy, he had not yet attained the vision of the Truths; having prostrated at the Buddha’s feet along with the great assembly, King Śuddhodana departed with reverence.
During the night, King Śuddhodana thought to himself:
"My only son possesses such majestic virtue that none others can equal him.

At that time, the World-Honored One, knowing the thoughts in King Śuddhodana’s mind and wishing to subdue the pride of his own royal lineage, waited until dawn and then addressed Mahāmaudgalyāyana, saying:
"You should observe and take pity upon your father, the King.
Maudgalyāyana replied to the Buddha, "So be it."
"World-Honored One!
Having thus taken up his robes and bowl, he went to King Śuddhodana’s residence.
When the king saw that Maudgalyāyana had arrived, he exclaimed, "Welcome," and bade him take a seat.
At that time, Maudgalyāyana entered *samādhi* according to his thought; having entered meditative absorption, he vanished from his seat and manifested in mid-air.

Then, the Great Maudgalyāyana first entered the fire-light *samādhi* in the eastern direction, manifesting various flames—blue, yellow, red, white, crimson, and the color of crystal. He further displayed supernatural powers, emitting water from the upper part of his body and fire from the lower part, or emitting fire from the upper part of his body and water from the lower part.
Just as it was in the eastern direction, so it was likewise in the south, west, and north.
He then withdrew his supernormal powers and reappeared at his original seat.
At that time, King Śuddhodana said to Mahāmaudgalyāyana:
“Does the Blessed One have any other disciples of such great majesty as this Venerable One?
At that time, Mahāmaudgalyāyana spoke these verses for the sake of the King, his father:
“The noble disciples of the Muni All possess great majesty.”
"In the three knowledges and the six supernormal powers, there is none who is not fully endowed with them.
At that time, King Śuddhodana thought to himself:
"It is not only my son who possesses great majestic power; there are other bhikṣus as well who possess such great supernormal powers."
The pride that had previously arisen was immediately severed.
At that time, King Śuddhodana again thought to himself:
"Now the World-Honored One accepts offerings only from humans; I do not see the devas."
At that time, Mahāmaudgalyāyana, knowing the king’s thoughts, addressed him, saying:
“Great King!
I now wish to return to the presence of the World-Honored One.”
He replied, "As you wish.
At that time, King Śuddhodana also went to where the Buddha was.
At that time, the World-Honored One, knowing the thoughts of his father, the King, immediately transformed the entire Kūṭāgāra forest into crystal (*sphaṭika*).
When King Śuddhodana wished to enter through the eastern gate, the gatekeeper reported,
"Great King, do not enter."
The king asked,
"What is the meaning of this?
The gatekeeper replied:
"The Buddha is now preaching the Dharma exclusively for the devas.
The king asked his gatekeeper:
"Worthy sir!"
"Who are you? The gatekeeper replied,
"Great King!"
"I am Dhṛtarāṣṭra, the Heavenly King of the East.
At that time, King Śuddhodana went toward the southern gate, wishing to see the World-Honored One; the gatekeeper addressed him, saying, "Great King, do not enter."
The king asked,
"What is the meaning of this?
The gatekeeper replied:
"The Buddha is now preaching the Dharma exclusively for the devas.
The king asked his gatekeeper:
"Worthy sir!..."
"Who are you? He replied, "I am Virūḍhaka,
the Heavenly King of the South."
Then King Śuddhodana went toward the western gate wishing to see the World-Honored One, but the gatekeeper said to him,
"Great King, do not enter.
The king asked:
"What is the reason?
The gatekeeper replied,
"The Buddha is currently preaching the Dharma exclusively for the sake of the devas."
The king asked the gatekeeper,
"Worthy sir! Who are you?"
The gatekeeper replied,
"I am the Heavenly King Ugly-Eyed from the West.
Then King Śuddhodana went toward the northern gate, wishing to see the World-Honored One, and the gatekeeper addressed him, saying:
“Great King, do not enter.
The King asked,
“For what reason?”
The gatekeeper replied,
"The Buddha is currently preaching the Dharma exclusively for the devas.
The king asked the gatekeeper:
“O noble one! Who are you?
The gatekeeper replied:
"I am Vaiśravaṇa, the Heavenly King of the North.

At that time, the World-Honored One, through his supernormal power, empowered King Śuddhodana so that from outside the gate he could see the Buddha, the World-Honored One, preaching the subtle and wondrous Dharma to the assembly of devas.
At that time, having witnessed this event, King Śuddhodana thought to himself:
"Now the Buddha, the World-Honored One, is not only being venerated by the multitude of people, but is also being personally served by the various devas who have come here."
Once King Śuddhodana’s pride had been quelled, [the Buddha] withdrew his supernormal powers.
Then, Mahāmaudgalyāyana led King Śuddhodana in to see the World-Honored One; having arrived at the Buddha’s presence and prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, he sat to one side.

At that time, the World-Honored One, in accordance with the inclinations, latent tendencies, and dispositions of King Śuddhodana and the other members of the assembly, taught the Dharma according to their respective faculties and capacities, causing King Śuddhodana to shatter the high mountain of the twenty types of *satkāyadṛṣṭi* (view of a self-identity) with the vajra-thunderbolt of wisdom and attain the fruit of a stream-enterer (*srotāpanna*).
Having realized the fruit, he addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!

That which I have now realized was not created by my ancestors, nor was it created by my parents; it was not created by kings, nor by devas, nor by śramaṇas or brāhmaṇas, nor could it have been created by any of my kinsmen."

It is solely by relying on the World-Honored One as my spiritual friend that I have now attained this state. From the three evil realms of hell, animals, and hungry ghosts, I have been rescued and established among humans and devas; I shall reach the ultimate limit of birth and death throughout the future, dry up the vast oceans of blood and tears, and cross over the great mountain of white bones. All those views of a self-identity (satkāyadṛṣṭi) accumulated since beginningless time—the dwelling place of such views—have now been entirely abandoned, and I have realized this wondrous fruit.
"Venerable One!
I have now emerged from the stream of birth and death; I now take refuge in the Triple Gem of the Buddha, Dharma, and Saṅgha as an upāsaka.

May the World-Honored One, out of compassion, deign to witness this: from this day forth until the end of my life, I shall not take the lives of sentient beings, nor shall I drink any wine, and I shall reverently accept the training rules prescribed by the World-Honored One."
Then King Śuddhodana paid homage to the Buddha and departed, proceeding to King Śuklodana and saying to him,
"The Prince may now accept the royal throne. He replied:
"What is your intention?
the king asked.
He replied, "Now that I have seen the Truth, I am unable to serve as king."
He asked, "On what day?
and he replied:
"Today," he replied,
"on the very day the Blessed One first arrived, at that moment I attained the vision of the Truth."
Next he went to King Droṇodana, and afterwards to King Amṛtodana, hoping they would accept the royal throne;
but both replied, "We have already realized the Truth."
King Śuddhodana said, "If this is so,
whom do I now wish to anoint on the crown of the head to receive the royal throne?
He then replied:
"The Śākya youth named Bhadrika shall be enthroned as king! Thereupon,
King Śuddhodana immediately performed the consecration and bestowed the royal throne upon Bhadrika.
At that time, the World-Honored One and the community of bhikṣus entered the royal palace day after day to receive his offerings.
Then King Śuddhodana thought to himself:

"Now these thousand followers of external paths who are disciples of the Buddha, though their minds are upright, their bodies are not well-proportioned; due to their former asceticism, their appearances are emaciated and haggard."
"How may we cause the disciples of the World-Honored One to possess such a pleasing appearance that their very sight gives rise to wholesome thoughts?
Only if the Śākyas accompany the World-Honored One will they be truly dignified and majestic, and thus be universally respected."
At that time, King Śuddhodana assembled the Śākyas and addressed them, saying:
"Gentlemen, you should know: if Prince Sarvārthasiddha had not gone forth from home, what would he have become?"
They all replied,
“He will become a wheel-turning monarch.
He asked again:
"What are you doing? they asked.
They replied, "We have declared ourselves subjects and serve as attendants."
The King spoke again, saying:
"Now that Prince Sarvārthasiddha has realized the Dharma of Ambrosia (amṛta), he shall likewise cause all sentient beings to partake of this flavor.
For what reason do you not follow him?"
They all replied,
"We have now gone forth into homelessness.
The king said:
"Go each according to your own wish.
The Śākyas said:
"Shall we all go together as a family?"
"Is it one person from each household?
The King replied,
"One person from each household."

At that time, King Śuddhodana immediately struck the bell and issued a proclamation to all the Śākyas, declaring that one person from each household must leave the home life to serve the Buddha; those who refused would surely incur blame and punishment.
At that very time, five hundred Śākyas among the Śākya clan, including Bhadrika and Aniruddha, all went forth as monastics.
As the Blessed One had said, those who renounce their noble lineage to go forth as monastics will generally receive much gain and support.
At that time, the five hundred Śākya bhikṣus were receiving an abundance of offerings and gains. Then the World-Honored One thought to himself:
"These Śākyas originally left the home life seeking liberation; now, however, they have abandoned fewness of desires and become attached to wealth and profit."
