The Blessed One, wishing to sever [the monk's] gain and offerings, immediately returned to Śrāvastī and resided as before in the Jeta Grove.

Then, during the first part of the day, the Venerable Udāyin took up his robes and bowl and entered Śrāvastī for alms in regular order, eventually arriving at the house of the former courtesan Guptā and standing at her door.

At that time, Gopā saw Udāyin approaching from afar; observing his appearance and features, she knew him to be her former husband, and she immediately struck her chest with her hand and said to him: "Udāyin!..."
"Noble sir, with what intention do you now abandon me to go forth into the homeless life?
Udāyin replied, "O fair lady!"

"When I, the World-Honored One, was a bodhisattva, I renounced sixty thousand court ladies—including the precious lady Yaśodharā (also known as Yecheng or Jucheng), Gopikā (also known as Mihu), and Mṛgajā (also known as Lüzizi)—and left the household life. Who could possibly sink into the mire with you, whose face is covered in dust and grime?"
Guptā replied, "Udāyin! If that is so, I too shall go forth."
He replied, “Excellent!
Guptā then said in response:
"I shall now settle my household affairs and immediately go forth into the religious life.
Udāyin said, "You should do so quickly; do not delay."
He then departed, leaving her behind.
However, Udāyin went to visit and inquire after her from time to time, saying to Gopā:
"You have not yet left the household life."
He replied, "My household affairs have not yet been concluded. Udāyin said:
"Must you wait until the Kingdom of Kośala has been reduced to ashes before your household affairs can be settled?
Gopā replied, "I shall gather my belongings this very day and go forth as a renunciant tomorrow."
Then Udāyin thought to himself:

"Even now, due to my past worldly ties, I am still held in contempt by my fellow practitioners who carry black alms-bowls; how much more so would it invite ridicule if I were to cause them to go forth, leading to the gossip that 'the six groups of bhikṣus are ordaining bhikṣuṇīs'?"
She immediately felt regret.
When dawn broke, she took up her robes and bowl and went to Rājagṛha; having arrived there, she entered the rains retreat.
At that time, after Guptā had entrusted her household affairs to others, she went to the Jetavana on another day and asked the bhikṣus:
“Where has he gone? A bhikṣu asked, “Who is he?”
He replied, "Venerable Udāyin!
The bhikṣus said in response:
"He has departed for the great city of Rājagṛha.
Having heard this, he immediately wept.
The bhikṣu asked:
"Guptā! For what reason are you weeping?
She replied:

“Noble Udayin! You promised me that you would allow me to renounce the world and go forth into homelessness; yet, once I had entrusted my household estate to him, he immediately abandoned me and departed.”
"I am neither living in a layman's house nor have I yet renounced the world; why then should I not be distressed?
Someone replied, "It is for the sake of a razor that he has gone toward the royal city, wishing to obtain a new blade to shave your new hair."
At that time, the community of bhikṣuṇīs came to the Jetavana to request instructions; seeing Guptā walking about weeping and dejected, they asked her, "Guptā!
Why are you so distressed?"
"For what reason are you weeping?
Gupatā related the previous events to the bhikṣuṇīs, and the nuns replied:
"You truly lack understanding; how could there be a bhikṣu who ordains a bhikṣuṇī?"
"She has even commanded the community of nuns to ordain you into the homeless life. You may come with me; we shall go to Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī’s place so that she may ordain you.
Then the nuns took Guptā to Mahāprajāpatī’s place and said to her:
"Noble Lady!"
"Guptā wishes to go forth from the household life.
Then Mahāprajāpatī immediately granted her the going forth.
At that time, Udāyin was in Rājagṛha and thought to himself:

"It was because I wished to protect those who carry black alms-bowls that I did not grant Guptā ordination; otherwise, I would have lost many waist-straps and various other requisites for sustaining the body."
"If anyone else with a black alms-bowl were to ordain Guptā, she would have no way to see me even for a moment.
Although she had entered the rainy season retreat, her mind was constantly dissatisfied.
At that time, there was an elder bhikṣu who, having completed the summer retreat at Śrāvastī, arrived at the Royal City.

Udāyin was standing outside the Veṇuvana Monastery near the main road, looking out, when he saw from afar that aged bhikṣu approaching; his hair was like reed blossoms, his eyebrows were long and drooped down over his face, and he walked with slow steps, his shoulders hunched and his arms hanging down.
At that time, Udāyin thought to himself,
"Who is this approaching elder?
Having drawn near, he addressed him, saying:
"Welcome! Welcome, Elder!
the old bhikṣu said.
"Homage to the ācārya! Homage to the upādhyāya!

When Udāyin saw that he lacked proper decorum and did not recognize his two teachers, he immediately knew he must be a mahallaka (an elderly or ignorant monk). He then led him into the monastery and asked:
“Where have you come from?
He replied,
“I have come from Śrāvastī.”
At that time, Udāyin thought to himself:
"If I were to ask about Guptā’s news first, those who hear it would find it shameful and disgraceful; I should ask the questions in their proper order."

Since you, Mahāra, have come from there, do you know whether the World-Honored One has little illness and little affliction, and whether he is living in ease, with his daily life light and comfortable?
He is currently observing the summer retreat at Śrāvastī.
He replied, "The World-Honored One is free from illness and dwelling in peace as he observes the rains retreat there.
He asked again:

"Are the assemblies of bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, and upāsikās all free from illness and dwelling in peace and comfort as usual? Do they, from time to time, pay their respects to the World-Honored One and listen to the True Dharma?"
He replied,
"The person you asked about has attained peace and security, and from time to time comes to hear the True Dharma.
He asked again:

“Are the venerable elders who have attained the stage of mastery—Ājñātakauṇḍinya, Mahākāśyapa, Śāriputra, Mahāmaudgalyāyana, and all the other senior disciples—as well as the Great Lady Gautamī, King Prasenajit, the householder Anāthapiṇḍada, the elder Mṛgāramātṛ Viśākhā, and the lady Sujātā—all dwelling in health and peace?”
He replied, "They are all dwelling in peace and well-being.
He asked again:
"Do you recognize the householder’s wife, Guptā? He replied, "I do."
"That was the former wife of the venerable Udāyin. Udāyin said,
"Could she still be the wife of the householder even now?"
He replied,
"I have already gone forth. Udāyin asked:
"Who allowed you to go forth?
He replied, "It was Mahāprajāpatī."
Udāyin then thought to himself,
"Since they have gone forth as renunciants, it is possible we may meet again.
He then called out to them:
"Mahallaka, come here and wash your feet.
Then Udāyin took his robes and bowl and hung them on a very high ivory peg; he then gave him much oil and told him to anoint his hands and feet, saying, "Now there is food and profit in this room;
you should dwell here in peace and with a joyful mind."
He replied, "I do not wish to stay here.
Then Udāyin took the keys and gave them to him, saying:
"As the Blessed One has said:
'A bhikṣu should not abandon his dwelling place and depart, leaving it empty. O Mahallaka!"
"This is the key; you shall know it for yourself.

Having said these words, he set out on the road and gradually reached the Jeta Grove in Śrāvastī. There, he swept the rooms and smeared them with soft cow dung. Then, closing half the door-panel, he lay down upon his bed and recited the True Dharma in a melodic chant.

At that time, there was a bhikṣuṇī who had come there to request instruction. Hearing this sound of recitation and recognizing its resonance, the bhikṣuṇīs immediately went together to Udāyin’s place and asked, “Venerable sir, you ran away previously; where have you been since?”
He replied,
"I must first go to the city of Rājagṛha.
Having learned this, the nun returned to the monastery and told Guptā:
"You are filled with joy now; the Ācārya has already arrived. Guptā asked, "Which Ācārya?"
He replied, "It is Udāyin! Guptā said:
"For what reason is he my preceptor?
How could I have received instruction and study from him?
The nuns replied:
"You are an ignorant person; many bhikṣuṇīs are closely associated with great bhikṣus. You should now go and inquire after their well-being.
He then took powdered incense, oil, and bathing requisites, went to her room, knocked on the door, and called out.
Udāyin asked, "Who is knocking at the door?
He replied:
"I am Gopā," she replied. Udāyin said, "Welcome!"
"Welcome!
Lady of the householder, please enter as you please.
At that time, Guptā entered and said:
"Venerable sir!
How could I possibly be a householder’s wife?
I have already gone forth."
He asked, "Who has ordained you? He replied:
"Noble One! Let Mahāprajāpatī grant me the going forth. Udāyin said:
"I have other business that requires me to go to the royal city; for what reason do you, in turn, so urgently seek to leave the household life?
He then replied, "Was it not the Venerable One who previously spoke these words:..."
"You should collect your family estate; I shall ordain you and let you leave the household life.
Following these instructions, I entrusted my family property to him, yet the Venerable One abandoned me and traveled far toward the royal city.
"If Mahāprajāpatī had not brought me across, I truly would be neither a layperson nor one who has gone forth.
Udāyin said, "How could I have ever imposed such a heavy burden upon myself as to promise to instruct you? For now, please sit down and I shall preach the Dharma for you."
Having prostrated, he sat down and listened to the Dharma with a composed mind.
At that time, Udāyin began to preach the Dharma; while preaching, he immediately recalled various instances of past laughter and asked Gopā:
"Do you remember how, in the past, at a certain grove in a forest shrine, we partook of such exquisite and delicious food?"
While they were conversing, lustful thoughts arose; once such thoughts had arisen, their emotions became greatly disordered.
Generally, there are five unique qualities possessed by wise women:
they know when men have intense lustful desires and when they do not.
Guptā, perceiving that Udāyin’s lustful mind was burning intensely, said to him:
"Noble One! I must go out for a moment; I shall return once my business is finished."
Udāyin thought to himself,
"Is he wishing to go out for the sake of relieving himself?
He then allowed him to go out for a moment.
Guptā, having emerged, lifted up her skirt and ran away in haste.
At that time, Udāyin heard the sound of her running and immediately went outside to follow after her, calling out:
"Bald śramaṇī, where are you running to?"
Again, he hurriedly pursued her until his organ touched her thigh, whereupon his semen was discharged.
Once his lustful mind had subsided, he stood there pacing back and forth.
Knowing this, Guptā also returned and said to him:
"Noble one! If I were to grant permission, I would no longer be a bhikṣuṇī, and you would no longer be a bhikṣu. Udāyin said:
"Sisters! As the Blessed One has said:
'If one protects oneself, that is protecting others; if one protects others, that constitutes protecting oneself.'"
How is it that protecting oneself is itself protecting others?
Because one is able to practice and cultivate repeatedly, there arises realization; through this, protecting oneself is itself protecting others.
How does protecting others become protecting oneself?

By not being vexed or angry, by having no heart of enmity or harm, and by constantly giving rise to compassion and sympathetic concern for all beings—this is called protecting others and thereby protecting oneself.
Guptā replied, "Noble One,
please take off your lower robe and bring it here; I shall wash it for you."
Then Udāyin immediately handed over the robe.
At that moment, seeing the semen on the robe, Guptā felt remorse and thought to herself:
"There is no part of my body that the noble Udāyin has not touched or seen; it was truly not a good thing that I did not comply with him."
Having formed this thought, his defiled mind became even more intense. As it is said in a verse from the Buddha’s sutras:
“Those who are addicted to desire Do not see what is meaningful and beneficial, Nor do they contemplate the wholesome Dharma; They always walk in the midst of darkness.”
At that time, because Guptā’s mind was agitated by desire, she took a single drop of the semen and placed it in her mouth; she then took another drop and inserted it into her female organ.
Through the inconceivable power of the karma of sentient beings, a sentient being with intermediate existence (*antarābhava*), who was in his final birth, came to take up residence there.
When Guptā arrived at the monastery, she proceeded to wash her clothes.
When the other nuns saw her and questioned her, Guptā explained the matter in detail.
The nuns then asked:
"I told you that you were going to the Great Virtuous One to seek the sublime Dharma; how could you have known that such an evil thing would happen?
Gupatā replied, "That Great Virtuous One is one who upholds the precepts; since he went forth, he has never again touched my body."
The nuns replied,
"If such a thing occurs even when there is no physical contact with the body, what would you do if there were actual contact?
When the bhikṣuṇīs learned of this matter, they went and informed the bhikṣus, and the bhikṣus in turn informed the Buddha.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"That nun has not committed a pārājika offense; since she is pregnant, she should be placed in a private room, provided with food and supplies so that her needs are not lacking."
When he gives birth to a son named Kumāra-Kāśyapa, he shall go forth as a renunciant within my Dharma and, having severed all outflows (āsrava), become an Arhat.
"Among my disciples, he is the foremost for his eloquence and skill in preaching.
At that time, the World-Honored One thought to himself:
"If there is a bhikṣu who has a bhikṣuṇī who is not a relative wash his old clothes, such a fault will arise."
The Blessed One, for these reasons, spoke at length as before, up until: "I now establish this training rule within the Vinaya for my disciples; it should be recited thus:
'If a bhikṣu should have a bhikṣuṇī who is not a relative wash, dye, or beat an old robe, it is a naiḥsargika-pāyattika.'"
"If there is again a bhikṣu" refers to Udāyin, or anyone else of a similar category.
Regarding "relatives," this means that from the two ancestors seven generations back, all are relatives; beyond this point, they are no longer so.
The "bhikṣuṇī" refers to Guptā.
"Old robes" refers to any one of the seven types of robes.
What are the seven?
First, wool;
second, *kṣaumaka* (which does not exist in this region);
third, *śāṇaka* (which does not exist in this region).
Fourth is *kapasika*, white cotton cloth;
fifth is *dukula*, linen cloth;
sixth is *karkatabhanga*, a fine woolen cloak that does not exist in this region.
Seventh, *āpalaṇḍaka* is the name of a region in the north; it is there that this garment is produced.
There is also an interpretation which states that it is simply a garment made of *śī* (silk) or *jiǎn* (raw silk).
Regarding "washing," it refers to at least immersing [the cloth] in water.
Regarding "dyeing," it refers to at least one application of color.
Regarding "beating," it refers to at least a single strike with the hand.
Regarding the *naiḥsargika-pāyattika*, the detailed explanation is as previously stated.
What are the characteristics of the offense and its specific instances herein?

If a bhikṣu knows that a nun is not a relative, and perceiving her as such, causes her to wash an old garment, he commits an offense of forfeiture (*naiḥsargika*). The same applies to dyeing and beating [the garment].
Regarding these three matters, one may cause all three to be performed together, or cause two to be performed, or cause only one to be performed;
furthermore, whichever of the three is undertaken first, if a nun who is not a relative performs it, she incurs the full offense.
If it is a non-relative nun and one suspects this, there is likewise an offense of expiation with forfeiture (*naiḥsargika-pāyattika*).
If it is a relative nun but one perceives her as a non-relative, one incurs an offense of wrongdoing (*dukkaṭa*).
If it is a relative nun and one entertains doubt regarding her status, one incurs an offense of wrongdoing.
Furthermore, there is no offense for one who is the very first offender, or for one who is insane, mentally deranged, or afflicted by intense pain.
The Fifth Training Rule: Regarding Taking Robes from a Nun Who Is Not a Relative. At that time, the Blessed One was staying in the Jeta Grove at Śrāvastī.

As the Buddha has taught, those who renounce their noble lineage to enter the homeless life generally receive abundant offerings; yet, since the Śākyas have received such great abundance of offerings after they went forth, they constantly attended to their clothing and regularly stored up extra robes, alms bowls, bags, and waist-bands.
The Blessed One, having understood this, thought:

"These sons of the Śākyas originally went forth from home seeking liberation, yet they have utterly abandoned the causes of renunciation; they do not cultivate wholesome qualities but are instead addicted to wealth and profit."
"I should now preach the Dharma for them so that they may relinquish their pursuit of wealth and profit.
At various times, the World-Honored One preached the Dharma for them, yet those Śākyas were unable to realize the Truth.
The World-Honored One further reflected:

"For what reason do these sons of the Śākya clan, though they have left the household life, fail to perceive the Truth? It is entirely because they are addicted to and attached to wealth, profit, and various material necessities for livelihood."

If I were now to employ reprimand or disciplinary punishment, the Śākya bhikṣu would have no means of attaining understanding; therefore, I should demonstrate the skillful methods of the Buddhas’ perfect enlightenment for subduing, transforming, and delivering beings.
At that time, the Blessed One addressed the bhikṣus, saying:
"You should know this: I wish to observe the summer retreat here; for the duration of the three months, I shall remain in secluded silence.
Let no bhikṣu come to see me, except for one bhikṣu who has been invited by me to provide a meal, and except on the day of the Poṣadha ceremony."
Then the bhikṣus respectfully received the Buddha’s instruction and together established a regulation:
"During this summer retreat, no bhikṣu shall see the World-Honored One at will, except for one bhikṣu who has been invited by the Buddha for a meal, and on the day of the Poṣadha ceremony."
"If anyone violates this regulation, we shall cause them to perform the confession for a *pāyattika* offense.

At that time, the World-Honored One remained in secluded silence for three months; not a single bhikṣu was able to see the Buddha, except for those invited to take a meal and on the day of the *poṣadha*.
At that time, there was a bhikṣu named Cūḍapanthaka who observed the first three months of the rainy season retreat at Rājagṛha, while the Buddha observed the final month of the retreat at Śrāvastī.

At that time, having completed his three-month retreat, Small-Army (Cūḍapanthaka) had finished his business as he pleased and completed the making of his robes; taking up his bowl and robes and practicing the dhuta ascetic virtues, he went with his disciples, dignified and composed, toward the city of Śrāvastī.
Having arrived there, the bhikṣu Cūḍapanthaka set down his robes and bowl, washed his hands and feet, and approached the Blessed One.
At that time, the group of six bhikṣus saw the bhikṣu Cūḍapanthaka coming toward the Blessed One from afar and said to one another:
"This visiting bhikṣu violates the regulations of the Saṃgha."
Furthermore, it is said:
"I shall cause him to confess his *pāyattika* offense.

Then, the bhikṣu Cūḍapanthaka went to the place where the Blessed One was staying; he gently knocked on the door-panel, and the Buddha opened the door for him. Having entered, Cūḍapanthaka prostrated at the feet of the Blessed One and sat down to one side.
It is the constant custom of the Blessed One, upon seeing a visiting bhikṣu arrive, to greet him with joyful words of consolation, asking:
"From where have you come?
Where did you spend the rainy season retreat?"
Seeing Little Army, the Buddha spoke with joyful words of greeting:
"From where have you come?
Where have you been dwelling?"
Kṣudraka replied:
"Venerable Sir, I have come from Rājagṛha; I observed the rains retreat there."
The Blessed One asked:
"Has the *pravāraṇā* ceremony already been performed by the bhikṣus of Rājagṛha?
They replied: "It has."
"It has been done," [he replied]. The Blessed One asked,
"Culla-kumāra!..."
"With what intention do you, who are yourself so dignified and majestic, surround those who are likewise dignified and majestic? Or it is said:
"I follow and circumambulate them."
Some said: "We shall follow him. Others said: [We shall follow him.]
“Retinue” and “entourage” are both of one and the same meaning.
Little Army addressed [the Buddha], saying:
“Venerable One!
If someone comes to me seeking to go forth, I reply to them:
‘O son of good family!’”
I praise such practices as dwelling in an araṇya, always begging for food, possessing only the three robes, wearing rag-robes from refuse heaps, and sitting at the foot of a tree.
"If you say you can, I shall ordain you and let you leave the household life;
if you say you cannot, let you go as you please.

If there are those who wish to receive full ordination (*upasampadā*), or seek a preceptor (*niśraya*), or seek instruction in recitation, or study according to the principle, and come to me seeking me with focused attention, mindfulness, and reflection, I respond to them all as previously stated.
If one says they are able, then according to their requests for full ordination or other matters, if one says they are unable, one should let them go as they please.
For this reason, my own person is dignified and handsome, and my disciples are likewise so.
The World-Honored One said:
"Excellent! Excellent!"
"Little Army!
You are able to vow to deliver immeasurable devas and humans, to benefit boundless classes of sentient beings, and to bring peace and happiness to those who come seeking the Dharma."
Kumāra, you should know this:
if one can praise the virtues of *dhūta* ascetic practices, it is no different from praising my own person.
If there is anyone who disparages the virtues of *dhūta* ascetic practices, they are disparaging my own person.
Why is this? Little Army!
Throughout the long night, I have praised and extolled such ascetic virtues (dhuta-guṇa) as the means of deliverance; yet you should not contravene the regulations of the Saṃgha.
Cūḍapanthaka said to the Buddha,
“I truly did not know what regulations the Saṃgha had established for this place.
The World-Honored One replied:
"Kṣudraka! During my summer retreat, I informed the bhikṣus, saying:

'You should know that I intend to observe the summer retreat here; for the duration of the three months, I shall remain in silent seclusion. Let no bhikṣu come to see me, except for one bhikṣu who has been invited by me for a meal, and on the day of the Poṣadha ceremony.'"

Then, having received my instruction, the bhikṣus further established a regulation: during this summer retreat, no bhikṣu shall see the World-Honored One at will, except for one bhikṣu who has been invited by the Buddha for a meal, and on the day of the Poṣadha ceremony.
"If anyone violates this regulation, we shall cause them to perform the confession for the *pāyattika* offense.
Little Army addressed the Buddha, saying,
"Venerable Sir!"
"My body is a guest, while they are the hosts; how could the regulations I have established for myself apply to me?
The Buddha told Little Army (Kṣullaka):
"Regardless of guest or host, all must comply with the regulations of the Saṃgha."
Nevertheless, from this day forward, I shall establish the rules of conduct for visiting bhikṣus.
Whenever a visiting bhikṣu enters a monastery, he should first ask the resident bhikṣus, saying:
"Venerable sir!..."
"What regulations does the Saṃgha have established within this monastery now?
If one asks this, it is well; if one does not ask, one incurs an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
If the host reports [the rules], it is well; if the host does not report them, one also incurs an offense of wrong-doing.
The Buddha said to Cūḍapanthaka:
"However, for a bhikṣu dwelling in an araṇya, there shall be benefit and exemption from the formal regulations of the Saṃgha.

If a person dwelling in an araṇya wishes to see me, they may come at any time as they please. Furthermore, those who are endowed with the thirteen dhūta-guṇas may also come to see me at their own convenience."

"O Little Army, you should know that these various people see me according to their own inclinations: those who wear rag-robes and those who possess only the three robes—these two correspond to clothing; those who always beg for food, those who beg in sequence, those who eat in a single sitting, those who eat from a single alms-bowl, and those who do not accept a second serving—these five correspond to food; those who dwell in forest hermitages, those who dwell at the foot of trees, those who dwell in the open air, those who dwell wherever they happen to be, and those who dwell in charnel grounds—these five correspond to dwelling places; and those who remain constantly seated—this one corresponds to diligent exertion."
At that time, having heard what the Buddha had said, the bhikṣu Kṣullaka rejoiced and practiced accordingly; he prostrated before the Buddha and withdrew.
Thereupon, the group of six bhikṣus went to where Kṣullaka was and said to him:
"Venerable One!"
"May I see if you will permit me to question you?
Little Army replied,
"Venerable One!"
"Among the five classes of offenses, you shall be questioned as you see fit.
He replied:
"You have committed a *pāyattika* offense; you must confess it according to the Dharma."
Cūḍapanthaka replied,
"Venerable sir!
I do not see my offense."
He replied,
"Do you not see that the rules for schism in the Saṃgha have been broken?
He answered:
"What regulations has the Saṃgha established?
He then informed him in detail of all that had been previously ordained.
Little Army said:
"Venerable one!
The Blessed One said to me:
'Cūḍapanthaka!'"
"I shall provide benefit for the bhikṣus dwelling in araṇya so that they may be exempt from the monastic regulations and enter to see the Tathāgata at their own pleasure.
When those Śākya renunciants heard this speech, each of them gave rise to this thought:
"O worthy ones, you should know!"
"Venerable Cūḍapanthaka has completed the summer retreat at Rājagṛha; having come to see the Blessed One, he has been able to attend upon him and converse with him personally.
We, however, remain here and are unable to receive his personal attendance. This is because we have been expelled by him due to seeing that we were full of excessive greed."
"We ought to regard our extra robes and bowls as a disease, as an abscess, and as an arrow, and we should cast them away.
Then, all those Śākya bhikṣus thought to themselves:
"We should take all our extra robes, bowls, and other belongings to the Venerable Ānanda, so that we may carry out whatever instructions he gives us."
At that time, the Śākya bhikṣus each took their own extra robes, long alms-bowls, bags, waistbands, and various other requisites, went to where Ānanda was, and spoke to him thus:
"Excellent, Venerable One!"
"We have these long robes, alms bowls, and other requisites for our livelihood; we pray that you will compassionately accept them.
Then the Venerable Ānanda replied to the Śākya bhikṣus, saying, "Virtuous ones, wait a moment; I shall inform the Blessed One."
Then the Venerable Ānanda went to where the Buddha was, prostrated at his feet, and stood to one side; he then reported the matter in its entirety to the World-Honored One.
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"You may accept these and place them in a large room, and then tell the bhikṣus:
'If there are any deficiencies in your requisites, you may take and use them as you please.'"

Then the Venerable Ānanda, having assented to the instruction, immediately returned to the place where those Śākyas were, received all their extra robes, bowls, and other belongings, placed them in the great hall as a single heap, and addressed the bhikṣus, saying:
"If anyone is in need, let them take these robes and bowls as they please."

At that time, the Śākyas regarded those extra robes as sores or arrows; having cast them aside, they distanced themselves from excessive seeking and delighted in cultivating few desires. They then went together to where the World-Honored One was, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and sat to one side.

At that time, the Bhagavat, on account of the bhikṣu Cūḍapanthaka, observed the inclinations, latent tendencies, and differences in the faculties of the Śākyas. He then preached the subtle Dharma suited to their capacities, whereby those five hundred Śākya bhikṣus, right there upon their seats, realized full perfection for themselves. They shattered the shell of ignorance, severed the delusions of the three realms, and attained the state of Arhat. Having accomplished the three knowledges, the six supernormal powers, and the eight liberations, they attained true knowledge: "Birth has been exhausted; the holy life has been established; what was to be done has been accomplished; there is no further existence."

The mind is free from obstruction, like a hand waving through space; whether cut by a blade or anointed with fragrance, neither love nor hatred arises; viewing gold and earth as equal and without distinction, one renounces all fame and profit, and even Śakra, Brahmā, and the various devas all pay him reverence.
At that time, the bhikṣus each gave rise to a doubt and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"It is rare, World-Honored One!

By what cause and condition, on account of the bhikṣu Cūḍapanthaka, were five hundred Śākya bhikṣus led to abandon great greed, practice few desires, and attain a distinguished fruit; crossing the sea of birth and death, they ascended to the shore of nirvāṇa, ultimately being established in the place of peace and security?"
The Blessed One said: "O bhikṣus!

At that time, I was free from desire, hatred, and delusion; without craving and without grasping, I completely eliminated all forms of conceit, was liberated from the links of existence, and attained the knowledge of all modes, realizing unsurpassed enlightenment."
"O Bhikṣus! It is not yet rare that because of Cūḍapanthaka I have praised fewness of desires, enabling five hundred Śākyas to emerge from the ocean of birth and death and realize great nirvāṇa."

Just as I was in the past—possessing desire, hatred, and delusion, with craving and grasping; while I had not yet eliminated pride, nor birth, aging, sickness, death, sorrow, lamentation, suffering, and affliction; and while I was still bound by the links of cyclic existence, not yet liberated, and lacking omniscience—it was also through my praising fewness of desires and censuring much greed for the sake of Cūḍapanthaka that these five hundred people were made to attain the five supernormal powers. You should listen to the causes and conditions of this!
In the past, in the kingdom of Vārāṇasī, there was a king named Brahmadatta, who was a great Dharma King.

At that time, the world was abundant and prosperous, and the population flourished. There were no wars, nor the use of weapons for punishment; there were no wicked or deceitful people who harmed one another, nor were there calamities or the sufferings of disease. Rice, sugarcane, cattle, and sheep were sufficient everywhere, and he regarded all his subjects with equal care, as if they were his only son.
At that time, the king’s queen was named Māyā; in this city there was also a great pond likewise named Māyā.
As the king had no son, he prayed to all the worldly deities and the gods born together with him, hoping for an heir.
The worldly say:
"By means of supplication, one obtains offspring.
This is truly false; if offspring were obtained through supplication, then every single person would have a thousand sons, just like a universal monarch (cakravartin).
Since this matter does not exist, one knows it is false.
Only when three conditions manifest will there be offspring.
What are these three?
First, the parents must possess a mind of passion;
second, the mother’s womb must be pure and ready for conception;
third, the intermediate state being (*antarābhava*) who is to take birth must appear before them. Only when these three conditions are met do sons or daughters come into existence.

While that king dwelt single-mindedly seeking a son, there was at that time a sentient being who, having vowed to cultivate and realize unsurpassed enlightenment, emerged from hell and took conception in Queen Māyādevī.
"Wise women possess five kinds of special knowledge, as explained in detail above.
At that time, having realized she was pregnant, the queen felt great joy and addressed the king, saying:
'Great King!'"
"You should know that the child I carry will surely cause Your Majesty to further glorify the royal throne.
Now that I am pregnant and the fetus dwells in my right flank, observing these signs, there is no doubt it is a male."
When the king heard this, he was filled with great joy and celebrated extensively as described above, ensuring that she remained constantly comfortable until the fetus was fully formed.
At that time, the chief queen had this thought:
"How wonderful!"

"I wish to extensively practice meritorious giving at the eastern gate of the city; likewise, I shall practice meritorious giving throughout the southern, western, and northern gates, as well as within the city itself, and release all prisoners who are confined and bound."

Then the chief queen reported the matter to the king; having heard this, the king granted all their wishes, providing extensive and unrestricted almsgiving within the four city gates and releasing all prisoners from the jails.
Once the Queen’s request had been fulfilled, that thought subsided.
The Queen then conceived another thought:
"I now wish to go to the flower gardens, groves, and springs for a brief excursion."
The king followed him out, and this thought immediately subsided.
Then another thought arose:
"I now wish to go to the pool of the Wondrous Brahmā, where famous flowers are spread everywhere, and to travel upon a boat together with my court ladies."

Having been informed by the messenger, the king had a light boat constructed and placed within the pond. He then commanded the queen and her handmaidens to board the boat for recreation. Once they reached the boat, she gave birth to a son; he possessed the knowledge of his past lives (*pūrvajātismara*), was handsome in appearance, and brought joy to all who saw him. His complexion was like gold, as described in detail above.
When they reached the point of asking, "What name should be given to this child?
his relatives deliberated and said, "Since this child was born in the water, we should give him a name; let his name be 'Water-born' (Jālinīputra)."
Then the king immediately entrusted the crown prince to eight nurses, as described in detail above, until it was said that he was like a lotus emerging from a pond.
At that time, once Prince Jālinīprabha had reached maturity, he thought to himself: "Where shall I die?"
"What karma did I create while in the Saṃghāta Hell?
In the past, during sixty years among the human realm, I was once a crown prince; because I committed various evil deeds, I fell into hell, and now I am born in the human path within a royal family."
"This is not a virtuous course; if you become king, you will surely fall back into hell.
He then devised a deceptive stratagem, remaining motionless and manifesting the appearance of a person with contracted limbs and lameness.
On the very day Prince Jālinīprabha was born, five hundred ministers all had sons born to them; each took the auspicious signs of the moment to establish their names.

As they gradually reached childhood and were able to enter and exit [the palace], the ministers brought them frequently to the King's presence. At that time, the King commanded the youths to play together with joyful games, leaping and bounding about.
Having seen this, the King thought to himself:
"If Prince Jalavāhana were not lame, he too would have joined us here in our leaping games.
Now, although my son knows his own lameness, he will ultimately become king."
At that time, having heard these words, Jālinīputra thought to himself:
"The king now seeks to force his gratitude upon me despite there being no cause; therefore, I should once again remain mute and say nothing."
Later, at another time, when the five hundred youths were gradually able to speak, they all went together to the king’s presence.
The king again thought to himself:
"If my crown prince were not mute, he too would be able to speak."
Previously he was named Prince Jālinīprabha; since he was both mute and lame, he was thereafter called the Mute-and-Lame Prince, and people no longer used the name Jālinīprabha.
On another occasion, the king sat with his cheek resting on his palm, sighing deeply. When the ministers saw this, they all addressed the king, saying:
"Great King, for what reason do you rest your cheek upon your palm as if burdened by sorrow?"
The king said:
"How could I not be filled with grief and lamentation at this time?

Having attained the status of a king with great wealth and power, honored throughout the land, I have no sons or daughters; though I have one son, his body is deformed, he is mute, and he is a cripple."
At that time, the ministers each summoned physicians to assemble in one place, instructing them to examine what ailment had struck the prince.
Then the physicians, having examined the prince together and finding no distinct symptoms of illness, came and said to the king:
"Great King!..."
"We have examined the Prince in detail; his faculties are clear and sharp, and there are no signs of illness.
We suspect this is likely due to a state of mental anxiety or fear, which is why he does not speak.

When King Brahmadatta had heard the physician’s words, he devised a stratagem to induce the Prince to move and to make him speak. He immediately summoned an executioner to a private place and commanded him, saying:
"This mute and lame prince of mine, whom I have ordered you to execute before the great assembly— you may take him away, but you must not kill him immediately.
The executioner replied,
"I respectfully obey the King's command."
Then, in the presence of the assembly, the king immediately entrusted the prince to the executioner and ordered him to carry out the law.
Thereupon, the executioner took up the prince, placed him upon a precious carriage, and departed from the city toward the place of slaughter.
At that time, the mute and lame prince looked about the city and, seeing its prosperity, spoke these words:
"Is this city now empty and devoid of things, or does it have inhabitants?"
At that time, having heard these words, the executioner immediately led the Prince back to the Great King and said:
"This Prince has spoken thus."
Then the king took the mute and paraplegic prince in his arms, placed him upon his breast, and said:
"Who is your enemy? I shall banish and put them to death for you."
"Who is your friend?
I shall bestow [a gift] upon him.
When the Prince heard these words, he remained mute and did not answer.

Then the king again commanded the executioner to take him back and kill him once more. The executioner, obeying the command, led him away as before. At that time, the prince saw a corpse being carried by four men and spoke these words:
"Is this one who has already died being killed again, or is it one who is alive yet dead?"
When the executioner heard these words, he returned the prince to the king.
The king again placed him upon his breast as before and questioned him in succession; yet the prince remained mute and did not answer.
The king again gave him over as before to be executed and led him out of the royal city.
At that time, the prince saw a great heap of grain and spoke thus:
"If this great heap of grain had not previously consumed its own root..."
At that time, having heard these words, the executioner returned him to the king. The king again questioned him in the same sequence as before, but the prince remained mute and did not speak.
The king again gave the same order as before, commanding the executioner, saying:
"You must go quickly to that cemetery and bury the prince in a pit."
Then that executioner, as before, led him away toward the deep forest charnel ground (śmaśāna) and dug a pit in the earth.
At that time, the Prince spoke this verse:
"For what purpose does the driver of the chariot hastily dig a trench here?"
"I have heard this; please answer me quickly: why have you dug this pit? The butcher replied:
"Great King, you have fathered a son who is mute and unable to walk."
"For this reason, I have sent someone to dig a pit, intending to bury my useless son.
At that time, the Prince who was Mute and Paralysed thought to himself:
"This executioner harbors a cruel and poisonous disposition; he holds a sharp sword in his hand, seeking only to kill people, making it his livelihood to sever the life-root of others."
His heart was immediately struck with terror, thinking:
"Perhaps they intend to fill this deep pit with me.
Having thought thus, he said to the executioner:
"If my father, the King, accords with my wish, I shall return to the city by means of speech and walking.
At that time, the executioner felt a sense of wonder and ran to inform the King.
The King said, "If the Prince requires the royal throne, I shall grant it to him immediately; how much more so regarding other requests—how could I not comply with his wishes?"
At that time, the Great King was filled with great joy and addressed his ministers, saying:
"You should immediately have the streets swept clean and strewn with fragrant flowers; hang silken banners and canopies, making them as magnificent and beautiful as possible."
As it is said: "Whatever words are spoken by the sovereign of the land, or by those of the celestial classes,
or by those who have realized meditative certainty— all such matters shall be accomplished according to their will."
Then the ministers, immediately following the King’s command, adorned the city walls and towers until they were all exquisitely beautiful.
At that time, immeasurable hundreds of thousands of people gathered like clouds in the streets and thoroughfares, gazing expectantly for the Prince to return to the city on foot.
At that time, the Prince who was mute and lame returned to the city on foot; having reached the Great King’s presence, he prostrated at his father’s feet and spoke this verse:
“Great King, you should now know: I am not truly mute or lame, Nor am I of a foolish or deluded nature;
It was only out of fear of suffering that I acted thus.”
"I have feet capable of walking, and I have a mouth that speaks clearly;
fearing the suffering of falling into the evil realms, I therefore perform such deeds.
The King said:
"Beloved son, if this is so, why do you not speak or walk with your own feet?
What is the meaning of these words of fear?
The Prince replied:
"May the King listen well; I shall explain the causal conditions for this.
In a previous life, for sixty years, I served as a crown prince and fully experienced the pleasures of the five senses."
Because of this, for six thousand years, he fell into the hells,
where he underwent all manner of sufferings beyond description;
only when his karma was exhausted did he emerge, to once again obtain a human body.
"Recalling such matters as these, I fear falling into hell;
I certainly do not wish to be king—release me into the forest wilds!
The King said:
"Dear child!

Previously, you performed sacrifices and cultivated sublime practices, establishing various assemblies of almsgiving to make offerings to the rishis, hoping thereby to obtain an offspring to succeed to the royal throne."
"For what reason have you now abandoned [the world] to go forth as a renunciant?
The Prince replied:
"I do not seek the enjoyment of desires; from them arise resentment and strife."
I vow to cultivate true brahmacarya; by this, one can destroy all enemies.
I do not seek the enjoyment of sensual desires, for they are like poisonous fruits;
I vow to cultivate true brahmacarya, always consuming the medicine of ambrosia.
The King said:
"That which is loved and cherished by the world, the kingship alone is most supreme;
for what reason do you now abandon it to seek renunciation?"
The Prince said:
"That which ultimately gives rise to suffering cannot be called happiness;
one must seek the place of true happiness, where all suffering can be brought to an end."
"I pray that the King will now release me, so that I may renounce the secular life and go to the forest.
The King said, "Dear son!"

At present, you dwell within this multi-storied pavilion, where the fragrance of incense and flowers is intense; your bedding is soft and supple, allowing for peaceful rest; you enjoy the sounds of stringed and wind instruments; you wear exquisite garments at the proper times; and you partake of sweet delicacies according to your desire.

If one leaves the household life, they must dwell in mountain forests and sleep upon withered leaves; they will be startled by the howling of foxes, wolves, tigers, and leopards; they will wear skins and grass for clothing and sustain themselves on roots and fruits; and when the water is hot and turbid, there will be no way to drink it. With what intention do you now renounce such honor and glory to take pleasure in dwelling in the wilderness?
The Prince said:
"I would rather dwell in the forest wilds clad in deer skins, living together with tigers and leopards while eating roots and fruits;
I will not become a king who constantly inflicts killing and punishment, for that would contradict the good fruits of future lives."
"I pray that Your Majesty will release me to hide in the mountain forests, so that I may diligently cultivate the path to nirvāṇa until my thoughts are fulfilled.
The King said,
"My beloved son!"
"First, you must resolve my three doubts for me; afterwards, it will not be difficult for me to leave the household life.
When you see all the wealth and prosperity within the city, do not speak thus:
'Is this city now empty and desolate, with nothing at all?'"
"Is there anyone living here?
"With what underlying intention do you speak these words?
The Prince replied:
"Great King, please listen!
Your Majesty has now ordered someone to kill me for no reason, yet not a single person speaks reasonably, saying:
'Why does Your Majesty now put this crown prince to death?'"
"I spoke these words for this reason.
The king said,
"Excellent!"
Furthermore, regarding your second view upon seeing a corpse being carried away, you say:
"Does one who is already dead die again, or does one who is alive die?
With what underlying intention do you speak these words?
The Prince said:
"Great King, please listen!
If a person commits evil deeds himself and then dies, this is called dying and dying again."
"If a person dies while performing wholesome deeds for themselves, this is called 'living yet dying.
It was with this intention in mind that I spoke these words.
The king said:
"This too is excellent!
Furthermore, for the third time you have seen a great heap of grain and made this statement:
'If one does not first eat the roots.'"
"What is the underlying intention behind your further making such a statement?
The Prince replied,
"Great King, listen well!

Those farmers borrowed grain from others to carry out their work; later, when the grain ripened and was gathered into a great heap, the creditors came to demand repayment, and they returned most of it to them.
If one does not consume others' property beforehand, it will not form a great accumulation.

Human beings are likewise: it is by practicing the ten wholesome actions that one obtains a human body. If one further commits evil and fails to cultivate goodness, the roots of merit from previous lives will immediately be exhausted. Because the roots of merit are exhausted, one loses the path of virtue; conversely, if one acts otherwise, they will not be lost.
"It is for this reason that I spoke these words.
Having heard these words, the king said:
"My beloved son!"
"This is even more excellent!
At that moment, the king immediately took the prince into his arms, sobbing and shedding tears, and said:
"Since you have already resolved your mind and your will cannot be shifted, I shall now follow your inclination to practice wholesome deeds; I too shall later go with you to the mountain forests."
Then King Brahmadatta addressed his ministers, saying,
"If my crown prince does not go forth into the homeless life, what will he become?
The ministers replied:
"You shall become kings.
[The father asked,] "And who are you, my sons?
They replied:
"These are his attendants.
The King said,
"Now that the Prince has already left the household life, why do none of you, my sons, follow him?"
The ministers replied,
"We respectfully carry out the King's command and cause him to renounce the world.
Not far from the city was a secluded place where there lived a seer endowed with the five supernatural powers, whose nature was compassionate and who felt pity for all beings.

At that time, the Prince departed from Vārāṇasī with five hundred men; leading his attendants, he went to the place where the seers were and requested ordination with great earnestness, and the seers all granted his wish.
After he had left the household life, he diligently practiced the essential Dharma, and before long the Prince attained the five supernormal powers (*pañcābhijñā*).
Later, when the seer passed away, the Prince followed the funeral rites and cremated his body.

At that time, the Prince who was mute and lame personally instructed the five hundred men; consequently, the name "Prince who was Mute and Lame" became obscured, while the eminent title "Great Master who was Mute and Lame" became widely renowned.
At that time, the master who was mute and lame had this thought:
"For what reason have my five hundred disciples not attained the five supernatural powers?

Is it not because they keep many deer skins and tree bark, maintain numerous sacrificial vessels, water containers, and various roots and fruits for their sustenance, and thus their four limbs are constantly exhausted, making the realization of the five supernatural powers difficult?"

If I were now to administer reprimands and punishments, those five hundred people would have no means by which to attain understanding; it would be more appropriate to demonstrate to them the supreme skillful methods of a Bodhisattva for transforming and delivering beings.
At that time, the Great Master addressed the young brahmins, saying:
"You should know this!

I wish to dwell in silent seclusion during these three months of the summer retreat; let no one come to see me at all, except for one person who gathers roots and fruits, and on the morning of the *poṣadha* ceremony on the fourteenth day of the month."

At that time, the disciples received his instruction and together established a regulation: for the duration of three months, no one was permitted to see the Great Master at will, except for the single person who provided fruit and vegetables and on the days of the *poṣadha*.
If anyone violates this regulation, we shall cause them to perform the *pāyattika* (confession) rite for repentance.
For three months, the teacher shall remain in secluded silence, and no one at all shall be permitted to enter and see him, except for those gathering fruit and on the day of the *poṣadha*.
At that time, the Great Teacher saw a flying bird at his dwelling place and addressed it, saying: "Welcome, bird!

What I am doing now is similar to what you are doing. Just as you seek food only to fill your belly and give rise to a mind of contentment, so too do I seek food only to fill my belly and cultivate a mind of contentment."
Next, he saw a deer and addressed it, saying:
"Welcome, wild deer!

What I am doing now is similar to yours. Just as you seek food only to fill your belly and give rise to a sense of contentment, so too do I seek food only to fill my belly and cultivate a mind of contentment."
At that time, when the disciples heard their teacher conversing with the birds and deer, each of them thought to themselves:
"Has the Great Teacher not abandoned his vow of silence?
They all went to where the teacher was, and after paying their respects, they sat down together; however, the teacher remained silent and did not speak with them.
At that time, the disciples again thought to themselves:
"Does our Great Teacher converse with animals and not speak with humans?
Thereupon, they abandoned him and departed.
Furthermore, there was another son of a brahmin named Nengshi (Capable of Giving) who happened to arrive there.
Seeing him from afar, the rishi called out to him, saying: "Nengshi!"
What I do now is similar to what you do: you carry only one deerskin garment and one sacrificial vessel, and I am the same.
You seek food only to fill your belly and give rise to a sense of contentment; I too seek food only to fill my belly and cultivate a mind of contentment.

"This place is not like that; there are many others who keep numerous leather garments, store a wide variety of miscellaneous vessels, and hoard all kinds of fruits and vegetables, exhausting themselves in their search for them.
When the disciples heard these words, each of them thought to themselves: "Now our Great Teacher praises having few desires and censures excessive seeking.

Observing his intent, it is clear that he has cast us out because he perceives our great greed. We should regard our surplus leather garments and miscellaneous vessels as diseases, arrows, or abscesses, and discard them in the river. We ought to wear only a single deerskin garment each and possess only one miscellaneous vessel each."
The assembly agreed together, and each discarded miscellaneous items into that river; they went to the teacher’s dwelling with only their basic requisites.
The teacher observed their faculties and expounded the Dharma for them, and they all realized the five supernatural powers.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
"Do not harbor other thoughts!
The mute and paraplegic seer endowed with the five supernormal powers at that time was none other than my own self, transforming all sentient beings through the practice of a bodhisattva."
Those who were the five hundred disciples in the past are these very five hundred bhikṣus of the Śākya clan; he who was able to give in the past is this very Sūkṣma.
Because of that ability to give in the past, I caused those five hundred people to abandon great greed, cultivate the practice of few desires, and attain the five supernormal powers.

Now, because of Cūḍapanthaka, five hundred Śākya bhikṣus have abandoned their greedy pursuits and followed the practice of contentment; they have become fully endowed with the six supernormal powers, attained arhatship, and dwell in ultimate peace within the city of nirvāṇa.
"You should know this!

Those who perform purely black deeds obtain purely black karmic results; those who perform purely white deeds obtain purely white karmic results; and those who perform mixed deeds obtain mixed karmic results."
Therefore, you should abandon purely black and mixed karma, and instead diligently cultivate purely white karma; observing these causes and conditions, you should practice and learn accordingly.
This was the origin of the matter; however, the Blessed One had not yet established a training rule for the bhikṣus.
At that time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park, and he had not yet prohibited bhikṣuṇīs from dwelling in forest hermitages (araṇya).
At that time, there were several bhikṣuṇīs who went to a quiet grove to practice meditative concentration and experience the bliss of superior dhyāna.

Then, the bhikṣuṇī Utpalavarṇā, together with her retinue of five hundred, went to the Dark Forest and sat in the half-lotus posture beneath a tree, entering the attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*).
At that time, after the sun had set, the other nuns each desired to return toward Śrāvastī, and one among them said:
"Noble Lady Utpalavarṇā!..."
"I shall call him to wake up.
Another said, "Noble one!"
"Endowed with great majestic power, she may perhaps be permitted to enter the monastery ahead of us.
Having said this, they did not call her up but each returned on their own.
When it was evening, the nun Utpalavarṇā emerged from meditative concentration and, surveying the nuns, saw that they had all departed. She then thought to herself:
"Shall I enter the city,
or shall I remain here? Having thus reflected,
he immediately entered meditative concentration.
At that time, a band of five hundred thieves, having completed their plundering, arrived at the edge of this forest. The thieves deliberated, saying:
"Let half the men divide the loot, while the other half acts as guards."
Thereupon, within the forest, they saw a nun who had entered meditative absorption; some said she was a tree, some said she was a human being, and some said she was a bhikṣu.
At that time, among the bandits was one who had returned to lay life, who reported:
"This is a bhikṣuṇī, not a bhikṣu."
Others asked, "How do you know this? He replied:
"The bhikṣus sit in the full lotus posture, whereas the bhikṣuṇīs sit in the half-lotus posture; since she is sitting in the half-lotus posture, it is clear she is a bhikṣuṇī.
At that time, the bandits were struck with a sense of wonder, thinking:
"You should know, sirs, that in such a terrifying, dense forest, a single bhikṣuṇī is able to stay here."
He immediately went to where the bandit general was, and the general asked,
"Have you seen anything extraordinary within the forest?
He replied:
"Look! In such a terrifying great forest of darkness, there is a bhikṣuṇī who is able to stay here.
Having heard this, the general said to the guards:

"I shall examine it," he said, and there he saw a bhikṣuṇī whose countenance was upright and pleasing to behold; her deportment was tranquil and composed, inspiring deep reverence upon being seen. He sighed in admiration, saying:
"In this grove today, there are two things that are lovely: [the grove itself and] this nun."
"It is the radiance of the bright moon and the countenance of the bhikṣuṇī.
The general said,
"You should have her roused so that I may offer her food."
The returned layperson replied,
"This is not eating at an improper time.
The general said:
"The bhikṣuṇīs in this grove possess two things that are admirable:
namely, their dignified appearance and their abstention from eating at improper times.
The general said:
"Make him drink wine.
He returned and reported,
"He does not drink wine."
The general said,
"In this grove, there are two further things that are lovely:
namely, that the bhikṣuṇīs possess upright and handsome countenances, and that they do not drink various wines."
The general said,
"Now that I have fortunately encountered this field of merit, yet I have failed to offer even a single meal.
He then wrapped exquisite food in a costly cotton cloth, hung it upon a tree branch, and spoke these words:
"Just as the Venerable One’s deportment is tranquil and composed, there is nothing you do not perceive and nothing you do not know.
I now leave these robes and food; I pray that out of compassion you will accept and make use of them."
Having spoken these words, she left them and departed.

When the night had turned to dawn, the nun Utpalavarṇā arose from her meditative absorption. She then saw the tracks where the great assembly had passed and entered a state of concentration; observing through meditation, she saw that those five hundred bandits had come to this place and then departed.
He further examined himself to see if there were any unseemly or improper acts,
knowing that he was without fault.
Then, seeing food wrapped and hung upon a tree, he thought to himself:
"This is brought about by the power of a pure heart and reverent faith. He further thought:
"If I wait for another person to offer the food, I fear that birds or beasts will come and spoil this pure offering."
"I should now take this superior food and offer it to the Saṃgha; for the Buddha has taught:
'If a nun has handled it with impurity and a bhikṣu is pure, it is pure; if a bhikṣu has handled it with impurity and a nun is pure, it is also pure.'"
Having said this, he took it himself in his hands and went to the Jetavana Grove.
It was the constant custom of the group of six monks for one or two of them to always remain stationed at the entrance of the monastery.
At that time, Upānanda was walking to and fro in front of the temple gate when he saw the bhikṣuṇī approaching from afar and asked her:
"O elder sister!
Is it not yet dawn that the city gates have already opened?
The nun said:
"Venerable sir!
I did not stay overnight in the city; I have come from the Dark Forest.
He replied:
“Sister! Once, during the day, I entered that forest and gave rise to a sense of fear such that the hairs on my body all stood on end.
Sister!”
"How is it that you dwell there alone, and what is the object held in your hand?
At that time, the bhikṣuṇī related the circumstances in full:
"At that time, a bandit, having purified his mind, left it for me."
Upānanda said, "Sister!

It was because of your dignified deportment that the thief conceived a sense of reverence and affection, thereby obtaining this object. Had he seen me, he would surely have given me a staff and forced me to carry the goods away."
Upānanda said: "Sister!

If one obtains this fine new white cotton cloth and sews it into a double-layered saṃghāṭī robe, then to dwell with few desires and cultivate all manner of wholesome qualities would indeed be excellent!"
The nun said,
"Venerable One,
do you require this robe?"
He replied,
"If there is indeed anything remaining, you may dispose of it as you see fit.
He answered:
"Wait a moment!
I shall take this first meal and offer it to the Saṃgha;
once I have returned here, I will give you this robe. Thus thought Upānanda:
"If there should be any other black-bowl wearer who sees this, they will surely beg for this robe,
and I shall have no means of obtaining it. She replied, "Sister!..."
"You may stay here; I shall go and summon someone to receive the first meal.
The nun consented.
Then Upānanda entered the monastery and saw that the person receiving the food was sitting there idly, so he said to him:
“Venerable one!
The donor has been toiling at the gate carrying food; you, however, are idly staying in your room with nothing to do. You ought to go quickly and receive that alms-food.”

He then took his vessel and went to the gate of the monastery, where he received the first portion of food from a bhikṣuṇī; after she had given him the food, she shook out her white cotton robe and offered it to him as a gift.
Having received the robe, Upānanda was delighted and offered this blessing:
"The object you have given is an ornament for the mind; it serves as an aid to the mind, adorned with concentration and wisdom, leading one to the realms of humans and devas."
"Enjoying excellent and exquisite garments according to your desire, you shall ultimately attain unsurpassed, peaceful Nirvana.
Having said this, she departed.
At that time, the bhikṣuṇī Utpalavarṇā thought to herself:
"Shall I now return to my original place,
or shall I pay homage to the World-Honored One?
Having come here now, I shall indeed prostrate at the Buddha's feet."
She then proceeded to the Buddha’s dwelling, prostrated before the World-Honored One, and sat to one side.
At that time, the bhikṣuṇī’s five robes were tattered and worn; seeing this, the World-Honored One said to Ānanda:
"Was the community of bhikṣuṇīs sufficiently provided with requisites during the rainy season retreat?"
Ānanda said to the Buddha,
“It is sufficient.
The Buddha said:
"For what reason is the nun Utpalavarṇā’s five robes so tattered?
Ānanda replied, "Venerable Sir!"

This bhikṣuṇī possesses firm and profound faith and a pure, virtuous intention; she joyfully relinquishes whatever she receives among the Three Jewels, never refusing the requests of those who come to beg from her.
"Today this nun obtained a fine, large piece of cloth and offered it to the Venerable Upānanda.
The Buddha asked Ānanda,
"Did the bhikṣu receive clothing from a nun who is not a relative?"
Ānanda said, "The bhikṣu has accepted the robe.
The Buddha told Ānanda:
However, a bhikṣu who is not a relative does not give rise to this thought:
"Does this bhikṣuṇī possess the five robes?
He accepts whatever is given to her at that time.
"If it were a bhikṣu who was a relative, it would not be thus; seeing his lack of necessities, one would be unwilling to accept the robe.
At that time, the World-Honored One said to Ānanda:
"From the place where robes are stored in the Great Hall, you should take five robes and give them to the bhikṣuṇī Utpalavarṇā."
Then Ānanda, having received the Buddha’s instruction, took five robes and presented them to Utpalavarṇā.
At that time, for this reason, the Blessed One addressed the bhikṣus:
“The full account, up to the point where he established a training rule (śikṣāpada) within the Vinaya, should be told as follows:”
"If a bhikṣu should take a robe from a bhikṣuṇī who is not a relative, it is a naiḥsargika-pāyattika.

After the Blessed One had established this training rule for the bhikṣus, there was a householder in Śrāvastī who was immensely wealthy, possessing great riches and abundant enjoyments; his entire estate was like that of King Vaiśravaṇa, and he took a wife from a family of equal standing.
Although they had lived together for a long time, no son or daughter was born; filled with sorrow and anxiety, he thought to himself:
"I now possess much wealth and treasure within my house, yet there is not a single heir to succeed me."
After my death, because I have no son, all my assets will be confiscated by the royal house;
furthermore, I have not yet prepared provisions for the journey to the next world.
He sat with his cheek propped upon his hand, sighing deeply.
His wife asked him,
"For what reason do you sit with such a sorrowful heart, propping your cheek upon your hand?"
He replied, "O worthy one!
How could I not be filled with sorrow now?"
He related the matter in detail.
His wife said,
"How can one cultivate the provisions for future lives?"
He replied, "O worthy one!

If you can provide excellent food and drink as an offering to the Buddha and the Sangha, and after they have eaten, present each person with a pair of fine white cotton cloths, this is called preparing the provisions for the journey to the next world and setting them in place beforehand."
The wife said, "Why do you not do so?

At that time, the elder went to where the Buddha was, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and sat to one side. Then the World-Honored One preached the sublime Dharma for the elder, instructing, exhorting, inspiring, and gladdening him, after which he remained silent.
At that time, the elder rose from his seat, adjusted his robe over one shoulder, pressed his palms together in reverence, and addressed the Buddha:
"World-Honored One,
I pray that out of compassion you and the community of bhikṣus will accept my humble offering at my home tomorrow."
The World-Honored One accepted by remaining silent.
Knowing that the Buddha had graciously accepted his invitation, the elder prostrated at his feet and departed.

That night, the elder prepared various kinds of exquisite food and drink; at dawn, he spread out seats and arranged water vessels, then sent a messenger to inform the World-Honored One that it was time.
In the early part of the day, the Blessed One dressed, took his bowl, and departed accompanied by a retinue of bhikṣus.
Upon arriving at the place where the householder had prepared the meal, he sat down upon the seat provided.
Once the elder had seen that the Buddha and the Saṅgha were seated according to the Dharma, he personally served them with exquisite food and drink until they were fully satisfied.
After they had rinsed their mouths and washed their hands, he presented the Buddha and each member of the Saṅgha with a pair of superior white cotton cloths.
Then that householder took a low seat and sat before the World-Honored One to listen to and receive the sublime Dharma.

The Buddha, according to his faculties and nature, instructed, exhorted, benefited, and gladdened him by preaching the sublime Dharma. Having recited the verses of blessing, he rose from his seat and departed.

At that time, having followed the Buddha out, the householder circumambulated him three times, prostrated at his feet, and withdrew. Standing upon a high terrace, he cultivated the mindfulness of renunciation and said to his wife, "O virtuous lady!
"You should feel great joy, for I have already prepared much of the provisions for the future life.
His wife then replied,
"Although you have now made them, I have not yet cultivated or prepared any."
The householder replied,
"Is not the merit being cultivated now shared?
His wife said:

"Although I know this is shared by all, it is my sincere wish to invite the Great Mistress (Mahāprajāpatī) and the community of bhikṣuṇīs to a meal at my home; once they have eaten, I shall offer each of them a pair of high-quality white cotton cloths. This shall serve as my provision for future lives."
The householder said:
"Excellent! Excellent!"
"Do as you wish.

Thereupon, the householder’s wife went to the bhikṣuṇī Mahāprajāpatī, prostrated at her feet, and sat to one side. Having listened to the sublime Dharma, she rose from her seat and said, "Noble Lady!"
"and the community of bhikṣuṇīs; I only pray that you will compassionately come to my home tomorrow.

[The request was made] in detail as previously described, until she had finished washing and rinsing herself. Then the householder’s wife took a large chest filled with fine white cotton cloth, opened it before the Elder, and stood there.
At that time, Mahāprajāpatī thought to herself:
"The World-Honored One has established the precepts, forbidding bhikṣuṇīs from accepting exquisite garments.
If I were to accept them now, I would be violating the training rules."
"If she does not accept it, she will obstruct the merit of the donor, and the bhikṣuṇīs will lose their offerings.
Each nun thought to herself:
"If Mahāprajāpatī were to accept this robe, it would truly be excellent!"
At that time, Mahāprajāpatī, having understood the thoughts of the assembly, thought to herself:
"The Blessed One should also, on account of this matter, permit the acceptance of fine robes.
Then Mahāprajāpatī accepted the robes on behalf of all; after reciting a verse of benediction for the householder’s wife, she rose from her seat and departed.
Approaching the World-Honored One with her usual dignified demeanor, she reported the preceding events in detail to the World-Honored One.
The Buddha said to Mahāprajāpatī: "Excellent!"
Excellent!
You have already understood the time when I had not yet granted permission.
From this day forward, I allow bhikṣuṇīs to accept robes of high value and exchange them with bhikṣus.
Then Mahāprajāpatī, having received the Buddha’s instruction, prostrated at his feet and departed. Upon arriving at the nuns’ residence, she distributed the upper robes and informed them:
“The World-Honored One has given this instruction: ‘Nuns are permitted to receive expensive robes; they may exchange them for coarse ones with the bhikṣus and use them as they please.’”
At that time, having received the robes, the bhikṣuṇī went to Jetavana and intended to exchange them with the bhikṣus.
Then the group of twelve bhikṣuṇīs took expensive robes and went to the place of the group of six, saying:
"Noble ones!"
The Blessed One has given this instruction: he permits bhikṣuṇīs to receive expensive robes and exchange them with bhikṣus.
Now, you should take this fine robe and give me yours, which is coarse.
The group of six replied, "Sisters!
We would not even accept a gift offered to us directly as it is; how much less would we exchange it with you, who are foolish, ignorant, and lack autonomy?"
The other nuns each took the robes they had received according to their own wishes and went to the elderly bhikṣu to report the matter as described above, offering to exchange them for his robes.
The elderly bhikṣu said,
"Sisters, wait a moment!"
"I shall ask the Buddha about this.
Then that bhikṣu went to where the Buddha was and addressed him, saying,
"Venerable Sir!"
"There is a bhikṣuṇī who, possessing fine robes and materials, has come to me seeking to exchange them for coarse ones; I do not know what to do.
The Buddha said, "I permit bhikṣus to receive robes from bhikṣuṇīs, with the exception of exchanging them."
"When changing clothes, one should cause the bhikṣuṇīs to be joyful and free from resentment.
At that time, the World-Honored One praised those who uphold the precepts, have few desires, and know contentment, and addressed the bhikṣus, saying:
"The previous [rule] was the original prohibition; this is a subsequent allowance. It should be stated as follows:"
"If a bhikṣu again takes a robe from a bhikṣuṇī who is not a relative, except in exchange, it is a naiḥsargika-pāyattika.
"If a bhikṣu" refers to Upānanda; the remaining meanings are as explained above.
Regarding the meaning of "one's own" versus "not one's own," there are seven kinds of robes, as explained in detail above.
With the exception of those obtained through trade, there is no offense in exchanging them.
As for the meaning of *naiḥsargika* (relinquishment), the method for relinquishing and confessing is likewise as explained above.
In this regard, what are the characteristics of the offense and its specific details?
If a bhikṣu, regarding a nun who is not a relative, perceives her as not being a relative or entertains doubt about it, and takes a robe from her, he incurs a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* offense.
If a bhikṣu perceives a relative bhikṣuṇī as a non-relative, or entertains doubt regarding her status, he incurs an *dukkaṭa* offense. Furthermore, there is no offense in the following cases:

if a bhikṣuṇī offers robes to the Saṃgha; or offers them for the purpose of preaching the Dharma; or offers them at the time of receiving full ordination (*upasampadā*); or offers them because she has been robbed by thieves; or if she obtained them by purchase or through exchange—in all these instances, there is no offense.
If a bhikṣuṇī who is widely known among the community and has received much gain takes her robes and clothing to a bhikṣu, places the garments on the ground, and speaks these words:
"Noble one!..."
"I now have much wealth such as this; I pray that you will compassionately accept it for my sake.
Having spoken these words, he abandons it and departs; even if one takes it, there is no offense.
Furthermore, there is no offense for one who is a first-time offender, or for one who is insane, mentally deranged, or overwhelmed by intense pain.
The Sixth Training Rule: Begging for Robes from a Householder Who Is Not a Relative. At that time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
In this city there was a householder who, not long after marrying his wife, said to her:
"O virtuous lady!
I wish to take various goods and travel to another region to trade and seek profit, so that I may preserve our family estate."
The wife said, "In one's youth, one should enjoy sensual pleasures; it is only when one has grown old that one may seek wealth.
The husband replied:
"O worthy one!

When one is young and strong, one should endure hardship and braving both cold and heat to seek wealth; it is only when one reaches old age and physical decline that one may sit back and enjoy its fruits."
The wife thought to herself:
"I did not urge him to do this, yet he seeks it for himself; I shall comply with his wish.
She replied:
"Seek it as you please.
He then immediately provided the necessary provisions for the journey and gave him full support for his departure.
Carrying his merchandise, he went to another place.
Later, his wife thought to herself:

"My husband has undergone hardships in seeking a livelihood, enduring all manner of suffering such as cold, heat, hunger, and thirst—all of this solely for the sake of seeking wealth and goods for my own benefit."
"I should not remain sitting idly now.
He then went to the marketplace and purchased fine cotton, spun it into superior thread, and wove it into exquisite cloth. He perfumed it with various kinds of incense and placed it inside a casket.

At that time, the elder returned to his home after seeking profit through trade; his wife prepared fragrant bathing water for her husband to wash and bathe, and she opened a chest, took out some fine cotton cloth, and presented it to him.
Having seen this, the householder thought to himself:
"Even if I were to sell the entire sum of money I previously set aside for food and drink, I still would not have obtained this robe. He asked:
“O noble one! Where did you obtain this upper garment?
He replied:
"You had better put it on.
He then put it on for him, and asked again:
"Where did you get this robe?"
His wife said,
"You should eat first.
After he had eaten, she asked again:
"Where did you obtain this robe?
His wife then related the circumstances in detail, and her husband said,
"Excellent, my dear!
"I shall act as the seeker of wealth, and you shall be the guardian who manages the household affairs well; in this way, before long, the resources within the house will surely become abundant.
His wife said, "This garment was obtained by my own hard labor; wear it yourself and do not give it to anyone else."
He replied, “So be it.

At that time, the householder’s faith was pure and wholesome; he went to the Jeta Grove to pay homage at the feet of the World-Honored One. As he was departing from the city, the gatekeeper saw him and thought to himself:
"Judging by the upper garment this householder is wearing, he will surely obtain great wealth and profit today.
At that time, a group of six monks were staying at the gate of the monastery; when Upānanda saw the householder approaching, he observed his clothing and thought to himself:
"Look at this householder wearing such fine garments; whatever wealth and profit he seeks, he will certainly obtain according to his wishes."
"If I do not manage to keep this robe now, I shall no longer be called Upānanda.
He then cried out,
"Welcome, householder!"
"From where have you come, O Benevolent One?
