You appear now like the crescent moon that manifests only after a long time.
He replied:
“Noble One!
I have traveled far abroad for trade and have only recently returned; that is why I have come to pay my respects to the Buddha. He asked:
“Householder, have you gained much profit?
He replied, “Depending on the circumstances, it has been more or less; at any rate, I have avoided returning empty-handed.”
He replied, "Householder!
I already knew this beforehand; seeing the water flowing from the pond, I knew it was clear and deep, and observing the fine garments, I knew you had gained much profit."

"However, you have recently been constantly preoccupied with greed and worldly business without ceasing, and you have never cultivated the provisions for future lives; come here, and I shall preach the Dharma for you."

At that time, the elder sat to one side to listen to the Dharma. Whenever Upānanda preached the Dharma, if he spoke on the causes and conditions of observing the precepts, those listening to the Dharma all thought that they themselves would immediately be reborn in the heavens;
if he spoke on the causes and conditions of giving, those listening to the Dharma even went so far as to cut flesh from their own bodies to offer as a gift;
and if he spoke on the causes and conditions of sinful karma, those listening to the Dharma immediately thought that they themselves were currently falling into the evil realms.
Upānanda taught the Dharma concerning generosity to that householder. Having conceived pure faith, the householder asked, "Noble One!
I am fortunate to have heard such sublime Dharma; I have a pair of white cotton cloths which I wish to offer as a gift."
Upānanda then offered a blessing for him, saying:
"The goods you have given are the provisions for the mind," and so forth, as explained above.
Having finished the blessing, he immediately asked the householder for his robe. The householder said:
"The robe is inside the house; bring it tomorrow.
He replied, "O virtuous one!"
As the Blessed One said:
"One should cultivate merit with haste; who knows if tomorrow will come?
In the end, one will certainly encounter the army of the King of Death."
Upānanda said: "Householder!
The garment you are wearing is made of exceptionally fine white cotton; you should offer it to me."
"I shall cut this into two new saṃghāṭī robes and live with few desires; by cultivating all manner of wholesome qualities, my merit will always support you.

The householder replied, "It is not that I am stingy and refuse to give, but rather my wife previously made a pact with me that she would wear these robes herself and must never give them to anyone else."
Upānanda said: "Householder!
I have heard that you are a virtuous, pure-faithed great man; how could I have known that you would now follow the words of a woman?"
He immediately stepped forward and forcibly pulled out a bundle of leaves; having obtained them, he examined them closely and, turning his hand toward his own face,
asked, "Noble One,
for what reason have you done this?"
He replied:
"You possess the merit of giving, but not the merit of enjoyment; the empty, ruined frame on the rack has no finished robe for use.
If I were to obtain another single bolt of cloth similar to this one, I would use it to make a saṃghāṭī, and your merit would be perfected."
The elder said,
"Would I return while naked?
He replied:
“Householder!

Why rely on external appearances as mere ornaments? Simply take the nature of dispelling stinginess and possessing a sense of shame as your garment. One who lacks a sense of shame is no different from one whose body is exposed, even if they wear clothes; do you have an undergarment?”
The householder said, "There is. [The other replied,] "If that is so,
then all these householders in this city today are wearing undergarments and carrying coarse staffs in their hands, returning at sunset from herding their cattle and livestock."
"You may now also enter the city wearing an undergarment and holding a staff in your hand, following behind another cow; when people see you, they will not find it strange at all."
He then forcibly took down the fine cloth, put on only his undergarment, and was given a staff; he followed the oxen and entered.
The gatekeeper asked:
“Householder!
Previously we saw you leaving the city dressed in fine white cotton cloth; now you have returned bare-bodied—have you perhaps encountered bandits?
The householder replied:
"We did not encounter any other bandits; rather, the venerable Upānanda preached the Dharma to us and forcibly took our robes.
Upon hearing this, the disciples were filled with extreme reproach and derision.
At that time, the householder Anāthapiṇḍada daily led five hundred attendants to pay homage at the feet of the Buddha and the venerable, senior bhikṣus.
Having arrived at the city gate, the gatekeeper said to him,
"Although you have many attendants, you must remain vigilant so that you do not fall prey to thieves.
The householder replied:
"Could there be bandits on the way to the Jeta Grove?
He replied, "O Householder!"
"Though there are no thieves on the road, there is one within the garden.
The elder said, "Ho! You man!"
Your innate nature is as evil as black wool, incapable of being altered; though this path has been constantly traversed by the Buddha and the Saṃgha for many years, you have not turned white.
The gatekeeper replied,
"Householder!
How could I not revere the dust trodden by the feet of the Blessed One, the Sugata, and the community of bhikṣus— dust which I regard as something to be worn upon my head?"

However, yesterday at dawn, there was an elder who, dressed in his upper garments, intended to go to the Jeta Grove; at that time, Upānanda preached the Dharma to him and forcibly took him away, making him enter with the oxen wearing only his undergarments, while he uttered insults and abuse—all of which everyone knows.
Having heard this, the householder thought to himself:
"On account of this, I shall go to the Jeta Grove today.
At that time, Upānanda saw him and said:
"Welcome, householder!
[The Buddha] replied,
"I am not welcome."
Upānanda said, "Previously you had smoke; now the fire has broken out.
The householder replied:
"How can I prevent myself from being consumed by fire?
While other renunciants all seek to abandon greed, the Venerable One's actions only cause my greed to increase further. Upānanda said:
"What have I done? the householder replied,

"Was it not yesterday that someone wished to see the Buddha, and you, for the sake of preaching the Dharma to him, forcibly seized his robe, made him wear only an undergarment, and sent him away following the oxen?"
Upānanda said, "The world says that when the devas delight in giving, the hungry ghosts obstruct them.
The householder replied:
"How could that person possibly pour water from a golden pitcher and offer it as a gift?
Upānanda said, "Householder, do not speak so much;
if you do not accept this, he will establish a rule according to his own whims."
The householder said, "How could I abandon him? He should stay for now!
Upānanda remained silent and stayed.
Then the householder Anāthapiṇḍada went to where the World-Honored One was, prostrated himself at the Buddha’s feet, sat to one side, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

Now these noble ones are seeking robes from householders and their wives who are not their relatives. I only pray that the World-Honored One will provide a reminder for the noble ones, so that they do not seek robes from householders and their wives who are not their relatives.”
At that time, the World-Honored One heard the householder’s words and granted his consent by remaining silent.
Knowing this, the householder prostrated before the Buddha and departed.
On account of these circumstances, the World-Honored One assembled the community of bhikṣus; as extensively described above, he questioned Upānanda, saying:
"Did you indeed beg for robes from a householder or a housewife who is not a relative?
He replied, "It is true."

At that time, after the Blessed One had rebuked Upānanda in various ways, he addressed the bhikṣus at length as previously described, up until: "In the Vinaya, for the sake of the bhikṣus, I shall establish this training rule, which should be recited as follows:
'If a bhikṣu should beg for a robe from a householder or a housewife who is not a relative, it is a naiḥsargika-pāyattika.'"
At that time, the World-Honored One first established the training rule for the bhikṣus while staying at Jetavana.
At that time, there were forty bhikṣus traveling through the countryside who were plundered by bandits and left without any clothing.
At that time, the bhikṣus deliberated together, saying:
"As the Blessed One has ordained:
'It is not permitted to beg for robes from a householder or a householder’s wife who is not one's relative.'"
"I have no kinsmen here; it would be appropriate for me to return to Śrāvastī to seek robes from my fellow practitioners of the holy life.
How can we depart with our bodies exposed?"
They deliberated, saying,
"We shall travel by night and remain hidden during the day.
Thus, they gradually made their way to the temple gate at nightfall.

At that time, the bhikṣu was practicing wakefulness and contemplation during the first and last watches of the night; hearing the sound of a knock at the door, he went out and saw a naked form, and said to him:
"O naked outsider, this is not a place for you to stay."
He said, "Venerable sir!
I am not a non-Buddhist."
“Who are you? “I am a bhikṣu. “Where could there be such a bhikṣu as this?”
"I have been robbed by bandits; what do you intend to do?
He asked, "What is your name?"
“I am one of the forty bhikṣus who have gone for alms.
He replied,
“Welcome, venerable sir!”
He then opened the door for them.

At that time, the bhikṣus vied with one another to provide for their needs, giving some *saṃghāṭī* robes, some *uttarāsaṅga* robes, some *antarvāsaka* robes, some *saṃkakṣikā* robes, *nivāsana* lower garments, *pātra* bowls, and water-strainers.
When daybreak had arrived, the bhikṣus reported the matter to the Buddha.
The Buddha said:
"For this reason, one should exclude other times."
"The exceptions are: if a bhikṣu’s robes have been stolen, lost, burned, blown away, or washed away by water—this is the proper occasion.
At that time, the Blessed One praised the observance of the precepts, and so forth, as explained at length.
He addressed the bhikṣus:
"What was previously established as a formal rule is now further supplemented by this allowance. For the sake of the bhikṣus, I establish this training rule:
'If a bhikṣu should beg for clothing from a householder or a housewife who is not a relative, except at the appropriate times, it is a naiḥsargika-pāyattika offense.'"
"Other times" refers to when a bhikṣu’s robes have been stolen, lost, burned, blown away, or carried off by water; these are the [permissible] times.
"If a bhikṣu" refers to Upānanda; the meaning of "robes" and so forth is as explained above.
"Begging" means to solicit from another.
"Robbed of one's robe" means being plundered by thieves.
"Lost one's robe" means losing it oneself.
"Burnt robes" refers to those burnt by fire.
"Blown-away robes" refers to those carried off by the wind.
"Floated-away robes" refers to those swept away by water.
If there are such difficult circumstances, one may request that there be no offense; otherwise, at the moment [the item] is obtained, one incurs the offense of *naiḥsargika-pāyattika*.
What are the characteristics of the offense in this case?
There are three types of matters:
This refers to price, color, and quantity. Regarding price:

if a bhikṣu, without being under duress, begs from a non-relative for a robe worth one *kārsāpaṇa*—the meaning of *kārsāpaṇa* having already been explained above in the section on the precept against taking what is not given—if he obtains a robe worth one *kārsāpaṇa*, there is an *dukkaṭa* (wrongdoing) at the time of begging, and a *nissaggiya pācittiya* (offense involving forfeiture) upon obtaining it.
In this manner, the number increases up to fifty *kārsāpaṇas*; the gravity of the offense in each case of begging and receiving should be understood according to the above principles.

If a bhikṣu begs from a non-relative for a robe worth one *kārsāpaṇa* and receives a robe worth two *kārsāpaṇas*, there is an *duṣkṛta* (wrongdoing) at the time of begging, but no offense at the time of receipt.
In this manner, up to fifty *kāṛṣāpaṇas* and so forth, one should understand that whether there is an offense or no offense when begging for little and receiving much follows the same principle.
Regarding color: if a bhikṣu begs from another for a garment of blue color and receives a blue garment in return.
When begging for it, one incurs a *duṣkṛta* offense; when obtaining it, one incurs a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika*.
As it is with blue, so it should be understood for yellow, red, and white, as well as for thick and thin fabrics.
If a bhikṣu requests a robe of blue color and receives one that is yellow, there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*) at the time of the request, but no offense at the time of receipt.
It should be understood that the same applies when other colors or thicknesses are mutually compared in this manner.

Regarding the measure: if a bhikṣu begs for a five-cubit garment from another and receives exactly five cubits, there is an *duṣkṛta* offense at the time of begging and a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* offense upon receipt.
Or, if he begs for five and receives ten, or even fifty, and so forth, it should be understood according to the above principle.
These are called the three matters.
If one asks for thread and receives a small piece, or if one asks for a small piece and the other gives a wide garment, there is no offense in either case.
Furthermore, there is no offense for the first offender, or for one who is insane, mentally deranged, or overwhelmed by intense pain.
The Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya, Volume Nineteen.
The Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya, Volume Twenty.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Yijing by Imperial Command. 7.

The Training Rule on Begging for Excess Clothing. The Seventh Training Rule on Begging for Excess Clothing. At that time, the Blessed One was staying in Śrāvastī at the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, Upānanda thought to himself:
"In all places where we seek our livelihood, it is solely due to the request of the householder Anāthapiṇḍada that the World-Honored One has established these rules of training."
"We have not even been able to obtain a small cloth towel through our humble requests, let alone a large one.

However, it may be that the Buddha, the World-Honored One, has made a special allowance because bhikṣus of few desires lack clothing. We should now seek out those of few desires to rely upon; perhaps by means of them, we may obtain something."
He immediately sought that person everywhere, yet despite his diligent search, he was unable to find him.
Someone informed him, saying:
"In an araṇya there dwell a community of forty bhikṣus who abide in fewness of desires."
He then went to that tranquil forest grove and saw a group of forty bhikṣus who were undergoing great hardship while mending their tattered robes.
At that time, Upānanda said to the bhikṣus:
"Venerable ones!..."

What I have heard does not accord with what I see. I had thought that you, the forty members of the assembly of bhikṣus, were dwelling in an araṇya, enjoying the supreme bliss of various dhyānas and liberations; how could I have known that you would be here, merely struggling with the hardship of mending tattered robes and having distracted minds?
The bhikṣus said,
"Venerable sir!
We have been plundered by bandits."
Upānanda said, "This is an unwholesome matter;
it will cause one to undergo extreme hardship.
The bhikṣus said:
"Venerable sir,
why do you appear so sorrowful? Upānanda replied:
"I do not worry about you, my virtuous friend; rather, I pity that thief who, driven by greed, has committed this wrongful act of robbery. After casting off this body, he shall surely fall into hell;
even if he should later obtain a human birth, he will receive the retribution of poverty."
"Venerable ones!
As the Blessed One has said:

'O bhikṣus, if a person, through the power of repeatedly practicing theft, shall after the end of life be born in hell to undergo various sufferings; even if they should obtain human birth, they will lack clothing and food.'"
"It is for this reason that I uttered words of sorrow.
However, venerable sirs!
You labor in vain with such hardship sewing these tattered rags; why do you not beg for new, fine cotton cloth?"
The people replied,
"Who would abandon the Three Jewels, the most excellent field of merit, to be so willing to give to us, mere paupers?
They reported this.
"Venerable ones!
The Blessed One praises your fewness of desires and contentment in every place.
Those with faith all delight in making offerings to you; why do you not go out to beg?"
He replied,
"Where do you wish to go to beg for robes? Upānanda said:
"If there is no place to beg, why not seek out someone who can exhort and convert others?
Such a person will be able to obtain clothing for you with ease.
He replied:
"Where could there be a virtuous bhikṣu recognized by all who would abandon his own wholesome qualities to seek on our behalf?
Upānanda said, "Each of us in the group of six bhikṣus has nine disciples, making sixty people in total; we shall together seek clothing for you."
"If you do not oppose me and comply with my wishes, our disciples will also obtain some clothing as a result.
He replied,
"What opposition could there be to us obtaining clothing together?"
Upānanda said, "How could we possibly go out to beg for alms ourselves and also search for robes?
If you can obtain a full meal without much hardship, I shall seek a robe for you."
The people replied, "This too is excellent!
Then, having returned to the monastery, Upānanda washed his feet and proceeded; once he had entered his cell, he reflected:
"What skillful means can I employ to convert everyone within this city, with the sole exception that the householder Anāthapiṇḍada does not enter his home?

If he were to see me, he would always harbor anger toward me; therefore, I should now first go to the houses of the poor, next proceed to the homes of the wealthy, and afterwards go to the residence of King Prasenajit, as well as to the houses of Queen Vārṣākārī, Queen Vaidehī, the householder Śroṇakoṭiviṃśa, the old lay devotee, the mother of Viśākhā, and the couple Sujāta."
Thus he went from place to place begging in succession.
At that time, a householder invited the Buddha and the Saṃgha to a meal at his home. Upon seeing this, Upānanda had a thought and said to his disciples:
"Venerable ones!..."
"Tomorrow, even if the monastic community assigns you tasks or labor, you must not accept them.
They replied,
"Our two teachers have few such duties for us."
When the next day arrived, he sent a disciple to summon the assembly of forty bhikṣus, saying:
"Venerable sirs, you may come; I wish to seek robes for you.
When the messenger reached them, he saw that all the bhikṣus were absorbed in meditative concentration (samādhi), and the messenger thought to himself:
"Who could harbor such a coarse and violent mind as to disregard the future life and cause one who is absorbed in meditative concentration to be startled awake by a physical touch?
He then returned to Upānanda and reported, "Ācārya!..."
"They have all entered meditative absorption; who could possibly startle them awake?
At that time, Upānanda said in anger: "Foolish and witless man!
Even if you now perform such a sincere act as this, how could it ever exhaust all the afflictions?"
He then went in person to the Hall of Meditative Concentration; as he stepped upon the door, the entire hall shook.
He rose from his meditation and asked, "Venerable sir, what is the meaning of this?"
He replied, "You forty people seek clothing; for what reason do you remain sitting here, neglecting your affairs?
Come, let us go together."
He replied, "Please wait a moment until I have finished chewing my tooth-stick. Upānanda said:
"You may come; we shall chew it together halfway.
The forty bhikṣus then followed him.
Upānanda then held a discussion with his own disciples, saying:
"Venerable friends!
We Six Groups are like white elephants; wherever we go, people flock there in competition.
We should not proceed as a crowd according to seniority, whether old or young; rather, we should travel separately, interspersing ourselves before and behind."

They then proceeded according to their plan; having traveled halfway and finished chewing their tooth-sticks, they entered the city of Śrāvastī and stayed together in a crowded area within the quarter of the poor.
The shopkeeper asked,
"Noble one!
Do you have some cause for sorrow today?"
He replied, "I have a matter of concern. Have you heard that there is a group of forty bhikṣus whom the Buddha has praised and extolled everywhere for their fewness of desires and contentment?"
He replied, "I have heard it. Upānanda said:
"This is that very man; his clothes have all been plundered by bandits.
Upon hearing this, the shopkeepers spoke to one another:
"Gentlemen, you should all take up bows, swords, shields, spears, and the like, and together seize the bandits."
The group of six monks replied, "It has been a long time since the robbery occurred; the thieves have scattered to other regions.
The people said:
"What do I wish to do?
The group of six replied,
"You may give away your robes."
Thereupon, those people immediately gathered their new and old cotton cloths (*kārpāsa*) and offered them as gifts.
At that time, the group of six [monks] bundled them into a large load and had several youths carry it back to the monastery.
Next, he went to where a group of wealthy people were gathered together and stood among them. They questioned him as before, and he answered as before.
Each of the men took a garment of high value and offered it to him as a gift, but he again had them return them to the monastery.
Next, they went to King Prasenajit’s location and stood gathered together. When the king saw them and questioned them, their reply was the same as before.
The king then commanded Virūḍhaka, saying:
"You should now assemble all the generals and go immediately to capture that rebel army."
The group of six monks replied, “It has been a long time since the robbery occurred; the bandits have dispersed to other lands.
The king said:
"If that is so, what do you holy ones intend to do?
The group of six replied,
"We shall give him a robe."
Then King Prasenajit immediately provided each person with thirteen sets of requisites and exquisite garments; at that time, the group of six monks had their disciples carry them away just as before.
At that time, the assembly of forty bhikṣus said to Upānanda, "Venerable One!
Considering the robes we have already obtained, we are fully provided for; do not seek any more."
Upānanda replied: "Venerable ones!
You are all people of indolence; do you not remember our previous agreement?"
"If you do not object to this, I shall likewise, on this account, seek some clothing for my disciples.
Why are you content with yourself and yet unwilling to seek more?
When the bhikṣus heard this, they all remained silent.

Thereupon, the group of six bhikṣus took him to the residences of Queen Vārṣākāra, Queen Vaidehī, the former acquaintance Amṛtodana, the mother of Viśākhā, and the couple Sūjāta; in each case, the questions and answers were exactly as described above.
At that time, they all provided them with the thirteen monastic requisites and exquisite garments, instructing their disciples to carry the clothing they had obtained back to the monastery.
Then the group of six monks said to the people:

"Yesterday, the World-Honored One accepted invitations for meals from various patrons along with the bhikṣus. If there were even a few hundred seats missing from the dining rows, the procession would appear sparse and the donors would surely find it strange. You should go and fill those dining rows, and you must also deliver our alms-food bowls."

Then, after those six groups of monks had sent away their attendants, they went themselves to the monastery, selected their upper robes, and set them aside; they then divided their old, tattered robes into forty portions.
At that time, after the forty people had finished their meal at the invitation and returned to the monastery, the six groups of monks, having finished eating, said to their disciples:
"You may call the forty people of few desires here."
They all came to him, and Upānanda said,
"Venerable sirs!
Am I your keeper of robes?"
"You should each take a robe.
Seeing their tattered robes, they looked at one another, and the group of six addressed them, saying,
"Why are you two looking at each other?"
He replied, "For what reason are all these given as tattered garments? Upānanda said:

"If these [robes] are used by layering them to make a *saṃghāṭī*, or by sewing them to make an *uttarāsaṅga* and an *antarvāsaka* or *saṃkakṣikā*, they will be sufficient for one's needs; why do you find fault with this?"
"If you are not satisfied, you may follow me and beg further.
He replied, "I have already obtained what is sufficient; do not seek anything more."
Thereupon, each of them took these tattered robes to a forest hermitage (araṇya) and mended them according to their needs.
Throughout the city and its environs, everyone heard the news that the assembly of forty bhikṣus, as well as the king and all the people, had obtained the thirteen requisites at all seven locations.
At that time, there was a bhikṣu who went to an araṇya and saw several bhikṣus, each of whom was diligently mending torn robes. He addressed them, saying:
"Venerable ones!..."
"What I have heard does not accord with what I see.
A bhikṣu in the forest asked,
"What is the meaning of these words?"
He replied, "I have heard that you venerable ones have obtained all thirteen types of requisites; for what reason, then, do you now still sew together tattered garments?
The bhikṣus replied:
“You have merely heard of it with your ears; I myself have borne it upon my shoulders.
“If that is so, where did you obtain these tattered robes?
At that time, the bhikṣus related the circumstances in full.
Upon hearing this, the bhikṣus felt extreme revulsion and contempt; they went to their residence and informed the other bhikṣus, who then reported the matter to the Buddha.
The Buddha addressed the bhikṣus and questioned the assembly of forty bhikṣus, saying:
"Is it true that you accept the gifts of others without knowing contentment?"
“It is truly so, World-Honored One!

At that time, the World-Honored One rebuked him in various ways for failing to accord with correct principle and for his lack of mental tranquility; he praised and extolled those who accord with principle and are well-disciplined. He spoke at length, even unto: “For the sake of the bhikṣus, I shall establish a training rule (śikṣāpada) in the Vinaya, which should be spoken thus:”
Furthermore, if a bhikṣu has had his robes taken away, lost, burned, blown away, or carried off by water, he may beg for robes from a householder or a householder’s wife who is not a relative.

If that person offers many robes and a bhikṣu requires them, he should accept two robes, one for the upper body and one for the lower body. If he accepts more than this, it constitutes a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* offense.
The textual passages concerning the confiscation of robes and so forth are all as stated above.
Regarding those who should receive the two garments, upper and lower, there are two types of such garments:
first, the upper and lower robes of a bhikṣu;
second, the upper and lower garments of a layperson.
Regarding the "upper and lower" robes of a bhikṣu: if it is a new garment, one should make the saṃghāṭī double-layered, with three vertical strips and five horizontal strips.
As for the nivāsana:
Two vertical and five horizontal [units].
For laypeople, the upper garment is twelve cubits long and three cubits wide;
the lower garment is seven cubits long and two cubits wide.
"Should receive" means to accept with a deliberate mind.
"If one receives in excess" means exceeding the aforementioned number.
At the moment one obtains the robe through begging, one commits an offense of forfeiture (naiḥsargika-pāyattika). The definition of "forfeiture and confession" is as explained extensively before.
Regarding this, what are the characteristics of the offense and how does it occur?
If a bhikṣu begs for a layperson’s upper and lower robes from another, he may obtain them according to the prescribed measure.
If he begs for more than that, he incurs a duṣkṛta offense; once he has obtained them, he incurs a naiḥsargika-pāyattika offense.
If one begs for the upper and lower robes of a bhikṣu, the matter is treated in the same way.

If one begs from a layperson for their upper and lower robes, even if they are smaller than the standard lay measurement, one should not beg for more; if there is any excess, it must be returned to the owner.
When begging for a bhikṣu’s upper and lower robes from another, if they are insufficient to meet the standard measure for a bhikṣu’s robes, one should beg for more;
if there is any excess, it should be returned to the donor.

If one asks for more secular clothing when one already possesses some, or if a bhikṣu has extra robes that he does not return, the gravity of the offense should be understood according to the specific circumstances.
If one originally intends to ask for more than allowed, one incurs a *duṣkṛta* (wrongdoing) at the time of requesting;
once the object is obtained, one commits a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* (offense involving forfeiture).
If, after having committed an offense involving forfeiture (*naiḥsargika-pāyattika*), one further acquires other items, all are likewise offenses; this is explained in detail as before.
Furthermore, there is no offense for the very first offender, or for one who is insane, mentally deranged, or overwhelmed by intense pain.

8. The Training Rule on Begging for Robes from a Layperson Who Has Offered Them. The eighth training rule concerning begging for robes from a layperson who has offered them. The Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
In this city there was an elder who, while already having his own wife, committed illicit acts with another woman.
His wife said to him, "Venerable sir, you ought not to commit such an illicit act."
Although his wife repeatedly admonished her husband, he did not follow her words; she became resentful and jealous, and began to engage in secret unions with other men.
Her husband constantly gave household goods to that illicit mistress, and his wife likewise gave household goods to that unfaithful husband.
The husband and wife exhausted their wealth until almost nothing remained.
By nature, the elder was violent and cruel; he beat his maidservants, constantly giving them tattered clothes and poor food, and scolded her, saying:
"It is because of you that my family's assets have been squandered."
The maidservant said,
"I have indeed known for a long time the reason for this dissolution.
However, as both are the masters of the house, I did not dare speak out."
At that time, the husband and wife, realizing the maidservant had been mocking them, both felt ashamed and remained silent.
When Upānanda learned of this matter, he went to the house of that elder and, for the sake of the couple, disparaged those who break the precepts and praised those who uphold them, saying:
"Good sons!..."
"Good woman!
As the Buddha has taught, those who engage in sexual misconduct will fall into hell after their lives end;
even if they should obtain human birth, their wives will not be chaste and faithful, and their husbands will harbor illicit thoughts."
"If one abstains from sexual misconduct, after the end of this life one will be reborn in the heavens;
if one is reborn among humans, one's spouse will be chaste and virtuous, and the husband will harbor no illicit thoughts.
He then spoke these verses:
"By hearing, one can know the Dharma; by hearing the Dharma, one leaves behind all faults;
by hearing the Dharma, one abandons evil friends; by hearing the Dharma, one attains Nirvāṇa.

When the husband and wife had heard the Dharma, they both abandoned their wrong conduct. Then Upānanda further explained to the couple at length the preeminent merits of taking refuge and paying homage, and said:
“You two should listen even more carefully!
As the Buddha has said:
‘Those who take refuge in the Buddha shall not fall into the evil realms.’”
Having cast off this human body, one shall be reborn in the heavens.
Those who take refuge in the Dharma will not fall into the evil realms;
having cast off this human body, they shall be reborn in the heavens.
"If one takes refuge in the Saṃgha, one will not fall into the evil realms;
having cast off this human body, one shall be reborn in the heavens.
At that time, those two men, hearing the Dharma with joy, conceived deep pure faith and immediately took refuge in the Triple Gem.
Furthermore, he praised the merits of the five precepts, saying: "Listen well:
as the Buddha has taught, there are five kinds of great giving."
What are these five? They are:
abstaining from killing, stealing, sexual misconduct, false speech, and drinking intoxicants; these constitute the five kinds of great giving.
For what reason is the renunciation of these five things called "great giving"?

Because by renouncing these five, one attains fearlessness and is free from all enmity and fetters; one's wife becomes chaste and virtuous, one's words are trusted and accepted, and one is never arrogant or dissolute.
"Because of these five [factors], one experiences immeasurable happiness and constantly dwells among humans and devas; therefore, it is called 'the great gift.
When those two men heard this Dharma, their deep faith redoubled, and they accepted the five precepts.
After Upānanda had caused those two to take the precepts of refuge, he abandoned them and departed.
Later, on another day, that householder again beat his maidservant with cruel punishment, whereupon his wife said:
"O Noble One!..."
"Previously, when I did not yet understand the ripening of karmic results, I constantly inflicted suffering and torture.
Now, through the holy Upānanda as my spiritual friend, I have come to recognize the maturation of karma; therefore, I should no longer inflict such suffering."
"However, as all people in the world receive the retribution of their own karma, there is no constancy in status—noble or base—who among them is truly a slave?
From this day forward, do not inflict corporal punishment.
The husband said:
"O virtuous one! Well said," she said,
and then commanded her maidservant:
“Little girl!
You may bathe and be given new clothes. He said:
"You must diligently attend to your household duties, and we shall grant you fearlessness.
The maidservant thought to herself:

"These two heads of the household were formerly both unkind; they delighted in inflicting punishments and tormented me with cruelty. Even coarse clothing and poor food did not suffice for my body. Now, their kindness and compassion are equal to those of my own parents."
He further reflected:
"Ever since the noble Upānanda entered this house, you have nurtured me with a benevolent heart and no longer struck me; what gift can I now offer to repay the noble one's kindness?"

If one were to steal a small amount of property from within the household in order to repay a kindness, the master of the house, upon discovering it, would undergo the same suffering as before; since there would be no way to recover the loss, he would only harbor a sense of shame.
Later, on another occasion, when Upānanda came and preached the Dharma to the husband and wife before departing, the householder’s wife said to her husband:

"Do you not know that the Venerable Upānanda is our spiritual friend? He has caused us to abandon evil deeds and abide in wholesome qualities; we have taken refuge in the Triple Gem and received the five precepts, and he further bestows the Dharma upon us from time to time."
"We ought to offer you some amount.
The elder asked,
"What do you wish to do?"
The wife said,
"Give her one white cotton shawl.
Upon hearing this, the maidservant thought to herself:
"I shall accept this speech as my repayment to the Noble One!
Then, at dawn, Upānanda entered the city and went from house to house for alms until he reached the house of the elder. When the maidservant saw him, she prostrated at his feet and said, "Noble One!"
I have some kind words I wish to offer you in return.
He asked, “What matters?”
The maidservant said,
"The householder and his wife wish to take this upper garment and offer it to the Venerable One!
Upon hearing this, Upānanda thought to himself:
"I shall count all those gluttonous people in the world; now that I have heard this gain of profit, it truly accords with my own heart.
Nevertheless, although this servant has spoken these words, I shall further interrogate him."
He then assumed an expression of anger and replied:
"Little girl!
For what reason have you suddenly been playing with me?"
He replied, "Noble One!
How could I dare deceive you?"
Upānanda replied, “Little girl! If what you say is true,
even if the head of the household should become angry, I shall intercede on your behalf to secure his forgiveness.”
"If it is false, I shall give you many lashes,
just as on previous occasions. He replied, "Noble One!"
"What is it that you must doubt?
Just enter the house and you shall know for yourself.
Then Upānanda entered his dwelling.
When the husband and wife saw him, they called out, "Welcome! They prepared a seat for him to sit upon; once he had prostrated at his feet, they took low seats and knelt to listen to the Dharma.
Having taught them the Dharma, he said:
"Householder, you promised me a large woolen blanket; I wish to see it now."
At that time, the husband and wife looked at one another. Seeing this, Upānanda asked, "Why are you two looking at each other like this?
They both replied:
"Noble One!
These were our private words spoken in secret; who would have informed you?
Could it be that the Noble One reads the minds of others?"
Upānanda said, "Since my youth I have maintained the alms-bowl and begged for food;
my teeth have fallen out and my hair has turned white—do you not believe me regarding such a minor matter as this?"
Then the householder presented him with the robe.
Having received it, Upānanda examined it thoroughly from all sides, then turned it over in his hands, his face wearing an expression of sorrow.
The householder asked,
"Noble One!
What is the reason for this?"
He replied, "Householder!

You possess the merit of giving, but not the merit of enjoyment; it is only fit for wiping shoes or for use as a curtain or window shade, for if placed upon a clothesline, it will naturally fall apart."
The householder asked,
"What do you wish to do?
He replied:
"Seek out something better to give me for making a robe.
He replied, "Noble one!"
"There is nothing more to be obtained. He replied,
"You may buy it and give it to me."
He replied, "I have no price.
The other said:
"Let us buy it on credit and we shall repay the price later.
At that time, the elder looked at his wife's face, and she said, "The noble Upānanda has truly shown us great kindness; you should purchase the robe for him so that his wishes may be fulfilled."
Then that householder took Upānanda with him to the marketplace and approached a shop;
thereupon Upānanda thought to himself, "I shall cause the shopkeeper to become conceited so that he will produce high-quality garments."
He replied to the householder, “Looking briefly at this shop, it appears that most of its patrons are poor people; how could they possibly possess such high-quality white cotton cloth?
You should seek it elsewhere.”
At that time, having heard these words, the shopkeeper gave rise to pride and brought out fine, high-quality cloth, saying:
"Noble One! Why do you slight me?"
"Look at this bundle.
Upānanda said, "It is truly a fine thing; what is its price?"
The merchant replied,
“It is worth fifty kārṣāpaṇas. Upānanda said:
"I shall take thirty.
The merchant said,
"Who will pay the price?"
He replied, "I shall return it to you, householder.
He then asked the householder:
"When will you give it?
The householder replied,
"I shall give it at such-and-such a time."
The merchant said,
“Excellent!
Take it as you please.”
The householder then handed it over to Upānanda.
Upānanda replied: "May the householder be free from illness and long-lived.
This gift you have now bestowed is an ornament for the mind and a support for the mind; adorned with concentration and wisdom, it leads one to the paths of gods and humans."
...and so forth, as extensively explained.
Upānanda then took this cloth and went to the Jetavana.
Because the householder was poor and unable to repay the price of the cloth on time, the merchant consequently stationed him in the scorching sun and would not let him leave.
A friend saw him and asked,
"For what reason are you standing in the middle of the sun?
Are you suffering from malaria, or have you been taking ghee?"
He replied, "I am not suffering from malaria, nor do I take ghee; I stand here because a debt has long remained unpaid. He asked:
"When did you incur this debt?
Did your grandfather owe someone a debt?
He replied:

"Because I conceived a heart of reverence and faith toward the son of the Śākyas, I offered him this robe, which he loathed and would not accept, forcing me to undergo this hardship of having to purchase a superior one."
When his friends heard of this matter, they immediately began to criticize him,
saying, "The śramaṇas, sons of the Śākyas, are insatiable in their greed.
When the bhikṣus heard this, they went in full detail to report the matter to the Blessed One.
For this reason, the Blessed One assembled the community of bhikṣus and spoke at length, until he addressed Upānanda, saying:
"Is it true that you have committed such an unseemly act, lacking contentment with whatever others offer, and further seeking fine things so as to cause them hardship?"
He replied, “It is truly so.
The World-Honored One, having rebuked him in various ways as before, addressed the bhikṣus:
"I now establish a training rule for my disciples within the Vinaya, which should be recited as follows:

'If a monk has a householder or a housewife who is not a relative, and they together provide the price for a robe, intending to purchase such a pure robe to give to a certain monk for him to use at the proper time.'"
This bhikṣu, having not previously received an invitation, upon being informed by another, went to that person's house and spoke these words: "Excellent!
O worthy one, you have prepared the price for a robe on my behalf; you may purchase such a pure robe and give it to me in a timely manner, so that it may be of good quality."
"If he obtains the robe, it is a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* offense.
"If a bhikṣu" refers to Upānanda. "One's own relative or one who is not a relative," and so forth, has the same meaning as explained above.
Regarding "the price of a robe," this refers to gold, silver, cowries, and so forth.
"Procuring" means storing or accumulating.
"Such a robe" refers to the seven types mentioned above.
"Buying" means purchasing from another.
"Pure" refers to obtaining such a robe as is fit for use.
"Giving" refers to the time when the robe is offered.
"Such-and-such a person" refers to Upānanda.
"Not having accepted the invitation" means he had not previously given his consent.
"Because another informed him, etc. means that seeing another person mention going there to seek robes, he forcibly demanded their price for the sake of obtaining something superior.
If one obtains the robe, one commits an offense of forfeiture and expiation (*naiḥsargika-pāyattika*).
What are the characteristics of this offense?
There are three types of cases:
This refers to price, color, and quantity.
What is meant by "price"?
If a bhikṣu obtains a robe worth five kārṣāpaṇas from a person who is not a relative, there is no offense at the time of receiving it.
If one does not accept this robe but seeks more than that, at the time of seeking, one commits an *dukkaṭa* offense; at the time of obtaining it, one commits a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* offense.
This applies even up to fifty *kārsāpaṇas*; whether seeking or obtaining, the gravity of the offense should be understood according to the above principles. This is what is meant by "price."
What constitutes the offense regarding color?

If a bhikṣu receives a blue-colored robe, there is no offense at the time of receiving it; however, if he does not receive this robe and subsequently requests one that exceeds [the permitted limit], there is an *dukkaṭa* (offense of wrong-doing) at the time of requesting it, and he incurs a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* (offense involving forfeiture) at the time of obtaining it.
Just as it is with blue, so it should be understood for all other colors accordingly; this is what is called "color.
What constitutes the measure?

If a bhikṣu receives a robe of five cubits in length, there is no offense. However, if he does not accept this robe and further requests one exceeding that size, he incurs an offense as previously described.
In this manner, even up to many cubits (*hasta*), the gravity of the offense is the same as previously described; this is what is meant by "measure.
The procedure for relinquishing these *naiḥsargika* robes is also the same as before.

There is no offense in the following cases: if one asks for thread or cotton and receives only a small fragment; or if one asks for a small fragment and the other gives a large robe—these are all without offense.
Furthermore, there is no offense for a first-time offender, or one who is insane, mentally deranged, or afflicted by intense physical pain.

9. The Training Rule Concerning Begging for a Robe from a Layperson Who Has Specifically Offered One. The ninth training rule concerning begging for a robe from a layperson who has specifically offered one. The Buddha was staying at Jetavana.

At that time, the bhikṣu Upānanda gave rise to the causes and conditions for transgression; the elder and his wife each had illicit affairs with outsiders. Consequently, he preached the Dharma to them so that they might abandon evil and cultivate goodness, and the circumstances were identical to those previously described.

The only difference was that two individuals had each provided the price for a robe; they caused those two prices to be combined into a single robe, which resulted in the elder undergoing great hardship.
The bhikṣu reported this matter to the Buddha, and so forth, until [the Buddha] established a training rule (*śikṣāpada*), which should be recited as follows:

"If a bhikṣu has a householder or a householder’s wife who is not a relative, and each intends to provide the price for a robe for the sake of that bhikṣu, saying, 'With these funds, buy such a pure robe and give it to a certain bhikṣu.'"
This bhikṣu, having not previously received an invitation, upon being informed by another, went to that person's house and spoke these words: "Excellent!
O worthy one, you may purchase such pure robes together with me; give them to me in a timely manner for the sake of their quality."
"If one obtains a robe [under such circumstances], it is a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika*.
Regarding this, the three types of transgressions are as previously explained.
The Tenth Rule on Soliciting Robes Beyond the Limit. The Buddha was staying at the Bamboo Grove Monastery in Rājagṛha.
At that time, Upānanda thought to himself:
"In all matters where we have sought instruction, it has been due to the request of the householder Anāthapiṇḍada that the World-Honored One has established these rules of training."
"We have not even been able to obtain a small cloth towel by begging for it; how much less a large one?
However, in the past, I studied under the same teacher as the brahmin Varṣākāra in the same schoolhouse. I should go to see him; perhaps he will grant me some clothing."
He then proceeded to that residence, but the doorkeeper stopped him, saying:
"Noble One, do not enter.
He replied:
“O worthy one!

The World-Honored One has prohibited me from going to five types of places: the homes of those who proclaim edicts, brothels, taverns, royal palaces, and butcher shops. Are these houses among those five places?”
The disciple replied,
"Venerable One!
Why must you engage in such excessive derision?"
"This is not the house of a courtesan or the like where one might call out for alms;
rather, it is the residence of the brahmin Varṣākāra. He said to the gatekeeper, "O man!"
"You should enter the house and inform the brahmin, saying:
'The venerable Upānanda is now outside the gate and wishes to see you.
The gatekeeper said:
"Judging by his demeanor, it seems he has come from the court of King Prasenajit.
He replied, "Fool!
"It would be well if you were to report this;
if you delay further, I shall certainly cause you to suffer the punishment of a heavy staff.
The disciple thought to himself:
"Observing his demeanor, he is entirely without fear; unlike others, there must be a reason for this, so we should inform him and not let him suffer humiliation.
He then entered and reported:
"The Venerable Upānanda is now outside the gate, saying that he must see you."
The brahmin said, "Call the Venerable One in; who would dare to obstruct him?
Having heard this, the gatekeeper thought to himself:
“For this reason, the eminent śramaṇa has no fear at all.
He then called him inside.

Upon seeing him, the brāhmaṇa cried out from afar, “Welcome! He prepared a seat and invited him to sit. Once he was seated, [the śramaṇa] uttered a beautiful voice, praising the sublime merit of the gate of giving.
If Upānanda, with a joyful mind, praises the act of giving, those faithful brahmins and others who are listening to the Dharma will think:
"How excellent is this sublime Dharma!"
"We ought to cut off our own flesh and offer it as a gift.
When the brahmin heard this Dharma teaching, he was filled with joy and spoke these words:
"Virtuous ones, on the day your summer retreat concludes, I shall respectfully offer you sixty gold coins."
Upānanda said, "Worthy one!
May you be free from illness and long-lived."
He then offered a blessing for her:
"May this gift you have now bestowed serve as an ornament for the mind, leading even unto peaceful Nirvana.
Having spoken thus, he took his leave and departed.
At that time, two bhikṣus traveled from Śrāvastī to Rājagṛha and went to the Bamboo Grove in order to pay homage to the Buddha.
Then the World-Honored One addressed the Venerable Ānanda, saying:
"You should now go and inform the bhikṣus: [as follows]"
“The Tathāgata wishes to travel to the human realm of Kośala to wander there; if there are any sentient beings who wish to follow him, they should prepare their robes.
Then Ānanda, having received these instructions, departed and informed the bhikṣus, proclaiming the World-Honored One’s teaching.
When the two newly arrived bhikṣus heard these words, they remained there with anxious hearts.
Upānanda asked them,
"You two youths, for what reason do you harbor such anxiety?"
The two of them replied:
"The Venerable Ānanda has informed the bhikṣus:
'The Tathāgata intends to travel among the people of Kośala; those who wish to go should prepare their robes.'"
"O Venerable One!
I have only just arrived and have not yet rested; how could I go further to Śrāvastī?
When Upānanda heard this, he became distressed and thought to himself:
"I have only received a meager gift after a long time; how could I have known that further obstacles would arise?
When morning came, he went at once to the house of the brahmin. Upon arrival, he took his seat and, with a voice full of sorrow and dejection, spoke of the merit of giving.
Then the brahmin asked, "Venerable One!
Previously your preaching of the Dharma was with such exquisite and beautiful tones, yet now your countenance seems clouded with sorrow and your voice is low; I pray you tell me the reason for this."
Upānanda said, "Worthy sir!
It has been a long time since we last met, and now before long we must part."
Having spoken these words, he remained there filled with anxiety. As the worldly saying goes:
"The people of Magadha understand by hearing the sound; those of Kośala know by seeing the form.
Those of Pañcāla understand from half a word; the people of other bordering kingdoms only comprehend after the speech is finished."
When the brahmin Vassakāra heard what Upānanda said, he thought to himself:
"He does not feel grief at our separation; he is merely distressed because of those sixty gold coins."
He replied,
"Venerable sir!
Wherever you may complete your *varṣā* retreat, I shall present you with sixty gold coins."
Upānanda said, "O worthy one!
May you be free from illness and long-lived."
"Excellent!
Your resolve in giving is firm from beginning to end; the merit you have performed shall surely bring forth a supreme fruit.
Having said this, he took his leave and departed.
At that time, the World-Honored One was surrounded by a great assembly, as described at length elsewhere; he traveled to Śrāvastī in Kośala and resided in the Jetavana Grove.
At that time, there was a merchant who departed from this city, taking various goods with him to travel toward Rājagṛha.

However, it was the ancient custom of Rājagṛha that whenever a great caravan of merchants arrived from another land, the king himself would inspect their taxes or delegate this task to the minister Vṛṣṭika.
At that time, Vassakāra examined the goods for customs duties and said to the merchant:
"If you return to Śrāvastī, you must inform me.
He replied: [as requested].
"So be it. Having finished his trade, the merchant went to the minister's residence and reported:
"I wish to return to my country."
He immediately gave him sixty coins and said,
"Take these goods and give them to the Venerable Upānanda.
Having accepted the items, he thought to himself:

"If he has been acquainted with the minister Vārṣaka in the past, he must certainly be a virtuous bhikṣu well-known to the public; I shall provide him with some small benefit to inspire his joy, and you may purchase fine cotton cloth and take it to that city."
He went to the Bamboo Grove and asked the bhikṣus,
"Which of these folded robes is suitable for a bhikṣu to wear?
The bhikṣus replied:
“O noble one!
Do you now intend to give a robe to the Saṃgha?
He replied:

"I have no leisure to give; however, the minister Caraka has sent sixty gold coins to me for the Venerable Upānanda. I now wish to purchase some cotton cloth with these coins and take it away, hoping to satisfy his wishes."
The bhikṣus said,
"You shall certainly now have to pay for the white cotton cloth and the gold coins.
The merchant thought to himself:
"Now this bhikṣu may have a grievance or enmity with him.
Thereupon, he went again to other bhikṣus and related the previous matter in detail.
The bhikṣus replied, "If you take it away without having had the gold coins sealed, he will certainly demand interest."
The merchant then thought to himself, "Since their words agree with one another, I must take precautions.
He went to the minister’s residence and requested that he affix his seal; the minister said:
"I now believe you; why trouble yourself with a seal?
The merchant said, "Though I place my trust in you, the law of merchants requires that matters be examined with great care."
Then the minister immediately affixed his seal and signature.
The merchant took it with him to Śrāvastī and went to the Jetavana Grove, where he asked the bhikṣus,
"Noble ones!..."
"Where is the room of Upānanda?
At that time, the bhikṣus showed him the location.
He went there but did not see him, and asked the bhikṣus:
"Venerable Upānanda, where are you going now?
He replied,
"I am going briefly to a quiet place outside the monastery."
The merchant replied, "This gold coin was entrusted by Varṣākāra, the minister of Rājagṛha; you may take it for him, and he shall give it to you when he arrives."
The bhikṣu replied:
"O worthy one!
Have you ever seen anyone with their head struck by a blazing torch emitting flames?"
The merchant then thought to himself,
"This man must surely have had some prior enmity with him.
He immediately went to other bhikṣus and said:
"Venerable sir!
These gold coins were entrusted to you by the minister Vassakāra of Rājagaha to be given to Upāli.
You may accept them; he will come and claim them."
The bhikṣus said, "If he brings it here without having it sealed, he will certainly demand interest from you; who could possibly accept such an item on his behalf?"
"I have entrusted it to you in person.
The merchant thought to himself:
"What he says is consistent; this must certainly be a difficult situation."
"I shall wait for that bhikṣu at my home; I myself will know how to respond.
He then informed the bhikṣu, saying, "If Upānanda returns here, you may inform him that I am at such-and-such a place; if he has need of anything, he must come and take it."
Having spoken thus, he departed.
Later, when Upānanda arrived at the monastery, the bhikṣus said to him,
"Venerable Upānanda!"
Excellent!
The World-Honored One has spoken thus:
"If one possesses virtuous conduct and a pure mind, whatever one wishes for will be accomplished according to one's heart's desire."
"Virtuous one, today you have obtained sixty gold coins while resting in the Grove of Tranquility,
and yet you have come from afar to make this offering. Upānanda replied,
"Long-lived one!"
"How could there be a donor who gives sixty gold coins each to the Buddha and the great assembly of one thousand two hundred and fifty [monks]?
The bhikṣu replied, "It was given to you alone, O worthy one; it was not distributed among the entire Saṃgha."
Upānanda said, "Who can bestow sixty gold coins upon me?
They replied:
"This was sent as a gift by the minister Vassakāra from Rājagṛha.
He replied, "He is an old friend of mine; he already had the intention to give me this thing."
"Who has received this? Examine it carefully;
do not let it be scratched, damaged, or broken, for this is a privately minted object unfit for use.
He replied:
"No one will accept it.
Upānanda said, "I have recently been living among evil friends; who would be willing to accept it?"
When these words were spoken, another person replied:
"Venerable sir, why are you distressed?
The merchant left this message:"
"I am staying at such-and-such a place; if you need it, you may come and take it.
When Upānanda heard these words, he immediately took his saṃghāṭī robe and went quickly to that person's house.
At that time, seeing him from afar as he walked with hurried steps, the merchant thought to himself,
"Judging by his appearance, this must certainly be a śramaṇa of noble lineage.
He then asked:
"Venerable sir, are you Upānanda? He replied, "I am."
He immediately took the money and said, "This was entrusted by the minister Varṣākāra; you may now take it.
He then offered extensive prayers of blessing for him.
The merchant said, "This is not my wealth;
do not perform the incantation for me. I pray that you may perform it for the minister Varsa. Upānanda said:
"What harm have I done to you?
You have also rendered me great service by traveling from afar with these goods.
Borrow a young boy and give him some money; send him back as soon as he reaches the marketplace."
“Noble one! I have no children.
He replied:
"You fool! You have carried it all the way from Rājagṛha, yet you are unwilling to send it back for the mere distance of a few steps.
He then ordered a young boy to deliver the money, saying to the boy:
"You must follow after me and not engage in any other activity;
if they offer you money for the cost of cakes and fruit, you must certainly not accept it.
At that time, the boy took the money and followed him to a shop, where he said:
"Noble one!
Place the money here.
Upon hearing this, Upānanda thought to himself:
"That merchant is instructing this boy not to follow me," he said,
and then addressed the shopkeeper:
"O worthy one!"
"Please take and keep this money for me.
He replied, "Noble One!"
"I have a head of the household. Upānanda said,
"May you never again be free."
He went again to another incense-seller boy and said to him,
"O worthy one! Please keep this money for a moment."
He replied,
"My honored master is away and not at home. Upānanda said:
"May your family never come here again.
He then approached a young incense-seller who had recently conceived faith and said to him, "O noble one!"
"Please entrust this money to me for a moment.
He replied, "I have a superior; I dare not accept your trust."
Upānanda said, "I thought you possessed at least a modicum of faith; how could I have known you were a rākṣasa of faith?
Had you not had even the slightest bit of faith from the start, I would have seized the bhikṣu by his feet and dragged him outside the gate."
He remained silent, and [the other] replied,
"Noble one,
you may place it here."
Upānanda then returned to the monastery.
At that time, the merchants had previously established a regulation: if anyone failed to assemble together by sunrise, they were to be fined sixty gold coins.
The mother said to the youth,
"You should depart early so that others do not punish you.
At that time, Upānanda conceived a thought in the night and felt a sense of remorse.
"The incense-selling youth has first conceived a heart of faith; perhaps he might allow me to entrust my belongings to his care.
Having said this, at daybreak, he took a young boy and went to that shop.
At that time, the shopkeeper was closing the door and about to leave when Upānanda said to him, "Good sir!
Give me back my gold coins."
He replied, "Venerable ones!
There is a regulation established here by the merchants: if anyone arrives for the assembly only after sunrise, they shall be fined sixty gold coins."
"Stay for a short while; I shall return only after attending the assembly.
Upānanda said, "Fool!"
"I am not your servant; who would endure the pain in their feet by standing here so long for the sake of their own money?
If you depart without returning it to me, you will be violating the command of King Prasenajit and shall further be fined sixty gold coins."
Upon hearing these words, he immediately became angry and abusive; he seized the money-wrapping and threw it to the ground, whereupon the clay seal broke.
Upānanda said, "You should stay here for a moment while I try to unravel it; has it not been rubbed away or damaged?"
"Is it not privately minted?
The shopkeeper replied,
"How could you have inspected it before handing it over to me?"
Upānanda said, "Even though I did not look at it, why is the seal broken?
At that time, the shopkeeper harbored resentment but remained silent.
When dawn broke, the appointed time had already passed; at that moment, the merchants came to their home and took away those sixty gold coins.
The mother said to them, "What have you done to violate the assembly's regulations such that you are fined sixty gold coins?"
The son replied to his mother,
“Because of my friendship with the Śākyaputra, the very first sprout of faith has been caused to wither.
He then gave rise to resentment and reviled him.
Having heard this, the bhikṣus reported it in full to the Blessed One.
On account of these causes and conditions, the Blessed One assembled the community of bhikṣus, and so forth, as extensively described.
He then questioned Upānanda, saying:
“Did you truly commit such an unseemly act? “It is true,
Venerable Sir.”
The Buddha rebuked him in various ways, and finally declared: "I now establish a training rule for my disciples within the Vinaya, which should be recited as follows:
'If a bhikṣu receives a messenger sent by a king, a high minister, a brahmin, a householder, or others, to deliver the price for a robe to that bhikṣu...'"
The messenger, carrying the price for the robes, went to where the bhikṣu was and said:
"Venerable Sir!
This item has been sent by such-and-such a king, minister, brahmin, householder, or others, and I have been dispatched to deliver it."
"Venerable sir, out of compassion, please accept this.
The bhikṣu says to that messenger:
"Good man, I should not accept this price for robes; however, if I obtain a pure robe appropriate for the season, I shall accept it."
The messenger said:
"Venerable Sir,
is there anyone who attends to your affairs?"
The bhikṣu said: "There are!
Whether they be monastic attendants (śrāmaṇeraka) or upāsakas, these are the persons who manage affairs for the bhikṣus."
The messenger went to the person in charge of goods, gave him the price for the robe, and said:
"You should use this price to purchase a timely and pure robe and give it to the bhikṣu so-and-so, so that he may wear it."
Having properly instructed the attendant, that messenger returns to where the bhikṣu is and says:
"Venerable One!
I have already given the price for the robe to the attendant you indicated; you should accept it when you obtain a pure robe."
"A bhikṣu who requires robes should go to the person in charge of affairs and, after reminding them two or three times, say:
'I require robes.'"
"If he succeeds, it is well;
if he does not succeed, he should go there up to four, five, or six times, remaining silent wherever he stands.
If he obtains the robe after four, five, or six visits, it is well."
If he does not obtain the robe, and seeks to obtain a robe beyond that [limit], it is a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika*.
If he still does not obtain the robe, that bhikṣu should go to the place where the price for the robe was sent, either going himself or sending a trustworthy person, and announce:
"The price for a robe was sent by you for the sake of the bhikṣu so-and-so; that bhikṣu did not obtain the robe. You should know this and ensure it is not lost; now is the time."
Regarding the term "bhikṣu," it refers to Upānanda.
Regarding the term "king," whether male or female, or even others who have been consecrated by the royal rite (rājavidhi), all such persons are called kings.
The ministers are those who hold the affairs of state and stand in mutual dependence upon the king.
The brahmins are of noble lineage and possess extensive learning.
The householders are those who are wealthy and affluent while remaining at home.
The term "and so forth" refers to various other miscellaneous types.
"Sending a messenger" refers to a woman, a man, or a eunuch.
"Sending the price for the robe" refers to gold, silver, money, and the like.
"Regarding that messenger who carries the price for robes and so forth": this means carrying the price for robes to the place where the bhikṣu is and declaring:
"Venerable Sir" (bhadanta) refers to addressing the person present.
"This object belongs to such-and-such a person" and so forth means describing the source from which it came and requesting that he accept it.
Regarding the phrase "these bhikṣus," it means that [the gift] should not be accepted as a reward.
Regarding "pure in accordance with the proper time," it means obtaining it in a manner consistent with reason.
Regarding the phrase "that messenger speaks to the bhikṣus," it refers to questioning the person in charge of affairs.
When the bhikṣu says "there is," he is referring to that person.
"If it is a saṃgha-upāsaka" means a lay attendant of the assembly.
"If it is an upāsaka" means one who has taken refuge in the Triple Gem and received the five precepts.
The phrase "those messengers" clarifies the intent of the messenger.
"Purchases" refers to either buying or weaving.
"To such-and-such a bhikṣu" indicates the person to whom it is given.
"Pure speech" means it is fit for use.
"Having instructed well" means having properly taught and shown.
"With two or three bhikṣus who have received the report" refers to the number of times one must speak back and forth to cause them to remember.
"To obtain what is good" means that it accords with the seeking mind.
If one does not obtain it, then even up to four, five, or six times, remaining silent and staying in whatever place one is, this refers to the count of silent dwellings.
Regarding "according to the place," there are four places: first, a dilapidated place;
second, a householder's place;
[third, a monastery; fourth, a forest].
Third, the place of fields;
fourth, the place of shops.
"Bastard" (bèi) refers to places where earthenware vessels and the like are made, or places for shaving hair.
"House" refers to a dwelling;
"field" refers to fields for rice, sugarcane, and the like;
"shop" refers to a place for selling goods.
There are six points of inquiry; one should examine those six statements and respond to them according to the specific circumstances.
What are the six? If someone asks:
"By what cause have you now arrived?
The bhikṣu replied,
"I have come for that matter."
If one says, "Welcome,
virtuous one; you should sit here," the reply is:
"I have come for that matter.
If he says, "To eat rice," [one should respond accordingly].
He replied, "I have come for that matter. If he says:
"Eat some cakes," [the other] replied,
"I have come for that matter."
If one says,
"I drink water," the reply is:
"If you have come for that matter.

If, among these six types of responses, one sees another speaking and immediately replies upon hearing the voice without answering slowly, thereby leaving the other person no opportunity to utter further words, this is not called a complete and excellent manner of speech.

Regarding the six kinds of interrogation: if, during any one matter, when you perceive another’s speech, you do not respond immediately upon hearing the words, but instead answer slowly and deliberately so that the other person has the leisure to formulate further remarks, this is called "perfectly excellent."
When seeking in this manner through the six kinds of interrogation, it is well if one obtains the robe;
if one does not obtain the robe, yet obtains it by seeking beyond this limit, it is a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika*.
"Exceeding" means that after three verbal requests and six silent entreaties have passed, one goes further to seek [the robe].
If one ultimately does not obtain the robe, one should either go personally or dispatch a trustworthy person to the place from which the robe originated.
Regarding those whose words are trustworthy: this refers to disciples and followers who may be entrusted with confidence.
One informs them so that they may know, dispatching them to retrieve [the items] so that nothing is lost in vain; this is the ritual procedure for returning a report.
If a bhikṣu has sent a messenger to inform [the donor], and that attendant comes to the bhikṣu's quarters and speaks these words:
"Venerable sir!
You may accept this price for a robe."
The bhikṣu should reply to him, saying:
"I have already relinquished this price for the robe; you should return it to the place from which the robe was sent.
If he replies in this manner, it is well; if he accepts the robe, he commits an offense of expiation involving forfeiture (naiḥsargika-pāyattika).
If the person in charge should speak thus:
"Venerable One!
You may accept this price for the robe; I shall consult with that donor together so as to make his heart rejoice."
"If it is done in this manner, there is no offense in taking the robe.
If a bhikṣu accepts a robe without following such a sequence, he commits an offense of expiation involving forfeiture (*naiḥsargika-pāyattika*).
Once the offense has been committed, the method for relinquishing and confessing it is explained at length as previously stated."
In this regard, what are the characteristics of the offense and how does it occur?

If one acts as the donor, one acts as the messenger, or one acts as the attendant, and thus obtains the robe in accordance with the Dharma, there is no offense; otherwise, it is a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* (an offense involving forfeiture).

If a human being acts as the donor, a human being acts as the messenger, and a non-human being acts as the servant, and one obtains a robe in accordance with the Dharma, there is no offense; otherwise, it is an act of wrongdoing (duṣkṛta).
If a human being acts as the donor, a non-human being acts as the messenger, and a non-human being acts as the attendant, it is an *dukkaṭa* (wrongdoing), as previously stated.

If a human being acts as the donor, a non-human being acts as the messenger, and a human being acts as the attendant, it is a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* (offense involving forfeiture), as previously stated.
If the donor is not a human being, the messenger is not a human being, and the attendant is not a human being, it is an *dukkaṭa* (offense of wrong-doing) as previously stated.
If the donor is not a human being, the messenger is not a human being, but the attendant is a human being, it is a *nissaggiya pācittiya* (offense involving forfeiture) as previously stated.
If a non-human is the donor, a human is the messenger, and a non-human is the attendant, it is the same as the previous offense of *naiḥsargika-pāyattika*.
If a non-human is the donor, a human is the messenger, and a non-human is the attendant, it is the same as the previous offense of *dukkaṭa*.
If a bhikṣu begs for the price of a robe from a non-human, he incurs an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa);
if he obtains it, he incurs an offense of expiation with forfeiture (nissaggiya-pācittiya).
If he begs for the price of a robe from a nāga, he incurs an offense of wrong-doing.
If he obtains it, there is an offense of expiation involving forfeiture (*naiḥsargika-pāyattika*).
If a bhikṣu sends a messenger, or requests by means of a letter or seal, there is an offense of wrongdoing (*dukkaṭa*);
if he obtains it, there is an offense of expiation involving forfeiture.
Furthermore, regarding those who are not at fault, the detailed explanation is as previously stated.
**The Eleventh Training Rule on Using Wild Silk to Make Bedding.** The summary verse says:
*Gauśeya, pure black, divided into six, and the *niṣīdana*.*
Carrying wool, washing gold and silver, pledging collateral, and buying and selling.
The Buddha was staying at the Jeta Grove in Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the bhikṣus were making new bedding out of wild silkworm silk; whether they made it themselves or had others make it, this material was difficult to obtain and was also of great value.

At that time, because the bhikṣus were engaged in many tasks for the purpose of construction, it hindered and interrupted their formal cultivation, recitation, and mental attention; they repeatedly requested wild silk from those brahmins and householders.
When the various non-Buddhist practitioners saw this, they looked upon it with disdain and spoke thus:

"All you people should know that these śramaṇa Śākyaputrīyas are killers who do not renounce the karma of harming; they themselves or by employing others use fresh wild silk to make bedding, and if one uses such things, many sentient beings are killed."
"How can one give fine food and clothing to those shaven-headed men who take the lives of living beings?
When the bhikṣus heard these words, they went to inform the Blessed One.
On account of this incident, the Blessed One assembled the community of bhikṣus and asked them:
“Are you indeed using new wild silkworm silk to make bedding? “It is so,
World-Honored One.”
The Buddha said:
"You are difficult to satisfy and difficult to support; you do not follow the practice of having few desires and knowing contentment.

Having rebuked them in various ways, he praised the merits of the dhūta ascetic practices, of having few desires, and of knowing contentment, and further declared: "I now establish a training rule (śikṣāpada) for my disciples within the Vinaya, which should be recited as follows:"
"If a bhikṣu should again make a bedding or mat from new *kośeya* silk thread, it is a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika*.
"If a bhikṣu" refers to one who is within this Dharma.
There are two kinds of "new":
first, that which is newly made; second, that which is newly obtained.
Here, "new" refers to that which is newly made.
Regarding the making of bedding from *kauśeya* silk, there are two types:
first, stuffing it into a mattress; second, sewing it into a finished garment.

This term "making bedding" includes both types of production, meaning whether one makes it oneself or instructs another to do so, one incurs a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* offense. The procedures for relinquishing the object and performing the confession are explained at length as previously described.
In this regard, what are the characteristics of the offense and how does it occur?

When a bhikṣu processes *jāṅgala* (wild silk), whether from a single cocoon, a small ball, or a large mass, if he spreads it out, tears it apart, or uses a bow to stretch it to make a bedding, he incurs an *dukkaṭa* (wrongdoing) while in the process;
when it is finished, he incurs a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* (offense involving forfeiture).
If a bhikṣu solicits *kauśeya* silk, or when he is processing it, he commits an *duṣkṛta* offense; once it is completed, he incurs the offense of *naiḥsargika-pāyattika*.
However, if he obtains what has already been made or items for prior use, or if he uses old items that have been newly processed, there is no offense in any of these cases.
Furthermore, there is no offense for one who is a first-time offender, or for one who is insane, mentally deranged, or overwhelmed by intense physical pain.
*Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya*, Fascicle Twenty. *Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya*, Fascicle Two.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Yijing by Imperial Decree. The Twelfth Training Rule:
On Using a Mattress Made Exclusively of Black Sheep’s Wool. At that time, the Blessed One was staying in Śrāvastī at the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the bhikṣus used pure black wool to make bedding for themselves or to have others make it for them;

however, because such wool was difficult to obtain and very expensive, the bhikṣus became preoccupied with many worldly tasks for its production. This hindered and interrupted their formal practice, recitation, and mental cultivation, as they repeatedly requested black wool from other brahmins and householders.

At that time, the bhikṣus who possessed few desires collectively felt disdain and contempt. They reported this matter in detail to the World-Honored One, as extensively described above, until [the Buddha said]: "For the sake of my disciples, I shall establish a training rule (śikṣāpada) within the Vinaya;
it should be recited as follows: 'If a bhikṣu makes a new bedding (niṣīdana) using pure black wool, it is a naiḥsargika-pāyattika.'"
"Furthermore, 'if a bhikṣu' refers to one who belongs to this Dharma.
Regarding 'pure black,' there are four kinds of black:
first, natural black; second, natural blue-black; third, clay-colored; and fourth, variegated."
"Wool" refers to wool and no other kind of hair.
"New" has two types: that which is newly made and that which is newly obtained;
here, the intention is to take that which is newly made.
The "maker" refers to one who makes it themselves or causes another to make it.
Regarding the "bedding," there are two types:
