namely, stuffed mattresses and those that are sewn; here, the intention refers to those that are sewn.
Regarding the offense of *naiḥsargika-pāyattika*, the procedures for relinquishing the object and the confession are explained in detail as previously stated.
What are the characteristics of the transgression and the specific circumstances therein?

When a bhikṣu processes wool—whether it be a single strand, a small ball, or a large heap—and fashions a mat by spreading it out, tearing it apart, or carding it with a bow, there is an offense of *duṣkṛta* at the time of making it.
When it is finished, one incurs a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* offense.
However, there is no offense if one obtains something already completed, or an item previously used, or an old item that has been refurbished.
Furthermore, there is no offense for the very first offender, or for one who is insane, mentally deranged, or afflicted by intense pain.
The Thirteenth Training Rule on Making Bedding Exceeding the Prescribed Dimensions. The Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.

The Buddha ordained that bhikṣus must not use pure black wool to make new bedding. At that time, the bhikṣus used four parts black wool and added a small amount of other colored wool as they saw fit to make new bedding.
The bhikṣus of few desires then censured him together and went to inform the Blessed One.
On account of this matter, the Blessed One assembled the community of bhikṣus; the exchange of questions and answers and the reprimand were as extensively described before.
"I shall now establish a training rule for my disciples within the Vinaya, which should be recited as follows:
'If a bhikṣu fashions a new woolen rug, he should use two parts of pure black wool, one-third part white, and one-fourth part coarse.'"
If a bhikṣu makes a new sitting mat without using two parts of pure black wool, one-third part white, and one-fourth part coarse wool, it is a naiḥsargika-pāyattika offense.
The meaning of "bhikṣu" is as explained above.
There are two kinds of "new," and there are two kinds of bedding materials; even down to the point that the intention here refers to what has been sewn together, all is as explained above.
Regarding what is called "pure black," there are four kinds of black, as already explained above.
What is called "white" refers to the hair on the flanks, along the spine, and at the sides of the neck.
What is called "coarse" refers to the hair on the head, feet, and belly.
Regarding the phrase "two parts, etc.," this indicates their respective quantities.

For example, if one wishes to make a woolen rug weighing ten *jin*, five *jin* should be pure black, two and a half *jin* white, and two and a half *jin* coarse; all other increases or decreases should be understood according to this principle.
Because black [wool] is divided into two parts, it constitutes four parts.
If it were otherwise, then regarding the latter two [parts], if one uses less than half a *liang* or uses pure black [wool], one incurs an *dukkaṭa* (wrongdoing) at the time of making it;
once it is completed, one incurs a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* (offense involving forfeiture).

If one does not do it for oneself, or if it was already accomplished beforehand, or if the black [substance] is easily obtained while the other is difficult to find, there is no offense regardless of whether the two quantities increase or decrease.
Furthermore, there is no offense in the case of the very first offender, or those who are insane, mentally deranged, or afflicted by intense pain.

14. The Training Rule on Making Bedding Last Less Than Six Years. The fourteenth training rule concerning making bedding last less than six years. The Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the bhikṣus kept many bedding materials and said to one another,
"Venerable sir,
this mattress is too long."
They would immediately cast it aside and make another;
thinking, "This mat is too short," "this one is too small," "this one is too wide," or "this one is entirely worn out and unfit for repair," they would discard them all and manufacture new ones.
Because he was burdened with the heavy task of making mats, the same faults as before arose.
Those of few desires collectively felt disdain and contempt for him, and reported the aforementioned matter in detail to the World-Honored One.
The Blessed One assembled the community and, after questioning and rebuking them, spoke at length as previously described, up until: "It should be stated thus:

'If a bhikṣu makes a new sitting mat, even if his heart is not inclined toward it, he must use it for six years. If he does not discard it before the end of six years and instead makes another new one, it is a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika*.'"
This was the first occasion on which the Blessed One established a training rule (*śikṣāpada*).

While the Buddha was residing at the Kalandaka Grove in Rājagṛha, a severe and biting wind arose and the bhikṣus suffered from the cold; yet those in charge of monastery affairs continued to hold onto their bedding and requisites for six years.
Because of the established precepts, they did not dare to undertake new construction; because of their endurance of the cold, all building activities were brought to a halt.
At that time, the Blessed One, knowing [the reason] yet asking out of formality, addressed the Venerable Ānanda:
"For what reason have the monks in charge of affairs ceased their building work?"
Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying:

“Because the Blessed One has established a training rule for the bhikṣus that one must not make a new bedding or mat for six years, the bhikṣus who are currently engaged in construction find their old bedding and mats worn out and unable to withstand the cold; consequently, all such labor has been brought to a standstill.”
The Buddha told Ānanda:

"If any bhikṣu serving as an administrator or engaged in construction work possesses bedding and requisites that, though not yet six years old, fail to protect him from the cold, that bhikṣu should request permission from the Saṃgha to have new bedding and requisites made within those six years."
One should request in this manner:

Having assembled the Saṃgha as usual, the *karmadāna* bhikṣu goes into the midst of the assembly, prostrates at the feet of the monks, and then squats before the *sthavira*, joining his palms and making the following announcement:
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!"
I, the bhikṣu [Name], who am engaged in construction, shall not make bedding or mats again for six years.

I, the bhikṣu [Name], wish to request from the Saṃgha permission to make new bedding and mats within these six years. May the venerable Saṃgha grant me, the bhikṣu [Name], permission to make new bedding and mats again within these six years.
"May those who are capable of compassion grant it out of their compassionate mercy.
This should be said a second and a third time.
"If the Saṃgha recognizes that person as being trustworthy, they shall grant him the Dharma."

Alternatively, he may be instructed to bring his old bedding to the midst of the Saṃgha; if it is too long, it should be cut short; if it is too short, it should be padded with wool; if it is too wide or too narrow, it should be adjusted according to the circumstances; if there are torn places, they should be patched with wool; if it is so completely shattered that it cannot be repaired, the Saṃgha should grant him the formal authorization for a new set.
One bhikṣu should perform the formal motion (*jñapti-karman*) as follows, in detail as explained in the *Ekottara-karman* (The Hundred-and-One Karmas):

"If a bhikṣu who manages affairs has been granted this legal authorization by the Saṃgha, he may act according to his own discretion within the six-year period; do not harbor any doubt regarding this."
At that time, the World-Honored One praised the observance of the precepts and those who revere the precepts; he then taught the Dharma accordingly and addressed the bhikṣus, saying:
"The former was the initial injunction; this is the subsequent allowance."
It should be stated thus:
"If a bhikṣu makes a new sitting mat, even if his heart is not inclined toward it, he must use it for six years.
If he does not discard the old one after less than six years and instead makes another new one, except by obtaining the formal authorization of the Saṃgha, it is a naiḥsargika-pāyattika."
The meaning of "bhikṣu" is as explained above.
Regarding "new," there are two kinds, as detailed previously.
This continues until it is taken up and completed.
Although one may feel no inclination to maintain it for the full six years, it is mandatory that one maintains it for exactly six years;
if the period is not completed, whether one relinquishes it or not, and then makes a new one, one incurs the offense of *naiḥsargika-pāyattika*.
The procedures for relinquishing and the subsequent confession are identical to those previously described.
What, then, are the characteristics of the offense in this case?

If a bhikṣu makes a new bedding or mat within this year, and further manufactures another during that same year, he incurs a *duṣkṛta* (wrongdoing) at the time of making the second one; once it is completed, he commits the offense of *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* (relinquishment and forfeiture).
There is no offense for the initial maker.
Even if it is not of the same year, if one makes another mat in the second year, and likewise in the third, fourth, or even fifth year, making a new one, the offense incurred is the same as before;
however, that very first mat involves no offense.

If a bhikṣu already possesses bedding and furniture, yet manufactures another set during that same year, he incurs an offense of expiation with forfeiture (nissaggiya-pācittiya) if it is completed within that year;
if it is not completed within that year but is only finished after five years, he likewise incurs an offense of expiation with forfeiture.
If a bhikṣu, within this year, has begun making a new bedding item but has not yet finished it when he begins another, and when both are completed, he says:
"I shall take the former and discard the latter," or "I may take the latter and discard the former."
If one commits the offense of *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* later,
there is no offense for those who committed it earlier.
If the initial construction was not yet finished, and in the second year— or even the third, fourth, or fifth year— it is completed simultaneously with the other, one says:
"I shall keep the former; I shall discard the latter.
This is explained at length as above.

If a bhikṣu has already made one mat and, within that same year, begins making another mat but stops before it is finished, and in the second year he again begins making another mat but stops before it is finished, and likewise in the third, fourth, and fifth years—if those [mats] remain unfinished, he incurs five *dukkaṭa* (offenses of wrong-doing).
There is no offense for the first maker.

If a bhikṣu has already made one mat and does not make another mat during that same year, and continues not to make a mat until the fifth year, such that he makes one again only in the sixth year, there is no offense.
Furthermore, there is no offense for one who is the very first offender, or for one who is insane, mentally deranged, or overwhelmed by intense pain.
The Fifteenth Training Rule: Making a New Bedding Without Dyeing It. The Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, after the World-Honored One had attained unsurpassed wisdom, his great fame spread throughout the four directions, and everyone heard that a Buddha had appeared in the Middle Kingdom.

Then, merchants from the north, hearing that a Buddha had appeared in the world—that anyone who could offer him worship would obtain a great fruit and great benefit, their fame would spread far and wide, and they would possess vast wealth—[were moved].
Having heard this matter, he thought to himself:
"I should now take my various goods and go to the city of Śrāvastī; first, so that I may seek profit, and second, so that I may pay homage to the World-Honored One."
Having formed this thought, he set out with five hundred merchants carrying northern goods toward the Middle Kingdom.
When the merchants arrived at Śrāvastī and had secured their merchandise, they went to the residence of the householder Anāthapiṇḍada and spoke to him thus:
"Householder, you should know!"
"We now wish to pay our respects and behold the World-Honored One.
The householder replied,
"Excellent!"
Excellent! You have been able to give rise to such a sublime thought.
The Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha is worthy of veneration; he is truly difficult to encounter, appearing but once in an age, like the udumbara flower.
Having spoken these words, the elder immediately led those five hundred merchants to where the Buddha was, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and sat to one side.

At that time, the World-Honored One preached the essentials of the Dharma for the elder and the five hundred merchants; having instructed, exhorted, benefited, and gladdened them so that they were filled with faith and joy, he remained silent.

At that time, the merchants, having heard the Dharma, rejoiced, prostrated before the Buddha, and withdrew. They then went to pay their respects to the senior bhikṣus and further desired to tour the dwellings and observe the assembly of bhikṣus.

At that time, as the householder Anāthapiṇḍada was leading the merchants around for an inspection, the merchants saw that the *niṣīdana* (sitting mats) upon the bedding of the bhikṣus had been torn through in their centers.
They asked the householder, "For what reason have the sitting mats of these venerable elder bhikṣus been torn through in their centers?"
The householder replied, "The venerable elder bhikṣus sit cross-legged for much of the night until dawn; it is because of this circumstance that they have all become worn through."
At that time, the merchants felt profound reverence and offered five hundred exquisite cotton cloths to the community of monks.

Once the bhikṣus had received the cloths, they made new *niṣīdana* (sitting mats) from them. As for the old ones, they placed them near an old room in an open space, piling them all together in one heap.
At that time, there was a householder who invited the Buddha and the Saṃgha to his home to provide an offering.
When the time arrived, all the bhikṣus departed, but the Blessed One alone remained at the monastery, instructing someone to fetch the food.
However, there are five causes and conditions for which the Buddha, the World-Honored One, does not go to the place where he has been invited.
What are these five?
First, he remains in solitary silence.
2. To preach the Dharma for the devas;
3. To visit and examine the sick;
4. To inspect the bedding and furniture.
5. He established the training rule (*śikṣāpada*) for the bhikṣus.
Herein, the Blessed One intended both to inspect their bedding and to establish a training rule for the bhikṣus regarding not attending invitations to lay households.

At that time, not long after the bhikṣus had departed, the World-Honored One took his key and went for a walk, surveying the various places until he arrived at an old dwelling. There he saw the bhikṣus having gathered their old sitting mats (niṣīdana) in one spot; they were mixed with refuse and scattered in disarray upon the ground.
Having seen this, the World-Honored One thought to himself:
"There are donors who, with deep faith and reverence, cut from their own flesh and blood to provide offerings and cultivate various meritorious deeds."
"However, the bhikṣus discard their old bedding without moderation in its use; lacking a sense of care, they cast it away wherever they please.
At that time, the World-Honored One took the old bedding, turned it over, shook it out, and placed it on a rack; he then washed his hands and feet outside the room and sat upright within the room.
Then the bhikṣu who had taken the food brought it to where the World-Honored One was; by the natural law of the World-Honored One, he joyfully inquired of the bhikṣu who had taken the food:
"Did the assembly of bhikṣus eat well and not fail to be satisfied?"
The bhikṣu who had taken the food said to him,
“World-Honored One!
The great assembly has all been fully satiated with food and drink.”
After the World-Honored One had finished his meal, he washed his hands and feet, returned to his chamber, and remained there in silent seclusion.
In the late afternoon, the World-Honored One arose from meditation and went to the great assembly, where he took his seat and addressed the bhikṣus:

"Not long after you had departed, I took my key and walked about, observing the various places until I came to an old room. There I saw that the bhikṣus had gathered their worn-out *niṣīdana* mats in one spot; they were mixed with refuse and littered upon the ground."
Having seen this, I then thought:
"There are donors who, with deep-seated pure faith, cut from themselves their own flesh and blood to provide offerings and cultivate various meritorious deeds."
"However, you bhikṣus, you have used old bedding and mats beyond measure, and without a sense of care, you have discarded them wherever you please.
This is not a virtuous matter. You, bhikṣus!"
"If one receives gifts offered out of faith by others, weighing them with care, protecting them, using them at the proper time, and knowing contentment—this is truly excellent!
At that time, after the Blessed One had praised the careful protection, timely use, and contented enjoyment of offerings given in faith, he addressed the bhikṣus:
"To explain at length, up until the formulation of the training rule, it should be stated as follows:"

"If a bhikṣu makes a new *niṣīdana*, he should take a worn portion from an old one, measuring one span of the Buddha’s hand in length and breadth, and patch it onto the new one for the purpose of discoloring it."
If a bhikṣu makes a new *niṣīdana* (sitting mat) and does not patch the old one onto the new one for the purpose of discoloring it, it is a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika*.
The meaning of "bhikṣu" is as explained above.
There are two kinds of "new":
first, that which is newly made; second, that which is newly obtained.
In this context, the intention refers to making something new.
"Naiṣidhana" (seating mat) refers to a bedding or sitting cloth.
"Making" means either making it oneself or having another person make it.
Regarding the phrase "one side of the old *niṣīdana*," this refers to taking a portion from one side of an old *niṣīdana* that is firm and of good quality.
"One span of the Buddha's hand" refers to the Great Teacher; one of his spans is equivalent to one and a half cubits (*hasta*) for a person of average height.
"Patch it over the new one" means that the patch should be placed over the new portion.
"For the sake of discoloration" means for the purpose of making it durable.
If one does not patch it, one incurs a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* offense; the procedure for relinquishing and repenting this offense is as explained above.
In this regard, what are the characteristics of the offense and how does it occur?

If a bhikṣu, when patching his old *niṣīdana* with a piece of cloth the size of one of the Buddha’s spans, uses a piece that is less than a finger’s breadth or half a finger’s breadth [in width], he also incurs a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika*.

There is no offense if one covers a new *niṣīdana* entirely with an old one, or if the [old] *niṣīdana* is so completely shattered that it is incapable of being patched onto a new one. There is no offense.
Furthermore, there is no offense for the very first offender, or for one who is insane, mentally deranged, or overwhelmed by intense pain.
The Sixteenth Training Rule on Carrying Wool on One's Own Person. The Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the six bhikṣus deliberated among themselves, saying:

"Nanda and Upananda, those black-bowl [śramaṇas] smear their feet with monkey fat; whenever they wish to depart, they receive offerings for the journey, and upon their first arrival from a long journey, they again receive provisions. Many people love and respect them, and they are well-known by all."
"However, we are like frogs in a well; having never traveled abroad, what could we possibly gain?
We too should travel in the four directions.
His companions asked:
"Where are you going? Upānanda replied,
"I am now going out for a short while to seek out some traveling merchants."
He further thought to himself:
"If all of us disciples were to depart together, the families who provide almsfood for me and my circle of disciples would all be seized and plundered by other black-bowl mendicants."
"It would be appropriate to leave one person behind; the rest may go as they please.
They then deliberated together:
"Who should remain here?"
"Venerable Udāyin, have him keep watch, and whatever profit is obtained shall be returned for our shared division.
Udāyin replied, "I shall remain here."
The other five men went out to seek traveling companions and saw a large group of people heading toward the country of Nepāla.
The bhikṣu asked them, "Where are you going?"
He replied,
"We wish to go to the country of Nepāla.
The bhikṣu said:
"We also wish to travel with you," said the merchants.
The noble one replied: "Venerable sirs!"
"The land of the country of Nīpāla is mostly rugged and stony, like the back of a camel; you, sirs, may not necessarily find it pleasant to dwell there.
The bhikṣus said, "We shall go together for now to try and observe that land."
“Noble One! If it is so, we shall go together.
He then accompanied the merchant along the road.

When that bhikṣu arrived in that country, he found no pleasure there at all; so on another day, he went into the marketplace and asked the merchants, "Sirs, when do you intend to return to your own country?"
The merchant said,
"Is it that your reverence does not find pleasure in this?
The bhikṣu replied:
"I have only just arrived, and on this very day my heart is devoid of joy and affection.
He replied, "Noble one!"

"Our goods have not yet been traded, so we cannot yet speak of returning home. I have a close acquaintance who wishes to return to the Middle Kingdom; you should entrust him with our affairs so that we may travel together."
The bhikṣu replied, "This is an excellent matter!
However, in the kingdom of Nepāla, there were two kinds of base commodities: namely, wool and realgar.
At that time, many merchants purchased large quantities of wool and departed with it on wagons.
The community of bhikṣus also traveled along with them; however, because the six bhikṣus were by nature averse to dust, they sometimes went ahead and sometimes followed behind.
At that time, the six bhikṣus were walking slowly behind them. Among the merchants, there was a single-horse cart whose axle suddenly snapped.

The merchants then deliberated among themselves, saying, "If we attempt to repair the axle now, the sound will be heard from afar and bandits will surely arrive; they will first kill us and then take our wealth."
"We ought to take our valuable goods and set out, discarding what we have loaded.
While they were deliberating thus, the group of six monks arrived and asked, "Virtuous ones,
for what reason do you remain here without proceeding, harboring such anxiety?"
He replied, "Noble one!
The axle of my cart has broken."
He related all that had occurred in detail.
The group of six asked,
"How could you possibly discard the wool?"
He replied,
"Throw it away.
The group of six replied:
“If my lords would grant me permission, I shall make hats, or boots and felt, or standing banners; I shall provide whatever I am able, however small or great.”
The merchant replied, "Take as much as you wish; it is of no use to me.
Then Nanda and Upananda consulted with one another, saying:
"Now there is an abundance of discarded refuse.
At that time, they had one of the five men carry all their robes and bowls, while the remaining four braided grass into ropes and tied them into four bundles, which they carried along the road.
Then the merchants saw him and said, "Noble One!
We wished to hire someone to come and fetch this wool, but now that you have brought it all here yourself, we wish to pay you a price and take the wool back."
The bhikṣu replied, "You are an ignorant person! Are we, by any chance, hired laborers?
If you act like this, I shall abandon you."
The merchants replied, "We were only speaking in jest; please do not take offense, you may take it with you.
At that time, there was a non-Buddhist (tīrthika) traveling with the caravan who teased the group of six monks, saying:
"Where shall this heavy burden be laid down? What profit shall we obtain?
Having heard this, the group of six replied in anger:
"We shall break open your belly and trample upon your head; only then will our burden be laid down, and we shall collect the profit as well."
He then kept his mouth shut and remained silent, offering no reply.
The group of six discussed among themselves, saying, "If we travel in the midst of a merchant caravan, we will attract much ridicule and mockery; we should instead go ahead."

Upon arriving at a village that was frequently plagued by bandits, the villagers stationed lookouts on the outskirts of the settlement. From afar, they saw the six companions of the group approaching carrying their loads and announced to one another:
"Virtuous ones, you should know that an elephant army is arriving."

When the people saw this, they were all struck with terror; abandoning their homes, they fled into the forest, leaving behind the strongest men to guard the village and town, and they said to one another:
"That was no elephant army; it was camels."
He said again, "That is not a camel; it must be an ox-cart.
He spoke once more:
"He is not a bullock-carrier; this man is carrying goods.
Having approached the village and recognized that he was a bhikṣu, they said:
"Noble One!"
"A most extraordinary burden! There is an unusual person here who has caused the entire village to flee in all directions.

The group of six replied, "You ignorant one, seeing someone carrying a load, you were terrified and called him a thief. If that 'thief' had known of you, he would have come to plunder you; yet you remained in constant flight, taking all your household property with you."
Upon hearing this, he remained silent.
Then, having witnessed this event, the group of six addressed one another, saying:
"Nanda and Upananda!..."
"We will likely draw much ridicule if we travel along the main road; let us instead go straight through the wilderness.
They then abandoned the path and departed.
At that time, the customs officers were stationed at various points guarding the route; seeing the load arrive, they said to them:
“You merchants have repeatedly evaded taxes; you travel by secret paths without paying the tax dues.
The group of six replied, “O witless one, do you take us for tax-evading merchants?”
He asked, "Who are you, sirs?
They replied:
"I am one of the six groups of bhikṣus. He replied,
"Noble one, please follow me."
They further consulted one another, saying, "If we go to the gate of Jetavana, those who carry black alms-bowls will all mock us; we should take a small side gate and enter carrying our loads."
Having entered through the small gate, an old monk (mahallaka) saw him and asked:
"You are a traveling porter; for what reason have you broken down the fence to enter the monastery?
He replied:
"Old man! Do you take me for a guest porter? he asked.
"What are you, sirs?
They replied, "We are bhikṣus."
He asked, "Venerable One,
are these the group of six?"
He replied, "It is I. He then said:
"Welcome! Welcome,
Venerable One!"
When he had entered, he placed all the bundles of hair within the monastery, piling them up like mountains; those who saw this marveled at the wonder and asked, "Venerable one!..."
"You, O virtuous ones, are able to bear such a heavy burden; do you not fear the derision and reproach of the worldly? They replied:
"Does our mouth merely consume food? If there are those who mock us, we shall mock them threefold."
At that time, the bhikṣus of few desires collectively raised criticism, saying these words:
"How can a bhikṣu carry such a heavy burden, taking shameless matters as his own competence and thereby giving rise to arrogance?"
At that time, the bhikṣus reported this matter in detail to the Blessed One.
The Blessed One then assembled the community of bhikṣus and, as extensively explained before, established the training rule, which should be recited as follows:
"If a bhikṣu, while traveling on a road, obtains wool and has need of it, he may take it."
"If there is no one to carry it, one may carry it oneself for up to three *yojana*s; if one exceeds this distance, it is a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* offense.
"Bhikṣu" refers to the group of six [monks], or others of a similar class.
"One traveling on a journey" means being on the road.
"Obtaining wool" means it is another's property.
"Desiring to have need of it" means having something to be done with it.
"Should take" means to take and carry as one pleases.

"Up to three *yojana*s" refers to the distance in *li*; it means that if there is no other person present, carrying it beyond this distance constitutes an offense of forfeiture (*naiḥsargika-pāyattika*).

The rules regarding the *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* (offenses involving forfeiture) are as extensively explained previously. What, then, are the characteristics of the offenses herein? They are as follows: seven atoms (*paramāṇu*) constitute one minute particle (*aṇu*);

seven of these constitute a copper-dust particle (*tāmra-rajas*); seven of these constitute a water-dust particle (*ab-rajas*); seven of these constitute a rabbit-hair dust particle (*śaśa-rajas*); seven of these constitute a sheep-hair dust particle (*avi-rajas*); seven of these constitute a cow-hair dust particle (*go-rajas*); seven of these constitute a mote floating in a sunbeam (*chidra-rajas*); seven of these constitute a nit (*likṣā*); seven of these constitute a louse (*yūka*); seven of these constitute a grain of wild barley (*yava*); seven of these constitute one finger-breadth (*aṅgula*). Twenty-four finger-breadths constitute one cubit (*hasta*); three and a half cubits constitute one person’s height; four cubits constitute one bow (*dhanus*); five hundred bows constitute one *krośa*; and eight *krośas* constitute one *yojana*.
If there are seven villages, with one *krośa* between each village, when one carries wool and travels halfway, one incurs an offense of wrong-doing (*duṣkṛta*) for each;
if one reaches a village, one incurs an offense of relinquishment and forfeiture (*naiḥsargika-pāyattika*) for each.
If one travels from a village toward the wilderness, for every half-krośa traveled, one incurs an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa);
for a full krośa, one incurs an offense of expiation with forfeiture (nissaggiya-pācittiya).
If one is already in the wilderness, there is no offense up to three yojanas.
If one exceeds this limit, one commits an offense of expiation involving forfeiture (*naiḥsargika-pāyattika*).
There is no offense if one secretly takes away [the material] for the purpose of making a cap, a *palla* (a type of cloth garment), or for erecting banners and the like.
Furthermore, there is no offense for the very first offender, or for one who is insane, mentally deranged, or overwhelmed by intense physical pain.

17. The Training Rule on Having a Non-Relative Nun Process Wool. The seventeenth training rule concerning having a non-relative nun process wool was established when the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the six bhikṣus said to one another,
"We should now divide the wool we possess. Nanda asked:
"How many portions should there be?
Should the venerable Udāyin, who is staying here, also receive a portion?
When the venerable Udāyin heard these words, he thought to himself:
"Our companions are receiving much gain and support; by what means can we obtain a share of it?
They asked, "What are you planning, sirs?"
"Whatever is obtained shall each be returned to its respective source; you shall receive your portion of merit, and I shall receive mine.
Having heard these words, Upānanda thought to himself:
"The World-Honored One, the Lord of Dharma, now resides here; surely we shall obtain much of the offerings brought by those who come."
For the sake of Udāyin, they spoke these words:
"We have always been the group of six since ancient times; how could we possibly become the group of five today?"
"You should divide it into six equal parts and give them to him.
Nanda said, "Who will do the dividing?"
Chanda replied, "Venerable Udāyin has been resting here for a long time; it would be appropriate to have him distribute [the goods] for me.
Everyone praised this as excellent.
Then Udāyin divided the goods into six portions and placed his own share in his room;
Aśvaka said, "Venerable Udāyin!..."
"Bring what has been obtained here so that we may divide it together. Udāyin said,
"Venerable friend!"

Since you have come and gone, we have not even once obtained twenty cowrie shells; if you do not believe this, why do you not ask the great assembly now present and your fellow practitioners of the holy life?
Punarnavasa said,
"How could we have known that Udāyin was deceiving us? Udāyin replied:
"If one were to obtain many things and not share them, that would constitute deception; yet I have never even obtained a few cowries—how could there be deception?
When those five heard this, they all remained silent.
At that time, Udāyin thought to himself:
"I have now obtained a great deal of wool; whom shall I send to process it?
If I give it to a skilled artisan, since he is difficult to trust and lacks moral discipline, there is a danger that both will be lost."

If it were given to the group of twelve nuns, they too would be difficult to trust, as they are meticulous calculators who would likely use it to pay for the cost of pastries and fruits brought from elsewhere.
As for the bhikṣuṇī Dharmadinnā, she is well-versed in the Sūtra Piṭaka; her followers likewise uphold the Sūtras, reciting them with diligence and cultivating all manner of wholesome qualities.
"As for me and that hair, we have spent a great deal of time without being able to finish the task.

That Gautamī is well-versed in the Vinaya-piṭaka, and all her disciples likewise uphold the Vinaya; they deliberate upon what constitutes an offense and what does not, weighing the gravity and lightness of each transgression. Therefore, even if I were to entrust the hair to her, I would still not be able to achieve my purpose."

"Since Mahāprajāpatī has made meditative concentration her primary concern and all her disciples are practicing tranquility, she may have a little leisure to allow me to request that my wool be processed.
Having thought this, Mahāprajāpatī came to pay homage to the World-Honored One;
seeing her, Udāyin asked, "Gautamī!"
As the Blessed One has said:
"For one who possesses the prohibitive precepts, whatever matters they contemplate in their mind shall all be accomplished; such is the fruit obtained through the power of pure morality.
This is well-spoken.
How is this known?
I have just had this thought:
"It would be truly wonderful if Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī were to come."
"Now that you have come, my deep wish has been fulfilled. He asked,
"Virtuous One!..."
"What do you wish to have done?
He replied, "I have a small amount of wool that requires processing; could you do it for me?"
He replied, "Venerable One!

I have come here specifically to pay homage at the feet of the World-Honored One. Once I have seen the Buddha, I shall have the two nuns come to my quarters so that we may meet; I will then hand over the articles they prepared for you."
At that time, Udāyin had tied all his wool into two bundles and placed them behind the door of his room.
When Gopikā, having paid homage to the World-Honored One, was about to return to the nunnery, she sent two nuns to the room to fetch the items, saying:
"Venerable Sir!"
The Noble Gautamī sent someone to fetch wool.
He replied, “Behind the door panels there are two bundles of wool; you may take them with you.”
He then entered the gate intending to take the wool away, but even when he pulled and tugged with his hands, he could not move it.
The two of them replied, "Venerable One!
Could there perhaps be a grinding stone within the wool?"
Udāyin said, "How could you young men possibly have your spines broken!
Then Udāyin took a bundle with his little finger and placed it upon one head, and again took another bundle and placed it between the waist of the other.

At that time, those two nuns, suffering from headaches and aching waists, arrived at the monastery in great distress. Once they had reached the monastery, they cast themselves upon the ground and lay prostrate upon their beds.
When the other bhikṣuṇīs saw them, they asked, "Have your spines broken, you two?"
"Carrying this small amount of wool has already caused me great exhaustion and suffering.
She said to the nuns,
"If you are stronger than I am, try lifting it up and see."
He then attempted to lift it, but in the end he could not move it.
The nuns replied,
"Is there a grindstone inside this bundle of hair?"
The two nuns, having entered meditative concentration, opened the bundle of hair, whereupon it became a massive heap. When the other nuns saw this, they laughed aloud.
At that time, Mahāprajāpatī heard their laughter and asked, "O venerable ones!
What is the cause of your laughter?"
Is this not a perversion?
Having shaved off your hair, a topknot has grown from your armpits; even until now you have been unable to attain tranquility.
Why do you engage in such clamorous laughter?
The nuns replied,
"Venerable Noble One!
If even 'a small amount of wool' spoken by Udāyin leads to such a consequence, what would happen if he were to say 'much'?"
Mahāprajāpatī said: "Sisters!
He has practiced evil deeds and constantly brings ruin to the Buddha's teaching, like a fine riverbank collapsing and causing things to fall."
However, the Buddha has spoken of two kinds of virtuous persons:
first, those who do not consent to a matter; second, those who, having consented, cause it to be fulfilled.
Since this is a case of having granted consent, the matter must be brought to completion.
"If you all can manage it together, take as much as you need, finish the task, and return it.
Since the hair was so abundant, it was difficult to complete the work in a hurry.
At that time, Udāyin thought to himself:
“Mahāprajāpatī always delights in tranquility; let us not cause the bhikṣuṇīs to be used as payment for flour.
Thus he remained, sighing in reflection.
At that time, two bhikṣuṇīs finished processing some wool and sent it to Udāyin, who replied:
"Noble One!
I have brought this wool; where do you wish to place it?
Udāyin replied:
"Since you still have some intention in your hearts to return my things," he then said to the bhikṣuṇī,
"Sister, you may keep them in your room."
She placed them inside a room and departed; once the remaining wool had been processed, she likewise sent it all there.
As Mahāprajāpatī had handled the wool, her hands became as red as a dyer of crimson; she then went to the Buddha’s dwelling, prostrated at his feet, and sat to one side.
At that time, the World-Honored One saw that her hands were red and asked,
“Gautamī, for what reason are your hands as red as those of a guest-dyer?”
He addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Venerable Sir!
As the Buddha has said:"
"What ought to be done was not done, and instead another matter was performed; now I shall do it.
The Buddha said:
"What was it that Mahāprajāpatī did?
Then Gopikā related the matter in detail to the Blessed One.
The Buddha said to Ānanda:
“Monks, did you have a nun who was not a relative process the wool?
Ānanda replied, “Venerable Sir!”
"Monks, have him prepare it.
Then the Blessed One, for this reason, assembled the community of monks and asked Udāyin:
"Is it true that you had a nun who was not a relative prepare the wool?"
He replied, “It is indeed so.
At that time, the World-Honored One rebuked Udāyin in various ways, as explained in detail above.
...down to: "I now establish this training rule, which should be recited as follows:
'If a bhikṣu should have a bhikṣuṇī who is not a relative wash, dye, or card wool, it is a naiḥsargika-pāyattika.'"
"Regarding 'if it is a bhikṣu,' this refers to Udāyin.
Regarding 'a nun who is not a relative,' the meaning of 'relative' and 'non-relative' is as explained above.
Regarding 'wool,' this refers to wool and no other fur."
"Washing" refers to even dipping it once into water.
"Dyeing" refers to even dipping it once into dye.
"Beating" refers to even a single stroke.
Regarding the *naiḥsargika-pāyattika*, it is explained in detail as stated above.

As for the characteristics of the offense herein: if a bhikṣu, regarding a nun who is not a relative, perceives her as not being a relative, or entertains doubt, and causes her to wash, dye, or card wool, he commits the offense of forfeiture and transgression (*naiḥsargika-pāyattika*).

If one washes and dyes but does not card, or washes and cards but does not dye, or dyes but does not wash and card, one likewise commits an offense of forfeiture and transgression (nissaggiya-pācittiya).

If one treats a nun who is a relative as if she were not a relative, or if one entertains doubt regarding her status, and causes her to perform the three tasks of preparing wool, one incurs an offense of wrongdoing (dukkaṭa) in each case.
The rest is as explained above.
There is no offense if one perceives the person as a relative.
Furthermore, there is no offense for one who is a first-time offender, or one who is insane, mentally deranged, or overwhelmed by intense pain.
18. The Training Rule on Taking Gold, Silver, and the Like. The eighteenth training rule concerning the taking of gold, silver, and the like. The Buddha was staying at the Bamboo Grove in Rājagṛha.
At that time, there was a village headman and householder named Ratnaśikhin who came to where the Buddha was, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, sat to one side, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!”
Recently, while the king and his ministers were assembled together in a great gathering, someone asked this question:
"Do you know, sirs, whether the śramaṇas, the sons of the Śākyas, are permitted to accept and possess gold and silver?"
Some people said:
"A bhikṣu may hold it.
Others further said:
"It is not permissible for a bhikṣu.
Of these two statements, which one accords with reason and which does not?
Who speaks the words of Dharma?
Who speaks what is not the words of Dharma?
Who slanders the Buddha?
Who is it that does not slander?
Who is it that is despised by superior persons?
Who is it that is not despised by superior persons?
The World-Honored One replied:
“Householder!

If someone were to say that the śramaṇas, sons of the Śākyas, are permitted to accept and handle gold and silver, this would not accord with reason; it is an unrighteous statement, a slander against me, and something for which superior persons would feel shame.”
Anything other than this is called "wholesome. Why is that?
Householder!
In truth, a bhikṣu must not accept or handle gold and silver.
If there is a bhikṣu who does not accept or handle gold and silver, this is the dharma of a śramaṇa, this is the way of a son of the Śākyas, and this is the purely wholesome dharma.
A second and a third time I speak thus:
whoever accepts [the robe] is not a śramaṇa, not a son of the Śākya, and does not possess the pure, wholesome Dharma.
"A second and a third time, I speak thus.
The householder said,
"Venerable Sir!"
This is my view:
if a bhikṣu does not accept or handle gold and silver, he is a true śramaṇa, a virtuous son of the Śākyas.
If he accepts or handles them, he is not a true śramaṇa, nor a son of the Śākyas.
The World-Honored One said:
"Excellent! Excellent!"
"Householder!
Your understanding is excellent; you have distinguished this well.
When the householder Ratnaśikhin had heard what the Buddha said, he received it with joy and faith, prostrated before the Buddha, and withdrew.
At that time, Ānanda was standing behind the Buddha fanning him. As soon as the householder had departed, [the Buddha] addressed Ānanda, saying:
"You should now go to all the bhikṣus present here and have them assemble entirely in the constant dining hall."

Then Ānanda, having received the Buddha’s instruction, summoned them all together; returning to the place where the Buddha was, he prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, stood to one side, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!”
"I have followed the Buddha's instruction and have recently summoned all these bhikṣus to assemble in the dining hall; only the Buddha knows the proper time.
At that time, the World-Honored One went to the dining hall, took his seat before the great assembly, and addressed the bhikṣus, saying:

"There was a village headman named Ratnaśikhin who came to my place, prostrated at my feet, and sat to one side, making this request as described above in detail, until he finally took his leave of me and departed."

"O bhikṣus! That village headman, amidst the assembly of the king, let out a lion’s roar and spoke with certainty: 'It is not fitting for the śramaṇa sons of the Śākyas to accept gold, silver, coins, and the like.'"
I have also declared:
"A śramaṇa, a son of the Śākyas, should not accept gold, silver, coins, or the like.
Therefore, O bhikṣus!
If for the purpose of constructing dwellings or similar tasks, one should seek grass, wood, vehicles, and manual labor; however, one should not seek gold, silver, coins, or the like.
I have not said that there is any expedient by which bhikṣus are permitted to possess or handle gold and such items.
This is the origin of the rule; at that time, the precept had not yet been established.

While the Buddha was staying in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park, the group of six bhikṣus took gold, silver, and coins with their own hands, or instructed others to take them for the construction of dwellings, or placed them upon beds and seats.
At that time, the non-Buddhists saw this and spoke with contempt:

"These śramaṇas, sons of the Śākyas, take hold of gold, silver, coins, and the like with their own hands, or instruct others to do so; as explained in detail above, even other laypeople act in this same way. What distinction is there between them and us?"
"How can you cause other brahmins and householders to conceive such deep respect and faith that they provide food and drink to these shaven-headed men?
When the bhikṣus heard this, they reported the matter in full to the Blessed One.
For this reason, the World-Honored One assembled the community of bhikṣus and spoke at length as previously described.
He then asked the group of six:
"Is it true that you yourselves took hold of gold, silver, coins, and the like, or that you instructed others to do so?"
He replied, "It is indeed so.
After the World-Honored One had rebuked him in various ways as described above, he established the training rule, which should be recited as follows:
"If a bhikṣu again takes gold, silver, coins, or the like with his own hand, or instructs another to take them, it is a naiḥsargika-pāyattika.
Regarding "if a bhikṣu again": this refers to the group of the six [monks].
"With one's own hand" means to grasp with the hand.
"Gold and silver" refers to gold, silver, and cowrie shells.
"Money" refers to coins made of gold and other metals.
Teaching others is likewise; all constitute an offense of forfeiture and transgression (*naiḥsargika-pāyattika*).
The method for relinquishing and repenting is explained in detail as above.
What are the characteristics of the offenses and their specific matters in this context?
If one instructs another to take [an object], there are eighteen different types of such acts, all of which constitute an offense.
That is to say, telling that person:
"Take this object";
"You take this from here;
you take that much from there.
You shall carry this object."
"Take this from here;
take that much from there.
Place this object here."
"Place this here;
place that many of these here.
Take that object."
"You took from that;
you took that much of it.
You carried away that object."
"You shall take that;
you shall take so much of that.
You shall set aside that object."
"Place that there for you";
"place that much of that for you.
Regarding the instruction "take this object," it means instructing another to take gold, silver, and so forth from a visible location; [if one does so], one incurs a *duṣkṛta* offense.
At the moment of seizing [the object], one commits an offense of expiation involving forfeiture (*naiḥsargika-pāyattika*).

To say, "Take this from here," means that if one instructs another to take an item from among various bags or containers made of iron, wood, or other materials, the offense incurred is the same as before.
Regarding the statement "Take this much," it refers to instructing another to take objects numbering in the hundreds of thousands of billions; the offense incurred is the same as before.
Regarding the statement "Bring this object," it refers to instructing another to bring items such as gold and silver; the offense incurred is the same as before.
Regarding the phrase "you take from this," it means instructing another to take an object from within a pouch, a box, or a container; the offense incurred is the same as before.
Regarding the phrase "you take this much," it means instructing another to take hundreds, thousands, billions, or more; the offense incurred is the same as before.
Regarding the statement "you place this object," it means that when one instructs another to place gold, silver, or the like, the offense incurred is the same as before.
Regarding the statement "you place this here," it means that one places it inside a chest, a vessel, or similar container; the offense incurred is the same as before.
"Setting aside this much" refers to when one instructs others to set aside hundreds of thousands of billions [of items] and so forth; the offense incurred is the same as before.
These nine cases all refer to instructing others to perform the act in a visible location.
Regarding the statement "you take that object," it means that if one instructs another to take objects such as gold or silver from a place where they are not visible, one incurs a *duṣkṛta* offense;
at the moment of seizing and lifting them, one commits a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* offense.
"To take from that" means instructing another to take items from bags or from chests and containers made of iron or wood; the offense incurred is the same as before.
"To take that much from that" means instructing another to take hundreds, thousands, billions, and so forth; the offense incurred is the same as before.
Regarding the statement "you shall bring that object," it means instructing another to bring items such as gold or silver; the offense incurred is the same as before.
Regarding the statement "you shall take from there," it means instructing another to take an object from within a pouch, box, or container; the offense incurred is the same as before.
Regarding the statement "you take that much," it means that when one instructs another to take hundreds of thousands of billions of items and so forth, the offense incurred is the same as before.
Regarding the statement "you set aside those objects," it means that when one instructs another to set aside gold, silver, and so forth, the offense incurred is the same as before.
"To place it there" means placing it within such things as chests or vessels; the offense incurred is the same as before.
"To tell another to place it there to such an extent" means instructing another to place it in quantities of hundreds, thousands, or billions; the offense incurred is the same as before.
These nine cases all refer to instructing another to perform the act in a place where one cannot see it.
If a bhikṣu personally grasps gold, silver, coins, or cowrie shells, he commits an offense of expiation with forfeiture (*naiḥsargika-pāyattika*).
If a bhikṣu grasps gold or silver, whether wrought or unwrought, he commits an offense of expiation with forfeiture.
If a bhikṣu takes hold of gold, silver, coins, or cowries that possess auspicious markings, he commits an offense of expiation involving forfeiture (naiḥsargika-pāyattika).
If a bhikṣu touches a mani-jewel or a beryl gem, he commits an offense of expiation involving forfeiture.
If a bhikṣu takes currency used in a particular country or region, he commits an offense of expiation involving forfeiture (naiḥsargika-pāyattika).
If he takes currency not used in that country or region, he incurs an offense of wrongdoing (duṣkṛta).
If he takes red copper, brass, bronze, iron, lead, or tin, there is no offense.

Thus, after the Blessed One had established the training rules for the śrāvakas, the Buddha was staying at Jetavana. At that time, there was a householder in the city of Campā who lived there; he was deeply faithful and purely virtuous, practicing generosity with excellent and superior things.

At that time, the elder constructed a dwelling for the Buddha and the Saṃgha, adorned with intricately decorated doors, windows, and railings; it was so exquisitely and magnificently embellished that it was a joy to behold, serving as a path to rebirth in heaven, and many monks resided there during the rainy season retreat.
Having completed the rains retreat and finished the *pravāraṇā* ceremony, they said to the elder:
"We now wish to go to Śrāvastī to pay homage at the feet of the Great Teacher and to the venerable, elderly bhikṣus; please grant us robes as we are currently lacking them."
The householder replied:
"Noble One! There are no superior, exquisite garments or fabrics here. However, I have heard that a caravan is about to arrive; when they arrive, I shall purchase some and offer them to you."
The bhikṣu said:
"Householder!
If you have no fine goods, give me something coarse and poor."
The householder replied, “Noble One!
It is my nature to always give excellent things; why should I now give you something of poor quality?”
"If you do not wait, you may take the money for the price of the robe with you.
He replied, "Householder!..."
“The World-Honored One has established precepts that prohibit me from handling money.
The householder replied,
“If that is the case, I would rather not give at all than bestow such base things upon others.”
At that time, the bhikṣus, having obtained nothing at all, abandoned it and departed, proceeding along the road until they reached Śrāvastī.
When the bhikṣus saw them, they said to them, "Welcome!"
"Welcome, venerable ones!
Did you not receive many robes at your place of retreat during the rainy season? Why have you come here wearing such coarse and tattered garments?"
He replied, "There are no robes to be obtained.
The bhikṣu said:
"In what place are you observing the rains retreat?
He replied,
"In the kingdom of Campā."
He asked again:
“Upon what do you rely for your dwelling? He replied:
"Householder So-and-so.
The bhikṣus said, "We have heard that this householder is fond of giving upper robes; will he not give one?"
He replied,
"It is precisely because of this that I have not obtained the robe.
The bhikṣu asked:
"What is the reason for this?
At that time, those bhikṣus related the matter in detail, and having heard it, the other bhikṣus informed the Buddha.
The Buddha thought to himself:
"When there are brahmins, householders, or lay devotees who, out of reverence and faith, joyfully wish to give the price for robes to the bhikṣus,
and my disciples desire to obtain robes, I should establish a rule so that the bhikṣus may receive them without any deficiency."
He addressed the bhikṣus, saying:

"If there is a gift of cloth-price offered by another, one may accept it as needed; having accepted it, one should then maintain possession of it with the mental attitude that it belongs to that person."
"However, the bhikṣus should seek out a person to serve as an attendant.
The bhikṣus did not know what kind of person they should seek;
the Buddha said:
"One should seek either a temple attendant (ārāmika) or an upāsaka.
A 'temple attendant' refers to a *kappiyakāraka* (a pure person).
An 'upāsaka' refers to one who has received the three refuges and the five precepts."
One should ask him:
"Are you able to act as my donor?
If he says he can, one may then entrust the matter to this person's mind and keep the items; one should have another person hold them and should not grasp them oneself.
At that time, there was a bhikṣu who, having gone to another region, thought to himself:
"I have now arrived here, yet I have no donor.
Feeling remorse, he reported the matter to the Buddha. The Buddha said:
"Even if he has gone far away, as long as his life remains, he shall always be the donor.
At that time, there was a bhikṣu who had not yet found a donor; when another person gave him an object, the bhikṣu was hesitant and did not dare to accept it.
He reported the matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"It should be accepted.
Having accepted it, one should hold the object and address a single bhikṣu as follows:"
"Venerable sir, please bear this in mind!
I, the bhikṣu [name], have obtained this impure object; I shall take this impure object and exchange it for pure wealth."
"Thus it has been said three times; you may use these things as you please, and do not harbor any doubts.
At that time, there was a donor who built a monastery in a remote border region and offered it to the Sangha; however, from time to time, bandits came to cause them alarm and fear.
Those bhikṣus departed from the empty monastery, whereupon thieves arrived and took the monastery's property.
The Buddha said:
"Whether it be the property of the Saṃgha, the property of a stūpa, or all gold, silver, money, jewels, and so forth, one should securely store them away before departing."
The Buddha said,
"Have it hidden.
The bhikṣu did not know whom he should send to hide it.
The Buddha said:
"If there is a *karmadāna* (pure person) or an *upāsaka* (lay follower), have them store and keep it.
When those who were storing it stole the items, the Buddha said:
"A lay follower (*upāsaka*) of deep faith should be made to store [the items]; if there is no one of deep faith, a novice (*śrāmaṇera*) should be made to do so.
If there is no novice, the bhikṣu himself should store them with his own hands."
The bhikṣus did not know how to store [the items] away.
The Buddha said, "One should dig a pit.
They did not know who should do it.
The Buddha said:
"One should employ a *kappiya-kāraka* (a pure person) or an *upāsaka* (lay follower).
If they should steal an object, one should instead employ a person of faith."
If there is no one [to do this], he should have a novice (śrāmaṇera) do it; if there is no novice, he should dig it up himself.
After the thieves have departed, he should take the items as before and return them to the Saṃgha.
The Buddha said:

"Regarding matters that I have permitted as exceptions, they should not be practiced after the exception has ceased; if one were to practice them then, one would incur an offense of wrong-doing (duṣkṛta)."
Furthermore, there is no offense for one who is a first-time offender, or for one who is insane, mentally deranged, or afflicted by intense pain.
