The Training Rule on Seeking Profit from Lending and Borrowing. At that time, the Bhagavān was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, the Garden of Anāthapiṇḍada. News had reached both far and near that a Buddha had appeared in the world in the Middle Kingdom, and that his śrāvaka disciples possessed great supernormal powers and performed various transformations, as described in detail above. It was further said that anyone who could make offerings to those disciples would obtain a great fruit of retribution, with vast benefit and increase.
At that time, there were merchants from the north who, having heard of this reputation, said to one another:
"Gentlemen, you should know!
We ought to go to the Middle Kingdom for trade; first, we shall gain great profit, and second, we shall make offerings to the Triple Gem."
Then the merchants, taking a great quantity of northern goods, set out for the Middle Kingdom and gradually arrived at Śrāvastī.

In this city there was a naked ascetic (*nirgrantha*) who was well-versed in celestial phenomena and skilled in mathematics and chronology. Hearing that merchants had arrived from the north, he thought to himself:
"I shall now go and examine and question these merchants; perhaps I may obtain something small from them."

He immediately took up his divination book to examine past events; observing it, he learned the names of the merchant leader’s parents, the goods they were carrying, and how much profit they would gain. He then went to where the merchant leader was and said, “Welcome! ”
"Welcome!

Merchant leader [Name], your father’s name was [Name] and your mother’s name was [Name]. You brought such-and-such goods to this region, and on such-and-such a day, you obtained such-and-such a profit."
Having heard this, the merchant leader thought to himself:
"I have previously heard that the disciples of the World-Honored One possess great supernormal powers, such as emitting smoke and pouring down rain; this must be that very person."

Having conceived a spirit of reverence and faith, the merchant leader took a crimson woolen cloak from the north and various rare fruits of the north, filled them into a vessel, and personally offered them with his own hands.
Having obtained it, he immediately donned the *kambala* and went to where his companions were.
When his companions saw him, they asked:
"From where have you come with this precious and high-quality article?"
He replied, "I went to see some merchants from the north; I told them the names of my parents, and they, having conceived faith and reverence in their hearts, bestowed a gift upon me."
His companions said to him:
"Venerable sir!
We are constantly held in contempt by the śramaṇas, the sons of the Śākyas, who always say to us:..."
"You have never associated with noble and excellent people, but have instead only been intimate with lowly laborers and the *caṇḍāla* class.
You should now put on these noble robes and go to the place of the śramaṇa sons of the Śākyas to pierce their hearts."
He replied, "So be it.
Thereupon, the naked ascetic put on a woolen cloak and went to the Jetavana Grove.
At that time, Upānanda was walking for exercise at the gate of the Jeta Grove when he saw him approaching from afar and thought to himself:
"The garment worn by this outsider is a fine and precious thing; if I cannot obtain this object, I shall no longer be called Upānanda."
Having gradually drawn near, he asked,
"O outsider!
Have you now perhaps recently returned to the lay life?"
He replied, "I shall not return to the life of a layman.
[The other] asked, "If that is so, why do you wear these robes?"
He replied, “I am a merchant from the north; I have mentioned the names of my kinsmen there because I felt great respect for them and thus offered this gift. Upānanda said:
"This is not a virtuous deed!
This is not a virtuous deed!
How can one who is advanced in years and physically decayed permit themselves to break the precepts?"
"You should sit for a moment and briefly listen to the essentials of the Dharma.
At that time, the non-Buddhist follower sat down immediately upon these words.

Then, with a joyful heart, Upānanda preached the Dharma to him; when Upānanda proclaimed the Dharma of renunciation and giving, those brāhmaṇas and lay devotees all desired to cut the flesh from their own bodies to offer it as a gift.
On the occasion of preaching the Dharma, Upānanda addressed him, saying:
"O outsider!

Your great teacher is by nature fond of what is coarse and wretched; he instructs his disciples to go naked, to pull out their hair, to practice much while dwelling little, and to constantly lie upon the ground."

"If your Great Teacher is fond of fine clothing and food, you should permit him to wear exquisite garments worth ten million [gold pieces], to eat and drink foods of a hundred flavors at his pleasure, and to dwell in a residence worth five thousand [gold pieces]."
Because of their narrow-mindedness, they could not tolerate this.

My Great Teacher, however, possessed a vast heart; he permitted me, his disciple, to wear robes worth ten thousand coins, to eat food of a hundred flavors, and to dwell in a residence valued at five thousand.
If you were to go begging for alms while wearing these expensive and fine garments, those who possess faith and reverence would think:
"Now this non-Buddhist practitioner has broken his moral conduct in body."
"As for food and drink, it is difficult to sustain myself with them.
You should give me this upper garment of yours; I have a woolen shawl which I shall exchange for it, and I will wear it as I go from house to house begging for alms."
If a person of pure faith should come and ask me,
"Venerable sir, where did you obtain this upper robe?
I shall answer him thus:
"There is a naked ascetic named so-and-so who has ceased [other activities] to give alms to you.
He will then recognize that you are a person of deep faith.
When you go begging for food, if he sees you, he will offer you a copper vessel filled to the brim with dregs of wine.
When the naked ascetic heard these words, he immediately felt faith and joy, and spoke thus:
"Venerable Upānanda! If it is so, you may take this robe."
Upānanda then uttered a blessing, saying:
"May you be free from illness and long-lived!
However, your followers are constantly in a state of poverty and suffering; when they hear that you are giving alms, they will surely snatch it away from you."
He said, "Venerable sir!
Is this woolen cloak indeed his property?"
"This is my own freedom; you need not worry.
Upānanda said, "If it is so, I shall accept it for you."
Having accepted it, he immediately gave him a coarse, stiff-haired blanket.
The outsider put it on and departed, going to where his fellow practitioners were.
He then asked,
"Virtuous one, where did you obtain this robe?
He immediately replied to him:
"He has exchanged it with me.
He asked, "Who is he?"
He replied,
"The Venerable Upānanda has exchanged goods with me.
Upon hearing this, they were all enraged and said in response:
"O virtuous one, this son of the Śākyas constantly intends to kill me; though he may deceive others, he is not like the group of six, and among those six, none surpasses Upānanda."
If you were to bestow [this] upon other virtuous ones, I would indeed rejoice; yet Upānanda wishes to drink my blood—if I were to give my robe to him, who could possibly endure it?
"You should go and demand it back immediately.
If you succeed, that is well; if you do not, I shall join you in censuring you, move your seat, cover your food vessels, and no longer speak with you."
He became terrified and went to where Upānanda was.
When Upānanda saw him coming from afar, he thought to himself:
"Judging by this non-Buddhist's movements and demeanor, he will surely seize my fine woolen cloak."
He immediately entered his cell, closed the door, and remained there.
When the non-Buddhist arrived and knocked on the door, calling out to him, Upānanda remained silent and did not respond. Seeing this, the bhikṣus asked, "Non-Buddhist!..."
"Why do you need to see Upānanda?
He replied,
"He came seeking me for the sake of my woolen cloak."
The bhikṣu replied,
“If you wish to obtain your old woolen cloak, go to the Blessed One and seek his compassionate favor.
Thereupon, that non-Buddhist went to where the Buddha was.
At that time, the World-Honored One saw the non-Buddhist practitioners approaching from afar and addressed the bhikṣus, saying:
"Do you see those non-Buddhist practitioners coming?
They replied to the Buddha: [We do.]
"I see," the Buddha said.
"He has come for the sake of the woolen cloak."
"If I can recover it, that would be well; if I cannot, I shall vomit hot blood and meet my end.
A non-Buddhist came to where the Buddha was and spoke these words:
"Venerable Upānanda has taken my woolen cloak; I pray only that the World-Honored One, out of compassion and pity, will cause him to return it to me."
"If he does not return, we, who are fellow practitioners of the holy life, shall expel me," he said,
as previously related in detail. At that time,
the Blessed One addressed the Venerable Ānanda, saying:
"Go yourself and say to Upānanda:
'May you be free from illness,' and further tell him:"
"You must return that woolen cloak to those non-Buddhists;
if you do not return it, these non-Buddhists shall vomit hot blood and meet their end.
When the Venerable Ānanda had received the Buddha’s instruction, he went to where Upānanda was. Seeing him from afar, Upānanda thought to himself:
"Seeing this non-Buddhist taking the Buddha’s attendant for a messenger, he will surely seize my woolen cloak.
Then the Venerable Ānanda replied to Upānanda,
"Venerable sir!"
“World-Honored One, may you be free from illness.
Having heard these words, Upānanda rose immediately from his seat and replied:
“I now pay homage to the Unsurpassed World-Honored One.”
Ānanda said: “The World-Honored One has given this instruction: ‘You should return the non-Buddhist woolen cloak.
If you can return it, that would be excellent.’”
"If he does not return, this non-Buddhist will vomit hot blood and meet his end.
Upānanda said, "I respectfully follow the Buddha's teaching; how would I dare to contravene it?"

If it were not for the Buddha sending me back, you would have caused the non-Buddhists to fill Jambudvīpa as densely as bamboo, reeds, or sugarcane, all vomiting hot blood and dying at once; yet not even a single hair of my Upānanda would have moved.
"Venerable Ānanda, you may go; I shall return there myself.
He then said to the non-Buddhist:

"Your great teacher previously practiced false speech to deceive the world; having passed away, he has fallen into the Avīci Great Hell, where five hundred plows are tilling his tongue day and night."
"Your current lie is twice as great as that one; you shall have a thousand plows constantly tilling your tongue.
Upānanda said, "You have already put on my woolen cloak, yet I never used your things."
The non-Buddhist replied, "I do not wear it either.

Then Upānanda took the woolen shawl, untied its knots, folded it into four layers, and placed it in his left hand; with his right hand he struck and beat it until the shawl was completely shattered to pieces. He then said to the non-Buddhist:
"Stretch out both your hands.
He then threw the woolen cloak over him, covering him from head to toe, and immediately fell upon him, kicking him in the ribs, saying: "Heretic!"
Go quickly! Go quickly!
Do not let excrement and filth defile my dwelling place.
The non-Buddhist replied,
“Venerable sir!
As long as I remain alive and am able to leave, I shall never again dare to enter the Jeta Grove.”
This was the origin of the event, yet the Buddha, the World-Honored One, had not yet laid down the precept.
At that time, the group of six bhikṣus engaged in various forms of lending at interest: they would either take or give, or produce profit, or pledge collateral;
they would exchange finished goods for finished goods, finished goods for unfinished goods, unfinished goods for finished goods, and unfinished goods for unfinished goods.

Regarding "taking": this refers to collecting all the goods that others cherish from other regions, loading them for transport and taking them away; seeking out guards and establishing various contracts—this is called "taking."
Regarding "giving" (*yāna*): this refers to giving another object on the eighth or tenth day and establishing a formal contract as proof; this is called "giving. Regarding "arising" (*jīvita*):

this refers to generating profit by giving a small amount of goods to another and taking back much grain or barley—increasing it by five percent, or one or two times its value—and storing it with measures such as *sheng* and *dou*, while establishing a promissory note; this is called "arising."

Regarding "pledge" (*pratigraha*): it refers to taking precious jewels or similar items as collateral, as previously stipulated in the contract, and requesting a reliable guarantor to provide those goods; this is called a pledge.
Regarding "taking what is already completed": it refers to using gold, silver, or other materials to take another's already finished vessel.
"Taking what is finished with what is unfinished" refers to taking another's gold vessel by means of a gold ingot.
"Taking what is unfinished with what is finished" refers to taking another's gold ingot by means of a gold vessel.
Regarding the phrase "taking what is unfinished with what is unfinished," this refers to taking broken gold in exchange for a gold ingot.
When monks engaged in such transactions to seek profit, the various non-Buddhists saw these matters and all felt contempt and disdain, saying:
"How is it that these śramaṇas, sons of the Śākyas, produce goods to seek profit? How are they any different from the laity?"
"Who can provide him with clothing and food?

When the bhikṣus heard this, they reported it all in detail to the Buddha. The Buddha spoke at length as above, until he reached the point of establishing the training rule (śikṣāpada), which should be recited thus:
"If a bhikṣu again seeks profit through various kinds of lending and borrowing, it is a naiḥsargika-pāyattika."
"Monks" refers to the group of six.
"Various kinds" means more than one matter.
"Seeking profit through lending and borrowing" means engaging in taking and giving with a covetous intent to seek financial gain.
Regarding the offense of *naiḥsargika-pāyattika*, the ritual procedure for its expiation is explained in detail as above.

As for the characteristics of the offense herein: if a bhikṣu, for the sake of seeking profit, collects goods and employs various means to drive carriages to other regions, enters into contracts with guarantors, and carries taxable goods, he incurs only an *dukkaṭa* (wrongdoing) as long as he has not yet obtained the profit; however, at the moment he obtains the profit, he incurs the *naiḥsargika-pāyattika*.

If a bhikṣu, for the sake of seeking profit, provides various goods such as gold, silver, and other valuables to another person and enters into a formal agreement or guarantee with them, he incurs an offense as extensively described previously.

If a bhikṣu, for the sake of seeking profit, takes various goods or grain and entrusts them to another, weighing them by measures such as *sheng* or *dou* and establishing a formal contract as evidence, he incurs an offense as extensively explained previously.
If a bhikṣu, for the sake of seeking profit, accepts precious gems, pearls, shells, or jade to calculate interest over time—whether he actually receives the profit or not—it is as explained above.

If a bhikṣu, for the sake of profit, exchanges his own robe for another’s robe, at the moment he seeks the exchange, he incurs a *duṣkṛta* offense; once the exchange is completed, he commits an offense requiring forfeiture and confession (*naiḥsargika-pāyattika*).

Furthermore, while the Blessed One was staying in the Multi-storied Hall by the side of the Monkey Pond in Vaiśālī, the Licchavis and others of that city saw that the dwellings of the bhikṣus were low and humble compared to their own residences, which were six or seven stories high; they immediately constructed for them well-constructed, magnificent houses six or seven stories high.
After the buildings had stood for a long time, many fell into ruin; seeing this, the donors all thought to themselves:
"The temples we currently maintain are all falling apart; what will become of them after our lives have ended?"
"We ought to provide inexhaustible materials for him to carry out the construction.
Having thus taken the materials, they went to where the bhikṣus were and said,
"Noble ones!..."
"This is an inexhaustible gift intended for the repair [of the monastery]; you may accept it.
The bhikṣus replied, "The World-Honored One has established the precepts; we are not permitted to accept it."
At that time, the bhikṣus reported the matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"If one is engaged in construction for the sake of the Saṃgha, one may accept inexhaustible goods."
"However, the vihāra for bhikṣus should be built with three stories, while that for bhikṣuṇīs should be built with two stories.
At that time, the bhikṣus obtained inexhaustible goods and placed them in the storehouse of the monastery. Then, a donor came and asked, "Noble ones!"
"For what reason has this monastery still not been repaired?
The bhikṣu replied,
"O noble one!"
"I have no money.
The owner said,
"Do I not give you inexhaustible goods?"
He replied, "O worthy one!
As for those inexhaustible goods, how could I have consumed them? They were placed in the monastery treasury and remain there to this day."
The donor replied, "It is not appropriate for such inexhaustible goods to be treated in this manner; surely there is no place for them in my home?
Why do you not exchange them to seek profit?"
The bhikṣus replied,
“The Buddha has prohibited us and does not permit us to seek profit.
Then the bhikṣus reported this matter in detail to the World-Honored One, and the World-Honored One said:
"If it is for the sake of the Saṃgha, one should seek profit.

Having heard these words of the Buddha, the faithful brahmins and householders offered inexhaustible goods for the sake of the Buddha, Dharma, and Saṃgha; these goods belonging to the Triple Gem should likewise be circulated to seek profit, and the profits obtained should be used to make offerings back to the Triple Gem.
Then the bhikṣus returned these items to those donors; when they sought interest on them, there was much contention and dispute, and [the donors] spoke thus:
"O Noble Ones!..."
"Could it be that we are quarreling over our own property?
Then the bhikṣus reported this matter in detail to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One said:
"You should not engage in lending at interest with them."
Furthermore, they entered into a loan agreement with those who were wealthy and noble; when it came time to reclaim the goods, [the debtors] refused to return them, relying on their official power.
The Buddha said: "One should not engage in transactions with such people."
Furthermore, when lending money at interest to a poor person and finding no goods upon demand, the Buddha said:

"When giving property, it should be done clearly; one should take a double deposit and record the terms on a formal document, establish guarantors, and note the year and month, as well as the name of the presiding elder and the title of the official in charge."
"Even if a lay follower with faith receives the five precepts, one should likewise take double their security deposit.
Furthermore, there is no offense for the very first offender, or for one who is insane, mentally deranged, or overwhelmed by intense physical pain.
20. The Training Rule on Trading. The twentieth training rule concerning trading: The Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the group of six bhikṣus engaged in various kinds of transactions, taking and giving, buying and selling.
At that time, the various non-Buddhist practitioners each gave rise to feelings of disdain and contempt, saying:
"These śramaṇas, sons of the Śākyas, do not give rise to a sense of weary detachment; yet now they engage in the business of trade, taking, giving, selling, and buying."
"What distinction is there between this shaven-headed śramaṇa and ordinary laypeople?
Who, moreover, would be able to provide offerings of food and drink to such a shaven-headed man as this śramaṇa, a son of the Śākyas?"
At that time, the bhikṣus reported this matter in detail to the Blessed One.

On account of this, the Blessed One assembled the community of bhikṣus and, having rebuked the group of six in the same manner as previously described, said: "I now establish this training rule, which should be recited as follows:
'If a bhikṣu engages in various kinds of buying and selling, it is a naiḥsargika-pāyattika.'"
"Furthermore, 'if a bhikṣu' refers to the group of six [monks].
'Various kinds' means more than one thing.
Regarding 'taking, giving, selling, and buying': 'taking' means that if goods are cheap in another place and expensive here, one takes them from there."

"Bestowing" means that if something is of low value here but of high value elsewhere, one takes it from this place with the intention of buying it during a time of plenty and selling it during a time of scarcity.
"Naiḥsargika" is explained in detail as previously stated.

Regarding the offense herein: if a bhikṣu engages in buying and selling for the sake of profit, it is an *dukkaṭa* (wrongdoing) at the time of buying, and a *niḥsargika-pāyattika* (offense involving forfeiture) at the time of selling.
If he buys for the sake of profit but does not sell for the sake of profit, it is an *dukkaṭa* at the time of buying.
There is no offense when selling.

If one buys without seeking profit but sells for the sake of profit, there is no offense at the time of purchase; however, there is an offense of expiation involving forfeiture (*naiḥsargika-pāyattika*) at the time of sale.
If one does not buy for profit nor sell for profit, there is no offense in either case.
If one buys goods in another region with the intention of departing and does not originally seek profit, then even if a profit is gained when selling at the destination, there is no offense.
Furthermore, there is no offense for one who is a first-time offender, or for one who is insane, mentally deranged, or overwhelmed by intense pain.
The third summary verse says:
Two bowls, two weavers, taking away robes, and urgent offerings.
The rain-cloak for forest-dwellers; the seven-day medicine diverted to the Saṃgha.
The Twenty-first Training Rule: Regarding the Obtaining of an Extra Alms-bowl and Not Distinguishing It within Ten Days. The Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, Upānanda thought to himself:
"The Buddha has prohibited us from all places where we seek profit; consequently, we have no means of seeking it, and all our gains and offerings have been cut off because of this."
He remained there in sorrow.
At that time, sixty men went out to a park for a picnic and social gathering. Seeing them, Upānanda thought to himself:
"If I do not obtain wealth from these people, I shall no longer be known by the name Upānanda."

He then took an excellent bowl—perfect, radiant, pure, and fit for use—and placing it in a cloth bag under his arm, went to the banquet hall; there, he taught the Dharma to a single person, causing them to give rise to deep faith.
Having gained faith, he asked:
"Noble One! For what purpose have you come here?"
Upānanda said, "O worthy one! I have come for the sake of the bowl."
He replied, "I have no bowl at present; if there is a place where one can be bought, I shall purchase one and give it to you.
Then Upānanda drew his bowl out from beneath his arm and presented it, asking:
"How much is this bowl worth?
He replied,
"It is worth sixty kārṣāpaṇas."
He said, "I will give you sixty kārsāpaṇas; you should buy it yourself. Upānanda replied:

“O noble one! May you live long and be free from illness. This gift is for the adornment of the mind; it is an aid to the mind and a provision for meditative concentration that leads to the attainment of supreme fruits, so that you may always be a vessel for the Dharma among humans and devas.”
Thus, each of these sixty men individually begged for sixty *kārsāpaṇas* and then departed.
When those men had each finished their feasting and gathered together in one place, one man said to the others: "Gentlemen, rejoice!

I have just seen the noble Upānanda, who has gone forth from the Śākya clan as a monk, a great leader of the Dharma, well-versed in the Tripiṭaka and possessed of unimpeded eloquence; I have used sixty *kārsāpaṇas* to provide the price for his alms-bowl."
When those people heard these words, they all said,
"I too shall give sixty kāṛṣāpaṇas to him," and they then deliberated together, saying:
"Do you know how many bowls a single bhikṣu ought to possess?
They each replied,
"We do not know."
At that time, a certain bhikṣu was passing by, and people asked him,
"Venerable One!
How many bowls does a single bhikṣu require?"
He replied,
"I require only a single bowl.
Upon hearing this, they all felt mutual contempt and disdain.
“The śramaṇas, sons of the Śākyas, are excessively greedy for gain and offerings.
This was the origin of the matter, at which time the precept had not yet been established.
At that time, the group of six bhikṣus obtained many long bowls; they did not use them themselves, nor did they give them to the other bhikṣus.
A bhikṣu of few desires, having seen this, felt disdain and reproached him, saying:
"How can a bhikṣu store up an extra alms-bowl, neither using it himself nor giving it to others?
For this reason, he reported the matter in detail to the World-Honored One.
For this reason, the Buddha assembled the community of bhikṣus and rebuked the group of six bhikṣus:
"How is it that you all keep so many extra alms bowls?
He spoke at length as above, until: "It should be said thus:..."
"If a bhikṣu keeps an extra bowl for more than ten days without making a formal distribution [of it], it is a naiḥsargika-pāyattika.
"Bhikṣu" refers to the group of six monks and others.
"Exceeding ten days" means exceeding ten nights.
"An extra bowl" refers to any bowl other than the one kept for regular use; it is called "extra.
"To possess" means to form the intention that it belongs to oneself.
If one keeps it further, one incurs the offense of *naiḥsargika-pāyattika*. The procedure for relinquishing it is as explained extensively above.
In this context, what are the characteristics of the offense and its specific details?
If a bhikṣu obtains a bowl on the first day of the month, he must, within ten days, either keep it, distribute it, relinquish it, or give it to another.
The sequence and the method of skipping [the stages] are explained in detail as in the initial section on the cloth precept; even the ritual for relinquishing it is entirely the same as before.
If the object is small, or white, or intended as a gift, there is no offense for one who wishes to receive the precepts.
Furthermore, there is no offense for a first-time offender, or for one who is insane, mentally deranged, or overwhelmed by intense physical pain.
22. The Training Rule on Begging for Alms Bowls. The second training rule concerning begging for alms bowls: The Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
In that city, there was a young perfume seller who possessed an excellent alms bowl—perfect, radiant, and pure, fit for use.
There was a bhikṣu who, during the first part of the day, entered the city to beg for alms and wandered through the marketplace. A young incense-seller saw him and said:
"Noble one!..."
"I have a fine alms bowl that is fit for use; if you require it, you may take it as you please.
The bhikṣu replied, "I already possess an alms bowl."
The youth said,
"If any other bhikṣus require a bowl, please send them here.
He replied:
"So be it. Then, having obtained food through alms, that bhikṣu returned to the Jetavana, finished eating, washed his bowl, and addressed the bhikṣus, saying:
"Venerable ones!..."
"At a certain shop there is a seller of incense who has a fine bowl.
If you need a bowl, you may go and take it.
At that time, Upānanda, being not far from there, heard these words and thought to himself:
"I ought to reprimand that mendicant bhikṣu so that he no longer spreads such rumors, lest the followers of the 'black bowl' hear these words and flee in agitation.
He then said to the mendicant:
"Venerable one!..."
He ate the food offered with faith without uttering a single word beyond it, but instead gave free rein to his greedy mind, discussing nothing but robes and alms bowls. A beggar thought to himself:
"Among those in this world who seek much and are constantly covetous, Upānanda is surely one such."

"If even this, upon hearing my words, leads to such derision and reproach, how much more so would it be for other elders of venerable seniority to hear these words of mine—they would surely rebuke me with even greater severity.
Thereupon, he remained silent and did not dare speak again.
Then Upānanda said to the mendicant:
"Venerable one!
Your preceptor is my friend; it was for this reason that I rebuked you, so do not harbor resentment."
He replied, "Venerable Sir,
if I were to speak further, I pray you would reprimand me again."
Upānanda said, "Venerable one!
I did not listen carefully just now; how can you speak of 'alms bowls' and 'non-alms bowls'?"
"Venerable sir, since I do not yet understand, why do you reprimand me?
Nevertheless, please explain further: where does that boy reside?
He replied:
"That person resides at such-and-such a shop; he has an excellent bowl that is perfectly fit for use.
He entrusted me with this message:
'If there is a bhikṣu who requires a bowl, please send someone to buy it.'"
Upānanda said, "I have heard these words,
yet I have not yet examined them with full detail.
Having spoken thus, he immediately donned his saṃghāṭī and went quickly to that marketplace.
At that time, seeing them approaching from afar, the boy thought to himself:
"I observe that those powerful and fierce bhikṣus will surely come here and seize my bowl."
He immediately took the bowl and placed it deep beneath the bed.
At that time, Upānanda saw him from afar hiding it and said:
"O worthy one!"
"Why have you hidden the bowl?
He then extended his hand and took the bowl himself, offering this prayer of blessing:
"May you be free from illness and enjoy long life."
The details are as previously explained.
The youth replied,
"Noble One!..."
"I am a merchant who lives by making a profit; I do not give things away for empty words, but rather take them after the price has been paid.
He replied, "How could you possibly sell the vessel of a seer?"
He spoke in verse:
"If one gives a clay vessel, they shall obtain a golden bowl;
this retribution is certainly not in vain—why, then, do you give rise to sorrow and suffering?"
The youth said, "Venerable sir!
Even if you speak at great length, it cannot be obtained except for its price."
Upānanda said, "Since you are now so stingy with this bowl,
in the future you will surely fall among the *mahāgalagaṇḍa* (gargantuan goiter) spirits.
While these harsh words were being spoken, an elder arrived at that place and said:
"I pay homage to the Venerable Upānanda.
Thereupon, Upānanda replied, "O noble one!"
"Who would require you to perform these empty prostrations?
The elder replied,
"When have I ever failed to follow the instructions and teachings issued by the Noble One?"
He said, "If that is the case,
you may purchase this bowl and give it to me as an offering.
Thereupon, the elder questioned the youth, saying:
“How much is this bowl worth?
He replied,
“It is worth that much.”
The householder said,
"I shall return the price for what has been discussed later.
At that time, the youth immediately handed the bowl to the householder, who took the bowl and offered it as a gift to Upānanda.
Upānanda then accepted his bowl and offered this blessing:
"May you attain long life and freedom from illness, and may you always serve as a vessel for the Dharma among humans and devas."
The full account is as related above.
The householder then departed.
Upānanda said to the youth:
"Stupid man!
You say that I, Upānanda, am unable to beg for even a small amount for the price of a bowl.
Because of this stinginess regarding the bowl, you shall certainly fall into the realm of the *mahā-ghaṇṭa* ghosts."
The youth said,
"What need is there for such boastfulness?
You have obtained the bowl, and I have now received the price."
"You should depart at once; why rely on further words!
Then Upānanda took that bowl and entered the Jeta Grove, where he showed the bowl to the bhikṣus and said, "Venerable ones!..."
"What do you think of this bowl?
At that time, a young bhikṣu asked Upānanda,
"Venerable One!..."
"Are there any other bowls remaining?
He replied, "There are."
"If that is the case, since you already have one bowl,
you ought to seek another. Upānanda said,
"I shall step upon the head of my enemy and still keep an extra bowl."
The youth asked:
"Venerable sir!
Could you possibly have an enemy?"
Upānanda said, "You are my foremost enemy,
for it was you who did not permit me to keep two alms bowls.
When the bhikṣus of few desires heard these words, they all felt resentment and contempt.
“How can a bhikṣu, while already possessing a bowl, seek another?
He then reported this matter in detail to the Blessed One.
On account of these causes and conditions, the Blessed One assembled the bhikṣus and questioned Upānanda, as explained at length above.
Having rebuked them in various ways, he addressed the bhikṣus:
"From this day forward, if a bhikṣu already possesses an alms-bowl, he must not seek another.

At that time, there was a bhikṣu who went on alms-round whose bowl had a hole. He took this bowl into the city to beg for food; when someone gave him roasted flour, he placed it in his bowl-sack. Next, he received some moist cakes with the bowl, whereupon the liquid from the hole leaked out, soaking the flour and staining the bowl-sack, so that many flies swarmed all around it.
Various young men and women followed after him, saying:
"Noble One!
You have cultivated karma that brings many attendants, like a great merchant leader, a householder, or a nobleman surrounded by a vast multitude; even so is the swarm of flies."
When the householder Anāthapiṇḍada saw the boys, he asked them,
"Why are you teasing the Noble One?
The boys replied:

"How could we dare to mock him lightly? However, this noble one cultivated the karma of having many attendants in former lives; just as a merchant leader, a householder, or a person of high status is surrounded by a multitude of followers, so too are his accompanying flies."
Having heard this, the householder said to the bhikṣu,
"Noble one! Having gone forth in the sublime and majestic teaching of the Buddha, the World-Honored One, for what reason do you perform such a shameful act?"
The bhikṣu replied,
"What kind of disgrace would that be?
For the Buddha, the World-Honored One, has ordained that bhikṣus who already possess one alms-bowl must not seek for another."
The householder said,
"Venerable One!
How can you keep only such a worn-out and broken bowl?"
When the bhikṣus heard this, they reported the matter to the Buddha.
The Buddha said: "Bhikṣus!
If a bowl has a hole, it should be repaired."

At that time, the bhikṣus used five kinds of molten and moist substances—namely, brown sugar, yellow wax, lac, lead, and tin—but when they applied them to hot objects, the coatings would immediately flake off.
Then the bhikṣus reported the matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"One should not use these to mend the bowl. Excluding these five kinds of molten or moist substances, one should instead employ five kinds of dry mending."
The bhikṣus did not know which five [methods] these were. The Buddha said:

"One should examine the size of the hole and act accordingly: one may drive in a nail; or insert an iron plate within the hole and hammer it down; or fix an iron plate around the four sides and drive in nails; or fashion it like the teeth of a makara fish; or fill it with powdered filings."
The bhikṣus did not know what kind of powder to use.
The Buddha said, "There are two kinds of powder: [powder for the body and powder for the face]."
"This refers to iron filings and stone powder;
iron bowls and earthenware bowls should be used accordingly.
When the bhikṣu ground the powder with water and placed it into the hole of the bowl, it immediately fell out. The Buddha said:
"One should apply oil and rub it into the opening.
After the bhikṣus had followed these instructions, [the bowl] still fell apart even when heated with a fierce fire, or it would likewise fall apart if the fire was too weak. The Buddha said:
"It should be heated with a moderate fire."
After it had been burned, it became rough and stiff.
The Buddha said, "It should be rubbed with an object.
When the bhikṣu rubbed it with water, the patch fell off. The Buddha said:
"Wipe it with oil and rub it thoroughly.
If the bowl has fine pores, mix sugar with clay, coat the pore areas entirely, and fire it according to the prescribed method.
If the bowl has cracks, one should drill holes and join them with a rivet; this is called the method for repairing a bowl."
The Buddha instructed the bhikṣus on five ways to mend a bowl.
At that time, there was a bhikṣu who went for alms; he dropped his bowl through a lapse of care, and it broke into five pieces.
That bhikṣu then drilled many holes in it and joined the pieces together with fine thread to carry it while seeking alms. The Buddha said:
"Whatever is a bowl must be thoroughly washed.
He then untied the cord used for washing, and having washed it, he tied it back together again; consequently, he spent the entire day neglecting his cultivation of wholesome qualities.
Other bhikṣus saw this and said to him,
"Venerable one!
Is it a virtuous practice to merely patch things with such an understanding, while neglecting to wash your bowls and utensils?"
He replied,
"Venerable sir!
As prescribed by the Buddha, if a bowl is broken, it should be mended with five types of dry patches."
At that time, the bhikṣus reported the matter to the Buddha. The Buddha said:
"If it is difficult to obtain a bowl, you may repair it as you wish; however, if it is easy to obtain elsewhere, you should discard it and seek a better one."

At that time, the Blessed One praised the observance of the precepts, as explained at length previously, up until: "I shall establish a training rule for the bhikṣus, which should be recited as follows:
'If a bhikṣu has an alms-bowl with less than five mends that is still fit for use, yet seeks another bowl for the sake of its excellence and obtains one, it is a naiḥsargika-pāyattika.'"
That bhikṣu shall relinquish this bowl within the assembly; the assembly shall take the lowest bowl among them and give it to that bhikṣu, saying: "This bowl is returned to you.

You must not keep it as a personal possession, nor may you distribute it, nor give it away to others. You should examine it carefully and use it slowly; you must maintain and protect it until it breaks. This is the proper rule."
"Furthermore, 'if a bhikṣu' refers to the group of six [monks].
The remaining meanings are as explained above.
'Less than five patches' means not reaching five patches."
"Fit for use" means having obtained and maintained [the bowl].
"Seeking another bowl for the sake of excellence" means seeking a second bowl out of a desire for something superior; "excellence" refers to being preeminent and exquisite.
"Obtained" means having sought it out and brought it into one's possession.
"Naiḥsargika" is explained in detail as above.
"That bhikṣu" refers to the person who has committed the offense.
That bhikṣu who must relinquish this bowl within the assembly should have one bhikṣu appointed from among the assembly to distribute the bowl of the offender.
If there is no one possessing the five virtues, he should not be appointed; even if appointed, he should not be made to perform the task.
What are the five? They are:
affection, malice, fear, delusion, and ignorance regarding what should and should not be done.
If one possesses these five qualities, one who has not yet been appointed should be appointed, and one who has already been appointed should be made to perform the duties.
What are the five? One should understand them as the reverse of the above; one should assign [the task] in this manner.
Ring the *gandi* to assemble the Sangha, and first ask whether he is capable.
"Can you, [Name], act as the distributor of the bowl for the Saṃgha that has been found guilty of an offense? He replies, "I can."
Next, one bhikṣu shall perform the formal motion (jñapti-karman); this should be done in detail as described in the *Ekottara-karman*.
The Buddha said:
"I shall now explain the rules of conduct for a bhikṣu who is practicing the use of a bowl that has been declared 'offensive'."
That bhikṣu should make the following formal announcement (*jñapti*) in the midst of the harmonious assembly:
"Venerable sirs!
I, the bhikṣu [Name], shall now proceed with the bowl that has been found guilty of an offense."
"Venerable ones!
Tomorrow, each of you should bring your own alms bowl to the midst of the Saṃgha.
When the following day arrived, the monk who was to distribute the bowls spread out the seats and struck the *gaṇḍī*; the monks each took their own alms bowl and went to the midst of the Saṃgha.
At that time, the bhikṣu who is walking with the almsbowl should hold his bowl, stand before the elder, and praise it, saying: "Elder!
This bowl is pure, complete, and fit for use; if you wish to have it, you may take it as you please."

If the senior monk (upādhyāya) takes this bowl, the person distributing the bowls should take the senior monk’s previous bowl and pass it to the second. If the senior monk does not take it, it is passed to the third.

When the third takes it, if the senior monk asks for it again, he should not give it on the first request, nor should he give it on the second request; however, on the third request, he should give it. If the senior monk [takes it] otherwise, he incurs an offense against the Dharma (dharmātikrama), which he must confess according to the Dharma.

In this manner, it continues down to the very last person in the assembly; when that person at the end of the line takes this bowl, the procedure for the third person from the end who requests the bowl is similar to that of the Elder.

When the distribution of bowls has been completed and a single bowl has been obtained, the monk who distributed the bowls should take that bowl, hand it to the other monk, and speak these words: "O monk!"

This bowl should not be kept as a personal possession, nor should it be distributed, nor given away to others; rather, one should use it carefully and gradually in accordance with the Dharma until it is destroyed—this is the proper rule.
"If a bhikṣu who goes for alms does not act according to the Dharma, he incurs an offense of transgressing the Dharma.
The Buddha said:
"I shall now prescribe the rules of conduct for a bhikṣu who has received an alms-bowl: he should keep two bowl-sacks."
The better bowl should be used for the long bowl, and the inferior one for the old bowl.
When going on almsround, one should carry both bowls; if one receives dry cakes, they should be placed in the long bowl, and if one receives moist cakes, they should be placed in the old bowl.

Having arrived at the dwelling place, one should construct a maṇḍala and arrange two bowls. After having eaten from the old bowl, one should first wash the extra bowl and then wash the old bowl; likewise, even up to the stages of drying and storing, the extra bowl always takes precedence.
When placing the inner reliquary chamber or when fumigating with incense, one should first place the extra bowl (*dīrgha-pātra*) in a secure location.
When traveling on a journey, one should have someone carry the old bowl while carrying the extra bowl oneself.
If there is no one to hold [the bowls], the long bowl should be placed on the left shoulder and the old bowl should be placed on the right side, which he should carry himself as he departs.
If a bhikṣu who possesses a bowl does not follow this rule of conduct, he incurs an offense of transgressing the Dharma.
"This disciplinary penalty shall last until the end of one's life or until the next [rainy season] retreat; it must be carefully observed.
Regarding what constitutes *naiḥsargika* (an offense requiring forfeiture), it is explained in detail as stated above.
Regarding this, what are the characteristics of the offense and the specific circumstances?

If a bhikṣu’s bowl is broken but can still be mended with a single patch, and although it has not yet been patched he is still able to use it, yet he seeks another bowl—when he seeks it, he commits an *duṣkṛta* (wrongdoing); once he obtains it, it is a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* (offense involving forfeiture).

If a bhikṣu’s bowl is broken such that it can still be mended twice, he may continue to use it even if it has not yet been repaired; yet if he seeks another bowl, he incurs an offense identical to the previous case.
This applies likewise for bowls that have been mended three or four times; the matter is the same as before.

If a bhikṣu’s almsbowl is broken such that it can still be mended with one patch, and having applied that one patch he is currently using it, yet he seeks another bowl—there is an *dukkaṭa* (wrongdoing) at the time of seeking, and upon obtaining it, there is a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* (offense involving forfeiture).
The same applies up to four patches; the offense incurred is likewise.
If a bowl is capable of being patched five times, whether it has been patched or not, or whether it remains functional or not, there is no offense in seeking another bowl.
If one acquires it by purchase or receives it as a gift, there is likewise no offense.
Furthermore, there is no offense for the very first offender, or for one who is insane, mentally deranged, or overwhelmed by intense physical pain.

23. The Training Rule on Requesting Thread and Having a Weaver Who Is Not a Relative Weave a Robe. The second training rule: "The Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park."
At that time, Upānanda thought to himself:
"It is all because of the householder Anāthapiṇḍada’s establishment of the training rules that I can no longer even succeed in soliciting the price for cakes and fruits."
"I should now enter the great city; perhaps there I may find some opportunity for teaching and conversion.

Thereupon, at dawn, he dressed in his robes, took up his alms-bowl, and entered the city to beg for food. In a grove of fragrant trees, he saw five hundred women spinning cotton thread. Having seen them, he thought:
"These women, all because of their own karma, must constantly pull white plows day and night, enduring hardship and toil to pay their taxes to the government."
Upānanda then approached them and addressed them all at once, saying: "Sisters!
May you all be free from illness and enjoy long life."
At that time, the women remained silent, and not one offered a response.
Upānanda said to them,
"Sisters!..."
There will come a time when a certain phenomenon arrives before long, which is disliked by many people and does not accord with their hearts; it is called death.
At that moment, though you may wish to speak, there will be no way to do so.
At that time, there was a woman of white complexion who rose from her seat and offered it to Upānanda.
Once Upānanda had taken his seat, the woman prostrated to him and sat down before him. Upānanda said to her, "Sisters!..."
"Have you ever performed even a small amount of wholesome deeds?
They replied,
"We have never done so."
He said to them:
"You should not fail to perform wholesome deeds.
This one woman possesses two kinds of roots of goodness that have been made to increase."
First, they are able to give rise to pure faith in me, planting the karma for physical excellence and causing it to increase;
second, upon seeing me approach, they immediately rise, prepare a seat, and pay homage with reverence, thereby causing the karma for rebirth in a noble family in future lives to increase.
"If you can give even a small amount more, you shall obtain precious wealth and enjoy abundant prosperity.
What will you all do, sisters? They all replied:
"We only know how to spin thread; what leisure have we to do anything else?
Upānanda said, "Have you ever prepared even a small amount of provisions for the journey to come?"
He replied,
"None of us have ever done so. Upānanda said:
"This too is unwholesome.
He then asked, "Venerable One!..."
"What is there to lament or sigh over?
She replied, "Sisters!..."
"In previous lives you did not cultivate meritorious deeds; thus, having been plundered by bandits, you now undergo this suffering.
Although you have obtained birth as a human, if you do not further cultivate merit, you will again be plundered by bandits."
The women asked,
"If that is so, O Noble One!
What action should we now perform so that it may serve as provisions for the journey in the future?"
Upānanda said, "Sisters!

If you can all deliberate together with one mind to produce a single large bolt of cloth and offer it to him who is of the Śākya clan, who has renounced the world to become a monk, who is proficient in all three Piṭakas, who is a great general of the Dharma, whose eloquence is unimpeded, and who is known by all— this would be for you to prepare in advance the provisions for the road in future lives."
The women replied,
“Noble one!
Where could we possibly obtain such large woolen cloths?”
"Furthermore, where can one encounter such a supreme field of merit?
Upānanda replied, "Do you not know?"

"I am of the Śākya clan, having renounced worldly life to become a monastic; I am proficient in all three Piṭakas and serve as a great leader of the Dharma. My eloquence is unimpeded, and I am well known to all.
As for what you said:
'Where could I possibly obtain a large woolen cloth?'"
"Do you not know this?
'Do not despise a small gift, thinking it brings no merit;
though a drop of water is minute, in time it fills a great vessel.'"
"Those who possess wisdom constantly cultivate even small merit;
within the field of excellence, they are able to summon great fruit. "Sisters!"
"Could you not give even one or two strands?
She replied, "I can."
Some said, "I shall give half a liang. Others said:
"I shall give one portion.
In this manner, all five hundred people followed suit and joyfully made their offerings.
Upānanda then said:
"Sisters! Since you possess a mind of renunciation, the thread must be fine and delicate. They said:
"Noble One!
We are all people who spin coarse yarn and cannot produce fine work; however, we have one daughter who can make fine yarn. Upānanda said:
"Try calling him here to look at him.
He was immediately summoned. Upānanda said:
“Girl, try rubbing it for me.
She then proceeded to rub it. Upānanda said:
"This is not yet well done; spin it better.
Thus he spoke up to three times.
The woman replied:
"Noble one!
Beyond this point, I am unable to go further. Upānanda said:
"Sisters! You all should spin this thread very finely.
They replied:
"Except for this young girl, we are unable [to do it].
Upānanda said, "Can you not exchange your tasks?
She shall spin the fine thread, and you shall spin the coarse."
He replied,
"If this girl is promised [to you], we shall do as you wish.
Upānanda then said to the young woman:
"You who delight in merit may twist this for me.
He then replied, "Noble One!"
"If it takes a long time to spin this fine thread, please do not urge us in haste.
Having received their consent, Upānanda offered them blessings and departed.
After many days had passed, he returned to inquire about the thread; the women all brought the thread they had spun and offered it to him.
Having received the thread, Upānanda offered this blessing:

"This gift is for the adornment of the mind; it is an aid to the mind and a superior provision for meditative concentration. By means of it, one shall obtain exquisite garments in the human and celestial realms."
Then Upānanda took the thread and returned to the monastery, where he said to the bhikṣus,
"Venerable ones!
Please examine how coarse or fine this thread is."
They all replied, “It is made of extremely fine thread; however, we do not know if the Venerable One can distinguish a skilled weaver. Upānanda said:
"Could it be that you, O Benevolent Ones, are deceiving and slighting me?
Had I not gone forth from home at that time, there would have been no craft or skill I had not mastered through diligent study; how much less could I, as a weaver, fail to distinguish these?"
The people replied, "How would we dare slight you? We only fear you may not know the way.

If you require a weaver, there is a weaver named Kākaṇḍaka in such-and-such a ward, who has a skilled wife capable of weaving fine cloth; if you obtain this thread, she will surely produce excellent garments."
He replied, "Excellent,
venerable sir!"
"Instructing a skilled craftsman means that you, my friend, shall weave this cloth for me.
Upānanda then took the thread to the weaver’s workshop; though they were not friends, he spoke this verse:
"The good man spreads a fine reputation; though far away, it is known and heard by all."
Like the Great King of Snowy Mountains, whom all people gaze upon together, the fool clings to delusion;
though close at hand, he neither knows nor hears.
Like an arrow shot in the dark, no one can see it.
"You have now attained great benefit and acquired great renown throughout the city of Śrāvastī; let us try to see what the appearance of this thread is like.
He looked at it and reported, "It is a most excellent thread!"
"If I were to weave it myself, I would surely produce a fine cloth. Upānanda said,
"O worthy one!"
"I shall weave it for you.
The weaver replied,
"Who will give me the price?"
Upānanda said, "You weavers always lack sufficient wages; you should prepare provisions for the future life.
At that moment, the weaver turned his face toward his wife, and she spoke to him.
"Virtuous one, have you not heard how this person of great virtue has deeply praised me? You should lend your hand to weave him a set of robes.
The weaver replied, "Noble one!"
"This thread is extremely fine and takes a long time to obtain; please do not urge me.
Having thus offered a blessing, he departed.
After many days had passed, [the king] came again to look, at which time the weaver presented him with the cloth.
At that time, having received the cloth, Upānanda offered a blessing and departed. Upon returning to the monastery, he showed it to the bhikṣus, saying:
"Venerable ones!
Observe this cloth; what do you think of its appearance?"
The people replied, "That is a most excellent white cotton cloth!

If you could obtain a second piece, you might sew them together to make a double-layered saṃghāṭī robe; thus, by simplifying your affairs, you could dwell there and cultivate various wholesome qualities—which would truly be wonderful."
Upānanda said, "Venerable ones!
Do you think I lack the power to obtain a second sheet?"
"Virtuous ones, observe how I shall now convert this weaver.

In the morning, having dressed and taken his bowl, he entered the city of Śrāvastī through a side gate. Seeking thread from others, he went to the house of the weaver Kaṇṭaka and spoke at length as before, showing him the thread.
He said, "Excellent thread!
If I were to weave it, it would become a fine, superior cloth."
“If that is so, I shall weave it for you. He replied,
“Who will pay the price?”
He replied, "Your weaver does not understand how to cultivate merit; his poverty will not cease in future lives. You ought to perform further deeds that serve as provisions for the journey."
He replied, "Venerable One!
Previously, while weaving robes for you, I consumed your food and drink; since then, I have been repaying these debts and have still not finished."
"Now that we have acted in vain once more, what shall we do?
Upānanda looked at the woman's face as her husband said,
"Venerable One!"
"Even if my wife were to desire it, I truly could not do so.
Upānanda said angrily, "You bald-faced weaver!
I swear by my own shaven head: if I cannot make you weave, I shall no longer be called Upānanda!"
Then that weaver, speaking with anger, said:
"You shaven-headed śramaṇa! I swear by my finger that I certainly cannot weave cloth for you."
Upananda then departed, his mind filled with anger and resentment.
At that time, King Prasenajit of Kośala had a trusted minister named Bhadra, who was an old friend of Upananda. The king sent him to visit Upananda;
having arrived at the gate, he asked, "Is Bhadra at home?"
He replied, "To the market.
Thereupon Upānanda went straight to the market to look for him; at that time, Bhadrika was at a tavern.
Upānanda went to his door and sent a messenger in to call him, conveying this message:
"Upānanda wishes to see you; please come out for a moment."
The messenger informed him, and Sudatta immediately went out and, joining his palms, said:
"I pay homage to the Venerable Upānanda.
Then Upānanda addressed him:
“Worthy one! May you be free from illness and long-lived.
I had thought you were constantly diligent in your public duties; how could I have known that in your leisure time you would frequent taverns?”
He replied, "Noble one!
I have come here on official business; for what reason has the Venerable One come here to seek me?"
He replied, "I have some thread with which you may weave a robe; you shall thereby obtain merit.
He replied:
"I shall fold this myself; why trouble yourself with weaving?
Upānanda replied, "That is indeed a virtuous thing to do;
however, these threads of mine are objects offered out of faith—how could they be cast away in vain?"
At that time, he immediately dispatched a messenger and instructed him:
"Go and tell the weavers: 'You should weave a fine white cotton cloth for the venerable Upānanda.'"
Upānanda said, "Virtuous one!
There is no need to trouble the weaver with this."
"However, in a certain ward there is a weaver named Kṛmuka, and he has a skillful wife; you may have him weave it.
At that time, Bhadra immediately sent a messenger with these instructions:
"You should now go to the weaver Kṛmuka and say:"
“‘Have the worthy Bhaddiya weave this cloth for me.
Then that messenger took the thread to him and said:
‘The minister Bhaddiya has sent this thread; you may use it to weave a garment.’”
When the weaver saw the thread, he immediately remembered and informed the messenger, saying,
"My turn has already been completed.
Then the messenger took the thread and returned, reporting the circumstances in detail to Bhadra.
The virtuous man replied,
"Go and tell him:
'As you weave this garment now, I shall release you at the next turn.'"
The messenger departed and reported these words.
The weaver replied, "The minister is virtuous and wields great power within the city; I would rather move elsewhere than remain here. Who could possibly skip their turn to weave for me?"
The messenger returned and reported these words in full to Bhadra.
Bhadra then replied to the messenger once more, saying:
"You may return and tell the weavers: 'Let them weave this cloth according to their established rotation.'"
Having heard this, Upānanda said, "No one else can do it; only Khaṇḍadravya can.
Then he sent a messenger back to Bhadra.
"You should go again to Kalandaka's place and tell him:
'Weave it for us, and we shall pay you the price.
" The messenger then departed, and Upānanda also followed right after him, saying to the messenger:
"You fool! Who told you to serve the king’s ministers?

You ought to be given many lashes of the cane and made to stand carrying firewood! How could it be tolerated that for the sake of some trifling task, you repeatedly send for a virtuous person to labor on your behalf?"
"Could you not go to the weaver's workshop and say this:
'Venerable sir, [the Master] has sent you to weave this white cotton cloth'? If he says:
To those who say, "I cannot," he shall bind their hair with his hand and strike them on the back with his fist.
If they cry out, he shall roll up their weaving implements so that they may not perform their work.
If a woman comes to call out, he should quickly pull her by her hair-knot and drag her out the door, saying to her:
"Since you have now disobeyed the virtuous command, King Śrīghoṣa will surely fine you five hundred gold coins."
He said: "Foolish man!
If you were able to weave this garment, they would give you a great deal for your hard labor; why must you go back to that empty place to exhaust yourself?"
Then that messenger returned to the weaver’s place and reported, saying:
"The virtuous one spoke thus:
'You should weave it for me; I shall pay you the price.'"
The weaver replied, "I cannot now skip ahead in my weaving to finish this cloth.

The messenger seized him by the hair with his hand and struck him on the back with his fist; he cried out loudly and immediately rolled up the loom. His wife called out in protest as the messenger grabbed him by the hair and dragged him away, saying: [to the king]...
"You have disobeyed the commands of the great minister; King Śrīghoṣa will surely fine you five hundred gold coins.
Upon hearing this, the wife was greatly terrified and said to her husband, "If we are imprisoned, who will rescue us?
We shall surely die bound in shackles. I should now weave this large cloth."
The weaver immediately replied to the messenger, saying,
"Do not take me away and hand me over to that judge.
I shall give you the wages for my labor."
"Leave the thread behind according to the intention with which you came.
The messenger left the thread and departed.
At that time, the weaver said to his wife:
“O virtuous one!
I am now weaving so that the threads may be lost and the cloth not finished.
The wife then replied:
"Look at this formidable and fierce śramaṇa! If he weaves coarse cloth, how could he possibly let us go?
Thinking thus, they worked with great hardship to weave the layered cloth.
Once the weaving was finished, Upānanda went to that house to demand the cloth, whereupon the weaver said:
“Venerable sir!
Will you not accept payment for this food and drink?
He replied:
"A destitute person is begging wine from me; why not drink poison or eat dregs instead?
At that time, the weaver gave rise to feelings of contempt and spoke words of revilement:

"These śramaṇa sons of the Śākya engage in evil conduct that is not the Dharma of a śramaṇa. How can they beg for thread themselves, or by means of preaching the Dharma, or by feigning the power of the king, cause those who are not their kin to weave robes for them, thus mutually harassing and disturbing one another?"
When the bhikṣus had heard these words, they reported them all in detail to the Buddha.
Thereupon, the World-Honored One assembled the community of bhikṣus and questioned Upānanda.
He replied:
"It is indeed so.
Having rebuked him in various ways, he spoke at length, up to: "I now establish this training rule, which should be recited as follows:
'If a bhikṣu himself solicits thread and has a weaver who is not a relative weave it into a robe, and if he obtains the robe, it is a naiḥsargika-pāyattika.'"
"If again a bhikṣu" refers to Upānanda; the remaining meaning is as above.
"To beg for thread himself" means one *tola*, half a *tola*, or the like.
Regarding "one who is not a relative," the detailed explanation is as above.
"Weaver" refers to a hired weaver.
There are seven kinds of robes, also as explained above.
If one obtains the cloth, one commits an offense of expiation with forfeiture (*naiḥsargika-pāyattika*); the method of relinquishment is as described above.
Regarding this, what are the characteristics of the offense and its specific details?
If a bhikṣu requests thread from a person who is not a relative and has a non-relative weave it, he commits an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*) in both instances.
At the moment one obtains the robe, one commits an offense of forfeiture (naiḥsargika-pāyattika).

If a bhikṣu requests thread from a person who is not a relative and has a relative weave the robe for him, there is an offense of wrong-doing (duṣkṛta) at the time of the request, but there is no offense upon obtaining the robe.
If a bhikṣu requests thread from a relative and has a non-relative weave it, there is no offense at the time of the request, but upon obtaining the robe, he commits a naiḥsargika-pāyattika offense.
If a bhikṣu requests thread from a relative and has a relative weave it, there is no offense in either case.

If a bhikṣu requests thread from one who is not a relative and weaves it himself into cloth: at the time of requesting, there is a dukkaṭa (wrongdoing); when the garment is completed, there is likewise a dukkaṭa offense.
If a bhikṣu requests thread from a relative and weaves it himself into cloth: at the time of requesting, there is no offense; when the garment is completed, there is a dukkaṭa.
If one weaves in exchange for payment, there is no offense.
Furthermore, there is no offense in the case of a first-time offender, or one who is insane, mentally deranged, or overwhelmed by intense physical pain.

The Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya, Volume Twenty-three.

The Training Rule on Exhorting Weavers. The twenty-fourth training rule on exhorting weavers. At that time, the Bhagavat was staying in Śrāvastī at the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, there was an elder in this city who had recently married; the husband and wife both engaged in improper conduct, committing adultery with outsiders, as detailed extensively above.
The account of requesting robes from a householder who was not a relative is told as the introductory narrative, up until the wife said to her husband:
"Noble son!

The Venerable Upānanda has frequently preached the essentials of the Dharma to us; we have not yet expressed our respect toward him, so it is fitting that we offer him support with food, clothing, and other necessities."
The householder replied,
"Worthy sir, excellent! You should do so."
The wife said, "I have some fine thread;
let such-and-such a weaver weave a *paṭa*—the term *paṭa* refers to a large cloth—as large as a *kāṣāya*, making it a single piece in total."

Since this term does not exist in the local language, it is simply referred to as "folding a robe. As for what was previously called "robe," the Sanskrit original in all cases uses the term *patta*, which here means "a strip of cloth"; he took it and gave it to the Venerable Upānanda, instructing him to wear it.
He then gave the thread to the weaver and said,
"O worthy one!
Weave a bowl-cover (*pātra*) with this thread, intended as an offering for the Venerable Upānanda."
The weaver replied, "I shall do so.
When the maidservant heard these words, she thought to herself:
"I shall tell the Venerable Upānanda these words so that he may be pleased.

Then, in the morning, Upānanda dressed himself, took his bowl, and entered the city to beg for alms. Arriving at her house, he saw the maidservant sweeping the courtyard; seeing Upānanda from afar, she set down her broom and prostrated herself, saying, "Noble One!"
"I have pleasant words that I wish to tell you. He replied,
"What is it you wish to say?"
The woman said,
"The master and mistress of this house wish to offer this *pata* to the Venerable One. Upānanda said:
"The world seeks to count me as one; this maidservant also knows this well.
He then said to the woman, "You are mocking me now."
He replied,
"How would I dare deceive you? Upānanda said:
"If it is true, when the head of the household becomes angry, you must seek his forgiveness on our behalf;
if it is false, I shall give you many lashes and restore your clothing and food to their former state, which will no longer suffice."
The woman replied again, “If you, Venerable Sir, do not believe me,
you should go to such-and-such a place, to the house of a certain weaver, and see for yourself with your own eyes.
She then went there and arrived at the weaver’s house, where she said:
“O noble one! For whom do you wish to weave this *pota*?
The weaver replied:
"This is the Venerable Upānanda," he said, and then asked,
"Have you ever known Upānanda?"
He replied, "I did not know him.
The other said:
"I am Upānanda. O worthy one!
This bowl-cover was originally woven for me; you should lengthen it and make it even more spacious."
He then replied, "Venerable One!
If the thread is so short, where could one seek more?"
He replied,
“The householder shall provide it for you himself, and I shall also give you wages for your labor.
Having said this, he immediately departed.

On a subsequent day, having dressed and taken up his alms bowl, he entered the city to beg for food. In due course, he arrived at the residence where Lady Śrīmālā lived; he prepared a seat for her and invited her to sit comfortably. The lady prostrated at his feet and sat to one side in order to listen to the Dharma.
Then Upānanda immediately preached the Dharma for him. Having heard the Dharma, he said:
"Venerable One!
Is there a place where you have been invited to eat today, or do you go from door to door to beg for alms?"
Upānanda replied,
“I am going on alms-round.
Queen Śrīmālā then thought to herself:
"Who is there who can surpass me in giving food?
Thinking thus, he took his bowl, filled it with excellent and delicious morsels, and presented it to him. Having received it, the other made this aspiration:
"May you be free from illness."
He went out and departed, immediately proceeding to the weaver’s house and saying,
“O noble one! You should extend your hand.”
Having seen that he had unfolded it, she took a fine lump of food and gave it to him to eat.
Once he had eaten, she asked:
"How was the flavor?"
He replied, "Noble One!
This modaka is exceedingly delicious."
He asked, "Have you ever obtained such excellent food before?
He replied:
"I have indeed never eaten before.
He replied, "You may spread out the hem of your garment."
He immediately spread out his hem and emptied all the fine balls of rice from his bowl into it, saying, "O worthy one!
Weave well for my sake;
I shall know of your hardships from time to time and shall further increase your wages from the total amount."
He replied,
"Who would ever add more thread? Upānanda said:
"I shall seek it from the donor.
Later, when the thread was exhausted, she went to the donor's house; at that time, the husband was present and the wife was not.
She said, "Householder!"
"I have now run out of thread; you should provide some for me.
The householder then gave him some thread.
Later, when the thread was exhausted again, he went to the house to ask for more. At that time, his wife was there while her husband was away, and she replied:
"Everyone! My thread is now exhausted; let me add some more.
His wife immediately gave him some thread.
When the thread was again exhausted, he went back to the house to ask for more. At that time, it happened that both husband and wife were present, and he said to them:
"Householder!
While weaving the *pota*, the thread has run out; you should add some more."
The wife said,
"Has the *pāṭha* you are weaving grown any larger?
Her husband asked his wife:
“Did I add a thread, and did you also add one?
He replied, “I added one.”
The householder said,
"How could the *pāṭa* possibly be made even more extensive?
The weaver replied:

"How could this be a new addition? On the day it was first drafted, the Venerable One came in person and instructed me to expand upon the broad and long [passage]; I then followed his words and further enlarged it."
The wife then thought to herself,
"I shall now go and see what that *pota* looks like.
She immediately took some thread to the weaver's house and, seeing that the *pota* was exceedingly vast, firm, and exquisite, she stared with wide eyes and spoke with indignation:
"I will not give this fine cloth to the bhikṣu; I shall weave another cloth for him.
Having said this, he departed.
Then Upānanda came from time to time to inquire:
“Ho! Man, is your robe finished?”
The weaver replied,
“Although I wish to finish it, you, sir,
have not yet finished. Upānanda said:
"What do you mean by that? He replied:
"The householder’s wife, upon seeing the *pūṭa*, glared with eyes wide and full of anger, and spoke these words:"
"I will not give this fine cloth to the bhikṣu; I shall weave another cloth for him.
Upānanda said, "O man!"
"Do you know that I have a debt of gratitude toward you?
He replied, "I know it very well;
the delicious morsels of food you left for me are still not yet finished."
He replied, "Man!
You saw me inside that householder's residence; you should take this cloth there and return it to me."
The weaver said,
"Noble One, you should depart;
wait a moment while I finish preparing the remaining cloth and send it to that house."
Upānanda immediately went to her house and sat down with his back toward the door. At that time, the elder’s wife came and prostrated at his feet, then sat down facing the door.

Then the weaver arrived carrying a *pata* (a garment), but when the wife saw him from afar, she raised her hand to stop him from entering. The weaver, pretending not to see her, lowered his face and entered; he then placed the *pata* inside the wife’s lap and said, "This is the *pata*."
Then Upānanda immediately took hold of her and offered a blessing for her, as described in detail previously.
The woman then replied,
"Noble One!..."
"Wait for the householder to arrive; we shall offer the gift with our own hands.
Upānanda said, "I will first dye it;
when the householder comes, I shall give him this garment of a seer as a gift in accordance with the Dharma."
The wife then replied:
"Noble One! The World-Honored One has said:..."
"White is superior," he replied.
[The other] said, "The seer’s garment is superior; I shall dye it."
He immediately left his seat, went out the door, and departed.
Then that weaver asked his wife for the payment, and she replied:
"O man!..."
"Now that you have lost my bowl-cloth (*pāṭa*) and seek its price from me, you should depart at once; as for the one who took the cloth, go to him and seek the money.
At that time, the weaver immediately went quickly to Upānanda’s place and reported, "Noble One!"
"Return me the price for the weaving. He replied,
"You should go to the householder and seek it there."
He immediately returned to the householder’s place and asked for the price of the weaving; the householder, as before, became angry and sent him away.
He then went to Upānanda and asked for the value of the robe, to which Upānanda replied:
"Go back again; he will return it to you."
He then departed once more and said to the householder,
"Give me back the price for my robe.
The man became greatly incensed and replied:
"If you cease [your practice], I shall say no more.
But if you come again, I will tie a broken clay bowl around your neck and lead you around the city of Śrāvastī to inform the public."
Having heard these words, he returned to Upānanda and said to him:
"Venerable One!
That householder’s wife has made an appointment with me."
"If you cease [your actions], I shall say nothing further.
But if you come again, I shall tie a broken earthen bowl around your neck and lead you around the city of Śrāvastī to inform the people."
"I only pray that the Noble One will have compassion for me, a poor man,
and return the price for the weaving. Upānanda replied, "O man!"
"If others were weaving robes for me and made me pay them back, how could I possibly have these three robes and bowl now?
Since you press me so hard, come and let us calculate together the value of those fine balls of food and other things you received from me."
Furthermore, when calculating the cost of the flour, and even the ghee, sugar, honey, and various fragrant substances, the total exceeded the price of the cloth;
he then said, "O man!..."
"You owe me money; why then do you demand the price for weaving?
Having stood long in the midday sun until he was exhausted, he was released.
Once the weaver had escaped, he felt extreme contempt and uttered words of abuse:

"The śramaṇas, sons of the Śākyas, do not know contentment; they have asked me for payment again for the kindness and favor [I showed them]. They are no true śramaṇas—what genuine Dharma do they possess?
When the bhikṣus heard this, they reported the matter to the Buddha.
On account of this, the Buddha assembled the community of bhikṣus and asked Upānanda,
"Is it true that you have committed such an undignified act?
He replied:
“It is indeed so.
The Blessed One rebuked him in various ways, and even established this training rule, which should be recited as follows:
“If a bhikṣu, for whom a householder or householder’s wife who is not a relative has commissioned a weaver who is not a relative to weave a robe, [and that bhikṣu...]”
This bhikṣu, having not previously received an invitation, conceived a contrary thought and went to the weaver’s workshop, saying these words: "Do you know?
This robe is being woven for me."
"Excellent!
Weaver, you should weave it well, comb and clean it thoroughly, select the fibers skillfully, and beat it very firmly.
I shall provide you with support by giving you a small or large portion of alms-food, or something similar to alms-food, or even the monetary value of such food."
"If a bhikṣu, by means of such items, obtains a robe from a weaver, it is a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika*.
As for "if a bhikṣu," this refers to Upānanda and others of his kind.
The meaning of "one's own" versus "not one's own," as well as the seven kinds of robes, are explained in detail as above.
"Having not previously received an invitation" means that one has never been informed in advance.
"Conceiving a divergent thought" means that the mind desires to obtain a robe.
Regarding the phrase "going to those weavers," this refers to expressing one's own intention.
The phrase "weave for me" clarifies that it is for one's own person.
The phrase "should be woven well" indicates the desire for the garment to be long and properly conform to the prescribed measurements.
"Thoroughly combing and grooming" means desiring to make the cloth wide and bright white.
"Skillfully selecting" means removing the knots to make it fine and delicate.
"Vigorously beating" means desiring to make it smooth, lustrous, and dense.
"When I shall give a small or large amount of bowl-food" refers to giving the five kinds of *khādaniya* (solid foods) and the five kinds of *bhojaniya* (soft foods).
"Or with types of bowl-food" refers to giving them raw grain and so forth.
"Or again, 'the price of food' means its value.
'Bhikṣu' refers to Upānanda.
'With such things' refers to the aforementioned matters."
"Obtaining the robe" means the robe has entered one's hand.
"Naiḥsargika" is as explained above.
What are the characteristics of the offense in this case?
