If a bhikṣu, for the sake of obtaining robes, rises from his seat, adjusts his clothing, and takes two sets of five kinds of food and other items to a weaver’s workshop to give them to him, urging him to weave well, he incurs an *dukkaṭa* (wrongdoing) for all of it; at the moment he obtains the robe, he commits the offense of *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* (requiring forfeiture).
The categories of "one's own kin" and "those who are not one's kin" are as explained above.
**The Twenty-fifth Training Rule on Taking Away Robes.** At that time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.

At that time, it was the constant practice of the six bhikṣus that, when they had granted others the going-forth or full ordination, or while living together with those disciples, they would continue to dwell with them even if they did not know whether their preceptors were practicing evil deeds;

yet, if they later discovered such conduct, they would immediately abandon them and dwell together with virtuous bhikṣus, with the sole exception that, following the Buddha’s instruction, they would come to their preceptors’ quarters three times each day to pay respectful homage.

At that time, the bhikṣu Nanda had a co-resident disciple named Dharma, who constantly maintained a sense of shame and remorse, and cherished and respected the various rules of training (śikṣāpada). He was unaware of Nanda’s evil conduct while living with him;
once he recognized Nanda’s behavior, he immediately abandoned him and lived together with virtuous bhikṣus, except for performing the three daily prostrations.
At that time, the Blessed One addressed the Venerable Ānanda, saying:
"Go and inform the bhikṣus:
'The Blessed One wishes to travel through the human realm of Kośala; those of you, venerable ones, who wish to follow him should prepare your robes.'"
Then the Venerable Ānanda, having received the Buddha’s instruction, went to where the bhikṣus were and announced it as commanded.
When the bhikṣu Nanda heard this instruction, he said to Upānanda:
"The World-Honored One has given us orders that we are to depart on a journey; while staying here, we have had to pass through a hundred doors before our bellies could be full."

If I were to follow the Buddha on his travels, although there would be eighteen kinds of rare and beneficial advantages, I would be surrounded by immeasurable hundreds of thousands of people; consequently, I would have no way to drink much of the turbid water or to sit beneath the trees.
"We should now take a certain elder monk whom we know well and go before him while praising the Triple Gem.
If we do so, we shall be able to travel in peace and security and obtain great gains and offerings."
When Upānanda heard this, he spoke these words:
"Ācārya! Have you now abandoned the golden bowl to seek an earthenware vessel?"

The Master’s disciple named Dharma constantly harbors a sense of shame and remorse, cherishing the precepts of training and joyfully upholding them; since even he refrains from coming out of shame, how could others be willing to follow him?
However, the Buddha, the World-Honored One, has taught the four means of integration:
namely, giving, kind speech, beneficial conduct, and cooperation.
If one practices these, others might perhaps come; yet among us, who is there willing to dwell together?
At that time, Dharmadatta’s *saṃghāṭī* had become somewhat worn out. Someone gave him cotton cloth, and wishing to make a new one, he thought to himself:
"I should now go and ask my upādhyāya that I wish to make a *saṃghāṭī*."
He then took the cotton cloth he had obtained and went to Nanda’s place.
At that time, a bhikṣu who was begging for alms saw Dharmadatta departing and asked,
"Venerable Dharmadatta, where are you going?"
He replied, "I have an old *saṃghāṭī*,
but now that I have obtained this cloth, I wish to go and ask my upādhyāya so that I may have a new one made."
Upon hearing this, the bhikṣu who was begging for alms said:
"If you are to make a new *saṃghāṭī*, you must bring these old ones to me.
He replied:
"Very well.
At that time, Dharma went to Nanda and said,
"Upādhyāya!..."
"Because my saṃghāṭī is worn out, I now wish to obtain this cotton cloth to make a new robe;
therefore, I have come to request your permission. Then Upānanda replied to Nanda, "O Ācārya!"
"Now is precisely the right time.
Nanda replied, "Venerable Dharma!"
"I have a saṃghāṭī; I now give it to you—what need is there to make a new one?
Dharmadatta replied, "There is no need."
"Upādhyāya! I shall simply sew this to make a great robe (saṃghāṭī).
Upānanda said to him:

“Dharma! What I heard of you in the past was one thing, but what I see now is quite another. I have recently heard that you have constantly maintained a mind of shame and remorse, and that you take joy in cherishing and upholding the various rules of training.”
"I truly did not know that you were violating your teacher’s instructions; how could it be that your teacher encouraged you to do evil?
At that time, upon hearing the Venerable’s reproach, Dharmā remained silent and offered no reply.
Nanda then presented him with his saṃghāṭī robe, which the other accepted,
saying these words: "Upādhyāya,
please accept this cloth."
Nanda replied, "Venerable Dharma!
How could I possibly exchange my robe with you?"
"Keep this cloth for your own use.
Dharma then thought:
"What use have I now for this foolish object?"
He then addressed his teacher, saying:
"I now wish to give this cloth to the Saṃgha; however, there was once a bhikṣu who went for alms and asked me for a saṃghāṭī, and I now wish to give it to him."
The teacher said,
"As you wish," and immediately bestowed his own saṃghāṭī upon the mendicant. He then gave his saṃghāṭī to the one who had requested it.
On another day, Dharmadatta put on his saṃghāṭī robe and prostrated at the feet of his preceptor. At that time, Nanda said to Dharmadatta:
"The Venerable Ānanda has transmitted the instruction of the Blessed One that he now wishes to travel through the human realm; those who can follow him should prepare their robes."
"If we remain here, we must pass through a hundred gates each day before our bellies are full.

If we follow the Buddha on his travels, although there are eighteen kinds of rare benefits, we will be surrounded by immeasurable hundreds of thousands of followers; thus, even if we drink much turbid water and sit beneath trees, we will have no means of obtaining it."
"We should praise the Triple Gem before proceeding; if we do so, we shall travel in peace and security and obtain great gain and offerings."
Dharma replied, "Upādhyāya!
Although there are eighteen kinds of benefits from following the Buddha, you, Upādhyāya, regard them as faults; therefore, my heart now delights in following the Blessed One."
Nanda replied, "Venerable one! Follow me."
Dharma replied, “Upādhyāya!
I shall not go ahead;
I wish to follow behind the Buddha.”
Nanda, filled with anger and resentment, immediately said:
"You foolish creature!
How could I have given you this great robe for the sake of merit? My original intention was simply to have you follow behind me."
"If you do not leave, return my robe to me; I will not give it to you.
At that time, Dharmadatta thought to himself:
"I would rather have no clothes than go along with these six people of evil conduct, for they may cause transgressions to arise."
He immediately returned that robe.
At that time, the World-Honored One, surrounded by a great assembly as described above, proceeded along the road.

It is the constant law of all Buddhas that when they are about to travel, they turn their whole body to the right like an elephant king, lest the members of the community be improperly dressed. He then saw Dharmadinnā wearing her upper and lower robes and intending to wander among the people; having seen her, he addressed the Venerable Ānanda, saying:
“Ānanda! Is it that after the *varṣā* (rainy season retreat), the bhikṣus do not receive the benefit of robes?
Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying:
“Venerable Sir!
A bhikṣu has obtained a robe.
The Buddha said:
"If he has obtained robes, for what reason does the bhikṣu Dharmadatta wear only the upper and lower garments when traveling among people?
Then the Venerable Ānanda related the circumstances in detail to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One said:
"How could a bhikṣu give a robe to another and then take it back?"
At that time, the World-Honored One, on account of these circumstances, questioned Nanda, saying:
"Did you truly take away his robe?
He replied:
"Truly he has taken it away.
The Buddha rebuked him in various ways as extensively explained before, up until: "I establish this training rule, which should be recited as follows:

'If a bhikṣu, having previously given a robe to another bhikṣu, later—out of malice, anger, or abuse, and with a mind of aversion or contempt—should take it back himself or cause another to take it back, saying:'"
"Give me back my robe; I will not give it to you.
If the robe is separated from that person's body and he uses it for himself, it is a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika*.
"If again a bhikṣu" refers to the Śākya son Nanda.
"To give to a bhikṣu" refers to [giving to] one who has attained the Dharma.
There are seven kinds of robes, as explained extensively above.
"To give robes" means to give them to a co-resident disciple, or to others of a similar class.
"At a later time" means on another day.
"Causing vexation, anger, abuse, or giving rise to a mind of disdain" refers to manifesting signs of malice through body, speech, or mind.
"Taking it oneself or causing another to take it away so that the robe is separated from the body" means it is completely removed from the body.
"Self-usage" means that which belongs to oneself.
"Naiḥsargika-pāyattika" is explained in detail as previously stated.
In this context, what are the characteristics of the offense and its specific circumstances?
There are three types of characteristics:
namely, those of the body, of speech, and of both together. Regarding the body:

if one first gives a robe and later, out of malice or resentment, personally seizes it—whether by pulling or dragging—without speaking a word, one incurs an *dukkaṭa* (offense of wrong-doing) as long as the corner of the robe has not left the body; at the moment it leaves the body, one incurs a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* (offense of forfeiture and confession). This is called bodily action (*kāyakarman*).
Regarding "by speech": this means that by uttering words one takes away another's robe without moving the body or hands;
the offense is established as before. Regarding "by both": this means that one takes away the robe by means of both body and speech; the offense is established as before.

Regarding "instructing another": if one instructs a bhikṣu to seize another's robe, as long as the robe has not yet left the body, both incur an *dukkaṭa*; if it has left the body, both incur a *pāyattika*.
The preceptor incurs the fault of negligence; if she instructs a nun to take it away, her offense is likewise the same.
The three lower assemblies all incur a *duṣkṛta* (wrongdoing);
if laymen or laywomen take it away, they incur immeasurable sin.
There are two kinds of cases where there is no offense:
first, for the sake of difficult circumstances; second, for the sake of following the teachings.

Regarding "difficult circumstances": if one's two teachers see their own disciples in places of terror and so forth, or crossing dangerous terrain at improper times on riverbanks, and fearing they might lose or fall [their belongings], they forcibly take back the robes; in all such cases, there is no fault.

Regarding "acting in accordance with the teaching": if one's two teachers see their own disciples associating closely with evil companions or traveling together with them, they may take away their robes so that they do not commit evil; this is called acting in accordance with the teaching.
Furthermore, there is no offense for the very first offender, or for one who is insane, mentally deranged, or afflicted by intense pain.
The Twenty-sixth Training Rule on Clothes Given in Times of Urgency and Distress. The Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.

In a certain village there was a householder of faith, virtuous and kind, who, within a forest hermitage, offered to the Saṃgha the construction of a dwelling place, fully equipped with all manner of adornments.
Sixty bhikṣus resided here, and the fourfold requisites for their support were provided in abundance.
At that time, the elder fell ill and passed away; from then on, the offerings were cut off.
Then the bhikṣus went to his son’s place and said to him, “O worthy one!
Your father built a monastery and provided sixty bhikṣus with abundant food and clothing; are you now able to perform such a deed?”
The son replied to him, saying:

“There are those who can give a hundred, or perhaps a thousand, even up to a hundred million; yet there are those who cannot save even their own selves. I am currently unable to provide for you as my father did.”
When the bhikṣus heard these words, they all departed.

At that time, there were two elderly bhikṣus who were natives of this village; having left the household life to become renunciants, they lived in this monastery, subsisting on alms they gathered for themselves.

Later, at another time, a caravan from the north, having seen the monastery, entered together and praised it aloud. They circled the stūpa and inspected the cells throughout, but finding them all empty, they thought:
"The bhikṣus must be dwelling here in silent meditation; perhaps we should go to the daytime forest grove and look more closely."
Seeing the two elders, he immediately addressed them, saying:
"Ācāryas! Where are the bhikṣus of this monastery now?"
He then related the matter in full.
Having heard this, the caravan leader said to his fellow travelers:
"For a long time, I have constantly harbored this thought:"
"How wonderful!
When shall I be able to construct a dwelling for the Saṃgha and provide robes and food as offerings for the bhikṣus?
Since this monastery has been completed and currently lacks a patron, I shall step in to provide for the community of monks.
He immediately spread out a large stack of cloth and placed an object upon it, addressing the people:
"If you all can rejoice in this with sympathetic joy, I would be grateful if you could each contribute a small or large amount according to your means to collectively seek merit."
At that time, the merchants each offered gifts and received many goods in return.
Then the caravan leader said to the elderly bhikṣu, "Ācārya!..."
This property is intended to provide for sixty bhikṣus during this rainy-season retreat to serve as the value of food and clothing.
This is the portion for the eighth day; this is the portion for the fourteenth and fifteenth days; this is the portion for medical supplies for the sick; and this is the profit from robes.
"There is a virtuous bhikṣu whom you may invite to dwell here; I shall return again at the end of the summer retreat, and I will provide offerings for one hundred bhikṣus according to my means.
Having spoken these words, he prostrated and departed.
An elderly bhikṣu said to his companion, "We have now gained much profit; who shall take charge of storing it?
The other replied:
"The junior one should lift it.
At that time, the junior one immediately lifted it.
"Who, moreover, should go to Śrāvastī to summon the bhikṣus to come and dwell here?"
He replied,
"The younger one.
The younger one answered:
"I have already taken charge of the robes; you, sir, should depart on your own.
Thereupon, the elderly bhikṣu proceeded toward Śrāvastī to go to the Jetavana Grove.

It was the constant custom of the group of six [bhikṣus] to always station one person at the entrance of the monastery. At that time, Upānanda was standing at the gate when he saw from afar the elderly bhikṣu approaching, his hair like that of a reed flower. Upānanda then thought to himself:
“From where has this venerable elder come?
He replied, “Welcome!”
"Welcome, Venerable One! He replied,
"I pay homage to the Ācārya!"
"I pay homage to my upādhyāya!
Upānanda then thought to himself:
"This is a mahallaka who cannot distinguish between the honorable and the lowly."
He then asked him, "Old man, from where have you come?
He replied:
"I have come from such-and-such a monastery!
[The other] replied,
"Old man, is this a monastery?"
"Is this for the sake of *vighāta*? He then asked:
"What is meant by *vihāra*?"
"What is meant by *vighāta*?
He replied, "'Abundant provisions' refers to a *vihāra*; 'lack of necessities' refers to *vighāta*."
He replied, "In the past it was Vikāta; today it is Vihāra. Upānanda said:
"What is your intention?

He replied, "Merchants from the north have come into the monastery and offered wealth for the purpose of making offerings; sixty persons are required, and I have now come specifically to summon the assembly of bhikṣus."
Having heard these words, Upānanda immediately thought to himself,
"I must not let this old man enter the monastery," and said:
"Do you not know, old man, that you wish to entice the bhikṣus here?

King Prasenajit provides the bhikṣus with various kinds of clothing and food, as do Queen Vaidehī, Queen Vārṣākārā, the Kṣatriyas, the householder Anāthapiṇḍada, Rāṣṭrapāla, the mother of Viśākhā, and Queen Sujātā; furthermore, there are many other faithful brahmins, householders, and laymen who daily offer prayers for their welfare."

All the bhikṣus who have not yet arrived desire to come; the present community of monks dwells with joyful hearts; the four types of requisites for their support have never been lacking; the Great Teacher, the World-Honored One, personally expounds the Dharma for them; and thus both the path of the Dharma and the path of material sustenance are entirely free from deficiency.
If the great assembly learns that you intend to come and entice the bhikṣus, they will certainly perform the *pravāsanīya-karman* (act of banishment) against you.
However, we brothers currently number six, each having ten disciples; out of compassion for you, we shall go.
Then the elderly bhikṣu replied to Upānanda, "Venerable sir!
I wish to go for a moment to pay homage at the feet of the World-Honored One before returning to my former residence."
Upānanda thought to himself,
"If there are others of the 'black-bowl' class who hear this announcement, they will depart ahead of me.
He then replied:
“Old man! Have you not heard the verse spoken by the Buddha:
‘All phenomena have the mind as their forerunner; the mind is supreme, the mind is swift.’”
"Because the mind is pure, through praise and prostration with the body,
one shall receive supreme and wondrous bliss, following the form like a shadow that never departs.
When Upānanda had spoken these words, he immediately seized him by the neck and pressed down to force his head low.
"You should recite aloud:
'Homage to the Buddha, homage to the Dharma, homage to the Saṅgha. He then said:
“Ācārya! I am now thirsty and should seek water to drink.
Upānanda replied:
“Old man! You may stay here;
I shall fill your pitcher with water for you to drink from this place.
He then fetched water and, once he had finished drinking, the other said to him:
"Old man! You should depart at once; do not linger any longer.
See him off as he sets out on his journey, ensuring that he does not turn back.
It was the constant custom of the group of six monks to gather together at the time of sunset, where they would inform one another of all matters, whether good or bad.
At that time, Upānanda entered the monastery and addressed the group of six, saying:
"Venerable friends!..."
"When shall we be freed from this hardship? He then asked,
"Venerable Sir!"
"Is there any news of anything particularly extraordinary?

He replied, "In a certain village there is a monastery (vihāra). Northern merchants have arrived there and, with a sincere desire to make offerings, they provide sixty bhikṣus with abundant food and clothing, lacking nothing."
Having heard this, everyone said:
"We shall go!
Shall we observe the rains retreat there?"
Upānanda said: "We shall not observe the rains retreat at that place;
we will go there, consume all our provisions during the preceding summer, and then return here to observe the latter rains retreat."
He then led his disciples along the road.
Having arrived there, the two original residents saw them approaching from afar and said, "Welcome!"
"Welcome, venerable ones! he said,
and immediately provided them with rooms, bedding, small seats, and vessels for water.
At that time, the group of six made this deliberation:
"We have come from afar seeking something; we should all observe together what is being done.
They then spoke to the elderly bhikṣu, saying:
"Bring forth whatever offerings of profit there are that can be brought out.
At that time, the two bhikṣus, being upright by nature, brought forth all the items for distribution, saying:

"This is the provision for the sixty bhikṣus for the duration of the rainy season retreat; this is for the regular meals; this is the cost for the eighth, fourteenth, and fifteenth days of each month; and this is the necessary medicine as well as the profit from the robes."
At that time, after the group of six had inspected the items, they said to one another:

"These two old men are so stingy that they are unwilling to provide excellent food and drink as offerings for the Saṃgha; yet these elders have already taken charge of protecting the monastic requisites, which has caused them considerable hardship. We ought to release them from their duties."
When the two elderly men were thus granted their release, they were filled with extreme joy. The group of six monks said to one another:
"We should appoint someone capable of supervision who can, day after day, prepare eighteen kinds of marvelous cakes and fruits for the Saṃgha to offer as alms."

He immediately appointed someone to serve as the administrator; following the instructions of the Saṃgha, that person daily prepared superior and exquisite food and drink, until before long their wealth and goods were completely exhausted.
At that time, the administrator addressed the Elder, saying:
"Venerable Sir!
The funds for the Sangha's meals are now entirely exhausted; only one day remains."
The Elder said: "Venerable one!
If one's precepts are incomplete, one may wait for a festival day; but since our conduct regarding the precepts is complete, why should we wait for such a day?"
"Those who intend to make offerings on the eighth, fourteenth, and fifteenth days should all consume [the food] in advance.
The person in charge, following these instructions, immediately prepared it accordingly.
When everyone had finished eating, he addressed the assembly again, saying,
"There is one day's worth of food remaining.
The Elder replied:

“The body of the five aggregates of clinging is constantly afflicted by the suffering of illness; even the value of all the medicines may be consumed, and the existing clothing and provisions must also be divided up, so that each may take their share and return along the road.”
They then divided the proceeds from the robes among themselves and addressed the assembly again, saying,
"There is one day's worth of gruel remaining."
Upānanda informed the official, saying,
"Call the old man here! The messenger reported this.
"You originally invited the Saṃgha, saying you would provide abundant offerings for three months; yet before even a month has passed, everything has been exhausted.
The two replied, "How could the donors have intended for us to eat eighteen kinds of wondrous cakes and fruits every day as our constant meal?"
The Elder replied, "Old man!
When you receive food, you should eat with your head bowed; now that it is all gone, you utter words of contempt."
Upānanda informed the official in charge, saying:
"The community should perform the formal act of banishment against these two old men.
Others further said:
“You two elders must quickly seek forgiveness; if you delay further, your heads will remain bowed for a long time and the tendons in your necks will stretch and snap.
Thereupon, the two immediately sought forgiveness from Paṇḍava before the assembly, addressing the great multitude:
“Venerable ones!...”
"These two elderly men are simple and straightforward by nature; may the assembly, out of compassion, grant them their pardon.
The assembly then immediately offered alms with joy.
Upānanda said to the old man:

“The people of this village have no faith or respect at all; it will be difficult for us to obtain alms here. If there is anything else remaining, you may carry it out; if there is none, we shall depart.”
The two of them replied,
"Venerable Sir,
there is nothing remaining."
Then the sixty men all followed the road to Śrāvastī; having arrived there, they all sat out the summer retreat.

When the three months had concluded, the former merchants returned to this place. As before, they entered the monastery to offer praise and prostrations, and while touring the cells, they again saw the two elderly bhikṣus and asked, "Where are the bhikṣus currently residing within the monastery?"
He replied,
"O worthy one! There are no bhikṣus here."
The merchant said,
"Did I not tell you that I invited sixty bhikṣus to observe the rains retreat here?
At that time, the two elderly men related the matter in full.
The merchant leader replied,
"In what place did you invite the bhikṣu?
He answered:
"The six bhikṣus together with their companions.
The merchant leader replied, "Virtuous sirs, you went to the great ocean to fetch artificial lapis lazuli; surely there are no others in the Jeta Grove—why did you request only the six bhikṣus?"
At that time, the caravan leader and the merchants each felt contempt and disdain, saying:
"The śramaṇa sons of the Śākyas have no sense of shame or remorse; they destroy the pure Dharma.
They cause the sprouts of faith we have just begun to grow to wither and break."
When the bhikṣus heard this, they reported the matter to the Buddha.
The Buddha said:
"Since such faults arise when distributing items during the summer retreat, bhikṣus should not distribute the property acquired during the summer retreat while the retreat is still in progress."
"If one does so during the middle of summer, one incurs an offense of transgressing the Dharma.
This was the origin of the rule, though the precept had not yet been formally enacted.
At that time, in this city, the Bhikṣuṇī Mahāprajāpatī constantly practiced meditative concentration, and all her disciples likewise remained in tranquil seclusion.
Dharmadinnā was always delighted to uphold the Sūtra-piṭaka, and all her disciples likewise upheld the Sūtra-piṭaka.
These two women lived together in the same monastery; whenever Mahāprajāpatī’s disciples arose from meditative concentration, Dharmadinnā would address her disciples, saying:
"Sisters!..."
The Blessed One granted permission for bhikṣuṇīs to go forth and receive full ordination; this was entirely through the power of Mahāprajāpatī’s exhortation.
As the Blessed One has said:
"If one can protect the minds of others, one shall generate great merit."
"O sisters! You too should practice the contemplation of impermanence.
At that time, the disciples followed the instruction and did so.
When the Dharma was being recited by the disciples, Mahāprajāpatī addressed them, saying: "Sisters!

The Tathāgata, the World-Honored One, cultivated various ascetic practices throughout three great kalpas; he brought the immeasurable hundreds of thousands of six pāramitās to complete perfection and realized unsurpassed wisdom—all of this was for the benefit of sentient beings."
As the Blessed One has said:
"If a person can protect the minds of others, they shall generate much merit. Sisters!
"You all should also recite the *Anityatā-sūtra*.
At that time, the disciples followed these instructions.

However, because the two bhikṣuṇīs and their disciples were preoccupied with looking after one another, they were unable to advance in their cultivation of wholesome qualities, just as flowers with little water fail to flourish.
There was a lay follower named Viśākha who conceived deep faith and reverence for the bhikṣuṇī Dharmadinnā; he provided her with all the requisites she required, according to her wishes.
At one time, Viśākhā went to the dwelling of the nun Dharmadinnā to pay her respects.
Having arrived at her place, the nun said to her, "Upāsaka!..."

When many bhikṣuṇīs dwell together in one place during the rainy season retreat, if they merely guard and cherish one another, their cultivation of wholesome qualities will fail to progress, like flowers with little water.
"Would you be able to build a separate monastery for the community of bhikṣuṇīs?
She replied, "Noble One!"
"I possess great wealth, yet I have no land; all land belongs to the King, so I have no means of obtaining it.
Dhamma replied, "If you are truly capable, I shall petition the King on your behalf in hopes of obtaining that land."
Viśākhā said, "If you obtain land, I shall have a monastery built for you.
Thereupon, the nun Dharmadinnā went to the residence of Queen Vaidehī.
At that time, seeing Dharmadinnā approaching, the lady said to her:
"Welcome! Welcome!"
“Venerable One, you may sit here.
Once the nun had sat down, she prostrated at his feet and said,
“Venerable One!”
"With what intention have you come?
He replied, "O Lady!"

"I now wish to construct a dwelling for the bhikṣuṇīs; however, since all the land belongs to the King, there is no place where I can build. For the sake of obtaining land, I wish to inform the King."
The lady replied, "Noble one!
You should go; I shall inform the king on your behalf."
Then the nun Dharmadinnā, having offered a blessing for his freedom from illness, rose from her seat and departed.
At that time, the queen went to the king's presence and said,
"Great King!..."
"Today Your Majesty has attained great benefit, for the noble lady Dharmadinnā Bhikṣuṇī has come to the royal palace.
The King said,
"Noble lady, why have you come?"
The lady replied,
"The Noble One intends to build a residence for the bhikṣuṇīs; he said,
'Since the entire earth belongs to the King, I wish to make a formal request in order to seek land.'"
The King then replied:
"If it is indeed a holy one who requires my inner palace for the purpose of building a monastery, I shall relinquish it and construct a separate residence for him."
"If you do not wish to do so, you may build it according to your own preference and wherever you please.
Having received the King's instruction, the lady sent a messenger to inform him:
"Noble One!..."
The King now followed his wish and said:
"If it is indeed the holy one’s requirement that I provide my inner palace for the construction of a monastery, I shall relinquish it and build a separate residence."
"If you do not wish to do so, you may build it according to your own preference wherever you please.
When the nun Dharmadinnā heard this instruction, she reported it in full to Viśākhā.
At that time, King Jayasena had two generals:
one named Suvīra and the other named Subāhu.
While Suvīra was away with his troops on a military expedition elsewhere, the king’s wife committed adultery with a paramour.
Near the vicinity of that house, there was a vacant and open space; Dharmadinnā sought land and consequently arrived there.
Dharmadinnā replied, "The location for building a monastery here is exceptionally beautiful and desirable."
At that time, Viśākhā immediately began construction on this site to build a monastery, and before long, the monastery was completed.
The bhikṣuṇī then took up residence there with her disciples.

When the army of Good-Sword returned from its expedition, the women went about as they pleased; when the men pursued and caught them, they brought them back to their homes and beat them with sticks, until all of them cried out in loud voices.
The bhikṣuṇīs all came and said to Dharmadinnā,
"Noble Lady! While we were avoiding the rain, we fell into the river."
When the nun Dharmadinnā heard these words, she thought to herself:
"Do these people possess any roots of goodness?
She then observed them and knew that they did indeed possess roots of goodness.
"To whom do they belong?
They all belong to me.
He then addressed his disciples, saying:
“Sisters! For the sake of converting and delivering others, you must endure this.
Thereupon, the nun Dharmadinnā placed a clay bowl in one spot and addressed her disciples, saying:
"Sisters! All leftover food should be placed here.
Then those nuns put all their leftover cakes and food there.
At that time, young boys and girls came into the monastery; if they were boys, the nun Dharmadinnā would place oil in their hands and have them rub their heads, then give them the leftover cakes;
if they were girls, the nun Dharmadinnā herself would take scented oil and smear it upon the crowns of their heads, giving them all the leftover cakes to eat.
When the boys and girls had received the cakes and fruits, they all took them home; upon seeing this, their mothers asked each of them, "Where did you obtain these cakes?"
He replied,
"The noble Dharma-datta gave it to me for me to eat.
When the mothers heard this, they all thought to themselves:
“Observing this affection, it is indeed the Dharma of the Noble Ones that assists me in raising my child.
Because of this matter, her reverence and faith toward the nuns became even deeper, and each of them formed this thought:
“If our husbands go forth again on military expeditions, we shall all go to the place of the Noble Ones to serve and make offerings.”

Subsequently, when their husband had departed for military service, the nun Dharmadinnā, knowing that those women were ready to be transformed and guided, sent her disciples to sweep the courtyard and smear it with fresh cow dung. She further provided scented powder and pure water, arranged fragrant flowers and offerings, and appointed those with beautiful voices to offer praises to the Buddha.
At that time, after their husbands had departed, those women called out to one another and entered the monastery, arriving at the place where Dharmadinnā was.
When the nun saw them, she said:
"Welcome, sisters!"

They all paid their respects and exchanged greetings; having been given powdered soap and poured with pure water to wash their hands, they were all provided with fragrant flowers and instructed to circumambulate to the right, making offerings at the caitya while singing hymns of praise.
Having completed the offerings, the nun Dharmadinnā took her seat before the great assembly.
Then all the women, having paid their respects, sat down before her in order to listen to the Dharma.

At that time, the bhikṣuṇī Dharmadinnā, observing the differences in their faculties, dispositions, and natures, taught the Dharma according to their inclinations, causing the minds of those women to attain awakening. Thereupon, while still on their seats, they used the vajra-pestle of wisdom to shatter the twenty-fold mountain of satkāyadṛṣṭi and all attained the fruit of srotāpanna, as described in detail previously.

Having departed from the three evil destinies and attained the path to nirvāṇa, she took refuge in the Three Jewels and received the five precepts—refraining from taking life up to refraining from drinking alcohol—and thus became an upāsikā.

Then the women, having paid homage to the community of nuns, each returned to their own homes. Once they had arrived at their dwellings, they swept and cleansed the courtyards, thoroughly smearing them with fresh cow dung; then, maintaining dignified decorum, they settled there in quietude.
Later, at another time, their husbands returned from the army; while each was on the road, they thought to themselves:
"With which man has the wife of my household committed an illicit act?"
At that time, when those wives heard that their husbands had returned, they all went out together to welcome them; having met one another, they said:
"Welcome! Welcome!"
"O noble son, you have undergone great hardship.
They then each led him back to their respective residences.
At that time, those wives each provided their husbands with fragrant oils for anointing the body, baths with warm water, and offerings of fine food, along with crowns, sashes, and flower garlands.
At that time, those people each thought to themselves:
"How extraordinary today are these manners and dignified deportment!
They all asked their wives, saying:
"For what reason have you provided me with such extraordinary service today?
The wife replied to her husband,
"Do you not know, noble son?"

"Having been blessed by the noble Bhikṣuṇī Dharmadinnā’s exposition of the sublime Dharma, we are now such that although we continue to wander within saṃsāra, our most heavy afflictions no longer manifest as they did in former days."
Then their husbands each had this thought: "The noble Dharma-yasas is able to tame those who are difficult to tame.

My wife has for many days committed many improper acts; though I have punished her with various whips and harsh words, she would not reform. Because she was granted the teaching by the noble one, she has now attained submissiveness. This is a great kindness bestowed upon us by the noble one; we ought to inform the King together and go to the monastery to pay our respects to the noble one."

At that time, the nun Dharmadinnā observed that their faculties were capable of being transformed and delivered; she immediately swept and sprinkled the dwelling and extensively expounded the Dharma as before, causing all those people to attain the vision of the Truths. She praised the rarity of such an occasion as previously detailed, until they took refuge in the Triple Gem and received the five precepts, whereupon she spoke these words:
"Noble Lady!..."
"From this day forward, we shall not intentionally take the life of even an ant; yet, we currently sustain ourselves by wielding the knife.
Now that we have ceased killing, what shall we do?"
The nun replied, "O worthy one!
Hold a barbless arrow, carry a stringless bow, and grasp a wooden blade; do not harbor thoughts of harm."
The people replied, "We shall carry this out.

Once those soldiers had realized the Truth, they abstained from drinking alcohol, refrained from gambling, and did not engage in sexual misconduct. Consequently, their household wealth and enjoyments became abundant, and all their elephants and horses were properly nourished and grew robust.

Later, at another time, a border region of King Prasenajit of Kośala rebelled against his command; he dispatched troops to campaign there, but every army sent out was defeated by the enemy, and even when he sent generals again, they likewise met with total defeat.
At that time, a high minister of the state came forward and addressed the king, saying:
"The troops at the frontier are flourishing while the royal army grows weaker by the day; if Your Majesty does not go in person, it will be difficult to subdue them.
Upon hearing these words, the king immediately issued a proclamation to inform all people:
“Within my kingdom, all those who live by the sword shall follow me to strike down that rebellious one.
The king had two armies:
the first was named Good Sword, and the second was named Good Bow.
Once the King had emerged, he ordered Sujāta to lead the vanguard and Suvarcā to serve as the rear guard.
Seeing that the men and horses of the vanguard were robust and flourishing, the King asked his minister,
"Whose army is this?"
The minister replied, "This is King Śūrasena’s vanguard, who has gone on ahead.
Then the king looked back and saw that the men and horses of his rear guard were emaciated; the king asked the minister:
“What army is this?
The minister replied,
“This is the King’s ‘Skilled Archers’ army, serving as the rear guard.”
The king said,
"How can you provide military provisions with such inequality?
The ministers replied:
"Grant them equal distribution.
The King said,
"Summon them."
He summoned him at once, and the king questioned him personally, saying,
"Was the grain not distributed equally among your troops?
He replied:
"Great King!
It is as you have surmised.
The king said:
"Why is it that the troops and horses of the vanguard are so robust and flourishing,
while your own army is so emaciated? He replied to the king, saying,

"If we were to hold arrows without shafts, carry bows without strings, and grasp wooden swords in our hands— refusing to cause harm— and instead sell all our weapons to provide for our food, then our soldiers would likewise be robust and flourishing."
Upon hearing these words, the king questioned his vanguard, saying:
"How can you possibly hold arrows without shafts, carry bows without strings, and grasp wooden swords in your hands, while having no desire to inflict harm!"
He replied, "It is indeed so.
The king said:
"Do you wish to take me there so that others may kill me?
They then replied, "How could weapons alone suffice for battle? Ultimately, it requires human strength to defeat that army."
Upon hearing this, the king became incensed and declared:
"If weapons cannot fight, and it is only men who can fight, then you should go and subdue and destroy that city.
Having spoken these words, the king turned his carriage back.
Then the vanguard soldiers went to the place of the nun Dharmadinnā and said to her, "Noble Lady!
The King has sent us to attack that city; what plan do we intend to adopt now?"
Dharmadinnā replied, "O noble ones!
You need only go; you shall certainly achieve victory at that frontier city. However, at every place where you stay, recite the Triśaraṇa Sūtra."
Having arrived at the frontier regions, they surrounded the city walls; then, throughout that entire night, they recited the scriptures and offered prayers by invoking the names of the gods, saying:

"May this merit be extended to Brahmā, Śakra, the Lord of this World, the Four World-Protectors, the eighteen kinds of Great Yakṣa Kings, the Yakṣa General Pañcika, the retinue of the King of the Staff-Holders, and the Great Nāga Kings Nanda and Upananda."

When those soldiers had heard the account spoken by the bhikṣuṇī Dharmadinnā, they immediately prostrated at her feet and departed with joy. At their respective dwellings, they recited the *Triśaraṇa* Sūtra; having arrived there, they surrounded the city walls on all sides and recited the sūtras throughout that entire night.

Then that general, in accordance with the Dharma, performed the ritual as instructed by the nun; he then extensively offered prayers of benediction as previously detailed, and prepared sacrificial food to make offerings to the celestial deities.

At that time, the Northern Heavenly King Vaiśravaṇa was about to go to the place where many yakṣas had gathered; hearing the sound of the various military hosts reciting incantations and prayers, he thought to himself:
"Who is invoking my name and offering these prayers?"
He then looked down and observed the various military hosts, and again thought to himself:
"This younger brother of mine in the Dharma is being driven toward an improper place.
He immediately addressed the yakṣa general Pañcika, saying:
"This army belongs to my Dharma-brother; it is improper for you to conscript them. You should instead subdue this city and hand it over to his troops.

The yakṣas respectfully assented and, not far from that place, manifested an army: elephants like great mountains, horses shaped like elephants, chariots like multi-storied pavilions, and men who were like yakṣas themselves.
At that time, the people within the city saw the army approaching from afar and were seized with great terror;
they said to one another, "Between the kingdom and our lives, which is more important?
If the kingdom is destroyed, it can be sought again; but once life is severed, it is difficult to restore."
"You ought to preserve your lives; why would you care for the city?
Thereupon, they each cast aside their weapons, opened the great city gates, and bound their own necks while entreating mercy and begging for their lives.

When Śūrasena saw this, he felt compassion for them and refrained from killing; instead, he took their generals and leaders along with all their territories and treasures, and returning in high spirits, he turned his banners toward home.
Arriving at the king's location, he said:
"Great King!
These are the troops and the goods for their maintenance."
The King, filled with extreme joy and celebration, addressed his soldiers, saying:
"The wealth of the fief I have brought shall be used to reward your diligent labors; as for the captives, let them be released after establishing an oath.
At that time, the soldiers of the Good Sword Regiment thought to themselves:
“Since we have returned safely from our military expedition, all of this is due to the majestic spiritual power of the Venerable Dharmadatta.
They then said to one another, “It was by the power of the Venerable that we achieved victory; we shall now offer these spoils of war as a direct gift to the Venerable.”
He immediately took the items and went to their location, saying:
"Noble ones!
We have returned from battle having preserved our lives; the King is delighted and has bestowed upon us abundant rewards."
"I have now brought this here to briefly express my sincere heart; I only pray that you will, out of compassion, accept this object.
Dharmadatta replied, "O noble one!"

If one does not offer worship to the Triple Gem, even if reborn in the heavens, one will still suffer the pains of poverty; you all should therefore offer worship to the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Sangha, so that you may always enjoy peace and happiness throughout the long night of saṃsāra.

Having received this instruction, those people all went to the Jeta Grove to invite the Buddha and the Saṃgha for the three-month summer retreat. They provided everything that was required, making offerings to the Triple Gem every day before each meal, listening to the sublime Dharma after the meal, and practicing mindfulness and contemplation during both the first and last watches of the night.
Later, at another time, there was again a border region that did not submit to the king's command; the king then issued an order to the soldiers skilled in archery, saying:
"You may go and subdue that border region."
Then Śaradhanus addressed the Great King, saying:
"Our troops are weak and their army is powerful; let them go first, and I shall take my turn later."
The king commanded the General of the Good Sword, saying:
"You may go and strike down those border regions.
That army addressed the king:
"My turn has ended; it is not yet time for the army to march.
The King said, "You must serve this one term for now; thereafter you shall be exempt."
Then, having received the king’s command, those soldiers deliberated among themselves, saying:
"Our previous submission to that city was due to the majestic power of the yakṣas; if we go there again now, our death is certain beyond doubt."
"However, we have invited the Buddha and the Sangha for three months, providing them with everything they require.
It would be appropriate for us to offer them these summer robes and then depart for the military campaign."
They then took the garments and went to the Jeta Grove.
At that time, the World-Honored One was sitting in silent seclusion. The people brought the items to the bhikṣus and said, "Venerable Sirs!"

"We have been dispatched to wage war against the border regions; having fallen in battle there, it would be difficult for us to return again. These are items offered during the summer retreat; we pray that you will accept them."
Then the bhikṣus replied, "Worthy friend!
The Great Teacher, the World-Honored One, has already established a training rule (śikṣāpada) forbidding us from distributing robes during the summer retreat; therefore, I do not dare accept them."
He replied, “Noble One!
Please accept this and set it aside in one place; when the summer retreat has ended, let the community divide it together.”
The people placed their robes in one room and departed.
At that time, those men emerged with their former weapons and military array. When the householder Anāthapiṇḍada saw them, he asked, "Where are you going?"
He replied, "Householder!
I wish to go on a military expedition."
The elder replied,
"Have you not already returned from your previous expedition?
They answered:
"It has been accomplished.
"If that is so, why did you set out on campaign once again?
He replied:
"The King has sent us; we must attend to this matter for now, but later you shall be exempted.
The elder replied, "Stay here for now."
"I shall inform the King.
Thereupon, the elder went to the King's presence and addressed him, saying:
"For what purpose does Your Majesty now employ the army of skilled swordsmen?"
The king said, "A certain city has rebelled; I am now going there to suppress it.
The elder said:
"Has he gone on duty yet?
The king replied,
"He has already gone."
The elder said, "If that is so,
why do you go there so frequently?
The king replied:
"The next time you shall be released.
The elder said,
"Does Your Majesty know this now?"
"Can one who wields a barbless arrow, holds a stringless bow, and grasps a wooden sword subdue others?

Indeed, those soldiers are all sons of the Buddha; they do not intentionally take the life of even an insect or an ant. Their previous expedition to wage war was actually the Yakṣa deities acting to subdue that city."
"Now that we are about to set out once more, I fear they will perish; would this not be for the Great King to harm the sons of the Buddha?
At that time, the Great King, recognizing them as the sons of the Buddha, told his ministers:

"Proclaim my command to the household of Vīradatta, letting him know that from this day forward, wherever there is a place of military expedition, he must no longer dispatch soldiers skilled with the sword."
Then, when the bhikṣus had completed their summer retreat, they went to various people and said:
"Virtuous ones! We have finished our *pravāraṇā*; if you have robes, please give them to us."
He replied, "Venerable One!
I gave it to him previously; he should take it from that place."
At that time, when the bhikṣus opened the room to retrieve their belongings, they saw only mounds of earth built up by ants.
The bhikṣus reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"You should appoint a bhikṣu to be in charge of storing the robes."
If a bhikṣu does not possess five qualities, he should not be appointed; even if appointed, he should not perform the duties.
What are these five? They are:
being subject to affection, aversion, fear, and delusion; and being unable to discern what has been concealed and what has not been concealed.
One who possesses five qualities should be appointed; once appointed, he should be made to perform the task.
What are these five? They are:
being free from attachment, aversion, fear, and delusion, and being well-versed in discerning what has been concealed and what has not been concealed. One who is thus qualified should be appointed.
First, one should exhort a single bhikṣu, saying:
"O [Name], are you able to store and protect the robes for the Saṃgha during the three months of the summer retreat? If he says:
Saying "I can," one should spread out the seating mats, then strike the *gandī* and announce the formal motion; once the Saṃgha has fully assembled, one bhikṣu shall perform the *jñapti-karman*.

At that time, the Blessed One praised the observance of the precepts and those who revere the precepts, as well as those of few desires, contentment, and the practice of the dhūta ascetic virtues; he extolled those whose deportment was dignified and who received alms with moderation. Having taught them in accordance with the dharma practiced by the bhikṣus, he addressed the bhikṣus, saying:
"The former was the initial injunction, and this is the subsequent allowance. For the sake of the bhikṣus, I establish this training rule (*śikṣāpada*), which should be recited as follows:

'If a bhikṣu, during the first three months of the summer retreat, when ten days remain until the end of the month or half a month remains until the end of the eighth month, should receive an urgent gift of robes (*ātyayika-cīvara*) if he requires it, he may keep it until the time for the distribution of robes.'"
"If one keeps [the robe] beyond this period, it is a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* offense.
"Bhikṣu" refers to one who is among the followers of the Buddha-Dharma.
"Ten days remaining before the middle of the eighth month" means that ten days remain until the time for the *pravāraṇā* ceremony.
The "first three months" of the summer retreat refers to the earlier retreat, not the later one.
Regarding "urgent robes for distribution," there are five types. What are these five?
Either giving for the sake of one's own illness, or giving for the sake of another who is ill; or giving at the time of death, or giving for the sake of the deceased; or giving when about to travel.
"A bhikṣu who requires it" means one whose mind desires it.
"Robe" refers to any one of the seven types.
"Should receive" means that having accepted and kept it, one should divide it according to one's wish.
"Even until the time for giving robes, one should store [the robe]" refers to its being kept in reserve.
What is meant by "the time for giving robes"?
It means that if the *kaṭhina* robe has not been spread, it is one month; if the *kaṭhina* robe has been spread, it is five months—this is what is called "the time."
Beyond this time, it is improper.

If one keeps an extra robe without making a formal determination (*vibhāga*) after this time has passed, one commits an offense of expiation involving forfeiture (*naiḥsargika-pāyattika*). The procedure for forfeiting it is explained at length as previously stated.
Regarding the characteristics of the offense herein, what are the specific matters?
If a bhikṣu distributes the summer gains during the rainy season retreat, or keeps them beyond the permitted time, he incurs the offense of *naiḥsargika-pāyattika*.
If one obtains five kinds of urgent offering robes within the ten-day period, there is no offense in dividing them.
If it is during the summer retreat, or if at any time a donor wishes to give with their own hands, there is likewise no offense in accepting them.
If a bhikṣu who has been designated to receive the stored robe, or the donor himself, should say:
"When I return from my journey, I shall personally offer it," then even if he keeps it beyond the prescribed time limit, there is no offense.
Furthermore, there is no offense for the very first offender, or for one who is insane, mentally deranged, or afflicted by intense pain.
*Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya*, Fascicle Twenty-three. *Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya*, Fascicle [Twenty-four].
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Yijing by Imperial Decree. 27.

The Training Rule on Six Nights in an Āraṇya. The twenty-seventh training rule concerning six nights in an āraṇya. At that time, the Blessed One was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
Not far from here there is a village; in it lived a householder who was immensely wealthy, possessing vast riches and many servants, and who was endowed with pure faith and a virtuous disposition.

For the sake of the Saṃgha, he constructed a dwelling place that was lofty and grand, featuring a magnificent stone gate and railings all around that were exquisitely adorned; it was like a stairway for ascending to heaven, bringing joy to all who beheld it.
Having invited sixty bhikṣus to this residence, they completed their summer retreat and departed as they pleased.
At that time, the donor, seeing the monastery empty, had people stationed to guard it so that bandits would not steal the beds, mats, and other belongings.
At that time, there were also sixty bhikṣus traveling through the countryside who arrived at this village seeking a place to stay.
Then a certain man said to the bhikṣus:
"Noble ones!..."
"Why do you not stay at the monastery?
He replied, "O worthy one!"
"Where is there a monastery? He replied,
"Outside the village, in the forest, there is a pleasant dwelling place."
The bhikṣu then went to see him; having seen him from afar, the guardian said:
"Welcome! Welcome!"
He then immediately provided them with dwellings in due order, along with bedding, pillows, seats, and three wooden props, saying:
"Venerable ones!..."
"You may first filter the water; I shall now go for a moment to inform the householder.
Having arrived, he said:
"Householder!"
"Now your merit and virtue have increased twofold, for sixty visiting bhikṣus have arrived at the monastery.
Upon hearing this, the elder was immediately filled with joy and surprise, and he said to his family members:
"You should now take butter, honey, granulated sugar, pomegranates, rock honey, grapes, and black pepper; [and prepare other offerings]."
Dry ginger and long pepper may be used to prepare non-time [afternoon] drinks and taken to the monastery.
Now that visiting *saṃghas* have arrived at their residence, we wish to prepare non-time drinks so that they may drink their fill.
Having heard this, the family members all brought him to the monastery. Once the bhikṣus had filtered their water, they each took their places, remaining wherever they were with dignified deportment.

At that time, the elder went into the monastery and saw from afar the bhikṣus filling the interior like a cluster of lotuses; his faith increased twofold and he turned toward them with great devotion, speaking these verses:
“In villages or in forests, In high places or low,”
"May those who dwell in the Saṃgha give rise to a heart of love and joy.

Having finished preparing the non-seasonal beverage (vikāla-pāna) and mixed it, he personally handed it out. Once the assembly of bhikṣus had drunk their fill, he prostrated at the feet of the Saṃgha, took up the incense burner himself, led the monks out to circumambulate the stūpa, and returned to the monastery.
He knelt for a long time before the Elder and remained there; the Elder then offered a blessing on his behalf.
When the blessing was finished, the householder said:
"At noon tomorrow, I pray that the Noble Assembly will deign to accept a modest offering at my residence."
The bhikṣus consented; he prostrated at their feet and departed.
On the following day, he prepared various exquisite foods to offer to the saṃgha. After the saṃgha had finished eating, each returned to his own dwelling place.
Furthermore, after midday, he served non-time-appropriate beverages; once they had rinsed their mouths and washed, he preached the sublime Dharma for them, and the Elder then offered a blessing.
At that time, the householder held an incense burner before the Elder and addressed the assembly, saying:
"O Noble Ones!"
"I have not built this dwelling for myself, nor for my relatives.
My original intention was solely to construct this dwelling for the Saṃgha; I pray that you will show compassion and spend the summer retreat here."
The bhikṣus said to the householder:
"The World-Honored One, the Lord of Dharma, is currently residing in Śrāvastī; from time to time he proclaims these predictions:
'A certain bhikṣu has realized arhatship; a certain bhikṣu has perfected the contemplation of impurity.'"
King Prasenajit, Queen Mallikā, the Mother Viśākhā—also known as Mṛgāramātṛ—and other householders and brahmins were all likewise filled with reverence and faith.
"When we arrive there, we shall equally enjoy both the Dharma and its meaning; we wish to go.
The elder replied, "As for receiving the benefits of the Dharma and its meaning, this is something only you gentlemen can know."
"I am willing to provide for your physical needs with clothing and food.
I pray that you will deign to remain here; we shall provide the four requisites of monastic life without any deficiency.
The Elder replied:
"Venerable ones!
As the Blessed One has said:
'If a donor possesses reverence and faith, one must increase their confidence through compassion.'"
"I now wish to dwell here.

Having thus resolved to remain, he immediately observed the interior and exterior of the place; he then saw trees filled with fragrant flowers and branches laden with beautiful fruit, while the clear ponds and lush forests were all delightful to behold.
The Elder said:
"Venerable ones!
This dwelling place is now abundant with flowers and fruits; since the fruits have not yet ripened for the preceding rains retreat, we should instead observe the subsequent rains retreat."
Having deliberated thus, they entered the later retreat (*paścimikā varṣā*).

At that time, that householder had built only a single monastery, and all his meritorious deeds were centered therein; there was no other monastery in this village or in other hamlets, so the meritorious deeds of all people likewise converged there.
At that time, the bhikṣus were receiving abundant offerings during this rainy-season retreat; having completed their随心 (suíyì) duties, they had not yet dispersed.
Then there was a band of Kāṣṭhavāṭaka thieves who deliberated among themselves, saying:
"What deed should we perform so that for an entire year we may have an abundance of food and clothing without the need for toil?"
Some among them said,
"We ought to steal the property of the bhikṣus.
The other bandits replied:
"He passes through a hundred doorways in a single day, begging with great hardship just to sustain his body; what does he possess?
One thief among them, who was intimately acquainted with the bhikṣu, said to the others:

"You do not know that he possesses great wealth. You should know this: because the donor who built this monastery is pure and virtuous in his faith, all the meritorious deeds resulting from the construction of this single monastery are concentrated within him. Since there is no other monastery in this village or in any other hamlet, the meritorious karma of all people has likewise converged upon him."
"At this time, the bhikṣus have received abundant offerings during their rains retreat here.
Those who do not believe may come together to witness it for themselves.
The people replied:
"If that is so, you may observe me first and I shall depart later.
He replied,
"I shall go on ahead for now."
He immediately adjusted his robes and proceeded with slow, composed steps, reciting verses as he circumambulated the stūpa before entering the monastery.
At that time, there was an elderly *mahallaka* bhikṣu at the gate; when the thief saw him, he prostrated at his feet and asked:
"Noble One!"
"Whose monastery is this?
Its chambers are so magnificently adorned that they inspire love and joy; it must be a staircase for those wishing to be reborn in heaven.
The bhikṣu replied:
“O noble one! This was established by the householder so-and-so. He asked:
“Noble one! Is this a vihāra,
or is it a vigata?”
The bhikṣu asked:
"What is meant by *vihāra*?
What is meant by *vighāta*?"
He replied, "If the requisites are abundant, this is a vihāra; if what is needed is lacking, this is a vigata.
The bhikṣu replied:
“O noble one! If it is so, this is a vihāra and not a vigada; the provisions at this dwelling place are abundant.
The thief then replied:
“Noble one!
If one has had enough food, one should not eat earth; if one has enough clothing, one should not wear tree bark. How much do you have of these robes?”
At that time, the mahallaka was by nature simple-minded and straightforward; he took the thief's hand and entered the room together, saying, "Look at the clothing and goods on the rack.
He asked again:
“Noble one! Is this your personal property,
or does it belong to the Saṃgha?”
He replied,
"O worthy one! This is my private property."
He asked, "Venerable One! Are you the Elder?"
"Are you this Dharma Master?
He replied, "O noble one!"
"I am not a senior elder, nor am I a Dharma teacher.
I am a śrāmaṇera, at the very end of the Saṃgha.
He replied:
“I already know all that you possess; however, do you have bedding and requisites for the community?
He replied, “O worthy one!”
"I am at the very lowest rank and yet possess seven things in full; how much more so for one of the Sangha?
He asked, "Noble One!"
"For the food being cooked inside the kitchens of various households, are earthenware vessels used,
or copper cauldrons?
The bhikṣu then showed him the storehouse and said:
"This storehouse is filled with copper vessels.
Having realized this, the thief was about to depart, but [the monk] addressed him, saying:
"Noble one!..."
"In the past, my practice of benevolence and goodness hindered my family business; now I shall take my leave for the time being and consult you further later.
He replied, "Go well."
The bandits then prostrated at his feet and departed;
they went to their fellow bandits and said, "I have observed the wealth in that monastery to be like a ship on dry land; it is fit to be stolen."
Among them, one man said to the bandits:

"I have heard it said that sixty men who were highly skilled in archery have gone forth as monks here; you must not rashly commit theft. Only when the assembly has gathered to listen to the sutras may you enter the temple."
Another person asked,
"I do not know on what day the assembly will gather to hear the sutra.
A monk who was well-acquainted with the details informed the bandits:
"Eight days have passed; since it is now the middle of the month, we should recite [the precepts].

Thereupon, they remained there counting the days on their fingers. On the fourteenth day, the presiding elder himself recited the *Prātimokṣa* for the purpose of the *Poṣadha* ceremony. Having done so, he had the reciter ascend the lion throne. As soon as the recitation began, he uttered a verse:
"The Buddha was in the Jeta Grove, Able to sever all fetters and delusions."
With all his faculties in perfect tranquility, he addressed the assembly with these words.
At that time, a band of thieves knocked on the door and called out; the bhikṣu asked, "Who are you?"
He replied, "Noble One!
I am a son of good family."
At that time, the bhikṣus thought to themselves:
"Perhaps people from the village will come here to listen to the Dharma; we shall open the gate for them.
Once the gate was opened, the bandits rushed in together, scrambling to seize the property. The bhikṣus said to them:
"You previously reported that this good man, having now entered the monastery, has stolen my property.
The thief said,
"Noble One!..."
"I have two names:
outside the monastery I am called a 'virtuous man' (kulaputra), but once I enter the monastery, I am called a 'thief'.
The bhikṣu said:
"The one who gave you that name was no good person.
Having stolen the object, he immediately left the monastery.
The bhikṣus discussed the matter, saying:
"Venerable sir!
As the Blessed One has said:
'One who milks a cow should not drain it completely.'"

"If this householder sees that we have encountered bandits and has already provided goods for the monastery, he will surely exhaust his entire fortune in giving to us once more; it would be best to go to Śrāvastī, to the place where our fellow practitioners reside, to seek clothing."
They said to one another, "Our bodies are exposed; how can we travel on this road?
One person said:
"Enter the grass thickets by day; at night, you shall travel along the road.
Without informing the elder, he set out and gradually reached Śrāvastī.

There, the bhikṣus were practicing meditation with vigilance and diligently cultivating wholesome qualities during the first and last watches of the night. Seeing a naked ascetic arrive before their gate, looking about in alarm and confusion, the bhikṣus called out from a distance:
"You naked ones who have plucked out your hair, for what reason have you come here?
This is where the Saṃgha resides; it is not your dwelling place.
They replied:
"Venerable one! I am a bhikṣu, not a naked heretic.
He asked again:
"How could there be such a bhikṣu with such an appearance?
He replied, "He has been plundered by bandits; what would you have him do?"
He asked, "What is your name? He replied:
“I am named Buddhagupta, Dharmagupta, Saṃghagupta,
and so forth. He then replied, “Welcome!”
"Welcome, venerable ones! he said,
and immediately opened the door.

He then entered the monastery and, according to what he possessed, provided for everyone: some were given the three robes (*tricīvara*), some a lower garment (*śāṭaka*), some a monastic vest (*saṃkakṣikā*), some a water-strainer (*parisrāvaṇa*), some a waistband (*mekhalā*), and some a bowl (*pātra*). He distributed everything he had to them all.
At that time, the bhikṣus reported the matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"If any bhikṣus dwell in an araṇya, they should leave one of their three robes behind in a layperson's house."
"As the Buddha has instructed, a forest-dwelling bhikṣu should leave one of his three robes within a layperson's house.

At that time, the bhikṣus, following the Buddha’s instruction, placed their robes in the village; because of the previously established precept, they returned to the village to stay overnight with the robes.
Then the brahmins and householders said to them:
"Venerable ones!
For what purpose have you stayed here tonight?"
He replied, "I have my own robe here.
The other then said:
"How could we possibly steal this robe?
If you do not trust us, you may take it with you.
Then the bhikṣus reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"You should not have stayed there overnight.
Then, before the dawn had broken, the bhikṣus went into the village and saw several women lying down naked;
they asked them, "For what reason, Noble Ones, did you come here before daybreak?"
The bhikṣu replied,
"I have my robe here. He then replied:
"How could we possibly steal this robe?
If you do not trust us, you may take it with you.
Then the bhikṣus reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"One should not go at night.
At that time, the bhikṣus went outside the village and waited for the appearance of the dawn light, whereupon they were terrified by thieves, tigers, wolves, and lions.
Then the bhikṣus reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"You should wait within the monastery until the appearance of dawn.
At that time, there were matters concerning the Three Jewels for which the bhikṣus needed to go outside the boundary; yet none dared to go, saying:
"I have a robe deposited in a layperson's house.
The bhikṣu informed the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"An araṇya bhikṣu may stay apart from his robe in another location for up to six nights."
At that time, the group of six bhikṣus went outside the boundary and remained there for seven nights. The other bhikṣus said to them:
"Venerable ones!
The Buddha permitted one to go outside the boundary and be separated from one's robes for six nights; for what reason have you remained there for seven nights?"
He replied,
"Venerable one!
Having been sent for six nights until the seventh night, would you have been drinking alcohol or eating garlic?"
When the bhikṣus of few desires heard this account, they all felt resentment and contempt, saying:
"The Buddha permitted bhikṣus to stay apart from their robes for six nights; how is it that these bhikṣus have actually stayed apart for seven nights?"
At that time, the bhikṣus reported the matter to the Buddha.
Then the World-Honored One, for this reason and on this account, spoke to the bhikṣus at length as above: "I shall establish a training rule (śikṣāpada), which should be recited as follows:

'If many bhikṣus are staying in an araṇya dwelling and are performing the later rains retreat in a place where there are fears and dangers, a bhikṣu may, from among his three robes, leave one robe behind in a village house.'"
If a bhikṣu has a reason to go outside the boundary of an araṇya, he may stay apart from his robe for up to six nights; if he exceeds this, it is a naiḥsargika-pāyattika offense.
"Furthermore, regarding 'a multitude of bhikṣus': a multitude refers to three or more persons. 'Bhikṣus' refers here to the group of six.

Regarding 'dwelling in an araṇya residence': five hundred bows from a village constitutes one *krośa*, which is called an *araṇya* residence; four *krośas* constitute one *yojana*. From the eighteen types of distinctions ranging from seven *paramāṇus* up to a *yojana*, it has been explained extensively as before."
"Residence" refers to a monastery.
"The later retreat" refers to that which begins from the sixteenth day of the sixth month.

Regarding "places with alarms, terrors, and hardships": "alarm" means fearing the arrival of bandits; "terror" refers to tigers, leopards, wolves, and the like; "hardships" refers to matters such as mosquitoes, gadflies, snakes, scorpions, wind, and heat.
Regarding the statement that a bhikṣu may, among his three robes, retain one robe within a village dwelling: the "three robes" refer to the saṃghāṭī, the uttarāsaṅga, and the antarvāsaka.
"Village" refers to a place where streets, lanes, and alleys can be identified.
"To place" means to set down.
"If there is a reason to go outside the boundary" refers to matters concerning the Three Jewels or matters concerning other individuals.
"To go beyond the boundary" means to depart from the limits of one's permanent residence.
"To obtain six nights" means to be permitted to remain for up to six nights.
"To stay apart from one's robes" refers to being separated from the robes deposited within the village.

If it exceeds [the limit], meaning until the appearance of the dawn on the seventh day, one commits the offense of *naiḥsargika-pāyattika*; the ritual for relinquishing and repenting is explained in detail as above.
In this regard, what are the characteristics of the offense and its specific circumstances?

If a bhikṣu wishes to leave one of his three robes within a village dwelling and remains separated from it beyond six nights while outside the boundary of the araṇya, he incurs the offense of naiḥsargika-pāyattika.
If any one of the eight difficulties should arise, it is not an offense to abandon [the precepts] and depart.
Furthermore, there is no offense for those who are first-time offenders, or those who are insane, mentally deranged, or overwhelmed by intense physical pain.

28. The Training Rule on Requesting a Rain-Bathing Robe in Advance and Using It Afterwards. The twenty-eighth training rule concerning the rain-bathing robe (*vassikasāṭikā*) which one requests in advance and uses afterwards. At that time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.

As the Buddha had instructed that bhikṣus should seek out rain-bathing robes, the group of six bhikṣus sought them in advance and used them after the rainy season had passed; their activities became so burdensome and complex that they obstructed and abandoned their formal practice.
The bhikṣus of few desires then felt contempt and said:
"How is it that you have intentionally contravened the Buddha’s words?
They reported this matter to the Buddha.
At that time, for these reasons and others, the Blessed One addressed the bhikṣus, saying: "I establish this training rule, which should be recited as follows:
'If a bhikṣu, when there is one month remaining of the spring season, seeks a rain-bath robe, he should use it until the end of the final half-month.'"
If a bhikṣu, when there is less than one month remaining until the end of spring, seeks a rain-bathing robe and continues to use it during the final half-month, it is a naiḥsargika-pāyattika offense.
"Furthermore, 'if a bhikṣu' refers to the group of six [monks], or anyone else of a similar class.

'When one month of spring remains' means that there is one month left until the commencement of the rainy season retreat (*varṣā*); specifically, from the sixteenth day of the fourth month to the fifteenth day of the fifth month."
"One who should seek a rain-bath robe" refers to bathing requisites.
"To be held and used until the last half-month" indicates the limit of usage; that is, one should perform the *pravāraṇā* ceremony while there remains a half-month [of the rainy season].
That is to say, from the first day of the eighth month onwards,

if a bhikṣu seeks out a rain-bath robe in advance before the final month of spring has arrived, and still continues to use it during the latter half of that month, he incurs an offense identical to the one mentioned previously.
The ritual for relinquishing [the robe] and the method for repentance are as explained extensively above.
Regarding this, what are the characteristics of the offense and its specific circumstances?
If a bhikṣu intends to enter the *pūrvavārṣika* (early) retreat, he must seek out a rain-bath robe during the final month of spring.
If a bhikṣu who intends to observe the later retreat (paścimā varṣā) should think,
"Since they still seek robes, why should I not seek one? and if he succeeds in obtaining one,
he commits an offense of expiation involving forfeiture (naiḥsargika-pāyattika).
If a bhikṣu observes the later retreat and carries his rain-bathing robe until the end of the eighth month, and still continues to carry it, a person observing the earlier retreat might think:
"Since he still carries his robe until the end of the eighth month, why should I not do the same?"
If one who holds [the robe] does so, they incur a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* offense.
However, there is no offense if the bhikṣus each seek robes according to their own summer retreat and hold them accordingly.
Furthermore, there is no offense for the very first offender, or for one who is insane, mentally deranged, or afflicted by intense pain.

29. The Training Rule on Appropriating Community Property for Oneself. The twenty-ninth training rule on appropriating community property for oneself: At that time, the Buddha was staying in the village of the reed-sellers in the region of the Śākyas.

At that time, there was a certain householder who, having conceived faith and developed deep affection and respect, constructed a dwelling place and offered it to the venerable Rāhula as a private residence.
At times, Rāhula would stay at this monastery, but on one occasion he had to travel to Śrāvastī due to some business.
At that time, when the elder heard that the Venerable Rāhula had left his residence and was heading for Śrāvastī carrying his robes and bowl,
he saw that the monastery was empty and immediately offered it to the Saṃgha.
At that time, when the venerable Rāhula had finished his business, he returned to his former residence and heard it said that the householder had offered his dwelling to the Saṃgha.
Having heard of this matter, Rāhula went to where the Buddha was, prostrated at his feet, and stood to one side. He then reported the circumstances in detail to the World-Honored One, saying:
"What should I do now?"
Then the World-Honored One addressed Rāhula, saying:
"You should now go to the householder’s place and speak these words:
'Householder!'"
“Could it be that you have found some unwholesome aspect in the bodily or verbal actions I have observed, such that you have conceived this contempt?
Then, having received the Buddha’s instruction, Rāhula went to the householder’s place and spoke these words:
“Householder!”
"Could it be that you have seen some unwholesome aspect in my bodily or verbal actions and thus conceived feelings of aversion or contempt?
At that time, the householder immediately prostrated at his feet and spoke these words:
