"I truly did not conceive any feeling of aversion or contempt toward the Venerable One upon seeing any unwholesome aspect in your bodily or verbal actions."
Then Rāhula offered a blessing to the elder, saying,
"May you be free from illness and live long," and immediately departed to return to the Buddha's presence. He prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, stood to one side, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
Having received your instruction, I went to the householder’s place and said to him:
‘Householder!’”
"Could it be that you have found some unwholesome aspect in my bodily or verbal actions and thus give rise to disdain?
The householder replied to me, saying:
"Noble One!"
"I truly do not harbor feelings of aversion or contempt toward the Venerable One regarding any unwholesome aspects of his bodily or vocal actions that I might perceive.
At that time, the Venerable Ānanda was standing behind the Buddha fanning him with a whisk. The World-Honored One then addressed the Venerable Ānanda, saying:
"You should now go to the village of the reed-sellers and inform all the bhikṣus, commanding them to assemble in the regular dining hall."

Then the Venerable Ānanda, having received his command, departed and proclaimed the Buddha’s teaching in full; once he had gathered that assembly of bhikṣus in the regular dining hall, he returned to the place where the Buddha was, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, stood to one side, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!”
"The assembly of bhikṣus in that village has all been gathered in the regular dining hall at my command; I only wish for you to know this.
At that time, the World-Honored One went to that hall, took the seat that had been prepared, and sat down. He addressed the bhikṣus, saying:

"If a donor gives a gift to one person, and later returns that same object to give it to another person, then this is an unrighteous act for the giver and an unrighteous act for the recipient; it is called 'impure enjoyment'."

If, in this manner, one further redirects [the gift] to two persons, or three persons, or to the Saṃgha, all such cases are termed giving that is not according to the Dharma, receiving that is not according to the Dharma, and impure utilization.

"O bhikṣus! If there is a donor who gives a certain object to two individuals, and later returns that same object to give it to one individual, then both the giver and the recipient are said to act contrary to the Dharma, and all such enjoyment is impure."
If, in this manner, one further diverts it to two people, three people, or to the Saṃgha, both the donor and the recipient are said to act contrary to the Dharma; all such enjoyment is impure.

"O Bhikṣus! If there is a donor who gives a certain object to three individuals, and later returns that same object to give it to one, two, or three other persons, or gives it to the Saṃgha, then both the giver and the receiver are said to act contrary to the Dharma; all such enjoyment is impure."

"O Bhikṣus! If there is a donor who gives a gift to the Saṃgha, yet later diverts that same object to give it to one, two, or three individuals, or to another group of monks, both the giver and the receiver are said to act contrary to the Dharma; all such enjoyment is impure."

"O Bhikṣus! If the Saṃgha has been split into two factions, and one first gives these items to one faction and then subsequently transfers them to the other faction, all such instances constitute impure utilization."

"O bhikṣus! If one gives to a single person and does not divert it to another, both the giver and the receiver are said to act in accordance with the Dharma, and all that is enjoyed is said to be pure."

In this way, if one gives to two persons, three persons, the Saṃgha, or a specific group, and does not subsequently divert it to others, then even its consumption is called pure, as explained extensively above.
"O bhikṣus! What preceded was a gift; what followed was not a gift. O bhikṣus!"
The land belongs to the king and the objects belong to the master; all items such as robes and alms bowls should be entrusted to the bhikṣus.
As for the temple and other property belonging to the donor, if it becomes dilapidated, one should repair it oneself and must not divert these goods to give them to others.
“O Bhikṣus! You should give Rāhula the dwelling place he previously occupied.
Then, having received the Buddha’s instruction, the bhikṣus immediately granted Rāhula his former residence.
This is the origin of the rule; however, the Buddha, the World-Honored One, had not yet established the precept.

While the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park, there was a bhikṣu who went for alms and granted a certain householder the three refuges along with the five precepts. At a later time, he further praised and explained to that householder the seven types of meritorious actions involving material things.
The householder said:
"Noble One!
I now wish, according to my ability, to perform some small amount of meritorious deeds."
The bhikṣu asked,
"What do you wish to do? He replied:
"I wish to make offerings to the Buddha and the community of bhikṣus.
He replied,
"Do you have even a small amount of clothing or other items to give?"
He said, "Noble One!

I am a poor man who possesses nothing but a single pair of white cotton cloths. Noble One, please go on my behalf and announce my name, requesting that the Buddha and the Sangha show their compassion by coming to my house tomorrow for a meal of alms."
The bhikṣu then went to the monastery garden and saw that all the bhikṣus were gathered there in great numbers.
At that time, the bhikṣu who was seeking alms announced the name of the elder and invited the Buddha and the Saṃgha to accept his offerings at his residence the following day.
Then the bhikṣus said to one another,
"This mendicant has now become a teacher within the homes of the laity.
At that time, someone asked:
"Does that householder's family have anything to give as an offering,
or do they have nothing? He replied:
"He is a poor man who has a pair of cloth garments which he wishes to offer as a gift.
When Upānanda heard this, he thought to himself:
"That person has invited the Buddha and the Saṃgha, intending to offer a pair of cloth garments; they must certainly be garments of great value."
"If I cannot take this robe away, I shall no longer be called Upānanda.
Having formed this thought, he exerted himself throughout that night until dawn; once day had broken, he put on his robes, took his bowl, and went to the householder's place.
Seeing that the elder had prepared food and drink, he asked him, "Elder!
What do you intend to do?"
He replied,
"I am now preparing a meal to offer to the Buddha and the Sangha. Upānanda replied:
“Householder!
As the Buddha has well said:

‘If there are sentient beings who, during the first division of the day, cultivate various wholesome karmas through body, speech, and mind, you should know that such persons are called “virtuous in the first division.”’”

If there are sentient beings who, at the time of midday, cultivate various wholesome deeds through body, speech, and mind, it should be known that such persons are called "those with wholesome [deeds] in the middle portion.

If there are sentient beings who, at the time of sunset, cultivate various wholesome deeds through body, speech, and mind, it should be known that such persons are called "those with wholesome [deeds] in the final portion."
“Virtuous one, you have now attained the initial goodness of the three karmas by personally preparing this offering for the Buddha and the Sangha; does the Elder have much left to give?
He replied, “My family is poor and destitute; I have only a pair of white cotton cloths.”
He replied, "Householder!
Bring it here for a moment so that I may examine its condition."
Then that householder immediately took the garment and said,
"Householder!
This new article is excellent!"
However, the householder possesses the merit of giving but lacks the merit of enjoyment. Why is this?

The Buddha’s assembly consists of one thousand two hundred and fifty members; they must wait until they have obtained one garment from you for each person—totaling one thousand two hundred and forty-nine garments—before they can share them. Yet now, this garment of yours has been consumed upon the drying rack.
Furthermore, as the Buddha said:
"When the Saṃgha obtains a small amount of food offerings, it should distribute them equally, like the leaves of a small tree.
If they obtain a small amount of clothing, they should divide it equally to serve as lamp wicks."
"Householder!
If the robes you have offered are divided and distributed in such a manner, what benefit or merit would there be in their use?
The householder replied:
“Noble one!
By what means may I now obtain the merit of giving as well as the merit of enjoyment?
Upānanda replied to the householder:

“If you can find among the Śākyas one who has gone forth, who is learned and proficient in the Tripiṭaka as a great Dharma-master, and who is skilled at expounding the teachings with unimpeded eloquence—if you take this robe and offer it to him, you will be able to fulfill both the merit of giving and the merit of enjoyment.”
The householder replied,
"Noble One! Where could there be such a field of merit for me to offer my gifts?"
Upānanda said, "I am that very person. Thereupon,
the elder prostrated at his feet, handed him the robe, and replied:
"Noble one!
Out of compassion, please accept this robe.
Upānanda replied:
“Householder!

Although you understand the act of giving, you have not yet mastered its proper ritual. You should wait a moment until the Buddha and the Sangha have finished their meal; then, holding this white cotton cloth before the presiding elder, express your sympathetic joy to the great assembly, and only after that should you give it to me.”
The householder replied, "I shall do so.

Thereupon, the householder immediately sprinkled and swept the courtyard, spread out seats, arranged fragrant flowers, and placed water vessels at the gate; he then dispatched a messenger to invite the Buddha and the Sangha, saying:
"The time has come.
At that time, the World-Honored One and the community of bhikṣus, during the first part of the day, took up their robes and bowls and went to the house of the elder, where they sat down in order.
When the householder saw that the assembly was seated, he personally served various kinds of fragrant and delicious food and drink to the Buddha and the great multitude.
Once they had eaten their fill, the householder took a piece of white cotton cloth and, standing before the assembly, proclaimed his sympathetic joy and gave it to Upānanda.
At that time, after the World-Honored One had himself offered a prayer of blessing, he rose from his seat and departed, returning immediately to the monastery.
Then the monk who was in charge of the robes said to the administrator:
"You should go to Upānanda and request some white cotton cloth."
The administrator went to seek it and said,
"Venerable One!
Please bring the items offered today to me."
Upānanda replied, "Venerable one!
Did you take this cotton cloth to the monastery and bring it back to me?"
He replied, "I will not return. Upānanda said:
"For what reason do you not return it? He replied,
"This is the property of the Sangha."
Upānanda said: "Venerable one!
Why do you not give me your robe and bowl?"
"I shall give my robes and bowl as an offering to the Saṃgha; I will not give them to you.
While that mendicant bhikṣu was at the householder’s home, he said to the householder, "Householder, what is your intention?
Why is it that there is thunder here while it rains there?"
The householder replied,
"Noble One! What fault have I committed?"
The bhikṣu replied, "Previously you intended to give this cotton cloth to the community of monks; for what reason, after the meal was finished, did you turn it over to Upānanda?
The householder answered:
"What shall I do? The Venerable Upānanda came to me and spoke these words:
'You possess the merit of giving, but not the merit of enjoyment.'"

Why is this? The Buddha’s assembly consists of one thousand two hundred and fifty members; having received your single garment, they must wait until they have obtained one thousand two hundred and forty-nine more garments before they can share them together.

"You have now worn out this robe of yours upon the clothesline; furthermore, the Buddha has taught that food and clothing should be shared equally, like the wick of a small oil lamp," and so forth, as explained at length.
"I said, 'I seek a virtuous person of great merit to whom I may give this robe; I am that very person, so you should express your sympathetic joy and give these bolts of cloth to me.
When I heard these words, I gave them to him exactly as he requested; how could there be any fault in this?"
When the bhikṣu who was begging for alms heard these words, he went inside the monastery.
Upon seeing him, the other bhikṣus said to him, "You, a beggar, have spent a long time teaching and converting only to win a single donor; yet there is thunder here while it rains elsewhere."
The mendicant replied:
"What fault have I committed against the householder?
However, there was a certain person who went to his home and informed the householder [of my arrival]."
"You possess the merit of giving, but not the merit of enjoyment," he said, explaining at length as above.
"Continue until you have expressed your sympathetic joy, and then you shall bestow it upon me.
At that time, the elder acted according to his words.
"What fault could there be for me or for him?
At that time, some bhikṣus of few desires, having heard these words, felt extreme revulsion and contempt, saying:
"How can a bhikṣu, knowing that an item was given by others to the Saṃgha, divert it for himself?"
Then the bhikṣus reported the matter to the Buddha.
At that time, the World-Honored One assembled the community of bhikṣus on this account and asked Upānanda:
"Is it true that you diverted monastic property for your own personal use?"
He replied, "It is indeed so. [The Buddha] spoke at length until he said:
"I shall now establish a training rule for the bhikṣus, which should be recited as follows:"
"If a bhikṣu, knowing that an item was given to the community, diverts it for his own personal use, it is a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika*.
"If a bhikṣu" refers to Upānanda, or anyone else of a similar kind.
"Knowing" means either knowing by oneself or being informed by another.
"Sangha" refers to the Buddha’s disciples.
"Various objects" refers to two kinds of objects:
This refers to gains consisting of food and gains consisting of clothing; what is spoken of here refers specifically to gains of clothing.
"To divert" means that an object already determined to belong to another is transformed and taken into one's own possession.
The *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* and the ritual for relinquishing and confessing it are explained in detail as above.
Regarding this, what are the characteristics of the offense and its specific instances?

If a bhikṣu knows that an object belongs to another bhikṣu, yet diverts it to his own possession: at the moment of diverting it, he incurs an *dukkaṭa*; once he has acquired it, he incurs a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika*.
In this manner, even if one knows that the property belongs to two persons, three persons, or the Saṃgha, and then diverts it for oneself, the offense incurred is the same as before.
If a bhikṣu knows that an object belongs to one bhikṣu, yet diverts it to another person, he incurs a duṣkṛta at the time of diversion, and he also incurs a duṣkṛta at the time of acquisition.

In this manner, even down to knowing that [an offering] belongs to one person, yet diverting it to two or three people, or diverting it to the Saṃgha, or diverting it into one's own possession—the offense incurred is the same as before.

If a bhikṣu knows that an object belongs to the Saṃgha and diverts it to give to a single person, he incurs a duṣkṛta offense at the time of the diversion and also incurs a duṣkṛta offense when he receives it.

Likewise, up to the point where he knows it belongs to the Saṃgha and diverts it to give to two or three persons, he incurs a duṣkṛta offense at the time of the diversion and also incurs a duṣkṛta offense when he receives it.
If a bhikṣu knows that an object belongs to one saṃgha and diverts it to another saṃgha, there is an *duṣkṛta* offense at the time of diversion and also an *duṣkṛta* offense upon its acquisition.
If he knows it is given to the bhikṣu-saṃgha and diverts it to the bhikṣuṇī-saṃgha;
or if he knows it is given to the bhikṣuṇī-saṃgha and diverts it to the bhikṣu-saṃgha; [the same applies].
Knowing that an object was intended for the Saṃgha of both divisions, one diverts it to the Bhikṣu-saṃgha;
knowing that it was intended for the Saṃgha of both divisions, one diverts it to the Bhikṣuṇī-saṃgha;
or if one knows that an object belongs to the Bhikṣu-saṃgha, one diverts it to the Saṃgha of both divisions.
Knowing that an object was intended for the community of bhikṣuṇīs, one diverts it to the community of both orders;
or, if the Saṃgha has split into two factions, knowing [the gift] was for this faction, one diverts it to that faction;
or, knowing [it was for] this monastery, one diverts it to that monastery.
If one knows that [an item] was given to this room and diverts it to that room;
or if one knows it was given to this corridor and diverts it to that corridor;

or if one mutually diverts items between rooms and corridors; or if one gives an item to this space between pillars and diverts it to that space between pillars; or if one diverts an item from between pillars to a doorway; or if one uses an item from a doorway to divert it to the upper story—thus explained in detail, even if they are diverted to one another in succession—all such acts constitute *duṣkṛta* (wrongdoing).
If a bhikṣu knows that an object was given for this particular image of the Buddha, yet diverts it to another image of the Buddha;
or if he knows that an object was given for this particular stūpa, yet diverts it to another stūpa;

or if he knows that an object was given for the first step of the staircase, yet diverts it to the second or third step, or diverts it to the body of the stūpa, or to the eaves and tiers; [he commits an offense].

Whether one diverts materials from this boundary to another boundary, or diverts them to a *pātra-nikubjana* (the overturning of the bowl), or to the first tier of a square pedestal or wheel-base, up to a jeweled vase, a Dharma-wheel pillar, or a foundation base; or whether one diverts them from here to those lower foundations—such mutual transferences as these all constitute an offense of wrong-doing (*duṣkṛta*).
If one turns [the gift] over due to the power of the king, there is no offense in any case.
If one gives an object intended for this poor person to that other poor person, one incurs an *dukkaṭa* (offense of wrong-doing);
however, if it cannot be found after searching, there is no offense in turning it over.
If a bhikṣu gives food to one animal and then diverts it to another animal, he incurs an offense of wrong-doing (duṣkṛta);
if he is unable to find [the intended recipient], diverting it is not an offense.
If one intends to give an object to an animal but instead gives it to a human, or intends to give an object to a human but instead gives it to an animal, one incurs a *duṣkṛta* offense.
If one intends to give an object to a renunciant but instead gives it to a layperson, or conversely, one incurs a *duṣkṛta* offense;
however, there is no offense if one searches for the intended recipient and cannot find them.

In this same manner, whether many or few, for women, men, *paṇḍakas*, bhikṣuṇīs, and the three lower assemblies, if they mutually exchange [robes] with one another, it should be explained according to the preceding rule.
If one cannot find [the object], there is no offense even if it contradicts one's original intention, provided it is given to someone else.
Furthermore, there is no offense in the case of the very first offender, or one who is insane, mentally deranged, or overwhelmed by intense physical pain.

30. The Training Rule on Taking Medicine for More Than Seven Days. The thirtieth training rule concerning taking medicine for more than seven days. At that time, the Buddha was staying in the Bamboo Grove at Rājagṛha.

At that time, the disciples and followers of the Venerable Pilindavatsa handled all kinds of medicines themselves or had others handle them; they mixed them with food or drink or with fine powders, or blended them with one another, or combined like substances together in one place. Not knowing whether they should discard them or not, they ate them at will, both at the proper time and at improper times.
When bhikṣus of few desires saw this, they gave rise to feelings of aversion and contempt, saying:

"How can a bhikṣu touch various medicines himself or cause others to touch them, or mix them with food and drink, or blend them together, or combine like substances in one place—whether discarded or not—and then eat them at will, regardless of whether it is the proper time or not?"
At that time, the bhikṣus reported the matter to the Buddha.

The Buddha, on account of this, assembled the community of bhikṣus; knowing the situation, he asked them intentionally, and after explaining it at length, he finally questioned the disciples and followers of Pilindavatsa:
"Is it true that you did so?"

Do you take all these medicinal substances—whether by touching them yourself or causing others to touch them, whether mixed with food and drink, or blended together with one another, or combined within a single place whether they have been relinquished or not—and consume them at will, regardless of whether it is the proper time or not?
He addressed the Buddha, saying:
“It is indeed so,
O Virtuous One!”

At that time, the World-Honored One rebuked various forms of excessive desire, which are insatiable and difficult to support or satisfy; he praised having few desires and being content, which are easy to support and easy to satisfy, and he taught the practice of the dhūta austerities by knowing the proper measure in receiving offerings.
He addressed the bhikṣus, saying:
"In detail, up to: 'I, having considered ten benefits, shall establish a training rule for my disciples, which should be recited as follows:
As the Blessed One has said:'"

It is permitted for sick bhikṣus to consume whatever medicines they require according to their needs—namely, clarified butter, oil, sugar, and honey—and to keep them in their possession for seven days, consuming them even if they have been stored overnight.
"If a bhikṣu consumes [it] beyond seven days, it is a naiḥsargika-pāyattika.
"As the World-Honored One" refers to the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha.
"To explain" means to provide instruction and clarification.
"A sick bhikṣu" refers to a bhikṣu within this Dharma who is afflicted by physical illness.
"All medicines that may be taken according to one's preference" refers to those that are suitable for the specific symptoms of the illness and are pure and fit for consumption.
"Ghee" refers to various types of ghee.
"Oil" refers to various types of oil.
"Sugar" refers to granulated sugar.
"Honey" refers to honey from bees.
"For seven days" means for seven nights and days.
"One may keep it oneself and eat it after it has been touched overnight" means that one may take it up oneself and consume it.
"Beyond seven days" means exceeding the limit of the period of restraint.
"Naiḥsargika-pāyattika" means that the object must be relinquished and the offense must be confessed; therefore, it is called *naiḥsargika-pāyattika*.
In this regard, what are the characteristics of the offense and how does it occur?

If a bhikṣu obtains medicine on the first day of the month, he must immediately take possession of that medicine himself within seven days; otherwise, he may either relinquish it or give it to another person.
If one neither retains, nor discards, nor gives it to another, then at the appearance of the dawn on the eighth day, one incurs a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* offense.

If a bhikṣu does not obtain medicine on the first day, does not obtain it on the second day, but obtains it on the third day up until the seventh day, he must, within those seven days, personally take formal possession (*parigraha*) of that medicine, or else discard it, or give it to another.
If one neither retains, nor discards, nor gives it to another person, then at the appearance of the dawn on the eighth day, one incurs the offense of *naiḥsargika-pāyattika*.

If a bhikṣu obtains medicine on the first day and also obtains it on the second day, within those seven days he should maintain the medicine obtained on the first day; as for the medicine obtained on the second day, he should either discard it or give it to another person. Alternatively, he may personally maintain the medicine obtained on the second day, and either discard the medicine obtained on the first day or give it to another person.
If one does not relinquish it, does not discard it, and does not give it to another person, then when the dawn of the eighth day appears, one incurs the offense of *naiḥsargika-pāyattika*.

If a bhikṣu performs the formal ritual in relation to [the robe] for one day or two days, and likewise for two days, three days, up to six or seven days, the remainder is as in the aforementioned rule.

If a bhikṣu obtains a large quantity of medicinal substances on the first day of the month, he must, within seven days, either formally take possession of them himself, relinquish them, or give them to another.

If one does not keep it, does not discard it, and does not give it to another person, then when the light of the eighth day appears, one incurs an offense of expiation involving forfeiture (*naiḥsargika-pāyattika*).
If a bhikṣu obtains many medicines over the course of seven days—just as he would on the first day—he must himself maintain them for those seven days, or else discard them, or give them to others.
If one neither retains, nor discards, nor gives it to another, until the appearance of the dawn on the eighth day, one incurs the offense of *naiḥsargika-pāyattika*.

If a bhikṣu obtains many medicines on the first day and also obtains many medicines on the second day, he should maintain the medicines from the first day within the seven-day period; as for the medicines from the second day, he should either discard them, give them to others, or maintain them himself. Alternatively, he may discard or give away the medicines from the first day, while maintaining those from the second day himself.
If one does not relinquish it nor give it to another person, by the time the dawn of the eighth day appears, one incurs the offense of *naiḥsargika-pāyattika*.

If a bhikṣu does not obtain a large quantity of medicine on the first day, nor on the second day, and so on until he obtains a large quantity of medicine on the sixth or seventh day, the medicine obtained on the sixth day must be formally maintained within the seven-day period; as for the medicine obtained on the seventh day, he should either relinquish it or give it to another.
If one neither discards it nor gives it away, when the dawn of the eighth day appears, one incurs an offense of expiation involving forfeiture (*naiḥsargika-pāyattika*).

If a bhikṣu has touched any of his medicines himself or caused another to touch them, or if they have come into contact with food or drink, or fine powders; or if they have been mixed together, or combined with similar substances in one place such that they can no longer be distinguished, these medicines should then be given to a lay attendant of the monastery or bestowed upon a *śrāmaṇera*.

Furthermore, if a bhikṣu does not touch these various medicines himself, nor causes another to touch them; if he does not allow them to come into contact with food or drink or fine powders; nor allows them to be mixed with one another, nor allows those of different kinds to be intermingled, nor allows them to be blended together in one place.

One should skillfully distinguish between what is relinquished and what is not, and between the proper time and the improper time; within seven days, one may keep it for oneself and take it for consumption.
It should be kept in this manner: before midday, having washed one's hands clean, one should receive that medicine and speak thus to a fellow practitioner of the holy life:
"Venerable one, please attend to me!..."
"I, the bhikṣu [Name], having this occasion of illness, now formally accept these pure medicines for my own use within seven days.
This should be said a second and a third time, as well as for one's fellow practitioners of the holy life.
If one has already taken it for one day, one should immediately inform one’s fellow practitioners of the holy life, saying:
"I have taken this medicinal medicine for my illness for one day; six days remain, and I shall continue to take it."
In this manner, one should inform others every day for up to seven days.
If, after the seven days have elapsed, there is still medicine remaining, it should be relinquished to a pure person (*pariśuddha*) or given to a novice (*śrāmaṇera*).
If one does not relinquish it, then when the dawn of the eighth day appears, one commits the offense of *naiḥsargika-pāyattika*.

If a bhikṣu possesses medicine subject to relinquishment and does not give it away to another, does not set it aside, and does not confess and repent for the offense, yet acquires further medicine, he commits the offense of relinquishment in its entirety due to the taint of the previous [offense].

If a bhikṣu commits an offense of forfeiture (nissaggiya-pācittiya) and, although he has already forfeited the medicine, has not yet created a separation [from the offense] nor confessed and repented the fault, if he obtains further medicine, he commits an offense of forfeiture for all of it, because of the prior defilement.

If a bhikṣu has committed an offense involving forfeiture (naiḥsargika-pāyattika) and, although he has already forfeited the medicine, there has been an interval [of time] and the offense has not yet been confessed and atoned for, should he obtain further medicine, he commits the offense of forfeiture in all such cases.

If a bhikṣu has committed an offense involving forfeiture (naiḥsargika-pāyattika) regarding medicinal requisites and has not yet performed the three prescribed actions, should he further obtain other items such as robes, bowls, nets for carrying them, or waist-bands—any of these being the articles or means of livelihood permitted for a śramaṇa—if he accepts and keeps them, he commits an offense involving forfeiture due to the influence of his prior transgression.

If a bhikṣu has committed an offense involving forfeiture (naiḥsargika-pāyattika) regarding medicine, and having already relinquished it, established an interval, and confessed and repented for the offense, he commits no offense if he subsequently obtains other medicine.
Furthermore, there is no offense for the very first offender, or for one who is insane, mentally deranged, or overwhelmed by intense physical pain.
"Venerable sirs, I have recited the thirty *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* dharmas. Now I ask the venerable ones: Are you pure in regard to these?
Thus it is asked three times."
"Venerable sirs, since you are pure in this matter, as indicated by your silence, I shall now hold it to be so.
*Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya*, Fascicle 24. *Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya*. Fascicle.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Yijing by Imperial Decree, Part 25.
The Summary Verse for the Ninety Pāyattika Dharmas states: [The summary verse follows. The Ninety Pāyattika Dharmas. [The individual rules follow.]
Therefore, regarding false speech, seeds, non-differentiation,
eating at the wrong time, water with insects, life, traveling with a companion, animals, thieves, and food:
the initial summary verse says:
False slander, divisive speech, Exposing faults, speaking in unison, Speaking of offenses, claiming superhuman states, And disparaging according to intimacy. 1.
The Training Rule on Intentional False Speech (Prathama-saṃprajāna-mṛṣāvāda-śikṣāpada). At that time, the Buddha was staying at Rājagṛha in the Bamboo Grove, by the Kalandaka Pond.
At that time, the Venerable Rāhula was dwelling in a grove of hot springs near this city.
Then, a great multitude of faithful brahmins and householders came to his place and asked:
"Venerable One!..."
“Where does the Blessed One reside now? If the Buddha,
the World-Honored One, was in the Bamboo Grove, Rāhula would immediately reply,
“He is on Vulture Peak Mountain.”
If he is on Vulture Peak Mountain, report:
"He is in the Bamboo Grove.
If he is in the Pipphalī Cave, report: [He is in the Bamboo Grove.]
"If he is in the Sīkara Cave.
If he is in the Sīkara Cave, report:
"He is in the Pippala Cave."
At that time, those people, wishing to pay homage to the Buddha but unable to see him, became physically exhausted and suffered great fatigue;
they then went to the place where Rāhula was. Rāhula asked the people:
"Sirs, were you able to see the World-Honored One?"
He replied, "I did not see it.
The people reported this, saying:
“Noble one!
For what reason do you trouble us?
He replied:
"It is indeed so; that is why I intentionally troubled you.
At that time, those people each felt resentment and contempt.
Then, the bhikṣus reported this matter to the Buddha.

At that time, having heard these words, the World-Honored One took up his robe and bowl during the first part of the day and entered the city of Rājagṛha to beg for food in sequence. Having returned to his original location and finished his meal, he proceeded after the meal to the Hot Springs Grove, to the dwelling place of Rāhula.

At that time, Rāhula saw the Buddha approaching from afar; he prepared a seat for the Buddha and set out a water jar along with a foot-washing basin. Having washed his feet and hands, he went out to welcome the World-Honored One, took his upper robe, and said:
"Welcome, World-Honored One!"
"I wish to sit upon this seat.

The Buddha then took his seat; having sat down, he immediately took water from a pitcher to wash his own feet. He poured out most of the water in the foot-washing vessel, leaving only a small amount remaining, and said to Rāhula:
"Do you see the little water left in the vessel?"
He addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Venerable Sir!
I have already seen it."
The Buddha said,
“Rāhula! If a bhikṣu intentionally utters a falsehood, lacking both a sense of shame and remorse— I observe that such a foolish person is said to be deficient in the qualities of a śramaṇa.”
The Blessed One again poured the little water remaining in the vessel onto the ground and said to Rāhula:
"Do you see that the little water has been entirely discarded upon the ground?"
He addressed the Buddha, saying:
“Venerable Sir!
I have already seen it.”
The Buddha said,
"Rāhula! If a bhikṣu intentionally speaks falsehoods, lacking both shame and remorse, I regard such a foolish person as one who has utterly abandoned the dharma of a śramaṇa."
The Blessed One again tilted the vessel until it rested on the ground and said to Rāhula,
"Do you see this vessel tilted?
Rāhula replied to the Buddha:
“Venerable One!
I have already seen it.
The Buddha said:
“Rāhula! If a bhikṣu deliberately utters a falsehood, lacking both shame and remorse, I regard such a foolish person as one who has caused the Dharma of the śramaṇa to fall into ruin.”
The Blessed One again overturned the vessel upon the ground and said to Rāhula,
"Do you see this vessel overturned on the ground?
Rāhula replied to the Buddha:
“Venerable Sir!
I have already seen it.
The Buddha said:
“Rāhula! If a bhikṣu intentionally speaks falsehoods, being devoid of shame and lacking remorse, I regard such a foolish person as one who has brought about the ruin of the Dharma of a śramaṇa.”
Furthermore, Rāhula!

It is like a drunken elephant king who possesses great power and majesty; his tusks are like chariot axles, he is stout, robust, and courageous, and he is skilled in combat. When he goes to the battlefield to fight with others, his four feet, two tusks, tail, back, and flanks all exert their full force, yet only his trunk remains curled and does not emerge.
"Rāhula! This elephant, for the sake of protecting its life, did not use its trunk to strike down those soldiers. Thereupon, the elephant trainer thought:
'This king of elephants cherishes its own life.'"

"Rāhula! When that elephant king engages in combat and extends its trunk to fight, the elephant trainer immediately knows that this elephant does not spare its own life; whether encountering its own army or another's, it will slaughter them at every opportunity and commit no evil deed."
Thus it is, Rāhula!
If a bhikṣu intentionally utters a falsehood, being devoid of shame and lacking remorse, I declare that such a person is capable of committing every kind of evil.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke these verses:
"If a person violates the true Dharma And intentionally utters false and deceptive speech,
Then until the end of their life, There is no evil they will not commit."
"It would be better to swallow a red-hot iron ball, blazing like a fierce flame,
than with a mouth broken by precepts to consume the food offered out of faith by others.
At that time, the World-Honored One again addressed Rāhula, saying:
"What do you think?
For what purpose do people of the world hold up a bright mirror?
Rāhula replied to the Buddha:
“World-Honored One!
That person holding the mirror does so in order to observe the auspicious or inauspicious marks of his own face.
The Buddha told Rāhula:
"So it is! So it is! You should repeatedly and thoroughly examine all the bodily actions you perform."

"Now, as I wish to initiate such bodily action, will this bodily action harm my own body and also harm the bodies of others? Is it an unwholesome matter, a painful and evil karma, capable of producing a bitter maturation in the future?"
"Does not harming oneself and not harming others constitute a superior and wholesome matter, a deed of peace and happiness, which can bring about a pleasant ripening in the future? Rāhula!"

When you perform this investigation, you will be able to recognize: "This bodily action that I now wish to perform would cause harm to myself or others; it is an unwholesome deed, a painful and evil karma, which will bring about a bitter ripening of suffering in the future. You should then restrain this bodily action and refrain from performing it.

Rāhula! When you perform this observation, you will be able to discern: "This bodily action which I now wish to perform is beneficial to myself and others; it is a supreme wholesome deed, a peaceful action that will bring about a pleasant ripening in the future. This bodily action should be initiated, and I shall cultivate this wholesome deed."
Furthermore, the Buddha told Rāhula:
"Regarding all the bodily actions you perform, you should repeatedly and skillfully examine them yourself:
'I am now performing such a bodily action; since this bodily action can harm myself or others and will result in the experience of suffering, I should not do it.'"
"If an action benefits oneself and others, one shall receive a pleasant retribution;
therefore, one should practice and learn accordingly. Furthermore, the Buddha told Rāhula:

"Regarding all the bodily actions you perform, you should repeatedly and skillfully observe them: 'I have already performed such a bodily action; this bodily action can harm myself and others, and I shall receive a painful retribution. All sinful karma should be confessed with utmost sincerity and compassion before the Buddha, or before pure fellow-practitioners of the holy life; one must disclose and repent for those transgressions, and henceforth refrain from committing them again under the new precepts."

If one performs wholesome deeds that can benefit oneself and others, one should experience joy at the prospect of receiving their pleasant retribution; throughout day and night, one should celebrate what has been done and not be negligent.
Rāhula! Just as you examine bodily action during the three stages of intending to act, acting, and having acted, you should know that verbal and mental actions are likewise to be examined.

Rāhula! You should know that all karmic actions of the past, future, and present arise from the mind; you should repeatedly examine them, abandon discursive thoughts, and constantly give rise to a virtuous mind.

Rāhula! If there are śramaṇas, brāhmaṇas, or others, when the actions of body, speech, and mind arise, they should skillfully examine them to make them utterly pure, and should constantly practice much cultivation while dwelling in accordance with that purity.
Rāhula! Just as you now observe the three types of action so that they abide in utter purity and accordance with reality, so too should you do for the past and the future.
"Therefore, you should now constantly and skillfully examine your three types of action, dwelling in accordance with extreme purity and never being negligent.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke these verses:
"Rāhula, you should know: Constantly examine the three types of action."
Do not allow yourself to commit various evils; this is to follow the teachings of all Buddhas.
This is the practice of the śrāvakas, which you should now cultivate.
When practicing this conduct, increase wholesome qualities and bring all evils to rest.

At that time, after the Blessed One had instructed, exhorted, inspired, and gladdened Rāhula by teaching this Dharma, Rāhula prostrated at the Buddha’s feet and joyfully practiced it; thereupon, the Blessed One rose from his seat and departed.
This is the origin [of the rule], though the precept had not yet been established.
The Buddha was staying at Jetavana.
At that time, the bhikṣu Dharmahasta, a son of the Śākyas, resided there; he was skilled in speech and capable of refuting the arguments of others.

At that time, there was a māṇavaka in the Middle Country who traveled to the South for the purpose of study; the details are as extensively explained previously in the account of the Kapphiṇa incident within the fourth Pārājika.

At that time, the teacher whom the Māṇavaka served was a Brāhmaṇa from the south, widely learned in all the treatises. Together with the Māṇavaka and his disciples, he traveled by stages through various cities and towns until he eventually arrived at the city of Śrāvastī.

At that time, there was a brahmin in that city who was the leader of the community; hearing that a great master of debate from the south had arrived, he addressed his disciples, saying: "Do you know?"
"There is a brahmin who is a great master of treatises from the south; he has now come here wishing to seek out an opponent in debate.
If that master establishes a thesis within his various treatises, you all should respond to it together, each according to what you have studied."
"If he is able to defeat him, it shall be said: 'Excellent!
If he is unable, you should lead him among the sons of the Śākyas and have him debate with them.
If that debater is able to defeat the sons of the Śākyas, then this will be my victory as a Brahmin."
If a son of the Śākyas were to defeat him, that too would be a victory for me, the Brahmin. Why is this?

It would cause my great fame to resound throughout the eight directions, such that it would be said: "In the south there is a great Brahmin, well-versed in the four Vedas and proficient in the eight arts, who has come to Śrāvastī seeking a formal debate."
"There is someone in the city who can refute his doctrine; none of us here shall suffer defeat.
Then, at dawn, that master of logic wrapped his belly in his robe, took a torch in his hand, and entered the city of Śrāvastī.
At that time, a son of a brahmin in that city asked,
"Great Master, for what reason do you wrap your belly with your robe?
The master replied:
"The learning I have received fills my belly; fearing it might burst, I wrap it with this cloth.
He asked again:
"For what reason do you hold a torch in your hand during the daytime?"
The Master replied, "I see that these people are foolish and obscured by darkness; I shall now illuminate them with the torch of wisdom so that they may attain clarity.

Thereupon, the Master engaged in debate with his disciples, challenging one another with polemical arguments. Wherever there was such spirited discussion, everyone else fell silent, and all the scholars within the city were utterly defeated.
The people asked, "Great Master,
why do you bring disgrace upon your own followers?
The master replied:
"Could there possibly be another companion here?
The people replied, "There is."
The Master of Treatises asked, "Who is he?
and [the other] replied:

"These śramaṇas, the sons of the Śākyas, have only recently risen to prominence; among the four castes, they alone claim to be most honored and supreme. Their great learning and eloquence are known to all; you, Master, should now go and engage them in debate."
He asked, "Where does he reside?
and was answered:
"Within the Jeta Grove in this city.
He asked, "Who among that assembly is the foremost king of debaters?"
He replied, "They are all widely learned, wise, and possess clear eloquence.
While he was speaking these words, the bhikṣu Dharmahasta arrived at that place on account of some other business. When the people saw him coming, they informed the master of dharma:
“Great Master, for now let us set aside all other śramaṇas and sons of the Śākyas; it would be fitting to engage in debate with this Bhikṣu Dharmapāṇi.
The Master of Treatises then looked directly at the bhikṣu and said to the assembly, “Judging by his appearance alone, he is certainly the proponent of the doctrine.”
He immediately went to him and said, "Bhikṣu!
I have studied a little under my former teacher; I wish to engage in a brief discussion with you, O virtuous one."
The bhikṣu replied, "This is truly excellent!
I have long harbored the intention to seek out debate; when shall I encounter an opponent with whom I may exhaust my humble mind?"
"Since you have come from afar, it deeply accords with my wishes; you may act as you please.
The Master of Treatises asked, "On what day shall we converse?"
The bhikṣu replied,
“It may be prepared tomorrow.
[The other asked,] “Where do you wish it to be?”
“At such-and-such a garden.
Having made this appointment together, they departed.

Then that master of treatises, having already made the appointment, spent that very night scrutinizing both systems; he prepared his arguments in advance, seeking out points for refutation and critique, contemplating without sleep until daybreak.
At that time, the bhikṣu Dharmahasta thought to himself:
"Even if I were to defeat this master of treatises, I would still not be exempt from visiting a hundred households for alms before my belly is full."
"If a brahmin should defeat me, all the fame and the flower-crown that I possess will utterly vanish.

At that time, the brahmin went to that garden at dawn and stood waiting for the bhikṣu to arrive; however, Dharmahasta did not go as previously arranged. Having waited a long time without his arrival, he finally returned to the city.
At that time, Dharmahasta, having observed that the appointed time had passed, entered the city to go on his almsround in due order.
Seeing him, a certain Brahmin asked:
"Monk, for what reason did you not go to the flower garden?"
He replied, "Where is the garden?
The brahmin said:
"Virtuous One, do you not recall our agreement yesterday that we would go back and forth to such-and-such a place?
Dharmahasta replied,
"I have forgotten that matter."
The brahmin thought to himself:
"Throughout the entire night I have been devising the points of this discourse,
yet the bhikṣu says:"
"I do not recall. He then thought further:
"However, there are only two possibilities for this bhikṣu: [either he has committed an offense, or he has not]."
"First, he is dull-witted and ignorant; second, his eloquence surpasses that of men.
He replied again, "I shall attend to the appointment tomorrow."
He replied, "So be it.
When the appointed time arrived, that brahmin went to the garden and waited for some time, but [the other] did not return; having waited in vain and lingering there, he finally returned to the city.
At that time, Dharmahasta, knowing that the appointed time had passed, entered the city to beg for alms. When the brahmin saw him, he asked again:
"Bhikṣu, why have you not come as agreed?"
Dharmahasta replied,
"How could I possibly have a wind-disorder?
Is it not the case that my only activity is debate, with no other work?"

Nevertheless, every morning I attend upon the Great Master, respectfully listening to and receiving the teachings I have not yet heard; furthermore, I instruct my own disciples and visit noble persons to welcome them and preach the Dharma.
The brahmin said,
"A bhikṣu should not intentionally speak falsehoods.
He replied:
"I truly am so.

Because of this, the bhikṣu Dharmahasta made an appointment with his interlocutor to go and meet him, yet he deliberately broke his word, causing that master of debate to laboriously travel back and forth many times.
When the various non-Buddhist practitioners heard this matter, they each gave rise to feelings of disdain and contempt, saying:

"You should know that these śramaṇas, the sons of the Śākyas, intentionally speak falsehoods; having made a pact with their opponents in the park, they deliberately utter empty words to cause those opponents to labor in vain through their repeated debates."
Having heard this, the bhikṣus reported it in full to the Blessed One.
On account of this matter, the Buddha assembled the community of bhikṣus and asked Dharmahasta:
“Is it true that you committed such an act of intentional lying, failing to go because of a prior agreement with another?”
He replied, “It is indeed so,
World-Honored One.”
At that time, having rebuked him in various ways, [the Buddha continued] up to: “I now establish this training rule for the bhikṣus, which should be recited as follows:
‘If a bhikṣu should speak a deliberate falsehood, it is a pāyattika.’”
"Furthermore, 'if a bhikṣu' refers to Dharmahasta; the meaning is as explained above.
'Intentionally' means that he knowingly understands the matter with a deliberate mind.
'Lying' consists of nine types of lying, with eight, seven, six, five, four, three, and two types of distinctions."
What are the nine kinds of false speech? They are:

making false claims based on groundless *pārājika*, *saṃghāvaśeṣa*, *pāyattika*, *pratideśanīya*, or *duṣkṛta* offenses; and making false claims based on groundless violations of morality (*śīla*), views (*dṛṣṭi*), conduct (*ācāra*), or livelihood (*ājīva*).
What are the eight kinds of false speech? They are:

[accusing another] with groundless cases of pārājika, saṃghāvaśeṣa, pāyattika, pratideśanīya, or duṣkṛta; and [accusing another] on the basis of groundless claims based on what was seen, heard, or suspected.
What are the seven kinds of false speech? They are:

[accusing another] of ungrounded violations of precepts, violations of views, violations of conduct, or violations of right livelihood; and [accusing another] based on ungrounded grounds of what was seen, heard, or suspected.
What are the six kinds of false speech?
If a bhikṣu intends to speak falsely, he forms this thought:
"I shall speak falsely."
While speaking a deliberate falsehood, one thinks:
"I am currently speaking a deliberate falsehood.
Or, having finished speaking the falsehood, one thinks: [as before].
"I have spoken falsely," based on groundless seeing, hearing, or suspicion.
What are the five kinds of false speech?
This refers to speaking falsely by means of groundless charges regarding the five classes of offenses.
What are the four kinds of false speech?
They are speaking falsely by means of groundless charges regarding broken precepts, broken views, broken conduct, and broken right livelihood.
What are the three kinds of false speech?
They are those based on groundless seeing, hearing, and doubt.
Furthermore, there are three other kinds of false speech, involving the following thought:
"I shall speak falsely," "I am speaking falsely," and "I have spoken falsely.
What are the two types of false speech?
They are: "I am speaking falsely" and "I have spoken falsely."
There is not a single kind that constitutes false speech.
Furthermore, there are five kinds of false speech; what are they?

There is false speech that incurs a *pārājika*, there is that which incurs a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*, there is that which incurs a *sthūlātyaya*, there is that which incurs a *pāyattika*, and there is that which incurs a *duṣkṛta*.
How does one incur a *pārājika* through false speech?
If a bhikṣu has not actually attained the state of a superior person (*uttarimanussa-dhamma*) yet claims to have attained it, this false speech constitutes a *pārājika*.
How does one incur a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* through lying?
If a bhikṣu, knowing that another bhikṣu is pure and free from transgression, yet slanders him with groundless charges of a *pārājika* offense, this lie constitutes a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*.
What constitutes a *sthūlātyaya* offense for lying?

If a bhikṣu, within the community of monks, intentionally utters a falsehood—speaking what is not Dharma as Dharma, speaking Dharma as not Dharma, speaking what is not Vinaya as Vinaya, or speaking Vinaya as not Vinaya—this lying constitutes a *sthūlātyaya* offense.
How does one incur a *duṣkṛta* for lying?
If, when bhikṣus perform the *poṣadha* every half-month and recite the *Prātimokṣa-sūtra*, someone asks, "Are you pure? [and he lies].
If, while actually being impure and knowing for oneself that one has committed an offense, one remains silent with the intention of concealing it, this false speech constitutes a *duṣkṛta* offense.
Apart from the four kinds of false speech previously mentioned, all other instances of lying result in a *pāyattika* offense.

The term *pāyattika* carries the meaning of being "scorched, boiled, and fallen"; that is to say, the offender falls into the evil realms of hell, the animal kingdom, or the realm of hungry ghosts, where they undergo the suffering of being scorched and boiled.
Furthermore, if this offense is not confessed and removed with earnestness, it will obstruct all wholesome dharmas; for these various reasons, it is called a *pāyattika*.
Regarding the characteristics of the offense herein, what are its specific details?
A summary verse states:
"If, in reality, one has not seen or heard, nor perceived or known, yet forms the notion [of having done so]..."
And to speak with doubt or with a divergent view—know that this is false speech.
If a bhikṣu has not seen, not heard, not sensed, and not known, yet forms such a thought and accepts it as such, saying:
"I have seen, I have heard, I have sensed, I have known."
When speaking in this manner, each and every word constitutes a *pāyattika* offense.

If a bhikṣu has previously seen, heard, sensed, or known a matter but has forgotten it, yet forms such a thought and such an acceptance, failing to remember the matter while saying, "I have not forgotten it."
For every such statement, one incurs a *pāyattika* offense.
If, after having actually seen, heard, sensed, or known something, one subsequently develops doubt, yet maintains the thought that it is so and endures it,
saying, "Regarding what was seen and so forth, I have no doubt," [one is likewise guilty].
For every single utterance made, one incurs a *pāyattika* offense.
If, while not actually seeing, hearing, perceiving, or knowing, one has the perception that one sees and so forth, and having formed that understanding, subsequently says:
"I truly have seen and so forth."
When each statement is spoken, one incurs the fundamental offense.
If one has not actually seen [the object] but has heard, sensed, or known it, yet forms the notion that one has seen it and accepts it as such, and later says:
"I saw it; there was no hearing and so forth."
When each such statement is made, one incurs the fundamental offense.
If, in reality, one has not heard but has seen, sensed, or known, yet forms the notion that it is so and assents accordingly, and later says:
"I have heard; I have no seeing, sensing, or knowing."
When each such statement is made, one incurs the fundamental offense.
If, in reality, one has not perceived [the object] yet claims to have seen, heard, or known it—and having formed that notion and accepted it as such—one later says:
"I perceived it, but I did not see, hear, or know it."
When each such statement is made, one incurs the fundamental offense.
If, while actually not knowing, one has seen, heard, or sensed something, yet forms such a thought and such an acceptance, and later says:
"I know it; I have no seeing, hearing, or sensing."
When each statement is spoken, one incurs the fundamental offense.
If one has actually seen but forgotten it, while having heard, sensed, or known without forgetting, yet forms the thought that this is so and later says:
"I have not forgotten what I saw, nor have I forgotten what I heard, sensed, or knew."
When each statement is spoken, one incurs the fundamental offense.
If one has actually heard but forgotten it, while having seen, sensed, or known without forgetting, yet forms the thought that this is so, and later says:
"I have heard it and have not forgotten it; I have also seen, sensed, and known it and have not forgotten it."
When each individual statement is made, one incurs the fundamental offense.
If one has actually perceived but forgotten it, while having seen, heard, or known it without forgetting, yet forms the thought that this is the case and later says:
"I have not forgotten what I perceived, nor have I forgotten what I saw, heard, or knew."
For every instance of speaking thus, one incurs the fundamental offense.
If one actually knows but has forgotten, yet does not forget what was seen, heard, or sensed, and then forms the thought that it has not been forgotten, saying later:
"I know it and have not forgotten it; I have also not forgotten what was seen, heard, or sensed."
When each statement is spoken, one incurs the fundamental offense.
If one has actually seen but doubts, while having heard, sensed, or known without doubt, yet forms the notion that it is otherwise, and later says:
"I saw without doubt, but I doubt what I heard, sensed, or knew."
When each statement is spoken, one incurs the fundamental offense.
If one has actually heard [the teaching] but doubts it, while having seen, sensed, or known it without doubt, yet forms this thought and later says:
"I heard it without doubt, but I have doubts about what I saw, sensed, or knew."
When each statement is spoken, one incurs the fundamental offense.

If one has actually perceived but doubts it, while having seen, heard, or known without doubt, yet forms the thought that "I have perceived without doubt, but I doubt what I have seen, heard, or known," and later says:
"I have perceived without doubt, but I doubt what I have seen, heard, or known."
When each statement is spoken, one incurs the fundamental offense.
If one actually knows but has doubt, or sees, hears, or perceives without doubt, yet forms the thought that it is otherwise, and later says:
"I know without doubt, but I have doubt regarding what I saw, heard, or perceived."
When each statement is made, one incurs the fundamental offense.

If one has not actually seen it but forms the perception that one did not see it, yet has heard, sensed, or known it and forms the perception that one has heard, sensed, or known it—forming such a perception, one later says:
"I saw it; I did not hear, sense, or know it."
When one speaks thus, the fundamental offense is incurred.

If, in reality, one has not heard it and forms the perception that one has not heard it, yet has seen, sensed, or known it and forms the perception that one has seen, sensed, or known it—forming such a perception—one later says:
"I have heard it, but I did not see, sense, or know it."
When one speaks thus, one incurs the fundamental offense.

If, in reality, one has not perceived but forms the perception that one has not perceived, yet has seen, heard, or known and forms the perception that one has seen, heard, or known—forming such a perception as that—and later says:
"I have perceived, but I have not seen, heard, or known."
When one speaks thus, one incurs the fundamental offense.

If, in reality, one does not know and forms the perception that one does not know, yet possesses perceptions based on what was seen, heard, or sensed, and while having those perceptions, one later says:
"I know; I have not seen, heard, or sensed."
When one speaks thus, one incurs the fundamental offense.
If one has actually seen, heard, sensed, or known, yet forms the notion that it was not so, and later says:
"I did not see, hear, sense, or know," [one incurs the offense].
When one speaks thus, one incurs the root offense.
If one has actually seen, heard, sensed, or known, and does not forget the matter, yet forms the thought that one has forgotten it and later says:
"I have seen, heard, sensed, or known, but I have forgotten the matter."
When one speaks thus, one incurs the fundamental offense.
If one has actually seen, heard, sensed, or known, yet without doubt, and while maintaining that perception, later says:
"I saw, heard, sensed, or knew, but with a doubting mind."
When one speaks thus, one incurs the fundamental offense.
If, having actually seen, heard, sensed, or known, one has the perception that one has seen, heard, sensed, or known, yet forms such a thought and later says:
"I have not seen, heard, sensed, or known."
When one speaks thus, one incurs the fundamental offense.
If one has actually seen but not heard, sensed, or known, yet forms the notion that one has heard, sensed, or known, and later says:
"I did not see it, but I have heard, sensed, and known it."
When one speaks thus, one incurs the fundamental offense.
If, in reality, one has heard but not seen, sensed, or cognized, yet forms the notion that one has, and later says:
"I did not hear it, but I saw, sensed, and cognized it."
When one speaks thus, one incurs the fundamental offense.
If one has actually perceived but did not see, hear, or know, yet forms the thought that one has, and later says:
"I did not perceive it, but I saw, heard, and knew it."
When one speaks thus, one incurs the fundamental offense (*mūlāpatti*).
If one actually knows, yet has not seen, heard, or cognized, and forms the thought that one has, then later says:
"I did not know, but I have seen, heard, and cognized."
When he speaks thus, he incurs the fundamental offense.
If he has actually seen it and does not forget it, but has forgotten what he heard, sensed, or cognized, yet forms this thought and later says:
"I have forgotten what I saw, but I have not forgotten what I heard, sensed, or cognized."
When he speaks thus, he incurs the fundamental offense.

If he has actually heard it and does not forget it, but has forgotten what was seen, sensed, or known, yet forms the thought that he has forgotten what he heard while not forgetting what he saw, sensed, or knew, and later says:
"I have forgotten what I heard, but I have not forgotten what I saw, sensed, or knew."
When he speaks thus, he incurs the primary offense.

If he has actually perceived and does not forget it, but has forgotten what he saw, heard, or knew, yet forms the thought that he has forgotten what he perceived while not forgetting what he saw, heard, or knew, and later says:
"I perceived it but forgot it; I did not forget what I saw, heard, or knew."
When he speaks thus, he incurs the fundamental offense.
If he actually knows but does not forget, yet has forgotten what was seen, heard, or sensed, and he forms this thought, later saying:
"I know it but have forgotten it; I have not forgotten what was seen, heard, or sensed."
When one speaks thus, one incurs the fundamental offense.
If one has actually seen without doubt, yet heard, sensed, or known with doubt, and forms this thought, later saying:
"I saw it with doubt; I heard, sensed, or knew it without doubt."
When one speaks thus, one incurs the fundamental offense.
If one has actually heard [the teaching] without doubt, yet sees, perceives, or knows it with doubt, and forms this thought, later saying:
"I heard it with doubt, but I see, perceive, and know it without doubt."
When one speaks thus, one incurs the fundamental offense.
If one has actually perceived without doubt, yet perceives, hears, or knows with doubt, and forms this thought, later saying:
"I perceived with doubt; I did not doubt what I saw, heard, or knew."
When one speaks thus, one incurs the fundamental offense (*mūlāpatti*).
If one actually knows [the fact] without doubt, yet has doubts regarding what was seen, heard, or sensed, and forms this thought, later saying:
"I know [it] with doubt, but I have no doubt regarding what was seen, heard, or sensed."
When he speaks thus, he incurs the fundamental offense (*mūlāpatti*).

If he has actually seen something and forms the perception that he saw it, yet regarding what he did not hear, perceive, or know, he forms the perception that he did not hear, perceive, or know it; and while forming that perception, he later says:
"I did not see it, but I have heard, perceived, and known it."
If one speaks at that time, one incurs the fundamental offense (*mūlāpatti*).
If one has actually heard it but perceives it as such, yet does not see, feel, or know it, and forms the perception that one does not see, feel, or know it, and later says:
"I did not hear it, but I have seen, felt, and known it."
When one speaks thus, the fundamental offense is incurred.

If one has actually perceived it and forms the perception that one has perceived it, yet has not seen, heard, or known it and forms the perception that one has not seen, heard, or known it—if one forms such a perception and later says:
"I did not perceive it, but I have seen, heard, and known it."
When he speaks thus, he incurs the fundamental offense.

If he truly knows [the act] and forms the perception that he knows it, yet regarding what was not seen, heard, or cognized, he forms the perception that it was not seen, heard, or cognized, and while forming that perception, he later says:
"I did not know; however, there was seeing, hearing, and cognizing."
When speaking thus, one incurs the fundamental offense.
If a bhikṣu speaks any words that contradict his own mind, he incurs a pāyattika offense in all cases.
If he speaks without contradicting his own mind, there is no offense in any instance.
Furthermore, there is no offense for the very first offender, or for one who is insane, mentally deranged, or overwhelmed by intense pain. 2.
The Training Rule on Slandering Speech (Kṣepaṇavāda-śikṣāpada). Second. At that time, the Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī at the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the group of six bhikṣus spoke disparaging words to other bhikṣus, saying:

"You one-eyed man! You lame man! You hunchback! You dwarf! You who are too tall! You who are too coarse! You deaf and blind man! You mute man! You who walk with a crutch! You with swollen feet! You with shaven arms! You with a large head! You with drooping lips! You with protruding teeth!"
At that time, the six groups of bhikṣus spoke such disparaging words.

When the other bhikṣus heard them, they were filled with shame and remorse, becoming sorrowful and unhappy; they neglected their recitation and contemplation entirely, remaining in a state of anxiety.
At that time, some bhikṣus of few desires, having witnessed this matter, all felt contempt and spoke words of disparagement:
"How can a bhikṣu revile another bhikṣu?"
"Regarding 'squint-eyed' and so forth, it is as previously described.
At that time, the bhikṣus informed the Buddha of these circumstances.
Thereupon, the World-Honored One, on account of this cause and condition, assembled the community of bhikṣus and even questioned the group of six monks, saying:
“Did you truly utter disparaging words, troubling the bhikṣus by calling them ‘one-eyed’ and so forth?
The group of six replied,
“It is true.”
"Venerable One!
The World-Honored One then rebuked him in various ways, explaining at length as above, up until: "This is not an act that a śramaṇa should perform."
Why is this? You should listen!
In times long past, there was an elder in a village who, shortly after marrying a wife, lived with her in mutual affection; they soon gave birth to a daughter who gradually grew up.

The elder was working the land with his own hands, single-handedly. At that time, there was the son of a householder whose parents had both passed away; he made his living by selling firewood in the forests and wilds.

Once, as the householder’s son was carrying a shoulder-pole of firewood and arrived at the field, he set down the pole under a tree at the edge of the field to rest his shoulders. Seeing the elder plowing the soil with his own hands, he approached him and asked:
"Uncle, why do you toil so hard yourself at this advanced age? You ought to be living in a village, yet you are instead out here in the fields."
He replied, "Welcome, nephew!
I have neither brothers nor children; how could I provide for my own food and clothing without farming myself?"
He replied, "Uncle, I shall plow for you for a while; you should rest for a moment.
He then took up the plow and plowed in his stead. When midday arrived and the meal was brought from the house, he called out:
"Nephew, please come and eat with me.
Once they had finished eating, he said, "Uncle, you should return home;
however, as I do not yet know the location of your residence, I shall go outside the village at the time of the afternoon meal to meet you on the road."
Having heard this, the elder immediately returned home.

At that time, the householder’s son had been plowing until evening; he released the oxen to graze on the green sprouts, personally took up a shoulder-pole with a load of grass and a bundle of firewood, and drove the livestock back toward the edge of the village.

The elder went out to meet him and immediately escorted him to his residence; at that time, the son of the house cleared the courtyard, spread dry earth over it, and prepared a fire with much smoke and fodder for the oxen.
Having seen this, the elder thought to himself:
"Because of this son, I now enjoy peace and happiness; I shall give my young daughter to him as a wife.
After having him eat, he said:
"Nephew, you should remain here and diligently attend to the family business; I shall give this young daughter of mine to you as a wife.
He replied, "Excellent!"
He then followed these instructions and established his livelihood through manual labor.
At that time, the elder’s household had two oxen whom he regularly employed:
the larger one was by nature gentle and well-behaved, while the smaller one possessed a greedy disposition; despite being restrained, it was its constant habit to act violently.
The youth, filled with indignation, hurled a stone from afar and broke off one of its horns; consequently, he was given the name "Bald-Horned.
On another day, as the animal continued to damage the crops in the fields as before, he released a sickle and cut off its tail; thus, it was thereafter named "Bald-Tailed Bald-Horned."
Later, at another time, the householder’s son said to the elder:
"Uncle, please fulfill the marriage alliance you previously promised.
At that time, the elder said:
"Very well," he replied, and then said to his wife,
"O virtuous lady!..."
"You should prepare the garments and ornaments; it will not be long before we wish to marry off our young daughter.
His wife then asked, "Since she has never been given in marriage before, how can you prepare these things?"
The elder replied,
"I have already given her away.
His wife said:
"Who is this? He replied,
"This is the son of a lay devotee."
The wife said, "I do not know this man's clan or lineage at all; he is like white pepper, whose place of origin is unknown. How can you rashly form a marriage alliance with him?"
"In all matters of marriage, when there is mutual visiting between relatives, feasting, and social calling, and when the lineages are compatible, only then shall I give my daughter.
He said to his wife:
"O virtuous one!..."
Since this son of a householder came to my home, I have been spared from labor and have enjoyed peace and comfort.
Had he not been here, I would once again be beset by hardship and could not avoid the toil of manual cultivation myself.
The wife replied to her husband, “I truly cannot give my beloved daughter to a servant.
People of the world generally follow the words of their wives; at that time, the elder thought to himself:
"If I were to reply that I will not give my daughter to him, this laborer would leave me this very day, and I myself could not avoid having to take up the plow.
For now, it would be best to employ some expedient artifice so as not to let him depart immediately."
At another time, that laborer said to the householder,
"Householder, you ought to arrange a marriage.
The householder replied:
"Nephew! My kinsmen are numerous;
when we gather, there will be a great need for food and drink. It would be best to wait until the autumn harvest of rice is gathered."
Once the grain had been gathered, he announced that the wedding was to take place, saying: "Nephew!
We require sugar; you should wait for the sugarcane."
Having accepted it, he further announced that the marriage was to be finalized, saying:
"Nephew! These flour and pastries are for your sustenance; you shall wait until the wheat is ripe."
Once the wheat had been harvested, he again announced that the wedding was to take place, saying:
"Nephew! The old rice is nearly exhausted; you should wait for the new *tāṇḍula*."
At that time, seeing the procrastination being practiced, the householder’s son conceived this thought:
"It is not possible for the grain in the field to ripen all at once; observing these circumstances, it is clear they are deceiving me."
"I should now go and inform the people; if they do not grant it, I shall take the matter to the authorities for a final decision.
He then addressed the assembly, saying, "Uncle, you may proceed with the marriage."
Having heard this, the people said to the elder, "It has been a long time since you gave your word; why have you not yet arranged the marriage?
At that moment, the elder spoke in anger:
"Friends, you should know!
This man is merely a hired laborer in my house; for what reason would I give him my daughter in marriage?
All the people agreed.
Then the householder’s son thought to himself:
"I have neither obtained the money nor the bride; time is being wasted in vain with no success to be seen.
I should now harm this man so that I may depart as I please."

He then drove the two oxen for half a day, beating them severely with a stick and tying them to a withered tree; having exposed them to the scorching sun, he was just about to say he was returning home.
"In times near the beginning of the kalpa, animals understood human speech. As the oxen were suffering such torment, the large bull addressed the householder’s son, saying: 'Ho, man!'"

Previously, you and I shared mutual affection and love; you were like a parent to me, knowing my hardships and toil. For what reason do you now inflict so many blows and whippings upon me, bind me to a withered tree, expose me to the scorching sun, and then abandon me to return home?
"What fault or offense have I committed against you?
The man replied, "You are without blame;
however, your master has committed an offense against me."
The ox asked,
"What fault has he committed?
The man replied:
"I previously promised my daughter to you, yet now you have broken your word.
The ox replied,
"Why do you not take this matter before the authorities?"
The man replied, "Because there is no witness.
The ox then said:
"We shall serve as witnesses for you. The man asked,
"Do you speak with human voices?"
"Shall I make the sound of a cow?
The ox replied, "I shall not speak human language; I will manifest signs so that people may recognize me."

"You should enter into an oath to cause others to believe you; you should cite me as a witness to cause others to know. Tie up my two oxen in the stable and give them neither water nor fodder. After seven days have passed, release me into a place on the ground where there is abundant water and grass, even to the point that passersby may come and see, so that they may verify that we have remained silent and have not eaten water or fodder."
"I shall manifest a physical appearance that will cause the king and his ministers to believe your words are true, and then I will eat and drink.
When the man heard this plan, he immediately released them both together into the lush grass.
He went in person to the king's presence, paid his respects, and said to the king: "Great King!
The elder of such-and-such a village agreed to give his daughter in marriage; yet after she had served for many years, he has now reneged."
The king summoned the elder and questioned him as to whether it was true or false. The elder replied, "I truly did not grant permission.
The king then questioned the man:
"Do you have any witnesses?
He replied to the king, "I do."
The king asked:
"Is it a human being?
Or is it a non-human being?"
He replied, "It is not a human being.
The king said:
"What is this? He replied,
"It is an ox."
The king asked:
"Is it spoken in human speech,
or is it some other kind of speech?"
He replied, "I do not speak the language of humans.
The king said:
"How can this be proven? He replied, "I have a reliable witness who can testify to it:

for seven days, tie that cow inside the barn and give it neither water nor grass. Once the seven days are complete, release the cow into a place where there is abundant water and grass in the ground."

"I bring this as my testimony that there must surely be extraordinary signs; until the Great King has yet to believe it, the ox shall not eat at all. If this should prove false, I shall deserve the death penalty."
The King commanded his minister, saying,
"You must follow these words and observe the resulting proof.
The minister, receiving the instruction, immediately took two oxen and tethered them inside a barn, providing them with neither water nor fodder.
Then the bald-tailed and bald-horned oxen said to the great bull:
"How could we have expected such a reversal? It is only us who, as the sun rises in the west, are confined within the stall, unable to hear the sound of water or grass?"
The great ox replied,
"Is it not true that I consented to act as a guarantor for the son of the householder, so that he might remain fasting for seven days, not eating water or grass until the king had gained faith?"
The bald-tailed and bald-horned ox replied to the great bull, saying, "If you release me, I would devour even a rock upon encountering it; how much more so water and grass?
The great bull replied:
"This son of a householder loves and cherishes us as his own parents; how could we violate our word and deceive him?
