The Bald-tailed and Bald-horned one said, "Though it is true that he loves and cherishes us with an affection equal to that for his own two parents, he constantly calls me 'Bald-tailed' and 'Bald-horned. Whenever I hear him call me thus, I wish to split open his belly with my horns."
Having heard this, the great ox remained silent.
Later, the son of that householder came again to look at it and asked the ox:
"Are you at peace?"
The great ox replied,
"I am at peace, but you are not at peace.
The householder’s son said:
"What is the meaning of this?
the great ox said.
"This shaven-tailed, shaven-horned one speaks thus:"
"If you release me, even if I encounter a stone I shall devour it; how much more so water and grass?
The son of the householder said, "If that is the case, I shall flee in haste this very night; having deceived the king, my life will last but a moment."
The great ox replied, "There is no need for you to flee;
I shall allow my tail to be shorn and my horns to be pierced for a nose-rope, and you must shorten the tether and fasten it to my horns."
On the day they are released, if they should break their vow and consume water or grass, I shall lift their noses upward with my two horns; you should then announce:
"Now these two oxen inform the fifth World-Protector—among those commonly acknowledged by the people of the world as the five protectors, namely earth, water, fire, wind, and the sun."

Then the householder’s son proceeded to pierce its nose; with its tail docked and its horns cut off, the bull said to the great ox, "Virtuous one, you should observe this cruel torment inflicted upon me."
The great ox said,
"What hardship is there in wearing the necklace?
and they immediately fastened the tether-rope around the head of the larger one.

When the seventh day arrived, the king and his ministers went together to observe the two oxen released into a field abundant with water and grass. Having seen the water and grass, the one with shorn tail and shorn horns immediately desired to eat them. At that moment, the great bull raised the nose of the young calf with both horns and gazed toward the sun.
The king asked his ministers, "For what reason are these two oxen gazing toward the sun?"
At that time, a wise minister addressed the king, saying: "Great King!

These two oxen now wish to inform Your Majesty of this matter. It is not merely we two who serve as witnesses; we also appeal to the Fifth Guardian of the World, so that the bright, clear sun may assist us in providing testimony."
When the king saw this matter, he was filled with extreme wonder and said to his ministers:
"Even animals, though lacking knowledge, can yet act as guarantors for human beings."
"Since the matter is not false, it is appropriate that I form a marriage alliance with her.
He then released the two oxen so they might both graze on water and grass.
At that time, having achieved victory, the householder’s son took the woman as his wife.
The Buddha addressed the bhikṣus:
“You should know this!
Even those in the realm of animals harbor thoughts of malice upon hearing disparaging words; how much more so, then, for human beings?”
"Therefore, monks, you should not speak ill of or disparage others.
This was the origin of the rule, though the precept had not yet been formally established.
At that time, the Blessed One again addressed the monks:
"When one utters disparaging speech, the undertakings of this present life cannot be accomplished.
Listen, all of you!
Long ago, in a certain village, there lived an elder whose profession was driving carts; he had two female oxen."
One was named Nandika and the other was named Rasagṛddhin.
During the spring season, each gave birth to a son with variegated coats.
As they gradually grew up, the son of Nandika had broad and long horns, while the son of Rasagṛddhin was bald-headed and hornless.
At that time, the elder gave them names:
the first was named Long Horn of Joy, and the second was named Bald Head of Fine Flavor; when they reached full maturity, both possessed great physical strength.
Later, at another time, various carriage-drivers gathered at the edge of a pond because they had each been drinking their oxen there, and spoke thus:
"Whose ox is the most excellent? Each said:
"My ox is superior," [the other] said. The elder replied,
"My ox is extremely superior."
The people replied,
"How can we know that your ox is the most excellent?
The elder said:
"Let us have a heavy carriage pulled up a steep slope," they said,
and together they made a covenant,
wagering five hundred gold coins.
Having made this resolve, he led his own oxen to the steep slope and hitched his heavy cart.
Then the elder called out to the oxen, saying:
"O Joyful Long-Horned One, you should pull swiftly; O Delicious-Tasting Bald-Headed One, you too must haul with haste!"
When the bald-headed ox heard these disparaging words, it immediately stopped and refused to pull the cart.
The elder grew furious and began to lash it with a heavy cudgel.
The others replied,
"Do you now intend to kill this ox?
Since it is not as you wish, you ought to release it."
At that time, the elder paid five hundred gold coins; filled with extreme rage, he beat the two oxen severely with a stick and tied them to a withered tree.
The oxen understood human speech as previously described.
At that time, the two oxen said to the elder:
"You, sir, raised us first, treating us like your own parents; what fault have we committed that you should inflict such cruel suffering upon us?"
The elder replied,
"It is because of you that I am now fined five hundred gold coins.
Huānxǐ Chángjiǎo then replied to the elder:
"Because of the fault of your own mouth, you have punished yourself with this fine;
what fault is there of ours? The elder said, "What fault is there in my mouth?"
The ox then replied,
"Why do you insult me before this crowd?
You do not call me 'good,' but instead address me as a 'bald-head'."

"If you say my reputation is good and that you do not disparage me, I shall pull twice as heavy a load up the steep slope once more, and we shall both establish a pact to wager twice the amount—a thousand gold coins."
The householder replied,
"Do you now wish to double my fine?
The ox said:
"Do not disparage me; I shall certainly exert my utmost effort.
Later, on another occasion, each spoke as previously described regarding the matter of drinking the cows' milk, and the elder replied:
"My cows are most excellent."
The people replied,
"Do you now seek further punishment?
The elder replied:
"Even if you were to further punish me, what would you lose?
You should instead double the load on heavy carts at this steep slope and wager one thousand gold coins; let us make a clear and binding agreement."
He then acted according to their words, using oxen to pull the cart up a steep slope, and called out to the oxen, saying:
"Joyful One, you should pull with haste; Delicately Flavored One, you must draw with speed!"

Upon hearing this, the two oxen were filled with joy; they exerted all their strength to pull the cart until it reached level ground, and having achieved victory, they obtained one thousand gold coins.
At that time, a deva in the sky spoke this verse:
"Though there be an extremely heavy load, And it rests upon a steep slope below;
If the two oxen are joyful in heart, They can pull this chariot out."
If one speaks words that accord with their wishes, the two oxen will hear them with joy;
drawing the cart out [of the mud] will not be difficult, and the master will obtain a reward of a thousand pieces of gold.
Therefore, always speak kindly and do not utter words that are harsh to the ear.
"When one utters words of loving-kindness, there is no fault and one is always at peace.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"When those of the animal realm hear such disparagement, they can still bring harm to their master; how much more so in the case of human beings?"
"Therefore, monks,
you should not speak disparagingly of others.
At that time, the Blessed One, having rebuked the monks in various ways, spoke at length as previously described.
"I now establish this training rule for my disciples; it should be recited as follows:
'If a bhikṣu speaks disparagingly, it is a pāyattika.'"
The meaning of "bhikṣu" is as explained above.

Regarding "derogatory speech," it refers to uttering words that manifest an act of disparagement or humiliation toward another; when the other person understands them, one incurs a *pāyattika* offense, as explained in detail above.
Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya, Fascicle Twenty-Five;
Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya, Fascicle Twenty-Six.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Yijing by Imperial Decree.
The remainder of the second section on the training rule concerning disparaging speech. What are the characteristics of the offenses herein?
A summary verse states:
Lineage and craft, karma, physical form, illness—these five;
offenses and the category of afflictions, with abusive speech as the last.
A summary verse says:
Weavers, wool-workers, and needle-makers;
those who work with iron, copper, and leather; potters and barbers;
wood- and bamboo-workers, as well as slaves—if a bhikṣu, with the intent to disparage, goes to a bhikṣu of Brahmin lineage and speaks to him thus:
"Venerable one!
You are one who has gone forth from the Brahmin caste; now you are neither a śramaṇa nor a brāhmaṇa.
When that bhikṣu hears these words, whether he is thereby distressed or not, this bhikṣu incurs an offense of wrong-doing (duṣkṛta).
If a bhikṣu, with the intent to disparage, goes to a bhikṣu of kṣatriya lineage and speaks thus:
"Venerable one!
You are one who has gone forth from a kṣatriya family; you are now neither a śramaṇa nor a brāhmaṇa."
When that bhikṣu has heard these words, whether he is thereby distressed or not, this [other] bhikṣu incurs an *dukkaṭa* offense.
If a bhikṣu, with the intent to disparage, goes to a bhikṣu of the Vaiśya caste and speaks thus:
"Venerable one!..."
"You are one of the Vaiśya caste who has gone forth; you are now neither a śramaṇa nor a brāhmaṇa.
When that bhikṣu hears these words, whether he is thereby distressed or not, this bhikṣu incurs a pāyattika offense.
If a bhikṣu, with the intent to disparage, goes to a bhikṣu of śūdra birth and speaks thus:
"Venerable one!
You are a śūdra who has gone forth; you are now neither a śramaṇa nor a brāhmaṇa."
When that monk has heard these words, whether he is thereby distressed or not, this monk incurs a *pāyattika* offense.
If a monk, with the intent to disparage, goes to the place of a weaver who is a monk and speaks thus:
"Venerable one!..."
"You are one born into the caste of weavers who has gone forth; now you are neither a śramaṇa nor a brāhmaṇa.
When that bhikṣu hears these words, whether he is thereby provoked to anger or not, this bhikṣu incurs a pāyattika offense.
If a bhikṣu, with the intent to disparage, goes to a bhikṣu of the wool-weaver caste and speaks thus:
"Venerable one!
You are a renunciant of the wool-weaver caste; you are now neither a śramaṇa nor a brāhmaṇa."
When that bhikṣu has heard these words, whether he is thereby distressed or not, this bhikṣu incurs a pāyattika offense.
If a bhikṣu, with the intention of disparaging another, goes to a bhikṣu who is a tailor and speaks thus:
"Venerable one!..."
"You are one of the cloth-sewing caste who has gone forth; now you are neither a śramaṇa nor a brāhmaṇa.
When that bhikṣu hears these words, whether he is thereby troubled or not, this bhikṣu incurs a pāyattika offense.

In this manner, up to and including the smiths by iron, the smiths by copper, the leather-workers, the potters, the barbers, the carpenters, the basket-makers, and the slaves—all these should be explained in detail according to the above; thus concludes this discussion on castes.
If a bhikṣu, with the intent to disparage, goes to a bhikṣu of Brahmin descent and speaks thus:
"Venerable one!
You are one who has gone forth from a Brahmin family; you are now neither a śramaṇa nor a brāhmaṇa."

"You should now learn your own crafts and various technical skills, namely: the dignified conduct and ritual protocols of a Brahmin; the practice of ritual purification, carrying the water-pitcher, and handling ashes and earth; the recitation of the rules and the four Vedas with their respective intonations—the *ghoṣa* and the *puṇya*; and the methods for performing various sacrificial assemblies and the procedures for giving and receiving."
When that monk has heard these words, whether he is thereby troubled or not, this [other] monk incurs an *dukkaṭa* offense.
If a monk, with the intent to disparage, goes to a monk of the Kṣatriya caste and speaks thus:
"Venerable one!..."
"You are one born of the Kṣatriya caste who has gone forth as a renunciant; yet now you are neither a śramaṇa nor a brāhmaṇa.

You should now properly train in your own crafts and various technical skills, as well as all the dignified deportment and formal protocols of a Kṣatriya—namely, riding elephants, horses, and chariots; wielding bows and arrows; maneuvering, advancing, and retreating; and the arts of handling hooks and ropes, the use of shields and spears, as well as the techniques of cutting, severing, hacking, stabbing, boxing, wrestling, and archery."
When that monk has heard these words, whether he is thereby disturbed or not, this [accusing] monk incurs an *dukkaṭa* offense.
If a monk, with the intent to disparage, goes to a monk of the Vaiśya caste and speaks thus:
"Venerable one!..."
"You are one who has gone forth from the Vaiśya caste; now you are neither a śramaṇa nor a brāhmaṇa.
You should now learn your own craft, namely the conduct and methods of a Vaiśya, such as plowing fields, tending cattle, and engaging in trade."
When that bhikṣu has heard these words, whether he is thereby distressed or not, this bhikṣu incurs a *pāyattika* offense.
If a bhikṣu, with the intent to disparage, goes to where a bhikṣu of the Śūdra caste is and speaks thus:
"Venerable one!..."
"You are one who has gone forth from the Śūdra caste; you are neither a śramaṇa nor a brāhmaṇa.
You should now learn your own craft—the conduct and customs of a Śūdra, namely, carrying firewood and fodder, and tending livestock."
When that monk has heard these words, whether he is thereby distressed or not, that monk incurs a *pāyattika* offense.
If a monk, with the intent to disparage, goes to the place of a weaver who is a fellow monk and speaks thus:
"Venerable one!..."
"You are one who has gone forth from a family of weavers; you are neither a śramaṇa nor a brāhmaṇa.
You should now learn your own craft: the making of large and small blankets, as well as cloaks for covering and garments made of hemp and jute."
When that monk has heard these words, whether he is thereby troubled or not, this monk incurs a *pāyattika* offense.
If a monk, with the intent to disparage, goes to a wool-weaving monk and speaks thus:
"Venerable sir!..."
"You are a renunciant of the wool-weaver caste; you are neither a śramaṇa nor a brāhmaṇa.
You should now learn your own craft, namely the weaving of large and small woolen rugs, whether thick or thin, and square or round cushions and mats."
When that monk has heard these words, whether he is thereby disturbed or not, this monk incurs a *pāyattika* offense.
If a monk, with the intent to disparage, goes to a monk of the *sewing-cloth* class and speaks thus:
"Venerable one!..."
"You are one who has gone forth from a family of tailors; you are neither a śramaṇa nor a brāhmaṇa.
You should now learn your own craft, namely: head-caps, shirts, tunics, and trousers of various sizes."
When that bhikṣu has heard these words, whether he is thereby distressed or not, this bhikṣu incurs a pāyattika offense.
If a bhikṣu, with the intent to disparage, goes to a bhikṣu of the blacksmith caste and speaks thus:
"Venerable one!..."
"You are one who has gone forth from the smith caste; you are neither a śramaṇa nor a brāhmaṇa.
You should now properly study your own craft, namely: large and small iron bowls, needles, knives, shaving tools, axes, mattocks, and other such implements."
When that monk has heard these words, whether he is thereby offended or not, this monk incurs a *pāyattika* offense.
If a monk, with the intent to disparage, goes to a monk who is a copper-smith and speaks to him thus:
"Venerable one!..."
"You are one who has gone forth from the copper-worker caste; you are neither a śramaṇa nor a brāhmaṇa.
You should now properly learn your own craft, namely the making of copper plates, jars, vessels, bells, and other such items."
When that monk has heard these words, whether he is thereby distressed or not, this [accusing] monk incurs a *pāyattika* offense.
If a monk, with the intent to disparage, goes to a monk who makes leather articles and speaks to him thus:
"Venerable One!..."
"You are one who has gone forth from a family of leather-workers; you are neither a śramaṇa nor a brāhmaṇa.
You should now learn your own craft, namely the making of boots, shoes, saddles, bridles, seats, and other such items."
When that bhikṣu has heard these words, whether he is thereby distressed or not, this bhikṣu incurs the same offense as before.
If a bhikṣu, with the intent to disparage, goes to a bhikṣu of the potter caste and speaks to him thus:
"Venerable one!..."
"You are one who has gone forth from the potter caste; you are neither a śramaṇa nor a brāhmaṇa.
You should now properly learn your own craft, namely the making of jars, pots, bowls, and other such vessels."
When that bhikṣu has heard these words, whether he is thereby troubled or not, this bhikṣu incurs the same offense as before.
If a bhikṣu, with the intent to disparage, goes to a bhikṣu of the barber caste and speaks to him thus:
"Venerable one!..."
"You are one who has gone forth from the barber caste; you are neither a śramaṇa nor a brāhmaṇa.
You should now learn your own craft, namely the tasks of shaving hair, clipping nails, grooming, and dressing."
When that bhikṣu has heard these words, whether he is thereby troubled or not, this bhikṣu incurs the same offense as before.
If a bhikṣu, with the intent to disparage, goes to where a carpenter-bhikṣu is and speaks to him thus:
"Venerable one!..."
"You are one who has gone forth from a family of carpenters; you are neither a śramaṇa nor a brāhmaṇa.
You should now properly study your own craft, namely such matters as beds, seats, doors, windows, and houses."
When that monk has heard these words, whether he is thereby distressed or not, this [accusing] monk incurs the same offense as before.
If a monk, with the intent to disparage, goes to where a bamboo-worker monk is and speaks to him thus:
"Venerable One!..."
"You belong to the lineage of bamboo-workers who have gone forth; you are neither a śramaṇa nor a brāhmaṇa.
You should now learn your own craft, namely the making of baskets, winnowing-fans, mats, fans, umbrellas, parasols, and nose-pipes."
When that bhikṣu has heard these words, whether he is thereby distressed or not, this bhikṣu incurs the same offense as before.
If a bhikṣu, with the intent to disparage, goes to a bhikṣu of slave descent and speaks to him thus:
"Venerable One!..."
"You are one who has gone forth from a lineage of slaves; you are neither a śramaṇa nor a brāhmaṇa.
You should now learn your own craft, namely such tasks as washing the feet and bodies of others, running errands, and performing menial service."
When that bhikṣu has heard these words, whether he is thereby disturbed or not, this bhikṣu incurs the offense as before.
This concludes the discussion on crafts.
If a bhikṣu, with the intent to disparage, goes to a bhikṣu of Brahmin descent and speaks these words:
"Venerable one!
You are one who has gone forth from a Brahmin family; you are neither a śramaṇa nor a brāhmaṇa."
"You should now perform your own duty, namely, the conduct and formalities of a brahmin, such as the tasks of ritual purification and carrying the water-pitcher," as explained at length previously.
When that bhikṣu has heard these words, whether he is thereby distressed or not, this [other] bhikṣu incurs an offense of wrong-doing (duṣkṛta).
Likewise, if one causes a kṣatriya to perform his own work, as explained at length above, he incurs an offense of wrong-doing.

If a Vaiśya, a Śūdra, or any other class of people, even down to a slave, performs work as previously described in detail—adapting the description according to the specific circumstances and including the tools used—this bhikṣu incurs a pāyattika offense.
This treatise on the performance of actions is concluded.
If a bhikṣu, with the intention of disparaging another, goes to a bhikṣu who is lame or crippled and speaks to him thus:
"Venerable one!..."
"You are a cripple who has gone forth; you are neither a śramaṇa nor a brāhmaṇa.
When that bhikṣu hears these words, whether he is thereby disturbed or not, this bhikṣu incurs a pāyattika offense.

In this manner, even if one speaks to those with squinting eyes, the blind, the sightless, the hunchbacked, the dwarfs, the deaf-mute, or those with loathsome appearances who walk with crutches—if that person, upon hearing these words, is either distressed or not distressed, this bhikṣu incurs a *pāyattika* offense in every case.
This concludes the exposition on the characteristics [of the offense].
If a bhikṣu, with the intention of disparaging, goes to a bhikṣu suffering from leprosy and speaks to him thus:
"Venerable one!..."
"You are a leprous renunciant; you are neither a śramaṇa nor a brāhmaṇa.
When that bhikṣu heard these words, whether he was thereby disturbed or not, this bhikṣu incurred the same offense as before.

In this way, there arise all manner of diseases of the body, such as scabies, balding sores, throat obstructions, vomiting, consumption, fevers with chills, wind-disorders, insanity, dropsy, hemorrhoids, fistulas, and tumors.
If a bhikṣu, with the intention of disparaging, goes to a bhikṣu who is ill and speaks to him thus:
"Venerable one!
You have gone forth while still afflicted by illness; you are neither a śramaṇa nor a brāhmaṇa."
When that bhikṣu has heard these words, whether he is thereby distressed or not, this bhikṣu incurs the same offense as before.
This concludes the discussion on illness.
What constitutes an offense?
If a bhikṣu, with the intent to disparage, goes to another bhikṣu and speaks thus:
"Venerable one!
You have committed a pārājika offense; you are neither a śramaṇa nor a brāhmaṇa."
When that bhikṣu has heard these words, whether he is thereby distressed or not, this bhikṣu incurs the same offense as before.
"In this way, you have committed a saṃghāvaśeṣa, a sthūlātyaya, a pāyattika, a pratideśanīya, or a duṣkṛta; you are neither a śramaṇa nor a brāhmaṇa."
When that bhikṣu has heard these words, whether he is thereby troubled or not, this bhikṣu incurs the same offense as before.
This concludes the discussion on the offense.
What, then, is affliction?
If a bhikṣu, with the intent to disparage, goes to another bhikṣu and speaks thus:
"Venerable one!
You are full of anger; you are neither a śramaṇa nor a brāhmaṇa."
When that bhikṣu has heard these words, whether he is thereby troubled or not, this bhikṣu incurs the same offense as before.

Likewise, if you harbor resentment, concealment, vexation, envy, stinginess, flattery, deceit, lack of shame, misconduct, or wrong views, you incur the same offense as before; this is called affliction (*kleśa*).
What is abusive speech?
If a bhikṣu, with the intention of disparagement, goes to where another bhikṣu is and utters various kinds of vulgar and offensive words as an insult,
then when that bhikṣu hears these words, he incurs an offense as previously described.

There is no offense if, at a single residence, there are many bhikṣus with the same name; if another asks about someone and does not recognize him, one should reply to him, "It is a bhikṣu of such-and-such a type," and in all such cases, there is no offense.
Furthermore, there is no offense for the very first offender, or for one who is insane, mentally deranged, or overwhelmed by intense pain.
The Third Training Rule on Divisive Speech. At that time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.

At that time, the group of six bhikṣus engaged in divisive speech toward other bhikṣus. Consequently, those bhikṣus harbored mutual resentment and felt great shame; each was filled with anxiety and could find no joy in their dwelling. They neglected the cultivation of right practice, recitation, and reflection, and the long-standing bonds of affection were thereby severed.
When the bhikṣus who possessed few desires heard of this matter, they felt revulsion and contempt, saying:
"How can a bhikṣu utter words of division among the bhikṣus?"
He then reported this matter in full to the Blessed One.
On account of these causes and conditions, the Blessed One assembled the community of bhikṣus and, though he already knew the facts, asked the group of six bhikṣus:
"Did you truly engage in such divisive speech?"
He replied, “It is indeed so.
Then the World-Honored One said:
“You are not a śramaṇa, you do not follow the practice, you are impure, you have done what should not be done; this is not what should be done by one who has gone forth.
After the Blessed One had rebuked him in various ways, he addressed the bhikṣus, saying:
“If you, monks, engage in divisive speech, you harm yourselves and harm others.”
Listen well!
Long ago, in a perilous forest, there lived a lioness who was pregnant. Whenever a lioness is about to give birth, she first takes a great deal of meat and only then brings forth her cubs.
At that time, the lioness, seeking meat, went to the herd of cattle and followed them.

There was a cow that had recently given birth to a calf; out of a desire to protect her offspring, she walked behind the herd. Then the lion killed the cow and dragged it away into a thicket of dangerous forest.
At that time, the calf, driven by greed for milk, followed its dead mother to her dwelling place.
When the lion saw this, he thought to himself:
"I shall take this little calf as well."
Later, he again had this thought:
"There is no need to kill him; if I have a son, I shall take him as a companion with whom to play and enjoy myself.
He then fathered a son, and both were nursed and gradually grew up together.
Later, at another time, when their mother, Siṃhī, was afflicted by illness and approaching the end of her life, she summoned both sons and addressed them, saying:

"You two children were nourished by the same breast; in my mind there is no distinction between you, and thus you have rightfully become brothers. You must know that there are those in the world who sow discord, weaving together words of flattery that fill the land of Jambudvīpa. After I have passed away, you should look after one another well; do not listen to or adopt words spoken behind each other's backs."
Having spoken these words, he immediately passed away.
O bhikṣus! Such is the constant nature of all phenomena.
He then spoke in verse:
"All accumulations come to an end; All that is lofty must fall;
All meetings end in separation; All who have life return to death."
After the lioness mother had passed away, her cub subsequently hunted fine deer; he sustained himself with their warm flesh and warm blood, and thus grew larger day by day.
Because of that lion’s strength, the ox grazed on the abundant grass as it pleased and its body became robust and well-fed.

At that time, there was an old jackal who constantly followed the lion in search of leftover scraps. Every time the lion had finished eating warm flesh and blood, he would quickly return to his dwelling and frolic with the great ox; meanwhile, the jackal would immediately devour all the remaining meat left over from other animals.
At that time, the old jackal thought to himself,
"I shall observe where this lion king dwells.
He followed after him until he reached the forest, where he saw him sporting and playing joyfully with the bull king.
Having seen this, he thought:
"Both of these shall enter my belly; I should now create a rift between them so that they may kill one another.
Then, the jackal waited for the lion to depart and approached the bull-king, standing there with his ears drooping.
According to the laws of the noble regions, the elderly are addressed as "uncle" (舅) and the young are called "nephew" (外甥).
Seeing that the jackal was old, the ox addressed him,
saying, "Uncle!"
"How can you allow yourself to be so exhausted by the warm breeze that you hang your head in dejection?
The jackal replied, "Nephew!"
"Why does the warm breeze alone blow upon my body, while these other sensations are like flames?
The Bull King replied,
"What are these sensations like?"
The jackal replied,
"I heard the lion say these words:
'Where can this heap of meat go?'"
"When I have no meat, I shall immediately kill it to satisfy my appetite.
The ox said, "Uncle!"
"Do not speak such words. When my mother was on her deathbed, she said to both of us:

'You two sons were nourished by the same breast; in my mind there is no distinction between you, and you are brothers in right. You must know that there are those in the world who sow discord and weave deceitful words throughout Jambudvīpa. After I have passed away, you should look after one another well; do not listen to or accept words spoken behind each other's backs.'"
The jackal replied, "Nephew! Look at your state;
your day of death is not far off. I speak words of benefit, yet you do not listen."
The ox said,
"Uncle! By what signs can you know that you will kill me?"
The jackal replied, "Nephew!

When this lion emerges from his cave, he thrashes his body, lets out three roars, and surveys the surroundings; when he approaches you in this sequence, you will know that he intends to kill you at that very moment."
Having spoken these words, he left the ox and went to the side of the lion, standing there with his ears drooping.
When the lion saw him, he asked:
"Uncle! Why do you stand here with such dejected ears?"
"How could it be that the hot wind strikes my body, leaving me so exhausted that my ears hang down?
The jackal replied, "Nephew, it is not only the heat that oppresses my body; there are also wicked words that are like flames."
The lion asked, "What is the news?
The jackal replied:
"Nephew! I have heard the Bull King speak these words:
'Where can this grass-eating lion go?'"
"This mother wrongfully killed my own mother in the past; I shall now certainly and resolutely tear open her belly.
The lion replied, "Uncle!..."
Do not speak such words; when my mother was dying, she said to both of us:

"You two sons were nourished by the same breast; in my mind there is no distinction, and you are brothers in right. You must know that there are those in the world who sow discord, filling Jambudvīpa with crafty and divisive speech. After I have passed away, you should look after one another well; do not listen to or adopt words spoken behind each other's backs."
The jackal replied, "Nephew!
I see that you believe your days of death are few; thus, though I have set forth what is beneficial, you do not listen."
The lion said,
"Uncle! By what signs can it be known that you have killed me?"
The jackal replied, "Nephew!

When this bull-king emerges from his lair, shaking his body, letting out a roar, and pawing the ground with his hooves— if he approaches you in such a sequence, you should know that he intends to kill you at that very moment."
Having spoken these words, he abandoned him and departed. "O Bhikṣus!

When the bull king and the lion emerged from their caves, they always engaged in such behavior and never considered it a fault. Later, on another occasion, the lion emerged from his cave, shook his body, let out three roars, and looking around in all directions, advanced toward the bull."
The ox also emerged from its cave, shook its body, and let out a roar; it pawed the ground with its hooves and approached the lion.
This was his habitual behavior, performed without conscious intent; yet when a thought of dissension arose within his mind, those two immediately recorded the deed that had been done.
Seeing the lion approaching with signs of intent, the ox thought to himself,
"He wishes to kill me.
Seeing the ox display such signs, the lion also thought to himself:
"This one wishes to kill me!
Thinking thus, the lion immediately seized the ox by the neck with its claws; the ox then gored the lion's belly with its horns, and in a mere moment, both passed away.
At that time, certain devas in the midst of the sky spoke these verses:
"If one listens to the words of evil people, There will certainly be no virtuous or wholesome matters;
The lion and the ox were friends, Yet the jackal caused them to fight to death."
“O bhikṣus! These animals, by listening to and adopting divisive speech, failed to remember their mother’s words and consequently came to kill one another.
How much more so, then, for humans to engage in divisive speech!”
"Therefore, you should not engage in divisive conduct toward others. This was the origin of the incident;
at that time, the training rule had not yet been established.
Then the Blessed One again addressed the bhikṣus:
"Furthermore, you should listen once more.
Long ago, in a vast and perilous forest, there lived a lioness and a tigress, each of whom raised a single cub; they dwelt within this forest without ever seeing one another."
Once, while his mother, a lioness, had gone out to seek food, her cub was wandering within the forest when he arrived at the dwelling place of a tigress.
Seeing [the deer] from afar, the tiger thought to himself:
"I shall kill this one to serve as food.
He then reflected further:
"There is no need to kill this one; I shall give it to my son as a companion with whom he may play and frolic together.
At that time, the lion cub, driven by hunger, went to the tiger's side and drank her milk together with him.
Then that lion returned to his dwelling and, not seeing his cub, began to search for him, wandering throughout the mountains and marshes until he saw it by the side of a tiger, drinking its milk.
At that time, seeing the lion approaching, the tigress mother was about to flee. The lion said to her, "Sister!

Please do not run away. Since you have been able to conceive a feeling of affection for my children, I shall now dwell together with you in one place; when I go out, you shall look after my two sons."
"If you seek food, I shall protect my two children; since good and evil are the same in this regard, it would be excellent!

Having thus reached a mutual agreement, they lived together. He then bestowed names upon his two children: the son of the lion was named Shanaya (Good Tusks), and the son of the tiger was named Shanbo (Good Shoulders). They were raised together and gradually grew up.
Later, at another time, both mothers fell ill and, as they approached the end of their lives, called their two sons together and said to them:

"You two children were nourished by the same breast; in my mind there is no distinction between you, and thus you have rightfully become brothers. You must know that those who sow discord fill the world; after I have passed away, do not listen to or accept words spoken behind our backs."
Having spoken these words, he immediately passed away.
O Bhikṣus! All phenomena are ever thus, as stated in the verse previously recited.
"At that time, after both mothers had passed away, the lion cub went outside to seek food; having eaten his fill of flesh and blood, he quickly returned to the forest thicket.

At that time, when the tiger cub went out on his rounds, he would only return after a long while. On another occasion, the tiger went out to seek food and, having eaten the remains of yesterday's meat, returned very swiftly."
Seeing this as strange, Siṃha asked him, "Brother!
You have been seeking food for a long time before returning; why have you come back so quickly today?"
The tiger said,
"I came after quickly devouring the remaining meat I had hidden.
The lion told him:
"Have you, perhaps, been eating stale and putrid meat? He replied, "I have."

The lion replied, "Whenever I go out, I take fine deer and eat my fill of their most excellent flesh and blood before returning; as for what remains, I have no intention of looking back upon it again."
The tiger said, "Brothers!
You possess the courage and strength to perform this deed; I lack the power to devour the remaining flesh."
The lion said, "If that is the case, go with me when you seek food; we may eat together whatever fresh meat you obtain.
Having made this arrangement, they frequently went together.
"Previously, when they were not traveling together, there was an old jackal who followed the lion and fed on its leftovers. Later, seeing a tiger following them, the jackal thought:
'Both of these shall eventually enter my belly; I should now create a rift between them so that they will kill one another.'"
Then, at a time when there were no tigers present, that jackal stood beside the lion with his ears drooping.
The lion then asked the jackal:
"Uncle! What is it?"
"How can you, with warm breezes blowing upon your body, remain so exhausted that your ears hang down?
The jackal replied, "Nephew!"
"Why does the warm wind alone blow upon my body, while there is also a sound and sensation like that of a blazing fire?
The lion replied,
"What is the meaning of these words?"
The jackal replied,
"I have heard the fierce tiger say these words:
'Where can this grass-eating lion go?'"
"Every time he gives me his leftover meat to eat, if I find an opportunity, I shall surely kill him.
The lion replied, "Uncle!..."
"Do not speak such words. When my mother was dying, she said to both of us:

'You two sons were nourished by the same breast; in my mind there is no distinction between you, for you are as brothers. You must know that those who sow discord fill the world; after I have passed away, do not listen to or accept words spoken behind one's back.'"
The jackal replied, "Nephew! Look at your state;
there are but few days left until your death, yet you will not listen to my words for your own benefit."
The lion said,
"Uncle! By what signs can you know that I am to be killed?"
The jackal replied, "Nephew!

When this fierce tiger emerges from its den, it stretches its body, lets out three roars, and surveys the surroundings with a gaze; as it approaches you in this sequence, you should know that at such a time it has the intention to kill."
Having spoken these words, he left him and went to the side of a fierce tiger, where he stood with his ears drooping.
Seeing him, the tiger asked:
"Uncle! Why have you come here?"
"How can you endure the hot wind touching your body while so utterly exhausted that your ears hang down?
The jackal replied, "Nephew!"
"Not only is my body oppressed by heat, but there are also evil words that are like flames.
The fierce tiger replied,
"What is the news?"
The jackal replied, "Nephew!
I have heard the lion speak these words:"
"Where can this leftover food of the tiger go?
It was with great hardship that I sought it out to give to him; if I find an opportunity, I shall kill it and eat its flesh.
The tiger then replied:
"Uncle! Do not speak such words. When my mother was on her deathbed, she told both of us:

'These two sons of yours were nourished by the same breast; in my mind there is no distinction between you, and you are brothers by right. You must know that those who sow discord fill the world; after I have passed away, do not listen to or accept words spoken behind one's back.'"
The jackal replied, "Nephew!
I see that your end is near; though I have offered you beneficial advice, you have not heeded it."
The tiger said,
"Uncle! By what signs can you know that it was I who killed?"
The jackal replied, "Nephew!
If you see the lion emerge from his cave, shaking his body and letting out three roars, looking about in all directions as he approaches you, then know that the lion has the intention to kill you."
After the jackal had spoken these words, he left them and departed. "O bhikṣus!
Whenever the lion and the tiger emerge from their cave, they always act in this manner, yet neither of them has ever considered it a fault."
Later, at another time, the lion emerged from its cave, shook its body, let out three roars, and looked around toward the tiger.
The tiger also emerged from its cave, shook its body, and let out three roars.
He looked around in the four directions toward the lion before him.

This was his habitual practice, never having consciously directed his attention to it; yet, when a thought of creating a schism arose within his mind, those two immediately recorded the deed he had committed.
Seeing the lion manifesting signs as he approached, the leopard thought to himself,
"He wishes to kill me.
Having seen the leopard and manifested his own signs, the lion also thought to himself:
"This one wishes to kill me," he thought, and further reflected:
"I possess great strength and peerless valor; how could this person possibly harm me?"
"I now ask you first: for what reason do you kill me?
He spoke in verse, saying:
"Your form is exceedingly beautiful and wondrous; You are valiant and possess many extraordinary powers."
"O Suvāhu, you ought not to harbor an evil mind to come and harm me.
Upon hearing these words, the tiger also spoke in verse:
"Your form is exceedingly beautiful, And you possess valor and many wondrous powers."
"O Sudaṃṣṭra, you ought not to come with an evil mind to harm me.
At that time, Sudaṃṣṭra asked Sudāman:
"Who has informed you that I have the intention to commit murder?"
Śubhaṅga replied,
“This is an old jackal.
At that time, Śubhaṅga also asked Śubhadanta:
"Who has told you that I have the intention to commit murder? Suxu replied,
"It was this old jackal."
Sundaradanta replied, "Because of this evil creature,
who incites strife between both sides, my kinsmen and acquaintances have nearly killed one another.
He then summoned the jackal, threw him down, and killed him.
At that time, various devas spoke these verses:
"Do not abandon your kinsmen and friends because of the words of others;
when you hear the words of another, you must carefully examine them."
The jackal dwells in an earthen burrow, And with a divisive mind gives rise to evil intent;
Therefore, a person of wisdom Should not hastily place their trust in it.
This wicked and deluded jackal Utters false words of strife and discord.
"By alienating the friends and relatives of others, one finds peace and happiness in killing them. "O bhikṣus!
This being in the animal realm brought about his own death by sowing discord."
"How much more so with human beings!
Therefore, you should not engage in divisive conduct toward others.

At that time, the Blessed One, having rebuked the group of six bhikṣus through various skillful means, addressed the bhikṣus at length as previously described, up until: "I, considering ten benefits, shall establish a training rule for my śrāvaka disciples, which should be recited as follows:"
"If a bhikṣu, moreover, speaks with divisive intent, it is a pāyattika.
The meaning of "bhikṣu" is as explained above; this refers to the group of six bhikṣus, or any others of a similar kind.
Regarding divisive speech: if a bhikṣu, with the intention of creating a rift, utters words toward another bhikṣu, he incurs a pāyattika;
the meaning of this is as explained above.
Regarding the characteristics of offenses herein, what are their specific matters?
A summary verse states:
"Lineage, craft, occupation, physical form, and illness—these five."
Offenses and the categories of afflictions, with abusive speech as the last.
A summary verse says:
"The castes refer to the four classes, down to the caste of slaves."
All crafts are alike, and their activities are likewise so.
Among them are various kinds: weavers, wool-workers, and smiths;
those who work with copper, leather-workers, and potters.
Shaven-headed men, those made of wood, and those made of bamboo—
these categories are distinguished as eleven types, with the slave ranked last. If a bhikṣu,
with the intent to cause division, goes to a bhikṣu of Brahmin lineage and speaks these words:
“Venerable one!
There is a bhikṣu who says:
‘You are one who has gone forth from a brahmin lineage; you are neither a śramaṇa nor a brāhmaṇa.’”
He asked, "Who is it? and she replied:
If one says, "So-and-so," by disclosing their name, one incurs an *dukkaṭa* offense; to disclose their clan (*gotra*) also constitutes an *dukkaṭa* offense.
The same applies to disclosing that they belong to the Kṣatriya caste.
If one reveals the name or the lineage of anyone from a Vaiśya down to a slave, one incurs a *pāyattika* offense.
The details therein are explained at length as in the training rule concerning disparaging speech (*paisunya-vākya-śikṣāpada*).
There is no offense for one who is the very first offender, or for one who is insane, mentally deranged, or overwhelmed by intense pain.
The Fourth Training Rule on Rebuking. At that time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the group of six bhikṣus, knowing that the harmonious Saṃgha had already settled a dispute in accordance with the Dharma, raised it again during the formal ritual (karmavācanā), saying:
"This matter of dispute was not properly extinguished; this is an improper adjudication. It should be investigated further and thoroughly resolved."
At that time, the bhikṣus again engaged in settling disputes and suppressing those matters, thereby neglecting the cultivation of wholesome qualities, the recitation of scriptures, and contemplation.
Bhikṣus of few desires felt contempt and spoke thus:

"How is it that these bhikṣus, knowing that the harmonious Saṃgha has already settled the dispute according to the Dharma, yet further raise the matter for a formal act (*karmavācanā*) as described above?"
Then the bhikṣus reported this matter in detail to the Blessed One, as previously described, up to the point where he said:
"Having considered ten benefits, I shall establish a training rule for my śrāvaka disciples, which should be recited as follows:

'If a bhikṣu, knowing that a harmonious Saṃgha has settled a dispute in accordance with the Dharma and that the matter has been extinguished, should later raise it again at the place of the formal ritual (karmavācanā), it is a pāyattika.'"
The meaning of "bhikṣu" is as explained above.
A "bhikṣu" refers to one of the group of six or others of a similar class.
"Knowing" means that having understood it oneself, one speaks of it to another.
"Harmonious" means being of one flavor.
"The assembly" refers to the disciples of the Buddha.
"Deciding according to the Dharma" means according to the Dharma, according to the Vinaya, and according to the Teacher’s instruction.
"Disputes" refers to the four types of disputes:
namely, disputes concerning legal matters (*adhikaraṇa*), disputes concerning verbal abuse (*abhivāda*), disputes concerning offenses (*āpatti*), and disputes concerning formal procedures (*kriyā*).
"Already eliminated" means that the matter has been extinguished.
"Subsequently raising the matter during the *karmavācanā* (formal ritual act)" means to raise the issue so that it does not cease.
The meaning of "falling [into an offense]" (*pātayantika*) is as explained above.
What are the characteristics of the offense in this context? How is the matter defined?

If a bhikṣu, regarding a legal case of censure, perceives it as a legal case of censure, and knowing that the case has been settled, perceives it as settled—or even if he harbors doubt—yet raises the matter again, it is a pāyattika.
If one perceives that a matter has not been settled as having been settled, and raises it again out of doubt, one incurs a *duṣkṛta*.

If a bhikṣu, regarding a legal case of censure (*adhikaraṇa*), perceives it as a legal case of verbal dispute (*bhāṣā-adhikaraṇa*), and knowing the matter has been settled, perceives it as settled—or if he entertains doubt—yet raises it again, it is a *pāyattika*.
The remaining offenses are the same as before.

If a bhikṣu, regarding a legal issue concerning censure (*adhikaraṇa*), forms the perception that it is a legal issue concerning an offense (*āpattādhikaraṇa*), and knowing that the matter has been settled, forms the perception that it has been settled—or if he entertains doubt—yet raises the matter again, it is a *pāyattika*.
The remaining offenses are the same as before.

If a bhikṣu, regarding a dispute over censure (*adhikaraṇa-śamatha*), forms the perception that it is a dispute over legal action (*kiccādhikaraṇa*), and knowing that the matter has been settled, forms the perception that it has been settled—or if he entertains doubt regarding this—he incurs an offense identical to the one mentioned before.

Just as taking *adhikaraṇa-śamatha* (settlement of legal issues) as the first [category] and comparing it with the other three types of disputes (*adhikaraṇa*) results in four permutations (*catuṣkoṭi*), one should understand that the same applies when taking the other disputes as the primary category; in full, there are sixteen permutations in total.
There are five types of individuals. What are the five? They are:
the host, the person performing the *karmavācanā*, the person giving consent (*chanda*), the person stating their own view, and the guest.
The "host" refers to one who understands the beginning, middle, and end of a legal dispute.
The "person who performs the *karmavācanā*" refers to one who presides over the formal ritual procedure (*karmavācanā*) regarding this legal dispute.
"One who gives their consent" refers to one who grants their consent at that time.
"One who states their own view" refers to one who articulates their own view during the performance of the *karmavācanā*.
Regarding "the guest" (the outsider): this refers to one who does not understand the beginning, middle, or end of a legal dispute (*adhikaraṇa*).
Among these five types of persons, if the first three know that the harmonious Saṃgha has rightfully settled the dispute, yet they raise the matter again, they incur a *pāyattika* offense.
If the latter two persons raise the issue again during a formal proceeding for settling a dispute, they incur a *duṣkṛta* offense.
The categories regarding the perception of the object (*ālambana-saṃjñā*) should be understood as usual.
Furthermore, there is no offense in the case of the very first offender, or one who is insane, mentally deranged, or overwhelmed by intense physical pain.

5. The Training Rule on Speaking Dharma Alone with a Woman for More than Five or Six Words. The fifth training rule: At that time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.

At that time, the Venerable Udāyin, who was skilled in interpreting bodily signs, took up his robes and bowl during the first part of the day and entered the city of Śrāvastī to beg for food. Arriving at the house of a brahmin householder, he saw a young woman and asked her, "How is your paternal aunt?"
He replied, "My mother-in-law is as impetuous and fierce as a rabbit struck by an arrow.
Udāyin responded:
"What fault do you have?
It is because between your two breasts and in your private parts there are signs of violence and wickedness—namely, black moles, red moles, and whorled hair; this is your fault."
Having spoken these words, he took the food and departed.
Later, at another time, he went to that house again and asked her mother-in-law:
"What is the character and conduct of your daughter-in-law?"

He replied, “My daughter-in-law is by nature very indolent and does not apply herself to respectful diligence; she is prone to harsh abuse and anger, and her speech is coarse and vulgar. Udāyin replied:
"What fault has the bride committed?
Her speech was just as before; this is her fault.
Having said these words, he took the food and departed.
Then, on another day, Udāyin entered the city of Śrāvastī to beg for alms in succession. While preaching the Dharma at the house of a brahmin householder, he asked the woman’s sister-in-law:
"How is your new daughter-in-law?"
He replied, "O Noble One!
My daughter-in-law is as filial as one's own daughter or like a younger sister."
Udāyin said, "It is not due to her virtue;
rather, it is because between her two breasts and in her private parts there are auspicious marks—namely, the signs of a vase, a fish, and coiled letters—that this is her merit."
On another day, he saw his daughter-in-law and asked her,
"How is your mother-in-law?
She replied:
"I regard my paternal aunt as a sister and as a mother.
Udāyin said, "It is not due to her virtue;
it is because the space between her two breasts is as it was before."
Having fully described all the signs and characteristics, he departed.

Later, at another time, that wife and her mother-in-law bathed their bodies together and rubbed each other; in the private parts, they each beheld the marks, which were identical to what the Venerable Udāyin had said.
Later, due to a dispute and mutual animosity, she spoke these words:
"Do you dare to contend with me?
You do not even realize that you have been having a private affair with another man."
He replied,
"I dare to swear an oath that such a thing is truly not the case.
He reported this, saying:
"If that is so, how did you allow other men to know of the moles and marks on your private parts?
At that time, the new bride also replied to her mother-in-law:

"I truly have no face to dare confront you, yet you dare say that the head of the household has been communicating with outsiders and allowed other men to know of my private features; please do not speak further and let this matter rest."
When those two had finished their mutual confession and apology, they asked one another:
"Who ever told you about the marks of our private parts? He replied:
"Noble Udayī! The aunt said,
"I too have heard Udayī speak thus."
At that time, the two of them both censured him together, saying:
"Venerable One!
For what reason do you trouble us?"
At that time, an elderly bhikṣu, while on his almsround, came to that house;
the aunt then asked him, "What kind of person is Udāyin?"
The bhikṣu replied,
"He is the son of a high minister who has left the home life and become a bhikṣu who upholds the precepts.
He answered:
“If this bhikṣu maintains the precepts, by what means could he know of such signs as moles on a woman’s private parts?
The bhikṣu replied,
“He understands the characteristics of the body and thus knows there are moles and such.”
He replied,
"How could one display such signs and inform everyone? Having heard this,
the bhikṣu returned to the monastery and informed the other bhikṣus, who then reported the matter to the Buddha.
The Buddha said:
"Because of preaching the Dharma [to women], such faults arise. From this day forward, you should not preach the Dharma to women in lay households.
Accordingly, as the Buddha had instructed, they did not preach the Dharma to women.
At that time, as the bhikṣus entered the village for alms, a woman said to them:
"Noble ones,
please teach me the Dharma."
The bhikṣu replied,
"Sister, the Blessed One does not permit me to preach the Dharma to women."
He replied, "If you, sir,
are unwilling to preach the Dharma for me, I likewise cannot offer you food.
The bhikṣus reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
“O bhikṣus, you should deliver a fivefold discourse on the Dharma to women, addressing them thus:
‘Sisters! Form is impermanent; even feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are impermanent.’”
When a bhikṣu entered a village to beg for alms, a woman said to him:
"Noble one! Please teach me the Dharma."
The bhikṣu then delivered a fivefold discourse on the Dharma for her, saying:
"Sisters! Form and the other aggregates are impermanent."
The woman requested again, saying,
"Please preach the Dharma once more.
The bhikṣu replied:
"Sisters! The Buddha permits only this much; he does not allow for excessive talk.
The women replied:
"I too shall merely give a small amount of food and drink.
The bhikṣus reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"Give him a teaching consisting of six phrases."
He replied:
"Sisters! The eye is impermanent, and so on, up to the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind—all are impermanent."
When a bhikṣu entered a village for alms, a woman said to him:
"Noble One! Please teach me the Dharma."
The bhikṣu delivered a sixfold discourse on the Dharma for her, saying:
"Sisters! The eye and so forth are impermanent."
The woman requested again, saying,
"Please preach the Dharma once more.
The bhikṣu replied:
"Sisters! The Buddha permits only this much; he does not allow for excessive speech.
The women replied:
"I too shall give only a small amount of food and drink.
The bhikṣus reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"A man should be stationed there so that [the donor] may speak as much as they wish."
A bhikṣu entered a village for alms, and a woman said to him,
"Noble one, please teach me the Dharma."
The bhikṣu replied,
“A man should be summoned. He said:
"What use is a man?
He replied: "The World-Honored One has established the precepts:..."
"One may respond by preaching the Dharma to a man as if he were a woman, speaking at length as one pleases.
The woman said, "Excellent!"
"I have protectors and you, O virtuous one, are likewise fearless; you may preach the Dharma to me as you please.
He then called for his men, and the bhikṣu preached the Dharma and departed.
At that time, the six bhikṣus went on their almsround in succession and arrived at the place of some women, saying to them:
"Sisters! Please sit; we shall preach the Dharma for you."
The woman said, "Noble one,
please wait a moment while I call a man."
The group of six replied,
"What need is there for a man?
It will suffice if there is but a single monkey, a rooster, a dog, a calf, or a young child."
He then preached the Dharma to the woman and departed.
At that time, an elderly bhikṣu arrived while begging for alms, and the woman said to him:
"Noble One!"
"Preach the Dharma for me.
The bhikṣu replied,
"A man should be summoned to preach the Dharma for you."
The woman said, "Noble One!
Here there are monkeys, chickens, dogs, calves, and small children; whenever any of them are present, you may preach the Dharma."
The bhikṣu replied,
“I should not preach the Dharma to a woman in the presence of such a man.
The bhikṣu then said:
"Who taught you to treat this as a male and preach the Dharma to it?
The woman said,
"Noble One!"
"The group of six [monks] taught me.
The bhikṣu replied,
"Who else but they could commit such evil deeds?"
The bhikṣus reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"One may preach the Dharma only in the presence of a man of intelligence.
As the Blessed One has taught, one should preach the Dharma to women in five or six sentences.
At that time, when the six bhikṣus intentionally taught the fivefold dharma to women until they reached the sixth point, and intentionally taught the sixfold dharma until they reached the seventh,
another bhikṣu saw them and said:
"Venerable sirs!..."
“As the Blessed One has said, one should teach the Dharma to women in five or six phrases; why then, Venerable Sir, do you now go on to seven or eight?
The group of six replied, “Do seven or eight phrases involve drinking alcohol or eating garlic?”
When the bhikṣus of few desires heard this, they felt aversion and contempt, saying:
"As the World-Honored One has taught:
'In preaching the Dharma to women, one should not exceed five or six phrases.'"
"Why did the group of six bhikṣus intentionally go as far as six or seven words?
They reported the circumstances to the Buddha.
On account of this, the Buddha assembled the community of bhikṣus and, eventually, questioned the group of six, saying:
"I have prescribed that one should preach the Dharma to women using only five or six phrases; why then do you intentionally use seven or eight?
They replied, "It is indeed so."
"Venerable Sir!
The Buddha rebuked him in various ways, as extensively explained before, up until: "I now establish this training rule for my disciples, which should be recited as follows:
'If a bhikṣu preaches the Dharma to a woman for more than five or six sentences, except in the presence of a man capable of understanding, it is a pāyattika.'"
The meaning of "bhikṣu" is as explained above; this refers to the group of six [monks], or others of a similar class.
"Woman" refers to one who has the capacity to understand speech that is either wholesome or unwholesome.

"One must not exceed five or six words" means that when speaking five phrases of the Dharma, if one intentionally reaches a sixth; or when speaking six phrases of the Dharma, if one intentionally reaches a seventh.
"Dharma" refers to that which is spoken by a Buddha or spoken by a śrāvaka.
"Spoken" means proclaimed with the mouth.
"Except for a man of wisdom" means excluding a man who lacks understanding and comprehension.
The meaning of *pāyattika* is as explained above.
Regarding the characteristics of the offense herein, what are the specific matters?
If a bhikṣu preaches the Dharma to a woman in an upper story using five or six phrases, and intentionally continues to the sixth or seventh phrase, he incurs a *pāyattika* for each instance.
When he had finished preaching the Dharma to the woman on the upper terrace and descended to the middle terrace, that woman also followed him down and spoke these words:
"Noble One!..."
"You may further proclaim for me the essential points of the Dharma.
At that time, that bhikṣu should reply to her, saying: "Sister!"
"I have finished speaking.
He replied, "Noble One!"
"Furthermore, I pray that you will proclaim the sublime Dharma for me.
At that time, the bhikṣu should preach the Dharma to him using five or six phrases; if he reaches seven or eight, he incurs a pāyattika offense.
In this manner, even if one goes as far as the courtyard, or to the door, or to the edge of the eaves, if one speaks beyond the permitted time, one incurs a *pāyattika* offense.

However, when instructing a woman to recite, or when she asks questions, or if there is a wise woman who can pose successive and varied questions, one should answer according to her inquiries; in such cases, there is no offense.
Furthermore, there is no offense for the very first offender, or for one who is insane, mentally deranged, or afflicted by intense pain.
The Sixth Training Rule on Reciting Verses Aloud Together with One Who Is Not Fully Ordained. At that time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove.

At that time, the six bhikṣus were reciting word-for-word with those who were not yet fully ordained; they made a great clamor in their dwelling, like Brahmins reciting various non-Buddhist treatises, or like a crowd of laypeople loudly practicing their lessons in a schoolhouse.
At that time, the World-Honored One, hearing the clamor and noise from their dwelling place, addressed Ānanda, saying:
"For what reason is there such great clamor at the dwelling place, like the sound of Brahmins reciting various non-Buddhist treatises, or like a crowd of laypeople reading aloud in a schoolhouse?"
Then Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying:

"World-Honored One, it is because these six bhikṣus are reciting the scriptures word-for-word with those who are not yet fully ordained that such a great clamor has arisen within this monastery, just as the brahmins and others have described."
The Buddha said to Ānanda:
"How could the bhikṣus recite the scriptures word-for-word with those who have not yet received full ordination?
Ānanda replied to the Buddha:
"Reciting word-for-word together.
At that time, the Blessed One, for this reason, spoke at length as before, and finally asked the six bhikṣus:
"Did you truly recite word-for-word together with those who were not yet fully ordained?"
He addressed the Buddha, saying:
“It is indeed so,
O Great Virtuous One!”
At that time, the Blessed One rebuked him in various ways, and finally declared: "I now establish this training rule for my disciples, which should be recited as follows:
'If a bhikṣu recites or instructs the Dharma in verse-by-verse correspondence with a person who has not yet received full ordination, it is a pāyattika.'"
"Furthermore, 'if a bhikṣu' refers to the group of six [monks], or others of a similar class.
Regarding 'one who is not fully ordained,' there are two types of full ordination:
namely, that of a bhikṣu and that of a bhikṣuṇī; all others are termed 'not fully ordained.'"
Regarding "phrases," there are parallel phrases and preceding phrases.
What are parallel phrases?
They refer to when one who is fully ordained says:
When [the preceptor] said,
"Commit no evil," those who were not yet fully ordained would all say at once:
"Commit no evil."
This is called a "corresponding phrase.
What is a "preceding phrase"?
It refers to when one who is fully ordained says:
Before the sound of the words "Commit no evil" had even ceased,
those who were not yet fully ordained chanted this phrase in unison, saying first:
"Practice all that is good."
This is called the preceding phrase.
What is the identical syllable?
It refers to when one who is fully ordained utters the syllable "pā" (evil).
When those who are not yet fully ordained simultaneously say "bad," this is called a "simultaneous word" (*sahakṣara*).
What is a "prior word" (*pūrvakṣara*)?

It refers to when the sound of the word "bad" has not yet ceased from the mouth of one who is fully ordained, and those who are not yet fully ordained simultaneously utter the word "bad"; because they speak it first, it is called a "prior word."
"Reciting and reading" means receiving and retaining the words through recitation.
"Dharma" refers to the teachings spoken by the Buddha and his disciples.
The meaning of *pāyattika* is as explained above.
Regarding this, what are the characteristics of the offense and how does it occur?
If a bhikṣu, perceiving a person who is not fully ordained as such—or having doubt about it—recites the Dharma with them, whether verse by verse or line by line, he incurs a root offense.

If one recites the Dharma with a person who is not fully ordained—whether perceiving them as such or being in doubt—and does so by using the same words or reading them out in succession, one incurs a root offense.

If one addresses a person who is not fully ordained with the thought that they are fully ordained, or with doubt, speaking to them using the same phrases as those used for the ordained and the same words as those used for the ordained, one incurs an *dukkaṭa* (offense of wrong-doing).

If, regarding one who is fully ordained, one perceives them as not fully ordained or entertains doubt, and speaks using the same phrase with the preceding phrase or the same word with the preceding word, one incurs an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
If one perceives a fully ordained person as being fully ordained, there is no offense.
There is no offense for those who stammer, those who are naturally impetuous, or those who speak rapidly.
There is no offense when teaching someone to recite or when instructing them on how to ask questions.
Furthermore, there is no offense for the following: one who is the very first offender;
those who are insane, mentally deranged, or afflicted by intense physical pain.
*Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya*, Fascicle 26. *Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya*, Fascicle 2.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Yijing by Imperial Decree. 7.

The Training Rule on Speaking of Gross Offenses to Those Not Yet Fully Ordained. The Seventh Training Rule on Speaking of Gross Offenses to Those Not Yet Fully Ordained. At that time, the Blessed One was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.

At that time, there were many bhikṣus, whether old or young, who, because they had not yet abandoned the afflictions of desire, engaged in unrighteous conduct and consequently committed saṃghāvaśeṣa offenses.

Later, he approached those who were learned in the Vinaya-piṭaka to study under them. Having recognized his transgressions, he felt remorse and sought to expiate his offenses. He then performed the *parivāsa* (probation) and *mānatva* (penance) according to the Dharma. Furthermore, he served the Saṃgha by providing drinking water or fanning them with a fan; or, at the stūpas containing the hair and nail relics of the Blessed One, he polished them with fresh cow-hide leather and performed other such tasks.
At that time, there were faithful and respectful brahmins and householders who, upon seeing this, discussed it among themselves, saying:
"In this world, there are those skilled at distinguishing precious gems; they examine various treasures and only accept and take up those that are not counterfeit or adulterated."

These bhikṣus were likewise; well-versed in cause and effect and having gathered various meritorious deeds, although they were advanced in years and aged, they personally provided water for the Saṃgha and performed all manner of tasks without declining the labor.
"However, these six groups merely nourish their own bodies and do not cultivate superior merit.
When those people treated them with contempt, the six groups heard this and said to the people:
"Do you suppose they provide for us because they take pleasure in merit?"
"However, he did not undertake this meritorious work out of a virtuous intent; rather, it was because the Saṃgha had assigned him a task of disciplinary labor.
The people asked, "What fault did he commit that the Saṃgha assigned him such disciplinary labor?"
The group of six monks replied,
"This old bhikṣu has himself committed such and such unrighteous acts.
When those brahmins and householders heard that he had practiced unrighteousness, they each felt revulsion and shame, saying these words:
"If even these venerable elders act unreasonably, what doubt can there be regarding the faults of other younger monks?
After the meal, the elder bhikṣus again went to the stūpa and wiped it down as they had done before.
At that time, the group of six monks went to the place where the śrāmaṇeras—the disciples of those elder bhikṣus—were staying, and asked them:
"Venerable ones!
Where have your two teachers gone now?"
The disciple replied:
"Venerable Sir!
My teacher practices various meritorious deeds."
He then asked, "What merit have you cultivated?
He replied:
"At the stūpa containing the hair and nail relics of the Blessed One, they have smeared and polished it with fine, soft cow dung.
Those disciples then asked the group of six:
"Venerable sirs!..."
“Virtuous ones, why do you not cultivate merit?
The group of six replied,
“Do you know or not?”
It was not that your two teachers sought merit for themselves by making offerings at the stūpa;
rather, it was the Saṃgha that imposed a punitive penance upon them, which they were made to undergo.
The disciple asked,
"What offense has our teacher committed that he should receive this punishment?
He then replied:
"Your preceptor himself committed such and such unrighteous acts.
Once that senior bhikṣu had been cleared of his offense, he compelled the śrāmaṇeras to perform various communal tasks.
He replied, "Why do you masters not do it yourselves?
The masters said:
"I should not do this. The śrāmaṇera replied, "If even you,
masters, perform such and such unrighteous acts, why would these actions be improper?"
The teacher then replied:
"Although such a transgression exists, we have already expiated it all in accordance with the Dharma.
However, who told you about this matter of offense?"
The novice replied,
“It was the group of six bhikṣus.
When the bhikṣus of few desires heard this, they felt aversion and contempt.
"How is it that a bhikṣu speaks of another's grave offense to one who is not yet fully ordained?
At that time, the bhikṣus reported this matter in detail to the Blessed One.
The Blessed One addressed the bhikṣus, and after speaking at length, he questioned the group of six:
“Monks, have you indeed told another person who is not yet fully ordained of his grave offense?
They replied to the Buddha,
“Venerable Sir!”
"It is indeed so.
At that time, the World-Honored One rebuked him in various ways, even saying, "This is not what one who has left the household life ought to do.
Having thus rebuked him, he addressed the bhikṣus, saying:
"Having considered ten benefits, I establish this training rule for the bhikṣus, which should be recited as follows:
'If a bhikṣu, knowing that another bhikṣu has committed a grave offense, should speak of it to one who has not received full ordination, it is a pāyattika.'"
After the Blessed One had thus established the training rule for the bhikṣus, there was a bhikṣu named Pūrṇamukha and a bhikṣuṇī named Śākhā in the city of Śrāvastī.
At that time, these two men performed defiling tasks in various lay households and manifested unwholesome appearances, causing people to lose their respect and faith.
The bhikṣus then reported this matter in detail to the Blessed One. The Blessed One said:
"Bhikṣus, you should appoint a bhikṣu to go to those lay households and inform the people, saying:"
"The actions of the bhikṣu Pṛthukola and the bhikṣuṇī Śākhā are unlawful.
If a bhikṣu does not possess five qualities, he should not be appointed; even if he has been appointed, he should not be sent away.
What are the five? They are:
being possessed of craving, hatred, delusion, fear, and ignorance regarding what has been said and what has not been said.
One who possesses these five qualities should be appointed; once appointed, he should depart.
In this manner, one should arrange the seats and strike the *gandī*. Once the assembly has gathered, one should inform them with words and first ask whether they are capable:
"Can you, [Name], go to the homes of laypeople and speak of the unlawful conduct of the bhikṣu Pṛthukūṭa and the bhikṣuṇī Śākhā?"
He replies, "I am able. Then,
one bhikṣu shall perform the formal act of motion (jñapti-karman) as follows:
“Venerable Saṃgha, listen!
These two—the bhikṣu Viśālakṣa and the bhikṣuṇī Śākhā—have committed various improper acts in the homes of laypeople, thereby causing people to lose their faith and respect.”
This bhikṣu, so-and-so, is capable of going to the homes of laypeople and proclaiming the unlawful conduct of the bhikṣu Pṛthukūṭa and the bhikṣuṇī Śākhā.

If it is the proper time for the Saṃgha and the Saṃgha is willing to listen, may the Saṃgha grant its permission: the Saṃgha shall now appoint this bhikṣu, so-and-so, to go to the homes of laypeople and proclaim the unlawful conduct of the bhikṣu Pṛthukūṭa and the bhikṣuṇī Śākhā.
The motion is thus made.
Next, the *karmavācanā* (formal ritual act) is performed:
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!"
This bhikṣu Viśālamukha and this bhikṣuṇī Śākhā have committed various improper acts in the homes of laypeople, thereby causing people to lose their faith and respect.
This bhikṣu, so-and-so, is capable of going to the homes of laypeople to speak of the improper conduct carried out by the bhikṣu Pṛthukūṭa and the bhikṣuṇī Śākhā.

The Saṃgha now appoints this bhikṣu, so-and-so, to go among the homes of laypeople as one who speaks of transgressions, to speak of the improper conduct carried out by the bhikṣu Pṛthukūṭa and the bhikṣuṇī Śākhā in the homes of laypeople.

If the venerable ones consent to this monk, so-and-so, speaking of the transgressions of the householder-superior in the presence of householders, and speaking of the unlawful conduct of the bhikṣu Pṛthukola and the bhikṣuṇī Śāṇakā in the presence of householders, let them remain silent;
if they do not consent, let them speak.

"The Saṃgha has now granted its consent to appoint this bhikṣu, so-and-so, as the one who shall speak of transgressions among the households of the laity, to go before those lay households and speak of the unrighteous conduct of the bhikṣu Pūrṇamukha and the bhikṣuṇī Śākhā."
"Because he remained silent, I now maintain it thus.
"O Bhikṣus! I shall now establish the rules of conduct for those who speak ill of bhikṣus in the homes of laypeople."
That bhikṣu should go to the house of a layperson and speak these words:
"O worthy ones, listen!

There are those who defile the household life and there are those who defile the life of renunciation. It is like a field of rice growing lushly in its furrows, which then encounters frost and hail, causing all the crops to be utterly destroyed."
Furthermore, it is like a stalk of sugarcane that flourishes with lush leaves and stems, yet when struck by the disease of red nodes, it is utterly ruined and destroyed without remainder.
You should know, O virtuous ones,
that those two evil persons are just like this!

Virtuous ones, do not dwell in association with him, lest you bring ruin to the Noble Teaching. You should know that this person has brought about his own destruction; like a scorched seed that can no longer sprout, he can no longer grow within the Dharma and Vinaya of the Noble Teaching.

"You all should contemplate the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha; and you should contemplate the Elder Venerable Ājñātakauṇḍinya, the Venerable Aśvajit, the Venerable Vāṣpa, the Venerable Aniruddha, the Venerable Bhadrika, the Venerable Mahānāman, the Venerable Yaśas, the Venerable Pūrṇa, the Venerable Vimala, the Venerable Gavāmpati, the Venerable Subāhu, the Venerable Śāriputra, the Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana, the Venerable Koṭīviṃśa, the Venerable Mahācunda, the Venerable Mahākātyāyana, the Venerable Upāli, the Venerable Nadīkāśyapa, the Venerable Gayākāśyapa, the Venerable Mahākāśyapa, and the Venerable Nandika—observe these and all such great bhikṣus!"
Then, having been thus instructed by that monk, the appointed bhikṣu should go to the house of the layperson and speak accordingly, and immediately depart from that dwelling.
When the bhikṣu Viśāṇa heard of this matter, he thought to himself:
"The Saṃgha has dispatched that bhikṣu to the house of a layperson to proclaim my faults."
He immediately went to that bhikṣu’s place and spoke these words:
"Did you speak of my faults while at a layperson's home?
The other replied:
"I have received the formal instructions of the Saṃgha.
Pṛthukūṭa replied:

"Regarding this matter, whether it be appropriate or not, I shall split open your belly and pull out your intestines to encircle the Jetavana Grove; I shall sever your head and hang it at the temple gate like a broken oil jar for all to see."
Upon hearing these words, he was struck with great terror and said to the bhikṣus,
"Viśālakṣa intends to slaughter me.
He then related the preceding events in detail to inform the assembly.
"I can no longer recount this matter in a layperson's house.
Then the bhikṣus reported this incident in detail to the Blessed One. The Blessed One said:
"That foolish man may be able to deceive an individual, but he cannot deceive the assembly. Therefore, the Saṃgha should perform a *jñapti* (formal motion) to explain his transgression in detail."
Having spread out the seats and struck the *ghanṭī*, once the assembly has gathered, one should inform them and instruct a single *bhikṣu* to act as follows:
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!
This bhikṣu Viśālamukha and this bhikṣuṇī Śākhā have performed improper acts in various lay households, thereby causing many people to lose their faith and respect.
At present, there is no one else capable of speaking of their faults while they are in lay households.
