If the time is right and the Saṃgha grants permission, then if the Saṃgha sees the bhikṣu Pṛthukūṭa and the bhikṣuṇī Śākhā acting improperly in the homes of laypeople, it should speak of their transgressions to them, saying:
"Venerable ones, you should know!..."
These sinful bhikṣus and bhikṣuṇīs bring ruin to the holy teaching.
You should know that such persons destroy themselves; they are like scorched seeds that no longer sprout, and can no longer grow within the discipline and law of the holy teaching.
"You all should contemplate the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, and you should also contemplate the conduct and traces of the elder Ājñātakauṇḍinya and all the other great bhikṣus."
"Thus it is announced.
Following the Buddha’s instruction, he ordered the great assembly to inform all lay households within that walking area.

At that time, the bhikṣus, whether they knew of the matter or not, went and informed everyone in the lay households. Consequently, this caused people to lose their respect and faith, making it difficult for those seeking alms to obtain food and drink. They reported these circumstances in detail to the World-Honored One, and the World-Honored One said:
"In lay households, one should speak of the faults of a bhikṣu or bhikṣuṇī who is known to have committed evil deeds; one must not do so in places where they are unknown.
From this it should be understood that this applies except in the case of a formal monastic decree (saṃgha-karman)."
At that time, the World-Honored One praised the observance of the precepts; having taught the Dharma of few desires according to the occasion, he addressed the bhikṣus, saying:
"The former was the original injunction; this is the subsequent allowance."
It should be stated thus:
"If a bhikṣu, knowing that another bhikṣu has committed a grave offense, should speak of it to one who is not fully ordained, except by formal authorization of the Saṃgha, it is a pāyattika."
"Furthermore, 'if a bhikṣu' refers to the group of six [monks]; the remaining meanings are as explained above.
Regarding the term 'fully ordained,' there are two types:
namely, bhikṣus and bhikṣuṇīs; all others are termed 'not fully ordained.'"
Regarding what is called "coarse and evil," there are two types:
those arising from the cause of a *pārājika* offense and those arising from the cause of a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense.
This "coarse and evil" has two characteristics:
First, coarseness in intrinsic nature;
second, coarseness in its origination.
"Speaking" refers to making the matter manifest and explicit.
"Except by formal monastic procedure (*saṃgha-karman*)" means except when the assembly performs the ritual act for one's sake.
The meaning of *pāyattika* is as explained above.
In this context, what are the characteristics of the offense and how does it occur?

If a bhikṣu, regarding a household that is unknown [to him], forms the perception that it is unknown or entertains doubt, and speaks of another’s grave offense to them, he incurs a *pāyattika* offense.
If a bhikṣu, regarding a household that is known [to him], forms the perception that it is unknown or entertains doubt, and speaks to them, he incurs a *dukkaṭa* offense.

There is no offense in the following cases: if one speaks to a lay family about something unknown to them while believing it to be already known; or if the matter has been discussed in detail by the assembly; or if at that time the people have all heard of it and know it universally—just as when people together view a mural on a wall, it is not something known by me alone. To speak in such circumstances carries no fault whatsoever.
Furthermore, there is no offense for the very first offender, or for one who is insane, mentally deranged, or afflicted by intense pain.

The Eighth Training Rule: Regarding the False Claim of Attaining Superhuman States to One Not Yet Fully Ordained. At that time, the Buddha was staying in the High Pavilion Hall beside the Monkey Pond in Vaiśālī.
At that time, there were five hundred fishermen living together as a group on the banks of the Vipāśā River.
Those fishermen possessed two great nets:

one named "Small-foot" and the other named "Large-foot," as described in detail previously in the fourth *pārājika* rule. Eventually, all five hundred of them went forth into homelessness, and through diligent practice, they attained the state of an Arhat.

At that time, the World-Honored One was staying at the Bamboo Grove Village. As it happened to be a time of famine and alms were difficult to obtain, they followed the World-Honored One’s instruction to observe the rains retreat in various locations.
Those bhikṣus all went to their home villages to observe the retreat, each thinking to themselves:
"Previously, we praised one another with untrue matters and were consequently rebuked; [we must not do so again]."
"We have now encountered a time of famine in this world where alms are difficult to obtain; we shall each praise one another for our actual virtues so that we may suffice ourselves.
They then went to their kinsmen and spoke these words, even saying:
"You, our relatives, have gained a great and wholesome benefit, for such a superior and wondrous assembly of monks has come to dwell in this very village during the rains retreat."
"This bhikṣu has attained the perception of impermanence; regarding the perception of suffering in what is impermanent, and so forth, he has even attained the eight liberations.
Later, at another time, when those kinsmen came to visit and inquire after him, the bhikṣus, seeing the kinsmen arrive, immediately began to praise one another:
"Your kinsmen have gained great benefit, for there is such a superior assembly of monks dwelling here in retreat near your village."
"This bhikṣu has attained the perception of impermanence," and so on, up to "he has attained the fruit of arhatship and the eight liberations.
When his kinsmen had heard this explanation, they said,
"Noble One!..."
"You, O virtuous ones, have realized such a supreme fruit.
They replied,
"We have all attained it."

At that time, when the common people heard that those who had attained the fruits [of the path] were being honored, they all conceived feelings of affection and joy; they failed to provide relief for their own parents, wives, children, and relatives, yet each provided food and drink to the bhikṣus.
However, while the Buddha dwelt in the world, he held two great assemblies with his disciples:

the first was on the fifteenth day of the fifth month, when they were about to enter the rainy season retreat (*varṣā*); the second was on the fifteenth day of the eighth month, when the retreat concluded and the *pravāraṇā* ceremony was performed.

The details are as previously explained; when the three months had concluded and the bhikṣus had finished making their robes, they were haggard in complexion and emaciated in appearance. Taking up their robes and bowls, they went to the Bamboo Grove Village, desiring to pay homage at the Buddha’s feet.
Having arrived at the village, the Venerable Ānanda saw the bhikṣus coming from afar; feeling a sense of compassion for his fellow practitioners of the holy life, he then cried out: "Welcome!"
He immediately went forward to receive him, taking up his robe, bowl, mendicant’s staff, water flask, and other miscellaneous items and requisites for a śramaṇa, and then asked:
"Venerable One!..."
"Venerable ones, where did you observe the rains retreat to come here?
"We observed the three-month rains retreat in the village of Pāṭaligrāma, and have now arrived here."
Ānanda asked, "Venerable sirs,
during your three-month rains retreat there, did you not find it burdensome to beg for food and drink?
They replied:
"Although one may dwell in peace and happiness there, obtaining food and drink is extremely difficult.
Then Ānanda replied, "It is indeed so."
"Venerable ones!
Seeing that [the others] are emaciated and their complexions are haggard, one can infer for certain that food and drink must be difficult to obtain here.

At that time, five hundred bhikṣus from the village of fishermen, having completed their summer retreat, also arrived at this village carrying their robes and bowls; their complexions were bright and healthy, and their countenances were plump and robust.
Then Ānanda immediately went out to meet him and questioned him as before:
"In this place of retreat, is food and drink easily obtained?
Are you living in comfort? He replied:
"I dwell there in true peace and happiness; the food and drink I seek are easily obtained and not difficult to find.
Ānanda said, "Venerable One!"
"Observing that he is well-nourished and his complexion is radiant, one can infer for certain that food and drink must be easy to obtain.
At that time, Ānanda questioned him in detail about these matters, and he replied:
"Among my own kinsmen, I have praised myself, saying:"
"This bhikṣu has attained the perception of impermanence, up to and including the eight liberations.
Ānanda asked: "Is what you have related true?"
"Is it false?
He replied, "It is true."
He asked, "Venerable ones!
Is it appropriate for you to proclaim to others the supreme state attained by yourselves merely for the sake of a little food and drink?"
He then reported this matter in full to the Blessed One.
Thereupon, the Blessed One assembled the community of bhikṣus and, knowing the reason, asked them as before in detail:
"Bhikṣus, did you, for the sake of food and drink, speak of what you yourselves had obtained to those who were not yet fully ordained?"
He said to the Buddha:
“It is indeed so,
Venerable Sir!”
At that time, the Blessed One, having rebuked the bhikṣus in various ways, even went so far as to establish this training rule, which should be recited as follows:
"If a bhikṣu, having actually attained a state superior to that of ordinary men, should speak of it to a person who has not yet received full ordination, it is a pāyattika."
"Furthermore, 'if a bhikṣu' refers to the five hundred fishermen who were bhikṣus; the remaining meanings are as explained above.
'Truly obtained' means that the matter is factual."
Regarding the "superior persons" and the "equality of dharmas," these are both as previously explained in the fourth *pārājika* and in the preceding detailed exposition.
What are the characteristics of the offenses herein?
A summary verse says:
Perceiving an aranya as such, one receives a sublime seat within a dwelling;
being able to know its own characteristics, one manifests its form through skillful means.
If a bhikṣu, with a mind free from falsehood, forms the perception that it truly exists and speaks thus to one who is not yet fully ordained:
"I see devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, asuras, bhūtas, piśācas, kumbhāṇḍas, and kaṭapūtanas."
If one says this, one incurs a *pāyattika*.
If one says:
"I saw a *pāṃśukūla-preta* (a ghost of rags)."
If a bhikṣu, without a deceptive intent and with the perception that it is true, speaks thus to one who is not fully ordained:
"I have heard the voices of devas, even down to the voices of kaṭapūtanas," he commits a *duṣkṛta* offense.
If one says this, one incurs a *pāyattika*.
If one says:
"I heard the voice of a *pāṃśukūla* ghost."
If one says this, one incurs an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*).
If a bhikṣu, without a deceptive intent, forms the perception that it is true and speaks these words:
"I have gone to the abodes of the gods, even to the abodes of the kaṭapūtanas."
If one says this, one incurs a *pārājika* offense.
Or if one says:
"Go to the place of the *vighna*-ghosts."
One who says this incurs an *dukkaṭa* offense.

These cases should all be explained in detail as previously set forth for the fourth *pārājika*; the distinction therein is that while the former was termed a "defeat" (*parājita*), here it is called "falling away" (*patanīya*).
What was previously called a "grave offense" (sthūlātyaya) is here called "misdeed" (duṣkṛta).
Furthermore, regarding those who are "without offense": this refers to the very first person to commit the act, or one who is insane, mentally deranged, or overwhelmed by intense physical pain.

9. The Training Rule on Slandering the Distribution of Community Property. This ninth training rule on slandering the distribution of community property was established at that time when the Buddha was staying at the Bamboo Grove, the Squirrels’ Feeding Ground, in Rājagṛha.
At that time, the bhikṣu Balavān was appointed by the community to distribute bedding and determine the order of meals.

Possessing faith and a virtuous disposition, he never declined the toil of overseeing the affairs of the community; he gave away all his own requisites to the field of the Three Jewels and to bhikṣus of superior conduct. Having given thus, his own three robes were entirely worn out and tattered.
When the bhikṣus had witnessed this event, they deliberated among themselves, saying:

"This venerable Sthavira Śrīgupta was appointed by the assembly to distribute bedding and to oversee the order of meals. He possesses faith and a virtuous disposition; he labors for the sake of the community without complaint. All his own requisites and possessions have been given away entirely to the field of the Three Jewels and to bhikṣus of superior conduct. Having given in this manner, his own three robes have all become worn and tattered."
"If there be anyone who offers a robe to the Saṃgha, it should be given to Śrīgupta.
At that time, the Saṃgha obtained some fine white woolen cloth. Then the bhikṣus reported this matter in detail to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One said: "O bhikṣus!"
A formal announcement (*jñapti*) should be made; having assembled the community, this robe should be granted to Śrīgupta, for there is truly no fault in it.
It should be done in this manner: having spread out the seats and struck the *ghanṭī*, the Sangha should be convened as usual, and the following should be recited:
"Listen, venerable Saṃgha!

This Śrīgupta possessed faith, reverence, and a virtuous disposition; he supervised the affairs of the community without shrinking from toil or hardship, and he gave away all his own requisites for life to the field of the Three Jewels and to monks of superior conduct until nothing remained.
Having made such a gift, his own three robes have all become worn and tattered.
Now the Saṃgha has obtained fine white woolen cloth; if the time is right for the Saṃgha and the Saṃgha permits it, may the Saṃgha now formally grant this white woolen cloth to Śrīgupta.
"Thus it is announced.
At that time, the bhikṣus, following the Buddha’s instruction, performed the single announcement (*ekajñapti*) and gave the saṃgha’s white cotton cloth to Sthūlanandika.

However, because the karmic conditions for the long-standing enmity between the Venerable Sthūlanandika and the two bhikṣus, Mitra and Pṛthivī, had not yet been exhausted, he spoke words of contempt and disparagement before the bhikṣus:
“Venerable ones!
For what reason can the Saṃgha receive offerings and then distribute them according to one’s personal acquaintances?
When the bhikṣus heard these words, they replied:
"Venerable one!
When the formal motion (*jñapti*) was being made, did you not assemble those who were of like mind and gave their consent?
He replied:
"Let us assemble together.
The bhikṣus said, "If that is so,
for what reason did you utter words of disparagement?"
He replied, "How could it be that even weeping is not permitted?
At that time, the bhikṣus who possessed few desires heard this and felt contempt; they collectively censured him.
"How is it that a bhikṣu who previously shared a common mind later speaks with discordant words, saying:
'Venerable sirs!
The gains acquired by the Saṃgha have been diverted to private individuals according to their personal friendships'?"
Then the bhikṣus reported this matter in detail to the Blessed One.
The Blessed One said:
“Your friends, the two men Māluṅkyaputra and Thera, truly spoke these words.”
"Venerable sirs!
The Sangha has received a gain and diverted it to private individuals according to their personal intimacy.
Those two replied:
"It is truly so, Venerable Sir!

At that time, after the World-Honored One had rebuked him in various ways and had explained at length as above, he continued until: "I now establish this training rule for the bhikṣus, which should be recited as follows:"
“If, moreover, a bhikṣu who has previously agreed with others later says:
‘Venerable sirs!
You have diverted the property intended for the Saṃgha to private individuals according to their personal intimacy.’”
...so saying, it is a *pāyattika* offense.
As for “if a bhikṣu,” this refers to the two individuals, namely the friend and the ground-dweller; the remaining meanings are as explained above.
“Having previously agreed” means having previously consented to that matter.
"Speaking thus later" means making such a statement at a subsequent time.
Regarding "those with whom one is intimate": what constitutes intimacy for a bhikṣu?

It refers to the preceptor and his disciple, the disciple and his preceptor; furthermore, the instructor (ācārya) and the student dependent upon him (niśrita-śiṣya), the student dependent upon him and his instructor; those who share the same preceptor or the same instructor, as well as other friends and relatives.
This "community of monks" refers to the disciples of the Buddha.
As for "material benefits," there are two kinds:
first, the benefit of clothing and requisites; second, the benefit of food and drink.
In this context, "benefit" refers to the benefit of robes.
"Having arrived among the assembly and diverting [the goods]" means transferring monastic property to another individual.
The meaning of *pāyattika* (offense of expiation) is as explained above.
In this regard, what are the characteristics of the offense and how does it occur?
If a bhikṣu, regarding whatever material goods for the Saṃgha there may be, having previously given his consent with a unified mind, later says:
"O Venerable Ones!..."
"To divert items intended for the community of monks to another individual based on personal intimacy" constitutes a *pāyattika* offense in all such cases. However,
if the Sangha has not actually granted the items and one diverts them oneself, there is no offense when the matter is reported.
Furthermore, there is no offense for the very first offender, or for one who is insane, mentally deranged, or overwhelmed by intense physical pain.
The Tenth Training Rule on Slighting and Reviling the Precepts (*Śikṣāpada-vinindana*). At that time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
The Buddha addressed the bhikṣus:
"Every half-month, you should recite the Prātimokṣa Sūtra.
Thereupon, the bhikṣus followed the Buddha’s instruction and recited the Prātimokṣa Sūtra every half-month.
At that time, when the six bhikṣus heard the exposition of the four *pārājika* rules, they remained silent and said nothing.

When the *saṃghāvaśeṣa*, the two *aniyata*, the thirty *naiḥsargika-pāyattika*, the ninety *pāyattika*, the four *pratideśanīya*, the numerous *śaikṣa* dharmas, and the seven *adhikaraṇa-śamatha* dharmas were being recited, the six bhikṣus spoke as follows:
"O Venerable Ones!"
If you know the matter and recognize the person, why do you repeatedly inflict further injury upon my wounds?
When you, venerable ones, recite even these minor and secondary precepts every half-month, you cause the bhikṣus to give rise to distress and provoke feelings of remorse.
When the bhikṣus heard these words, they replied:
"Venerable one!
It is not for your sake that we recite the Prātimokṣa Sūtra every half-month; rather, we recite it because we uphold the instructions of the Great Teacher."
At that time, although the group of six heard these words, they still did not cease their disparagement and criticism, saying:
"Why do you speak of these minor and lesser precepts, causing the bhikṣus to give rise to distress and feel regret?"
The bhikṣus replied,
"If you did not wish to hear it, what transgression had you previously committed that now causes you remorse?
At that time, those bhikṣus of few desires felt aversion and shame, speaking as follows:

"How is it that during the half-month, when the four *pārājika* rules were being recited, you remained silent and said nothing; yet when the *saṃghāvaśeṣa* rules up to the seven methods for settling disputes were being recited, you spoke thus:
'Venerable ones!'"
"If one knows the matter and recognizes the person, as explained in detail previously, up to the point of giving rise to remorse.
At that time, the bhikṣus reported this matter in its entirety to the Blessed One.
The World-Honored One asked:
"Did you, O group of six, truly speak these words at the time of the recitation of the precepts?
He questioned them extensively regarding the matter.
He replied:
"It is indeed so,
Venerable Sir!"
After the Blessed One had rebuked him in various ways, he established the training rule, which should be recited as follows:
"If a bhikṣu, when the Prātimokṣa Sūtra is being recited every half-month, should speak thus:
'Venerable friend!'"
"What is the use of teaching these minor and secondary rules of training?
When these precepts are being taught, they cause the bhikṣus to feel remorse, distress, and regret.
If one thus disparages the precepts, it is a *pāyattika*.
"Furthermore, 'if a bhikṣu' refers to the group of six [monks]; the remaining meanings are as explained above.
'Half-month' means that one month is divided into two parts.
'Precepts' refers to the rules beginning from the four *pārājika* offenses and ending with the seven methods for settling disputes (*adhikaraṇa-śamatha*)."
"Sūtra" means the sense of sequential correspondence.
"To speak" means to proclaim.
"O Venerable Ones! [is the address].
"Those" refers to describing their circumstances to manifest a state of distress and affliction.
"To revile the precepts" means to utter disparaging words to inform another person.
The meaning of "falling" is as explained above.
In this regard, what are the characteristics of the offense and how does it occur?

If a bhikṣu, during the fortnightly recitation of the four *pārājika* rules, or when the *saṃghāvaśeṣa* rules are being recited, up until the recitation of the seven methods for settling disputes, should speak as follows:
"Venerable one!..."
"If one says, 'Why is it necessary to speak of these minor and very minor precepts?
They cause the bhikṣus to feel remorse,' one commits a pāyattika offense."
Or "giving rise to vexation, regret, sorrow, and feverish distress. Or it says:
"recalling worldly affairs."
Some said, "I do not delight in leaving the household life. Others said:
"Return to the life of a layperson.
To utter such words as these constitutes an offense of falling (pāyattika).

One should understand it thus: when these matters are being discussed in the context of the other sixteen categories, the *Kṣudrakavastu* (Miscellaneous Matters), the *Nidāna*, the *Mātṛkā*, and so forth, as well as in the *Sūtras* associated with the Vinaya teachings or in other *Sūtras*, if a bhikṣu speaks in this manner:
"Venerable one!
What is the use of reciting these minor and lesser precepts?
When they are recited, they cause the bhikṣus to give rise to remorse."
If one says this, one incurs a *pāyattika*.
If, when proclaiming it during the recitation of other sūtras, one speaks thus:
"Venerable One!"
Regarding the statement, "What is the use of relying on this sūtra to speak of such matters as to cause people distress and regret," one incurs an *dukkaṭa* (offense of wrong-doing).
Furthermore, there is no offense for the very first offender, or for one who is insane, mentally deranged, or overwhelmed by intense physical pain.
The second summary verse says:
Seeds, lightness, and instruction; Arranging beds, grass mats, and pulling;
Insisting on staying, and beds with removable legs; Sprinkling grass—these should be three and two.

11. The Training Rule on Destroying Living Seeds. This eleventh training rule on destroying living seeds was established at that time when the Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī, at the Jeta Grove, in Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, there was a certain mahallaka bhikṣu who was foolish and ignorant; wishing to construct a great monastery for the saṃgha, he proceeded to cut down magnificent, noble trees.

At that time, there was a deva dwelling in a tree; having passed the first watch of the night, his bodily radiance surpassing all others, he approached the Buddha, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and sat to one side.
The radiance of this deva’s body illuminated the Jeta Grove on all sides, and he addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

There is an elderly bhikṣu who is ignorant and lacks discernment, failing to understand the proper timing. He wishes to construct a great monastery for the Saṃgha, and has consequently cut down magnificent, large trees.”
"This tree has been my dwelling place for a long time.
Venerable Sir!

Now that it is the height of winter, the cold wind splits the bamboo; our young sons and daughters have no refuge at night. I pray only that the World-Honored One will look upon us with compassion; what plan do you suggest I take?"
At that time, the World-Honored One immediately commanded another great tree deity, saying to him:
"The dwelling place you occupy may be made to accommodate this homeless deva."
Then that tree deity, having received the instruction, made the necessary arrangements.
At that time, when the night had turned to dawn, the World-Honored One gathered the bhikṣus at his usual seat; having sat down composedly, he addressed the bhikṣus:

"Last night, a tree deity of surpassing radiance came to my place, prostrated at my feet, and sat to one side. The light from her celestial body illuminated the entire Jeta Grove, and she spoke thus:"
“World-Honored One!

There was an elderly mahallaka bhikṣu, ignorant and lacking discernment, who did not understand the proper timing. He wished to construct a great monastery for the Saṃgha and consequently began cutting down magnificent, large trees.”
"This tree has long been my dwelling place,
O Venerable One!
Now that it is the season of midwinter, the cold wind splits the bamboo, and the young boys and girls have no shelter at night."
"I only pray that the World-Honored One will compassionately examine me; what course of action should I take now?
"O Bhikṣus! This act committed by this Mahallaka is contrary to the Dharma.
By felling that great tree which was the dwelling place of a deity, he has caused that deity to feel resentment and contempt, thereby violating the discipline of the Śākya-sons."
The Buddha thought to himself:
"Because this bhikṣu has cut down a great tree, a transgression has arisen; for this reason, from this day forward, bhikṣus should not cut down trees."
"If anyone cuts down [trees], they shall incur an offense against the rules.
This was the origin of the matter, yet the precept had not yet been formally established.
While the Buddha was in the Āṭavī forest, the World-Honored One instructed the bhikṣus that they should not cut down trees.
At that time, because of this matter, all the *vaiyāvṛtyakara* bhikṣus suspended their various construction activities.
Then the World-Honored One, knowing [the reason], intentionally asked the Venerable Ānanda:
"For what reason have all the construction works of the *vaiyāvṛtyakara* bhikṣus been brought to a halt?"
Then Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
While residing in Śrāvastī, the Buddha informed the bhikṣus that they should not cut down trees.”
"For this reason, there is no wood to be found, and thus the construction must be abandoned.
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"I shall now explain the proper conduct for a bhikṣu engaged in construction."

Whenever a person appointed to oversee construction is about to fell a tree, seven or eight days prior, they should construct a maṇḍala beneath that tree, arrange incense and flowers, provide various sacrificial offerings, and recite the Triśaraṇa Sūtra. An elder bhikṣu should perform the *tikīṇa* (special) blessing, preach upon the ten paths of wholesome action, and extol virtuous deeds.
Furthermore, one should inform them:
"If there are devas who have long resided in this tree, you should seek another dwelling elsewhere.
This tree is now being prepared for the sake of the Buddha, Dharma, and Sangha; after seven or eight days have passed, it shall be felled."
"If, when felling a tree, some unusual sign appears, one should praise the merit of giving and renunciation and explain the faults of stinginess and greed.
If such unusual signs still appear, one should not fell it; if no such signs are present, it may be felled."
"If a monk engaged in construction does not act in accordance with what I have prescribed, he shall incur an offense of transgression against the Dharma.
This was also an introductory narrative (nidāna), yet at that time the precept had not yet been formally enacted.
The Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.

At that time, the group of six bhikṣus personally or by means of others cut down trees and various kinds of living grass, even including flowers and fruits, taking whatever they desired for their use.
At that time, when the various non-Buddhists saw this, they each felt contempt and shame, and deliberated thus:
"These śramaṇas, the sons of the Śākyas, have themselves or through others cut down grasses and trees."

"However, we laypeople, including brahmins and even hired laborers, ourselves or through others, cut down trees and kill grasses; the śramaṇas, sons of the Śākyas, do these same things as well. Even though they have left the household life, how are they different from the laity?"
"Who would ever make offerings to such shaven-headed śramaṇas?
At that time, the bhikṣus reported this matter in detail to the Blessed One.

On account of these causes and conditions, the Blessed One assembled the community of bhikṣus. Through questions and answers, he rebuked them at length as previously described, and said: "I shall establish a training rule for the bhikṣus, which should be recited as follows:"
"If again a bhikṣu himself destroys a village of seeds or sentient beings, or causes another to destroy them, it is a pāyattika.
"If again a bhikṣu" refers to the group of six; the remaining meanings are as explained above.
Regarding the "village of seeds," there are five kinds of seeds: first, root-seeds;
second, stem-seeds; [third, joint-seeds;
fourth, node-seeds; fifth, seed-seeds].
Third, propagation by joints;
fourth, propagation by cuttings;
fifth, propagation by seeds.
What are root-propagated plants?
They refer to nut-grass, sweet flag, yellow ginger, white ginger, *ākanda*, and *vatsanābha* and so forth; since these things all grow from planted roots, they are called root-propagated plants.
What are stem-propagated plants?

They refer to the pomegranate tree, the willow tree, the grapevine, the bodhi tree, the udumbara tree, the nyagrodha tree, and so forth; because these all grow from stems, they are called stem-propagated plants.
What are joint-propagated seeds?
They refer to sugarcane, bamboo, reeds, and the like; since these all grow from joints, they are called joint-propagated seeds.
What are split-propagated seeds?

This refers to the seeds of plants such as *lānxiāng* (Cymbopogon), *yúnsuǐ* (Coriandrum), and *júyòu* (citrus fruits); because these various seeds are produced through the splitting open [of the fruit], they are called "splitting seeds" (*kai-zhong*).
What are "seed-seeds" (*zi-zhong*)?
This refers to rice, wheat, barley, various beans, mustard seeds, and the like; because these various fruits arise from seeds, they are called "seed-plants.
All such things are collectively termed a "seed-village."
What is the village of sentient beings?

"Sentient beings" refers to grasshoppers, butterflies, mosquitoes, gadflies, dung beetles, ants, snakes, scorpions, and various bees; these sentient beings all rely upon grasses, trees, and wood to make their dwellings.
If a bhikṣu pulls up, breaks, or cuts grass, trees, or wood, it constitutes a pāyattika offense; the meaning is as explained previously.
What are the characteristics of the transgression in this case? How is the matter defined?
The summary verse says:
Perceiving seeds in roots and so forth, Cutting trees, grass, and flowers,
Walking paths near trees and the like, And green moss, jars, and shelves.
If a bhikṣu perceives a plant that is a root as being a root, and perceives what has grown as having grown, and he cuts it himself or instructs another to cut it, he incurs a pāyattika;
if he does so while in doubt, he incurs a pāyattika.
If one perceives dry wood as being alive, or entertains doubt regarding it, in both cases one incurs a *duṣkṛta* offense.

If a bhikṣu perceives a root-plant as a stem-plant, or perceives it as living, or entertains doubt regarding it, and then cuts it himself or instructs another to cut it, he incurs a *pāyattika* offense in all such instances.
If one perceives dry matter as being living or harbors doubt regarding it, at the time of cutting or destroying it, one incurs an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*).
In this same manner, for each of the four types of seeds—root-seeds, joint-seeds, node-seeds, and seed-seeds—one should apply the analysis according to the preceding rules.
Furthermore, regarding the seed from a stalk, and likewise for each of the other four types of seeds, there are four cases for each.
Whether it be a thought of desire or doubt, one incurs both a *pārājika* offense and an *dukkaṭa*; this is explained in detail according to the specific circumstances.
If a bhikṣu himself or causes another to cast five kinds of seeds into fire, thinking:
"May these seeds all be destroyed."
If [the seeds] are destroyed, one incurs five *pārājika*-level offenses; if they are not destroyed, one incurs five *dukkaṭa* offenses.
If a bhikṣu himself or causes another to cast the five types of seeds into water, it is also as previously stated.
If a bhikṣu places five types of seeds into a mortar and pounds them with a pestle so as to damage the seeds, he incurs five *pārājika*-like offenses (*sthūlātyaya*);
if they are not damaged, he incurs five *duṣkṛta* offenses.

If a bhikṣu places the five types of seeds on dry ground or in a warm place, and mixes them together with alkaline water, *gomeya*, dry soil, and so forth, thereby causing them to be damaged, he incurs an offense according to the gravity of the act, as previously described.
If a bhikṣu places the five types of seeds into the broth, soup, or rice-water so as to cause them to be damaged, he incurs an offense identical to that mentioned previously.
If a bhikṣu cuts down a tree using a single method, he incurs one *dukkaṭa* (wrongdoing) and one *pāyattika* (offense of expiation).
If one strikes two trees with a single blow and they are both severed, one incurs one *duṣkṛta* (wrongdoing) and two *pāyattika* (offenses involving forfeiture).
If a bhikṣu severs many trees with a single blow, he incurs one *duṣkṛta* and numerous *pāyattikas*.
If a bhikṣu cuts down one tree with two strokes, he incurs two *duṣkṛta* offenses and one *pāyattika* offense.
If he cuts down two trees with two strokes, he incurs two *duṣkṛta* offenses and two *pāyattika* offenses.
If one cuts down many trees with two strokes, one incurs two *dukkaṭa* offenses and numerous *pācittiya* offenses.
If one cuts down a single tree with many strokes, one incurs many *dukkaṭa* offenses and one *pācittiya* offense.
If one cuts down two trees with many strokes, one incurs many offenses of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa) and two offenses of downfall (pācittiya).
If one cuts down many trees with many strokes, one incurs many offenses of wrong-doing and many offenses of downfall.
As it is with trees, so it is with wild grass, lotuses, and the like; according to the facts, the degree of the offense incurred is the same as before.
If a bhikṣu pulls up the roots of a tree, he incurs a *pārājika* offense (a downfall).
If one damages the rough bark of a tree or its non-solid, moist parts, one incurs an *dukkaṭa* (offense of wrong-doing);
if one damages its solid, moist parts or its wounded and broken areas, one incurs a *pāyattika* (offense involving forfeiture).
If a bhikṣu damages a tree or grass that has grown leaves, he incurs a *pāyattika* offense;
if he damages yellowing leaves, he incurs a *dukkaṭa* offense.
If he damages an unopened flower, he incurs a *pāyattika* offense.
If one destroys a flower that has already blossomed, one incurs an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
If one destroys fruit that is not yet ripe, one incurs an offense of falling (pācittiya);
if it is already ripe, destroying it incurs an offense of wrong-doing.
If one pours hot water, cow dung, mud, or the like onto a patch of growing grass, causing it to be damaged, one incurs a *pāyattika* offense;
if it is not damaged, one incurs a *dukkaṭa* offense.
If one pours out substances with no intention of causing damage, there is no offense whatsoever.
If a bhikṣu, while walking upon a patch of living grass, forms the thought of damaging it, he incurs a *pāyattika* offense for every blade of grass destroyed.
If one merely performs the practice of walking meditation (caṅkrama), there is no offense.
If, while on living grass, one drags firewood or pulls a mat with the intent to damage it, one incurs a downfall (pāyattika);
if there is no intent to damage it, there is no offense.
If one performs walking meditation on ground covered with green moss, there is an offense or no offense as previously stated.
If one drags firewood, spreads mats, or handles other objects on such ground, the resulting offense is the same as before.
If one picks up duckweed leaves or green moss from within water, one incurs a *duṣkṛta* offense as long as they have not yet been removed from the water;
once they are removed from the water, one incurs a *pāyattika*.
If one pulls up a fungus from the ground, one incurs an offense of wrongdoing (*dukkaṭa*).

If a bhikṣu, with the intention of causing damage, removes green mold or white mildew found upon jars, pots, clothing, bedding, mats, or racks for robes, he incurs an offense of wrongdoing in all such cases.
If one causes another to know that [the seeds] have been purified before using them, there is no offense.
If one causes another to know that five types of living seeds have been purified, there is likewise no offense in all such cases.
Furthermore, there is no offense for the very first offender, or for one who is insane, mentally deranged, or afflicted by intense pain.
The Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya, Volume Twenty-seven;
The Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya, Volume Twenty-eight.

The Training Rule on Contemptuous Disparagement. The Twelfth Training Rule on Contemptuous Disparagement. At that time, the Blessed One was staying at Rājagṛha in the Bamboo Grove, by the Kalandaka Pond.
At that time, the bhikṣu Ghaṭīkāra was appointed by the assembly to distribute the bedding and requisites for the Saṃgha and to oversee the sequence of meals.
At that moment, the two bhikṣus Mitra and Bhūmija and Ghaṭīkāra had not yet exhausted the karmic conditions of their enmity spanning many generations.
While these two bhikṣus were conversing together with Upānanda in one place, the venerable Śrīgupta passed by their side.
At that time, the two bhikṣus said to Upānanda,
"Venerable sir!..."
If you, Venerable One, were assigned by the community to distribute bedding and determine the order of meals, you too would have caused me mutual distress, just as Sāriputta was deceived by me.
Upānanda said, "Venerable ones!
You all know that this bhikṣu has been appointed by the harmonious Saṃgha to distribute bedding and determine the order of meals."
"For what reason do you show such contempt and revilement in our very presence?
The two replied,
"Venerable Elder!..."
"Is it not permissible for me to weep out of my own distress?
At that time, the monks of few desires heard this and felt contempt and shame, saying:
"How can a monk, knowing that another monk has been assigned by the harmonious Saṃgha to distribute bedding and determine the order of meals, openly express such disdain and disparagement?"
Having reported these circumstances in detail to the Blessed One,
the Blessed One said: "You,
monks, should perform the formal act of censure against the monks Mitra and Bhūmi for their face-to-face disparagement and contempt."
If there are others of a similar class, they too should be reprimanded by performing the ritual procedure.

The *gaṇḍī* should be struck as usual to assemble the Saṃgha; once the assembly has gathered, it should be announced with words, and one bhikṣu should perform the *jñapti-karman* (motion) in this manner:
"Listen, venerable Saṃgha!..."

These two bhikṣus, Citta and Gopa, knowing that the Saṃgha had appointed those bhikṣus to distribute the bedding and furniture of the Saṃgha and to determine the order of meals, spoke words of disparagement and reproach before the Venerable Sthavira Śrīgupta.
If it is the proper time for the Saṃgha and they grant permission, may the Saṃgha allow that the Saṃgha now reprove the two bhikṣus, Yu and Di, for their face-to-face disparagement and reviling.
The motion is thus made.
Next, perform the *karmavācanā*:
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!

These two bhikṣus, Yu and Di, knowing that the harmonious Saṃgha has appointed those bhikṣus to distribute the bedding and furniture of the Saṃgha and to determine the order of meals, have expressed their resentment and disparagement toward them in the presence of the venerable Śrīgupta."
The Saṃgha now censures the two bhikṣus, Upāli and Bhūmi, for their face-to-face disparagement and abuse.
If the venerable ones consent to the censure of the two bhikṣus, Upāli and Bhūmi, let them remain silent; if they do not consent, let them speak.
"This is the first *karmavācanā*.
The second and third are likewise spoken.

"The Saṃgha has now finished its face-to-face censure and reproach of the two bhikṣus, Mitra and Bhūmi. The Saṃgha has granted its consent, as indicated by their silence; thus do I now uphold this decision."

At that time, once the Saṃgha had finished performing the formal act of censure against the two, Upāli and Cūḍapanthaka, for their face-to-face disparagement and slandering, on another occasion the two were conversing together with Upānanda in one place. As Śrīgupta passed by their side, the two of them said to Upānanda:
"Venerable One!"

"If you, Venerable One, were appointed by the Saṃgha to distribute bedding and determine the order of meals, you too would have been as troublesome to me as one person is to another. Upānanda replied:

"You two know that this bhikṣu was appointed by the harmonious Saṃgha to distribute the monks' bedding and determine the order of meals; yet now, under the pretext of some other matter, you do not mention his name and instead express your resentment and disparagement."
The two of them replied,
"How could we harbor resentment or contempt based on names or clan lineages? Upānanda said:
"If you can harbor resentment and disparagement without mentioning another's name or clan, then I too shall likewise revile the entire assembly without mentioning their names."
When the bhikṣus of few desires heard these words, they were filled with resentment and shame, and spoke thus:

"How can a bhikṣu, knowing that the Saṃgha has appointed him to distribute bedding and determine the order of meals, use some pretext not to mention his name, but instead show open contempt and disparage him?"
They immediately reported this matter in detail to the World-Honored One.
The World-Honored One told them:

"You, bhikṣus, should perform a formal act of censure against the two bhikṣus, Mitra and Bhūmi, for falsely using other matters as a pretext to disparage them face-to-face without mentioning their names."
As previously prescribed, it should be performed in this manner:
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!
These two bhikṣus, Yu and Di, know the harmonious Saṃgha to have appointed them as the bhikṣus who shall distribute the bedding and furniture of the Saṃgha and determine the order of meals."
These two bhikṣus, in the presence of the Venerable Sthavira, have under false pretenses avoided mentioning his name and instead openly censured and reviled him.
If the Saṃgha deems the time right and grants its permission, may the Saṃgha authorize that the Saṃgha now reprimand the two bhikṣus, Mitraka and Bhūmika, for their false pretenses and open censure.
The motion is thus made.
Next, the *karmavācanā* (formal ritual act) is performed:
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!
These two bhikṣus, Mittra and Bhūmija, knowing that the Saṃgha had appointed those bhikṣus to distribute the bedding and furniture of the Saṃgha and to determine the order of meals,
slandered them before the Venerable Sthavira Śrīgupta, falsely alleging other matters while failing to mention their names.
The Saṃgha now censures the two bhikṣus, Upāli and Daṇḍapāṇi, for pretexts and for expressing contempt and disparagement in their presence.
If the venerable ones consent to the censure of the two bhikṣus, Upāli and Daṇḍapāṇi, let them remain silent; if they do not consent, let them speak.
"This is the first *karmavācanā*.
The second and third are likewise spoken.

'The Saṃgha has now finished censuring the two bhikṣus, Mitra and Bhūmi, for their face-to-face disparagement under the pretext of other matters. The Saṃgha has granted its consent, as indicated by their silence; thus do I now uphold this.'"

Later, at another time, because the two bhikṣus, Mitra and Bhūmi, had slandered [the Saṃgha] both face-to-face and by means of false pretexts, the Saṃgha performed the formal act of censure (tajjanīya-karman) against them in two ways.
Due to the power of their past karma, these two bhikṣus continued unabatedly to disparage Sthūlananda face-to-face.
When the bhikṣus of few desires heard these words, they were all filled with resentment and shame, saying:
"How can a bhikṣu disparage another face-to-face, or even resort to indirect disparagement?"
He then reported this matter in detail to the Blessed One.
Having assembled the Saṃgha as was his custom for such occasions, the Blessed One addressed the bhikṣus Mitra and Bhūmi:
"Did you two truly engage in face-to-face pretension to disparage the person in charge of distributing bedding and determining the order of meals?"
He replied, “It is indeed so,
Venerable Sir!”
The Blessed One rebuked him in various ways, as extensively explained before, up until: "I shall establish a training rule, which should be recited as follows:
'If a bhikṣu again shows contempt for, reviles, or treats a bhikṣu with disdain, it is a pāyattika.'"
"Furthermore, 'if a bhikṣu' refers to the two individuals, Mitra and Bhūmi; the remaining meanings are as explained above.
'To disparage, revile, or treat with contempt' means either to speak directly to one's face or to manifest such intent by speaking under the pretext of other matters."
The meaning of *pāyattika* is as explained above.
What are the characteristics of the offense and what are its specific instances?

If a bhikṣu has been subjected to the formal act of censure by the Saṃgha, and while the matter concerning those twelve types of persons appointed by the assembly has not yet been concluded, he disparages them out of resentment, it is a *pāyattika*.
If one treats another with contempt, it is a *pāyattika*;
if one treats another with resentment, disparagement, or contempt, it is a *pāyattika*.

Furthermore, if a bhikṣu who has been subjected to the formal act of censure by the Saṃgha treats with resentment or disparagement those among the twelve types of persons appointed by the assembly—even when their duties have ceased—it is a *pāyattika*.
If one treats [a fellow monk] with contempt, it is a *pāyattika*;
if one reviles, slanders, or treats [him] with contempt, it is a *pāyattika*.

If a bhikṣu has not been formally censured by the Saṃgha through a ritual act, yet he reviles or slanders those among the twelve types of persons who have been appointed by the Saṃgha while their duties have not yet ceased, he incurs an *dukkaṭa* offense.
If one treats another with contempt, one incurs an *dukkaṭa* offense;
if one feels resentment, slanders, or treats another with contempt, one incurs an *dukkaṭa* offense.

If a bhikṣu has not been formally reprimanded by the Saṃgha through a ritual act, yet feels resentment or slanders those among the twelve types of persons who have been appointed by the Saṃgha—even if their duties have ceased—he incurs an *dukkaṭa* offense.
If one treats another with contempt, one incurs an *dukkaṭa* offense;
if one treats another with resentment, disparagement, or contempt, one incurs an *dukkaṭa* offense.
The categories of objects and mental perceptions should be understood according to the specific circumstances.
Furthermore, there is no offense for one who is the very first offender, or for one who is insane, mentally deranged, or afflicted by intense pain.
The Thirteenth Training Rule on Contradicting and Annoying through Speech. The Buddha was staying at the Ghoṣitārāma in Kauśāmbī.
At that time, the bhikṣu Chanda had committed numerous offenses and did not confess them according to the Dharma.
Desiring to bring him benefit, peace, and happiness, the bhikṣus said to him:
"Venerable Chanda!"
"You yourself have committed an offense; you should confess it according to the Dharma.
He then replied, "Venerable sirs!"
"Those who have committed offenses should themselves confess and repent.
The bhikṣus said, "Since you yourself have committed the offense,
whom do you intend to send to confess and repent on your behalf?"
Candaka replied,
"If he feels regret, he will know it for himself.
The bhikṣus said:
"You have committed the offense yourself;
whom do you send to repent on your behalf? Chanda replied, "Venerable sirs!"
"Virtuous ones, do not confess your offenses before me; you should confess them before others. Why is this?
You all have gone forth from home, having been born into various lineages and various families."
Just as the trunks and leaves of various trees, though distinct from one another, are gathered together in one place when blown by the wind;
so too it is with you, venerable ones, who have gone forth from home despite being born into various clans and various families.
"Because our World-Honored One has realized Great Enlightenment, you all have come here to rely upon him together.
When they spoke these words in opposition to and in vexation of the instruction, the bhikṣus of few desires, having heard this speech, were filled with mutual disdain and shame, saying:
"How can a bhikṣu, when seeing another provide instruction in accordance with the Dharma, utter such coarse and vulgar words to oppose and vex him?"
He then reported this matter in detail to the Blessed One.
The Blessed One said:
"O bhikṣus, you should perform a formal ritual (karmavācanā) to rebuke the bhikṣu Chanda; should there be others of a similar kind, they should be dealt with in the same manner."
As is the usual procedure for assembling the Saṃgha, one bhikṣu should perform the formal motion (jñapti-karman) as follows:
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!
This bhikṣu Chanda has committed an offense himself but has not confessed it according to the Dharma."
At that time, the bhikṣus, wishing to bring him benefit and cause him to dwell in peace and happiness, informed him according to the Dharma; yet he rejected the instructions of the community.
If the Saṃgha deems the time has come and grants its consent, may the Saṃgha permit that the Saṃgha now reprove the bhikṣu Chanda.
"Thus it is announced.
Next, perform the *karmavācanā*:
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!
This bhikṣu Chanda has committed an offense and does not repent in accordance with the Dharma.

Although the bhikṣus, wishing to bring him benefit and cause him to dwell in peace and happiness, have admonished him according to the Dharma, he has instead opposed and vexed the community’s instruction.
The Saṃgha now censures the bhikṣu Chanda for his refusal to comply with the instruction of the assembly.
If the venerable ones consent to the censure of the bhikṣu Chanda for refusing the instruction of the Saṃgha, let them remain silent; if they do not consent, let them speak.
The second and third times were spoken in the same manner.

"The Saṃgha has now finished its formal censure of the bhikṣu Chanda for his defiance of the community's instruction. The Saṃgha has granted its consent, as indicated by their silence; thus do I now uphold this."
When the bhikṣus had performed the *karmavācanā* exactly as the Buddha had instructed, at that time Chanda thought to himself:
"This is my fault, for I engaged in verbal exchange with these people."
As it is said: "Those who possess wisdom Guard well the four kinds of speech;
Observe the birds of the mountain forests: Though they can speak, they are caught in cages."
Having formed this thought, he thought:
"I should now remain silent and say nothing.
Later, on another occasion, he committed an offense again. At that time, the bhikṣus, wishing for his benefit and for him to dwell in peace and happiness, said to him:
“Cchanda! You have now committed an offense; you should repent according to the Dharma.
He remained silent and did not respond, thereby causing annoyance. Even when spoken to a second and a third time, he remained silent and said nothing.
A bhikṣu of few desires, seeing this, felt disdain and reproach, saying:
"How can a bhikṣu commit an offense himself and remain silent when another points it out, thereby causing him distress?"
He then reported this matter in detail to the Blessed One.
The Blessed One said:

"O bhikṣus, you should perform a formal act of censure against the bhikṣu Chanda for silently harassing others; should there be others of a similar kind, you should likewise perform such a formal act."
As is the usual procedure for assembling the Saṃgha, one bhikṣu should perform the formal motion (*jñapti-karman*) as follows:
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!
This bhikṣu Chanda has committed various offenses and has not repented in accordance with the Dharma."
At that time, the bhikṣus, wishing to bring him benefit, peace, and happiness, addressed him, saying:
"Venerable Chanda, you have committed an offense yourself; you should confess it according to the Dharma."
He then remained silent and without speech, merely causing annoyance through his silence.
If it is the proper time for the Saṃgha and the Saṃgha is willing to listen, may the Saṃgha permit this: the Saṃgha shall now reprove the bhikṣu Chanda for causing annoyance through his silence.
"Thus it is announced.
Next, perform the *karmavācanā*:
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!
This bhikṣu Chanda had committed various offenses and did not repent according to the Dharma.
At that time, the bhikṣus, wishing to bring him benefit and cause him to dwell in peace and happiness, said to him:
"Venerable Chanda, you have committed an offense; you should confess it according to the Dharma."
"When the bhikṣus spoke according to the Dharma, he remained silent and disturbed them with his silence.
The Saṃgha now censures the bhikṣu Chanda for disturbing others with his silence."
Venerable sirs, if you consent to the censure of the bhikṣu Chanda for his silent harassment, remain silent; if you do not consent, speak.
This is the first *karmavācanā*.
A second and third time, he spoke likewise:
"The Saṃgha has now finished censuring the bhikṣu Chanda for his silent harassment; the Saṃgha has granted its consent, as indicated by its silence. Therefore, I now hold it thus."
When the bhikṣus had received the Buddha’s instruction, they rebuked Chanda for silently causing them distress.

Although the assembly performed the formal act of censure against him for his silent harassment, at another time Chanda again committed an offense, and the bhikṣus addressed him with the same words as before.
At that time, whether speaking or remaining silent, Chanda harassed them both.
When the bhikṣus of few desires saw this, they felt revulsion and shame, and spoke thus:
"How can a bhikṣu, having committed an offense himself, fail to repent according to the Dharma, yet when exhorted by another, harasses them by either speaking or remaining silent?"
He then reported this matter in full to the Blessed One.
On account of these causes and conditions, the Blessed One assembled the community of bhikṣus and, eventually, established a training rule for the bhikṣus, which should be recited as follows:
"If a bhikṣu again violates or disregards verbal instructions, it is a pāyattika."
"Furthermore, 'if a bhikṣu' refers to Chanda; the remaining meanings are as explained above.
'Contrary to and vexing the verbal instruction' means expressing oneself with words intended to cause vexation to others."
*Pāyattika* has the meaning as explained above.
What is the nature of the offense and what are its specific circumstances?
If there is a bhikṣu who goes to another bhikṣu and speaks as follows:
"Venerable sir!

Have you seen a bhikṣu with freshly shaven hair and beard, wearing a crimson outer robe, carrying a bowl substituted by another object and holding a mendicant’s staff, or perhaps one who has filled his bowl to the brim with ghee, honey, granulated sugar, or rock honey, and is departing while carrying it?"
When questioned by him, he replied:
"I truly did not see any such signs,
O Bhikṣu!"
"I see a bhikṣu walking away on two feet.
If a bhikṣu intentionally speaks these words to disturb or annoy another, he commits a pāyattika offense.
If someone else comes and asks:
“Did you see a bhikṣuṇī passing by here with the appearance of robes and bowl as previously described?
She replied, “I truly did not see a bhikṣuṇī with such an appearance of robes and bowl passing by; I only saw a bhikṣuṇī walking away on her two feet.”
If a bhikṣu intentionally speaks such words to disturb another, he incurs a pāyattika.
The same applies, through the same questions and answers as before, for śikṣamāṇās, śrāmaṇeras, and śrāmaṇerīs; they also incur a pāyattika.
If someone else comes and asks:
"Have you seen any laypeople passing by here carrying sugarcane, bamboo, reeds, firewood, grass, or jars of ghee?"
He then replied:
"I truly did not see such a person; I only saw someone walking away on two feet.
If a bhikṣu causes such vexation, it is a pāyattika offense.
If someone were to ask:
"Have you seen any laymen wearing garments of blue, yellow, red, white, or other colors, carrying vessels of ghee and the like, passing by this way?"
...and so on, until he replies:
"I only saw a layperson walking away on two legs.
Just as it is with men, one should understand that the same applies in detail to seeing women and others; when spoken with an agitated mind, one incurs a *pāyattika* offense in all such cases.
As it is with speaking, so it is with remaining silent; in both cases, one incurs an offense of downfall (*pāyattika*).
There is no offense if, for instance, a bhikṣu sees hunters pursuing deer or other game entering the monastery, and after the bhikṣu has seen them, the hunter asks:
"Noble One!..."
"Have you seen any deer running past here?
The bhikṣu should not answer, "I have seen one.
If it is a cold season, he should reply to the butcher:
"O virtuous one!
You may enter the heated room for a short while to warm yourself by the fire.
If it is hot, he should say:
"O noble one!
You may enter the cool chamber for a moment, drink some clear cold water, and rest for a short while.
If the hunter says:
"I am not weary; I shall ask the fleeing deer.
He should first examine his own fingernails and then reply to that person, saying:
"Nokha-paśyāmi. (I see [the deer].)
If asked again, one should look at the great void and reply to that person:
"Namo bhasme. According to the Sanskrit pronunciation: [Namo bhasme].
*Nakha* means "nail" and also means "not"; *paśya* means "seeing"; and *mi* means "I. Thus, it refers to "my seeing with the nails," which also signifies "my not seeing."
When a bhikṣu examines his own fingernails with his eyes, it immediately demonstrates that he is not speaking falsely.

When that person hears it said that "non-existence" is taught, they will conclude that there is nothing that is not seen; thus, the Buddha opens the gate of skillful means to save suffering sentient beings.
If translated literally, it says:
"I observe the fingernail.
There is no principle that is not mutually perceived; therefore, I have retained the original Sanskrit term, which can only be explained in detail through oral instruction.
The term *naba* carries two meanings:
first, it refers to the great void; second, it signifies "not.
It likewise cannot be translated into an Eastern language; regarding this, one should not adhere to [the interpretation of] *nakha*. Consider this in detail as explained in the extensive commentary.
It is just as when one observes the hair on one’s arm here in this world and says, "I see hair";
this, too, refers to its lack of intrinsic meaning. If a hunter were to say:
"I do not ask about the fingernails nor the ether; rather, I ask whether it is permissible to kill a sentient being here or not?
The bhikṣu should then survey the four directions and reflect thus:
"In the ultimate sense (*paramārtha-satya*), all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) are fundamentally devoid of a sentient being."
He immediately replied to him,
"I do not see any sentient beings.
In all such cases, there is no offense.
If a bhikṣu, when questioned by others, does not speak according to the facts, he incurs a *pāyattika* offense in all such cases.
Furthermore, there is no offense for the very first offender, or for one who is insane, mentally deranged, or afflicted by intense physical pain.
At that time, all the bhikṣus were filled with doubt and together went to where the Buddha was, saying to him:
"World-Honored One!

For what reason did the bhikṣu Chanda, when fellow practitioners of the holy life exhorted him in accordance with the Dharma, fail to heed their words and instead disturb them with his speech, ultimately causing the Saṃgha to perform a formal act of censure against him and subjecting him to such distress?"
The World-Honored One said:

"This Chanda has not only troubled the bhikṣus and disobeyed the words of his virtuous friends today; in the past as well, he troubled and disturbed his virtuous friends because of his speech, thereby bringing suffering upon himself."
"You all should listen!
In the distant past, there was a large pond where a flock of geese and various turtles lived together.
Among them was one turtle who formed a close friendship with two geese, and they were deeply affectionate toward one another."
Later, at another time, a great drought occurred and the waters of the pond were nearly exhausted. Then those two geese both went to the place where the turtle was and said to him:
"Friend! You may dwell here safely in this mud; we shall seek out other ponds in other directions."
The turtle said to the goose:
"We have lived together for a long time and our bond is one of mutual affection; that you would abandon me and depart elsewhere when I am about to face calamity is truly unacceptable!"
The goose asked,
"What do you wish to do?
The tortoise replied:
"You all should take me along with you.
The geese said,
"How can we take you?"
The turtle said, "If you all hold a staff together at its ends and I bite it in the middle, we shall reach the clear pond together; would this not be a good thing?
The geese said:
"I have no objection to traveling together with you;

however, because your natural disposition is to engage in idle talk and you cannot guard your speech, you will surely drop the staff and fall through the air. When we see this happen, our grief and suffering will only increase."
The turtle said,
"I shall guard my mouth and hold the staff in my beak without speaking.
The goose said:
"This is a good plan," they said, and immediately sought out a staff, each biting one end. The turtle bit the middle, and they soared into the air and flew away, eventually passing over a city.
At that time, those people saw in the sky a goose carrying a turtle; filled with wonder and astonishment, they said to one another:
"Sirs, look! Those two geese are stealing a single turtle together."
Upon hearing these words, the turtle remained silent and endured them without speaking.
He then arrived at another city and again passed through the marketplace; when the men and women there lamented as before, the turtle thought to himself:
"How much longer must I endure this hardship, constantly holding my neck out and guarding my mouth so that I cannot speak?"
He immediately replied, "I intended to leave of my own accord; I did not come here as a thief.
As he spoke these words, his staff suddenly slipped from his hand and fell to the ground. The boys beat him together until he died.
Having seen this, the two geese were filled with sorrow and resentment, and they flew away through the air.
At that time, there was a deva in the sky who, having witnessed this event, spoke a verse:
"If one cannot rely upon or act according to the beneficial words of a good friend;..."
"Falling and suffering hardship, just like the tortoise that let go of its staff.
"O bhikṣus, do not harbor other thoughts: the tortoise of that time was none other than Chanda; the geese of that time were none other than Nanda and Upananda."
In the past, having heard the words of a virtuous friend, you refused to rely upon or act according to them, which ultimately led to your death.

Even now, it is the same: you refuse to rely upon the words of your fellow practitioners of the holy life (*brahmacārin*), whether by speaking or remaining silent, thereby harassing and disturbing others and causing the Saṃgha to perform a formal act of censure against you.

14. The Training Rule on Placing Monastic Bedding in the Open Air. The fourteenth training rule concerning the placement of monastic bedding in the open air. At that time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, the Garden of Anāthapiṇḍada.
At that time, the householder Sudatta invited the Buddha and the Saṃgha to his home for a meal.

When the bhikṣus, during the first part of the day, took up their robes and bowls and proceeded to the householder’s residence, the World-Honored One remained within the monastery and sent someone to fetch the food.
The Buddha has five reasons for eating in the monastery.
What are these five?
First, he requires personal quietude and silence.
2. Preaching the Dharma for the devas;
3. Visiting those who are ill;
4. Inspecting the bedding and furnishings of the Sangha.
5. He established the training rules for the bhikṣus.
At that time, the Buddha wished to inspect the monastic bedding and furnishings and to establish the training rules; for this reason, he remained within the monastery and had people bring him food.

At that time, after the World-Honored One and the assembly of monks had departed, he took the keys and inspected all the dwellings within the monastery, and even observed all the groves and gardens in the vicinity outside the monastery.
Next, he went to an old dwelling where many bedding materials were placed out in the open air. Suddenly, an unseasonable wind and rain arrived in thick torrents. The Buddha thought to himself:

"These bedding materials were all offered by faithful brahmins and lay devotees who, through self-denial, reduced their own portions and even those of their wives and children to give to the Saṃgha in pursuit of supreme merit."
"When the bhikṣus use [the bedding], they do not know its proper measure, nor do they guard it well, but discard it wherever they please.

Having seen this, the World-Honored One exercised his supernormal powers to dispel the wind and rain; yet heavy clouds gathered and spread, hanging low without dispersing, awaiting the World-Honored One’s withdrawal of the bedding.

At that time, the World-Honored One personally took his bedding and arranged it within the chamber; he then took his rain-cloak and went outside the monastery, intending to bathe. He immediately withdrew his supernormal powers, whereupon thunder and lightning darkened the day and a torrential rain fell, moistening both the high and the low ground alike.
After the Buddha had washed his body, he washed his feet, entered his room, and remained there in silent meditation.
At that time, the bhikṣu who was to take food arrived carrying the meal; having set it aside, he approached the World-Honored One and prostrated at his feet.
It is the constant custom of the Blessed One to exchange friendly greetings with those who bring food, asking:
"Has the community of bhikṣus received sufficient food and drink to be satisfied?
They replied:
"Venerable Sir!
All have been fully satisfied.
He then offered the food to the World-Honored One.
At that time, when the Blessed One had finished his meal, he went outside the cell, chewed a tooth-stick, and washed his feet; he then re-entered the cell and remained there in silent meditation.
Later, when the sun had reached the hour of *pradoṣa*, the Blessed One sat down upon his usual seat and addressed the bhikṣus, saying:
"Just after the Saṃgha had gone to take their meal, I took the keys and inspected the dwellings throughout, seeing many bedding mats laid out in the open air."
At that time, as it was about to rain, I used my supernormal powers to clear away all the clouds and personally gathered up [the water].
Then I addressed the bhikṣus, saying:

"There are donors who, through great hardship to their own bodies, give to the Saṃgha in pursuit of merit; yet you are unable to use these offerings in accordance with the Dharma, thus wasting the gifts of faith."
He then spoke in verse:
"Regarding the gifts of others' faith, one should know the proper measure in their enjoyment;
thus one attains peace for oneself and causes the merit of others to increase."

At that time, the Blessed One, having praised contentment and the proper use of offerings made out of faith in accordance with the Dharma, addressed the bhikṣus at length as previously stated, up until: "I now establish this training rule for the bhikṣus, which should be recited as follows:
'If a bhikṣu places monastic bedding and various seats in an open area and, upon departing, neither puts them away himself nor instructs another to put them away, it is a pāyattika.'"

Thus, after the Blessed One had established the training rules for the bhikṣus, there were many bhikṣus who, traveling through the countryside following a caravan, arrived at a certain city where there was a residence for bhikṣus.
At that time, the bhikṣus wished to seek a place to stay. Then a certain man said to the bhikṣus:
"Noble ones! Why do you not go to the monastery to stay the night?"
He replied, "O worthy one!
I am bound by my travel with a caravan and have no freedom of action; if I were to stop at the monastery, I would lose my companions."
He said, "Noble one!
Simply stay overnight at the monastery; when the merchants depart, I shall call for you."
Then the bhikṣus went to the monastery and spread out the monastic bedding, staying there to sleep wherever they found space.
During the latter part of the night, the traveling merchants departed; only one pack animal remained, and when its keeper finally woke up, he rose quickly in alarm and called out to the bhikṣus:
"The merchants have already left; you should depart at once!"
When the bhikṣus heard his call, they immediately rose quickly; having first washed their hands, they prepared the bedding.
Because this took so much time, the merchants eventually moved far away.
At that time, the bhikṣus pursued them from behind, but they were subsequently plundered by bandits and lost their robes and bowls; they then arrived at the Jetavana Grove.
Upon seeing them, the resident bhikṣus said:
"Welcome! Welcome!"
"Are you all traveling in peace and safety?
They replied,
"How could there be peace and safety?"
"I have been robbed by bandits. He asked,
"For what reason?"
Then the visiting bhikṣu related the matter in full.
When the bhikṣus had heard this, they reported the entire incident to the Blessed One.
The Blessed One said:
"If there is a bhikṣu at the place where one is staying, one should entrust [one's affairs] to him before departing.
When the bhikṣus heard this instruction from the Buddha, whenever they had a reason to leave, they all entrusted their affairs before going.
At that time, there were two householders in the city of Śrāvastī who were mutual enemies:
one possessed faith, while the other was devoid of faith.
The one who possessed faith thought to himself:
"What cause have I now for increasing enmity?
I should abandon hatred and evil and go forth into homelessness.
He then went to the Jeta Grove, approached a bhikṣu, and requested to rely upon him for the sake of the dharma of going forth.
Then that faithless householder asked one person:
"Do you happen to know where that certain householder is now?
He replied:
"He has already abandoned the secular life and gone forth into homelessness. He asked, "Where?"
He replied,
"Among the śramaṇas, the sons of the Śākya.
He reported this, saying:
"Is that place truly the City of Fearlessness?
I shall go there and punish him according to the law for his harmful actions.
At that time, a person who was a close friend of that bhikṣu heard these words and went to inform him, saying:
“Venerable sir!
Do you know?
That faithless householder has made a solemn appointment with me, speaking these words:”
"Is Jetavana Grove the City of Fearlessness?
I shall go there and punish him according to the law for performing such unbeneficial acts.
Upon hearing this, the bhikṣu thought to himself:
"Out of fear of him, I have come forth into the homeless life; how could I encounter that same fear again in this very place?
It would be best for me now to flee to another region.
Having thought thus, he went to his teacher and said:
“Upādhyāya! It was out of fear of him that I sought ordination; now I have heard that he has come intending to harm me.
The preceptor asked:
"Who is that person? He replied,
"He is an old enemy."
The teacher said,
"If it is so, where do you wish to go to escape this calamity?
He replied:
"I now wish to go toward the city of Rājagṛha.
The teacher said,
"Go as you please."
He then took leave of his teacher, took up his robes and bowl, and set out for the royal city.
At that time, the faithless elder went to the Jeta Grove and asked a bhikṣu,
“Noble one!
"Do you know that the householder named So-and-so has come here to renounce the world? Where is he now?
He replied, "He has already departed."
Question:
"In which direction?
Answer: "He replied:"
"Head toward Rājagṛha.
He replied, "That too is not the City of Fearlessness; I shall go there to perform deeds that bring no benefit."
Then that householder took provisions for the journey and pursued him.
The bhikṣu departed at the proper time and did not depart at improper times;
the layman, however, proceeded without ceasing, whether at the proper time or at improper times.
Along the way, there was a monastery. At that time, the elder caught up with the bhikṣu and saw from afar that the bhikṣu had entered the monastery.
The elder thought to himself:
"If he enters the monastery intending to speak with me, there are many people there who will surely harm me."
"I shall know for myself when it is time to set out on the road.
Having had this thought, he sought another place to rest.
Then, when dawn had broken, that bhikṣu said to the other bhikṣus:
"You may now inspect the bedding; I wish to proceed ahead.
The bhikṣus asked, "Where do you wish to go?"
He replied,
"I wish to go to the royal city.
The bhikṣu said in response:
"You should seek this path; do not travel by other ways.
He replied, "Farewell."
He then proceeded forward.
At that time, the elder entered the monastery at dawn and asked a bhikṣu,
"Where is the bhikṣu so-and-so now?"
He replied,
"I have already headed toward the royal city. He asked:
"Which road shall we take?
He replied, "This road."
Then that householder hurried along the road, caught up with the bhikṣu, and said to him:
"Hey! Shaven-headed śramaṇa, where do you intend to go?"
The bhikṣu replied,
"O worthy one!
I have already gone forth from home, desiring to eliminate enmity and strife."
He replied, "I am here now to eliminate this enmity and dispute.
He then struck the bhikṣu severely with a staff until he was nearly dead; the monk's robes and bowl were all shattered, and with only his life remaining, he crawled back toward the monastery.
A bhikṣu saw him and asked:
"Venerable one!
For what reason do you bear such a distressed appearance?"
He then asked the bhikṣu:
"Did you see any layperson come here?
What did they say?"
Then that bhikṣu related the matter in full and said to the bhikṣus:
"If I had not informed the Venerable One of his destination, I certainly would not have encountered such suffering."
The bhikṣus then reported this matter in detail to the Blessed One. The Blessed One said:
"Except for specific circumstances, one must otherwise entrust [one's bowl] to another.

At that time, the Blessed One praised those who uphold the precepts, those who revere the precepts, and those who are content with few desires; having delivered a teaching in accordance with the Dharma, he addressed the bhikṣus:

“I perceive ten benefits as explained at length above; the former was the original enactment, while this is a subsequent allowance. For the sake of the bhikṣus, I establish this training rule, which should be recited as follows:

‘If a bhikṣu, having placed monastic bedding or various seats in an open area, departs without lifting them himself or instructing another to lift them, and if there is no other bhikṣu to whom he has entrusted them—unless there is a special reason—this is a pāyattika.’”
"Furthermore, 'if a bhikṣu' refers to one among those in this Dharma;
the remaining meanings are as explained above. 'The Saṅgha' refers to the disciples of the Tathāgata.
'Requisites' (śayanāsana) refers to large beds, woolen rugs, blankets, quilts, carpets, pillows, and so forth."
"Miscellaneous items" refers to small beds, stools, and other requisites.
"In an open space" means in a place that is not covered.
"When departing" means when one has left the boundary of influence.
The Venerable Upāli addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Bhadanta, when one is separated from bedding and furniture, at what distance does it constitute the 'sphere of influence'?"
The World-Honored One replied:

"It is like the method by which the Brahmin Jātiśroṇa plants mango trees: he plants one tree every seven *vyāmas*, so that their branches grow tall and lush and their flowers and fruits are abundant; within the space of seven trees, there are forty-nine *vyāmas*."
"When bedding and seats are placed in an open space, one must entrust them to someone else for a distance equal to this [specified] range; once beyond this boundary, they must be gathered up.
"Not lifting them oneself" and "not instructing another to lift them" refers to not gathering them up.
"Regarding 'there being a bhikṣu,' this refers to a person currently present who is capable of receiving an entrustment.
There are five kinds of entrustment. What are the five?"
One should reply to the host, saying:
