"Venerable one! This is the dwelling; this room may be inspected. These are the bedding and furnishings; these should be kept. This is the key to the door."
If there are no bhikṣus at that place, one should entrust [the keys] to a śrāmaṇera;
if there is none of these, one should entrust them to a layperson;
if there is none of these, one should look around in the four directions for a secure place to hide the door key, and only then depart.
If one encounters a bhikṣu along the way, one should inform him, saying:
"I have hidden my door-keys in such-and-such a place; you may take them.
Regarding the phrase "except for special circumstances," this refers to excluding cases involving difficult conditions.
The meaning of *pāyattika* is as explained above.
Regarding the characteristics of the offense herein, what are the specific circumstances?

If a bhikṣu has arranged bedding or seating for the Saṃgha and intentionally departs without entrusting it to another, he incurs a *duṣkṛta* (wrongdoing) as long as he has not yet left the boundary (*sīmā*). Once he has left the boundary, he incurs a *pāyattika*.
If, at the time of first departing, one forgets to entrust the matter and remembers it while on the road, one should form this thought:
"I have placed the monastic bedding and requisites in such-and-such a place; when any fellow practitioner of the holy life comes and sees them, they should lift and store them away."
The bhikṣu practicing this course of conduct should reflect in his mind and say aloud:
"I shall never again commit such an act; I shall confess according to the Dharma whatever offense I have committed."
If he should encounter a bhikṣu on the road, he should say to him:
"Venerable one!
I have been using the bedding and furniture belonging to the Saṃgha at such-and-such a place; you should collect and put it away."
Reflecting that this bhikṣu will certainly be restrained, one should further mentally resolve and verbally declare:
"I shall never again commit such an act; I must repent for my offense according to the Dharma."
If one only remembers it upon arriving at the dwelling place, one should form this thought:
"I have placed the bedding for the Saṅgha in such-and-such a place; when any fellow-practitioner of the holy life sees it, they shall pick it up and store it away."
This bhikṣu should reflect in his mind and speak these words:
"I shall never again commit such an act.
When he arrives at his residence, if he sees a bhikṣu who intends to go to that place, he should say to him:
"Venerable one!
I have used the bedding and furnishings belonging to the Saṃgha at such-and-such a place in such-and-such a monastery;
you should collect and put them away. Thinking that this bhikṣu will certainly take care of them, one should further mentally reflect and speak these words aloud:
"I should not act in this manner.

If a bhikṣu places monastic bedding in an open space and enters his room with the intention of sitting in stillness to pacify a distracted mind, he may leave at his own discretion only after he has attained meditative concentration; if he does so until the first watch of the night without damaging the bedding, he incurs a *dukkaṭa* (offense of wrong-doing); if he damages it, he incurs a *pāyattika* (offense of falling).
The Venerable Upāli addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Bhagavān, Great Virtuous One!
How many kinds of damage are there to bedding and seating materials?"
The Buddha told Upāli:
“There are two kinds of destruction:
namely, wind and rain.”
"If the wind blows it so that it becomes crumpled, this is called destruction by wind.
If the rain makes it thoroughly damp, this is called destruction by rain.

If a bhikṣu leaves his bedding exposed at dusk and fails to retrieve it by the time of the middle watch, nor does he guard it himself or have someone else do so, if it is not damaged he incurs a *duṣkṛta* offense; if it is damaged, he incurs a *pāyattika* offense.

In this manner, there are one watch, one and a half watches, two watches, two and a half watches, three watches, three and a half watches, four watches, and four and a half watches. Since the night in the west consists of three periods, these are divided into ten segments for the sake of clarity; however, following the convention of this region, they are counted as five watches so that those who seek [this knowledge] may easily understand them: the time of sunrise, the time of the light meal, the time of mid-morning, the time approaching noon, the time of exact noon, the time past noon, the time of the sun’s apex, the time of the afternoon snack, the time after the afternoon snack, and the time of dusk.

If a bhikṣu, having arranged the bedding and mats for the Saṃgha during the day, does not inspect them within that same period, he incurs an *dukkaṭa* (offense of wrong-doing) if they have not been damaged, and an *pāyattika* (offense of falling) if they have been damaged.
The summary verse says:
Reciting the sūtras while seated on a small bench; because of listening [to the Dharma], one may sit on a lion throne;
when a layperson borrows a seat, it should be lent to them at the appropriate time.
If these items were given by someone else, they may be taken back once their use is finished;
one should record the name of the donor and fashion Buddha images according to one's inclination.
When attending to a sick person, one must observe them closely and not entrust them to the five types of persons.
When receiving the Dharma, act as a representative for the teacher; failing to rely [on the teacher] is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*).
When a youth fasts due to illness, one should collect his requisites upon seeing him sitting among laypeople.
Regarding damage by fire or water, and when it is the proper time, one should first collect one's own belongings.
At that time, there were brahmins, householders, and others who came to the dwelling place of the bhikṣus and spoke these words:
"Noble ones!
Please expound the sublime Dharma for us."
The bhikṣus replied, “O noble ones!
The Blessed One is currently present; for what reason do you not go to listen to the Dharma?”
They said, "Noble ones!

Our sole Great Teacher has many who come to seek him; he proclaims the essentials of the Dharma for devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, humans, and non-humans. We have had no opportunity to listen and receive it in our haste; you should recite the Dharma for us."
The bhikṣus replied,
"The Blessed One has not yet permitted one to recite the Dharma for another.
Then the bhikṣus reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"One should recite the scriptures for them.
The bhikṣus addressed the Buddha, saying:
"We do not know how to recite the scriptures for them."
The Buddha said,
"They should sit on small seats and recite the Dharma for him.
When the householder Anāthapiṇḍada heard that the Blessed One had permitted the bhikṣus to sit on seats while reciting the sūtras, he immediately offered five hundred small seats to the Saṃgha.
At that time, all the bhikṣus were reciting the sūtras loudly in one place, creating such a great clamor that it was impossible to listen or contemplate.
The bhikṣus reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"You should have one person recite the sūtra for the assembly, while the others should listen."
At that time, he did not know whom he should have recite it:
the elder or the younger?
He went at once to inform the Buddha, who said:
"They should be arranged in order from the oldest to the youngest.
At that time, the youths were placed at the end of the procession to proclaim the essentials of the Dharma, which caused the minds of the audience to lack reverence.
The World-Honored One said:
"One should recite the scriptures while seated in the place of the senior elder.
At the time of expounding the Dharma, an elderly bhikṣu failed to maintain an air of reverence. The Buddha said:
"One should set aside two or three senior elders and have [the reciter] sit and chant the sūtra.
At that time, the Dharma master felt his majestic authority was diminished and lacked sufficient dignity. The Buddha said:
"Place a lion throne in the position of the senior elders and have him chant the sūtra there."
When ascending and descending was somewhat difficult, the Buddha said:
"If it is a fixed location, one should use bricks to construct a stepped path; if the location is not fixed, one should make a wooden ladder."
The Dharma Master spat, which caused others to feel resentment. The Buddha said, "One should place a spittoon.
Many flies gathered there, so the Buddha said:
"Place grass inside, or put sand and soil there.
After a long time, it became foul-smelling. The Buddha said:
"It should be washed at the proper time and dried in the sun."
At that time, those listening to the Dharma sat in a single row; those at the end of the row could not hear the teaching. The Buddha said:
"One should arrange the seats in two rows, either in the shape of a half-moon or in the form of a square pond."
At that time, there were lay followers of faith and reverence who invited the bhikṣus to their homes for a meal; the bhikṣus did not accept, whereupon the brahmins and householders said:
"Noble ones!..."
"If the Buddha, the World-Honored One, had not appeared in this world, the various non-Buddhist practitioners would have been our field of merit.

Now that the Buddha has appeared in the world, you, sirs, are our most excellent and sublime field of merit. If we come to invite you and you do not grant us permission, how could we possibly abandon the provisions for the journey on the path to the next world?"
At that time, the bhikṣus reported the matter to the Buddha.
The Buddha said, "If someone comes to invite you, you should accept it.
When that host was preparing the offerings, he lacked sufficient seating; he went to the bhikṣus to request a temporary loan of some, but the bhikṣus would not give them. The Buddha said:
"It should be given.
After the bhikṣus had finished eating, they took [the food] themselves and returned;
the laypeople said to them, "You gentlemen should go on your way; we shall take it back ourselves."
The bhikṣus, being afraid, were unwilling to leave it with him.
The Buddha said, "Leave it with him. The donor replied:
"Noble One,
please stay and drink some non-timely beverage.
The bhikṣu did not consent, and the Buddha said:
"One should remain seated until after one has finished drinking before departing.
At that time, when laypeople encountered matters requiring their presence and were unable to return the seats they had left behind, the Buddha said:
"They should be taken [back]."
At that time, the bhikṣus did not know whom to send to fetch it.
The Buddha said:
"The ghaṇṭā should be struck to have a junior monk fetch it."
Furthermore, there were laypeople who, having prepared offerings, came to the bhikṣus to borrow items for sitting; the bhikṣus did not give them.
They then replied, "We have prepared these offerings for your sake; why do you not give us the seats yourselves to sit upon?"
The Buddha said, "It should be given.
At that time, the bhikṣus finished their meal and departed, leaving [the food] behind, whereupon it was stolen by thieves. The Buddha said:
"It should be commanded that a bhikṣu act as the guardian.
That guardian lived together with laypeople, and people asked him:
"Noble one!..."
"How could you possibly wish to eat a second meal?
The bhikṣu replied, "I do not do so for the sake of food;
I am merely looking at the seating materials."
The layperson replied,
"How could I possibly steal the seat you left behind?
If you do not believe me, you may take it yourself."
He was unable to maintain [the practice], so the Buddha said:
"You should stay in a separate area; do not mingle with worldly people.
At that time, worldly people called out for food as before, so the Buddha said:
"If there is one reciting the sūtras, they should remain to one side while reciting.

If there is one practicing meditative concentration, they should sit to one side and contemplate with focused attention on dhyāna, continuing to observe their seat until the laypeople have dispersed, at which point they may depart."
At that time, there were remnants of food and oily impurities defiling the sitting mats; the bhikṣus discarded them. The Buddha said:
"If they are defiled by remnants of food, they should be washed with water; if they are defiled by oil, one should use soap powder (sādu)."
"If it is defiled by impurities, you must scrub and wash it with earth and cow dung before you may take it away.
As the Buddha had thus instructed those who were to recite the Dharma, at that time the bhikṣus sat in the open air and were oppressed by the sun's rays;
the Buddha said, "You should cover them with a canopy."
At that time, having encountered wind and rain, they abandoned it and departed; consequently, it was damaged.
The Buddha said, "It should be brought inside.
[The monks] did not know who should bring it in.
The Buddha said:
"Let the great assembly collect [the seats] carefully.
Since many were spread out at the seating places for the elders, the aged, being weak in strength, were unable to lift them up. The Buddha said:
“The junior monks should collect [the items], while the senior and elder monks may set aside those for later distribution.
At that time, they were gathered in one place until they became moldy and spoiled. The Buddha said:
“Distribute them and store them separately.”
At that time, the bhikṣus no longer recited the scriptures.
The Buddha said, "Whether in an open space or under cover, you may recite the scriptures according to your preference.

At that time, there were among the lay followers those who possessed faith and reverence; they all used genuine pearls, precious objects, gold, and silver for ornamentation, and covered the lion throne with exquisite garments.
At that time, the bhikṣus did not dare to sit down. The Buddha said:
"If you conceive of the objects as mundane things or as impermanent, there is no fault in sitting.

Later, when they encountered wind and rain, the bhikṣus placed only the monastic property inside while leaving their secular clothes outside; consequently, the latter were damaged. Thereupon, the Buddha said:
"It should be placed inside.
At that time, there was a donor who constructed two dwellings:
one within a village and one in an araṇya (forest hermitage).
In that village monastery, bedding and requisites were abundant, whereas in the *āraṇya* (forest hermitage), the beds and mats were sparse.

Later, at another time, a great assembly was to be held within the *āraṇya*. When the bhikṣus saw there were no seats, they went to the village monastery to borrow some temporarily; however, the residents there refused to give them any. The Buddha said:
"They should give."
If one suspects that it will rain or while it is actually raining, one should not give [the robe].
At that time, if one encounters rain while on the road, one should place it under a tree or by a wall, covering it with a single cloth.
They used fine cloths to cover [the offerings], and the Buddha said:
"One should use coarse ones to cover them.
Once the offerings had been prepared, they did not immediately return them, and everyone thought to themselves:
"Both of these are the property of a single donor.
The Buddha said:
"This belongs definitively to him; it should not be used for anything else."
As the property of the two monasteries became intermingled and difficult to distinguish, the Buddha said:
"One should write the name of the monastery upon the items, and also write the name of the donor, stating: 'This is the gift of so-and-so.'"
Then the householder Anāthapiṇḍika approached the Buddha, prostrated at his feet, sat to one side, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!
When the Buddha, the World-Honored One, sits at the head of the assembly, the assembly becomes majestic and solemn."
"If the assembly does not sit [in this manner], it will lack majesty and virtue.
If the Blessed One would grant permission, I wish to create an image of Jambudvīpa and place it at the head of the assembly.
The Blessed One replied:
"You may fashion it as you wish and place it at the head of the assembly.
At that time, while the great assembly was seated in the open air, they encountered rain from the heavens; the bhikṣus then abandoned the image and entered the monastery.
At that time, some brahmins and householders, having seen this, mocked them, saying:
"Why, sirs, do you cast away the Great Teacher?
The Buddha said:
"You should have laypeople or śrāmaṇeras move the image and bring it inside.
If none of these are available, you bhikṣus should lift it in yourselves, conceiving of yourselves as the Great Teacher."
At that time, there were many bhikṣus who each encountered illness but had no one to attend to them.
The Buddha said, "If there is one who is ill, they should be attended to."
The Buddha sent [monks] to attend to the sick, but the bhikṣus did not know whom to appoint for the care. The Buddha said:
"From the senior-most monk down to the junior-most, everyone should attend to the sick."
At that time, there were elder bhikṣus who all came to inquire after his illness and stood waiting; because he was suffering from the affliction, the Buddha said:
"You should sit and look after that sick person."
At that time, the bhikṣus took their seats with them. When some laypeople who lacked faith saw this, they asked in astonishment, "Noble ones, do you wish to view a dance and music performance now?
The bhikṣus reported this to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"Those who attend to the sick should not take their own seats with them; rather, the caregivers should provide many seating items for the patient.
At that time, the group of six bhikṣus also came to inquire after the sick, but they engaged in much idle talk by the patient's side. Then the caregiver said to them:
"Venerable sirs!"
"You had better leave now and cease providing for the sick.
The group of six replied, "Do as you wish;
who would ever obstruct you?"
He replied, "Venerable sir,
you should observe that I wish to travel elsewhere.
The group of six replied:
"If the patient dies, you shall take possession of the six types of requisites; why then do you have me attend to this sick person?
Having thus reviled him, he made the patient examine his miscellaneous belongings and then departed immediately.
At that time, the patient was unable to maintain self-restraint and consequently suffered harm. He reported this matter to the Buddha.
The Buddha said:
"There are five kinds of persons whom one should not entrust with the task of observing [the patient]."

What are the five? First, those who lack a sense of shame; second, those with whom one has a grudge; third, those who are aged and infirm; fourth, those who are ill and weak; and fifth, those who have not yet received full ordination.
Then the Venerable Upāli asked the Blessed One:
"If two bhikṣus are sitting together on one seat, when they rise and depart, who should collect and put away [the bedding]?"
The Buddha said:
"Those who arise later should collect and put it away; if they arise at the same time, those who are younger should collect it, and if they are of the same age, they should lift it together."

At that time, there were two teachers—the preceptor and the instructor—who went outside for walking meditation (caṅkrama), while their disciples and followers remained inside the monastery; consequently, they were unable to increase their wholesome qualities (*kuśaladharma*), like lotuses deprived of water. The Buddha said:
"When the two teachers go out, the disciples should follow them."
At that time, those two teachers carried their own seats while their disciples followed behind with their hands hanging down. The Buddha said:
"Disciples and followers should carry the seats and follow along."
At that time, those two teachers were sweeping the walking path themselves while their disciples stood idly by. The Buddha said:

"If a disciple or follower sees his teacher holding a broom, he should step in to do it for him so that the teacher may rest. However, if the teacher has been assigned by the community to perform the sweeping, there is no fault in not assisting him."
If those two teachers are engaged in needlework and sewing while the disciple remains idle, the Buddha said:
"You should assist them so as not to let them suffer hardship."
"If the teacher is assigned by the community to sew robes, there is no fault in [the disciple] not acting as his substitute.
At that time, when the disciples received their lessons, they would begin reciting and practicing them immediately in the presence of their teacher. The Buddha said:
"Once you have received your lesson, you should move away from where you can hear [the teacher] and practice your recitation in a place where you can see him."
Those who practice meditative concentration, having received and attained the Dharma, may proceed to another location to engage in quiet reflection and settle their minds.
If they see the two teachers being sent on errands for the community, they should also inquire after them at the appropriate time and take turns assisting them with their labors.
"If you go for a walking meditation together with two teachers and take a seat with you, you should bring it back.
At that time, a disciple went ahead while the teacher remained behind; encountering some other business, the teacher was unable to follow. The Buddha said:
"When the disciple returns, he should ask the teacher, saying:"
"Does the Master wish to return?
If he says, "I shall return," [then proceed].
In such a case, one should take the seat and depart.
If they say, "I have not yet returned! [one should wait].
"You need not carry seats.
O bhikṣus, as I have prescribed, those who do not act accordingly commit an offense against the Dharma.
— *Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya*, Fascicle 28.
The Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya, Scroll Twenty-nine,
translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Yijing by Imperial Decree.
The remainder of the Fourteenth Training Rule on Not Folding Bedding. At that time, the Blessed One was staying in Śrāvastī at the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
Then, a householder invited the Buddha and the Saṃgha to his home for a meal.
At that time, there was a young bhikṣu who, exerting himself in body and mind, cultivated various wholesome qualities. He then thought to himself:

"Today the Buddha and the Saṃgha have accepted an invitation; I shall not enter the city to beg for food and drink, but will instead recite my prayers and wait until midday to proceed to the place of the invitation."
Having formed this thought, he took his bench and went outside the monastery to a secluded spot to work as he pleased.
Meanwhile, the other bhikṣus departed early for their invitations; they locked the door and left for the donors' homes.
At that time, the bhikṣu who was engaged in recitation arrived at the appointed hour and saw that the temple gate was already locked.
He then thought to himself: "I would rather fast than abandon the monastic furnishings and thereby incur transgression."
He consequently did not go to the invitation and immediately undertook a fast.

When the other bhikṣus had finished eating and were returning, this bhikṣu also followed them into the monastery; as long as the strength of his meal remained, he applied his mind to wholesome qualities, but once the power of the food was exhausted, he lay down on his side.
When the bhikṣus saw this, they asked,
"Venerable one!
While the food belongs to another, is your belly not also another's?"
"Why do you greedily eat until you are so full and distressed that you neglect the cultivation of wholesome qualities?
He replied, "I did not attend the meal; how could I be full and distressed?"
Then the bhikṣus asked him the reason for this, and he told them everything in detail.
When the bhikṣus had heard his account, they reported the matter to the Buddha.
The Buddha said:

“Bhikṣus should not go to an invitation too early, causing others to miss their meal; they should observe the time, wait for the *ghanṭī* to be struck, and depart only after the assembly of monks has gathered and looked upon one another.”
The preceptors and masters should all observe whether their disciples know of their departure.

If, after the gates have been closed, a bhikṣu arrives, and there is a small seat available, he should place it under a tree or by the wall and proceed to the place where the meal is being served; he should not hastily and abruptly undertake a fast.
"If one fasts without a valid reason, one incurs an offense of transgressing the Dharma. 'Fasting' refers to abstaining from food for one day.

At that time, there were brahmins and householders who came to the monastery and used the monks' seating materials; when they departed, they left them abandoned in the open air, and because no one took them up, they became damaged. The Buddha said:
"The person who first sees them should immediately take them up."
At that time, there was an elderly and infirm bhikṣu who saw a monk’s seat abandoned in the open air; being unable to lift it, he reported this to the Buddha. The Buddha said:

"The elder should inform the *vaiyāvṛtyakara* (officer in charge of affairs). That *vaiyāvṛtyakara* should, with a respectful mind, lift and place the seat back on its stand. If he does not lift it, he commits an offense of transgression against the Dharma (*dharmāpatti*)."

At that time, there was a bhikṣu who placed the monastic bedding and requisites in the open air; after going out for alms, wind and rain began to fall. The bhikṣus already present should have taken them up, so that when he returned from his meal, mindful of them, he would find them ready.

At that time, there was a donor who, out of reverent faith, constructed a dwelling in a mountain forest. Later, a hunter seeking to capture birds and deer set fire to the wilderness; the flames grew fierce and intense, burning through villages and towns until they eventually reached and consumed the monastery.

At that time, when the bhikṣus saw the fire burning the monastery, they vied with one another to enter and take their own robes and bowls; however, as for the property belonging to the Saṃgha, no one took charge of it, and it was all consumed by the flames.
Having heard this, the donor came to the monastery and asked the bhikṣu,
"Noble One! Was the property not burned?"
The bhikṣu replied,
"One has not been burned.
Another reported:
"However, the property of the Sangha has been burned away without a single remnant remaining.
The donor said, "If the property of the Sangha is completely exhausted, how can you say it was not burned?"
The bhikṣu said,
"My belongings were not burned.
The donor asked:
“If the property of the Saṃgha were also distributed together with these, would it not be excellent!

For a long time I have undergone hardships as if cutting the flesh from my own body and diminishing the portions of my wife and children, making offerings to the field of the Saṃgha in the hope of attaining supreme merit.”
"Why do you, venerable sirs, take only your own belongings while disregarding the property of the Saṃgha?
Having expressed this reproach, they left him.
Then the bhikṣus reported this matter in detail to the Blessed One.
The World-Honored One declared:
"If the monastery is being burned, one should also retrieve the property belonging to the Saṃgha.

Later, on another day, there were other bhikṣus whose monastery was set on fire. Hearing the Buddha’s instruction to bring out the property of the Saṃgha, they each discarded their own belongings to retrieve the communal goods; consequently, their own possessions were all consumed by the flames, leaving them destitute.
The Buddha said:
"One's own deficiencies and afflictions are grave and cannot be compared to those of the Saṃgha.
If a fire breaks out, one should first take out one's own belongings and only afterwards take those belonging to the Saṃgha."

Furthermore, there was an instance where a fire broke out and the bhikṣus all brought out their own belongings and placed them outside; while they had entered to retrieve the property of the Saṃgha but had not yet emerged, all the clothing and goods were stolen by bandits. The Buddha said:
"Once you have brought out your belongings, you should have someone keep watch."
At that time, the bhikṣus sent the stronger ones to guard [the goods] while the weaker ones went out to fetch them, but they were unable to lift them. The Buddha said:
"Let the weaker ones guard [them], and let the stronger ones lift the goods."
At that time, although the bhikṣus saw the blazing fire, they entered to retrieve the property out of fear of damaging the Saṃgha's goods; consequently, they were burned by the fire. The Buddha said:
"If the fire is raging, one should not enter; even if the goods are burned, there is truly no fault in this."
At that time, there was a donor who had constructed a dwelling place in the midst of a mountain valley. When heavy rains from the heavens occurred, floods overflowed and the monastery was swept away.
At that time, the bhikṣus each took their own personal belongings and disregarded those belonging to the Saṃgha; the circumstances were identical to those mentioned previously.
The only difference lies in [the use of] water and fire; this should be understood through the detailed explanation. The Buddha said:
"If one does not act in accordance with what I have prescribed, one incurs an offense against the Dharma."
The remaining meaning is as above.
**The Fifteenth Training Rule on Not Putting Away Grass Mattings.** The summary verse says:
Two bhikṣus from the south, Two villages, two residences.
Dyeing the *mṛdvīkā* grass by the well, walking in meditation beside the stacked earthen bowls.
At that time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, there were two bhikṣus from the south:
one old and one young. For the purpose of paying homage to the Buddha, they were traveling toward Śrāvastī; as evening fell while on the road, they entered a monastery to stay the night.
When the bhikṣus saw the elder from afar, they said to him, "Welcome, Venerable One!
They then assigned him a cell and bedding according to seniority; however, for the younger ones, they provided only cells without any bedding.
This young bhikṣu was by nature diligent and industrious; he gathered much dry grass, standing as high as his knees, to serve as bedding.
The old bhikṣu then thought to himself:
"Let me see if the young one has any bedding."
He then went to see that the grass matting was thick and warm, and he immediately thought to himself:
"If I were to return the bedding to the Sangha tomorrow morning, it would hinder my journey; I should return the bedding now and stay the night here with him."
He immediately returned his bedding and stayed in one place through the night; at dawn, he departed.
Later, a swarm of ants took refuge in this grass matting and burrowed through the dwelling.
At that time, a householder invited the Buddha and the Sangha to his home for a meal.

At that time, during the first part of the day, the bhikṣus took their robes and bowls and went to the house of the elder; the World-Honored One did not go himself, but sent someone to receive the food. There were five reasons for this, as explained at length previously in the rules concerning the open air (ābhyavakāśika).

At that time, the Buddha, wishing to inspect the bedding and seating of the Saṃgha and to establish a training rule (śikṣāpada), remained within the monastery for this purpose and had someone fetch food.

Then, after the World-Honored One and the assembly of monks had departed, he took the keys and inspected all the dwellings within the monastery, as well as the gardens and groves situated nearby outside the monastery.
Next, he came to a room; within that room he saw the straw strewn about in disorder, with many insects and ants boring through it both inside and out.
Having seen this, he thought:

"These dwellings were all offered by faithful brahmins and householders who, mortifying their own bodies and diminishing the portions of their wives and children, bestowed them as fields of merit for the Sangha in order to seek supreme blessings."
When the bhikṣus were using it, they did not know its capacity and failed to guard it well, resulting in excessive damage by insects and ants.

The World-Honored One then used his supernormal powers to separate the earth and the ants, placing each on one side. With his two exquisite hands, adorned with the hundred blessings and complete with webbed fingers and wheels, he gently took up the ants and moved them outside the room to a cool, shaded place, ensuring they would suffer no harm.

At that time, the World-Honored One, having swept the room and gathered the refuse and soil to discard it outside the chamber, washed his hands and feet and entered the room to sit in silent meditation.
When the bhikṣu who had gone for alms arrived with the food, it was as described in detail previously.
Then, when the Blessed One had finished his meal, he went outside the room, chewed a tooth-stick, and washed his feet; he then returned to the room and remained there in silent seclusion.
At that time, when the sun had set and it was late afternoon, the World-Honored One took his seat as usual. Once seated, he addressed the bhikṣus, saying:
"After the Saṃgha had finished their meal earlier, I took the keys and inspected the dwellings; I have informed you all of everything that occurred therein."

"O Bhikṣus! There are donors who, by afflicting their own bodies, give to the Saṃgha in pursuit of merit; yet you are unable to enjoy these offerings in accordance with the Dharma, thereby wasting the gifts of faith."
He then spoke in verse:
"Regarding the gifts of others' faith, one should know moderation in their use;
thus one attains peace for oneself and causes the merit of others to increase."

At that time, the Blessed One, having praised contentment and the lawful enjoyment of offerings made out of faith, addressed the bhikṣus at length as previously related, up to: "I now establish this training rule for the bhikṣus, which should be recited as follows:
'If a bhikṣu, within a monastery cell, having himself spread or caused another to spread grass or leaves, departs without himself removing them or causing another to remove them.'"
"If there is a bhikṣu who does not give formal notice, except for other extenuating circumstances, it is a pāyattika.

Thus the Blessed One, having established this training rule for the bhikṣus, at that time a great number of bhikṣus were traveling through the countryside with a caravan of merchants and arrived at a certain village.
As the sun was about to set, wishing to find a place to stay, he asked an elder:
"Is there perhaps a lodging where I might be accommodated?
The elder replied:
"One must first establish a formal agreement before we can tolerate one another.
The bhikṣu asked,
"In what manner should this be done?"
The elder said,
"I shall not depart until you have accepted food at my house.
He replied:
“Householder!
I am not independent due to my business with the caravan; if my traveling companions stop and accept an invitation for a meal, I shall follow them as soon as they depart.”
The elder said,
"This is also excellent!
and immediately provided him with a place to stay.
The bhikṣu said to the householder,
"Is there bedding in your residence?
He replied:
"There are none.
At that time, that bhikṣu had many laypeople and śrāmaṇeras as his companions; they all sought out much dry grass to serve as bedding, piling it up knee-high and lying down together in one place.
At that time, the merchants departed under the stars during the night; having seen them go, the bhikṣu discarded the grass and left. When day broke, the elder thought to himself:
"I shall observe the bhikṣu; if he remains, I will provide him with food."
Not seeing any bhikṣus, they saw the grass strewn about in disorder.
At that time, the elder and his wife spent nearly half a day clearing away the tangled grass.
This was the origin of the incident; at that point, the precept had not yet been established.
Furthermore, a great number of bhikṣus, traveling along with a caravan of merchants, arrived at this village and went to the elder to seek lodging.
The elder replied,
"Only after we have established an agreement may you be permitted to stay overnight."
The bhikṣu asked, "How should this be done?
The householder replied:
"One who does not take dry grass as bedding may stay at will.
A bhikṣu asked,
"Is there any bedding or furniture for sleeping in the house of this householder?"
He replied, "There is none.
The bhikṣu said:
"On hard and rigid ground, how can one sleep peacefully?
The elder said,
"O Noble One!"

Previously, fellow practitioners of the holy life such as yourselves came to stay with us; you piled up a great deal of dry grass in a most disorderly and improper manner, causing my husband and me to toil for half a day clearing away the mess. For this reason, we now enter into a formal agreement together.
At that time, the bhikṣus had endured hardship throughout the night; when dawn broke, they set out and traveled by stages until they reached Śrāvastī.
Upon seeing them, the bhikṣus there greeted them, asking, "Are you well?"
He replied, "How can there be peace and security?
The other asked him the reason for this.
He replied, "In this village, sleeping on straw is not permitted; I slept only upon the hard ground, enduring hardship throughout the entire night.
The bhikṣu asked:
"In which village did you undergo such hardship?
He replied,
"In a certain village."
He asked, "In whose house did you stay overnight?
He replied:
"At such-and-such an elder’s house.
One person replied, "I stayed there and slept peacefully upon a grass mat; what fault have you committed that you alone must suffer this flogging on the ground?"
The bhikṣu asked,
“Who has cleared away the grass upon which you slept?
He replied:
"I have already traveled a long distance since dawn; after I arrive, he will surely cast you out.
The bhikṣu replied, "Because of this disturbance, he has caused me to be reviled and made me lie on the ground all night long, striking it with my staff."
Then the bhikṣus reported this matter in detail to the Blessed One.
The Blessed One said:
"Even when using grass mats in a layperson's house, they should likewise be discarded."

Having heard the Buddha’s teaching, at that time a great number of bhikṣus followed a caravan of merchants on their journey through the countryside until they reached a village. There, an elder had constructed a guest house for the sake of śramaṇas, brahmins, and others, and he had sought out soft grass from afar to serve as bedding.
After the bhikṣus had stayed there for the night, they all discarded the grass in a place of filth and each set out on the long journey.
When daybreak arrived, the elder went to inquire after the bhikṣus; seeing only the grass discarded in the impure ground and unable to retrieve it again, he felt resentment and contempt.

Furthermore, a great number of bhikṣus traveling with a caravan arrived at this village; they went to that elder to seek a place to stay, and the elder replied, "I have a guest-house where you may dwell as you please."
The bhikṣu asked,
"Is there any bedding or furniture available?
He replied:
"There is none," the bhikṣus replied,
"How then shall we lie upon such hard ground?"
The householder replied, "Noble ones!
I have built this house of merit for traveling śramaṇas, brāhmaṇas, and others; I have sought out soft grass from afar to provide for those guests who stay overnight."

In the past, there were fellow practitioners of the holy life who came here to stay overnight; when dawn broke, they all discarded their soft grass in the midst of filth, so that if one wished to seek more, it was ultimately impossible to find.
At that time, the bhikṣus passed the night with great hardship on the hard ground.
As this bhikṣu traveled by stages and eventually arrived at Śrāvastī, the bhikṣus there asked him,
"Was your journey safe?"
He replied,
"When one lies sleeping on the bare ground, how can there be any peace or happiness? He asked:
"In what place did you stay that you endured such hardship?
He replied,
"In a rest-house in a certain village."
The bhikṣu replied, “I once stayed overnight in that house of merit; all the bedding grass was discarded by me at dawn.
He answered:
"Because you discarded the grass, it caused us to be treated with contempt, and consequently we had to sleep on the bare ground.
Then the bhikṣus reported this matter in full to the Blessed One.
The World-Honored One told them:

"As for the grass upon which you lie, let the white donor know; if he says it should be discarded, you should immediately remove it; if he says it should be left, you should leave it according to his word."
"If anyone violates this command, they shall incur an offense of transgression against the Dharma.
In a certain village there was a monastery where the bedding and furniture were scarce.
At that time, the bhikṣus, in order to provide for guests, sought bedding and grass from a distant place and settled them in one room.
At that time, a large number of bhikṣus were traveling through the human realm and arrived at this monastery.
They asked the host, "We wish to stay overnight; do you have sufficient bedding and requisites?"

The bhikṣu replied, "This monastery was previously poor and lacked good bedding; for your sake as guests, I have sought out soft grass from afar. If you do not find it objectionable, you may stay and rest as you please."
After he had stayed the night, he wished to discard the grass mat;
the host replied, "I sought this grass from afar for the sake of you, my guest; it is truly difficult to obtain, so you should not discard it lightly."
The visiting bhikṣus said, "You yourselves are ignorant and have committed an offense; do you wish to cause us to commit an offense as well?
Having rebuked them thus, they immediately took the grass and threw it outside before departing, causing it to rot and be damaged.
Later, a large number of bhikṣus, while traveling through the human world, arrived at this monastery seeking lodging.
They asked, "Are there bedding and requisites available? The host replied:
"There are no bedding materials here; for the sake of a guest like me, I have traveled a long way to seek soft grass.
Previously, a bhikṣu came here to stay the night and wished to collect and discard all the straw mats, but we did not permit it."
"Refusing to comply with my words, he instead rebuked me and departed, leaving everything behind; therefore, at this time, there is nothing more to be found.
He then lay down on the ground.

At dawn, he proceeded to the Jetavana Grove. When the bhikṣus saw him, they questioned him one another, and the details were recounted as before, up until: "I stayed there overnight and forcibly discarded his grass," to which he replied:
“Because of this circumstance, those who come to stay as guests undergo great hardship.
At that time, the bhikṣus reported the matter to the Buddha.
The Buddha said:

"This should not be discarded. If there is a bhikṣu who departs after having given instructions [to leave it], one may discard it only after being dispatched to do so; the detailed explanation is as before.
If one acts otherwise, one incurs an offense of transgressing the Dharma."
Furthermore, there were many bhikṣus traveling among the people with a caravan of merchants who, upon reaching the side of a well, stopped there to stay the night.
At that time, the bhikṣus used mostly dry grass as bedding, and not far from there, a brahmin was also staying.

At that time, the merchants set out at dawn; the bhikṣus and brahmins remained behind with the grass mats and followed along with the caravan. On the road, they encountered another caravan approaching from afar.

At that time, the brahmin encountered those merchants; having had all his requests fulfilled to his heart's content, he immediately returned with them and, upon reaching the site of the former well, halted there for the night.
At that time, there were certain naked ascetics who settled down in the dwelling place of the bhikṣus.
Then the naked ascetics said to one another,
"We do not know what creature is biting our bodies?"
The others replied, "Yesterday you ate much dregs of wine; driven by evil desires and discursive thoughts, we bit and gnawed at one another.
As they held a torch to look, they saw a swarm of ants and spoke these words:
"Who was this ignorant person who stayed here and, upon departing, did not know how to fold up this grass mat?
When the brahmin heard this, he replied:
"A son of the Śākyas stayed here previously and departed."
The naked ascetic reviled him, saying,
"Among all people, the śramaṇa sons of the Śākyas claim to possess wisdom, yet they do not clear away the grass mats where they have stayed overnight.
The brāhmaṇa said:
"The śramaṇas, sons of the Śākyas, do not abstain from taking life; they fall asleep wherever they happen to be without performing observation.

Once the assembly had gathered, they saw Udāyin himself carrying bricks and tiles; the other bhikṣus also joined him in carrying them. They all worked together throughout the day without ceasing, and said to one another:
"Venerable ones!
In the past, all those in this monastery diligently practiced meditative concentration; how can it be that today we are all engaged in such labor? Let us abandon this place and go to Śrāvastī."
When those long-term residents saw the visiting bhikṣus arrive, they each cried out,
"Welcome! and addressed them, saying:
"Venerable sir!
I have heard that all those in that monastery practice meditation; I have long wished to go there to join in their joy and meet them.
For what reason have you ceased your practice of meditative concentration to come here?"
The visiting bhikṣu replied, "In the past, all at that monastery were diligent in the practice of meditative concentration; by today, they have all come together to engage in manual labor. He asked:
"What is the reason for this?
He replied,
"It was Udāyin who sent word to do so."
He related the matter in full. At that time, the bhikṣus reported the matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"If any bhikṣus intentionally cause distress to others, they all incur an offense of falling (pāyantika)."
The circumstances were as before; eventually, Udāyin arrived at a monastery where many bhikṣus made recitation their primary practice, and upon seeing Udāyin, they all refused to speak with him.

The temple was not yet completed; [the text] describes at length how he informed the temple’s master and had the bhikṣus work there all day long, after which they all abandoned their tasks and departed for the Jeta Grove.
The bhikṣus informed the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"The offense is the same as before.
Furthermore, the causal origin is the same as before, up until the time when Udāyin arrived at a monastery; at that moment, there was a threat of robbers in the monastery.
When the bhikṣus saw Udāyin approaching, they recognized his evil conduct and none of them spoke with him.
Seeing this, Udāyin then sought to cause them disturbance; when evening fell, he threw wide the temple doors and stood in the doorway.
Then the administrator replied,
"Venerable sir,
do not stand in the doorway; I wish to close the door."
He replied,
"You may close the doors of your own quarters securely, but what business is it of yours regarding the gate of the Great Assembly?
At that time, the bhikṣus were terrified throughout the night and could not sleep.
The bhikṣus informed the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"To intentionally cause distress to others constitutes a *pāyattika* offense.
Furthermore, the narrative context is the same as before, up until the point when Udāyin arrived at the monastery; since there was no fear of thieves, many doors were left open during the night.

At that time, a bhikṣu went out from the monastery to attend to his bodily needs. Seeing that he did not speak to him, Udāyin became enraged; he then firmly locked the door and lay down across the threshold.
At that time, when the bhikṣus needed to relieve themselves at night, they said, "Venerable sir!
Do not stand by the threshold; we shall go out to relieve ourselves."
He replied, "Venerable one!
You emerged by breaking through the wall of your own room; I am utterly exhausted from walking—whom could I possibly have gotten up for?"

At that time, as the bhikṣus had no place to dispose of it, they discarded their impurities either in front of the eaves, or beneath the gateway, or at the drainage openings, or in the middle of the courtyard.
When dawn had broken and those with faith entered the monastery to pay their respects, Udāyin saw them and said:
"Look at these fellows with black bowls! They leave the monastery in such a state of filth and disorder; how could such a place ever be fit for the dwelling of a sage!"
When these words were spoken, the lay followers all felt resentment and contempt.
The bhikṣus reported this to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"If a bhikṣu intentionally causes distress to another bhikṣu, he commits a pāyattika offense."
Furthermore, there is no offense for one who is the very first offender, or for one who is insane, mentally deranged, or afflicted by intense pain.
*Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya*, Fascicle 29; *Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya*, Fascicle 3.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Yijing by Imperial Decree. 18.

The Training Rule Concerning Sitting or Lying Down with the Body Unrestrained on a Bed with Detachable Legs. The eighteenth training rule concerning sitting or lying down with the body unrestrained on a bed with detachable legs. At that time, the Bhagavān was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
Then the Venerable Upānanda went to where those many young bhikṣus were and exhorted them, saying:
"Come with me to travel through the human world; we shall surely subdue the doctrines of other schools and attain renown for ourselves."
"If you wish to recite, chant, or practice meditation, as well as for whatever you require for food, clothing, or medical needs, I shall ensure that nothing is lacking.
Although the youths heard this exhortation, they all knew that Upānanda was by nature of evil conduct and unfit to live with; consequently, not a single one of them consented to go together with him.
At that time, a bhikṣu who lived on alms heard that he was seeking companions and said to Upānanda,
"I shall travel through the human world together with the Venerable One.
A fellow traveler then informed the alms-collecting bhikṣu:
"This Upānanda is of evil conduct; if you follow him now, you will surely encounter distress and provocation.

He then said to his fellow practitioners of the holy life, "I have completed ten years of seniority and do not rely upon others for dependence, nor do I go to him to request instruction in the teachings; what could he possibly do to me?"
The acquaintance replied, "I will not speak with you; you shall know for yourself later.
Though he did not accept this advice, he nevertheless went along with him, and they departed until they reached the boundary outside the realm.
Then Upānanda replied, "O alms-seeker, you may carry my robe-bag for me;
my years have grown old and infirm, so you should assist me."
The mendicant replied, “Venerable sir! Having received the Buddha,
Dharma, and Sangha— the supreme and wondrous field of merit— as an offering, how can you store up such things that cause affliction?”
He replied to the mendicant, saying:
"It was not unreasonable that you were unwilling to carry my belongings when I sent you to do so.
However, it was not fitting for you to reprimand me without the authority of my two teachers; how could this be appropriate?"
Then Upānanda thought to himself:
"I need not speak with this alms-seeker yet; let us endure it for now and go together, and later I shall know for myself."
They then gradually traveled on until they reached a village, where they went to the edge of a well and pond outside the woods to rest together.
In the village there was a monastery, and the sound of the *gandī* drum was heard; having heard the sound, the alms-seeker reported, "Venerable Sirs!..."
"The temple bell has been struck; I wish to go and see.
He replied, "Venerable one!"

These are mostly of the "black bowl" type who are too lazy to cultivate wholesome qualities; they ring the gong to assemble the monks for some other labor. Since we are already exhausted from the road, who would be willing to join them in such manual work?
The alms-seeker said, "Perhaps this is the distribution of the *gaṇḍī*; since I have reached the boundary, it is only right that I receive it. Upānanda said:
"You should go; if this is a *gaṇḍī* for the distribution of shares, take my portion as well.
He replied, "So be it."
He then went into the monastery and inquired, learning that it was indeed the *gaṇḍī* for distributing bedding.
The resident bhikṣu replied,
"Āyuṣman, you should receive your bedding."
He replied, "I have some large ones; would you also accept those?
He asked:
"Who is he? He replied,
"It is the Venerable Upānanda."
He replied,
"That person is well-known to the assembly and is entitled to a share as well.
Thereupon, he accepted both of their bedding and requisites.
At that time, Upānanda was at the well, extensively questioning the people and preaching the Dharma for them, as described in detail above.
Once the people had dispersed and the sun was about to set, he entered the monastery and called out loudly.
The mendicant was lying down with his door closed in a room below the pavilion; having heard the call, he replied:
"Venerable sir, why do you raise your voice?
I have already prepared bedding and washing materials for you in the upper room, all set aside; you should go there and lie down."
He replied, "You may open a room for this mendicant; I wish to have some deliberation with him.
He then thought to himself:
"If you enter the room and we cannot finish our conversation until daybreak, I shall now lie down and not open the door for you.
He replied,
"Venerable Sir!"
"I am utterly exhausted from my journey and have no leisure for discussion; if there is anything to be deliberated upon, let us wait until daybreak.
At that time, Upānanda, knowing his intention, did not open the door. He immediately went up to the upper room, washed his feet, entered the chamber, and asked:
"I have some oil for anointing my feet; where is it kept?"
He replied, "It is just by the side of the bed. Upānanda,
being skilled in discerning signs from sound, observed the place where he lay and immediately shifted the leg of the bed toward his head, then sat down, leaning back against it.
He caused the legs of the bed to fall off and struck him on the head, saying:
"Venerable Sir!
You have broken my head; it is extremely painful."
Upānanda replied,
"Why has the head of this alms-seeker been broken?
He then thought to himself:
"If I speak harshly, he might strike me again," he thought,
and so he remained silent.
When dawn had broken, he went to take his leave.
He replied,
"Venerable sir!
I wish to depart now."
He asked, "Where do you wish to go?
He replied:
"Head toward Śrāvastī.
He replied,
"Wait for a moment!"
"I shall provide you with whatever medicinal requisites you need for your illness.
He replied,
"Venerable Sir!"
"I was originally free from illness when you broke my head;
if I were to fall ill again, how could you possibly care for me?
Having spoken these words, he abandoned him and departed, returning to the Jeta Grove.
Then his fellow practitioners saw him and cried out, "Welcome!
and asked:
"Are you at ease?
He replied, "My head has been beaten until it is split open; how could there be any ease?"
He related the circumstances in full.
When the bhikṣus heard this matter, they all felt revulsion and contempt, saying:
"How can a bhikṣu lie upon an upper loft, knowing that the bed has removable legs, yet let his body fall onto it while sitting down, causing the legs to detach and strike another's head?"
He reported these circumstances in detail to the Blessed One.
The Blessed One assembled the community and asked Upānanda:
"Is it true that you committed such an act of harassment?"
He replied, “It is indeed so.
The World-Honored One rebuked him in various ways, and after speaking at length, he established a training rule for the bhikṣus, which should be recited as follows:

"If a bhikṣu, in a dwelling belonging to the Saṃgha, knowing that it is an upper story or a loft with removable legs, should sit or lie down by throwing his body onto it, or upon other seating objects, it is a pāyattika."
"Furthermore, 'if a bhikṣu' refers to Upānanda; the remaining meanings are as explained above.
'In the monastery of the Saṃgha' is also as explained above.
'Knowing' means either acting on his own initiative or being instructed by another."
"Multi-storied rooms" refers to living in multi-leveled pavilions that are dilapidated and decaying.
"Ladders with detachable legs" refers to beds whose legs are not fixed to the upper frame, as well as other types of seating.
"Leaving the body unguarded while sitting or lying down" means to allow the body to be completely unrestrained, whether sitting or lying, such that the feet protrude and cause injury to others.
The term *pāyattika* (波逸底迦) is explained in detail as above.
Regarding this, what are the characteristics of the offense and how does it occur?

If a bhikṣu, knowing that there is a bed with detachable legs in a monastic dwelling, sits or lies down upon it recklessly with the intent to annoy others, he incurs a *pāyattika* offense in all such cases.
If it is a wooden shelf, or a brick floor, or if the feet are supported by a board, or if [the bed] is lying face up, in all these cases there is no offense.
Furthermore, those for whom there is no offense include the very first offender, or one who is insane, mentally deranged, or overwhelmed by intense physical pain.

19. The Training Rule on Using Water Containing Living Beings. The nineteenth training rule concerning the use of water containing living beings. The Buddha was staying at the Ghoṣitārāma in Kauśāmbī.
At that time, the Venerable Chanda used water containing living beings to sprinkle grass, soil, cow dung, and so forth. When the bhikṣus saw this, they said to him:
"Venerable Chanda!"
"Do not water grass, soil, cow dung, or the like with water containing living creatures. Chanda replied,
"Did anyone summon all these living beings here?"
How could there be anyone else to whom I might entrust these teachings?
How can you wish to leave me when I do not permit your departure?
The four seas are vast and wide; for what reason do you not go?
"Why do the rivers, streams, ponds, pools, jars, pots, and vases not all flow away?
When the bhikṣus who possessed few desires heard these words, they all felt resentment and contempt, saying:
"How can a bhikṣu take water containing living beings and pour it over grass and such, doing so himself or employing others, regardless of the loss of life?"
At that time, the bhikṣus reported the matter to the Buddha.
On this account, the Buddha assembled the bhikṣus and asked Chanda:
"Did you indeed use water containing living beings, or did you instruct others to sprinkle it on grass and such?"
"It is truly so, Venerable Sir!

The World-Honored One rebuked him in various ways for doing what is not appropriate for one who has left the household life; he praised those with few desires and those who revere the precepts, as extensively explained before, up until: "The training rule is established and should be recited as follows:"
"If a bhikṣu, knowing that water contains living organisms, personally sprinkles it on grass or soil, or mixes it with cow dung, or instructs another to do so, it is a pāyattika offense."
"Furthermore, 'if a bhikṣu' refers to Chanda; the remaining meanings are as explained above.
'Knows' means either knowing by oneself or being informed by another.
'Water' refers to water from wells, ponds, and so forth."
There are two kinds of insects:
those visible to the eye and those caught by a strainer.
Whether one uses them oneself, or causes another to sprinkle them on grass or soil, or mixes them with cow dung and so forth, one incurs a *pāyattika* offense; the meaning is as explained above.
Regarding this, what are the characteristics of the offense and how does it occur?
If a bhikṣu perceives water containing living beings as having living beings, and whether using it himself or instructing another to use it for watering grass and so forth, he incurs a pāyattika;
the same applies if he is in doubt.
If there are no insects in the water, but one uses it while perceiving them as being present, one incurs an *dukkaṭa* (offense of wrong-doing);
the same applies if one is in doubt.

If a bhikṣu, at a pond or river where there are many insects and fish, intends to kill them and diverts the water, he incurs a *pāyattika* (offense of falling) for every insect or fish whose life is cut off.
If they do not die, all incur the offense of *dukkaṭa*.
If one causes the flow to be cut off at this water source, then for every insect whose life is severed downstream—or even if they sometimes do not die—the offense incurred is the same as before.
If there was no intent to kill, there is no offense.
Furthermore, those for whom there is no offense include the very first offender, or one who is insane, mentally deranged, or overwhelmed by intense physical pain.

20. The Training Rule on Building a Great Monastery Beyond the Limit. The twentieth training rule concerning building a great monastery beyond the limit was established when the Buddha was staying at the Ghoṣitārāma in Kauśāmbī.
At that time, the group of six bhikṣus would frequently give rise to feelings of contempt for other monasteries, saying:
"This monastery is dilapidated, like a guest house or a stable for elephants and horses."
Having heard this, the bhikṣus said to them:
"Venerable ones!
You have taken up residence in another's dwelling place, yet you yourselves cannot even lay down a single foundation stone; instead, you rely on that location to forcibly incite derision."
When the group of six heard this, Nanda and Upananda said to one another:
"We are constantly treated with contempt by those 'black-bowl' types, who say:
'You always dwell in others' monasteries and have no residence of your own; you cannot even find space for a single stone.'"
"We should now build a monastery together so that those with black alms-bowls shall never have seen its like.
Then Nanda said to Upānanda:
"If all six of us undertake this work, the other holders of black alms-bowls will find fault with us and say: '..."
"The six bhikṣus of the group do not cultivate wholesome qualities but instead devote themselves entirely to worldly labor.
They have persuaded all our families who provide us with almsfood to change their minds.
We ought to select one person from among the six who is of sharp intellect, skilled in expounding the Dharma, and capable of inserting a fine needle into a thick staff."
"Among us six, who is capable of doing such a thing? Upānanda said,
"Venerable Channa!"
"He is renowned among the assembly, possesses unimpeded eloquence, and is capable of acting as a companion to you like a needle and a staff.
Aśvaka said, "If that is the case,
we should go in detail and together invite him to exhort us to appoint him as the administrator."
He then went at once and informed Cchanda, saying:
"Venerable sir, you should know that we have been constantly mocked by those who carry black alms-bowls, who say:
'We always dwell in other monasteries and cause much derision; we cannot even settle ourselves upon a single stone.'"
"Now we should build a monastery together, so that those black-bowl monks have never before seen or heard of it.
If we manage this together, we fear they will invite criticism, saying:
'In the past these were the six groups of monks; now they are working as hired laborers.'"
Having fully related the circumstances of what could and could not be done, they together entreated him, saying:
"Virtuous One!
You should rouse a courageous resolve to serve as the overseer of affairs and construct a dwelling place for the Saṃgha."
He replied, "Excellent!
Since this is a field of supreme merit, I shall perform it for you."
Then, having received the exhortation of the assembly, Chandaka washed his feet, entered his own cell, and sat cross-legged; he remained awake throughout the night, reflecting thus:
"By what means can I construct a great monastery for the Saṃgha?"
He further reflected:

"Now, among the multitudes of gods and humans in this world, all have conceived universal respect and faith toward the World-Honored One; yet, that certain family has conceived particular respect and faith toward Aśvajit, that family toward Vairāṭīputra, that family toward Vāṣpa, that family toward Mahānāman, that family toward Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra, that family toward Vimala, that family toward Gavāmpati, that family toward Śāriputra, and that family toward Mahāmaudgalyāyana—and likewise for other great bhikṣus, each has donors who have conceived particular respect and faith."
"Since I have no other donor, upon whom shall I rely to be able to build this monastery?

At that time, there was an elder in this city who was immensely wealthy and possessed great riches, yet he was by nature so miserly that he would not even give away the turbid water used for washing dishes to others.
"If you can convert them and cause them to give rise to faith and reverence, you may build a great monastery for the Saṃgha.
At that time, after dawn had broken, Chanda put on his robes, took up his bowl, and entered Kauśāmbī to wander for alms.
Having first obtained some parched grain by begging at other houses, he then proceeded toward the house of that elder, wishing to enter his residence.
At that time, the gatekeeper said to him,
"Noble One!..."
"This is the home of a great householder; it is not appropriate to enter without invitation.
Chanda replied, "According to the Blessed One, the World-Honored One, those who beg for alms are forbidden from only five places:"
1. The house of a public announcer;
2. The house of a courtesan;
3. The house of a wine-seller.
Fourth, the family of a caṇḍāla;
fifth, the royal family.
How could these families be any of the aforementioned five types!
Then the gatekeeper replied, "Noble one!
This is a great cause for ridicule. This is not a place where proclamations are made, nor even a royal palace; rather, it is the residence of a certain householder. You need not enter."
At that time, Channa thought to himself:
"If they will not even allow me to approach when I seek to grasp the hem of his robe, how could I possibly obtain anything else?
Just then, there was an elder who had recently given birth to a child; in great celebration, he had drummers and musicians play, and a large troupe of dancers passed by the front of his gate.
The gatekeeper, distracted by his eager observation of the music and performance, left his post; at that moment, Chanda entered furtively.
Then the Venerable One, whose deportment was composed and dignified like that of one free from desire, was seen from afar by the householder, who said to him:
"Welcome, Great Virtue Chanda!"
"You should sit here for a short while.
As he had not yet found an opportunity to begin his discourse, he said to the elder, "I have already gone from door to door begging and obtained some parched grain; you may prepare a sieve for it."
The householder told the maidservant, "Prepare some parched flour," and she prepared it for him.
At that time, Chanda looked at the parched flour, and the householder asked him,
"What are you looking at, venerable sir?"
Chanda replied, "I wish to examine for insects; if there are any insects, I should not eat it.
The householder responded:
"If one eats insects, what fault would there be?
He replied, "As the World-Honored One has said:..."

"If one who takes life practices this habitually, at the breaking up of the body after death, they will fall into the hells, the realm of hungry ghosts, or the animal realm to undergo various sufferings; even if they are born among humans, they will have a short life and many ailments."

However, the bhikṣu Chanda was thoroughly proficient in the Tripiṭaka and possessed unimpeded eloquence; being skilled in discerning the proper timing and preaching the Dharma according to the capacities of his audience, he immediately expounded the essentials of the Dharma for the elder, praising the cultivation of the ten wholesome actions and censuring the practice of the ten unwholesome actions.

At that time, having heard the Dharma, the elder conceived a heart of reverence and faith; he immediately entered his house and had various kinds of exquisite foods and drinks, along with diverse delicacies, prepared. He filled platters and vessels with them and brought them forth to offer as a service.
Upon seeing this, Chanda immediately thought to himself:
"I have heard that wooden pots are used for cooking only once; if I accept this offering, it will serve as both my morning meal and my evening provision."
He then addressed him, saying: "Donor!
I have already accepted the flour offered by another; how could I possibly discard it to eat this fine food?"
The householder said,
"According to our worldly custom, if one first obtains coarse food and later encounters something exquisite, there is truly no fault in discarding the former inferior food.
Chanda replied:
“Householder!

A layperson who lacks the precepts acts as they please; how could I, having received the categories of precepts, be like them in accepting the faithful offerings of others and then recklessly casting them aside?”
When the householder heard these words, his profound faith doubled; Candana then took his leave and departed.
The householder said to him, "Venerable One!"
"Please come to my house from time to time. He then replied,
"I truly wish to visit you frequently, yet the gatekeeper is like a violent and cruel warder of Yama's hell, not permitting me to advance."
At that time, the householder called the gatekeeper and said,
"When you see the venerable Channa entering, you must not stop him.
He replied:
“As you command.
At that moment, Channa thought to himself:

“If other black-bowl monks enter here, they will not recognize the proper occasion and will cause him to lose his faith; I should now prepare a skillful means in advance to prevent them from entering.”
He replied to the gatekeeper, saying: "Ho!
Man, do you know this now?"
"I shall cause this head of the household to develop respectful faith through a great means.
The gatekeeper replied,
"I already know this."
He told him:

"From this day forward, do not allow any other members of the 'black-bowl' class to enter this gate. If you let one in, I shall have the Elder strike you with a heavy staff and replace you with someone else."
He replied, "It was not my desire that you enter this gate; how could I have allowed others to advance so abruptly?
Please do not worry."
At that time, Channa would visit their home from time to time and proclaim the sublime Dharma to the elder and his wife, causing them to receive the three refuges and observe the five precepts.
Then the householder replied, "Noble One!
If you have any need for requisites or provisions, please take whatever you require from my home as you wish; do not seek them elsewhere."
At that time, although Channa heard this announcement, he did not accept anything at all.

Later, on another occasion, he came to visit the householder’s residence and, for the sake of that elder, praised and explained the seven types of meritorious actions pertaining to material things (*sāmiṣa-puṇya-kriyā-vastu*).
Upon hearing this account of the benefits, the householder felt profound joy and said to Chanda,
"Noble One! I now wish to cultivate meritorious deeds involving material things."
He replied, "O worthy one!
Now is precisely the right time; you may do as you please."
The householder asked,
"What do you wish to do? Chanda replied:
"One may construct a dwelling for the community of monks.
The elder then thought:
"I have repeatedly offered my household wealth as alms, yet even when I offered a single thread, they would not accept it."
"Although it is now permitted for you to serve as a member of the Saṃgha once again, observing this contentment of yours,
I hold you in deep respect. He replied,
"Venerable Sir!"
"Now my household possesses much wealth, and I am able to provide a dwelling place for the Saṃgha; however, I have no one to assist me in its supervision.
Chanda replied, "I wish to assist you in accomplishing this meritorious deed."
Then Chanda replied to the householder,
"You should now go to the place where the Saṃgha is gathered, consult the assembly, and request that they appoint me as the person in charge."
The householder replied,
"Excellent! I shall go."
He then accompanied Channa toward the monastery and entered the midst of the great assembly. Having prostrated at the feet of the Sangha, he respectfully addressed the assembly:

"This venerable Channa desires to construct a dwelling for the community of monks; I shall serve as the donor. I pray that the Sangha, out of compassion, will grant permission to appoint him as the official in charge of construction."
At that time, Śāriputra was the senior elder among the assembly; seeing that the householder had made his request, he thought to himself:

"These six groups of monks have recently been constantly harassing the community even without being assigned to such duties; how much more so now that they have been specifically appointed—there is no doubt they will continue to trouble us."
He replied, "Venerable Chanda!
I myself established the Jeta Grove; who else could have assigned me this task?"
The Venerable Mahācunda constructed this Ghoṣitārāma; by whom was he appointed to do so?
If you wish to construct a dwelling for the Saṃgha, you should manage it yourself; why wait for an appointment by the assembly?
Upon hearing this, Chanda thought to himself:
"The followers of the Black Bowl do not even wish to see me, much less would they appoint me as an administrator.

Since the assembly did not appoint him, he departed together with the elder at that very moment; having gone to the elder’s house, he took a great quantity of money and goods and went to the brick-makers, where he said:
"O noble sirs!
Is it possible for you all to construct one hundred three-storied monasteries with matured bricks within a single day?
The brick-makers replied:
"If we provide a large amount of money and act together with many people, this can surely be accomplished.
He then gave them as much money as they requested.
Next, he went to the bricklayer and said:
“O noble ones! Could you possibly construct a three-story temple using fired bricks by scraping them down within a single day?
Next, he went to the carpenters and said:
"O worthy ones!
Could you all gather together in a single day and construct a three-storied temple?
Next, he went to the masons and the painters, asking each according to their respective crafts; the questions and answers were the same as before.
Next, he sought out many laborers and led them into the monastery, where they worked together to construct a three-story temple that was completed in a single day.

However, at the time of its construction, there were no drainage pipes below and no conduits above; neither doors nor windows were installed, leaving no openings for ventilation. Its shape resembled a square basket, with only a small door just large enough for people to pass through.
Once the construction was completed, he went to the house of that elder and announced:
"Elder, the temple has been finished; you should hold a celebration."
The householder replied, "I am not prepared at this time; I shall do so tomorrow.
At that moment, the World-Honored One thought to himself:

“The monastery built by the six groups of monks and Chanda will surely collapse during the latter part of the night. If I and the Saṅgha do not accept the use of this monastery, its donor, seeing the temple destroyed, will give rise to great anguish and will surely die from vomiting hot blood.”
The World-Honored One addressed Ānanda, saying:
"You should now go to the bhikṣus at the Ghoṣitārāma and tell them: 'O bhikṣus!'"

I have often taught you to practice secret virtuous deeds and to confess all transgressions. If any among you attain superior meditative concentration, you should, by the power of that concentration, go during the first watch of the night to the monastery built by Canda and each cultivate wholesome qualities there.
Then Ānanda, having received the Buddha’s instruction, addressed the bhikṣus, saying:
"Venerable ones! The Blessed One has given this command:"

"Whenever I have taught you to practice secret virtuous deeds and confess all transgressions, if any among you have attained superior meditative concentration, you should, by the power of that concentration, go during the first watch of the night to the monastery built by Canda and each cultivate wholesome qualities there."
When the bhikṣus heard these words, those who had attained superior concentration went to that monastery as instructed by the Buddha and practiced the wholesome qualities accordingly.
Then, at midnight, the World-Honored One also went to the monastery and gave rise to a mundane thought.
It is the constant law of all Buddhas that whenever they give rise to a mundane thought, Śakra and the various devas all know their intention.

At that time, Śakra and the various devas came to where the Buddha was; having prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, they sat to one side. The Buddha then expounded for them the impermanence of all phenomena. Having prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, they suddenly vanished from sight.

Then the bhikṣus departed together with the Buddha. When the latter part of the night arrived, clouds arose on all four sides; the wind howled and thunder shook the earth as a great rain poured down, filling the monastery until it resembled a massive granary, with no outlet for the water. As the water soaked through, the monastery collapsed.
When dawn broke, the group of six monks heard of this and were all struck with terror; they fled in every direction.
At that time, the donor, on that very day, loaded various kinds of excellent food and drink onto a cart and came to the monastery wishing to offer his congratulations.
He asked the bhikṣus, "Which one among these is the monastery I have built?"
There was a bhikṣu who had gone forth late in life; having a prior grievance with those six groups [of monks], he said to the householder:
"This is your monastery; it is like a camel that has collapsed while crouching."
"You must be mindful when entering your own monastery; do not let the lintel of the gate strike your topknot.
Upon seeing this, the elder thought to himself:
"I have given away immeasurable wealth and treasures, yet I have never enjoyed them, and now they have fallen into ruin."
He then fell to the ground in a swoon of grief and despair.
At that time, his kinsmen sprinkled cold water on his face, and he regained a little consciousness.
Then the Blessed One addressed the Venerable Ānanda, saying:
