"You should now go and tell that householder:

'There are many donors who have offered to construct dwellings for the Tathāgata; yet, although the Buddha, the World-Honored One, has not made use of them, merit nevertheless accrues to those donors accordingly.'"

How much more so for your monastery, where during the first watch of the night, elder bhikṣus of venerable virtue all enter to enjoy its use; and during the final watch of the night, the Blessed One himself goes there, as do Śakra and the various devas, who all gather like clouds to enter your monastery together to enjoy its use and proclaim the sublime Dharma.
"Your merit and benefit shall be immeasurable and boundless; you ought to rejoice and not be distressed.
Then, having received the Buddha’s instruction, Ānanda went to the householder and informed him of the Buddha’s words in full.
Having heard this, the householder said to Ānanda:
"Venerable Sir,
has the World-Honored One, out of great compassion, entered my monastery for the sake of making use of it?"
Ānanda said, "It has already been used.
The householder said:
“Venerable Sir!
If the Buddha, the World-Honored One, enters my monastery and accepts its use, I shall be able to provide this dwelling place for the World-Honored One every day.”
At that time, the householder asked the people,
"Where is my spiritual friend, the group of six bhikṣus, now?
Hearing that the householder had inquired after them, the group of six all hurried to the place where the householder was.
The householder then invited him for a meal and presented each monk with a new cotton cloth; furthermore, he provided whatever requisites the monks required according to their wishes.
When the bhikṣus saw this, they said to the group of six:
"Virtuous ones, you have been able to construct a great monastery for the elder; it is truly solid."
The group of six replied, "Why do you mock us?

We six men can cause the elder to give rise to deep respect and faith; even though he may suffer a loss of wealth, his reverence and faith toward us will only increase further. He will provide us with superior food, offer each of us a piece of fine cotton cloth, and supply whatever requisites a śramaṇa needs according to our wishes."
When those bhikṣus of few desires heard these words, they all felt resentment and contempt, saying:
"How can the group of six bhikṣus, regarding matters for which they ought to feel shame, instead further exalt themselves?"
Then the bhikṣus reported this matter in detail to the Blessed One.
The Blessed One assembled the Saṃgha and addressed the group of six monks, saying:
"Did you truly commit such unseemly acts?"
The group of six monks replied,
"It is indeed so,
Venerable Sir!"
The Blessed One rebuked him in various ways as extensively described above, up until: "For the sake of all bhikṣus, I shall establish a training rule (śikṣāpada), which should be recited as follows:
'If a bhikṣu constructs a large dwelling, he must install a cross-bar at the side of the door-frame, provide windows, and also install a drainage outlet.'"
"If, when building a wall, it is made of wet mud, it should be two or three layers high, level with the place where the horizontal cross-bars are set.
If it exceeds this, it is a *pāyattika* offense.
Regarding "if there is again a bhikṣu," this refers to the group of six monks (*ṣaḍvargika*).
"Large" is of two kinds:
first, largeness of the object given; second, largeness of physical dimension.
This refers to largeness of physical dimension.
"Residence" refers to a place where one may perform the four modes of deportment: walking, standing, sitting, and lying down.
"One who acts" refers to either doing it oneself or causing another to do it.

Beside the door pivots, one should install horizontal bolts, as well as windows and drainage channels; if the walls are to be built of wet clay, one should begin by preparing the ground, laying the foundation, and then erecting the walls.
Regarding this moist mud, one should apply it to the mold or brick-form in two or three layers.
If more than that is applied, one incurs a *pāyattika* offense; the explanation of the meaning is as stated above.
In this regard, what are the characteristics of the offense and how does it occur?
If a bhikṣu constructs a large monastery for the Saṃgha and uses wet mud, brick molds, or mud-slurry forms to build more than two or three stories, he incurs a *pāyattika* (offense of falling).
If the bricks are fired, or if they are made of stone or wood, or if the donor wishes for a rapid completion, there is no offense even if the weight limit is exceeded.
Furthermore, there is no offense for the very first offender, or for one who is insane, mentally deranged, or overwhelmed by intense physical pain.
At that time, all the bhikṣus were filled with doubt and requested the World-Honored One, saying:
"When the Venerable Chanda requested the Saṃgha to appoint him as the *vaiyāvṛtyakara*, for what reason did the Venerable Śāriputra employ skillful means to prevent it and not allow him to do so?"
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"It was not only today that Śāriputra used skillful means to restrain Cchanda; in the distant past, he also restrained him."
"You all should listen!
In a past age, in an extremely deep and perilous place within the Snowy Mountains, there lived a great flock of birds.
Among them was a king of birds who ruled over them all; however, having been stricken by illness, he eventually met his death."
At that time, as the flocks of birds were without a leader, they began to deceive one another and act to their mutual disadvantage.
The birds gathered in one place and said to one another:
"We cannot survive for long without a leader; we wish to seek a king of birds to perform the consecration and establish him as our ruler together. Where might we find such a one?"
Not far from there lived an old owl, and the assembly all deliberated, saying:
"This bird is venerable and fit to be our leader; if we support him, there will surely be great benefit."

Not far from here there is a parrot, whose nature is intelligent and wise, and who well understands the requirements of the situation; let us all together ask him whether this matter of supporting the owl as our leader is acceptable or not.
They immediately went together to where the parrot was and asked, "We wish to establish the owl as our leader; would this be acceptable?
At that time, the parrot looked at the owl's face and spoke this verse:
"I do not love the owl, yet I regard it as the king of birds;
I am not angry with one whose face is thus, so how could anger arise? How could it be provoked?"
“When the flock of birds heard these words, they did not appoint him as their leader, but instead appointed the parrot as their leader.
O bhikṣus, do not harbor any doubts: the parrot of that time was none other than Śāriputra, and the old owl was none other than Chanda.”
"In the past, when Fu was made king, I used skillful means to prevent it;
now that he has been appointed to an office, I likewise use skillful means to refuse him.
Furthermore, there is no offense for the very first offender, or for one who is insane, mentally deranged, or afflicted by intense pain.
The third summary verse says:
Not sending [a messenger], until sunset, two kinds of robes for food,
traveling together and riding in a boat, and the two types of secluded invitations for food.

21. The Training Rule Concerning Not Appointing a Bhikṣu to Instruct Bhikṣuṇīs. The second training rule concerning not appointing a bhikṣu to instruct bhikṣuṇīs. A summary verse within this section states:
The Buddha commanded Nandaka To instruct and admonish the bhikṣuṇīs;
For them he preached the profound sūtras, And they all realized arhatship.
At that time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
He was observing the summer retreat there together with five thousand bhikṣus.

There were also elder bhikṣuṇīs who were observing the rains retreat at this same Jeta Grove Monastery; namely, the bhikṣuṇīs Cundā, Mṛdvīkā, Mallapā, Mahākāśyapī, Sucarita, Āraṇyikā, Candraprabhā, Kṣemā, Alpakalpā, Gautamī, Utpalavarṇā, and Mahāprajāpatī—the great śrāvakī bhikṣuṇīs—all of whom resided there.
At that time, the Bhikṣuṇī Mahāprajāpatī, accompanied by five hundred bhikṣuṇīs as her retinue, went to where the Buddha was, prostrated at his feet, and sat down to one side.

At that time, the World-Honored One expounded the essentials of the Dharma for Mahāprajāpatī and the others, instructing, benefiting, gladdening, and inspiring them with joy; having done so, he addressed them, saying:
"Mahāprajāpatī!
"The time has come; you may depart.
Then Mahāprajāpatī, having heard the Buddha’s teaching, received it with reverence, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and immediately departed.
At that time, after Mahāprajāpatī had left, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus, saying:
"You should know this!
I am now old, decrepit, and my strength is exhausted; I can no longer proclaim the essentials of the Dharma for the fourfold assembly of bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, and upāsikās."
"From this day forward, you senior bhikṣus should take turns in instructing the bhikṣuṇīs.
When the bhikṣus had heard the Buddha’s instruction, they immediately began to provide instruction according to their seniority.
At that time, it was the turn of the Venerable Nandaka to provide instruction, yet he was unwilling to go and instruct the bhikṣuṇīs.

Then the Bhikṣuṇī Mahāprajāpatī, together with five hundred bhikṣuṇīs, went to the place where the Buddha was; she spoke at length as previously described, until finally she paid homage to the Buddha and departed.
After the Great Leader of the World had seen her depart, he addressed Ānanda, saying:
"Who now should be appointed to instruct the community of nuns? Ānanda replied:
"Until now, it has always been the turn of the senior bhikṣus to instruct [the nuns], but now that it has come to the venerable Nandaka, his mind is disinclined to teach the community of nuns."
At that time, Nandaka was also present among the assembly by the Buddha's side.
Then the Buddha addressed Nandaka, saying:
"You should instruct the bhikṣuṇīs; you ought to proclaim the essentials of the Dharma to them."
For what reason? Nandaka!
I shall instruct the bhikṣuṇīs according to my ability, and you, too, shall instruct the bhikṣuṇīs.
I have proclaimed the essential points of the Dharma for the bhikṣuṇīs; you, likewise, shall proclaim the essential points of the Dharma.
By this cause and condition, you will bring great benefit and great radiance to that community of bhikṣuṇīs, enabling them to increase extensively and attain the ultimate state.
“You should not decline to instruct that community of nuns.
Having received the Buddha’s instruction, Nandaka accepted it in silence.
Then, when the night had passed and dawn had broken, the Venerable Nandaka dressed in the first part of the day, took up his bowl, and entered the city of Śrāvastī to beg for food in regular order.

Having received the food, he returned to his original location; when he had finished eating, he put away his robes and bowl, chewed a tooth-stick, and washed his feet. He then entered his room and remained there in silent meditation.

Then, in the late afternoon, Nandaka arose from meditative concentration, donned his saṃghāṭī robe, and, taking a single bhikṣu as his attendant, proceeded toward the Rājārāma monastery intending to instruct the bhikṣuṇīs.
Having arrived there, the community of nuns saw Nandaka coming from afar and said,
"Welcome, Venerable One!
They immediately prepared a seat and invited him to sit.
Then the bhikṣuṇīs, having prostrated at the feet of Nandaka, sat down to one side. At that time, Nandaka addressed the bhikṣuṇīs, saying:
"I shall now explain to you sisters the Dharma-gate of Question and Answer; listen well."

If one understands, one should say that one understands; if one does not understand, one should say that one does not understand. One should thoroughly comprehend the meaning and practice in accordance with the principle; if there is uncertainty regarding the meaning, one should certainly ask further questions.
“Venerable One! I am unable to understand the meaning of these words.
Having heard this instruction, the bhikṣuṇīs said to Khanda-daka:
“Virtuous One!

Having received your excellent instruction, we are filled with a sense of wonder and boundless joy. Since you have thus excellently instructed us, Virtuous One, we shall all follow the matters taught and engage in dialogue and practice in accordance with the principles.”
Then the Venerable Nandaka said to the bhikṣuṇīs:
"Sisters! Do you know whether there is 'I' or 'mine' in the internal sense-base of the eye?"
The nuns replied,
"Venerable sir,
we do not see anyone."
He asked again: "Sisters!
Just as it is with the eye, do the internal bases—up to the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind—possess a self or what belongs to a self?"
He replied,
"Venerable sir,
I do not see any."
Why is this? Venerable sir!

We follow and practice right conduct, truly forming this understanding; with right wisdom and vision, we observe that within the six internal bases there is truly no self, and because our minds have given rise to faith and understanding through the realization of non-self.
Then Nandaka replied to the bhikṣuṇīs, saying:
"Excellent, sisters!
You have well understood the meaning expressed by these words; one should know that within these six internal bases there is neither self nor what belongs to a self."
"Furthermore, is there a self or what belongs to a self within external forms?
The nuns replied,
"Venerable Sir!"
"I do not see any.
She asked again:
"Sister!..."
"Just as it is with form, so it is with the external bases of sound, odor, taste, tangibles, and mental phenomena: is there a self or what belongs to a self therein?
He replied, "Venerable sir!"
I do not see that it exists. Why is this?
Venerable sir!

We, practicing in accordance with the correct conduct, truly hold this understanding: through the vision of right wisdom, we observe that within the six external sense bases there is truly no self; because we have given rise to faith and understanding, we realize the non-existence of a self.
Then Nandaka replied to the bhikṣuṇīs, saying:
"Excellent, sisters!
You have well understood the meaning expressed by these words: that beyond these six sense bases there is no self and nothing belonging to a self; thus it should be known."
"Furthermore, sisters!
Eye and visible forms serve as conditions to give rise to eye-consciousness. Does this nature of consciousness possess a self or what belongs to a self?
"Venerable Sir!"
"No. "In this way, up to the point where mind and mental phenomena serve as conditions to give rise to mental consciousness—do these types of consciousness possess a self or what belongs to a self?
He replied:
"There is none. Why is this?
As explained at length above."
...and so on, up to: "In this way it should be understood.
Furthermore, sisters, with the eye and visible forms as conditions, eye-consciousness arises; from the coming together of these three, contact arises."
"Does this contact possess a self or what belongs to a self? ...
Up to: when the triad of mind, mental objects, and consciousness gives rise to contact, does this contact possess a self or what belongs to a self?
He replied:
"There is none.
Why? As explained at length above."
...and so on, up to: "In this way it should be understood.
Furthermore, sisters!
This eye, form, and visual consciousness—these three meeting in harmony give rise to contact, which is capable of producing feeling."
"Does this feeling possess a self or what belongs to a self?
And so on, up to the last three types of feelings born from contact as their cause—do these feelings possess a self or what belongs to a self?
He replied:
"There is none.
Why? As explained extensively above."
"...and so forth, up to: 'In this way it should be known. Furthermore, sisters!

From the coming together of these three—the eye, forms, and visual consciousness—contact arises; from contact, feeling arises; from feeling, craving arises. Does this craving possess a self or belong to a self?'"
"Is there even in the latter three types of craving any sense of 'I' or 'mine'?
He replied, "There is not."
Why is this? As explained extensively above...
up to: "In this way, it should be understood."
"Furthermore, sisters!
It is just as, for example, it is because of a vessel, oil, a wick, and fire that a flame arises.
Sisters!"
Just as a flame is impermanent, so too are the wick, the oil, and the vessel impermanent.
Sisters! If, moreover, someone were to speak thus:
"Although the vessel, oil, wick, and flame are impermanent, the flame produced in dependence upon these must certainly be a firm, unchangeable, and eternally abiding phenomenon."
"When this is said, could it be said that this person speaks the truth? He replied,
"Venerable Sir!"
This is not true speech. Why?
Because these vessels, oils, and so forth are all impermanent; how could the flames produced by them possibly be permanent?
"Sisters! Thus, the six internal sense bases are impermanent.
Furthermore, if someone were to speak as follows:"
"Although these six internal sense bases are impermanent, the joy and pleasure arising in dependence upon them are certainly firm, indestructible, and eternal dharmas."
When this is said, can it be said that this person speaks the truth?
He replied, “Venerable Sir! [No.]”
"This is not true speech.
Why is that? [It continues] at length."
"Venerable Sir!
We have followed and practiced the right conduct, truly forming this understanding: with right wisdom and vision, we contemplate that the six internal sense bases are all impermanent.

We give rise to faith and resolve that through the arising of this or that phenomenon, this or that phenomenon arises; and through the cessation of this or that phenomenon, this or that phenomenon ceases. In the end, we are able to attain the state of peace, coolness, and liberation."
Nandaka replied to the bhikṣuṇīs, saying:
"Excellent! Excellent!"
Sisters!

If you can understand the meaning expressed by words and give rise to faith and understanding that this is impermanent—that from the arising of such and such phenomena, this and this phenomenon arises; and from the cessation of such and such phenomena, this and this phenomenon ceases—then you will ultimately attain the state of peace, coolness, and liberation.
“Furthermore, sisters!

It is like a great tree that is fully endowed with roots, trunk, inner and outer branches, leaves, flowers, and firm fruit. Of this great tree, the roots are impermanent, and even the flowers and leaves are likewise impermanent.”
Furthermore, if someone were to say:
"The roots and other parts of this tree are all impermanent; however, the shadow of the tree is certainly a firm, indestructible, and eternally abiding phenomenon."
"When this is said, can it be said that this person speaks the truth? He replied,
"Venerable Sir!"
This is not a true statement. Why is this so?

This great tree—its roots, trunk, branches, leaves, and even its flowers and fruits—is entirely impermanent. If there were no supporting objects such as the roots and so forth, the shadows that depend upon them could not exist.
Nandaka said: "Sisters!
It is likewise that all six external sense bases are entirely impermanent."
Suppose someone were to come and say this:
"The six external sense bases are all impermanent; however, the pleasant contact that arises in dependence upon them is certainly a firm, unchanging, and eternal phenomenon."
"When this is said, could it be said that this person is speaking the truth? He replied,
"Venerable Sir!"
This is not true speech.
Why? As explained extensively before, it ultimately enables one to attain the state of liberation.
"Furthermore, sisters!
I shall speak another parable;
you should listen!"
Those who possess wisdom can understand its meaning through analogies.

It is like a skilled butcher or his apprentices, who, holding a sharp knife in their hands, sever the life of an ox; yet, through skillful means, they skin and flay the outer hide without damaging the flesh within.

However, within the belly, one carefully cuts, slices, and severs the liver, stomach, intestines, and bowels, discarding them all entirely, and then takes the skin again to cover [the body] completely.
Sisters!
If someone, upon seeing it, were to say:
"This ox is still joined to its hide and not separated from it;
this is a living ox," could one say that this person is speaking the truth?
He replied,
"Venerable Sir,
this is not the truth."

Why is this? When these ox-slaughterers and their disciples grasp sharp knives in their hands and sever the life of an ox, although they do not damage its hide or flesh, they nonetheless cut out and discard the liver, stomach, intestines, and entrails within its belly; they merely take the hide and cover it all over, so that this flesh and the hide are no longer connected.
“Sisters! I have raised this analogy in order to clarify another meaning; you should understand it according to the principle.
What is called ‘the ox’ refers to the physical body composed of the coarse and heavy four great elements, formed through the aggregation of the parents’ semen and blood, the *kalala*, and so forth.”
Furthermore, though they are mutually sustained by food and drink, and temporarily supported by ointments, perfumes, bathing, and the like, they ultimately end in decay, destruction, and dissolution.
What is called "inner flesh" refers to the six internal sense bases (*ṣaḍ-āyatana*).
The "outer skin" refers to the six external sense bases (*bāhyāyatana*).
The "five viscera within the belly" refers to sensual desire and so forth.
The "skilled butcher and his apprentices" refers to the śrāvaka disciples who are learned and possess sharp wisdom.
The "whetted blade" refers to the sword of wisdom.

It means that the disciples of the Buddha hold the sword of wisdom in their hearts to sever the afflictions and secondary defilements bound to those [objects] through association; having counteracted and destroyed them, they are entirely eliminated and discarded.
Therefore, you all, having understood this matter, should diligently practice and study; do not be negligent, lest you later give rise to regret.
Sisters! Regarding those things to which your minds are attached and for which you feel desire and delight, you must skillfully guard your hearts.
Because attachment has not yet been abandoned, one should skillfully guard the mind against objects that provoke aversion.
Because aversion has not yet been abandoned, one should skillfully guard the mind against objects that provoke delusion.
Because delusion has not yet been abandoned, one should skillfully protect the mind within the four foundations of mindfulness, dwelling in right contemplation.
Having cultivated the foundations of mindfulness, one should skillfully cultivate and frequently practice the seven factors of enlightenment.

Once these factors of enlightenment have been cultivated and frequently practiced, through the accomplishment of right mindfulness within the Eightfold Path, one is able to eliminate the outflow of sensual desire.

Having eliminated the outflow of sensual desire (*kāma-āsava*), one should cultivate revulsion toward and relinquish the outflows of existence (*bhava-āsava*) and ignorance (*avijjā-āsava*). Through the arising of revulsion and relinquishment, one attains liberation; having attained liberation, one realizes the knowledge and vision of liberation, whereby one is able to understand:
"Birth has been exhausted, the holy life has been established, what was to be done has been accomplished, and there is no further state of existence."
"Sisters! You should train yourselves in this way.
Then, the Venerable Nandaka, having instructed, exhorted, inspired, and gladdened the community of nuns with a discourse on the Dharma, rose from his seat and departed.

When the next day arrived, Mahāprajāpatī, together with five hundred bhikṣuṇīs, returned to the Buddha’s dwelling; having listened to the sublime Dharma with their customary deportment, they prostrated before the Buddha and departed.
After the Great Lady Mahāprajāpatī had departed, the Buddha addressed the bhikṣus, saying:
"Observe this Nandaka, who has provided correct instruction and admonition to those five hundred bhikṣuṇīs, causing them to attain liberation, though they have not yet realized the ultimate goal."

If they were to pass away this very day, I do not see a single one of those bhikṣuṇīs who has not severed the fetters of affliction; because these bonds of delusion serve as their shackles, they would return to this world to undergo birth once again.
"O Bhikṣus! It is like the fourteenth day of the waxing moon when the moon is in the sky; all people behold it and harbor doubts, saying:
'Is this bright moon full or not full?'"
"However, this bright moon is not yet full because it has not reached its ultimate limit.

In the same way, although the bhikṣu Cūḍapanthaka has correctly instructed and admonished those five hundred bhikṣuṇīs, leading them to attain liberation, they have not yet realized the ultimate goal."

If they were to pass away this very day, I do not see a single one of those bhikṣuṇīs who has not severed even the most subtle fetters of affliction; because these bonds and delusions serve as their shackles, they would return to this world once more to undergo rebirth.
At that time, after the Blessed One had declared that those five hundred bhikṣuṇīs had attained the fruit of non-returning, he addressed Nandaka, saying:
"You should instruct and admonish the bhikṣuṇīs, preaching the sublime Dharma so that they may swiftly attain liberation."
"Why is this? It is I and you who instruct the bhikṣuṇīs so that they may attain liberation.
Having heard the Buddha's teaching, Nandaka accepted it in silence.

Then, when the night had passed and the next day arrived, during the first watch, the Venerable Nandaka dressed himself, took his bowl, and entered the great city to beg for alms in sequence. Having returned to his own quarters and finished his meal, he put away his robes and bowl, chewed his tooth-stick, and rinsed his mouth. Having washed his feet outside, he entered his cell and sat in meditative seclusion.

When the time of the afternoon meal arrived, he arose from meditative concentration, donned his saṃghāṭī robe, and, taking a single bhikṣu as an attendant, went to the Rājaka-vihāra to instruct the bhikṣuṇīs.
Having arrived there, the community of nuns saw Nandaka coming from afar and said,
"Welcome, Venerable One!
They then prepared a seat for him and invited him to sit.

Then the bhikṣuṇīs, having prostrated at the feet of Nandaka, sat down to one side. At that time, Nandaka proclaimed the essentials of the Dharma to the assembly of bhikṣuṇīs, instructing, exhorting, inspiring, and gladdening them. Having finished preaching the Dharma, he rose from his seat and departed.

At that time, the Bhikṣuṇī Mahāprajāpatī, leading a community of five hundred bhikṣuṇīs, went to where the Blessed One was, prostrated at his feet, and related everything in detail as before, until she had paid homage to the Buddha and departed.
At that time, after the community of nuns had departed, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus, saying:
"Do you see how this bhikṣu Nandaka, having already correctly instructed five hundred bhikṣuṇīs, has caused them all to attain liberation and reach the ultimate state?"
If these members of the community of nuns were to pass away this very day, I do not see a single one among them who would again tread the path of birth and death;
therefore, at this moment, they shall reach the end of all suffering.
"O Bhikṣus! It is like the full moon on the fifteenth day, situated in the midst of the sky; all people behold it and no longer harbor any doubt, wondering:
'Is this bright moon full or not full?'"
"Furthermore, this Candraprabha is perfectly full because he has reached the ultimate.

Likewise, the bhikṣu Cūḍapanthaka has provided correct instruction and admonition to those five hundred bhikṣuṇīs, causing them to attain liberation and reach the ultimate state; if they were to pass away this very day, the path of saṃsāra would be severed and they would no longer undergo rebirth."

At that time, after the World-Honored One had prophesied that the five hundred bhikṣuṇīs would attain the fruit of arhatship, the assembly of bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and accepted it with faith.
The Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya, Scroll 30; The Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya,
Scroll 31.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Yijing by Imperial Decree.
The Twenty-first Section on the Precept Against Teaching Bhikṣuṇīs Without Being Appointed, Part Two. The Summary Verse states:
The Six Groups Teaching Improperly, The Great Road and the Small Road.
The Buddha, wishing to manifest his supreme virtues, extensively explained the causes and conditions of the past:
how the Physician King had given rise to pride upon obtaining great wealth from a mouse;
and how he then spoke of the matter of the Wise Horse, teaching that one should not attempt to evaluate those who are not noble.
At that time, the World-Honored One commanded the senior bhikṣus to provide instruction to the bhikṣuṇīs in due order.
On the following day, the group of six bhikṣus went to the place where those bhikṣuṇīs were, conversing and laughing with them, or touching one another with their hands and bodies;

among those nuns, those who felt desire engaged in unrighteous acts, while those who did not feel desire would not comply, and consequently walked up and down in the corridors uttering words of reproach and abuse.

At that time, those bhikṣuṇīs who delighted in few desires and upheld the precepts went and informed the bhikṣus of the matter; having heard it, the bhikṣus reported it in full to the World-Honored One.
The World-Honored One declared:
"Although there should be a proper sequence, you must not allow those six bhikṣus to instruct the community of bhikṣuṇīs.
Although the six bhikṣus heard this instruction, they continued to instruct the bhikṣuṇīs according to their own sequence, once again engaging in unrighteous conduct as before.
The Buddha said,
"If one is not appointed by the assembly, one should not provide instruction.
When the group of six heard these words, they all went outside the boundary to appoint themselves, thereby repeating their previous transgression.
The Buddha said,
"One should not designate and dispatch someone from outside the boundary.
Having heard these words, the group of six then took the requisites for the sick person within the boundary, without consulting anyone else.
The Buddha said:

"One should not appoint a person for the instruction of nuns by convening a separate assembly; rather, when the Saṃgha has gathered on the fifteenth day for the poṣadha ceremony, one should appoint a person to instruct the nuns."
One should appoint them in this manner, first asking whether they are capable:
"O so-and-so, are you able to instruct the bhikṣuṇīs? He should reply:
"I can. Then, he should have one bhikṣu perform the formal motion (*jñapti-karman*) in this manner:
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!..."
This bhikṣu, so-and-so, is a person appointed to instruct bhikṣuṇīs; this so-and-so desires to instruct the bhikṣuṇīs.

If it is the proper time for the Saṃgha, may the Saṃgha grant its permission: the Saṃgha now appoints the bhikṣu, so-and-so, as the instructor of bhikṣuṇīs, and this so-and-so desires to instruct the bhikṣuṇīs.
The motion is thus made.
Next, the *karmavācanā* is performed:
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!
This bhikṣu, so-and-so, is the person appointed to instruct the bhikṣuṇīs; this so-and-so desires to instruct the bhikṣuṇīs.
If the Saṃgha permits that the bhikṣu so-and-so be appointed as the instructor of the bhikṣuṇīs, this so-and-so shall indeed instruct the bhikṣuṇīs.
"If the Venerable Ones consent to appoint such-and-such a person as the instructor of bhikṣuṇīs, let them remain silent; if they do not consent, let them speak.
"The Saṃgha has now completed the appointment of such-and-such a person to instruct the bhikṣuṇīs; because of their silence, I now hold it to be so."
When the bhikṣus heard the World-Honored One’s instruction that someone should be appointed to instruct the bhikṣuṇīs, they proceeded to appoint someone without any discernment.

The Buddha said: “It is impossible for one who is not self-disciplined to discipline others; for one who is not himself tranquil to bring tranquility to others; for one who is not himself at peace to bring peace to others; for one who has not himself attained cessation to bring cessation to others; or for one who is himself mired in the mud of desire to rescue others.”
He addressed the bhikṣus, saying:
"One should not hastily appoint someone without first exercising careful discernment.
If a bhikṣu possesses seven qualities, the Saṃgha should appoint him as an instructor of bhikṣuṇīs."
What are the seven? First, maintaining the precepts;

second, being learned; third, abiding in the status of an elder; fourth, being skilled in the language of the capital; fifth, never having defiled a bhikṣuṇī with one’s body; sixth, being well-versed in distinguishing the eight pārājika rules; and seventh, being able to skillfully explain the eight rules of respect.
What is meant by "upholding the precepts"?
It refers to not committing even a single transgression against the four *pārājika* rules.
What is meant by "being learned" (*bahuśruta*)?
This refers to being able to recite the two sections of the Prātimokṣa Sūtra well.
What constitutes dwelling in the status of a senior elder?
It means having received full ordination for twenty rainy-season retreats (*varṣa*) or more.
What is skillful speech regarding royal capitals?
It refers to being able to skillfully understand the sounds and languages of a royal capital and communicating fluently across various regions.
What is not defiling a bhikṣuṇī with one’s body?
That is to say, he has never touched a bhikṣuṇī with his body; even if he has previously touched her, he has already confessed this offense according to the Dharma.
How are the eight pārājika dharmas distinguished?
This refers to skillfully discerning what is permitted and what is prohibited regarding the first eight [precepts].
What is meant by being skilled in understanding the eight rules of respect?
It means being able to skillfully explain and expound upon these eight matters.
"If a bhikṣu possesses seven qualities, the Saṃgha should appoint him as a teacher of bhikṣuṇīs.
As the Blessed One said:
"If he possesses seven qualities, the Saṃgha should dispatch him to teach the community of bhikṣuṇīs."
At that time, although they had not been appointed, the group of six bhikṣus went to instruct the nuns. When the bhikṣus of few desires heard of this, they felt resentment and shame, saying:
"How can a bhikṣu, without being appointed by the Saṃgha, go of his own accord to instruct the community of nuns?"
He reported these circumstances in detail to the Blessed One.

On account of this, the Blessed One assembled the community of bhikṣus and questioned the group of six; he then rebuked them extensively as previously described, saying, "I now establish a training rule for the bhikṣus, which should be recited as follows:
'If a bhikṣu, not having been appointed by the Saṃgha, goes of his own accord to instruct a bhikṣuṇī, it is a pāyattika.'"
Thus, after the Blessed One had established the training rule for the bhikṣus,
he was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park. In that city,
there was a brahmin who, after marrying a wife, found that every son she bore would die immediately.
Later, at another time, his wife again became pregnant. When the brahmin learned of this matter, he sat with his cheek propped up by his hand, brooding in sorrow.
An old woman from a neighboring house came to him and said, "Brahmin, for what reason do you sit here brooding in sorrow with your cheek propped up?"
He replied, "My wife has little merit; every son she bears dies immediately.
Now she is pregnant again; even if the child is born, it will surely die. How could I not be distressed?"
The old woman replied,
"When the day arrives for your wife to give birth, you should summon me.
Later, when her wife reached the day of birth, she immediately summoned the old woman.

The mother went to her daughter-in-law’s quarters and saw that a son had been born. The old woman took the child, bathed him thoroughly, wrapped his body all around in fresh white cloth, placed excellent fresh butter in his mouth, and handed him to a maidservant, instructing her:
"You should carry this infant to the main road at the crossroads. When you see śramaṇas or brāhmaṇas passing by, you should respectfully pay homage and say to those people:
'This small child pays homage at the feet of the Noble Ones.'"
"When evening comes, if he is still alive, you may take him back with you.
If he is no longer alive, you should leave him wherever he lies and return home."
At that time, the maidservant followed her instructions and took the child to the intersection of the four great roads, placing him by the side of the path.
A group of non-Buddhist practitioners (tīrthikas), who were passing along the road at dawn to pay homage at the temples of the various devas, came upon him.
At that time, the maidservant saw him approaching from afar and, having paid her respects, pointed to the child and said:
"Noble One! This little boy pays homage at your feet."
He offered this blessing:
"May your child be free from illness and long-lived, protected by the devas, and may all the wishes of your parents be fully realized.
Furthermore, many senior bhikṣus, wishing to enter the city of Śrāvastī to beg for alms, also passed by that way.
When the maidservant saw him, she likewise reported it as before, and at that time the bhikṣus offered the aforementioned prayers of blessing.
Then, during the first part of the day, the World-Honored One donned his robes, took up his bowl, and entered the city of Śrāvastī to beg for food, passing by this very spot as well.

At that time, seeing the World-Honored One approaching, the maidservant paid him homage with the utmost sincerity by prostrating herself with her five limbs touching the ground. She then pointed to the infant, joined her palms, and said to the Buddha:
"This little child pays homage at the feet of the World-Honored One."
The World-Honored One replied, "May your child be free from illness and long-lived, protected by the devas, and may all the wishes of his parents be fully realized.

Having paid such respects, when evening fell, he went to visit the child and saw that his life still remained. He took the child in his arms and returned home; when the family members saw him, they asked:
"Is the child alive?
He replied, "He lives."
He asked again,
"Where did you place this child while holding him?
She replied:
“By the side of the great road.
His parents were filled with joy and gathered their kinsmen for a grand banquet;
wishing to bestow a name upon the child, they deliberated and said, “Since this child was placed by the great road immediately after birth, it is fitting that he be named Mahāpanthaka (Great Road).”
This youth Mahāpatha grew rapidly through excellent nourishment; he studied various arts and skills, such as writing and arithmetic, as described at length above.

Regarding all the Brahmanical rites, including the protocols for dressing, eating, and ritual purification, as well as the melodies of recitation, he mastered every excellence. He was proficient in the four Vedas (*catur-vidyā*), understood the six types of action (*ṣat-karman*), possessed great wisdom, and five hundred youths came to him to study under his guidance.
At that time, the brahmin was unable to abandon desire, as it has been said:
"If a person driven by thirst drinks salt water, their thirst increases all the more;
likewise, when one who lusts indulges in desire, their craving grows even greater."
The brahmin’s lust did not cease, and his wife became pregnant again. When she was about to give birth, he sent for his elderly mother once more.

Upon her arrival, the mother attended the delivery; seeing that a son had been born, she bathed him thoroughly as before, wrapped him in white cotton cloth, and handed him to a maidservant, instructing her:
"Take this child and place him by the side of the great road, just as you were previously instructed."

At that time, the maidservant was by nature indolent; she took the child and placed him by the side of a small path. Whenever she saw śramaṇas, brāhmaṇas, followers of external paths, followers of internal paths, or great masters, she pointed him out as before, and they all offered blessings for him, as described in detail above.
When evening arrived, the child was still alive; she carried him back home, and her parents, filled with joy, asked the maidservant:
"Where did you keep this child while you were carrying him?"
He replied,
"It was placed beside a small path.
His parents immediately prepared a grand assembly and conferred a name upon their son, saying:
"Since this child was placed by the side of a narrow path because they desired long life for him, he should be named Cūḍapanthaka—
'Cūḍa' being 'small' and 'Panthaka' being 'path'."
"The former name, Zhouli Panteka, is an erroneous transcription.

Once he had gradually grown up, his teacher was made to instruct him in learning; first, the teacher taught him to recite the *Sitan* chapter. By nature he was dull-witted: when he recited the *Sitan*, he would forget the *Xitan*, and when he recited the *Xitan*, he would forget the *Sitan*.
Then the preceptor replied to his father, saying, "In the past, I have taught many young boys, yet I have never seen one as dull-witted as this child.

When the boy Mahāpatha was first instructed, he understood much; however, this boy forgets what he has studied when it comes time to speak, and forgets what he has spoken when it comes time to study. I truly cannot teach him learning."
Having heard these words, the father thought to himself:
"Not all brahmins possess literary learning; it would be appropriate to have him teach the son to recite the *Vidyā* treatises from memory."

He was entrusted to a master to be taught the recitation of the mantras. The master then instructed him in the *Vidyā-śāstra* (Science of Knowledge). Regarding the phrases "dào péng wàng wèng" and "dào wèng wàng péng," these two sounds, "péng" and "wèng," are secret syllables within the four *Vidyā-śāstras* of the Brahmins; they can contain manifold meanings and encompass both humans and deities. Those who practice their recitation generate vast merit and wisdom. For all beginners, one uses the hand to follow the sound to facilitate their recitation and study; this is also called *chánduó shēng* (Chandas-svara), which carries the meaning of rhythmic division.
However, as the characters "xī," "tán," "péng," and "wèng" cannot be translated, their Sanskrit phonetic forms have been retained.
At that time, the teacher said to the boy's father:

"In the past, I have taught many children, yet I have never seen such a dull-witted child; he forgets 'péng' when reciting 'wèng,' and forgets 'wèng' when reciting 'péng. I truly cannot teach him to master his lessons."
When the brahmin had heard these words, he further thought to himself:
"Not all brahmins are able to recite and study; those who are merely brahmins by birth naturally obtain their livelihood, so why should they undergo such hardship?"
Because this boy was by nature dull-witted, the people of the time all called him Mūḍharatha (Stupid Road).
His father held a particular affection for Mūḍharatha and would invariably take him along whenever there was an invitation or summons.

Later, at another time, his father, the brahmin, fell gravely ill; though medical treatment was administered, he gradually grew weak and emaciated. He said to Mahāpatha, "After I have passed away, you need have no anxiety.

However, as for the foolish Patha, who lacks discernment, do not treat him with contempt. Share in both prosperity and adversity, assist one another from beginning to end, and fulfill the duty of brotherhood; you must remember my words."
As the Buddha has said:
"All accumulations are subject to dispersal; what is lofty must fall.
Meetings end in separation; all who have life return to death."
Having spoken these words, he immediately passed away.
The two sons wailed in grief and prepared the funeral rites; they escorted him to the forest, and once the cremation was completed, they returned home filled with sorrow.
At that time, Śāriputra and Mahāmaudgalyāyana, together with five hundred bhikṣus, traveled through the human realms in the kingdom of Kośala and arrived at the city of Śrāvastī.
When the people within the city heard that Śāriputra and Mahāmaudgalyāyana, together with five hundred bhikṣus, were about to arrive there, they went out of the city to welcome them.

At that time, Āḍavala was outside this city under a tree, leading five hundred men and teaching them their studies. Seeing the great multitude all going out of the city together, he asked his students:
"Where are these people intending to go now?"
The disciples replied,
"When these people heard that Śāriputra and Mahāmaudgalyāyana, together with five hundred bhikṣus, were about to arrive here, they have all come out to welcome them."
Mahāpatha asked, "What is there to behold in those two?
I have heard that they both abandoned the most eminent Brahmin caste to go forth as śramaṇas under Gautama of the second caste, the Kṣatriyas; why is it worth welcoming them?"
Among his disciples was a māṇavaka who held the Triple Gem in high esteem; he came before his teacher and said, "Master, do not speak such words.
He has attained the fruits of holiness and possesses great majestic power; if you, Master, were to hear him preach the Dharma, you would surely follow him and seek to go forth into homelessness."
At that time, whenever there was a holiday, the various disciples would either tour the city, or go to the Immortal Canal, or gather firewood for sacrifices, or pay homage at the celestial temples.
Later, while on a break from his studies, Mahāpanthaka thought to himself as he was traveling along the main road:
"Maṇavaka praises the Buddha’s Dharma; I should now go there in secret to listen."
He then went outside the city and saw a bhikṣu walking to and fro beneath a tree; he approached him and said, "Bhikṣu!
How much of the World-Honored One’s sublime Dharma have you been taught?"

Then that bhikṣu extensively explained for him the ten paths of unwholesome action and the karmic results of the ten wholesome actions. Having heard this, Mahāpatha conceived a heart of reverence and faith, and said:
"Bhikṣu!..."
"I shall return again before long.
Having said this, he departed.
Later, on a holiday, he went once more to that bhikṣu’s dwelling and again requested him to preach the Dharma.
The bhikṣu then explained the twelvefold dependent origination in detail for him. Having heard this, his deep faith redoubled, and he said:
"Noble One!
May I be permitted to go forth in this well-spoken Dharma and Vinaya, to practice the holy life under the Tathāgata?"
Then that bhikṣu thought to himself:
"I should now allow him to go forth, so that he may be made to yoke the chariot of the Dharma and carry the torch of the Dharma.
He said to the brāhmaṇa:
"Do as you wish," [the Buddha said].
The brahmin replied, "I am well-known here among the people; I cannot go forth into homelessness."
"You should go to another region for the sake of going forth.
The bhikṣu then took him to another place, granted him the going forth and conferred full ordination upon him, saying:
"Venerable one!"
"As the Buddha has taught, there are two kinds of practice:
first, recitation; second, meditative reflection. Between these two, which do you prefer?
He replied:
“Upādhyāya! I shall do both. Thereupon, during the day, he recited and studied the various sūtras;

before long, he became well-versed in the Tripiṭaka. During the first and last watches of the night, he observed and contemplated, severing all afflictions and realizing arhatship. Possessing the three knowledges, the six supernormal powers, and the eight liberations, he attained knowledge in accordance with reality:

Birth has been exhausted, the holy life has been established, what was to be done has been accomplished, and there is no further existence. My mind is unobstructed like a hand waving through space; whether cut by a blade or smeared with sandalwood paste, neither love nor hatred arises. I regard gold and earth as equal and without distinction; I have renounced all fame and profit, and even Śakra, Brahmā, and the various devas all pay me reverence.
At that time, having attained the fruit, Mahāpanthaka thought to himself:
"Through my diligent recitation and arduous contemplation, that which was to be attained has now been obtained by me."
"I should now go to Śrāvastī to pay homage at the feet of the World-Honored One and serve him with offerings.
Thereupon, together with five hundred disciples, he took up his robes and bowl and traveled by stages until he reached Śrāvastī.

At that time, when the people of this city heard that the Venerable Mahāpanthaka was traveling through the human realms of Kośala with five hundred followers and intended to come here, the entire multitude went out to welcome him.
At that time, after parting from his elder brother, Mṛgāra’s family fortune declined day by day until he fell into poverty and had to beg for his livelihood.
Seeing a great crowd of people coming out, he asked them,
"For what purpose are you all leaving the city?"
The people replied, "Venerable Sir, the Great Road (Mahāpanthaka) has arrived here from Kośala with five hundred followers; for this reason, the people have come out of the city to welcome them."
Having heard this, Upāli thought to himself:
"These people are neither his brothers nor his kinsmen, yet they have come out to welcome him.
I am his younger brother; why should I not go?"
He immediately went out with him and met his elder brother.
His brother greeted him with concern, saying, "Uluva, it has been a long time since we last parted; how have you managed to survive?"
He replied,
"I live by hard labor. He asked:
"Why do you not leave the household life? He replied,
"Since I am both utterly foolish and extremely dull-witted, who would be willing to instruct me in leaving the household life?"
The elder brother then thought, "I do not know whether this younger brother possesses any roots of goodness.
He immediately observed him and saw that he did possess roots of goodness; yet, although such roots existed, with whom were they associated?
Perceiving that they belonged to him, he said to them,
"Come, I shall grant you ordination.
They replied:
"Excellent! he said, and immediately granted him the going-forth and the full ordination. He then gave him a single verse to diligently study and recite:
"Do no evil with body, speech, or mind; Do not afflict any sentient beings in the world."
"With right mindfulness, observe that the realm of desire is empty; one should distance oneself from this fruitless suffering.
At that time, although Upāli recited this gāthā for three months, he was unable to master it.

There were some cowherds who, upon hearing his recitation, all mastered it by ear; at that time, Śroṇakoṭīviṃśa conceived a heart of reverence, went to the cowherds' place, and requested that they teach him the verses (gāthās), whereupon they explained them to him.
However, it is the constant law of all Buddhas that their śrāvaka disciples assemble from all quarters on two occasions:
first, on the fifteenth day of the fifth month when they are about to enter the rains retreat; second, on the fifteenth day of the eighth month at the time of the *pravāraṇā* ceremony.
If they have come from the first assembly, each receives their studies from their respective teachers—namely, reflection, reading, and recitation.
Having received these instructions, they then enter the rains retreat in cities and villages.

If there were those who arrived for the later assembly, they were tested on the scriptures they had previously received and requested to undertake new studies; whatever realizations they had attained, they reported them all.

At that time, when the disciples and followers of the Venerable Mahāpanthaka had each completed their retreats in their respective locations, they went to where Mahāpanthaka was during the later assembly; they were tested on the scriptures they had previously received and requested to undertake new studies, reporting all their realizations as they had done before.
If there were those who were dull-witted, they would serve the group of six monks together.
At that time, Maudgalyāyana was also close to the group of six, and the six monks said to him,
"Maudgalyāyana!"
"Your fellow students have each gone to their teacher to request and receive their studies; why do you not go to request new lessons?
He replied, "I have spent three months reciting a single verse and am still unable to master it; how could I find the leisure to seek out something new?"
The group of six said:
"Venerable ones!
Have you not heard it said:..."
"If the karma one has received is not practiced, it will grow increasingly coarse and harsh day by day.
How could it be that you have not yet mastered this verse?
You should now seek out someone to teach you how to recite it.
At that time, having seen the hardship of his exhortation, Upananda went to his preceptor and said:
"Great Master,
I pray that you will grant me a teacher for my recitation."
Having heard this, Mahāpatha thought to himself:
"Did Mṛgāra himself give rise to this thought,
or was he incited by others?"
Furthermore, he observed that [the disciple] had been encouraged and praised by others;
he then examined Mārgika to see whether he was capable of being transformed through encouragement and praise,
or whether he could be converted through censure.
Observing that he could only be transformed through reprimand, [the Buddha] then seized him by the neck with his hand and pushed him out of the room, rebuking him, saying:
"You are the most foolish and the most ignorant, the most dull-witted and the most obtuse; what do you intend to do within the Buddha’s teaching?"
At that time, Upāli stood outside his cell, tears streaming down his chest as he sighed deeply and said:
"I am neither a layman nor have I become a renunciant; now that I endure such hardship, to whom can I appeal?"

It is the constant custom of the Blessed One to spend his time either wandering among mountain streams, or wandering through groves and thickets, or going to the charnel ground, or wandering within the monastery.
At that time, for a certain reason, the World-Honored One went to the dwelling of Udayin; having arrived, he saw Udayin weeping outside his room and asked:
"For what reason are you now weeping outside your room?"
He addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
By nature I am dull-witted and lack the power of intelligence. Driven out from my room by my preceptor, I am neither a layman nor a renunciant; now I endure hardship with no place to appeal.”
The World-Honored One replied:

"The principle is not so. The holy teaching of the Muni is not your teacher; it was brought forth through the perfection of the six pāramitās, having undergone immeasurable hundreds of thousands of ascetic practices over three incalculable great kalpas."

"However, this sacred teaching is something I have personally maintained by practicing the myriad deeds for a long period of time; are you able to receive it from me directly through oral recitation?"
At that time, Mṛgāra addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
Since I am already the most foolish and the most dull among the foolish, how can I possibly receive and study the teachings directly from the Great Master?”
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed them with these verses:
"The fool who calls himself a fool is called wise;
The fool who falsely claims to be wise is truly deluded."
"However, it is impossible for the Buddha, the World-Honored One, to personally instruct a student in the words and syllables.
At that time, the Buddha said to Ānanda:
'You may instruct Upananda.'"
Then Ānanda, having responded "So be it" to the command, instructed him in recitation; however, he was unable to master the lessons.
Thereupon, Ānanda went to where the Buddha was, prostrated at his feet, stood to one side, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!..."

Since I have personally attended upon the Great Master to receive and uphold the treasury of the Dharma, and am directed by him to preach the Dharma to the assembly of disciples, including the Brahmins, it is not appropriate for me to instruct Mṛgāra.
At that time, the World-Honored One called out to Mūḍharatha and bestowed upon him two lines of Dharma:
"I sweep away the dust; I remove the defilements.
Yet he was likewise unable to remember them as they were spoken.
The World-Honored One, having perceived this and knowing that his hindrance was heavy, instructed him to eliminate it, and said to Upananda:
"Are you able to sweep and wipe the shoes for the bhikṣus?"
He addressed the Buddha, saying,
"I can. "You should now go and wipe the shoes of the bhikṣus," [the Buddha said].
He then followed the instruction and acted accordingly, but the bhikṣus would not permit it. The Buddha said:
"You must not obstruct him; you should desire to cause this person to remove his karmic obstructions, and you should teach him these two lines of Dharma."

At that time, the bhikṣus had him sweep the shoes and taught him two lines of Dharma. Maudgalyāyana applied himself with diligence and constantly recited this teaching; through his unremitting accumulation of merit, he eventually attained mastery.
Then, during the latter part of the night, the bhikṣu Māluṅkyaputra had this thought:
"The Blessed One has instructed me to recite these two lines of Dharma: 'I sweep away the dust; I remove the defilements. What is the meaning of these words?"
There are two kinds of defilement:
first, internal; second, external.
Does this Dharma teaching intend to represent the internal?
Is it intended as an external indication?
Is it a direct exposition?
Or is it a cryptic teaching?

While reflecting thus, he was suddenly enlightened; his roots of goodness were aroused and his karmic obstructions were eliminated. Three sublime verses, which he had never studied before, then manifested from his mind:
"This dust is desire, not the dust of the earth; It is taught in secret that this desire is the dust of the earth.
The wise are able to remove this defilement of desire; It is not for those who are shameless and heedless."
This dust is anger, not the dust of the earth; it is spoken of cryptically as the dust of the earth.
The wise are able to remove this anger; they are not shameless or heedless people.
This dust is delusion, not the dust of the earth; it is spoken of cryptically as the dust of the earth.
The wise are able to remove this poison of delusion; they are not shameless or heedless people.

At that time, Upāli recalled the meaning of this verse and practiced in accordance with the truth, thereby eliminating the three poisons. With diligent effort and without indolence, he severed all afflictions and in an instant realized the fruit of Arhatship. He maintained an impartial mind in which love and hatred were non-dual; having shattered the shell of ignorance, he forever emerged from the cage of worldly existence. Śakra, Brahmā, and the various devas honored and made offerings to him, as described in detail above.
He remained seated there in the full lotus posture without rising.

As Mahāpanthaka was walking by, he saw him sitting thus; however, since an Arhat does not give rise to knowledge and vision unless he applies deliberate attention, Mahāpanthaka pulled his arm and called out, "Venerable one!..."
"Furthermore, first arise and practice recitation, and only then engage in contemplation.

When the bhikṣu Elapattra saw his elder brother compassionately beckon him by the arm to rise, he did not leave his seat but extended his hand long, following after him like the trunk of an elephant king. Having turned back to look and seen this marvel, Mahāpanthaka asked:
"Venerable One!"
"Are you able to realize and witness this sublime virtue?
Maudgalyāyana remained silent and offered no reply.
At that time, after the bhikṣu Maudgalyāyana had attained the supreme fruit, the various non-Buddhist practitioners collectively raised criticisms and disparagement:
“The śramaṇa Gautama himself claims:

‘I have realized a profound and sublime Dharma that is difficult to know and difficult to awaken to; it cannot be fathomed by those who rely on mere ratiocination, but can only be understood by those of great wisdom.’”
Such a statement is indeed a false teaching. Why is this?
Even one as foolish, most foolish, dull, and most dull as this Mūḍha can now realize and enter [the path]; how could it be so profound?
The World-Honored One, having known this, thought to himself:
"This disciple of mine possesses virtues as sublime as Mount Sumeru; why do all these people harbor such resentment and slander?
It is now fitting that I should manifest and proclaim his virtues."
At that time, the World-Honored One said to Ānanda:
"Go now and command Cūḍapanthaka to instruct the bhikṣuṇīs.
Having received the Buddha’s instruction, Ānanda went to where Cūḍapanthaka was and said to him:
"Venerable One!
The Great Teacher has given this command: 'Let the Venerable One instruct the bhikṣuṇīs.
Upon hearing this, Maudgalyāyana thought to himself:
"For what reason has the Blessed One set aside the elder and highly venerable bhikṣus to have me instruct the community of bhikṣuṇīs?
His intention is that I shall manifest my own superior virtues; therefore, I ought now to fulfill the Great Teacher's wish."
At that time, a bhikṣuṇī came into the monastery to request a teacher for instruction and asked the administrative bhikṣu,
"Venerable sir!
Who shall serve as our instructor?"
He replied,
"The Venerable Mūḍha.
Having heard this, the nuns said to one another:

"Virtuous ones, you may observe how these bhikṣus have shown contempt for women; having not mastered even a single verse during the three-month retreat, how can they wish to be sent to instruct the bhikṣuṇīs?"
However, those nuns are experts in the Tripiṭaka with unimpeded eloquence; they are great Dharma masters. How can we have them come to instruct us? We should instead go to pay homage at their feet.
Having arrived, she paid her respects and said:
"Venerable Ācārya, please attend to me!

The community of bhikṣuṇīs from the Rājaka-vihāra pays homage at the feet of the bhikṣu-saṃgha of Jetavana. They inquire after the Venerable One’s health, asking if you have little illness and little affliction, and whether your daily life is light, easy, and peaceful."
"Now let us request a teacher to instruct us.
Upāli replied, "Aubhika."
"Translated as 'expedient means' (upāya), the meaning of these words is:
'All that you have set forth are expedient means for proceeding toward nirvāṇa.
If translated as:
Regarding the use of "Good" or "So be it," although these do not differ from the traditional forms, they nevertheless deviate from the principle of skillful means (*upāya*).
These original characters were retained for the sake of the present time. Upon hearing this, those nuns said to one another:
"This too explains the profound meaning of the Way," he said,
and then took his leave and departed.
Upon arriving at the nunnery, the bhikṣuṇīs asked him:
"Sisters! Who wishes to come and instruct us?
She replied:
"This is the noble Mūḍha.
When the twelve bhikṣuṇīs heard this, they said to one another:
"Venerable sirs, observe how you all despise women! That bhikṣu has not mastered even a single verse in three months; how can you wish to send him to instruct the bhikṣuṇīs?"
The full account is as related above.
They then said to one another:
"Sisters!..."
"We six shall prepare a lion throne twelve cubits high.
Six of us shall go to Śrāvastī and, at all crossroads and thoroughfares throughout the various villages, give public notice so that all people may know:

'Tomorrow, at the Royal Garden Monastery, there will be a great Dharma master whose eloquence is unimpeded, coming to instruct the nuns and preach the sublime Dharma. Those who are able to listen shall attain the vision of the Truth (satyadarśana) and no longer wander in saṃsāra.'"
When these people came to listen to his teaching, if the bhikṣu Mūḍha had remained silent without offering any response, the great assembly would have laughed at him.
For this reason, he caused those fools to no longer come to instruct the community of nuns.
Having deliberated thus, six men prepared a high seat while the other six went throughout the city to announce it; everything was completed exactly as they had envisioned.
Then, during the first part of the day, Upananda put on his robes, took up his bowl, and entered the city of Śrāvastī to wander for alms.

Having received the food, he returned to his original location; after finishing his meal, he put away his robes and bowl, washed his feet, and entered his cell to dwell there with focused mindfulness.
When the afternoon had passed, he arose from meditative concentration and, taking a bhikṣu with him, went to the King’s Garden Monastery.

At that time, there was a vast assembly of immeasurable hundreds of thousands gathered within that temple; some were awakened by the roots of goodness from their past lives, while others were mutually inspired to enlightenment by present conditions.
At that time, the great assembly saw the Venerable Mūḍha coming from afar and asked one another:
"Both have arrived; which of them is the Dharma teacher?"
Someone informed them, saying,
"The one before you is the Dharma Master.
At that time, the great assembly each gave rise to feelings of contempt and spoke as follows:
"These bhikṣuṇīs intentionally vexed me; this foolish Road has not mastered even a single verse in three months—how could he possibly instruct me or preach the Dharma for me?"
Some said this: "Let us observe them first; if they can preach the Dharma, we shall listen.
If they merely intend to mock us, it will do no harm for us to leave, and it will not be too late to depart."
All the people sat together and observed the outcome.
At that time, the Venerable Mūḍhaka, seeing that the lion throne was high, thought to himself:
"Is this intended as a joke?"
"Is it out of respect?

He perceived that they were merely provoking him and had no intention of showing reverence. Then, the Venerable Mūḍha extended his right hand like the trunk of an elephant king, pressed down the high seat until it was low, and sat upon it with composure.
At that time, because the assembly was so large that they could not see everywhere, the Dharma Master immediately withdrew his mind and entered meditative concentration (*samādhi*).

Having entered concentration, he concealed his body so it was no longer visible; he then ascended into the air from the east, manifesting the four dignified postures (*catur-īryāpatha*), emitting water and fire from his body, and performing the eighteen transformations. He did likewise in the south, west, and north.
Having manifested these supernormal powers, he returned to his original seat and addressed the bhikṣuṇīs, saying:
"I have received a single verse over the course of three months; do you wish to hear its meaning?"
"Even if I were to spend seven days and seven nights analyzing the meaning of each individual word and phrase, I could not exhaustively complete it.
He then explained the meaning of the verse:
"One who does not commit evil through the actions of body, speech, and mind—this is what the Buddha taught regarding not causing sentient beings to engage in various unwholesome karmas."
What are called the three evils committed by the body:
killing, stealing, and sexual misconduct.
Those of speech constitute four offenses:
False speech, divisive speech, harsh speech, and frivolous speech.
The three mental offenses:
covetousness, malice, and wrong view.
“Regarding these various transgressions, the Blessed One does not wish for sentient beings to act according to their own whims.

While this half-verse, which served as an excellent metaphor, was being explained, twelve thousand sentient beings within the assembly were all freed from dust and defilement, attaining the pure Dharma-eye and clearly seeing the Truths; some attained the stage of Heat (*uṣmagata*), some the Peak (*mūrdhan*), some Patience (*kṣānti*), or the Supreme Worldly Dharmas (*laukikāgradharma*); some attained the fruit of Stream-enterer (*srotāpanna*), Once-returner (*sakṛdāgāmin*), or Non-returner (*anāgāmin*); some left the household life and realized the fruit of Arhatship; some set out toward the enlightenment of a Śrāvaka, some toward Pratyekabuddha enlightenment, and some toward Unsurpassed Enlightenment (*anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*).
At that time, the great assembly all took refuge in the Triple Gem—the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha—and marveled at such an unprecedented occurrence.

Then, the Venerable Mūḍha, having proclaimed the essentials of the Dharma to the people, instructed, exhorted, benefited, and gladdened them, rose from his seat and departed. The community of bhikṣuṇīs received it with joy and practiced accordingly.
At that time, the twelve bhikṣuṇīs, their intentions unfulfilled, remained silent and said nothing.
Then the six [companions] saw Mūḍharatha approaching from outside and each thought to themselves:
"Today Mūḍharatha will cause many people to lose their faith."
The group of six could not speak to him face-to-face, so they instead asked a monk who was his attendant:
"How many sentient beings has Upananda caused to lose faith today?"
He replied:
"It was truly extraordinary!
Not a single person among them gave rise to a lack of faith."

However, at Vārāṇasī in the Deer Park, the Buddha, the World-Honored One, turned the Wheel of Dharma three times for the sake of the assembly of devas and humans; now, at this time, Upāli has likewise followed in turning it. Even before half a verse in gāthā had been spoken, he caused the great assembly to attain boundless fruits, leading them toward the three types of enlightenment and taking refuge in the Triple Gem.
At that time, Upāli went to where the Buddha was, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and sat to one side.
Then the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus, saying: "O bhikṣus!..."
"Among my śrāvaka disciples, he whose mind is well-liberated is Udraka.

At that time, the World-Honored One praised the observance of the precepts as leading swiftly to liberation and censured the breaking of the precepts as sinking into the cycle of birth and death. He addressed the bhikṣus, saying:
"The former was the initial injunction; this is a subsequent allowance. I now re-establish a training rule for the bhikṣus, which should be spoken thus:"
"If a bhikṣu, without being dispatched by the Saṃgha, goes himself to instruct a bhikṣuṇī, except when he has attained a superior dharma, it is a pāyattika.
"If a bhikṣu" refers to the group of six; the meaning of "Saṃgha" is as explained above.
"Not having dispatched" means not performing the *jñapti-dvitīya-karman* (the formal act consisting of a motion and one proclamation).
"Bhikṣuṇī" refers to a nun within this Dharma.
"Instruction" (*anuśāsana*) refers to teaching and instructing them by means of the dharmas of ethical discipline (*śīla*), meditative concentration (*samādhi*), and wisdom (*prajñā*).
"Except for one who has attained the supreme Dharma": if one has attained a particularly sublime Dharma that is unerring and faultless, one is therefore "excepted"; the rest is explained as above.
What are the characteristics of the offense and its specific instances herein?
If bhikṣus appoint a person outside the boundary, the assembly incurs an offense of wrong-doing (duṣkṛta);
if the person so appointed goes to provide instruction, he incurs an offense of falling (pāyattika).
If one appoints a person within the boundary but it is not the day of the *poṣadha*, the assembly incurs an *āpatti* of wrong-doing (*duṣkṛta*);
if the appointed person goes to provide instruction, they incur an *āpatti* of falling (*pāyattika*).
If, although within the boundary and on the day of the *poṣadha*, the assembly does not gather, the offense incurred is the same as before.
If the procedure for appointing [an official] is faultless, yet the person is not one who maintains the precepts, the offense incurred is the same as before.
Although he maintains the precepts, he is not widely learned and has not yet completed twenty years of summer retreat;
although he has completed twenty years of summer retreat, he is not well-versed in the dialects of the capital;
although he is well-versed in local dialects, he once defiled a bhikṣuṇī and failed to perform the proper expiation.
Even if she is pure, if she cannot discern and instruct the nuns regarding the eight *pārājika* rules;
or even if she can explain them, if she cannot discern the eight *gurudharma*s;
if these various dharmas are not fully possessed, the assembly incurs the offense of *duṣkṛta*.
Those who are dispatched all incur an offense of downfall (*pāyattika*).

However, if the dispatching is performed according to the Dharma, the assembly is endowed with perfect virtues, the monks are without fault, and the instructor commits no transgression, [there is no offense].
If there is no one at the residence to provide instruction to the bhikṣuṇīs, a brief method of instruction should be performed.
When a bhikṣuṇī comes to request an instructor, the elder or the administrator should say to her:
"Sister!..."
Is the Bhikṣuṇī Saṃgha harmonious, pure, and free from transgressions?
Now that no one among this assembly desires to go and instruct the Bhikṣuṇīs, you members of the Saṃgha should be diligent and not be negligent.
She replied,
“Aubhika. The nun should then pay homage at her feet and depart.
Furthermore, there is no offense for one who is the very first offender, or for one who is insane, mentally deranged, or overwhelmed by intense pain.
At that time, all the bhikṣus were filled with doubt and, wishing to request the World-Honored One to sever their doubts, addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
By what causes and conditions did the group of twelve bhikṣuṇīs come to exist?
Furthermore, for what reason did the group of twelve bhikṣuṇīs intend to bring harm to the venerable Mūḍha, yet instead achieve great benefit for him?
"I only pray that the Blessed One will explain the causes and conditions for this.
The Blessed One told them: "O bhikṣus!"
Not only today do these nuns, intending to cause harm, instead bring about great benefit; even in the distant past, these very same nuns intended to cause harm but instead invited benefit.
"You all should listen!

In the past, in a certain village, there was a brahmin who married a wife. Not long after, he had a son, and subsequently another son was born. In this manner, twelve sons were born; when they had all grown up, each took a wife and built a separate residence."
Not long after, his mother fell ill and passed away. His father, already advanced in years, was blind in both eyes and could see nothing at all.
At that time, while her husband—the son—was away, the new wife engaged in illicit and evil acts with a man from outside the family.
The brahmin was skilled in discerning the characteristics of sounds; when he heard the sound of walking, he knew whether it was his own son or another’s.
Hearing that sound of walking and knowing it was not his son, he immediately rebuked the bride, saying:
"Do not commit such wicked deeds."
At that time, the bride, perceiving his anger, said to one another:
"This brahmin will bring us harm; we should now deprive him of his fine food."
He then gave them coarse rice mixed with sour gruel; as the Brahmin was already advanced in years and frail, he could not bear to eat it.
The Brahmin then said to his sons:
"You sons-in-law have given me this coarse food mixed with sour gruel; how can this possibly sustain my life?"
Then those sons said to their wives:
"For what reason have you given our father coarse rice mixed with sour gruel?
The wives replied to their husbands:
"The Great Elder’s merit is exhausted; what fault is ours?
Whenever we cook rice, we cast white grains into the cauldron, yet they turn into red rice;
when mixed with fine curd, it turns into sour gruel."
Her husband replied,
"How could such a thing be possible?
His wife then answered:
"If you do not believe me, you may observe for yourself.
The women deliberated and said, "We have already informed our husbands; we must now seek to avoid being caught."
He then went to the potter’s place and said,
“O worthy one!
Could you perhaps make two earthen cauldrons, each with one opening and two bellies, each with a capacity of several *śu*?”
The potter said,
"If you give me double the price, I shall make it for you.
He replied:
"Very well!
Having finished his work, the potter’s wife paid him the wage and took the vessels home to prepare food for her husband.

In a private place, she placed red rice in one compartment of the two pots and vinegar in the other; then, in the presence of her husband, she placed white rice in one compartment and delicious curd in the other.
When both pots were cooked, she said to her husband,
"Shall I give the food first to my father-in-law,
or shall you eat first?"
The husband said,
"First serve my father.
His wife then poured red rice from one cauldron and served it, followed by pouring vinegar broth from another cauldron and serving it.
Next, he went to his husband’s side and served him white rice along with fine curd. Once the son had seen this, he said to his father:
"Father, your merit has truly been exhausted; for within the same pot, though you placed white rice and added fine curd, once it was cooked, it turned into red rice and sour gruel."
Upon hearing this, his father thought to himself:
"Since my youth, I have never practiced deception; I have established my livelihood by seeking wealth entirely in accordance with the Dharma."
"Why is it that my meritorious karma has now been exhausted?
It must be this wicked woman who, through her own deceit, has deceived me.

Thereupon, while the people were away, the old man entered the kitchen alone and felt around among the pots and vessels. He then groped in the dark and seized two pots, both of which had partitions inside; he immediately took the pots and hid them in a secluded place.
When the sons had arrived, he took up the cauldron and said to them:
"You should know this!
It is not that my merit has been exhausted; rather, it is the cauldron that causes merit to be exhausted."
He spoke in verse:
"O sons, you should know: Another’s cauldron feeds but one belly;
Now that my merit and karma are exhausted, One cauldron must feed two bellies."
At that time, when those sons saw this matter, each became incensed with their wife and severely beat her, saying:
"If you act like this again, we shall give you a heavy flogging and drive you out of the house."
