When the women heard these words, they said to one another:
"This old brāhmaṇa is plotting with his son to harm us; we ought to employ some other expedient to sever his life-force."
At that time, a snake charmer came into the house, and the women asked him,
"Do you have any poisonous snakes for sale?
He replied:
"What kind of snake do you require?
Is it dead or alive?"
He replied, "He is dead.
The other thought to himself:
"What is the meaning of these women seeking a dead snake?
Is it not because they intend to kill this old brāhmaṇa? He asked.
"How much do you wish to be paid?
He replied, "Whatever you ask."
"When venomous snakes are provoked and distressed, their poison is located in two places: namely, the head and the tail.
The snake charmer then produces a black snake, strikes it with a staff until it becomes enraged, severs both its head and tail, and takes the middle section of its belly to give to the woman."
Then, having obtained it, he prepared it as a soup; once the soup was cooked, he took it to his grandfather and said, "Grandfather, you have this fine meat soup; would you be able to eat it?"
At that time, the brahmin thought to himself:
"Where can I obtain meat to make a soup for me? Is this not a ruse intended to kill me?
Then he further thought:
"I am now old and infirm, with no one to provide for me; what is the use of living?
Whether right or wrong, I shall eat.
He then spoke to his daughter-in-law:
"I must have some meat broth brought for me to eat.
Once the food was served, because of the aroma of the broth, the cataracts over his eyes cleared and he gradually became able to see objects; nevertheless, he feigned, saying, "I am dead!"
"I am dying!
When the wives heard this, they wished for his life to end quickly and said,
"Is there any remaining soup that you can finish eating?"
He replied, "I can eat.

His wife gave him all of it, and he ate it again. His eyes became bright and clear; looking left and right, he could see everything with perfect clarity. Joyful in his heart, he feigned sleep and did not rise.
When those brides, like those suffering from an eye disease, committed various unrighteous acts in the presence of the Brahmins, the Brahmins would seize their staffs, rise up abruptly, and declare:
"I have now seen you; do not do so again!"
At that time, the wives remained silent and offered no reply.
"O bhikṣus, do not harbor any other thoughts: the brahmin of that time was none other than Maudgalyāyana, and the twelve wives were none other than these twelve bhikṣuṇīs."
"In the past, when he sought to take his life, it instead resulted in great benefit; now, when he seeks to bring him shame, it further manifests his holy virtue.
At that time, the bhikṣus again had doubts and asked the World-Honored One:
"Venerable One, what karma did the Elder Mūḍha previously commit to receive a human body so utterly foolish and dull-witted?"
The Blessed One said:
"This action formerly committed by the bhikṣu Cūḍapanthaka has increased, reached its maturity, and its retribution has now manifested before him. You bhikṣus!"

For all sentient beings, the karmic fruition of the wholesome and unwholesome deeds they themselves have committed does not ripen within the external elements of earth, water, fire, or air; rather, it ripens solely within their own aggregates, elements, and sense bases.
He spoke in verse:
"Though a hundred eons may pass, the karma one has created does not perish;
when the causes and conditions meet, the retribution must be experienced by oneself."

"O bhikṣus! In the distant past, when the lifespan of humans was twenty thousand years, there appeared in the world the Buddha Kāśyapa—a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Vidhyācaraṇasaṃpanna, Sugata, Lokavid, Anuttara, Puruṣadamyasārathi, Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām, Buddha, Bhagavān."
At that time, there were twenty thousand members of the assembly of śrāvakas, all of whom resided in the kingdom of Vārāṇasī.

Mūḍha was among their number; he was well-versed in the Tripiṭaka and served as a great Dharma teacher, yet by nature he was stingy with the Dharma and never instructed others, not even explaining a single four-line verse.

After his life ended, he was reborn in a celestial palace; having died there, he fell into the human realm, being born into a family of pig-sellers, where he gradually grew up and took up the profession of slaughtering pigs.
Beside that village there was a large river, and not far from the riverbank lay another settlement.
When the day of the festival arrived, the butcher thought to himself:

"If I were to slaughter many pigs now and carry their meat to sell, should there be no buyers, the meat would all rot and I would suffer a financial loss. It would be better to take the pigs alive to that village; on the day itself I shall slaughter them for sale. In this way, there will be no loss and the profit will be much greater."
He then bound the pig with ropes and placed it upon the boat.
As the pig butted and jostled one another, the boat’s hold shook violently; the pig and the boat were simultaneously capsized and submerged. With no means of rescue, the pigs all perished.
At that time, the butcher also went along with the current. On the riverbank, there were five hundred pratyekabuddhas dwelling in dependence upon a forest.
Then, one pratyekabuddha who had gone to the river’s edge to fetch water saw a man floating downstream from afar and thought to himself:
"Is this person drifting with the current dead?"
"Is he alive?

Having observed him closely and knowing him to be a living person, he immediately manifested his supernatural powers; extending his right hand like the trunk of an elephant king, he seized the man and departed, leaving him face-down on the dry sandbank.

When that drowning man had finished vomiting out all the water, he immediately stood up and looked in the four directions around the city. Seeing human footprints, he followed the tracks until he reached the place where the pratyekabuddha was staying; having paid his respects, he requested to remain there as a dependent disciple.
Day after day, he gathered flowers, picked fruits, and collected various roots and leaves to serve the pratyekabuddhas.
In turn, those pratyekabuddhas provided for him with their leftover food. At that time, all the pratyekabuddhas sat cross-legged and remained absorbed in meditative concentration.
Upon seeing this, the butcher also learned to sit in the full lotus posture; by practicing it repeatedly and without ceasing, he attained the state of non-conceptual absorption (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*).
Later, when his life ended, he was reborn in the Heaven of Non-conceptual Beings (*asaṃjñisattva-deva*), and after passing away from there, he was born here among humans.
"O bhikṣus, do not harbor other thoughts!

The pig-slaughterer of that past time was none other than this very bhikṣu, Mūḍha. Because in former times he was stingy regarding the Dharma—to such an extent that he did not explain even a single four-line verse to others—and because he frequently slaughtered various animals, and furthermore because he was born in the Heaven of No-Thought (asaṃjñisattva-deva), through those karmic conditions he has become utterly foolish and dull-witted."
Therefore, you bhikṣus should not be stingy with the Dharma; you should train yourselves thus: to preach the Dharma to others with a pure mind;
to always give rise to compassion for all sentient beings; and to remain far removed from those of wrong determination. You should train yourselves thus.

The Twenty-first Section, Part Three: The Training Rule on Not Teaching Bhikṣuṇīs Without Being Appointed. At that time, the bhikṣus, having witnessed the events as described above, were all filled with doubt and addressed the Buddha once more, saying:
“World-Honored One!”
With what intention did the bhikṣu Cūḍapanthaka, through a brief instruction, exert himself with right diligence and quickly manage to transcend saṃsāra, realizing the ultimate peace of nirvāṇa?
The Blessed One said:
"You should know this!

It is not only today that the bhikṣu Cūḍapanthaka has been able to realize awakening through brief instruction; in the past as well, by applying himself with right diligence due to brief instruction, he attained great wealth, honor, and lived in peace and happiness."
"You all should listen!

In the distant past, in a certain village, there was an elder who was immensely wealthy, possessed of great riches, and enjoyed abundant prosperity. Not long after he had married his wife, a son was born to him, whose physical appearance was handsome, as described in detail previously."
He said to his wife, "O virtuous lady!
I now have a son for whom there are many expenses; I wish to go to the ocean to seek out precious treasures."
The wife said,
"As you wish.
The elder then thought to himself:
"If I were to leave much wealth with my wife, she would surely become arrogant and extravagant, and I fear she might commit unrighteous acts.
Thus, he gave her but little.
In that village, there was a merchant leader who was his friend; he entrusted all his remaining goods to him, saying:
"I now wish to travel abroad to seek my fortune, though the date of my return is yet uncertain; if my wife should lack food or clothing, you should provide for her.

He then took his wealth and entered the great ocean, where he encountered a storm that wrecked his ship, and having gone forth, he did not return; the man to whom he had entrusted his affairs paid no heed to him.
At that time, the elder’s wife, relying on the strength of her kin and through her own efforts, raised her son. As he gradually grew up, he asked his mother:
"What kind of livelihood did my father and grandfather pursue to maintain our family estate?"
The mother thought to herself:
"If I were to reply that he has gone to sea to engage in trade, I fear this son might also go out to sea; should he meet with disaster and fail to return, I would suffer in solitary misery."
He then replied,
"Your grandfather engaged in trade here as a means of livelihood.
The son said to his mother:
"I shall give you money so that you may learn the art of commerce.
His mother replied to him,
"Where would I have any money to give?"
"I have merely supported you with the meager resources of my kinsmen; I possess no other wealth to fulfill your desires.
However, the merchant leader Somagiri is your father’s old friend and acquaintance; you may seek goods from him and carry out your business as you please."

Having heard this, the son went to the merchant’s residence. At that time, someone from the merchant’s household was taking money; having failed three times, the merchant was in the midst of angrily rebuking him, and there was no opportunity for the son to enter.
The maidservants of his household were carrying out some refuse, among which was a dead mouse; they all intended to discard it.
The elder, harboring resentment, said to the man who had taken his money:
"Do you know this now?"
"In this world, there are those who understand how to seek profit; they can, because of a mouse discarded by this slave girl, achieve abundant wealth.
When the son of the householder heard these words from afar, he thought to himself:
"This great merchant leader will certainly not speak falsely; surely it is because of this dead mouse that one can obtain wealth and happiness."
He then followed the maidservant to observe her dwelling.
The maidservant had discarded a dung-rat into a pit; the boy took the rat and went to the great marketplace, where he saw a hungry cat with its neck tied to a pillar, and showed the rat to it.
Seeing the mouse, the cat immediately sprang forward; at that moment, the cat’s owner said to the boy, "Give him a dead mouse.
The boy replied:
"How can you expect to obtain another object with mere empty words?
If you pay the price, I shall give you the mouse.
The cat's owner then paid a handful of peas as the price.
At that time, the boy left the mice behind and took the beans; he then roasted them on a tile until they were cooked. He then thought to himself:
"If I eat them all, I will have nothing left of my original goods."
He then wrapped the beans in the hem of his robe, took a flask of cold water, and went outside the village to wait for their return at the place where the wood-sellers rested.
At that time, the wood-sellers arrived together as evening fell; seeing them approach, the youth said to them, "Elder brothers!
Since the weather is already scorching hot, you should rest for a while."
At that time, the wood-seller immediately paused for a moment; the boy then took some cooked beans and distributed them to the people, giving them cold water as well.
The people asked, "Younger brother!..."
"Where do you wish to go?
He replied,
"I wish to gather firewood."
He replied, "I left the city this morning and have only just now arrived. If you were to go now, you would not return until evening; your toil would be in vain and you would surely gain nothing."
Then those people each reduced their own firewood by one piece and offered it to him in exchange.

The youth took the wood and combined it into a single load; he went to the market and sold it, using the cowries he obtained to purchase mung beans, which he roasted until they were thoroughly cooked. Carrying a jar of cold water, he returned to his former location to await the wood-gatherers.
When the people had arrived and were distributed as before, the woodcutter saw them and said joyfully, "I am relieved;
thank goodness I have recovered.
He then replied:
"You should look after this place every day; we shall each provide you with an extra load of firewood as wages for your labor.
Because of this, the youth subsequently gained great profit.
At that time, the youth replied to the men, saying:
"Brothers, do not take these firewood to sell in the market; pile them all together at my house, and I shall sell them for you, paying you the price by the bundle."
The people agreed, giving him firewood for its price.
Later, at another time, he encountered overcast skies and rain; after seven days of continuous downpour, the price of firewood had increased, and he obtained even greater profit.
The youth thought to himself:
"Though I have gained profit, it will not endure for long; living by selling firewood, I am held in contempt by others.
He immediately purchased various miscellaneous goods and established a small shop of his own, whereby his profits increased even more.
He further thought:
"These miscellaneous goods are a source of shame for a merchant.
He then placed them in a perfume shop and sold them at their respective prices, thereby obtaining twice as much money as before.
He further reflected:
"This has no great utility.
He then established a gold shop that yielded even greater profit and eclipsed all other shops.
The merchant, out of envy, gave him the nickname "Rat" and called him the "Gold-Shop Owner.
The assembly deliberated together, saying:
"Gentlemen, you should know!..."

"Because this rat has eclipsed our gold shop owner, our trade has not been successful. We should go together to his place, incite him to go to sea to seek many treasures, and cause him to die there instead of returning because of it."
They immediately approached the vicinity of the shop where they had heard the voice and deliberated together, saying:
"Do you all know? Observe how those in the world who do not carry on their lineage see their conduct decline day by day."
It is like a man who first rode an elephant, then a horse, then abandoned the horse for a carriage, and finally abandoned the carriage to travel on foot.

This owner of the jeweled shop was just like this: from his grandfather’s time onward, he had always entered the great ocean to seek fine treasures, providing for himself and being praised by people near and far.
"This boy cannot support himself today; he has opened a small gold shop and must toil to earn a living by trading in ivory—how truly pitiable!
Upon hearing these words, he asked the people:
"What were you discussing just now?"
The people answered him fully regarding the matter.
Having heard these words, he returned home in silence and asked his mother:
"Did my grandfather once enter the great ocean, seeking precious jewels as a master merchant?"
The mother thought to herself:
"Could it be that this son has heard or learned of this elsewhere? Now I ought not to deceive him myself; it is fitting that I inform him of the matter according to the truth."
"Your ancestors and forefathers all went out to sea, serving as great merchants and being praised by all.
He said to his mother,
"I now also wish to go to the islands of the sea to seek precious treasures."
The mother said, "You need not go.
Before long, he petitioned her again; the mother, knowing his resolve was firm, finally did not stop him.
Having obtained his mother’s permission, he immediately ordered that it be proclaimed throughout the city:

"Gentlemen, if any among you wish to enter the great ocean to seek precious jewels, you should follow the merchant leader Mūṣikakanaka; by paying no taxes on your goods, you shall go and return in safety. You should prepare in advance the merchandise required for the voyage."
At that time, there were five hundred merchants who, having heard the announcement, each prepared sea goods and awaited the departure date.

Then, the merchant leader Suvarṇamūṣika consulted on an auspicious day for a favorable occasion; subsequently, together with the others, they took their various wares and transported them by means of carts, horses, and porters toward the seashore.
Having reached the sea, the merchants, filled with fear upon beholding the ocean, all intended to retreat and were unwilling to board the ship.
At that time, the caravan leader, fearing they would all return home, said to the helmsman:
"Good sir, you should report truthfully regarding the precious goods within the sea."
The helmsman then addressed the people, saying:
"You people of Jambudvīpa, each of you should listen well!

Within this great ocean there are many extraordinary goods and rare treasures, namely: mani-jewels, pearls, vaidūrya gems, coral, shell-jade, gold, silver, red pearls, and exquisite right-turning conch shells; such various jewels are beyond counting."

If you are able to enter the great ocean and obtain this treasure, you shall personally enjoy it with joy throughout this single lifetime; your parents, wife, children, kinsmen, acquaintances, and all your servants shall likewise be free from hardship. From time to time, you will be able to provide for śramaṇas, brāhmaṇas, and others; as a result, you shall be reborn in the happy realms where rewards follow you, and you shall go to the celestial palaces to experience various pleasures, gradually cultivating supreme merit and ascending the path to nirvāṇa.
"If you would enjoy this, you should board the ship together and enter the great ocean.
When the people of the world heard that they could attain such wealth and prosperity, their hearts were filled with joy, and they all boarded the ship together.
The crowd was large and the ship was heavily laden;
the merchant leader thought to himself, "Since they have already personally urged me to board, how can I now make them disembark?
He then said to the helmsman:
"You should now speak of the dangers and calamities within the great ocean.
At that time, having heard the words of the merchant leader, the helmsman immediately informed the people with the truth, saying:
"O people of Jambudvīpa, you should listen!

Within this great ocean there are great terrors: namely, the makara, the great fish that swallows ships and spews forth waves; vast surging billows that swirl and eddy boundlessly; river otters and sea boars that pose dangers everywhere; and sudden black winds that arise, drifting one to the corners of mountains, where sails are torn, banners are shattered, and there is nowhere to cry out for help.

Furthermore, there may be blue-bannered pirates who suddenly and unexpectedly arrive, smashing your great ship and severing your lives, thereby forcing you all to abandon your beloved bodies so that you and your parents and kinsmen shall never see one another again.
"You all should reflect upon yourselves and do what is good.

At that time, the multitude of people were mostly timid and few were courageous; having heard this proclamation, many disembarked from the ship, whereupon the vessel became light and balanced, ready to cross over. After the announcement had been made three times, they removed the submerged stones. Stirred by a long wind, the great ship surged upon the waves like a swift cloud soaring upward, and everyone reached the treasure island in safety and security.
The helmsman said:

"All merchants from Jambudvīpa must know this: in these treasure islands, many counterfeit lapis lazuli closely resembles genuine jewels. You should carefully test them before taking them; do not arrive back in your own land only to feel regret."

Furthermore, on this jewel island there dwell cranes and rākṣasas who, upon seeing you, will employ various stratagems and speak with soft words to deceive you, ultimately causing you all to lose your lives.

Furthermore, in this continent there are many "intoxicating fruits"; if a person eats them, they will be unable to regain consciousness for seven days. You must take note of this and exercise caution.

Furthermore, this continent is frequently inhabited by non-human beings who dwell there; for seven days they tolerate one another, but once the seven days have passed, they unleash a great wind that blows their merchant ships to pieces.
When the merchants heard these words, they each fortified their positions and gathered vast quantities of precious treasures—like rice, hemp, grain, and beans—and heaped them into the ships.
Then, the helmsman awaited a favorable wind and set sail back for Jambudvīpa.
In this manner, he returned safely seven times.
His mother said to him,
"You should take a wife and establish a household."
The son said to his mother,
"I shall follow your instructions only after I have repaid my debt.
His mother told her son:
"Your grandfather did not have any prior debts or interest; why do you say today that you must repay a debt?
He replied, "I myself know that I have one."

He immediately fashioned four mice out of the four precious substances and, having filled a silver platter with golden grain, placed the four mice upon it and went to the house of his father’s acquaintance, the merchant leader.
Then that merchant leader discussed the matter of the "rat-gold" with the assembly:
"Gentlemen, do you know?
The merchant leader Ratna has great merit; if he takes up a tile or a stone, they all become precious gold."
When these words were spoken, the gatekeeper informed the merchant leader, saying,
"The merchant leader Mūṣikakanaka has arrived outside the gate.
He replied:
"Call him in! He must not be turned away.
The gatekeeper led him inside and immediately presented a golden tray containing a precious rat before the merchant leader, saying:
"This is the principal, and this is the interest," [the mouse] said.
The merchant leader replied, "I do not recall ever giving you any wealth; why do you now speak of repaying principal and interest?"
He replied, "I do remember it.
He then related in detail to the merchant leader the circumstances concerning the mouse he had discarded in the past.
The merchant leader asked,
"Whose son are you? He replied:
"He is the son of such-and-such a householder.
The merchant leader said, "He is the son of my own friend; I ought to give him [the goods] to you—how could you possibly repay me?"
"Your father, on the day he departed, left various goods with me which I have not yet returned.
He then gave his eldest daughter to him as a wife, adorned her body with necklaces and jewels, and escorted her to his home.
The World-Honored One said:
"O bhikṣus, do not harbor any other thoughts. The merchant leader of that time was none other than myself; the merchant leader Gold-Rat was none other than Maudgalyāyana."
In the past, I spoke of a minor cause regarding a dead mouse, which ultimately enabled [the recipient] to attain great wealth and prosperity.

Now, by means of my brief instruction, he has exerted himself to sever all afflictions, crossed over the shore of birth and death, and attained the supreme, wondrous fruit of the eternal realization of Nirvana.

At that time, the Venerable Mūḍha, having gone forth within the well-spoken Dharma and Vinaya, attained the fruit [of Arhatship]. In the city of Rājagṛha there was a great physician-king named Jīvaka. Hearing that the Blessed One had granted the going-forth to the Venerable Mūḍha—who was extremely dull and slow-witted—he thought to himself:
"If the Blessed One comes here, I shall invite the Buddha and the community of bhikṣus, with the sole exception that Mūḍha is not included in the invitation."

At that time, the World-Honored One, desiring to transform and deliver all sentient beings, traveled gradually from Śrāvastī until he reached the city of Rājagṛha and stayed in the Kalandaka Bamboo Grove.

At that time, Jīvaka, having heard that the Buddha had arrived at the Bamboo Grove Monastery, went to the Buddha’s dwelling, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and sat to one side. The Buddha then taught him the essentials of the Dharma, instructing, exhorting, inspiring, and gladdening him.
Having heard the Dharma, he rose from his seat, bared his right shoulder, placed his right knee on the ground, and with palms joined in reverence, addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One, I only pray that the World-Honored One and the community of bhikṣus will come to my home tomorrow to accept my humble offering."

The World-Honored One accepted by remaining silent. At that time, Jīvaka, having personally witnessed the World-Honored One’s majestic and solemn presence, did not dare to speak face-to-face except to mention Cūḍapanthaka; he paid homage to the Buddha and withdrew, then went to Ānanda and respectfully said to him:
"Venerable Sir!..."
"Tomorrow I have invited the Buddha and the Saṃgha, wishing to provide a modest offering; out of respect for the Buddha’s majesty, I did not dare to face him personally and said:
'With the exception of Pūramāla.
At that time, Ānanda replied to Sīvaka:
"Act according to the prince's wishes so that his merit may increase.
Then the prince prostrated at his feet and departed.
After the prince had left, Ānanda went to Mṛgāra and said to him:
"Venerable sir!
You should know this: tomorrow Prince Upāli will invite the Buddha and the Saṃgha to his residence for a meal, with the sole exception of you, Venerable sir."
At that time, having heard these words, Upāli replied to Ānanda, "Let it be according to the prince's wish, so that his merit may increase.
Thereupon, that prince immediately prepared various kinds of excellent food and drink that night; at dawn, he arranged and set out water basins and sent a messenger to inform the Buddha:
“The meal is now prepared; we pray that you will know the time.

At that time, during the first part of the day, the World-Honored One donned his robes, took up his bowl, and set out with the great assembly, with the sole exception of the foolish Rādha. Having arrived at the prince’s residence, he inspected the water to ensure it was free of insects, washed his feet, and sat down upon the seat.
The Buddha said to Ānanda,
"You should set aside a seat for Upananda. Then Ānanda,
having received these instructions, set aside a place for him.
At that time, the prince held a golden pitcher filled with clear water and was about to proceed from above.
Then the World-Honored One was unwilling to accept it. Jīvaka addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One, why do you not accept the water?"
The Buddha said,
"Prince! The community of bhikṣus has not yet fully assembled."
The prince asked the Buddha,
"Who has not yet arrived?
The Buddha said:
"The bhikṣu Śāriputra has not yet arrived.
The prince said to the Buddha,
"I did not invite him."
The Buddha said,
"Prince, did you not take the Buddha as your head and universally invite the Saṃgha?
He replied:
“World-Honored One!
Please summon the great assembly.
The Buddha said:
“Prince! Is that foolish Māṭhara outside the assembly?
The prince replied:
"He is not outside the assembly.
The Buddha said,
"If that is the case, you should go and summon him."
Then Jīvaka thought to himself, "Out of respect for the Buddha, I have sent someone to summon him; I cannot show him such honor as to provide him with food and drink.
He then commanded his messenger, saying:
"You should now go to the Bamboo Grove and summon the Venerable Maudgalyāyana.

At that time, Maudgalyāyana, perceiving the prince's intention within the Bamboo Grove, then manifested himself as one thousand two hundred and fifty bhikṣus, all of whom were identical in appearance to Maudgalyāyana himself.
When the messenger arrived at the monastery and called out,
"Venerable Mūḍha, Venerable Mūḍha," all the bhikṣus responded at once.
The messenger did not know which one was the actual Mūḍha.
He immediately returned and reported to the prince, saying, "Within the bamboo grove there are bhikṣus filling it; I truly do not know which one is Maudgalyāyana.
The Buddha said to the messenger:
"Go to the monastery and say these words:
'The truly foolish Mārga should come forth.
The messenger went immediately to the Bamboo Grove and called out:
"Let this truly foolish Mārga come forth.
At that time, Mārga used his supernormal powers to go to the place where he was to stay and took his seat.

When Upavāna saw that he had arrived, he served food to the Buddha and the Saṅgha in due order; however, when it came to Mārga’s turn, he did not treat him with respect, and although he gave him food, he did so without any faith or reverence.
The World-Honored One then thought:
"My disciple is of profound virtue and most sublime; yet this Upavāṇa, out of folly, has brought harm upon himself. I should now manifest his superior excellence."
At that time, when the World-Honored One had finished his meal, Ānanda wished to take the Buddha’s bowl, but the World-Honored One did not give it to him.
Now, it was the constant custom of the World-Honored One that as long as he had not yet put away his bowl, none of the assembly of bhikṣus would put away their bowls.
When the foolish Māṭhara saw that the bhikṣus had finished their meal but had not yet put away their bowls, what was his motive?

He perceived that [the monks] wished to manifest his own virtue; he then shifted half of his seat, extended his hand like the trunk of an elephant king, and went to where the World-Honored One was to take his bowl.
At that time, the prince was standing beside the Buddha; having seen his hand, he asked, "Which great virtuous one has manifested this supernatural power?
Following the bowl as it moved, he wished to observe its form and recognized it to be Pūrṇa Maitrāyaṇīputra.

Having seen this, he was overcome with great anguish and fell to the ground in a faint. At that time, his kinsmen sprinkled water on his face, and only then did he regain consciousness. He then approached Mūḍharatha, grasped his feet, and prostrated himself in worship, seeking mercy and offering an apology while speaking these verses:
"The nature of sandalwood is ever cool; The essence of the *utpala* flower is perpetually fragrant;
A golden platter always emits wondrous light; A lapis lazuli gem is forever fresh and pure."
The evil person is constantly prone to anger and harm, Just like a drawing on stone that is difficult to remove;
The sage is always accompanied by wondrous goodness— I pray you will have compassion for me and grant me forgiveness!
At that time, Mṛgāra replied to the prince, saying, "I have always maintained patience; how could I harbor any resentment?
Thereupon, the prince went to where the Buddha was, prostrated at the Buddha's feet, and withdrew after paying his respects.
When the bhikṣus had arrived at their dwelling place, they were all filled with doubt and requested of the World-Honored One:
"Venerable Sir,

by what cause and condition did Prince Śivaka fail to show respect when he did not yet know the true virtues of the Venerable Mūḍha, yet upon coming to know them, prostrated at his feet and sought forgiveness through repentance?"
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"It is not only today that such a thing has occurred; it was also thus in the past.
You should listen!"
In a past age, there was a great king named Brahmadatta. At that time, there was a horse-dealing merchant from the north who drove five hundred horses toward the central kingdom.
At that time, the caravan leader had a mare who suddenly became pregnant; she was of the breed of wise horses.
From the day she conceived, the other horses in the herd no longer neighed. The caravan leader then thought:
"Is there something wrong with these horses of mine?"
"For what reason have they not neighed nor pranced for many days?
Later, when the mares had given birth to foals, the five hundred horses stood with their ears drooping, not daring to make a sound by sneezing or coughing.
At that time, having witnessed this event, the caravan leader immediately thought to himself:
"For what reason has this being of meager merit been born within the horse herd? Because of this fault, all my horses have become afflicted with disease."
He habitually rode this mare, yet he never gave her the finest grass or grain.
Traveling south by stages, he reached the borders of the Central Kingdom and arrived at a village named Gongshi.
Just as they were there, it happened to be the rainy season; the caravan leader then thought:
"If I depart now, my horses will all suffer from sore hooves, which will lead to illness and much loss. It would be best for me to remain here for the time being."
Once they had halted, the people of the nearby villages and towns, according to their respective crafts, each brought rare and wonderful objects to present to the caravan leader.

When the summer retreat ended and the merchants were about to depart, all the craftsmen came to see them off; the caravan leader recompensed them in accordance with the goods he had previously received from them.
At that time, there was a potter who had previously presented earthenware vessels to the merchant leader;
hearing that he was about to depart, his wife said to him, "You should now go to see the merchant leader again, so that perhaps he may remember you and reward you with goods."
At that time, having heard his wife’s words, the potter immediately took a lump of clay and fashioned it into an auspicious seal (mudrā). He then went to see the merchant leader.
Upon seeing him, the merchant leader said: "O man!..."
"You have arrived far too late; my wealth and property have already been spent. What thing can I give you to express my remembrance?
However, the merchant leader had no affection for the small foal, considering it an inauspicious omen, and said to the potter:
"I now have only this small foal; if you require it, take it as you please."
The potter replied:
"I have expended great effort in crafting various vessels; why would I need this useless colt to trample them into pieces?"

At that time, having heard these words, the colt knelt before the potter and licked his two feet; seeing this, the potter felt a surge of affection and immediately took him, leading him back to his house.
When his wife saw him, she asked,
"What goods did you obtain from the merchant leader?
Her husband replied:
"I have obtained this foal.
His wife said,
"Excellent indeed is this thing!"
"It tires me to make vessels that are trampled and ruined as soon as they are finished.
Upon hearing these words, the horse went to his wife's side and licked her two feet; when she saw this, she too conceived a heart of affection.
At that time, the colt moved about and circled among the various fired and unfired clay vessels without causing a single breakage. The wife reported to her husband, saying:
"This lovely little colt is truly skillful in its attentiveness; it has walked within the clay vessels without sustaining any injury whatsoever."
At that time, the potter went a distance away to fetch earth, and this young colt followed behind him.
When the potter filled his bag with earth, the little colt lowered its back to approach it; the potter placed the bag upon its back, and it slowly carried the earth back to the house.
The husband said to his wife:

"My beloved foal shall relieve me of my labors; I will place it on its back with an earthen bag upon it in the field, and you may carry it down from there into the house. You must always provide it with food made of rice bran mixed with the dregs of sesame oil."
“At that time, King Brahmadatta of Vārāṇasī had a wise horse that died of illness.
When the distant border kingdoms heard that the king’s horse had died, they each dispatched envoys to inform the king:
‘Your Majesty should now pay tribute to our countries; if you do not, do not pass through our city gates.’”
"If anyone comes out again, bind them with ropes and bring them here.
Although the king heard these words, he did not give him the goods, fearing that [the horse] would not leave the city.
At that time, a horse-dealing merchant arrived in the kingdom of Vārāṇasī. Having heard that horses from the north had arrived in great numbers, the king told his ministers:
"Recently, all my victories were due to this intelligent horse; now that the horse has died, I am being treated with contempt.
How much longer must I remain hidden within the city? You gentlemen should seek out an intelligent horse for me."

The ministers, having received these instructions, entered the caravan of horse-merchants together with the horse-trainer and inspected five hundred horses. They recognized that these horses had been trained by the Wise Horse, yet though they searched everywhere, they could not find the Wise Horse.
At that time, the horse-trainer saw the mare and said to the stable-keeper:
"Do you know now?
This mare will surely give birth to a wise colt; for what reason has it not been seen?"
Together they asked the caravan leader,
"Have you ever sold or given away any of these horses?
He replied:
"I have never sold a horse; however, there was one colt which I considered inauspicious, so I requested it from a potter's house in a certain city.
Then the horse-evaluator said to the ministers, "You should know that he is a wise horse.
The merchant leader is dull-witted and cannot distinguish a noble steed; he has discarded the finest essence of ghee for useless dregs."
Having spoken thus together to the king, they went to the city of Saṃsevaka and approached the potter, asking:
"For what purpose do you now require this colt?
He replied:
"I shall have him carry the earth.
The horse appraiser said,
"I will trade my donkey for yours."
He replied, "It cannot be.
The minister reported this, saying:
"Would you be willing to exchange these four oxen along with the cart?
He replied, "I cherish this colt;
the oxen and the cart are of no use to me."
The ministers said, "You should reflect carefully; we shall come again tomorrow.
Thereupon, they took their leave and departed.
Although the colt belonged to the class of animals, his intelligence surpassed that of humans; sensing the opportune moment, he spoke in human language.
After the ministers had departed, the colt said to the potter, "What was that man seeking when he came here just now?"
He replied, "I am looking for you. [The other] said,
"If you are seeking me, why not give it to him?"
"O Benevolent One, you should not now entertain such thoughts as: 'May I spend my entire life carrying earth for you, with rice husks and hemp dregs as my sustenance.

If there were a Kṣatriya Great King who had received the consecration of his rank, and whose body was shielded by a hundred-branched golden parasol being held aloft—such a superior person as that, I would carry and support."
"When it is time for me to eat, I will eat as much as I wish from a golden basin, mixing honey with husked rice.
If those people come tomorrow and ask about the colt, you should reply to them:
'Why do you treat one another with such contempt?'"
If you call him a wise horse while pretending not to recognize him, you shall call him a colt.
As for his price, demand one hundred million gold pieces; or else, place the gold in a pouch and pull him here with all the strength of my right foot.
"If you obtain this, we shall give it to you.
On the following day, the ministers came and asked the potter: "O man!"
"Have you reflected upon this? He replied,
"I have already reflected and reached a decision."
He asked,
"Will you give me the colt?
The potter then answered everything exactly as the intelligent horse had said.

When the horse trainers heard these words, they said to one another, "This potter is obstinate, foolish, and lacking in discernment; how could he possibly know whether this horse is intelligent or not?"
"It must be that this horse, wishing to repay its debt of gratitude, instructed him to devise this plan during the night.
The minister said, "O potter!"
"The value can be discussed in terms of whether it corresponds to wisdom or lacks wisdom.
The potter said, "I shall give you one hundred million pieces of pure gold, as much as you desire; or else, let a bag filled with gold be pulled by the horse's right hoof—that shall be the measure."
The ministers deliberated and said, "He possesses great strength, pulling up double the amount of gold; it is fitting that we reward him with one hundred million [pieces of gold] as a fixed standard.
The ministers then dispatched an envoy to inform the Great King:
"Now that this wise horse has been obtained, I demand one hundred million in gold.
Having received this message, the king told the messenger:
"Give him whatever price he demands and bring it back here."
He then took a billion pieces of gold and sent a messenger to fetch the horse.

Once the messenger arrived there and had delivered the gold, he brought the wise horse to Vārāṇasī, led him into the stable, placed him in the foremost stall, and fed him with unhusked barley and grass.
The horse refused to eat; the king personally observed that it was not eating and said to the groom:
"Could it be that this wise horse has fallen ill?"
He replied, "Great King!
The horse is truly not ill; I should now inquire."
He spoke in verse:
"Do you not remember the potter’s house, Where grain, water, and fodder were always lacking?
Your body was emaciated, nothing but skin and bone, And in hunger and exhaustion, you ate the wild rice from the fields."
Day and night you always followed the potter’s will, constantly carrying earth and enduring humiliation;
now you are the chief charioteer for the king—by what cause do you not eat, as if harboring sorrow?
At that time, the wise horse, harboring indignation in his heart, replied in anger:
"I possess swift feet and a courageous mind; in careful deliberation and wisdom, none surpass me.
You know all my excellent virtues; for what reason do you cause others to treat me with such contempt?"
Only you can distinguish between good and evil, yet you do not follow or honor the ancient laws;
I would rather die now with my mouth closed than live while being held in contempt by others.
Even if I am long deceived and treated with contempt by fools, I shall not give rise to a mind of sorrow or vexation;
yet seeing those I know well treat me with even momentary slight, it causes me such grief that I have no hope of living.
When the horse-keeper heard these words, he said to the Great King:
"Your Majesty should now provide for the wise horse according to the sequence prescribed by the ancient seers;
if the sequence is not followed, he will certainly refuse to eat."
The King asked,
"In what order? He replied:

"You should prepare for his arrival at a distance of three *yojanas* from the city, leveling the roads and adorning them with banners and canopies. The King, accompanied by his fourfold army, shall personally go out to welcome him. The ground where he is to be stationed shall be paved with sheets of red copper. The Crown Prince shall personally hold a golden parasol with a thousand ribs to shade him from above. The King’s eldest daughter shall hold a fly-whisk adorned with gold and jewels to drive away mosquitoes and flies. The Queen Mother shall take polished rice smeared with honey on a golden platter, holding it in her own hands to provide him with food. The Chief Minister shall personally hold a golden winnowing fan to receive his excrement."
The king said, "If one is provided with such service as this, that person is effectively the king; what further use would I have?
The groom replied:
"This is not merely a matter of whim; rather, for the ritual of welcoming [the Buddha] after a seven-day fast, the principle dictates that it must be done in this way.
The King said, "What has already passed cannot be repeated; as for what remains before us, it should be performed according to the Dharma."

He immediately spread a sheet of red copper upon the place where the horse stood in the stable; the Prince himself held a golden parasol with a thousand ribs to shade it, the King’s eldest daughter held a fly-whisk to brush away flies, the Queen-mother presented food on a golden platter, and a high minister held a winnowing basket to receive the horse's dung.
Upon seeing such exquisite provisions, the horse immediately began to eat them.
Then, the stable keeper spoke this verse:
"The Great King now provides you with these most excellent offerings; [The horse] has accepted them all."
"Whatever you require shall be according to your wishes; toward the King, you must exert your utmost sincerity.
The horse replied to that man:
"I shall follow your words; whatever needs to be done, my mind will be free from indolence."
At that time, the Great King wished to go to the pleasure grove; his ministers, having prepared a saddle and bridle of various exquisite jewels, brought the wise horse to the King's presence.
At that time, when the wise horse saw that the king was about to mount it, the horse arched its back.
The king asked,
"Is the horse suffering from its back?"
The charioteer replied, "It is not that he is suffering from a sore back; I fear the King will find it difficult to mount, which is why he has arched his spine.
The King then took the reins and proceeded to the riverbank, but the horse refused to advance.
The king asked his charioteer,
"Is it because the horse has a fearful mind that it refuses to enter the water?
He replied:
"This is not a river of fear; I do not enter it for fear that it might moisten or splash upon Your Majesty's person.
Thereupon, he tied up its tail and placed it in a golden bag, and crossed over the water.

The king remained within the park, indulging in his pleasures for many days; when the various kingdoms from afar heard that the king was residing within the park, they raised large armies and marched toward the city gates.

When the king heard that the troops from the bordering kingdoms had all arrived, he mounted his intelligent horse and intended to enter the city through a rear gate. On the way, there was a great pond called Brahmāvatī, which was completely covered with many lotuses, utpalas, and other such flowers.
At that time, the wise horse reached the edge of the pond; treading upon lotus flowers, he proceeded slowly and entered the city, causing the border rebels to flee and scatter.
The King was greatly delighted and said to his ministers: "Do you all know?"
"If there were one who could save the life of a consecrated Kṣatriya great king, how should he repay that debt of gratitude?
The ministers replied,
"He ought to be granted half the kingdom."
The King said:
"He is but an animal; how can I grant him a reward equal to half the kingdom?

It would be more appropriate to arrange for him a grand *pañcavārṣika* (unrestricted) feast within seven days, providing him with a *kūpodaka* assembly at an unusual time, giving him everything he requires."
The ministers, having received these instructions, all performed the task accordingly.
At that time, a horse-dealing merchant chieftain, seeing that a great assembly had been convened, asked the people:
"For what reason is this great assembly being held at an improper time?"
The people replied, "Do you not remember how, in the city of Saṃsevya, you begged a horse colt from a potter?
That was an intelligent horse, prized by the whole world; the King purchased it from him for one hundred million gold pieces, and it saved the King's life."
"Because of this auspicious occasion, we have established an unrestricted festival (amogha-pūjā).
Upon hearing this, the merchant leader thought to himself:
"Could it be that the horse I left behind is this wise steed?"
"I should now go and observe his appearance.
Having arrived at the stable, the wise horse saw him and asked,
"O Merchant Lord!"
"How much was obtained from the sale of the many horses?
I alone have already repaid the potter with one hundred million gold pieces.
Upon hearing this, the merchant leader fainted and fell to the ground; only after water was sprinkled on him did he revive. He then clasped the horse's feet in gratitude and departed.
At that time, the Buddha addressed the bhikṣus:
"Do not harbor any other thoughts!
The merchant leader of that past time was none other than Prince Jīvaka; the wise horse of that past time was none other than the bhikṣu Maudgalyāyana."

In the past, when the caravan leader did not recognize the superior qualities of the wise horse, he treated him with contempt; yet once he knew of those superior qualities, he apologized and departed.

Now, while Śivaka did not know that Māṭhara possessed superior qualities, he gave rise to pride; but upon learning that he was endowed with such virtues, he prostrated at his feet and offered his apologies.
Therefore, O Bhikṣus!

Ordinary persons, lacking the eye of wisdom themselves, should not hastily give rise to contempt for others; rather, they should observe all things with wisdom wherever they may be—thus you should train yourselves.

22. The Training Rule on Instructing Bhikṣuṇīs until Sunset. This is the twenty-second training rule concerning instructing bhikṣuṇīs until sunset. The Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
The Buddha commanded Nandaka to instruct the bhikṣuṇīs by preaching the Dharma to them.

At that time, the bhikṣuṇī Utpalavarṇā, together with a retinue of five hundred, went to the venerable Nandaka; having prostrated at his feet, they sat to one side and requested instruction and the proclamation of the sublime Dharma.
Then Nandaka, using complete phrases and meanings with exquisite and beautiful words, preached the Dharma for her; the listener forgot her fatigue until sunset.
When the nuns finally departed and reached the gate, the city gates were already closed.
Then the community of nuns called out for the gate to be opened, but the gatekeeper said,
"The gate has already been closed.
The nuns spoke again, saying:
"Your father is full of reverence and faith; for what reason does he obstruct me?
You should open it for me. He replied:
"The keys have already been entrusted to the royal household; there is no way we can gain entry.
Since the nuns were unable to enter, they said to one another, "Not far from here is an empty grove;
let us go there to spend the night together."
As the Blessed One said:
"Even when dwelling under trees, one should divide [the provisions] according to the established order.
He then divided them and gave them out according to that order.
"This is the tree of the noble one [Name], and this is the ground of [Name]," they cried out, making a clamor that was heard outside.
At that time, there were five hundred thieves who, intending to go near the city to commit robbery, heard the sound of those nuns and said to one another:
"We must not approach the city yet; let us first plunder these old palace women."
At that time, the nun Utpalavarṇā perceived through her insight that the bandits were approaching and thought to herself:
"Let not these bandits plunder my fellow practitioners while they are in this loathsome state; I shall observe them so that no noise from this may give rise to lack of faith among others."

Observing that a band of five hundred thieves was about to come and plunder, he then manifested himself as the military forces of King Vīradatta, with the sound of drums resounding from all four sides.
The thieves said to one another, "This is the king's army surrounding us on all sides; they will surely kill us, and our lives depend on a mere moment."
"We ought to flee in the four directions.
Once the bandits had dispersed, the nun Utpalavarṇā addressed the other nuns, saying:
"Sisters!..."
"A band of five hundred thieves heard the sound of voices in the night and intended to come and plunder us; by my supernatural power, I have caused them to flee.
You all should distribute yourselves while keeping your voices low."
Having stayed there overnight, she entered the city at dawn.
At that time, when the brahmins and householders saw the bhikṣuṇī entering from outside, they immediately gave rise to derision and spoke thus:
"The Śramaṇas, sons of the Śākyas, possess truly marvelous teachings; men and women dwell together while practicing pure conduct."
The bhikṣus of few desires heard this and felt revulsion and shame; they immediately reported the matter in detail to the Blessed One.
The Blessed One assembled the bhikṣus and asked Nandaka:
"Is it true that you actually instructed the bhikṣuṇīs until sunset?"
He replied, “It is indeed so.

The World-Honored One reproached those who were ignorant of the proper time and lacked tranquility in various ways; he praised those who knew the proper time and were able to cultivate tranquility, and addressed the bhikṣus, saying:
"I now establish this training rule, which should be recited as follows:
'If a bhikṣu, though appointed by the Saṃgha to instruct bhikṣuṇīs, should provide instruction until the time of sunset, it is a pāyattika.'"
"Furthermore, 'if a bhikṣu' refers to Nandaka; the remaining meanings are as explained above.
'Appointed by the assembly' means by means of a *jñapti-dvitīya-karman* (a formal motion followed by one proclamation).
'To instruct' means to instruct them by means of the teachings of the Threefold Training (*tri-śikṣā*)."
Regarding the characteristics of the offense herein, what are its specific instances?
If it is evening and one perceives it as evening, or if there is doubt, one incurs a *pāyattika* (offense of falling).
If it is not yet evening but one perceives it as evening, or if there is doubt, one incurs a *dukkaṭa* (offense of wrong-doing).
If it is not yet evening and one perceives it as not yet evening, or if it is already evening but one perceives it as not yet evening, there is no offense.
If one preaches the Dharma throughout the night, or if the temple gate is nearby, or if the city gates are not closed, in all such cases there is no offense.
Furthermore, there is no offense for one who is the very first offender, or for one who is insane, mentally deranged, or afflicted by intense pain.
At that time, the bhikṣus requested of the World-Honored One, saying:
"Bhadanta!..."
"For what reason did the nun Utpalavarṇā protect five hundred nuns and cause them to escape the danger of bandits?
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"It was not only today that they rescued one another; in the past as well, they saved one another."
"You all should listen!
In the distant past, there was a merchant leader in a certain village who, not long after marrying his wife, told her:
'I now wish to go to another region to engage in trade and business.'"
The wife said:
"Excellent! Since there are no children, I shall go along with you as well."
The husband said:
"The road ahead is long and perilous; who will provide for you?
You should stay here and not follow me."
When his wife saw that he was being blocked, she immediately began to weep.
Her traveling companion said to her,
"For what reason must you weep?"
He replied,
"I wish to accompany you, but you will not take me with you.
The traveling companion said to the merchant leader:
"You may go together with us.
The merchant leader asked,
"Who will provide for you?"
The companion said,
"I shall look after it for you," and immediately took it away.
Having traveled a long distance, they stayed overnight in a mountainous and perilous place. While everyone else was asleep, only the merchant’s wife remained awake.
At that time, a lion entered the merchant's camp; the woman then whirled a torch in her hand and drove the lion away.
A deity in the sky saw this and spoke a verse:
"Not all undertakings can be accomplished by men alone!
Though she be but a woman, she possesses the wisdom to drive the lion."
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"The merchant's wife of that past time was none other than the bhikṣuṇī Utpalavarṇā.
Just as she once saved the traveling merchants during the night in the past, she is now likewise able to protect five hundred bhikṣuṇīs by driving away the bandits."

23. The Training Rule on Accusing Another of Teaching Bhikṣuṇīs for the Sake of Food and Drink. The twenty-third training rule concerning accusing another of teaching bhikṣuṇīs for the sake of food and drink. The Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
The Buddha commanded Nandaka to instruct the bhikṣuṇīs and preach the Dharma to them.

At that time, the bhikṣuṇī Mahāprajāpatī, together with a retinue of five hundred, went to Nandaka’s place; having prostrated at his feet, they requested him to preach the Dharma and then sat to one side.

At that time, Nandaka expounded the meaning of the verses with a profound and wondrous voice; however, the women, possessing little wisdom, were unable to understand them immediately, and filled with fear, they did not dare to inquire further.

Then Mahāprajāpatī and her retinue, having heard the Dharma, prostrated at his feet and departed; they then proceeded to where the Buddha was, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and sat down to one side.
The Great Lady (Mahāprajāpatī) addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

We recently went to the place of the Venerable Nandaka to request that he preach the Dharma. At that time, the Venerable one expounded the meaning of the verses with a profound and wondrous voice; however, we women possess little wisdom and were suddenly unable to comprehend it. Filled with fear and trepidation, we did not dare to ask him questions.”
As the Buddha has said:
"Through giving, one attains fearlessness.
If the Blessed One permits the community of nuns to provide offerings to the bhikṣus, I shall provide offerings according to my ability.
The Buddha said,
"You may do as you wish.
At that time, the bhikṣuṇī did not know with what she should make an offering.
The Buddha said:
"One should provide five kinds of solid food, or five kinds of chewable food, or items such as a waistband.
At that time, there was a bhikṣuṇī who personally carried milk porridge and delicious rice balls into the Jeta Grove, going to the place of the Venerable Nandaka.

At that time, the six bhikṣus would each take turns standing in front of the monastery gate to practice walking meditation. One day, at the monastery gate, Upānanda saw a bhikṣuṇī and asked her: "Sister!"
"What do you have with you? He replied,
"It is milk porridge and some fine dumplings."
He asked, "With whom do you wish to share this meal?
He replied:
"I shall offer it to the Venerable Nandaka. Upānanda said, "Sister!"
"If I, Upānanda, were always to receive milk-rice porridge and fine rice-balls, I too would be able to constantly instruct the community of nuns.
Subsequently, another nun arrived carrying curd-rice porridge or various cakes;

seeing her, Upānanda said in reply, "I had previously thought that Nandaka was teaching the Dharma to the nuns with a mind of righteousness; who would have known that he was merely instructing them for the sake of such trivial matters as food and drink?"
When the bhikṣus of few desires heard these words, they felt revulsion and shame, saying:
"How can a bhikṣu speak thus:
'I instruct the bhikṣuṇīs for the sake of food and drink'?"
Having reported these circumstances in detail to the World-Honored One,
the World-Honored One assembled the community of bhikṣus and asked Upānanda:
"Did you truly speak these words?"
"Is it true, monks, that you instruct the nuns for the sake of food and drink?
Upānanda replied:
"It is indeed so, Venerable Sir!
Having rebuked him in various ways, the Blessed One said: "I shall now establish a training rule (śikṣāpada), which should be recited as follows:"
"If again a bhikṣu speaks thus to other bhikṣus:
'You instruct bhikṣuṇīs for the sake of receiving food and drink offerings,' it is a pāyattika."
"Furthermore, 'if a bhikṣu' refers to Upānanda; the remaining meanings are as stated above.
'Food and drink' refers to the five kinds of solid food and the five kinds of chewable food; the rest is the same as previously explained."
In this regard, what are the characteristics of the offense and how does it occur?
If a bhikṣu says to another bhikṣu:
"You teach bhikṣuṇīs for the sake of food and drink."
Those who [speak thus] all incur a *pāyattika* offense.
However, there is no offense if one speaks knowing that a bhikṣu is actually instructing a bhikṣuṇī for the sake of food or drink.
Furthermore, there is no offense for the very first offender, or for one who is insane, mentally deranged, or overwhelmed by intense physical pain.

24. The Training Rule on Giving Robes to a Bhikṣuṇī Who Is Not a Relative. The twenty-fourth training rule concerning the giving of robes to a bhikṣuṇī who is not a relative. The Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
In this city there was an elder who lived with his wife; they had no children. As they grew old, their relatives, friends, wealth, and means of subsistence were all exhausted. He said to his wife:
"O virtuous lady!..."
"I am now old and can no longer manage my affairs; I wish to leave the household life to become a renunciant.
His wife said, "I shall also leave the household life."
He replied, "As you wish.
They then followed him to the place of Mahāprajāpatī; having prostrated at her feet, they said:
“Venerable sir!
My wife wishes to go forth in the well-expounded Dharma and Vinaya; I only pray that you, venerable sir, will grant her the going forth and confer upon her full ordination.”
Then, the Great Mistress (Mahāprajāpatī), having learned that there were no obstacles, immediately granted her the going forth and the full ordination.
Then the Great Mistress said to her husband, "O Noble One!"
"The nature of women is to be largely prone to attachment; you, sir, should come from time to time to visit and inquire after her.
He replied, "Very well!"
The man immediately went to a certain bhikṣu in the Jeta Grove and sought refuge to leave the household life.
After the bhikṣu had questioned him, he granted him the going forth and conferred full ordination upon him.

At that time, when the people within the city heard that the elder had left the household life, they marveled at such a rare occurrence; everyone provided him with offerings of food, drink, clothing, bedding, and medicinal requisites, hoping thereby to attain superior merit.
At another time, he put on his upper robe and went to the nunnery to visit two former female companions.
After the nuns had prostrated at his feet, they sat to one side; they looked up repeatedly to gaze at his *saṃghāṭī*. Then the bhikṣu said to them, "Sisters!"
"Do you wish to have this great robe?
He replied,
"If there is indeed a surplus, it would be excellent to give it away!"
The bhikṣu then thought:
"This intention is difficult to refuse; I shall give him this robe and make another for myself.
He then gave him the robe and departed.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Ānanda, saying:
"You may inform the bhikṣus:
'The World-Honored One intends to travel among the people of the world. If there are any who wish to follow the Buddha, they should take up their robes.'"
Then Ānanda, having received these instructions, announced them. The Blessed One, surrounded by the great assembly in silence as described at length above, desired to go to the kingdom of Magadha.

It is the Blessed One’s constant custom that when about to set out on a journey, he turns his entire body to the right and gazes back, like a great elephant king surveying his herd, lest the robes of the bhikṣus be disarrayed.
Seeing that bhikṣu intending to go abroad while wearing only his upper and lower robes, the World-Honored One, having seen this, said to Ānanda:
"Could it be that the bhikṣu has not obtained summer robes at the place where he is observing the rains retreat?"
He addressed the Buddha, saying,
“I have obtained it.
The Buddha said:
"Why is it that this bhikṣu has no saṃghāṭī, but travels with me wearing only two robes?
Ānanda then related the matter in full, and the Blessed One said,
"Did the bhikṣu give his robe to a nun who is not a relative?"
He addressed the Buddha, saying,
“I shall give it.
The Buddha said:
"One who is not a relative does not know how to deliberate; whether she has robes or not, she accepts them as soon as they are offered.
A relative, however, is not like this. For this reason, the World-Honored One asked that bhikṣu:
"Did you truly give a robe to a nun who is not a relative?"
He replied, "It is truly so.
The World-Honored One rebuked him in various ways, as extensively explained before, and continued until he established the training rule, which should be recited as follows:
"If a bhikṣu gives a robe to a bhikṣuṇī who is not a relative, except in exchange, it is a pāyattika.
Regarding "if a bhikṣu": this refers to one within this Dharma; the remaining meanings are as explained above.
There are seven kinds of robes, all as described above.
Regarding this, what are the characteristics of the offense and its specific details?
If one gives a robe to a person who is not a relative, while perceiving them as not being a relative or having doubt about it, one incurs a *pāyattika* (offense involving falling).
If one gives a robe to a relative while perceiving them as a non-relative, or while being in doubt about it, one incurs an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*).
If one gives a robe to a relative while perceiving them as a relative, or to a non-relative while perceiving them as a relative, there is no offense.
If one sees someone in distress who lacks clothing, there is no offense in giving it to them;

or, perhaps while preaching the Dharma, out of appreciation for eloquent speech, one gives a large cotton cloth (*karpāsa-śāṭī*); or perhaps one gives it because of receiving the precepts; or again, one sells it to them or exchanges it with them.
Furthermore, there is no offense for one who is the very first offender, or for one who is insane, mentally deranged, or overwhelmed by intense physical pain.
*Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya*, Fascicle 32. *Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya*, Fascicle 3.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Yijing by Imperial Decree. The Twenty-fifth Training Rule:

Making Robes for a Bhikṣuṇī Who Is Not a Relative. The Twenty-fifth Training Rule: Making Robes for a Bhikṣuṇī Who Is Not a Relative. At that time, the Blessed One was staying in Śrāvastī, at the Jeta Grove, in Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the bhikṣuṇī Gupitā’s five robes were worn out, yet she had many other robes;
she then thought to herself, "Who will sew a great robe for me?"
While she was reflecting thus, other nuns came to her place and said,
"Guptā! Why do you appear to have a look of sorrow?"
He replied, "Sisters!
My five robes are all worn out and tattered, and my saṃghāṭī is especially torn to pieces."
"I now have many cotton garments, but I do not know whom I should send to make them.
The nuns replied,
"Do you intend to carry a golden bowl and beg for food from others?"
"You have the noble Udāyin, who is well-known to the assembly; how could you possibly worry that no one will stitch your robe?
He replied, "He is a person of venerable virtue; how could he do it for me?"
He replied, "Perhaps it may be for you.
He reported this, saying:
"He certainly could not. He replied,
"How could anyone about to cross a river remove their boots upon merely hearing the sound of flowing water?"
"You may take this cotton cloth and perhaps sew it for me.
At that time, Gupta took the white cotton cloth and went to Udāyin’s place, where she prostrated at his feet and sat down.
At that time, Udāyin saw the large piece of cloth and said to her, "Guptā!
If a person obtains such a fine,
new white cloth and sews it into a double-layered saṃghāṭī robe for use as occasion demands, they will increase their cultivation of all wholesome qualities day by day."
Guptā said, "Venerable Sir, if you require it, it is only right that I should offer it to you.
However, my great robe is extremely tattered; I shall now entrust this bolt of cloth to you so that you may have a robe made from it."
At that time, Udāyin thought to himself: "I am the one who sews;
whenever the group of twelve nuns needs to have a robe sewn, they all come to rely on me. How can I continue to endure such toil for others?"

"If she does not have it sewn, Guptā will harbor resentment. I should now employ a method to sew it so that it becomes like a wooden cauldron—destroyed by a single boiling—and thus she will not come again to have me sew and stitch it."
He replied to Guptaka, "You may leave the cotton cloth behind.
At that time, the six bhikṣus arrived; seeing the large cotton cloth, they asked:
"Venerable sir!
Whose cloth is this?
He replied:
"This is the person who is beloved.
He asked, "Who is the beloved?"
He replied,
"It is Guptā. [The other] said, "If that is so, we shall do it together."
He immediately cut the cloth and finished embroidering it on the spot.

Then Udāyin took this great robe (*saṃghāṭī*) to the walking path (*caṅkrama*) and, using thread of five colors, embroidered upon it the image of himself and the nun Gopikā embracing one another. He then took the great robe and placed it on a rack inside his cell.
When Guptā arrived, she asked,
"Is the robe finished?
He replied:
"As soon as the robe is finished being embroidered, you shall come here.
He then placed the robe upon the other's shoulder and said, "Until it has been dyed, you must not open it at all; if you open it, you will incur an offense."
At that time, Guptā took the robe and departed.
A fellow nun said to her, "Guptā, bring the robe here;
let me examine it to see how the Venerable One has embroidered it."
Guptā replied, "Have you not heard the Venerable Udāyin say:
'As long as the cloth has not yet been dyed, do not open it prematurely; if you open it, you will incur an offense.'"
Upon arriving inside the monastery, the nuns said, "Let us examine the robe; how has it been embroidered?
They replied:
The noble Udāyin spoke thus:
"Until it has been dyed, one must not open it at random; if one opens it, one incurs an offense.
At that time, a bhikṣuṇī with whom he was on intimate terms forcibly pulled the great robe (saṃghāṭī) from his shoulder and opened it.
When the nuns saw this, they all laughed loudly and said:
"The noble Udayin and Guptā have not been able to see one another for a long time; only today have they finally managed to join necks and dwell together."
Then Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī replied to the nuns, "Your heads are hairless and the hair in your armpits is long; what joy can there be for you to be so noisy and laughing?"
The nuns said, "Venerable One!
Udāyin has committed an unrighteous act; it is because of this that we are laughing."
He then asked for the reason, and the nun reported the matter to him.
At that time, Mahāprajāpatī addressed the nuns, saying:
"That man constantly commits evil deeds and brings ruin to the Holy Teaching, causing the riverbanks of the Dharma to crumble day by day."
The bhikṣuṇīs reported this matter to the bhikṣus. Upon hearing it, the community of bhikṣus felt revulsion and shame, and they reported the matter in full to the Buddha.
The Buddha asked Udāyin, "Is it true that you made a robe for a bhikṣuṇī who is not a relative?"
He replied, "It is truly so,
Venerable Sir!"
The Blessed One assembled the bhikṣus and, after reprimanding Udāyin in various ways, established this training rule, which should be recited as follows:
"If a bhikṣu makes a robe for a bhikṣuṇī who is not a relative, it is a pāyattika."
"Furthermore, regarding the phrase 'if a bhikṣu,' this refers to Udāyin; the remaining meanings are as explained above.
What are the characteristics of the offense and its specific details?
The six points concerning the gravity of the transgression are the same as before, and the cases of non-offense are as stated above."
26. The Training Rule on Traveling with a Bhikṣuṇī. The second training rule on traveling with a bhikṣuṇī. The Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the six bhikṣus, Nanda and Upananda, thought to themselves and said to one another:

"These black-bowl holders smear their feet with monkey fat and constantly travel in the four directions; when they are about to depart, they receive offerings from others, and upon their return, they again receive provisions, being loved and respected by many."
"We are like frogs in a well who have never traveled abroad; therefore, we lack the opportunity to receive the offerings of others.
We should now inform our sisters.
At the first part of the day, she put on her robes, took her alms bowl, and went to the place where the group of twelve bhikṣuṇīs was, saying to them:
"Sisters! Remain well-established; I wish to travel abroad to teach and transform beings wherever I go.
When those nuns heard this, they all wept.
Udāyin asked, "Sister,
why are you weeping?"
He replied,
"Great Virtue has departed!
The pleasure grove is now empty."
He replied: "Sisters!
The Great Master dwells in this world with hundreds of thousands of noble disciples; why do you recklessly claim that he is empty and void?"
He replied:

"When those who carry black alms-bowls even hear my name, they are not pleased; how could they possibly allow me to sit at their place, grant me conversation, or permit me to proclaim the sublime Dharma?"
Upānanda said, "If it is so,
you may go together with me.
The nun Khujjuttarā said:
"Is it appropriate for a bhikṣu to travel along the same road as a bhikṣuṇī?
Upānanda replied, "According to reason, it is appropriate to go; who would ever obstruct you?"
"You should prepare a large amount of provisions for the journey so that you may accompany us.

At these words, the bhikṣuṇī prepared everything accordingly. Then the group of six bhikṣus put on their robes, took up their bowls, entered the city to beg for food, and having obtained it, went to the nunnery.
The group of twelve saw him and said,
"Venerable One,
please partake of some light food."
The group of six accepted [the invitation], and having consumed all their provisions for the journey, they said to the nuns, "Sisters!
You have prepared provisions for the journey; should you not bring them here so that we may see whether they are good or not?"
The nun replied, "The light meal we had earlier was all travel provisions; it has now been completely consumed.
The group of six said:
"If it is thus, how can we sustain one another over such a long journey?
You should prepare more; if you lack sufficient provisions, you will surely suffer from hunger.
He then prepared further supplies, and they both joined a caravan of merchants.
At that time, there was also a bhikṣu who went on alms-round and wished to follow along;
the people informed him, saying, "These six men are all of evil conduct; if you go with them, you will undoubtedly be troubled."
The mendicant said:
"I did not receive instruction from him, nor do I rely upon him as my teacher; for what reason does he trouble and disturb me?"
Not accepting their exhortations, they nevertheless went along with them.
When the group of six had reached the boundary outside, they said to one another:
"How can we continue to serve these models for long?"
"You should each act according to your own inclination regarding your deportment.

At that time, Nanda, together with the bhikṣuṇī Nandā, Nanda’s disciples and the disciples of the bhikṣuṇī, down to the śrāmaṇeras and śrāmaṇerīs, traveled along the road together in one place; Upānanda and the others did likewise.
At that time, there were brahmins, householders, and others who, seeing such a mixture of people, spoke thus:
"This is the wife of the śramaṇa; this is a son; this is a daughter; this is a daughter-in-law; this is a grandson. This is no different from the laity; how can there be any True Dharma here?"
Upon hearing this, Upānanda said to him:
"You wretched and evil Brahmin!
Even if I were to trample your throat with my foot right now, what does it matter to you whether I have many wives and children, or whether my actions are lawful or unlawful?"
When that mendicant bhikṣu heard this, he thought to himself:
"I would rather die than travel together with such a person of evil conduct."
He then immediately returned to the Jetavana Grove.
When the bhikṣus saw him, they asked, "Welcome! "
"Are your belongings secure and at ease?
He replied,
"Venerable sir!"
"How could there be peace and happiness?
I was traveling along the same path as the group of six monks; they committed evil deeds that bring ruin to the Buddha-dharma. He asked:
"What did he do? they asked, and he answered them in detail.
Upon hearing this, the bhikṣus of few desires felt revulsion and contempt.
“How is it that a bhikṣu travels through inhabited areas on the same road as a bhikṣuṇī?
Having reported this matter in detail to the Blessed One, the Blessed One,
knowing the situation, waited for the group of six to arrive, assembled the community, and asked:
“Did you six truly commit such unseemly acts?
They replied,
“It is indeed so.”
The Blessed One rebuked him in various ways, and even went so far as to establish this training rule, which should be recited as follows:
"If a bhikṣu travels along the same path with a bhikṣuṇī, it is a pāyattika."
Thus, after the Blessed One had established the training rules for the bhikṣus,
he was staying at Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, a large number of bhikṣuṇīs were observing the three-month rains retreat at the Rājaka-vihāra in Rājagṛha.
When summer had ended, she wished to go to the Jeta Grove to pay homage at the feet of the World-Honored One; she went out to seek a caravan.
Among the merchants, she saw some bhikṣus, whereupon she said to them:
"Sisters!..."
"There is a bhikṣu here; it is not appropriate for us to go together, so we must seek another way.
Among the various merchant caravans, there were likewise bhikṣus, and they told one another, "Although we have searched for a long time, every caravan has a bhikṣu; we cannot travel with them."
She merely watched from afar as the caravan departed behind her.

As the bhikṣuṇī traveled along in the rear, she could not catch up with her companions and was consequently plundered of her robes and belongings by bandits. She gradually made her way to Śrāvastī and went to the bhikṣuṇī convent.
Having seen her, the nun said:
"Sister, have you traveled in safety and peace?"
He replied, "How could there be peace and happiness?
