On the road, I encountered bandits who plundered my clothes and belongings."
The nuns replied,
"Is there no merchant caravan with whom you might travel together?
She answered:
“There was. “If that is so, for what reason were you robbed?
He replied:
“There was a bhikṣu who should not have gone with us; because he stayed behind for that reason, we were subsequently robbed by bandits.

The nuns said, “Of the ninety-six kinds of non-Buddhist sects, all show compassion and do not abandon women; yet only the Buddha, the World-Honored One, has alone abandoned us, leaving us without refuge and causing us to be plundered by bandits.”
When the bhikṣuṇīs heard this, they informed the bhikṣus, and the bhikṣus informed the Buddha.
The Buddha said:
"Except in cases of special circumstances."
On another occasion, there were many bhikṣus traveling among the people following a caravan; as they lacked food and drink, the Buddha said:
"You should carry provisions for the journey."
Regarding the Buddha’s instruction that provisions for the journey should be carried, the bhikṣus did not know whom to send to carry them.
The Buddha said:
"One should have a male *kappiyakāraka* (a pure person) or a female *kappiyakāraka* do so."
If these are not available, the male novices (śrāmaṇera) and female novices (śrāmaṇerī) should do so;
if these are not available, the bhikṣus and bhikṣuṇīs should carry [the food] back and forth for one another and mutually distribute the food.
Furthermore, there were many bhikṣus traveling through the human realm who became afflicted with illness; the other bhikṣus abandoned them and departed. The Buddha said:
"You should not abandon them and leave; you should carry them on a litter."
The bhikṣu’s strength was insufficient to carry her away, so the Buddha said:
"If there is a bhikṣuṇī, she should accompany him on a litter.
When the bhikṣu stayed near the head and the bhikṣuṇī was at the feet, a defiled mind arose; the Buddha said:
"The bhikṣus were at the patient's feet, while the bhikṣuṇīs were at his head.
When they traveled to a village and all went to attend to the sick person, they failed to go out for alms and consequently lacked food and drink. The Buddha said:
"One person should be left to guard the sick person, while the rest should go out for alms."
"If a bhikṣuṇī is ill, she too should be taken along according to this same principle.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus, saying:
"The former was the original regulation; this is a subsequent allowance."
...up to: "If a bhikṣu travels together with a bhikṣuṇī as part of a caravan, except at other times, it is a pāyattika."
"Other times" refers to occasions when there is fear or danger; these are the [permissible] times.
"If it is again a bhikṣu" refers to the group of six bhikṣus.
"Ni" (nun) refers to the group of twelve.
"Agreed upon" means having formed a companion group together.
"Traveling" means proceeding by way of the road.
Regarding the "exceptional circumstances," this refers to when there are difficult conditions that allow one to travel together with a caravan; if no caravan is available, one cannot go.
The details concerning fear, dread, difficulties, and even the determination of the offense are all as explained above.
Regarding this, what are the characteristics of the offense and how does it occur?
If a bhikṣu travels along the same road as a bhikṣuṇī as part of a caravan, if they travel half a krośa or more, he incurs an *duṣkṛta* (wrongdoing) for each;
if they travel a full krośa, he incurs a *pāyattika* (offense of falling).
Whether traveling from a village to the wilderness or from the wilderness to a village, the calculation of the distance in *li* for determining the offense follows these same principles.
Furthermore, there is no offense for the very first offender, or for one who is insane, mentally deranged, or overwhelmed by intense physical pain.

27. The Training Rule on Traveling in the Same Boat with a Bhikṣuṇī. The twenty-seventh training rule concerning traveling in the same boat with a bhikṣuṇī. The Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the six bhikṣus, Nanda and Upananda, said to one another:
"These black-bowl holders have smeared their feet with monkey fat."
Thus it was explained in detail as before.

Even unto informing the twelve assemblies, they wept; he then prepared provisions for the journey, and so they embarked together on the same boat, men and women intermingled, which drew the ridicule of all people.
The bhikṣus heard this and reported the matter to the Buddha. The Buddha then rebuked them and, having done so, established a training rule (śikṣāpada), which should be recited as follows:
"If a bhikṣu travels in the same boat with a bhikṣuṇī, it is a pāyattika."
Thus, after the Blessed One had established the training rule for the bhikṣus,
there was a river not far from the Jeta Grove called Durgavāha.
Outside this river there was a village named White Pigeon.

In that village lived an elder who had constructed a great monastery; once its construction was complete, he wished to offer it to the Saṃgha and invited the two divisions of monks and nuns to come and receive offerings there.
At that time, there was a nun who diligently cultivated wholesome qualities. She thought to herself:
"I shall not go out for alms today; instead, I will perform some work so that when midday arrives, I may attend the offering."

Having practiced meditation and recitation, he saw that the sun was about to reach its zenith, so he went to the riverbank. There he saw several bhikṣus already on a boat; at that time, the boatman addressed him, saying:
"Noble One!"
"It would be appropriate for you to board the ship.
The nun said,
"O worthy one!"
"It is not appropriate for me to go; I should wait for the next boat.
The boat turned back again, took people on board, and called for the nun to come up as well.
When the nun saw the bhikṣu, she spoke once more:
"I will follow later.
Once the boat had reached the opposite shore and moored,
the bhikṣuṇī then called out to the boatmen:
“O boatman! Please come and take me. The boatman refused;

the nun then stood by the riverbank, and seeing that the sun had passed noon, she returned to the monastery. There, as long as her strength from the meal remained, she was able to engage in recitation; but once the hunger and exhaustion pressed upon her, she leaned against one side and lay down.
At that time, after the other nuns had returned from the meal offering, they asked this nun:
"Venerable one!
The food is another's property; can the belly truly be another's?"
"Eating too much and greedily gluttoning over, one lies down drowsy and oppressed.
He replied, "I do not go out to eat; how could I have such oppression?"
She was asked,
"For what reason do you not eat?
She then related the matter in detail to the nuns.
The bhikṣuṇīs informed the bhikṣus, and the bhikṣus informed the Buddha.
The Buddha said:
"Except for crossing directly."
For this reason, the Blessed One addressed the bhikṣus, saying:
"The former was the initial prohibition; this is the subsequent allowance.
To establish the training rule, it should be spoken thus:"
"If a bhikṣu again makes an appointment with a bhikṣuṇī to ride in the same boat, whether going downstream or upstream—with the exception of crossing directly across—it is a pāyattika."
"Furthermore, 'if a bhikṣu' refers to the group of six; the remaining meanings are as explained above.
'Agreeing to ride in the same boat' means to board a vessel together to cross a ferry."
"Following the waves" refers to going downstream.
"Going against the current" refers to going upstream.
"Crossing directly" refers to proceeding straight toward the opposite bank.
Regarding this, what are the characteristics of the offense and how is it determined?
If a bhikṣu travels on the same boat as a bhikṣuṇī, the gravity of the offense—calculated according to the distance traveled—is the same as that for traveling together on land.

If the oars or paddles break and drift away with the current, or if the rudder breaks, or if one avoids a sandbank or shoal, or if the helmsman does not follow one's instructions—in all these cases, there is no offense.
Furthermore, there is no offense for one who is a first-time offender, or for one who is insane, mentally deranged, or overwhelmed by intense pain. 28.

The Training Rule on Sitting Alone with a Woman in a Secluded Place. The twenty-eighth training rule concerning sitting alone with a woman in a secluded place was established when the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.

At that time, the Venerable Udāyin, during the first part of the day, dressed himself, took his bowl, and entered the city to beg for food; he eventually arrived at the house of the former courtesan Guptā.
Seeing Udāyin approaching from afar, Guptā immediately prepared a seat for him and said, "Welcome! Welcome!"
"Venerable One, please sit here.
He then sat down facing Gupta.
At that time, Udāyin preached the Dharma for him; then, recollecting their former shared pleasures, he said to Gupta:
"Do you remember how, in the past, in that garden or at that temple, you prepared such bedding, lit such lamps, partook of such food and drink, and engaged in such amusements?"
He replied, "I remember.
At that time, a bhikṣu who was begging for alms also arrived at Guptā’s house; seeing him, Guptā had this thought:
“I fear that if I rise now to give him food, our conversation will be interrupted.
He then waved his hand to dismiss him.
When Udāyin saw him wave his hand, he said:
"Guptā! You have no sense of shame before me that you could beckon another man with your hand.
She replied:
“Noble One!
It is not that I am idly gesturing to dismiss outsiders; rather, there was a bhikṣu seeking alms who wished to come for food, and I thought to myself:
‘If I rise to give him food, our conversation will surely be interrupted.’”
He then gestured with his hand, having no other intention. Udāyin said,
“Did I fear that you would cut me off while I was teaching you the Dharma of the Four Noble Truths?”
"In the past, I used to raise my own hand and beg from others to acquire this property, which I then renounced and left home for.
Yet now, you are unable to assist in accomplishing meritorious deeds by giving to a beggar."
Then Guptā immediately called out to the beggar once more and gave him a bowl filled with the finest food.
Having received the food, the beggar departed; and after Udāyin had finished eating this meal, he returned to the Jetavana.
That alms-seeker then thought to himself:
"I should now go to the Venerable Udāyin and assist him in his joy.
He went there and said:
“Venerable sir, you should feel great joy; today I have received your sublime offering.
Udāyin said, “When you first entered the house, what did you see being done?”
He replied,
"I saw him shielding it with his hand. He asked:
"What did he do afterward?
He replied,
"He brought forth excellent food and offered it as a gift."
He replied, "At that time, I was inside my house; I instructed them to give you food. He asked:
“Venerable sir, did you sit in one place with a woman at that time?
He replied, “Yes.”
He asked,
"Is this matter appropriate?
He replied:
"I have already finished what was to be done regarding whether we are in harmony or not; how does this concern you?
If you cannot tolerate it, you should inform the bhikṣus so that they may establish a training rule (śikṣāpada) for him."
He replied,
"How could I ever abandon you!
He then reported this matter to the bhikṣus.
Those of few desires, upon hearing this, each felt aversion and shame, saying:
"How can a bhikṣu sit alone in a secluded place with a woman?

Then the bhikṣus reported this matter in detail to the Blessed One. The Blessed One questioned Udāyin at length, as previously described, and established the training rule, which should be recited as follows:
"If a bhikṣu again sits alone with a woman in a secluded place, it is a pāyattika.
"If a bhikṣu" refers to Udāyin; the remaining meaning is as explained above.
"A woman" refers to a woman capable of engaging in sexual intercourse.
"Alone" means that there is no third person present. There are three types of secluded places:
[the private place, the concealed place, and the dark place].
This refers to walls, fences, and curtains.
Regarding "sitting," it means sitting with the body extended within a distance of one *vyāma*. The offense is established as before.
In this context, what are the characteristics of the transgression? What are its specific details?
If a bhikṣu sits alone with a woman in a secluded place, even if he merely leans his body against her and there is no third person present, he incurs a pāyattika offense.

However, if they are under a porch or in front of a room door, or if he causes the woman to grind or boil various medicines alone in that place while the door stands wide open such that all people passing by can see them, there is no offense.
Furthermore, there is no offense for one who is the very first offender, or for one who is insane, mentally deranged, or afflicted by intense pain.
The Twenty-ninth Training Rule: Sitting in a Secluded Place with a Bhikṣuṇī. The Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, having already gone forth, Guptā was next in line for the administrative duties.
When the community of nuns, during the first part of the day, put on their robes, took up their alms bowls, and went out to beg for food, Guptā alone remained in the monastery.
At that time, Udāyin entered the city to beg for alms and arrived at the bhikṣuṇī convent.
Just then, Guptā was personally sweeping and cleaning; seeing Udāyin approaching from afar at the entrance of the convent, she said to him, "Welcome, Noble One!"
He immediately set aside his broom, went forward to prostrate at his feet, and stood to one side.
At that time, Udāyin preached the Dharma for him; after he had been preaching for some time, he recalled their former shared pleasures and said to Gopikā:
"Do you remember those days in that garden? He then spoke at length as before.
...until she replied,
"I remember. At that time,
there was an elderly and sick bhikṣuṇī sitting beneath the porch, who had this thought:
"These two even discussed matters as far back as their mothers' marriages.
As time passed, Guptā replied,
"Venerable Sir!"
"You should go.
When the bhikṣuṇīs wish to enter the monastery, they may see that it has not been swept and fear they will harbor resentment;
I shall sweep and sprinkle it. Thus, Udāyin departed.
Guptā was sweeping and sprinkling water; seeing this, the nuns asked her, "Why is the floor being swept so little?
She replied:
"Since you departed, I have remained standing and not sat down.
Upon hearing this, the old nun replied,
"It is indeed true that Guptā did not sit down after you all left."
"However, the Venerable Udāyin has come here and stands conversing with Guptā as he pleases, even discussing such matters as her mother’s marriage.
The bhikṣuṇīs asked Guptā,
"Is it true that you have committed such unseemly acts?"
She replied,
"It is indeed so.
When the nuns heard this, they were all filled with revulsion and shame.
"How is it that a bhikṣu stands alone in a secluded place with a bhikṣuṇī?
Having reported this matter to the bhikṣus, the bhikṣus informed the Buddha.

For this reason, the Buddha assembled the community of bhikṣus. After the questions and answers and the reprimand had been extensively explained as before, he continued until: "In order to establish a training rule, it should be spoken thus:
'If a bhikṣu sits alone with a single bhikṣuṇī in a secluded place, it is a pāyattika.'"
“Furthermore, ‘if a bhikṣu’ refers to Udāyin; the remaining meanings are as explained above.
The detailed explanation of the meaning of ‘alone’ and so forth is as previously stated.
Regarding the characteristics of the offense herein, both sitting and lying down constitute an offense; the rest is as previously explained.”

30. The Training Rule on Knowing that Food Was Obtained through a Bhikṣuṇī’s Praise. The third training rule, "The Training Rule on Knowing that Food Was Obtained through a Bhikṣuṇī’s Praise," was established when the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.

At that time, the Venerable Mahākāśyapa was staying in the Eastern Park at the residence of Mṛgāramātṛ in the city. Then, having arisen from meditative concentration in the late afternoon, Kāśyapa went to where the Blessed One was, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and withdrew to sit at one side.
At that time, the Buddha said to Kāśyapa:
"You are now advanced in years and decayed with age; the rag-robes you wear have become extremely heavy and cumbersome, and these should be discarded."

"You should dwell in accordance with my instruction, relying upon the community; you may accept special invitations for meals and robes offered by donors, but you must cut them with a knife, dye them into a discolored hue, and then maintain them."
Then Kāśyapa, having received these instructions with joy, paid homage to the Buddha and departed.
In this city there was an elder who, throughout the long night, had been thinking thus:
"How wonderful!..."
"Mahākāśyapa is worthy of receiving the respectful offerings and veneration of gods and humans; when shall I be able to prepare a modest offering in my own home and invite him there to eat?"

When the householder heard that the Buddha had instructed Kāśyapa to dwell among the community and accept individual invitations, he went to his place, prostrated at his feet, and sat down to one side.
At that time, Kāśyapa taught the subtle Dharma to the elder, instructing, exhorting, benefiting, and gladdening him. The elder then thought:
"If I were to invite the Venerable One alone to my home for a meal, he might perhaps decline; it would be better for me now to invite all four of them together."
The householder immediately rose from his seat, bared his right shoulder, joined his palms in reverent salutation, and said:
"Noble One!
I pray that you, Great Virtue, along with these four others, will accept my humble offering at my home tomorrow."
At that time, the Venerable One accepted the invitation by remaining silent.
Having seen that he had accepted, the householder prostrated at his feet and departed. Once he had reached his home, he said to his wife:
"O virtuous lady!..."
For a long time, I have thought thus:
"How wonderful!
Mahākāśyapa is worthy of receiving the respect and offerings of gods and humans; when shall I be able to provide a modest offering in my own home and invite him to come and eat?"
"I have previously invited four virtuous monks who are masters of the Abhidharma; they shall come to my house tomorrow to receive offerings.
Since they have compassionately accepted my invitation, O noble sir, you should prepare many pure and excellent foods and drinks."

Upon hearing this, his wife immediately prepared everything accordingly: those foods that were suitable to be served cold she prepared that day, while those that required heating she intended to prepare the following morning.
Then, at dawn on the next day, the householder thought to himself:
"If I were to arrange the seating mats beneath the three-storied house now, the various beggars would create a great commotion."
"If we were on the third floor, crows and birds would fly about in disorder, fearing they might defile the food and drink; it would be better to spread our mats and seats on the middle floor.
Once the preparations were complete, he sent a messenger to inform the Venerable Kāśyapa:
"O Mahāsthavira!..."
"The food and drink are prepared; we pray that you will know it is time.
As the Buddha has taught:
"If one is the foremost person to accept another's invitation, one should go there first."
Then, during the first part of the day, Mahākāśyapa went with three others to the house of the elder; having arrived there, he ascended to the middle story and took his seat.

At that time, the householder, having prostrated at the feet of the Venerable Kāśyapa, sat to one side; then Mahākāśyapa preached the Dharma to him, instructing, exhorting, inspiring, and gladdening him.
At that time, the bhikṣuṇī Dhanika also came to beg for alms and entered the house of the elder ahead of her, saying to his wife:
"O lady of excellent appearance, may you be free from illness and long-lived; please grant me a fine meal."
When the householder’s wife saw him,
she replied, "Noble one!
Today I am somewhat busy and have no leisure to converse with you."
He asked, "For what purpose?
and he replied:

“Venerable Mahākāśyapa is honored and supported by all gods and humans; now, within my home, I have prepared a simple offering and invite those four to come here to receive their meal. As the time is nearly upon us, you may depart for now.”
The nun then replied, "He is a renunciant of the non-Buddhist sect, utterly foolish and dull-witted.

There are many others from the noble Śākya clan who have left home to take up the precepts and serve as great Dharma masters, proficient in all three Piṭakas and possessing unimpeded eloquence; why do you not make offerings to them, but instead bestow gifts upon this man?"
At that time, upon hearing the sound of these words, Mahākāśyapa thought to himself:
"Let not this nun commit extensive evil karma.
He therefore made a coughing sound, which was as melodious and clear as the ringing of a golden bell, its resonance filling the entire house.
Hearing the wondrous voice, the nun knew it was Kāśyapa and spoke these words:
"That great elephant has already arrived at our home.
Upon hearing this, the elder then thought to himself:
"Previously you said:
'The non-Buddhist renunciants are utterly foolish and dull-witted.
Yet later you spoke again, saying:"
"He is a great nāga-elephant!
Thinking thus, he gave rise to a mind of anger and descended from the upper story.
As he hurried down the stairs, his footsteps made a loud thudding sound; hearing the noise of his descent, the nun thought to herself:
"Listening to the sound of her footsteps, it is different from usual; she will surely do me some harm. I ought to leave quickly so that she does not see me.
She immediately lifted her skirt and hurried out of the house with rapid steps. The elder said to her:
"Shaven-headed śramaṇī!"
"Why did you flee?
You shall not come back into my house again.
The nun replied from afar:
“Your home is like a latrine, a prison, or a dwelling for outcasts; yet I, by the grace of the King, am like a member of the royal harem and face no obstacles.
If you so much as touch me, I shall cut off both your wrists.”
The householder said, "Shaven-headed śramaṇī!
It is the elder nuns who have received the king’s bounty and grace, not you—a greedy, hateful, and ignorant person. Now, let you go."

The elder himself provided offerings of various kinds of excellent food and drink with sincere devotion. When the meal was finished, he withdrew the bowl, washed his hands, and used a tooth-stick. Then the elder and his wife sat on low seats to listen to the sublime Dharma.
Then Mahākāśyapa, having taught the essentials of the Dharma to inspire, instruct, benefit, and gladden them, rose from his seat and departed.
Having reached his dwelling, he went to the place where the Buddha was, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and sat down to one side. He addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!...”

Having received the Buddha’s instruction to dwell among the community and accept separate invitations for meals, I am thus a most foolish and dull-witted renunciant of the non-Buddhist path, yet among the disciples of the Buddha, I am a great nāga-elephant.
Today, O Venerable One, I have received such praise and blame:

for dwelling myself in the forest (*araṇya*) and praising the dwelling in the forest; for being myself a constant alms-seeker (*piṇḍapātika*) and praising the practice of constant alms-seeking; for dwelling myself at the foot of a tree and wearing rag-robes (*pāṃsukūla*), and praising the dwelling at the foot of a tree and the wearing of rag-robes.
The Buddha said to Mahākāśyapa:

"What benefit do you see in dwelling in the forest (*araṇya*) and praising the forest; in always begging for food and praising begging for food; in dwelling under a tree and praising dwelling under a tree; and in wearing rag-robes (*pāṃsukūla*) and praising rag-robes?"
Mahākāśyapa addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!
I see two benefits."
What are these two?
First, attaining a state of peaceful dwelling in the present life; second, being able to act as a great lamp for many people in future lives to show them the correct path.
At that time, all those people heard and learned of this together, and spoke thus:
"When the Buddha was in the world, there were bhikṣus of great virtue who left the household life to become renunciants and purely cultivated the holy life."
"Praised by the Great Master and extolled by the wise, he dwelt in the Āraṇya and even showed them the true path.

When the bhikṣus heard these words, they each exerted themselves and practiced according to the teaching, diligently seeking the way out; thus, for a long night, they attained peaceful and happy dwelling.
Having spoken these words, the Buddha addressed Mahākāśyapa:
"Excellent! Excellent!"

By being able to do so, you will bring great benefit to your fellow practitioners of the holy life throughout the long night of future ages; out of compassion for the world of humans and devas, you shall bestow welfare upon all and cause them to attain liberation.
Kāśyapa! If there are those who disparage the practice of dhūta, I disparage them;
if there are those who praise the practice of dhūta, I praise them.
Why is this? Kāśyapa!
Throughout the long night, I have praised the practice of these dhūta qualities, extolling and proclaiming them as the most excellent among all practices.
Kāśyapa! From this day forward, you should always dwell in the forest (*araṇya*), praise others for dwelling in the forest, and so forth, as explained at length.
You all should diligently cultivate and train yourselves in this.
At that time, Kāśyapa received the instruction and practiced accordingly.
This was the origin of the story, though the training rule had not yet been established.
The Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.

At that time, there was a famine, and it was difficult to obtain food through begging. There were, however, brahmins, householders, and lay devotees of pure faith who regularly provided offerings to the venerable and senior bhikṣus.
At that time, the group of six bhikṣus entered the city to beg for alms and went to where the group of twelve bhikṣuṇīs were.
When those bhikṣuṇīs saw the six bhikṣus arrive, they addressed them, saying:
"Noble ones!..."
"Take a seat and you may eat some light refreshments.
Upānanda said, "Who shall serve me?"
He replied, "We do. He answered:
"Even though it is so today, whom shall I send tomorrow?
He replied,
"I shall return it myself."
He replied, "Sisters!
Even if we were to obtain this food, it would not suffice to sustain us."

If you can act in accordance with our wishes for our benefit, then regarding the various offerings previously provided by the brahmins and others to the great bhikṣus, you should exhort them to redirect those gifts to us.
"If you can provide such excellent offerings as these,
I shall support you. Then the nun Tullānandā said,
"Noble One!"
"Is it appropriate for me, a bhikṣuṇī, to perform this task?
Upānanda replied, "It is most certainly appropriate; who else could possibly prevent you?"
"How could we allow ourselves to die of hunger?
The nun said,
"We shall follow your instructions."
At that time, the bhikṣuṇī Pūtanā entered the city to beg for food. Arriving at the house of the donor, the Venerable Kauṇḍinya, she went inside the residence and spoke these words:
"To whom have you been providing food offerings lately?"
He replied,
"The noble Kauṇḍinya, I have always made offerings to him.
He [the monk] said in response:

"If you can renounce the world within the Śākya clan, becoming a great Dharma master who is learned and proficient in the Tripitaka with unimpeded eloquence, and serve as a provider of offerings, you shall surely obtain most excellent merit."
He then asked: "Who among the Śākyas possesses such a multitude of virtues?
He replied:
“The noble Nanda is that very person.
He replied,
“I act according to his instructions.”
The householder then took the offerings intended for Kauṇḍinya and redirected them to Nanda.
In this manner, he redirected all the offerings belonging to the other senior and venerable elders to the group of six bhikṣus.

At that time, during the first part of the day, the group of six monks put on their robes, took up their alms bowls, and entered the city to beg for food. Upon reaching a household where food was being given, they received various kinds of food and drink; they filled their leather bags with items such as cakes and fruits, and returned to their residence carrying their rice bowls.
The bhikṣus saw him and asked, "What is contained in this bag? Where did you bring it from?
He replied:
"May my sisters be free from illness and long-lived; it is because of their instruction that I have obtained this fine food.
The bhikṣus said, "Venerable one!"
"Is it appropriate to send various nuns to teach and convert [the laity] so that they may receive and enjoy food and drink?
He replied: "On what grounds would it be inappropriate?"
"Your profound sincerity is indeed consistent with reason;
how could I die of starvation simply because I do not eat?
When the bhikṣus who possessed few desires heard this, they felt disdain and contempt.
“How is it that a bhikṣu accepts food provided through the solicitation of a bhikṣuṇī?
For this reason, they reported the matter in detail to the Blessed One.
The Blessed One then engaged in an extensive exchange of questions and answers, and for the sake of establishing a training rule (śikṣāpada), he declared: “It should be stated as follows:”
“If, moreover, a bhikṣu, knowing that food was obtained through the cause of a bhikṣuṇī’s praise, should eat it, it is a pāyattika.
Thus the Blessed One, having established this training rule for the bhikṣus.
In the city of Śrāvastī there was an elder who engaged in two types of work:
first, commerce; second, agriculture.

Having finished plowing his fields in the wilderness, he sowed them with parched barley seeds and immediately constructed a small hut at the site of the field. He then took his wealth and went elsewhere to engage in trade.
At that time, there was a bhikṣu wandering for alms who, while traveling through the human realm, arrived at Śrāvastī.
Upon leaving the city to look about, he saw that small hut and thought to himself:
"This place is secluded and quiet; it is fit for staying overnight."

Thereupon, he entered the city daily to beg for alms and temporarily stayed in a small hut; because of the presence of human beings, other birds and deer did not come to damage the crops, and furthermore, thanks to the timely rains, the seedlings and grain grew to full maturity.
At that time, the householder, having traveled to another place in search of goods and arrived safely, stored his merchandise, bathed, ate, and then said to his wife:
"Previously, I sowed seeds of husked barley in a certain field and subsequently went away in search of goods."
"I wonder if it is possible to plant [seeds] at this time?
He then went into the field and saw that the stalks and grain were fully matured, whereupon he thought to himself:
"The seedlings I planted were not enclosed by fences, nor was anyone appointed to guard them."
"Why is it that at this time my mind has not yet reached maturity?

He then set out on foot and, seeing tracks of human presence, followed the trail until he reached the old grass hut. Peering through the door, he saw the mendicant sitting cross-legged in meditative silence, absorbed in dhyāna.
The householder then thought,
"It is by this man's labor that my field has been brought to fruition.
He then went forward and asked:
“Noble one, do you dwell here?
He replied:
"So be it," the householder replied, saying,
"Noble One!"
"This is my field; you may happily rely upon it for your stay.
If you require flowers, leaves, or tooth-sticks, you may take them as you please. Tomorrow, come to my home so that I may offer you a simple meal."
The bhikṣu replied,
“I am a mendicant who does not accept invitations from others,” and thus he did not grant his permission.
Then that householder prostrated at his feet and departed; having reached home, he said to his wife, "O virtuous lady!
You should attend to the storehouses, for the field barley has ripened."
The wife said,
"Are you deceiving me, my lord?
Her husband replied:
"I previously sowed the seeds without securing them with fences, nor did I have anyone guard them; now they have reached full maturity.
Why do you deceive me?
Do not harbor any doubt!"
The wife asked for the reason, and he replied:
"I built a grass hut by the side of the field, and there dwelt a mendicant; it was through his power that the crops ripened."
The wife said, "If that is so,
why not invite him to our home to receive food?
He replied:
"I have already extended an invitation, but he was unwilling to accept.
He said of himself:
'I am a mendicant; I do not accept invitations from others.'"
The wife said,
"That mendicant wanders through a hundred households every day, begging with great hardship before he can fill his belly.
Because you were not earnest, he did not accept."
"It would be fitting for you to go once more; since he has pressed me so earnestly, I must surely accept.
When the elder heard his wife's exhortation, he went back again. Upon arrival, he prostrated at [the monk's] feet and said, "Noble One!"
"I pray that you will show me your compassion and come to my home tomorrow to accept my humble offering.
The bhikṣu replied,
"Householder, I am a mendicant who does not accept invitations from others."
The householder replied, "I pray that you will deign to come to my home tomorrow; please accept a simple meal and do not refuse my request.
Seeing that the householder was insistent and would not desist, the mendicant finally accepted in silence.
Having seen him accept [the invitation] and prostrate at his feet before departing, the householder returned to his home and said to his wife:
"O virtuous lady!
The bhikṣu who begs for alms has already accepted my invitation and promised to come tomorrow; you should prepare excellent food and drink for him."
Upon hearing this, his wife immediately made preparations: she prepared those foods that could be eaten cold on that very day, and those requiring heating was to be done the following day.
At that time, another bhikṣu who was wandering for alms arrived at the grass hut in the field; he called out to the one seeking alms, saying, "Come, let us go together."
The mendicant replied, "A certain elder has come to invite me for a meal; when the time arrives, I shall go there, so I cannot accompany you.
The other mendicants spoke thus:
"You possess great merit and are able to obtain offerings; having been invited for the sake of sentient beings, you should go when the time arrives.

At that time, the bhikṣuṇī Pūtanā, during the first part of the day, put on her robes, took up her alms bowl, and entered the city to beg for food. Proceeding by turns, she arrived at the house where the offering was being prepared and entered the residence. Seeing the wife of the elder, she addressed her:
"O lady of exquisite features!"
“May you be free from illness and long-lived; please grant me some food.
The woman replied, “Noble One!”
"Furthermore, I am currently beset by sorrow; there is no room for me to accept food.
He asked, "What is your sorrow?"
He replied, "I invited the alms-seeker to come to my house; since he has not yet arrived, I fear he will go without food, and for this reason I am filled with anxiety.
The nun then responded:
"If I summon him, will you give me food?
He replied, "I will give it."
The nun said,
"Although I have received food, what about my companions?
She replied:
"I shall give it as well.
[The nun asked: "Which nun in charge of the temple should be given the food?
She replied:
"I shall give it as well.
Then Tullānandā thought to herself:
"The beggars who entered the city have now all departed; the one who has just arrived is surely that person."
The nun went to the city gate and stood there gazing into the distance.
The alms-seeker thought to himself:
"Since I have accepted the invitation, I shall not go begging for alms but will instead cultivate wholesome qualities; I shall go when the time arrives."
When the time for the meal arrived, he put on his robes, took up his bowl,
and went into the city. Seeing him, Pūrṇaśikha thought to herself,
"This person who has come here is the one invited."
He then stepped forward and asked,
"Venerable One,
have you accepted an invitation to the house of so-and-so?"
She replied, “Yes. The nun said:
"I have already praised that family for you.
She replied, "Sister!..."
“Did I previously command you to praise me?
Then he thought: “As the World-Honored One has said:”
"If a bhikṣuṇī praises [the food] so that one may obtain it, one should not eat it.
I would rather endure hunger and abstain from food than commit an offense for this reason.
She immediately wished to turn back.
When Utpalānandā saw that she was about to leave, she said to her,
"Noble Lady!..."
"I do not know your name, clan, or lineage; why do you suddenly praise me in this way?
At that time, the mendicant replied, "Sister!"
"If what was said before is true, then what follows is false;
if what follows is true, then what was said before is empty.
Having spoken these words, he returned to his original place.
The nun was deeply ashamed and immediately went out to beg for alms.
When the bhikṣu returned to his grass hut, he devoted himself to various wholesome practices as long as the strength of his meal remained; once that strength had faded, he leaned back and lay down.
Other mendicants came and asked him:
"The food is another's property; is the stomach, then, not yours?
He replied:
"What have I done? he asked.
They replied, "You were excessively greedy for food; consequently, you were unable to cultivate the various categories of wholesome qualities."

Question: "Who is it that craves a full meal? Answer: [The Buddha said: "It is the fool who craves a full meal. Question: "What is the fool like? Answer: "He is one who, having committed evil deeds, does not repent; he is one who, having done what is unwholesome, does not abandon it; he is one who, having fallen into calamity, does not seek deliverance; he is one who, having encountered a wise person, does not ask about the Dharma; he is one who, having heard the Dharma, does not practice it; he is one who, having received instruction, does not follow it; he is one who, having been admonished, does not accept it; he is one who, having seen the path, does not enter it; he is one who, having seen the fruit, does not attain it; he is one who, having seen the truth, does not realize it; he is one who, having seen Nirvana, does not enter it. This is called a fool. Furthermore, he is one who, when seeing others enjoy wealth and status, gives rise to envy and covetousness; he is one who, when seeing others suffer from poverty and lowliness, gives rise to contempt and disdain; he is one who, when seeing others receive praise and honor, gives rise to jealousy and resentment; he is one who, when seeing others suffer censure and disgrace, gives rise to malice and hatred. This is called a fool. Furthermore, he is one who, when seeing others give alms, does not rejoice; he is one who, when seeing others perform meritorious deeds, does not follow suit; he is one who, when seeing others observe the precepts, does not respect them; he is one who, when seeing others break the precepts, does not feel shame. This is called a fool. Furthermore, he is one who, when seeing others practice generosity, does not offer anything himself; he is one who, when seeing others uphold the precepts, does not maintain them himself; he is one who, when seeing others cultivate patience, does not practice patience himself; he is one who, when seeing others exert vigor, does not exert vigor himself; he is one who, when seeing others practice meditation, does not practice meditation himself; he is one who, when seeing others cultivate wisdom, does not cultivate wisdom himself. This is called a fool. Furthermore, he is one who, when seeing others attain the fruits of the śrāvaka, does not seek them himself; he is one who, when seeing others attain the fruits of the pratyekabuddha, does not seek them himself; he is one who, when seeing others attain the fruits of the Buddha, does not seek them himself. This is called a fool. Furthermore, he is one who, when seeing others attain the stage of stream-enterer, does not aspire to it himself; he is one who, when seeing others attain the stage of once-returner, does not aspire to it himself; he is one who, when seeing others attain the stage of non-returner, does not aspire to it himself; he is one who, when seeing others attain the stage of arhat, does not aspire to it himself. This is called a fool. Furthermore, he is one who, when seeing others attain the stage of pratyekabuddha, does not aspire to it himself; he is one who, when seeing others attain the stage of Buddhahood, does not aspire to it himself. This is called a fool. Furthermore, he is one who, when seeing others attain the dhyānas, does not seek them himself; he is one who, when seeing others attain the samādhis, does not seek them himself; he is one who, when seeing others attain the liberations, does not seek them himself; he is one who, when seeing others attain the supernormal powers, does not seek them himself. This is called a fool. Furthermore, he is one who, when seeing others attain the four foundations of mindfulness, does not seek them himself; he is one who, when seeing others attain the four right efforts, does not seek them himself; he is one who, when seeing others attain the four bases of psychic power, does not seek them himself; he is one who, when seeing others attain the five faculties, does not seek them himself; he is one who, when seeing others attain the five powers, does not seek them himself; he is one who, when seeing others attain the seven factors of enlightenment, does not seek them himself; he is one who, when seeing others attain the eightfold noble path, does not seek it himself. This is called a fool. Furthermore, he is one who, when seeing others attain the emptiness liberation, does not seek it himself; he is one who, when seeing others attain the signless liberation, does not seek it himself; he is one who, when seeing others attain the wishless liberation, does not seek it himself. This is called a fool. Furthermore, he is one who, when seeing others attain the knowledge of the destruction of outflows, does not seek it himself; he is one who, when seeing others attain the knowledge of non-arising, does not seek it himself. This is called a fool. Furthermore, he is one who, when seeing others attain the stage of non-retrogression, does not seek it himself; he is one who, when seeing others attain the stage of certainty, does not seek it himself; he is one who, when seeing others attain the stage of the irreversible wheel-turning king, does not seek it himself. This is called a fool. Furthermore, he is one who, when seeing others attain the stage of the śrāvaka, does not seek it himself; he is one who, when seeing others attain the stage of the pratyekabuddha, does not seek it himself; he is one who, when seeing others attain the stage of the Buddha, does not seek it himself. This is called a fool. Furthermore, he is one who, when seeing others attain the stage of the bodhisattva, does not seek it himself; he is one who, when seeing others attain the stage of the Tathāgata, does not seek it himself. This is called a fool. Furthermore, he is one who, when seeing others attain the stage of the dharmakāya, does not seek it himself; he is one who, when seeing others attain the stage of the sambhogakāya, does not seek it himself; he is one who, when seeing others attain the stage of the nirmāṇakāya, does not seek it himself. This is called a fool. Furthermore, he is one who, when seeing others attain the stage of the ten stages, does not seek it himself; he is one who, when seeing others attain the stage of the ten paramitas, does not seek it himself; he is one who, when seeing others attain the stage of the ten powers, does not seek it himself; he is one who, when seeing others attain the stage of the four fearlessnesses, does not seek it himself; he is one who, when seeing others attain the stage of the eighteen unique qualities of a buddha, does not seek it himself. This is called a fool. Furthermore, he is one who, when seeing others attain the stage of the great compassion, does not seek it himself; he is one who, when seeing others attain the stage of the great joy, does not seek it himself; he is one who, when seeing others attain the stage of the great equanimity, does not seek it himself; he is one who, when seeing others attain the stage of the great kindness, does not seek it himself. This is called a fool. Furthermore, he is one who, when seeing others attain the stage of the three gates of liberation, does not seek them himself; he is one who, when seeing others attain the stage of the three knowledges, does not seek them himself; he is one who, when seeing others attain the stage of the six supernormal powers, does not seek them himself; he is one who, when seeing others attain the stage of the four analytical knowledges, does not seek them himself. This is called a fool. Furthermore, he is one who, when seeing others attain the stage of the ten powers of a buddha, does not seek them himself; he is one who, when seeing others attain the stage of the four fearlessnesses of a buddha, does not seek them himself; he is one who, when seeing others attain the stage of the eighteen unique qualities of a buddha, does not seek them himself; he is one who, when seeing others attain the stage of the great compassion of a buddha, does not seek it himself. This is called a fool. Furthermore, he is one who, when seeing others attain the stage of the dharmakāya of a buddha, does not seek it himself; he is one who, when seeing others attain the stage of the sambhogakāya of a buddha, does not seek it himself; he is one who, when seeing others attain the stage of the nirmāṇakāya of a buddha, does not seek it himself. This is called a fool. Furthermore, he is one who, when seeing others attain the stage of the ten stages of a bodhisattva, does not seek them himself; he is one who, when seeing others attain the stage of the ten paramitas of a bodhisattva, does not seek them himself; he is one who, when seeing others attain the stage of the ten powers of a bodhisattva, does not seek them himself; he is one who, when seeing others attain the stage of the
"You are excessively greedy," he replied,
"I have never eaten."
He asked, "What is the cause and condition for this?
Then the mendicant related the matter in detail to the bhikṣus, and the bhikṣus reported the circumstances to the Buddha.
The Buddha said,
"Except when one has previously accepted an offering with the donor’s intention, there is no offense in eating.
At that time, the World-Honored One praised those who uphold the precepts and rebuked those who violate them, and addressed the bhikṣus, saying:
"The former was an original enactment; this is a subsequent allowance.
For the sake of the bhikṣus, I establish this training rule (śikṣāpada), which should be recited as follows:
'If a bhikṣu, knowing that food was obtained through the cause of a bhikṣuṇī’s praise, should eat it—except when the donor had a prior intention—it is a pāyattika.'"
"Furthermore, 'if a bhikṣu' refers to the group of six; the remaining meanings are as explained above.
'A bhikṣuṇī' refers to Khemā (Turu-nan-da).
'Praising' is of two kinds:"
First, praise for upholding the precepts; second, praise for extensive learning.
There are two kinds of food, as already explained above.
"Food" refers to that which is swallowed.
Except when the donor has a prior intention—that is, if the donor has previously intended to invite this bhikṣu—there is no offense even if one praises the food.
What are the characteristics of an offense in this regard? What are the specific details of the matter?
Suppose a large number of bhikṣus have been invited by a lay family, and a bhikṣuṇī arrives at that house beforehand and says:
"Virtuous ones, which bhikṣus have you invited for this offering?"
She replied, "So-and-so. The nun said:
"What kind of coarse gruel do you wish to serve?
The donor replied,
"I wish to serve coarse gruel."
The nun said, "You should give fine flour.

Among those bhikṣus, there were some who had realized the fruit of stream-entry, some who had attained the fruit of once-returning, some who had attained the fruit of non-returning, and some who had realized the fruit of arhatship. The nun said:
"What kind of ghee do you wish to take? He replied,
"Lamb's ghee."
The nun said:
"One should give cow's ghee, for that bhikṣu has attained the four fruits.
The nun said:
"What kind of salt do you wish to buy? He replied, "Salt."
The nun said:
"One should give rock salt, for that bhikṣu has attained the four fruits [of the path].

If one were to offer fermented rice gruel, one should instead offer curdled milk; likewise, regarding all vegetables, cakes, and fruits, one should encourage the giving of the most excellent and superior varieties. When wishing to give molasses syrup at an improper time, the nun said:
"One should give honey syrup.
When she wished to give millet rice, the nun said,
"One should give non-glutinous rice."
When she wished to give vegetable soup,
the nun said, "One should give meat soup, for that bhikṣu has attained the four fruits [of the path].
If bhikṣus know that when a bhikṣuṇī sees a donor serving coarse food, she encourages and praises the serving of fine food, praising that bhikṣu for having obtained a superior fruit.
If a bhikṣu knowingly partakes of food offered as a result of such false praise, he incurs a pāyattika offense.
If a bhikṣuṇī praises a bhikṣu by saying that he maintains the Tripiṭaka and thus deserves excellent food, she incurs a duṣkṛta offense.
If a bhikṣu has truly attained the various fruits [of the path] and truly understands the Tripiṭaka, there is no offense for a bhikṣuṇī to eat while praising him.
Furthermore, there is no offense in the case of the very first offender, or one who is insane, mentally deranged, or afflicted by intense pain.
The Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya, Scroll Thirty-three.
The Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya, Scroll Thirty-four.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Yijing by Imperial Command.
The fourth summary verse says:
Frequent eating and staying one night; Receiving a bowl and not for the sake of another.
Eating after having finished one's meal, eating separately, eating at an improper time, touching food, and eating exquisite food without it being offered.

31. The Training Rule on Successive Eating (Saṃnipātika-bhojana-śikṣāpada). The thirty-first training rule on successive eating. At that time, the Blessed One was staying at Rājagṛha in the Bamboo Grove, by the side of the Kalandaka Pond.

At that time, the Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana would, from time to time, constantly go to the realms of hell-beings, animals, hungry ghosts, humans, and devas to observe them with compassion. In the hells, he saw sentient beings undergoing various sufferings, such as having their bodies hacked and cut by swords and blades, or being burned and boiled in corpses, excrement, hot ashes, fierce flames, and glowing coals.
In the animal realm, he saw them suffering from preying upon and devouring one another.
In the realm of hungry ghosts, he saw them oppressed by various forms of hunger and thirst.
In the realms of the gods, one sees the suffering of separation from loved ones as they are about to fall;
in the human realm, one sees various hardships such as the toil of seeking the necessities of life—food, clothing, and shelter—as well as the sufferings of execution and punishment.
Having seen this, he proclaimed to all within the fourfold assembly:
"All you people, you should know!
As I have seen the distinctions among the five destinies, the retributions of suffering and happiness are entirely not in vain."
You all should believe this and harbor no doubts.

Those who undergo the retribution of suffering are summoned by their own evil karma—namely, killing, stealing, sexual misconduct, and even wrong views; failing to respect the Triple Gem; deceiving and being arrogant toward one's elders and kin; lacking a heart of compassion; and not observing the prohibitions and precepts. It is due to these evil deeds that they obtain such bitter maturation.

The experience of pleasant retribution is induced by wholesome karma; that is to say, by abstaining from killing and stealing up to and including wrong view, by reverently believing in the Triple Gem, honoring one's elders and kin, possessing a heart of compassion, and upholding the prohibitive precepts—through such virtuous conduct, one obtains the ripening of pleasure.
Upon hearing this, the people marveled at such an unprecedented occurrence; they all raised their hands and cried out in a loud voice: “Excellent!

O Noble One, you have been able to act for us who are blind and ignorant—those who see only the present and do not perceive the future, being intimately bound to the five destinies. By observing good and evil deeds and returning to inform us of them, we now finally understand that retribution and its consequences are never in vain.”
"From this day forward, we shall reform our evils and cultivate merit, aspiring to be reborn in the good realms and not fall into the evil destinies.
At that time, having heard these words, the fourfold assembly all thought to themselves:
"Our sons, daughters, or disciples constantly engage in evil deeds and do not diligently practice the pure holy life."
Desiring to cause them to abandon all evil karma, he brought them all to the presence of the noble Mahāmaudgalyāyana to have them hear the Dharma.
Having heard the Dharma, they hoped to cultivate virtuous conduct, avoid falling into the evil realms, and realize the sublime fruit.
At that time, the fourfold assembly had gathered like clouds to hear the essential teachings, and the crowd was making a great clamor.
The World-Honored One, knowing this, intentionally asked the Venerable Ānanda:
"For what reason has a great cloud-like assembly gathered around Mahāmaudgalyāyana?"
Then Ānanda said to the Buddha:

“World-Honored One, the Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana traveled through the five realms of existence and witnessed various sufferings; he recounted these matters in detail before the fourfold assembly, and because of this, these people have all gathered here to hear the Dharma.”
At that time, the Blessed One addressed Ānanda:

“It is not the case that Mahāmaudgalyāyana is always present at all times and places; such individuals as he are indeed rare to find. Therefore, I now command all the bhikṣus to paint the Wheel of Birth and Death beneath the eaves of the monastery gate.”
At that time, the bhikṣus did not know the method of painting. The World-Honored One told them:
"One should draw a circular wheel shape according to its size, with a hub placed in the center; next, install five spokes to represent the characteristics of the five destinies."
Beneath the hub, one should paint the hell realms (*naraka*); on its two sides, the animal and hungry ghost realms. Next, above those, one may paint humans and devas;
within the human realm, one should depict the four continents:

Pūrvavideha in the east, Jambudvīpa in the south, Aparagoyānī in the west, and Uttarakuru in the north. At the center of the hub, one should make a white circle, in which a Buddha image is painted. In front of the Buddha image, three types of forms should be depicted.

First, one should depict the form of a pigeon to represent excessive passion; next, the form of a snake to represent excessive hatred; and finally, the form of a pig to represent excessive delusion. At the rim, one should fashion the image of an irrigation wheel, upon which many water jars are placed, painted as the image of the birth and death of sentient beings.
The living emerge from the jar with their heads out, while the dead emerge from the jar with their feet out; in each of the five destinies, they are depicted according to their respective forms.
Around the perimeter, one should further paint the signs of the arising and ceasing of the twelve links of dependent origination (*dvādaśāṅga-pratītyasamutpāda*), namely:

ignorance conditions volitional formations (*avidyā-pratyaya-saṃskārāḥ*) up to old age and death. The link of ignorance should be depicted as the form of a *rākṣasa*, and the link of volitional formations...
One should depict the link of formations (*saṃskāra*) as a potter’s wheel; the link of consciousness (*vijñāna*) as a monkey; the link of name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*) as a person riding in a boat;
the link of the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*) as the six sense organs; the link of contact (*sparśa*) as a man and a woman touching one another;
the link of sensation (*vedanā*) as a man and a woman experiencing pleasure and pain; and the link of craving (*tṛṣṇā*) as a woman.
A person should hold an image of a male and female; the *āśraya* branch should be made as a man holding a flask and drawing water;
the *sattva* branch should be made as the image of Mahābrahmā; the *jāti* branch should be made as a woman giving birth;
the *jarā* branch should be made as men and women in a state of senility; the *vyādhi* [branch] should be made as men and women afflicted with disease; and the *maraṇa* branch should be made...
The "carrying of a corpse" should be depicted as men and women carrying a corpse; "sorrow" (*śoka*) should be depicted as men and women in a state of grief;

"lamentation" (*parideva*) should be depicted as men and women weeping; "suffering" (*duḥkha*) should be depicted as men and women undergoing suffering; and "despair" (*upāyāsa*) should be depicted as men and women struggling to lead a refractory camel.

Upon that wheel, one should depict the Great Ghost of Impermanence with disheveled hair and a gaping mouth, stretching out both arms to embrace the wheel of birth and death. On both sides of the ghost’s head, one should write these two verses:
"You should seek liberation, And diligently practice the Buddha's teaching;
Subdue the army of birth and death, As an elephant destroys a house of straw."
"Within this Dharma and Vinaya, by always practicing heedfulness,
one can exhaust the ocean of afflictions and reach the ultimate end of suffering.
Next, one should construct a white circular mandala upon the ghost of Impermanence to represent the image of the perfect purity of Nirvana.
"As the Buddha has instructed, the wheel of birth and death should be made beneath the gateway. Thereupon, the bhikṣus followed the instruction and made it.
When the faithful brahmins and householders saw the painted image of the wheel, they asked, "Noble ones!..."
"What does this painted wheel intend to signify?
The bhikṣu replied,
"I too do not know what it represents."
The people replied, "If you do not understand it, for what reason did you paint it?
At that time, the bhikṣus remained silent and had no response; they then reported this matter in detail to the World-Honored One.
The World-Honored One said:
"A bhikṣu should be appointed to sit beneath the gatehouse and point out to the various people, brahmins, and others who come and go, the causes and conditions for the cycle of birth and death."

When the Buddha instructed that they should be directed, the bhikṣus did not exercise discrimination, but instead had those lacking understanding guide the matter; this failed to inspire faith in others and instead invited ridicule and disgrace. The Buddha said:
"Have those who possess knowledge and understanding direct the people."
At that time, there was a householder in the city of Rājagṛha who, not long after marrying his wife, fathered a son whose countenance was so upright and handsome that all who saw him were delighted.
He said to his wife, "O fair lady!..."
"I now have a son who has many expenses; it would be fitting for him to enter the great ocean to seek out precious goods.
His wife replied, "Very well."
The elder then took various goods and set out upon the great ocean; however, his ship was wrecked by the winds, and he went forth but did not return.

His wife endured great hardship, sometimes relying on her kinsmen and sometimes using her own strength to raise her young child. Because she raised him in such solitary poverty, he was named "Born of Poverty" (Daridra-jāta).
At that time, the youth Daridraputra, having gradually grown up, was entrusted to a teacher to receive his training; he then went with his fellow students to the Bamboo Grove Monastery.
Upon arriving at the monastery gate, he saw a painted wheel of the cycle of birth and death across the five destinies and asked, "Noble One!..."
"What is this called? The bhikṣu replied,
"This is the wheel of birth and death within the five destinies."
He said, "Noble One! Please explain it for me."
The bhikṣu said: "Listen well!
These are the distinct realms of existence: hell-beings, animals, hungry ghosts, humans, and devas."
He asked again:
"Noble One!
What karma did these sentient beings of the hells previously commit to undergo such suffering as being cut, hacked, and having their bodies crushed?"
The bhikṣu replied, “Worthy one!
This is because he repeatedly committed these ten paths of unwholesome action with an extremely heavy mind without ceasing; by the power of that karma, he now undergoes this suffering.”
He asked again:
"Noble One!
What karma did these beings in the animal realm previously perform to undergo such suffering as bearing heavy burdens and devouring one another?"
The bhikṣu replied, "O worthy one!

This is due to having committed the ten paths of unwholesome action; because you performed them repeatedly with a slight degree of mind without ceasing, by the power of that karma you now undergo this suffering."
He asked again:
"Noble One!
What karma did these beings in the realm of hungry ghosts previously commit to undergo such suffering as being scorched by hunger and thirst?"
The bhikṣu replied, "Worthy sir!

This is due to your stinginess regarding your own possessions and your refusal to give in charity; when you saw others giving, you obstructed them. You lacked the intention to share with the Triple Gem, your parents, or your kinsmen, and having practiced this habit repeatedly, you now undergo this suffering through the power of that karma."
He asked again:
"Noble One! What karma did this being in the heavenly realm perform to receive such supreme and wondrous bliss?"
The bhikṣu replied: "O noble one!

This is because you cultivated the ten wholesome karmas with a sincere heart, revered and placed faith in the Triple Gem, and observed the prohibitive precepts; by the power of that karma, you have now been born in heaven to enjoy supreme and wondrous bliss."
He asked again:
"Noble One!
Having performed what kind of karma in this human realm did you receive this intermediate pleasure, yet still experience the suffering of striving for a livelihood and so forth?"
The bhikṣu replied: "O worthy one!

This was due to repeatedly practicing the ten paths of wholesome action with a feeble mind; by the power of that karma, you have now obtained a human body and experienced middling pleasures, yet you still endure the sufferings of seeking a livelihood and the like."
The youth replied, "Noble One!
I do not desire rebirth in the three lower miserable realms; my heart aspires to be born among humans or devas."
"Noble One!
What karma did I perform to be born in that heavenly realm?
He replied:

"If you are able to go forth within the Buddha’s true teaching, skillfully expounding the Dharma and Vinaya, then by exerting yourself in practice during this present life, you shall sever all afflictions and reach the end of suffering."
"If one does not attain the fruit and passes away while still possessing residual afflictions, one will be reborn in the heavens.
"Noble One! What kind of karma should one who has gone forth perform?"
He replied,
"Until the end of my life, I shall not let my holy life (brahmacarya) decline. He said:
"I am unable to do that; what other karma might lead to rebirth in the heavens? [The Buddha replied:
"If one observes the eight precepts and the five training rules, one becomes a lay follower (upāsaka) who dwells near [the Dharma]."
He asked, "What is this doing? He replied:
"If for one day and night, or even until the end of one's life, one refrains from killing, stealing, sexual misconduct,
false speech, and so forth," he said, "I am unable to do even this. What other karma must I perform to be reborn in heaven?"
He replied,
“If one provides food and drink to the Buddha and the Sangha, by virtue of this meritorious cause, one shall be reborn in the heavens.
[The other asked], “Noble One!”
"How much wealth can be used to provide food and drink as offerings for the Buddha and the Sangha?
He replied,
"Five hundred gold coins may be used."
“Noble One! This matter can be accomplished.
Having said this, he rose from his seat, prostrated at his feet, and departed.
Returning home, he said to his mother:

"Earlier, I went to the Bamboo Grove Monastery and saw beneath the temple gate a painted wheel of the cycle of birth and death in the five destinies—namely, the hells, animals, hungry ghosts, humans, and devas."
"The three lower miserable realms are not what I desire; as for the two higher realms, my heart has affection for them. Mother, do you now wish to be born among humans or devas?
The mother replied, "I do."
"If it be so, you should give me five hundred pieces of gold to offer as a single meal to the Buddha and the Sangha; thus, I shall be reborn in heaven."

The mother said, "You lost your father while young and were raised in solitude; you have relied either on your own strength or on your kinsmen. Now that you have finally reached adulthood and are being entrusted to a teacher to receive instruction, even the fee for your tuition has not yet been met—how could you possibly obtain five hundred gold coins so suddenly?"
He said, "If I am poor and have nothing, I shall seek money by working as a hired laborer.
His mother said:
"You are currently young, yet your strength is slight; how can you seek out precious wealth through labor?
He replied, "I shall exert all my effort, hoping to equal others."
Seeing her persistence, her mother released her and let her go. She went to the marketplace and sought employment for herself.

At that time, there were Brahmins, householders, and others coming to seek laborers; she had not seen or been asked about them until evening. Standing among the passersby, when all the people had dispersed, she finally returned home.
The mother asked,
"Have you found a place to work for hire?
He replied:
"I have never before seen or heard of such a thing.
His mother said,
"How can there be a man who acts like you, even when fastening his belt?"
"Whenever one works as a laborer, one’s head is covered in dust and dirt and one wears tattered, worn-out clothes; when others see this while working, they will ask about it.
On the following morning, he did exactly as his mother had said, putting on coarse clothing and staying among the laborers.
At that time, there was an elder who wished to build a residence and came to the marketplace to seek laborers; he took other men away without even asking after the poor man.
Then the poor man said to the elder, "I am also a hired laborer; why do you not employ me?"
The householder said, "Your appearance is so delicate; how could you possibly perform manual labor?
He replied:
"How can one who hires laborers pay them in advance?
The elder replied,
"The wages are paid at the end of the day."
The poor man said, "I shall work for you;
when the time comes for the afternoon meal, if my labor is deemed satisfactory, you should pay me the wage; if it does not meet your expectations, there is no need to give me anything."
The elder took him back and assigned him labor; while the other workers were not all of one mind, this poor man alone performed his tasks with all his might.
The others said to him, "Judging by your appearance, you do not understand the nature of hired labor; you should merely pass the time—why trouble yourself so?"
The poor man replied, "Do you brothers not know?
Because of my evil karma, I was born into a poor family; if I now further deceive others, in what realm shall I be reborn?"
The men replied, "You do not yet understand;
for now, apply yourself with diligence, lest in no long time you become more lazy than we.

At that time, the poor youth was skilled at conversation and spoke skillfully to the laborers according to their needs. The men delighted in his words and followed him as he worked; they were so eager to listen to his talk that they had no leisure to walk slowly. The youth led them on until the end of the day, such that the work done in one day by him was twice that of others.
At dusk, the elder came in person to inspect the work; seeing that what had been done was twice as excellent as usual, he asked the laborer:
"Did you employ additional workers today?"
He replied, "I have not added anything.
[The other asked,] "If that is so, why is it now double what it was before?"
The man who was to perform the task reported the matter in full; upon hearing it, the elder felt extreme joy and consequently gave the poor man twice the price.
The poor man asked, "Are you paying two days' wages all at once?"
The elder said,
"I feel ashamed before you, and therefore I shall double the price.
The poor man said:

"If it is to your satisfaction, even until the house is completed, you may always allow me to work; as for the price, there is no need to repay it yet—it shall be paid all at once when the work is finished."
The elder said, "Excellent!

He then regularly had him perform manual labor. When the work at his residence was completed, the elder calculated the money to pay for the wages, but he received only four hundred and fifty, which fell short of what had been promised.
Upon seeing this, the poor man immediately began to weep. The elder said, "Why do you weep?
Have I perhaps wronged or deceived you?"
He replied:

"O Great Householder, it is not possible that you would deceive me; however, my original intention was to seek five hundred coins to offer as an act of worship to the Buddha and the Sangha. Since the money was not yet sufficient, I have further subjected myself to hardship. It is for this reason that I weep."
The householder said,
"If it concerns a meritorious deed, I am willing to assist in its completion.
The poor man replied:
"The householder has filled [the bowl] to the brim, which constitutes a meritorious deed for himself; it contradicts my original vow, and thus I shall not be reborn in heaven.
The householder said, "Did you offer [this] to the Buddha and the Sangha with a faithful heart?"
He replied, “It is so.
[The other] said, “If that is the case, you should go and ask the World-Honored One; you should practice according to what the Buddha teaches.”
Then that poor man went at once to where the Buddha was, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, sat to one side, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

In order to provide for the Buddha and the assembly of monks, I hired out my own labor to seek five hundred gold coins. I worked as a day laborer for a certain elder for a long time, yet when the work was finished, the five hundred were not fulfilled.”
"If the elder sees that it is insufficient and fills it for me,
should I take it, or should I not?
The Buddha said:
“O youth! You should take it.
He addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
If one relies on the assistance of others, I fear they will not be reborn in heaven.
The Buddha said:
“Young man!
When you first resolved your mind [on awakening], you were destined for birth in the celestial realms; how much more so now that you have practiced giving—will you not be born in the heavens?
Having received the Buddha’s instruction, he departed with joy. Arriving at the elder’s house, he took five hundred gold coins and returned to his mother’s place, saying:
“O compassionate mother!
Here are five hundred gold coins; I pray that you will use them to prepare offerings for the Buddha and the Sangha.
The mother said:
"Do you not realize that our household has long been poor and lacks provisions for every need? We have no food, utensils, or mats; how could we possibly provide for the Buddha and the Sangha?"

"You may now go and inform the householder at the place where you work for wages, so that he may know; perhaps his residence is spacious enough and he might be able to assist you. Having heard this advice, the poor man went to the householder’s place and said:

"My family is currently impoverished and destitute in every respect; we lack food, utensils, and seating. I wish to invite the Buddha and the Sangha, but I am unable to manage it. I venture to request your assistance in providing what is necessary within this very house; would it be possible to invite the Buddha and the Sangha to a meal here?"
The householder then thought, "I have built this new residence; it would be a virtuous deed to offer it to the Buddha and the Saṃgha.
He then said:
"You may leave some goods behind to invite the Buddha and the Sangha; they shall come to our home to accept our offerings.
At that time, the impoverished man left the goods and departed. Then, on the following day, he went to where the Buddha was, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, knelt with palms joined, and said:
"World-Honored One!..."
"I only pray that you will deign to accept a modest offering at my residence tomorrow.
At that time, the World-Honored One accepted the invitation by remaining silent.
Seeing that the Buddha had accepted, he prostrated at his feet and departed to inform the elder of the news.

The householder immediately prepared various kinds of excellent food and drink; at dawn, he spread out seats and mats, set out large water vessels, and arranged fragrant flowers. He then sent a messenger to inform the Buddha:
"The meal is ready; may the Buddha know that it is time."
At that time, during the first part of the day, the World-Honored One dressed in his robes, took up his alms bowl, and went with the assembly of noble ones to the house of the elder.
At that moment, the six bhikṣus asked the official in charge of affairs,
"Whose house has invited the Buddha and the Saṃgha today?"
He replied,
“I am the son of a certain elder.
The group of six [monks] deliberated, saying:
"What food and drink does that hired laborer have?
It would be appropriate for me now to go to another acquaintance's place to seek some light refreshment.
Having arrived at that house, he said:
"Noble one!
You may eat some light refreshments.
They then ate their fill before proceeding to the place where they were invited.
At that time, the World-Honored One, together with the great assembly, arrived at the house of the elder. Having each washed their feet, they took their seats.

Then, the impoverished man personally served them pure and exquisite food and drink until everyone was fully satisfied. Seeing that the six bhikṣus were unable to eat the food well, he went to where the Buddha was and said:
"World-Honored One!"
"I see among the assembly some noble ones who cannot eat fine food; could it not be that this is an obstacle preventing me from being reborn in heaven?
The Buddha said, "Worthy One!
"Merely by offering a seat or a mat, one will certainly attain rebirth in heaven; how much more so when providing food and drink for the Buddha and the Sangha.

At that time, having seen that the Buddha and the assembly of monks had finished their meal and withdrawn their bowls, the poor man took a small mat and sat before the Buddha to hear the sublime Dharma.
The Buddha taught them, instructing, exhorting, inspiring, and gladdening them, after which he rose from his seat and departed.

At that time, five hundred merchants were traveling from the great ocean through the city of Rājagṛha; on their first day there, they encountered a great festival, and as no one would trade for the precious goods they had brought, they deliberated among themselves, saying:
"Since there is no business for trading, what shall we do?"
"There is no need to seek out where food and drink are required.
Among them was one man who had previously associated with bhikṣus and was well-acquainted with their formal procedures;
he said to the others, "We should go about and inquire: 'Where will the Buddha and the Sangha be provided for this morning?'"
"There must be leftover food and drink in that household; let us go there to seek it.
Having learned that a certain householder’s residence had already provided for the Buddha and the Sangha, they said, "Let us go there and redeem it by paying its value."
He then went to the house and said, "Householder!
The Buddha and the Sangha have finished their meal and there must be some leftovers; how much would you ask for them?"
The householder replied, "This is not my food; it is the meal prepared by this youth.
The merchant then approached him and made the same request as before.
The poor man replied, "I do not need money; simply grant me this favor.
Then the merchants ate as much as they desired; once they were fully satiated, they all offered praise and said to the elder:
"You have obtained great and excellent benefit today, sir, in that you have provided offerings of food within your own home for the Buddha and the Saṅgha; we merchants, too, have been satiated.
The householder replied, "This is not my food; it is an offering prepared by this youth."
He asked, "Whose son is this youth?
and she replied:
"This is the son of such-and-such a householder.
The merchant leader replied,
"This person is the son of my own friend."
He then spread a large cloth upon the ground and placed precious jewels upon it, addressing everyone present:
"Gentlemen, you should know!
I have heard that even a single thread completes a garment and a single drop fills a vessel; therefore, if any among you possess the virtue of giving, you should place your offerings here."
In an instant, it became a heap of jewels.
The merchant leader replied,
"You shall receive these goods."
The poor man said, "I merely gave food; I had no intention of seeking anything in return.
The merchant leader said:
"This is not the price for the food; a single jewel within this [pile] can provide a hundred offerings. It has nothing to do with the value of the meal, but is a gift exchanged out of a heart of joy.
He replied, "I have now prepared this food seeking rebirth in heaven. Although you offer it to me, I dare not accept it; let us not, on account of this, obstruct my attainment of heaven."
The merchant leader asked,
"Do you have faith in the Buddha?
