He replied:
“I believe. “If you believe in the Buddha, you may go and ask him; you should practice according to whatever the Buddha teaches.
Thereupon, the son of the elder went to where the Buddha was, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and said:
“World-Honored One!
I recently prepared an offering and had food remaining, with which I satisfied five hundred merchants.
They were so delighted that they bestowed many rare treasures upon me. Should I accept these items or not?”
The Buddha said, "Accept it. He replied:
“World-Honored One!
Let not this jewel obstruct my rebirth in heaven!
The Buddha said:
“This is but the flower-retribution; the fruit-retribution shall follow later.
At that time, the son of the elder prostrated before the Buddha and departed to receive precious jewels.
Now, in the city of Rājagṛha, there was a preeminent elder who had fallen ill and passed away without leaving any heirs. The multitude deliberated, saying:
“The elder has passed away, and our leaders and guarantors are all gone; whom can we seek to take charge of us collectively?
We ought to seek together a person of great merit and virtue and establish him as our leader.”
The people deliberated, saying,
"How can we know that he possesses such great merit?
Among them was a wise man who addressed the others, saying:
"One should place many kinds of seeds into a single jar and have those people reach their hands in to draw them out.
If one draws out a seed of a single color, that person shall be established as the leader."

They then acted according to their plan, placing various kinds of seeds into a single jar; when everyone drew one out, they all obtained mixed varieties, yet this poor man alone obtained seeds of a pure color.
Although everyone saw this, they all deliberated together, saying:
"How could we possibly appoint a hired laborer as our leader?
They then had him take three more [draws], and he obtained pure-colored [wool] each time.
When the people saw this, they were all filled with wonder and said, "This must be the protection bestowed by a celestial deity; we should now unite our hearts and request him to be our leader."
At that time, the people of the town and its outskirts all bowed to the poor man, regarding him as their leader.

When the elder who had provided the offerings saw this, he immediately adorned his daughter with various precious necklaces and gave her in marriage to him. Due to the power of the poor man’s wholesome karma, treasures suddenly appeared spontaneously within his house; because of this, the people called him "Śrīsaṃbhava" (Born of Good Fortune).
At that time, the householder Śrīgupta thought to himself:

"The rewards currently being experienced within my home are all due to the majestic spiritual power of the World-Honored One. I should now invite the Buddha and the Sangha to come to my home and accept my offerings."

At that time, the householder Śreṣṭhin approached the Buddha; having prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, he sat to one side. Once the Buddha had preached the Dharma for him, and he had heard it, he immediately rose to his knees, adjusted his robe over one shoulder, and with palms joined in reverence, addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
"I only pray that out of compassion, you and the bhikṣus will come to my residence tomorrow to accept a modest offering.
At that time, the World-Honored One accepted by remaining silent.
Having seen that the Buddha had accepted, the elder Śreṇika prostrated at the Buddha’s feet and departed from his seat.

At that time, the householder Śreṣṭhin immediately prepared various kinds of superior and exquisite food and drink during that very night—as described in detail previously—and personally carried the food to offer it to the Buddha and the assembly of monks.
Having seen that his bowl had been taken away, the elder wished to hear the Dharma and took a small mat to sit before the Buddha.

At that time, the World-Honored One, knowing the elder’s inclinations and faculties, taught the Dharma according to his capacity, causing the elder’s mind to attain awakening; immediately upon sitting there, both husband and wife used the vajra-wisdom mallet to shatter the twenty-fold mountain of *satkāyadṛṣṭi* and attained the fruit of stream-entry (*srotāpanna*).
Having realized the truths, they addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

It is through the Buddha that we have attained the fruit of liberation; this was not something that could be accomplished by our parents, ancestors, kings, nor by the hosts of devas, śramaṇas, brāhmaṇas, friends, or kinsmen.”

Because I encountered the World-Honored One, the Great Spiritual Friend, he has rescued me from the realms of hell, animals, and hungry ghosts and established me in the superior and wondrous states of humans and devas. I shall reach the end of suffering and attain the bliss of nirvana; I have dried up the ocean of blood, transcended the mountain of bones, and completely eradicated all views of a self accumulated since beginningless time, thereby attaining the first fruit of the path.

I now take refuge in the Triple Gem of the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha. May the World-Honored One bear witness that I am an upāsaka and an upāsikā; from this day forth until the end of my life, I shall observe the five precepts:
abstaining from taking life, and so on, up to abstaining from drinking intoxicants.
Having spoken these words, they both prostrated at the Buddha’s feet and joyfully practiced his teaching.

Then the World-Honored One expounded the essentials of the Dharma for that husband and wife; having instructed, inspired, benefited, and gladdened them so that they attained the supreme fruit, he rose from his seat and departed.
When they had arrived at their dwelling place, all the bhikṣus were filled with doubt and requested the World-Honored One, saying:
"What karma did that elder, Śreṇika, previously perform?"
"By the power of that karma he became a hired laborer; what further karma did he perform such that precious jewels emerged spontaneously within his house?
The Blessed One replied, "This very Sunakṣatra performed deeds in the past; when the conditions converged and matured, the fruit of retribution was not lost."

Whatever wholesome or unwholesome karma sentient beings have previously performed in former bodies does not ripen within external elements such as earth, water, fire, or wind; rather, the fruits of karma ripen within their own aggregates, elements, and sense bases.
Then he spoke in verse:
"Even if a hundred eons pass, the karma one has created does not perish;
when the causes and conditions meet, the retribution is inevitably experienced by oneself."
"O Bhikṣus! You should listen to this causal connection.

In a past age, there was a householder in a village who was immensely wealthy, possessing great riches and abundant enjoyments. During the month of spring, when all the flowers were in full bloom, the lush forests and clear ponds were all delightful; birds of various colors, such as śāris, parrots, and thrushes, emitted harmonious and elegant sounds."
At that time, the elder took his sons and daughters to a flower grove to enjoy a stroll together.

At that time, there was no Buddha in the world; instead, a Pratyekabuddha had appeared in the world. He always harbored compassion for those who were poor and destitute, dwelling in humble lodgings and subsisting on coarse food, appearing in the world alone like a rhinoceros horn.

At that time, out of compassion for sentient beings, this Pratyekabuddha traveled through the human world and arrived at this village. During the first part of the day, he put on his robes, took up his alms bowl, and intended to go begging for food. He then reflected to himself:
"For what reason do I now undergo such hardship with this body, which is so difficult to satisfy, entering the village and seeking food in many places?"
"You should stay within the garden.
If people come for festivals or celebrations, you may use whatever they provide to satisfy your own needs.
At that time, the Pratyekabuddha went to the garden.

Seeing from afar that the elder’s body and mind were serene and tranquil, and his deportment was dignified and orderly, the householder’s faith and respect increased all the more; he gave rise to a heart of yearning and approached to prostrate at the elder’s feet, saying:
"Noble One!..."
"You practice benevolence for the sake of seeking food, while I seek merit; it would be fitting for you to dwell in this grove and accept my offerings.
At that time, the Pratyekabuddha silently consented, and the elder provided him with food and drink every day.
Later, when the householder had business requiring him to go to another village, he said to his wife, "My dear lady!
I now have business that requires me to go to such-and-such a village; you must continue to provide for the Noble One as usual, without any deficiency."
Having spoken thus, he departed.
Then, at dawn, the elder’s wife rose early and prepared food and drink. Her son asked:
"Mother, for whom do you labor so diligently every day?"
The mother said,
"They are the supreme field of merit.
Having heard this, he spoke in anger:
"He accepts food from others without performing labor," his mother then rebuked him,
"Do not commit such a grave offense of verbal karma."
Later, when the householder returned, he asked his wife,
"Did the noble ones lack for food and drink?
His wife replied to him:
"The food and drink provided here are never lacking whenever they are needed; yet my child has committed a verbal offense against the Noble One.
He then related his son's words in full.
The elder then thought to himself:
"A child lacks discernment and thus brings harm to his own person; he is destined to fall into the evil realms.
He then took the boy and went to the place where the venerable one was.
At that time, the Pratyekabuddha saw from afar that the elder had arrived with his son, and he thought to himself:
"The householder has come alone recently; why does he come today accompanied by a companion?

Having observed this, [the Buddha], knowing the situation, did not rely on verbal speech but taught the Dharma through his body out of compassion for him. He leaped into the air like a king of geese, manifesting great supernormal powers and performing the eighteen transformations: red flames surged upward while clear water flowed downward, expanding and contracting with ease, causing [the householder] to give rise to deep faith.

When ordinary people saw the supernatural powers, they were swiftly awakened as if a great tree had been toppled; bowing their heads in refuge, they prostrated from afar at his venerable feet and said:
"O Venerable One, with a compassionate and pure mind, we pray that you will take pity on us and descend quickly to accept our humble sincerity and receive this brief offering."

At that time, out of compassion, the noble one lowered his body and descended. The elder immediately made diligent offerings of seasonal incense and flowers; both father and son prostrated themselves at the venerable one's feet and made this aspiration:

"This great field of merit is worthy of veneration, yet we instead reviled him with evil words and spoke of hiring him for labor. We pray that in the future he may not suffer the retribution for this."

By all the merit of my diligent and sincere offerings, I pray that in future lives I may be born into a great wealthy family and attain such sublime fruits; furthermore, may I serve a teacher even more excellent than this one, never becoming weary of or turning away from him.

“O bhikṣus, do not harbor any other thoughts. The son of a householder at that time was none other than the present householder Śrīgupta. Because he gave rise to a mind of anger toward a pratyekabuddha and spoke words of contempt while performing labor for hire, he was constantly a hired laborer for five hundred lifetimes; even until now, his evil karma of hired labor has only just been exhausted.”

Furthermore, through the merit of making offerings with utmost sincerity, he was born into a great wealthy family; because of his former vow that such a sublime fruit might be attained, he has now, in my presence, perceived the Truths.

Furthermore, regarding the vow: "May I serve this Great Teacher, never giving rise to weariness or aversion"—I am a hundred thousand billion times superior to the Pratyekabuddhas, yet those who make offerings to me do so without weariness or aversion.
Therefore, O bhikṣus!

If you perform purely black karma, you will obtain a purely black maturation; if you perform purely white karma, you will obtain a purely white maturation; if you perform mixed black-and-white karma, you will obtain a mixed maturation.
"O bhikṣus! You should abandon entirely black and mixed karma; you should cultivate entirely white karma so as to obtain entirely white retribution. Thus you should train.
This was the origin of the rule, yet the precept had not yet been formally enacted.
At that time, the World-Honored One departed from the city of Rājagṛha and proceeded to Vaiśālī, where he stayed in the High Chamber Hall beside the Monkey Pond.

At that time, there was an elder named Vīradatta who heard that the Buddha had arrived and was staying in the High Chamber Hall. He went to the Buddha’s location, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and withdrew to sit to one side. The Buddha preached the Dharma for him, instructing, exhorting, benefiting, and gladdening him; having brought him to a state of joy, the Buddha remained silent.
Then the householder Śūradatta rose from his seat, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and said:
“World-Honored One,
I pray that out of compassion you and the assembly of monks will come to my home tomorrow to accept a modest offering.”
The World-Honored One accepted by remaining silent.
At that time, the elder, seeing that the Buddha had accepted, prostrated at his feet and departed. Having reached his home, he addressed his family members, saying:

"I have invited the Buddha and the Sangha for a meal tomorrow. However, the Buddha and the assembly of monks will be weary from the journey; therefore, you must prepare many excellent and exquisite foods."
Then the family members prepared everything according to his instructions.
At dawn, the householder arranged seats and mats and set out a large water vessel; he then sent a messenger to inform the Buddha:
"The food and drink are ready; may the Buddha know that the time has come."
The group of six bhikṣus arrived at this city and went to the residence of their disciples; seeing them, the disciples paid their respects and said,
"Venerable ones,
please partake of some light food."
He replied, "I have accepted an invitation from another.
He spoke again, saying:
"You may eat a small amount of āmra cakes.
He replied, "Very well."
He then ate his fill.
At that time, a bhikṣu seeking alms passed by the gate; the elder came out, saw him, and also invited him to eat the cakes.
The bhikṣu replied, "I eat in one sitting; I should not go to two places."
The householder said,
"If that is the case, take it as you please and go to eat with them.
He then took it in a small bowl and went to the house where he had been invited.
At that time, the World-Honored One did not go to accept the invitation, but the bhikṣus all went.
There are five causes and conditions for which the Buddha sends someone to fetch food. What are these five?

First, for his own quiet seclusion; second, to preach the Dharma to the devas; third, to visit the sick; fourth, to inspect the bedding and furniture; and fifth, to establish rules of training for his disciples.
In this context, the training rule was established because, while staying in the hall, he had people fetch food for him.

At that time, the householder Vīradatta, seeing that the assembly was seated, personally offered various kinds of pure and exquisite food and drink with his own hands, ensuring that everyone was fully satisfied.

At that time, while the householder was distributing food, he saw the alms-food held in the small bowl of the mendicant; as the distribution of food was nearly finished, he stood before the mendicant bhikṣu, who thought to himself:
"Now this householder gazes at me alone, intending to say something; before he has even spoken, I shall speak first."
He replied, "Householder!
Why should I eat these amra cakes alone?"
"The six bhikṣus of that group have also all finished eating.
The householder replied,
"Noble ones!"
"What do you mean by that?
The alms-seeker replied, "It is not only I who have eaten the *āmra* cakes; those six groups [of monks] have also finished eating them."
Having heard this, the householder’s face flushed with anger, and he said,
"Noble One! Is it that there are no such cakes within my own home?"
He said to his family members,
"You may take these mango cakes.
They immediately took the cakes.
When the bhikṣu who had taken the food had received it, he went to where the Buddha was, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and stood to one side.
It is the constant custom of the World-Honored One to exchange greetings with those who bring food, asking:
"Have the community of monks eaten their fill today?"
He addressed [the Buddha], saying:
"World-Honored One!
We have all been fully satiated with the most excellent food and drink; however, that householder Vīradatta harbors resentment toward the Saṃgha."
The Buddha asked,
"What is the reason?
At that time, the bhikṣu reported the matter in detail.
The Buddha said, "It is reasonable that the householder Vīradatta spoke words of resentment.

At that time, the World-Honored One, having finished his meal, put away his robes and bowl; after rinsing his mouth, he went outside to wash his feet, then returned to his room and sat in silent meditation.
In the late afternoon, he arose from meditative concentration, went to the regular assembly hall, sat down before the community of monks, and addressed the group of six:
"Did you truly engage in successive meals?"
The group of six monks replied,
"It is indeed so,
Venerable Sir!"
The World-Honored One rebuked them in various ways:
"This is not proper conduct, it is not a compliant practice, it is not a pure dharma, and it is something you ought not to do.
Why do you engage in successive meals?"
Having thus rebuked him, he addressed the bhikṣus at length as previously described, up until: "In order to establish a training rule, it should be stated thus:
'If a bhikṣu eats in succession, it is a pāyattika.'"
Thus the Blessed One established this training rule for the bhikṣus.
While the Buddha was staying in the High Chamber Hall in Vaiśālī, there was a bhikṣu afflicted by the suffering of illness, and a physician skilled in medicine came into the monastery.
Having seen him, the bhikṣu replied,
"O noble sir!
You should examine my illness and prescribe a remedy."
The physician said:
"Venerable sir!
You may eat a light meal."
He replied,
"O worthy one! The World-Honored One does not permit it."
The physician said, "This itself is the medicine; nothing else can cure it.
The bhikṣu replied:
"The World-Honored One has established the precepts and does not permit me to eat," [the monk] said.
The physician replied, "The World-Honored One is greatly compassionate; for the sake of the condition of illness, he must surely grant permission to eat."
When the bhikṣus heard of this matter, they reported the circumstances to the Buddha.
The Buddha said, "Except in cases of illness.

Furthermore, there were bhikṣus who, while attending to monastic affairs or performing services for a stūpa, became physically exhausted and hungry, and consequently lay down to rest, neglecting the cultivation of wholesome qualities.
At that time, some brahmins and householders of pure faith entered the monastery and, seeing him lying prostrate, spoke these words:
"Venerable One!
The teaching of the World-Honored One is to be practiced with constant diligence; for what reason do you now remain lying prostrate?"
He replied, "O worthy one!
I am extremely emaciated and weak."
He replied,
"One should eat light food.
He answered:
"The Buddha has prohibited it.
The bhikṣus informed the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"Except when there is a specific cause or condition."
At that time, the World-Honored One departed from Vaiśālī for the Anāthapiṇḍada Monastery.
There was a bhikṣu who, exhausted by the road, his body weakened and emaciated, said to his companions:
"My body is weary."
"If the Buddha, the World-Honored One, would permit us to eat light meals, we could travel long distances without our bodies becoming weary.
They reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said,
"Except when traveling on the road."
At that time, the World-Honored One arrived at the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park, in the city of Śrāvastī.

At that time, there was a householder in this city who had made a personal vow: on the eighth, fifteenth, twenty-third, and the final day of every month—on these four days—he would observe the eightfold noble precepts of the upavāsa fast.
Furthermore, he made a solemn vow, inviting the bhikṣus to his house for a meal, resolving that he would not eat beforehand until the bhikṣus had arrived and eaten.
On that same day, another householder invited the Buddha and the Saṃgha to his house to receive a meal.
After the Buddha and the assembly of monks had accepted the invitation, the elder dispatched a messenger to the monastery to invite the monks for a meal.
When the messenger arrived at the monastery, he did not see any bhikṣus and returned to report to the elder:
"I did not see a single person within the monastery."
The householder asked,
"Where has he gone?
They replied:
“Another householder has invited the Buddha and the community of monks to his home for a meal.
The householder said,
“Whichever bhikṣu that householder calls, take one from him.”
The messenger went to summon them, but seeing that all those bhikṣus had already finished their meal and were leaving the house, he said to them:
"Venerable ones!
A certain householder has prepared a meal; we pray that out of compassion you will not refuse our invitation."
The bhikṣu said,
"I have already finished eating," and reported this back to the elder.
"The bhikṣu has finished eating.
The householder said,
"Go back quickly again and say:..."
"Noble One!
Please come and take your meal; after you have finished eating, we shall offer you a great cotton cloth.
The messenger went again and reported to the bhikṣu:
"Please come and take your meal; after you have finished eating, we shall offer you a large cotton cloth (*karpāsa-śāṭaka*).
The bhikṣu said, "I have already had enough to eat; regardless of the size of the cloth, it is not appropriate for me to go further."
The messenger reported to the householder:
"The bhikṣu has had enough to eat and is unwilling to come again; it is not appropriate for him to eat again regardless of the size of the robe.
At that time, because the householder waited for the bhikṣu, the time for his meal had already passed, and he consequently went without food for an entire day.
When the neighbors heard of this matter, they all felt resentment and contempt, saying:
"How is it that these śramaṇa sons of the Śākyas refuse to eat even when others offer them clothing?"
"You have violated that householder’s heart of faith and reverence; by not accepting his invitation, you have caused him to go without food.
When the bhikṣus heard this, they reported the matter in detail to the Blessed One. The Blessed One said:
"Except during the time for the distribution of robes."
At that time, the World-Honored One praised those with few desires who maintain the precepts and honor the precepts; speaking in accordance with the Dharma, he addressed the bhikṣus, saying:
"The former was the original prohibition; this is the subsequent allowance."
The detailed explanation is as before.
"I now establish this training rule for the bhikṣus, which should be recited as follows:
'If a bhikṣu eats in succession (transitively), except at the [proper] times, it is a pāyattika.'"
"Other times" refers to the time of illness, the time of work, the time of traveling on a road, and the time of receiving robes; these are the [permissible] times.
"If it is again a bhikṣu" refers to the group of six [monks]; the rest of the meaning is as explained above.
"Successive eating" refers to eating repeatedly.
"Except at other times" means excluding those specific occasions.
In this context, "time" refers to the time of illness.
"Time of illness" refers to when a bhikṣu is unable to satisfy his hunger during a single sitting.
"Time of work" refers to when there is construction at a stūpa or business for the Saṃgha, such as sweeping an area as large as a mat, or plastering an area the size of a cow's resting place.
Regarding the time of traveling on a journey: if one travels half a *yojana* and returns, or travels directly for one *yojana*, it is permissible.

Regarding the time of giving robes: this refers to items such as a wiping cloth, the dimensions of a lower garment (*nivasana*), or the dimensions of a waistband (*mekhala*); in all these cases there is no offense, and the determination of the transgression is the same as previously stated.
In this regard, what are the characteristics of the offense and how do they manifest?
At the time of giving robes, there are many kinds of invitations, namely sixteen variations such as giving with robes or giving without robes.
If a bhikṣu receives two invitations—both the first and the second providing food and clothing—and accepts both invitations and eats at both locations, he commits no offense in either case.
If a bhikṣu has been invited first to a meal where robes will be provided and invited later to one where no robes will be provided, he should accept the former invitation and not accept the latter.

If he has already accepted the latter, he should transfer it to another person; if he does not transfer it, he incurs a *duṣkṛta* (wrongdoing) at the time of acceptance, and if he eats the food, he incurs a *pāyattika* (offense of downfall).
If a bhikṣu receives an initial invitation for robes and a subsequent invitation for both robes and the value of robes, accepting both is not an offense.

If a bhikṣu receives an initial invitation for robes and a subsequent invitation for neither robes nor the value of robes, he should accept the initial invitation and must not accept the subsequent one.

If one has accepted [the food], one should transfer it to another person; if one does not transfer it to another, there is an *dukkaṭa* (wrongdoing) at the time of acceptance, and one incurs a *pāyattika* (offense involving forfeiture) upon eating it. This is the first case; all subsequent phrases should be understood according to this principle.
If a bhikṣu is first invited to a meal without robes and later invited to a meal with robes, he may accept both without offense.
If a bhikṣu is first invited to a meal without robes and later invited to a meal without robes, he should accept the former and relinquish the latter.
If a bhikṣu receives an initial invitation for food without clothing and a subsequent invitation for food with clothing or the value of clothing, he may accept both without offense.

If a bhikṣu receives an initial invitation for food without clothing and a subsequent invitation for food without clothing or the value of clothing, he should accept the initial invitation and not accept the subsequent one.

If one has received [the food], one should transfer it to another person; if one does not transfer it to another, there is an *dukkaṭa* (wrongdoing) at the time of receiving, and one incurs a *pācittiya* (offense entailing confession) upon eating it. This is the second set of four cases.
If a bhikṣu receives both an invitation with robes and an invitation with the value of robes for the former, and an invitation with robes for the latter, he may accept both without offense.
If a bhikṣu receives an invitation with robes and the value of robes for the former, and an invitation without robes for the latter, he should accept the former and relinquish the latter.
If a bhikṣu receives both an earlier invitation for robes and their value, and a later invitation for robes and their value, he may accept both without offense.
If a bhikṣu receives an earlier invitation for robes and their value, and a later invitation for neither robes nor their value, he should accept the earlier invitation and not accept the later one.

If one has accepted [the food], one should transfer it to another person; if one does not transfer it to another, there is an *dukkaṭa* offense at the time of acceptance, and one incurs a *pāyattika* offense upon eating it. This is the third set of four cases.
If a bhikṣu has been previously invited to receive clothing or the value of clothing, and is subsequently invited to receive clothing, it is not an offense to accept both.

If a bhikṣu has been previously invited to receive clothing or the value of clothing, and is subsequently invited to receive clothing [but no value], he should accept the former and relinquish the latter.

If a bhikṣu receives an initial invitation for clothing or the value of clothing that provides no clothing, followed by a subsequent invitation for clothing or the value of clothing that does provide clothing, it is not an offense to accept both.

If a bhikṣu receives an initial invitation for clothing or the value of clothing that provides no clothing, followed by a subsequent invitation for clothing or the value of clothing that also provides no clothing, he should accept the initial invitation and must not accept the subsequent one.

If, having accepted it, one does not transfer it to another person, there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*) at the time of acceptance, and one incurs an offense of falling (*pācittiya*) upon eating it; this is the fourth set of four.
Furthermore, there is no offense for the very first offender, or for one who is insane, mentally deranged, or afflicted by intense suffering.
*Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya*, Fascicle 34. *Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya*, Fascicle 3.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Yijing by Imperial Decree. 32.

The Training Rule on Receiving More Than One Meal at a Single Place. The thirty-second training rule concerning receiving more than one meal at a single place: At that time, the Bhagavān was staying in Śrāvastī, in the Jeta Grove, the Anāthapiṇḍada Park.

In a great village in a remote region, there was an elder of profound faith who constructed a dwelling for śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas from the four quarters; he provided food and drink to anyone who stayed there.

At that time, the World-Honored One manifested great supernormal powers in the city of Śrāvastī; all the non-Buddhist practitioners were driven out, and both humans and devas were filled with deep joy and venerated the World-Honored One with profound respect.
However, among the followers of external paths who frequent the borderlands, sixty naked ascetics arrived at this village and went to where the householder was, speaking these words:
"May you obtain the benefit of the Dharma!"
"Virtuous ones, you have obtained the benefit of the Dharma! The elder asked,
"Virtuous ones, who are you that have come here now?"
He replied, "I am a renunciant.
The elder said to him:

"Welcome! I have constructed this dwelling for śramaṇas, brāhmaṇas, and others from the four quarters; you may stay here as you please, and I myself shall provide whatever food and drink you require."
At that time, the various non-Buddhist practitioners remained right there, receiving the provisions provided by the householder.
Meanwhile, a lay devotee from Śrāvastī, carrying various goods, arrived at this village and also stopped at the householder’s shop, where he formed a close bond of friendship with the householder.
At that time, the elder personally handed over cakes, fruits, and food to the naked ascetics; he then sent a messenger to the householder, saying:
"Venerable sir, please come for a moment so that we may together make offerings to these supreme fields of merit."
Having heard this, the householder thought to himself:
"These words are most earnest; they must belong to a disciple of the Buddha. I should now go and prostrate at his feet."
Having arrived there, he saw those shameless, naked ascetics; however, being unable to rebuke them face-to-face, he remained silent.
When those ascetics had finished eating and departed, the elder said to the householder, "Excellent field and excellent seed—how could this not be good?"
The householder replied:

"Though the seeds sown are excellent, the field is inferior and poor—saline, barren, and stony—and thus there will ultimately be no harvest; likewise, those who go naked without shame constantly harbor evil views."
The householder replied,
"Is there any field superior to this?
The lay devotee said:
"There are! Namely, the śrāvaka disciples of the Tathāgata, the Great Teacher.
The householder said:
"If he should come, I shall provide for him with the four requisites.
When that householder heard these words, he took them to heart in silence; having exhausted his old stock, he purchased new goods and immediately returned to Śrāvastī.
Having delivered the goods and settled them within the market shop, he went to the Jetavana Grove to pay homage at the feet of the bhikṣu-saṃgha.

Now, it was the constant habit of the group of six to practice walking meditation (caṅkrama) mostly at the entrance; at that time, Upānanda was standing outside the gate when he saw the householder approaching from afar. He then went forward to greet him and said, "Welcome, householder!"
"It is like the new moon, which only gradually appears after a long time; compared to what place could one arise and seek it through trade?
The householder replied, "I pay homage to the Ācārya!"

Recently, in a certain village, there was an elder who constructed a dwelling place and invited śramaṇas from the four quarters, providing them with excellent food and drink as constant offerings; he harbored a heart of deep longing and veneration for the disciples of the Buddha.
Having heard this, Upānanda thought:
"If any other members of the Black-bowl faction hear these words, they will surely come before me to that dwelling place."
"I should now reprimand that householder so that he does not speak of this to others. He said,
"Householder!"
"Do you always think that I do not practice meditative reflection, am not diligent in reading and reciting, and constantly dwell on food and clothing merely to sustain myself?
The householder then thought:
"In this world, many are greedy and do not know contentment; Upānanda is surely one such person."

"If even upon hearing my words they give rise to such derision and suspicion, how much more so for other venerable elders who hear this teaching of mine—how could they not reproach me with even greater severity?
Thereupon, he remained silent and did not speak further.
At that time, when Upānanda saw that the elder had departed, he went to the six bhikṣus and said,
"Venerable ones!
How can we continue to endure such hardship living here for so long?"
The people said,
"Venerable sir!
Is there any good news?"
He replied, “Venerable sir, there are also some.”
Udāyin asked, "What is the news? Upānanda replied:

"In a certain village there is an elder who, with a mind of faithful giving, has constructed a dwelling place and provides food and drink for the śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas of the four quarters for their unrestricted enjoyment; it would be fitting for us to go together and receive his offerings."
The people asked,
"Is it possible that all six of you will go there?
He replied:
“Furthermore, what harm is there in going together?
Thus, the six men set out together for that village.
At that time, the naked ascetics said to one another:
"We ought to go out for a time to observe and transform [the people]; there must be a favorable location where we may move and settle.
Thereupon, they left one person behind to guard the place while the rest all departed.
At that time, the group of six monks traveled by stages until they reached that village. Upon arriving at the house of the elder, they greeted him and said:
"May you be free from illness and enjoy long life."
The householder asked,
"Who are you, sirs?
They replied:
"He is a disciple of the Buddha, the World-Honored One.
The householder said,
"Welcome, Noble One!"
"I have long held a longing heart, wishing to see the Buddha and his assembly; that you have now arrived, O virtuous one, deeply accords with my original aspiration.
I have long intended to construct a dwelling place and provide food and drink, intending it as a place of rest for śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas from the four quarters; you may now dwell here."
The group of six replied,
"Is there perhaps any bedding, mattresses, covers, or pillows in that place?
They answered:
"There was none before.
The group of six said,
"If there were none there, how could he have been sitting on the ground?"
The householder then sent various couches and seats, along with rugs and mats.
At that time, the six men went to his residence, where one of the non-Buddhist practitioners saw them and said:
"Why have you Śramaṇas, sons of the Śākyas, come here so abruptly?"
"This dwelling is not a place for you to stay.
They replied,
"O non-Buddhist!"
"This is not your dwelling place; what do you mean by this?
If you remain silent, you may stay for now; but if you speak further, you shall certainly be punished.
The non-Buddhist then thought to himself:
“There are six men here, while I am all alone; who could confront and resist them?
We must flee to avoid being humiliated.
These six men ate daily at the house of the elder.
Later, when the householder had business requiring him to travel elsewhere, he addressed the group of six monks, saying:
"I have a minor matter to attend to in a certain village; you should continue to accept my offerings in my home as you have done before, until my return."
The householder then addressed his family members, saying, "As you have done in the past, provide for the noble ones as usual; do not let them lack anything until my return.
The householder then departed, and the group of six received their food as was customary.
Then Udāyin replied to Upānanda:
"Who could remain silent and speechless for such a long duration while following another's rules? It would be better to manifest one's own dignified demeanor."
Upananda said, "This is also excellent! Then,
as the women came forward to offer food and drink, Udāyin said to Nanda and Upananda:
“You all observe this beautiful woman; her eyes, ears, mouth, nose, waist, thighs, hands, and feet are all perfectly formed and truly worthy of enjoyment.
When the women heard this, they were each filled with shame and withdrew into their rooms, waiting for him to finish eating so that they might take back his bowl and depart.
When the elder had finished his business and returned home, he asked his family members:
"Did you provide for the fields of merit without deficiency or lack during my absence?"
The family members replied,
"What use is there for such an evil field of merit?
The elder asked:
"Why did you utter such coarse words?
The woman replied, "Recently,

I have seen those who are foolish, mad, and engaged in frivolous dancing and music uttering coarse and vulgar speech, yet none of their words can compare to the words uttered by the Field of Merit of your honorable family."
The householder asked, "What did he do? He replied:
"This is a vulgar utterance, never before spoken even by jesters or courtesans; having heard it, we are filled with shame and remorse.
The elder then thought:
"Whenever women gaze upon men, those of exposed form satisfy their defiled minds; through this cause and condition, affection and desire arise."
"The conduct and appearance of the śramaṇa Śākyaputrīyas are dignified and their robes cover their bodies;
women do not find them pleasing. She then said:
"You heretics who go naked are what you all enjoy seeing, but as for these śramaṇas whose bodies are covered, my heart has no desire to look upon them."
His wife replied, "If you do not believe me,
I shall allow you to verify it for yourself.
The elder then thought to himself:
"I shall personally investigate whether this is true or false.
After staying there for several days, he said to the group of six:
"Venerable ones!..."
"I have some business and must depart for a short while; you may accept the provisions as usual.
He then hid himself in a secret room to observe from within.
When the time arrived, the group of six went to the place where the food was served, and the elder’s wife personally handed them the meal. As before, the group of six spoke words of flirtation:
"One may observe that this woman’s countenance is upright and handsome, her eyebrows and eyes are slender and long, and her physical form is perfectly proportioned; she is truly worthy of affection.
Having heard this, the elder thought to himself:
"As this woman says, she is not a field of merit."
"I should not now abruptly cut off my provisions; rather, I ought to employ a skillful means to cause him to leave of his own accord.
When the next day arrived, he reduced the number of cakes by one. Chandaka informed Nanda and Upananda:
"Regarding this morning's cakes and fruit, for what reason have they become so meager?"
Nanda said, “Venerable one!
I have been giving the leftover cakes from day to day as alms to poor children; from this day forward, I shall no longer give them.”
On the second day, he removed another cake, and Aśvaka said:
"Venerable one!
This morning’s cakes and fruits are entirely lacking."
Upānanda said, "In recent times, after I had finished eating, there was leftover cake in my bowl; from now on, there shall be no more leftovers.
Thus he gradually reduced his intake until he subsisted on nothing but plain cakes and sour gruel.
Punarvasu said,
"Venerable ones!
Since our food and drink are finished, we may depart."
Udāyin said, "Venerable one!
Since you have lost all hope, you should depart now!"
Before he had departed, [the Buddha] said to the outsider guarding the gate:
"The cessation of our excellent food is due to you; you should leave."
He then went out to wander and encountered other non-Buddhist practitioners who had previously gone out;
he asked them, "Virtuous ones, during your recent travels in the four directions seeking disciples, have you managed to find many fine followers?"
The people said, "We have ordered you to keep watch; why have you gone out?
He replied:
"He drove me out. He asked,
"Who was this person?"
He replied,
"This is a śramaṇa, a son of the Śākyas. He asked:
"How many people are there currently?
He replied, "There are only six."
The non-Buddhists deliberated, saying:
"How could we sixty not be able to restrain these six?
Beat them until they are thoroughly subdued and drive them out!"
Then that Elder addressed the people, saying:

"Let us now go together to that house. When I raise my voice to announce what must be done, you all—ten of you for every one—shall beat him thoroughly until he is well-taught, then drag him out to the edge of the village; having made this agreement, let us enter the village together."
The Elder replied,
"We should first go to see that householder.
Having arrived there, they asked after his well-being.
He then asked,
"For whom was this dwelling originally intended by you,
O Householder? He replied:
“I have built a dwelling for those whose minds lack a fixed standard; whoever stays therein shall be provided with food and drink.
The outsider said, “The Elder’s mind is impartial and free from favoritism.”
They then went together to the place where he was staying and asked him:
"You, śramaṇa son of the Śākyas, this is no place for you to stay; you ought to leave at once and not remain here any longer. If you do not depart, we shall deal with you by our lethal hands."
Upon hearing this, Upānanda said:
"The hair-pulling heretic has uttered these meaningless words:
'This is no place for the śramaṇa sons of the Śākya.'"
"If it is not mine, does it perhaps belong to you?
Then that naked ascetic spoke in anger:
"This is your business."
At that time, ten non-Buddhist practitioners each seized one [of the monks] and began to beat them.
Nanda said to them:
"Venerable sirs!..."
"Each of you must protect your own eyes and ears; do not let them be damaged or blinded so that you are ridiculed by your fellow practitioners of the Brahma-faring life.
He addressed the non-Buddhists, saying:
"Practitioners, you may strike [the drum] upon the shoulders, the waist, and the hips."
At that time, the non-Buddhist practitioners were exhausted from beating their staffs, and their hands and feet were all weary; they consequently stopped to rest.
Chandaka said to them:
"Venerable sirs!..."
"Next, it is my turn to act.

At that time, those six men were all possessed of great strength; when they extended their right hands, they struck down five of the non-Buddhist practitioners, and then, extending their left hands, they toppled another five. Whether with their mendicant staffs or with their hands and feet—punching, kicking, and striking them at will—they beat them thoroughly as they pleased.
Udāyin said, "Venerable ones!
You must guard against the fundamental offense; do not cause your lives to end, lest we incur a *pārājika*."
Once they had beaten them thoroughly, they all drove them out.
When the brahmins saw this, they said to one another, "Look at the son of the Śākyas fighting with the outsiders; surely the heavenly deities will now send down a great rain!"
At that time, after the group of six had driven out the non-Buddhists, Aśvaka said:
"Venerable ones!
We have now emerged victorious in battle without bringing disgrace upon the Saṅgha; we should all go together to Śrāvastī."

At that time, there was a non-Buddhist teacher from the south named Udāyin, a follower of the Lokāyata school who frequently asserted that there is no future life. Seeking debate, he came to the city of Śrāvastī and entered the Jetavana Grove.
He went to the Venerable Ājñātakauṇḍinya and spoke these words:
"Bhikṣu! I have received a small amount of training from my own teacher; I wish to establish a point of debate with you."
Then the Venerable Kauṇḍinya replied:
"Brahmin, you may debate with those who delight in philosophical discourse; such talk as this is not to my liking."

Then the brahmin went to all those great virtuous ones—the Venerable Aśvajit, the Venerable Bhadrika, the Venerable Mahānāman, the Venerable Yaśas, the Venerable Pūrṇa, the Venerable Vimala, the Venerable Gavāmpati, the Venerable Subāhu, and others—and having arrived at their respective places, he sought to engage them in debate; yet with each, as with the Venerable Kauṇḍinya, his discourse was entirely without commonality.
Next, he went to where the Venerable Śāriputra was and spoke these words: "Bhikṣu!
Previously, I practiced a certain amount of study; I wish to establish a point of debate with you."
When Śāriputra heard these words, he thought to himself:
"Let me examine whether this person possesses any roots of goodness.
He then perceived that they possessed some slight roots of goodness. Although they had such roots, he wondered: "Upon whom do these roots depend?"
He then contemplates that this person is connected to him.
He further reflects:
"Are there other such classes of sentient beings who, by observing these discourses and debates, might be able to receive transformation?"
He observed and knew that there were others to be converted;
he then perceived when they would assemble,
knowing that they would all gather on the seventh day.
On that very day, he established his thesis with some points left unfinished; this continued in the same manner for six days.

By the seventh day, it was heard throughout the four quarters that a Southern Master of Logic—a non-Buddhist who claims there is no life after death—had arrived there and engaged in debate with Śāriputra, yet neither could claim victory over the other.
At that time, hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of sentient beings were all filled with joy; some, awakened by the roots of virtue from previous lives, all came to assemble.
Then Śāriputra, knowing the assembly had gathered and observing that the opportune moment had arrived, immediately subdued those non-Buddhists with the profound Dharma, rendering them speechless.
At that time, having been thus defeated, that non-Buddhist follower gave rise to a mind of respectful faith. Joining his palms in reverence, he addressed him thus:
"Virtuous One!
I wish to go forth within the well-spoken Dharma and Vinaya, and having received full ordination to become a bhikṣu, I shall practice the holy life under the World-Honored One."
Then Śāriputra immediately ordained him, conferred full ordination (*upasampadā*) upon him, and instructed him in the rules of conduct.

He then applied himself with single-minded diligence to sever all afflictions and realized arhatship. Possessing the three knowledges (*trividyā*), the six superknowledges (*ṣaḍabhijñā*), and the eight liberations (*aṣṭavimokṣa*), he attained knowledge in accordance with reality:

"Birth has been exhausted; the holy life has been established; what was to be done has been accomplished; there is no further existence. His mind was unobstructed like a hand waving through space; whether cut by a blade or smeared with fragrance, neither love nor hatred arose. He viewed gold and earth as equal and without distinction, renouncing all fame and profit without exception, and was revered by Śakra, Brahmā, and all the devas.
At that time, the great assembly all felt a sense of wonder and spoke thus:
"All you people should know!

This great master of treatises, who was without rival among men, has now been subdued by Śāriputra through his unimpeded eloquence; he has been granted the precepts and has realized the fruit of Arhatship."
The great assembly that had gathered felt a devotion and faith far exceeding their usual measure.

At that time, Śāriputra, knowing the inclinations, latent tendencies, and dispositions of the various members of the assembly, taught the Dharma according to their individual capacities. Consequently, twelve hundred million sentient beings either realized the stages of Heat, Peak, Patience, or the Supreme Mundane Dharma; or attained the fruit of Stream-entry, up to ordination and the attainment of the fruit of Arhatship.

At that time, among the great assembly, some gave rise to the mind of a śrāvaka, some gave rise to the mind of a pratyekabuddha, and some gave rise to the unsurpassed mind of great bodhicitta; all of them conceived deep reverence and faith toward the Triple Gem.
At that time, Śāriputra had defeated those non-Buddhists during the first part of the day; then, after the meal, the group of six bhikṣus came from that village to the Jeta Grove.
When the bhikṣus had seen one another, they said:
"Welcome, venerable one!
It has been some time since we last met; from where have you come?"
He replied,
"I have come from such-and-such a great village.
The people said to him:

"Virtuous ones, due to your meager merit, you did not witness this great event. Recently, Śāriputra subdued the non-Buddhist teachers and outsiders of the south, causing them to renounce worldly life and attain arhatship; hundreds of millions of their followers have likewise attained the fruits [of the path] and resolved their minds upon enlightenment."
At that time, having heard these words, the group of six replied:
"Venerable ones! This is not at all surprising."
Why is this? Śāriputra is the second of the great Dharma Generals who assists the Buddha in turning the Wheel of Dharma; what is there to praise in his subduing of a single non-Buddhist?
"If even when Śāriputra was overcome by others, there was still our Great Teacher to provide mutual rescue and relief, that would not be considered extraordinary.
What we have accomplished is truly rare: that we six persons have subdued sixty non-Buddhists."
The bhikṣu asked,
"By what occult art? Nanda replied:
"He uses the staff technique exclusively.
He asked again,
"What Dharma teachings does he expound?"
He replied,
"I preach the Dharma with my body. He asked:
"Will we both die,
or shall we survive?
He replied:
"At that time his life was still with him; who knows whether he is alive or dead by this day?
When the bhikṣus had fully learned the circumstances, they each felt revulsion and contempt, saying:
"How can a bhikṣu commit such an utterly evil deed? It is only right that he should feel shame, yet instead of this he has become even more arrogant and insolent because of it!"
Then the bhikṣus reported this matter in detail to the Blessed One.
At that time, the Blessed One assembled the bhikṣus and questioned the group of six:
"Did you truly commit such unseemly acts as to bring harm to my Dharma?"
He replied, "It is indeed so,
Venerable Sir!"
The Blessed One rebuked him in various ways, as extensively explained above, and continued until: "In order to establish a training rule, it should be stated thus:
'If a bhikṣu stays at a dwelling place of non-Buddhists for even one night and takes one meal, should he receive anything further, it is a pāyattika.'"
Thus, after the Blessed One had established the training rule for the bhikṣus,
that faithful householder returned with his merchant goods to the aforementioned village and placed them at the shop of the former elder.
The elder still made offerings even to the naked ascetics; he sent a messenger back to summon that householder to join him in expressing sympathetic joy and providing food for the field of merit.
Upon hearing this, the householder thought to himself:
"I shall go and observe them; they are likely disciples of the World-Honored One."
Having seen them there, he observed that they were still naked heretics, devoid of any sense of shame.
The householder was unable to say anything to them face-to-face; he remained silent.
Having finished eating in the nude, he departed from his seat.
Then the elder addressed the householder, saying:
"Excellent field, excellent seed," and so forth, as extensively explained before.
"One who is most excellent and supreme is a disciple of the Blessed One.
Having heard this, the householder spoke these words:
"My friend!"
"Do not even mention his name; I do not wish to hear it, much less desire to see him.
He asked, "Has he already arrived?"
He replied, "I have come.
He asked again:
"Who are these people? He replied,
"The group of six."
The householder asked,
"What business did he have here?
The elder reported the matter in detail, and the householder said:
"Go to the great ocean and collect some imitation lapis lazuli.
The householder said,
"Does the World-Honored One not have excellent disciples?"
The householder said, "There is. The elder said:
“What characters are these? He replied, “They are Śāriputra, Mahāmaudgalyāyana, and others.
If you, O Noble One, should see them, you will surely give rise to a mind of extraordinary faith and reverence, and attain a rare and marvelous thing.”
The elder said,
"If he should come, I shall provide him with offerings.
The householder then thought to himself:
“If I return there, I shall inform the Blessed One.

At that time, the householder finished his trading and took further goods back to Śrāvastī. Having settled his merchandise, he went to where the Buddha was, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and said to the Buddha:
“Blessed One!”

In a certain village there was an elder who constructed a dwelling for śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas from the four quarters; he provided them with food and drink whenever they came, and he felt deep admiration and devotion toward the disciples of the Buddha.
Excellent,
World-Honored One!
Out of compassion for them, please send a bhikṣu to fulfill their faith.
The World-Honored One then granted his consent by remaining silent.
At that time, the householder, knowing that the Buddha had consented, paid homage, took his leave, and departed.
Thereupon, the World-Honored One thought to himself:
"Who has a karmic affinity from a previous life with this elder, his retinue, and the assembled multitude?
He then perceived through insight that only Śāriputra had such an affinity and was able to bring them to spiritual transformation.
The Buddha addressed Śāriputra, saying:
"You should go to such-and-such a village to deliver that elder, his retinue, and the multitude of people there.
Having heard this from the Buddha, Śāriputra immediately followed the Buddha's instruction and, surrounded by five hundred bhikṣus, proceeded to that village.
Having arrived there, they rested at the place where the elder had provided alms-food.

When the elder heard that the Venerable Śāriputra, accompanied by a retinue of five hundred followers, had come to his residence, he immediately went to where Śāriputra was, prostrated at his feet, and sat to one side.
Then Śāriputra expounded the sublime Dharma to that householder, instructing, encouraging, benefiting, and gladdening him, and then remained silent.
Thereupon, the householder rose from his seat, adjusted his robe to bare his left shoulder, joined his palms in reverence, and bowed his head to the ground, saying:
"Venerable One and great assembly!..."
"Please come to my home and compassionately accept a modest offering.
At that time, Śāriputra accepted by remaining silent.
Seeing that Śāriputra had accepted by his silence, the elder prostrated at his feet and departed.
That very night, he prepared various kinds of excellent food and drink; when dawn broke, he arranged the seats and set out large water jars.
He then dispatched a messenger to inform Śāriputra and the great assembly:
"The meal is ready; please be aware that it is time."
Then, during the first part of the day, Śāriputra dressed himself, took his bowl, and together with the great assembly, went to the house of the elder and sat down upon the seats.
When the elder saw that the assembly was seated, he personally served them food until they were all fully satisfied.
Then, Śāriputra, knowing that the assembly had finished eating and had completed their washing and rinsing, collected the alms bowls.
At that time, the elder took a small mat, sat before the senior monk with palms joined, and addressed Śāriputra:
"Venerable One!..."
"I shall preach the Dharma for you.
Then Śāriputra replied to the elder:
"If you wish to hear the Dharma, you should prepare many seats in a wide, spacious, and open place, beat the drum, and proclaim it to all people:"
"If you, sirs, would like to hear the sublime Dharma, you should assemble tomorrow morning to listen as the Venerable Śāriputra proclaims its meaning.
Having thus instructed the elder, he offered him a timely blessing by reciting this verse:
"Whoever practices generosity, Will surely obtain its benefit; Whoever upholds the precepts, Will surely attain peace and happiness."
"If one gives for the sake of happiness, one will surely attain peace and joy in the future.

With such verses as these, he taught how to provide for the welfare of both the living and the deceased, so that all sentient beings might be freed from obstacles and attain liberation. Having offered these prayers of blessing, he rose from his seat and departed.

Now, this elder was the most eminent among the great community. Following the Venerable One’s instruction, he prepared many seats upon an open space and beat a drum to proclaim the announcement to all:

"Tomorrow, the Venerable Śāriputra, the General of the Dharma, will preach the sublime Dharma. If you, sirs, desire to hear it, assemble all together; may you hope to realize the Truths and not remain long submerged in the cycle of birth and death."

Then, when the next day had arrived, at the time for the morning meal, the Venerable Śāriputra, together with the assembly of monks, ascended the seat at the site of the Dharma assembly. An immeasurable multitude of hundreds of thousands gathered like clouds; all sentient beings felt joy and happiness, and some were awakened by their roots of merit from previous lives so that they delighted in hearing the Dharma.

At that time, Śāriputra, knowing the inclinations, latent dispositions, and the diverse natures of the great assembly, taught the Dharma according to their capacities. Consequently, he caused that elder, along with his kinsmen and hundreds of thousands of sentient beings, to attain the four roots of goodness and realize the four supreme fruits; they turned toward the three types of enlightenment according to their conditions, and their reverent faith in the Triple Gem became even more profound.

At that time, Śāriputra had been preaching the Dharma for a long duration and suffered from a wind-disorder in his back. Furthermore, because the Buddha had previously established the precept against eating after the proper time had passed, he did not eat.
Then, the householder invited Śāriputra and the great assembly, saying:
"I pray that you will deign to remain in my home for some time; I shall provide for all of you with the four requisites."
Then Śāriputra replied to the householder:
"Taking you as the occasion, the Buddha will establish a training rule for the bhikṣus; I now wish to depart."
At that time, Śāriputra was afflicted with a wind-related ailment; having fasted and become physically weak from hunger, he set out for Śrāvastī with a great assembly of followers.
Upon his arrival there, the bhikṣus asked Śāriputra’s disciples, "Welcome, venerable ones!"
"Are your belongings secure?
He replied, "Some are secure, and some are not."
He asked: "For what reason? He replied:
“O my Upādhyāya! You have extensively brought about our deliverance and established us in peace and happiness.

However, because the time spent preaching the Dharma was long, you suffered from a wind-disorder (vāta-roga) in your back; furthermore, having gone without food for a day, you have traveled a great distance—this is not peaceful or happy.”
When the bhikṣus heard of this matter, they reported the circumstances to the Buddha. The Buddha said:
"I permit the bhikṣus to keep a waistband (kaṭicāpaka) for their own comfort; furthermore, at places where food is distributed, one should set aside those who are ill."
At that time, the World-Honored One praised those who uphold the precepts as extensively explained before, and addressed the bhikṣus:
"The former was the initial prohibition; this is the subsequent allowance."
It should be stated as follows:
"If a bhikṣu stays at the dwelling place of non-Buddhists for more than one night and takes more than one meal, except when there is a cause such as illness, it is a pāyattika."
"Furthermore, 'if a bhikṣu' refers to the group of six [monks]; the remaining meanings are as explained above.
'In the dwelling place of non-Buddhists' means that if a donor has previously given that dwelling to non-Buddhists, one may accept a single meal at such a location."
Regarding "except for the cause of illness": if there is a reason of illness, eating beyond [the prescribed limit] is not an offense.
If one is not ill, eating beyond [the limit] incurs a *pāyattika* (offense of falling). The rest is the same as before.
Regarding this, what are the characteristics of the offense and how does it occur?
If a bhikṣu has already accepted one meal at a separate residence and stays overnight again, he incurs a duṣkṛta offense;
if he accepts food [after staying overnight], he incurs a pāyattika offense.
If one stays overnight in this place but receives food elsewhere, there is an offense of wrong-doing (*duṣkṛta*) at the time of staying, but no offense at the time of eating.
If one stays overnight elsewhere but eats here, there is no fault at the time of staying, but one incurs an offense of downfall (*pāyantika*) at the time of eating.
If one stays in another place and eats in another, coming here only briefly, there is no offense.
If this location is a communal dwelling for many, or if the donor requests that one remain, or if this residence was built by a relative, there is no offense in eating beyond the prescribed time.
Furthermore, there is no offense for one who is the very first offender, or for one who is insane, mentally deranged, or overwhelmed by intense physical pain.
The Thirty-third Training Rule: Regarding Receiving Food in Excess of Three Alms-Bowls. The Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, there was a great merchant leader from the north who arrived at the outskirts of this city and halted there.
When the group of six heard of this, they said to one another:
"Nanda and Upananda!..."

"I have heard that a great merchant leader from the north has arrived and is resting outside this city wall. I shall now go for a moment to visit him; if he is willing to receive me, I shall exhort and convert him to some small extent."
Nanda replied, "This too is excellent!
and they immediately went together, saying to one another:
"If those merchants should invite us to eat, we should reply:
'We already have sufficient food and drink for our sustenance; however, if you would grant us robes, that is what we truly need.'"
Having arrived there, he asked,
"Merchant leader, have you not grown weary from traveling such a great distance?
He replied:
"Noble one! We have troubled you by asking this.
The group of six said:
"One who possesses such composure may briefly listen to the Dharma.
At that time, the merchant leader respectfully joined his palms and immediately listened to the Dharma.
Having heard the teaching, the merchants requested:
"Noble one!
Please eat here.
He replied:
"O Noble One! I am already fully provided for; do not trouble yourself with such hardship.
On another day, he went again to visit him and preached the Dharma for him. The merchant leader earnestly invited him to accept a meal, but he replied once more:
"I have no need for food.
Later, at another time, the merchants deliberated, saying:
"There is a shortage of grass here; we shall go to such-and-such a village to graze our cattle there."
They then took the oxen and horses and departed for that region.

On the following day, the group of six returned there, intending to preach the Dharma to those merchants; however, having arrived, they did not see the merchants and remained there filled with anxiety.
At that time, someone came and asked,
"Venerable sir,
why are you so sorrowful?"
Upānanda said, "There was a merchant here who was an acquaintance of mine; his goods were abundant, yet he departed without even bidding me farewell."
He replied, "Venerable sir!
He has not gone away entirely;
for lack of grass, he has gone temporarily to a certain village to graze his cattle in search of fodder and to sell his goods, and he will return before long."
Upānanda said, "May you be free from illness and long-lived.
Having spoken these words, he went to that village and, seeing the merchants from afar, spoke this verse:
"One should not travel on dangerous paths in remote regions; even if one must go, do not remain there.
Not only are such places unfit for travel, but one should not form intimate friendships with the people there."
The inhabitants of the perilous mountains first appear impressive, like gold freshly polished on stone;
those dwelling in the central lands are not so, remaining as immovable as mountain peaks from beginning to end.
When the merchants heard these words, they replied to the noble ones,
"For what reason do you harbor resentment and treat us with such bitter derision?
The group of six replied:
“O noble one! We have already briefly expressed our mutual sentiments with you, and I have set aside my own virtuous practices to frequently preach the Dharma for you.
Why did you not say your farewells and instead come here in private?”
He replied, "Noble One!
It is not that I have come from afar; it is simply because I am following the grass."
"When the day of our departure arrives, we shall return to the city of Śrāvastī and bid each other farewell.
Chandaka said, "O noble one!"
"You may also come for a moment to hear me preach the Dharma.
Then those people together paid their respects, each taking a low seat to sit and listen to the teaching.
Having finished preaching the Dharma, the merchant leader said:
"Noble one!
Please eat here.
He replied:
"No need. Then that caravan leader said to the people:
"Gentlemen, you have repeatedly invited us to accept food, yet each time we replied that there was no need; is it not because the Noble Ones lack clothing?"
"You all should each offer robes for alms according to what you possess.
The people replied,
"This is also excellent!"
Thereupon, each person offered one high-quality woolen shawl as a gift. Chandaka then recited a blessing:
"May the merit and benefit of this offering be boundless."
Having received the items, Udāyin said to him:
"O worthy one!
You have repeatedly invited me to accept food; bring it now—what offering is this?"
Then the merchant immediately took the cakes and fruits and arranged them before him; Udāyin then extended his large alms-bowl and said,
"O worthy one, place them within this."
The merchant thought to himself, "This bowl is exceptionally large;
if it were filled to the brim, it would suffice for six people to satisfy them with a single midday meal.
He immediately filled the bowl to the top and presented it to Udāyin.
Then the bhikṣu Aśvajit again extended his bowl, and the merchant filled it once more.
This continued until all six of them had extended their bowls, and the merchant, with some reluctance, gave to each of them.
All their provisions for the journey were completely exhausted, even the food and drink in their cooking pots were used to provide for them.
Then the merchants said to the bhikṣus,
"Noble ones!..."
"The provisions for our journey that we have prepared have all been exhausted," they said.
Then the merchants replied to the bhikṣus:

"We wish to send someone along with you to the city to seek further provisions for the road; you should oversee the purchase. On your return day, we hope you will provide us with escorts so that we do not encounter bandits on the way."
Nanda replied, "I shall look after it for you.
Then the merchant sent a man to follow him; once they had arrived at the monastery, Aśvajit said:
"O worthy one! You may perform such a task for me.
He did as he was told, and immediately thereafter [the other] spoke again:
"To perform this task.
Thus they passed the time from one stage to the next until evening approached, when he said,
"Man, you may return home."
Then that messenger departed from the city, but on his way through a perilous place, he was plundered by bandits.
Once he had entered the camp, the people there asked him,
"How was your journey and your provisions?"
He replied, "I have nearly lost my life; how could I possibly have provisions for the journey? He asked:
"Does not the Noble One assist you by providing human aid?
He replied, "By this logic,
it is he who has incited the bandits to plunder."
Question: "For what reason? Answer:

"He went to the monastery and ordered me to perform manual labor; he relied on me to oversee the market transactions but said nothing at all. It was not until evening that he sent me out of the city, and because I had to travel by night, I was subsequently robbed by bandits."
When the merchants heard these words, they all spoke in reproach:
"These sons of the Śākyas have lost their conduct as śramaṇas.
How can they entrust a deposit and then be deceived in return?"
This is the origin of the rule; at that time, the precept had not yet been established.
The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī at the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, there was a householder in this city who, shortly after marrying his wife, gave birth to a daughter who was blind in her right eye.

Later, as she gradually grew up, her female companions of the same age were all married off one after another; however, this girl alone had squinting eyes and lacked auspicious features, so although she was of marriageable age, no one would take her as a wife.
Within this city there was also a householder who took a wife from a family of equal standing; before long his wife died, and he married a second wife, who likewise passed away.
In this manner, it continued until he married a wife for the seventh time, and each one died.
At that time, people all called him "the husband-killer" (*bāngfù*), and it was because of this incident that his name was established.
At that time, the elder Bhārgava wished to take another wife, but no one would give her a daughter to him, saying:
"How could we possibly cause our daughter to die?"
"I cannot give you [my daughter].
He then sought a widow to take as his wife, but she replied, "How could I not cherish my own life? How could I enter your house?"
At that time, the elder was unable to find a wife for himself and personally managed the household with great labor.
Later, on another occasion, an old acquaintance came to his home; seeing him performing manual work, he asked, "What are you doing, sir?"
He replied,
"I am attending to my household affairs.
The other then said:
"What do you mean, benevolent sir, that you now personally attend to the affairs of your household?
He replied, "I have already taken seven wives, all of whom have passed away; there is no second person left by whom I may know the business of the family."
The friend replied,
"Why do you not seek something else?
He answered:
"Although we have sought you these past days, no one has granted us their consent, all saying:
'How could we not cherish our daughters?
We would rather give them in marriage to your family so that they might die early.'"
“If that is the case, why not seek out other widows?
The elder replied in detail regarding the matter:
“Although I sought out widows, they were unwilling to come.”
A friend said, "There is a daughter in such-and-such a family who is blind in her right eye; why not seek her?
He replied:
"He will not give it to you either.
His friend said, "Try going to ask him; perhaps he might grant it to you."
At that time, the elder went to that household; having arrived, he asked the head of the family, "Have you been well lately?
He asked in return:
"For what purpose have you come?
He replied,
"I wish to seek your daughter in marriage."
He asked, "Which girl? He replied:
"He has his right eye gouged out.
His father said,
"Marry him as you wish."
He asked, "On what day do you wish to take [her]?
The father said:
"On such-and-such a day, at an auspicious hour, the marriage rites may be performed.
Having received this permission, he departed with joy and returned home to await that favorable day.
At that time, having finished his exhortation, the friend thought to himself:
"It would be improper for me to cause my friend to seek out a one-eyed woman as a wife."
"She has an unwholesome appearance; do not let her come to our house, for she will hinder my acquaintances.
Having thought this, the friend went to the elder's place and asked, "Have you obtained the girl with the squint?"
He replied, "I have obtained it.
At that time, his friend spoke this verse:
"If one uses *pāruṣaka* twigs to clean one's teeth, or if a person sleeps with their head toward the west;
if one marries a woman who is blind in her right eye—even these can cause harm to Śakra, Lord of the Devas."
When two evils meet, there will surely be harm, Just like a blade and a stone cast together;
If both husband and wife are people who cause injury, Marriage will certainly lead to a matter of death.
Having spoken these words, he replied to the elder:
"The fact that the girl’s right eye is squinted is undoubtedly a hindrance; if you, sir, were to marry her, I fear you would meet with an untimely death, so you should abandon her."
"I have a younger sister who has been a widow for some time; if you are a suitable match, we shall become husband and wife.
The elder said, "I already have a verbal agreement with her and cannot simply abandon it; you should employ skillful means so as not to lose her affection."
The acquaintance replied,
"Very well.
Then the parents of the one-eyed man, wishing to reach an auspicious day, immediately prepared and arranged various kinds of feasts and offerings.

The group of six bhikṣus had previously been acquainted with that householder. At the time for the morning meal, the six bhikṣus put on their robes, took up their bowls, and entered the city to beg for food.
Upon arriving at the householder’s home, they saw him preparing exquisite cakes and delicacies; Nanda asked, "Sister!..."
"What festival is being celebrated?
His mother replied,
"Noble One!"
"My dear niece wishes to marry into another clan, and as the auspicious day approaches, we are making these preparations for her.
Nanda replied, "Sister!..."
"Have I been able to taste even a little today?
The mother said,
"Noble one!"
"This is your own property; why wait for it to be bestowed by another?
Nanda replied, "Giving gifts at other times is indeed the common practice, but today, please give me some of these delicacies."
At that time, the woman was by nature broad-minded and forgiving, so she gave all the cakes to the six men.
Having received them, they immediately offered this blessing:
"May you be free from illness and enjoy long life."
He went out from the house.
At that time, the elder came and saw that the cakes were gone, and asked:
"For what reason?"
The wife said, "Whenever a field of merit appears, I offer everything to them. You may now go and inform your husband's family; we shall wait for another occasion to prepare [the feast] separately."
The elder replied, "He will certainly not agree to postpone it until another day; let us first marry off our daughter and afterwards arrange the feast for our kinsmen.
His wife said:
"Since he has already obstructed my wife, who would give their daughter to him?
Let her wait for another day so that we may spend all the expenses at once.
Having accepted his wife's persuasion, the elder went to his husband's house and said:
“O worthy one! The preparations for our family’s ancestral rites have been undertaken by us; however, the six groups of field-of-merit recipients have all taken what was intended for them.
We are currently unable to complete the offerings; you may wait for a later time.”

The man replied, "An auspicious day has already been divined and cannot be changed; if I marry her on that original date, she shall become my wife, but if it is later than that, she will surely be rejected."
The elder returned home and told his wife of this;
the wife said, "He has many wives; who would finally give their daughter to him?
Let her stay until another day before we arrange the marriage."
The wife then gradually prepared the cakes and food, eventually exceeding the appointed time.
Upon hearing this, the husband’s family took the younger sister of a close friend—a widow living alone—as his wife.
When his wife had finished preparing the cakes and food, she sent the elder once more to invite him for the wedding, reporting to her husband's family:
"My cakes and food are all prepared; you may now perform the rites of hospitality."
The man replied, "Since the previously agreed time has passed, I have no need for the girl.
The elder became enraged and took him to the authorities; the judge ruled according to the principles of the law, and the elder was defeated.
Upon returning to inform his wife, she wept aloud:
