"My daughter has lived here for a long time and was finally about to be married, yet because of the Six Groups [of monks], the marriage was ruined.
Hearing this, her neighbors all felt resentment and contempt.
"The group of six bhikṣus has lost the dharma of a śramaṇa and corrupted the pure saṃgha, causing a woman who had been married to be abandoned by her husband.
When the bhikṣus heard this, they reported the matter to the Buddha.
The Buddha then assembled the community and questioned those six men; he rebuked them as before, up until: "In order to establish a training rule, it should be spoken thus:
'If a number of bhikṣus go to the home of a layperson, and there is a faithful brāhmaṇa or householder who earnestly invites them to receive cakes and parched grain.'"
A bhikṣu who requires it should accept two or three bowls; if he accepts more than that, it is a pāyattika offense.
Once he has received them and returned to his residence, if there are other bhikṣus present, they should share the food together; this is the proper occasion.
"Furthermore, 'if a bhikṣu' refers to the group of six [monks].
'More than two' is termed 'a multitude.
'Lay families' refers to the households of white-robed laypeople, Brahmins, and so forth."
"To go" means to arrive at that place.
"Pure faith" means to believe in the Triple Gem with a profound heart of devotion and respect.
"Diligent" means that the mind has reached its ultimate limit.
"Requests" refers to extending an invitation by speaking.
"Requests for flour-cakes" refers to the food being offered.
"Needs" refers to a personal desire or preference.
Regarding "two or three bowls," there are three types of bowls:
namely, superior, middling, and inferior.
The superior bowl is one that can receive two *śrona* measures of cooked rice from the kingdom of Magadha.
The "medium" [portion] refers to receiving one and a half *sheng* of cooked rice;
the "small" [portion] refers to receiving one *sheng* of cooked rice.
The instruction that "one should receive two or three bowls" indicates the limit of the amount.
"Returning to one's dwelling place" means arriving at the monastery.
"If there are bhikṣus with whom the food should be shared" means distributing it among fellow practitioners of the holy life (brahmacārin).
Regarding the offense of *pāyattika* for receiving more than the permitted amount, the explanation of the transgression is as previously stated.
What are the specific characteristics of the offense in this case?
If a bhikṣu receives food from another using three large alms bowls, he incurs an *dukkaṭa* (wrongdoing).
If one swallows and eats it, one incurs a *pāyattika*.
If one receives food from another using two large bowls and one medium bowl, one incurs the offense of *duṣkṛta*;
at the time of swallowing and eating it, one incurs a *pāyattika*.
If one receives food from another using two large bowls and one small bowl, one incurs a duṣkṛta offense;
at the time of swallowing and eating it, one incurs a pāyattika offense.
If one receives food from another using two medium bowls or one large bowl, the gravity of the offense is the same as previously stated.
In short, if a bhikṣu takes food from another and it exceeds the quantity of four and a half *śē* of cooked rice, he incurs a *pāyattika* offense.

If one takes one large bowl, one medium bowl, and one small bowl; or two large ones; or two medium ones and one small one; or two small ones and one large one; or two small ones and one medium one; or three of each size; or three small ones, and so forth—in all these cases, there is no offense.
Furthermore, if the donor permits one to take as much or as little as desired, there is no offense in taking it.
Moreover, there is no offense for the very first offender, or for one who is insane, mentally deranged, or overwhelmed by intense physical pain.
The Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya, Scroll Thirty-Five.
The Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya, Scroll Thirty-Six.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Yijing by Imperial Decree.
**The Training Rule on Eating to Satiety, Number Thirty-Four** At that time, the Blessed One was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park. He addressed the bhikṣus, saying:
“When I eat in a single sitting, I always remain free from excessive desire, free from illness, with light and agile movements, strong in physical vigor, and dwelling in peace and happiness.”

You all should also practice eating in a single sitting; by eating in a single sitting, you will likewise attain few desires and freedom from illness, and you shall dwell in ease, with light and agile movements, robust physical strength, and well-being.
"As the Buddha has taught, there are such merits in eating in a single sitting; thus, all the bhikṣus ate in a single sitting.
However, while they were eating, if they saw their ācāryas, upādhyāyas, or other senior elders arrive at that place, they would immediately leave their seats."
Having already left his seat, he considered himself to have had enough to eat and did not dare to eat more.
Because he ate so little, his complexion became sallow and his body grew emaciated.
When the World-Honored One saw this, he knew the reason and intentionally asked Ānanda:
"I eat in a single sitting until I attain a state of dwelling in comfort, and I instruct the bhikṣus to likewise eat in a single sitting so that they may dwell in comfort.
For what reason are the bhikṣus' complexions so sallow and their bodies so emaciated?"
Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
As the Buddha has said:”
"I dwell in comfort by eating in a single sitting; you all should also dwell in comfort by eating in a single sitting.

At that time, the bhikṣus followed the Buddha’s instruction and ate in a single sitting. While they were in the midst of eating, they saw two teachers and various elders approaching, and they immediately rose from their seats.
Having already left his seat, he considered himself to have finished eating and did not dare to eat further.
Because he ate so little, his complexion became sallow and his body grew emaciated.
The Buddha said to Ānanda:
“If a bhikṣu, while eating, eats to his heart’s content until he is no longer hungry, once he has finished receiving food, he should not rise again.

According to the Buddha’s instruction that one may eat to one’s satisfaction until no longer hungry, but once the meal is received should not rise again, the bhikṣus at that time—upon obtaining even a small amount of soup, vegetables, or cooked beans—considered themselves to have had enough and, having risen, did not dare to eat further.
Due to these causes and conditions, their bodies became emaciated.
Having seen this, the World-Honored One asked Ānanda:

"I have instructed the bhikṣus that when they wish to eat, from the time the salt is served until they are no longer hungry, they may eat as much as they desire to their satisfaction; however, once they have finished eating, they should not rise again."
"For what reason are the bodies of the bhikṣus so emaciated and unable to find satisfaction?
Then Ānanda immediately reported the preceding circumstances in detail to the World-Honored One, up until the point that their bodies were emaciated and unable to find satisfaction.
For this reason, the World-Honored One said to Ānanda:
"There are five kinds of *khādaniya* food, which has the sense of being chewed and bitten; if one eats these, it does not constitute having had enough to eat."
What are the five?
They are: first, the root; second, the stem; third, the leaf; fourth, the flower; and fifth, the fruit.
Eating these five does not constitute having finished one's meal.
There are five kinds of *pūsaṇī* food, which means food that is chewed and swallowed; when one has eaten these, it constitutes a full meal (*kṛtabhaktakṛtya*).
What are the five? First, rice; second, barley and bean porridge; third, parched grain flour; fourth, meat; fifth, cakes. When one chews and swallows these five, it is called having had a full meal.
If a bhikṣu has first eaten the five kinds of chewed foods, he may later eat the five kinds of masticated foods.
If he has first eaten the five kinds of masticated foods, he should not further eat the five kinds of chewed foods.
"If one eats further, one incurs an offense of transgressing the Dharma.

When the Blessed One stated that five kinds of chewed food do not constitute a full meal, whereas five kinds of masticated food do constitute a full meal, at that time the bhikṣus, having received food and eaten only a small amount before rising due to some circumstance, believed they had already reached satiety and did not dare to eat more; consequently, their bodies all became emaciated.
The World-Honored One, having seen this and knowing it, intentionally asked Ānanda:
"I have taught that five kinds of chewed food do not constitute a full meal, whereas five kinds of masticated food do constitute a full meal; in all cases, one should eat until satisfied."
"For what reason, Bhikṣu, is your body so emaciated?
Ānanda replied to the Buddha:

"As the Buddha has taught, the five kinds of chewed food (khādanīya) do not constitute 'sufficient food' (paryāpta-bhakta), whereas the five kinds of masticated food (bhojanīya) do. When the Bhikṣus receive food, they eat only a small amount; once they have risen from their seats due to some business, they consider it sufficient and dare not eat further."
"For this reason and these conditions, his body has become emaciated.
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"There are five causes and conditions by which one’s meal is considered sufficient, and there are another five causes and conditions by which it is not considered sufficient."
What are the five conditions that constitute having finished eating?

First, knowing it is food; second, knowing there is a person who bestows the food; third, knowing one has received and is eating it; fourth, knowing the prohibition against further food; and fifth, knowing one has abandoned the formal posture.
How does one know food?
It means knowing these five kinds of chewed food and five kinds of masticated food.
How does one know there is a person who bestows the food?
This refers to knowing whether the recipient is a woman, a man, or a *paṇḍaka*.
How does one know that food has been received before eating?
It means eating two kinds of fivefold foods after having received them from another.
How is it known that food is being refused?
It refers to refusing two sets of five kinds of food.
How is it known that one is relinquishing formal deportment?
That is to say, when one leaves this seat and rises, possessing these five conditions, it is called "having finished eating.
What are the five cases that do not constitute having finished eating?

They are: knowing it is not food; knowing there is no person to offer it; knowing one has received it but has not yet eaten it; knowing there is no prohibition against eating; and knowing one has not yet left the seat. These are called the five cases of not having finished eating.
Furthermore, there are five kinds of "completed meal" (*pūrvabhakta*). What are the five? First, pure food;

second, food mixed with a small amount of impure food; third, food not touched by what is unwholesome; fourth, food mixed with a small amount of what is touched by the unwholesome; fifth, having left one's original seat—these are called the five kinds of completed meal.
Furthermore, there are five kinds of food that do not constitute "having finished eating. What are these five? First, impure food;

second, food mixed with much that is impure; third, food touched by what is unwholesome; fourth, food mixed with much that is touched by what is unwholesome; and fifth, when one has not yet left one's original seat.
These are called the five kinds that do not constitute having eaten one's fill.
Furthermore, there are five kinds of having eaten one's fill. What are these five?
That is to say, when seeing someone distributing food, a bhikṣu replies,
"I do not need it," or says:
"Go! Or he might say: "Cease!"
Some said, "I have already finished eating. Others said:
"I have finished.
These five [expressions] are all definitive statements of non-acceptance without remainder; when these words are spoken, it is called "having eaten enough.
Furthermore, there are five kinds of cases where one has not yet eaten enough.
What are the five?
They are as follows: when one sees someone distributing food, a bhikṣu replies, "I do not yet need any."
Some said, "Go for now. Others said:
"Stop for now," he said; or,
"Wait until you have eaten."
Or one might say, "Wait until it is finished.
These five cases are all instances where the matter has not been definitively resolved; when such words are spoken, it is not termed "having finished eating" (*paryāpta-bhakta*).
As the Blessed One has said:
"A bhikṣu should not, having already eaten his fill, receive further food.

At that time, the group of six bhikṣus ate again and again, regardless of whether they were full or not. When the bhikṣus of few desires heard this, they felt disdain and reproach, saying these words:
“How is it that a bhikṣu, contrary to the Buddha’s instruction, accepts and eats more food than he requires?
He then reported this matter in detail to the World-Honored One.

On account of these causes and conditions, the World-Honored One assembled the community of bhikṣus. After questioning and ascertaining the facts, he extensively rebuked him in various ways as described above, and addressed the bhikṣus, saying: “For the sake of ten benefits, I shall establish a training rule (śikṣāpada). It should be recited as follows:”
"If a bhikṣu, having finished his meal, eats again, it is a pāyattika.
Thus the Blessed One established this training rule for the bhikṣus.
At that time, a householder invited the Buddha and the Saṃgha to his home for a meal. Many bhikṣus were afflicted by the suffering of illness.
Their attendants also went to the meal; having finished eating themselves, they returned carrying food for the sick.

At that time, the sick were unable to finish their food, and the attendants, having already eaten their fill, did not dare to eat more. Furthermore, as there were no śrāmaṇeras or lay attendants (karmadāna) with whom they could share the food, they simply set aside the leftovers to one side, where they formed a great heap.
At that time, various crows and birds vied with one another to come and feed upon [the remains], resulting in a clamorous noise.
When the World-Honored One heard this sound, he knew the cause and intentionally asked Ānanda:
"Why are these birds making such a noise?"
Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!
Today a householder has invited the Buddha and the Saṃgha to his home for a meal; however, there are many sick bhikṣus at this residence."

At that time, the attendant brought food for him, but the sick bhikṣu was unable to finish it all. Having already eaten his fill, the attendant did not dare eat more; furthermore, there were no śrāmaṇeras or lay attendants (karmadāna) with whom he could share it. He cast the remaining food outside the monastery, where it formed a great heap. Consequently, crows and birds vied with one another to devour it, causing a great clamor.
When the Blessed One heard these words, he thought to himself:

"Now, for the sake of ensuring the bhikṣus dwell in comfort and so that those donors may receive the merit of their offerings, I shall permit the practice of the *yavāpūrvaka* (remaining-food) rite before eating."
He addressed Ānanda:
"I now permit the bhikṣus to perform the *kṛta-śeṣa-kalpa* (the ritual for leftover food) and eat as they please.
As the Buddha had spoken, he permitted them to eat by performing the *kṛta-śeṣa-kalpa*.
At that time, the bhikṣus did not know how to perform the *khalupaścādbhakti* (the rite of leftover food).
They went to the Blessed One and reported this matter to him.
The Blessed One said:
"If there is a bhikṣu who has already finished his meal, and a donor further offers him five kinds of chewable foods and five kinds of masticable foods that are choice and remaining;

at that time, if those bhikṣus desire to eat, that bhikṣu should wash his hands clean, receive the food, and go before a bhikṣu who is currently eating and has not yet left his seat, standing in front of him and speaking these words:
'Venerable one, please take heed!'"
I, the bhikṣu [name], having already finished eating my fill, now receive these *khādanīya* foods, *bhojanīya* foods, and so forth, and my mind desires to eat further.
"Venerable one, please perform the *kṛtapiṇḍa* rite for me.
At that time, the bhikṣu should immediately perform the *kṛtapiṇḍa* rite for him; having eaten two or three mouthfuls, he should say:
"You may go; this is yours, you may eat it as you wish."
When that bhikṣu has completed the ritual procedure, he should take it to one side and eat as much as he desires until satisfied.
If a bhikṣu, having already eaten his fill, desires to eat more but eats without performing the remaining ritual procedure, he commits an offense of transgression against the Dharma (dharmātikrama).
There are five causes and conditions by which the *kṛtapiṇḍapāta-vidhi* (the formal procedure for declaring food as "leftover") is not accomplished.

What are these five? They are: being outside the boundary; being at a distance or in a screened place; being behind [the recipient]; being at the side; or if the person addressed has already left their original seat. In all these cases, the *kṛtapiṇḍapāta-vidhi* is not accomplished.
There are five conditions for performing the *kṛtapiṇḍapāta* (the ritual of making food "leftover").

What are these five? They are: being within the same boundary (*sīmā*); being in close proximity in an unobstructed place; not being behind [the recipient]; not being at the side; and the person facing one must also not have left their seat. When these are met, the *kṛtapiṇḍapāta* is accomplished.
Furthermore, there are five conditions under which the *kṛtapiṇḍapāta-vidhi* (the ritual for leftover food) is not established.

What are these five? They are: being outside the boundary (*sīmā*); being at a distant or obstructed location; not using a vessel to hold the food; not holding it up with the hands; or the person addressed having already left their original seat. These are not called performing the *kṛtapiṇḍapāta-vidhi*.
There are five conditions for performing the *kṛta-śeṣa-bhakṣaṇa-dharma* (the ritual for declaring food as leftover).

What are these five? They are: being within the same boundary (*sīmā*); being in close proximity without obstruction; holding it in a vessel, or holding it in the hand or with an object; and the person addressed has not yet left their original seat. This is called performing the ritual for declaring food as leftover.
If one person has performed the *kṛta-śeṣa* rite and many bhikṣus subsequently arrive to eat together with him, none of them commit an offense; do not harbor any doubt regarding this.

At that time, the World-Honored One praised the observance of the precepts and those who revere the precepts; for the sake of the bhikṣus, he taught the Dharma in accordance with the truth and addressed the bhikṣus, saying:
"The former was the original prohibition, while this is a subsequent allowance."
For the sake of the bhikṣus, I re-establish this training rule, which should be spoken thus:
"If a bhikṣu, having finished eating his fill, should eat again without performing the *kṛtapiṇḍapāta* rite, it is a *pāyattika* offense."
"Furthermore, 'if a bhikṣu' refers to the group of six; the remaining meanings are as explained above.
'Having finished eating' means that after having eaten one's fill, one has left one's original seat."
"Without performing the *kṛta-śeṣa-dharma* (the rite of making food remain)" means not performing the ritual procedure for two or five types of food in the presence of another person.
"Eating further" refers to swallowing.
In this context, what are the characteristics of the offense and its specific details?
If a bhikṣu has eaten his fill and perceives that he has eaten his fill, or if he is in doubt about it, he incurs a pāyattika offense.
If he has not eaten his fill but perceives that he has eaten his fill, or if he is in doubt about it, he incurs a duṣkṛta offense.
If one perceives food as insufficient when it is insufficient, or perceives food as insufficient when it is sufficient, there is no offense.
At that time, Upāli addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!”
"What kind of gruel is called 'sufficient food'?
The Buddha told Upāli:

"If the gruel is freshly cooked such that a spoon placed upright does not fall over, or if the traces of lines drawn with a finger or the like do not disappear, eating this gruel is called 'sufficient food.'"
“Venerable Sir! What kind of flour-based food (*saktu*) must one eat to be considered having finished eating?
The Buddha said:

"If, when first mixing with water and stirring, the spoon remains upright without falling over, or if the traces [of the spoon] do not disappear when hooked by the five fingers, eating this gruel is called 'having had enough food' (paryāpta-bhakta)."
Furthermore, Upāli!
Any thin gruel or thin flour paste is not considered sufficient food.
Moreover, there is no offense for the very first offender, or for one who is insane, mentally deranged, or overwhelmed by intense pain.

35. The Training Rule on Exhorting Another to Eat Until Satiated. The thirty-fifth training rule on exhorting another to eat until satiated. At that time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, there was an elder in this city who, despite having been married for a long time, had no son or daughter; all his relatives had also passed away.
As his household grew increasingly impoverished and he himself reached the decline of old age, he said to his wife:
"O virtuous lady!..."
"I am now old and can no longer manage a livelihood; I wish to abandon worldly affairs and go forth as a renunciant.
His wife replied, "If you have the necessary faith, you may go as you please."
The elder then departed for the Jetavana Grove; upon seeing a young bhikṣu there, he prostrated at his feet and said:
"Venerable Sir!
I wish to go forth into the religious life; I pray that out of compassion you will grant my request."
The bhikṣu replied, "I am young;
it is not fitting for me to perform the work of a householder on behalf of others.
The elder said:

"I have now come for the first time to the presence of the Venerable One; I pray that you will kindly guide and instruct others so that they may fulfill their original intention of undertaking the life of a renunciant.

At that time, the young bhikṣu had a preceptor who constantly cultivated meditative concentration while dwelling in the empty forests and wilds. He then led the elder to his teacher's location, and after prostrating at his feet, he said: "Upādhyāya!..."
This son of good family desires to go forth in this well-expounded Dharma and Vinaya; may the Preceptor, out of compassion, grant him the going forth and bestow upon him full ordination.
Then the preceptor replied to the disciple,
saying, "Venerable one!
I have no leisure."
As the Blessed One said:
"It would be better to be a butcher who constantly commits acts of killing than to allow others to go forth and receive full ordination and then fail to instruct them."
The disciple said:
"I pray that the Preceptor will grant me the going-forth and the full ordination; I shall provide instruction in recitation and perform the necessary tasks."

Upon hearing these words, the Master granted his permission; having then questioned him on the difficult points of the Dharma and ascertained his purity, he subsequently ordained him and conferred full ordination (*upasampadā*), saying:
"O noble youth!
"This is your ācārya!
You must approach him to receive all your studies; you must consult him regarding every movement and action.

At that time, the ācārya instructed him in recitation and various duties, but because the elderly disciple was already advanced in years, he could not retain them in memory and frequently committed transgressions.
The preceptor repeatedly commanded him to kneel for a long time and confess his transgressions. At that time, the elderly disciple thought to himself:
"This ācārya makes me kneel before him every day to recount my faults; by what means can I cause him to kneel before me and recount his own?"
At that time, there was an elder who invited the Buddha and the Sangha to his home for a meal.
Thereupon, the World-Honored One donned his robes, took up his bowl, and, accompanied by the great assembly, proceeded to the elder’s residence.
When the meal was finished and he had preached the sublime Dharma to that householder, he and the great assembly rose from their seats and departed.
At that time, the instructor went out accompanied by his elderly disciple to the home of an acquaintance. Upon arrival, the host addressed them, saying:
"Noble One!"
"You may eat.
The bhikṣu said,
"I have already finished eating."
The elder said, "If that is the case, the time has not yet passed; take it as you please and, having performed the *kṛtāvadāna* rite, eat it out of compassion.
The teacher asked the elder:
"Do you wish to obtain it?
He replied,
"I wish to obtain it."
He then took two portions and went to the edge of a pond outside the monastery; there, the instructor said to his elderly disciple,
"Will you filter the water,
or will you perform the ritual for leftover food?"
The senior disciple said, "I shall perform the *śeṣa-bhakta-vidhi* (the ritual for leftover food).

The teacher then took some water, and he immediately went to the monastery to visit a bhikṣu who had not yet finished his meal; there, he performed the *śeṣa-bhakta-vidhi* on his own portion, but not on the teacher's portion.
Having taken water, the teacher entered the monastery and asked,
"Venerable one,
have you performed the ritual for leftover food?"
He replied,
"It has been prepared," and immediately took the food.
Once the teacher had finished eating, the elder addressed him, saying:
"I pray that you will grant me leave; I wish to interrogate him regarding his offense.
The teacher replied:
"As you wish," the elder said.
"The Master now has an offense and should repent according to the Dharma."
The teacher said,
"I do not see any offense.
He replied:
"I have eaten without performing the *kṛtapiṇḍapāta* rite.
He replied,
"Venerable one!"
Did I not ask you: "Have you performed the ritual for leftover food?
and did you not say: [yes]?
“I have already finished.
With what intention did you say “I have not finished” only after having eaten? He replied:
"I have already performed my portion; it is not the portion of the ācārya.
The teacher said, "Venerable one!"
"I am truly without fault; according to this principle, you must be at fault.
He then reported this matter to the bhikṣus. Having heard it, the bhikṣus all felt disdain and spoke thus:
"How can a bhikṣu, knowing that another has not performed the *śeṣa-kāraṇa* (the ritual for leftover food), intentionally cause him to eat it?"
At that time, the bhikṣus reported this matter in detail to the Blessed One.
The Blessed One, on account of this, assembled the community of bhikṣus. The sequence of questions and answers is as explained at length above, up to:
"How is it, bhikṣus, that you eat what has been prepared by another without having performed the *kṛta-śeṣa* (remaining-food) rite?"

After the Blessed One had rebuked him in various ways, he addressed the bhikṣus, and so forth, until: "For the sake of ten benefits, I establish this training rule, which should be recited as follows:
'If a bhikṣu, knowing that another bhikṣu has finished eating and has not performed the *kṛtāvadhi* (the rite of leaving food remaining), should urge him to eat more, saying:
"Venerable one!..."
"You should eat this food.
If, by such means, one intends to cause another to commit an offense and thereby produce distress and affliction, it is a *pāyattika*.
"If again a bhikṣu" refers to an elderly bhikṣu; the remaining meanings are as explained above.
"Knowing" means either knowing by oneself or being informed by another.
"Another bhikṣu" refers to one who is a member of this Dharma.
"Having finished eating" means having already eaten to satiety.
"Without performing the *kṛtapiṇḍapāta* (the ritual for leftover food)" means not taking food from another person in their presence.
"To urge" means to send [them] to eat more.
With this as the condition, one intends to cause another to commit an offense; the determination of the offense and the explanation of its meaning are both extensive as previously described.
In this regard, what are the characteristics of the offense and how does it occur?

If a bhikṣu knows that another has finished eating, and without performing the *kṛta-śeṣa* rite (the ritual for leftover food), he encourages that person to eat or chew these solid foods, it is a *pāyattika*.
Furthermore, regarding those who are not at fault, the detailed explanation is as previously stated.
The Thirty-sixth Training Rule on Eating in a Separate Group: The Buddha was staying at Rājagṛha, in the Bamboo Grove, by the Kalandaka Pond.
At that time, Devadatta and a large number of bhikṣus were eating separately from the community in a location near the monastery.
The bhikṣus of few desires felt resentment and shame, saying:
"How can a bhikṣu eat separately from the community in a location so close to the monastery?"
He reported this matter in detail to the Blessed One.
The Blessed One assembled the community of bhikṣus and, as explained at length above, engaged in a dialogue regarding the circumstances.
[The Buddha said: "How is it, bhikṣus, that you eat apart from the assembly?"
After the Blessed One had rebuked him in various ways, for the sake of ten benefits, he established a training rule for the bhikṣus, which should be recited as follows:
"If a bhikṣu eats in a separate group, it is a pāyattika."

Thus, after the Blessed One had established the training rule for the bhikṣus, there were many bhikṣus who were afflicted by the suffering of illness. A physician came to the monastery, and the bhikṣus asked him:
"O worthy one!"
"This bhikṣu is afflicted by illness; please prescribe a remedy.
He replied, "Noble one!"
"You should take such-and-such medicine, along with a small amount of food.
The sick bhikṣu asked,
"Who will provide these?"
The physician said,
"I am able to give it.
The bhikṣu said:
"Is the entire Saṃgha able to give?
He replied, "It is not the entire Saṃgha; you should give to the one who is ill."
He replied,
"The World-Honored One has established a precept that does not permit eating in a separate group.
The physician said:
“Your Great Master is always possessed of compassion; for this reason, he will surely grant permission.
Then the bhikṣus reported this matter in detail to the Blessed One. The Blessed One said:
“Except in cases of illness.”
Furthermore, when the bhikṣus, for the sake of stūpa affairs or communal business, became utterly exhausted and lay down wherever they were, neglecting the cultivation of wholesome qualities,
a faithful householder entered the monastery, saw them, and asked: "Noble ones!..."
"The Buddha's teaching emphasizes diligent effort; for what reason do you sleep during the day instead of cultivating wholesome deeds?
The bhikṣu replied, "O noble one!"
"My body is hungry and exhausted.
The elder replied,
"Why do you not eat a little?"
He replied,
"O worthy one! Who would give it to me?"
He replied, "I shall give it.
The bhikṣu said:
"Can the entire Saṃgha grant it?
He replied, "It is not the case that all the Saṃgha can; you should give it when you are in need."
He replied,
"The World-Honored One has established a precept that does not permit eating in a separate group.
The householder responded:
“Your Great Teacher is always possessed of compassion; for this reason, he will surely grant permission.
Then the bhikṣus reported the matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
“Except in cases of a specific cause or condition.”
Furthermore, while some bhikṣus were traveling together with a caravan of merchants, they arrived at a village to beg for alms. When the time came, they said to the people: "O worthy ones!
Please wait a moment; we wish to enter the village to beg for a little food and drink."
The merchant said, "O Noble One!
This place is a perilous road with many thieves and robbers; you may follow me, and I shall provide you with food."
The bhikṣu asked,
"Can the entire Saṃgha grant it?
He replied:
"I cannot; perhaps I may give two, three, or four according to my ability.
The bhikṣu said, "The World-Honored One has established a precept that does not permit [eating] apart from the assembly."
At that time, all the bhikṣus abstained from food; the full account is as previously related, until the Buddha said:
"Except when traveling on a journey.
Furthermore, some bhikṣus traveled by boat and, while wandering through the human world, arrived at a certain village. Then the bhikṣus addressed the boatmen, saying:
“I wish to stay for a short while and enter the village to beg for food and drink.
The boatman replied, “The river here is treacherous and there are many bandits; you should go together with me, and I will give you food.”
The bhikṣu replied,
"Is it for one person,
or for the community?"
He replied, "I cannot give much; perhaps three, four, or five [measures].
The bhikṣu said:
“The Blessed One has established a precept that does not permit eating in a separate group.
At that time, all the bhikṣus fasted for an entire day.
They reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"Except when traveling by boat.
As the Blessed One had said that every five or six years a Śikha-mahāpariṣad (Topknot Great Assembly) should be held, at that time immeasurable bhikṣus gathered together.
There were lay devotees of pure faith who separately invited the bhikṣus, saying:
"Noble ones!
Come and eat."
The bhikṣu replied:
"Is it for one, or for all?"
The householder replied, “I am not equal to the assembly;
I can only provide offerings according to my means, perhaps twenty or thirty [measures].
He answered:
“O noble ones! The World-Honored One has established the precepts and does not permit separate meals.
Then the bhikṣus reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"Except during the time of a great almsgiving assembly.

At that time, King Bimbisāra had not yet attained the vision of the Truths; he had given the Bamboo Grove Park to the naked ascetics (nirgranthas). However, once he had given rise to pure faith and attained the vision of the Truths, he subsequently discontinued his offerings to the heretics and instead offered them to the Buddha and the Saṅgha for their use.
At that time, King Bimbisāra’s maternal uncle had gone forth among the non-Buddhist ascetics. The king addressed the Saṅgha, saying: “This is my uncle;

I pray that he be permitted to remain for a while. As long as no transgression has arisen, let him stay as he pleases; but if a transgression occurs, he shall be sent away. I myself will provide him with food.”

At that time, as the bhikṣus remained awake and engaged in contemplation during the first and last watches of the night, the non-Buddhists saw them and conceived a heart of reverence and faith, saying to the bhikṣus:
"We shall provide food for the bhikṣus."
The bhikṣu said:
"Excellent!
Is it for one?"
"For the sake of the multitude? He replied, "I cannot provide much;
my food and drink come from the King's quarters, whether ten or twenty portions, which is sufficient to sustain me."
The bhikṣu replied,
"The World-Honored One does not permit eating in a separate group.
The bhikṣu informed the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"Except when receiving food as an offering from a śramaṇa.
At that time, the Blessed One praised those with few desires and those who respect the precepts; having taught the Dharma to them, he addressed the bhikṣus:
"The former was the original prohibition; this is a subsequent allowance."
I shall now establish this training rule, which should be recited as follows:
"If a bhikṣu eats separately from the community, except at the appropriate times, it is a pāyattika offense."

The exceptions are: when one is ill, when working, when traveling on a road, when traveling by boat, when a great multitude is eating, and when a gift of food is being offered to śramaṇas; these are the appropriate times.
"Furthermore, 'if a bhikṣu' refers to Devadatta; the remaining meanings are as explained above.
'Eating in a separate group' means eating individually.
'Except at other times' means excluding specific occasions."
"Being ill" means being unable to sit at ease during the single mealtime.

"Being occupied with work" refers either to stūpa-related matters or communal affairs, ranging down to sweeping a patch of ground as large as a mat, or occasionally scrubbing and plastering an area the size of a cow's resting place.
Regarding the time for traveling by land: it refers to traveling half a *yojana* or one *yojana* to and fro.
Regarding the time for traveling by boat: it refers to embarking on another vessel or traveling half a *yojana* or one *yojana*.
"Great assembly" refers to a gathering of many people.
"Śramaṇa" refers to various types of non-Buddhist practitioners outside the Buddha-dharma who are also called śramaṇas, because they toil their bodies in pursuit of the Way.
This is a concession granted according to circumstances; the offense incurred is the same as previously stated.
In this context, what are the characteristics of the transgression and how does it occur?
If a bhikṣu, within the same boundary, perceives it as being within the same boundary—or harbors doubt—and partakes of a meal apart from the community, he incurs a *pāyattika* offense.
If one is outside the boundary but perceives it as being inside, or is in doubt about it, one incurs an *dukkaṭa* offense.
If one is outside the boundary and perceives it as being outside, or if one is inside the boundary but perceives it as being outside, there is no offense.
Generally, there are two kinds of residences:
first, the primary residence; second, the extramural residence.
When the bhikṣus at the primary residence are about to eat, they should ask the bhikṣus from the extramural residence whether they will come to eat together.
If one eats without having asked, one incurs an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*).
When a bhikṣu outside the monastery is eating, he should ask the bhikṣus residing in that place whether they will come to eat together with him.
If one eats together with four people without having asked whether they have been informed, one incurs a *pāyattika* offense.
If three people eat and one does not eat, or if three are fully ordained (*upasampanna*) and one is not yet fully ordained, there is no offense in any case.
If one sends food to them—even a single spoonful of salt or a handful of grass leaves—to be shared among that community, there is no offense.
Or, at times, a donor may say:
"I shall give food to everyone who enters."
Alternatively, if a donor constructs a separate room and offers it, saying,
"I shall provide food for all who reside within my room," there is likewise no fault.
Furthermore, there is no offense for the very first offender; the rest is as explained above. 37.
The Training Rule on Eating at Improper Times. The thirty-seventh training rule on eating at improper times: The Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, Mahāmaudgalyāyana ordained seventeen followers and granted them full ordination.
With the young Upāli as their leader, they were all youthful and vigorous; at the time for the morning meal, they donned their robes, took up their alms bowls, and entered the city to beg for food.

The conduct of women is primarily driven by craving and attachment. At that time, there were many young women who, seeing the group of seventeen young bhikṣus begging for alms with their bowls, all struck their breasts with their hands and spoke these words:

"These bhikṣus have grown from childhood to adulthood under the laborious care and nurturing of their mothers, yet they never repaid their debt of gratitude; instead, they abandoned them to go forth into homelessness—what benefit or fruit is there in this?"
"Why did you not, before it was born, fill its mouth with earth and cast it into a pit or ditch?
When the group of seventeen heard these words, they were all filled with shame and said to one another,
"We would rather starve ourselves to death and endure hunger than go from house to house again and hear such malicious talk about others."

Each returned to their respective monasteries and remained there abstaining from food; they cultivated various wholesome qualities as long as the strength of their previous meal lasted, but once that strength was exhausted, they all lay prostrate.
At that time, Upānanda saw them and asked, "You seventeen novices, the food you eat belongs to others; is your belly also another's?
Why do you lie down after eating your fill instead of cultivating wholesome qualities?"
He said, "Venerable sir,
who has eaten their fill?"
He replied, "It was you all.
Then the group of seventeen informed him of what had occurred; having heard this, Upānanda departed in silence.
At that time, there were various laypeople enjoying themselves with games and banquets in a grove; the sun had already passed its zenith.
Then the group of seventeen monks also arrived within the grove and, before the crowd, rubbed their own bellies and spoke these verses:
“The Buddha has spoken words of exquisite beauty, Which pervade the entire world;”
"Among all forms of suffering, none exceeds hunger; this statement is most true.
Having seen this, the people asked, "Noble One!..."
"Do you wish to obtain food? He replied, "I do."

People brought them excellent food and drink, and they all ate their fill; having finished eating and being fully satiated, they each returned to their respective places and recited their lessons aloud, two by two.
At that time, Upānanda heard the sound of their recitation and came to their location, asking:
"You group of seventeen, why have you now begun to exert yourselves with such vigor, reciting so loudly as to be twice as exceptional as usual?"
The group of seventeen replied,
"Have you not heard the Blessed One say:
'One whose mind is joyful is able to expound the meaning of the Dharma'?"
Upānanda said, "Did you obtain good food today?
He replied:
"You have obtained a meal that satisfies you within that garden.
Upānanda said, "I asked you just now whether you were both hungry and famished; why do you say now that you are satisfied?"
"How can it be that you all eat at improper times?
They replied, "We do not eat before midday, nor do we eat after midday; how could we endure hunger and let our lives come to an end?"
When the bhikṣus of few desires heard this, they felt revulsion and shame, and spoke among themselves:
"How can a bhikṣu eat at an improper time?
They reported these circumstances in detail to the World-Honored One.
The Blessed One immediately assembled the community of bhikṣus and, after the exchange of questions and answers regarding the origin of the matter as explained above, said:
"How is it, bhikṣus, that one eats at an improper time?"
The Blessed One, having rebuked them in various ways, addressed the bhikṣus:
"For the sake of ten benefits, I establish this training rule, which should be recited as follows:
'If a bhikṣu eats at an improper time, it is a pāyattika.'"
"Furthermore, regarding the phrase 'if a bhikṣu': this refers to the group of seventeen [monks]; the remaining meanings are as explained above.
As for the term 'improper time' (*akāla*), there are two kinds:
first, that which has passed the midday limit; second, that which precedes the appearance of the dawn light (*aruṇodaya*). The determination of the offense is the same as previously stated."
Regarding this, what are the characteristics of the offense and how does it occur?
If a bhikṣu eats at an improper time while perceiving it as such, or while in doubt, he commits a pāyattika offense.
If he eats at a proper time while perceiving it as improper, or while in doubt, he incurs a duṣkṛta offense.
If one perceives it as the proper time when it is the proper time, or perceives it as the improper time when it is the improper time, there is no offense.
Furthermore, there is no offense for the very first offender; the rest is as explained above.

38. The Training Rule on Eating Food Touched by Others. The thirty-eighth training rule concerning eating food touched by others. The Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.

At that time, it was the constant custom of the Venerable Kāla that whenever he resided in a village or town, he would dress in his robes and take up his alms bowl at the time of the morning meal, enter the village or town to beg for food in sequence, with dignified and careful deportment, guarding his sense faculties and dwelling securely in mindfulness.
When obtaining food, if it is moist rice, one should receive it with the alms bowl; if it is dry rice, place it inside the bowl-cloth.
Once the food has been obtained, all moist rice should be eaten on that very day, while the dry rice should be dried in the sun and stored in a jar.
If they encounter wind, cold, or rainy weather, they immediately moisten it with warm water and use it as their food.
Once they have eaten their fill, they experience the subtle bliss of meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), liberation (*vimokṣa*), samādhi, and meditative attainment (*samāpatti*).

It is the constant law of all Buddhas, abiding in the world, that from time to time they go to the various realms of hell-beings, animals, hungry ghosts, humans, and devas, as well as to mountain forests, river valleys, charnel grounds, or the dwellings of bhikṣus, in order to observe them; in this particular instance, the purpose was to observe the dwelling place.
At that time, the Blessed One went to the dwelling of the Venerable Kāla and, seeing dried rice being sun-dried, said to Ānanda:
"Whose dried rice is this being sun-dried here?"
Then Ānanda related in detail, as before, the matter of Kāla’s alms-gathering, up until the point where he experienced sublime bliss.
The Buddha said to Ānanda,
“Is there any bhikṣu who eats food that has been previously touched?”
Ānanda said to the Buddha, “There were.

The World-Honored One assembled the community and reprimanded them in various ways for their lack of tranquility and for their reproachable conduct; he praised the practice of contentment and addressed the bhikṣus, saying:
"I now establish this training rule for the bhikṣus; it should be recited as follows:
'If a bhikṣu eats food that has been previously touched, it is a pāyattika.'"
"Furthermore, 'if a bhikṣu' refers to the bhikṣu Kāla; the remaining meanings are as explained above.
'Having already touched' refers to two kinds of touching:
first, receiving [food] before midday and consuming it after noon; second, receiving [food] after noon and consuming it after the watch of the night."
If a bhikṣu knows that food has been previously touched by another and swallows it again without performing the proper ritual, the offense is established as before.
What are the characteristics of the transgression in this case? How does the matter unfold?
If a bhikṣu eats food that has been previously touched, whether perceiving it as such or suspecting it to be so, he commits a pāyattika offense.
If the food has not been previously touched, yet he perceives it as such or suspects it to be so, he incurs a duṣkṛta offense.
If it was not actually touched but one perceives it as not touched, or if it was touched but one perceives it as not touched, there is no offense.
The Buddha said:

"If any bhikṣus use for drinking or eating bowls that they have previously handled and have not yet thoroughly cleansed—whether small bowls, spoons, bronze cups, or salt containers—they all incur a pāyattika offense."

If one touches a bowl-bag, a wiping cloth, a mendicant’s staff, a door-key, or a lock, and having thus touched or grasped such objects, fails to wash the hands clean before grasping other food or drink, even down to fruit, at the time of swallowing it, one incurs a *pāyattika* offense in every case.
If a bhikṣu wishes to drink water but has not thoroughly cleansed his mouth, he incurs a duṣkṛta offense at the moment of swallowing.
If he rinses and washes with soap-nuts, earth, or other such pure substances, there is no offense.
Furthermore, there is no offense for the very first offender; the rest is as explained above. 39.
The Training Rule on Not Accepting Food. The third and ninth training rule regarding not accepting food: The Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.

At that time, the Venerable Mahākāla Bhikṣu always used at all times an almsbowl from a *śmaśāna*—the term formerly translated as "Śītavana" is an error, referring here to a place where corpses are discarded—as well as robes from a *śmaśāna*, food from a *śmaśāna*, and bedding and seating from a *śmaśāna*.
What is a *śmaśānapātra*?
If someone has died and been abandoned in a wilderness field, and the relatives at that time use a clay bowl as a sacrificial vessel, Mahākāla takes it to serve as his almsbowl.
What is meant by "clothes of the dead"?
When kinsmen present garments to the deceased and discard them in the wilderness, Mahākāla takes them, washes, dyes, and sews them to make his own clothes.
What is the food of the dead?
When these kinsmen offer five morsels of food as a sacrifice to the deceased spirits, Mahākāla takes them and uses them for sustenance.
What is the bedding of the dead?
This Mahākāla always sleeps and lies down in the place of corpses;
this is what is called the "corpse-forest bowl-food and bedding.
When many people die, Mahākāla’s body becomes plump and robust, and he no longer goes to the city frequently to beg for food.
When there were no deaths, Mahākāla’s body became emaciated, and he frequently went through the city, wandering from door to door begging for food.
At that time, the gatekeepers took note of this and thought:
“If many people die, the bhikṣu Mahākāla’s body becomes plump and robust; if few people die, his body becomes thin and weak. Could it not be that the venerable Mahākāla eats the flesh of the dead?”
At that time, there was a brahmin in this city who, not long after marrying a wife, gave birth to a daughter. When the girl had grown up, her father passed away.
Then his kinsmen prepared the funeral rites with full solemnity and escorted him to the charnel ground; having cremated him, they returned home, while his wife and daughter wept at one side.
At that time, Mahākāla was watching over the burning corpse;
when the girl saw him, she said to her mother, "This venerable Mahākāla is like a blind crow, sitting there guarding the corpse."
At that time, someone who had heard this came to inform the bhikṣus, and the bhikṣus reported it to the Buddha. The Buddha said:

"That brahmin woman, for her own harm, spoke coarse and evil words to disparage my śrāvaka disciple whose virtue is like Mount Sumeru; by reason of this evil karma, she shall remain a blind crow for five hundred lifetimes."
At that time, people from near and far all heard the World-Honored One’s prediction that the Brahmin girl would always be a blind crow for five hundred lifetimes.
Upon hearing this, her mother spoke these words:
"The Buddha has predicted that my daughter will always be a blind crow within five hundred lifetimes; how extreme is this suffering!"
The mother then took her daughter to the World-Honored One; having prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, she addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

I pray that out of your compassion you will forgive this young girl. Because she lacked understanding, she uttered these words without any intent to cause harm; I pray that you will graciously pardon her.”
The World-Honored One said:
"Did I cast an evil spell so that she would suffer this?
It is because this woman spoke harsh words with a frivolous mind that she has fallen among the animals; had her mind been heavy with evil, she would have fallen into hell."
Having heard this, the woman rose from her seat and departed.
At that time, the people of the city saw the gatekeeper and said,
"The venerable Mahākāla eats the flesh of the dead."
Hearing the wicked words uttered by the young girl, the people immediately said to one another:
"We ought to go to the charnel ground to see whether the venerable Mahākātyāyana’s eating of corpses is true or false."
They further deliberated together, saying:
"How can we know whether this is true or false?
Let one person act the part of a dead man, and let us all carry him together to the charnel ground."
He then dispatched one man to serve as the corpse;
the man replied, "Do you intend to have him eat my flesh? The others replied:
"You need not worry; I shall protect you.

Thereupon, he immediately assumed the appearance of a dead man, smeared his entire body with yellow ginger oil, lay down upon a bed, and placed five lumps of sacrificial food beside him. Together they carried him out of the city toward the charnel ground.
At that time, Mahākāla entered the city to beg for alms; seeing a corpse being carried out, he thought to himself:
"I shall now turn back and eat these five morsels; why should I trouble myself to wander from door to door in search of alms?"
At that time, the man feigning death saw the bhikṣu turn back and said to the people, "The Great Brother has come; he surely intends to eat me!
The people replied:
"We shall protect you together; you need not worry.
They then carried him to the charnel ground and set him down upon the earth, each entering the thickets to wait for the bhikṣu.
There was a jackal who intended to go toward the place of the corpse to eat those five morsels; at that time, Mahākāla thought to himself:
"If this jackal should devour these sacrificial offerings, it will cause me to suffer from hunger for an entire day."
He immediately hurried away, driving off the jackal.
At that moment, the person feigning death saw the bhikṣu approaching and let out a great cry: "Eat me!"
"Eat me!
At that time, those people each took up clubs and staffs and came to where he was, saying to the bhikṣu:
"Noble One!..."
"You have donned the robes of a great seer and left the household life to become a renunciant,
yet now you commit such a grave evil deed. The bhikṣu replied, "What have I done?"
The people said,
"You eat human flesh.
He replied:
"Do you all see me holding a knife, cutting off my flesh,
and eating it? They replied, "We do not."
The people asked, "If that is so,
for what reason did you run so quickly toward the side of the dead? Kāla replied:
"I saw a jackal coming to feast upon the sacrificial offerings; had it eaten them, I would have suffered from hunger. I intended only to drive it away quickly and harbored no ill intent.
The people replied, "We leave it to you to say whatever you wish and to eat whatever you please; however, let your voice resound throughout the city, saying:"
"You are an eater of humans!
Having spoken these words, they went away together and informed the bhikṣus.
When the bhikṣus heard these words, they reported them in full to the World-Honored One. Upon hearing this, the World-Honored One reflected thus:
"Whenever bhikṣus incur this fault because they do not accept food, I now command all bhikṣus: you must accept and eat it so that others may take cognizance of it."
“As the Buddha has taught, one should receive [the food] before eating it.
The bhikṣus did not know how this receiving was accomplished,
so the Buddha said:
"There are five kinds of receiving:
first, receiving with one's own body;
second, receiving with an object."
3. Receiving an object with the body;
4. Receiving an object with an object;
5. Receiving by placing it on the ground.
What is receiving with the body by means of the body?
It refers to receiving with the hand what has been handed over by another hand.
What is receiving an object with the body?
This means that another gives with the hand, and one receives with the bowl.
What is meant by "giving with the body and receiving"?
This means that another gives with the bowl, and one receives with the hand.
What is receiving an object from an object?
It means that another person gives with a bowl and one receives it with a bowl.
What is receiving by placing on the ground?

"O bhikṣus, you should know that there is a borderland country where people are exceedingly malicious and contemptuous; even toward their parents, brothers, and sisters, they harbor much hatred and dislike, refusing to have them near."

When a bhikṣu arrives in this country, he should construct a small maṇḍala altar at the place where he begs for alms in the streets and lanes; having placed his bowl there, he should stand to one side with his mind focused upon the bowl.
When someone offers food and places it within the bowl, this is called "receiving.
Furthermore, there are five ways of receiving:
either on a bed, or on a seat, or on a stool, or on one's robes, or in the bowl.
A bhikṣu should apply his attention, cupping one side of the vessel with upturned palms to allow it to be suspended; all such acts are termed "receiving.
There are five ways in which the receiving of food is not validly accomplished.
What are the five? They are: being outside the boundary;
being at a distance where one is obstructed from view; being at the side; being behind; or joining the palms [at improper times]. These are the five ways in which receiving food is not valid.
"There are five ways of accepting [offerings]; one should understand them as the reverse of the above.
At that time, there were brahmins and householders of pure faith who offered various excellent fruits to the bhikṣus, but the bhikṣus did not accept them.
The people replied, "If the Buddha had not appeared in the world, we would have all taken non-Buddhist practitioners as our field of merit.

Now that he has appeared in the world, we take you, O Benevolent One, as our field of merit. If you do not accept what we offer, how could we abandon the provisions for goodness as we set out for the next life? We pray that you will compassionately accept it for us."
Then the bhikṣus reported this matter to the Buddha. The Buddha said:
“You should accept it for them; having performed the purification (pariśuddhi), you should eat it.
The bhikṣus did not know how to perform the purification.
The Buddha said:
"There are five kinds of purification.
What are the five?
These are: purification by fire, purification by knife, purification by fingernail, purification by withering, and purification by pecking by birds; these are called the five.
Furthermore, there are five kinds of preparation for purity:
purification by uprooting, purification by breaking by hand, purification by cutting off, purification by splitting, and purification by removing the seed.
What is purification by fire?
It refers to contact with fire.
What is purification by the blade?
This refers to damaging [the object] with a blade.
What is purification by means of the nails?
This refers to injuring it with fingernails.
What is "withered and dried up" (*pūti*) purification?
It refers to seeds that have withered and dried out on their own, becoming unfit for planting.
What is "pecked by birds" (*vighāta*) purification?
This refers to damage caused by a bird’s beak;
the subsequent five cases are easy to understand.

As the Buddha had taught that food should be eaten only after it has been purified (*kappiya*), the bhikṣus proceeded to purify each item individually, and consequently failed to eat anything after midday. The Buddha said:
"All fruits and such should be gathered into a single heap and damaged by touching them with fire or a knife at three or four places; this is called 'purification.

As the Blessed One said that one should eat the fruit after it has been received, the bhikṣus each received their portions individually, and the day consequently passed the midday hour. The Buddha said:
"One may take as much as needed for eating collectively; one should not receive them individually."
Furthermore, when members of the Saṃgha who maintain purity were distributing fruit, they could not do so with equality. The Buddha said:
"You should have a śrāmaṇera distribute it.
When this, too, was not done with equality, the Buddha said:
"The great bhikṣus should accept [the robes] and distribute them themselves.
Still, they were unable to divide them equally. The Buddha said:
"They should be divided into three grades—namely, superior, middling, and inferior—and they should be distributed by observing their quality and distributing them equitably."

Regarding the fruits of their practice, one should only distribute the portions due to a person after they have completed their practice; otherwise, they may receive something inferior, or perhaps nothing at all. The Buddha said:
"One should first set aside the portion."
He then brought out the better ones; when the bhikṣus saw them, they felt aversion.
The Buddha said, "Those two masters should receive their share.
Still, upon obtaining the better ones, he gave rise to a sense of regret. The Buddha said:
"As for the order of seating, one should receive [the offerings] there.
At that time, the bhikṣu sitting nearby rose to receive them. The Buddha said:
"One should not rise to receive; one should receive them wherever they reach one's hand."
When he placed it in the bowl, the fruit rolled away; the bhikṣu received it again. The Buddha said:
"One should not receive it again. One should take and eat it as far as one's hand can reach; if it is beyond the reach of the hand, one must receive it again."
When the bhikṣu was walking with his alms bowl, the vessel was so heavy that he could not lift it alone. A layperson saw him and said, "Venerable Sir!
Let me assist you in carrying it."
The bhikṣus did not permit it. The Buddha said:
"You should go together.
When the bhikṣu and the layperson each held one end, with the layperson holding the front and the bhikṣu following behind, the Buddha said:
"It should not be done thus.
A bhikṣu should first receive it; having grasped one end, he should then have a layperson grasp it, and afterwards they should walk together.
When the layperson let go first and the bhikṣu remained behind, the Buddha said:
"It should not be done thus; the bhikṣus should release [the food] first, and the layperson should follow behind.
When the bhikṣus were walking, other bhikṣus received and ate it again. The Buddha said:
"If one receives it from a bhikṣu, it constitutes a prior acceptance (pūrvaparigraha)."
"If one receives [an offering] from a layperson, it constitutes a new acceptance.

At that time, there was a faithful donor who came with a jar filled with ghee, honey, oil, and sugar to offer to the present assembly of monks. The bhikṣus were unwilling to accept it, but the Buddha said, "You should accept it;
the bhikṣus should distribute it."
While walking, his robes became soiled. The Buddha said, "You should use grass as a substitute.
When he placed them on the ground, the jars rolled over. The Buddha said:
"Place the supporting items below.
Having distributed the ghee and honey, he returned the jars to their original owners, who said:
"Noble One!"
"Is it that you give the jar of ghee and honey, but do not give [the vessel]?
"This too shall be used according to what you require.
The bhikṣu did not know whether this would constitute a pure (kalpa) acquisition.
The Buddha said:

"You should take it and place it in deep water to soak for seven or eight days, waiting until all the fish and turtles have consumed the oily fat; then it should be used by the Sangha in the clean kitchen."
Regarding what the Buddha has taught—that one should accept food before eating—the group of six bhikṣus would take and eat it regardless of whether they had accepted it or not.
When the bhikṣus of few desires saw this, they felt revulsion and shame, saying:
"How can these bhikṣus willfully contravene the holy teaching by eating without having accepted the food?"

He reported these circumstances in detail to the Blessed One. The Blessed One assembled the bhikṣus and questioned them regarding the truth of the matter; the full account is as previously related, up until: "For the sake of the bhikṣus and for ten benefits, I establish this training rule (śikṣāpada), which should be recited as follows:
'If a bhikṣu, without having received food, places it in his mouth and swallows it, it is a pāyattika.'"
Thus, after the Blessed One had established this training rule,
there was a bhikṣu dwelling in the forest who, finding no one to provide him with water or tooth-sticks, abandoned his secluded retreat and went into the village.
The Blessed One, having perceived this with his own knowledge,
asked intentionally: "Ānanda,
from which forest hermitage did those bhikṣus come to enter the village?"
Then Ānanda said to the Buddha:

“In accordance with the rules established by the Buddha, one must not place anything that has not been formally offered into the mouth to swallow. For this reason, these forest-dwelling bhikṣus—since no one offers them water or tooth-sticks—have all come into the village seeking someone to give them these things.”
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"Except for water and tooth-sticks.
At that time, there were some bhikṣus traveling through the countryside who passed through a perilous road where no one offered them food.
At that time, there was a bodhisattva who, for the sake of taming sentient beings, manifested as a wise horse, a monkey, and a bear, and gave fruit and food to the bhikṣus.
The bhikṣus did not accept it, and upon returning, they informed the Buddha.
The Buddha said, “If sentient beings know whether food has been offered or not yet offered, all may receive the food; do not harbor any doubt.”
For this reason, he addressed the bhikṣus, saying:
"The former was the original prohibition; this is a subsequent allowance. It should be stated thus:
'If a bhikṣu, without having received food, places it in his mouth and swallows it—except for water and tooth-sticks—he commits a pāyattika offense.'"
"Furthermore, 'if a bhikṣu' refers to Mahākāla; the remaining meanings are as explained above.
'Not having received' means not having obtained it from another."
"Eating" refers to the two sets of five [types of food] and so forth.
"Chewing and swallowing" refers to the act of ingesting.
"Excluding water and tooth-sticks" means that, with the exception of these items, all else must be formally received; the offense for failing to do so is the same as previously stated.
Regarding the characteristics of offenses herein, what are the specific matters?

If a bhikṣu, regarding food not received, forms the perception that it was not received, or harbors doubt, etc., there are two grave offenses and two light offenses; for the latter two cases, there is no offense.
As well as the matters concerning non-offenses, as explained in detail above.
At that time, all the bhikṣus were filled with doubt and requested the World-Honored One, saying:
"Venerable Sir!..."

What karma did the Venerable Mahākāla perform such that he always delighted in dwelling in charnel grounds, left the household life under the Buddha, severed all afflictions to become an Arhat, yet was slandered, saying, "You eat human flesh"?
The World-Honored One replied:
"This Mahākāla has performed his own karma, whether good or evil.

When the conditions converge and the fruit ripens, it is experienced by him within his own aggregates, elements, and sense bases; it does not ripen within external elements such as earth, water, fire, or wind."
He then spoke in verse:
"Though a hundred eons may pass, The karma one has created does not perish;
When causes and conditions meet, One must experience the retribution oneself."
"Listen well!

In a past age, there was a Pratyekabuddha named Kāśyapa living outside the city of Vārāṇasī at the dwelling place of an ancient seer. He was constantly followed by a retinue of immeasurable hundreds of thousands of millions of devas."
Whenever he entered the city to beg for alms, he would always stay near the charnel ground.
Beyond this place where corpses were discarded lived a yakṣa who resided there, feeding on the flesh of the dead.
If a Pratyekabuddha, who was held in high esteem, passed by the forest, this yakṣa spirit would immediately flee due to the majestic power of the devas;
at that time, the corpses would then be devoured by jackals, wildcats, and dogs.
The yakṣa thought to himself:
"This renunciant constantly troubles me; I should now perform an inauspicious act so that he will not return."
He then took a human hand and threw it into the alms bowl so that the people could see it; at that time, the people of this city all spread an evil rumor:
"This renunciant eats human flesh whenever he eats."
Having understood this, the Pratyekabuddha thought to himself:
"I must not allow this ignorant yakṣa to undergo such bitter retribution.

Out of compassion, he immediately leaped into the air before him and manifested great supernormal powers; smoke and flames issued from his upper body, while pure water flowed from his lower body, performing inconceivable feats to inspire right faith in him.

When the various classes of ordinary beings saw the supernormal power, they were quickly moved to repentance; they threw themselves upon the ground like great trees being toppled, prostrating from afar at the holy feet and seeking mercy through confession, speaking thus:
"May the Great Field of Merit quickly release us from below; we, ignorant and sunk in the mire of evil deeds, pray that you will descend with compassion and extend a helping hand to rescue us."
Then that holy man immediately lowered his body; the yakṣa then took a dead human hand from the bowl and cast it outside. He addressed the people of the city, saying:
"It was not an ordained one who truly ate human flesh; it was my own evil mind that caused this slander. I prostrate at his feet to offer my apologies."

I have committed evil deeds that have troubled the supreme field of merit; may I not suffer the retribution of great suffering in the future. Through the merit of this profound heart of reverence and repentance, may I encounter a Great Teacher even more supreme than this one in future lives, and by serving and making offerings to him, may I attain the fruits of sainthood.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus: "Do not harbor doubts!
The yakṣa of that time was none other than Mahākāla.
Because he slandered the pratyekabuddha with an evil mind and brought forth a foul reputation, he later gave rise to regret and sought to offer a repentant apology."

Due to his evil karma, he was constantly slandered with ill repute throughout five hundred lifetimes; however, because he gave rise to a mind of remorse and made a solemn vow, he encountered me, went forth into homelessness, severed all afflictions, and realized the fruit of Arhatship.
I surpass hundreds of thousands of millions of Arhats; having encountered them, I have honored and made offerings to them with a mind free from weariness or abandonment.

You bhikṣus! If you perform purely black karma, you will obtain a purely black maturation; if you perform mixed black-and-white karma, you will obtain a mixed maturation; if you perform purely white karma, you will obtain a purely white maturation. Therefore, you should abandon the other two types of karma and cultivate only the purely white; this is how you should practice.
The subsequent summary verse says:
He constantly dwelt in the charnel ground, as well as acting as a gatekeeper;
people feigned death, and together they observed whether his powers were real or false.
There are five ways of receiving food; for bhikṣus, it is permitted to take it oneself.
On dangerous paths, keeping domestic animals is allowed; the case of Kāla is the last.
*Vinaya-vibhaṅga of the Mūlasarvāstivāda*, Scroll 36.
The Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya, Scroll Thirty-Seven.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Yijing by Imperial Command.

40. The Training Rule on Soliciting Delicate Food. The forty-first training rule: At that time, the Blessed One was traveling through the human realm in the residence of the Śākyas and arrived at the Nyagrodha Grove in the city of Kapilavastu.
At that time, Mahānāma the Śākya, hearing that the Buddha, the World-Honored One, had now arrived at this Veṇuvana Grove, immediately went to visit him.
Having arrived there, he prostrated at the Buddha’s feet and sat to one side; the Buddha preached the Dharma for him, instructing, benefiting, and gladdening him, after which he remained silent.
Then the Śākyan Mahānāma rose from his seat, bared his right shoulder, joined his palms in reverence, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!
Out of your compassion, I pray that the Buddha and the Saṃgha will accept my humble offering at my home tomorrow."
At that time, the World-Honored One accepted by remaining silent.
Seeing that the Buddha had accepted his invitation through his silence, the Great Māhānāman, son of the Śākyas, paid homage to the Buddha and departed.
Having arrived at his home, he addressed his family members, saying:
"The Buddha and the assembly of monks have newly arrived here; their journey was arduous. You should prepare excellent food so that they may relieve their fatigue.
Having received these instructions, the family members immediately prepared various kinds of superior and exquisite food and drink that very night.
At that time, after rising early in the morning, the six bhikṣus gathered together in one place. The Elder Nanda said to them, "Venerable friends!
Should we go to the homes of our relatives and acquaintances to see how they are faring?"
The people replied, “It should be done in this manner.
At that time, the group of six monks went together to a layperson’s house; when their friends saw them, they said:
"Noble one!
Please eat here.
The group of six replied:
"We have already accepted an invitation for a meal from the great and renowned son of the Śākyas.
The people said, "If that is so,
you shall come to eat tomorrow."
He replied, "So be it.
Then the Śākyan Mahānāma sent a messenger to announce:
"The food and drink are prepared; may the Noble One know that it is time.
Thereupon, the World-Honored One, together with the great assembly, proceeded to the house of Mahānāman and sat upon the seats that had been prepared for them.

When the Great Name (Mahānāman) saw that the Buddha and the Saṃgha were seated, he immediately served them various kinds of excellent food and drink. When the assembly had finished eating, the Buddha preached the Dharma for him; thereafter, the Buddha and the great assembly rose from their seats and departed.

At that time, the Śākya son Mahānāma followed behind the Buddha; having exited the house, he circumambulated the Buddha three times and then re-entered the house, whereupon he ascended to a high tower and practiced the meditation on giving.

At that time, after the family members had gathered up the seats, mats, and the remaining food, the group of six monks, having finished soliciting food from thirty households, said to one another: "The time for the meal is approaching;
we should go to the house where the invitation was made."
Having arrived at the residence of the Śākya Mahānāma, he saw that there was neither a seat nor food or drink.

Chandaka reported, "I invited the Buddha and the Saṅgha to receive offerings at this house, yet I see no seats laid out and no food or drink; do you wish to cause the Buddha and the assembly to fast for an entire day?"
The family members replied, "Venerable sir, were you perhaps napping during the day and unaware that others had departed? The Buddha and the assembly of monks have finished their meal and all left.
Chandaka said:
"Judging by your demeanor, you will not give me food," the family member replied,
"O Noble One!"
"I shall wait here for a moment to inform my master.
He then entered and announced,
"The group of six bhikṣus has now come to request food."
The Great Name said, "Let whatever remains be given to him for him to eat.
He then ordered him to sit down and served him food and drink; seeing that he was destitute, they spoke to one another:

“The son of the Śākyas, Mahānāma, has opened his mouth wide and invited the Buddha and the Saṅgha to receive offerings at his home; that such a trivial person should succeed in inviting the Buddha and the Saṅgha—well, I, Udāyin, could also invite the Buddha and the Saṅgha every day. But what would this poor man have to chew and eat?”
He addressed his family members, saying: "Ho, men!
Go to such-and-such a house and fetch fine milk; from another house, fetch curd; from another, fetch clarified butter; and from another, fetch fish, meat, dried meat, and so forth."
The family members immediately brought it for them; once they were fully satiated, they returned to the monastery.
The bhikṣus asked, "Venerable sirs, where did you receive your meal this morning?"
He replied,
"I dwell together with you,
O virtuous ones. The bhikṣus said:
"I have not seen you," [the other] replied,
"I arrived later."
He asked, "What food and drink do you consume?
He replied:
"Milk, curd, ghee, and meat— these things are abundant there.
The bhikṣus said,
"We do not have such food at that house."
Aśvaka said, "How could that poor man possibly have such food? I obtained it from the house of a relative and friend of his and ate my fill.
The bhikṣus said:
"Virtuous ones, how could it be appropriate for you to seek such excellent food and drink from the homes of laypeople?
The group of six replied, "Whether it was appropriate or not, we have already finished eating; would you rather have us spend the night with empty stomachs?"
When the bhikṣus of few desires heard these words, they were filled with mutual reproach and shame, saying:
"How can a bhikṣu solicit such fine food and drink from the homes of laypeople?"
They reported the matter to the Buddha.
On account of this, the Buddha assembled the community of bhikṣus and asked the group of six: "O bhikṣus!..."
Regarding the exquisite and superior delicacies I have mentioned—
namely, milk, curd, fresh butter, fish, meat, and dried meat— did you go to the houses of the laity to beg for such fine foods?
He replied, “It is indeed so,
Venerable Sir!”

At that time, the World-Honored One rebuked them in various ways, as extensively explained before, and addressed the bhikṣus, saying: "For the sake of ten benefits, I establish this training rule, which should be recited as follows:
Regarding the excellent and exquisite foods spoken of by the World-Honored One—milk, curd, fresh butter, fish, and meat—"
"If a bhikṣu, for his own sake, goes to another's house to beg for food, it is a pāyattika.
Thus the Blessed One established this training rule for the bhikṣus.
At that time, there was a bhikṣu afflicted by illness who asked a physician,
saying, "O worthy one!
Please prescribe a remedy for me, hoping to cure this disease."
The physician replied,
"Venerable one,
you should drink milk."
He replied, "O worthy one!
Who will give me milk?"
He replied: "Noble One!
I shall go to the house of a disciple and beg for it to drink."
He replied, "O worthy one!
