The World-Honored One has established a precept that does not permit begging from others."
The physician said,
"The Buddha should grant permission based on the causes and conditions of this illness.
The bhikṣu reported the matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
“There is no offense for one who begs for fine, delicious food on account of being ill.
At that time, the World-Honored One praised the observance of the precepts and those who respect the precepts; having taught the Dharma, he addressed the bhikṣus, saying:
“The former was the initial prohibition; this is the subsequent allowance.”
The precepts were again established and should be recited as follows:
"As the Blessed One has spoken of superior and exquisite foods:
milk, curd, fresh butter, fish, and meat."
"If a bhikṣu, being without illness, goes to another's house for his own sake to beg for food, it is a pāyattika.
As for "as spoken by the Blessed One," this refers to the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha.
"Exquisite food and drink" refers to milk, curd, and so forth.
"One who is not ill" refers to one who is free from the suffering of illness.
"For oneself" means desiring to obtain it for one's own sake, not for others.
"Other families" refers to those of the four castes and so forth.
"Begging for" means to solicit.
"Eating" means to swallow.
The determination of the offense is the same as before.
What are the characteristics of the transgression in this case?

If a bhikṣu who is not ill requests delicious food and eats it while not being ill, there is an *dukkaṭa* (wrongdoing) at the time of requesting, and the offense of a *pāyattika* (offense requiring expiation) upon eating.
If a bhikṣu begs for food when he is not ill but eats it while ill, there is an *dukkaṭa* (wrong-doing) at the time of begging, but no offense at the time of eating.
If a bhikṣu begs for food while he is ill but eats it when he is not ill, there is no offense at the time of begging, but he incurs a *pāyattika* (falling offense) at the time of eating.
There is no offense if one begs for food while ill or if one eats food while ill.

If a bhikṣu enters a village to beg for alms and arrives before a certain door, and a woman, having seen him, comes out holding rice, the bhikṣu, if he requires something else, shall not accept that rice but remain silent.
The woman asked,
"Noble one! What do you require?"
When these words are spoken, it expresses that [the gift] is according to one's own wishes; if a bhikṣu requires it, he may seek it accordingly, and there is no offense.
Furthermore, if a donor sees a bhikṣu and says:
"Noble One!..."
"Whatever you may require, you should ask for it as you wish.
Whatever a bhikṣu seeks in accordance with this, there is no offense.
Furthermore, there is no offense in the case of the very first offender, or one who is insane, mentally deranged, or afflicted by intense pain.
The fifth summary verse says:
Water containing insects, the two kinds of food, and the house; not wearing robes, going to view an army, seeing soldiers on patrol for two nights;
striking, threatening, and concealing a grave offense.

41. The Training Rule on Using Water with Living Beings. This forty-first training rule concerning the use of water containing living beings was established when the Buddha was staying at the Ghoṣitārāma in Kauśāmbī.
At that time, the bhikṣu Chanda used water containing living organisms. When the other bhikṣus saw this, they said to him:
"Venerable Chanda!
For what reason do you intentionally use water containing living organisms?"
Chanda replied,
"Who assigned me this water containing insects?
Why not go instead to the other jars, pots, rivers, streams, ponds, and even the waters of the four great oceans?"
"What fault is it of mine that I am born and die of my own accord?
When the bhikṣus of few desires heard these words, they felt mutual disdain and shame, and spoke thus:
"How can a bhikṣu knowingly consume water that contains living beings?"
At that time, the bhikṣus reported this matter in detail to the Blessed One.
On account of this cause and condition, the Blessed One assembled the community of bhikṣus and questioned them as to whether it was true;
the full account is as related above.
After the Blessed One had rebuked them in various ways, he addressed the bhikṣus, saying: "For the sake of ten benefits, I establish this training rule, which should be recited as follows:
'If a bhikṣu, knowing that water contains living organisms, should use it, it is a pāyattika.'"
"Furthermore, 'if a bhikṣu' refers to Chanda; the remaining meanings are as explained above.
'Knowing' means either knowing by oneself or being informed by another.
'Water with insects'—there are two kinds of insects:"
First, it is seen immediately upon inspection; second, it is seen only after straining with a filter.
"Water" refers to all types of water.
There are two ways of using water:
First, internal enjoyment; second, external enjoyment.
What is internal enjoyment?
This refers to all that is used by the internal body, such as bathing, drinking, eating, chewing tooth-sticks, or washing the hands and feet.
What is external use?
This refers to all external requisites for use, such as washing robes and bowls, laundering and dyeing robes, sprinkling the ground, or smearing it with cow dung and so forth.
*Pāyattika*: the explanation of the term is as above.
Regarding the characteristics of the offense herein, what are its specific instances?
If a *bhikṣu* uses water containing living beings while perceiving it as such, or while harboring doubt, he incurs a *pāyattika*.

If one perceives water as containing insects when it is actually free of them, or if one suspects it contains insects, one incurs an *āpatti* of wrongdoing (*dukkaṭa*); in the other two cases, there is no offense.

If a bhikṣu knowingly consumes flour, honey, oil, vinegar, water-gruel, sour milk, curd, cakes, fruits, or similar items that contain insects, he incurs an *āpatti* of falling [into a transgression] (*pāyattika*).
Furthermore, there is no offense for one who is the very first offender, or for one who is insane, mentally deranged, or overwhelmed by intense physical pain.
The Forty-second Training Rule: On Sitting Forcefully in a House Where Food Is Being Served. The Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.

At that time, the Venerable Udāyin, who was skilled in worldly arts and sciences and possessed the power of foreknowledge regarding the affairs of others, dressed in the morning, took his bowl, and entered the city to beg for alms.
At that time, there was a young perfume merchant in this city who had recently married.
Upon arriving at his shop, as soon as he opened it, a wicked thought arose in him: he wished to return home to enjoy sexual union with his wife, so he closed the shop.
At that time, Udāyin saw this and thought to himself:
"While all the other shops have only now opened their doors, for what reason has this young man closed his?";
he then observed him with the supernormal power of reading others' minds and knew that he wished to return home to enjoy amorous play with his wife.
"I should now abandon that lustful desire.
He then went to the youth's house, sat down upon a seat, and said to the woman:
"Come here and sit; I shall preach the Dharma for you."
The wife then paid her respects and listened as he taught the meaning of the Dharma.
While he was preaching the Dharma, the young man arrived and said to his wife,
"You should take some food and give it to the noble Udāyin so that he may return to the monastery."
Then Udāyin replied to the youth: "O worthy one!
I have abandoned my virtuous practices to come to your home; I have increased your faith and preached the Dharma for you. Since you do not wish to listen, what do you intend to do?"
He then forcibly summoned him to sit and made him listen to the Dharma; after he had listened for a long time, his lustful thoughts ceased. Knowing this, Udāyin rose from his seat and departed.
At that time, the young man felt extreme contempt and spoke these words:
"How can a bhikṣu, knowing that a layperson has lustful intentions, intentionally disturb him to cause him to lose heart and deprive him of mastery over his own wife?"
"In that case, what trace of the Dharma of a śramaṇa remains?
Upon hearing these words, the bhikṣus of few desires were filled with revulsion and shame, saying:
"How can a bhikṣu, knowing that it is a family’s mealtime, insist on staying there?"
He then reported this matter in detail to the Blessed One.
On account of these causes and conditions, the Blessed One assembled the community of bhikṣus and questioned Udāyin extensively, as described above.
After the Blessed One had rebuked them in various ways, he addressed the bhikṣus, and so forth: "For the sake of ten benefits, I establish this training rule, which should be recited as follows:
'If a bhikṣu, knowing that a family is engaged in a meal, should sit down forcefully, it is a pāyattika.'"
"Furthermore, 'if a bhikṣu' refers to Udāyin; the remaining meanings are as above.
'The meaning of "knowing" is as above.
Regarding 'having food': men take women as their food and women take men as their food; because they mutually desire one another, it is called 'food.'"
"Household" refers to the four castes and so forth.
"Forcefully" means acting according to one's own will despite the disapproval of others.
"Sitting" means sitting with the body relaxed; the offense is established as described above.
In this regard, what are the characteristics of the offense and how does it occur?
If a bhikṣu, knowing that a man and a woman have lustful intentions, sits down forcibly within their home, he incurs a pāyattika.
If one knows that the mind is free from desire, there is no offense.
Furthermore, there is no offense for the very first offender, as described above.
**The Forty-third Training Rule: Regarding Insisting on Standing in a House Where Food Is Being Consumed.** The Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.

At that time, the Venerable Udāyin went for alms in the early morning and saw a young man selling incense who had just married; having opened and closed his incense shop, the youth returned home with a mind stained by lustful thoughts.
Having seen this, Udāyin went to her house and spoke at length as before.
Once Udāyin had entered the house, he hid his body behind the door panel. There was a maidservant in the household who saw the bhikṣu and remained silent.
Then that young man returned home from the market; seizing his wife by the arm, he led her to a secluded place, intending to commit an illicit act.
His maidservant reported this, saying: "O Master!"
Behind this door-panel is the Venerable Udāyin!
Having heard this, the youth stood there with a changed expression and said to his maidservant,
“The Noble One Udāyin!”
"While I was practicing various meditative concentrations in my own room and experiencing the bliss of *samādhi*, for what reason have you come here?
Looking behind the door-panel, he saw Udāyin; his lustful desire immediately subsided, and he spoke these words:

"How is it that a bhikṣu has lost the dharma of a śramaṇa, coming to a secluded place in a layperson's house to stand there so forcefully, causing another layman to lose his self-mastery over his own wife?"
When the bhikṣus of few desires heard these words, they all felt resentment and contempt, and reported the matter in detail to the World-Honored One.
The World-Honored One immediately assembled the bhikṣus; the questions and answers were as before.
After the Blessed One had rebuked them in various ways, he addressed the bhikṣus, and so forth: "For the sake of ten benefits, I establish this training rule, which should be recited as follows:
'If a bhikṣu, knowing that there is a household where food is being served, should stand insistently in a secluded place, it is a pāyattika.'"
"Furthermore, 'if a bhikṣu' refers to Udāyin; the remaining meanings are as explained above.

To explain the characteristics of this precept, the detailed exposition is the same as before, with the sole difference being that he stands in a secluded place. All else may be understood as previously stated, up to the phrase 'being tormented by painful afflictions.'"

44. The Training Rule on Giving Food to Naked Ascetics, Male and Female. The forty-fourth training rule: The Buddha was staying at the Bamboo Grove, the Squirrels’ Feeding Place, near the Kakrandaka Pond in Rājagṛha.
At that time, there were several merchants within this city who came to where the Buddha was, prostrated at his feet, and sat to one side.
Then the World-Honored One taught the subtle and wondrous Dharma to the merchants, instructing, encouraging, benefiting, and gladdening them, before remaining silent.
At that time, having heard the Dharma, the merchants were filled with deep joy in their hearts; they prostrated to the Buddha and departed.
They then went to the Venerable Ānanda, and after prostrating, they sat down.
The Venerable One expounded the essentials of the Dharma and then remained silent.
When the merchants had heard the Dharma, they rose from their seats and said:
"Venerable Sir!..."
"Where will the Blessed One go once this summer retreat has concluded?
Ānanda replied,
"People may go and ask the Blessed One themselves."
The merchants replied, “The Great Master, the World-Honored One, possesses such majestic and solemn authority; how would we dare to pose questions to him at our own initiative?
Then Ānanda said to the merchants:
“I too have seen the Buddha’s majestic virtue and profound dignity; how could I presume to address him with a question on my own initiative?

The merchant said, “Venerable Ānanda, if you do not inquire, how will we know that the Great Teacher, the Tathāgata, has completed his three-month summer retreat and intends to travel to a certain place?”
Ānanda said, "By observing his physical appearance and his speech, one can know that the World-Honored One intends to go to a certain place.
The merchant asked:
"By observing what signs and what speech can one know that the Tathāgata intends to go to a certain place?
Ānanda replied,
"If he sits facing that direction while chewing his tooth-stick, this is the sign."
"If one praises the people and things of that region, this is mere talk.
The merchant asked again:
"In recent times, toward which direction has the Blessed One turned to chew his tooth-stick?"
"Furthermore, in what place was that person praised?
Ānanda replied, "Recently,
when the Blessed One was chewing his tooth-stick near Kośala, he praised all the people of Śrāvastī."
When the merchants heard these words, they knew that the Buddha, the World-Honored One, would soon be heading toward Śrāvastī; they prostrated at his feet and departed.
Thereupon, the merchants immediately began to gather all the goods and merchandise required for entering Śrāvastī.
At that time, when the three-month summer retreat had concluded, the World-Honored One addressed Ānanda, saying:
"You should inform the bhikṣus:
'The World-Honored One now intends to travel among the people of Kośala. If there are any who wish to follow the Tathāgata on this journey, they should prepare their robes.'"
Then Ānanda, having received the Buddha’s instruction, informed the bhikṣus, recounting everything as previously stated, up until the preparation of their robes.
When the merchants heard Ānanda inform the assembly of bhikṣus:
“The World-Honored One intends to go to the city of Śrāvastī in the kingdom of Kośala,” they [prepared accordingly].
Then those merchants went to where the Buddha was, prostrated at his feet, and sat down to one side.
At that time, the World-Honored One taught the sublime Dharma to the merchants, instructing, exhorting, inspiring, and gladdening them, after which he remained silent.
The merchants all rose, bowed their heads to the ground, joined their palms, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

We have heard that the Tathāgata intends to travel to Śrāvastī. Whatever four requisites are required for the journey along the road, we shall provide them all for the Buddha and the Saṃgha. We only pray that, out of compassion, you will graciously accept our offerings.”
At that time, the World-Honored One accepted by remaining silent.
When the merchants saw that the Buddha had accepted, they paid homage to him and departed. They then went to the Venerable Ānanda, and after paying their respects, they said to him:
"Virtuous One!..."
"How far can the World-Honored One travel in one day?
Ānanda replied,
"Just like a Wheel-Turning King."
He asked again:
"How much does the Dharma of a Wheel-Turning King travel each day?
He replied:
"Every two *yojanas*.

At that time, the merchants established necessary provisions at intervals of every two *yojanas* along the route; during the first part of each day, they provided for the Buddha and the Saṃgha, and once the meal was finished, the merchants would proceed further. In this manner, they made arrangements all the way to Śrāvastī.

At that time, the World-Honored One, leading the great assembly, traveled along the road; being himself serene, he was surrounded by those who were serene; being an Arhat, he was surrounded by Arhats—and so on, as described at length previously—as he proceeded toward Śrāvastī.
At that time, there was also a naked ascetic among the traveling merchants who accompanied them. As the ascetic was constantly oppressed by hunger and thirst along the way, he thought to himself:
"How can I now employ some skillful means to escape this suffering of hunger?"
He then thought to himself:
"If I join the disciples of Śākyamuni as their companion, I may escape hunger and thirst; though I must travel a long distance, I shall not grow weary.
He immediately went to where the bhikṣus were and said to them:
"Noble One!

Your Great Master is by nature fond of what is beautiful and fine; he constantly uses a golden plow for his cultivation, permits disciples such as yourselves to partake of food of a hundred flavors and wear garments worth a thousand pieces of gold, and provides superior dwellings with a value of one hundred million."
"By this, you honorable ones shall dwell in peace and happiness in the present life; after the end of your lives, you will certainly be reborn in heaven and attain liberation.

My Great Teacher is by nature fond of harshness and austerity; he does not even plow with a ploughshare made of hemp dregs. He causes his disciples to pluck out their hair, go naked, beg for alms among the people, and sleep upon the bare ground."
"Because of this, we have constantly suffered in our bodies throughout the present life, and after the end of our lives, we were born in the hells, long submerged in the ocean of suffering.
When the bhikṣus heard these words, they thought to themselves:
"This non-Buddhist possesses a heart of faith and reverence."
He said to him:
“O outsider!
Do you now take pleasure in what belongs to the bhikṣus; would you be able to eat the remains of the food from their alms bowls?”
Having heard this, the non-Buddhist practitioners thought to themselves,
"If we do not eat the leavings of these bhikṣus, we will surely die of hunger and starvation.
They then said to the bhikṣus:
"Noble One! I am able to eat it.
The bhikṣu replied:
"When the community of monks is eating, you may stay wherever you wish within sight; the bhikṣus shall offer you the remains from their alms bowls.
He replied, "Excellent!"
He then took a large copper bowl and stood by as instructed.
When the bhikṣus had finished eating, each of them gave their leftovers to the naked ascetic; the vessel was filled to the brim with cakes, fruits, and other such items.
When that non-Buddhist practitioner had filled his bowl and was carrying it out, the merchant leader saw him at the entrance of the gate and asked in surprise,
"Who has bestowed these cakes and fruits upon you?"
He replied to the caravan leader, "Regarding those whom you hold in high esteem as fields of merit, I have acted as a field of merit for them; they have presented me with cakes and fruit."

Having heard this, the merchant leader said to the non-Buddhist practitioners, "The bhikṣus have conceived a heart of compassion for you and brought these to give as gifts; yet you now speak of them as being their field of merit—this is not a virtuous thing."
"If the World-Honored One hears these words, he will surely take this matter as the occasion to establish a training rule for the bhikṣus.
Having heard this, the non-Buddhists felt ashamed and said to the merchants, "That was merely a joke; do not take it to heart."
He then took his leave and departed.
At that time, there was another caravan arriving from Śrāvastī, and within that caravan was a naked ascetic (nirgrantha).
Having seen him, he asked:
"Virtuous one, do you have provisions for the journey on your path?
He replied:
"It exists.
He asked, "From what is it obtained?"
He replied,
"A shaven-headed householder has provided for me. At that,
those non-Buddhist practitioners became angry and said:
"You are ungrateful; having received his bounty and been spared from hunger and exhaustion, you have uttered coarse words, calling me 'shaven-headed householder.

Yet, I have seen that there are five hundred śramaṇa bhikṣus among the Śākyas who have attained arhatship and entered parinirvāṇa. Among us followers of external paths, have you ever seen even a single one who has attained nirvāṇa?"
Having spoken these words, he uttered this verse:
"Why does your body not sink into the earth?
Why does your tongue not split into a hundred pieces?"
Why did the various deities, upon witnessing this matter, not strike your body with a thunderbolt?
The jackal, though constantly eating the leftovers of the lion, always harbors the intent to harm the lion;
you, who have been sustained by the food provided by the Noble Ones of Ten Powers, now revile them and fail to recognize their kindness.
He has certainly realized all-knowledge; his mind is equal toward friend and foe.
Even you, O outsiders and loathsome persons, still rely upon him and receive his aid and sustenance.
If a person does not recognize kindness and righteousness, know that such a type is inferior even to a dog;
for a dog understands how to repay the favors bestowed upon it by humans, whereas you are like a venomous snake, constantly spitting out poison.
When that naked ascetic had finished reciting the verse, he abandoned [the child] and departed; this was the origin of the event, at which time the precept had not yet been established.
At that time, the Blessed One was wandering through the human realm in the kingdom of Kośala and gradually arrived at the city of Śrāvastī.
At that time, in a certain grove within this city, there were five hundred women who made their living by spinning cotton thread in that park.

Then those women beheld the Buddha, the World-Honored One, with his thirty-two marks and eighty minor characteristics, all the qualities of merit fully manifest; his body was like a mass of fire emitting great radiance, like a golden wheel reflecting the brilliance of torches. He advanced slowly and gravely, like a moving mountain of jewels, or like a golden pillar adorned with various gems; his light was pure and his wisdom fearless.

When the women saw the Buddha, their hearts were filled with great joy. It was as if someone who had diligently practiced sublime meditative concentration for twelve years suddenly attained realization and felt delight in their heart; or like a poor person encountering a treasure trove, or a childless person obtaining an offspring, or a seeker of sovereignty attaining the rank of consecration—the joy of these women exceeded even that.
Then those women went to where the Buddha was, prostrated at his feet, and withdrew to sit to one side.
At that time, the World-Honored One expounded the sublime Dharma for those women, instructing, encouraging, benefiting, and gladdening them. Having finished preaching the Dharma, he remained silent.
Then the women said to one another:

"Now that the Blessed One has entered the royal city, we will have no opportunity even to seek his presence for a moment of worship; we ought, therefore, to invite the Buddha and the Saṅgha at this very time to accept a modest offering."
Having deliberated thus, they all rose from their seats, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“We pray that the World-Honored One and the assembly of bhikṣus will accept the offerings we have prepared tomorrow.”
At that time, the World-Honored One accepted [the invitation] by remaining silent.
When the women saw that the Buddha had accepted, they took their leave of the Buddha and departed. The women then went to the Venerable Ānanda, prostrated at his feet, and said:
"O Prince! [We wish to offer our services to you.]"
"How much will it cost to provide offerings for the Buddha and the assembly of monks? Ānanda replied,
"It would require five hundred gold coins."
Then those women each left one coin as a fee for their offerings and spoke these words:
“Prince! We are poor people and possess neither utensils nor seats.”
"We only pray that the Prince will provide the offerings and all necessary requisites; when the time comes, we ourselves shall serve the food with our own hands.
Ānanda replied, "I shall prepare them for you."
Then the women left the money behind and departed.

At that time, the householder Anāthapiṇḍada heard that the Buddha, the World-Honored One, had arrived there on his journey of transformation. He went to the Buddha’s dwelling, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and sat to one side. The Buddha preached the Dharma for him until he remained silent.
At that time, the elder rose from his seat, adjusted his robe to bare his left shoulder, joined his palms in reverence, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"I pray only that the World-Honored One and the assembly of bhikṣus will come to my home tomorrow to accept my humble offering."
The World-Honored One said:
"Householder!
I have already accepted the invitation from those five hundred women for tomorrow's meal."
Having heard this, the householder rejoiced in his heart, paid homage to the Buddha, and departed.
Then, the householder Anāthapiṇḍada went next to the Venerable Ānanda; having paid his respects and prostrated at his feet, he sat to one side. Seeing those gold coins, he asked:
"Venerable sir, whose property are these?"
He replied,
"Five hundred women have left this gold money here, intending to invite the Buddha and the Sangha for a single meal tomorrow.
You may take this gold money and add your own goods to it, preparing a sublime offering to bring tomorrow."
The householder then took the money and departed; having arrived at his home, he added his own goods to it, prepared the superior offerings, and sent them to the Jeta Grove.
At that time, Ānanda dispatched a messenger to inform the women, saying:
"The preparations are now complete; you may come to receive the food."
The women all went together and said to Ānanda, "Venerable sir, you are our true spiritual friend;
we pray that you will look upon us with compassion and personally assist us in making offerings to the Buddha and the Saṅgha."
Then Ānanda proceeded to distribute the food.
There were two women, one old and one young; the younger was a naked ascetic who came to beg for alms.
The women replied,
"This is an offering for the prince.
At that time, a naked woman approached Ānanda and begged him for food and drink, saying:
“Prince! We are famished;
we pray that you grant us the remains of your meal. Ānanda said:
"Sit down and I shall give you food.
The two of them sat down.
When Ānanda was serving the food, he did not examine it carefully; seeing that the cakes were stuck together, he gave one to the elder and two to the younger.
At that time, after the elder had finished eating the cakes, he asked the younger one,
"How many cakes did you receive?
He replied:
"You have received two," the elder said.
"The prince gave me one cake, and you have received two."
"I know for certain that you have conceived a feeling of love toward me; you should adorn yourself.
The youth replied, "Do not speak such words!"
Now this prince has abandoned the imperial palace and left the household life out of weariness with the mundane world; he has cast off the dust of worldly toil as if discarding snot or spittle.
How could he possibly deign to cast a glance upon my defiled appearance?
The old woman said, "Do you not know that men’s affections for women differ? Judging by his demeanor, it seems he seeks you."
When the bhikṣus of few desires heard this account, they each felt revulsion and shame, saying:
"How can a bhikṣu give food, drink, cakes, fruits, and the like with his own hands to naked ascetics and other male and female followers of external paths?"
At that time, the bhikṣus reported this matter in detail to the Blessed One.

Thereupon, the Blessed One assembled the community of bhikṣus and spoke at length as previously described. After engaging in a dialogue of censure, he praised various means of practicing tranquility and condemned the lack of tranquility. He addressed the bhikṣus, saying: "I, having considered ten benefits, shall establish a training rule for the bhikṣus, which should be recited as follows:
'If a bhikṣu, with his own hands, gives food to a naked ascetic or to any other male or female non-Buddhist ascetic, it is a pāyattika.'"
"If there is again a bhikṣu" refers to Ānanda.
"With one's own hand," and so forth, means to give food with the hand.
The meaning of "food" is the same as previously explained.
"Those without clothing" refers to the naked ascetics and other miscellaneous classes of non-Buddhists; for these, it constitutes a *pāyattika* offense. The remaining meanings are as explained above.
Regarding this, what are the characteristics of the offense and how does it occur?
If any bhikṣu gives food with his own hand to male or female followers of other paths, he incurs a *pāyattika* offense.
However, if they are relatives or if they are sick, there is no offense in giving to them.
If one wishes to eliminate that person's wrong view by means of food, there is no offense in giving it to them.
Furthermore, there is no offense for one who is a first-time offender, or one who is insane, mentally deranged, or overwhelmed by intense physical pain.
45. The Training Rule on Viewing Armies. The forty-fifth training rule on viewing armies. The Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.

At that time, the border regions of the kingdom of Kośala rebelled, and King Prasenajit dispatched a great general to lead an army to suppress them. When his army arrived there, it was defeated by the enemy; this happened a second and a third time, and each time they were utterly routed.
At that time, the Great General returned and addressed the King, saying:

"The rebels' forces are strong while the royal army is weak; unless Your Majesty personally leads the troops, there is no way to subdue them. I pray that Your Majesty will marshal the banners and eliminate this insubordinate faction."
At that time, King Prasenajit beat the drum to proclaim his decree to the people of the kingdom, saying:
"All those who are skilled in martial arts may join the army; there shall be no exemptions. Should any fail to go, they shall be fined five hundred gold coins."
At that time, when the six bhikṣus heard that the army was about to depart, they said to one another:
“Nanda and Upananda! We should go and observe what these soldiers of King Mahāsena are like.”
"Are the fourfold army you have mobilized capable of fighting?
Then, as they were traveling along the road, they saw an elephant corps approaching. Nanda asked, "Where are you going?"
He replied, "Noble One!
There is currently a rebellious border region that does not submit; by the King's command, we have come to eliminate those traitors."
Nanda replied: "Fool! How could an elephant army such as this ever subdue him?
I observe that your elephants are like pigs, while the great elephants of the borderlands are shaped like mountain peaks; looking at your current situation, you have only departure and no return."
"You may return for a moment to bid farewell to your kinsmen; only after performing a ritual sacrifice together with *kṛsara* water may you join the army.
When those people heard these words, they were filled with sorrow and stood to one side.
Next, he saw the cavalry approaching, and Upānanda asked,
"Where are you headed?
They replied:
“Noble One!
There is currently a frontier region that does not obey the royal command; we wish to go and subdue those rebels.
He replied:

"O fool! How could such a cavalry as this possibly defeat them? I observe that your horses resemble dull oxen, while the horses of the borderlands are like elephants in form. Looking at your current situation, you have no hope of returning; you had better go home."
The details are as extensively described above.
Next, they saw an army of chariots approaching; upon seeing it, the six groups of monks engaged in the same dialogue as before.
He replied:

“Fool! How could a chariot army such as this possibly defeat them? I observe that the form of your chariot is decayed and ruined, whereas their chariots are sturdy and shaped like peaked towers; you should return home.”
The details are as extensively described above.
Next, the infantry approached; having seen them, the group of six monks questioned and answered as before, and then replied: "Fools!"
"I observe you soldiers to be like straw figures bound together; those enemy troops are like valiant yakṣas. You should return home.
It was explained at length as above.
At that time, King Prasenajit arrived with his army in full array;
seeing that the troops were not advancing, he asked, "Soldiers, for what reason do you not proceed? They replied:
"Great King!

We were sent forth on this expedition by command, fearing it might prove disadvantageous; now these shaven-headed śramaṇas, clad in tattered robes, have uttered meaningless words that cause us distress."
The king asked, "Who is this?
They replied:
"Noble Sixfold Assembly," the King said,
"They are haughty and noble śramaṇas who speak according to their own whims; you should depart and not heed what they say."
At that time, King Prasenajit thought to himself,
"Let not these śramaṇas trouble one another so frequently.
He then commanded his messenger, saying:
"You should now go to the place where the World-Honored One is, and after prostrating at his feet, you should convey my words:
'I respectfully inquire after the World-Honored One:
Are you free from illness and affliction? Is your daily life light and easy? Are your physical strength and energy well-adjusted? Are you dwelling in peace and happiness?'"
"Furthermore, convey my words:
'I only pray that the Venerable One, out of some consideration for the assembly of noble ones, will establish a training rule so as not to allow bhikṣus to go and observe military arrays.'"
Then that messenger, having received the king’s command, went to the place where the Buddha was; after prostrating at the Buddha’s feet, he stood to one side and said:
“World-Honored One!
"King Prasenajit has sent me here specifically to pay homage at the feet of the World-Honored One and respectfully inquire after him:
Are you free from illness and affliction? Are you light and agile in your daily life? Is your physical strength well-adjusted? Do you dwell in peace and happiness?"
At that time, the World-Honored One said to the messenger:
"Is the Great King Śreṇika enjoying peace and well-being?
Are you yourself in good health?"
The messenger said:
"The King has a request:
'Now that the assembly of noble ones has come to view the military array, they have caused great disturbance.'"
"I only pray that the Blessed One will take some thought for this and establish a training rule (śikṣāpada), so as not to allow bhikṣus to go and observe military arrays.
When the World-Honored One had heard the messenger's words, he gave his silent assent.
When the messenger knew that the Buddha had granted permission, he prostrated at his feet and departed.
On account of this incident, the World-Honored One assembled the community of bhikṣus and asked the group of six:
"Did you truly go to observe the army as it was being arrayed?"
He replied, “It is indeed so.

The World-Honored One then rebuked him in various ways, as extensively explained before, up until: “For the sake of ten benefits, I establish this training rule for the bhikṣus, which should be recited as follows:”
"If a bhikṣu goes to view an army in full array, it is a pāyattika.
Regarding "if a bhikṣu": this refers to the group of six; the remaining meanings are as explained above.
To "array the army" means that when one intends to go to war, one arranges the troops, fastens armor and helmets, and prepares the military regalia.

There is a type of army consisting solely of elephants; there is a type of army consisting of both elephants and horses; there is a type of army consisting of elephants, horses, and chariots; and there is a type of army consisting of elephants, horses, chariots, and infantry.
"To go and watch" means to head toward that place; the offense is established as described above.
What are the characteristics of the transgression in this case?
If a bhikṣu watches an army preparing for battle, he incurs a pāyattika.

If a bhikṣu, while on his almsround, sees an army approaching; or if the monastery is near a main road and an army enters the monastery; or if a bhikṣu is summoned by a king; or if he is invited by a queen, a crown prince, a minister, or other such persons—should he see an army in these circumstances, there is no offense in any case.
When seeing an army, one should not speak of its strengths or weaknesses.
Furthermore, there is no offense if any one of the eight difficult circumstances (aṣṭāvakṣaṇa) has manifested.
Additionally, there is no offense for the very first offender, or for one who is insane, mentally deranged, or overwhelmed by intense physical pain.
46. The Training Rule on Staying Two Nights in an Army. This is the forty-sixth training rule. The Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, a border region of the kingdom of Kośala rebelled. The King ordered a punitive expedition, but as before, they were defeated. A minister said to the King:
"To speak at length... [the details] ...until finally, a fine of five hundred coins was imposed."
At that time, the Great King personally led his army to the border city; having arrived there and surrounded it, the inhabitants had still not surrendered.
A minister addressed the King, saying:
"The householder Anāthapiṇḍada possesses great power of merit; if he were to come, they might perhaps surrender."
The king said:
"This is also excellent!
You should issue an imperial decree commanding him to come here, and send a messenger bearing the decree to the householder's residence."
The householder accepted the command with reverence and, having addressed the World-Honored One, proceeded immediately to the royal camp. Although he was among the troops, they still did not submit.
At that time, the householder Anāthapiṇḍada’s body was emaciated; when the king saw him, he asked:
"Householder!..."
"How could you, Elder, be thinking of sons or daughters?
The elder replied, "I am not thinking of sons or daughters; I am only thinking of the Noble Assembly."
Then King Prasenajit immediately wrote a letter to the assembly of monks, saying:
"I now have a minor matter for which I wish to see the noble assembly; send a messenger into the community to proclaim this royal decree."
Having heard this, the great assembly immediately dispatched messengers to distribute voting sticks (*śalākā*). The elder *bhikṣus* spoke thus:
"We are decrepit with age and no longer capable of traveling; those who are young likewise say they are incapable. How could we go there to fill jars for others and fetch water?"
"We do not understand the Dharma being preached for the king; what benefit is there in going there in vain?
Then those six groups of monks said to one another, "Nanda and Upananda!"
Now that the Great Master remains in the world and we ourselves still exist, the unsurpassed True Dharma flows widely to transform the world.
If the Great Master were to enter nirvana and his disciples followed him in extinction, all the true teachings would likewise perish and vanish.
"At this time, we are fortunately still possessed of remaining strength; we shall pull the yoke of the Noble Teaching without weariness.
Thereupon, they took up their counting-sticks and proceeded to the king's army.
Having arrived there, they preached the Dharma for the king, who was greatly delighted.
The Queen, the Crown Prince, and the great ministers were all taught the Dharma, and they were all filled with joy and celebration.
The King commanded his generals, saying:
"Prepare the troops well and together defeat the border rebels."
Having heard this, the group of six immediately said to one another:

"How could we continue to adopt the deportment of others for so many days? We should now resume our own customary ways and dwell as we please; let us go together and observe what the appearance of King Mahāsena’s arrayed army is like."
He then went to the road and saw an elephant army approaching;
he asked the soldiers, "What do you intend to do? They replied:
"I wish to fight.
[The opponent] said to him:
"These elephants of yours look like pigs; how can you wish to fight?"
He then seized the elephant’s tusk and dashed it to the ground.
Seeing the cavalry approaching, he asked the same questions as before:
"This horse is like an ox."
He immediately seized the tail and threw it aside.
Seeing the chariot-warriors approaching, he said,
"This is a broken chariot."
He immediately seized the axle and pulled it to the side of the road.
Seeing the infantry approaching, he said,
"They are like straw men."
He then seized him by the neck and threw him outside the army.
At that time, those four soldiers, having been thus humiliated, were helpless and each stood to one side, dwelling in sorrow.
The King arrived later with his retinue and asked, "Why did you not proceed?
The soldiers replied:
"Great King, you should know: how could we possibly subdue these rebels? Now these shaven-headed śramaṇas have utterly humiliated us with their wicked bodies and speech.
The King asked, "Who are they?"
He replied,
"The group of six.
The king said:
"You all should fight; he is a noble and eminent śramaṇa, so there is no need to pay him any heed.
At that time, King Prasenajit thought to himself:
"Let not that holy one trouble us again and again."
He addressed the messenger, saying:
"Take my words to the World-Honored One and speak at length as before.
I only pray that the World-Honored One, out of compassion for the noble assembly, will establish a training rule [śikṣāpada] so that they do not remain within the army for any longer."
The messenger departed, and as previously described at length, having inquired after the Buddha’s well-being, he took his leave and went away.

At that time, the World-Honored One, on account of these circumstances, assembled the community of bhikṣus. The questions and answers were the same as before, up until: “I, observing ten benefits, shall establish a training rule for the bhikṣus, which should be spoken thus:
‘If a bhikṣu has a reason to go into an army, he may stay for no more than two nights; if he stays longer, it is a pāyattika.’”
"Furthermore, 'if a bhikṣu' refers to the group of six; the remaining meanings are as explained above.
'Having a reason' refers to being summoned by anyone from kings down to the common people."
"Within the army" refers to when the soldiers are about to engage in battle.
The four types of troops are as previously described.
"For two nights" means one should remain on duty for two nights; beyond this, it is not required.
If one stays overnight beyond [the permitted limit], it is a *pāyattika*.
In this regard, what constitutes the nature of the offense?
If any bhikṣus stay overnight for more than two nights within an army, they all incur a *pāyattika*.
If the king or others request that one remain for lodging, or if there are the eight difficult circumstances, staying overnight is not an offense.
Furthermore, there is no offense for the very first offender, or for one who is insane, mentally deranged, or afflicted by intense pain.

47. The Training Rule on Disturbing Military Troops. The forty-seventh training rule concerning disturbing military troops. The Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park. As before, there was a rebellion on the borderlands.

Once the royal army had departed, he commanded the householder Anāthapiṇḍada to send a messenger to inform the assembly. He then conducted a vote by lot before the assembly; the group of six monks drew the lots, and when he preached the Dharma for them, they were all filled with joy and celebration.
When the king arrayed his troops and was about to go forth to battle, the group of six monks went together to observe how the army appeared—whether it was brave or cowardly.
They then hid in advance within a dense forest; as soon as the four divisions of the army were about to arrive, they let out a great shout, causing all the military commanders to flee in terror.
The group of six approached and asked,
"Why are you so startled?
They replied:
"The enemy's city troops have come out; we are fleeing!
The group of six replied, "It is not that enemies have arrived; it was merely our laughter."

If that enemy city knows you to be cowardly and weak, they will tie a rope around your neck every day and drag you into their city; yet, I desire to arrange my military formations for your sake, hoping surely that we shall achieve victory.
The people consented and provided him with an elephant army. When they saw a young elephant, he asked, "What is this for?
and immediately threw it to one side.
Next, he gave it to the cavalry; seeing a horse with a lame leg, he asked, "What is this for?
and seizing its tail, he cast it away.
Next, he was given the chariot army and saw an old chariot;
asking, "What is this for?
he immediately seized its axle and cast it aside.
Next, he gave it to a foot soldier, who saw a bald-headed man and said:
"Bald-headed man! What is this for?"
He then gripped him by the neck, cast him aside, and departed.
When the fourfold army had thus been humiliated, they each remained on one side, dwelling in sorrow.
When the King’s army arrived, he asked his men,
"Why have you not deployed the battle array? The men replied:
"What sentient beings do we have to rely upon that we should deploy our armies and seek a decisive victory?
The King asked,
"For what reason?"
He answered at length as before, up until: "That is a noble and eminent bhikṣu; why should his words be heeded?
You all should instead deploy your own military formations."
The King thought to himself:
"Let not the group of six monks cause further disturbance; I should now inform the World-Honored One.
He then commanded a messenger to respectfully inquire after the World-Honored One’s welfare, and having reported on his own well-being, addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

The group of six bhikṣus have long been lodging within military camps and disturbing the troops. We only pray that the World-Honored One will take this into consideration and establish a training rule (śikṣāpada), so that although the noble assembly may stay overnight in a military camp for up to two nights, they shall not observe the soldiers and cause mutual disturbance.”
The messenger, having received the King’s words, went to the Blessed One and reported everything in full; the Blessed One gave his silent consent.

After the messenger had departed, the Buddha assembled the community of monks and questioned them, reprimanding them as extensively explained previously, up until: “I, considering ten benefits, establish a training rule for the bhikṣus, which should be spoken thus:
‘If a bhikṣu stays within an army for two nights, and observes an arrayed army, sees the vanguard troops, or watches the deployment of battle formations, it is a pāyattika.’”
"Furthermore, 'if a bhikṣu' refers to the group of six; the remaining meanings are as explained above.
'To stay for more than two nights' means to exceed two days and two nights.
'An arrayed army' refers to one that is about to go to battle and is positioned at the site of the formation."
There are four kinds of banners:
first, the lion banner; second, the great ox banner; third, the makara banner; and fourth, the garuḍa banner.
There are four kinds of troops:
namely, elephants, cavalry, chariots, and infantry.
There are four kinds of battle arrays:
First, the spear-point formation; second, the chariot-pole formation; third, the half-moon formation; fourth, the garuḍa-wing formation.
If a bhikṣu observes such military arrays, he incurs a pāyattika offense.
Regarding this, what are the characteristics of the offense and its specific details?
If a bhikṣu stays within an army for two nights and observes the fourfold forces when they have not yet donned armor or taken up weapons, he incurs a duṣkṛta offense;
if he observes them when they are fully equipped, he incurs a pāyattika offense.
If the king or others request that one remain, or if one encounters the eight difficult circumstances (*aṣṭāvakṣaṇa*), seeing [these] constitutes no offense.
Furthermore, there is no offense for the very first offender, or for one who is insane, mentally deranged, or afflicted by intense physical pain.
48. The Training Rule on Striking Bhikṣus. The forty-eighth training rule concerning striking bhikṣus. The Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
Mahāmaudgalyāyana ordained seventeen individuals and conferred full ordination upon them; these seventeen all drew close to the group of six bhikṣus and associated with them intimately.
Then Udāyin replied,
"You all should come and perform such-and-such tasks.
They then answered him:
"Are you all truly my preceptors and instructors that you cannot carry out my instructions? At that,
Udāyin grabbed one person and said:
"You fools!
What further deeds will you perform that you do not accept my words?
At that time, all seventeen men fell prostrate and wept, saying:
"Strike me!
When the bhikṣus saw this, they asked Udāyin,
"For what reason did you strike that young man?"
He replied,
"I struck only one, yet seventeen all fell down and wailed aloud.
The bhikṣu asked:
"He struck me only once; why are you all crying?
He replied, "Venerable Elder!..."
"If they do not all cry out together, they shall all be beaten.
When the bhikṣus of few desires heard this matter, they each felt revulsion and spoke thus:
"How can a bhikṣu, with a mind of anger, strike another bhikṣu?"
On account of these circumstances, they went to inform the World-Honored One.

Thereupon, the World-Honored One assembled the community of bhikṣus, engaged in a dialogue of inquiry and reprimand, and finally declared: "I, having considered ten benefits, shall establish a training rule for the bhikṣus, which should be recited as follows:
'If a bhikṣu, out of anger and displeasure, strikes another bhikṣu, it is a pāyattika.'"
"Furthermore, 'if a bhikṣu' refers to Udāyin; the remaining meanings are as explained above.
'Angry' means when one's mind is entangled in resentment and gives rise to indignation and vexation.
'Striking' means to strike or beat."
"A bhikṣu" refers to one who has received full ordination within this Dharma.
The explanation of the offense is as above.
What are the characteristics of the transgression and its specific details?
If a bhikṣu uses a part of his own body, or an external object, or both together [to strike another],
what constitutes "using a part of one's own body"?
If a bhikṣu, with a mind of malice, strikes another bhikṣu with even a single finger, he incurs one *pāyantika* offense.
If two strikes result in two offenses, up to the point where striking with five fingers results in five *pāyattika* offenses.
Whether using the fist, elbow, head, shoulder, hip, knee, or even the toes of the feet, one incurs a *pāyattika* offense in each case; this is referred to as "the internal body."
What are external objects?

If a bhikṣu, with a mind of malice, takes a fine blade of grass, or an arrow shaft, or other implements—even down to a jujube pit—or a handful of mustard seeds and hurls them from afar at another, he incurs a *pārājika* offense for every single instance they strike; these are called external objects.
What is meant by "both"?

If a bhikṣu takes up a sword or staff in his hand to strike another person, or any other kind of weapon, even down to a blade of grass or a leaf from a tree, he incurs a *pāyattika* offense for whatever strikes its mark; this is called "both."
If one strikes another person in order to frighten them, or to accomplish a spell or incantation, there is no offense in any of these cases.
Furthermore, there is no offense for the very first offender, or for one who is insane, mentally deranged, or overwhelmed by intense physical pain.
The Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya, Volume Thirty-seven;
The Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya, Volume Thirty-eight.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Yijing by Imperial Decree. 49.

The Training Rule on Pointing with the Hand Toward a Bhikṣu. The Training Rule on Pointing with the Hand Toward a Bhikṣu, the Forty-ninth. At that time, the Blessed One was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.

At that time, the Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana ordained seventeen people and conferred full ordination upon them, as described in detail previously; he then assigned them their duties, but they did not follow his instructions.
At that time, Udāyin became enraged and lashed out with his hand toward one person; those seventeen people all fell down at once and wailed loudly.
The other bhikṣus asked him the reason:
"For what cause did you become angry with only one, yet seventeen all fall down together?"
He replied,
"If we did not all fall to the ground together, I fear we would all be beaten.
The bhikṣus felt contempt for him and reported the matter to the Buddha.
The Buddha then rebuked him, and so forth, until he said: "Having considered ten benefits, I shall establish this training rule, which should be recited as follows:
'If a bhikṣu, out of anger and displeasure, makes a threatening gesture toward another bhikṣu, it is a pāyattika.'"
Regarding the phrase "if, moreover, a bhikṣu... and so forth, the circumstances are identical to those previously described.
To say "brandishing the hand" means to raise the hand in a threatening gesture toward another.
The explanation of the offense is the same as before.
In this regard, what are the characteristics of the offense and how do they manifest?
There are cases involving both the internal and the external.

"Internal" refers to when a bhikṣu extends one finger toward another bhikṣu; he incurs one *pāyattika* offense, and so on up to five fingers, for which he incurs five *pāyattika* offenses. Alternatively, using the fist or the elbow from head to foot—following the same principle as before—is what is meant by "internal."
Regarding "externally": it refers to throwing grass, stalks, or the like toward another person, as explained in detail above.
Regarding "together": it means holding a staff or similar object in one's hand and brandishing it toward another person; in all such cases, one incurs a *pāyattika* offense.

If one acts for the sake of benefiting others by causing them fear, or if one intends to achieve the efficacy of a mantra or incantation by directing it toward another person, there is no offense in either case.
Furthermore, there is no offense for a first-time offender, or for one who is insane, mentally deranged, or overwhelmed by intense physical pain.

50. The Training Rule on Concealing Another’s Offenses. This fiftieth training rule concerning the concealment of another’s offenses was established when the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the six bhikṣus ordained others and, having conferred full ordination upon them, lived together with them as their companions.
At first, when those disciples did not yet know that their teachers were practitioners of evil conduct, they all served, attended upon, and made offerings to them.

Later, once they had come to know this, they abandoned them and departed, associating instead with virtuous bhikṣus; nevertheless, out of reverence for the Buddha’s teachings, they continued to pay homage to their former teachers three times every day.
The bhikṣu Nanda had a close disciple named Dharma; not yet knowing that his teacher was a man of evil conduct, he lived together with him.
Later, having come to know this, he abandoned him and departed to dwell with virtuous bhikṣus.
Out of reverence for the Buddha’s teachings, he came daily at the three times of the day to pay his respects, and thus addressed his teacher:
"Venerable Upādhyāya, please take note!
I now wish to request permission to go to a quiet place within the monastery grounds to engage in my work as I see fit."
Nanda replied, "You must be careful.
Having heard these words, Upānanda said to Dharma:
"Take my seat and go together with me. Dharma replied,
"Does the Ācārya also seek solitude by visiting the forest retreats during the day?"
Upānanda said: "Fool!
You think in your mind that my heart is always distracted and devoid of awareness."
"In what meditative absorption am I not proficient?
Dharmā replied, "I truly did not dare to think such a thing; I was merely asking whether the preceptor had gone out for his midday stroll."

At that time, Dharmadatta took that seat and went to his daytime walking grounds, placing it beneath a tree; he then withdrew his body to a secluded spot, sat cross-legged, and focused his mindfulness in contemplation.
Upānanda arrived shortly after; seeing him from afar, Dharmadatta said, "Great Master!
He has already taken his seat beneath that tree; you should go there and dwell in peace."

Then Upānanda went there and sat down upon the seat; however, with his head and face covered by his robe, he concentrated his mind in contemplation but could find no peace, so he rose from his seat and looked around in all four directions.
Seeing a woman tearing down a fence to enter, Upānanda called out to Dharma from afar, saying:
"Dharma! Do you know this now?"
"Someone has destroyed the fence," Dharma replied, "Ācārya!"
"You should fortunately reflect upon the *Jetavana Sūtra*. Upānanda said, "Fool!"

Only now do you understand how to abide according to the sūtras; have you not heard the World-Honored One’s teaching that one must not abandon property belonging to the Saṃgha? I shall go there myself to restrain that woman.
He immediately rose from his seat, and having arrived there, he asked:
"Young woman!
For what reason have you destroyed the fence?"

The woman then laughed, whereupon Upānanda’s lustful mind was immediately aroused; he seized her by the arm, embraced her body all over, kissed her mouth, and having let her go, departed for Dharmā’s place, asking her:
"What did you see?"
He replied,
"Except for the act of sexual intercourse,
I see all other matters. Upānanda said:
"Venerable one!
Although you know this, do not tell anyone else. He replied:
"O Great Master!
Until I have seen a virtuous bhikṣu arrive, I shall never speak [of this]. Upānanda said:
"You have committed a base and evil deed against your preceptor; I shall conceal it for you. Do you not see my own faults and fail to protect them by concealing them?
Dharmā replied, "O Great Master!"
"Knowing that others conceal one another's gross and evil offenses, I shall speak of such matters first.
Dharma then departed and informed the bhikṣus.
Those of few desires heard this and felt contempt and disdain, reporting the matter to the Buddha.
The Buddha assembled the bhikṣus and, after considering ten benefits, established a training rule, which should be recited as follows:
"If a bhikṣu, knowing that another bhikṣu has committed a grave offense, conceals it, he commits a pāyattika."
"Furthermore, 'if a bhikṣu' refers to Upānanda; the remaining meanings are as above.
The meaning of 'knowing' is also as above.
'Bhikṣu' refers to Nanda."
There are two kinds of grave offenses (*sthūlātyaya*):
namely, the *pārājika* offense and the *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense.
For what reason are these two called "grave"?
Because both its own nature and its cause are coarse, inferior, and loathsome, it is called "coarse and evil" (*audārika*).
"Concealing" (*pracchādana*) means to hide or cover up.
The explanation of the offense is the same as before.
In this regard, what are the characteristics of the offense and how does it occur?
If a bhikṣu, upon seeing another bhikṣu commit a pārājika offense, intentionally conceals it until the appearance of dawn has not yet occurred, he incurs a duṣkṛta offense;
once the appearance of dawn has occurred, he incurs a pāyattika offense.
If one conceals another’s residual offense, it is treated in the same manner.
If a bhikṣu sees a bhikṣu commit a *pāyattika* offense and intentionally conceals it until the appearance of dawn, he incurs a *duṣkṛta* offense;
once the dawn has appeared, he likewise incurs a *duṣkṛta* offense.
The same applies to the method of individual confession for offenses down to the *dukkaṭa* (wrong-doing), as it does to concealing them.

However, if one confesses a transgression because they fear others will create obstacles for them, or because it would cause difficulties for their holy life (*brahmacarya*), or if it would otherwise lead to a schism in the Saṃgha, then concealing it constitutes no offense.
Furthermore, there is no offense for one who is a first-time offender, or for one who is insane, mentally deranged, or overwhelmed by intense pain.
The sixth summary verse says:
"Companions, vexation, touching fire, desire, sleeping together, the Dharma, and non-obstruction."

51. The Training Rule on Going Together to a Layperson’s Home When Food Is Not Given. The fifty-first training rule: The Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.

The bhikṣu Nanda had a disciple named Dharma, who was by nature modest and felt remorse for his transgressions; as explained in detail previously, he even paid homage to his teacher three times each day out of deep respect for the Buddha’s teachings.
Then Upānanda said to Nanda, "Venerable one,

you should know that Dharma has a long-standing enmity toward me. I shall certainly, before the Buddha, the Saṅgha, and the rest of the assembly, expose his ill repute and perform acts of harm, perhaps even causing him to go without food for a day and suffer from hunger."
Nanda replied, "This Dharmā is by nature observant of the precepts; he harbors a sense of shame and maintains remorse in his heart, having never committed any transgression."
"How can I do anything harmful to him? Upānanda replied,

Having heard this, Nanda thought to himself,
"It would be better for me to starve to death than to allow him to publicly expose my other transgressions.

At that time, Nanda replied to Upānanda,

"Now is precisely the right time.

"I now wish to go out for alms.

He then said to his teacher,
"Have I ever followed behind you recently to accept an invitation for a meal?

For what reason do you now disobey his superior command?”
At that time, having received the Great Virtuous One’s reprimand, Dharmadatta fell silent; he then addressed his teacher, saying:
"I shall take my water filter and alms bowl before departing from you, Master."
Upānanda replied, "Venerable one!
What further need is there for a water filter or a bowl? That house already possesses pure vessels; the water has been filtered beforehand and is free of insects, so you may simply accompany me."
At that time, Dharmadatta followed after his teacher.
A bhikṣu who was begging for alms saw him and asked,
"Venerable Dharmadatta!
"Where do you wish to go?
He replied,
"I wish to go to the place where I am invited."
The alms-seeker replied,
"Venerable one,
eat with moderation."
Dharma said: "Virtuous One!
The matter is not yet certain; will we actually obtain food?"
"Or has he gone on a fast?
Then the mendicants followed one another and entered the city of Śrāvastī.
At that time, Nanda and Upananda, together with their disciples, arrived at a shop; there, Nanda and Dharma remained.
Upānanda went immediately to the donor’s house; having eaten his fill, he returned to the shop, while Nanda followed next to the house to eat.
Dharma then said to Upānanda, “Ācārya, the time for our meal is nearly upon us; I shall now depart.”
Upānanda replied, "The household of that donor has completed all their preparations;
when we arrive, we shall simply eat. What need is there for further anxiety? Wait until midday, and I shall go together with you."
Dharma immediately stood up and measured his shadow with his feet.
Upānanda replied to Dharma, saying, "Fool!"
"Do you mean to say that I do not protect my ethical discipline (*śīla*), that my mind is always indolent and arrogant, and that I eat at improper times?
You should leave now!
Your presence here makes me unhappy; whether speaking or sitting together, there is no joy in my heart. It would be better for us to dwell alone; do not remain here."
Dharma thought to himself:
"If I had brought my water-strainer and alms bowl here, I would have gone out to beg for food; but now that I lack both the strainer and the bowl, what am I to do?"

He then returned to the monastery; until the power of the food had not yet faded, he devoted himself exclusively to the cultivation of wholesome qualities, but when the strength of the food declined, he lay down on his side.
At that time, the alms-collector returned to the monastery, saw Dharmadatta lying there, and said to him:
"Venerable Dharmadatta!..."
"The food is another's property; how can your belly be another's?
You eat to your heart's content until you are unable to perform your work.
He replied:
"Venerable sir!
Who has eaten their fill?
He replied:
"Did you not accept an invitation to eat today?
He replied, "I did not eat."
He asked, "For what reason?
and he immediately related the preceding circumstances in their proper sequence.
At that time, the alms-seeker informed the bhikṣus; having heard this, the bhikṣus each gave rise to feelings of disdain and spoke these words:

He reported the circumstances to the Buddha.

The Buddha assembled the community of monks and questioned them regarding the facts; the details were explained at length as before, until he said: "I, considering ten benefits, establish this training rule, which should be recited as follows:
'If a bhikṣu speaks to another bhikṣu in such a manner:'"
"Venerable one!
Let us go together to a layperson's home; there we shall provide you with fine food and drink until you are fully satisfied.
When that bhikṣu arrived at the layperson's home, they gave him no food at all, but said:
"Venerable one! Go away.
I do not find pleasure in sitting or speaking with you; I find pleasure in sitting and speaking alone."
"When one speaks these words with the intent to cause vexation, it is a *pāyattika*.
As for "if there is again a bhikṣu," this refers to Upānanda; the remaining meanings are as explained above.
"Other bhikṣus" refers to those within this Dharma.
"Going together to a layperson's home" refers to the households of the four castes.
"Delicious food and drink" refers to the five types of chewed food (*khādya*) and the five types of masticated food (*bhojya*).
"To cause them to be fully satiated" means to eat to one's heart's content.
"Go away," and so forth, are words of dismissal.
"Speaking" refers to recitation; "sitting" refers to meditative reflection.

Regarding "sitting alone and waiting for pleasure": this clarifies that one intentionally causes distress so as to make the other person abstain from food; with this as the motive, and for no other purpose.
The explanation of the offense is the same as before.
In this regard, what are the characteristics of the offense and how does it occur?
If a bhikṣu intentionally causes another bhikṣu to abstain from food, he commits a pāyattika offense.
If, however, for the sake of illness a physician has prescribed fasting, there is no offense in not providing food.
Furthermore, there is no offense for one who is a first-time offender, as described above. 52.
The Training Rule on Touching Fire. The fifty-second training rule concerning touching fire was established when the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, there were several merchants in this city who went to where the Buddha was, prostrated at his feet, and then proceeded to Ānanda’s place, asking him:
"World-Honored One!..."
“Summer has ended; where do you intend to go?
Ānanda answered in detail, as previously described, observing the omens that he intended to go to Rājagṛha.
The merchant leader asked:

they asked, and immediately prepared all that was required for the offerings.

Ānanda replied:
"Venerable Sir!
Here are now two paths:
one is a direct road, but it is difficult to traverse due to the many terrors of lions, tigers, and leopards."
"One is a winding path, peaceful and unobstructed;
I do not now know which path I wish to take.
The Buddha told Ānanda:

Thereupon, the World-Honored One took the direct road and arrived at a village.

When the two boys saw the World-Honored One approaching, they immediately prostrated at his feet and said to the Buddha:
"World-Honored One!"
Welcome! Welcome!
For what reason does the World-Honored One wish to travel along this perilous path?

One went ahead, beating a drum as he departed, while the other followed behind, carrying a bow and arrows.
When the World-Honored One saw them depart, he thought to himself:

He then said:

One man beat a drum before the Buddha, while the other drew his bowstring in the presence of the Buddha. Having prostrated at the Buddha's feet, they both returned to their original places.

These lights either descended or ascended; those that descended went as far down as the Saṃjīva (Reviving) Hell, the Kālasūtra (Black Rope) Hell, the Saṃghāta (Crushing) Hell, the Raurava (Wailing) Hell, the Mahāraurava (Great Wailing) Hell, the Tapana (Heating) Hell, the Pratāpana (Great Heating) Hell, the Avīci (Unrelenting) Hell, and the eight cold hells.
When the light reached them, those sentient beings who were suffering from the heat all attained coolness, while those dwelling in the icy cold obtained warmth.
Free from suffering and established in peace and happiness, those sentient beings all spoke these words:
"Have you and I died in hell and been reborn in another place?"

At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to inspire faith and joy in those sentient beings, dispatched a transformation body to enter the hells. Upon seeing the transformation body, they all said:

"We have not died here to be reborn elsewhere; it must be due to the majestic power of this extraordinary Great Being that our bodies and minds are now freed from suffering and have attained happiness."

Having thus given rise to faith, they are able to extinguish all the sufferings of the hells and receive superior and wondrous bodies within the realms of humans and devas; constantly serving as vessels for the Dharma, they are able to perceive the principles of the Truths.

Those who ascended went upward as far as the Heaven of the Four Great Kings, the Heaven of the Thirty-three, the Yāma Heaven, the Tuṣita Heaven, the Nirmāṇarati Heaven, the Paranirmita-vaśavartin Heaven, the Brahmakāyika, the Brahmapurohita, the Mahābrahmā, the Parīttābha, the Apramāṇābha, the Ābhāsvara, the Parīttaśubha, the Apramāṇaśubha, the Śubhakṛtsna, the Anabhraka, the Puṇyaprasava, the Bṛhatphala, the Avṛha, the Atapa, the Sudṛśa, the Sudarśana, and the Akaniṣṭha Heaven.
Wherever he went, light emanated from him as he expounded the dharmas of suffering, emptiness, impermanence, and non-self, and further recited these two gāthās:
"You should seek renunciation, And apply yourself with diligence to the Buddha's teaching;
Subdue the army of birth and death, Just as an elephant destroys a thatched hut."
"In this Dharma and Vinaya, by constantly practicing heedfulness,
one can exhaust the ocean of afflictions and reach the ultimate end of suffering.
Then that radiance, having illuminated the trichiliocosm, returned to the presence of the Buddha.

if he speaks of future events, the light enters through his chest;
if he speaks of matters concerning the hells, the light enters through the soles of his feet.

if he speaks of matters concerning hungry ghosts, the light enters through his toes;
if he speaks of matters concerning humans, the light enters through his knees.

if he speaks of the affairs of a Cakravartin Universal Monarch, the light enters through the palm of the right hand;
if he speaks of celestial matters, the light enters through the navel.

if he speaks of the matters concerning pratyekabuddhas, the light enters between his eyebrows;
if he speaks of anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, the light enters through the crown of his head.
At that time, the light circled the Buddha three times and entered through the crown of his head. Then the Venerable Ānanda, with palms joined in reverence, addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!”
"The Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, does not manifest a joyful smile without cause or condition.

Having subdued all afflictions and adversaries, the Tathāgata does not smile without cause or condition.
The Muni, who has personally realized the true and wondrous awakening, is heard with joy by all who listen;
may he, the most supreme, proclaim his resolve and resolve the doubts of the great assembly.
The Buddha told Ānanda: “So it is! So it is!”
"The Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha does not manifest a smile without cause or condition.
Did you see the two youths who guided me?
He addressed the Buddha, saying:
“I see it.
The Buddha told Ānanda:

“By virtue of these roots of goodness, for thirteen kalpas into the future, he shall not fall into the evil realms but will be born among humans and devas. In his final existence, he shall attain unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment; one shall be named Dharmadundubhisvara Tathāgata, and the other shall be named Abhayada Tathāgata.”
At that time, having delivered this prophecy, the World-Honored One departed along the road and stayed for the night in a grove at the edge of a village.
As the Buddha had taught, even dwellings for bhikṣus, down to those under trees, should be shared out in due order.

Ānanda replied to the Buddha:

"You all should listen!

"Generally, when the heat of these animals intensifies and they can no longer endure their hunger, they pass away and are reborn in the Heaven of the Four Great Kings.

He then immediately knew for himself that he had died from the animal realm and was now born among the Gods of the Four Great Kings.
"What karma did he perform?
He gave rise to pure faith toward the Buddha.
At that time, this devaputra again thought to himself:
"I should now go to the place where the Buddha is to attend upon and make offerings to him.

At that time, the devaputra adorned his body with celestial necklaces and filled the corners of his robe with exquisite celestial flowers. Past the end of the night, he emitted a great radiance and approached the Buddha's dwelling. He then arranged celestial *utpala*, *kumuda*, *padma*, and *puṇḍarīka* flowers before the Buddha as an offering, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and sat to one side.
Because the radiance of this celestial body was so magnificent and pervasive, the entire forest of *araṇya* became clearly illuminated.

At that time, the World-Honored One, in accordance with that devaputra’s inclinations, latent tendencies, and differences in faculties, preached the Dharma for him, enabling him to realize and enter into the principle of the Four Noble Truths.

At that time, having heard the Dharma, the devaputra, while still upon his seat, used the vajra-pestle of wisdom to shatter the twenty-fold mountain of satkāyadṛṣṭi and attained the fruit of stream-entry.
Having realized the truths, he addressed the Blessed One, saying:
"Venerable Sir!
It is because of the Blessed One that I have attained the fruit of liberation."

This was not something that could have been accomplished by my parents, ancestors, kings, celestial hosts, śramaṇas, brahmins, friends, or kinsmen; rather, because I encountered the World-Honored One as a spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitra), he rescued me from the realms of hell, animals, and hungry ghosts and established me in the superior and wondrous states of humans and devas. I shall now exhaust birth and death and proceed upon the path to nirvāṇa. Having dried up the ocean of blood and crossed over the mountain of bones, I have shattered with the vajra-pestle of wisdom the mountain of the view of a self-entity (satkāyadṛṣṭi) accumulated since beginningless time, and have attained the fruit of stream-entry (srotāpanna).
I now take refuge in the Triple Gem of the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha.

May the World-Honored One deign to bear witness that I am an upāsaka; from this day forth until the end of my life, I shall observe the five precepts, from abstaining from taking life to abstaining from drinking intoxicants.

Having spoken these words, that devaputra was filled with profound joy at having attained what he had never experienced before; he paid homage to the Buddha and departed, returning to his celestial palace.

At that time, the bhikṣus, remaining awake during the first and last watches of the night, dwelt in contemplation with focused minds. Seeing a great radiance from the World-Honored One that illuminated the entire Jeta Grove, they conceived this doubt:
"Which assembly of devas has come to the place where the Buddha is?"
"By the power of that merit, light pervaded the entire grove.
When dawn had broken, he went to the place where the Buddha was, prostrated at the Blessed One’s feet, sat to one side, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Last night I saw a great radiance filling the grove, and I immediately thought to myself:"

"Is it not that the devas of the Brahma world, or Śakra, Lord of Devas, or the Four Great Kings, or other distinguished devas of great majesty and power, have come to the Buddha’s presence to personally receive and make offerings; by their power, the light pervades the grove?"
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus, saying:

"The radiance last night was not due to the majestic power of Brahmā, Śakra, or any other host of devas. Did you not see the Great Lion King in the forest personally hear the Dharma of three phrases from my side?"
The bhikṣus said to the Buddha,
“We have already seen it.
The Buddha said:
"That lion king, having heard the Dharma from me, passed away here and was reborn in the Heaven of the Four Great Kings.
Having received a celestial body as a reward for his gratitude, he came to my presence to present heavenly flowers as an offering, and I preached the Dharma for him."
