Having heard the Dharma, he immediately attained the vision of the Truths (satyadarśana) and returned to his original celestial palace; it was by the power of that merit that light pervaded the grove.
When the bhikṣus heard these words, they requested of the World-Honored One, saying:
"We do not know what karma the deva Siṃha had previously performed?"
By what karma was he drawn to undergo the ripening retribution of falling among lions?
Furthermore, by what karma did he, after the end of his life, take birth in the Heaven of the Four Great Kings?

And by what conditions did he, having heard the Buddha’s Dharma, attain the fruit of stream-entry (*srotāpanna*), experience what he had never before known, and return to his original celestial palace?
The World-Honored One said:
"Listen, all of you!

Regarding the karma performed by this devaputra in a previous life, when the convergence of causes and conditions reached its point of maturation, it did not ripen within the external elements of earth, water, fire, or wind; rather, he experienced the retribution for his wholesome and unwholesome deeds within the internal aggregates, elements, and sense-bases of his own body."
He then spoke in verse:
"Even if a hundred eons were to pass, The karma one has created does not perish;
When the causes and conditions meet, One must experience the retribution oneself."
“O bhikṣus, you should listen with a sincere mind!
In the past, when the human lifespan was twenty thousand years, a Buddha appeared in the world named Kāśyapa, fully endowed with the ten titles.”
He had twenty thousand disciples as his retinue and resided in the kingdom of Vārāṇasī.
Before that Buddha Kāśyapa appeared in the world, there was in this city a brahmin who had mastered the four Vedas and was widely learned in all the treatises.
At that time, the people of the world developed the utmost respect for him; with one mind they looked up to him in veneration as their Great Teacher.
After that Buddha Kāśyapa appeared in the world, everyone revered the Buddha and no longer went to serve him collectively.
At that time, the Perfectly Enlightened One Kāśyapa was proclaiming the sublime Dharma amidst an assembly of immeasurable hundreds of thousands.
A certain brahmin, passing by the edge of the crowd, saw the Blessed One preaching the Dharma to those hundreds of thousands and, conceiving jealousy, uttered these disparaging words:
"This śramaṇa knows no fear; he is like a lion preaching the Dharma to others in the midst of a great assembly, while the other listeners are like small beasts respectfully receiving his teaching."
At that time, having heard these words, the World-Honored One addressed the brahmin, saying: "Brahmin!
Since you have uttered harsh and evil words toward the Teacher of Gods and Humans, you shall undergo various bitter retributions in the hells."
"You should now come to me and confess your transgressions with a sincere heart; thus your offenses shall be lightened.
When the brāhmaṇa heard the Buddha’s instruction, shame and remorse arose within him, and he confessed his own faults before the World-Honored One.
Having thus confessed his transgressions, he immediately took refuge in the Three Jewels before the Buddha and received the five precepts as an upāsaka.
O bhikṣus! Do not harbor any other thoughts.

The Brahmin of former times, because he used harsh speech and uttered words of contempt in the presence of the Buddha, still has residual retribution remaining from that evil karma despite having confessed his transgression; for five hundred lifetimes he was constantly a lion, and even now other retributions have not yet ceased.
Because he gave rise to right faith upon hearing the Dharma of the three phrases from me, he was reborn in the heavens.

Because he took refuge in the Triple Gem and received the five precepts before the Buddha Kāśyapa, through the power of that karma, he has now realized the principle of the True Dharma under me, attained the fruit of Stream-enterer, and returned to his original celestial palace.
Therefore, bhikṣus, you should know this:

by performing purely black karma, one obtains a purely black maturation; by performing purely white karma, one obtains a purely white maturation; and by performing mixed karma, one experiences a mixed maturation.
"From this day forward, you all should abandon black karma and mixed karma; you must not be negligent, but should cultivate pure white karma. Thus should you train.
When the bhikṣus and the assembly of humans and devas had heard what the Buddha said, they received it with faith and practiced accordingly.
At that time, the World-Honored One traveled by stages until he reached Magadha, arriving at the city of Rājagṛha where he stayed in the Bamboo Grove near the Kakrandaka Pond.
At that time, the six bhikṣus of the group were at a place where fire was being kindled; they each played with the tips of the flames, fashioning them into the shapes of the sun and the moon.
When the non-Buddhists saw this, they each felt contempt and spoke thus:
"Do you not know, sirs?
The fire-worshipping Śramaṇas of the Śākya clan are acting with frivolity; what difference is there between them and those common children?"
"How can one diminish the portion set aside for one's wife and children to provide for this shaven-headed man to fill his alms bowl?
When the bhikṣus heard these words, they reported them in full to the World-Honored One.

At that time, the Blessed One assembled the bhikṣus and spoke at length as previously described, up until: "Having considered ten benefits, I shall establish a training rule for the bhikṣus, which should be recited as follows:
'If a bhikṣu himself kindles a fire, or instructs another to kindle one, it is a pāyattika.'"
At that time, the Blessed One established a training rule for the bhikṣus: "One must not touch fire.

Consequently, the community of bhikṣus no longer burned incense or lit lamps as offerings at the Tathāgata’s stūpas; nor did they serve their preceptors and instructors with warm water, nor perform such tasks as fumigating their bowls or dyeing their robes.
At that time, the Blessed One, knowing [the reason] yet asking out of formality,
addressed the Venerable Ānanda: "Ānanda,
why is it that the bhikṣus do not offer incense and light lamps as an offering at the stūpas of the Tathāgata, nor provide services such as hot water for the two teachers?"

Ānanda said: "Because the Blessed One has established a training rule prohibiting the touching of fire, for this reason the community of bhikṣus has consequently ceased all activities such as making offerings."
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"If one touches fire while performing an act of formal maintenance (*dhāraṇā*), there is no offense despite the contact.
At that time, the bhikṣus did not know how to perform the formal maintenance when acting.
The Buddha said:
"Whenever you touch fire, you should form this thought:
'I must now touch fire for the sake of making offerings to the Buddha.'"

Or it may be said: "For the sake of the Dharma, for the sake of the Saṅgha, for the sake of my upādhyāya, ācārya, and myself, as well as for the sake of my fellow practitioners of the holy life, I must now touch fire for a certain purpose."

The bhikṣus repeatedly touched fire for such matters as dyeing robes and fumigating bowls; while touching it, they forgot their mindfulness and failed to maintain mental vigilance, whereupon regret arose and they felt remorse, thinking:
"How is it that I have now intentionally committed this offense?"
He then reported this matter in detail to the World-Honored One, and the Buddha said:
"One should say:
'...and shall maintain it for as long as the matter remains unfinished.'"
At that time, a certain bhikṣu suffering from a wind-related illness went to a physician and said to him,
"O worthy one! Prepare a prescription and medicine for me according to this ailment."
The physician replied, "In all cases of wind-disorder (*vāta*), fire is beneficial; you must stay near a fire.
He then said:
“O worthy one! The World-Honored One has established a precept that does not permit [monks] to approach fire.
The physician said:
"Noble One! The Blessed One is greatly compassionate; for this reason, he will certainly grant permission.
Having reported the circumstances to the Buddha, they said: [the matter].
The Buddha said:
"What was previously established as a prohibition is now further relaxed; it should be stated thus:
'If a bhikṣu, being not ill, for the sake of his own body, should kindle a fire himself or instruct another to kindle one, it is a pāyattika.'"
"Furthermore, 'if a bhikṣu' refers to the group of six; the remaining meanings are as explained above.
'Not being ill' means excluding those who are sick.
The meanings regarding oneself and others, etc., are as extensively explained previously."
In this regard, what are the characteristics of the offense and how does it occur?
If a bhikṣu uses the tip of a flame to play with one another, or fashions the shape of the sun or moon discs, he incurs a pāyattika offense in all such cases.
Whenever a bhikṣu kindles a fire, he should observe the purpose and maintain it with mindfulness;
if he kindles or touches it without such mindfulness, he incurs a pāyattika offense.
If one extinguishes the fire, one also incurs a *pāyattika* offense.

If a bhikṣu grasps the tip of a flame and moves it forward, or pulls back the tip of the flame, or turns over burning coals, or turns over fires such as those made of husks or chaff—whatever action he performs, whether for cooking food, boiling water, lighting lamps, or burning incense—at the moment of contact, he incurs an *dukkaṭa* offense.
If one discards hair, body hair, nails, saliva, or similar substances into fire, one incurs an offense of wrongdoing (*dukkaṭa*).
However, if these actions are performed while maintaining the formal resolve (*saṃvara*), there is no offense.
Furthermore, there is no offense for one who is the very first person to commit the act, or for one who is insane, mentally deranged, or overwhelmed by intense physical pain.
**The Fifty-third Training Rule: Regarding Withdrawing After Having Granted Consent** The Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.

At that time, when the Venerable Udāyin had severed all afflictions and attained the fruit of Arhatship, the Bhikṣu Chanda went to the country of Kauśāmbī to dwell in seclusion. Both Aśvaka and Punarvasu had passed away, while Nanda and Upananda remained in the Jeta Grove, both having reached an advanced age.
As those seventeen bhikṣus grew older, they became courageous, strong, and proficient in the Tripitaka. They then deliberated together and all spoke thus:

"For a long time we have been constantly deceived and slighted by the group of six; among them, Nanda and Upananda have always acted with malice, and of these two, Upananda is even more cruel and harsh. We ought to perform the *jñapti-karman* of suspension against him."
One person said to the assembly, "The Elder Nanda is his elder brother; he is well-versed in monastic affairs, so how could we possibly perform the *karmavācanā* against him?"
One person proposed:
"We should now employ a stratagem to lure him away so that he does not enter the assembly; we shall then perform the *karmavācanā* together.
Having made this proposal, they went to his location and said to him:
“Vandāmi ācariya! He replied, “May you,
Venerable One, be free from illness!”
He said, "The *cīvara* worn by the Elder is extremely soiled and greasy; why do you not wash it?
He replied:
“Venerable one!
I am now old and decrepit; seeing me thus aged, my disciples and followers have all begun to treat me with contempt. Who, indeed, would be willing to wash my robes?”
He then replied,
"Venerable sir,
please give me the robe; I shall wash it for you."
At that time, Nanda gave him a garment and told him to wash it.
He replied, "Since the labor involved is the same,
you might as well give me all the garments together so they may be washed at once."
He then took one tattered robe and gave it to all three of them together.
Having received the robes, they all soaked them in lye; they then went to the assembly hall, spread out the seats, and struck the *gaṇḍī* gong.
They went together to Nanda and said to him, "Venerable One!
There is business for the Saṃgha;
the signal mallet has already been struck. You should enter the assembly for a moment to observe the matter together with us."
Nanda replied, "Venerable one!
With my appearance as it is now, how could I enter the assembly?"
"If there is any matter concerning the Saṃgha that accords with the Dharma within this assembly, I shall grant my consent (*chanda*).
He then granted his consent.
Taking that consent, he went into the midst of the assembly and, having announced it, one person immediately rose and approached the Elder Upānanda, speaking as follows:
“Venerable sir, you have committed an offense; I wish to interrogate you, so please grant me your permission.
He replied, “As you wish.”
He said: "Venerable Sir!
Do you perhaps recall that at such a time and in such a place, you yourself spoke these words?"
"I shall split open your bellies, pull out your entrails, and encircle the Jetavana Grove with them!
Is this statement true? Having heard these words, Upānanda replied:
"Venerable sir!
Is it not as if you have already inflicted further injury upon a wound that has been healed? This matter is in the past; why trouble yourself to speak of it? He replied:
"Venerable One!
The Great Teacher, the Tathāgata, also established rules of training for his disciples based on past events.
Having said this, they forcibly performed the *jñapti-caturtha-karman* of suspension against him.
When the great assembly had dispersed, Upānanda went to Nanda’s place and stood there weeping.
Nanda asked him, "What is the matter that you have suddenly begun to weep?"
He replied,
"I have been subjected by those black-bowl monks to the *jñapti-caturtha-karman* of suspension (*pratikṣepa*). Nanda replied:
"He who performed the *karmavācanā* for my younger brother was merely expelling his person from within the village, city, and the three realms; what fault was there in that toward my brother?"
"However, I must now offer my apologies.
Furthermore, that Saṃgha performed a formal act (karmavācanā) as a separate assembly; the procedure was invalid, and I did not attend the gathering.
The others replied:
"Is it not the case that you, Venerable Sir, previously gave your consent?
Nanda replied,
"If such an undesirable matter were to occur, I would not have given my consent."
"An expression of consent that is not valid is an evil expression of consent.
When the bhikṣus of few desires heard these words, they each felt revulsion and contempt, saying:
"How can a bhikṣu first express his consent and later, in regret, speak such words?"
"Return what you wish to have; I will not give you what you desire.
At that time, the bhikṣus reported this matter in full to the Blessed One.

On account of this, the Buddha questioned the bhikṣus regarding the facts of the matter and provided a detailed explanation, concluding: "I, having considered ten benefits, shall establish a training rule for the bhikṣus, which should be recited as follows:"
"If a bhikṣu, having already given his consent to another bhikṣu, later regrets it and says:
'Give me back my consent; I will not give it to you,' it is a pāyattika."
"Furthermore, 'if a bhikṣu' refers to Nanda; the remaining meanings are as explained above.
Moreover, 'a bhikṣu' refers to one who belongs within this Dharma.
'Having already given his consent' means that he has previously stated that he gives it."
The phrase "afterwards, then equally" refers to the words for requesting [the fulfillment of] one's desire.
The explanation of the offense is the same as before.
In this context, what are the characteristics of the transgression and its specific details?
If a bhikṣu has previously given his consent (*chanda*), but later feels regret and informs the assembly, saying,
"Return my consent to me; I do not wish to give it," he incurs a *pāyattika* offense.
Furthermore, there is no offense for one who is the very first person to commit such an act, or for one who is insane, mentally deranged, or overwhelmed by intense physical pain.
*Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya*, Volume 38. *Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya*, Volume 3.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Yijing by Imperial Decree. Precept 54:

The Training Rule on Staying Overnight for More than Two Nights in the Same Room with One Who Has Not Yet Received Full Ordination. At that time, the Blessed One was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, the Garden of Anāthapiṇḍada.
At that time, many devoted lay patrons came to the monastery and said to the bhikṣus, "Noble ones!
We pray that you will proclaim the True Dharma for us; we long to hear it."
The bhikṣu replied:
"O noble sirs!
If you have the desire to hear the Dharma, you should go to where the Buddha is; the Buddha himself will preach it for you."
He said, "Noble One!

There is but one Great Master, and those who gaze upon him are many; gods, nāgas, humans, and spirits all wish to hear the Dharma. Do you know for whom he intends to expound the essentials of the Dharma?"
"You may also recite the sūtras for me, O virtuous ones.
The bhikṣus replied,
"The World-Honored One has not yet permitted this."
When the laypeople heard this, they all rose up in derision and departed, leaving them behind.
The bhikṣus then reported this matter to the Buddha, who said:
"I now permit the bhikṣus to recite the sūtras at appropriate times."
Once the Blessed One had granted permission for the bhikṣus to recite the sūtras, they began reciting them every day without ceasing.
Those who possessed merit and leisure came daily to listen; having returned home, they would then speak thus during the night to those laborers who lacked merit:
"You should know this!..."

Those noble assemblies constantly recite the True Dharma day after day; their speech is so exquisite that it brings joy to all who hear it, and the listeners forget their weariness as bees savor honey.

When the supervisor heard these words, he replied to the people, "Virtuous ones, you possess great merit to have encountered the appearance of a Buddha in the world, to have heard the essentials of the Dharma, and to have obtained such great benefit; day by day, you experience what has never been known before."
He said to the laborer,
"Why did you not listen?
The man replied:

“You possess merit and virtue; though you listen to the sutras during the day, your family members are able to survive. We, however, have meager merit and must labor to earn our living; if we constantly go to hear the sutras, we will surely starve to death.”
"If those noble ones recite the sūtras at night, I too would delight in listening.
When the bhikṣus heard these words, they went and informed the Buddha.
The Buddha said, "One may indeed recite the Dharma even during the night."
He then recited the scriptures throughout the entire night; consequently, he became exhausted and distressed. The Buddha said:
"One should not recite the scriptures day and night.
When the bhikṣus taught the Dharma for only short periods according to the occasion, those who came to listen all conceived feelings of dissatisfaction. The Buddha said:
"One should not teach according to convenience; rather, one should explain in full.
Thereupon, the bhikṣus recited [the scriptures] every night, and the laborers had no opportunity to come constantly.
At that time, a person of merit, having arrived home, recounted the matter as before. The laborers sighed to themselves:
"We are of little merit and have not been able to hear the sutras.

If the noble ones would recite them throughout the night on the eighth, fifteenth, twenty-third, and the final day of every month, we could constantly hear them and thereby generate merit and benefit."
The bhikṣus reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"On the eighth day, the fifteenth day, the twenty-third day, and the final day of the month, you should recite the sūtras throughout the entire night."
At that time, there was a bhikṣu who lived as a mendicant in an araṇya; he said to his fellow residents:
"Today is the fifteenth day; I wish to go to the monastery to perform the poṣadha together with you and also listen to the sūtras."
He then proceeded to the monastery and listened to the Dharma with great earnestness until midnight. At that time, the alms-collector thought to himself:
"Since it is now not the proper time, there is no opportunity for me to go to the forest hermitage; I shall remain here for now and sit to one side."
The laypeople who were listening to the Dharma were also staying there.
At that time, when the temple attendants were about to extinguish the lamps and candles, the laypeople said:
"Noble ones!..."
"Do not extinguish the lamp; I shall provide oil and a candle.

There was a mahallaka bhikṣu who lay down with him and did not sleep mindfully; he then saw in a dream that he was engaging in sexual union with his former wife, whereupon he immediately began to mutter improper words.
Having heard this, the laypeople immediately went to look all around and saw the mahallaka lying on his back with his belly up, speaking incoherent words and discussing unrighteous matters.
Upon seeing him, the laypeople deliberated together:
"O sirs, look at this aged bhikṣu; even he still engages in such behavior."
"What will those others who are young and vigorous do?

At that time, the alms-seeker heard the common people’s disparaging remarks. The next morning, he went into the forest, where a person practicing meditative concentration within a *araṇya* saw him and asked:
"Venerable one! [What has happened?]"
"When fellow practitioners of the holy life in that monastery recite the scriptures at night, are they able to inspire pure faith in the laypeople?
He replied, "Upon hearing the sublime Dharma, all give rise to joy and faith; however, there is one elderly bhikṣu who provokes the censure and suspicion of the laity."
He asked, "For what reason?
He then answered in full detail regarding the matter. When the bhikṣus heard this, they reported the circumstances to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"Because monks have stayed in the same room as those who are not fully ordained and have lit lamps and candles, such faults have arisen.
Therefore, I now forbid monks from staying in the same room as those who are not fully ordained or from lighting lamps and candles."
This is the origin of the rule; at that time, the training precept had not yet been established.
The Buddha was staying in the Kūṭāgāraśālā at the Miśrakāvana park in Kauśāmbī.
At that time, the Venerable Śāriputra had two śrāmaṇeras.
The first was Cunda, and the second was Rāhula.

At that time, Rāhula had business requiring him to go to a daytime recreation area. A visiting bhikṣu arrived at the monastery and, having seen the administrator (vaiyāvṛtyakara), sought a place to stay.
When the administrator saw that Rāhula had gone outside and was not present, he immediately asked the guest to stay temporarily in the room.
The guest bhikṣu then took Rāhula’s robes and bowl and placed them outside the room.
Then Rāhula returned from a secluded place outside to his own room; seeing his robes and bowl lying outside the door of the room, he stood there dejectedly.
At that time, Cunda came to where he was and asked, "Venerable one!..."
"Why do you look so somber, as if bearing a trace of sorrow?

He replied, "I went out for a brief stroll, and when I returned, a guest had arrived and left my robes and bowl in front of my room. As the day is drawing to a close and the heavens are about to rain, where shall I lie down tonight?"
Cunda replied,
"Whenever and wherever one may find space for a body to lie down, why trouble oneself with anxiety and linger before the door?
He answered:
“You, O Benevolent One, possess merit and great spiritual power; you could transform this into a grass hut fit for dwelling.
As for me, I lack such power—what can I do?
Having heard this, Cunda departed in silence.
At that time, there was a faithful donor who, for the sake of the Buddha and the Saṃgha, smeared the latrines with exquisite fragrant clay. Upon seeing this, Rāhula thought to himself:
"To see the Buddha at an improper time in order to have some questions to ask—such a thing is not possible."
"I should now sleep here tonight to pass the night.
He then entered the latrine hut and lay down for the time being.
That very night, a heavy rain fell from the heavens; not far from there, within a hole in the ground, lived a large venomous snake.
When the hole was filled with water, the snake emerged and went straight to the latrine.
The Great Teacher, the Tathāgata, possessing a mind free from forgetfulness, thought thus:
"If that venomous snake were to bite Rāhula, he would surely die and exist only in name."
Furthermore, those of the Śākya clan, relying on their own high status and arrogance, gave rise to disbelief and spoke these words:

"If Rāhula had not gone forth into homelessness, he would have succeeded to the position of a Wheel-Turning King; now that he has gone forth and has no one to rely upon, he lies upon a latrine and has been bitten by a snake, meeting an unjust and painful death."

Having formed this thought, he extended his right hand like the trunk of an elephant king, reached the place where Rāhula was, lifted him up, and brought him into his own room to place him upon his own bed.
During that night, the Buddha remained walking or sitting until daybreak.
At dawn, another bhikṣu, having finished cleansing his teeth with a tooth-stick and rinsing his mouth, went to where the World-Honored One was to pay him homage.

It is the constant custom of the Blessed One that, when he intends to establish a training rule for the śrāvakas, he does not allow those bhikṣus who have already arrived to depart until all have assembled.
Then the śrāmaṇera Cunda went to where Rāhula was, snapped his fingers to rouse him, and said: "Rāhula!
Where are you sleeping?"
Having awakened and realized it was the Buddha’s bed, he immediately sprang up in alarm and stood there trembling with fear.
Cunda said to him: “Rāhula!
Had the World-Honored One not taken thought for you, you would have been bitten by a venomous snake and certainly met with death, leaving nothing but an empty name behind.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus, saying:
“For all śrāmaṇeras who have neither father nor mother, there are only those like you—fellow practitioners of the holy life—who should show mutual compassion and concern.”
Most of these are Arhats who are about to emerge from the womb of existence; if you do not show mutual compassion and protection toward them, who would feel concern?
Therefore, I now permit the Bhikṣus to stay overnight for up to two nights with those who have not yet received full ordination, without committing an offense.

At that time, there was a bhikṣu who suddenly suffered from diarrhea; his feet became defiled with impurity, and as there were no lamps or candles in his room, he had no means to wash them. He consequently left his feet hanging at the edge of the bed and lay down to sleep through the night.
As dawn was about to break, the disciples and attendants entered the room to inquire:
"We wonder, Upādhyāya, whether your four great elements are at ease?
He replied:
"I am uneasy. He asked,
"For what reason?"
He informed them of his ailment in full so that they would know. When the bhikṣus heard this, they reported the matter to the Buddha.
The Buddha said, "A lamp should be placed there.
At that time, after the bhikṣus had placed the lamp, a certain patient could not sleep, and because of this, his illness became even more severe. The Buddha said:
“If a bhikṣu has an illness and requires a lamp to be lit, there is no offense in sleeping face-to-face with another; do not harbor doubts about this.
At that time, the attendant nurse also did not dare to sleep, and consequently fell ill. The Buddha said:
“Even if the attendant nurse sleeps while the lamp is burning, there is likewise no offense.”
At that time, the sick person required medicine and food, but as there was no one to administer them, his needs were neglected. The Buddha said:
"One who has not yet received full ordination should be permitted to stay overnight with him."
At that time, after two nights had passed, the bhikṣus did not dare to sleep, and because of this, further illness arose. The Buddha said:
"Even if a sick person stays together with others for more than two nights, there is no offense."
There was a sick bhikṣu who was unable to eat by himself; he had a person who had received full ordination (upasampadā) feed him before he would eat.
At that time, the one who had received full ordination went out and was absent. The Buddha said:
"It is also permitted for one who has not yet received full ordination to feed him."
"If such a person is not present, even a great bhikṣu may take [the food] himself and eat it.
At that time, the bhikṣus did not dare to sleep under the light of the sun or moon. The Buddha said:
"The light of the sun and moon is not something to be avoided; there is no offense in sleeping during these times."
As the Buddha had prescribed:
"A bhikṣu must not stay overnight for more than two nights with one who has not received full ordination.
At that time, after staying for more than two nights, the bhikṣus were driven outside the monastery and suffered injury from thieves, wild beasts, mosquitoes, ants, and the like. The Buddha said:
"One should not send him out of the monastery.
At that time, the bhikṣus sent him out onto the porch; the Buddha said, "One should not drive him out onto the porch;
rather, one should have him stay overnight at a distance from the range of the door of the room."
At that time, there was a bhikṣu who kept a śrāmaṇera and had him go out to sleep for the night. A wicked bhikṣu came from outside and asked the śrāmaṇera, "Where will you sleep tonight?"
He replied,
"Under the porch of the gate.
At that time, the master heard the sound of his voice and asked:
"What did he say? The disciple answered in full detail.
Having heard this, the master summoned him into his room to stay the night together; throughout the entire night, whether walking or sitting, he remained there until the break of dawn.
At that time, his disciples and followers came together to inquire:
"We wonder, Upādhyāya, whether since last night your daily activities have been light and easy, and whether your strength and vigor are at peace?"
He replied, "I am not at ease. He asked:
"Why is that? At that time, the preceptor answered the disciple in full detail regarding the matter.
Having heard this, the disciple said to the preceptor:
"Master, have you not heard what the Buddha said:
'There are two things by which one becomes a great person:
first, knowing that a certain matter should not be done, one does not do it;'"
"Second, once a task has already been undertaken, one should not abandon it, but rather bring it to completion.
Since the Master has already taken pity on that śrāmaṇera and accepted him for his upbringing, he ought to see the matter through from beginning to end; how could he possibly decline such labor?
Upon hearing this, the Teacher remained silent.
When the bhikṣus heard of this matter, they reported it to the Buddha, who said:
"If such a person of evil conduct should come, those capable of expelling him ought to drive him away together."
If it is not possible, one should take the śrāmaṇera to another monastery.

If, after the summer retreat has concluded, an evil bhikṣu comes to the monastery, the preceptor should share a room with the śrāmaṇera until the end of the summer; do not entertain any doubt regarding this.
When the summer retreat concluded, those capable of driving him away should have expelled him; if that was impossible, they should have taken the śrāmaṇera to another monastery.
At that time, there were many bhikṣus who traveled along the road together with the śrāmaṇera; after two nights had passed, they made him sleep outside, whereupon he was harmed by a predatory beast.
They reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"You should not allow them to leave. You should divide the bhikṣus into two groups; as long as the night has not yet ended, staying together is not an offense."
At that time, when the śrāmaṇeras arose at night, they fell asleep on the road; the bhikṣus abandoned them and departed, whereupon they were also harmed. The Buddha said:
"One should not abandon them and leave; one should have them go ahead."
At that time, the śrāmaṇera requested food and drink during the morning meal, but the bhikṣu did not give it to him. The Buddha said, "You should give it to him.
When he requested it again at midday, the bhikṣu replied:
"Why do you seek more food after having already been given the morning meal?
He then refused to give him any food.
The Buddha said:
"The youth's appetite is strong; he may be given more food.
Furthermore, when traveling on a journey with an unordained companion, the bhikṣus said to one another:
"As the Buddha has ordained:"
"After two nights have passed, it is not permitted to stay overnight with one who has not yet received full ordination.
He then remained awake throughout the entire night without sleeping, and consequently became exhausted. The Buddha said:
"One should guard against the appearance of dawn; there is no need to stay awake all night long."
At that time, the bhikṣus were still exhausted.
The Buddha said, “If you are traveling on a journey, you should sleep throughout the night; do not harbor any doubts.
At that time, Upānanda had two śrāmaṇeras.
One was named Kṣurapra and the other was named Dīrgha; he stayed with these two disciples for more than two nights.
When the bhikṣus saw them, they said to him:
"Venerable One!..."
The Buddha has established a precept forbidding two people from staying together for more than two nights.
For what reason do you now willfully contravene the Buddha’s word?
You ought to change this.
Upānanda said: "What difference is there between this second night and the third night?
Furthermore, how could one possibly drink alcohol or eat onions and garlic on the third night?"
At that time, there were bhikṣus of few desires who, having heard these words, felt revulsion and contempt, saying:
"How can a bhikṣu fail to uphold the Buddha’s teaching?

The World-Honored One did not permit staying overnight for more than two nights in the same room as one who has not received full ordination; yet he willfully violates the holy instruction by staying with such a person."
He then reported this matter in full to the Blessed One.

The Blessed One assembled the community and questioned them regarding the facts of the matter. Then, up to the point where he said: “I, considering ten benefits, shall establish a training rule for the bhikṣus, which should be recited as follows:
‘If a bhikṣu stays in the same room with a person who has not yet received full ordination for more than two nights, it is a pāyattika.’”
"Furthermore, 'if a bhikṣu' refers to Upānanda; the remaining meanings are as explained above.
There are two types of those who have received full ordination: namely, bhikṣus and bhikṣuṇīs."
The others are not fully ordained, namely those such as śrāmaṇeras; the rest of the meaning is understandable.
There are four types of dwellings:
first, those that are completely roofed and completely enclosed, such as various rooms, guest halls, and multi-storied pavilions, where the top is entirely covered and all four walls are screened.
2. Fully covered with many obstructions: having few windows or doors on the four walls;

3. Fully covered and fully obstructed: namely, a house on four sides, with walls erected on the four edges, pillars standing in the middle, and the four eaves recessed inward, being either low or level;
4. Fully covered and many obstructed: referring to a house on three sides, which lacks one side of the four-sided house.
If it is half-obstructed and half-covered, or mostly covered with little obstruction, or at the edge of an eaves and so forth, there is no offense in any such case.
Furthermore, there is no offense for the very first offender, or for one who is insane, mentally deranged, or overwhelmed by intense physical pain.
55. The Training Rule on Refusing to Abandon Wrong Views Despite Being Admonished. The Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, there was a bhikṣu named Animitta who, having conceived a wrong view, spoke as follows:
"As the Buddha has taught:
'Dharmas that constitute obstacles should not be practiced.'"
"I know that when this dharma is practiced and cultivated, it does not constitute an obstacle.
At that time, a great number of bhikṣus, having heard these words, went to inform the Blessed One.
The World-Honored One said:
"O assembly of bhikṣus!
You should carry out a formal admonition against that bhikṣu Niḥsanimitta."
If there should be others of such a kind, one should act in this manner:
go to their place and say to them,
"You who lack the marks, do not speak these words."
"As the Buddha has said:
'Dharmas that constitute obstacles should not be practiced.
Yet I know that when these dharmas are practiced, they do not constitute obstacles."
"Do not misrepresent the Blessed One; it is unwholesome to misrepresent the Blessed One.

You are without grounds, for the Blessed One has not said that obstructive factors are not obstructive factors. By means of various skillful methods, he has declared these to be obstructive factors, and if one practices them, they are certainly obstructive factors."
"O signless one!
You should now abandon such an evil view.
Thus should he be admonished.

The bhikṣus, having received their instructions, went to where Niḥsanimitta was; when they exhorted and admonished him as the Buddha had instructed, he remained obstinate in his evil views and refused to relinquish them, saying:
"What I say is the truth; all else is false."
At that time, when the bhikṣus saw that their admonition was not heeded, they went to where the Buddha was and spoke to him thus:
"Venerable Sir!
We have already admonished Aśmaka separately as the Buddha instructed; yet while we were exhorting him, he remained obstinate regarding his evil view and would not relinquish it."
...and so forth, as extensively explained.
The Buddha said:
"You bhikṣus!..."
One should perform a formal motion with three proclamations (*jñapti-caturtha-karman*) to admonish that bhikṣu.

It should be done in this manner: having struck the gong to assemble the community, once the assembly has gathered, one bhikṣu should perform the formal motion (*jñapti-karman*), which should be done as follows:
"May the venerable Saṃgha listen!..."
This bhikṣu, Animitta, gave rise to an evil view and spoke these words:
"As the Buddha has said:
'Dharmas that constitute obstacles should not be practiced.'"
"I know that when this dharma is practiced, it does not constitute an obstacle.
At that time, the bhikṣus offered him a formal admonition.
During the formal admonition, he stubbornly clung to his evil views and refused to relinquish them, saying:
"I say this is the truth; all else is false.
If it is the proper time for the Saṃgha and they grant permission, may the Saṃgha allow that the Saṃgha now perform the *jñapti-caturtha-karman* for you, the bhikṣu Niḥsīmā, to clarify the matter.
“You who are without marks, do not speak these words:
‘As the Buddha has taught,
“One should not practice obstructive dharmas.”’”
"I know that when this dharma is practiced, it is not an obstructive dharma.
Do not slander the Blessed One; to slander the Blessed One is unwholesome.
You are without signs!
The World-Honored One has, through various skillful means, taught that sensual desires are obstructive dharmas; if one practices them, they will certainly constitute an obstruction.
You must relinquish such an improper and evil view.
"Thus is the motion (*jñapti*) made.
Next, the formal ritual (*karman*) should be performed according to the established motion.
At that time, when the monks performed the *jñapti-karman* and offered their exhortation, the monk Asaṃvarika stubbornly clung to his evil views and refused to relinquish them, saying:
"This matter is true; all else is false.
When the bhikṣus saw that he would not change his mind, they reported to the World-Honored One in detail how they had failed to follow their advice.
The World-Honored One said:
"O bhikṣus! You should perform the formal act of suspension for the bhikṣu Niḥsāmānya on account of his refusal to relinquish his evil view."
It should be performed in this manner, and the same applies to the others.
Having struck the gong to assemble the community and so forth, one bhikṣu should perform the formal motion (*jñapti-karman*):
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!..."

This bhikṣu Niḥsīmā has personally given rise to evil views, as explained at length above, up to: "If the Saṃgha deems it the right time and grants its consent, the Saṃgha should authorize the performance of the *pratisaṃharaṇīya-karman* (act of suspension) against the bhikṣu Niḥsīmā for not relinquishing his evil views. Until this bhikṣu Niḥsīmā has relinquished such evil views, the community of monks shall not converse with him nor engage in discourse with him; he is to be regarded as utterly detestable and most wicked, like a *caṇḍāla*."
“[The motion] is thus announced.
Next, the *karmavācanā* (formal ritual act) should be performed according to the announcement.
At that time, although the bhikṣus performed the *pratisāraṇīyakarman* (act of reconciliation/suspension) against Asaṃvaraka, he remained obstinate in his evil views and did not relinquish them.
At that time, the bhikṣus reported the matter to the Buddha.
The Buddha assembled the community of monks and questioned Animita, saying:
"Is it true that you spoke these words?"
"Regarding the obstructive dharmas spoken of by the Buddha, I know them to be non-obstructive; when I practice them, they do not constitute an obstruction.
He addressed the Buddha, saying, "It is truly so."
"Venerable Sir!

The World-Honored One rebuked him in various ways, as extensively described above, up until: "I, considering ten benefits, shall establish a training rule for the bhikṣus, which should be spoken thus:
If a bhikṣu should speak these words:"
"If I understand the Dharma taught by the Buddha, those things which are obstacles when one indulges in them are not obstacles when one practices them," then the bhikṣus should say to that bhikṣu:
"Do not speak such words."
"I understand what the Buddha has taught: that which he declared to be obstructive dharmas is not an obstruction when one practices them.
Do not misrepresent the Blessed One; it is unwholesome to misrepresent the Blessed One.
The Blessed One does not speak thus; the Blessed One has, by way of countless approaches, declared all sensual desires to be obstacles. You should abandon such an evil view.
"When the bhikṣus have admonished him in this manner, it is well if he relinquishes [the matter];

if he does not relinquish it, they should admonish him earnestly and correctly a second and third time, and following their instructions, they should interrogate him to make him relinquish that matter."
"It is well if he relinquishes it; if he does not relinquish it, it is a *pāyattika* offense.
Regarding "if there is again a bhikṣu," this refers to one who is without signs (*animitta*); the rest of the meaning is as explained above.
"One who speaks such words" refers to the statement of that matter.

"I know the Dharma taught by the Buddha" means that the Buddha—namely the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha—has taught it; "Dharma" refers to what was spoken by the Buddha or spoken by a Śrāvaka, and it signifies the meaning of an obstacle.

The obstructing dharmas refer to the four pārājikas, the saṃghāvaśeṣas, the two aniyatas, the thirty naiḥsargika-pāyattikas, the ninety-one pāyattikas, the four pratideśanīyas, and the śaikṣa-dharmas.
That which does not constitute an obstacle during the time of practice means it cannot hinder the noble fruits of a śramaṇa.
"Slander" refers to uttering irrational speech.
"Unwholesome" means that it brings about a negative karmic maturation.

When the bhikṣus see such speech, they should perform a formal admonition; if he does not relinquish it, they should perform a *karmavācanā* admonition, continuing until the conclusion of the formal act, as explained in detail previously.
In this regard, what are the characteristics of the offense and how does it occur?
If a bhikṣu speaks thus:
"I know that which was spoken by the Buddha," and so forth.
When the bhikṣus see him speak these words, they should perform a formal admonition (pratyekapratideśanā).
If he relinquishes [the position], it is well; if he does not relinquish it, he incurs an offense of wrong-doing (duṣkṛta).

When performing the formal ritual (karmavācanā) of admonition, if he does not relinquish it during the proclamation (jñapti) or during the first two proclamations of the motion (karmavācanā), he incurs an offense of wrong-doing in each case.
If the threefold *karmavācanā* is completed, one incurs an offense of downfall (*pārājika*).
However, if one performs an illegal *karmavācanā* and so forth, there is no offense.
Furthermore, there is no offense for the very first offender, or for one who is insane, mentally deranged, or overwhelmed by intense physical pain.

56. The Training Rule on Following One Subjected to the *Pratiniḥsarga* (Act of Suspension). This is the fifty-sixth training rule. At that time, the bhikṣu Animitta had been subjected to the *pratiniḥsarga-karman* (act of suspension), and he went to the place of Upānanda and remained there weeping.
Upānanda said to him:
"Venerable Animitta!
Why are you weeping?"
He replied,
"The Black-bowl monks have performed the *jñapti-karman* of suspension against me. Upānanda said:

"If one were to perform the formal act of setting aside (*sthāpanīya-karman*) against cities, villages, and the sentient beings of the three realms, would that imply that cities and such do not exist?
Do not be distressed; you should instead seek to offer an apology."
Having been thus instructed, they conversed with him, partook of food and clothing with him, and lay down in the same room.
When the monks of few desires saw this, they were filled with resentment and contempt, saying:

"How can a monk, knowing that another monk is a person of evil views and that the Saṃgha has performed the formal act (*karmavācanā*) against him without yet having carried out the legal procedure of reconciliation, converse with him and engage in the duties of communal living?"
He then reported this matter in detail to the Blessed One.

The Blessed One assembled the community and questioned him regarding the truth of the matter, reprimanding him in various ways. Furthermore, [the Buddha declared]: "Having considered ten benefits, I shall establish a training rule for the bhikṣus, which should be recited as follows:

'If a bhikṣu knows that a person who speaks in such a manner has not yet acted in accordance with the Dharma nor abandoned his evil views, yet he converses with him, dwells together with him, shares resources with him, or sleeps in the same room with him, it is a pāyattika.'"
"Furthermore, 'if a bhikṣu' refers to Upānanda; the remaining meanings are as explained above.
'One who speaks thus' refers to one who is without signs (animitta).
'Not having performed the conforming dharma' means not having carried out the dharma of conforming confession (*pratideśanā*)."

"Regarding 'not abandoning an evil view while engaging in conversation with them,' etc.: this refers to performing acts such as providing instruction or serving as a formal preceptor (*upādhyāya*), staying together in one of the four types of rooms until dawn; the offense is established as described above."
In this regard, what are the characteristics of the offense and how does it occur?

If a bhikṣu knows that such a person has not yet performed the *anuvartana-dharma* (the act of compliance), yet engages with them in matters such as discussion or communal residence, he incurs a *pāyattika* (offense of falling).
If that person is ill, there is no offense in attending to them.
Or, if one causes a co-resident to abandon wrong views, this also entails no offense.
Furthermore, there is no offense for the very first offender, or for one who is insane, mentally deranged, or overwhelmed by intense pain.

57. The Training Rule on Accepting Those with Evil Views and Not Expelling a Śrāmaṇera. The fifty-seventh training rule concerning accepting those with evil views and not expelling a śrāmaṇera. The Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, Upānanda had two novices:
one named Śaṇḍa and the other named Phalgu.
Then, many bhikṣus from various places came to his location and lived together with those two novices; they engaged in playful banter, agitation, and physical contact with one another.

At that time, the bhikṣus felt subsequent remorse and reproached themselves for the offenses they had committed. Those [offenses] requiring mental repentance, they repented with mental remorse; those requiring confession before another, they confessed and thereby removed them. Arousing a mind of heroic vigor and a resolute intention, they severed all afflictions, realized arhatship, and attained great supernormal powers.
Later, on another occasion, while those two novices were gathering flowers in the forest, they saw that bhikṣu traveling through the air and called out from afar:
"Who are you, sirs?"
The bhikṣu replied, “I am so-and-so.
The two of them answered:

"Virtuous ones, did you not formerly dwell together with us, engaging in jesting, frivolity, and physical contact, thereby committing various sinful deeds? How is it that you have now attained such superior realization?"
He replied: "This is indeed true;

however, at a later time, remorse arose within me, and I deeply reproached myself for the transgressions I had committed. As previously described in detail, I eventually attained the fruit of the Path."
Upon hearing this, the śrāmaṇera thought to himself:
"In the past, these bhikṣus engaged in such and such unrighteous acts together with us; how is it that they have now obtained such superior fruits?"
"For this reason, I know that when the Buddha taught the Dharma, saying,
'To indulge in various sensual desires is an obstacle,' this is not actually an obstacle.
He related this entire matter to the bhikṣus.
At that time, those of few desires, having heard these words, neither censured nor rejoiced in them, but reported the matter in its entirety to the World-Honored One.
The World-Honored One then addressed the bhikṣus:
"What these two śrāmaṇeras have said is unreasonable; you should perform the rite of separate admonition to enlighten them."
If there should be another person who acts in this manner, they should likewise be admonished and told:
"You, Li-ci, stop and do not speak such words as:
'I know that what the Buddha taught regarding the obstructive nature of sensual desires is not actually an obstruction.'"
"Do not speak such words to slander the Blessed One; it is unwholesome to slander the Blessed One.
The Blessed One does not speak thus. By means of various skillful methods, the Buddha has said:
'The pursuit of sensual desires is an obstructive dharma.'"
"You two must now abandon these evil views.
When the bhikṣus had received the Buddha’s instruction, they went to the two śrāmaṇeras and exhorted them regarding the matter just as the Buddha had taught.
When they were thus admonished, those two novices stubbornly clung to their evil views and refused to relinquish them, saying:
"This alone is the truth; all else is false."
Then the bhikṣus reported this matter in detail to the Blessed One:
"When we followed your instructions and separately admonished those two śrāmaṇeras, their evil views remained stubbornly held and were not relinquished;
they said, 'What I say is the truth; all else is false.'"
The Buddha said:
"O bhikṣus! You should perform a formal proclamation followed by three motions (jñapti-caturtha-karman) to admonish those two śrāmaṇeras."
It should be done in this manner: strike the gong to assemble the community.
Once the assembly has gathered, have two novices move to a place where they can see but cannot hear. One person should then perform the formal motion (*jñapti-karman*) as follows:
"Listen, venerable Saṃgha!
These two novices, Kaṇṭaka and Dīrghāyu, gave rise to such an evil view and spoke thus:
"I know that which the Buddha taught as 'an obstacle'—namely, sensual desire—is not actually an obstacle."
When the bhikṣus were giving him a formal admonition, those two stubbornly clung to their evil views and refused to relinquish them, saying:
"This alone is the truth; all else is false."

"If it is the proper time for the Saṃgha and the Saṃgha is willing to listen, may the Saṃgha permit that the Saṃgha now perform the formal motion and three proclamations (*jñapti-caturtha-karman*) to instruct those two persons in this matter."
"You two should not speak these words: 'As the Buddha has said,
"one should not practice obstructive dharmas," yet I know that when this dharma is practiced, it is not an obstruction.'"
"Do not misrepresent the Blessed One; it is unwholesome to misrepresent the Blessed One.
The Blessed One does not speak thus; rather, the Blessed One has taught through various skillful means:
'Sensual desires are obstructive states; if one practices them, they will certainly become obstacles.'"
"You two should abandon such evil views.
This is the formal announcement (*jñapti*).
A single bhikṣu then addressed the two individuals, saying:
"The Sangha has performed the formal motion (*jñapti*) and the fourfold proclamation (*karma*) for you; the motion having been completed, you should now abandon this evil view.
If he abandons it, that is well.
If he does not abandon it, that bhikṣu should return to the midst of the assembly and announce:
"He does not relinquish his evil view.
Next, the *karmavācanā* is performed:
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!..."
"The formal announcement (*jñapti*) should be made as prescribed, up until the completion of the first *karmavācanā*.
As before, let the questioning be conducted.
If [the offender] does not relinquish [the offense], report this back to inform the assembly."
"Next, when the second and third proclamations have been completed, you should act exactly as before in making the inquiry.

When the bhikṣus had received the Buddha’s instruction and were summoning those two men to perform the *jñapti-caturtha-karman* (the formal ritual of four proclamations) to admonish them, they stubbornly clung to their evil views and refused to relinquish them, saying:
"This alone is the truth; all else is false."
Then the bhikṣus reported this matter in detail to the Blessed One:
"We have already performed the formal procedure of *jñapti-caturtha-karman* to admonish those two, yet they stubbornly cling to their evil views and refuse to relinquish them, saying:
'This alone is the truth; all else is false.'"
The Buddha said: "O bhikṣus!
You should perform the formal act of suspension for not relinquishing evil views against those two śrāmaṇeras."
It should be done in this manner:
strike the gong to assemble the community.
Once the assembly has gathered, have one bhikṣu perform the formal motion (*jñapti-karman*):
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!
Those two śrāmaṇeras, Tiṇṭha and Bhaddali, have given rise to evil views, as previously explained in detail.

When the Saṃgha performed the formal admonition and the *jñapti-caturtha-karman* to instruct them, they obstinately clung to their position and refused to relinquish it, saying: [Insert the specific content of their refusal here]"
"This matter is true; all else is false.

If the Saṃgha deems the time appropriate and grants its consent, the Saṃgha should authorize the performance of the *pravāsanīya-karman* (act of banishment) for these two individuals for not relinquishing their wrong views, and should address them as follows:
"From this day forward, you two must no longer say:..."
"‘The Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha is my great teacher’—
furthermore, you should not follow behind a bhikṣu and travel along the same path.
Just as other śrāmaṇeras may stay overnight in the same room with a great bhikṣu for two nights, you now have no such privilege."
"You foolish man!
You may depart now!
Thus he spoke.
One bhikṣu should go to the two individuals and announce:

"The Saṃgha is now performing the formal act of suspension (pravāsanīya-karman) against you two by means of a jñapti-caturtha-karman; the announcement has been completed. You two should abandon such evil views."
"If he relinquishes it, that is well; if he does not relinquish it, he should return to the assembly and report the matter in full, as explained above.
Next, one should perform the *karmavācanā* (formal ritual act) for him, proceeding according to the formal announcement (*jñapti*)."
Once the formal procedure has been completed, he should again instruct the bhikṣu to go before that assembly and declare:
"The community has already performed the first *karmavācanā* for you; you should abandon this evil view.
This is to be explained in detail as above.
"Up until the completion of the third *karmavācanā*, the concluding formula should be applied accordingly.
The bhikṣus said to the Buddha,
"Venerable One!"
"You should act in this manner.

Having received the Buddha’s instruction, the bhikṣus summoned the two śrāmaṇeras and performed the formal ritual of expulsion against them; yet, as they did not relinquish their evil views, they went to Upānanda’s place and remained there weeping.
Upānanda asked:
"You two venerable ones!
Why are you weeping?"
He replied, "The Black-bowl monks have already performed the *pravāsanīya-karman* (act of banishment) against us;
what do you intend to do now? Upānanda said:
"If they have performed the *pravāsanīya-karman* against those villages, towns, cities, and even against the triple world, does it mean that the villages and so forth do not exist?
Do not be distressed; you should go and confess (*pratideśayitavya*)."
He then accepted their offerings and hospitality, conversing with them and staying overnight.
When the bhikṣus of few desires saw this, they felt revulsion and contempt, saying:
"How can a bhikṣu accept the service and hospitality of such a śrāmaṇera of evil views who has been subjected to the *pravāsanīya-karman* by the Saṃgha, and stay overnight conversing with him?"
He then reported this matter in detail to the Blessed One.

The Blessed One assembled the community and questioned Upānanda, as explained at length above, until he said: "I, considering ten benefits, shall establish a training rule for the bhikṣus, which should be recited as follows:
'If a bhikṣu sees a śrāmaṇera speaking in such a manner:'"
"If I understand the Dharma taught by the Buddha, that 'sensual desires are obstructive dharmas,' when one practices them, they are not actually obstructions.
The bhikṣus should say to that śrāmaṇera:
"Do not speak such words:..."
"I understand what the Buddha has taught: 'Sensual desires are obstructive dharmas'—when one practices them, they are not obstructive.
Do not misrepresent the Blessed One; it is unwholesome to misrepresent the Blessed One.
The Blessed One does not speak thus; the Blessed One has, by means of countless methods, declared all sensual desires to be obstacles. You should abandon such an evil view.
When the bhikṣus speak to that śrāmaṇera, it is well if he abandons this matter;
if he does not abandon it, they should, up to two or three times, admonish him properly and instruct him properly to abandon this matter.
If he relinquishes it, that is well; if he does not relinquish it, the bhikṣus should say to that śrāmaṇera:
"From this day forward, you must not say:
'The Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha is my teacher.'"
"If there are elders or fellow practitioners of the holy life, you should not follow after them.
Just as other novices are permitted to stay overnight with bhikṣus for two nights, you now have no such privilege."
"You foolish man!
Depart at once!
If a bhikṣu, knowing that a śrāmaṇera has been thus expelled, should nevertheless accept him, support him, or share a room with him, it is a pāyattika offense.
"Furthermore, 'if a bhikṣu' refers to Upānanda; the remaining meanings are as explained above.
'There is a śrāmaṇera' refers to Li-ci (Kaṇṭaka) and Chang-da (Bṛhat)."
"Buddha" refers to the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha.
"Teacher" (śāstṛ) has the meaning of one who guides and instructs.
"Dharma" refers to that which was spoken by the Buddha or that which was spoken by the Śrāvakas.
"Desire that constitutes an obstacle" refers to the five objects of desire (*pañca-kāmaguṇa*).
"One who practices them" refers to one who performs those acts.
"That which does not constitute an obstacle" refers to that which cannot obstruct the noble fruits of a śramaṇa (*śrāmaṇyaphala*).
"Bhikṣu" refers to one who belongs to this Dharma.
"Speaking to that śrāmaṇera and others" means recounting their evil views and then administering both individual admonition and communal admonition to them.
If he does not relinquish [the offense], one should perform the formal act of banishment (*pravāsanīya-karman*) by saying:
"From this day forward, you must explain the matter in detail; you are not permitted to travel or stay overnight together with [the community]."
"You are a foolish person!
You should depart quickly.
As for the "bhikṣu," this refers to Upānanda.
"Knowing" means either knowing by oneself or hearing from another.
"Accepting" means providing a basis for reliance.
"Benefiting" refers to supplying food and clothing.
Regarding "sharing a room": if one sleeps in the same room as any of the four types of persons mentioned, the offense is established as previously described.
What are the characteristics of the offense in this context?
If a bhikṣu knows that a śrāmaṇera has been expelled and yet sleeps in the same room with him, it is a pāyattika.
If they are kinsmen, or if they are currently afflicted by illness, or if one intends to cause them to abandon wrong views, there is no offense even if one temporarily accepts them.
Furthermore, there is no offense for the very first offender, or for one who is insane, mentally deranged, or overwhelmed by intense physical pain.
58. The Training Rule on Wearing Uncolored Robes. The fifth and eighth training rule concerning the wearing of uncolored robes. The Buddha was staying at Rājagṛha in the Bamboo Grove.
At that time, there were two dragon kings in this city, one named Kṛīla and the other named Bāḍu.

By virtue of the majestic spiritual power of these two dragons, there were five hundred hot springs and various ponds in the city of Rājagṛha that flowed incessantly; they sent down sweet rain in due season, causing the five grains to ripen in abundance.

At that time, after the Blessed One had tamed the two nāga kings Nanda and Upananda, these two nāga kings would regularly emerge from the great ocean on the eighth, fifteenth, twenty-third, and final day of the month, ascending the peak of Mount Sumeru to approach the Buddha’s dwelling for the purpose of making offerings and listening to the Dharma.
At that time, the two nāga kings Kṛkī and Vatsa, seeing Nanda and Upananda coming to the Buddha’s presence to present their offerings, said to one another:
"These two nāga kings come from afar to this city every month on the four fast days (upoṣadha) to serve the World-Honored One and hear the sublime Dharma."
"How can we remain in this city without offering our respects?
We should now go to make offerings to the World-Honored One.
At that time, the two dragon kings came to where the Buddha was, prostrated at his feet, and sat to one side.

At that time, the World-Honored One expounded the essentials of the Dharma for those two nāgas, causing them to take refuge in the Triple Gem and receive the five precepts; from then on, their bodies and their wealth both flourished and increased.
Once they had increased and flourished, they deliberated together, saying:
"We ought to go into the great ocean and dwell wherever it is vast and expansive.
Having made this deliberation, they went to where the Buddha was; having paid their respects, they sat to one side and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“Venerable Sir!
Since we received the precepts of refuge from the World-Honored One, our bodies and our resources have both flourished.
If the Greatly Compassionate World-Honored One would look upon us with pity and grant us permission, we now wish to go to the great ocean to dwell there as widely as possible.”
Having seen their request, the Buddha addressed the two nāgas, saying:
"King Bimbisāra is the sovereign of this kingdom; if you wish to depart, you should inform him."
Then the two nāga kings took their leave of the Buddha and departed, whereupon they said to one another,
"As the Buddha has spoken, it seems we are not permitted [to remain].
Thereupon, they returned to their former dwelling.
However, if the two dragon kings come to see the Buddha at night, they appear in their original forms; if they do so during the day, they take the form of householders.

On a later occasion, while the dragons were listening to the Buddha’s teaching at the World-Honored One’s residence during the daytime, King Bimbisāra also went to the Bamboo Grove Park at that same time. Upon arriving at the gate, he commanded his attendants, saying:
"Go to where the Buddha is and observe who is there."

Then his attendants, having received these instructions, departed for the Buddha’s location. Upon arriving, they prostrated at the Buddha’s feet and, seeing the two elders there with the World-Honored One, immediately returned to the king and said:
“Great King! [...]”
"There are two householders present with the World-Honored One.
The king thought to himself:
"Those two householders are my own countrymen; seeing that I have arrived, would they dare not rise?"
At that time, King Bimbisāra was about to go to where the Buddha was. When those two nāga kings saw the great king approaching, they addressed the World-Honored One, saying:
"Venerable Sir!
Should we first pay respect to the Dharma?"
"Is it out of respect for the King?
The World-Honored One replied,
"All Buddhas, World-Honored Ones, as well as Arhats and others, all revere the Dharma."
For this reason, he spoke three verses:
"Whether they be the Buddhas of the past, Or those of the future;
The World-Honored Ones of the present, They are able to sever all sorrow."
All together they revere the Dharma—in speech, in conduct, and in stillness;
at all times, they honor the True Dharma.
Therefore, those who seek benefit and desire abundant prosperity and happiness [should do likewise].
"One should revere the Dharma and constantly reflect upon the teachings of all Buddhas.
At that time, when those two nāgas heard the World-Honored Buddha speak on the matter of revering the Dharma, although they saw the king arrive, they did not pay him homage.
Having seen them, the king thought to himself:
"These two householders are my own subjects; seeing that I have arrived, they do not show me respect.
Thus, he gave rise to resentment.

Having approached the World-Honored One and prostrated at his two feet, he sat to one side; the Buddha, knowing that the king’s mind was possessed by anger, spoke other words instead of preaching the Dharma for him.
Then King Bimbisāra requested of the World-Honored One, saying:
"I pray that the Great Master will preach the Dharma for me.
At that time, for this reason, the World-Honored One spoke these verses:
"If one lacks a pure mind and harbors thoughts of anger and resentment,
one will be unable to understand the subtle and wondrous Dharma taught by all Buddhas.
One must subdue the mind of contention and eliminate all impure intentions."
"Only one who can eliminate anger and malice / Shall understand the subtle and wondrous Dharma.
When King Bimbisāra had heard this verse, he thought to himself:
"Because of these two elders, the World-Honored One has been unable to expound the essentials of the Dharma for me at the proper time."
He then rose from his seat, paid homage to the Buddha, and departed. He commanded his attendants, saying:
“When those two elders leave the presence of the Buddha, you should inform them, saying:
‘By the command of the Great King, you two should depart at once; do not remain within my kingdom.’”
Thereupon, the messenger received his orders and departed.
Having heard the sublime Dharma, the two nāga kings paid homage to the Buddha and were about to leave the Bamboo Grove when the messenger reported:
"The Great King has issued a command: 'You two should depart at once; do not remain in my kingdom.
Upon hearing this, the two nāgas thought to themselves:
"That which we have long cherished in our hearts can now be fulfilled without further toil."

Immediately, dense clouds arose and a torrential rain fell; following the various channels and ravines, it entered the rivers and streams, flowing successively until it reached the great ocean, where his person and his wealth increased even more abundantly.

After the dragon had departed, five hundred hot springs on the outskirts of Rājagṛha all dried up; from time to time, sweet rain did not fall, the five grains failed to ripen, and the people were filled with sorrow and grief.
At that time, King Bimbisāra, having witnessed this event, thought to himself:
"Within the city of Rājagṛha there are two nāga kings, one named Giri and the other named Jaya, who constantly dwell in this city."

By his majestic power, he was able to cause five hundred hot springs and various ponds to flow incessantly; from time to time, sweet rains fell, causing the five grains to ripen in full abundance without any deficiency.

Suddenly, at this present time, the hot springs and ponds have all dried up; for a long time there has been no rain and the five grains have failed to grow. Could it be that the two dragon kings have passed away?
"Perhaps he has fled to another land, or is being held by a dragon-conjurer, or has been devoured by the King of the Garuḍas.
However, the Buddha, the World-Honored One, possesses all-encompassing wisdom and observes everything; I should now go to him and ask about the cause."
Then King Bimbisāra went to the Bamboo Grove, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and sat to one side. He addressed the Buddha, saying:
“Venerable Sir!
There are two nāga kings who dwell in this city; they have described their powers and the reasons for their waxing and waning. I do not know where they reside at present.”
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed King Bimbisāra, saying:
"Great King, you should know this!
It is not that those two nāgas have died or passed away, nor have they been consumed by a garuḍa; rather, it is because you yourself have driven them out."
The King said,
"I do not recall ever having met with him, much less expelling him.
The World-Honored One replied:
"I recall for Your Majesty the matter of your expulsion.
Do you not remember that once, when you came to my place and saw two elders sitting beside me, what conversation did you have with them at that time?"
Bimbisāra said to the Buddha, “World-Honored One!
I did not speak with them myself; I sent a messenger to convey this message to the two elders:”
"Do not reside in my kingdom.
The Buddha said:
"Those two elders were actually nāga kings who manifested in human form to come and listen to the essential Dharma."
The King asked,
"Where have those two dragon kings gone now?
The Buddha said:
"Go to the great ocean.
Having heard these words, the king’s face was immediately suffused with sorrow, and he addressed the Buddha, saying:
"O Virtuous One!..."
"Will my kingdom fall into decline?
The Buddha said, "The king's realm has not yet reached a state of decline; however, you ought to offer an apology to those two nāga kings."
The king said, "He is at sea while I dwell in the city; since we do not see one another, there is no way for me to offer my apologies.
The Buddha said:

"Whenever the four fast days arrive, you come to my place to pay your respects; on these days, Your Majesty should come in person, and I shall instruct you so that you may offer your repentance and gratitude."
The King asked,
"When I offer my apology, should I prostrate at his feet?
The Buddha said:
"You should not prostrate at his feet; rather, you should extend your right hand and say to the dragon kings:
'I pray that you will forgive me and harbor no resentment for my previous words.
Those two dragon kings will surely grant you their forbearance."
Later, at another time, on the day of the *poṣadha*, those two nāga kings came to where the Buddha was; having prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, they sat to one side.
On that same day, King Bimbisāra also came to prostrate at the Buddha’s feet and sat to one side.
At that time, the World-Honored One manifested a sign to indicate their location,
saying, "These are the two great nāga kings. Then King Bimbisāra extended his right hand and addressed the two nāgas, saying, "Nāga Kings!"
"I pray that you will grant me your forgiveness.
The Dragon King replied,
"I forgive you."
"Great King!
The king said,
"If you will grant me your pardon, I pray that you return here to dwell within my kingdom."

The two nāgas replied, “Once we have reached the great ocean from this place, our bodies and our possessions will become exceedingly vast; if we were to come here, there would be no room to accommodate us.”
The king said,
"If it is so, I shall lose my kingdom.
The nāga said:

“I only pray that Your Majesty do not worry about losing the kingdom; you may build two shrines for deities outside the city—one named the Shrine of the Kṛtī Dragon Deity, and the second named the Shrine of the Vajra Dragon Deity.”
"I have commanded my retinue to reside within this hall; every six months, they shall once hold a grand assembly, and we ourselves will come to inspect the king's realm so that it suffers no lack."
The King said,
"Excellent!
It shall be done accordingly."

At that time, King Bimbisāra immediately constructed two divine shrines in a grove by a spring outside the city. Every year, on the days of the seasonal festivals, all the people from the six great cities would gather there like clouds.
Once, on the occasion of a festival, musicians from the south arrived at the royal city. At that time, those musicians said to one another:
"By what means can we cause the hearts of the people to feel joy and affection, so that we may obtain much wealth and profit to provide for ourselves?"
At that time, there was one person who made this proposal:
"If we recount the extraordinary and sublime deeds of a Great Man, it will cause the people's hearts to feel joy and affection, and they will obtain much wealth."
The people replied, "If that is so,
there is nothing more excellent in the world than the Buddha, whom all sentient beings alike revere.
If I were to praise him to attract the multitude, I would thereby obtain wealth and never lack for anything."
Then those musicians went together to the place where the group of six monks was, prostrated at their feet, and said:

"We pray that the Venerable Ones will explain for us how, in the past, when the Buddha was a Bodhisattva, he made four kinds of observations while in the Tuṣita Heaven palace, just before he was about to descend to be born within Jambudvīpa."

Please recount all such circumstances as follows: how he performed his various duties according to the needs of each of the six heavens of the desire realm; his descent into his mother’s womb and his birth; his gradual growth to childhood and his departure from the city for excursions where he beheld old age, sickness, and death; his subsequent retreat into the forest to practice austerities for six years; and how, finding those paths to be of no benefit, he attained perfect enlightenment to universally deliver the deluded masses. Please explain all such events.
The group of six replied,
"Having heard this, what do you intend to do?
The musicians said:
"I wish to set this to music and arrange it as a song.
When Udāyin heard this, he said: "Fool!..."
“You must take these supreme matters of our Buddha’s Dharma and set them to song and melody; you may depart at once, for I cannot explain them to you.
Then the musicians departed in silence and went to a nunnery, where they approached the bhikṣuṇī Ghosilā (Tulānanda) and, having paid their respects, said:

“We pray that the Noble One will proclaim for us: how the Buddha, in the past when he was a bodhisattva, descended from Tuṣita Heaven to be born here below, and so forth, until he universally rescued all deluded beings. We pray that you will tell us this.”
When Tullanandā heard this, she said, "You wish to hear this; what do you intend to do?
The musician replied:
"I now wish to take this matter and set it to strings and pipes to compose a dance.
The nun then replied, "We must first establish an agreement; only then may I recount it."
"If you give me the price for the cakes and fruit, I shall preach for you," the musician said.
"This is a small matter; I shall certainly pay it."

The nun Tullānandā, who was possessed of great learning and well-versed in the Tripitaka, then expounded for them the account from the stage of birth up until the attainment of enlightenment; having heard it, the musicians all took those events and incorporated them into their songs.
At that time, the musicians said to one another:
"This excellent event causes those with faith and reverence to feel great joy; by what means can we cause even those who lack faith to give rise to a joyful heart?"
"I shall perform both arts simultaneously, so that those who believe and those who do not will all cry out, 'Excellent!

He then went everywhere searching for something extraordinary and returned to the monastery. There he saw the bhikṣu Chanda, who, having finished eating his fill, had abandoned his dignified deportment; suddenly, a donor arrived with exquisite food and drink to give to Chanda.
At that time, Chanda, desiring to eat more, washed his hands, received the food, and went to where Udāyin was.
Udāyin had not yet risen from his meal; Chanda immediately crouched down before him and spoke these words:
"Venerable Udāyin, please take heed!"

"I, the bhikṣu Chanda, have already finished my meal; yet having obtained such excellent food and drink as this, I now wish to eat more. I pray that you will perform for me the ritual of 'leftover food' (paryuṣitakalpa)."
Then Udāyin took two or three mouthfuls and said, "Go;
this is your food, so eat it as you please.
When that musician saw this, he thought to himself:
"By means of this favorable opportunity, if I were to perform it, I could cause even those who lack faith to give rise to joy.

Thinking thus, he went to that place of entertainment; there, shaking a hand-drum (*tāla*), he gathered a great multitude and performed various musical arts. Beginning from the Bodhisattva’s descent from Tuṣita Heaven down to his universal salvation of all deluded beings, he rendered everything into orchestral music and performed grand dances.
