Those who were respectful and faithful gave rise to a sense of wonder, all saying:
"How marvelous!
This musician is truly skilled at singing."
He bestowed many gifts and bribes, which were extraordinary compared to others of his station.
At that time, the musician thought further:
"Those who do not believe must ultimately be drawn toward the truth."
He then had one person assume the form of Chanda and sent another to take on the appearance of Udāyin; they sat back down and began to eat.
The one in the form of Chanda took a clay bowl, filled it with ashes, and placed sugar-candy on top;
he then crouched before Udāyin and said, "Venerable Udāyin, please attend to me!"

"Venerable Ānanda, I have already eaten my fill, yet I have obtained such excellent food and drink that my heart desires to eat more. I pray that you will perform for me the ritual of 'leftover food' (paryuṣitakalpa)."
At that time, the musician Udāyin took some granulated sugar and, placing a bowl of ash over the man's head, said to him:
"This is your property; eat it as you please."
At that time, those who were faithless saw this rarity and all laughed aloud, shouting words of praise and joy, and bestowed much precious wealth upon him.
After the crowd had dispersed following the performance, the spectators recounted the events to others in the places they went, in the same sequence as before.
The six bhikṣus heard the report from one another and discussed it among themselves, saying:
"Ignorant performers have imitated our forms and used them as a spectacle of curiosity within the theater."
"I should now do something unbeneficial for that son of a courtesan.
They then said to one another,
"We ought to go before our sisters and reminisce about our past playthings."
He then went to her and said, "Sister!

Regarding the deeds performed by our World-Honored One when he was a Bodhisattva, there was at that time a musician named Gālavā who took those Bodhisattva practices and set them to song and instrumental music."
"Although we may forget some things while watching, we shall immediately sing them together so that nothing of the matter will be lost.

They then went to the site of the two shrines; not far from there, they set up a performance arena, shielding the sides with blue cloth and covering it above with red curtains. Once the arrangements were complete, the group of six monks arrived together.

At that time, Upānanda immediately donned secular clothing, wrapped his head with a multicolored cloth, and beat a hand-drum (*tāḍa-kaṃsika*); the rest of his companions all performed as dancers and musicians.
As soon as the sound of the drum arose, the great assembly rushed there like clouds; they abandoned the site of the performance and gathered at this place.
At that time, the musicians heard their sounds as marvelous and extraordinary; they also came together to witness what they were doing, and all were struck as peerless.
They said to one another, "Are these beings gods?"
"Have nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, and others come here to sing and play?
Each person felt a sense of wonder and together they relinquished their wealth.
At that time, the group of six monks finished their performance and dispersed; they collected all the money and took it away with them.
At that time, the musicians also followed after them to observe their dwelling place; they saw the group of six enter the Bamboo Grove and remained at the gate to watch their activities.
At that time, Udāyin was outside the monastery gate with yellow orpiment still on the side of his ear.
When a musician saw him, he asked, "Was it you who performed the music just now? Are you not a noble one?"
He replied,
"It was my deliberate intent to humiliate you, you foolish man!
How could I allow you to rely upon my majestic power to sustain your livelihood, only to turn around and mock me, imitating my appearance before the assembly as a cause for derision?"
"If you go anywhere, I shall surely follow you, so that for a long time you shall have nothing at all to gain.
We will not lend you playthings to serve as a substitute;
you will find it exhausting to carry all these things."
Having seen these words, the man who was seeking favor entreated him, saying,
"I only pray that the Noble One will forgive me for this one transgression. Udāyin replied:
"If you obtain any wealth, you must give it all to me; let us make this solemn pact, and then I shall not follow you.
The musician deliberated and said, "If I do not give [the wealth] to you, my harassment will never cease."
"Therefore, at this time, we give everything to whoever receives it; consequently, we have returned to our original place and are all filled with grief.
A friend of theirs came and asked them, "Virtuous ones, for what reason do you each bear such sorrowful expressions?"
He replied, "I have now been punished; how could I not be distressed? He asked:
"Who is it? He replied,
"A son of the Śākyas."
He asked, "For what reason?
and she immediately informed him of all that had occurred in full detail.
At that time, his acquaintances were simultaneously filled with disdain and contempt, saying:
"How can a bhikṣu wear the white robes of a layperson and personally perform such acrobatic feats? Even though he is a musician, does he not still have to pay his dues?"
When the bhikṣus had heard these words, they reported them in full to the Blessed One.

At that time, the Blessed One assembled the community of bhikṣus and, having learned the facts through questioning regarding the worldly reproach, he said: "I, considering ten benefits, shall establish a training rule for the bhikṣus, which should be recited as follows:
'If a bhikṣu obtains new cloth, he must apply one of three types of discoloring dye.'"
Whether it be blue, mud-color, or red, it must be discolored by one of these;
if one uses it without having discolored it in these three ways, it is a pāyattika offense.
"Furthermore, regarding 'if a bhikṣu': this refers to the group of six; the remaining meanings are as explained above.
Regarding 'new clothing,' there are two kinds of new:
first, the substance of the garment is new; second, it is newly obtained from another."
In this context, "new" refers to new clothing.
There are seven types of clothing, as fully described above.
"Blue" refers to the color blue.
"Clay" refers to red stone.
"Red" refers to the red bark of trees.
"Dyeing it a discolored color" means to spoil its original white color.
If one uses [the garment] without disfiguring it with dye, the offense is the same as before.
What are the characteristics of the transgression in this case?
If any bhikṣus obtain a new robe and do not disfigure it with one of the three prescribed colors, they all incur a *pāyattika* offense.
There is no offense for one who is the very first offender, or for one who is insane, mentally deranged, or afflicted by intense pain.
*Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya*, Scroll 39; *Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya*, Scroll 40.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Yijing by Imperial Decree. 59.

The Training Rule on Taking Precious Objects. At that time, the Blessed One was staying at Vulture Peak Mountain near the city of Rājagṛha. During the first part of the day, he took up his robe and bowl, descended from Vulture Peak Mountain, and entered the city to beg for alms, with the Venerable Ānanda serving as his attendant.

At that time, encountering heavy rains from the heavens, the cliffs were washed away and collapsed, revealing a treasure-store deposited by people at the beginning of the eon, its radiance shimmering brilliantly.
The World-Honored One said to Ānanda:
"You should observe this: it is a great black serpent; it is a most deadly poison."
Ānanda said, "This is a fearsome poison. As he spoke these words,
a poor man who lived nearby, constantly gathering roots and fruits to sustain his life, heard the mention of "poison" and immediately thought to himself:
"I shall go and observe for myself what the nature of this so-called 'poisonous sting' is, lest it bite and harm me at night.
Having arrived at that place, he saw a hidden treasure whose radiance shone forth from the outside. Upon seeing it, the poor man was filled with joy and secretly thought to himself:
"May this venomous serpent always sting me; I shall not shrink from the pain even for the sake of my parents, wife, children, or any of my kinsmen.

Having thus covered it with leaves, he carefully carried it home and gradually built a dwelling. There, he provided for food and clothing, and together with his relatives, they enjoyed its benefits as they pleased, until he became exceedingly wealthy and prosperous.
At that time, Ajātaśatru had killed his father and established himself as king. He then dispatched messengers to travel throughout the kingdom and cities to see who possessed great wealth.

When those messengers encountered someone who had discovered a hidden treasure—whose house was flourishing and whose food, clothing, and possessions were abundant, with servants, cattle, and sheep unlike any other day—they asked him:
"In former times you were poor, lacking both food and clothing; for what reason have you suddenly become so wealthy and prosperous today?"
"Is this not a case of having stolen the royal treasury?
He was immediately seized and brought before the king.
The king then asked:
“You have suddenly become wealthy; have you discovered my hidden treasure?
He then denied it. The king said, “This man has disobeyed my command;
according to the law, he deserves death. All his kinsmen shall be seized and imprisoned, and he himself must be executed.”
Then that jailer, intending to take the man away to be executed, spoke these words while on the road:
"Ānanda! This is a great black snake; this is a great and deadly poison."
Ānanda said, "This is a fearsome poison.
Now, according to the laws of the kingdom, whatever the person condemned to death says must be reported back; having seen these words, he immediately informed the king.
The king said,
"Summon him here.
Once he had arrived at the king's presence, the king questioned him himself:
"What is the meaning of what you have said?
The man related the events of the past in full detail.
At that time, the king conceived faith in the Blessed One for the first time and asked the man:
"Hey! Man, do you believe the Buddha's words?
He replied:
“Great King!
I truly have deep faith.
When the king heard this, his tears fell and soaked his robes, and he replied to that person, saying:
"I give this property to you; all your kinsmen are released.
When that man had been liberated, he was overcome with joy and thought to himself:
"All the wealth and prosperity of my household are due to the Blessed One. I should now pay homage at the feet of the Blessed One and invite the Buddha and the Sangha to take a meal at my home."

The full account continues until it is said that after he had eaten and heard the Dharma, he perceived the Four Noble Truths on that very seat and attained the fruit of stream-entry, as described at length elsewhere.
This was the origin of the event; at this point, the precept had not yet been established.

The Buddha was staying at Vulture Peak Mountain in the city of Rājagṛha. At that time, during the first part of the day, Upānanda took up his robes and bowl and entered the city to beg for food. On the way, he saw an archery instructor but did not pay him homage. Continuing his rounds from house to house, he eventually reached the archery hall, where he saw no master, only the students.
Upānanda said to the people, "You students of archery are wasting your days in vain; you have not yet achieved mastery."
He then took up his bow and arrows himself and shot to the left and right; every arrow he released hit its mark, and he declared:
"You all should seek out a preeminent master and learn these skills."
Having spoken thus, Upānanda departed.
When the archery master returned to the hall, the people saw him and failed to show him respect, asking:
"Why are you so exceptionally arrogant?"
The people replied,
"We have abandoned our livelihoods in order to learn skills, yet observing this situation, it seems we are merely wasting our days.
The Master asked them the reason for this, and they answered him fully regarding the matter.
Having heard these words, the teacher went to the monastery to seek out Upānanda. Upon finding him, he prostrated at his feet and spoke thus:
"Ācārya! This is the very means by which I sustain my life; I pray that you will show me compassion and not destroy it."
Upānanda replied, "Fool! Archery is my craft;
you have sought your livelihood from me without offering any honorarium."
The man prostrated and apologized, saying, "As for what has already passed, please do not hold me accountable. From this day forward, I shall strictly obey your instructions.
He immediately sold his archery equipment and sent the proceeds to Upānanda, then went to the archery hall and remained there with a heavy heart.
His friends asked him, "Why are you so sorrowful?
He answered them with the facts of the matter; when the people heard this, they immediately began to criticize him.
“The Śramaṇas, sons of the Śākyas, act contrary to the Dharma; how is it that they have caused those who teach archery to fall into such poverty?
This was also an occasion for the origin [of a rule], yet the precept had not yet been established.

The introductory circumstances were the same as before. Having entered the city to beg for alms, Upānanda eventually made his way through the houses until he reached a music hall. Seeing that the master was not there, he took the musical instruments himself and performed the eightfold orchestra. The full account is as related previously, until it came to pass that the man who had sold the musical instruments fell into poverty.
This was also a case of dependent origination, and the precept had not yet been established.
At that time, the World-Honored One, teaching and transforming beings according to conditions, traveled from Rājagṛha to Vaiśālī and stayed in the High-Roofed Hall.

At that time, during the first part of the day, Upānanda took up his robes and bowl and entered the city to beg for alms; on the way, he saw many young boys of the Licchavis who had set aside their ornaments and were playing together.
When Upānanda saw the necklace, he assumed it was the property of a yakṣa and immediately took it.
When the children saw him take the necklace, they all rushed forward in competition to pull at his hands and feet, scattering dust and dirt over him, until he finally returned the necklace.
When Upānanda returned to the monastery with his body covered in dust, the bhikṣus saw him and asked, "Did you play together with the children?
Upānanda answered the matter in detail; this was also the origin of the incident, though the precept had not yet been established.

The Buddha was staying in Vaiśālī. When the six groups of bhikṣus entered the city to beg for alms, they passed by the Āmrapālī Garden; entering the garden, they saw various musical instruments and immediately took up drums and cymbals, playing them according to the proper method, producing sounds like the music performed by King Śuddhodana and the resonance of the war drums of Ajātaśatru.
When the people within the city heard this sound, they were all greatly terrified and spoke thus:
"It must surely be King Ajātaśatru who has come to attack our country."
They immediately arrayed their weapons and armor and went out through the great city gate to confront the enemy.
At that time, the group of six monks abandoned the drums and music and all went outside the garden. When the people saw the group of six monks approaching, they asked:
"Noble ones!..."
"Where are the troops belonging to King Ajātaśatru now?
The group of six replied,
"For what reason would that Ajātaśatru come here?"
He asked, "If they have not come, for what reason does that war drum resound?
The group of six replied:
"We were merely joking; these are not the King's troops.
The others replied, "You should depart at once and stay not here; when the Vṛji people arrive, they will surely humiliate you."
He immediately returned to the monastery.
The bhikṣus asked him,
"For what reason have you returned with an empty bowl?"
He answered with the facts as they were.
Upon hearing these words, the bhikṣus of few desires all felt resentment and contempt, saying:
"How can bhikṣus together perform such unseemly acts?"
...and so on, until he reported this to the Buddha, explaining it in detail as before.
The Buddha said:
"Observing ten benefits, I shall establish this training rule (śikṣāpada). It should be recited as follows:"
"If a bhikṣu should himself take hold of, or cause another to take hold of, precious objects or things belonging to precious objects, it is a pāyattika.
At that time, the World-Honored One departed from Vaiśālī and traveled to Śrāvastī in the kingdom of Kośala, where he stayed at the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.

At that time, Viśākhā Mṛgāramātṛ, hearing that the Buddha had arrived and wishing to pay him homage, prepared various necklaces and ornaments to adorn her body completely. However, as she was by nature modest and felt a sense of shame upon about to see the Buddha, she eventually removed her ornaments and entrusted them to her attendants; she then put on fresh white garments and entered to see the World-Honored One.
Having prostrated at the Buddha’s feet and heard the sublime Dharma, he rose from his seat and departed.
At that time, his attendant placed the necklace beneath the flowering tree and subsequently forgot to take it home.
At that time, Ānanda, seeing those necklaces, thought to himself:
"The prohibition established by the World-Honored One shall now be relaxed because of this.
He immediately took them up and went to inform the Buddha. The Buddha said:
"Excellent! Excellent, Ānanda!"
Although I have not yet granted you permission, you already know the time.
When reciting the precepts, one should say:
"Except for the causes and conditions of the time."
At another time, Viśākhā asked her attendant,
"Bring me the necklace.
He replied:
"I forgot to bring it from under the tree in the monastery," he replied,
"I shall go to fetch it."
Having heard these words, the son said to his mother, "Would it not be better to have him bring it from the storehouse?
There are many people in the monastery, and that object would surely be lost.
His mother said:
"I have never lost anything since birth; you need only go and take it, and you will certainly obtain it.
Following these instructions, the attendant went to the monastery, and upon seeing him, Ānanda handed over the necklace.
The attendants brought it there, and the mother said to her son, "I have not lost my wealth; these words are not false.
The son thought to himself:
"I shall test whether this is true or not," he thought,
and he took his mother's gold-sealed ring and threw it into the well;
when the water was drawn, it was recovered along with the water.
The son threw it back into the river again, where a fish saw it and swallowed it;
a fisherman caught it and took it to the market to sell, and the family bought it home and cut open its belly to find [the jewel].
He further discarded a golden bag on the road; those who saw it at the time all thought it was a snake and avoided it, but the son returned to pick it up.
After conducting various such tests, he finally realized that his mother had not lost any of her belongings.
Furthermore, there was a bhikṣu who, while walking outside the monastery, saw a discarded purse of gold; he took it and departed.
Later, someone came along, and the bhikṣu asked him, "Is this your purse?"
The man replied,
"Yes," and then gave it to him to take away.
Next, a man came running up in haste and asked the bhikṣu,
"Did you see my gold bag?
He replied:
"I have already entrusted him to him.
Upon hearing this, the man died in deep distress.
The World-Honored One, knowing this, addressed the bhikṣus:
"One should not give it away to others so hastily.
One should give it only to those whose responses correspond to the signs of its provenance; do not give it to those who do not.
Furthermore, there was a bhikṣu who saw a bag full of gold being discarded and left the place; the Buddha said:
"One should not discard it; rather, one should cover it with leaves.
He covered it with leaves, discarded it, and departed. The Buddha said:
"One should not discard it; it may be covered with some other material."

One should remain at that location for seven or eight days, coming and going to keep watch; if someone comes to claim it, one should question them and, if they are the rightful owner, give it to them.
If they are not the rightful owner, one should bring it back to the monastery and store it in the monastic treasury.
If, after five or six months, someone comes to claim it as their own, it should be returned to them if they can identify it correctly;
if no one comes to claim it, one should purchase durable goods with this property and put it to use.
If a claimant appears later and the description matches, one should show him the object, saying:
"This is your property that you purchased; take it as you please.
If he demands interest, one should reply to him:
"Your property was rightfully lost; that you have recovered it should bring you joy.
Why do you fail to recognize this kindness and instead seek further gain?
At that time, the World-Honored One, for these reasons, assembled the community of bhikṣus and, praising the observance of the precepts, declared:
"The former was an original enactment; this is a subsequent allowance.
Furthermore, having considered ten benefits, I establish this training rule for the bhikṣus, which should be recited as follows:

'If a bhikṣu should himself take hold of a jewel or anything belonging to a jewel, or cause another to take hold of it, except when inside a monastery or in the house of a layperson, it is a pāyattika.'"
If one sees jewels or things belonging to the category of jewels within a monastery or in the house of a layperson, one should form this thought before taking them:
"If there is anyone who recognizes these, I shall give them back to him."
"This is the proper time.
As for "if it is again a bhikṣu," this refers to the group of six [monks].
"Jewels" refers to the seven precious gems.
Regarding "precious objects," this refers to various weapons such as bows and swords, as well as musical instruments such as drums and flutes.
Whether one takes them up oneself or causes another to do so, the offense is established; the details are as explained above.
If a bhikṣu, whether in a monastery or in a layperson’s house, sees such things as precious objects, he is permitted to take them up after first forming this thought:
"Should the owner come, I shall hold this for him and return it."
In this regard, what are the characteristics of the offense and how does it occur?
If a bhikṣu takes various precious objects with his own hand or causes another to take them—whether they have been polished or not—he incurs a *pāyattika* offense.
If they have not been polished, he incurs only a *dukkaṭa* offense; this applies even to taking imitation lapis lazuli, for which there is also a *dukkaṭa* offense.
If one grasps ornaments for adorning the body, such as necklaces and so forth, one incurs a *pāyattika* offense;
even grasping a garland made from barley stalks constitutes a *dukkaṭa*.
If one grasps various musical instruments such as the lute (*vīṇā*) that possess strings and frets, one incurs a *pāyattika* offense.
To play a stringless instrument is an *dukkaṭa* (offense of wrong-doing); even to play a one-stringed lute made from a bamboo tube, holding it is also an *dukkaṭa*.
If various conch shells are fit to be blown, grasping them constitutes a *pācittiya* (offense entailing confession);
if they are not fit to be blown, it is an *dukkaṭa*.
Whether musical instruments are fit for use or unfit, the gravity of the offense incurred is explained in the same manner.
If one holds a bow that has a string and a grip, one incurs a *pārājika* (defeat) offense;
if it lacks these, it is an *dukkaṭa* (wrongdoing).
If a knife has a blade or an arrow has a point, one incurs the full offense;
otherwise, it is an *dukkaṭa* (wrongdoing).
This applies even to bows made of hair or arrows made of grass stalks; these also all constitute *dukkaṭa*.
If the image contains relics, one commits an offense of downfall (pāyattika) by taking hold of it;
if it contains no relics, it is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
There is no offense if one lifts and carries it while perceiving it as the Great Teacher.
Furthermore, there is no offense for one who is the very first offender, or for one who is insane, mentally deranged, or overwhelmed by intense pain.
At that time, all the bhikṣus had doubts and asked: "By what causes and conditions did Mother Viśākhā not lose her wealth?"
The Buddha addressed the bhikṣus:
"Listen, all of you!
In the distant past, after the parinirvāṇa of Kāśyapa Buddha, there was an elderly woman who faithfully observed the precepts."

At that time, King Kṛkin’s palace women were playing in a garden when they lost their pearl necklaces. An old woman there found these necklaces and, intending to seek out their original owners, tied them to the top of a bamboo pole.
At that time, the king sent men to search for this necklace; having found it with the old woman, they presented it to the king.
When the king saw the object, he was delighted and marveled at its extraordinary nature. He sighed in praise of the old woman and asked her:
"Since you possess such a virtuous heart, you are worthy of noble reward; what do you desire now?"
The old woman said to the king:
"I have no further desires and seek no immediate benefit; my only wish is that, by virtue of this cause, I may attain the fruit of never losing my wealth in whatever place I am born in future lives."
"Because of that pure mind in the past, he now receives this fruit. The old mother of former times was none other than the present mother Viśākhā.
Because she did not conceal another's property and made a vow through the power of that resolve, although she lost precious wealth in life after life, she ultimately recovered it."
"Therefore, monks, when you obtain another's property, do not steal it and hide it away; thus you should train yourselves. 60.
The Training Rule on Bathing at Improper Times. The Buddha was staying in Rājagṛha. At that time, there were three hot springs near this city.
First, the king bathes himself; second, the palace attendants; third, various other people.
Where the king bathes, the bhikṣus also bathe; where the palace attendants bathe, the bhikṣuṇīs also bathe.
At that time, while the six bhikṣus were bathing, they thought to themselves:
"We shall now test the depth of the king's faith.

Intending to cause him annoyance, they lingered for a long time and did not emerge promptly. Consequently, the king sent men to fetch water elsewhere and bathed using that, rather than entering the hot spring.
Having bathed, he went to where the Buddha was, prostrated at his feet, listened to the sublime Dharma, and took his leave of the Buddha to depart.
When the Venerable Ānanda heard of this matter, he went to inform the Buddha. The Buddha said:
"Because the bhikṣus have been bathing, this fault has arisen; therefore, the bhikṣus should not bathe."
At that time, the bhikṣus had not washed their bodies and were covered in much grime and oiliness. When they went for alms, brahmins and householders saw them and asked, "Noble ones!..."
"Is it that you, O virtuous ones, carry filth upon your bodies while considering yourselves pure?
For what reason do you not wash?
At that time, the bhikṣus reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"One should bathe every half-month.
During the hot season, because those bhikṣus did not wash frequently, their bodies became withered and pale.
When people saw them, they asked:
"Noble one, why do you appear to be ill?
He replied, "It is because the Blessed One does not permit frequent washing of the body; due to that, I have become thus afflicted by heat."
The people said, "The World-Honored One,
out of great compassion, will surely grant permission for this occasion.
They reported the matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"One should wash during the heat.
A certain bhikṣu was ill, and his physician told him to wash;
he replied, "The World-Honored One does not permit it."
They reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said, “When one is ill, one should wash.

Later, when bhikṣus were engaged in communal work or at a stūpa and their bodies became soiled and impure, people saw them and spoke with contempt. They reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"One should wash while performing [the task].

When the bhikṣus were traveling on the road, they became utterly exhausted from the coming and going and lay down, casting their bodies upon the ground. People saw this and, finding it strange, asked:
"Virtuous ones, why do you not exert yourselves in cultivating wholesome qualities, but instead remain here sleeping during the day?"
The bhikṣus reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said, "When traveling on the road, you should wash.

When the bhikṣus were blown by the wind and their bodies became covered in much dust and filth, making them unclean, people saw them and mocked them. They reported this again to the Buddha as before, and the Buddha said:
"When it is windy, one should wash.
Again, when touched by rain, and again when touched by wind and rain, the body became soiled with mud; they reported this to the Buddha as before, and the Buddha said:
"Whether it is raining or there is wind and rain, you should wash as you please."

At that time, the Blessed One praised the observance of the precepts, and so forth, until he said: "Having considered ten benefits, I establish this training rule for the bhikṣus, which should be recited as follows:
'If a bhikṣu bathes when it is not the half-month period for bathing, and does so intentionally, except during the [permitted] special times, it is an *pāyattika* offense.'"
The exceptions are: during the heat, during illness, during work, while traveling, during a windstorm, during rain, or during both wind and rain; these are the appropriate times.
"Furthermore, 'if a bhikṣu' refers to the group of six [monks].
'Should bathe every half-month' means that bathing once every fifteen days is permitted.
'To willfully contravene this' means to act in a manner that does not conform to the instruction."
"Except at other times" means that if it is at another time, there is no offense.

"The hot season" refers to the remaining one month and a half of spring—meaning the one month and a half during which one should enter the rains retreat, from the first day of the fourth month to the middle of the fifth month—as well as the first month of summer—meaning the month of entering the rains, from the sixteenth day of the fifth month to the middle of the sixth month. These two and a half months are called the period of extreme heat.
"Regarding 'when one is ill,' it refers to when a bhikṣu is sick such that he cannot remain at ease unless he bathes frequently.

Regarding 'when performing work,' it refers to tasks for the sake of the Triple Gem, even as small as sweeping a patch of ground the size of a mat, or occasionally scrubbing and smearing it like a cow's resting place."
"Time of walking" refers to one who travels one *yojana* or half a *yojana* and returns.
"Time of wind" refers to when the wind blows until even the corner of one's robe is shaken.
"During rain" refers to when even two or three drops of rain fall upon one's body.
"During wind and rain" means that both are present.
Regarding "this is the proper time," it refers to listening to the Dharma as permitted; the offense for violating this is the same as previously stated.
Regarding this, what are the characteristics of the offense and how does it occur?
Whenever a bhikṣu bathes during the permitted time, he must always maintain the observance through mental reflection and verbal declaration, saying:
"During such-and-such a period, I am now bathing."
If one does not maintain the vow, when washing the body with water that has not yet reached the navel, one incurs an *dukkaṭa* (wrongdoing);
when the water reaches the navel, one incurs a *pāyattika* (offense entailing expiation).
If one enters the water to wash, it should be understood that this applies accordingly.
If one first uses warm water and subsequently uses cold water as when bathing above, the offense incurred is the same as before.
Whether one first uses a pond and subsequently a river, etc., the matter is likewise the same.
At that time, there was a bhikṣu who had an invitation to attend on the other side of a river; not daring to enter the water to go to that invitation, the Buddha said:
"You should go; do not harbor any doubt."
A bhikṣu was crossing a river on business when he tripped and fell into the water; he felt doubt and regret, and the Buddha said, "There is no offense.
A bhikṣu fell from a bridge while crossing and fainted; seeing this, others sprinkled him with water, and once the bhikṣu had risen, he immediately felt doubt and regret. The Buddha said:
"There is no offense.
Furthermore, "no offense" refers to the very first person to commit the act, or one who is insane, mentally deranged, or overwhelmed by intense physical pain.
The seventh summary verse says:
Killing animals, causing distress, Prodding, and waking those sleeping together in water;
Frightening, concealing requisites, and seeking a robe; Groundless [accusations], and traveling the same road with a woman.
61. The Training Rule on Killing Animals, the sixty-first. The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī.
At that time, the Venerable Udāyin entered the city for alms during the first watch of the day and eventually arrived at an archery hall.
The master had gone out, leaving only the students behind; they saw that the targets set up in the archery area were not properly aligned with the mark.
Then Udāyin took five arrows and looked up into the sky; at that moment, a crow was flying overhead.
Udāyin shot four arrows to block the four sides of the bird’s path, causing it to fly upward; he then pierced it with an arrow from its mouth as it emerged.
He said to the students, "Young men, you should seek such a teacher and learn this craft."
Later, when the archery instructor returned to the archery hall with his disciples, they related the matter in detail. The master thought to himself:
"I must not allow these bhikṣus to come here frequently and disturb me."
He immediately devised a stratagem, having those youths take a dead crow, tie it to a bamboo pole, and follow behind Udāyin, so that its foul odor would pervade the ten directions as they spoke thus:
"Venerable sirs, you should know!..."
"The Venerable Udāyin possesses such skill that he can drop feathered arrows from the air into the bellies of crows.
When the brahmins and householders witnessed this, they each gave rise to derision and reproach, saying:
"How can a bhikṣu take up bows and arrows himself to kill various birds?"
"In this case, the meat is unfit for consumption and the sinews and skin are useless; thus, you have committed an evil deed in an improper place.
When the bhikṣus of few desires heard this, they felt revulsion and shame, and reported the matter to the Buddha.
At that time, the Blessed One spoke at length as before, up until: “Having considered ten benefits, I establish this training rule for the bhikṣus, which should be recited as follows:
‘If a bhikṣu intentionally takes the life of an animal, it is a pāyattika.’”
"Furthermore, 'if a bhikṣu' refers to Udāyin; the remaining meanings are as explained above.
'Intentionally' clarifies that it was not an error.
'A beast' refers to a flying bird or any other species of fowl or animal."
"Taking life" means severing the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*).
The explanation of the offense is the same as before.
In this context, what are the characteristics of the transgression and its specific details?
Regarding the statement "taking the life of a sentient being," it refers to employing the three modes—
internal, external, and both— to apply the means of terminating that life-force.
If a bhikṣu, with the intent to kill, harms even a single animal as little as with a finger, and because of this the animal's life ends, he incurs a *pāyattika* offense.
If one does not die at that time but dies later as a result of it, one incurs a *pāyattika* offense;
if one does not die later either, one incurs a *dukkaṭa* offense.
Thus it is explained in detail, as fully set forth previously in the training rule concerning the taking of human life.
Furthermore, there is no offense for one who is a first-time offender, as explained extensively before.

62. The Training Rule on Intentionally Annoying a Bhikṣu. The sixth and twelfth training rule concerning intentionally annoying a bhikṣu. The Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.

At that time, Mahāmaudgalyāyana ordained seventeen individuals and conferred upon them full ordination (*upasampadā*). Those seventeen individuals then began to associate with the group of six monks (*ṣaḍvargika-bhikṣu*).
Then Udāyin said to the seventeen individuals:
"Venerable ones!..."
"You all must perform such and such tasks for me.
They replied, "We cannot do it;
how could you, O Venerable One, be our ācārya or upādhyāya and command us to perform manual labor?"
When Udāyin saw these words, he immediately expelled them and would not allow them to dwell with him.
Thereupon, the group of seventeen monks went to another place to engage in recitation. Udāyin then went to Upānanda and said:
"Does the Elder know?..."
"These young novices do not accept my words; what should be done about this?

Upānanda said, "You should now cause those young novices to each feel vexation and regret so that they abandon their studies. You must speak these words, explaining at length the causes of their distress."
When Udāyin had heard these instructions, he acted exactly as told and said to the group of seventeen:
"Venerable ones!
Are you truly able to attain the exhaustion of outflows and enter the assembly of those fixed in rightness?"

"Since you have all received full ordination by misrepresenting your age, you lack the foundation of the precepts and thus no wholesome qualities can arise; such is the detailed explanation, continuing until it says that the ritual procedure is invalid."
Then the group of seventeen monks reported this matter to Mahāmaudgalyāyana.
At that time, Mahāmaudgalyāyana, in order to dispel their doubts and remorse, addressed them again, saying:
"The Buddha has declared that the first person [to commit such an act] is not guilty; how much more so is it that you have committed no transgression?"
"Furthermore, who spoke such words to you all as to cause you to feel regret?
They replied, "Venerable Udāyin!"
When the bhikṣus of few desires heard these words, they felt contempt and disparagement, saying:
"How can a bhikṣu intentionally cause another bhikṣu to feel regret and distress?
They reported this matter to the Buddha, and after the full explanation, [the Buddha] established the training rule, which should be recited as follows:
"If a bhikṣu intentionally harasses another bhikṣu, even to the extent of causing him a moment of displeasure, and acts with this as his motive, it is a pāyattika.
"If a bhikṣu" refers to Udāyin; the remaining meanings are as explained above.
Thus, "distress" means causing the mind to give rise to remorse and initiate regret.
"Displeasure for a short time" refers to the state where the mind is not at ease for even a brief moment.
That which serves as the condition for this is nothing other than these matters.
The offense is established as described above.
In this context, what are the characteristics of the transgression and the specific details of the case?
This refers to questioning him about specific matters and questioning him regarding what is consistent with the Vinaya teachings.
What is meant by questioning him about specific matters?
If a bhikṣu, with a mind intent on causing disturbance, approaches another bhikṣu and speaks as follows:
“Venerable one!
Do you remember such-and-such a king and such-and-such a householder?
He replied:
"It has been a long time since he was here; I do not remember him.
He replied, "Venerable sir!"
"If it was not a long time ago and you do not remember, then he must have received full ordination before reaching the age of twenty; he should be ordained again.
Even if that bhikṣu does not feel resentment when these words are spoken, this [accusing] bhikṣu still incurs a *pāyattika* offense.
He asked him thus:
"Do you remember such-and-such a time when there was a solar eclipse, a lunar eclipse, a year of famine, or a year of plenty?
He spoke at length as above.
What is questioning in accordance with the Vinaya teachings?
For example, one asks with a mind of malice, saying:
"Venerable sir!..."
"In what place did you previously receive full ordination?
He replied, "In such-and-such a place."
He replied:

"In that place there was originally no great boundary (mahā-sīmā), nor was a formal boundary established for the assembly; thus, they became separated in residence, and your full ordination (upasampadā) was not properly received. You should receive it again."
He asked again:
"Venerable one!
Who are your ācārya and upādhyāya?"
He replied,
“They are my two teachers.
He [the other] responded:
"That person has broken the precepts and is unfit to be your teacher; therefore, you cannot be said to have properly received full ordination.
He asked again:
"Did you go to such-and-such a place?"
He replied, "I am going.

[The other] said, "If you go to that place, it will be filled with people who are foolish and immoral, or those of base and evil character; they are not virtuous companions, and you will certainly break the precepts."
When one speaks such words as these to disturb another, whether that person is actually disturbed or not, if they merely hear and take it to heart, one incurs a *pāyattika* offense.
Again he asked:
"Venerable One!"
"Did you take the robes of the two teachers? He replied, "I did."
He replied:
"If you take it, because you have a thieving intent, you will commit a defeat (pārājika). He asked:
"Venerable one!
Have you ever spoken of the impermanence of all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*), the selflessness of all phenomena (*dharma*), and the tranquility of nirvāṇa?
He replied:
"I say so. He replied:

"If you claim such a state of superior human attainment, you commit a *pārājika* offense; if you speak thus with a mind intent on causing confusion and disturbance, you all incur a *pāyattika* offense."
In this regard, there is no offense if, for example, a bhikṣu goes to another bhikṣu and asks:
"Venerable friend,
do you remember such-and-such a king or such-and-such a householder?"
He replied, "I do not remember.
The other said:
"Venerable one!
A long time has passed since he was ordained; even if you do not remember it, he has indeed completed twenty years and has properly received full ordination.
Furthermore, regarding solar and lunar eclipses, as well as years of abundance or famine, these should be understood as explained above.
This is called asking about a specific matter.
For example, if a bhikṣu goes to where another bhikṣu is and asks:
"Venerable sir!..."
"In what place did you previously receive full ordination?
He replied, "In such-and-such a place."
He replied, "I know a certain place where there was previously a great boundary (mahā-sīmā) and an established site for ordination; you may then properly receive full ordination.
He asked this of the two preceptors.
Question: Where is he going?
Question: Is he taking his teacher's robe?
Answer: [He is]...
"This is all without fault.
He asked again:
"Venerable sir!"
"You have spoken of the impermanence of all conditioned phenomena, up to the tranquility of nirvāṇa.
He replied, "I have spoken."
He replied,
"Did you not claim for yourself that you had attained this state of a superior person?
He answered:
"No. If one speaks according to what has been said, there is likewise no fault; this is called a question that accords with the Vinaya teachings.
Furthermore, regarding "one who has not committed an offense," this refers to the very first person to commit such an act, as explained in detail above.
63. The Training Rule on Probing with Fingers. The sixth and thirtieth training rule concerning probing with fingers. The Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.

At that time, after Mahāmaudgalyāyana had ordained the group of seventeen, as described at length, whenever there was any task to be performed, those seventeen would inspect one another and assist each other in its completion, as detailed in the previous section on the precept concerning killing.

At that time, sixteen people begged one man for his forgiveness; seeing that he remained silent, they all began poking him with their fingers until he burst into loud laughter, which resulted in his death.
A bhikṣu of few desires heard of this and felt revulsion and shame, thinking:
"How can a bhikṣu use his fingers to poke and tickle, thereby severing another's life-faculty?
He reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"Expounded at length, up to: 'I, having considered ten benefits, shall establish this training rule for the bhikṣus, which should be recited as follows:
If a bhikṣu should tickle another with his finger, it is a pāyattika.'"
"Furthermore, regarding 'if a bhikṣu': this refers to the group of seventeen [monks]; the remaining meanings are as explained above.
'Striking with a finger' refers to a physical act (kāyakarman); the determination of the offense is as explained above."
Regarding the characteristics of the offense herein, what are its specific details?
If a bhikṣu strikes or tickles another with a single finger, he incurs one *pāyattika* offense;
up to five fingers, he incurs five offenses.
If one strikes or tickles with a fist, one incurs one *pāyattika* offense.
If one uses a toe, it should be understood that the same applies as for the hand.

If one points with the tip of a finger toward a freckle, or points toward a sore, or points toward a mosquito or insect, or points toward a whorl of hair (*āvarta*), there is no offense in any such case.
Furthermore, there is no offense for one who is the very first person to commit such an act; the details are as explained above.
The Sixty-fourth Training Rule: Sporting in Water. The Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, among the group of seventeen, there was a senior bhikṣu named Upāli. Having severed all afflictions and realized the fruit of arhatship, he thought to himself:
"I shall first examine those with whom I have long lived together in the holy life; who among this assembly possesses roots of goodness?"
"Who lacks roots of goodness?
Having observed this, he already knows that there are those who are bound;
he knows they belong to him.
At that time, Upāli acted as his guide, and by means of this skillful arrangement, they went together to the Aṭṭhala-vati River.
Having strained the water and filled the jars, and having observed the water with right mindfulness and focused attention for the purpose of bathing, he finished his bath and stood to one side.

At that time, the sixteen men also all bathed; having entered the river, they now floated and now submerged, sometimes going to the opposite bank and sometimes returning to this one; they followed the waves or went against the current, some beating water-drums, some striking water-frogs, some making water-ropes, and some making water-mortars. Performing various such musical entertainments, their bodies and hands agitated, they laughed and played together.
At that time, King Śrīghana, from atop his high tower, saw their performance from afar and said to Queen Vaśavattī:
"Observe for a moment this field of merit to which you hold such great esteem."
The lady said to the king: "Great King!
These youths possess full and vigorous countenances, yet they are able to practice the holy life; Your Majesty does not marvel at this."
"Although the King is advanced in years, he has not yet attained tranquility; why then should his playing in the water be censured?
At that time, the Venerable Upāli, observing the King's mind and perceiving that he had conceived a sense of contempt, wished to inspire faith in him and said to the people:
"Gentlemen, each of you should adjust your robes and, taking water jars together, let us return to our residence."
Then, by means of his supernormal powers, Upāli and his fellow practitioners of the holy life each ascended into the air and flew past above the king’s palace.
At that time, Queen Vaidehī looked down at their shadows and gazed up at this marvel, whereupon she said to the king:
"Your Majesty, behold these most excellent fields of merit as they soar through the sky."
The king said,
"My lady! How could there be one who has realized arhatship playing in the water?"
The lady replied, “This is indeed what Your Majesty has heard and known; however, there are matters you have not yet heard and do not know.
The king said:
"What do you mean?

The lady replied, "The mind is like a flash of lightning, changing in an instant; yet with firm concentration as steadfast as a diamond, one shatters the delusions of ignorance in a single kṣaṇa. Your Majesty should not find this strange."
Having heard these words, the King remained silent and gave no reply.
Then, Lady Śrīmālā, having witnessed this event, sent a messenger to pay homage to the World-Honored One and to submit this request:
"I have seen the noble ones sporting in the water; I pray that the World-Honored One will take heed of these noble ones and ensure they do not continue their playful diversions in the water."
At that time, having heard this matter, the Blessed One—up to—"I, considering ten benefits, shall establish a training rule for the bhikṣus, which should be spoken thus:
'If a bhikṣu again plays in water, it is a pāyattika.'"
"Furthermore, regarding 'if a bhikṣu': this refers to the group of seventeen [novices]; the remaining meanings are as explained above.
If a bhikṣu plays in water—performing such acts as floating, submerging, or tossing about as described above—he incurs an offense of defeat (pārājika)."
In this regard, what are the characteristics of an offense and how does it occur?
There are nine matters that can give rise to an offense.
What are these nine?

That is to say: taking pleasure oneself and inciting others to take pleasure; playing oneself and inciting others to play; leaping oneself and inciting others to leap; agitation, dallying with shadows, and mutual striking or slapping of the body.

If a bhikṣu, with the intention of playing in water, rises from his bed, takes up his robes, goes to a river or pond, removes his upper garment, puts on a bathing skirt, and enters the water, he incurs a *duṣkṛta* (wrongdoing) for everything from the moment he enters until he has not yet submerged;
once his body is submerged, he incurs a *pāyattika* (offense involving forfeiture).
The same applies when exiting [the water].
If one acts with the intention of seeking coolness, there is no offense whether entering or emerging.
However, if one goes from this shore to the other shore, from the other shore to this shore, or travels with or against the current, in all such cases, one commits a *pāyattika* (offense of falling).
If one acts with the intention of learning to swim, there is no offense.
However, if one beats the water like a drum—as extensively explained before—down to even making a sound by snapping the fingers, one incurs a *pāyattika* (offense of falling).
If one plays with water contained in jars, pots, bowls, or vessels, it is a *pāyattika* offense;
even snapping one's fingers [in such a manner] constitutes a *dukkaṭa* offense.
If one beats a sound like a drum on a soup bowl, or even draws patterns with one's finger while harboring a playful intent, one incurs a *dukkaṭa* offense.
There is no offense for one who intends to cool [the fever].
Furthermore, there is no offense for a first-time offender, as explained in detail above.

The sixty-fifth training rule: On sleeping in the same room as a woman. The sixty-fifth training rule on sleeping in the same room as a woman. The Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the Venerable Āniruddha severed all fetters and delusions and realized arhatship. Having personally attained the supreme bliss of liberation, he thought to himself:
"The World-Honored One has bestowed great kindness upon me; what deed might I perform for the World-Honored One to repay his virtue?"
"I should now benefit sentient beings; this is what is called the most excellent way of repaying their kindness.
Having formed this thought, he took up his robes and bowl and traveled among the people until he reached a certain village.
In this village there was an elder who had two sons and one daughter.
When the daughter reached maturity, her conduct was not chaste or disciplined. Because the two brothers were competing with others, those others said to them:
"Your sister, though not yet married, has been having illicit relations with an outsider."
Having heard this, the brothers questioned their sister as to its truth or falsehood.
The sister replied immediately, "I am indeed pure and disciplined; it is the people of the world who speak falsely."
Not long thereafter, she became pregnant. Her brothers asked her, "You claimed to be pure and disciplined; where did you obtain this?
The sister replied:
"Once, a bald man forced himself upon me, and because of that, I became pregnant.
Later, she gave birth to a son; people of the time called him "Baldy," and the mother was known as "Mother Baldy."
At that time, when the Venerable Āniruddha had arrived at this village and the sun was about to set, he sought a place to stay for the night.
Then the youths replied,
"Noble One!..."
"There is the house of a woman with a bald son in that place; you will surely be allowed to stay there for the night.
Then the Venerable Aniruddha went immediately as instructed and sought lodging in that household.

At that time, the son of the shaven-headed woman consented to cohabit with him; she then conceived an illicit thought and, during the night, approached the Venerable One with the intent to embrace and seize him.
At that moment, the Venerable One, perceiving her evil intent, ascended into the air by means of his supernormal power.
Upon seeing this, the woman was struck with wonder; seeking his compassion and offering her apologies, she looked up and said, "I pray that the Noble One, out of pity for me, will descend."

At that time, for the sake of benefiting her, the Noble One lowered his body and preached the Dharma to her; having heard the Dharma, the woman’s mind was awakened and she realized the first fruit of the path.
When the next day arrived, her sister came back and was ridiculed, saying:
"Your sister is not only dragged away by worldly travelers; even a son of Śākyamuni has been ensnared."
Upon hearing this, the two of them were simultaneously seized with rage and went to his dwelling, intending to kill the bhikṣu.

At that time, the Venerable One, observing that the faculties of the two youths and all sentient beings had ripened, ascended into the air and manifested the eighteen transformations as a rare and wondrous feat.
At that time, the people from the four surrounding villages of that settlement all rushed there like clouds to witness this extraordinary phenomenon.
Once the Venerable One had resumed his seat, he immediately proclaimed the essentials of the Dharma for the assembly, enabling those brothers and twelve thousand others to all realize the Truth.
To speak at length, even Āniruddha, having seen such faults, no longer stayed overnight in the homes of laypeople.
On another occasion, Āniruddha was staying overnight in a garden at the edge of a village. That very night, a band of thieves intended to plunder the village by passing through the garden;
seeing the bhikṣu staying there, they consulted one another, saying, "We wish to steal wealth, yet we have encountered an inauspicious omen. We should now kill this bhikṣu."
At that time, the bandit general had previously been a laborer within the Venerable’s monastery; seeing him from afar, he recognized him and said to his men, "Gentlemen, you should know this!"

In the past, there was a merchant who entered the great ocean and encountered various perils and hardships; those who invoked his name returned in safety and well-being. Such a person as this should not be summarily put to death.
"Let us go into the village for now; it will not be too late to kill them on our way back if we do not obtain any goods.
The bandits followed one another into the village to plunder, and having acquired much wealth, they returned to the garden.

At that time, the Venerable One preached the essentials of the Dharma to the bandits, instructing, exhorting, benefiting, and gladdening them, causing them all to realize the Truth and attain the fruit of Stream-entry (*srotāpatti*).
Thereupon, those men left behind their stolen goods and returned them to the villagers of that village.
That night, a deity told the villagers:

"The goods stolen by the thieves from you all were preserved by the majestic spiritual power of the Venerable Āniruddha; all the property remains within the grove outside the village and has not been taken away. At daybreak, each of you should go there to retrieve it."

At that time, having heard the divine proclamation, the villagers waited until dawn and then proceeded to the grove. Upon reaching the Venerable One’s dwelling, they each prostrated at his feet and sat to one side. The Venerable One preached the Dharma for them, causing twelve thousand people to likewise realize the Truth.
At that time, there were five hundred members of that band of thieves who sought ordination under the Venerable One.

Then Āniruddha led those five hundred men to the presence of the World-Honored One. Upon seeing them arrive, the World-Honored One addressed them, saying, "Come, Bhikṣus. They all became ordained and immediately received full ordination; having received the Buddha’s instructions and admonitions, before long they all realized the fruit of Arhatship.
At that time, the bhikṣus asked the Venerable Āniruddha,
"Are you dwelling in peace and comfort?
He replied:
“There is the practice of peace and happiness, and there is also the practice of suffering.
He asked, “In what way?”
He replied:
"To benefit sentient beings is what constitutes my joyful practice; to have been beheaded many times is what constitutes my ascetic practice. He asked:
"Why? he replied, explaining in detail how he had stayed overnight at the courtesan's lodging.
The bhikṣus said:
"Is it appropriate to sleep in the same room as a woman?
He replied,
"It is precisely because it is inappropriate that this fault arises."
Upon hearing this, the bhikṣus of few desires felt revulsion and contempt, saying:
"How can a bhikṣu sleep in the same room as a woman?
They reported the matter to the Buddha, who said: "I shall consider ten benefits and establish a training rule for the bhikṣus, which should be recited as follows:"
"If a bhikṣu again sleeps in the same room as a woman, it is a pāyattika.
"If a bhikṣu" refers to the Venerable Āniruddha; the remaining meaning is as explained above.
"Together" means including the other person.
"A woman" refers to either a wife or a young girl, meaning one who is a suitable object for sexual intercourse.
"Sleeping in the same room" refers to the four types of rooms as described above.
The explanation of the offense is the same as before.
What are the characteristics of the transgression in this case?

If a bhikṣu stays overnight with a woman, and his body is on the upper floor while the woman is on the floor below, he should remove the ladder so she cannot ascend, or secure the door with a bolt and lock, or dispatch someone to keep watch.
If it were otherwise, until the appearance of the morning light, one incurs the offense of *dukkaṭa*;
if the morning light has passed, one incurs the offense of *pāyattika*.

Whether the bhikṣu is on the lower floor and the woman is on the middle floor, or the bhikṣu is on the middle floor and the woman is on the upper floor, or the reverse of these cases, the full explanation is as stated previously.
Alternatively, if the bhikṣu is in the room and the woman is under the eaves, with the single exception of the ladder, all other matters are as previously stated.
If the woman is inside the room and the bhikṣu is under the eaves, he should fasten the door from the outside; the rest is as explained before.

If one is beneath a gatehouse, with the bhikṣu inside the gate and the woman outside the gate, he should place the bolt inside; if it were otherwise, he would fasten it on the outside. All other matters are the same as previously stated.
Even if they share the same room, there is no offense if there is a husband who guards her.
Furthermore, there is no offense for one who is a first-time offender; the details are as explained above.
At that time, all the bhikṣus were filled with doubt and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

What karma did the venerable Āniruddha perform in the past such that he was born into a wealthy and noble family, left the home life to sever his afflictions and realize arhatship, and extensively transformed sentient beings for their great benefit?”
"I only wish that you would explain this for me.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus: "Listen well!

In the distant past, during the time of Kāśyapa Buddha, there was a bhikṣu who resided in a village. He constructed a great monastery and personally oversaw its management, making supreme offerings with the aspiration to attain liberation; he had five hundred disciples living together with him.
At that time, all the people in the village possessed deep faith and reverence toward the bhikṣus, as described at length.
Because he had previously overseen and made offerings to the Saṃgha, he was born into a wealthy and noble family; and by the power of his aspiration, he realized arhatship.
Those five hundred disciples are none other than the five hundred arhats present here today.
All the inhabitants of that village in the past are those very people who have been converted.
He asked again:
"By what cause did you obtain the wondrous divine eye, becoming the foremost among the Buddha’s disciples?
The Buddha said:

"Formerly, at the site of the Caitya of Krakucchanda Buddha, a great offering was being performed. At that time, a band of thieves intending to commit robbery entered the caitya; seeing that the lamps were dim, they raised them up. Beholding the venerable countenance of the Buddha, joy arose in their hearts, and they immediately made this great vow:
'May we, in a future life, encounter the Great Teacher and serve him without weariness, and may we obtain the wondrous divine eye, foremost among men.'"
"By the power of that vow, he has now attained the divine eye, which is foremost among all.
You bhikṣus, you should train yourselves in this way.
*The Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya*, Fascicle 40.
The Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya, Scroll Forty-one.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Yijing by Imperial Decree.
66. The Training Rule on Terrifying Bhikṣus. The sixty-sixth training rule on terrifying bhikṣus. At that time, the Blessed One was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana had ordained the group of seventeen, granting them both the going-forth and full ordination.
These seventeen individuals then lived together with the group of six, receiving instruction in the Dharma and its meaning from them. They said to one another:
"We are ignorant and unacquainted with the scriptures; we are constantly held in contempt by the group of six. We ought each to exert ourselves and diligently practice recitation."

Once the group of six had learned this, at the beginning of the night while they were engaged in recitation and study, Udāyin turned his woolen cloak backward over his shoulders and, making a terrifying sound, said:
"A yakṣa has come to harm you!"
They terrified one another, and at that time the group of seventeen was each greatly struck with panic.

On another day, those seventeen men, resentful of having been frightened by one another, immediately beat Udāyin together until he was nearly deprived of life; they smeared his body with oil and left him lying there, utterly exhausted.
Having seen this, a bhikṣu asked,
"For what reason?
He replied:
"I have brought this humiliation upon myself for the sake of a mere trifle of amusement.
He related the circumstances in full.
Upon hearing these words, the bhikṣus of few desires all felt contempt and disdain.
"How does a bhikṣu terrify another bhikṣu so as to cause him distress?
The bhikṣus reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said: "I shall now, for the sake of ten benefits, establish a training rule for the bhikṣus, which should be recited as follows:
'If a bhikṣu, whether by himself or by instructing another, should terrify another bhikṣu—even if done in jest—he commits a pāyattika offense.'"
"Furthermore, regarding the phrase 'if a bhikṣu': this refers to Udāyin; the remaining meanings are as explained above.
Regarding the phrase 'another bhikṣu': this refers to one who is a member of this Dharma.
In this context, what are the characteristics of the offense and how does it occur?"

If a bhikṣu, with the intention of terrifying others, creates various kinds of fearsome forms—such as various colored objects resembling charred stumps, or even the images of ghosts and spirits—and says:
"Come and eat you! Cut off your life-force!"
Regardless of whether that bhikṣu was frightened or not, this bhikṣu incurs a pāyattika offense.

If a bhikṣu, with the intent to terrify another, produces various frightening sounds—namely, the sounds of lions, tigers, leopards, and various spirits and ghosts—saying, "Come and eat you! [he incurs an offense].
The rest is the same as before.
If a bhikṣu, with the intention of terrifying others, produces various kinds of fearsome odors—namely, the odors of feces and urine, or the odors of spirits and ghosts—and says:
"These things are coming to harm you."
The rest is the same as before.

If a bhikṣu, with the intention of terrifying another, creates an unpleasant tactile sensation—such as by using coarse and stiff mats or bedding, or by employing objects that have a malignant touch associated with spirits and deities—and says:
"He will come to harm you."
The rest is the same as before.
If a bhikṣu, with the intention of terrifying others, creates various attractive forms—namely, the likenesses of kings, ministers, elders, householders, devas, and so forth—and says:
"This one comes to harm you."
Whether that bhikṣu feels fear or not, he incurs an offense of wrong-doing (duṣkṛta).
If one makes pleasant sounds— such as the sounds of the lute, the reed organ, the flute, or those of devas and nāgas— and says,
"These various sounds are coming to harm you," [he incurs an offense].
If they produce a pleasant fragrance—such as the scents of sandalwood, aloeswood, camphor, saffron, or celestial and nāga perfumes—they think:
"They wish to come and harm you."
If there are pleasant tactile sensations—namely, exquisite touches such as those of fine silks, brocades, and the like, or those of devas and nāgas—one should say:
"These various tactile desires are coming to harm you."
Whether that bhikṣu feels fear or not, he incurs an offense of wrong-doing (duṣkṛta).

However, if he intends to cause the other person to develop a sense of weary detachment (nirveda), and speaks of the various sufferings and pleasures found in the realms of hell-beings, animals, hungry ghosts, humans, and devas, thereby inducing a sense of dread, there is no offense in any of this.
Furthermore, there is no offense for the very first offender; the details are as explained above.

The sixty-seventh training rule concerning the concealment of the robes and bowls of other bhikṣus, etc. The sixty-seventh training rule concerning the concealment of the robes and bowls of other bhikṣus, etc. The Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, a householder invited the Buddha and the Saṃgha to his residence for a meal.
While the bhikṣus went to accept the invitation, the World-Honored One did not go.
The group of six bhikṣus and the group of seventeen bhikṣus followed behind at a leisurely pace until they reached a pond. Thereupon, the group of six addressed the group of seventeen, saying:
“Venerable ones!
There is no need to hurry away; let us enter the pool together and bathe at our leisure.
Having entered the pool, he addressed the group of seventeen:
"If we both sink together, who will emerge with their head last?
Once the group of seventeen had submerged, the group of six immediately emerged quickly; they seized their clothes, hid them beneath a thicket of grass, and fled in haste.
After a long time, the group of seventeen finally raised their heads; looking around in all directions, they did not see their robes and remained standing where they were.

At that time, the Venerable Śāriputra and Mahāmaudgalyāyana, returning from their travels through the human realm, arrived there. Seeing them from afar, the people recognized them as their teachers and said: "Upādhyāya!..."
"We have all had our robes hidden away by the group of six; thus we have no means to go to lay households to receive offerings.

What should we do now? At that time, Mahāmaudgalyāyana immediately performed an inspection and saw that their clothes were hidden beneath a thicket of grass. He then retrieved the robes and gave them to the group of seventeen.
Having put on his robes, he went to the place where the invitation was being held; once he arrived at his seat, he caused the bhikṣus to rise.
The bhikṣus asked in astonishment, "Why have you come so late and caused such a commotion?"
The group of seventeen replied to the people, saying,
"Venerable sirs!
If we do not have an upādhyāya, we shall all fast entirely for the whole day."
He asked, "For what reason?
The monk then answered him in full detail. Upon hearing this, the monks of few desires felt revulsion and shame.
“How is it that a bhikṣu conceals another’s robes and causes mutual disturbance?
Then the bhikṣus returned to the monastery and reported the matter to the Buddha.
The Buddha said: “...up to: ‘I, considering ten benefits, shall establish a training rule for the bhikṣus, which should be recited as follows:’”

"If a bhikṣu, knowing that it is the robe, bowl, or other requisites belonging to a bhikṣu, a bhikṣuṇī, a śikṣamāṇā, a śrāmaṇera, or a śrāmaṇerī, should hide them himself or cause another to hide them, it is a pāyattika."

Thus, after the Blessed One had established the training rule for the bhikṣus, there was a time when one bhikṣu entrusted his robe to another bhikṣu; however, that bhikṣu stored away only his own robe and did not store the other's robe.
At that time, thieves arrived and stole the robes of others; consequently, the bhikṣus were deprived of their clothing. The Buddha said:
"Except in cases of such circumstances, there is no offense for one who stores [the robe]."
The former was an original enactment; this is a subsequent allowance.
It should be stated thus:

"If a bhikṣu himself hides the robes, bowl, or other requisites of a bhikṣu, a bhikṣuṇī, a śikṣamāṇā, a śrāmaṇera, or a śrāmaṇerī, or causes another to hide them, except for other extenuating circumstances, it is a pāyattika."
"Furthermore, 'if a bhikṣu' refers to the group of six [monks]; the remaining meanings are as explained above.
The five groups beginning with the bhikṣus are all persons within this Dharma.
There are seven kinds of robes and three types of waist-bands; the rest of the text is as explained above."
Regarding this, what are the characteristics of the offense and its specific instances?
If a bhikṣu conceals the robes, bowl, or other requisites of another bhikṣu or similar person, or instructs another to conceal them, he incurs an offense of downfall (pāyattika) in all such cases.
"Except for other circumstances" refers to the eight difficult conditions (*aṣṭāvakṣaṇa*) and so forth;
in these cases, there is no offense. Furthermore, "no offense" refers to a first-time offender, as explained in detail above.

68. The Training Rule on Wearing a Robe Entrusted by Another Without Asking the Owner. The sixth and eighty-first training rule: When the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.

At that time, having severed all afflictions and delusions and realized arhatship, Udāyin’s story is to be told at length as in other accounts; Nanda and Upananda, however, remained living in dependence upon the community.

At that time, Upānanda was advanced in years and frail with age; none among his disciples or followers would attend to him. His robes were soiled and greasy, and wishing to wash and dye them, he took them and gave them to a disciple, saying:
"I have no further use for these clothes; take them and go."
At that time, because his heart was greedy for the robe, the disciple took it, washed, dyed, and finished preparing it.
Then, as the World-Honored One wished to travel through the human realm, the disciple immediately took the washed robe and entrusted it to his preceptor, following after the Buddha.
Later, Upānanda took that robe, put it on, and after it became soiled with grease, he placed it back in its original location; this continued until the World-Honored One returned.
At that time, a donor invited the Buddha and the Saṅgha to his house for a meal.
At that time, Upānanda’s disciple thought to himself:
"I should now take my newly washed and dyed robes and eat at a layperson's house.
Upon opening his bag, he saw that the robes were entirely soiled and greasy, unfit for wearing; he thus put on some suitable, tattered, and worn-out clothes and went to the place of the invitation.
Other bhikṣus asked,
"For what reason have you come to receive offerings wearing these soiled robes?
He then related the matter to them exactly as it had happened.
A bhikṣu of few desires heard of this and felt revulsion and shame, saying:
"How can a bhikṣu receive a robe entrusted to him by another and put it on without asking permission?
He reported this matter to the Buddha.
The Buddha said: "I shall now, having considered ten benefits, establish a training rule for the bhikṣus, which should be recited as follows:
'If a bhikṣu receives a robe from another as a deposit, and later, without asking the owner, should wear it himself, it is a pāyattika.'"
"Furthermore, 'if a bhikṣu' refers to Upānanda; the remaining meanings are as explained above.
'Without asking the owner' means that he took it for wear according to his own will, without borrowing it with permission."
Regarding the characteristics of the offense herein, what are the specific cases?
If a bhikṣu accepts a robe entrusted by another and uses it without asking permission, the offense is established as previously described.

However, if they are close friends who understand each other’s intentions, or if they have heard that the other would be pleased by its use, there is no offense in wearing or using it even without asking permission.
Furthermore, there is no offense for one who is a first-time offender; the details are as explained above.
The sixty-ninth training rule: Regarding the accusation of a pure bhikṣu with a saṃghāvaśeṣa offense. The Buddha was staying at Rājagṛha, in the Bamboo Grove, by the Kalandaka Pond.
At that time, the Venerable Sthavira Śrīgupta was staying on Vulture Peak Mountain, walking back and forth for exercise by the side of the Śilāpuñja Pond.
Then, the Bhikṣuṇī Utpalā saw the Elder from afar and came forward to pay her respects.

Not long after that bhikṣuṇī had shaved her hair, as she was bowing her head in prostration and rising up, she rose with the great robe of Śrīgupta upon her head. When the two bhikṣus, Mitra and Bhūmi, saw this occurrence, they returned to their residence and informed the bhikṣus, saying:
"Venerable ones!..."
"In whom do you wish us to place our faith?
For we ourselves have seen the venerable Sthavira Śrīgupta touching the body of the bhikṣuṇī Utpalā."
He related the matter in detail.
When the bhikṣus had heard it, they informed the Buddha, and the Buddha said to the bhikṣus:
"You should thoroughly investigate what those two bhikṣus have seen."
"How did you see it?
For what reason did you go there to see the physical forms touching one another?
When the bhikṣus had received the Buddha's instruction, they questioned those two men regarding the truth or falsehood of what they had seen. The two replied:
"Venerable sirs!
We truly did not see the Venerable Sthavira Śāriputra making physical contact with the body of the nun Utpalavarṇā; we only saw him prostrating by raising his head to her robe."
"I spoke thus because I harbored anger, hatred, and a resentful mind.
Upon hearing these words, the bhikṣus of few desires were filled with mutual reproach and shame, saying:
"How can a bhikṣu slander a person who is pure and free from offense by means of a groundless *saṃghāvaśeṣa* charge?"
He then reported the matter to the Buddha.
The Buddha said, "Up to this point, I shall establish a training rule for the bhikṣus out of consideration for ten benefits. It should be recited as follows:
'If a bhikṣu, out of anger, knowing that another bhikṣu is pure and free from offense, should defame him with a groundless *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense, it is a *pāyattika*.'"
"Furthermore, 'if a bhikṣu' refers to the two individuals, Mitra and Bhūmika; the remaining meanings are as explained above.
'Malicious' means harboring resentment and hatred.
'A pure bhikṣu' refers to Sthavira."
"Groundless" means that there is no basis in the three grounds—seeing, hearing, or suspicion. The rest is as explained above.
Regarding this, what are the characteristics of the offense and its specific instances?
It refers to knowing that a pure person is being slandered by means of groundless charges; in ten instances there is an offense, and in five instances there is no offense.
What are the ten? They are:
not having seen the matter, nor heard it, nor suspected it, yet forming such false and deceptive conceptions, and though there is in fact no seeing and so forth, falsely claiming:
"I have seen, heard, and suspected."
When one speaks thus, one incurs a *pāyattika* offense.
Or, having heard [the teaching] but forgotten it, or having doubted it and forgotten it, one forms such an understanding and such a conception as to say:
"I have not forgotten what I heard or what I doubted."
When one speaks thus, one incurs a *pāyattika* offense.
Whether one has heard it and believes it, or has heard it and does not believe it, yet says, "I have seen it";
or whether one has heard it and doubts it, or has heard it and does not doubt it, or merely suspects it oneself, yet says:
