"If I saw it"—when one speaks thus, one incurs a *pāyattika* offense; this is called the commission of an offense through ten matters.
What are the five matters for which there is no offense?
That is to say, one who has not seen, heard, or suspected, yet possesses the understanding that they have seen and so forth, and the perception that they have seen and so forth, speaks these words:
"I have seen, heard, and suspected."
There is no offense in these cases.

Or, if one has heard but forgotten, or suspected but forgotten, yet speaks as if one had heard and so forth while maintaining the perception that one had heard or suspected, there is likewise no offense.
As when slandering a pure person, there is an offense in ten matters and no offense in five matters.
If one slanders a person who is pure as if they were impure, it is likewise.
If one slanders a person who is impure, there is an offense in eleven instances and no offense in six instances.
What are the eleven?
They are as follows: not having seen, not having heard, and not having suspected, yet forming such an understanding and such a conception, one falsely declares:
"I have seen, heard, and suspected," when in reality there is no seeing and so forth.
When one speaks in this manner, one incurs a *pāyattika* offense.
Or, having seen but forgotten, or heard but forgotten, or suspected but forgotten, one forms such an understanding and such a conception as to say:
"I have not forgotten what was seen, heard, or suspected."
When one speaks in this manner, one incurs a *pāyattika* offense.
Whether one has heard it and believes it, or has heard it and does not believe it, yet says:
"I have seen it."
Whether one hears it and doubts, hears it and does not doubt, or merely doubts oneself, yet says,
"I have seen it," when one makes such a statement, one incurs a *pāyattika* offense.
These are called the eleven matters that constitute an offense.
What are the six matters that do not constitute an offense?
They are as follows: one has not seen, heard, or suspected; yet, having the conviction that one has seen and so forth, and the perception that one has seen and so forth, one speaks in this manner:
"I have heard it with doubt": there is no offense.

Or having seen but forgotten, or having heard but forgotten, or having doubted but forgotten; if one has the perception of having seen and so forth, and the understanding of having seen and so forth, yet says "I saw," "I heard," and so on, there is likewise no offense. These are called the six matters involving no offense.
Furthermore, there is no offense for one who is a first-time offender, as explained in detail above.
The Seventieth Training Rule: Traveling on the Same Road with a Woman. The Buddha was staying at the Bamboo Grove, the Kalandaka Pool, in Rājagṛha.

At that time, there was a weaver in this city who was by nature coarse and fierce, making him difficult to live with. Because the other weavers knew his evil character, they would not give their daughters in marriage to him. Consequently, he went to the city of Śrāvastī and married the daughter of a weaver; taking her back to his native village, he resided in the royal city, where he constantly inflicted cruel treatment upon her, leaving her perpetually without joy.
At that time, there was an old woman in a neighboring house. Her daughter went to her and said, "Mother!
I married far away to this man and have obtained a wicked husband who constantly beats me with a staff; I have no heart for pleasure here. I wish to run away—what do you think of this?"
The mother remained silent and gave no reply.
The daughter went outside and saw a bhikṣu traveling toward Śrāvastī; she immediately accompanied him and followed along the road.
At that time, the weaver pursued their tracks in haste and saw a bhikṣu walking with his wife along the path.

The weaver saw him from afar; when they reached a certain village, he summoned his acquaintances and together they beat the bhikṣu until he was nearly dead. After regaining consciousness for a short while, he gradually made his way to Śrāvastī.
A bhikṣu saw him and asked,
"Have you traveled in safety and comfort?
He replied:
"How can there be peace and happiness?
he asked, and upon being questioned about the reason, he related the circumstances in detail.
The bhikṣus said:
“Is it not fitting for you to travel along the road with a woman and no other man?
She replied,
“It is precisely because this was improper that I have encountered such misfortune.”
The bhikṣus of few desires, hearing this, felt reproach and shame, saying:
"How can a bhikṣu travel along a road with a woman who lacks a male companion?
They reported this matter to the Buddha.
The Buddha said: "I shall now consider ten benefits and establish this training rule for the bhikṣus, which should be recited as follows:
'If a bhikṣu travels along the same road with a woman without another man present, even for the distance between two villages, it is a pāyattika.'"
"Furthermore, 'if a bhikṣu' refers to one among those in this Dharma; the remaining meanings are as explained above.
'A woman' refers to one who is capable of engaging in sexual intercourse.
'There is no other man' means that there are only two persons present."
"Road" refers to a remote and distant path.
Regarding this, what are the characteristics of the offense and how does it occur?
If a bhikṣu travels alone with a woman along a remote and distant road, he incurs a pāyattika.
If there is one *krośa* between two villages, and so on up to seven; if it is less than a full *krośa*, one incurs an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*);
if it is a full [distance], one incurs an offense of falling (*pācittiya*).
Whether traveling from village to wilderness or from wilderness to village, the number of *krośas* required for the offense is similar to that stated above.
If, at such a place, another person dispatches a woman to act as a guide, there is no offense.
If at times a bhikṣu becomes lost on the road and a woman comes to provide directions, there is likewise no offense.
Furthermore, there is no offense for a first-time offender; the details are as explained above.
The eighth summary verse says:
Robbers, age not yet reached, Digging the earth, invitations, and contravening the instructions;
Eavesdropping, departing in silence, Lack of respect, alcohol, and untimely food.

71. The Training Rule on Traveling with Thieves. The seventy-first training rule concerning traveling with thieves was established when the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
There was a bhikṣu residing in the Bamboo Grove at Rājagṛha who was observing the rains retreat.
When that bhikṣu had completed the retreat and finished making his robes, he wished to go to Śrāvastī to pay homage at the feet of the World-Honored One; thus, he set out in search of a caravan.

At that time, there was a merchant who wished to go toward Śrāvastī; this merchant was a smuggler, but the bhikṣu did not know it and accompanied him. As they were about to reach the customs station, he took a different road and traveled by way of a shortcut.

At that time, the tax official, having observed and learned of their evasion of the toll road, seized them and bound them both together to bring them before him; realizing the bhikṣu was without fault, he immediately released him.
Having gained his freedom, he gradually arrived at the Jeta Grove.
The bhikṣus saw him and asked,
"Welcome! Has your journey been peaceful and pleasant?"
He replied,
"How could there be peace and happiness? He asked:
"Why is that? they asked, and he answered them by relating the matter in full.
The bhikṣus then questioned him, saying:
"Venerable sir!
Is it appropriate to travel together with bandits?
He replied:
"It is solely due to not seeing this difficulty and suffering.
Upon hearing this, the bhikṣu of few desires felt disdain and shame, saying:
"How can a bhikṣu travel along the same path as bandits?"
He reported the matter to the Buddha.
The Buddha said, "I shall observe ten benefits and establish this training rule for the bhikṣus, which should be recited as follows:
'If a bhikṣu travels along the same road with a caravan of thieves, even for the distance of a single village, it is a pāyattika.'"
"Furthermore, 'if a bhikṣu' refers to one within this Dharma.
'With a thief' refers to one who destroys villages or steals customs duties.
'Traveling together on the same path' means being companions over a long distance, even as far as the interval between two villages; for this, one incurs a *pāyattika* offense."
Regarding this, what are the characteristics of the offense and its specific details?
If a bhikṣu travels together with thieves, he incurs a pāyattika.
If there is one krośa between villages, up to seven villages—as explained in detail above—he incurs a pāyattika offense in all such cases.

If one takes a thief as a protector or guide, there is no offense in traveling together; nor is there any offense in traveling along the same path if the person comes to provide directions when one has lost one's way.
Furthermore, there is no offense for one who is a first-time offender; the details are as explained above.
The Seventy-second Training Rule on Ordaining Those Under Age. The Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, Mahāmaudgalyāyana ordained seventeen youths and conferred upon them full ordination (*upasampadā*).
Once they had received full ordination, the young novices did not eat throughout the entire night until dawn; scorched by the fire of hunger, their bodies became emaciated, and they began to weep.
At that time, the World-Honored One, hearing the sound of a young boy crying within a side room, addressed Ānanda, saying:
"For what reason is there the sound of a boy crying within the side room?"
Then Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
These seventeen groups of newly ordained monks, having received full ordination, were unable to endure hunger from not eating at improper times; for this reason, they wept.”
The Blessed One asked,
"Did the bhikṣus confer full ordination upon one who was less than the required age, thereby establishing him in the status of a bhikṣu?
They replied:
“World-Honored One!
Please grant him full ordination.
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"If a person is not yet twenty years of age, they cannot endure cold and heat, hunger and thirst, nor can they perform such tasks as wandering from house to house to beg for alms.
For this reason, and having considered ten benefits, I establish this training rule for the bhikṣus, which should be recited as follows:
'If a bhikṣu, knowing that a person is less than twenty years of age, confers full ordination upon them and causes them to become a bhikṣu, it is a pāyattika.'"
"This is not full ordination; all the bhikṣus incur an offense.
As for "if there is another bhikṣu," this refers to one within this Dharma; the remaining meanings are as explained above.
"Not yet twenty years old" refers to a person of deficient age who is incapable of receiving the full precepts.

Regarding the statement "the nature of a bhikṣu is not accomplished": although one has received the precepts through the formal procedure of the *jñapti-caturtha-karman*, one does not become a bhikṣu.

This is not the attainment of full ordination (*upasampadā*). As for the statement that "all other bhikṣus incur an offense," this means that, with the exception of the preceptor, all others incur an *duṣkṛta* (wrongdoing) offense.
In this regard, what are the characteristics of the offense and how does it occur?
If a person who is not yet twenty years old forms the perception that they are not yet twenty and desires to receive full ordination (*upasampadā*), and the bhikṣus ask him:
"Are you twenty years old?"
He replied, "It has not been completed.
If a bhikṣu confers full ordination upon such a person, that individual fundamentally does not obtain the precepts; the preceptor commits a pāyattika offense, and the others commit duṣkṛta offenses.
If others who dwell together and share in common use [of the same dwelling] are also involved, they likewise all incur an *dukkaṭa* (wrongdoing).
If a person who has not yet reached twenty years of age forms the perception that he has not reached them and desires to receive full ordination (*upasampadā*), and the bhikṣus ask him:
"Have you reached twenty years of age?"
He replied, "I recall from my own mind that I have no doubt; I am not yet twenty years old.
The bhikṣus conferred full ordination upon him; this person did not obtain the precepts, and the offense incurred is the same as before.
If a person who is not yet twenty years of age forms the perception that they have reached twenty and desires to receive full ordination (*upasampadā*), and the bhikṣus ask him:
"Have you reached twenty?"
He replied, "I am twenty years old.
The bhikṣus conferred full ordination upon him; this person attained the precepts and became a bhikṣu by nature. There was no offense for the preceptor, nor was there any offense for the others.
If a person who is not yet twenty years of age forms the perception that they have reached twenty and desires to receive full ordination (*upasampadā*), and the bhikṣus ask him:
"Have you reached twenty years of age?"
He replied:
"I myself recall knowing that my mind was free from doubt when I reached twenty years of age.

The bhikṣus conferred full ordination upon him; this person obtained the precepts and attained the nature of a bhikṣu. There was no offense for the preceptor, nor was there any offense for the others.

If a person is not yet twenty years of age, yet does not know this for themselves and has no doubts, and they desire to receive full ordination (*upasampadā*), and the bhikṣus neither inquire about it nor provide an answer when questioned, yet the bhikṣus nevertheless confer full ordination upon them.

This person has obtained the precepts and attained the nature of a bhikṣu. If the preceptor commits an offense, others may also commit offenses, yet there is no offense regarding communal residence and so forth.
If a person who is actually twenty years old forms the perception that he is not yet twenty and desires to receive full ordination (*upasampadā*), the bhikṣus ask him:
"Are you twenty years old?"
He replied, "It has not yet been completed.

At that time, the bhikṣus conferred full ordination upon him; this person obtained the precepts and attained the nature of a bhikṣu, while both his preceptor and the assembly were guilty of an offense, though there was no offense regarding matters such as communal residence.
If a person who has reached twenty years of age forms the perception that they have not reached it and desires to receive full ordination (*upasampadā*), the bhikṣus shall ask:
"Have you reached twenty years of age?"
He replied, "I recall from my own mind that I had no doubts, yet I was not yet twenty years old.

When the bhikṣus conferred full ordination upon him, this person obtained the precepts; the preceptor was guilty of an offense, as were the others, but there was no offense regarding communal residence and so forth.
If a person is twenty years of age and perceives themselves as being twenty, desiring to receive full ordination (*upasampadā*), the bhikṣus ask him:
"Are you twenty years of age?"
He replied, "I am twenty years old.
The bhikṣus conferred full ordination upon him; this person attained the precepts, and neither the preceptor nor the assembly committed any offense.
If a person who is actually thirty years old forms the perception that he is twenty and desires to receive full ordination (*upasampadā*), and the bhikṣus ask him:
"Are you twenty years old?"
He replied, "I myself remember with a mind free from doubt that I have reached the age of twenty.
The bhikṣus conferred full ordination upon him; this person obtained the precepts, and the bhikṣus were not at fault.

If a person has reached twenty years of age, yet does not know for themselves whether they are free from doubt, and desires to receive full ordination (*upasampadā*), and the bhikṣus do not question them—or even if they do question them, the candidate does not answer—and the bhikṣus nevertheless confer the full ordination upon them.
This person has obtained the precepts; if other bhikṣus commit an offense while living together with him, they are not at fault, as explained in detail previously.

Among these, the first two have not received full ordination (*upasampadā*); if they stay in the same place as virtuous bhikṣus and perform the *poṣadha* ceremony two or three times, they are considered "living like thieves" (*cora-vāsa*) and must be expelled.
If a person who is not yet twenty years old forms the perception that they are twenty and thus completes the full ordination (*upasampadā*), and a relative comes and asks:
"This person is not yet twenty years old; who conferred the full precepts upon them?"
Regarding this, one should calculate for this person the months spent in the womb as well as the intercalary months; if they are complete, it is well.
If they are not complete, he shall be demoted to the status of a *śrāmaṇera* and the precepts shall be conferred upon him again.

If one does not retreat to the status of a śrāmaṇera and does not receive the precepts again, yet stays in the same place as virtuous bhikṣus and performs the poṣadha ceremony with them two or three times, this person is a "thief-dweller" (cora-vāsika) and must be expelled.

If a person who is nineteen years old receives full ordination (*upasampadā*), and before a year has passed, he himself remembers that he was not yet twenty, one should calculate the months spent in the womb and the intercalary months; if these complete [the age], it is well. If they do not complete it, he should be demoted to the status of a novice (*śrāmaṇera*) and then receive full ordination again.
If it is not so, and he remains in the same place as virtuous bhikṣus, performing the poṣadha ceremony with them two or three times, he should be expelled by the *pratisāraṇīya-karman*.
If, however, after one year has passed, he remembers and recognizes [his status], he is said to have properly received full ordination (*upasampadā*).
"O Bhikṣus! If a person goes forth and receives full ordination (upasampadā) to become a bhikṣu within this well-expounded Dharma and Vinaya, it is indeed difficult to encounter such an opportunity.

If a person is eighteen years old when given full ordination, but recalls before the first year has passed that they were not yet of age, they should be demoted to the status of a śrāmaṇera and ordained again."
If it is not so, and he stays in the same place as virtuous bhikṣus and performs the *poṣadha* ceremony with them two or three times, he should be expelled.

If after one year he remembers that he has not yet completed [the required time], one should calculate the months spent in the womb and the intercalary months; if they complete the full period, it is well; if they do not, he should be moved from that location and receive the full ordination (*upasampadā*) again.
If it is not so, he shall be subject to the same expulsion as before.
If he only recalls and realizes this after two years have passed, he is then said to have properly received full ordination; the details are as explained above.

Because the sublime teaching is difficult to encounter, if a person who has not yet reached twenty years of age harbors doubts, one should act to remind them by calculating whether their years are actually complete or not, thereby removing their state of uncertainty.

If [the age] is not yet full, it should be calculated by including the intercalary months of the womb; if it is full, that is well. If it is not full, the detailed explanation is as previously stated.

If a person who has reached twenty years of age forms the perception that they have not reached it, yet seeks the full precepts and receives the higher ordination (*upasampadā*), this is called a "proper reception" [of the precepts].

If a person who has reached twenty years of age forms the perception that they have reached twenty, and seeks the full precepts to receive ordination (*upasampadā*), this is called "properly received.
Furthermore, there is no offense for those who are first-time offenders, or those who are insane, mentally deranged, or afflicted by intense pain.

73. The Training Rule on Destructing Uncultivated Ground. The seventy-third training rule concerning the destruction of uncultivated ground. The Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.

At that time, the six bhikṣus dug the earth with their own hands or instructed others to do so; they constructed embankments or destroyed anthills and the like. When the various non-Buddhists saw this, they all reviled them together, saying:
"How can these renunciant bhikṣus engage in such worldly affairs, digging the earth and taking life without any feeling of compassion?"
Having heard this, the bhikṣu of few desires informed the Buddha.

The Buddha assembled the bhikṣus and, through various skillful means, praised the observance of the precepts, having few desires, and being content; he censured those with many desires who engage in useless activities. He spoke at length until: "I, considering ten benefits, shall establish a training rule for the bhikṣus, which should be recited as follows:
'If a bhikṣu digs the earth with his own hand, or instructs another to dig it, it is a pāyattika.'"
"Furthermore, 'if a bhikṣu' refers to the group of six; the remaining meanings are as explained above.
'Self and others' are as previously stated.
As for 'ground,' there are two kinds:"
This refers to cultivated ground and uncultivated ground.
What is cultivated ground?

It refers to ground that is naturally cultivated, or ground that has been excavated and has undergone heavy rains from the heavens during the three months [of the rainy season]; this is called cultivated ground.
If there is no rain, it is only after six months have passed that it is said to have "arisen.
The explanation of the offense is as above.
In this context, what are the characteristics of the transgression and its specific details?
The summary verse says:
Perceiving life, lifting, the earth’s surface, Driving in stakes, and drawing lines on the ground;
Cow dung, crumbling riverbanks, Mud walls, and the nature of moisture and continuity.
If the painted walls are damaged by green-clad attendants, or if sand, gravel, and soil are mixed together,
and there is no pure person (kappiya-kāraka) available on an auspicious day, one may drive a wooden peg into the ground to a depth of four finger-widths.
If a bhikṣu digs into and damages the earth, he incurs a pāyattika offense.
If it is not native soil, one incurs an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*).
When a bhikṣu lifts up a layer of earth, if it remains connected to its original nature as soil, it is a *pāyattika*;
if it is no longer connected, one incurs an offense of wrong-doing.
If a bhikṣu drives in a peg, it is a pāyattika;
if he pulls out a peg, he incurs a duṣkṛta offense.
If a bhikṣu carelessly draws on the ground, he incurs a duṣkṛta offense.
If one reckons them lightly, there is no offense.
If a bhikṣu picks up cow dung that has been placed on the ground, he incurs an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa);
if he merely takes up cow dung [that is not so placed], there is no offense.
If a bhikṣu causes damage to native soil when the riverbank collapses, it is a pāyattika;
if there is a fissure that subsequently collapses, one incurs a duṣkṛta offense.
If a bhikṣu stirs up the mud in a river or pond, he incurs an offense of wrong-doing (duṣkṛta).
If he lifts up a jar while it is situated in the mud, he incurs an offense of wrong-doing.
If one drives a stake into a wall, it is a *pāyattika*.
If one lifts up dried cow dung attached to a wall, one incurs a *dukkaṭa* offense.
If one pushes a wall that is connected to dampness, one incurs a *pāyattika*.
If there are cracks or fissures, one incurs an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*).
If one paints on a wall, one incurs an offense of wrong-doing;
however, if one forms the intention that it is merely a numerical mark, there is no offense.
If one damages or disturbs green plants growing on a wall, one incurs an *dukkaṭa* offense.
If one digs into a stony ground where stone predominates and earth is scarce, one incurs a *pāyattika* offense;
if earth predominates, one incurs an *dukkaṭa* offense.
If it is pure stone, there is no offense.
If one digs into sandy ground where the sand is scarce and the soil is abundant, one incurs a *pāyattika*;
if the sand is abundant, one incurs a *dukkaṭa*.
If it consists purely of sand, there is no offense.

When a bhikṣu engaged in construction wishes to establish the foundation and encounters a favorable astrological alignment and an auspicious day, but has no lay attendant (śrāmaṇera) available, he may himself drive a stake into the ground to mark the boundary; if it is four finger-widths deep, there is no offense.
Furthermore, there is no offense for one who is a first-time offender, as described above.

**The 74th Śikṣāpada: The Rule Concerning Seeking Food After Four Months.** The Buddha was wandering among the people in the realm of the Śākyas and gradually arrived at the city of Kapilavastu, where he stayed in the Nyagrodha Grove.

At that time, the renowned Śākya, knowing that the Buddha had arrived, went to where the Buddha was, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and sat to one side; the Buddha then preached the Dharma to him, instructing, exhorting, benefiting, and gladdening him.
He immediately rose from his seat, joined his palms toward the Buddha, and said:
"World-Honored One!
I pray that the Buddha and the Sangha, out of compassion and pity, will accept my offerings of food and drink for three months, as well as all other necessary requisites."
The World-Honored One accepted by remaining silent; seeing that the Buddha had accepted, he rose from his seat and departed.
Having arrived at his home, he addressed his family members, saying:
"I have invited the Buddha and the Saṃgha for three months of offerings; you must prepare them so that nothing is lacking."
When the six bhikṣus heard of this matter, they thought to themselves:
"How might we enjoy fine food and drink for three months, while always digesting it well, remaining physically light, at ease, and free from the suffering of illness?"
He immediately went to a physician and asked for a prescription.
The physician told him:
"First consume oily and fatty foods, and afterwards you shall suffer diarrhea; thus, even if you eat much, it will be digested."

When Upānanda heard these words, he followed the physician’s instructions and ate fine food throughout the three months. When the three months had ended, he still requested fine, delicious food from the cook—such as meat broth—but was unable to obtain it.

Then that cook went to inform the great donor, Mahānāman; having heard this, the donor immediately gave rise to criticism and disdain. When the bhikṣus of few desires heard these words, they felt extreme shame and reproach, saying:
"How can a bhikṣu, having already accepted another's invitation, demand what is not his due?"
They reported this matter to the Buddha.
The Buddha said,
"You must no longer forcibly beg from other donors, thereby giving rise to resentment and distress."
"You all should listen!
Long ago, in the past, in a tranquil forest by the side of a great pond, there was a rishi who sat cross-legged, fixing his mindfulness in contemplation."
At that time, a nāga youth emerged from the pond and coiled his body around the rishi to shield him from the suffering of the cold, further asking,
"What do you require, O Benevolent One? In this manner,
he coiled his body around him every single day.
At that time, because of this affliction, the seer fell ill and remained there dwelling in sorrow.
Another seer came to his place and asked:
"For what reason has your body become so emaciated and suddenly reached such a state?"
He answered in full detail regarding the matter, and the seer told him:
"If the dragon prince comes again, he will have a bright jewel upon his head; you should ask for it from him. Because he will cherish that jewel, he will not come again."
Having heard this, the ṛṣi saw the nāga approaching and begged for the jewel with such persistent earnestness that the nāga eventually departed, speaking this verse:
"Food, drink, and clothing— All are brought about by means of this jewel.
Though you, O virtuous one, insistently beg for it, I truly cannot give it to you."
"You begged me for my jewels; your words were like a sharp sword.
Like being crushed by a great boulder, from this day forth you shall not come again.
"O Bhikṣus! You all..."
That nāga son belongs to the class of animals; yet, upon hearing a forceful request, he immediately departed to a distance—how much more so should this be for humans?
Therefore, you all should not seek anything from others by means of coercion.

Furthermore, you should listen further: in times past, there was a rishi who practiced meditative concentration in a great forest. At that time, many birds were in that forest, their clamorous cries disturbing the rishi so that his mind could not attain stability.
Another seer came to his place and, seeing that he could not attain concentration, asked:
"Why are you not concentrated?
He then answered him with the facts of the matter.
The seer said to him:
"Virtuous one, you should now kindle a great torch during the night and speak these words beneath that forest:
'You must give me wings, as well as eggs and fledglings, to serve as my food.'"
When those birds heard these words, they took the eggs and their young and moved away to various places.
O bhikṣus! Those were merely birds;
when they heard such forceful begging, they all fled far away—how much more so would humans do?

At that time, the Blessed One, having extensively cited various analogies and rebuked them in many ways, addressed the bhikṣus, saying: "I shall observe ten benefits and establish this training rule for the bhikṣus; it should be spoken thus:
'If a bhikṣu receives an invitation for four months, he may accept it when necessary.'"
"If one receives more than this, it is a *pāyattika*.

Thus the Blessed One, having established this training rule (*śikṣāpada*), traveled by stages until he reached the city of Rājagṛha, where he stayed at the Bamboo Grove Monastery for the summer retreat.
At that time, King Bimbisāra invited the Buddha and the Saṃgha for three months of offerings.
During this time, the brother-in-law of the Venerable Pilindavatsa’s sister also invited them for offerings. Pilindavatsa then informed the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"I now grant permission for this."
"If invitations are made individually, a bhikṣu may accept them without offense.
Furthermore, when a visiting bhikṣu arrives, he might think:
"I have not been invited by the king."
He then went out to beg for alms.
When the king saw him, he asked, "I have invited the assembly of monks;
for what reason are you begging for alms?"
He replied,
"I did not accept the invitation.
The king said:
"I shall further invite those bhikṣus.
He reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"If they are invited again, the bhikṣus should accept."
At that time, the bhikṣus thought to themselves:
"The King has many affairs of state; he might perhaps neglect or forget [this matter], so we shall go for alms.
The King, in turn, saw them from afar.
"What further intention have I for which I have requested alms?
The bhikṣu replied, "The affairs of state are many; perhaps you have neglected or forgotten."
The king said, "I entreat you most earnestly once more; I pray that you will accept my food.
He reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"If you are invited with earnest and repeated entreaty, you may accept.
At that time, King Bimbisāra invited the Buddha and the Saṅgha for a meal.
When the [usual] period was complete and [the monks] were wandering for alms, the king saw them from afar once again.
"For what reason does the Noble One still go on alms-round?
He replied, "The King has already invited me to eat; therefore, I am going on alms-round."
The King said,
"I now invite you constantly.
At that time, the bhikṣus reported the matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"If it is a regular invitation, a bhikṣu should accept it.
At that time, the World-Honored One praised those who maintain the precepts and have few desires, and rebuked those with many desires, saying to the bhikṣus:
"The previous [rule] was the initial regulation; this is a subsequent allowance."
For the sake of his disciples, he established this training rule anew, which should be recited as follows:
"If a bhikṣu receives an invitation for four months, he may accept it when necessary; if he accepts it beyond that period, except during other [permitted] times, it is a pāyattika offense."
"Other times" refers to a special invitation, a repeated invitation, an earnest invitation, and a regular invitation;
these are the [permissible] times. "If a bhikṣu" refers to Upānanda.
"Four months" refers to a period of exactly four months.
"Invitation" refers to being extended an invitation by another.
"Acceptance" refers to consenting to that matter.
"Exceeding [the time]" means exceeding the appointed limit.
"Except for other times" refers to the time of a special invitation, which means that others are not included.
"Repeated invitation" means inviting again and again.
"Entreated with earnestness" means to entreat again and again with utmost sincerity.
"Constantly entreated" means to invite for a long duration.
"This is the proper time" refers to the time when permission has been granted.
The explanation of the offense is as above.
Regarding the characteristics of the transgression herein, what are the specific circumstances?

If a bhikṣu, having been invited by another to a coarse meal, requests something fine and delicious, there is a *duṣkṛta* (wrongdoing) at the time of requesting; upon eating it, he falls into an offense.
If another person gives one fine food, yet one asks for coarse food, there is an *duṣkṛta* offense at the time of asking, but no offense at the time of eating.
Likewise, if one is given milk and so forth, yet asks for curd and so forth, there is an *duṣkṛta* offense at the time of asking, but a *pāyattika* offense at the time of eating;
however, there is no offense for one who is ill.
If a bhikṣu goes on his alms-round from house to house and a woman, having seen him, comes out holding food,
and if the bhikṣu has some desire for it, he should say to her:
"There is no need for more rice."
If the woman asks in return,
"Venerable sir, what else do you require?
this constitutes a formal request.
If one seeks out whatever is required for that purpose, there is no offense.
Furthermore, there is no offense in the case of a first-time offender; the details are as explained above.
The Seventy-fifth Training Rule: Prohibiting the Transmission of Teaching. The Buddha was staying at Rājagṛha, in the Bamboo Grove, the Squirrels’ Feeding Ground, by the Kalandaka Pond.
It is the natural law of the World-Honored One that when a training rule (śikṣāpada) common to both divisions is being established, the Saṃghas of both divisions must assemble together.
Although this training rule is shared by both divisions, the community of nuns did not assemble.
The Buddha addressed the Venerable Ānanda:
"You should say to Cūḍapanthaka:
'You must take these rules of training and go before the community of bhikṣuṇīs to proclaim them.'"
Then Ānanda went to Cūḍapanthaka and related the Buddha’s words in full.
Having received the Buddha’s instruction, Cūḍapanthaka set out for the nunnery intending to proclaim the Buddha’s teaching; on the way, he encountered the six bhikṣus and said to them:
“Venerable ones!...”
The Buddha has now established this training rule for the dual monastic community.
The group of six asked:
“What is this training rule?”
He then explained for him:
"If a bhikṣu receives an invitation for four months, he should accept it when necessary.
If he accepts it beyond that period, except during other [permitted] times, it is a pāyattika offense."
"If there is a separate invitation, a repeated invitation, a persistent invitation, or a regular invitation—this is the proper time.
Having spoken thus, he addressed the group of six monks, saying:
"Venerable ones!"
"You should train yourselves in this rule of training.
The group of six replied, "You are foolish, lacking in discernment, and not well-behaved; how could we possibly adopt this rule of training based on your words and conduct?"
"If I see another bhikṣu who is well-versed in the Tripiṭaka, I shall follow his words and undertake the training rules.
Having spoken thus in reproach, he then departed.
At that time, Khaṇḍā again went to the place where the group of twelve bhikṣuṇīs was, and they likewise spoke such unlawful words.
When the rest of the monks and bhikṣuṇīs heard this, they rejoiced, received it with reverence, and set out to practice accordingly.
When Khaṇḍadravya had returned to his dwelling, he immediately reported this matter to the bhikṣus.
When those of few desires heard these words, they reported the circumstances to the Buddha.
The Buddha said, "I shall establish a training rule for the bhikṣus after considering ten benefits; it should be spoken thus:
'If a bhikṣu hears other bhikṣus speaking in this way:
"Venerable one!'"
"Virtuous one, you should now train in such precepts. He replies:
"I truly cannot accept and practice the precepts according to the words spoken by you, who are foolish, lacking clarity, and unskilled in understanding."
"If I were to see another who is well-versed in the Tripiṭaka, I would accept and practice according to his words," [if one says this], it is a *pāyattika*.
If that bhikṣu truly desires to seek understanding, he should inquire about the Tripiṭaka; this is the proper occasion.
"Furthermore, 'if a bhikṣu' refers to the group of six [monks]; the remaining meanings are as explained above.
'Venerable sir!
You should now train in such a precept' refers to the precepts as they have been transmitted."

Regarding the phrase "one cannot employ your foolishness and so forth": it means that to contemplate what is evilly contemplated, to speak what is evilly spoken, and to perform what is evilly performed is termed "foolishness."
If one does not uphold the Sūtras, Vinaya, and Abhidharma, this is called "delusion.
If one does not understand the meaning of the Tripiṭaka, this is called "lack of clarity.
If one is not skilled in making definitive distinctions regarding the Tripiṭaka, this is called "lack of proficiency"; the rest of the text is easy to understand.
The explanation for the offenses up to this point is as stated above.
In this context, what are the characteristics of the transgression?
If a bhikṣu says to another bhikṣu:
"Venerable one!
You should practice and observe such training rules. He then replied:
"I cannot accept your words.
If one speaks of each of the four matters, such as being foolish, one incurs a *pāyattika* offense.
However, if the person before one is actually foolish and so forth, there is no offense in speaking.
Furthermore, there is no offense for one who is a first-time offender, as explained in detail above. 76.

The Training Rule on Listening in Silence to Quarrels. The Training Rule on Listening in Silence to Quarrels, the seventy-sixth. The Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.

At that time, Udāyin severed all fetters and delusions and realized arhatship; the Venerable Chanda went toward Kauśāmbī to attend to his affairs; Aśvaka and Punarvasu both passed away together; and Nanda and Upananda remained dwelling with the great assembly.
When the group of seventeen saw this, each gave rise to a resolute mind intent on seeking revenge, and they deliberated together:
"Among the six groups, he who most frequently deceives and harasses us is always Upānanda, who stands as the leader."
"We ought to perform the *jñapti-caturtha-karman* of suspension against them.
They then went to the refectory to deliberate together.
At that time, Upānanda went to the window and listened by pressing his ear against it; hearing their discussion, he immediately entered the hall and severely rebuked them, speaking as follows:
"I shall surely inflict a great punishment upon you all! How could you not have heard the verse of the ancient seers, which says:
'Just as when an elephant’s leather tether has rotted, Having been blown by the wind and scorched by the sun for a long time;
Though it lacks the strength to hold him as before, It is still sufficient to bind five hundred sheep.'"

At that time, the group of seventeen monks, knowing that Upānanda had become aware of the matter, went out together to the heated hall to deliberate on the case, intending to carry out the formal act of suspension (niḥsargika).
At that time, Upānanda again listened to their conversation from a secluded spot; he then entered the hall and spoke further malicious words.
Then those seventeen went up to the upper terrace, while Upānanda remained on the middle terrace.
While he was on the middle gallery, Upānanda stayed below the gallery;
while he was inside the room, Upānanda then stayed under the eaves—or rather, it may be the reverse.
He was beneath the portico, while Upānanda was at the corner of the gate; sometimes it was the reverse.
At that time, the group of seventeen monks deliberated together:
"We cannot perform the *jñapti-karman* of suspension against that old man; our labor would be in vain, so we should go to him and collectively offer an apology."
He then went to that place and requested forgiveness; having already offered his apologies, he asked, "Venerable Sir!
By what means did you know that we intended to perform the *pratisāraṇīya-karman* against you?"
He then answered each point in detail:
"Wherever you go, I shall follow and listen.
When the bhikṣus of few desires heard these words, they all felt resentment and shame.
“How is it that a bhikṣu, knowing that other bhikṣus are engaged in a dispute and are deliberating together, goes there in secret to eavesdrop on their conversation, thinking:
‘According to what they discuss, I shall bring it to light’?”

At that time, the bhikṣus reported the matter to the Buddha. The Buddha said: “...up to this point—having considered ten benefits, I shall establish a training rule for the bhikṣus, which should be recited as follows:

‘If a bhikṣu, knowing that other bhikṣus have engaged in a discussion concerning a matter, and are dwelling in a state of seeking faults, agitation, and contention, should silently go there to listen to what they say.’”
If one forms the thought:
"After I have listened, I shall cause discord and strife," and acts with this as the motive, it is a *pāyattika*.
"Furthermore, if a bhikṣu— referring to Upānanda, with the rest of the meaning as above—
and 'other bhikṣus' meaning those within this Dharma—
should engage in 'discussing matters,' which means beginning to discuss a matter upon first seeing something disagreeable."
To "seek out faults" means to search for transgressions and to speak of them to one another.
To be "disturbed" means that, unable to contain one's feelings, one brings the matter to light.
To "engage in contention" means that, through these matters of dispute, one enters the gate of strife, forming factions and mutually inciting one another.
To "dwell in contention while listening in silence" means to eavesdrop on their words and follow along with what they say.
To "cause strife" means to desire that the conflict shall not cease.
The explanation of the offense is as above.
What are the characteristics of the transgression and the specific circumstances involved?
If a bhikṣu is engaged in discussion on an upper story, when another bhikṣu ascends the story, he should make a sound while treading upon the steps, or cough, or snap his fingers.
If one ascends the pavilion without performing such actions, merely hearing the words without understanding their meaning constitutes an offense of wrong-doing (duṣkṛta);
if one understands the meaning of the words, one incurs an offense of downfall (pāyattika).
The detailed explanation is as previously stated; one should understand the gravity of the offenses regarding gate-houses according to the specific circumstances.
This should likewise be recognized by applying the same principles to walking paths and forest retreats.

If there are bhikṣus traveling along a road who consult together, it should be understood that when a bhikṣu arrives later, all the rules of conduct for travel shall follow those prescribed for ascending a multi-storied pavilion;
if he does not act accordingly, the gravity of his offense shall be as described above.

If a bhikṣu has no prior enmity or grievance, and upon hearing such things—or even after having heard them—seeks through skillful means to extinguish a dispute with the intent of bringing about reconciliation, there is no offense.
Furthermore, there is no offense for one who is a first-time offender, as explained in detail above.
*Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya*, Fascicle 41. *Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya*, Fascicle 4.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Yijing by Imperial Decree. 77.

The Training Rule on Departing in Silence Without Having Granted Consent. The seventy-seventh training rule on departing in silence without having granted consent. At that time, the Blessed One was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.

At that time, Udāyin severed all fetters and delusions; the details are as explained above. Furthermore, the group of seventeen monks held a consultation together, and having assembled the community of bhikṣus, they approached the Elder and made this announcement:
"We now have a matter to interrogate him about, even to the point of wishing to perform the *jñapti-karman* of suspension against Upānanda."
Then the Elder Nanda spoke these words: "Upananda is an elder;
how could we possibly permit him to be subjected to the formal act of *jñapti-caturtha-karman* (the act of suspension) so hastily?"
The group of seventeen monks said to the great assembly:
"If one associates with and instigates evil persons, the assembly shall likewise perform the *jñapti-karman* of suspension (*pratikṣepa*) against them.
Having heard this, Nanda became terrified; he gathered his woolen cloak into a shape resembling a human form upon his seat and departed in silence.
The assembly, unaware of the situation, subsequently performed the *jñapti-caturtha-karman* of suspension against Upānanda. Thereupon, they went to Nanda and said to him with tears:
"How could it be that this Black Bowl has suddenly carried out the act of suspending us?"
Nanda replied, "You need not worry;
since that assembly has not gathered, the ritual cannot be accomplished. Upānanda said:
"Who has not gathered? He replied,
"I am not among the assembly."
When the bhikṣus of few desires heard these words, they all felt resentment and shame, saying:
"How can a bhikṣu, knowing that the assembly has gathered and that a formal act according to the Dharma is being performed, depart in silence?"
The bhikṣus reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said: "I shall observe ten benefits and establish a training rule for the bhikṣus, which should be recited as follows:
'If a bhikṣu, knowing that the Saṃgha is engaged in a formal discussion on a matter according to the Dharma, should rise from his seat and depart in silence, it is a pāyattika.'"
Thus, after the Blessed One had established the training rule for the bhikṣus,
the bhikṣus remained in the assembly for long periods, causing neglect and deficiency in the duties of those who cared for the sick and those who managed communal affairs.
On account of this, the Buddha further permitted that if there is a valid reason, one should depart after having made a formal entrustment.
The World-Honored One praised the observance of the precepts, and so forth, in detail:
"The former was the original prohibition; this is a subsequent allowance. It should be stated as follows:"

"If a bhikṣu, knowing that the Saṃgha is engaged in a formal discussion of matters according to the Dharma, should rise from his seat and depart in silence without having instructed another bhikṣu—unless there is a special reason—it is a pāyattika."
"Furthermore, 'if a bhikṣu' refers to Nanda; the rest of the meaning is as explained above.
'The assembly' refers to the disciples of the Buddha.

'Discussion in accordance with the Dharma' refers to formal procedures consisting of a single motion (*jñapti*), a motion followed by one proclamation (*jñapti-dvitīya-karman*), or a motion followed by three proclamations (*jñapti-caturtha-karman*) that are performed in accordance with the Dharma."
"To depart from one's seat in silence" means to go beyond the bounds of propriety.
"Without having made an announcement" means that although there is a bhikṣu present, one departs without informing him.
The explanation of the offense is the same as before.
In this regard, what are the characteristics of the offense and how does it occur?

If a bhikṣu knows that the Saṃgha is engaged in a formal discussion and deliberation on a matter in accordance with the Dharma, and another bhikṣu departs from his seat in silence without having informed [the assembly], he incurs a *duṣkṛta* (wrongdoing) for every step taken until he reaches a place where his voice can no longer be heard;
at the moment he leaves that place, he incurs the fundamental offense (*mūlāpatti*).
Furthermore, there is no offense for one who is a first-time offender, as explained in detail above. 78.

The Training Rule on Lack of Reverence. The seventy-eighth training rule concerning lack of reverence was established when the Buddha was staying at the Bamboo Grove, the Squirrels’ Feeding Ground, near Rājagṛha.
At that time, there were two bhikṣus:
one named Citra and the other named Hastisiṃha. Knowing that the bhikṣus had gathered in the dining hall, they intended, in accordance with the instruction of the Blessed One, to settle the dispute.
Of these two individuals, one complies with the command of the assembly;

the other, however, defies the instruction and fails to attend the assembly. Once the assembly has finished its deliberation, he shows no respect, causing the proceedings to become disordered and turbulent.
The bhikṣus of few desires collectively felt disdain and contempt, saying:
"How can it be that when the community of bhikṣus is resolving a dispute, one does not attend the assembly oneself, nor show respect upon witnessing the deliberation?"
The bhikṣus reported the matter to the Buddha.
The Buddha said, and after speaking at length, continued: “I, having considered ten benefits, shall establish a training rule for the bhikṣus, which should be recited as follows:
‘If a bhikṣu is disrespectful, it is a pāyattika.’”
"Furthermore, 'if a bhikṣu' refers to one of variegated color; the remaining meanings are as explained above.
'Lack of respect' is of two kinds:
first, toward the great assembly; second, toward an individual."
If one fails to show respect in these two instances, one incurs an offense of downfall (pāyattika) in both cases.
What are the characteristics of the transgression in this regard?
If a bhikṣu knows that the assembly has gathered for a formal discussion and, having been summoned to attend, does not come, he incurs an offense of downfall.

If one calls someone to stay but they do not stay, or sends them away but they do not go; if one sends for bedding and requisites but they refuse to take them, yet when not sent for them, they take them by force; and if the same occurs regarding matters such as requesting a room—when one acts in opposition to the community's instructions in these ways, one incurs a *pāyattika* offense.

If a bhikṣu sees his upādhyāya or ācārya speak in such a manner—such as calling him to come when he does not, or regarding matters concerning his cell and so forth—and he disobeys the instructions of that individual, he incurs an offense of wrong-doing (duṣkṛta) in every instance.
If one makes a formal announcement based on the correct reasoning and does so without disrespect, there is no offense in any of these cases.
Furthermore, those who are without offense include the first-time offender, as explained in detail above.
79. The Training Rule on Drinking Alcohol. The seventy-ninth training rule concerning drinking alcohol. The Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, there were many villages at the foot of Mount Śiśumāra in Kauśāmbī.

There was an elder named Pútú who was immensely wealthy with abundant riches and ample provisions for food and clothing. Not long after he had taken a wife, a daughter was born to them; she was of such upright and beautiful countenance that all who saw her found her pleasing to behold.
When he had grown up, he was married to the son of the householder Anāthapiṇḍada as his wife.
Not long after, the householder Puṭṭa gave birth to another son whose appearance was lovely; on the day of his birth, the father saw him and rejoiced, exclaiming: "Welcome!"
"Welcome! At that time, his kinsmen gave him a name based on these words, calling him Svāgata (Welcome).
Due to the power of this child's meager merit, all their family property gradually perished; both his parents passed away, and he had nowhere to flee for refuge.
When the multitude of people saw him in such a state, they named him "Evil-Come" (Ēlāya).
He became a companion to beggars, seeking his livelihood by begging.
At that time, there was a man who was an old friend of Evil-Come’s father; seeing his poverty and suffering, he gave him a single gold coin to provide for food and clothing.
From there they parted and gradually reached Śrāvastī.
A maidservant of the elder sister saw him and recognized him, returning to report to her mistress:
"I just went outside and encountered Āgata; he is extremely impoverished."
Upon hearing this, his sister was deeply moved by compassion and sent a messenger with cotton cloth and gold coins to temporarily relieve his destitution.
Because he possessed little merit, these were immediately stolen by thieves. Hearing of this matter, the sister sighed in lamentation, saying:
"What use have I for such a person of evil karma and meager merit?"
He immediately cast it aside and did not inquire further.

At that time, the householder Anāthapiṇḍada invited the Buddha and the Saṅgha to his residence for a meal; having prepared various kinds of exquisite and fragrant delicacies, he remained there gazing longingly at the Buddha and the Saṅgha with thirsting devotion.
At that time, E-lai and his fellow beggars, having heard that the elder was providing offerings in hopes of scavenging leftover food, went together to the place where the meal was being served.
When the elder saw the poor men from afar, he commanded his attendants, saying:
"The Buddha and the Sangha are about to arrive; drive these poor people away."
At that time, each of the fellow beggars thought to themselves:

"This great householder previously possessed a compassionate heart; we were solitary and have always relied upon him as our protector. For what reason does he now treat us with such harshness and drive us away?"
"Is it not because the power of this evil one's unwholesome karma has brought calamity upon us?
They then all lifted him up together and threw him onto a heap of filth.
Having been thus slighted by his companions, Evil-Come (Pāpāgata) lay weeping upon the heap of filth.

The elder sent a messenger to announce that the time had arrived; at that moment, during the first part of the day, the World-Honored One took up his robe and bowl and, surrounded by a great assembly, proceeded to the house of the elder, intending to go to the place where the meal was being served.
At that time, the World-Honored One, drawn by the power of great compassion, led them toward the place of evil rebirth and stood there, addressing the bhikṣus:

"You should cultivate weariness for the boundless ocean of suffering within the various realms of saṃsāra, and you should further cultivate weariness for the requisites of life within birth and death."
"Observe this person in his final birth; he shall no longer transmigrate to undergo such suffering and distress, nor shall he have to provide for himself.
He then said to Ānanda:
"Today, for the sake of Svāgata, you should set aside half of your food."
At that time, the World-Honored One entered the house of the elder and took his seat.

Once the elder saw that the great assembly was settled, he immediately provided various kinds of pure and exquisite food and drink to the Buddha and the Sangha, ensuring they were all fully satisfied.
At that time, due to the power of that previously committed evil karma, Ānanda forgot to set aside the half-portion of food he had promised.

The Great Teacher, the World-Honored One, being free from forgetfulness, knew that Ānanda had forgotten not to leave the food behind; he then took half of his own portion and set it aside in his own bowl.
Then, after Ānanda had finished his meal, the thought arose in him:
"Today my mind was disturbed, and I have contravened the instruction of the World-Honored One.
The Buddha said to Ānanda:

"Suppose Jambudvīpa, extending to its four boundaries and filled with oceans, were entirely full of Buddhas; and suppose each of these Buddhas were to preach the profound Dharma, which you would receive and uphold in its entirety without any forgetfulness."
"Now, because of the power of your meager merit, Svāgata, you do not remember.
You should now go and summon that Svāgata.
Then Ānanda, having received these instructions, went to him and said:
"Welcome! Welcome!
He did not recall the name "Welcome," and so remained silent, without response.
Ānanda spoke again, saying:
"This son of a stūpa was formerly named Svāgata; he is no ordinary man.
Having heard this, Svāgata thought thus and spoke these verses:
"I have lost the name 'Welcome'; from where have I come now?
Is it not that my evil retribution has ended, and virtuous karma has arisen at this time!
The Buddha possesses all-encompassing wisdom; he is the refuge for all beings."
Because of his affectionate and kind words, it is fitting to call this "Welcome.
Yet I am a man of no merit; all my kinsmen have abandoned me. Alas!
I am oppressed by manifold sufferings; how can this be called a "Welcome"?
Then Ānanda led Svāgata to the place where the Buddha was; having prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, he sat to one side.
The Buddha said to Ānanda, “Give him half of my meal.”
Ānanda took the bowl and handed it to him.
At that moment, when Svāgata had seen that half of the food remained, he shed tears and spoke these words:
"Though the Blessed One has set aside a portion for me, how could even this small fragment suffice to satisfy my hunger?"
The World-Honored One, knowing the thoughts of Svāgata, addressed him with words of consolation:
"Even if your belly were as vast as the great ocean, and you were to consume mouthfuls as large as Mount Sumeru, no matter how long you ate, you would never finish."
"You should now eat; do not harbor any anxiety.
Svāgata then ate, and having finished his meal, he was filled with joy.
The World-Honored One said to him:
“What is this object in the corner of your robe?

He then opened it and saw a gold coin. He said to the Buddha, “This gold coin was given to me by a paternal acquaintance who, seeing my poverty and suffering, brought it to present to me; however, due to my meager merit, I forgot and did not remember it.”
The World-Honored One said,
"You may take these gold coins and purchase blue lotuses to bring back.
After Svāgata had departed, the Buddha and the assembly of monks returned together to their original location.
At that time, Svāgata, having received the Buddha’s instruction, went to the dwelling of the flower-seller Lambā and entered her garden.
Upon seeing him, the owner of the garden said:
"Svāgata, you may depart; do not enter my garden. Let it not be because of you that the trees and ponds become withered."
Svāgata replied:
“The Blessed One has sent me to purchase blue lotuses.
He then spoke this verse:
“I have no use for these blue lotuses;
it is the Great Teacher, the Omniscient One, who has sent me to purchase them.
Hearing this message from the Buddha’s messenger, Lampā felt deep reverence and spoke this verse:
“The Sage of Great Tranquility is honored by both devas and humans;
as you are the Buddha’s messenger, take as many flowers as you wish.
At that time, after Suvāgata had been given the gold coins, he took many blue lotuses and returned to the place where the Buddha was.
Having seen this, the World-Honored One said:
"Welcome! You may take these lotuses and go present them to the community of monks."
"Welcome," he said, as he passed the flowers from the Buddha to the Saṅgha in succession.
At that time, none of the bhikṣus dared to accept them.
The Buddha said, "Out of compassion for this donor, you should accept and use them; furthermore, all such fragrant substances benefit the faculty of sight, and there is no fault in smelling them."
At that time, all the bhikṣus accepted [the flowers], and they immediately blossomed.

Having seen the blue lotuses, Svāgata recalled his previous life, during which he had cultivated the meditation on the blue (*nīlavarṇa-bhāvanā*) in the presence of various Buddhas; the images then appeared before him. The World-Honored One further expounded the essential points of the Dharma for him, instructing, benefiting, and gladdening him, whereupon he realized the vision of the Truths (*satyadarśana*).
At that time, having attained the first fruit, Svāgata spoke these verses to express his own celebration:
"The Buddha, with the supreme noose of skillful means, Has drawn me forth and established me in the vision of the Truths;
He rouses compassion for those in the evil realms, Like pulling an old elephant from deep mud."
In former times my name was Svāgata; later, people called me Duḥsvāgata.
Now this name Svāgata is no longer false, because I abide within the holy teaching of the Muni.
Having spoken these verses, he rose from his seat, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and said:
“World-Honored One!
I now wish to leave the household life and renounce the world to practice the holy life within the well-expounded Dharma and Vinaya of the Tathāgata.”
The World-Honored One addressed him with a Brahma-like voice, saying:
"Welcome, bhikṣu!
Practice the holy life."
Having spoken these words, he immediately went forth; his hair and beard fell away naturally, the dharma-robes clothed his body, and he was fully ordained, becoming a bhikṣu.

From that time forward, Svāgata exerted great vigor and maintained a firm mind; through meditation during the first and last watches of the night without weariness, he severed all fetters and delusions and realized the fruit of arhatship.

He spoke this verse: "In the presence of the Buddhas of the past, I merely sustained a body of clay or iron; Now, having encountered the Buddha, the World-Honored One, I have attained the state of an Arhat."
Now having heard the World-Honored One’s teaching, I am transformed into a body of pure gold.
Within the cycle of birth and death, I shall no longer undergo future existence;
upholding the untainted Dharma, I peacefully proceed toward the city of Nirvana.
"If a person desires precious jewels, Or birth in heaven and liberation,
They should draw near to virtuous friends, And all their wishes will be fulfilled as they intend.

After the World-Honored Buddha had delivered Śāriputra, Mahāmaudgalyāyana, Mahākāśyapa, Pilindavatsa, and others, those among the people of the world who lacked faith and respect began to harbor resentment and speak thus:

“The śramaṇa Gautama is a thief who steals the world’s precious jewels; from time to time, such dragon-elephants among men appear within this great earth, yet he entirely seduces and entices them to leave the household life so that they may serve as his attendants.”

The Buddha had also previously ordained Niṭṭha, a man of low caste, Cūḷapanthaka, Gopaka, Paṇḍita, the five hundred fishermen by the riverbank, Svāgata, and others. Those who lacked faith and respect again gave rise to slander, saying:
"The Śramaṇa Gautama greedily seeks disciples without ceasing; even those in the world who are poor, low-born, and foolish, he ordains as monks to serve as his attendants."
Having heard this, the World-Honored One thought to himself:

"My great disciple is as virtuous as Mount Sumeru, yet the assembly, being ignorant, has treated him with casual disregard; thus, for no reason, they have brought upon themselves the fault of harming his person."
"Now I ought to initiate this excellent and sublime virtue of 'Welcome' (svāgata).
It is the natural law of the World-Honored One that if there is a disciple possessing true and superior virtue whom others do not recognize, the Buddha employs skillful means to manifest that virtue.
At that time, the Blessed One, wishing to manifest the virtue of "Come, Bhikṣu," addressed Ānanda, saying:
"I now wish to go to Mount Śiśumāragiri; if there are bhikṣus who wish to follow me, let them take their robes and bowls."
The full account continues until they reached Mount Siṃhala.
At that time, there was a venomous dragon dwelling in a grove of mango trees at that residence; it constantly damaged all the crops located near the edge of this mountain.

When the people of this mountain heard that the Buddha had arrived, they all gathered like clouds and proceeded to the Buddha’s dwelling. There they prostrated at the Buddha’s feet and sat to one side.
At that time, the World-Honored One expounded the sublime Dharma for the multitude, instructing, inspiring, benefiting, and gladdening them, before remaining silent.
Then the assembly rose from their seats, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and said:
“World-Honored One!
We pray that you will compassionately deign to come to our home tomorrow to accept our humble offerings.”
The World-Honored One, having understood this, accepted by remaining silent.

When the people knew that the Buddha had accepted, they rose from their seats and departed. That very night, they prepared various kinds of excellent offerings, along with water vessels; having completed the arrangements, in the morning they sent a messenger to announce that the time had arrived.

In the early part of the day, the World-Honored One took up his robe and bowl and, surrounded by a great assembly, proceeded to the place where offerings were prepared; he then sat down at the head of the assembly, and the people of the mountain, including brahmins, provided him with full offerings.

When the Buddha and the assembly of monks had each finished their meal and were fully satiated, they all proceeded to where the Buddha was and sat down wherever space allowed. The Buddha preached the Dharma for them, and with deep joy in their hearts, they addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!..."
We have often heard that the World-Honored One is well able to subdue extremely wicked yakṣas, such as the yakṣas Vana, Śarama, and Khara;
furthermore, he has likewise subdued female yakṣas, such as Ālikā and Hārītī;
and he has also brought under control various venomous nāgas, such as the nāga kings Nanda, Upananda, and Apalāla.
“World-Honored One!

However, beneath this mountain dwells the poisonous dragon Āmra, who constantly and unjustly treats us as enemies and inflicts harm upon us at will. Every day at the three appointed times, he perpetually exhales foul vapors; all birds and beasts within a radius of one hundred *li* die upon smelling his toxic breath, and the complexions of all men and women turn dark and sallow, losing all their luster.”
"We only pray that the World-Honored One will take pity on us and subdue this venomous dragon.
When the World-Honored One had heard these words, he addressed Ānanda, saying:
"You may distribute voting sticks to the great assembly; whoever is able to subdue the dragon shall take one."
At that time, as none among the great assembly would take it up, the World-Honored One addressed him, saying, "Come hither!
You should take up the tally and subdue that poisonous dragon Āmrapālī for the sake of the assembly."

At that time, having heard the Buddha’s command, Svāgata immediately took up his tally. During the first part of the day, he took his robes and bowl, entered the village, and went on almsround; having finished his meal, he proceeded to the dwelling place of the Naga Āmra.

At that time, the dragon king saw Sudinna entering his abode from afar; overcome with great rage, he raised clouds that darkened the day and caused thunder to shake the earth, then sent down rain and hail, intending to harm Sudinna.

At that time, Svāgata entered the meditative concentration of loving-kindness (*maitrī-samādhi*); consequently, all the wind and rain that fell were entirely transformed into powdered aloeswood (*agaru*), powdered sandalwood (*candana*), and powdered *tamāla*, which descended from the sky.

At that time, the Āmra dragon became even more enraged and again brought down sword-wheels, spears, lances, and other weapons; yet upon reaching Svāgata, they all transformed into exquisite celestial lotuses and descended from the sky.

The dragon again emitted smoke, and Svāgata also emitted smoke; the dragon again emitted fire, and Svāgata immediately entered the fire-light samādhi (*tejodhātu-samādhi*), whereby through his supernormal power his body became like a mass of fire, filling the dragon’s palace and all other dwellings with flames.

At that time, the venomous dragon, seeing the great blazing fire, was struck with extreme terror; his body hair stood on end as he sought to flee, only to find that fierce flames had spread everywhere in all other directions, leaving only the place where he was welcomed as peaceful, serene, and cool.
The venomous dragon then went to pay homage at the feet of Svāgata and spoke these words:
"May you grant me protection!
May you grant me protection!"
Śubhāgatā said:

"In a previous life you committed defiled and impure karma and fell among the animals; now, having once again caused harm and performed many unwholesome deeds, where will you fall when your life here ends?"
"On what do you wish to rely?
You will certainly fall into hell; there is no need to doubt this.
At that time, the venomous dragon said to Svāgata:
“Venerable sir!
Please grant me your instruction; what should I do now? Svāgata replied:
"One should receive the Three Refuges along with the Five Precepts, vowing in heart not to transgress them for as long as life lasts.

At that time, the venomous dragon immediately received the Three Refuges and the Five Precepts, pledging for as long as life lasts not to kill, not to steal, not to engage in sexual misconduct, not to drink intoxicants, and not to speak falsely.
Having made this solemn covenant, he prostrated to Svāgata and suddenly vanished.
At that time, having subdued the venomous dragon, Svāgata went to where the Buddha was, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and said:
“World-Honored One!”
"I have already subdued that venomous dragon and caused him to receive the three refuges along with the five precepts.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"Among my disciples, the śrāvakas, Svāgata is foremost in subduing venomous dragons."

At that time, all the people, brahmins, and others living near and far around Mount Śiśumāra, seeing that the assembly of venomous dragons had been subdued and were no longer causing harm, were all filled with great joy at such an unprecedented occurrence.
Each carrying incense, flowers, and articles for offering, they went to where the Buddha was to express their joy; having prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, they each stood to one side and said:
“World-Honored One!
"By the grace of the Buddha’s power, that venomous dragon has been eliminated; we wish to present our offerings and pray that you will graciously accept them.
The Buddha addressed the brahmins, householders, men, and women:
"You should know that this venomous dragon was converted from evil and caused to receive the precepts of refuge by the bhikṣu Svāgata, the son of the Stūpa; it was not through my power."
"You all should take these various items to offer as a gift to Svāgata, thereby repaying his kindness.
At that time, having received the Buddha's instruction, the people took the offerings and went to where Svāgata was; they prostrated at his feet and said, "Noble One!"

"O Benevolent One, you have bestowed great compassion upon us and granted us fearlessness, enabling all living beings to find relief. We pray that you will deign to give us your instructions: what do you wish for us to do?"
Svāgata replied, "Each of you should provide offerings to the Triple Gem according to your means.
At that time, because of Svāgata, the Brahmins and others invited the Buddha and the Saṃgha to partake of a meal for seven days; the Buddha accepted by remaining silent.

When the people there knew that the Buddha had accepted [the invitation], they prostrated at his feet and departed. That very night, they prepared various kinds of exquisite food and drink, arranged seats and mats, and in the morning sent a messenger to announce that the time had come:
"The offerings are prepared; may the Buddha know that the time is right."
At that time, during the first part of the day, the World-Honored One, accompanied by the great assembly, proceeded to the house of the donor where the meal was prepared.

When the various brāhmaṇas, householders, and others saw that [the Buddha] was seated, they immediately provided the Buddha and the Saṃgha with various kinds of exquisite food and drink. Once everyone had eaten their fill, they sat before the Buddha to listen to the essential teachings of the Dharma.
As it was on the first day, so it was for all seven days.
There was a brahmin who had been a long-standing friend of Svāgata’s father; being able to charm venomous dragons, he went to Śrāvastī out of fear of the dragon and lived there under a changed name.

At that time, King Prasenajit had appointed a man as his chief elephant-minister; this man, having come to the foot of the mountain on some business, was filled with great joy upon hearing that Sudarśana had already subdued the venomous dragon.
Having approached the place where he was staying and prostrated at his feet, they said:
"Noble One! We were all terrified and fled together.

Now, hearing that the Venerable One has aroused a heart of compassion to eliminate our enmity and harm, we are filled with joy beyond measure. We wish to offer you our service; we pray that you will deign to show us favor by accepting a meal tomorrow."
"Welcome," he replied, but did not accept.
Then the brāhmaṇa requested again, saying:
"If you are unwilling, I only pray that when the Venerable One returns to the city, you will first accept my offerings."
At that time, Svāgata took pity on them and accepted [the offerings].
Then, after the donors at the foot of the mountain had provided for the Buddha and the Saṃgha for a full seven days, they all prostrated at the Buddha’s feet and listened to the sublime Dharma.

At that time, the World-Honored One expounded the essentials of the Dharma for them, instructing, benefiting, and gladdening them; immediately upon these seats, immeasurable sentient beings had their doubts removed and attained the fruits [of the path].

The Buddha and the assembly gradually arrived at the city of Śrāvastī. Then, the householder Anāthapiṇḍada went to the place where the Buddha was, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and sat to one side.
At that time, after the World-Honored One had finished preaching the Dharma, he remained silent. Then the elder rose from his seat and said:
"World-Honored One, I pray that the Buddha and the Sangha will come to my home tomorrow to accept a modest offering."
The World-Honored One accepted by remaining silent.
Having understood this, the householder paid his respects and departed.
At that time, the brahmin went to Svāgata and said:
“Venerable One!
I have already made a request that when you arrive at my native city, you first accept my meal.
Svāgata informed the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"You have already accepted an invitation previously; you should now go to that banquet. Thus, Svāgata went to the house of that brāhmaṇa.

At that time, the brāhmaṇa served him with excellent food and drink with sincere devotion, and after having him eat his fill, he wished for the food to be digested quickly. He therefore placed a small amount of *hasti-mada* (elephant-liquor) into the drinking water. Svāgata, unaware of this, drank the water, then immediately chewed a tooth-stick and rinsed his mouth before departing.
Having reached the middle of the road, he was scorched by the sunlight and fell asleep intoxicated upon the ground.
Since the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, never lose mindfulness at any time, they immediately manifested a grass hut over the place where he lay, covering his body so that no one would see him.
At that time, after the World-Honored One had finished his meal at the house of the elder and had preached the Dharma for him,
he returned to the place called "Welcome" (Svāgata) and addressed the bhikṣus, saying:
“You all should observe what has been accomplished by Svāgata; in the past, at the place of Mount Gaṅgāśīrṣa, he subdued the poisonous nāga Āmra.
How much more so now could he not tame a small loach?”
“O bhikṣus, if you drink alcohol, such great loss will ensue. At that time,

the World-Honored One used his hand— adorned with the marks of a thousand-spoked wheel and webbed fingers, and distinguished by immeasurable hundreds of thousands of merits— to stroke the crown of Svāgata’s head and said, “Welcome!”
"Why do you not observe that you have fallen into such distress?
At that time, Svāgata regained a small measure of clarity and followed behind the Buddha to the Jetavana Grove.
After the Buddha had washed his feet, he sat down upon his usual seat and addressed the bhikṣus, saying:
“You all should observe that those who drink alcohol possess such faults.
Having praised the observance of the precepts, he spoke at length until: “I, having considered ten benefits, shall establish this training rule for my disciples, which should be recited as follows:
‘If a bhikṣu drinks any kind of intoxicant, it is a pāyattika.’”
"Furthermore, regarding the phrase 'if a bhikṣu': this refers to one who has been ordained by the command 'Come, Bhikṣu' (svāgata), while the remaining meanings are as explained above.

As for the term 'various liquors,' it refers to rice-based fermented liquor (*surā*), or liquors produced by blending roots, stalks, bark, leaves, flowers, and fruits; these various liquors cause intoxication and stupor when consumed."
"Drinking" refers to swallowing.
The explanation of the offense is as before.
In this context, what are the characteristics of the transgression and its specific details?
If a bhikṣu drinks various types of liquor that can cause intoxication, it is a pāyattika offense;
if it does not cause intoxication, drinking it constitutes a duṣkṛta offense.
