If a bhikṣu sees such liquor possessing the color, smell, and taste of liquor, and it is capable of causing intoxication, it is a pāyattika offense.
If one does not become intoxicated, one incurs three *duṣkṛta* offenses.
If a bhikṣu drinks various types of liquor that possess the color, smell, and power of intoxication of liquor, if it is capable of causing intoxication, it is a *pāyattika*;
if it is not capable of causing intoxication, one incurs two *duṣkṛta* offenses.
If a bhikṣu drinks various types of liquor when it possesses only the color of liquor, if it is capable of causing intoxication, it is a pāyattika offense;
if it is not capable of causing intoxication, he incurs one duṣkṛta offense.
If one eats dregs of wine and becomes intoxicated, it is a *pāyattika* offense;
if one does not become intoxicated, one incurs an *dukkaṭa* offense.
If one eats a lump of fermenting agent (*mukha*), one incurs an *dukkaṭa* offense.
If a bhikṣu eats any roots, stalks, leaves, flowers, or fruits that can intoxicate a person, he incurs an offense of wrongdoing (dukkaṭa).
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"If you take me as your teacher, you must not drink any kind of liquor yourselves, nor give it to others, nor even place a drop of liquor on the tip of a blade of grass and put it into your mouth."
"If one willfully violates this, one incurs an offense of transgression against the Dharma.
If a bhikṣu drinks vinegar that has the color of alcohol, there is no offense in drinking it.
If he drinks alcohol that has been thoroughly boiled, this likewise constitutes no offense.
If a physician causes one to swallow wine or applies it to the body, there is no offense.
Furthermore, there is no offense for a first-time offender; the details are as explained above.
At that time, having witnessed these events, all the bhikṣus were filled with doubt and questioned the World-Honored One:

“Welcome, Bhikṣu! What karma did you previously perform to be born into a wealthy and prosperous family, yet later encounter such poverty and suffering that you were constantly begging for alms, called by the name ‘Evil-Coming,’ and abandoned by your companions in a heap of refuse?”
"Furthermore, by what karma did he encounter the World-Honored One, sever all afflictions, and attain arhatship?
The Buddha told the bhikṣus: "Listen well!

In the distant past, before a Buddha had appeared in the world, there was a Pratyekabuddha who had manifested in the world; though his heart was filled with compassion, he did not preach the Dharma with his voice.
At that time, there was an elder who went to a fragrant garden intending to enjoy himself in play.
There was a Pratyekabuddha who, being afflicted by illness, entered the garden wearing coarse and tattered robes for the sake of begging for alms.
Upon seeing him, the householder immediately gave rise to anger and, with an impatient mind, told his messenger:
"This wicked person must not be allowed to enter."
The messenger, feeling pity for him, did not immediately drive him forward; the elder rose up himself, seized the Venerable One by the neck, and pushed him toward a heap of filth, saying:
"Why do you not go among the beggars to be their companion?"
At that time, out of compassion for him, the Venerable One rose into the air like a king of geese and performed the eighteen miraculous transformations.

When those of the class of ordinary beings witnessed such supernatural power, they quickly gave rise to a sense of remorse as if a great tree were collapsing. Prostrating from afar at the Venerable One’s feet, they cried out:

“Welcome, O Noble One! You are a true field of merit. We pray that you will lower your body and, out of pity, accept our repentance for us ignorant people, so that we do not sink into suffering for eternal kalpas.”
At that time, seeing his sincere devotion, the Venerable One lowered himself from the air.
After the elder had paid his respects, he prepared various kinds of exquisite food, drink, flowers, and incense as offerings. He repented for his evil karma and made a great vow:

"By the roots of goodness from this offering I have now made, may I be born into a wealthy family in a future life; may I find a supreme guide to serve without weariness, who shall awaken me and lead me toward the gate of liberation."
"O Bhikṣus! The householder of that time was none other than Svāgata.
He once committed an act of malice against a Pratyekabuddha, calling him 'Durbhāga' and pushing him into a heap of dung."
Due to this karma, for five hundred lifetimes he was constantly a beggar, known by the name Makarakṣa (Evil-Coming), and was abandoned by his companions in a heap of filth.
Because of the power of his former offerings and his aspiration, he was born into a great wealthy family; within my Dharma, he left the household life, severed his delusions, and became an Arhat.
"O bhikṣus, the karma you yourselves have created must be experienced by yourselves as its retribution; it does not perish.
Therefore, you should cultivate wholesome conduct and refrain from evil deeds; thus should you train."

[80] The Training Rule on Entering a Village at an Improper Time Without Informing a Bhikṣu. The eightieth [training rule]: Entering a village at an improper time without informing a bhikṣu. At that time, the Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī at the Jeta Grove, in Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, there was a brahmin from another region who came to this city to marry a wife and returned to his ancestral home.
Before long, he gave birth to a daughter; as she gradually grew up, her father took her to her maternal uncle’s house.

This girl wished to pay homage at the Jeta Grove; as soon as she stepped out the door, she saw various Brahmins and the wives of householders also intending to go there to pay their respects, so she went in and informed her father.
When the father saw his companions depart, he immediately ordered the young girl to follow them until they reached the gate of the monastery.

At that time, Udāyin saw the women being led into the monastery; he led them through the successive prostrations to his own room, where he preached the sublime Dharma to them at length, as described above.
At that time, seeing the girl’s beautiful countenance and graceful form, Udāyin gave rise to a defiled mind; he immediately touched her body and kissed her mouth.
At that moment, the girl wished to engage in unrighteous conduct, but Udāyin would not consent to it.
Filled with rage and resentment, the girl tore at her own body with her fingernails;
having returned home, she said to her father, "The bhikṣu Udāyin has violated me, a maiden."
The father immediately informed the five hundred brahmins.
When those men heard this matter, each harbored resentment and anger; they gathered in one place, intending to beat Udāyin.
When the five hundred men arrived at that place, they all pulled and dragged him together, yet they were unable to move him even by the shift of a foot.
Having known this, the World-Honored One thought:
"This is the final instruction for Udāyin."

The Buddha diminished his strength so that he was rendered incapable of resistance; when the brahmins saw his weakness, they beat him together until he was nearly dead and dragged him to the king’s gate.
At that time, the king was sleeping during the day atop a high tower.

Then, by means of his supernormal powers, the World-Honored One extended his hand adorned with the merits of a hundred blessings, went to the place where the king lay, and made a sound by snapping his fingers to awaken him, saying:
"Great King!"
"In matters of judicial inquiry, one must observe well and observe thoroughly; one should not act with haste.
Upon hearing this, the king was startled awake and realized it was the voice of the Buddha.
At that moment, the brahmin let out a great cry at the foot of the king’s gate.
"There is an improper matter!
There is an improper matter!
the King commanded his messenger to inquire, saying:
"What is unreasonable about this?
The messenger went to the gate, investigated the matter thoroughly, and reported it all to the king.
Upon hearing these words, the king thought to himself:
“The World-Honored One has instructed me to observe thoroughly and not act precipitately; this was my intention.
The king summoned the young girl and questioned her as to its truth or falsehood;
she replied, “It is true.”
The king then sent her into the palace, ordering Queen Śrīmālā to personally examine whether her body had sustained any injury.
Queen Śrīmālā immediately called the young girl, laid her upon her breast, and questioned her with the truth; the girl likewise spoke the truth.
The lady then ordered an elderly palace attendant who was skilled in examination to inspect her eyes to verify whether she was truly intact or not.
After the attendant had observed her, she informed the lady, saying, "This girl has no injuries at all."
He immediately reported the matter to the king.
The king became greatly incensed and ordered that the brahmin and this woman be handed over to the judicial officials for severe punishment.
Then, King Prasenajit, having rebuked Udāyin three times, released them both in order to manifest the respect due to the holy teaching of the Tathāgata.
Queen Śrīmālā covered [the window] and sent a messenger to summon Udāyin, saying to him:
"Venerable One!

The Unsurpassed World-Honored One, our Great Compassionate Father, made solemn vows and commitments throughout incalculable kalpas; he exerted diligent effort and practiced the pure conduct with a steadfast mind. He renounced the rank of a Wheel-Turning King, his kingdom, city, wife, and children, setting his will upon detachment from desire to rescue and deliver the ignorant sentient beings within the three realms."

If even we, who are but worldly folk, still aspire to renunciation, how much more so should you, who have left the household life through the well-spoken Dharma and Vinaya? Yet now that your hair is shorn and your robes dyed, you have grown old and decrepit; unable to cast off the burden of transgressions, you personally commit evil deeds with a defiled heart, causing laypeople to lose their faith and reverence.
Alas! How painful! This is the height of base depravity.
"From this day forward, you ought to repent.

When Udāyin heard this reprimand, he was overcome with such shame that he had no place to set his body; he then went to the Venerable Śāriputra, prostrated at his feet, and reported the matter in its entirety.
At that time, Śāriputra observed their faculties and dispositions and taught the Dharma accordingly, providing them with instruction.
Having heard it, they deeply reproached themselves and gave rise to a courageous mind; before long, all their delusions were severed and they realized the fruit of Arhatship.
The Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya, Scroll Forty-two;
The Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya, Scroll Forty-three.
The Tripiṭaka Master Yijing, by Imperial Command, translated [the remainder of] the Eightieth Chapter:
The Training Rule on Entering a Village at an Improper Time Without Informing a Bhikṣu. At that time, having attained the fruit, Udāyin thought to himself:
"The World-Honored One, my compassionate father, has indeed bestowed great kindness upon me; what deed can I now perform to repay his virtue?"
"Except for benefiting sentient beings, there is no other fruit of retribution.
Thereupon, Udāyin proceeded to travel about and teach according to the circumstances.
At that time, the Blessed One addressed the bhikṣus, saying:
"Among my disciples in the assembly of Śrāvakas, he who teaches and transforms sentient beings, causing them to attain the fruits of sainthood, is foremost Udāyin.
The summary verse says:
Mahādeva, Mahāśikha, Maṇi, the Physician, and the Belly of the Saṃgha.
The ladder, the two-fold enjoyment, the violent and the childhood;
the bowl and the wrestler—these are called the thirteen matters.
He extensively transformed eighteen billion beings, causing them all to cross over from the ford of suffering.
Regarding Mahādeva: at that time, the Venerable Udāyin thought to himself, "Among all these sentient beings now, who is connected to me such that I may first bring them to spiritual transformation?
He observed a certain Brahmin serving Mahādeva and saw that he was fit to be delivered.
At that time, during the first part of the day, Udāyin took up his robe and bowl and entered the city of Śrāvastī to wander for alms; he saw that the brahmin had prepared a full array of offerings.
Seeking out a brāhmaṇa to whom he might give food and drink, he called out in a loud voice: "Who is a brāhmaṇa?
To him I shall give food."
Udāyin said, "I am a brāhmaṇa;
my Great Teacher is the supreme brāhmaṇa.
That person replied:
“You are not a brāhmaṇa; you are a shaven-headed śramaṇa.
Udāyin said, “I shall now go with you to ask Mahādeva whether or not I am a brāhmaṇa.”
The two of them went together to the shrine of Mahādeva, and Udāyin asked: "Am I a brāhmaṇa?
Then the image of Mahādeva spoke and said:
“Noble Udayin! You are truly a brahmin, and your teacher is an even more eminent great brahmin.

Upon seeing the image of Mahādeva speak, he was struck with great wonder and marveled at such an unprecedented occurrence; he conceived deep faith and reverence for the Buddha’s teaching and immediately invited Udayin to his home to offer him hospitality.

When the meal was finished, he immediately preached the Dharma for him, instructing, exhorting, benefiting, and gladdening him. Having heard the Dharma, he perceived the Truths and attained the first fruit; he took refuge in the Triple Gem and received the five precepts, vowing to abstain from taking life and so forth for as long as he lived.
He then said: "Noble One!..."
"I vow to provide for all your needs—food, drink, clothing, bedding, and medicine—for as long as I live; I pray that you will graciously accept them.
He replied, "I have not yet finished my work of transforming others; I should not accept this."
Having spoken these words, he rose from his seat and departed.
As for Mahāśikha, on another occasion, the Venerable Udāyin again surveyed all sentient beings to see who was capable of being converted.
He saw a certain brāhmaṇa who also served Mahādeva and did not believe in the Triple Gem;

knowing that he was capable of being converted, [the Blessed One] took up his robes and bowl at dawn and entered the city of Śrāvastī. There he saw that brāhmaṇa preparing food as before, searching for a brāhmaṇa with the hope of making an offering.
He cried out:
"Who is a brāhmaṇa?
To him I shall give food."
Udāyin said, "I am a brahmin;
my Great Teacher is the supreme brahmin.
That person replied:
"You are not a brāhmaṇa; you are a shaven-headed śramaṇa.
A true brāhmaṇa does not have such a physical appearance. Udāyin said:
"What are the physical characteristics of a brahmin?
He replied,
"A brahmin’s topknot is tall and large, just like a crown or hat."
Udāyin said, "If it is so, I am that very person.
As he stroked his head with his hand, a great topknot like a crown suddenly appeared.
Having seen him, the man conceived deep faith and, with a sense of wonder, invited him to enter and accept a meal.
After he had eaten, [the Buddha] preached the Dharma for him, instructing, inspiring, benefiting, and gladdening him; both the Brahmin and his wife attained the first fruit of the path.
Having attained the fruit, he took refuge in the Triple Gem and received the precepts, vowing to provide the four requisites for as long as he lived.
The Venerable One said:
"I have karmic obligations to fulfill."
Having abandoned it, he departed.
On another day, the Venerable Udāyin went to observe which sentient beings were capable of being converted.
He saw a brahmin who also worshipped Mahādeva and did not believe in the Triple Gem;
knowing that he was capable of being transformed, he took up his robes and bowl at dawn and entered the city, standing outside the gate of the brahmin’s house.

Knowing that the woman desired fine pearls, he immediately transformed himself into a pearl merchant and entered her house to show her excellent pearls—resplendent with brilliant luster and lovely in form—and said:
"I am selling these pearls; if you require them, take whichever you please."
Then the brahmin asked for its price, and Udāyin said,
"It shall be whatever you offer.
He offered a price that was less than even one-hundredth of the value, yet Udāyin immediately accepted it.
At that time, the husband and wife were struck by what they had never before experienced and sighed to themselves, saying, "For what reason is this precious jewel being taken at such a low price?

When Udāyin perceived that their faculties were ripe, he resumed his original form; thereupon, the husband and wife felt redoubled faith and reverence, and proceeded to provide him with offerings of the finest food and drink.

After they had finished eating and rinsed their mouths, [the Buddha] recited for them the verses on giving and further expounded the profound Dharma. Having heard this, the husband and wife both realized the first fruit [of the path], took refuge, and received the precepts; they vowed to provide offerings for the rest of their lives, as described in detail previously.
Then Udāyin abandoned him and departed.

As for the physician, there was at that time in Śrāvastī a brahmin who harbored no faith or reverence toward the Triple Gem. He had been afflicted by a chronic illness for many years, and every physician had abandoned him, saying, "This is a malignant disease; it cannot be cured."
At that time, the brāhmaṇa no longer sought a physician and waited for death with composure.

Udāyin, observing that he was ready to be converted, took his robes and bowl and entered the city. Arriving at the man's house, he stood outside the gate and transformed himself into a physician, saying:
"I am skilled in medical treatment."
The family members called him inside, and the patient told them:
"I have been ill for a long time, and all physicians have abandoned me; I know only how to await death, with no one left to rely upon."
The conjured physician replied, "You need not worry;
the power of incantations and excellent medicines is inconceivable, and in a mere moment, you shall be restored to health."
Upon hearing this, the patient felt profound joy and gratitude.
Udāyin then recited incantations and invoked the names of the Triple Gem; once the brahmin had heard the spells, all his ailments were eliminated, and he was restored to his former health.

Having seen this, the Venerable One returned to his original form; the husband and wife of that household felt redoubled faith and reverence, marveling at such an unprecedented occurrence, and prepared exquisite food and drink to invite him to accept their offerings.

After they had eaten, he preached the Dharma, and both [the king and his retinue] realized the first fruit of the path. For their reception of the refuges and precepts, the detailed account is as previously described, up until the point where he left them behind.

Regarding the "monastic community": at that time, there was a brahmin in Śrāvastī who harbored no faith or reverence toward the Triple Gem. Though immensely wealthy and possessing vast riches, he was by nature miserly and lacked the intent to give; he delighted only in amassing great stores of wealth.

At that time, Udāyin, knowing that the man's faculties were ripe for conversion, went frequently to his house to beg from him; yet despite his repeated coming and going, he ultimately obtained nothing.
On another day, carrying his robe and bowl, he entered the man's house again and emerged with an empty bowl. Just as he reached the gateway, the brāhmaṇa came out from within and asked: "Bhikṣu!"
"Is there anything to be obtained within my house?
Seeing that he lacked faith and respect, the Venerable One spoke to him in secret, saying:
"Since you yourself have nothing, what can you possibly give?"
Upon hearing this, he became enraged and replied: "Śramaṇa!
I possess wealth and food sufficient to provide for everyone; why do you and your followers say we have nothing, and why do you so lightly despise us?"
He replied,
“If that is the case, I shall come to you tomorrow to receive food.
The brahmin said:
"This is indeed a virtuous deed.
At that time, Udāyin went to other households again; having obtained food through alms, he returned to his original location. After finishing his meal, he paid homage to the Buddha and said:
"World-Honored One!..."
There was a brahmin who did not believe in the Triple Gem; by nature he was stingy and devoted to the accumulation of wealth, lacking any intention to practice giving.
Today, he suddenly requested me, the Buddha, and the assembly of monks to come for a meal tomorrow morning.
The Buddha accepted by remaining silent.
When the next day arrived, that brahmin had made no preparations whatsoever within his house.
At that time, Anāthapiṇḍada and other elders, having heard that the Buddha and the Saṅgha had been invited, all went to that residence; seeing that nothing was prepared, they said to the brahmin:
"You invited Udāyin along with his retinue; this means that the Buddha and the community of monks have come to your residence to receive a meal at one time.
Why is it that you now make no preparations?"
He replied,
"I will not give you food.
The people said to him:
"If the Buddha and the community of monks come to your home today and you do not offer them food, King Śrīghoṣa will surely punish you and will not tolerate or overlook it."

When the brahmin heard this, he was greatly terrified; however, due to the manifestation and awakening of roots of goodness from past lives, he subsequently provided a great quantity of goods, preparing superior offerings intended for the gift to the Buddha and the Sangha.
At that time, during the first part of the day, the World-Honored One, surrounded by a great assembly, went to that house and sat down calmly upon the seat prepared for him.
Then the brahmin personally offered excellent food and drink; when the Buddha and the Sangha had finished eating and completed their ritual rinsing, they rose from their seats and departed.

At that time, Udāyin remained seated alone and expounded the sublime Dharma for the husband and wife; they both attained the vision of the Truths while still on their seats, took refuge in the Triple Gem, and received the five precepts, as described in detail previously.
As for "Belly," there was a brahmin in the city of Śrāvastī who likewise lacked respectful faith in the Triple Gem; his wife was so exceptionally beautiful that she had few equals.
That man felt such intense affection for his wife that he never permitted anyone to enter their home unannounced.

At that time, Udāyin, as before, observed those capable of being converted and saw that the moment for the liberation of that couple had arrived; thus, taking up his robes and bowl, he went on his almsround in due order.
Upon arriving at the gate of that house and wishing to enter, the brahmin saw him and refused permission;

Udāyin then went to urinate. At that moment, Udāyin caused the brahmin’s urine to flow out incessantly. He then entered the house and stood face-to-face with the wife; however, out of arrogance, she did not look upon him. Udāyin then transformed her intestines, causing them to protrude from her abdomen.
When the brahmin arrived and saw this, he was struck with terror and felt a sense of revulsion; he then prostrated before the Venerable One and requested forgiveness.
Udāyin immediately withdrew his supernormal powers, restoring the woman’s body to its former state, whereupon the husband and wife marveled at such an unprecedented occurrence.

Udāyin then preached the Dharma for them, saying that the body is impure and not worth cherishing. Upon hearing the Dharma, both husband and wife realized the first fruit of the path; the full account is as previously described.
Regarding "one who climbs the ladder": there was a brahmin in the city of Śrāvastī whose wife was beautiful, yet she lacked faith and respect in her heart.
Udāyin thought to himself, "Who should receive my instruction?"

Observing that the roots of goodness of that couple from their past lives were connected to him and that they were ready to be transformed through his influence, he took up his robes and bowl and went to their home.
At that time, the Brahmin had gone out on prior business, so the Venerable One entered the house.
Seeing him from afar, the woman avoided him and entered the room; the Venerable One followed her inside.
The woman then climbed the ladder up to the high gallery, and the Venerable One ascended as well.
The woman immediately pushed the ladder upright, whereupon the Venerable One fell to the ground and entered the meditative attainment of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*).
At that time, the wife watched from afar and, seeing that there was no breath, concluded he was dead.

She descended by means of a ladder and tried to lift him with her hands; though she exerted all her strength, she could not move him at all. She then ordered her family members to come together and lift him, yet he remained motionless.

At that time, a Brahmin came from outside; astonished by the incident, he questioned briefly and learned what had happened. He immediately tried to support him himself, but could not even lift him up. His family was filled with terror and, having no other recourse, devised a plan.
At that time, a Brahmin lay follower who was a close acquaintance of his arrived from outside.
Seeing the Venerable Udāyin, he said to the host: "This man has not died;
rather, he has entered a sublime meditative absorption. He has come to your house to deliver you from suffering, and thus he has manifested this transformation."
"You should earnestly seek compassion through repentance and apology.

At that time, the brahmin grasped the Venerable One's feet, prostrated himself, and sought compassion through repentance. The Venerable One emerged from meditative concentration and preached the Dharma for him; he immediately attained the first fruit of the path. The details are as previously explained.

Regarding the one who enjoys [the gains]: there was a brahmin in Śrāvastī who had married a woman from a prominent family as his wife; she was exceptionally beautiful in appearance and fond of boasting about herself.

At that time, Udāyin observed that this woman’s faculties and disposition had ripened and she was capable of being transformed; thus, taking up his robes and bowl, he entered the city according to his circumstances and arrived at her residence.
At that time, the brahmin had some business and had already departed. His wife was arrogant; although she saw the bhikṣu, she gave him nothing at all, nor did she speak with him.
The Venerable One, following her karmic disposition and past-life circumstances, spoke this verse:
"You now enjoy the fruits of your past karma, Yet in the present you have no mind to practice giving."
"I have seen beautiful women with tears soaking their robes; before long, they too shall weep for themselves.
Having spoken this verse, he departed through the gate.
At that time, the woman, not understanding the meaning of the words, thought to herself:
"This śramaṇa reviled me," he thought,
harboring resentment and vexation. When the brāhmaṇa returned and saw him, he asked,
"What trouble do you have?"
The wife said, "Just now a śramaṇa came and insulted me; if he remains alive, my life will not be preserved.
Upon hearing this, her husband glared with fury and shouted, seizing a sharp sword in his hand, he pursued that bhikṣu, intending to take his life.
At that time, Udāyin saw him approaching from afar; he transformed himself into a small room and sat with the door closed. The brahmin called out for him to open the door, and the Venerable One said:
"You may cast away your sword, and I shall open it for you."
The brahmin then thought to himself,
"I shall simply seize him by the neck and beat him to death with my fist.
He then cast aside his sword and, driven by intense rage, cried out urgently for the door to be opened.
The Venerable One replied,
"I shall open it for you once you have abandoned this angry and violent disposition.
Having heard this, he thought to himself:
"This holy man has perceived my evil intent," he thought, and immediately repented and reproached himself, abandoning his harmful mind and opening the door.
Once the man had entered, [the holy man] preached the sublime Dharma to him; he then attained the first fruit of the path, received the three refuges and the five precepts, and was told:
"I have not uttered any harsh words toward your wife; rather, I spoke these verses to cause her to reflect upon past events, but she, being foolish, did not understand and instead gave rise to anger.
Now, listen attentively!
I shall explain this for you.
In the distant past, there was a poor woman who saw another beautiful woman, exquisitely adorned and attended by her own retinue, whom all people loved and revered.
The poor woman, weeping in distress, thought to herself:
"By what means can I now obtain such a thing as I desire?
At that time, there was an upāsikā who was her close friend, and she said to her:
"Why do you grieve and suffer?
The woman explained the matter to him, and he replied:
"Grief and affliction are of no benefit; the karmic retribution of another arises from their own causes."
The poor woman asked, "What is its cause?
He replied:
"If one bestows food and drink upon a supreme field of merit and makes a vow with utmost sincerity, one will surely obtain its fruit.
At that time, a Pratyekabuddha saint came to beg for alms; the woman offered him the food, her heart harboring a specific aspiration.
Then that Pratyekabuddha manifested a supernatural transformation, and the poor woman, conceiving faith, made this aspiration:
"By the roots of merit from this offering, may I never encounter poverty or suffering in whatever place I am born."
"If one attains a human body that is upright, beautiful, and exquisite, such that all who see it rejoice, and whose enjoyments are never lacking.

Because of the power of the vows made by your wife through her previous acts of giving, she has obtained the retribution of physical beauty and enjoys abundant wealth; she was born into a noble family and is beloved and esteemed by all people.
"Now that you do not believe me, how could I have attained this?

At that time, the Brahmin, having obtained the supreme fruit and heard the account of his past-life causes and conditions, invited the Venerable One back to his own residence and prepared for him various kinds of excellent and sublime food and drink.

After he had eaten, he preached the essentials of the Dharma for her; having heard the Dharma, the wife also realized the first fruit of the path (srotāpanna). She requested to receive the Three Refuges and the Five Precepts, as explained in detail previously. Regarding the "twofold" case:

In the city of Śrāvastī, there was a Brahmin whose family was immensely wealthy but who harbored a stingy disposition. Having some business that required him to travel elsewhere, he calculated his wife’s portion of food and departed, sealing the rest of the storehouse with clay.

At that time, Udāyin, knowing that the woman was ready to be converted, entered her house to beg for alms. The woman took her own portion of one *śu* of cooked rice and offered it to the bhikṣu; when she looked back into the vessel, the food remained as it had been before.

Then, on the following day, Udāyin again brought a companion to her house; when the woman saw them, she invited both to eat, yet the rice vessel returned as it was the day before, without having diminished.
The husband sent four men, and thus the number doubled until sixty-four men came; he gave each of them one *sheng* of cooked rice, no less than usual.
As these sixty-four men came to eat every day, the others saw this and felt jealousy. When the husband returned home, they told him: "Your wife is being wasteful at home;
she constantly provides food for a hundred people every day. Look at what she is doing—your family will surely be ruined."
When the brahmin had heard these words, he returned home and rebuked his wife:
"Why did you spend so extravagantly while I was away for but a moment?"
The wife then said, "Venerable sir, you need not be angry;
the portion set aside for me has been used to provide for the Sangha, while not a single thing among the remaining storehouse goods has been diminished."
When her husband heard this, he was deeply perplexed by what she said and wished to test it to verify its truth or falsehood.
At that time, as it was mealtime, Udāyin returned and brought in that same number of bhikṣus; after they had finished eating as before, the rice vessel remained full.
Upon seeing this, the brahmin felt even greater wonder and developed deep faith; he immediately invited the assembly of monks and prepared an extensive offering.
After they had eaten, he listened to the Dharma, whereupon both husband and wife realized the Truths (satyāni). Having received the refuges and precepts, they took their leave and departed.
Regarding the "violent and wicked": In the city of Śrāvastī, there was a brahmin whose wife was violent and wicked by nature.
On the day of a festival, the brahmin thought to himself:
"Today, many relatives and acquaintances will surely come; it would be deeply shameful and disgraceful if my wife were to revile them in the presence of these guests."
Having had this thought, he took his young child and fled toward another village.
Udāyin, perceiving that the time for converting that woman had arrived, took his robes and bowl and went to her house, where he saw the woman preparing food and drink.
The Venerable One stood not far away, and the woman said to him:
"If you wish to find food, even were you to stare with eyes as large as alms-bowls, food would still be difficult to obtain."
At that time, the Venerable One opened both eyes, which were as large as alms bowls;
the woman spoke again, saying, "Even if you were to divide your body into two parts, I would still not give it to you."
The Venerable One’s transformed body was then split into two pieces.
At that time, the maidservant said to the woman:
"If you kill a bhikṣu, you will violate the laws of the land; you shall become a state slave and be put to labor for the rest of your life."

The wife was struck with terror and wished to take the corpse and discard it in a deep pit; however, as the Venerable One had entered the meditative absorption of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*), she was unable to move him. She then grasped his feet and offered a sincere apology, praying that he would restore his original form and allowing her to take the rice cakes as she pleased.
The Venerable One immediately rose and asked her for some cakes.

The woman, wishing to find one of poor quality to give him, examined the basket and found that they were all excellent. She took one and gave it to the Bhikṣu; however, as she did so, all the cakes came out.
She asked the Venerable One, "Are you taking them all?"
He replied, "There are many of us who practice the holy life together; it would be a great kindness if you were to go there yourself.

The woman took the cakes and went to the house of the householder Anāthapiṇḍada. She saw the Buddha and the assembly of monks sitting in solemn dignity; she offered a cake to each person, yet the cakes were still not exhausted.

Upon seeing this, the woman marveled at such an unprecedented occurrence and gave rise to profound faith and reverence; as he then preached the Dharma for her, she immediately attained the first fruit of the path. When she returned to her home, she saw that the cakes were just as they had been before.

When the day for the festival had passed, the brahmin, accompanied by his son, arrived. Seeing that his wife’s deportment was composed and her silence profound, and observing that her actions were unlike those of ordinary times, he spoke this verse:
"Your former disposition was wild and reckless; For what reason has your mind now changed?"
"I observe what you have done, and it is not the same as your past conduct.
His wife replied:
"In the past I was not mad; now I have no other intent."
"Only through the teaching of the World-Honored One, one perceives the Truth and enters the True Stream.
His wife then related the matter in full.

Upon hearing this, the Brahmin husband marveled at such an unprecedented occurrence and his reverence and faith deepened even further. He then went to the Jeta Grove and invited Udāyin, along with the Buddha and the community of monks, to take a meal the following day.

Having accepted [the invitation], Udāyin informed the Buddha and the Saṃgha, as was extensively related in the usual manner; eventually, after the Buddha and the Saṃgha had finished eating, they returned to their residence.
At that time, Udāyin remained alone in the house to teach the essential points of the Dharma, causing [the host] to realize the fruits of the path and perceive the Truths.
At that time, the husband and wife invited him to receive offerings for as long as they lived; however, the Venerable One would not accept. The wife said to him:
"I have prepared a seat; I only pray that the Venerable One will beg for alms elsewhere and eat here."
The Venerable One, out of compassion, accepted [the invitation] and departed.
As for the "youths," there were five hundred sons of brahmins in Śrāvastī who, on the day of a festival, each took food and drink and went to a grove intending to assemble there.
At that time, Udāyin thought to himself:
"Who now is capable of being transformed?

Knowing that the faculties of those five hundred sons of brahmins were nearing maturity, he took his robe and bowl in the early morning and entered the park, going to the place where those youths had gathered.
Having seen him, the people asked one another,
"Of what lineage is this bhikṣu that he has gone forth?
One who knew the details replied to the crowd:
"This is one of the Brahmin caste, who has abandoned his noble lineage to become a śramaṇa.
Having heard this, the people asked the Venerable One:
"Your Honor is the son of a high minister of noble descent; why have you renounced it to go forth among these common and lowly folk, where food is indiscriminate and seating lacks order?"
The Venerable replied:

"The brahmins of the world possess the name but lack the substance. Those to whom I have turned— the Unsurpassed Great Teacher and the assembly of noble ones who can eliminate evil—are truly all genuine brahmins."
When the young men heard these words, they clapped their hands and laughed.

Thereupon, the Venerable One, by means of his supernormal powers, caused the flower garlands upon the heads of all the youths to transform into wreaths of scallions and garlic; all the cakes and food became ox-hide, and all the various delicacies turned into beef; the milk and drinking gruels were entirely transformed into wine—all of which are not things fit for the consumption of those of the Brahmin caste.
Then that Venerable One, having miraculously produced various kinds of pure food within his own alms bowl, addressed the people, saying:
"Behold my bowl and my physical form; compared to what you have done, which of us is truly pure?"
"Who is it that lacks discernment?
When the youths heard these words, each reflected upon themselves and realized their own baseness and wickedness.

They then said to one another, "It must be that venerable one who, by means of his supernormal powers, has caused our flower garlands and all our food and drink to become foul and unfit for consumption."
"At this time, we have no other recourse; it is fitting that we go before him to offer our confession and apology.
They then prostrated at his feet and said:
"Noble One!..."

We are a foolish lot, possessing only the ignorant physical eye; relying on our noble lineage, we have uttered base and evil words, rashly insulting and provoking you, O Noble One. We pray only that, out of compassion, you will accept our repentance.
With one voice, they spoke these verses:
"Skin, flesh, blood, and excrement; The faculties of suffering and pleasure are no different.
All are alike this defiled body; How can there be distinctions among the four castes?"
One whose body is free from all evils, whose speech is likewise without transgression,
and whose mind is utterly pure— such a one is called a true Brahmin.
Adorned with the sublime Dharma, they have skillfully disciplined themselves and cultivated the holy life.
"One who can eliminate all evil karma is a true Brāhmaṇa.

When Udāyin heard these verses, he knew that their faculties were ripe; he then preached the Dharma to them, instructing, exhorting, inspiring, and gladdening them. Thereupon, the five hundred youths, while still on their seats, severed their afflictions and realized the Truths.
Their bodies and their food and drink became pure as before; each received the refuges and precepts, as explained in detail previously. Regarding the bowl:

in the city of Śrāvastī there was a brahmin who was skilled in the mastery of incantations but did not believe in the Triple Gem. He constantly used the power of his spells to command spirits and deities, making them drive his chariot so that he could travel wherever he pleased.
At that time, Udāyin again observed sentient beings to see who was capable of being guided and led into the True Dharma.

Seeing that this Brahmin’s faculties were nearing maturity, he took his robes and bowl and went to the man’s house. He saw the Brahmin reciting incantations to command a spirit to drive his chariot as he was about to depart; the man had briefly stopped, descended from the vehicle, and was just about to urinate when Udāyin caused him to urinate without pause. He then immediately broke the spell and released the deity.

After a short while, the Brahmin returned and saw that the spirits had all dispersed and the chariot could not be moved; although he recited his incantations and arts, none proved effective, and his resources being exhausted, he was at a loss for a plan.
He said to the bhikṣus,
"Since your mastery of mantras has failed to achieve its purpose, whom do you wish me to send now to serve me?
The Venerable One took his bowl, opened it to show them, and said:
"This shall serve as your attendant.
The brahmin said,
"How can this black iron bowl serve me?"
The Venerable One said, "Whatever you think of shall emerge from this.
Upon hearing these words, he immediately tested his mind by thinking of food and drink of a hundred flavors; as soon as he thought of them, the various flavors were fully present within the bowl.
Seeing this event, he marveled at such an unprecedented occurrence and said:
"Great Sage! I pray that you will grant me this wondrous art."
The Venerable One then spoke a verse to him, saying:
“I do not bestow my secret spells upon those who do not offer them;
I give them only in exchange for spells, or when one provides me with sustenance, or when one acquires a great deal of precious wealth.”
"If it is not so, even if I die, I shall not transmit it.
When the brahmin had heard this verse, he reflected deeply in order to obtain the mantra:
"I know that the power of divine mantras possesses inconceivable qualities; since it has not been transmitted to anyone, by what means could I possibly obtain it?"
He addressed the Venerable One, saying:

"I possess no wondrous arts with which to exchange [for yours], nor do I have precious wealth to offer as an endowment; I have only my physical strength to serve you. I pray that, out of compassion, you will teach me the vidyā-mantra."
The Venerable One replied:
"If you wish to obtain it, you may go forth as a renunciant within the well-expounded Dharma and Vinaya of the Tathāgata; I shall then grant you the *ṛddhi-mantra* (如意神呪)."
For the sake of the mantra, he went forth according to the instructions; having shaved off his hair and beard and donned the dharma robes, he said to his preceptor:
"Upādhyāya, grant me the vidyā-mantra."
The Master said,
"You may accept it.
The disciple said:
"What does this mean?
The Master replied,
"It means that all conditioned phenomena are impermanent, all dharmas are without self, and nirvana is true quiescence."
"This is the vidyā-mantra within the bowl; if you practice it diligently for three nights, there will surely be a divine manifestation. You should contemplate the meaning of these phrases well.

At that time, the disciple, seeking a sign of success and hoping for its accomplishment, focused his mind continuously day and night on these three phrases of the Dharma. He profoundly understood the true source, severed all delusions, and realized arhatship.

He then went to his teacher’s place, prostrated at his feet, and said: "I have now truly attained the unsurpassed vidyā-mantra. I know according to reality: 'Birth has been exhausted, the holy life has been established, and there will be no further existence.'"
Udāyin said: "Excellent! Excellent!"
"You have truly repaid the Buddha’s kindness and benefited both yourself and others; you shall no longer transmigrate within the ocean of the three realms of existence.
As for the wrestler: at that time, a powerful man came from the south, seeking someone in the Middle Kingdom with whom to compete in strength.
Upon arriving at the city of Śrāvastī, he removed his clothes beneath the city gate, slapped his thighs, and cried out in a loud voice:
"I have come from afar seeking someone to wrestle with; if there is anyone capable, please come forward to take my hand."
At that time, there was no one in this city to oppose him.

Then Udāyin, knowing that this strongman was capable of being transformed, took up his robe and bowl at dawn and, wishing to go for alms, arrived beneath the city gate and saw the strongman, saying to him: "O man!"
"Are you a strong man who wishes to seek a wrestling match?
He replied, "It is so."
Udāyin said, "Will you wrestle with me?
Or will you wrestle with one whom I have already defeated?"
The strong man replied,
"If you, sir, can wrestle him down,
I shall wrestle him down as well. Udāyin said:
"He possesses great power that you cannot restrain.
The warrior said,
"One must wait until facing the enemy to know who is strong and who is weak."
Udāyin said, "Greed, hatred, and delusion—these three are what I have subdued; you may try to strike them down.
The warrior replied:
"This man possesses great power and deceives everyone; by what means can I act as his adversary?
Udāyin replied, "First you must leave the household life; only then can you oppose him."

He immediately shaved his hair and donned the dyed robes, intending to subdue the three poisons. Before long, all his fetters and delusions were eliminated, and having realized arhatship, he went to where Udāyin was and said to him:
"Great Master!..."
"I have subdued the three types [of defilements], and as a hero, I have brought the four matters to completion.
As explained at length above, in this way the bhikṣu Udāyin, in the city of Śrāvastī, converted eighteen million households, causing them all to attain liberation.

At that time, Udāyin transformed the violent and wicked woman so that she attained the vision of the Truths; the details are as previously explained, up until he accepted her invitation for food and a seat.
Not long after, the violent and wicked woman took a wife for her son, but when she herself was afflicted by illness and approaching death, she told her family members:
"After I have died, whatever may happen, do not let the meal and seat for the noble Udāyin be neglected."
Having spoken these words, he passed away in an instant.
That brahmin died in due course; his son, after grieving for some time, gradually abandoned his sorrow and left his wife to seek learning in other lands.
Later, as her afflictions intensified, the wife secretly engaged in unrighteous conduct with the leader of the bandits.
Whenever the Venerable One came to her house to eat at his seat, he perceived that this woman was of a highly afflicted nature and constantly preached the Dharma of detachment from desire for her.
The wife then thought to herself:
"The Venerable One possesses the power of holiness to discern the minds of others; he knows of my illicit affair with this man. When my husband arrives, he will surely inform him."
"Now I ought to take his life beforehand.
He then feigned illness and said to a maidservant, "I am currently ill;
you may go now and inform the Venerable One that he is requested to come to my residence."
The maidservant went to report this. At that time, the Venerable One, without prior observation, came to her house and insisted on staying until nightfall.
She then summoned the leader of the bandits; when he arrived, she told him:
"If this bhikṣu remains alive, I shall certainly not survive."
At that time, the leader of the bandits, fearing his crime would be exposed, became enraged and took a knife to sever the Venerable’s life. He then cast the corpse into a heap of refuse.

This was the ripening of karma previously created by the Venerable; now, as the fruit has matured, it is experienced within his own aggregates and physical vessel, and not in any other place—thus it is explained at length.
At that time, on the fifteenth day during the poṣadha ceremony, the World-Honored One was seated among the assembly; the great multitude had all gathered, yet only Udāyin had not arrived.
At that time, the one in charge of the assembly said,
"I do not see the Venerable Udāyin!
Since the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, possess no forgetfulness, he immediately addressed the assembly, saying:
“I have declared Udāyin to be the foremost among those who convert others; now that he has been killed and cast away in a dung heap, you should perform the Poṣadha ceremony.”
When the bhikṣus had completed the poṣadha ceremony, the Buddha said:
"You all should go together and perform the final offering of the śarīra for Udāyin."

At that time, the World-Honored One, surrounded by a great assembly, arrived at the city gate at night and emitted a great radiance that filled the entire city; the gate opened of its own accord, and everyone thought it was dawn.
Everyone rose, but the night-watchman knew that day had not yet dawned.
At that time, King Prasenajit, Queen Vimaladattā, and the others were struck with wonder and alarm at the event;
the gatekeeper reported, "Now the Buddha, the World-Honored One, and the assembly of noble ones have all arrived at the entrance."

When the king had heard this, he summoned his ministers, Queen Vaśiṣṭhā, and the entire retinue of men and women from the palace and the city; they all rushed together to the city gate and prostrated at the feet of the World-Honored One.
The King first prostrated himself and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!
For what cause and condition has the Unsurpassed Great Teacher come here in person?"
The Buddha said to the Great King:

"Among those who convert people, I declare the bhikṣu Udāyin to be foremost; yet he has now been killed by another and cast into a dung heap. I have come here specifically to cremate his body and perform the rites of offering for him."

When King Prasenajit and Queen Vaidehī heard of these matters, they adorned a funeral bier with the four precious gems. They personally followed the Tathāgata to the charnel ground, where they bathed the Venerable’s body with fragrant water and placed it within the precious bier. As various musical instruments were played, banners and streamers filled the road, and incense smoke pervaded the sky, the king, his ministers, and the men and women of the city escorted the Buddha and the Saṅgha outside the city walls. Arriving at a secluded spot, they piled up various kinds of fragrant wood, doused them with ghee and oil, and cremated the body. After reciting the *Anityatā-sūtra*, they collected the relics and placed them inside a golden jar, constructing a stūpa beside a crossroads.
With various kinds of fragrant flowers and manifold musical instruments, they made offerings of unprecedented magnificence.
The King, the ladies of the inner palace, and all the commoners and officials, along with the Buddha and the assembly of noble ones, each returned to their respective abodes.
At that time, having arrived at his dwelling place, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:

"This great transgression was brought about by traveling at an improper time. [The Buddha spoke] at length, up to: 'I, considering ten benefits, shall establish a training rule for the bhikṣus, which should be recited as follows:
"If a bhikṣu enters a village at an improper time, it is a pāyattika. "
Thus, after the Blessed One had established this training rule for the bhikṣus, they were not permitted to enter a village at an improper time.
Consequently, those bhikṣus who were attending to the sick were deprived of the opportunity to provide care, and those managing monastic affairs found their duties neglected.
He reported the matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"If there is a bhikṣu present, you should entrust him with your affairs before departing; you should tell him:
'Venerable one, please bear this in mind!'"
"I have a reason for visiting a sick person, or there are various matters that require me to enter the village at an improper time.
I inform you, Venerable One. He replies:
“*Aucitya* (it is improper).

At that time, there was a bhikṣu who had previously deposited his robes and bowl inside a layperson’s house. Suddenly, a fire broke out in that house at an improper time. The bhikṣu immediately went to retrieve his robes and bowl; while on the way, he thought to himself:
“It is improper for me to enter a village at an improper time without having announced my intention.”
He immediately turned back to find someone to give him formal authorization (*anuśāsti*), but in a mere moment his robes and bowl were completely consumed by the fire.
The bhikṣus then reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"Except in cases of such circumstances."
He addressed the bhikṣus:
"The former was the original injunction; this is a subsequent allowance.
It should be stated thus:"
"If again a bhikṣu enters a village at an improper time without having informed another bhikṣu, except for other circumstances, it is a pāyattika.
"If again a bhikṣu" refers to one who is among those in this Dharma; the rest of the meaning is as explained above.
Regarding the term "improper time," there are two boundaries: from after noon until the appearance of the morning light has not yet occurred.
The meaning of "village" is as explained above.
"Entering" means arriving at a village.
"Other bhikṣus" refers to those bhikṣus who are actually present at that location but have not been informed.
"Except for timely causes and conditions" refers to the presence of difficult circumstances.
The remaining meanings are as explained above.
Regarding this, what are the characteristics of the offenses?
If a bhikṣu, when it is not the proper time, perceives it as such or has doubt about it, he incurs the root offense.
If it is the proper time, but he perceives it as not being so or has doubt about it, he incurs an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
The other two cases involve no offense.
Furthermore, those for whom there is no offense are explained at length as above.
At that time, Queen Śrīmālā, knowing that the Venerable Udāyin had been unjustly killed by the bandit teacher, earnestly petitioned the King to capture him, so as to protect future bhikṣus.

At that time, the king immediately commanded the relevant officials to strictly apprehend him; once the master thief was captured, the king dispatched him to be cast into a cauldron of boiling oil to end his life.

The bandit’s companions numbered five hundred; they all had their hands cut off. As for the woman with whom he had committed adultery, they tied her hair to the hoof of a restless horse and set it loose to trample her to death.
At that time, all the bhikṣus were filled with doubt and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!
What karma did that heretical teacher commit such that he killed Udāyin, suffered [the consequences], and died?"
"And why were five hundred women with whom he had illicit relations and his band of five hundred thieves all executed?
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:

"Because of the karma they themselves created in previous lives, those kings must experience the results for themselves; there is no other entity that can undergo retribution on their behalf," as explained at length elsewhere.
"You all should listen!

In the distant past, in the city of Vārāṇasī, there was a king named Brahmadatta. A high minister of that king was wise and learned, and he had five hundred disciples. Out of greed for profit, they went before the king and falsely claimed to have had a prophetic dream, saying:
'In our dream we saw that for twelve years the heavens will not send rain; the land will fall into ruin and chaos, the people will suffer from famine, and the royal throne will be endangered.'"
The king said:
"If this is the case, what should be done?
What plan can be devised to escape this calamity?"
The minister replied, "One must slaughter five hundred oxen to hold a *yaśas* feast; only by providing for the brahmins can this disaster be averted."
The king then issued an order to assemble five hundred oxen in one place; the oxen bellowed loudly.
Hearing their cries, the king was moved by compassion and said to his ministers:
"Are you going to slaughter all these oxen?"
The minister, discerning the king’s intention, said:
"Great King!
Observe these cattle as they are about to be slaughtered; among them, those that have committed sexual intercourse should be put to death."
At that time, as he was preparing for the assembly and inspecting all the cattle, it happened that a bull and a cow engaged in sexual intercourse.
The minister said,
"This one ought to be killed."
Then those five hundred disciples all raised their hands at once and said,
"This ox deserves to die.
The minister’s wife also said:
"Let them be put to death.
He then slaughtered two oxen to provide for the assembly. You bhikṣus!

The minister of former times was none other than this bandit master; his wife was this woman with whom he had illicit relations; and his five hundred disciples were these five hundred accomplices of the bandit.
The two oxen of former times were none other than King Prasenajit and Queen Vimalā; having been killed in the past, they have now returned to kill him.
You bhikṣus! For all sentient beings, the karmic retribution for one's own actions does not perish; even after passing through many kalpas, it will still be experienced when the conditions converge.
Therefore, you should know: do not commit evil deeds, but cultivate all categories of wholesome qualities.
Furthermore, O bhikṣus, listen!
What karma did Udāyin previously create, by the power of which he is now killed by another and cast into a heap of refuse?
Long ago, in a certain village, there was a hunter who made his living by the profession of slaughter.
At that time, a Pratyekabuddha came to the forest and rested there for a while.
On that very day, the hunter had caught nothing at all, which caused him to wonder:
"In the past, I have always obtained many birds and beasts in this forest; why is it that today I have gained nothing?"
He then saw human footprints and followed them; seeing a Pratyekabuddha sitting upright in meditation, the hunter thought to himself:
"Because of this man's arrival, I have gained nothing."
Thereupon, he gave rise to a fit of rage and immediately drew his bow to its full extent, discharging a poisoned arrow at the vital point of the sage.
Seeing this foolish man, the Pratyekabuddha Saint conceived a heart of compassion and manifested a supernatural transformation, leaping upward into the air like a king of geese.
At that time, having witnessed the supernatural power, the hunter was filled with deep remorse and spoke, looking up to him:
"I am a foolish man who did not recognize a noble sage; I pray that you will lower your body to receive my repentance."
At that time, out of compassion, the noble one lowered his body to accept the hunter’s repentance and subsequently passed away.
The hunter then cremated his body with fire, collected his relics, and erected a stūpa, making various offerings and forming this great vow:
"May I not suffer the retribution of the hells due to this transgression; in a future life, may I encounter a supreme Great Teacher and personally receive and serve him."
"O bhikṣus! The hunter of that past time was none other than Udāyin; because he killed another in the past, he is now killed in turn.
Furthermore, O bhikṣus!"
"You all should listen!
What karma did this Udāyin previously create, such that he attained arhatship and attended upon me personally, yet after being killed, was cast into a heap of filth;

and how is it that the Buddha, the Saṃgha, the king and his ministers, Queen Vaidehī along with the palace ladies, and the citizens and commoners of the city, all went to the side of the corpse, adorned a precious palanquin, moved it to a superior location, and once the cremation was completed, took up the śarīras to construct a stūpa and extensively offer worship?"
In the distant past, there was a potter who saw a Pratyekabuddha afflicted with illness as he approached his house for alms.

At that time, the potter did not recognize a noble being; he seized the Pratyekabuddha by the throat, pushed him out, and discarded him in a heap of refuse. The Pratyekabuddha, lacking physical strength, passed away on the spot.
Another Pratyekabuddha was crossing through the air; seeing his corpse, he dropped his body down from the sky and made offerings of various fragrant flowers as the occasion required.
When the potter saw this, he inquired in detail about the cause and, realizing it was a holy man, felt remorse and regret, thinking:
"I am foolish and did not recognize a noble sage."
Realizing that they lacked the power to perform the cremation according to the Dharma, they then addressed the King, requesting that he conduct the funeral rites together with them.

When the King heard that the Great Sage had entered *nirvāṇa* against the natural order, he issued a command to all his officials, the ladies of the inner palace, and the citizens of the city. The multitude gathered like a dense throng, each carrying ghee, oil, and various scented waters, and proceeded to the site of the Noble One to perform the offering of cremation.

Then that potter fashioned a golden jar to contain the remaining bones; placing them upon a multicolored carriage, he went to the side of a crossroads and constructed a stūpa, making offerings according to his means.
He then made this great vow:
"May I not, on account of these grave deeds of immediate retribution, fall into the *naraka* hells.

By virtue of this earnest act of making offerings, may I in future ages encounter a supreme Great Teacher, personally receive his instructions without weariness, and attain such sovereign mastery of supernatural powers (*abhijñā*)."
"O bhikṣus! That potter at that time was none other than Udāyin.
Due to the residual retribution of evil karma committed in the past, for five hundred lifetimes he was constantly killed by others and cast into heaps of excrement."
By the power of that offering and the force of his aspiration, he has now encountered me and attained arhatship.
Due to this karma, even after my parinirvāṇa, I, together with the great assembly, the king, and the people, will all gather like clouds to perform the offering of cremating his body.
"You should know this!
Furthermore, for what reason is this Udāyin the foremost among those who convert others?

In a past life, during the time of Kāśyapa Buddha, Udāyin went forth as a monk; he was a great Dharma master, skilled at preaching the Dharma, and converted immeasurable billions of sentient beings. By the power of that karma, he is now the foremost in converting the masses."
Therefore, O bhikṣus!

You should contemplate such retributions for good and evil; like a shadow following a form, they never fail to manifest. Diligently cultivate wholesome karma and abandon unwholesome deeds; you should train yourselves in this way.
The ninth summary verse says:
Food, the appearance of dawn, and present knowledge; the needle-case, the measurement of bed-legs, storing flowers, and the sitting-mat;
the sore, the rain, and the Master’s robe.

81. The Training Rule on Going to Other Houses Before or After a Meal Without Informing [the Monks]. The eighty-first training rule concerning going to other houses before or after a meal without informing [the monks]. At that time, the Blessed One was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, there was an elder in this city who was immensely wealthy, possessing great riches and enjoying abundant prosperity.
On one occasion, the Venerable Upānanda, while wandering for alms, arrived at the elder’s house; the elder then immediately took some rice and offered it to him as a gift.
Because he preached the Dharma, the person who provided the food obtained five merits: namely, longevity, physical beauty, strength, happiness, and eloquence.
Having heard this, the elder was filled with deep joy; he prostrated at his feet, took refuge in the Triple Gem, and received the five precepts.
Then, on another day, Upānanda went again to the house of the elder, who addressed him, saying:
"Noble One!
Because you, Virtuous One, have been my spiritual friend, I now wish to invite the Buddha and the Saṅgha to my home for a meal."
"I only pray that the Noble One will inform [the Buddha] on my behalf.
Then Upānanda returned to his residence and, calling out the householder's name, requested the Buddha and the Saṅgha on his behalf.
At dawn, Upānanda went to the householder’s residence and informed him, saying:
"I have some business and am going briefly to another house; if I do not return, you need not serve the meal.
Having spoken these words, he left them and departed.

At that time, the World-Honored One, knowing that the elder was unfamiliar with the proper etiquette and had not come to inform him, immediately led the great assembly to the elder’s house and proceeded to the place where the meal was being served.
Then the bhikṣus said to the elder,
"You should announce the invitation for the *pravāraṇā* ceremony. The elder then replied:
“Noble One! I have prepared these seats and mats for the great assembly.
The Buddha said:
"This constitutes the completion of the *pravāraṇā*; you should now take your seats.
Although the Buddha and the great assembly had been seated for a long time and midday was approaching, no food was being served.
The Buddha said to Ānanda:
"Inform the householder that the time has arrived and he should serve the meal.
Once the time has passed, what would be the purpose of eating?"
The Venerable Ānanda, having received these instructions, informed the householder,
saying: "Noble one,
Upānanda has not yet arrived."
When this had been said three times, Ānanda asked,
"If Upānanda does not come, do you wish to serve the food?
He replied:
"So it is," the Venerable Ānanda said, reporting the matter to the Buddha. Thereupon, the World-Honored One spoke these verses:
"Because of others, all suffer; By being free from them, one attains happiness."
"When there is a deficiency in common provisions, the wise should not perform [the meal].
At that time, as it was nearly midday, Upānanda finally arrived, whereupon the food was served.

At that time, some of the bhikṣus ate a little while others did not eat at all. After the Buddha had recited the verses on giving for the sake of the elder, he rose from his seat and departed; however, Upānanda remained right there and did not go to the monastery.

At that time, on the fifteenth day, the community of monks wished to perform the *poṣadha* ceremony; however, only Upānanda did not come to join the assembly. Furthermore, as there was no one to carry his proxy consent (*chanda*), the assembly sat for a long time, which hindered and obstructed the religious rites. They searched for him but could not find him, causing the assembly to become weary.
At that time, the bhikṣus collectively felt resentment and contempt, saying:
"How can a bhikṣu, having accepted an invitation to a layperson's home, fail to come promptly before or after the meal, but instead remain for a long time in a lay dwelling?"
He reported the matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"Since such faults arise before or after a meal, I shall, having considered ten benefits, establish a training rule for my disciples, which should be recited as follows:
'If a bhikṣu, having accepted an invitation to a lay family's home, should go to another house either before or after the meal, it is a pāyattika.'"
Thus, after the Blessed One had established these training rules for the bhikṣus,
there were occasions when a bhikṣu tending to the sick neglected his nursing duties, and those managing monastic affairs found their oversight to be deficient.
Then the bhikṣus reported the matter to the Buddha. Having heard this, the Buddha addressed the bhikṣus:
"The former was the initial prohibition; now I grant a further concession. It should be stated thus:
'If a bhikṣu, having accepted an invitation to a meal at a layperson's home, goes to another house before or after the meal without having informed [the host], it is a pāyattika.'"
"Furthermore, 'if a bhikṣu' refers to Upānanda; the remaining meanings are as explained above.
'Invited to a meal by a family' means being summoned by another to a family for a meal; the meaning is as explained above."
"Before eating" refers to the period before noon.
If one goes out on a journey and passes by two households, one incurs an offense of falling (pāyattika).
"After eating" refers to the period after noon has passed.
If one passes by three houses while traveling, one incurs a *pāyattika* offense.
"Not having informed" means not reporting to someone; one should inform the donor, saying:
"I am going to such-and-such a place."
Or if one instructs a bhikṣu, saying,
"Go to such-and-such a place," the offense is established as described above.
In this regard, what are the characteristics of the offense and how does it occur?

If a bhikṣu has accepted an invitation to a meal and, before the meal, passes by more than two households, or after the meal, passes by more than three households, without having informed [the host], he incurs a *pāyattika* offense.
If one invites [a guest] without making this bhikṣu the primary person of honor, there is no offense.
Furthermore, there is no offense for a first-time offender; the details are as explained above.
The Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya, Scroll Forty-three;
The Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya, Scroll Forty-four.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Yijing by Imperial Decree.
82. The Training Rule on Entering the Royal Palace. The First of the Eighty-Two: The Training Rule on Entering the Royal Palace.
A Summary Verse at the Beginning: First, the two Nandas; Seven days, and also Sudatta.
The five persons and the four wonders; Śrīmālā instructing the Great King.
The two cities, one flourishing and one declining; Candraprabha white in the night.
Having gone forth upon the path of the sages, Bimbisāra asked for verses.
Mūrdhaja took the life of his father and shall be reborn in the Avīci Hell;
Having accepted the words of two sycophantic ministers, he slandered two Arhats.
The two ministers seized the treasures and departed; dust and sand filled the city.
The Great Minister gave his daughter and son, each to a master;
The dark-complexioned youth followed his teacher away, through causes and conditions such as the path of the immortals;
The circumstances of Sudhana building a temple, and Cunda’s discourse on the seven merits.
The hero of the wilderness, the dark-complexioned one who realized non-returning;
the peerless acupuncturist, who extensively recounted the story of the lion.
When the two men spoke of good and evil, the dark-complexioned one was consumed by flames.
The Hunchbacked One served the monks and entered the royal palace as a consort.
As for Nanda and Upananda: when the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus, saying:

"You should dwell in forest hermitages, beneath trees, in empty rooms, in mountain clefts or caves, within straw huts, in the open air, in charnel grounds, in other groves, or in peripheral quarters, using coarse and inferior bedding. In such places, you should eliminate external conditions, straighten your minds, and practice meditative concentration to seek the severance of afflictions. Do not be negligent, lest you later fall into sorrow and regret; this is my true and authentic instruction."
Thus the Blessed One taught the monks about the practice of reflection in order to cause them to abandon worldly bustle.
At that time, there was a monk who had attained mundane supernormal powers (*abhijñā*) and went to Mount Sumeru to practice meditative concentration (*dhyāna*).
The Buddha addressed the bhikṣus:

"Mount Sumeru, the King of Mountains, extends eighty thousand yojanas downward from the golden wheel to the level of the ocean waters, and it likewise rises eighty thousand yojanas above the surface of the water."

Its shape is square with four sides, each measuring two thousand yojanas; its appearance is so upright and handsome that humans and devas delight in beholding it. Above it are the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, composed of four kinds of jewels:
crystal on the eastern side, vaidūrya on the southern side, white silver on the western side, and gold on the northern side.
Beneath this mountain, within the great ocean, there is a palace of the nāga kings, likewise composed of the four precious substances and provided with all necessary enjoyments.
There dwell two nāga kings named Nanda and Upananda, each having eighty-four thousand nāgas as their retinue.
These two nāga kings cannot be harmed even by the king of the garuḍas; all their food and drink are like the exquisite offerings of the devas.
At that time, out of craving and attachment, each of the two nāga kings wound his body seven times around the mountain and remained there with his head raised, both thinking:
"All these enjoyments are brought forth solely by the power of my own meritorious karma."

Out of a mind of malice and envy, he emitted his poisonous breath three times each day; within a radius of two hundred and fifty *yojanas*, all birds and beasts that encountered this poisonous breath perished.
After the dragon had finished exhaling its breath, it fell fast asleep.
At that time, those bhikṣus who were practicing meditative concentration found their skin and flesh changing color, becoming withered and jaundiced due to the poisonous vapor of the dragon.
As the Blessed One said:

"O bhikṣus, those of you who desire the purity of the precepts should perform the poṣadha every half-month; for the sake of seeking the removal of transgressions, you should perform the pravāraṇā ceremony."
Then, when those bhikṣus gathered together on the day of the poṣadha, the long-term residents, finding it strange, asked them:
"For what reason, venerable sirs, do your complexions appear so unusually withered and pale?"
The bhikṣu practicing dhyāna informed them of the circumstances, and the bhikṣus asked,
"Since this nāga is causing such affliction and harm,
why do you not subdue him? He replied:
"This can only be subdued by the World-Honored One or a Great Śrāvaka; it is not something I am capable of.
Then the bhikṣus reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha thought to himself:
"Among my disciples, who is capable of subduing those two great Nāga Kings?"
The Buddha, knowing that Mahāmaudgalyāyana was certainly capable of subduing them, addressed Mahāmaudgalyāyana, saying:
"You should observe the two great nāga kings, Nanda and Upananda."

Then Mahāmaudgalyāyana, having accepted the instruction with a simple "So be it," immediately employed such skillful means as to enter meditative concentration; he vanished from Śrāvastī and appeared on Mount Sumeru, walking back and forth upon the bodies of the nāgas.
The dragon slept and did not wake; as [the nāga] again walked upon its head, it likewise remained unaware.
Maudgalyāyana then entered its belly and shook forth a great thunderclap, yet the dragon still did not awaken.
At that time, the Venerable One thought to himself:
"A nāga can be subdued only under two conditions. What are these two?"
First, it causes them to become enraged; second, it arouses a sense of terror.
If I were to cause them to give rise to anger, it would make the entire Jambudvīpa tremble.
"I should now cause them to be terrified.
He immediately transformed himself into the body of a dragon three times larger than theirs, coiled his body seven times around the two dragons, and remained there with his head raised.
The dragon, feeling his body heavy, immediately awoke from sleep; seeing that massive form, he was struck with extreme terror and anxiety, losing all composure, and thought to himself:
"The place where I dwell has now been seized by treachery."
He then transformed himself into a small body and fled from the palace.
The Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana immediately resumed his original form, stood before the nāga with a composed countenance to block his path, and asked:
"What do you two nāga kings intend to do? They replied: [as above].
He replied:
"A dragon of great virtue has come to my dwelling, wishing to take my life and seize the palace where I reside. Due to these perilous circumstances, I have fled to another place."
The Venerable One replied,
“I went to your palace earlier and did not see this.
The nāga said:
“We have seen him with our own eyes.
The Venerable One said,
“You may return to the palace and show me his form.”
The dragon said,
"Virtuous One!
Do you truly intend to kill me?"
The Venerable One said:
"Let us go together to see; who would dare kill you?
It is better that you turn back and show him your appearance."
The two nāgas and the Venerable One returned to their dwelling, but they saw only an empty palace with nothing else remaining.
The two nāgas asked,
“Did the Noble One perhaps see our arrogance and violence and become terrified?”
The Venerable One said, “It may be so.
That nāga replied:
"Noble one!
For what reason have you come here?
The Venerable One replied:
"Listen, all of you!
In the past, you committed base and evil deeds and fell among the animals to undergo this bitter retribution.

Now, you have once again given rise to a mind of fierce venom, killing sentient beings without a thought of compassion; after passing away from here, there will be no place for you to be born other than the hells."
The two dragon kings both came and prostrated at his feet, saying:
"What task do you wish us to perform?
The Venerable One replied:

"You should now take refuge in the Triple Gem and receive the five precepts, vowing for as long as life lasts not to kill living beings and so forth, up to not drinking intoxicants. To all birds, beasts, and other creatures who dwell upon Mount Sumeru, grant them fearlessness and do not cause them alarm."
The nāgas replied, “We were ignorant and lacked self-aware wisdom;
