we are now fortunate to have been rescued from the depths of suffering by the Noble One. We make a solemn vow in our hearts to diligently follow your instructions.”

From this day forth until the end of my life, I take refuge in the Triple Gem and receive the five precepts; I shall not cause suffering to any living beings, loving them as my own children and eliminating the poison of anger.
When Mahāmaudgalyāyana had subdued the two nāgas and was about to return to his own abode, the two nāga kings prostrated at the Venerable One’s feet and said:
“Virtuous One!

We have fallen into the abyss of delusion and have received your grace in being rescued. When you reach the World-Honored One, we pray that you will respectfully convey our words and prostrate at his two feet, asking: ‘We wonder if the World-Honored One has little illness and little affliction?’”
"Are you comfortable in your daily activities? Is your physical strength at ease?
He further addressed him, saying:

"I only pray that the Great Master, out of compassion and pity, will—when the bhikṣus and bhikṣuṇīs have finished their meal and recite the verses of merit—mention my name so that I may be granted the benefit of this merit and, abandoning these evil karmas, be reborn in a happy realm."
Maudgalyāyana replied, "I shall inform you.

Then, having completed his task, the great Maudgalyāyana—just as a strong man might extend or contract his arm—disappeared from Mount Sumeru and appeared in the Jeta Grove. Having approached the World-Honored One and prostrated at his feet, he addressed him, saying:
“World-Honored One!
I have already subdued the two Nanda nāgas, causing them to receive the three refuges and the five precepts, and I have given rise to compassion for all sentient beings dwelling upon Mount Sumeru.”
Those two dragon kings respectfully offer their salutations at the feet of the World-Honored One: We wonder if the Great Teacher has little illness and little affliction;
whether your daily life is light and easy, and your physical strength is secure?
"Due to my evil karma, I have fallen among the animals and am undergoing various sufferings and hardships; I only pray that the World-Honored One will compassionately rescue me.
She related her plea in full detail.
Having heard this, the World-Honored One praised her, saying:
“Excellent! Excellent!
Those two nāga kings have been able to give rise to weary detachment.”
He then addressed the bhikṣus, saying:

"From this day forward, whenever my disciples—the bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, and others—have finished their meal, they shall recite the *daurmanasya-gāthā* and invoke the names of those two nāga kings to offer a prayer of blessing, so that they may abandon the evil realms and be reborn in the happy destinies; you must act in this manner."
"If you do not rely upon my teaching, you shall incur the offense of wrongdoing (*dukkaṭa*).

From that time forward, on the eighth, fifteenth, twenty-third, and the final day of each month, these two nāga kings would assume their original forms at night and take human form during the day; they would go to the place where the World-Honored One was and together offer him salutations and receive the eightfold precepts (*aṣṭāṅga-śikṣā*).
Furthermore, each time he arrived, from Mount Sumeru to the city of Śrāvastī, dragon troops were arrayed along both sides of the road, filling the void of space to serve as his retinue.
Later, at another time, the nāga assumed the form of a householder and came to where the Buddha was to listen to and receive the sublime Dharma.
At that same time, King Śreṇika Bimbisāra also came to where the Buddha was; having reached the gate, he commanded his attendants, saying:
"Go to where the Buddha is and observe who is there?"

Then his attendants, having received these instructions, departed; after prostrating at the Buddha’s feet, they saw the two elders in the presence of the World-Honored One listening to the Buddha’s teaching of the Dharma. They immediately returned to the king and said:
“Great King!...”
"There are two householders present with the World-Honored One.
The King thought to himself:
"Those two householders are subjects of my kingdom; when they see me coming, how would they dare not show respect?"
At that time, King Prasenajit was about to go to where the Buddha was staying. When the two dragon kings saw the lord of the land approaching, they addressed the World-Honored One, saying:
"Venerable Sir!

Since we have seen the lord of the land arrive, it is fitting that we alter our usual protocol: shall we now sit and listen out of respect for the Dharma, or shall we rise to stand out of respect for the king?"
The World-Honored One said:
"All Buddhas, World-Honored Ones, as well as Arhats and others, all revere the Dharma.
For this reason, he spoke three verses:
"The Buddhas of the past, as well as those of the future,
and the World-Honored Ones of the present, who are able to sever all sorrow—
they all together revere the Dharma in their speech, their conduct, and their dwelling."
At all times, one should always revere the True Dharma.
Therefore, those who seek benefit and desire the joy of abundant prosperity should honor the Dharma and constantly contemplate the teachings of the Buddhas.
When those two nāga kings had heard the Buddha’s words, although they saw the king approaching, they did not perform acts of respect.
Having seen this, the king thought to himself:
“These two elders are subjects of my kingdom; seeing that I have arrived, they show me no reverence.”
He then gave rise to anger and resentment, went to where the World-Honored One was, prostrated at his feet, and sat to one side.
Knowing that the king’s mind was possessed by ill will, the Buddha spoke of other matters instead and did not preach the Dharma for him.
At that time, King Prasenajit requested of the World-Honored One, saying:
"I pray only that the Great Teacher will preach the Dharma for me.
On account of this occasion, the Buddha spoke these verses:
"If one lacks a pure mind and harbors thoughts of anger and resentment,
one will be unable to understand the subtle and wondrous Dharma taught by all Buddhas.
One must subdue the mind of contention as well as impure intentions."
"One who can eliminate anger and harm / Only then understands the Buddha's Dharma.
When King Prasenajit heard this verse, he thought to himself:
"It is because of these two elders that the World-Honored One has not yet expounded the essentials of the Dharma for me at this time."
He immediately rose from his seat, prostrated before the Buddha, and departed. He then commanded his attendants, saying:
"When you see that elder leave the presence of the Buddha, wait until he reaches the gate and cut off both his heads."
When the followers of those two dragon kings saw that the king harbored such resentment and spoke these words, they were all struck with astonishment and, in their anger, deliberated, saying:
"We possess the power to shatter high mountains and drain the great ocean; by what strength does this king dare to speak such words?"
Immediately, thick clouds suddenly gathered and thunder and hail crashed down; from the midst of the void, swords, staves, wheel-blades, arrows, and spears all fell.
Before they had even reached the ground, the World-Honored One, having attained the state of non-forgetfulness, addressed Mahāmaudgalyāyana:
"You should quickly bring to mind King Prasenajit and all the sentient beings within this city."

Then Mahāmaudgalyāyana, having responded "So be it" and accepted the instruction, immediately entered the concentration of loving-kindness (*maitrī-samādhi*). No sooner had he entered this meditative state than celestial flowers, such as *kumuda* and others, rained down everywhere throughout the void and fell upon the earth; indeed, from the time King Prasenajit entered his palace until that moment, celestial flowers fell continuously.

The King, marvelling at this extraordinary marvel, exclaimed that it was unprecedented. He then summoned the ladies of the inner palace, the queens, the princes, the ministers, as well as the brahmins and all the commoners, and having assembled them all, issued this command:
"From the Jetavana Grove until my palace, celestial flowers have fallen like rain—something never seen before. I do not know by whose power this has been wrought."
At that time, there was a courtier who spoke pleasing words to the King, who addressed him, saying:
"It is because Your Majesty governs people according to the Dharma and does not practice injustice or cruelty that the devas rejoice and rain down these exquisite flowers."
The king said, "I have always brought peace to people through the Dharma; this must be due to the power of my merit.
The women within the palace spoke as follows:
"We have lived in chastity, serving only our lord; toward other men, we have forever severed all improper thoughts. May the celestial deities take note of this and grant us auspicious omens.
The Prince said, "I have served my parents with the utmost filial devotion; it is through the resonance of the spirits that these auspicious signs have been brought about."
The minister said,
"I have received the King’s command that I must fully carry out his instructions to assist in transforming the people of the nation, so as to cause celestial flowers to fall.
The brāhmaṇa said:
"I have followed the four seasons in reverently sacrificing to Heaven and Earth without fail in my pure conduct,
thereby bringing forth these fresh flowers," the fierce general said.
"When there was a powerful rebel in the land, I first dispatched my army to bring peace to the masses, and thus obtained this auspicious response."
The people of the country said:

"We have personally cultivated the land to provide the kingdom’s taxes without failing our seasonal duties; this is known to the gods, who have observed our reverence and diligence, and thus auspicious flowers have scattered everywhere."
When the king heard the assembly’s deliberations as each recounted their own capabilities, he thought to himself:
"This is wondrous, spiritual, and marvelous, never before seen in the world; I do not know whose power of merit this is."
"I should now go to inquire of the World-Honored One;
I shall accept and uphold whatever the Buddha says.
At that time, King Prasenajit filled the hem of his robe with celestial flowers, mounted the Great Elephant King to the outskirts of the Jeta Grove, and then proceeded on foot.
Having paid homage to the World-Honored One, he sat to one side and reported the aforementioned matter in detail to the World-Honored One.
The Buddha said,
"Great King!"

These celestial flowers are not due to the power of Your Majesty, nor are they brought about by the majesty of the inner palace, the princes, or the ministers and commoners; rather, they are due to the awesome spiritual power of Mahāmaudgalyāyana.
"Great King!
Had Maudgalyāyana not observed us and given rise to compassion, in a mere moment the King and the citizens of Śrāvastī would all have been reduced to dust."
Due to the power of his profound compassion and meditative concentration, celestial flowers consequently filled every place.
Therefore, both the king and his subjects should all offer worship to Mahāmaudgalyāyana.
Then King Prasenajit addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

By what causes and conditions did it come about that solely through the Noble Maudgalyāyana, myself, those within my palace, and the people of my kingdom and cities were spared from being covered in dust and preserved in our lives?”
"This power of grace belongs neither to the World-Honored One nor to any other disciple.
The Buddha said,
"Great King!"
"This is not by my power, nor by that of any other śrāvaka disciples;
it is solely due to Maudgalyāyana.
If Your Majesty has any doubt, you may place the heavenly flowers upon the ground with the hem of your robe."
The king followed the Buddha’s instruction and cast the flowers upon the ground; they all transformed into swords, blades, wheels, and spears.
Having seen this, the king was greatly terrified and struck with wonder and alarm, and he said to the Buddha:
“World-Honored One!
“From where do these weapons come?
The Buddha said,
“Great King!”

"Does Your Majesty not recall that previously you commanded your attendants, with hearts full of poisonous malice, to utter violent and evil words to the two nāga kings Nanda and Upananda, dispatching them to end their lives?"

At that time, all the followers belonging to that dragon king, having heard these words, became enraged; they immediately raised dense clouds in the sky and rained down various swords, arrows, and spears.

At that time, having witnessed this event, Mahāmaudgalyāyana immediately entered the samādhi of loving-kindness so as not to allow the king’s retinue and all the people of the land to be utterly destroyed; he then transformed the weapons into celestial flowers, bringing peace and happiness to the multitude.
The king said, “World-Honored One!
I have never seen those two dragon kings; how could I have sent someone to take their lives?”
The Buddha said,
"If Your Majesty does not remember, I shall cause you to remember.
Do you not recall how, when two elders saw you and you did not rise for them, you became enraged and commanded your attendants to take their lives?"
The king said,
“I remember.
The Buddha said:
"Those two elders were actually dragon kings; for the sake of hearing the Dharma, they manifested in human form and came to where I was.
The King said, "Because of my fleshly eyes, I did not recognize these divine dragons. Since I have committed an offense, what should I do?"
The Buddha said,
"Go to the place where the two nāgas are and offer them an apology.
The king said:
"How can I offer my apologies when he is on Mount Sumeru and I am dwelling in the kingdom of Magadha, separated by such a vast distance?
The Buddha said, "Those two dragon kings come to me every month on the eighth day and on the day of the *poṣadha* ceremony for the sake of hearing the Dharma; you, O King, must also go there."
"I shall manifest that dragon king's body so that Your Majesty may seek his pardon.
The King asked,
"When I seek his pardon from that dragon, shall I prostrate at his feet?"
The Buddha said, "Great King, you should not prostrate at their feet; rather, you should extend your right hand toward those nāgas and say:
'O two Nāga Kings!'"
"I have spoken harsh words; I hope you will graciously forgive me.
Thus, those two dragon kings mutually showed forbearance.
The King said:
“I respectfully accept the Buddha’s teaching and shall act accordingly.
Having prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, he returned to his own palace.

Later, on the day of the *poṣadha*, the nāga assumed human form and came to where the Buddha was; the king also arrived to behold the World-Honored One, and the Buddha manifested signs to point out the nāga king to him.
At that time, King Prasenajit, seeing the signs manifested by the Buddha, rose from his seat, adjusted his robes, and approached the two nāgas. Extending his right hand, he spoke these words:
"I pray that the two Nāga Kings will grant me their forgiveness."
The two of them replied:
"Excellent, Great King!
Let us mutually grant each other our pardon."
Regarding the "seven days": at that time, King Prasenajit had this thought:
"Because I distressed those dragon soldiers with harsh words, clouds, rain, and thunder have caused these swords and blades to fall."
"By virtue of the power of the noble Mahāmaudgalyāyana’s meditative concentration of loving-kindness, he transformed celestial flowers to sustain our lives.
Desiring to repay his kindness, I invite the Buddha and the Saṅgha to receive my offerings for seven days."
He immediately rose from his seat, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and said:
“World-Honored One!
I pray that the Buddha and the Saṃgha will deign to accept my humble offering by coming to my residence for seven days.”
At that time, the World-Honored One, seeing that the king had made his request, accepted it by remaining silent.
Having seen that he had accepted, the king paid homage to the Buddha and departed. Once outside, he addressed his ministers, saying:

"On account of the noble Mahāmaudgalyāyana, I have invited the Buddha and the Saṃgha to take their meal at my residence for seven days. You should sweep and adorn the roads, decorate the city walls, and prepare food of the finest flavor to await the Buddha and the Saṃgha."

The ministers, having received the command, prepared everything in full; from within the royal palace to the Jeta Grove, the space between was filled everywhere with jeweled banners, streamers, canopies, incense, and flowers.
Once the preparations were complete, the King sent a messenger to announce:
"The food and drink for the Buddha and the Sangha are ready; may the Buddha and the assembly know that it is time.

At that time, during the first part of the day, the World-Honored One took up his robe and bowl, and followed by the great assembly, proceeded to the King’s residence and arrived at the place where the meal was served. He took the seat that had been prepared beforehand and sat down upon it.
When King Prasenajit saw that the assembly was seated, he personally presented various kinds of pure, excellent, and sublime food and drink to the Buddha and the community of monks.

Once they had finished eating and the procedures for rinsing the mouth were completed, the Buddha recited verses on the merit of giving for the sake of the Great King, expounded the sublime Dharma, and returned to his own abode.
As it was on the first day, so it was for all seven days.
After the noble assembly had eaten and preached the Dharma to the king, they returned to their own abodes.
Later, during the night, King Prasenajit’s elephant was lost and burned to death by fire. The king then ordered the drum to be beaten to proclaim to the people of the country, saying:

"From this day forward, you must not light lamps or fires at night on your own initiative; anyone who violates this shall be fined sixty gold coins, and those who have no money shall be imprisoned indefinitely."
At that time, all the bhikṣus were filled with doubt and requested of the World-Honored One, saying:
"Venerable Sir!
What karma did these two nāga kings, Nanda and Upananda, previously commit to fall into the realm of animals?"

Furthermore, what karma did he perform such that his palace and residence are all composed of the four precious substances, his food and drink are of the same quality as those of the devas, eighty-four thousand nāgas serve as his retinue, and even the King of the Garuḍas cannot cause him any harm?
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"The karma created by these two nāga kings must be experienced by their own bodies as its retribution; there is no one else who can act as a substitute."
And so it is said at length:
"Even if a hundred eons should pass, the karma one has created does not perish;
when the causes and conditions meet, the retribution is received by oneself."
"Listen, all of you!
In the distant past, during this Bhadrakalpa when the human lifespan was twenty thousand years, the Tathāgata Kāśyapa appeared in the world, fully endowed with the ten titles."
At that time, there was a king ruling over the city of Vārāṇasī named Kṛkī; his realm was prosperous and joyful, and its people were peaceful and secure.
At that time, there were two brothers who both served as ministers:
one was named Nanda and the other Upānanda. These two ministers governed the kingdom by means of both righteous and unrighteous methods.

"I have a nephew named Aśoka who has gone forth within the teachings of the Buddha Kāśyapa. Having renounced worldly life with diligent and tireless devotion, before long he severed all afflictions and realized the fruit of arhatship."
Every day at the three appointed times, he went to his maternal uncle’s residence to preach the Dharma to him, speaking these words:
"I only pray that you, my uncle, will not employ unrighteous means to assist the King in governing the state; for by reason of this, you shall receive an evil retribution in future lives."
The two uncles replied:
"O Noble One!
According to the laws of governing a kingdom, one cannot transform the people through purely virtuous deeds alone."
The Arhat said, "If that is so,
you should cultivate and accumulate the provisions for future lives.
The two maternal uncles replied:
"What should I do now? he asked.
He replied, "You should construct a dwelling place for the Saṃgha."
He replied, "I shall construct it.

He then built a great monastery for the Sangha of the four directions, providing the four requisites without deficiency; the food and non-timely beverages he offered were all fully endowed with excellent color, fragrance, and flavor.
The bhikṣus within the kingdom were as unimpeded as the crown prince, and the bhikṣuṇīs were like those in the inner palace, none daring to intrude or disturb them.
Those two ministers, having assisted the king in governing the country through both righteous and unrighteous means, fell among the animals due to their evil karma.
Because he constructed monasteries and offered them to the Sangha of the four quarters, all his dwellings are composed of the four precious substances.
Because he provided the community of monks with exquisite food and drink, the food and drink he receives are equal in flavor to those of the devas.
Because they cause no harm to the bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, and others, they obtain eighty-four thousand nāgas as their retinue; even the King of the Garuḍas cannot inflict injury upon them.
"O bhikṣus! If one commits evil karma, one will in turn encounter bitter retribution; all virtuous causes shall yield virtuous fruits.
You should train yourselves in this!"

Regarding "Sudatta": In the city of Śrāvastī there was an elder named Sudatta, who was immensely wealthy with abundant riches and enjoyments; his assets were such that he could rival Vaiśravaṇa, the Heavenly King of the North. Because he was benevolent, free from stinginess, and supported the poor and destitute, he was known by the name Sudatta.
At one time, that householder came to where the Buddha was, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and sat to one side. Having heard the sublime Dharma, he rose from his seat and said to the Buddha:
“World-Honored One!
“I only pray that, out of compassion, the Buddha and the assembly of monks will accept my humble offering at my home tomorrow.
The World-Honored One accepted by remaining silent.

When the elder saw that the Buddha had accepted, he prostrated at his feet and departed. That very night, he prepared various kinds of excellent food and drink, and at dawn, he sent a messenger to announce that the time had come.
At that time, the World-Honored One donned his robes and took up his alms bowl, followed by the noble assembly, as they proceeded to the house of the elder and took their seats.

When the elder saw that the assembly was seated, he personally served various kinds of food and drink with his own hands; once the assembly had finished eating to their satisfaction, they completed their ritual rinsing of the mouth.

The elder and his wife immediately prostrated at the Buddha’s feet before him and remained kneeling. The World-Honored One, observing the differences in their faculties and dispositions, preached the Dharma according to their capacities; thereupon, while still on their seats, they both perceived the Truth and attained the fruit of Stream-entry. The sūtra continues with a detailed account of how they took refuge in the Triple Gem and received the five precepts.

The Buddha and the assembly of noble ones each returned to their respective dwellings. On the very night that the householder’s wife attained the fruit [of her aspiration], she perceived that she had conceived. From then on, she made regular offerings to the Buddha and the Sangha. When nine months had passed, she invited the Buddha and the Sangha to her home for a meal, and the Buddha preached the Dharma for them.
The husband and wife both attained the fruit of non-returning (*anāgāmiphala*). On that very day, their son was born, his appearance extraordinary and beloved by all who saw him.

His forehead was broad, his eyebrows long, and his nose high and straight; his crown was rounded like a parasol and his complexion as beautiful as gold. His hands reached down past his knees, a sight for which he was praised by the multitude.
After twenty-one days had passed, he held a gathering with his kinsmen. His father addressed the relatives concerning his son, saying, "What name should be given to this child now?
The entire assembly replied in unison:

"On the very day his parents attained the fruit [of enlightenment], this child entered his mother's womb; and at the time of his birth, he likewise attained a supreme fruit. Such a convergence of fortune has never been heard of in this world."
"If he possesses supernatural powers (*ṛddhi*), it is only right that we praise him; this son should be named 'Supernatural Power' (*Ṛddhimat*).
The elder raised the child, entrusting him to eight nurses:
two to provide milk and food, two to carry him in swaddling clothes, two to bathe him, and two to play with him joyfully.
He was provided with nourishment and sustenance without any deficiency, as described in detail above.
At that time, the youth Ṛddhimat, having reached adulthood and possessing a most extraordinary appearance, departed along the road from beneath the royal city.

At that time, there was a palace lady on an upper terrace who saw him from afar; her mind became enamored by his appearance, and she immediately cast a flower garland down from above, which fell upon the youth's head.
A supervisory official, having witnessed this event, went to inform the king:
"Does Your Majesty know?
The youth Ṛddhiputra harbored improper lustful thoughts toward the women of the inner palace; as he passed below the city, a court lady threw a flower garland at him."
Having heard this, the king did not reflect upon it carefully, but immediately gave rise to anger and commanded his judicial officers, saying:
"This youth has had illicit relations with those within the palace; since he has committed a crime punishable by law, his life shall be taken."
The judge, following these instructions, bound the youth and went to the place of execution, where he immediately severed his head.
When the multitude of people in the city saw that this youth had been unjustly put to death, they all raised a great cry and spoke thus:
"This unrighteous king has failed to investigate thoroughly; one who possesses no fault and is beyond reproach has been subjected to execution."
When the king saw that the people were speaking of his unreasonableness, he reflected to himself:
"It was I who acted with haste and failed to examine the legal statutes; you all, sirs, shall be pardoned for this one transgression."
At that time, the householder Sudatta, having seen his son dead, thought to himself:
"I have sought out precious wealth with great hardship, all for the sake of supernatural powers to ensure the prosperity of my family estate."
"Now that my life has come to an end, what use would wealth be?
It is fitting for me now to bestow all my precious possessions upon śramaṇas, brāhmaṇas, and the poor, reserving only a single gold coin as the foundation for food and clothing."
Having formed this thought, he then had a drum beaten in the city of Śrāvastī to proclaim:

"Gentlemen, you should know that the householder Sudatta currently possesses wealth and goods which he gives away without restriction; his male and female slaves and various livestock are all released to follow their own fortunes. If anyone has need of anything, let them come and take it as they please."
Upon hearing this, people gathered from near and far; the elder distributed all his goods as alms, and everyone, their wishes fulfilled, marveled at such an unprecedented occurrence.

At that time, the elder purchased various commodities for a single gold coin, and by selling them the following day, he would always obtain four coins. Every day at noon, he would purchase various fragrant substances with one gold coin, grind them into incense paste, and smear it upon the Buddha hall.
Furthermore, he used one coin every day to make offerings to the monastic community in turn, and used another coin for the clothing and food of the inhabitants of his house;
the remaining single coin was kept as capital.

Once the householder Sudatta had exhausted his family estate and was destitute of wealth and food, he nevertheless provided for all who came to beg according to their needs; because of this, he was called "Sudatta the Coarse."
Then the householder Raudrākṣa went to where the Buddha was, prostrated at his feet, and sat down to one side.
The Buddha said to the householder:
"Are you able to give alms regularly from within your home?"
The householder said, “World-Honored One!
Although I have daily bestowed food and drink upon my household, because I am poor and lack resources, I am unable to provide what is refined; most of it is coarse and inferior.”
The Buddha told the householder:
"Householder, whether the object given is excellent or inferior, both shall result in a ripened fruit.
Householder!"

If a person, when giving, acts according to their whims—whether good or bad—lacking faith and failing to show respect; if they do not give with their own hands, at the improper time, or with impurity; then when such a person receives the karmic retribution, they cannot enjoy it as they wish like that great wealthy householder. Regarding their houses, servants, vehicles, food, drink, clothing, beds, and bedding, as well as forms, sounds, scents, tastes, and textures, their minds remain stingy and they are unable to enjoy them.
"Householder!
Such is the retribution obtained from practicing generosity out of lack of faith and other such motives.
Householder!"

Furthermore, whether the objects given are excellent or inferior, if one gives with deep faith and profound reverence, personally offering pure things at the appropriate time to another, such a donor, when receiving the fruit of their reward, will enjoy them at will like a great householder. They will extensively love and enjoy many possessions within their home—slaves, vehicles, food, drink, clothing, couches, bedding, and the objects of the senses: forms, sounds, smells, tastes, and tangibles.
For this reason, Elder, you should listen!
In the distant past, there was a most noble and eminent great Brahmin named Vairocana.

He would constantly bestow upon the Brahmins eighty-four thousand great elephants, each equipped with golden saddles, bells, and banners all made of gold, and covered atop the elephants with golden nets, which he gave as gifts.
Furthermore, there were eighty-four thousand horses, all equipped with saddles and bridles made entirely of gold.

There were also eighty-four thousand chariots, each constructed from the four treasures—gold, silver, lapis lazuli, and crystal—with canopies and nets made of gold, and adorned with the variegated patterns of lions, tigers, and leopards; within them were spread cushions of skins and fine carpets.
Furthermore, there were eighty-four thousand exquisite pavilions, likewise composed of the four precious substances;
there were also eighty-four thousand couches and bedding, likewise made of the four precious substances.
All the mats, rugs, and blankets spread out were rare and exquisite items from all quarters; at both ends of the beds, vermilion pillows were placed.
Furthermore, eighty-four thousand golden bowls were filled with silver grain, and eighty-four thousand silver bowls were filled with golden grain.
Furthermore, there were eighty-four thousand pairs of exquisite, superior cotton garments of four kinds:
namely, fine Kāśika cotton, fine kṣauma cotton, fine hemp, and fine kośamba cotton.
Furthermore, he took eighty-four thousand cows, all of which had horns adorned with gold and were accompanied by their calves, each covered with fine cotton cloths.

He also took eighty-four thousand youths, all wearing necklaces made of gold, silver, and various precious gems. All such items as these he offered as gifts to the brahmins, let alone the remaining superior and exquisite foods and various kinds of clothing!

Householder, you should know that the merit obtained by that great brahmin Mahāsamudra when he bestowed such eighty-four thousand wonderful things upon the brahmins is not equal to that of a person who provides food and drink as an offering to even one hundred non-Buddhist seers who have abandoned desire and possess the five supernormal powers; the fruit and retribution of this latter merit far surpass those of the former.
Furthermore, householder!

Suppose that Great Tide were to give such eighty-four thousand wondrous and rare objects as these to the brahmins and to one hundred hermits of non-Buddhist paths; this would not equal the merit of someone who gives food and drink to a single ordinary person—a bodhisattva who has not yet abandoned desire—sitting beneath a jambu tree. The fruit and reward of this latter merit far surpasses that of the former merit.
Furthermore, householder!

Suppose that Great Tide were to give such eighty-four thousand marvelous things as these to the brahmins, to one hundred hermits of the non-Buddhist paths, and to ordinary bodhisattvas beneath the Jambu tree; this would not equal the merit of someone who gives food and drink to even a single person entering the stream. The fruit and reward of this latter merit far surpasses that of the former.
Furthermore, householder!

Suppose that Great Tide were to give such eighty-four thousand wonderful and marvelous things as these to the brahmins, and to one hundred hermits of the non-Buddhist paths, and also to ordinary bodhisattvas and those entering the stream under the Jambū tree; this would not equal the merit of someone who gives food and drink to a single stream-enterer. The fruit and reward of this latter merit would be far more excellent than the former merit.

Thus it is explained in detail regarding the candidate for the fruit of Once-returner, the fruit of Once-returner, the candidate for the fruit of Non-returner, the fruit of Non-returner, and the candidate for Arhatship. However, this merit is not equal to that of someone who gives food and drink to a single person who has attained the fruit of Arhatship; the fruit and retribution of this latter merit are far more excellent than those of the former. This is fully contained in the Sanskrit original, but I have abbreviated it here for fear of being too prolix.
"Furthermore, householder!

Suppose that Great Tide were to bestow such superior and exquisite articles of pleasure upon brahmins, one hundred *ṛṣis*, ordinary bodhisattvas, as well as those on the four paths and those who have attained the four fruits—this would not equal the merit of someone who gives a magnificent garden to the Saṃgha of the four directions; the fruit and retribution of this latter merit are far more excellent than the former."
Furthermore, householder!

Suppose that Great Tide were to bestow such excellent and sublime articles of pleasure upon brahmins, one hundred *ṛṣis*, ordinary bodhisattvas, as well as those on the four paths and in the four fruits, and were to give a magnificent garden to the Saṃgha of the four directions; this would not equal the merit of someone who builds a monastery within this very garden and offers it to the Saṃgha—the fruit and retribution of this latter merit would be far more distinguished than that of the former.
Furthermore, householder!

Suppose that Great Tide were to bestow such superior and exquisite articles of pleasure upon brahmins, even to the point of constructing monasteries within his gardens; this would not equal the merit of someone who, within such a monastery, provides couches, bedding, and various types of seats, mats, blankets, and pillows. The fruit and retribution of this latter merit far surpass those of the former.
Furthermore, householder!

Suppose that Great Tide were to bestow such superior and exquisite articles of pleasure upon brahmins, even providing beds, couches, bedding, and various types of seats, mats, covers, and pillows within that monastery; this would not equal the merit of someone who provides the Sangha with regular meals in this monastery. The fruit and reward of this latter merit far surpasses that of the former.
Furthermore, householder!

Suppose that Great Tide were to bestow such superior and exquisite articles of pleasure upon brahmins, even providing the Sangha with regular meals in monasteries; this would not equal the merit of someone who, for as long as life lasts, takes refuge in the Buddha, takes refuge in the Dharma, takes refuge in the Saṅgha, and upholds the precepts. The fruit and retribution of this latter merit far surpass those of the former.
Furthermore, householder!

Suppose that Great Tide were to bestow such superior and exquisite articles of pleasure upon brahmins, even to the point of leading them to take refuge in the Three Jewels and undertake the training precepts; this would not equal the merit of someone who, for even a short time, practices the meditation on loving-kindness toward all sentient beings. The fruit and retribution of this latter merit are far more excellent than those of the former.
Furthermore, householder!

Suppose that Great Tide were to bestow such superior and exquisite articles of pleasure upon brahmins, and so forth, as extensively described, even practicing the meditation on loving-kindness toward all sentient beings; this would not equal the merit of someone who, for even a brief moment, understands that all conditioned phenomena are entirely impermanent, entirely subject to disintegration, and are to be reviled, and thus cultivates the perception of renunciation. Compared to the former merit, the fruit and retribution of this latter merit are far more excellent and cannot be measured against it.

For this reason, householder, you should know that constantly cultivating the contemplation of impermanence and so forth regarding all conditioned phenomena to seek the practice of deliverance is an essential gateway to the Dharma, through which one swiftly attains liberation.
"In this manner you should train; in this manner you should practice; do not be negligent.

At that time, the householder Suyātra and the great assembly, having heard the Buddha’s teaching, prostrated at his feet with deep joy in their hearts, accepted it with faith, and departed from their seats to put it into practice.
At that time, having arrived at his home, the elder lit bright lamps and read the Buddha’s teachings during the night.
Meanwhile, the king’s messengers were regularly patrolling the houses at night to inspect for open fires; seeing a lamp light in the elder’s room, they reported: "Elder!..."
Is it not because Your Majesty has sounded the drum and issued a proclamation to all people, decreeing that no one shall go out at night without holding a lamp?
Anyone who violates this instruction shall be fined sixty gold coins.
"If one has no money, they shall be imprisoned for life; have you not heard this?
The elder replied, "I have long been aware of this."
The night watchman said,
"If that is so, why have you lit this lamp?
He replied:
"I have been receiving the Buddha’s words throughout the night.
He replied, "Even if you recite the Buddha's teachings, how can you avoid paying the fee? Bring it here at once."
The householder replied, "I am now poor and destitute; where could I seek money?
He [the deity] reported this, saying:
"If that is so, you may come and be bound forever in a heavy prison.
He replied, "I have no other plan; I shall follow you accordingly."
The messenger then led him and placed him inside the prison.
The prison tower built by the king had three levels:
those of high rank were placed on the upper level, those of intermediate status were settled on the middle tier, and commoners of lowly station were confined in the lower building.
At that time, the householder Cūḍapanthaka, being of noble lineage, resided on the upper story.

Then the Four Great Kings, knowing that this householder lived near those who were beyond training (*aśaikṣa*) and was diligent and ardent in his practice, came to his dwelling during the first watch of the night.
He asked,
"Is it not improper for a householder to remain in prison?
The householder replied:
"O Great Seer!
I have committed this because I violated the laws of the kingdom;
it was not my own desire. He asked:
"What offense have you committed?
He replied, "Last night my lamp was fined sixty coins; as I am poor and have no means, I must be imprisoned."
The Four Heavenly Kings said,
"Householder!
Where do you wish to place these gold and jewels?"
"We have brought these for you to enjoy as you please.

The elder said, "I only pray that the Great Seer does not worry; if the King learns of this, he may perhaps grant us leave, so that the Great Seer might find the leisure to listen briefly to the sublime Dharma."
Then the Four Heavenly Kings prostrated themselves and requested permission to hear the teaching; out of compassion, the Elder proclaimed the essentials of the Dharma for them.
The bodily radiance of the Four Heavens was like four great masses of fire; seeing them from afar, the King thought to himself:
"Who is this person setting such a great torch ablaze within the prison?"

When the middle of the night arrived, Śakra, Lord of the Devas, came; the radiance he emitted outshone that of the assembly of the Four Heavenly Kings. Their questions and answers were just as those of the Four Heavenly Kings, continuing until [the king] requested to hear the sublime Dharma.

When the latter part of the night arrived, the Brahmā King came forth; his bodily radiance was so brilliant that it surpassed that of all the devas. After exchanging greetings and requesting permission to listen, he heard the Dharma with joy and returned together with the others to their respective palaces.
At that time, during one night, the Great King saw from afar this extraordinary radiance; when dawn had broken, he asked the prison official:
"Who lit a fire in the prison last night?"
The jailer replied, "There was no lighting within the prison during the night.
The king ordered a high minister to go in person to inspect it; they questioned everyone throughout the prison, but there was nowhere where a fire had been lit.
He returned and reported to the king, saying,
"No one has lit a fire.
The king said:
“Who is imprisoned within the third chamber?
The jailer replied,
“The man named Sthūlakoṣṭhaka is confined in the upper chamber.”
The king said, "Summon him here; I shall question him myself.
The messenger summoned him, and the king questioned the elder:
"Previously, when you were confined in prison by King Rāṣṭrapāla, why do you now kindle a fire again?
The elder replied,
"I do not recall kindling a fire during the night."
The king said:
"In the first watch of the night I saw four masses of fire, at midnight five, and in the last watch six.
For what reason does the elder speak falsely, saying there are none?"

The elder then explained in full that it was because the Four Heavenly Kings, Śakra, and Mahābrahmā had come to listen to the Dharma that his body possessed this radiance, and not from lamps or candles.
Upon hearing these words, the king felt a profound sense of reverence, admiration, and wonder, and said:
"Elder!..."
"You, O Benevolent One, possess great power; what do you now wish to seek?
Whatever you desire, I shall provide and bestow upon you.
The elder replied:
"I now venture to beg a boon from the King.
The King said,
"Whatever you require, according to your wish."
The elder said, "I wish to study the Buddhist scriptures at night; I only pray that Your Majesty will not prohibit the use of lamps.
The king replied:

"Following the elder's wish, let lamps be lit at night; furthermore, let others also do as they please, lighting fires during the night to read the Buddhist scriptures, and all shall be exempt from their offenses."
At that time, the householder Cūḍapanthaka and the people of the country, having been granted amnesty by the king, were all filled with great joy.
*Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya*, Fascicle 44. *Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya*, Fascicle 4.
The Eighty-second Chapter, Part Two:

The Training Rule on Entering the Royal Palace Gate, translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Yijing by Imperial Command. At that time, the Blessed One was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, there were three elders in this city:
the first was named Sudatta, the second named Suvīra, and the third named Śīlavant.

Each of these three elders had a distinct virtue by which they were named: the elder Sudatta was so called because he was able to give extensively; the elder Suvīra was so called because his speech was free from falsehood; and the elder Śīlavant was so called because the multitude trusted and submitted to him.
The one who was well able to endure and forgive was King Prasenajit; the one who was free from the mind of illicit desire was Prince Gopa.
At that time, in the kingdom of Kośala, after the middle of the eighth month, there were many thieves and robbers known as the "autumn bandits."
Those bandits gathered together and deliberated thus:
"How might we, with little exertion during this time, obtain much wealth so that we may enjoy it as we please for the duration of one year?"

One man said, "In this city there is the householder Sankha, who possesses great wealth and an abundance of treasures; we should go to the householder's place and together fabricate a false accusation against him."
He replied:
"Householder!
We previously deposited one hundred million gold coins with you; we now require them for use, so please return them to us."
"If you say it was false, we shall jointly cite the merchant Vīradatta as our witness.
Having acquired this wealth, they enjoyed it in abundance for one year.
One man said,
"How could that eminent layman Śreṣṭhin Śīlavant act as a witness for us?
The others deliberated, saying:
"I compelled him by force to provide testimony.
He asked: "What constitutes force?"
He replied, "This precept is superior because the Elder is naturally possessed of great shame; when he must defecate, he will certainly go far outside the village and enter the deep forest thickets."
I shall wait for the moment he intends to depart and take my stand in the thicket with a sharp blade in hand.
When he arrives, I will seize him and say:
"Householder, if you provide me with testimony, your life shall be spared; if you do otherwise, I shall surely cut off your head."
Upon hearing this, everyone said,
"A wise plan!
It will not be difficult to provide proof through such a stratagem."
They each took up their swords and went to the place where the elder Śīlavatī defecated, hiding themselves and sitting amidst the thickets.
When the elder arrived at that spot to relieve himself, he was seized by the thieves within the grassy thicket, who said to him:
"Elder, would you rather die?"
"Are you seeking a livelihood?
The elder replied,
"I truly do not know what your intentions are."
The bandits said,
"You must follow our instructions. He replied:
"Do as you wish," the bandits said.
"If you follow our words, your life will be spared; if you stubbornly oppose us, the blade will soon be plunged into you."
The elder asked,
"What instructions do you have?
The thief replied:
"Be my witness," [the monk said].
The householder replied,
"What matter requires a witness?"
The bandits said, "The householder Sāḷha previously deposited one hundred million gold coins with us; we now wish to reclaim them.
Fearing that he might not acknowledge it, we require human witnesses."
The elder said,
"Is this a genuine entrustment,
or is it empty talk?"
The thief said,
"This is a falsehood.
Having heard this, the elder thought to himself:

"I would rather die upholding the Dharma than perform an act of injustice; how could I avoid the suffering of a single lifetime by undergoing the retribution for various evils throughout immeasurable kalpas?
Having formed this thought, he spoke a verse to the bandits:
"Better to meet death by upholding the Dharma, Than to preserve life by betraying the Dharma."
"By upholding the Dharma, one surely attains the joy of ascending to heaven; by turning one's back on the Dharma, one shall be born within the hells.
When the elder had spoken this verse, he briefly proclaimed the essentials of the Dharma to the bandits, saying:

"Gentlemen, you should know that all of you, due to the causes and conditions of evil karma in previous lives, committed acts of deception; thus, though you have obtained human bodies, your food and clothing are constantly lacking."
"Now you have again committed unwholesome deeds; when your life here ends, in which realm will you be reborn?
There is nowhere other than the three evil destinies that can accommodate you.
Thus he exhorted him with various such admonitions.
Upon hearing this, the bandits conceived a heart of faith and reverence; they immediately came together to prostrate at the elder’s feet and said: "Elder!
We were foolish and unacquainted with good and evil, and we intended to defame one another through unlawful means."
"Having received your instruction, we are filled with profound joy and gratitude. What should we do now?
The elder replied, "Nothing surpasses taking the three refuges and observing the five precepts as the cause for a fortunate rebirth."
He immediately conferred upon them the Three Refuges and the Five Precepts, including the lifelong abstention from taking life; the bandits were delighted and took their leave.
Furthermore, King Prasenajit had a younger brother named Kāla, whose countenance was so handsome and dignified that all people loved and respected him.
On the day of the Poṣadha ceremony, he went to the Buddha’s dwelling; having prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, he requested and received the precepts.
Once he had received them, he rose from his seat and departed for a secluded place to restrain and collect his inner mind.
At that time, a demoness, having adorned her appearance, came to his side and said:
"Prince, since you are now in the prime of youth, you ought to enjoy sensual pleasures; it is only after you have reached old age that you may restrain your mind."
Having heard this, the prince said to the demoness:
"You delude beings with a mind of folly, but I uphold the pure precepts and do not practice the path of the heterodox.
At that time, the demoness, knowing that the prince’s intent was firm and rooted in ultimate sincerity, failed in her purpose and departed, concealing her form.
At that time, the householder Śubhadatta came to where the Buddha was staying; having prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, he sat to one side to listen to the Buddha’s teaching.
Then King Prasenajit also came to the Buddha’s dwelling to pay his respects; upon reaching the gate of the Jeta Grove, he commanded his attendants, saying:
“Go to where the Buddha is and see who is there?”
The messenger entered and saw the elder Sāḍha listening to the Dharma by the Buddha’s side, as described in detail above.
When the king reached the gate, he said to his attendants:
"When you see that elder coming out, inform him thus:"
"The Great King has issued a command: 'May the elder depart quickly from within my kingdom!
At that time, there were various devas who felt deep reverence for the elder; having heard these words, they each harbored indignation and released poisonous bees upon the king's body.
Having been stung by the bee, he hurriedly entered the palace, but the bee would not leave him and followed him inside.
With no other recourse as he suffered from the venomous sting, the king immediately returned to the Buddha’s presence, prostrated at his feet, and said:
"I have suddenly been stung by a bee; I do not know what the cause could be."
“I only pray that the World-Honored One will rescue and deliver me.
The Buddha said,
“Great King!”
"Because the King conceived a mind of malice toward the householder Sudatta and desired to expel him from the country, the devas, filled with indignation, released these venomous bees.
The King said, "I have committed this transgression; what should I do now?"
The Buddha said,
"Great King,
you ought to go to him and offer an apology."
The King asked,
"Am I to feel shame and apologize by prostrating at his feet?
The Buddha said:
"One should not offer formal salutation; rather, one should go before him, take his hand, and say:
'Householder!
I have spoken harsh words; I pray you will graciously forgive me.'"

At that time, King Prasenajit, having received the Buddha’s instruction, went to the householder’s place and offered his apology. Upon seeing him, the householder granted him mutual forgiveness. All those swarms of bees dispersed in every direction, and all who witnessed it were filled with wonder.
At that time, King Prasenajit addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
That I, occupying the throne of a king, should seek repentance and forgiveness from a commoner—is this not indeed extraordinary?”
The Buddha said,
"Great King, for a person of great sovereignty to seek repentance and apology from those of lowly status is truly rare.
Having heard this, Śreṇika addressed the World-Honored One, saying:
"I am poor and have nothing, yet I constantly give whatever I possess.
Is this not indeed a rare and extraordinary thing?
The Buddha said:
“It is truly rare to be able to practice giving despite being poor.
At that time, the elder Śīlavant and Prince Kāla were also by the Buddha’s side. The elder Śīlavant reported the matter of the autumn bandits in detail to the World-Honored One:
“I did not commit a wrongful act for the sake of saving my life; is this not indeed a rare occurrence?”
The Buddha said, "Though faced with the peril of death, his mind remains sincere and upright; this too is rare.
Prince Kāla addressed him, saying:
“World-Honored One!
A demoness, beautiful and seductive, came to delude and confuse me; yet, restrained by my observance of the precepts, I did not engage in unrighteousness.
Is this not indeed a rare and marvelous thing?”
The Buddha said:
"If a person of wealth and status is able to receive the prohibitive precepts and distance themselves from perverse desires, this is truly rare among all those in the world.
At that time, the World-Honored One, for this reason, spoke these verses:
"If a person occupies a position of honor, yet seeks to apologize to those of humble station;
or if they possess little wealth, yet practice giving according to their means;
even when encountering the calamity of death, they do not give rise to a heart of deception."
"Wealth, nobility, simplicity, and the absence of worldly passions—these four are all rare.

At that time, the elder Sudatta, the elder Śīlavant, and Prince Kāla each questioned the Buddha regarding profound meanings in his very presence; the World-Honored One answered them appropriately according to their respective matters.

At that time, King Prasenajit was also among them; seeing him pose the question but failing to understand its meaning, he merely gazed up with a heart full of anxiety and dejection, then paid homage to the Buddha and withdrew.
Having returned to the palace, he rested his cheek in his hand and was filled with sorrow and anxiety. At that time, Queen Śrīmālā, seeing the King’s dejected countenance, asked him:
"Great King, from where have you come? Your appearance is so haggard and distressed."
The king reported the matter to his consort. She said,
"Because Your Majesty is of little learning and unacquainted with the Buddha-dharma, you should read the Buddhist scriptures during the intervals between state affairs."
The King said:
"I am now advanced in years and cannot practice recitation; furthermore, the affairs of state are so numerous that I have no leisure to seek out the scriptures.
If you, Queen Śrīmālā and Lady Vārṣākārī, were to read the Buddha’s sutras, I would listen to and receive their textual meanings during the night."
The lady said,
"Excellent.
Then Queen Śrīmālā addressed the king, saying:
“I was born in the kingdom of Kośala, and the noble Udāyin was also born in the kingdom of Kośala; I shall go to him to receive the scriptural teachings.
Then Queen Vārṣākārī also said to the King:
“I was born in the kingdom of Magadha, and the noble Śāriputra was also born in the kingdom of Magadha; I shall go to him to engage in recitation and study.”
The King said,
"Let each person do as they please. Then,
King Prasenajit went to where Śāriputra was, and having extended his respectful greetings, he said:
“Venerable sir!
Lady Vāsavadattā wishes to receive the Dharma from you; we pray that out of compassion you will deign to grant her instruction.
Śāriputra replied:
"I should now go and inform the World-Honored One.
He immediately went to where the Buddha was, prostrated at the Buddha's feet, and said:
"World-Honored One!"
"The King wishes to invite me to serve as Lady Xingyu to receive the Buddha’s teachings of the Dharma; will this matter be permitted?
The Buddha said, "She should be instructed."
Śāriputra returned to the king and reported:
"The World-Honored One, out of compassion, has granted me permission to instruct you.
Having received this permission, King Prasenajit then went to the Venerable Udāyin and said:
“Noble One!
Lady Śrīmālā wishes to receive instruction on the Buddha’s sūtras from you, Venerable Sir,” she said, as related at length above, until she added, “Please grant me your permission to teach her.
Having received this permission, the King returned to the palace and informed his two queens:
"The two Great Virtuous Ones have consented to provide instruction.

Thereupon, the two Great Virtuous Ones came into the palace every day to teach the Dharma to the two ladies. Later, at another time, the border regions of King Prasenajit’s kingdom rebelled; the king dispatched his generals to attack them, but they were defeated and returned home. This occurred a second, a third, and even up to seven times, each time being utterly routed by the enemy and forced to retreat with their backs to the foe.
Upon hearing of the defeat, the king thought to himself:
"The border rebels have already been subdued by the dispatched army; it is not that I must go in person to suppress them.
Thereupon, the king arrayed his fourfold army and set out with his forces during that very night.

The Venerable Śāriputra was well-acquainted with the proper timing, whereas Udāyin did not recognize the shifting circumstances. Hearing the sound of the bells of the troops at night, he immediately woke up and thought to himself:
"Could it be that the king’s retinue has some business and is departing elsewhere?"
Before dawn had even broken, he perceived it as daybreak, took up his robe and bowl,
and entered the royal palace. At that time, a woman of the inner quarters informed Queen Vaidehī,
saying, "The Ācārya Udāyin has now arrived here."
Having heard this, the lady put on a light silk garment and went out the door to receive him; at that moment, Udāyin saw the lady’s body revealed and gazed intently at her.

When the lady realized this, she felt shame and remorse; she returned to the palace, changed into other clothes, and went to where Udāyin was to respectfully receive his instruction on the scriptures. She repeated this process two or three times before dawn broke.
When the palace attendants saw this, they all began to speak in derision, saying:

"Although the King’s faith and respect are sincere and unflagging, this bhikṣu lacks awareness of the proper time; he has arrived at midnight. Before the King has even put away his treasures and various precious objects, he has rashly and precipitately come to the palace gate."
At that time, Udāyin instructed her in recitation until dawn. Then Queen Vaśiṣṭhā asked,
"Noble One, where shall you eat this morning?"
Udāyin said, “I shall eat wherever I happen to find it.
The lady then took his bowl, filled it to the brim with food, and gave it to Udāyin; having received the bowl, he made this aspiration:
"May you be free from illness.
Having taken it and departed, he arrived at the king's gate and saw Śāriputra coming from outside. Udāyin asked:
“Virtuous One!
If one applies such diligence and mental focus as this, how can one possibly sever all afflictions?
I rose before dawn and entered the palace to instruct the queen in the Dharma, and having received my alms-bowl of food, I am now departing through the palace gate.”
"Venerable one, you have only just arrived now;
why are you so very late? Śāriputra replied, "O Āyuṣmat!"
"You may go.
On account of this matter, the Buddha shall establish a *śikṣāpada*.
When the bhikṣus of few desires heard this, they went and informed the Buddha.
For this reason, the Blessed One addressed the bhikṣus:
"There are ten kinds of faults for those who enter the royal palace.
What are these ten?"
First, the king and his consort were staying in one place. When a bhikṣu entered, the consort smiled, and the king immediately became suspicious:
"Could it be that my consort and this bhikṣu have committed some vile and evil act in a private, secluded spot?"
"If it were not so, for what reason would he smile?
Or could it be that he has some evil intent in his heart?
Second, when a bhikṣu enters the palace and the queen is pregnant, the king gives rise to this thought:
"Could it not be that the bhikṣus engaged in misconduct together, causing her to become pregnant?
Thirdly, when the bhikṣus entered the palace, the king lost his precious treasures and various other valuables; the king then thought:
"Could it not be that the bhikṣus have stolen my things?"
"Fourth, the King has secret words that have leaked outside; the King thinks to himself:
'Could it not be that the bhikṣu has transmitted these secret words?
Fifth, when a bhikṣu enters the palace, the King becomes angry with the Crown Prince and demotes him from his position; the Crown Prince thinks to himself:"
"Could it not be that the bhikṣu slandered me to the king, causing me now to fall into such grief?

Or, when the bhikṣu entered the palace and the prince committed an act of treachery against his father, did people not hear of it and say that the bhikṣu transmitted secret words, thereby causing the loss of filial piety and righteousness?"
Seventh, when a bhikṣu enters the palace, a high-ranking minister whom the king holds in great esteem may be dismissed from his position and think to himself:
"Could it not be that this bhikṣu has slandered me to the king, causing me to fall into such an undesirable state?"
8. When the king bestowed heavy rewards upon a minister of low rank, the people discussed it, saying:
"Is it not because a bhikṣu acted as his intermediary? 9.
When the king frequently went forth with his army to wage war, the people of other countries all discussed it, saying: [as above].
"Is it not because the bhikṣus have been discussing matters with the king that they have repeatedly caused us the exhaustion of military expeditions?
Tenth, when a bhikṣu enters the palace, the king, about to set out on a campaign, says to his warriors:
"Whatever is acquired shall belong entirely to yourselves."
After they had been completely suppressed, the king then reclaimed [the property].
The people deliberated, saying:
"This was done because the bhikṣu instructed the king to seize it from us."
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"For this reason, you should not enter the palace grounds without due cause, as it may cause the fourfold army to lose its peace and security; this is not something that a bhikṣu ought to do."
The summary verse says:
The Queen’s laughter, pregnancy, and jewels; leaking words, anger toward the Crown Prince;
harming the King, dismissal, and the matter of appointments; frequent expeditions, returning, and the seizure of wealth.
Thus, up to: "Having considered ten benefits, I shall lay down a training rule for the bhikṣus, which should be spoken as follows:

'If a bhikṣu, while the dawn has not yet appeared and before the consecrated Kṣatriya king has hidden his treasures or treasure-like objects, should enter past the threshold of the palace gate, except for other circumstances, it is a pāyattika.'"
Thus, while the Blessed One was staying at the Bamboo Grove Monastery in Rājagṛha, having established the training rules for the bhikṣus, he addressed the bhikṣus, saying:
"Within Jambudvīpa there are two great cities:
the first is named Puṣpapura, and the second is named Jayapura."
These two cities alternately experience decline and prosperity:
when the city of Puṣpapura prospers, the city of Jayapura declines; when the city of Jayapura prospers, the city of Puṣpapura declines.

At that time, the city of Jyotiṣka was prosperous and flourishing. It had a king who ruled the world, named R̥ṣidatta; he governed the people with the True Dharma, and the land was abundant and joyful, free from military conflicts and devoid of the suffering of illness.
The Dragon King rejoiced, and the five grains ripened to perfection, as described in detail above.
That king’s queen was named Candraprabhā; her countenance was exceptionally beautiful, and she was beloved and respected by all.
The king’s crown prince was named Śikhin.
He had two ministers:
the first was named Hitaiṣin, and the second was named Ātaṅkavyupaśama.

At that time, the king of Rājagṛha in Magadha was named Bimbisāra; he governed the people according to the Dharma, and the kingdom was free from calamities and afflictions, as described at length elsewhere.
His queen’s name was Vaidehī, whose appearance was so transcendent that she was peerless within the realm.
The king’s crown prince was named Ajātaśatru.
There was a high minister named Varṣākāra, who was of the most eminent and noble lineage among the great Brahmins.
At one time, while King Rāmagrāma was assembled in a grand court, he addressed the multitude, saying:
"Is there any other country that is as prosperous, joyful, and flourishing as our own?
At that time, among the assembly was a merchant from the kingdom of Magadha who spoke these words:
"Great King!"
"In this eastern direction, there is the great city of Rājagṛha in Magadha, where the king is named Bimbisāra.
That kingdom is prosperous and joyful, resembling that of the King.
When King Ṛṣipatya heard these words, he conceived a feeling of affection for King Bimbisāra and asked his ministers:
"What is lacking within that king's realm?
He replied, "There is no treasure there."
The king said,
"Summon experts in appraising jewels to select the finest ones.
He then filled a golden casket with exquisite gems, attached the royal decree, and dispatched a messenger to send them to King Bimbisāra of Magadha, saying to the messenger:
"You should reply to that king:
'From this day forward, may Your Majesty be my ally; whatever you may require, I shall provide for you.'"
The messenger, carrying the king’s letter, arrived at Rājagṛha and presented the letter and the national gifts to King Bimbisāra.
Once the king had read the letter and opened the national gifts, he was filled with great joy.
The king asked,
"What is lacking in that country?
The people replied:
"He has no fine cloth.

Thereupon, the King immediately took a chest filled with the finest cloth produced in the kingdom of Magadha and, in accordance with the aforementioned protocol, sent it to King Ṛṣidatta along with a letter stating:

"I have respectfully read your letter and received your national treasures; though we have not yet met in person, I am deeply moved by your distant kindness. Should he require anything, I shall provide it for him."
The messenger, carrying the king’s letter, arrived at the city of Jyotiṣprabha and presented the letter and the national credentials to King Rṣidatta.
Upon seeing them, the king was filled with joy and asked the messenger,
"What is the king's appearance and what is his stature?"
He also inquired about his character and conduct.
The messenger replied, "King Bimbisāra is similar to Your Majesty in stature; he is valiant and fierce by nature, personally leading military expeditions."
The king immediately had a superior suit of armor made according to these specifications and sent it off by messenger.
What were the five qualities?

First, when worn during the height of the heat, it became cool; second, blades could not penetrate it; third, arrows could not pierce it; fourth, it effectively warded off all poisons; and fifth, it was capable of emitting light.
Having had the armor fashioned, the King also drafted an imperial decree, saying:
"I now present these precious armor, complete with its five virtues. If you have any regard for me, I hope you will wear them yourself; I trust you will not bestow them upon others."
He then gave these fingernails to the messenger.
The messenger took them and went to the city of Rājagṛha, where he presented the fingernails to King Bimbisāra and said:
"Great King!..."
"This precious armor is endowed with five virtues; it was sent here by the Great King of the Immortal Path.

At that time, King Bimbisāra read the letter and examined the armor, his heart filled with wonder. He summoned the appraisers of jewels and ordered them to determine its value. The jewel appraisers replied, "Great King!..."
"Each of these jewels is priceless; nevertheless, by common consensus, they are valued at ten billion gold coins.
Upon hearing this, the king was filled with anxiety and thought:
"A dear friend from afar has sent me these precious armors. Since the value of each individual jewel is difficult to ascertain, how shall I repay him, as my kingdom possesses none such?"
With his hand supporting his cheek, he sat with a downcast face.
At that time, the minister Varṣākāra entered and saw that the Great King appeared to bear a look of sorrow, and asked:
"Great King!"
"Why does your face bear an expression of sorrow?
The king replied,
"How could my heart not harbor sorrow now?"
"A distant king has presented me with precious armor; the value of each of these jewels is beyond measure.
My kingdom possesses no other extraordinary treasures to offer in return, and for this reason, I am filled with anxiety."
The minister replied, "May Your Majesty not worry; there is a fine gift.
The king said:
"Where could such a thing be found?

The minister replied, "That king has bestowed only a single suit of precious armor. However, within Your Majesty's realm dwells the Buddha, the World-Honored One; he is the most exquisite treasure among men, revered by all sentient beings, and there is no one equal to him throughout the worlds of the ten directions."
The king said,
"If this is indeed true, what do you wish for me to do?
The minister replied:
"One may paint an image of the World-Honored One upon a cloth and dispatch a messenger to deliver it.
The King said, "If this is so, I shall inform the Buddha; I will carry out his instructions according to his teaching."
Then King Bimbisāra went to where the Buddha was, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, sat to one side, and reported the matter to the Buddha.
The Buddha said, “Great King, excellent! Your intention is most wonderful!”

One may paint a set of Buddha images and present them to that king. Regarding the method for painting these images: once the image has been painted, one should write the Three Refuges beneath it, saying:

"From this day forth until the end of my life, I take refuge in the Buddha, the most honored among two-legged beings; I take refuge in the Dharma, the most honored among those free from desire; I take refuge in the Saṃgha, the most honored among all assemblies."
Next, he wrote down the five precepts:
first, not to kill; second, not to steal; third, not to engage in sexual misconduct; fourth, not to speak falsely; fifth, not to drink any intoxicants.

Next, write the forward and reverse progression of the twelve links of dependent origination, namely: "Because this exists, that exists; because this arises, that arises," from ignorance as a condition for volitional formations, up until their accumulation and arising.

"Because this does not exist, that does not exist; because this ceases, that ceases. From the cessation of ignorance up to the simultaneous cessation of all accumulations, all of these were written out in detail.
Furthermore, on the upper edge of the image, two verses were inscribed:
"You should seek renunciation, And exert yourself diligently in the Buddha’s teaching."
Subdue the army of birth and death, as an elephant tramples a thatched hut.
Within this Dharma and Vinaya, you should practice heedfulness;
you shall exhaust the ocean of afflictions and reach the end of suffering.
"When the painting has been thus completed, it should be handed over to the messenger, who should be told:

'When you take this painted image to your own country, you should hang silk banners and canopies in a spacious place, arrange incense and flowers in profusion to create a magnificent display, and only then open the image.'"
If someone should ask,
"What is this? one should answer them as follows:
"This is the image of the World-Honored One, who renounced the rank of a Wheel-Turning King to achieve Perfect Enlightenment.
He asked again:
"What is the meaning of the inscription below this?"
He replied:
“Taking refuge in the Three Jewels is the cause for transcendence.
[The interlocutor asked: “What follows next?”
He replied,
"I teach them to uphold the five precepts so that they may be reborn in the human or heavenly realms.
[The other asked,] "What follows after that?"
He replied:

"This refers to dependent origination (pratītyasamutpāda), which clarifies the principle of cause and effect regarding the flow and cessation of transmigration within the three realms and five destinies.
If one asks what the meaning of the two preceding verses is:
The answer is:

"These two verses clarify the exhortation for all sentient beings to practice according to the teachings, to destroy the army of birth and death, and not to be negligent, but to swiftly proceed toward Bodhi."
At that time, King Bimbisāra, having received the Buddha’s instruction, joyfully accepted it with his head bowed, prostrated at his feet, and departed.

The king then had an image painted, inscribing the account of these events upon its upper and lower borders. He thoroughly perfumed the venerable image with various exquisite incenses; thereafter, he rolled it up finely and placed it within a golden casket, then placed that golden casket within a silver casket, and finally placed that silver casket within a copper casket.

Furthermore, he wrapped this casket tightly in exquisite, fine incense-cloth and placed it upon a fragrant elephant. With the streets solemnly adorned and banners and streamers leading the procession, they departed from the city of Rājagṛha.
At that time, King Bimbisāra also composed a royal decree to inform King Ṛṣipatya, saying:
"Though we have not yet met, upon receiving your messenger and perusing your letter, I have received the gift of a precious breastplate such as is rarely seen in the world."
Now, having painted an image of the World-Honored One, the Most Honored in the Three Realms, you should have it carried there so that offerings may be presented.

Once you have arrived there—having traveled two and a half *yojanas* from the royal city—you should level the roads, adorn the city walls and moats, and personally lead the fourfold army. At a spacious location, set up the sacred image with banners, streamers, flowers, and canopies, and offer diligent worship; thus you shall obtain great merit and virtue.
Having finished sealing the letter, he handed it to the messenger and commanded him:
"You must remember my instructions and carry them out to the fullest extent.

Having received these orders, the messenger took his respectful leave and departed. After traveling for many days, he gradually reached the city of Śabdavatī; having stayed there for about two and a half *yojanas*, he dispatched a scout to inform the king and carried the letter with him.
Having received the letter and read it, the king was filled with indignation and said to his ministers:
"I do not yet know what extraordinary or magnificent gift that country possesses.

Yet the letter says that the roads for two and a half *yojanas* must be leveled and the city walls adorned; flowers, parasols, banners, and streamers must be gathered, and all the people assembled, so that I may personally lead the fourfold army out to welcome them from afar."
"Judging by these circumstances, they intend to treat us with contempt; you all should assemble the fourfold army, and I shall personally go to wage war against the kingdom of Magadha.
The ministers replied, "We have heard that the king there possesses great magnanimity; one should not provoke the Great King with a mere ordinary diplomatic gift."
Your Majesty should now follow his words and go in person to observe.
If it accords with Your Majesty’s wishes, it will be excellent; if not, it will never be too late to mobilize the army.
The King said, "Truly there is such a principle; let us act according to the letter.

He had the roads leveled for one and a half stations, even going so far as to inspect them in person. Following the instructions in that letter, he prepared elaborate offerings and led [the Buddha] to the city, arriving at a level place where hundreds of thousands of people gathered in immeasurable numbers, with incense and flowers spread everywhere, filling the streets.

The king opened the portrait and stood gazing upon it with reverence; at that time, merchants from the Central Land came together to view the image, and they all joined their palms, raising a great sound in unison with one voice.
He cried out:
"Namo Buddhāya! Namo Buddhāya!"

When King Ṛṣipatya beheld the Honored One’s majestic form and heard the name of Buddha—seeing what he had never seen before and hearing what he had never heard before—the hairs on his entire body stood erect with awe.
The king then asked,
"What does the name 'Buddha' signify?
The merchant leader replied:
"Great King!
In the Middle Kingdom there is a city named Kapilavastu. Within it dwells King Śuddhodana, who has fathered a crown prince endowed with the thirty-two major marks and eighty minor signs."
The physiognomist gazed at him and said:

"If this prince remains at home, he shall become a Wheel-Turning Sage King (Cakravartin Rāja), possessing the perfection of the seven treasures and a full thousand sons; he will bring the four continents under his sway and transform the world through the Dharma."
"If one leaves the household life, they shall realize the state of a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, and be called a Buddha among gods and humans.
This is his true likeness.
Upon hearing this, the king was delighted and asked:
"What is the meaning of these subsequent words?
The merchant replied:
"Great King!
This is the taking of refuge in the Triple Gem.
The king said:
"Next, what follows? He replied:
"This clarifies the five precepts."
He asked again:
"What comes next? He replied:
"This is the forward and reverse progression of the twelvefold dependent origination.
[The interlocutor asks: "What follows this? He replied:
"This clarifies the exhortation to cultivate weary detachment from saṃsāra and the aspiration for nirvāṇa.
This was the extensive explanation.
