At that time, King Ṛṣipatya, having heard the merchant explain the principle of the arising and ceasing of the twelve links of dependent origination—ignorance, formations, and so forth—recited the text well and returned to his palace. There, during the first watch of the night, he contemplated according to the text; then, during the latter watch, he set aside all worldly affairs. As dawn approached, he sat cross-legged, straightening his body and maintaining right mindfulness, fixing his attention on the present to contemplate and investigate the principle of the arising and ceasing of the twelve links of dependent origination.

That is to say: because this exists, that exists; because this arises, that arises. From ignorance as a condition, volitional formations arise; from volitional formations as a condition, consciousness arises; from consciousness as a condition, name-and-form arise; from name-and-form as a condition, the six sense bases arise; from the six sense bases as a condition, contact arises; from contact as a condition, feeling arises; from feeling as a condition, craving arises; from craving as a condition, clinging arises; from clinging as a condition, existence arises; from existence as a condition, birth arises; and from birth as a condition, old age, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair arise. In this way, this entire great mass of suffering comes into being through accumulation.

That is to say: because this does not exist, that does not exist; because this ceases, that ceases. From the cessation of ignorance, volitional formations cease; from the cessation of volitional formations, consciousness ceases; from the cessation of consciousness, name-and-form cease; from the cessation of name-and-form, the six sense bases cease; from the cessation of the six sense bases, contact ceases; from the cessation of contact, feeling ceases; from the cessation of feeling, craving ceases; from the cessation of craving, clinging ceases; from the cessation of clinging, existence ceases; from the cessation of existence, birth ceases; from the cessation of birth, old age, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, and despair cease. In this way, this entire great mass of suffering, having been accumulated, is utterly extinguished.

At that time, King Ṛṣidatta, having gained a profound realization of the principle of dependent origination, did not rise from his seat; with the vajra-pestle of wisdom, he shattered the twenty peaks of the mountain of satkāyadṛṣṭi and attained the fruit of stream-entry.
Having seen the Truths, he rejoiced in his heart from afar and, longing for the World-Honored One, spoke this verse:
"Homage to the Great King of Physicians, Who skillfully cures the maladies of the mind;
Though the World-Honored One is far away, He can cause the eye of wisdom to be clear."
At that time, the king was filled with joy and immediately composed a letter to report to King Bimbisāra, saying:

"By relying on your benevolence, I have come to know the Three Jewels; I have awakened to the principle of dependent origination and attained insight into the True Dharma. Having been submerged in the ocean of suffering, the further shore is now within reach. To be pulled from the mire—how can my celebration be expressed?"
"However, I wish to see the bhikṣu in person; therefore, employ a skillful means to cause him to come here.
The messenger took the letter to King Bimbisāra. After the king had finished reading it, he went to the Buddha's dwelling, prostrated at the Buddha's feet, and said:
"World-Honored One!..."

The King Ṛṣidatta of the city of Jyotiṣa beheld the image of the Buddha and attained realization of the True Dharma; he has dispatched a messenger bearing a letter to this place to seek an audience with the bhikṣus, praying only that the World-Honored One will compassionately grant him leave to go.
Having spoken these words, he paid homage to the Buddha and departed.
At that time, the World-Honored One thought to himself:
"Who has a karmic connection with that city, such that they could go there and extensively bring about its transformation and deliverance?"
Perceiving through his insight that the noble Kātyāyana had the karmic affinity to teach and transform those there, the World-Honored One commanded Kātyāyana, saying:
"You should observe the Great King Ṛṣidatta within the city of Jyotiṣpura, along with all his retinue and the various classes of people."
Then Kātyāyana, having responded "So be it" and accepted the instruction, observed [the situation] and took his leave of the Buddha.
Taking up his robes and bowl, he entered the city to beg for food.
Having finished his meal and assigned the bedding and seats, he set out on the road with five hundred bhikṣus toward the city of Jayapura.
At that time, King Bimbisāra composed a royal decree and dispatched a messenger to deliver it to King Rājagṛha, saying:
"I have learned that you have realized dependent origination and attained the fruit of a stream-enterer; furthermore, I desire to meet with you, O Bhikṣu."

The Buddha has commanded five hundred bhikṣus to travel a great distance to attend your invitation; you should treat them with earnest devotion as if they were the Great Master himself. At a distance of two and a half *yojanas* from the city, prepare the roads and array fragrant flowers; then, having readied the fourfold army, come yourself to welcome them.

Furthermore, he constructed a great monastery in a secluded spot within the city, providing five hundred rooms equipped with beds, couches, and bedding so that nothing was lacking; all necessary provisions, including food and drink, were prepared in advance.
"If one performs such acts of offering as these, one shall obtain immeasurable merit.
The messenger took the letter and delivered it to King Śrīdhara; having read the letter, the king performed everything exactly as instructed.

Once the bhikṣu had arrived, the host welcomed him into the city; then, in a spacious and secluded place, they hung silk banners and canopies and solemnly prepared a ritual site (maṇḍala), inviting the bhikṣu to take his seat.

At that time, a great assembly of immeasurable hundreds of thousands gathered like clouds; then the noble Kātyāyana, according to their individual capacities and conditions, expounded the essentials of the Dharma for them.

May the entire great assembly receive benefit: some may attain the fruit of stream-entry, others may attain further fruits, and even those who have gone forth may attain the fruit of arhatship; some may set their minds upon the vehicle of the śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas, while others may set their minds upon the Mahāyāna.
At that time, there were two elders in the city of Jayapura:
one named Tiṣya and the other named Puṣya. They went to the place where the noble Kātyāyana was staying; having arrived, they prostrated at his feet and said:
"Noble One!..."
"I now wish to go forth in this well-spoken Dharma and Vinaya, and to practice the holy life under the guidance of the Noble One.

At that time, Kātyāyana, perceiving the sincerity of his resolve, immediately granted him the going-forth and the full ordination. He examined his faculties and instructed him in the essential teachings; the two of them then practiced with diligence day and night without weariness, severing all afflictions and realizing the fruit of Arhatship.

He immediately ascended into the void and manifested various miraculous transformations; water and fire issued from his body, and he then entered the realm of the wondrous *nirvāṇa* without remainder.
His kinsmen then cremated him with fire as an act of offering, and having collected his remaining bones, they constructed two *stūpas*.
At that time, King Rṣidatta went daily to the place of the noble Kātyāyana to hear the sublime Dharma.
Having heard it, he returned to the palace and told his court ladies:
"The noble Kātyāyana constantly expounds the profound and wondrous Dharma for me."

The palace attendants replied, "Great King, you possess great merit to have encountered the appearance of a Buddha in the world; thus, with causes fulfilled and conditions met, you have been able to hear the True Dharma.
The King said to the palace attendants:
"Why do you not go to listen to the Dharma?
The palace women replied,
"We women of the inner quarters have no means of going out frequently."
"If the noble Kātyāyana would enter the palace and preach the Dharma for us, we would listen.
Having heard these words, the king went to the noble one, prostrated at his feet, and said:
"Noble one!..."
"The women of the inner palace desire to hear the Dharma; I only pray that the Venerable One will give rise to a heart of compassion and enter the palace for a short while to fulfill their wishes.
Then Kātyāyana replied, "Great King!"
"The World-Honored One has established a precept that does not permit bhikṣus to enter the royal palace to preach the Dharma to women.
The king said,
"Noble One!..."
"If that is so, who will enter the palace to preach the Dharma for the women?
He replied,
"There is a bhikṣuṇī permitted to enter and preach for them."
When King Ṛṣipatya heard these words, he immediately wrote a letter to inform King Bimbisāra, saying:
"The women within my palace desire to hear the Dharma; is there perhaps some means by which bhikṣuṇīs might be allowed to come?"
At that time, King Bimbisāra, having read the letter, went to the Buddha’s presence, prostrated at his feet, and said:
“Venerable Sir!

That King Ṛṣidatta has again sent a letter stating that the queens and consorts of the inner palace wish to hear the True Dharma and desire to see the bhikṣuṇīs; what should be done regarding this matter?”
At that time, having heard these words, the World-Honored One thought to himself:
"Which bhikṣuṇī might have a karmic connection with those women of the palace in the city, such that they may meet and mutually deliver one another?"
Observing that the bhikṣuṇī Śailā was capable of converting them, the Buddha said to the bhikṣuṇī Śailā:
"You should observe those women of the palace in the city of Jyotiṣka."
The nun replied to the Buddha, “I respectfully accept the holy instruction!

Having prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, she went to her former residence; after entrusting her bedding and requisites to others, she took up her robes and bowl and, together with five hundred bhikṣuṇīs, set out for the city of Jeta-vana.

King Prasenajit again sent a letter to him, ordering that he be welcomed and received; he constructed five hundred dwellings to provide for all his needs, and established a place of practice where he preached the Dharma to the assembly, whereby many attained realization and resolved to attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
At that time, the Śrāmaṇerī went to the royal palace every day to expound the essential teachings of the Dharma for the queen and her attendants.

"That Great King Ṛṣidatta is skilled at playing the vīṇā, and Queen Candraprabhā is adept at dancing. Once, while the king was within the palace, he played the vīṇā with his own hands and Queen Candraprabhā rose to dance. During the course of her dance, [the Śrāmaṇerī] perceived signs of impermanence upon the queen’s body, indicating she would surely pass away on the seventh day."
When the king saw this, distress arose in his heart, and he cast the lute he was playing to the ground. Seeing this, Candraprabhā said to him:
"Great King!
Is it that my dance does not accord with the strings and pipes of the music, such that you have cast your lute to the ground?"
The king said, "It has nothing to do with the wickedness of your dancing; rather, I see the signs of death upon your body, and you shall certainly pass away within seven days.
Candraprabhā said to the king:
“If it be so, I pray you let me go; I wish to leave the household life.

The King said, “We shall establish a covenant so that your desire may be fulfilled: if, once you have left the household life, you sever all afflictions and realize the fruit of Arhatship, then my hope shall be severed.”
"If there be any remaining fetters or afflictions such that you pass away, you should inform me of your destination.
The lady replied, "So be it."
Then King Ṛṣipatya led Candraprabhā to the bhikṣuṇī Śailā; having prostrated at her feet, he said:

"Noble Lady! Lady Candraprabhā wishes to go forth in this well-spoken Dharma and Vinaya. I pray that the Noble Lady will compassionately accept her, grant her the going-forth, and confer upon her full ordination."
Śaila replied, “Excellent, Great King!

He immediately granted him the going forth and the full ordination. Observing his karmic retribution, he knew that his life was about to end, so he instructed Candraprabha in the practice of the contemplation on impermanence.
Candraprabha acted according to his word; on the seventh day, he suddenly passed away and was reborn in the Heaven of the Four Great Kings.
It is the natural law of the gods that at the moment of their first birth, three thoughts necessarily arise: "Where did I die?"
"Knowing that he was among humans, [the deity asked],
'Where have you been born this life? He replied,
'I have been born in the Heaven of the Four Great Kings.'"
"What karma did you perform?
[The Buddha replied: "I cultivated the pure life (brahmacarya) within the Buddha's teaching.
At that time, the goddess Candraprabhā thought to herself, "If I do not go to pay homage to the World-Honored One, it would be improper."
He immediately took necklaces to adorn his body and filled a cloth bag with various kinds of exquisite celestial flowers. At night, he went to where the Buddha was.
The divine light shone brilliantly, filling the Bamboo Grove Monastery; he then scattered the exquisite flowers everywhere around the Buddha, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and sat to one side.

At that time, the World-Honored One observed their spiritual capacities and preached the Dharma for them. Having heard the Dharma, they attained the fruit of stream-entry (*srotāpanna*) and spoke these verses:
“The world’s humans and devas all offer worship to you, Who can eliminate karma, delusion, birth, aging, and death;
Difficult to encounter throughout hundreds of thousands of lifetimes, I have now fortunately met you—truly a rare occurrence.”
Relying on the Great Master, I have eliminated the fetters and delusions; Now, at this time, I have attained the pure eye.
Having crossed the torrent of suffering and ascended to the other shore, I shall ultimately enter the city of Nirvana.
When that goddess had spoken these verses, she prostrated at the Buddha’s feet and went to King Ṛṣidatta in the city of Jayasvara.

At that time, the king was sleeping alone on an upper terrace; upon her arrival, the goddess’s body emitted a great radiance, and she snapped her fingers to make a sound that awakened the king from his sleep.
Upon hearing this, the king sat up in alarm and asked,
"Who is making that sound?
They replied:
"I am Candraprabhā.
The king said, "Lady!"
"Come and lie down with me," the celestial maiden replied,
"O Great King!"
"I have already died and been reborn in the Heaven of the Four Great Kings. Since the affairs of humans and devas differ, it is logically impossible for us to dwell together.
If Your Majesty wishes to enjoy union with me, you must leave the household life and practice the Way within the Buddha’s teaching."
If all afflictions are forever severed, all worldly expectations will utterly cease.
If one passes away while still possessing residual delusions, they shall be reborn in the Heaven of the Four Great Kings and meet with me there.
Having spoken these words, he ascended into the air and departed.
When King Śrīdhara heard this instruction, he was filled with a mixture of wonder and joy.
He thought of the matter of renouncing the world and remained awake throughout the entire night; when dawn arrived, he addressed his great ministers, saying:
"Go and ask where Lady Candraprabhā is now.
The minister replied,
"She has already passed away."
Upon hearing this, the king thought to himself:

"I should not remain at home, heedless of the celestial warning and disregarding its words. I shall appoint Prince Śikhin as king and entrust him with the affairs of state, so that I may go forth into homelessness within the well-expounded Dharma and Vinaya."
Then King Śikhin said to his two ministers: "You should know this!

My affection for Śikhin is deep, and my sense of duty toward you two is likewise great; therefore, you may remain by Śikhin’s side to restrain him from evil and encourage him toward good, for I wish to renounce the household life."
Upon hearing this, the two ministers shed tears that drenched their robes.
The King then addressed Cūḍāpanthaka, saying:

"As you have followed my instructions until now, from this day forward you should likewise heed the words of these two ministers. Rule over the people of all lands according to the Dharma; I wish to renounce the world and go forth into homelessness."
Upon hearing this, the Prince wept with such grief that he could hardly endure it.
Then, King Ṛṣipatya, having completed his instructions, beat the drums and issued a proclamation to announce to all the people of the kingdom:
"I entrust all affairs of state to the Prince; I wish to renounce the world."
"I have compared myself to a king who was unable to rule according to the Dharma; may you, the people of this land, each grant one another forgiveness.
When the multitude heard this proclamation, they were moved by the king's benevolence and all wept, unable to restrain themselves.

The king established his crown prince to oversee the affairs of state; he distributed vast quantities of wealth and treasures to extensively provide for the *asaṃvara* (unrestricted) offerings, such that no one among the śramaṇas, brāhmaṇas, or the poor and lowly was left without being fully provided for.

Taking a single attendant, he traveled on foot toward Rājagṛha; at that time, King Śikhaṇḍin and the multitude of the people all followed him for a short distance to see him off before returning home.
The king gradually proceeded toward the city of Rājagṛha; having rested for a short while in a garden, he addressed that man, saying:
"You should now go and inform King Bimbisāra, saying:
'The seer-ruler Rāja is currently outside the city.'"
The messenger immediately went to the king’s presence and reported the matter in full detail.
Upon hearing this, the king rose in alarm and said to his ministers:
"King Ṛṣidatta possesses a vast army; why did you not inform us beforehand of his sudden arrival here?"
The messenger reported to the king:
"He has no military forces; he has only a single attendant.
Upon hearing these words, the king thought to himself:
"He is a Kṣatriya great king who has received the consecration; I ought not now to lead him alone into the city without preparation.

Thereupon, they repaired the roads and adorned the city walls. They personally led the fourfold army to the place where King Ṛṣidatta was, and with joyful words and a handshake, they exchanged greetings. Together they mounted a single elephant and entered the city of Rājagṛha, where he was immediately bathed with fragrant water and presented with exquisite garments.
Having finished eating and drinking, he asked:
"For what reason has Your Majesty now abandoned the great position of sovereignty and, accompanied by only a single attendant, traveled such a long distance on foot to arrive here?"
He replied, "Great King! I have no other business;
my original intention was to come before the World-Honored One to seek to go forth and receive full ordination, so as to purely cultivate the holy life with the resolve to attain liberation."
Then King Bimbisāra, raising his body and joining his palms, spoke these words:
"Excellent, O Buddha!
Excellent, O Dharma!"
Excellent, O Saṃgha!

Possessing great compassion and supreme power, you have enabled this Kṣatriya, an anointed Great King, to relinquish his exalted station and come to the Buddha’s presence to seek renunciation, receive full ordination, and practice the conduct of a bhikṣu.
Then King Bimbisāra immediately led King Śuddhodana to the place where the World-Honored One was.

At that time, the World-Honored One, surrounded by an immeasurable multitude of hundreds of thousands of the fourfold assembly, was expounding the sublime Dharma. Seeing from afar King Bimbisāra and King Śuddhodana approaching to enter the assembly, he addressed the bhikṣus:
"That King Bimbisāra has come to my presence, bringing offerings."
"You all should know!
Among all offerings made to the Tathāgatas, none surpasses that which guides and transforms sentient beings.
Having spoken these words, he remained silent.
At that time, King Bimbisāra and King Rājagṛha went together to the place where the Buddha was. Having prostrated at his feet, they stood to one side and said:
"World-Honored One!

This is the Great King Rājagṛha from the country of Jyotiṣprabha, who has come here on foot. He desires to go forth in the well-expounded Dharma and Vinaya of the Tathāgata, to receive full ordination, and to practice the conduct of a bhikṣu."
"I only pray that the World-Honored One will compassionately accept me.
The World-Honored One then addressed King Rṣidatta, saying:
"Welcome, Bhikṣu!"
"You may practice the holy life.

Upon hearing these words, the king's hair and beard fell away of their own accord; dharma robes appeared upon his body and a bowl and almsbowl were in his hands, and his dignified deportment was like that of a bhikṣu of a hundred years' standing.
At that time, King Bimbisāra paid homage to the Buddha and departed, while the bhikṣu Ṛṣipatya remained with the assembly.
In the early morning, he donned his robes, took up his alms bowl, and entered the city of Rājagṛha to wander for alms.

At that time, a multitude of hundreds of thousands of men and women, hearing that he had entered the city, all came together to gaze upon him; the ladies of the inner palace likewise ascended their towers and pavilions, looking out with utmost sincerity to behold this rare wonder.
When that bhikṣu had finished eating, he returned to his original place; having finished his meal, he put away his robes and bowl, washed his feet, and sat down.
At that time, King Bimbisāra, accompanied by his ministers and retinue, went to the place where the bhikṣu Ṛṣidatta was, personally prostrated in respect, and spoke this verse:
"The Great King of the Land of Excellent Sound Relinquished hundreds of thousands of cities;”
Now begging for leftover scraps of food—does this not give rise to toil and hardship?
Previously you used a wondrous golden plate, adorned with various jewels;
now you merely hold a clay alms bowl—does this not give rise to toil and hardship?
Formerly you ate fragrant non-glutinous rice, with exquisite delicacies provided according to your desire;
now you eat coarse and sparse food—does this not give rise to weariness and hardship?
Formerly you wore garments of Kāśī, fine cotton cloths and various silks;
Now that you wear the rag-robe of a scavenger, does it not cause you toil and hardship?
Formerly you dwelt in magnificent palaces, attended by many servants;
now you live alone beneath a tree—does it not cause you toil and hardship?
Formerly, you rested upon exquisite couches and cushions, enjoying fine, soft textures as you pleased;
now you lie upon a bed of grass—how could this not give rise to weariness?
Formerly, you were entertained by the ladies of the inner palace, with pleasures always following your heart's desire.
Sleeping alone at this time, how could it not give rise to weariness?
Formerly you rode a priceless elephant, a precious horse, and a magnificent carriage;
now you travel on foot—how could it not give rise to weariness?
"Your treasuries were once overflowing, and you always enjoyed whatever you desired;
now that you have nothing at all, does this not give rise to weariness and suffering?
When the bhikṣu Ṛṣidatta heard these words, he also replied with a verse:
"All those matters that are difficult to subdue, I have now humbled and eliminated;
I beg for food to sustain my body, like an ox bearing a yoke."
King Bimbisāra said:
"What is the meaning of your current words of sorrow?
Whatever is on your mind, I shall provide it all to you."
The bhikṣu Ṛṣidatta said:
"Those who delight in the Dharma have no sorrow or longing in their hearts;
those who do not know the Dharma pass from darkness into darkness."
"Great King, listen well!
I shall now proclaim the True Dharma;
by understanding the True Dharma, one is born in heaven and attains Nirvāṇa."
This body is not to be cherished; yet one virtue should be known:
by skillfully training it to abide within its proper sphere, one finds peace and happiness according to the mind.
Even if one lives for a hundred years, this physical life ultimately comes to an end.
Why do you constantly crave and cling to wife, children, wealth, and food?
A wife and children are like enemies; precious wealth is always feared as being lost.
I now renounce them all, liberated from every sorrow and affliction.
When human life is about to end, neither incantations nor medicine can save it;
neither gods, immortals, nor any holy ones can resist its course.
Though the heavens possess great power and long lifespans in superior realms, [they too must eventually pass away].
When the signs of decay appear before one, death is certain and none can save.
Though kings attain sovereign power, their majesty is unrivaled by any man;
though they possess great wealth and renown, in the end they enter the gate of death.
Even if one practices asceticism with valor surpassing all men,
or possesses the strength of a vast multitude of troops, how could one transcend the suffering of death?
Neither in the sky nor within the ocean, nor even amidst the mountains and rocks, can it be found.
There is no place on earth, Where one is not harmed by death.
Neither in the sky nor within the ocean, Nor even amidst mountain crags;
There is no place on earth, Where one is not harmed by karma.
After death, the body swells; skin and flesh gradually separate;
only white bones remain—what is there to find attractive in this?
When all the bones have crumbled away, there is nothing but an empty skull.
The form and color are most loathsome; who could give rise to love and delight?
Whether staying in a cool palace during the heat, or dwelling in a warm chamber during the cold;
Though one constantly protects and sustains body and life, one cannot avoid the invasion of death.
If a person performs the causes of wholesome deeds, the fruit is not shared with others;
kings and the like cannot harm it, therefore one should cultivate merit.
If one dies having committed the ten unwholesome actions, neither wife nor children will weep for them.
Funeral rites performed according to convenience are called a "bad death.
If one dies having practiced the ten wholesome deeds, wife and children will all remember them;
when the enshrinement and burial are both conducted according to the Dharma, this is called a "good death."
At birth one comes alone; at death one departs alone.
One experiences suffering and joy by oneself; there is no one with whom to share them.
When the Lord of Death arrives to take one away, father and son cannot save each other.
Neither kinsmen nor precious treasures can ransom one’s life.
Birth, old age, sickness, and death constantly pursue one day and night;
there is no place to hide or escape, for in the end, one is led away by the King of Death.
The wise one, seeing these things, Leaves them behind and seeks to go forth;
He shall cross the ocean of afflictions And no longer suffer the pains of the womb.
I have abandoned all enmity and suffering, And attained the nature of a bhikṣu.
"Ultimately escaping the prison of birth and death, one shall forever proceed toward the city of Nirvāṇa.
At that time, King Śuddhodana, having been taught this sublime Dharma by the bhikṣu Ṛṣidatta, listened with reverence and a heart of profound yearning, and addressed him, saying:
"Noble One!..."

"Birth and death are long and far-reaching, making it ultimately difficult to escape them. My position as a king is contrary to tranquility; I can only rejoice [in your teaching], yet I am unable to untie my bonds.
Having spoken these words, he prostrated himself and departed.
The Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya, Scroll 45. The Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya,
Scroll 46.
The Third Part of the Eighty-second Chapter on the Training Rule Concerning Entering the Royal Palace, translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Yijing by Imperial Decree:

"At that time, King Mūrdhaja of the city of Jayasvara, having succeeded to the throne from his father, initially transformed the people through the True Dharma; however, before long, he began to practice what is not the Dharma."
Those two ministers, seeking his welfare and removing his afflictions, addressed him, saying:
"Great King!
You should transform the people through the True Dharma and not through what is contrary to the Dharma."

Why is this? The people of the king’s realm are like flowering and fruit-bearing trees; if they are irrigated at the proper time and not allowed to wither, then it may be expected that their branches, trunks, flowers, and fruits will grow lush and abundant.
"The king's subjects are likewise; he nurtures them with righteousness, and their tax obligations are never in arrears.

Although he offered righteous admonitions when they practiced what was contrary to the Dharma, they refused to repent or change. When this had happened up to three times and they still would not heed his words, the king gave rise to anger and said to his other ministers:
"If there is one who intentionally opposes the commands of an anointed king, what punishment should be meted out to him?"
At that time, there was a sycophantic minister who came forward and said to the king:
"What need is there for further words? In principle, he deserves death.
He then spoke this verse:
"If a minister resists the king's command, or if one's teeth are loose,
or if poison is mixed in one's food— only by removing these can one find joy in life."
“If a minister possesses great wisdom, is well-versed in all laws and regulations,
and is wealthy with a strong military force— if he does not eliminate [the king], he will surely bring about his own destruction.
When the king heard these words, he said to that minister:
"If it be so, those two elder ministers were entrusted with my charge by my late father; I cannot now bear to inflict punishment upon them myself.
From this day forth, let there be no further meeting between us on such grave terms."
He immediately ordered his gatekeepers to block him and not allow him entry, and appointed two sycophantic ministers as his chief counselors.
Having gained the king’s favor, these sycophants would regularly recite verses in the king’s presence, saying:
“*The mustard seed has not been parched or steamed,* *Nor has it been ground or pounded;”*
"Without applying effort and pressure, one cannot obtain oil through mere conditions.
"The affairs of the people within the kingdom are likewise: only by inflicting severe and bitter hardship can state affairs be accomplished."
The king said, "I now entrust the administration of the state to you two; whatever you do shall be considered the final authority.
Thereupon, the two sycophantic ministers drove the common people with harsh laws.
At that time, there was a merchant who, carrying various goods from the city of Śabdavatī, arrived in the kingdom of Magadha at the dwelling of the bhikṣu Ṛṣipatya. Recognizing him, Ṛṣipatya asked:
"The King Śabdavajra-śikhin, His ministers and his military hosts— Are they free from illness and fear? Does he govern the people according to the Dharma?"
The merchant replied:
“‘The king and his ministers, along with the entire host of soldiers, are all at peace;
though they have no other fears, they govern the people through unrighteous means.’”
When the bhikṣu Ṛṣidatta heard these words, he asked in succession:
"Who is the chief minister?
Whose words does the king follow to oppress the common people?"
He replied:
"Venerable ones!

Previously, two ministers blocked us and would not allow us to enter. Furthermore, they appointed two other sycophantic ministers; the King followed their words and constantly practiced cruel oppression, causing the people of the land to find no peace or security."
Having heard this, the Rishi told the merchants:
"Go to that country and say to all the people:
'Do not be distressed!'"
"Wait until my three-month summer retreat is concluded; I shall go there in person to instruct the king.
At that time, the merchant prostrated at the feet of the bhikṣu, took his leave, and departed. Gradually arriving at the city of Śrāvastī, he informed the people, saying:
"The old king will arrive here before long to instruct the young king, forbidding him from practicing illegal acts or inflicting suffering upon the populace."
When the sycophantic minister heard these words, he said to King Śikhaṇḍin:
"Does Your Majesty not know?
Formerly, the old king came here with the intention of greedily seizing the sovereignty once again."
The king said, "My father has already left the household life; how can I seek the throne?
The minister said:
"By means of a heart of greedy attachment, I shall cause him to feel regret.
The King asked,
"How do you intend to do this?"
The minister said,
“One should take his life.
The king said:
"He is my father; how could I bring him harm?
The minister then spoke for him in verse:
"If they be one's parents, brothers, Or even daughters or sons;..."
Evil thoughts act as enemies; one must surely cut off their heads.
Even if one has a thousand sons, all riding together on a single boat—if even one son acts as an enemy, all the sons must sink.
"To preserve one's family, one may kill a single life; to rid the village of its troubles, one may destroy a family;
to rid the city of its troubles, one may destroy a village; and for one's own sake, one may abandon an entire kingdom.
At that time, the sycophantic minister offered such various exhortations, and the king approved of his words.
The sycophantic minister immediately commanded the butchers, saying, "You may now go and kill that old king; I shall reward you.

At that time, those butchers felt such deep affection for the old king that, although they were dispatched, their hearts were unwilling to leave. Thus it was repeated two or three times, and even after being granted rewards of gold, silver, precious jewels, and even entire villages, they still refused to go.
The sycophantic minister, filled with rage, told the jailer:
"You must now go and arrest that butcher, along with his family, and bind them in prison.
Having heard this, the jailer fled in alarm and went to the butcher's location; he seized both the butcher and his entire family and brought them back in shackles.
Terrified, the butcher said:
"Do not bind me; do as you please.
The prison official replied:
"You have killed the old king; I now release you," said the executioner.
The man replied, "I am going."
Thereupon, they all took up sharp swords in their hands and sought out the old king, traveling along the road toward the kingdom of Magadha.
At that time, the Venerable Ṛṣipatana, having completed his summer retreat, went to the place where the Buddha was, prostrated himself at the Buddha’s feet, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!...”
"I now wish to go to the city of Adhiśobhā.
The World-Honored One said, "Go as you please;
however, you must keep in mind that the power of karma is difficult to evade."

At that time, the Rishi-da bowed and took his leave of the Buddha, then went to his dwelling. Having entrusted his bedding and taken up his robes and bowl, he set out for the city of Jyotiṣka; when he had traveled halfway there, he encountered the butcher and recognized him.
He asked, "Have you come from the city of Jyotiṣka?"
He replied, “It is so.
[The Buddha asked:
“Are the king and the common people there each at peace?”
He provided a full account of the dialogue, explaining it at length as before, up until the point that he would not wish to see the Great King because the kingdom was being governed unrighteously.
Having heard this, the Seer said:
"O Noble Sir!"
"If it be so, I shall turn back.
Then the butchers spoke in verse:
"O valiant Great King, where are you going?"
"Since the Crown Prince did not wish for the King to live, he sent us to execute him together; now that the King's life has ended, there is no place for escape.
Upon hearing this, the Seer said to those men:
"O Noble Sir! Is it because of the topknot that you have sent you all to take my life?
They replied:
"So be it," thought the seer Ṛṣidatta:
"As the Blessed One has said:..."
"One must reflect that the power of karma is difficult to contravene"—
it was for this reason that he spoke these words in secret.
He then replied to the butcher, saying:
"O noble ones! You should pause for a moment.

The purpose for which I originally went forth as a renunciant has not yet been accomplished, despite my shaving of the hair and donning of the dyed robes. You should stay here for a short while while I seek to fulfill that objective."
The people replied,
"Great King, do as you wish.
Then the Venerable Ṛṣipatana sat cross-legged beneath a tree like a coiled nāga king, and spoke as the Buddha had said:
"A person of great learning has five kinds of benefits.

What are these five? First, skillfulness regarding the aggregates; second, skillfulness regarding the sense bases; third, skillfulness regarding the elements; fourth, skillfulness regarding dependent origination; and fifth, not seeking from others the instructions and exhortations that one requires."

At that time, the bhikṣu Ṛṣidatta was thoroughly proficient in these five matters. He understood that there is no fixed nature in the saṃsāra of the five destinies and that all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) are impermanent. Having observed this well, he severed all afflictions (*kleśa*) and realized the fruit of Arhatship. He viewed gold and earth as equal and indistinguishable; whether his body were cut by a blade or anointed with fragrance, he had no dualistic perception whatsoever.

With a mind free from obstruction, like a hand waving through space, he was able to shatter the shell of ignorance with great wisdom. He was fully endowed with the three knowledges, the six superknowledges, and the four kinds of unimpeded eloquence. Having renounced all attachment within the triple world, as well as gain, offerings, and honor, he realized the bliss of liberation and spoke this verse:
"All fetters and bonds have been severed; The many poisoned arrows have been well-pulled out.
I, the bhikṣu of the path of the sages, Yet still cannot escape the king’s law."
Having spoken these words, he said to the butcher:
"O worthy one! That which was to be done by me has now been completed; you may do as you please with what remains."
The butcher replied: "Great King!
If I return to my country, Crown Prince Mūrdhaja will ask me:"
"What were the final words spoken by the Great King at the time of his death?
How shall we report this? He replied:
"You should reply to him with these words:
'You have committed many evil deeds; by killing your father out of greed for the throne, you shall fall into the Avīci Hell, while I shall attain supreme Nirvāṇa.'"
“Furthermore, one should tell him:
‘You have committed two deeds of immediate retribution:
first, you killed your father; second, you killed an Arhat whose outflows were exhausted. You shall undergo extreme suffering and fall into the Avīci Hell.’”
"You should repent of your transgressions with utmost sincerity and earnestness, hoping that they may be lightened.
Xian Dao thought again:
"I shall use my supernatural powers to travel through the air; let me not suffer such extreme calamity because of this."

He immediately gave rise to right mindfulness and desired to manifest supernormal powers; however, regarding the object he sought, his mind became confused and disordered, such that he could not even remember the word "supernormal power," let alone ascend into the air and travel far away.
He further thought to himself:
"The World-Honored One has commanded me to contemplate the power of karma, from which there is no escape.
He then spoke this verse:
"Even if a hundred eons should pass, The karma one has created does not perish;
When the causes and conditions meet, One must experience the retribution oneself."
Then that butcher immediately drew a sharp blade and severed the king’s head; as it fell to the ground, a verse was spoken from mid-air:
“The power of inconceivable karma, though distant, inevitably draws one near;
when the fruit of retribution ripens, one seeks escape but can never be released.”
At that time, the World-Honored One suddenly smiled while in the Bamboo Grove Monastery.
It is the natural law of the World-Honored One that when he smiles, five-colored rays of light issue from his mouth; some descend downward, while others ascend upward.
The light that descended reached as far as the Avīci Hell and other hells; those suffering from intense heat all attained coolness, while those dwelling in freezing ice obtained warmth.
Those sentient beings each attained peace and happiness, and all thought to themselves:
"Have you and I died from hell to be born in another place?
Once they had developed faith, he again manifested other signs.
Having seen those signs, they all thought:
"We have not died here to be reborn elsewhere; rather, it must be due to the power of the majesty of this rare and great sage that our bodies and minds now experience such peace and happiness."

Having given rise to reverent faith, they were able to extinguish all the sufferings of the hells and receive superior, wondrous bodies within the realms of humans and devas; as vessels for the Dharma, they were able to perceive the principles of the Truths. Those who ascended rose as far as the Akaniṣṭha Heaven, where amidst the light they expounded the dharmas of suffering, emptiness, impermanence, and non-self.
And he further spoke these two verses:
"You should seek renunciation And apply yourself with diligence to the Buddha’s teaching;
Subdue the army of birth and death As an elephant destroys a thatched hut."
"In this Dharma and Vinaya, by constantly practicing heedfulness,
one can exhaust the ocean of afflictions and reach the end of suffering.
At that time, those rays of light, having pervaded the trichiliocosm, returned to the presence of the Buddha.
If the Buddha, the World-Honored One, speaks of past events, the light enters through his back;
if he speaks of future events, the light enters through his chest;
if he speaks of matters concerning the hells, the light enters through the soles of his feet.
If he speaks of matters concerning animals, the light enters through the heels;
if he speaks of matters concerning hungry ghosts, the light enters through the toes;
if he speaks of matters concerning humans, the light enters through the knees.
If he speaks of the affairs of a Cakravartin King of Power, the light enters through the palm of the left hand;
if he speaks of the affairs of a Cakravartin Universal Monarch, the light enters through the palm of the right hand;
if he speaks of celestial matters, the light enters through the navel.
If he speaks of the matters concerning śrāvakas, the light enters through his mouth;
if he speaks of the matters concerning pratyekabuddhas, the light enters between his eyebrows;
if he predicts the matter of anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, the light enters through the crown of his head.
At that time, the light circled the Buddha three times and entered beneath his feet.
Then, the Venerable Ānanda joined his palms in reverence and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!”
"The Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha smiles with a joyful countenance; it is not without cause or condition.
He then spoke a verse to request [an explanation] from the Buddha:
"Various wondrous rays of light issue from your mouth, Filling the great trichiliocosm in manifold forms; [Please explain this matter to us. "
Pervading all lands throughout the ten directions, like the sun’s light illuminating the entirety of space;
the Buddha is the most supreme cause for sentient beings, able to remove pride as well as grief and sorrow.
Without a cause, he does not open his golden mouth; this smile shall surely proclaim something rare and marvelous.
The serene and discerning Honored One of the Munis, who delights in speaking for those who wish to hear,
like a lion king letting forth his sublime roar, we pray that you resolve our doubts.
The Buddha is like the great ocean and the King of Wondrous Mountains; Without cause or condition, he does not stir.
Out of sovereign compassion, he manifests a smile, And for those who thirst and yearn, he explains the causes and conditions.
The Buddha told Ānanda: “So it is! So it is!”
"It is not without cause or condition that a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha suddenly smiles.
You should now listen!
He then spoke these verses:
“Though he has severed all fetters and bonds, and skillfully extracted the many poisoned arrows, that bhikṣu Ṛṣidatta still cannot escape the king’s law.
“Ānanda! [the Buddha said.]

Due to the influence of evil associates, King Śikhi of that city of Jyotiṣprabha will perversely commit the murder of his father—the former king who had attained arhatship and was free from all fault—and he is certain to fall into the Avīci Hell.
Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One,
has the bhikṣu Ṛṣipatya, who had attained arhatship, now been killed?”
The Buddha said,
"He has been killed.
Upon hearing this, Ānanda shed tears, overcome with grief beyond measure.
Then that butcher took the old king’s head, along with his robes and alms bowl, and went to the city of Jyotiṣka to the place of the sycophantic minister, saying:
"I have seen the old king; I have carried out the execution as commanded."
"This is his head, along with his robes and bowl.
When the two sycophantic ministers saw this, they were filled with great joy; they went to Mūrdhaja and said, "Great King!"
"The King may rejoice; within his kingdom there shall no longer be any enemies.
The King asked, "Who are my enemies?"
He replied,
“An old king. The king said:
"Has the former king's life already come to an end?
He replied,
"He has now been executed."
The king asked,
"How can this be known?
The sycophantic minister immediately pointed to the butcher:
"These people have personally taken his life.
Śikhaṇḍin asked,
"How many troops did my father, the former king, intend to bring here?"
The butcher replied,
"How could that renunciant bhikṣu have an army?
He has come along the road alone, walking on his own."

He then took the robes, the bowl, and the king’s head to show them to Śikhaṇḍin. Upon seeing them, Śikhaṇḍin fainted and fell to the ground. After cold water was sprinkled over him for a long while, he revived;
rising up, he wept bitterly and asked the butcher, "When my father, the King, died, what final instructions did he leave?"
He replied: "Great King!
When the former king passed away, he personally spoke this verse and sent word to inform Your Majesty."
"You have committed many sinful deeds, killing your father out of greed for the throne;
I have attained supreme nirvāṇa, while you shall fall into the Avīci Hell."
He said again: "You have committed two acts of immediate retribution:
first, you killed your father; second, you killed an Arhat whose outflows were already exhausted."
"You shall fall into the Avīci Hell and undergo extreme suffering; you should now sincerely and earnestly eliminate your remorse, hoping that [the punishment] may be lightened.
At that time, having heard these words, Kūṭāgāra felt as if an arrow of sorrow pierced his heart; his complexion grew haggard, like a living reed cut down, its stalks and leaves withering away.
He even dispatched a messenger to summon his two former ministers, and upon their arrival, he said to them:
"For what reason did you two fail to restrain me when I was committing such extremely grave evil deeds?"
The two ministers replied, "The King has commanded that we may not see one another; what means is there for us to counsel and dissuade him together?

Thereupon, Mūrdhaja issued an edict that the two sycophantic ministers were no longer to have audiences with him, and he reinstated the two former ministers as chief counselors. From then on, they gradually exhorted King Mūrdhaja to govern the kingdom according to the True Dharma.
At that time, once the two sycophantic ministers had lost their favor, they devised another stratagem to change the king’s mind.

They took two small cats—one from the stūpa of the elder Arhat named Tiṣya and one from the stūpa of the elder Arhat named Puṣya—and placed each inside a small hole made on one side of the respective stūpas. Every day they fed them with meat and taught them to understand speech; they would regularly carry meat to the edge of the holes and call out loudly:
“Tiṣya! Puṣya! Come out, each of you!”
The cat then emerged.
He spoke to them again:

"If it is true that you have deceived the world with deceitful and sycophantic acts, receiving the food and clothing of the faithful to sustain your lives, and by this evil karma have fallen into the state of cats—if this matter is not false, each of you take a piece of flesh, circumambulate your own stūpa, and return to your original burrows."
Having spoken these words, he finally threw down the meat; the two kittens took the meat, each circumambulated the stūpa, and returned to their burrow.
In this manner, he daily instructed the two kittens at the site of the stūpa until they were thoroughly matured and understood human speech.
When the two sycophantic ministers had performed this deed, they went to Queen Mūrdhaja and said to her:
"O Great Queen!
The King is now so emaciated that his life is at its end; how can you now abandon him and fail to inquire after him?"
The Queen Mother replied: "What can I do?
It was because of you two who taught her to commit such an extremely grave evil deed."
The two ministers said,
"How could we discard the rope as well simply because the water jar has fallen into the well?
The mother replied:
"Knowing that such a thing exists,
what should I do? The sycophantic minister said:
"The grief over killing your father you have already dispelled yourself; now, as for the remorse arising from killing an Arhat, we shall remove it for you.
The mother asked, "How do you wish to remove it?"
The minister said:

"Tiṣya and Puṣya claimed for themselves that they had attained arhatship, which was known to all; this was merely to deceive and delude others by asserting that there is no future life. How could they have known that after death they were reborn among cat offspring? By this evidence, one knows that there are no arhats."
The mother said, "If this is indeed true, you may let him verify it for himself; that would suffice to dispel my grief.
Her mother then went at once to Cūḍāmaṇi and asked:
“Dear child!
Why is it that your body is now so extremely emaciated, jaundiced, and gravely ill?
She then addressed her mother, saying:
"How could I now possibly avoid suffering in body and mind?

Because these two sycophantic ministers incited me to commit two acts of immediate retribution—first, the wrongful execution of my innocent father, and second, the killing of an Arhat whose outflows were exhausted—he will surely go straight to the Avīci Hell."
The mother said, "You need not worry; I shall explain it for you.
The king asked:
"I pray that you will explain this for me and dispel my deep sorrow.

His mother said, "The former king of this country was not your father. While I was bathing, I had intercourse with a stranger, and because of that, you were born. Although he was executed, it does not constitute the crime of parricide."
The king said, "I know that were it not for my father, there would have been no grave karma of rebellion; yet, could the sin of killing an Arhat truly be absolved?
His mother said:
"In this matter, you should consult those who possess wisdom to ascertain the truth.
At that time, the Queen Mother took her leave of her son and departed, commanding her two sycophantic ministers, saying:
"The anxiety my son felt regarding the murder of his father has already been dispelled; as for the sin of killing an Arhat, you yourselves shall know it well."
At that time, King Śikhaṇḍin immediately commanded all his ministers to assemble in one place, and he also summoned all those who were wise.
The two sycophantic ministers arrived along with the crowd, and the king asked them:
"I have heard that killing an Arhat constitutes a crime of immediate retribution (ānantarya); what do you think of this matter?"
At that time, someone from within the great assembly addressed the king, saying: "Great King!
Who else could know that he has attained arhatship?"
Furthermore, some say:
"An Arhat travels through the air with the clear and penetrating vision of the Way-eye; knowing that there was a threat to his body, why did he not avoid it from afar?"
The two sycophantic ministers said:
"Why does Your Majesty appear so distressed?
Is there no Arhat in this world, such that by killing him you would incur the crime of parricide?"
The King said:

"I and all these people have witnessed with our own eyes how Tiṣya and Puṣya attained arhatship, ascended into the void, transformed their bodies into water and fire, performed various supernatural powers, and entered the realm of the wondrous nirvana without remainder."
"How can you say that it is not real?
The sycophantic ministers replied,
"We pray that Your Majesty will pardon their offense and allow them to complete their task."
The king asked,
"What do you wish to do?
The minister replied:
"They were all hypocrites who deceived the world; they have truly taken rebirth again, yet they claim there is no further existence.
If it were truly non-existent, for what reason would they be born among the kittens, each dwelling beneath a stupa?"
The king asked,
"How can this be known?
The minister replied:
"Your Majesty should verify this for yourself.
Thereupon, the king immediately commanded his ministers, saying:
"I wish to go there to observe whether it is true or false."
The king then prepared his carriage, and together with a great multitude of hundreds of thousands of people, proceeded to the site of the stūpa.
At that time, the sycophantic minister took a piece of meat and, standing beside the stūpa, called out in a loud voice:
"Tiṣya and Puṣya, each of you come forth!"
The cat then emerged.
He spoke to them again:

"If it is true that you have deceived the world with deceitful and sycophantic conduct, and have sustained yourselves by receiving the food and clothing of the faithful, and if it is not false that you have fallen among cats due to this evil karma, then each of you take a piece of meat, circumambulate your own stūpa, and return to your original burrows."
Having spoken these words, he finally cast down the meat.
The kittens, having obtained the meat, each circled their respective stūpas and returned to their holes.
The sycophantic minister said:
"Does Your Majesty see it now?
The King replied, "I see it."
The sycophantic minister said, "In this world today there are no arhats; there are only empty words.

At that time, the king immediately abandoned his view of the arhats and gave rise to a perverted mind, severing all offerings of food and drink to the bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, and others that he had previously provided through his acts of generosity.
At that time, as the five groups of disciples had no food or drink, they all dispersed in the four directions; only Mahākātyāyana and the bhikṣuṇī Śailā remained in this city.
At that time, the bhikṣu Kātyāyana took up his robe and bowl in the early morning and entered the city of Śrāvastī to go for alms.
He encountered King Śikhaṇḍin as he was going out on a hunting expedition; upon seeing the king, the Venerable One thought to himself:
"Perhaps the king will see me and feel displeasure, and thus avoid me and depart."
When the king encountered him, he asked his sycophantic minister:
"For what reason did the bhikṣu avoid me from afar?
The sycophantic minister replied:
"That bhikṣu thought to himself:
'Let not one who has committed the parricidal crime of patricide touch my body with even a speck of dust; for this reason, I have gone far away.
When the king heard this, he was greatly incensed and commanded his soldiers to each scatter a handful of earth upon the bhikṣu."
At that time, having understood this matter, the Venerable One immediately manifested a small chamber and sat cross-legged within it.
Each of those people took dust and threw it upon the Venerable One, until it formed a great heap.
At that time, the two great loyal ministers, Hita and Amṛta, seeing that this was contrary to principle, immediately removed the earth and asked:
"Venerable One!
Now that the people of this city have committed such unwholesome deeds, what retribution shall they receive?"
The bhikṣu replied,
"In seven days there shall be a rain of dust and soil, which will fill and crush all the city walls and towers without leaving a trace.
At that time, the son of the minister Hitārtha, named Anjanavaktra, was given to the Venerable Mahākātyāyana to serve as his attendant.
The minister’s daughter, named Gaurī, was given to the bhikṣuṇī Śailā to serve as her attendant.
On that very day, it rained precious jewels from the heavens, and for six days thereafter, precious jewels continued to rain down.

At that time, the two great loyal ministers, Hita and Ahita, each gathered precious treasures and filled two ships with them. During the night, they departed the city to escape, traveling downstream until they reached an excellent location where they each built a city to dwell in:
one named Hita-pura and the other named Ahita-pura.

On the seventh day, the bhikṣuṇī Śailā took her handmaid and, by means of her supernormal powers, went to the city of Kauśāmbī; she then entrusted the handmaid to the elder Ghoṣila, instructing him to raise her.

On the seventh day, the Venerable Mahākātyāyana saw dust and earth raining down within this city. Knowing that its karmic power was such that it could not be saved, he took leave of the goddess who had long resided in the city of Jayasvara, along with his attendant youth, and departed through the air. Seeing that the city was filled with dust and no survivors remained, he went to a great village and rested for a short while in a threshing floor. Having adjusted his robes and bowl, he entered the village to beg for alms.
By the power of the goddess, the rice in the threshing floor naturally became full to overflowing; when the owner of the field saw this, he spoke these words:
"The fact that the rice in my field is so abundant is entirely due to the majestic spiritual power of the goddess."
He then took the keys and handed them to the celestial maiden, saying,
"Until I return once more, please do not abandon this place.
He then went to a gathering place in the village and announced to all the people:

"A goddess has arrived at my field, and by her power the grain in the field has increased. If you can together establish my son as the village headman, I shall keep that goddess here to protect you all, so that you may always enjoy peace and happiness."
Having heard this, everyone said, "Excellent!
and immediately installed that boy as the village headman. His father then went to a secluded place and committed suicide by cutting his own throat with a sharp knife.
When Kātyāyana had finished begging for food and returned to the threshing floor to share it with his companions, he finished eating, put away his robes and bowl, and said to the celestial maiden:
"I wish to proceed ahead; you have been entrusted to another and may not follow me."
The goddess said,
"What is there that I may not follow?
The Venerable One replied:
"If one takes the keys of another's house and then departs before the owner arrives, it is a violation of trust and righteousness.
After a short while, the people of the village and town each brought incense and flowers to offer worship, and they entreated the goddess, saying:
"We are fortunate that a holy being has come to us; we pray that you will compassionately deign to remain here. Whatever you require, we shall provide for you all."
The goddess replied:

"If you, my lords, insist on detaining me against my will, you may build a monastery for the Venerable Kātyāyana and also establish a separate shrine for me; provided that the four requisites of worship are offered without deficiency, I shall remain here."
The people replied,
"This was all done for that purpose.
They immediately constructed a monastery and, not far from it, established a shrine hall, providing offerings without fail.

At that time, every midnight, that goddess would carry a torch and approach the Venerable One to listen to the sublime Dharma. When the villagers saw this, they began to mock and criticize her, saying:
"How can a goddess come to a bhikṣu at night to engage in unrighteous conduct?"

Upon hearing this, the goddess gave rise to a mind of anger and cast spells upon the villagers, causing them all to fall ill. When the people learned of this, they all went to the goddess’s shrine to offer collective repentance and apology, whereupon their suffering was finally removed.

Having understood this, the Venerable One took his leave of the goddess and left behind a small copper bowl as a memento; he then had the youth Gāṇaka hold the corner of his dharma robe and ascended into the air to depart.
At that time, the goddess exhorted the villagers to construct a stūpa and place a cup inside it; this was named the Tāmraśarāva-caitya (Copper Cup Stūpa), which still exists today.
Then, the youth Gopāla grasped the corner of his teacher’s robe and suspended himself from it as he departed. People seeing him from afar all cried out:

"Laṃbate, laṃbate!"—this being the meaning of "to hang down. Because of this, the regions and kingdoms through which he passed were called Laṃpā, a country which can still be found today in North India.
"The Venerable One gradually traveled on until he reached a small kingdom; its king had passed away, leaving no heir.
At that time, all the people there knew of the Venerable One’s sublime and far-reaching spiritual virtue, so they invited the youth to be established as their sovereign."
The Venerable One granted his permission and consequently appointed King Kanaka as the regent to oversee state affairs; from there, he proceeded again to the kingdom of Pukkaṇa.
The Venerable One’s mother was born in this country, named the maiden Bhadrā; the Venerable One went to her residence and preached the Dharma for her, enabling her to realize the Truths.
He gave him a *khakkhara* staff as a memento; that stūpa (*caitya*) constructed for the staff is still venerated today.
From there, the Venerable One wished to travel toward the Middle Country, passing through the Snowy Mountains. The devas of the north all came to request of him:
"We pray that out of compassion you will leave behind some small memento in our dwelling place."
The Venerable One then thought:
"As the World-Honored One has said:
'In the Middle Kingdom, one does not wear a *pātra*.'"
He then gave the sandals to the deity.
Having received them, the deities constructed a caitya on a high and open piece of ground, which they named the Pūla-caitya.
At that time, the Venerable One crossed the Vakṣu River and arrived within the city of Puṣya, where he went from house to house to beg for food.
Having finished his meal, he shaved off his hair and beard and clipped his nails.
When the people saw this, they requested his hair and nails to create a hair-and-nail caitya for perpetual veneration.
The Venerable One then proceeded south from there to the city of Śrāvastī;
when the bhikṣus saw him, they addressed him, saying, "Welcome, Great Virtuous Kātyāyana!"
"Have you all traveled with ease and found well-being?
He replied,
"Venerable sir!"
"There was suffering and there was joy.
At that time, the bhikṣus asked him in detail for the reason, and he replied:
"Transforming people wherever I went was my joy; being crushed by dust and soil in the city of Jyotiṣka constituted my suffering."
Then the bhikṣus inquired as to the cause, and the Venerable One answered them in detail regarding the matter.
Having heard this, the bhikṣus spoke thus:

"That man who killed his father has given rise to the most extreme wrong views; he already undergoes such a karmic retribution in his present life, so who else shall take upon himself the bitter fruits of the future?"
Then, having washed his hands and feet, Kātyāyana went to where the Buddha was, prostrated himself at the Buddha’s feet, and sat to one side.
At that time, the World-Honored One, knowing [the answer], asked him nonetheless: “Kātyāyana!”
"Did you find peace and happiness in the places you traveled?
At that time, Kātyāyana reported in detail all the events he had experienced to the World-Honored One; having heard this, the World-Honored One remained silent.
When the bhikṣus heard his words, they were all filled with doubt and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One, we pray that out of your compassion you will explain this for us."

For what reason did the bhikṣu Ṛṣidatta serve as a sovereign of a kingdom and enjoy great happiness, yet renounce this superior station to go forth under the Buddha, sever all afflictions to attain arhatship, and still not escape being killed by a blade?
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
“Listen, all of you!
The karma created by the bhikṣu Ṛṣidatta must necessarily be experienced by him in person when its causes and conditions ripen; there is no place to escape it. This was explained at length as above.
He spoke in verse:
"Even if one were to dwell for a hundred kalpas, the karma one has created does not perish;
when the causes and conditions meet, one must receive the retribution oneself."

“O Bhikṣus! In the distant past, before a Buddha had appeared in the world, there was a Pratyekabuddha who appeared in the world. His heart was filled with compassion as he sought to rescue and relieve the poor and destitute; he was content with what he received and took no pleasure in seeking much.”
The sole field of merit was like a rhinoceros horn; having come to dwell in the forest thickets with few desires, he found that many deer had previously taken refuge there.
At that time, a hunter set snares in this place and usually caught many deer, but suddenly he caught none at all. He wondered why this was so.
He then followed the tracks of a person until he reached the dwelling of a Pratyekabuddha; filled with a surge of anger, he shot him with an arrow.

Out of compassion for the hunter, the Noble One ascended into the realm of space. The hunter begged him to descend, whereupon the Noble One passed away. The hunter then cremated the remains with fire, pouring over them the milk of eight cows, and collected the remaining bones to construct a stūpa, making various offerings, prostrating, and wailing in grief.

"I pray that you do not suffer the retribution of the three miserable realms because of this. May all the merit of these offerings cause you to be reborn into a great royal family with abundant wealth; may you obtain such rare merit as this, which surpasses the service and offerings rendered to this Great Master, performed with a mind free from weariness."

"O Bhikṣus! The hunter of that past time was none other than the Bhikṣu Ṛṣidatta. Because he shot a Pratyekabuddha with an arrow in the past, he suffered the torments of hell for many lifetimes; subsequently, even when born as a human, he was constantly killed by blades and arrows for five hundred births."
"By the power of his past vows, he encountered me and attained arhatship; yet, because he could not avoid being harmed by swords and blades, he entered nirvana.
At that time, the bhikṣus again had doubts and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"

For what reason did Prince Śikhaṇḍin and the men and women of the city of Jayasvara see Kātyāyana being buried under dust and earth, while they themselves emerged from the city carrying jewels for their benefit and to ward off calamity?
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"For these individuals, the convergence of causes and conditions has brought their karmic fruits to manifestation; as explained at length above, they shall experience the retribution themselves."
"You all should listen!
In the past, there lived an elder in a certain village. Not long after he had married, a son was born to him, followed by a daughter; both gradually grew up."
Once the man had taken a wife, yet this girl had not yet been married; while all her other female companions were already wed, this one girl remained without anyone asking for her hand.
At that time, a Pratyekabuddha Arhat appeared in the world, as described at length above.
A certain Pratyekabuddha was traveling through the human world when he arrived at this village to beg for alms.
At that time, a young girl who had not yet been married saw the noble one approaching; she took some refuse and threw it upon his body. On that very day, someone came to inquire after her relatives.
Her elder brother asked her in surprise,
"For what reason did someone question you this morning?
She replied:
"I just now cast foul refuse upon a bhikṣu. When her elder brother heard this, he laughed;
the girl then told her companions what had happened, and upon hearing it, all the women desired to marry him, vying with one another to hurl refuse at the bhikṣu.
In this manner, the process continued until all the inhabitants of the great village had become possessed of such wrong views, regarding this [practice] as virtuous.
At that time, the noble one, fearing that he would bring sin upon the multitude, subsequently departed.
Furthermore, there were rishis possessing the five supernatural powers who came to this place; when the people again threw refuse and filth at them, the rishis, having seen this, likewise departed.
Everyone conceived the thought:
"One gains merit by discarding excrement upon the Venerable One.
Consequently, they began to discard filth even upon their own parents.
At that time, there were two elders in this village who, seeing that [the people] were practicing what was contrary to the Dharma, announced to them all:
"The deeds you have performed truly violate the laws of the Dharma; because of these evil karmas, you will inevitably bring forth bitter fruits."
"Although the people of the village heard these words, their wrong views increased all the more and their malicious intent did not cease. 'O Bhikṣus!
She who was the daughter of the elder at that time was none other than Śikhaṇḍinī; those people of wrong views in that village were the many inhabitants of the city of Jayasvara.'"

The two elders who at that time exhorted and restrained the people were none other than the two ministers, Li-yi (Benefit) and Chu-huan (Dispelling Suffering); because they had previously urged others to refrain from wrong views, they have now escaped calamity and avoided being crushed by the dust.
The brother of the young girl who was seen laughing was none other than Kātyāyana; because of his past habit of laughing, he has now met his end by being buried under earth. O Bhikṣus!
Had Kātyāyana not realized the fruit of Arhatship, he would certainly have lost his life today due to this burial under earth.
"Therefore, O bhikṣus!
If one performs purely black karma, one will obtain a purely black ripening; as explained at length above, you should train yourselves accordingly.
At that time, there was a householder in the city of Kauśāmbī named Sudhana, whose voice was like the sound of gold and who possessed one hundred million gold coins.
At dawn, he let out a great voice and commanded his laborers, saying:
"O worthy ones! You should all rise and attend to your work."
This householder’s residence was near the royal palace; when people heard his voice, they thought to themselves:
"The sound of this man's voice indicates that he will arrive at the court assembly with one hundred million gold coins."
Then the king commanded his ministers, saying,
"I have heard that this elder Sudhana possesses one hundred million gold coins according to the laws of signs.
Thereupon, the king summoned Sudhana and questioned him, saying:
“Householder!
How many treasures and riches do you possess within your residence?
He replied:
"Great King!
There is one hundred million gold coins.
When the ministers heard this, they recognized the king’s excellent marks and marveled at what they had never before seen.
Because the king knew that he possessed a wondrous voice, people of the time immediately called him the Elder Wondrous Sound (*Ghoṣila*).

That elder never uttered a falsehood from his mouth even at the cost of his life; seeing this, the king marveled and appointed him as the state minister. As the elder assisted in governing with the Dharma, outshining all others, the other ministers became envious and said to the king:
"The minister Wondrous Sound practices much deception."
Having heard this, the king immediately put him to the test; he lent him half a hundred million gold coins and ordered him to collect them from the common people as he saw fit.
At that time, the elder collected exactly according to the amount, not taking a single coin unjustly.
When the king investigated and understood this, he was struck with profound wonder and further elevated his rank.

At that time, the minister Sudarśana realized that wealth and food are entirely impermanent; he consequently constructed a hall of righteousness to provide clothing and food, appointing people to guard and manage it, and addressed them, saying:
"If you see anyone whose appearance or demeanor is unusual, you must inform me."

At that time, there were five hundred recluses from the south who had withdrawn from worldly life; they wore tattered and worn-out robes and were devoted to having few desires. Having traveled far across hardships and perils, they wished to go toward the kingdom of Kauśāmbī, but finding no water to seek along their path, they went together beneath a great tree and said:
"Give us water."

At that moment, a hand suddenly extended from between the branches of the tree, adorned with bracelets and bangles, holding a vessel and pouring water. After those five hundred people had all drunk their fill, they asked:
"Who are you, O deity?"
He replied:
"In a previous life, I lived not far from the house of the householder Anāthapiṇḍada, working as a tailor for travelers.
Whenever there were those who were destitute and did not know the location of the householder’s residence, I would point out the way to them with my hand."
"Furthermore, because we have observed the eightfold precepts, we have now been reborn here among the Gods of the Four Great Kings.
When the five hundred people saw this occurrence, they said to one another,

"Since it is through the observance of the precepts that one gains the retribution of birth in heaven, we too should go to the house of the householder Anāthapiṇḍada and receive the eightfold pure precepts for the poṣadha."

They proceeded in succession until they reached the hall for the Dharma established by the householder Sudatta. Having accepted the offerings, the attendants returned home and informed the householder, saying:
"There are five hundred men who say they have come from the southern kingdom; their appearance and deportment differ from our own customs. You should summon them and question them."
The elder commanded his attendants to ask,
"From where have you noble ones come?
They replied:
“We have come from the south.
He asked again,
“Where do you intend to go now?”
He replied,
"I wish to go to the house of the householder Anāthapiṇḍada in Śrāvastī to receive the eightfold precepts.
Mañjughoṣa said to him:
"You may stay here and wait until the end of the three-month summer retreat; I shall go with you.
They replied, "So be it."

When the summer retreat had concluded, the householder Sudatta, accompanied by five hundred people, went to the residence of Anāthapiṇḍada; having offered his greetings, he related the matter in full detail.
Then that elder led these people to the place where the Buddha was, and together they prostrated at the Buddha’s feet and sat to one side.

At that time, the World-Honored One, observing their faculties and dispositions, taught the Dharma according to their capacities and ordained them. They severed all afflictions and realized the fruit of Arhatship, while the Elder Wonderful Sound attained the fruit of Stream-entry.
Having realized the Truths, he prostrated at the Buddha’s feet and said:
“World-Honored One, I pray that you will out of compassion go to Kauśāmbī; I shall construct a vihāra for the Buddha and the assembly of noble ones.”
The World-Honored One accepted the invitation with silent compassion and addressed Mahācunda, saying:
"You should now go together with the householder Ghosila to Kośambī to construct a vihāra."

Then Mahācunda, having received the Buddha’s instruction, took up his robes and bowl and went together with Rāhula to Kauśāmbī. Once he had completed the construction of a residence, he sent a messenger to inform the Buddha:
“The work on the monastery is finished; I only pray that the World-Honored One and the assembly of bhikṣus will deign to come out of compassion.”

When the World-Honored One had finished his meal in the early part of the day, he took up his robe and bowl and, accompanied by the great assembly, proceeded toward the city of Kauśāmbī and arrived at the Garden of Exquisite Sound. Outside the monastery, by the pond, he washed his hands and rinsed his feet before entering the temple.
At that time, the elder Gadgadasvara immediately poured water from a golden pitcher, and the Buddha accepted it.
He invited the Buddha and the Sangha to accept this dwelling place; when the following day arrived, the elder prepared an abundant array of offerings and served them to the Buddha and the Sangha.

When the meal was finished, and the bowls and utensils had been washed, and the tooth-sticks used and the mouth rinsed, Mahācunda and the householder Ghosila, together with their retinues, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet and sat to one side. For the sake of hearing the Dharma, Cunda addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!..."

We pray that you will reveal and expound for us: what meritorious deeds must be performed to obtain great fruits and benefits, such that one’s merit is brilliantly manifested without end, constantly increasing, and continuing in an uninterrupted succession?
The Buddha told Cunda:
"There are seven kinds of meritorious deeds with material basis and seven kinds of meritorious deeds without material basis. I shall explain them to you; listen with a single-minded focus!"

If there are sons or daughters of good family with pure faith who accomplish these seven meritorious deeds, whether walking, standing, sitting, or lying down, or whether sleeping or awake—at all times—such meritorious deeds will yield great fruits and benefits, manifesting boundlessly, and their merit will constantly increase in an uninterrupted succession.
What are the seven? Cunda!
