If there are sons or daughters of good family who offer a fine garden to the Sangha of the four quarters.

This is the first meritorious action involving material things, which yields great fruits and benefits, its radiance manifesting without end. By virtue of this merit, whether walking, standing, sitting, or lying down, or whether sleeping or awake, at all times such meritorious action yields great fruits and benefits, its radiance manifesting without end; the merit constantly increases, continuing in an uninterrupted succession.
Furthermore, Cunda!
If there are sons or daughters of noble family with pure faith who construct monasteries within this grove and offer them to the Sangha of the four quarters—
this is the second meritorious action involving material things, which yields great fruits and benefits, manifesting infinitely, and whose merit constantly increases in an uninterrupted succession.
Furthermore, Cunda!
If there are sons or daughters of noble family with pure faith who provide various kinds of couches, seats, bedding, and requisites for śramaṇas within this monastery.
This is the third meritorious action involving material things, which yields great fruits and benefits that are infinitely radiant; its merit constantly increases, continuing without interruption.
Furthermore, Cunda!

If there are men or women of pure faith who constantly provide offerings of exquisite food and drink according to the season to the assembly of monks within this monastery, this is the fourth meritorious deed involving material things;
it yields great fruits and benefits that shine forth inexhaustibly, and their merit constantly increases in an uninterrupted succession.
Furthermore, Cunda!
If there are men or women of pure faith who provide offerings and support to newly arrived bhikṣus as well as those about to depart on a journey.

This is the fifth meritorious action based on material things, which yields great fruits and benefits, its radiance manifesting without end; its merit constantly increases and continues without interruption.
Furthermore, Cunda, if there are faithful sons or daughters of good family who provide offerings and support to the sick and to those who tend to them.

This is the sixth meritorious action with a physical basis, which yields great fruits and benefits, its radiance manifesting without end; its merit constantly increases, continuing in an uninterrupted succession.
Furthermore, Cunda!

If there are men or women of pure faith who, during times of wind, cold, rain, snow, or heat, bring various seasonal foods and even gruel to the monastery to offer to the assembly of monks, thereby ensuring they are free from hardship and may dwell in peace after having eaten.

This is the seventh meritorious action involving material things, which yields great fruits and benefits that shine forth without end; its merit constantly increases, continuing in an uninterrupted succession.
Cunda, you should know this!

Regarding these seven types of meritorious actions involving material things, if any man or woman were to undertake them with a formal commitment and vow, performing them continuously, the measure of this merit would be impossible to calculate or know.
Having obtained such merit and attained such a fruit, and having brought forth such a sublime and wondrous body, it can only be called a great mass of merit, Cunda!
It is like five great rivers that merge into one place, flowing together toward the great ocean; their names are:
the Gaṅgā River, the Yamunā River, the Sarayū River, the Aciravatī River, and the Mahī River.
The quantity of this water cannot be known; it consists of so many hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of *hu* that it cannot be calculated, and can only be called a great mass of water.
At that time, Cunda again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
We have already heard about meritorious deeds involving active engagement and meritorious deeds without active engagement; we pray that you will further explain them for us.”
The Buddha told Cunda:
"You should know that there are seven types of merit-making actions concerning the 'unconditioned' (anārambha).

If any man or woman accomplishes these seven meritorious deeds, whether walking, standing, sitting, lying down, sleeping, or awake—at all times—such meritorious deeds will yield great fruits and benefits, manifesting boundlessly, with merit constantly increasing and continuing without interruption."
What are the seven? Cunda!

If there is a son or daughter of good family with pure faith who hears that a Tathāgata or a disciple of the Tathāgata is dwelling in dependence upon a certain village or hamlet, and having heard this, they rejoice and give rise to the mind of renunciation.
This is the first meritorious action of the "unconditioned" (*anārambha*); it yields great fruits and benefits, its radiance manifesting without end.

Because of this merit, whether walking, standing, sitting, or lying down, or whether sleeping or awake—at all times—such meritorious action yields great fruits and benefits, its radiance manifesting without end; the merit constantly increases, continuing in an uninterrupted succession.
Furthermore, Cunda!

If there are sons or daughters of noble family with pure faith who hear that a Tathāgata or a disciple of the Tathāgata intends to come here, having heard this, they will rejoice and give rise to the mind of renunciation.

This is the second type of meritorious action without a physical basis, which yields great fruits and benefits that shine forth infinitely; its merit constantly increases, continuing without interruption.
Furthermore, Cunda!

If there are men or women of pure faith who hear that a Tathāgata or a disciple of the Tathāgata is traveling along the road, upon hearing this, they will rejoice and give rise to the mind of renunciation.
This is the third meritorious action without a physical basis, which yields great fruits and benefits that shine forth inexhaustibly; its merit constantly increases, continuing without interruption.
Furthermore, Cunda!

If there are sons or daughters of noble family with pure faith who hear that a Tathāgata or a disciple of the Tathāgata has arrived at a certain village or hamlet, and having heard this, they rejoice and give rise to the mind of renunciation.

This is the fourth type of merit-making action without a physical basis, which yields great fruits and benefits that shine forth inexhaustibly; its merit constantly increases, continuing in an uninterrupted succession.
Furthermore, Cunda!

If there are men or women of pure faith who go to that Tathāgata or to the disciples of that Tathāgata wishing to pay their respects, upon seeing them, they will rejoice and give rise to the mind of renunciation.

This is the fifth type of meritorious action without a physical object, which yields great fruits and benefits, its radiance manifesting without end, and its merit constantly increasing in an uninterrupted succession.
Furthermore, Cunda!

If there are sons or daughters of noble family with pure faith who, upon seeing that Tathāgata or a disciple of the Tathāgata, immediately listen to and receive the sublime Dharma with a single-minded focus; having heard the Dharma, they give rise to great joy and develop the aspiration for renunciation.
This is the sixth merit-making action without a physical basis, which yields great fruits and benefits, manifesting boundlessly, and wherein merit constantly increases in uninterrupted succession.
Furthermore, Cunda!

If there are sons or daughters of noble family with pure faith who, having heard the Dharma from that Tathāgata or a disciple of the Tathāgata, take refuge in the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha, and receive and uphold the pure precepts.

This is the seventh merit-making action without a physical object, which yields great fruits and benefits that shine forth inexhaustibly; its merit constantly increases, continuing without interruption.
Know this, Cunda!

Regarding these seven kinds of meritorious actions without a physical basis, if any man or woman should undertake them with a formal vow and perform them continuously, the measure of this merit cannot be calculated or known. One obtains such merit and reaps such fruits, and brings forth such a sublime and wondrous body; it can only be called a "great mass of merit."
Cunda! It is like the five great rivers that converge in one place and flow together toward the great ocean; their names are:
the Gaṅgā River, the Yamunā River, the Sarayū River, the Aciravatī River, and the Mahī River.

The volume of this water cannot be known; it consists of so many hundreds, thousands, tens of thousands, millions, and billions of *hu* that it cannot be calculated, and can only be called a great mass of water.
At that time, having spoken this Dharma, the World-Honored One spoke these verses:
"The five rivers are pure and cleanse all things; The wondrous ford conceives jewels and guides the myriad streams.
It enables humans and beasts alike to take refuge, Each vying to rush toward it without ceasing."
If a person can cultivate meritorious deeds involving material things, as well as those free from material things, they will give rise to joy;
supreme merit will constantly flow back to this person, just as the many rivers pour into the vast ocean.

At that time, Mahācunda, the householder Susvara, and the great assembly of devas and humans, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, each gave rise to a sense of wonder; they prostrated at the Buddha’s feet and joyfully put his teachings into practice.
At that time, all the bhikṣus were filled with doubt and requested the World-Honored One, saying:
"Venerable Sir!
What karma did this elder Ghosila previously perform such that when the Great King heard his voice, he recognized the matter and consequently named him 'Ghosila' (Wonderful Sound)?"
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"In the distant past, in the city of Vārāṇasī, there was no rain for twelve years due to a drought.
There was a householder named Suvihita who appointed a man as his steward to regularly distribute gifts; every day, he provided excellent food and drink as offerings to one thousand Pratyekabuddhas."

The person in charge of preparing the food would always go with a dog every morning to announce that the time had arrived; however, on one particular day, he forgot to inform them. Seeing that it was nearly noon, the dog immediately ran toward the place where the thousand sages were and began to howl loudly.

At that time, the noble ones heard the dog’s distinct sound and knew it was coming to invite them; they all went together to the householder’s residence. The dog then went to where those who were to be served at the appointed time and made a sound there. Upon seeing this, those people thought to themselves:
"Could it be that this dog is summoning the noble ones to come?"
He then proceeded to make offerings to the various noble ones as was his custom. You bhikṣus,
you should know this!
In the past, the householder Supāraga was none other than myself;
the treasurer was none other than Anāthapiṇḍada;
and the one who announced that "the time has come" was King Udayana.
The dog was none other than Gadgadasvara.
Because he went to the Sound and addressed the Noble One, he now possesses this excellent voice.
Thus, all of this is the experience of the fruit in the present due to causes and conditions from previous lives.
At that time, the bhikṣus rejoiced and accepted it with faith.
*Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya*, Scroll 46 (Part 4). *Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya*, Scroll 4.
The Seventeenth [Section]:
The Vinaya-mātṛkā translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Yijing by Imperial Decree.
Chapter Eighty-two, Part Four: The Training Rule on Entering the Royal Palace. At that time, the Bhagavat was staying in the Bamboo Grove Monastery at Rājagṛha.

At that time, there was a warrior from the south whose strength equaled a thousand men; he came to this city and approached King Bimbisāra, declaring himself to be brave and robust, with peerless skill in archery and horsemanship.
Upon seeing this, the King was filled with joy; he bestowed upon him a generous stipend and appointed him as a great general.

At that time, in a vast wilderness situated between the two kingdoms of Magadha and Kośala, there were five hundred bands of bandits who slaughtered traveling merchants, such that the passage of people between these two realms was cut off.
When King Bimbisāra heard of this matter, he commanded his great general, saying:
"You should go to that wilderness between the two kingdoms, clear away the bandits, and stay there for the time being."

Then, having received the king’s command, that great general led his attendants into the wilderness; seeing those bands of bandits, he advanced alone and, with sword against sword and arrow against arrow, struck down one hundred men.
Four hundred others were still coming forward to fight, so their general told them:
"Do not advance; let us not all die together. You should cast off your armor and weapons, remove the arrows from the wounded, and observe whether they live or not."

Upon hearing this, the bandits examined those who had been struck; as soon as they removed the arrows, the men all died. Only then did they realize that the general was so skilled in the art of archery that they dared not fight again, and the remaining four hundred men sought mercy, entreating him to spare their lives.

The Great General took pity on them and, with a heart of compassion toward them, immediately constructed a new city at the junction of the two realms. He gathered all the people together so they might dwell therein; from that time forth, it was named the City of the Wilderness (Khaṇḍava-nagara).
At that time, the people of this city had established a common rule: whenever there were marriages, they would all invite the Great General first to eat, and only then hold their celebratory banquet.
Now, there was a family who was extremely poor; wishing to marry off their son, they found themselves unable to provide food to entertain the Great General.

They thought to themselves: "I am poor and have no means to invite the Great General. Yet, this new bride has not yet touched my body; it would be fitting to present her to him as an offering to express my sincere heart."
He then had his wife enter the general’s chamber before returning home; from that time on, all the people within the city took this as their standard practice.
At that time, there was a woman who wished to marry and thought to herself:
"The people of this city have long practiced such unrighteousness, giving away their own wives to others before they themselves take them. By what means can I put an end to this custom?"
Thereupon, during the day, she stood naked in a public gathering place to urinate. When the people saw her, they all rebuked her, saying:
"You are a young girl; it is only right that you feel shame. For what reason do you perform such indecent acts before the multitude?"
The woman replied,
"If one may feel shame in the presence of a husband, what cause for shame or modesty is there in the presence of other women?
The others replied:
“Am I not a man? The woman replied, “If you were truly a man,
how could you marry your own wife and then allow another to violate her first!”
Having heard this, the people were each filled with deep shame and immediately consulted one another, saying:
"We should devise a plan to kill that great general.
While he was entering the pond to bathe, the people gathered together and stabbed him with their swords. As his life was about to end, he thought to himself:
"This was not my original intention; you took pleasure in doing it yourself. Now, though truly innocent, you have unjustly taken my life.
He then made an evil vow:
"I pray that after I cast off this body, I shall be reborn as a violent and malevolent yakṣa, devouring all the men and women within this city."
Having made this vow, he immediately passed away and was reborn with the body of a yakṣa, dwelling in these wilderness thickets.
Due to the karmic enmity of his previous life, he wrought great calamities within this city, causing many people to die of disease.
Once the people learned of this, they all went to the forest to repent for their past transgressions and requested that one person be provided daily to serve as food for them.
Whenever someone was next in line to die, a notice would be hung upon their door to inform them; either the head of the household would go in person or send a son or daughter to provide the meal.

At that time, there was an elder who, after praying to a hundred deities, obtained a son. At the moment of his birth, a placard was seen above the gate; the mother, filled with sorrow, held the infant in her arms and stood weeping.
A man arriving from outside saw the notice and entered; learning that his wife was suffering in grief, he said to her:
"Since our karma has led us to this state, what can be done?
You need not worry; do not harbor attachment, for you should deliver your son to the yakṣa."

Having spoken these words, he took his child and carried him to the forest. The couple returned home and ascended to the high tower; looking out in all four directions, they paid reverent homage and spoke this verse:
“Divinities pervade the world; Those who have subdued their own senses can deliver others.
For the sake of our child, we offer this prayerful salutation: May you look upon us with compassion and grant us protection.”
At that time, the World-Honored One constantly observed sentient beings with his Buddha-eye, as described at length elsewhere, even like a mother cow following her calf.

Out of compassion for the householder’s wife and children, as well as the men and women in the city of Kāpilavastu, the Buddha knew that those in the city were capable of receiving instruction. He traveled by stages until he reached the wilderness, where he preached the subtle and wondrous Dharma to the fierce yakṣa so that he might give rise to pure faith. The yakṣa then received the three refuges and the five precepts, and finally spoke a verse in request, saying:
“What is the most supreme wealth for a man?”
How is it that through practice one can bring benefit and happiness?
What is foremost among flavors?
What is most excellent among life-spans?
The World-Honored One said:
"Faith is the most excellent wealth for a man; By constantly practicing wholesome dharmas, one gains benefit and joy.
Among all flavors, truthful speech is supreme; Among all forms of life, wisdom is the best."
The yakṣa asked:
"In what way does one possess precious wealth?
In what way does one have a good reputation?"
"How does one become respected by others?
How does one increase in virtuous friends?
The World-Honored One replied:
"One who is generous possesses abundant wealth; one who upholds the precepts has a good reputation;
one who speaks truth is respected by others; and one who is free from stinginess increases their circle of virtuous friends.
The yakṣa then requested:
"By how many births does the world arise?
By how many is it given its designation?
By how many is it established?"
"By how many factors is one brought to ruin?
The Blessed One replied:
"The world arises by means of six; it gains its reputation by means of six."
"By six things one is established; by six things one is brought to ruin.
The yakṣa asked:
"How does one leave behind delusion, remaining unshackled day and night?"
"Able to dwell not upon conditions, / Not fearing the deep abyss?
The World-Honored One replied:
"With concentration and wisdom, one leaves behind folly; / Having abandoned attachment, one is free from fetters."
"Not dwelling upon objective conditions, one maintains the precepts and crosses over the deep pit.
The yakṣa asked:
"Who is able to cross the torrential flood?"
Who is able to cross the great ocean?
Who is able to leave all suffering behind?
Who attains purity of mind?
The World-Honored One said:
"Faith can cross the torrent; heedfulness can traverse the great ocean;
diligence brings freedom from all suffering; and with wisdom, the mind is purified."
"You may all now ask: among śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas, is there any teaching superior to truthful speech and generosity?
The yakṣa replied:
"Why should I now consult other śramaṇas or brahmins?
The World-Honored One is an ocean of great wisdom, able to preach the truly wondrous Dharma.
From this day forward, I shall wander throughout the human world."
I constantly pay homage to the Buddha, the World-Honored One, and revere the True Dharma.
Out of great compassion and pity, the World-Honored One has descended to my dwelling place;
I now know with certainty that I shall reach the end of birth and death.
At that time, the yakṣa presented this boy to the World-Honored One; having accepted him, the World-Honored One bestowed him upon his parents and spoke these verses:
"The Secret Trace (Guhyapada) handed him to my hand, And from my hand, I gave him to his parents;
Because he was passed from hand to hand, He should be named 'Hand of the Wilderness' (Āṭavika-hasta)."
Because of this, the child was named Āṭavika (Forest-Hand), and as he gradually grew up, there was no sovereign in the city of Āṭavī.
The people deliberated together and said, "This youth Āṭavika possesses great merit and virtue, having been personally protected by the World-Honored One’s mindfulness;
we ought to consecrate him as king."

At that time, the bhikṣuṇī Śailā took the daughter of the minister Vyādighāta from the city of Rājagṛha, named Anupamā, and entrusted her to the elder Sumaṅgala to be raised. When she had grown up, her appearance was so upright and beautiful that she was beloved and respected by all, being without peer in the kingdom.

At that time, King Bimbisāra of Magadha, King Prasenajit of Kośala, King Virūḍhaka of Kauśāmbī, as well as the Licchavis of Vaiśālī and other nobles, all brought gifts and dispatched envoys to request the maiden Gaurī from Guṇasvara.
The elder, distressed and troubled, thought to himself:
"Most of those who come to seek my daughter are kings; if I do not grant her to them, they will all harbor resentment and may bring harm upon me."
He replied to Gaurī:
"I shall now follow your wishes; since you are a worthy match, you may choose for yourself.
At that time, the envoys of the various kings and other nobles gathered there by chance and took up residence within the garden of the elder Mādhava.

Then the elder immediately adorned Gāndhārī with various kinds of exquisite garments and priceless pearl necklaces, had her mount a great elephant, and taking a flower garland in her hand, went to where the crowd was gathered, saying:
"Whomever you love and desire as a husband, you should cast this flower upon his body."
Viśākhā immediately went to where the people were and asked,
"Where does King Āṭavika reside?
The people pointed him out, and the woman then cast a flower toward him, speaking these words:
"The young boy whom the Buddha received from the hands of the yakṣa shall be my husband.
Upon hearing this, all the people dispersed in every direction.

Knowing his daughter’s resolve, the Elder Svaramañjari immediately prepared excellent elephants, horses, servants, and carriages, and adorned her with various garments and jeweled necklaces. He escorted Anurādhā to the Vindhya wilderness; however, as night fell and the gates were closed, she had no way to enter and was forced to stay temporarily at the gate, dozing through the entire night.

At that time, the World-Honored One perceived that Kalandaka was ready to be transformed; [the text continues] at length until: "If Kalandaka were to meet with Indrasenā, he would be bound by the fetters of defiled passion and would not yet be able to escape from within birth and death, nor would he have the means to attain the fruits of holiness."

At that time, the World-Honored One, having understood this matter, departed from Rājagṛha for the city of Āṭavī. Upon reaching the corner of that city, the sun set; that very night, he lay down upon a patch of ground as large as a cow’s footprint.

At that time, having heard that the Buddha, the World-Honored One, had arrived outside the city and was lying in a cow’s footprint at dawn, the man of the wilderness set out from the city gate to pay homage to the World-Honored One. There he saw the woman Gaurī with her chariot, horses, and attendants.
Question:
"Whose daughter is this who has been staying at this city gate?
At that time, the maiden Śyāmāvatī related her intentions in detail to Pāṇḍuka, and upon hearing this matter, the king ordered her to go to the palace.
Then the king went to where the Buddha was, prostrated himself, and said:
"World-Honored One!
I wonder, Great Master, whether you have dwelt peacefully in that desolate field during the night?"
The Blessed One said:
“Kāḷakaṇṭha! In this world, I am the foremost of those who sleep in peace.”
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke these verses:
"One who can eliminate evil deeds, And is not bound by desire;
Who leaves defilement behind to return to parinirvāṇa— That person shall sleep in peace."
"Able to eliminate the disease of feverish affliction, All hopes and desires are severed;
His mind is ever tranquil, And he attains peaceful sleep.

At that time, the World-Honored One taught the Dharma to Pāṭaliputra in various ways, instructing, exhorting, benefiting, and gladdening him. Thereupon, while seated on that very seat, he realized the fruit of non-returning (*anāgāmiphala*). The details are as extensively explained in the *Āgama Sūtra*.
Having prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, he rose from his seat and departed. Once he had returned to the palace, he said to Gaganagañjā:
“I have renounced all desires and shall no longer indulge in pleasure; though you have come here, you may go or stay as you wish—no one shall obstruct you.”
Gāndharī said, "I wish to dwell here;
I pray to become an attendant to the Son of the Buddha.

At that time, Vana-pāṇi built a monastery for the Buddha and the Saṅgha outside this city, providing the four requisites of support without any deficiency. [The account continues] at length until King Vana-pāṇi fell ill and died, being reborn in the Avṛha Heaven. Having given rise to the three thoughts, he came to the place where the Buddha was, prostrated at his feet, and sat down.
The Blessed One asked,
"Āṭavika, by what karma were you reborn in the Heaven Free from Heat?
He then replied to the Blessed One with these verses:
“Having seen the World-Honored One, and having heard the True Dharma,
I have never felt satiety in making offerings to the Saṅgha.
Practicing the Dharma of the Supreme Person, I remain far removed from craving and attachment.”
"By constantly practicing these three things, I am born without fever.
Then the deva Hastaka Āṭavika prostrated at the Buddha’s feet and suddenly vanished.
At that time, the bhikṣus, seeing the radiant light during the night, were all filled with doubt. At dawn, they requested the World-Honored One, saying:
"What karma did that Pāṃśupradāna previously perform such that, upon merely beholding your azure countenance, he thereafter attained the fruit of non-returning?"
The Buddha addressed the bhikṣus:
"Listen, all of you!

In the distant past, there were two brothers who were sons of a high minister, dwelling in a forest. The elder was named Jālinīpāda (Webbed-Feet), and the younger was named Ajālinīpāda (Unwebbed-Feet)."
The elder among them had cultivated the five supernatural powers (*pañcābhijñā*), while the younger attended his teacher to receive instruction.
The teacher had a daughter named Miaorong (Wondrous Beauty), whose countenance was upright and dignified.
As she gradually grew older, she longed to marry; thus, she went to where the student was and spoke these words:
"My parents have commanded me to be your wife.
Upon hearing this, he refused; the girl then became enraged.
The student, terrified, fled immediately, but the girl pursued him closely, seeking to take him as her husband.
The student remained steadfast and would not comply with her wishes; the woman then took up a sword, intending to cut off his head.
At that moment, the student, realizing he could not escape this peril, immediately joined his palms and spoke thus:
"Homage to the Great Seer, whose hands and feet are marked by webbed fingers and toes."

As soon as he had taken refuge, the seer arrived; he immediately took him away to the mountain forest, ordained him at the site of the cow’s footprint, taught him the sublime Dharma, and he attained the five supernormal powers.

"O bhikṣus! The elder brother of those times, the seer endowed with the five supernormal powers, was none other than myself. The younger brother was none other than Āṭavika-hasta. And that woman of exquisite beauty was none other than Śyāmāvatī."
In the past, I saw her being led away to be harmed in the mountain forests; I enabled her to attain the five supernormal powers and escape the enmity of women.
Today, I shall again cause her to be freed from the oppression of Kanakāvatī, so that she may attain eternal liberation from the ocean of birth and death.
"Therefore, you should all seek to swiftly abandon that which is subject to outflows (*sāsrava*).
At that time, the bhikṣus again had doubts and requested of the World-Honored One:

"By what causes and conditions did the World-Honored One arrive there and cause this Wilderness-Hand (*Āṭavika*)—who had just been born and was about to be given to a yakṣa for food—to escape his calamity?"
The Buddha addressed the bhikṣus:
"Listen well! I shall speak for you."

In the distant past, there was a king in a certain city who was fond of eating meat. At that time, a man wishing to serve the king desired to offer him a chicken; once the king had obtained the chicken, he gave it to the cook to be used for his soup and stews.
The one who had offered the chicken was naturally compassionate by nature and thought to himself:
"I ought not now to present this live chicken to him so that he may slaughter it.
He immediately paid double the price at the butcher's shop to redeem it and set it free, whereupon he further reflected:
"This chicken is innocent; because I offered it for sacrifice, it was nearly killed. May I not suffer the retribution for this evil karma.
Furthermore, by the merit of my act of ransoming and releasing it, may I, when encountering calamities in future lives, find a supreme teacher to come and rescue me."

"Do you understand? The one who offered the chicken in the past was none other than this very person, Hastaka Āṭavika. It should be known that by virtue of his former vow, he has now been spared from calamity."
At that time, after the death of Araṇyaka, Śyāmā returned to the house of the elder Ghosila in Kauśāmbī.

When King Udayana, the ruler of Kauśāmbī, heard that the maiden Śyāmā had not yet been touched by a man and had returned to her own home, he asked the minister Ghosila to marry her in a formal ceremony. He provided her with a tower of exquisite flowers and a thousand female attendants so that she lacked for nothing, and granted her one thousand gold coins every day.
Among his attendants was a woman with a hunchbacked back, and he named her accordingly.

Every day, this woman Hunchback would spend a thousand coins to purchase incense for his supply; at the incense shop, she engaged in a secret affair with the man who sold the incense. She would set aside five hundred coins to cover the cost of her food, while using the remaining five hundred to buy incense before returning home.

Later, at another time, the man who sold incense and his wife joined their hearts in preparing an offering, inviting the Buddha and the Sangha; as extensively described, they partook of the meal and listened to the Dharma.
Having heard the Dharma, they both attained the first fruit of the path while still seated upon their mats.
Having realized the truth of the Dharma, he immediately used one thousand coins to purchase incense and brought it back to the palace.
When Lady Gāndharī saw that the ointment was more abundant than on other days, she asked him the reason.
The hunchbacked woman reported all these matters in full and with truth. At that time, seeing her rare appearance, Gaurī said to her maidservant:
"I have a physical ailment and cannot go out at will; you should go daily to the World-Honored One's place, and after listening to the sublime Dharma, come back and tell it to me."
He immediately went to listen and returned to the palace; there, Lady Gāndharī sat upon a superior seat and ordered him to preach the Dharma.
Kubjottarā said to him, "The ritual for listening to the Dharma should not be like this."

Having understood this, the lady prepared an excellent seat for him and, seating herself in a humble position below him, requested him to preach the Dharma. Upon hearing the sublime teaching, she realized the fruit of Non-returning (Anāgāmi).
At that time, there was a non-Buddhist Brahmin from the kingdom of Mathurā named Aśoka, whose wife’s name was Śrī.
Later, she gave birth to a daughter whose appearance was so upright and dignified that all who saw her were filled with affection;
thus, she was named Anupamā. As she gradually grew up, she formed this thought:
"If there is a man whose countenance and deportment resemble mine, I shall take him as my husband."
At that time, the World-Honored One arrived at Kauśāmbī and, having completed his alms round, returned to his quarters; after finishing his meal, he stayed in a secluded grove.
Then the non-Buddhist ascetic Aśoka came to where the Buddha was; observing that the Buddha’s countenance and deportment were beyond compare, he thought to himself:
"How wonderful it would be if this man, whose appearance is so exceptionally distinguished, were to become my daughter's husband!"
The non-Buddhist returned home and told his wife, "My daughter has found a husband whose appearance resembles her own; we should prepare the necklaces and ornaments and arrange their marriage.
His wife then asked:
“Who is that person? He replied,
“He is the śramaṇa Gautama.”
Having heard these words, the wife spoke in verse:
"I once saw a great seer in the kingdom begging for alms;
As he walked upon uneven ground, his feet followed its rises and falls."
"How could such a great man as this think of wife and children?
When the brahmin Aśoka heard these words, he spoke with anger:
"The śāli is no auspicious omen; the words of Śrī are signs of evil."
"Even if she possesses a mind of diligence and great majestic power, upon seeing the peerless woman, she will immediately give rise to a heart of love and attachment.

Having spoken these words, he adorned the woman with exquisite garments and various necklaces and ornaments. Her parents followed her as they escorted her toward the Buddha’s dwelling; along the way, they saw the Buddha’s footprints marked with the thousand-spoked wheel sign. Upon seeing them, Aśoka said to his wife:
"This is the path of a woman's husband.
Śāri observed that the Buddha’s footprints were dignified and majestic, and he reported this in verse:
"The tracks of those stained by desire are not upright; Those of impatient and wrathful nature tread firmly upon the earth."
"The tracks of the deluded are indistinct; this is the path frequented by those who have abandoned desire.
Observing these signs, it is certain that he is not one who lacks a counterpart."
Aśoka repeated the first verse and replied:
"The śarīra is no auspicious omen; the words of the Auspicious One [the Buddha] speak of evil signs.
Even if it were complete with its thousand spokes, and possessed great majestic power,"
"If one sees the peerless woman, one immediately gives rise to a heart of love and delight.
Continuing further on his way, he saw the place where the Buddha, the World-Honored One, had lain upon a bed of grass, and he said to his wife:
"This is the bed of grass where the woman's husband lay."
Śāriputra observed that the grass mat was not disarrayed and replied:
“The mat of one who lies down with lustful desire is full of holes; The place where one who dwells in anger lies has a hard grass spread;
The mat upon which the foolish lie is strewn haphazardly; This, however, is the sleeping place of one who is free from desire.”
"I observe these signs; this is certainly not a place where a husband would sleep with his wife. We ought to turn back at once and return to our former home.
Without Regret (Aśoka), filled with renewed indignation, replied:
"The śarī is no auspicious omen; the words of Śrī are but evil portents."
"Even if those grasses were not disarrayed, he possessed great majestic power;
yet, upon seeing the peerless woman, he immediately gave rise to a heart of craving and delight.
Having spoken these words, they went together to the place where the Buddha was. Then Aśoka spoke this verse:
"O Benevolent One, you should observe this woman, whose beautiful form is fully adorned;
as a wife for me, she is bestowed upon you,
her countenance so exquisite that she resembles the moon and stars shining together on the fifteenth night."
Having heard this, the Blessed One thought to himself:
"If I speak words of compassion to this peerless woman, she will surely feel a sense of longing and attachment as she departs from me, and because of that, her life will end."
"I should now manifest an appearance of anger and speak with my father.
Having formed this thought, he immediately addressed Aśoka in verse, saying:
"The Māra-king offered three daughters, Beautiful beyond compare in the world; [The original text continues here.]
Though adorned with magnificent necklaces and ornaments, I do not give rise to desire for them;
how much less so for this lowly body, filled throughout with impurity?
Even if my toes were brought close to it, such a thing would never occur.
When the maiden Anupamā heard these words, her heart was filled with resentment. She observed her father with his head bowed, while Aśoka gazed up at the venerable countenance and spoke in verse:
“My daughter’s beauty is flourishing, Her grace and dignity are peerless;
What have you done now, O Noble One, That you have no heart for love and affection?”
The World-Honored One replied:
"The foolish people of the world give rise to attachment toward sense objects;
if they behold such a beautiful woman, their minds consequently become deluded and overturned."
"I am the seventh Buddha, having attained the unsurpassed fruit;
like a lotus emerging from the water, I am not defiled by the dust of desire.
At that time, the Brahmin Aśoka and the maiden Anupamā, having heard these words, departed from the Buddha.

At that time, there was an elderly bhikṣu who had formerly been a non-Buddhist renunciant; seeing the girl Anupamā not far from the Buddha, he conceived a lustful attachment and addressed the World-Honored One, saying:
“Your Buddha-eye is all-pervading and luminous; Please accept this peerless maiden.
Take her as my wife, And enjoy her according to your desire.”
When the Buddha heard these words, he remained silent and did not answer.
At that time, because his mind was overcome by defilement, the elderly bhikṣu spoke again to the Buddha:
"These are the Buddha’s robe and bowl, the mendicant’s staff and water flask."
"Give back both the precepts and our mutual vows; I shall now follow this woman.
That elderly bhikṣu immediately cast aside his robes and bowl, renounced the precepts, and went to the father of Aśoka, saying:
"Give me Anupamā to serve as my wife."
Her father reviled her and refused to speak with her; when her wish was not fulfilled, she vomited hot blood and died because of it.
At that time, all the bhikṣus were filled with doubt and requested the World-Honored One, saying:
"By what causes and conditions did you present the maiden Anupamā to the World-Honored One, yet He did not accept her?"
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"It is not without cause or condition!
You should listen."
In the distant past, there was a blacksmith’s household that had only one daughter. Although she had grown up, she would not marry anyone out of pride in her own craftsmanship.
This blacksmith, however, was able to place a single iron needle upon the water so that it did not sink.
At that time, there was a young Brahmin boy who was exceptionally skilled in this art; he cast seven needles through a single eye of a needle, causing them to float upon the water without sinking.
At that time, this youth, wishing to humble the smith, went to his door and cried out:
"I have needles for sale; let those who need them take them.
The girl then stepped out of the door and replied with a smile:
"You are a foolish person, or perhaps you lack consciousness;
having come now to the smith's house, you say, 'I am selling needles.'"
The youth also laughed and replied:
"O noble one, I am not foolish, nor am I without consciousness;
wishing to quell your pride, I have come here to sell needles."
"If your father knew that I possessed such superior skills,
he would surely betroth you to me, along with all the wealth belonging to his household.
When the smith heard these words, he asked the youth:
"Is your craft real or false?
He then immediately floated up a single needle himself.
He then floated seven times.
The boy felt affection and delight toward him, and consequently consented to give his daughter in marriage to him as a wife.
The boy said:
"I am of the Brahmin caste, of noble and superior lineage; how could I take a blacksmith as my consort?
Having said this, he abandoned her and departed. O Bhikṣus!
The brahmin of that time was none other than myself; the blacksmith was none other than Aśoka; and the woman was none other than Anupamā. You bhikṣus!

"In the past, when I was still possessed of afflictions, I abandoned my own daughter; how much more so now that I am free from desire and have become a supreme teacher—how could I give rise to lustful attachment?
Thus it should be understood."
Then the bhikṣus again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
By what causes and conditions did the elder bhikṣu meet his death because of the girl Anupamā?”
The Buddha told the bhikṣus: "Listen well!
It is not only today that this elderly bhikṣu brought about his own death on account of Anupamā; in the past as well, he met his end because of her."
In the past, there was a city named Siṃhakalpa. Its king was named Siṃhaśikhara, who was a great Dharma King.

At that time, the world was abundant and joyful, and the population was flourishing. There were no enemies, disputes, weapons, or punishments; there were no deceitful or wicked people who harmed one another. Furthermore, there were no calamities or various sufferings of disease. Rice, sugarcane, cattle, and sheep were sufficient everywhere, and he regarded all his subjects with equal vision, as if they were his only son.

At that time, there was a merchant leader in this city named Siṃha, who was immensely wealthy with abundant resources and enjoyments. His precious goods and various assets, as well as his servants and laborers, were never lacking; his treasuries overflowed like those of King Vaiśravaṇa, and he had taken a wife from among his own kindred clan.

Although they had lived together for a long time, no son or daughter was born; therefore, seeking an heir, they offered prayers to the gods and spirits, visiting all the temples, mountains, forests, rivers, and ponds, as well as the heavens where beings are born together, hoping for a descendant.
"O bhikṣus! When people of the world say that one obtains a son by means of begging, this is truly false.
If it were true, everyone would have a thousand sons, just like a wheel-turning monarch."
However, it is only through three conditions that a child is conceived:
first, the union of the father and mother; second, the mother’s body being pure and ready for conception; and third, the presence of an intermediate state being (*antarābhava*).

Due to the convergence of karmic conditions and destiny between the merchant leader and his son, a certain deva descended from the Subhakṛtsna Heaven and, destined for a noble station, took conception within the womb of the wife.
A wise woman possesses five special knowledges:

first, she knows whether a man has a mind of passion or a mind free from passion; second, she knows the proper season; third, she knows from which person [the conception] was obtained; fourth, she knows it is male; and fifth, she knows it is female.
If it is a male, he dwells on the right side; if it is a female, she dwells on the left side.
At that time, the wife was endowed with keen intelligence and, knowing the fetus was on the right, joyfully said to her husband:
"Do you know, merchant lord?"
"The child I carry will surely bring glory to our clan; he dwells now at my right side.
There is no doubt that it is a son.
Upon hearing this, the merchant leader was filled with great joy and spoke these words:

"For a long time I have constantly contemplated the matter of succession, wishing to obtain a virtuous son who would inherit my family estate and ensure that our lineage does not fall. Once I have raised him to maturity, I intend to repay his kindness by practicing extensive acts of charity for the benefit of my kinsmen."
After my passing into this world, may those who invoke my name and offer prayers on my behalf wish that all my honored ancestors and parents, in whatever place they are reborn, be adorned with merit.

He then placed his wife in a magnificent pavilion where she could dwell at her leisure; he provided for all her needs according to the changing seasons of coolness and heat, constantly employing female physicians to prepare her food and drink so that the temperature was perfectly balanced, the six flavors were never lacking, and she was never made to eat anything that was unsuitable for her.

Adorned with wondrous necklaces and ornaments, she was like a celestial maiden wandering in the Garden of Joy; from the time of her birth until now, she has remained upon her couch without her feet ever touching the ground, her eyes never beholding unwholesome sights, and her ears never hearing unwholesome sounds.

When nine months had passed, he gave birth to a son whose countenance was upright and handsome, bringing joy to all who saw him. His body was the color of gold, his head was as round as a parasol, and his hands hung down past his knees; his eyes were like blue lotuses, his forehead broad, his eyebrows long, and his nose high and straight.
Endowed with all the marks of perfection and praised by all people, after twenty-one days had passed, the caravan leader gathered his kinsmen and addressed them concerning the child:
"What name should be given to this child?"
The assembly deliberated together and said:
"Since this is the son of the merchant leader Siṃha, he shall be named Siṃhala.
His father then entrusted the child to eight nurses:
Two nurses provided him with milk and food; two carried him in their swaddling clothes; two bathed and cleansed him; and two played joyfully with him.

Thus, as this son was attended by these eight nurses, he lacked for nothing. He was constantly nourished with milk, curd, fresh butter, clarified butter, and the finest essence of clarified butter (*sarpis*), as well as other exquisite and delicious foods and drinks, so that he grew rapidly like a lotus emerging from a pond.

Gradually reaching childhood, he studied various arts, arithmetic, writing, and seal-engraving; in matters of taking and giving, income and expenditure, he mastered every subtlety. He was eloquent and insightful, possessed of keen intelligence, and was highly skilled in the eight types of divination—namely, regarding men and women, elephants and horses, precious garments, and wooden dwellings.

At that time, his father constructed for him three palaces and three gardens for each of the seasons—spring, summer, and winter—and provided him with three classes of women, namely superior, middling, and inferior; he would ascend these exquisite towers and pavilions to enjoy himself with various musical performances.
“Sārthavāha Siṃha personally attended to his household affairs every day, forgetting to eat until late in the day.
Seeing his father laboring with his own hands, his son said to him:
‘The sun is already setting; why do you not eat at the proper time?’”
The father then said to him,
"How can one attend to the family business while constantly enjoying pleasure?
Upon hearing these words, the son had this thought:

"My father is advanced in years and manages the household affairs himself; how could I afford to be idle and indulge in pleasure? It is fitting that I seek my own livelihood to sustain our family business.
He then said to his father:
"The burden of food and sustenance must be sought through one's own efforts; it is improper to sit idly and consume my father's wealth."
"I now wish to go into the great ocean to seek out precious treasures.
His father said to his son:
"You should not now undergo such hardship to seek them yourself; there is much wealth within my storehouses, including gold, silver, and precious goods for you to enjoy as you please."

"Even if one were to spend rice and barley every day, they could not be exhausted; as long as I remain, you may take and use them as you please, and after I have passed away, you may seek and obtain them as you wish."
The son repeatedly petitioned his father,
saying, "I wish to board a ship and travel briefly to a treasure island.
Seeing his earnestness, the father granted his wish and said:
"Go as you please; you must endure whatever hardships may come.
His father then immediately struck the drum to proclaim an edict, announcing throughout the city and to merchants from near and far:
"Gentlemen, you should know this!"

Those who seek precious treasures may enter the great ocean together with the caravan leader Siṃhala; wherever they pass through, they shall pay no taxes, and all goods for the sea voyage must be prepared.
At that time, there were five hundred merchants who, having heard this announcement, gathered at the merchant leader’s place to collectively set a date for their journey.

Once they knew the date, each took leave of his parents and bid farewell to his relatives and acquaintances. Selecting an auspicious day, they took their various goods—some carried on men’s shoulders and others loaded on horses—and followed the merchant leader. Traveling through successive cities and towns, they eventually reached the seashore.
The merchant leader then hired a ship for five hundred gold coins to enter the sea, and sought out five men:

first, one capable of distant observation; second, one capable of rowing; third, one capable of repairing the ship; fourth, one capable of swimming underwater; and fifth, one capable of steering the rudder.
At that time, the captain, intending to raise the sails, addressed all the merchants, saying:

"Within the great ocean, perils are manifold: perhaps a fierce wind will suddenly arise and cast us adrift upon a mountain peak, or a whale with scales like armor and teeth like saws may pierce our ship and sink it."
"You all should not be without a means of reliance during times of urgent distress; you ought each to protect yourselves by holding onto floating objects.
When the merchants heard this instruction, they said to one another, "The safety or peril of the great ocean is difficult to foresee in advance; we should follow the words of our helmsman."
Each person sought floating objects to protect themselves, taking either wooden planks, leather bags, or hollow gourds, and all arrived at the ship.
Once they had entered the great ocean, they encountered a makara fish that shattered their vessel.

At that time, the multitude of people, each relying on floating objects, rose and fell with the waves; as their remaining life-span was not yet exhausted by the movement of past karmic conditions, they encountered a north wind and were漂流 (drifted) to the southern shore, arriving at the Copper-Red Island (*Tāmradvīpa*), where many *rākṣasīs* known as "Sounding Cranes" resided.
At that time, the rākṣasī could transform her appearance at will; seeing the ruined merchants, she would employ sweet words to deceive and entice them. Above the city, she erected two banners:
one named "Joy" (Saumanasya) and the other named "Fear" (Bhaya).
"If this banner moves, it portends signs of good or ill fortune; now that the merchants have arrived, the joyous banner has moved.
The women deliberated and said:
"Since the auspicious banner has moved, we may go to the seashore; there must certainly be people from Jambudvīpa who have drifted here."

He then immediately transformed himself into a beautiful woman of exquisite appearance; together they walked along the seashore, strolling about and looking in all directions, until he saw various people relying on floating objects to reach the shore.
Each of the women transformed herself into a jeweled necklace to adorn her body; holding superior offerings, they addressed the people, saying:
"Welcome, O noble ones!
You have drifted upon the great waves and endured extreme hardship; you should come to our residence to relieve your fatigue together."

At that time, there were some wandering merchants within this city who had previously been captured and confined in the iron city, where they were gradually taken as food; they then accompanied those other merchants and went together to the residence.
The women said:

"Halls, garments, and all that you may require—enjoy these as you please. Furthermore, we have no husbands and now depend on you for our livelihood; we wish to be your companions with hearts free from any discord. Our many gardens and groves are all delightful."
He then pointed to the treasury and said:

"These are the precious objects required within Jambudvīpa—gold, silver, lapis lazuli, pearls, mani-jewels, musaragalva, agate, conch shells, jade, red pearls, and right-spiraling shells. You may take and use such items as you please; dwell with me in joy without harboring any doubts. However, you must not go toward the south of this city on a whim."
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus, saying:

"I do not see a single thing that deludes and intoxicates the world, or that binds it through craving and attachment, more than female form. You should know that women are capable of drowning all men."

When men see women, they immediately become bewildered and infatuated, losing their resolve through lustful passion; they forget the sequence of all their tasks and no longer apply their minds to sublime and virtuous qualities.
Therefore, O bhikṣus!
Those who seek liberation should diligently cultivate the practice of detachment from desire and perform the contemplation of impurity regarding all defiled objects; in this manner you should train.
At that time, the merchant spent many years in amorous dalliance and feasting with the rākṣasī, and they gave birth to a son and a daughter.
Then the merchant leader Siṃhala thought to himself:
"For what reason do these women not allow people to pass on the southern road of the city?"
"I should wait until my wife has slept soundly at midnight, then withdraw quietly, rise, draw my sword, and travel south to observe what is happening.
He then rose in the night and traveled south as he had intended, hearing a great multitude of people wailing and crying out, saying:
"Alas for Jambudvīpa!"
"How painful it is for my parents and brothers!
At that moment, having heard this cry, the merchant leader was struck with great terror, and the hair on his body stood on end.

Continuing further forward, he saw a great iron city, towering and solid, which he searched all around but found no gates; nor did he see any sign of humans or animals. To the north of this city stood a śirīṣa tree, rising high above the corner of the wall.
The merchant leader ascended and saw the people in the city; calling out from afar, he asked them,
"Who are you that wail here, thinking of your parents and brothers in Jambudvīpa?"
They all replied:

"We are people from Jambudvīpa who went to sea to retrieve treasures. On the day we were to board the ship, fearing we might encounter maritime calamities, each of us took wooden planks and flotation bags to protect ourselves, hoping to escape such misfortune."

Having entered the great ocean, our ship was struck and shattered by a makara fish; with no way to lodge our grievances, we each took hold of bags and planks and drifted with the wind until, our karmic lifespans not yet exhausted, we were blown to the southern shore.
At that time, there were many women of exquisite beauty who, bringing offerings, came to where I was and spoke these words:
"Welcome, O Noble One! We have no refuge;

we take you as our husband. All our houses, clothing, food, drink, and the rare treasures of the seven jewels are for your use as you please. They spoke at length as before, even concluding with: "Do not give rise to doubt or hesitation."
He further told us:
"It is not appropriate for you to go anywhere south of this city; let us dwell together in joyful banquets.
After many years had passed, each of us gave birth to a son by our own wives, and subsequently, each also gave birth to a daughter.

At that time, those women saw the auspicious banners fluttering and knew that a ship from Jambudvīpa had arrived after being wrecked; they immediately seized us and ate us one after another in succession, placing those who remained uneaten within an iron city.

While they were eating, they manifested as rākṣasas, their appearance terrifying, with long claws and saw-like fangs that tore apart human bodies; they devoured flesh, blood, hair, nails, sinews, and bones until not a trace remained, even picking up drops of blood that fell to the ground with their fingers and swallowing them along with the soil.
"In the iron city where it is my turn next, one person is eaten every day; those women there are not human beings, but are all rākṣasīs.
You should guard yourselves well, for before long you too shall meet with this same calamity."
At that time, having heard these words, the merchant leader was greatly terrified and said to the man:
"Is there any expedient by which you and we may escape this calamity and reach Jambudvīpa again in safety and peace?"
He then replied:
"I have no means by which I may return to Jambudvīpa to see my native land once more. Why is this?"

"I know that my karma is heavy and there is no way for me to seek liberation; let us all together focus our minds to pierce this iron city and create an opening, so that we may seek refuge and hope to escape these bonds. As they spoke, the city immediately expanded several times wider.
When they further attempted to leap over and exit the city, the walls rose even higher; thus they knew that there was no way for them to escape and waited for their lives to end.
"You gentlemen may yet have some expedient means by which you can return to your own country."
The merchant leader asked,
"What is the matter? He then replied:
"I have heard that on the fifteenth day, during the poṣadha ceremony, various devas in the sky spoke these words:
'O people of Jambudvīpa!'"
Because you lack wisdom, you remain in ignorance; on the fifteenth day of the *poṣadha*, you do not understand how to travel north to seek a way out.

Every fifteen days, there is a celestial horse king named Balaha who emerges from the ocean and wanders along the shore. He feeds on naturally fragrant rice, is free from disease, is full of vigor, and possesses great power. Raising his head and looking in all directions, he proclaims three times:
"Who wishes to go to the other shore and return to Jambudvīpa?"

"You all should, on the fifteenth day during the poṣadha ceremony, go to where the divine horse is by the great ocean at the northern edge of the city. When the horse speaks, you must immediately say to him:
'We wish to return to the other shore in Jambudvīpa; we pray that you will lead us across in safety.'"
"You should carry out what the horse has said.
By this expedient means, you may return to your own country.

When the merchant leader Siṃhala heard these words, he received them with deep sincerity, praised their rarity, immediately descended from the tree, sought the path, and returned to lie down as before.
When dawn had broken, he went to where those five hundred merchants were and addressed them, saying:
"Gentlemen, you should all assemble together at a certain garden; there is a matter requiring deliberation. You must not bring your wives and children with you."

When the merchants heard the words of the caravan leader, they all gathered together in a garden. The caravan leader then informed the entire assembly of the aforementioned matters and further addressed them, saying:
"These women are all rākṣasīs; you should each guard yourselves with great care."
The Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya, Volume Forty-seven;
The Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya, Volume Forty-eight.
When the merchants heard these words, they were all seized with great terror and knew not what to do.
*The Vinaya of the Mūlasarvāstivādins*, translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Yijing by Imperial Decree, Chapter Eighty-two, Part Five: The Training Rule on Entering the Royal Palace.
When the fifteenth day arrived for the poṣadha ceremony, they all went toward the north of the city to the place where the divine horse was.
At that time, the divine horse emerged from the great ocean and was eating naturally fragrant rice by the seashore.
At that time, there was an ignorant merchant who did not recall what had been said before;
having seen the Horse-King, he spoke these words: "Do you know?
This is the divine horse-king Brahā, who feeds upon fragrant rice. We ought to approach and prostrate at his hooves, saying:"
"I am returning to Jambudvīpa from the other shore.
Then that merchant leader said to the people:
"I received this message within the iron city; the matter is not as you say!"

Until the Horse-King has spoken, it is not appropriate to draw near; one must wait until the Horse-King has eaten his fill of fragrant rice, his body is refreshed and satisfied, and he raises his head, looks around in the four directions, and utters these words three times:
"Who is going to the other shore to return to Jambudvīpa?"
Upon hearing these words, they proceeded to the horse’s location to request passage across the great ocean.

When the horse had finished eating, he looked around in all four directions and made his proclamation three times. Having heard this, the people approached to prostrate at his feet; with palms joined in reverence, they spoke thus:
“We seek to go to the other shore and return to Jambudvīpa.”
Then that horse-king addressed the people, saying:

"If you wish to cross the great ocean safely and return to Jambudvīpa, you must follow my instructions, receiving them with careful attention and reflection; if you do not follow them, there is no way for you to cross over."
That rākṣasī transformed her appearance into one of exquisite beauty, far surpassing her usual form, and bringing along her sons and daughters to entice and deceive him, saying these words:
"I have lived depending on you and have taken refuge in you; now that you abandon me and depart, where do you intend to go?"
"As I have described above, I have fully detailed the houses and treasures; if you do not wish to stay, your sons and daughters may take them with them.

When you hear such a proclamation, if you give rise to thoughts of attachment, regarding them as your wives and children, and if your hearts feel longing and desire to return to those treasures and gardens, then even if you climb upon my back, you will surely fall, just like ripe fruit that cannot remain upon its branch.

Then those women resumed their forms as rākṣasīs and vied with one another to devour his skin, flesh, sinews, and bones; his intestines, stomach, blood, marrow, hair, fur, nails, and teeth were all consumed until nothing remained. As described in detail previously, they even took up every drop of blood that fell upon the ground and ate it all.
If you all follow my teaching and do not give rise to such thoughts of attachment, even a single hair of mine will not fall away, and we shall be able to cross the great ocean and reach Jambudvīpa.
Then that horse king, having given good instructions to the merchants, immediately lowered his body so they could draw near, allowing them to grasp his mane, tail, or body hair as they pleased.
Then that celestial horse leaped into the void and galloped through the path of the clouds toward Jambudvīpa.
At that time, as the banner of fear fluttered, the rākṣasa saw this marvel and thought to himself:
"Now that this banner flutters, could it be that the people of Jambudvīpa have abandoned me and fled?"

Having searched all the rooms and seen no one there, they immediately transformed their appearances into those of beautiful women; taking both men and women with them, they went together to the great ocean to search for the merchants.
Having seen him from afar, she followed behind him weeping and said,
"O noble one! For what reason have you treated me with such neglect and abandoned both me and our children to depart?"
"If you all collectively wish to turn your backs on me, then each of you may take your young children with you.

When the merchants heard these words, they each felt a sense of longing for that house, as well as for the gardens, ponds, and various precious treasures; at the moment their thoughts of attachment arose, they fell from the celestial horses, their bodies dropping just like ripe fruit falling from its branch.
At that time, the rākṣasīs seized and devoured them as the Horse King had described;
only the caravan leader, his mind free from attachment, relied upon the divine horse and reached the seashore, arriving safely and without hindrance in Jambudvīpa.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus, saying:
"Observe these people; because they gave rise to attachment and did not follow my instructions, they have all fallen."
You should know that if you conceive such thoughts regarding yourselves as:
"The eye is my self; I possess the eye," and so on, up to "the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind are likewise my self; I possess them."
Furthermore, one thinks: "Form is my self; I possess form," and so on up to sound, odor, taste, touch, and mental phenomena (*dharma*).
Furthermore, one thinks: "The earth element is my self; I possess the earth," and so on up to the water element, fire element, wind element, space element, and consciousness element (*vijñānadhātu*).
Furthermore, one might think: "The aggregate of form is my self; I possess the aggregate of form. The same applies to feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness. O Bhikṣus!

If you give rise to such notions of "I" and "mine," you will develop attachment toward yourselves and others, turn your backs on the sublime teaching, and take delight in false paths. You will then fall into the ocean of birth and death, undergoing all manner of suffering and affliction with no prospect of escape.
For example, it is like an unwise merchant who abandons the instructions for the celestial horse, falls in love with rākṣasī women, and plunges into the great ocean.
You bhikṣus! If you do not direct this thought toward yourselves:
"The eye is my self; I possess the eye," and so on up to "the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind.
"Form is my self; I possess form," and so on up to "sound, odor, taste, tangible objects, and mental phenomena."
"The earth element is my self; I possess the earth element," and so on up to "the water element, the fire element, the wind element, the space element, and the consciousness element.
"The aggregate of form is my self; I possess the aggregate of form," and the same applies to feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness.

"O bhikṣus! If you can refrain from such notions of 'I' and 'mine,' and remain free from attachment toward yourselves and others; if you accept and practice the true teaching while rejecting and turning away from the heterodox paths, you will not fall into the ocean of birth and death, but will dwell in peace and happiness, proceeding toward the city of Nirvāṇa."
"It is like a wise and capable leader who, having received the instruction of a divine horse, abandons the rākṣasī women, is able to cross the great ocean, and reach Jambudvīpa.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke in verse:
"All those people who lack wisdom, And do not have faith in the Buddha’s teaching..."
When undergoing the sufferings of saṃsāra, one is like one who loves a rākṣasī;
if there is a person of wisdom who reveres the Buddha’s teaching,
they shall emerge from the ocean of birth and death, just as one follows the words of the divine horse.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
"Because those merchants were unable to uphold the instructions of the divine horse, they all fell into the great ocean and were devoured by rākṣasī women."
Only the caravan leader Siṃhala, having received the instruction of the divine horse, remained firm and single-minded; he was able to reach Jambudvīpa safely from the great ocean.
At that time, Siṃhala’s wife, a great rākṣasī, did not seek out her husband but remained within the city. All the other rākṣasīs came together and said to her:
"Just as we have been searching for our runaway husbands, we shall seize them and bring them back so that we may all devour them together."
"Your husband has not gone far; based on these circumstances, I shall send you back to Jambudvīpa.
It would be well if you can find him immediately upon your return, but if you cannot, I shall consume you—do not harbor resentment."
Having heard this, he was overcome with extreme anxiety and fear, and said to the rākṣasīs:
"If you are so determined to force me to search for her, I shall now go to Jambudvīpa myself to capture her and bring her back."
The rākṣasīs said, "This is most excellent. Then the merchant’s wife immediately soared into the air and crossed the great ocean;

in the time it takes to bend and stretch one’s arm, she reached Jambudvīpa, where she transformed herself into the likeness of a terrifying yakṣa—twice as fierce and harmful as usual—and stood before Siṃhahanu, blocking the road.
At that time, Siṃhavijaya saw the yakṣa image and immediately drew his sharp sword, intending to strike the yakṣa; the latter then fled in terror, stepping aside from the path to avoid him.
Thus they pursued one another without ceasing until, midway along the road, they encountered a caravan of merchants.
That merchant leader and Siṃhala had been old friends; their affection was so profound that they took leave of one another with joyful banquets and conversation.

At that time, the rākṣasī transformed herself into a beautiful woman, carrying her young child and adorned with exquisite finery. She went before the merchant leader in the central land, prostrated at his feet, and spoke thus: "I am the daughter of the King of Tāmradvīpa.

My parents betrothed me to the merchant leader Siṃhala as his wife, and we were returning to Jambudvīpa together. Within the great ocean, we encountered a makara that struck and shattered our ship; all our precious treasures were lost without remainder. Because they deemed me an ill omen, they subsequently abandoned me."
"It is my great fortune to have met you today; I only wish that you would take mother and son to him to offer our thanks.
He then replied, "I shall send you there."
At that time, seeing how earnest and sincere this woman was, the merchant leader went to Siṃhahanu’s son and said:
"My friend! Your wife is lovely in appearance and is moreover a princess."

"A match such as this is difficult to find in all the world; since she has committed no great transgression, you should not abandon her so hastily. You ought to take her in and live together with her.
Then Siṃhavijaya replied, "She is not a princess;
she is a fierce Rākṣasī from the Copper-Colored Continent (Tāmradvīpa), a great devourer of human flesh and blood among her kind, and she is not my wife."
The merchant leader replied, "If that is so, for what reason have you come here?

Then Siṃhavijaya fully related the circumstances; having heard this, the merchant leader remained silent for a moment, then gave him provisions for the journey along with various other goods, and departed.

Then Siṃhala gradually returned to his own home, and the rākṣasī followed after him; taking the young boy with her, she arrived at Siṃhala’s residence and stood to one side, leaning against the side of the gate.
At that time, when the crowd saw his son, they said to one another:
"O virtuous ones, you should know!
Judging by this boy’s appearance and features, it is no lie that he is the son of Siṃhahanu."
The rākṣasa replied, "You may judge by their appearance that they are not false; it is due to the meager merit of their past karma that they have been abandoned by their father.
He then said:
"Sister, from where have you come?
Whose wife are you?
The rākṣasī replied:

"I am the daughter of the King of the Copper-Colored Continent. My parents betrothed me to the merchant leader Siṃhaketu as his wife, and we traveled together toward Jambudvīpa. Within the great ocean, we encountered a makara that struck and shattered our ship; all our precious treasures were lost without remainder. Because they deemed me an ill omen, they abandoned me, and after enduring the hardships of wandering, I have arrived here."
"I pray that you gentlemen will take me and my son to the merchant leader and offer our apologies.
Then those people went to the merchant leader's parents and reported the matter to them.
At that time, his parents said to Siṃhavijaya, "She is a princess of noble lineage who has followed you from afar;
this is truly lamentable. Furthermore, she brings her young child with her, which only serves to deepen our grief."
"You ought to have pity on him and not abandon him; a man of virtue such as you would not act contrary to his heart.
Then Siṃhavijaya bowed his head and prostrated three times, saying to his parents:
"She is not a princess, but a wicked rākṣasī. On the island of Tāmradvīpa, she commits great acts of cruelty, seizing and devouring all the merchants who drift there."
"We of this company have all been devoured, yet by my remaining merit, I have been granted the fortune of beholding your honored countenance.
His parents replied, "All women are rākṣasīs;
why do you alone ascribe this evil reputation to your wife? You ought to take her in and bring her into our household."
He addressed his parents again, saying:

"I know that I am not a human being and cannot live together with you; since you surely love me and will accept this according to your wishes, I shall go to another household to seek a separate dwelling."
The parents said, "We brought you into our household for your own sake; since you find us so distasteful, what use are we to you?
It is best that you follow your own wishes and let this mother and son pursue their livelihood according to their own conditions."
He immediately dispatched a messenger to drive them away.

Once the mother and son had been expelled, they went to the king’s gate. All the ministers gathered there and marveled at their beauty; they then entered together and addressed the Great King, saying:
“There is a woman at the gate whose appearance is rarely matched. She has suddenly arrived here, and we do not know her origin.”
The king said, "Bring her in;
I shall question her myself.

The minister immediately summoned her forward. Upon seeing the woman’s appearance—her peerless beauty and incomparable grace—the king was overcome by lustful thoughts and conceived an intense attachment. He addressed her, saying:
"Welcome, beautiful lady!
From where have you come?
For what reason have you arrived here?"
The woman then bowed her head to the ground and said to the Great King:
"I originally resided on the southern shore of the great ocean in the land of Red Copper Island; I am the daughter of that king.

When Siṃhavijaya was cast adrift by the wind, his ship was destroyed without a trace, and he drifted with other merchants to my country. My parents betrothed me to him as his wife, built a new residence for us, and bestowed upon us many precious jewels."

After years had passed, a child was born; we, mother and son, traveled far across the vast blue ocean, where we encountered a makara fish that shattered our ship. Having endured great suffering, we reached Jambudvīpa, but because they regarded me as an ill omen, they cast me away.

Now that I have returned to my own home, I am no longer tolerated; having no place to survive, I have come to submit this petition. I only pray that Your Majesty’s compassionate grace will be stirred, and that you summon the merchant leader to offer me an apology on your behalf.
Upon hearing these words, the king gave rise to a heart of compassion and said, "Do not grieve;
you should set your mind at ease.
He immediately dispatched a messenger to summon the merchant leader.
When Siṃhavijaya had arrived and paid his respects to the king, he stood to one side.
The king said to Siṃhavijaya:
"This is the king's daughter!"
"You took me as your wife and we have borne children together; we have followed you here.
For what reason do you unjustly and abruptly cast us out?
Even if there were a fault, it could still have been tolerated."
Then Siṃhavijaya advanced and addressed him:
“Great King!

This is not the daughter of the Great King of the Copper-Colored Continent; she is a wicked rākṣasī who has brought harm to living beings. He related in full detail everything that had occurred during their journey across the ocean islands.”
"All my companions have been completely devoured, and I alone remain alive.

Yet this rākṣasī still does not release me; she flies across the great ocean and transforms herself into a beautiful woman. Your Majesty should examine her closely and drive her away, lest she continue her wanton violence."
The king said, "All women are rākṣasīs; why should this woman alone be viewed with such dislike?
If it is truly that you do not love her, she ought to be given to me."
He addressed the King, saying: "Great King!
I have heard that filial piety is perfected within the family and loyalty is exhausted within the state; I fear this will invite great calamity, for the matter is no trivial one."
"Great King, if there is one toward whom you feel affection, I dare not advance, nor do I dare to stop; surely some calamity will arise, yet it shall not be my fault.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus, saying:

"You should know that for all men, women are a place of bondage and a place of drowning. They become greedily attached to physical beauty, do not believe in loyal advice, and do not contemplate the resulting disaster; you all should understand this."
At that time, King Siṃhacūḍa conceived a deep attachment and immediately ordered the girl to enter the inner palace.
Then, Prince Siṃhadatta, knowing the king’s intent and seeing no way to offer counsel, went before the hall and addressed the ministers, saying:
"Gentlemen, you should know!"
"The King loves this rākṣasī; if she enters the inner palace, it will surely bring about great calamity. Know that this is not my fault.
Having said these words, she wept and departed.
