Later, the King conceived a deep affection for the rākṣasī woman, which was far greater than that of ordinary men. He became so immersed in and infatuated by her that he neglected the affairs of state.

At that time, the rākṣasī unleashed all manner of seductive charms, bringing the royal palace under her total control so that it was no longer independent; then, at midnight, she ascended into the void and returned to the abode of the rākṣasīs on the Copper-Red Island.
When the women saw him approaching, they were all filled with joy and asked,
"Where is the merchant leader now?
He replied to the women:
"Sisters! Why do you think of that single merchant leader?

After parting from you all, I went to Jambudvīpa and arrived at the city of Siṃhapura, where King Siṃhacūḍa resided. He then received me and admitted me into his inner palace, and he installed me as his queen."

"I have unleashed my seductive charms so that the people within the city are no longer self-possessed, and the King neglects his governance, his mind intoxicated and deluded by debauchery. You all may go together to that city; there, you may eat as you please and carry away whatever you desire."
Upon hearing this proclamation, the rākṣasīs leaped for joy and flew up into the air; that very night they went to Siṃhala Island and devoured all the people within the city.

When dawn broke, the city gates remained unopened. From atop the royal palace, they saw vultures and eagles feeding on human flesh filling the air as they flew about; the state ministers gathered at the gate and stood waiting for a long time, yet the gates did not open.

Together they raised their voices and proclaimed throughout the city: "The night has long since dawned, yet the royal gates remain unopened; within the inner palace, many *manuṣyāda* birds (carnivorous raptors) are swooping down in chaotic flight, snatching flesh and bone in their beaks. The people were all struck with terror, and though they devised plans, they had no recourse.
When Siṃhahanu heard this report, he drew his sharp sword and rushed to the city gate, addressing the people:
"What are you discussing?

I have already informed you previously that the King’s acceptance of the rākṣasī would surely bring disaster. Now the city gates do not open and birds fill the sky; observing these omens, calamity shall extend to the royal house."
The ministers asked,
"What plan do you have in mind?
The merchant leader replied:
"It would be well to place a high ladder against the wall to observe from above.

Once the ladder was secured, the merchant leader drew his sharp sword and ascended to the corner of the wall. Looking far into the palace, he saw corpses strewn about in disorder; he immediately leaped down, recited a divine mantra, and brandished his sword. He struck the five hundred rākṣasas, who scattered and fled in all directions—some clutching human hands, some holding up feet, and others carrying heads or bellies as they flew away.
All the people outside the city saw this from afar.

At that time, the merchant leader threw wide the city gates, and the people vied with one another to enter and behold the desolation. The ministers and high officials wailed throughout the city, and together with the multitudes, they shed tears within the palace; each then returned to their own homes, bewildered and without order.
Later, on another day, they gathered all the people together and deliberated among themselves, saying:
"The Great King, our sovereign, brought this calamity upon himself; having taken in a rākṣasī woman and refusing to heed loyal advice, he has now perished along with everyone."
"What plan do you intend to adopt?
The chief minister addressed the people, saying:
"The former king has passed away and there is no heir apparent; the precious throne is vacant and the people have no sovereign."
"A ruler cannot be established without a sovereign; whom shall we now enshrinementally appoint?
A subordinate minister replied, "Only one who possesses both wisdom and valor is fit to ascend the throne."
The people replied:

"The merchant leader Siṃhala entered the sea with five hundred men to retrieve treasures; all the others were slain by rākṣasīs, and he alone returned to his native land. However, having been pursued by a rākṣasī woman to his home city, he did not succumb to her seductions."

The king took this woman as his consort; though she offered firm words and direct admonition, he would not accept her loyal counsel. Through his debauchery and loss of the Way, he brought about his own ruin and extinction.
The Merchant Leader drew his sword and entered the city alone to rid our countrymen of the host of calamities; in great courage and great wisdom, none can surpass him.
The ministers deliberated and said, "It is exactly as you have said;
it would be fitting to appoint that man as our sovereign.
They then went together to the merchant leader's place and, with one mind, entreated him, saying:
"Caravan leader, do you not know?
The Great King has passed away and there is no heir apparent; the royal lineage is vacant and cannot remain without a sovereign.
The people of the land now wish to offer the imperial decree to invest you as king; please deign to accept out of compassion."
At that time, the merchant leader said to the people:
"I am but a merchant who seeks his livelihood through trade; how could I possibly endure such a heavy burden as being the sovereign of the nation?
You should seek another person to occupy this precious throne."
The multitude again entreated him, saying:
"There is no one else capable; we pray that you will compassionately accept our invitation.
At that time, the merchant leader declined so firmly, yet the people of the country repeatedly and persistently sought his favor with prostrations.
At that time, the merchant leader, having been unable to decline the request, addressed the assembly, saying:

"I am truly incompetent and have no desire for this position; however, in accordance with the wishes of the people, let us together establish a covenant: that I shall not disobey any command issued by the king hereafter, and I shall accept my investiture."
After the multitude had bowed their heads in gratitude, they all said, "We shall carry out your commands.

Thereupon, the ministers immediately swept and cleansed the city walls and adorned the palace halls; they consecrated him as king with exquisite perfumed water, and he assumed authority over the myriad affairs of state in a single day.
The king then thought to himself:
"In the past, when I was a merchant entering the sea to seek treasures, my companions were devoured by rākṣasas.

At that time, I lacked the power to eliminate those harmful enemies; now, as the sovereign of the land, I may act according to my will, and I shall rid myself of these rākṣasas to fulfill my long-held vow."

He immediately issued an order to summon extensively all mantra-masters capable of commanding spirits and deities; those from near and far assembled, and through their further recitation of efficacious mantras, the rites were solemnly accomplished.
Furthermore, he selected soldiers and banners and ordered them to practice with bows and arrows. He then commanded his great ministers, saying: "Do you know?
I have an old enemy far across the great ocean whom I wish to go and exterminate. We shall require many ships and oars, which you should prepare; we shall set out before long."

At that time, the ministers constructed many ships; having selected an auspicious day and calculated the timing, they arrayed the fourfold army and proceeded to the great ocean mouth, where they encountered a favorable wind and boarded their vessels, intending to reach the southern shore.
At that time, ominous banners fluttered within the rākṣasī city. When the women saw this, they said to one another, "Sisters!

You should know that now that these ominous banners move, there must be people from Jambudvīpa who, harboring memories of past enmity and malice with cruel and violent intent, have come to slaughter us. We should go to the seashore to observe what they do."
He summoned his entire retinue to the seashore together; seeing the various ships covering the sea as they approached, everyone was struck with alarm and prepared for battle.

At that time, King Siṃhavijaya ordered the mooring lines to be cast off, and the four divisions of his army descended together, raising their arms and shouting loudly as they fought the rākṣasas. He then unleashed divine mantras to bind the rākṣasas in darkness; as spears and arrows crossed, more than half of them were slain.
Due to the power of the vidyā-mantra, they had no means of escape; those who remained alive begged for their lives and sought deliverance.
The King then declared:
"Only by establishing a solemn covenant shall your lives be spared. From this day forward, you must move to other places and must not return here again to be slaughtered once more."
"If you follow our instructions, you shall preserve the remainder of your life.
The rākṣasīs bowed their heads in prostration and said, "In the past, we have extensively committed violent and evil deeds;
from this day forward, we shall respectfully obey your teachings, move far away, and dare not cause you further injury."
At that time, having paid his respects and taken leave of the king, the rākṣasī departed for another region.

King Siṃhala then leveled the old city and demolished the Iron City prison; he reopened the frontiers and established a new city. He summoned various people to dwell upon this Jewel Island and gathered vast quantities of pearls and jade to bring back to Jambudvīpa. Because of the king, that country was named after him as the Lion Island (Siṃhaladvīpa).
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
"Do not harbor any other thoughts!
The King Siṃhahanu of former times was none other than myself; the King Siṃhaśīrṣa was this elderly bhikṣu; and that rākṣasī was none other than Anupamā."
In the past, Siṃhottama met his end because of his attachment to a rākṣasī; now, this Anupama has likewise brought about his own death through greed.
You bhikṣus!
"In the past, I have already rejected those rākṣasīs; how could I possibly fulfill their desires today?

Therefore, you all should reflect well upon this: recognize that women are objects of drowning, conceive of them as impure, develop a profound sense of weary detachment, and single-mindedly uphold my instructions."
At that time, the bhikṣus and the great assembly, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, rejoiced, practiced accordingly, paid homage to the Buddha, and departed.
Then the brahmin Aśoka took the maiden Anupamā and went to Kauśāmbī, where he gave her in marriage to King Udayana.

The king then placed Anupamā in the Pavilion of Exquisite Flowers, provided her with five hundred female attendants and five hundred gold coins daily; [the account continues] at length until the king appointed Aśoka as his chief minister.
At that time, there were two men who came to the king’s presence to serve him:
one was able to speak of joyful matters, and the other was able to speak of sorrowful matters.
Once, while the king was sitting together with his two wives, King Udayana sneezed, and Queen Śyāmāvatī said:
“Homage to the Buddha!
May the King enjoy long life and freedom from illness.
Thus spoke Queen Anupamā.
"Homage to the Great King!
May Your Majesty live long and be free from illness.
At that time, Anupamā, filled with jealousy, addressed the king, saying:
“Kāṇamukhī ate the King’s food while thinking of the Buddha.
Having heard these words, the King remained silent and offered no reply.
On another day, she again sowed seeds of slander against her at the King’s court. Consequently, the King established a rotation system for attending to the two queens in order to receive their food.
Next, they arrived at Gāndharī. At that time, Queen Anupamā secretly devised a plan, having the bird-catcher bring a live bird to present to the king.
The king asked, "With whom shall I dine today?"
Anupama replied,
"Next is Gāndharī.
The king said:
"You may take this bird to serve as food.
When Gāndharī saw that it was alive, she refused to accept it and returned it to the hunter.
When the King saw this, he spoke with astonishment:
"Why do you not slaughter them?
The king reflected again; because he had cultivated wholesome thoughts, his mind remained intent on protecting life.
Anupama said to him:
"If it is for the sake of the Buddha and the Sangha, he will then kill the birds to provide the offering.
The King said,
"Inform Gaurī that she should prepare food for the Buddha."
The Peerless One immediately instructed his attendants, saying:
"You may kill the bird and present it to the lady.
They killed it and brought it to her; seeing it dead, Kanakāvatī accepted it to serve as kitchen fare. The attendants returned and reported that the lady had already received it.
The king became greatly enraged and said,
"If you will not accept it for me, then kill her for the sake of others!
Taking his bow and arrows, the king went to shoot Kan-yung.

Upon seeing him from afar, the lady immediately entered the meditative concentration of loving-kindness (*maitrī-samādhi*). The arrow shot by the king fell midway through its flight, and its barb turned back toward the king.
The king then shot again, whereupon the lady said to him, "Do not harm yourself, O King."
The King asked,
"What is the meaning of this?
The Queen replied:
"I have realized the state of non-returning and am free from further transgressions; yet, O King, you have conceived evil intent, which will surely bring upon you grave retribution.
When the King learned the truth of this, he immediately went to pay his respects and apologized for his previous faults, treating the Queen with great affection as if she were his own sister.
From this time forward, whenever there were new grains or new fruits, he would invariably offer them first; every day he personally inquired after his well-being.
At that time, a city on the king’s border rebelled, so the king personally led his troops to go and punish it, subsequently decreeing that the minister Aśoka remain to guard the capital.
The two ladies were charged with presiding over the inner palace, and the King said:
"You two must not harbor mutual jealousy; from dawn until dusk, never be negligent in guarding the palace gates."
The lady said,
"Very well.
At that time, Anupama repeatedly urged her father to harm Ghanarūpā, and so Anuśaya immediately devised a means to kill her.
At that time, Lady Gāṅgārī was reading Buddhist scriptures at night and required further transcription. She told her ministers:
"Birch bark, palm leaves, pens, ink, and lamps—these essentials must be supplied in abundance."

The minister followed these instructions and respectfully presented them; he secretly placed burning coals inside a birch bark pouch and set it at the palace gate. At night, the wind blew upon it and the fire suddenly flared up, its light piercing through to the upper stories of the palace. The city folk all gathered there, each carrying water, to together extinguish the fire.
Then the minister Aśoka drew a sharp sword and blocked them, preventing them from proceeding, and addressed the people, saying:
"Do you intend to plunder the inner palace?
Thereupon, the people dispersed.
At that time, Lady Gāṅgarājadhītā ascended the pavilion together with five hundred court ladies and addressed them, saying:
"I and you all have been summoned by our own karma; it is difficult to escape its consequences."
He spoke in verse:
"In a gap between the city walls, I gazed afar upon the World-Honored One;
Relying on the Dharma and practicing with diligence, I have already attained the truth of reality."
All the women threw themselves into the mass of flames like moths; they perished simultaneously, while the hunchbacked maidservant escaped the disaster by exiting through a water drain.
When the night had turned to dawn, the minister Aśoka gathered the bones of the women and cast them away in the cemetery.
When a bhikṣu entered the city to beg for alms, he witnessed this event and returned to inform the World-Honored One.
The Buddha then explained this in detail, as in the *Pañcavarga Sūtra*.
Eventually, the World-Honored One led the bhikṣus to a charnel ground and, observing the remains of the five hundred women, addressed the bhikṣus with these verses:
"Bound by delusion in the world, They take evil matters for good."
The fool, bound by craving, dwells perpetually in the dark prison.
Taking what is unwholesome to be wholesome, he fails to perceive that all things are ultimately empty and void.
One should give rise to a mind of weary detachment and not produce further stained attachment.
At that time, the people of the country and the ministers left in charge, seeing that Gāṇḍī was dead and having no plan for what to do, called upon those skilled at recounting tragic events, saying:
"You have received the king's stipend; now is precisely the time [to exercise it]."
He went and informed the Great King, saying:
"Lady Gāṅgarūpa has died by entering the fire.
[The account continues] at length until the man immediately deliberated with the ministers and others:

"One scroll should be painted depicting the circumstances of Lady Ganyong’s self-immolation, as well as five hundred elephants and horses, five hundred boys and girls, one hundred million pieces of pure gold, and a separate array of the four divisions of the army; once these have been prepared, I shall depart."
The ministers immediately prepared everything for him.
Then the man who had been speaking of the distressing matter led this military host to the king's camp; not far from the camp, he dispatched a messenger with a letter to address King Udayana, saying:
"I am the Great King of such-and-such a country!"
"I have but one son who has been taken away by death; seeking death myself, I have come to this country, wishing to ransom my son's life with elephants, horses, and even gold and jewels."
"If you grant this, it will be well; if you do not, I shall go to war against you, and I pray that Your Majesty will assist me.
At that time, the king opened the seal and read the letter, whereupon he laughed and dispatched a messenger to summon the foreign king to come.
Having arrived as commanded, after exchanging greetings, he asked:
"Friend! Have you ever seen anyone who was carried off by death and subsequently recovered?"
He replied,
"If you are led away by death and can no longer find it, you may open this scroll and examine it carefully.
The king then opened and looked at it, saying:
"How could Gāndharī have been burned to death by fire?
He replied, "She is already dead.
I pray that Your Majesty will pardon her crime and not hold me accountable; I devised this stratagem only for fear that Your Majesty might fall into grief and distress."
He spoke in verse:
"I am neither the king nor the son who died; I am the king’s minister, subsisting on the king’s bounty.
There was a matter that was not pleasing, which I reported to the king for his knowledge; I only pray that Your Majesty will show mercy and forgive my offense."
Upon hearing this, the king immediately turned his army back toward the kingdom of Kauśāmbī and commanded his judicial officers:
"Seize Aśoka, smear his body with lac, place him inside a heated kiln, and take his life."
"Furthermore, bind the horse of the unruly one with the hair of Anupamā and trample it to death.
Thereupon, the minister who served as judge killed Aśoka and cast Queen Anupamā into a dungeon.
When the king had not seen Anupama for seven days, he became deeply distressed with grief.
The king asked,
"Where is Anupama now?"
The minister said,
"The King has issued an order for his execution.
The King said:
"Gāndhārī has already been consumed by fire, and now Anupamā has also died.
Do you intend for me to renounce the world?
All the ministers remained silent and offered no reply.

The minister, knowing the King’s thoughts, brought forth the peerless woman to see him. At that time, the King was greatly pleased and inquired in detail about the circumstances, marveling at the rarity of the event.
With a mind full of doubt, the King went to question the Buddha. He explained the matter at length and finally entreated the World-Honored One, saying:

“By what causes and conditions did Kan-yung (Gambhīravarṇā) attain the fruit of the Non-Returner, yet she and her five hundred court ladies, who served as her attendants, were all simultaneously burned to death by fire?”
"Only the woman with the curved spine alone has survived; I pray that the World-Honored One will explain her past causes.
The Buddha said, "Great King, you should know!"
In the distant past, there was a king in the kingdom of Vārāṇasī named Brahmadatta.
Once, the king’s principal consort, accompanied by five hundred court ladies, went to visit a flower garden and entered a fragrant pool to bathe.
Having emerged from the pond, she sought fire as it was cold.
Not far from there lived a Pratyekabuddha, who had constructed a grass hut and resided within it.
At that time, the lady commanded a maidservant:
"You may burn that grass hut with fire.
The woman then went there; seeing the renunciant dwelling within the grass hut, she could not bear to set it on fire.
The lady herself then went there and set the fire ablaze; when the women saw this, they all laughed together and said, "What a fine fire!
When the Noble One saw this, compassion arose in his heart, and he soared from within the flames into the great void, manifesting great supernormal powers in the hope of uprooting their suffering.
When the women saw this, they called out from afar for her to descend, seeking her compassion and offering their apologies; they prepared food and drink to present as an offering and each made a vow.
The lady at that time was none other than Gāṅgā, and those maidservants were none other than the five hundred palace women.

Due to the power of that karma, although she attained the fruit of the Noble Path with her exquisite beauty, she was nevertheless burned to death by fire during five hundred lifetimes along with five hundred female attendants.
That messenger girl was none other than this hunchbacked woman; because she refused to burn [the offerings], she has always escaped calamity.
Great King, you should know that such is the retribution for good and evil.
The king further asked:

"By what causes and conditions did that hunchbacked woman receive the retribution of being hunchbacked; why is it that she attains realization upon hearing a sutra but once, yet her body remains in a lowly station?"
The Buddha said to the Great King:
"In the past, there was an elder in Vārāṇasī named Sunetra.
At that time, the elder invited five hundred Pratyekabuddhas to his home for a meal."

At that time, there was a pratyekabuddha among this assembly who suffered from a wind disorder; while eating, his hand trembled so violently that his alms bowl was about to fall. At that moment, the elder Bhadraśreṣṭhin had a young daughter who, seeing his hand trembling, took off her armlet and used it to steady the bowl. Seeing that the bowl remained motionless, she immediately made this aspiration:
"Just as this bowl does not waver again, may my mind never waver when listening to the sublime Dharma in future lives, and may I comprehend it without forgetting."
Furthermore, there was another noble one who suffered from a hunched back; consequently, he was not seen on the day of the meal.
The daughter asked her father, "Why has a certain noble one not come to eat?"
The father asked, "What is the appearance of a sage?
The girl, with a playful mind, bent her back to imitate the form of a sage; yet such a person was not to be seen among the assembly.
Furthermore, he constantly addressed his own relatives as "slaves.

Great King, you should know that by the power of the vow he made upon offering the alms bowl, he has now attained the capacity for hearing and retaining [the teachings], as well as intelligence and quick comprehension.
"Because he treated the Noble One with a disrespectful mind while training under him, he now receives the retribution of a hunched back.
Because in the past he called others 'slave-girls,' he constantly dwells among the lowly classes.
The King again invited the Buddha:
"For what reason did he remain within the dungeon for seven days without peer, neither obtaining food nor drink, yet his countenance remained unchanged?
The Buddha told the Great King:
"In a past life, there was a Brahmin woman who was a close friend of a Kṣatriya woman."
That Kṣatriya woman possessed faith and reverence, and she regularly offered the bhikṣus food and drink whenever they required it.

Later, a Brāhmaṇa woman invited the Kṣatriya woman to her house for a meal. Once they had arrived at the house, a Pratyekabuddha came to that home seeking alms. The Kṣatriya woman said to the Brāhmaṇa woman, "Give food to this Noble One."
The woman said,
"I cannot give it to you.
He replied:
"If you do not give it away, I shall return home myself and offer him food.
Then the Brahmin girl, following her friend's wish, took the food and gave it as an offering.
When the Kṣatriya woman saw that the food had been given, she instructed her to make a vow, and she immediately made this vow:
"By means of this merit, may I not receive superior rewards in this life or in future lives; when I encounter times of calamity and distress, may I not suffer the pain of hunger."
"By the power of that vow, she does not suffer from hunger now, and her facial features have not changed.

Later, on another occasion, when the householder Svaghoṣa was making offerings to the Buddha and the Saṅgha, he had a maidservant who was constantly assigned to provide service. This woman fell ill and died; as her life was ending, she made this aspiration:

"By the merit and karmic conditions of my labor in serving the Buddha and the Saṅgha, after I cast off this body, may I be conceived in the womb of the principal wife of the householder Svaghoṣa, with a beauty of countenance equal to that of Sundarī, and may King Udayana take me as his queen."

Having made this vow, he immediately passed away and took rebirth in the womb of a noble lady. When nine months had elapsed and it was time for his birth, the chamber was filled with radiance; therefore, he was named Śrīmati.
Recalling the events of her previous lives, as she gradually grew older, she cultivated faith from past lives.
When the Venerable Ānanda went on his almsround and happened to arrive at her house, the maiden Śrī bowed at his feet and said:
"Noble One!"

"Please convey my words to pay homage to the World-Honored One and the assembly of noble ones, and inquire whether they are free from illness and affliction, and whether their daily life is light, easy, and peaceful.
When Ānanda had returned to his dwelling and conveyed the words of Śrīmati to pay homage to the World-Honored One and the great assembly, and had extended his greetings, the Buddha said to Ānanda:
"Do you know that Śrīmati?"
He replied, "I do not know.
The Buddha said:

"She was a servant girl who made offerings in the Garden of Wondrous Sound. Because of the power of her vow made while offering to the Saṃgha, she has been reborn in the house of the Elder Wondrous Sound.

This is explained at length until it is said that once she had grown up, she looked down from a high tower at King Udayana; the king saw her from afar and, thinking her to be Anupamā, summoned the elder and asked:
"Why have you kept Anupamā hidden within your home for so long?"
He replied, "It is not.
The king did not believe his words and questioned him again:
"Who is it? He replied, "It is my daughter."
The king said,
"Whichever of these two proves right, she shall be taken as my bride.
He then prepared grand ceremonies to welcome her into the inner palace, providing her with five hundred court ladies to serve her.
At that time, Śrīmati, wishing to see the World-Honored One and the assembly of bhikṣus, informed the king of her intention.
The king, complying with her wish, immediately prepared offerings and invited the Buddha and the monastic community, intending for them to receive food within the palace for seven days.
The King went there in person; having arrived at the Buddha’s dwelling and performed all the proper rites of deportment, he addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
Śrīmatī requests that the Buddha and the Sangha accept a meal at her palace.”
The Buddha accepted by remaining silent; the king paid his respects and departed.

Upon returning, he informed the queen to prepare various kinds of exquisite and superior food, and went to announce that the time had come. The World-Honored One did not go himself, but commanded Śāriputra to proceed together with the assembly.
Having arrived at the royal gate, he did not dare to enter abruptly. When the king commanded him to proceed, Śāriputra thought to himself:
"The World-Honored One has established a precept forbidding unauthorized entry into the palace gates;
yet now that I have received the king's command, I must not disobey it. Perhaps the Buddha will grant permission on account of these circumstances."
He then entered the palace and took his seat.
At that time, Lady Śrīmatī and the King personally presented him with exquisite food and drink.

After he had eaten, they listened to the Dharma; immediately upon sitting, the lady attained the fruit of stream-entry (*srotāpatti*). After seven days had passed, the community of monks took their leave.
When the bhikṣus had arrived at the Buddha’s dwelling and prostrated at his feet, they related the aforementioned matter.
The Buddha said to Śāriputra:
“Excellent!”
I have not yet granted you permission; you already know the time.
You should all understand this!
What preceded was the original prohibition, whereas this is a subsequent allowance. For the sake of the bhikṣus, I re-establish the training rule (śikṣāpada), which should be stated as follows:

"If, moreover, a bhikṣu enters past the threshold of the palace gate before the dawn has appeared and before the Kṣatriya consecrated king has hidden his treasures and precious objects, except for other circumstances, it is a pāyattika."
"Furthermore, 'if a bhikṣu' refers to Udāyin; the remaining meanings are as explained above.
'Before the dawn has appeared' means that the sky has not yet lightened; there are three types of such signs."
The king and the jewels are as previously described.
Regarding the threshold of the palace gate, there are three distinctions:
namely, the city gate, the royal gate, and the palace gate.
"Transgressing" means to step over with the feet.
"Except for other circumstances" refers to cases such as obtaining superior dharmas like Śāriputra and others.
The explanation of the offense is as above.
Regarding the offenses herein, what are the specific cases?
If a bhikṣu, while it is not yet dawn, perceives it as not yet dawn—or has doubt—and crosses the city gate, he incurs a *duṣkṛta* (wrongdoing).
If it is already dawn, but he perceives it as not yet dawn—or has doubt—he likewise incurs a *duṣkṛta*.
The royal gate is treated in the same way.
If one passes through it with the thought that it is the palace gate, or if there is doubt regarding this, it constitutes the root offense.
For the next two cases, it is an *dukkaṭa* (wrongdoing); for the final two cases, there is no offense.
If the king, the queen, the crown prince, or a high minister summons one, there is no offense.
Furthermore, there is no offense for the very first offender, or for one who is insane, mentally deranged, or overwhelmed by intense physical pain.
The Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya, Volume Forty-Eight.
The Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya, Volume Forty-Nine.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Yijing by Imperial Decree.
Precept 83: The Training Rule on Pretending Not to Know. At that time, the Blessed One was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
The Buddha addressed the bhikṣus:
"Every half-month, you should recite the Prātimokṣa precepts.
At that time, the bhikṣus followed the instruction and recited them.
When the six groups of bhikṣus were listening to the precepts, they spoke these words:
"Venerable ones!
It is only now that we have learned that this rule is recited within the Prātimokṣa Sūtra."
The bhikṣus replied,
"Could it be that the Venerable One did not listen when the Prātimokṣa Sūtra was recited every half-month?
The group of six answered:
"How can I now merely listen to this and have no other matters, nor even contemplate the objects of sensual desire?
The bhikṣus informed the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"These foolish people treat the training rules with contempt. Therefore, for the sake of ten benefits, I shall establish a training rule for my disciples, which should be recited as follows:"
"Furthermore, if a bhikṣu, when the Prātimokṣa Sūtra is being recited every half-month, should speak thus:
'Venerable sir!
Only now do I know that this rule is taught in the Prātimokṣa Sūtra.'"
If the other bhikṣus know that this bhikṣu has performed the *poṣadha* together with them two or three times, let alone more than that, they should say to him:
"Venerable one!..."
"It is not because you were unaware that you may escape your offense; you must confess and repent for the offense you have committed according to the Dharma.
One should then exhort them, saying:
"Venerable one!"

This Dharma is rare and difficult to encounter; yet when you recite the precepts, you listen without reverence, without focused attention, without earnestness, without mental engagement, without one-pointed concentration, without lending an ear, and without applying mindfulness.
"Whoever [does so], it is a *pāyattika* offense.
"If again a bhikṣu" refers to the group of six; the remaining meanings are as explained above.

"When reciting the Prātimokṣa Sūtra" means reciting in succession from the four *pārājikas* down to the seven rules for settling disputes (*adhikaraṇa-śamatha*), thereby elucidating their essential meanings.

Regarding the phrase "I now only know for the first time," etc.: this refers to the six *bhikṣu*s who repeatedly listened to the precepts together with other *bhikṣu*s, yet they intentionally said, "I do not know," intending to cause others to feel remorse and regret, and to disturb the assembly at that time.
Regarding the phrase "the bhikṣus should exhort [him] with words," etc., this clarifies that there is a deficiency due to a lack of respect and so forth.

As for the characteristics of an offense herein: when a bhikṣu sees the four *pārājika* rules being recited, and likewise up to the thirteen *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offenses and the seven methods for settling disputes (*adhikaraṇa-śamatha*), if he speaks in such a manner, he incurs a *pāyattika* offense for each individual statement.
If one truly does not understand [the rule] and is like a foolish person, there is no offense in speaking the truth.
Furthermore, "no offense" is explained in detail as above.
The Eighty-fourth Training Rule: On Making Needle Cases. The Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.

There was a craftsman named Dharma, skilled in ivory and bone carving, who previously felt reverence and faith toward the Nirgrantha ascetics. Later, he came to the monastery to listen to the essential teachings from a bhikṣu seeking alms, and consequently developed a profound faith in the Buddha’s teaching.
He further expounded for them the seven types of meritorious actions involving material things. Having heard this, they thought to themselves:

"Previously, out of ignorance, we took refuge with the naked ascetics; they take the plucking out of hair as their practice and mortify the body in their cultivation. Thus, they dwell on the extreme of error and do not traverse the Middle Way."
I should now abandon those false teachings and align my thoughts with the True Dharma, hoping for deliverance in both the present and the future.
However, as my family’s estate is poor and destitute, it is difficult to cultivate meritorious deeds; therefore, I ought to exert myself, laboring for my own sake and bestowing benefits upon others.
He then informed the bhikṣus of his own craftsmanship, saying:
"I am skilled at working ivory; if you require an ivory needle-case, I shall provide my services.
At that time, there was a bhikṣu who had an ivory needle-case made for him; it was so exquisitely crafted and lovely that other bhikṣus marveled at it in admiration and requested him to make more.
In this manner, as it was passed on from one to another until many people had handled it, the ivory of the craftsman was completely exhausted.
Furthermore, he had them work with bone until the bone was finished, and used horn until the horn was likewise brought to an end.
At that time, the artisan fell into poverty; his clothes did not cover his body and his food was insufficient for his mouth.
When the naked ascetic saw him, he said to him:

"In former times, when you took refuge with us, your household was prosperous and abundant; now, by following the tonsure, you have fallen into such destitution. Judging by this, which of us is the superior companion?"
When the bhikṣus who were of few desires heard these words, they all felt resentment and contempt, saying:
"How can a bhikṣu cause a craftsman to build without knowing the proper measurements, thereby leading to poverty and bringing about ridicule and disgrace?"
He reported the matter to the Buddha. The Buddha told the bhikṣus, as explained at length above, up until: "I shall establish a training rule, which should be recited as follows:
'If a bhikṣu makes a needle case from bone, ivory, or horn, once it is finished, it must be smashed; this is a pāyattika.'"
"Furthermore, 'if a bhikṣu' refers to one among those in this Dharma.
As for the bone, ivory, and horn [needle cases], they should be understood according to the facts.
There are two kinds of needle cases:"
First, cylindrical cases; second, joined cases.
If these are made from bone, ivory, or horn, both types are prohibited.
Whether for oneself or for others, one should not make them under any circumstances.
If it has been completed, one should immediately break it; the offense must be confessed.
The person to whom the confession is made should ask:
"Have you broken the needle case?"
If one does not inquire, one incurs an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*); only after inquiring may one repent.
A bhikṣu should use bamboo or reed tubes, or pieces of felt and the like, to store his needles.
One may inspect it at appropriate times so as not to allow dust or grime to accumulate;
in these cases, there is no offense. Furthermore, those for whom there is no offense are explained in detail as above.
The Eighty-fifth Training Rule: On Making Beds of Excessive Dimensions. The Buddha was staying in the Jeta Grove at Śrāvastī.

At that time, there was a bhikṣu traveling through the human realm who arrived at the gate of the Jetavana Monastery as evening fell and the gates were closed. He sat upon a low-legged stool beneath the gatehouse.

Having washed his feet, he withdrew his body into meditative concentration (*samādhi*). A snake, fond of coolness, stayed before the bed; seeing the bhikṣu with his head hanging down, it bit him on the forehead, causing his death. Consequently, he was reborn in the Heaven of the Thirty-three (*Trāyastriṃśa*), where he sat with hands folded in reverence.

At that time, Śakra, Lord of the Devas, dispatched five hundred celestial maidens to serve him; the necklaces of these goddesses emitted exquisite sounds, which caused those who heard them to feel love and joy in their hearts.
At that time, although the deva-son heard her voice, he did not look at her; snapping his fingers, he said to her:
"Sister! For what reason do you trouble me?"
Having seen this, the goddesses marveled at its extraordinary nature and went to inform Śakra.
The Lord of Devas replied,
"You should take a large mirror and place it before him."

The woman then set down the mirror, and at that moment the celestial being beheld himself, fully adorned with various necklaces and ornaments. Deeply moved by a sense of weary detachment, he spoke this verse:
“In this world, a human body is most difficult to obtain;
To have right faith in the Tathāgata’s teaching, And to leave the household life is even more difficult.”
Such a difficult matter as this, I have already experienced;
why then have I lost the eye of Dharma and fallen into the prison?
Until I attain right view, I shall never again accept sensual pleasures.
Liberated from these obstacles, one would otherwise fall into the evil realms.
Dwelling amidst these celestial maidens, I am as if surrounded by malevolent spirits;
having entered this forest of delusion, how shall I escape?
It is the natural law that when the gods are first born, they obtain three kinds of recollections: "Where did I die?
Where have I now been born?"
"Furthermore, by the power of what karma?
He then perceived that [the being] had died among humans and been reborn in the Heaven of the Thirty-three, as the result of the wholesome karma of purely maintaining the precepts.
Having formed this thought, the celestial maidens said to the devaputra:
"Great Seer!
You should now go to pay homage to Śakra, and only then shall you join us in our joyful play."
The deva-son replied:
"Sister! Has the Lord of Devas, Śakra, already been able to distance himself from passion, hatred, and delusion?"
He replied,
"I have not yet left it.
The devaputra said:
"Sister! In the past, I took refuge in the Great Teacher, the World-Honored One, and paid homage while remaining free from passion, hatred, and delusion.
Why is it that now I pay homage while still possessing the three poisons?"
"Sisters!
Is there any cause or condition by which Śakra could be made to pay homage to me?
The goddess replied:
“There is a superior grove named *Sudharmā*, within which is a dwelling place inhabited by celestial seers (*ṛṣi*).
If one goes forth as a renunciant while staying therein, Śakra himself will go to pay him homage.”
At that time, the devaputra conceived the notion of the celestial maidens as malevolent spirits (*bhūta*) and abandoned them to depart.
He went to the Abode of the Celestial Rishis (*ṛṣi*) in the Wondrous Land and entered the religious life among that assembly.
At that time, having heard of these matters, Śakra went to the park and personally paid his respects, praising him before withdrawing.
The devaputra thought to himself:
"If I do not go to pay my respects and visit the World-Honored One, yet continue to enjoy celestial pleasures, it would be improper."
"Now I shall first pay homage at the feet of the World-Honored One.

At that time, the deva-son placed four celestial flowers within the hem of his robe, adorned his body with various exquisite necklaces and ornaments, and like a strong man bending and extending his arm, vanished from the celestial palace and appeared in the Jeta Grove.
By the majestic spiritual power of that celestial light, a brilliant radiance shone forth, illuminating the entirety of the Jeta Grove.

She approached the Blessed One, prostrated at his feet, and immediately scattered heavenly flowers before the Buddha as a mark of devout offering. After circumambulating the Buddha three times, she sat to one side and addressed the Blessed One with these exquisite verses:
"Residing among the goddesses, I am as if surrounded by malevolent spirits."
"Having entered the dense forest of ignorance and darkness, how should one cultivate the way out?
The World-Honored One replied:
"There is a wondrous, level, and straight path; where it leads, there is no fear."
The patience of the Dharma is the great ox, pulling the chariot without a jarring sound;
shame and remorse fill the seat and cushions, while focused mindfulness serves as the attendants;
wisdom is the driver of the chariot, and right view leads the way before him.
"If there are sons or daughters of good family who ride this vehicle of peace and security;
with a single mind free from other distractions, they shall be able to reach the most supreme place.
At that time, the World-Honored One, observing the inclinations and faculties of that devaputra, preached the Dharma according to his capacity so that he might attain awakening.
Immediately upon his seat, using the vajra-pestle of wisdom, he shattered the twenty-fold mountain of satkāyadṛṣṭi and attained the fruit of stream-entry (srotāpatti).
Having seen the truths, he addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!..."

It is because the Buddha has enabled me to attain the fruit of liberation amidst all hardships; this is not something that could have been accomplished by my parents, ancestors, kings, the hosts of devas, śramaṇas, brāhmaṇas, friends, or kinsmen.

Because I encountered the World-Honored One, the Great Spiritual Friend, he has rescued me from the realms of hell, animals, and hungry ghosts and established me in the superior and wondrous states of humans and devas. Having brought an end to the suffering of birth and death and attained the path to Nirvana, I have dried up the ocean of blood and crossed over the mountain of bones; with the vajra of wisdom, I have shattered the mountain of the view of a self accumulated since beginningless time and attained the first fruit [of the path].

I now take refuge in the Triple Gem of the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha; from this day forth until the end of my life, I shall undertake the five precepts, from abstaining from taking life up to abstaining from drinking intoxicants.
"I only pray that the World-Honored One will bear witness that I am an upāsaka.
Then, before the Buddha, he spoke this verse of self-congratulation:
"By the power of the Buddha, I have forever closed the gates to the three evil realms."
Having opened the wondrous gate to heaven, I shall forever ascend the path to Nirvana.
Relying upon the World-Honored One, I have now attained the pure eye;
having realized and beheld the true Path of the Sages, I have transcended the shore of existence.
The Buddha transcends humans and devas, having left behind the faults of birth, old age, and death;
difficult to encounter within the ocean of existence, I have met him today and attained the fruit.
With my body adorned, I worship the Buddha’s feet with a joyful heart.
"Having circumambulated the One who Eliminates Enmity, I shall now proceed to the celestial palace.

At that time, that deva attained what he had never before attained within the cycle of birth and death; having prostrated at the Buddha's feet, he further made offerings with celestial flowers with utmost sincerity, and then departed for his celestial palace, suddenly vanishing from sight.

At that time, when dawn had broken, the monastery steward of Jetavana opened the temple gates and saw that monk sitting upright on a small bed, having passed away; he also saw a venomous snake staying beneath the bed.
He immediately went to inform the World-Honored One of this matter, and the World-Honored One said,
"You may cremate it.
He further addressed the bhikṣus, saying:
"One should not lie down to sleep on a low or small bed, nor should one wash one's feet at the foot of the bed; anyone who violates this incurs an offense of transgression against the Dharma.
When the group of six bhikṣus heard this regulation, they subsequently constructed high beds with legs seven cubits long, which they ascended and descended by means of ladders.
When the various brahmins and householders saw this, they felt contempt and disdain. The bhikṣus reported these circumstances to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"I shall now, on account of this matter, speak extensively to the bhikṣus and even establish a training rule (śikṣāpada), which should be recited as follows:
'If a bhikṣu makes a large or small bed, the legs should be no higher than eight finger-breadths of the Buddha.'"
"If one exceeds [the prescribed measure], it should be cut off;
this is a *pāyattika* offense.
Thus the Blessed One established this training rule for the bhikṣus. At that time, the Venerable Udāyin, being tall in stature, sat upon that bed.
At that time, [the Buddha] rested his chin upon his knees. A bhikṣu informed the Buddha, who said:
"The previous rule was the initial prohibition; this is now further permitted as an exception. It should be stated thus:

'If a bhikṣu makes a large or small bed, the legs should be eight finger-breadths high according to the Buddha’s measure, excluding the depth of the mortise."* *Note: "E-bu" (梐木) refers to the wooden tenon or mortise joint.*
"If it exceeds [the prescribed measure], it shall be cut down; this is a *pāyattika* offense.
Regarding "if a bhikṣu": this refers to the group of six monks (*ṣaḍvargika*).
Regarding "making large or small beds": this means when one makes such a large bed or small seat either by one's own hand or by employing others to do so.
"Eight finger-breadths of the Buddha" refers to the Buddha, meaning the Great Teacher; these eight finger-breadths are equal in length to one cubit of a person of average stature.
"Excluding what enters the frame" means excluding the portions of the bed legs that enter the frame; these are not to be included in the measurement.
Regarding "exceeding [the measure]": if the measurement exceeds [the limit], it should be cut off.
The confession for the offense should be performed as previously described.

As for the characteristics of the transgression herein: whether a bhikṣu is making it for the Saṃgha or for himself, if it exceeds the measure of eight finger-breadths, it must be cut off, and the offense is cleared by the confession.
One who is being addressed regarding an offense should be asked:
"Has the leg of the bed been cut off?
If one does not ask, one incurs an *dukkaṭa* (offense of wrong-doing).
The offense for this should not be confessed;
if one acts according to the prescribed measure, there is no transgression.
Furthermore, regarding what constitutes no transgression, it is as explained in detail above.

86. The Training Rule on Using Cotton from Trees or Grass to Stuff Beds. The eighth and sixty-sixth training rule concerning the use of cotton from trees or grass to stuff beds. The Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
Upānanda received a large bed, which he stuffed with cotton wool and used as a mattress upon which to lie down.

An elderly bhikṣu arrived from another location and was entitled to a bedding set; the assigner of duties distributed them in order, and when he reached Upānanda’s room, he gave the bed to him because of his advanced age and his right to it.
Upānanda then went away, distributed the cotton wadding from the inner garment, and had him lie down to rest.
Once the bhikṣu was asleep, at dawn he emerged from his room with both body and robes entirely white.
When the other bhikṣus saw him, they said to him, "Elder, could you really have been sleeping amidst a heap of reeds?"
Having related these circumstances in detail to the bhikṣus, the bhikṣus informed the Buddha.
The Buddha said:
"I shall now establish a training rule for the bhikṣus, which should be recited as follows:"
"If a bhikṣu, moreover, should store cotton wool or the like upon a monastic bed or seat, it must be removed; [otherwise, it is] a pāyattika.
"If a bhikṣu, moreover" refers to Upānanda; the remaining meanings are as explained above.
Regarding "stored items," there are five kinds:
first, cotton; second, grass-cotton; third, reed-down; fourth, *karpāsa* (cotton); and fifth, wool.
Furthermore, if a bhikṣu stores five kinds of items himself or instructs others to store them, he incurs an offense of downfall (pāyattika), which must be confessed.
Regarding the transgression herein: if a bhikṣu, whether for the sake of the Saṃgha or for himself, scatters cotton or similar materials upon a bed or seat, he incurs an offense of downfall.
The stuffing should be removed, and the offense should be confessed.
One who is to be confronted regarding the offense should be asked:
"Has the stuffing been removed?"
If one does not inquire, one incurs a *dukkaṭa* (offense of wrong-doing).
This offense should not be confessed; the full explanation is as above.
The Eighty-Seventh Training Rule on Making a *Naiṣīdana* (Sitting Mat) of Excessive Size. The Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
As the Blessed One said: "O bhikṣus!
When you use bedding belonging to the Saṃgha, or other people's property, even down to private items, you must use an under-linens."
The bhikṣus, not knowing its proper dimensions, made them too large and discarded the smaller ones, or complained about their length and breadth.

Their labors became so numerous and their constant busywork such that it hindered their cultivation of wholesome qualities. [The Buddha] spoke at length until he established a training rule for the bhikṣus, which should be recited as follows:
"If a bhikṣu makes a *niṣīdana* (sitting mat), he must make it according to the prescribed measurements."
Regarding the measurements therein: the length shall be two spans of the Buddha’s hands, and the width one and a half spans.
If it exceeds these dimensions and is completed, it must be cut down;

this constitutes a *pāyattika* offense. Thus, after the Blessed One had established this training rule for the bhikṣus, the Venerable Udāyin, whose body was tall and large, would, whenever he went to sleep, use various tree leaves as a cushion at the edge of his feet in order to protect his bedding.
The World-Honored One, while inspecting the dwellings, saw that the leaves were strewn about in disarray. Having questioned the administrative officials, he addressed the bhikṣus, saying:
"This was originally established as a regulation, and now it is being restated. [The full explanation] continues until:
'If a bhikṣu is making a *niṣīdana* (sitting mat), he must make it according to the prescribed measurements.'"
Regarding the measurements therein: the length shall be two spans of the Buddha’s hands, and the width one and a half spans; the length may be increased by one further span.
If it exceeds these dimensions, it must be cut down; this constitutes a *pāyattika* offense.
"Furthermore, 'if a bhikṣu' refers to one within this Dharma.
'Niṣīdana' refers to a sitting mat.
Whether he makes it himself or causes another to make it, the offense is incurred in both cases."
Regarding "of measured proportions," this may be understood from the text.
If one *hasta* (span) of the Buddha is equivalent to three *hastas* of a person of average height, the total length is nine *hastas*, which equals four and a half *cubits*;

the width of one and a half *hastas* is equivalent to four *hastas* of a person plus six fingers. The intention behind this regulation is that the *niṣīdana* was originally intended as a protective layer for bedding; fearing it might be damaged, it was not meant for any other use.
However, its length is equal to one's own body, with a span (*vitasti*) remaining above the head; this is precisely what corresponds to the bedding.
Furthermore, since the Buddha’s body is three times the size of an ordinary person’s, the mention of "twice" refers to the specific traditions of different schools.
If one relies on the double measure for the *niṣīdana*, its size is entirely too small to serve as a substitute for lying down, spreading on the ground, or prostrating.
Since no scriptural authority is seen to support this, it contradicts the words of the Sage; who would take responsibility for such a transgression? Is this not worthy of detailed discussion?
As explained in detail elsewhere:

if a bhikṣu constructs something exceeding these measurements, the excess material should be cut away and the offense should be confessed. All other questions and answers are as extensively set forth above.
88. The Training Rule on Making Garments for Covering Sores. This is the eighty-eighth training rule concerning the making of garments for covering sores.
When the Buddha was staying at Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park, the Blessed One prescribed that monks should make garments for covering sores; however, the bhikṣus did not know how they should make them.
Its dimensions were sometimes too large or sometimes too small.
The bhikṣus informed the Buddha, and the Buddha said: "Up to this point, it should be stated thus:
'If a bhikṣu makes a wound-covering cloth, he must make it according to the prescribed measurement.'"
Regarding the measurements therein: the length shall be four spans of the Buddha’s hands, and the width two spans.
If one makes it exceeding these, it should be cut down; [otherwise] it is a *pāyattika* offense.
"If again a bhikṣu... and so forth, the meaning is as explained above.
Regarding "covering sores," this refers to covering sores or scabies on the body.
The Buddha’s measurement of a span (*vyāma*) and the rules concerning exceeding it, as well as the explanation of the offense and so forth, are detailed at length as previously stated.
The Eighty-ninth Training Rule: On Making Rain-Bathing Garments. The Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.

During the three-month summer retreat, Viśākhā Mṛgāramātṛ went to the place where the Buddha was staying; having prostrated at his feet, she sat to one side. The Buddha taught her the Dharma, instructing, benefiting, and gladdening her, after which he remained silent.
Then Viśākhā rose from her seat, joined her palms in reverence, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!
I pray that the Buddha and the Saṃgha will come to my home tomorrow to accept my humble offering."
At that time, the World-Honored One accepted by remaining silent.
Knowing that the Buddha had accepted, Viśākhā prostrated at his feet, took her leave, and departed.
Having arrived at her home, she immediately prepared various kinds of excellent and sublime food and drink during that very night.

That night, as dawn was approaching, the Buddha saw many clouds rising in the eastern direction, shaped like a round bowl and filling the void of space; such clouds were capable of bringing down a great rain that filled the ditches and channels.
At that time, the Buddha addressed Ānanda, saying:
"You should now go and inform the bhikṣus:
'Now these clouds have arisen and will surely send down heavy rain; this rain, once it falls, possesses great power.'"
"If one bathes, it can eliminate various ailments.
If any bhikṣus wish to bathe, they may do so as they please in an open space.
Having received these instructions, Ānanda related the Buddha’s words to the bhikṣus in their entirety.
At that time, all the bhikṣus were standing in the rain on open ground to wash themselves.
When Viśākhā had prepared the food and drink, she arranged the seats and set out jars of pure water, then sent her maidservant to Jetavana to invite the Buddha and the Saṅgha, saying:
"The time has come."

The maidservant went to the gate to look for the bhikṣus; at that time, the bhikṣus had closed the doors to bathe. From a crack in the door, she saw from afar the bhikṣus bathing naked within the monastery, and she thought to herself:
"There are no bhikṣus here; these are all naked heretics."
He immediately returned home and said to his mother, "In the monastery, I did not see a single person who was a bhikṣu; I saw only naked heretics standing and washing themselves in the rain."
At that time, Viśākhā thought to herself:
"It is raining today, and many of the Noble Ones are bathing in the open air amidst the rain; these are not outsiders."
He then sent another person to go knock on the door and call out, saying:
"Venerable One!
Mother Viśākhā sends word that the time has arrived."

At that time, the Buddha, together with the great assembly, donned his robes and took up his alms bowl, proceeding to the residence of Viśākhā. Once they were seated, pure water was first served, followed by exquisite food; there was no kind of delicacy or rare delicacy that was not provided.
When the assembly had finished eating, received water and tooth-sticks, and completed their cleansing and rinsing, they all put away their bowls.
Then Viśākhā, standing before the Buddha, poured water from a jar; after he had granted her permission to recite her vow, she prostrated at the Buddha’s feet and addressed him, saying:
“World-Honored One!”
"I only pray that, out of your compassion, you will grant my humble wish.
The Buddha said, "I shall grant whatever you seek; what wish do you desire to make?"
Viśākhā said: "I have eight wishes: first, I wish to give rain-bathing robes to the community of bhikṣus;

second, I wish to give rain-bathing robes to the community of bhikṣuṇīs; third, visiting bhikṣus who come shall eat first at my house; fourth, departing bhikṣus shall eat at my house before they leave; fifth, I will provide food and drink to sick bhikṣus; sixth, I will also provide food to those bhikṣus who are nursing the sick; seventh, I will provide medicine to any sick bhikṣu who requires it; eighth, I will constantly provide rice porridge to the Saṃgha."
The Buddha said to Viśākhā,
“For what reason do you offer this rain-bathing robe?
She replied:
"Venerable Sir!
Today, when the time arrived, I sent a maidservant to the gate, and she saw the bhikṣus bathing with their bodies naked; she thought they were non-Buddhist outsiders (tīrthika).
Venerable Sir!"
"It is for this reason that I give rain-bathing robes so that the noble assembly may cover their bodies while bathing.
"Furthermore, Viśākhā!
For what reason do you give rain-bathing robes to the bhikṣuṇīs?"
He replied, "Venerable Sir!

I recall having seen various bhikṣuṇīs bathing naked in the river water. Laypeople mocked and reviled them, speaking words of disdain; it was for this reason that I gave these robes so they might conceal their physical imperfections while bathing in any location."
“Furthermore, Viśākhā!
For what reason do you give food to visiting bhikṣus who have newly arrived?
She replied:
“Venerable Sir!
These newcomers do not yet fully understand the proper sequence for begging for alms, and moreover, being exhausted, they require fine food; for this reason, I am making this offering.”
“Furthermore, Viśākhā!
For what reason do you provide food and drink to the bhikṣu who is about to travel far?
She replied:
"Venerable One!
When my fellow bhikṣus go out for alms, I offer this food so that they may not lose their companions.
"Furthermore, Viśākhā!"
"For what reason did you give food to the sick bhikṣu?
He replied,
"Venerable sir!"
"If the sick bhikṣus were not permitted to eat, their illnesses would only worsen; therefore, I give this gift.
"Furthermore, Viśākhā!
For what reason do you give food to those who tend to the sick?"
He replied,
"Venerable sir,
if the attendant were to go out for alms, the nursing would be neglected and the necessary medicinal decoctions would miss their proper timing; therefore, I am making this offering."
“Furthermore, Viśākhā!
For what reason do you provide the necessary medicines for a sick bhikṣu?
She replied:
“Venerable One!
If there were no medicine, illness would be difficult to cure; one would carry the affliction for a long time and be unable to cultivate the categories of wholesome qualities.
For this reason, I give this gift. Furthermore, Viśākhā:
"For what reason did you offer rice gruel to the community of bhikṣus?
He replied,
"Venerable Sir!"
"If there are bhikṣus who do not eat gruel, they will be oppressed by hunger and thirst; for this reason, I offer it.
At that time, Viśākhā again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"

"I have heard that a bhikṣu has passed away at such-and-such a place; the Buddha has declared that this person attained the fruit of stream-entry, and others have been declared to have attained the fruits of once-returner, non-returner, or arhatship."
"Venerable Sir!
Have those noble ones ever come to Śrāvastī to accept my offerings and support?
The Buddha said:
“Has it been accepted?
“If it has been accepted, then by this cause and condition, the merit of my gift will certainly result in the perfection of merit and wisdom.
The Buddha told Viśākhā:
"Excellent! Excellent!
The merit and virtue of your gift are perfectly fulfilled."
Then Viśākhā rose from her seat, paid homage to the Buddha, and departed.
On this occasion, the Buddha addressed the bhikṣus:
"I allow the bhikṣus to keep a rain-bathing robe for bathing anywhere."
At that time, the bhikṣus did not know the proper measurements; [some made them] too long and others too narrow.
The Buddha said: "It should not be done in this way. One must make it according to the prescribed measurements. This is explained at length, concluding with:
"If a bhikṣu makes a rain-bath robe, he must make it according to the prescribed measurements."
Regarding the measurements therein: the length shall be six spans of the Buddha’s hand, and the width two and a half spans.
If it exceeds these dimensions, it must be cut down;
[otherwise, it constitutes] a *pāyattika* offense.
"If, furthermore, any bhikṣu or others [should act as described], it shall be as explained above.
Regarding the *vassikasāṭikā* (rain-bathing robe), this refers to that which is used during the rainy season.
Whether making it oneself or instructing another to do so, it must be made according to the prescribed measurements; its length and width are as stated in the text."
If one exceeds [the prescribed measure], the offense is the same as before; the detailed explanation for the confession, questioning, and answering is as stated above.
90. The Training Rule on Making Robes the Size of the Buddha’s Robes. The setting and circumstances are the same as before.
At that time, Upānanda made a robe equal in size to the Buddha’s; he wore it with only one side draped over him, while the rest was gathered upon his shoulder.
When the bhikṣus saw this, they thought he was a newly arrived guest and wished to relieve his fatigue, so they said to him:
"We did not know you had just arrived; we have made this *cīvara* according to the same measurements as the Buddha's."
The bhikṣus criticized and disparaged him,
saying, "How can one make such an oversized robe?
They reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"On this account, I shall establish a training rule for the bhikṣus, which should be recited as follows:
'If a bhikṣu makes a robe the same size as the Buddha’s robe, or larger than it, it is a pāyattika.'"
Regarding the measurement of the Buddha’s robe therein: it is ten spans of the Buddha’s hand in length and six spans in width.
This is the measurement of the Buddha’s robe.
"If any bhikṣu" refers to Upānanda.
The "Buddha’s robe" refers to the Master’s robe.
Its length is ten *hasta* (hand-spans) of the Buddha, which corresponds to thirty *hasta* for an ordinary person, or fifteen *cubit* (*aratni*).
Its width is six [hand-spans], which corresponds to eighteen *hasta*, or nine *cubit*.
Or if it exceeds this amount, one commits a *pāyattika* offense; the rest is as explained in detail above.
The Summary Verse for the Four *Pātideśanīya* Dharmas says:
Receiving [food] directly from a nun who is not a relative, and eating food distributed within a house.
Do not go uninvited to families to receive food outside the monastery. 1.

The Training Rule on Receiving Food from a Non-Relative Nun. Regarding the first training rule on receiving food from a non-relative nun: The Buddha was staying at the Bamboo Grove Monastery in Rājagṛha.
At that time, there was an elder in the city of Takṣaśilā who, not long after marrying his wife, gave birth to a daughter. Her body possessed three virtues like those of a blue utpala lotus:

first, her body was golden-yellow in color, just like the filaments of the flower; second, her eyes were deep blue, just like the petals of the flower; and third, her fragrance was exquisite, just like the scent of the flower.
When twenty-one days had passed since his birth, his relatives gathered for a naming ceremony and said, "This child's body is like a blue lotus; he should be given the name 'Blue Lotus'."
When he had grown up, she was married to the son of an elder from the same city, and he was brought to her home.
Not long after, the father of the Blue Lotus met with illness and passed away; subsequently, his mother could no longer maintain her chastity and began to have secret relations with her son-in-law.
That Blue Lotus Maiden had previously given birth to a daughter who was still in her childhood.
Suddenly, while in a secluded place, she saw her mother and husband engaging in unrighteous conduct together; consequently, she gave rise to intense anger.
She then took her young daughter and said to her husband,
"You worthless man!
Why do you not join me in this unrighteous act?"
She then threw it onto the wood; it struck the woman’s head, causing blood to flow. Unperturbed by her anger, the Blue Lotus covered her head with a cloth and went out to seek traveling companions.
Seeing a caravan heading toward the city of Amitābha, she immediately entered the camp and followed them.
At that time, the caravan leader, seeing that the Blue Lotus was of upright and beautiful appearance, asked:
"To whom do you belong?"
She replied, "If there is anyone who can provide me with clothing and food to support me, I shall belong to him.
The merchant then provided her with clothing and food and took her as his wife; he brought her to his own home, and they lived together for a long time.
The merchant leader, carrying his goods, was returning toward the city of Takṣaśilā when a companion and friend said to him:
"Having wealth yet not enjoying it—when do you intend to wait?"
"Seek out another who is beautiful and elegant so that we may marry her.
The merchant leader replied,
"If there is one whose appearance resembles that of the blue lotus, only then may we marry her."
His companion said, "A certain family has a daughter who surpasses the blue lotus twofold.
They went together to see her; she met with their approval, and they immediately prepared the wedding rites to take her as his wife.
Having returned, they went together toward the city of Abhyavakāśa; not far from home, he left his young wife behind and left half of their goods.
Once they had reached their home, the wife said, "Why is the wealth so small?"
He replied,
"I was robbed by bandits.
His wife said:
"Why do you not search for him more urgently? He replied,
"I am now going to pursue and seek him out for this very reason."
After the caravan leader had departed, a friend came and asked,
"Where is the caravan leader going?
He replied:
"Go and search for the thief," his friend said.
He replied, "It has nothing to do with searching for a thief; it is only because I am searching for my wife."
He reported the matter in full to Utpalavarṇā.
Before long, the merchant returned home, and Utpalavarṇā said, "Did you not deceive me by claiming you had been robbed? Since you have another wife, why did you not bring her here?"
The husband said, "I have two wives in the house; I have no leisure even to drink water, for I fear there will be quarrels.
That is why I did not bring her. He replied:
"I can endure [them] without anger or contention; if their age is similar to mine, I regard them as sisters, and if they are much younger, I look upon them as daughters."

Her husband accepted her words and subsequently brought the young woman back to their home. Upon hearing this, Queen Utpalavarṇā, who was from the same hometown, felt a particular sense of compassion for her; one day during a leisure moment, she combed the young woman’s hair and noticed a scar upon her head.
He asked,
"Daughter-in-law, how did you come to sustain this wound?
The young woman replied:

"I do not clearly remember this myself, but I have heard it said at home that when I was a child, my mother, having become angry with my father over some matter, threw me onto a wooden beam; I was injured at that time, which is why these scars exist."
He asked again:
"In which courtyard do you reside?
In which direction does your gate face?"
The woman then related everything in detail.
Utpalavarṇā, recognizing her as his own daughter, was deeply moved by grief and thought to himself:
"Since she is my own daughter, what shall I do?"
In the past, she shared a husband with her mother; now, she shares a husband with her daughter.
Alas, how tragic!
How extreme is this evil!
She then covered her head with a cloth once more and sought to leave, finding a companion to travel with her to Vaiśālī.
Once they arrived there, she ceased being a courtesan and instead engaged in secret affairs with men; before long, everyone spoke of her with admiration.
Then the courtesans all went to his house and said to him:
"You have stolen our arts to sustain your own life, yet you do not speak with us or engage in sexual intercourse."
He immediately snatched away his outer robe and towel and dragged him away by force.
They all came together and asked, "What sorcery do you possess that you can entice so many people? He replied:
"There is no other method; if there is a youth who merely allows me to see him, there is none who will not comply.

The women said, "If that is so, there is currently a man selling incense in this city who has perfected the contemplation of impurity (aśubha-bhāvanā) and has long since developed weary detachment toward all women."
"If you can break that practice, we shall establish you as the most honored among courtesans;
if you do not break it, you shall be fined sixty pieces of gold.
He then asked the women:
“Is he a great man? He replied, “He is.”
"If that is so, why is he not sufficient to attract her?
She then drew near to him and stayed there, feigning various means of endearing herself to her husband, and had her maidservant go to purchase scented ointments.
She further purchased various medicines, saying, "These are required for my husband's illness.

When the incense-seller heard this, he thought to himself, "This woman must surely be chaste and prudent, for she is able to devote her whole heart to her husband. Thereupon, he conceived a deep affection for her.
The Blue Lotus then feigned that her husband had died; wailing and weeping bitterly, she passed by the door of the perfume seller.
Upon seeing her, the man’s attachment grew even more intense. [As extensively described,] he was ultimately ruined in his meditative practice by this woman.
The courtesans all saw her together and marveled at her, whereupon they immediately established her as the most honored among them.
Having long been in a relationship with the incense-seller, she consequently became pregnant.
At that time, there were gatekeepers stationed at both the eastern and western gates of Vaiśālī. Out of mutual affection, they deliberated together:
"The two of us have been companions for many days; if we should have sons and daughters, we must certainly arrange their marriage."
Not long after, Utpalavarṇā gave birth to a son. She then thought to herself:
"If I raise this child, my body will no longer be pure; I fear that men will find me repulsive and refuse to come. I should now abandon this infant."
She then handed the infant to a maidservant and gave her a lamp, instructing her:
"Take this and place it in the middle of the road; stay hidden nearby and watch who takes the child away."
At that time, the maidservant abandoned him near the eastern gate and set up a lamp there.
When the gatekeeper saw the light from afar, he came to investigate and saw the child; taking him back, he gave him to his wife and said, "You should raise him with great care; he shall be your son."
Then the gatekeeper held a great assembly and announced to his kinsmen,
"My wife has given birth to a son.
When the people from the western gate heard that a child had been born to the man at the eastern gate, they brought ceremonial gifts and went there to offer their congratulations.

Later, that Blue Lotus again gave birth to a daughter; as before, she thought of her and could not bear to raise her herself, so she had a maidservant discard the child at the western gate during the night.
At that time, the gatekeeper, as before, took him in and raised him for the sake of celebration and joy.
The sons and daughters of both families grew up together until they were all of marriageable age.

Once, during a seasonal festival, the son of the eastern gatekeeper was invited by his friends to go out for a pleasure excursion; they gave him sixty gold coins and blue lotuses and went together to a fragrant garden to enjoy themselves.
The assembly collectively established a regulation:
"If anyone does not assemble together on this day, they shall be fined sixty pieces of gold.
The son of the eastern gate did not wish to join in the festivities; when the others wished to fine him, he had no money or goods and thus humbly complied, following along with them.
Having already shared intimacy with her, he developed a deep affection for her and took the blue lotus flower home to live together.
At that time, the people of Vaiśālī all discussed it, saying:
"How is it that the son of the gatekeeper has taken these many courtesans into his own home alone?"
Having heard these words, the son of the East Gate apologized to everyone and prepared a grand feast, subsequently taking her as his wife.
The man of the East Gate then informed the man of the West Gate, saying:
"Your daughter has grown up; you may now fulfill your previous request."
He replied, "Your son is now marrying a courtesan; why do you seek this marriage?
He answered:
"Even if one marries many wives, what fault is there in that?
He then followed her request and betrothed his daughter to him, who returned to his residence at the Eastern Gate.
At that time, the Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana came to his house and said to the newly arrived woman:
"Do you know now?
Your husband's former wife is your mother, and your husband is your brother. Do not harbor further mutual jealousy toward one another, lest you thereby generate extensive evil karma."
Having spoken these words, she abandoned him and departed.
Later, at another time, Utpalavarṇā gave birth to a son; at that time, the woman from the western gate was playing with this infant before her door.
At that time, a Brahmin physiognomist came to where she was and asked in verse:
"Your countenance is like a wondrous flower, And you have deep faith in the Triple Gem;
As for this child you are fondling, What kinship does he have to you?"
Then that woman immediately replied in verse:
“O Brahmin, listen well!
This is my younger brother, as well as my elder brother’s son, and also my own son.”
"He is again my husband’s younger brother; this father is my father, yet he is both my father and my husband—thus spoke the Noble One with compassion.
Having heard this, the brahmin laughed and departed.
At that time, from within the Blue Lotus Chamber, she heard these words and, wondering at their significance, asked her handmaid:
"What was this woman discussing with the Brahmin while holding her child?"
Then that maidservant related the matter in full to Utpalavarṇā.
Having heard these words, Utpalavarṇā thought to herself:
"By what karma did I previously share a husband with my mother, and later share a husband with my daughter?"
"Now you take my son as your husband, and furthermore, share a husband with my daughter?
