Having thought this, she threw herself to the ground, unable to bear her shame and humiliation; she immediately left the house to seek companions for the royal city, abandoned them, and departed for Rājagṛha.
Not long after she had rested, five hundred men who regularly gathered for recreation in this city heard that a blue lotus had arrived;
they said to one another, "That woman’s beauty is rare in the world; since she has now come here, we should invite her to share our pleasures."
He then gave five hundred gold coins to Utpalavarṇā and, taking her with him, went to a fragrant garden where they dwelt in pleasure.
At that time, the Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana, knowing that Utpalavarṇā was ready to be transformed by the Dharma, went to that garden and walked back and forth beneath a tree.
At that time, there was a young man among the assembly who said to Utpalavarṇā, "Do you see that venerable one?
He possesses great majestic power and pure conduct; the mud of lust cannot defile him. Are you able to cause him to give rise to a mind of passion?"
The Blue Lotus said: "What is there to say about this?
Once, when a man selling incense had achieved mastery in the contemplation of impurity, I caused him to give rise to feelings of passionate attachment; how much more so, then, in this case?"
The people replied, "O Noble One, you are firm and cannot be moved.
Then the Blue Lotus approached the Venerable One, displaying various seductive gestures and pressing her body against him; the Venerable One leaped into the air and addressed her with a verse:
"You shall surely grow weary of this skeletal body, pervaded by veins and sinews entwined;
originally accomplished from semen and blood, it has lived off others to come and treat me with contempt."
This leather bag is constantly filled with impurities, entering and exiting day and night without ceasing;
from its nine orifices, pus and sores flow perpetually without healing, as foul odors pervade the body in every direction.
If you cause all people to awaken to this knowledge—just as I recognize your body to be impure;
like a summer latrine that cannot be approached—you should cast it far away with a mind free of attachment.
Because they are blind and dark, lacking the eye of wisdom, and are constantly shrouded by the cataracts of ignorance;
for this reason their minds are deluded and they take pleasure in you, just like an old elephant sinking into deep mud.

At that time, Utpalavarṇā, witnessing the wondrous supernatural power of the Venerable One, realized with certainty the impurity of her own body. She prostrated from afar to the Venerable One and spoke this verse:
"I now know this loathsome body, a skeleton bound all over by sinews;
Originally accomplished from semen and blood, it lives dependent on others—yet I have rashly treated it with contempt."
My body is perpetually filled with impurity, Entering and exiting day and night without ceasing;
Nine orifices constantly flow with discharge, this ulcer never heals, And foul odors pervade my frame from every side.
If those people were to understand this body as the Great Sage knows it to be impure—
like a summer latrine that one cannot approach, which one abandons and leaves far behind with no attachment of heart.
Because they are blind, ignorant, and lacking understanding, they are constantly shrouded by delusion;
thus their minds are bewildered and they take delight in the self, like an old elephant mired in deep mud.
I only pray that the Great Sage will deign to descend, And for my sake, expound the subtle and wondrous Dharma;
Seeking to leave the household life within the most supreme teaching, I vow to constantly practice the conduct of detachment from desire.

Then, out of compassion for him, Mahāmaudgalyāyana descended from the air; observing his faculties, he preached the Dharma so that he might perceive the True Truth. Having attained the fruit [of the path], he prostrated at the Venerable One’s feet, seeking permission to go forth, and went to the people to return their gold coins, apologizing to them with mutual shame.
The people rejoiced and all came at once to pay homage at the feet of the Venerable One.
Then Mahāmaudgalyāyana took blue lotuses and went to the place where the World-Honored One was; having prostrated at his feet, he related the matter in detail.

At that time, the World-Honored One wrote a letter to the Great Mistress Bhikṣuṇī (Mahāprajāpatī) in Śrāvastī on behalf of Utpalavarṇā, granting her ordination and instructing her to provide guidance; he then commanded Utpalavarṇā to go according to the letter.

At that time, King Bimbisāra sent a messenger to escort him to Śrāvastī. Having arrived there, he went to the place of Mahāprajāpatī; he left the household life and received instruction, practicing with unremitting diligence until, before long, he attained the fruit of arhatship.
The Buddha praised her as having the greatest supernormal power among the bhikṣuṇīs, being foremost of all.
At that time, the Buddha addressed the bhikṣus:
"You should contemplate that within the ocean of birth and death, saṃsāra is unstable; who has not been your father or mother?"
Who among them is not male or female, or some other relative or acquaintance?
Just as one clearly sees such unrighteous conduct being committed even among one's own kinsmen—as if with blue lotuses—how much more so across different lifetimes?
Without realizing the fruits of sainthood, you will sink into the depths of saṃsāra without rest.
Therefore, you all must strive with diligence for deliverance from the three realms as if your hair were on fire. The objects of sensual desire in the world know no end to one's craving;
you should quickly abandon them, cultivate the perception of impermanence and the perception of a putrid corpse, and train yourselves by binding the mind to these reflections day and night.
At that time, all the bhikṣus were filled with doubt and requested the World-Honored One, saying:

"By what causes and conditions did the nun Utpalavarṇā possess these three virtues: she was never lacking in men who constantly disturbed her in private; yet after going forth, she attained the fruit of arhatship and was praised by the Buddha as the foremost among those with supernormal powers?"
The World-Honored One said:
"Listen well, all of you, to this account of the nun Utpalavarṇā.

Long ago, there was a merchant leader who took various goods to seek profit in another land. His wife, meanwhile, was oppressed by afflictions and her heart consumed by the fire of desire. Not far from where she lived was the house of a courtesan."
Whenever she saw a man enter that house, a feeling of love and desire arose within her, and she asked an old woman:
"What meritorious deed must one perform so that all that is sought accords with one's heart's desire?"
The old woman said,
"If one offers food, drink, and various offerings to those who have accomplished the practices of the supreme beings, all that is sought shall be fulfilled according to one's heart."

At that time, there was a Pratyekabuddha sage whom the old woman provided with food and drink, and she offered him an offering of blue lotuses. Witnessing his supernormal transformations, the woman conceived deep faith and immediately made this aspiration:

"By this merit of mine, may I obtain a beautiful body in a future life, with the color and fragrance of a blue lotus fully perfected; may I find no lack of men according to my thoughts and desires, and even attain great supernatural powers, so that upon encountering a Great Master, I may personally serve him."
Furthermore, in previous lives, she frequently acted as a matchmaker, causing parents, brothers, sisters, sons, daughters, and their kin to engage in unrighteous conduct together.
By virtue of her offerings and her aspiration, she has now attained this superior and wondrous body, possessing the three qualities of a flower, and she never lacks for men.
Because of acting as a matchmaker for relatives, she now receives this evil retribution from her own kin.

Furthermore, through the power of her vows, she encountered Maudgalyāyana and met me; having renounced the household life and left secular society, she has become an Arhat. Thus it should be understood.
The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī.
At that time, after the bhikṣuṇī Utpalavarṇā had attained the fruits [of the path], she revered the Triple Gem and constantly made this vow:
"Whatever food I first obtain by begging, I shall offer to the Saṃgha; whatever I obtain next by begging, I shall use for my own sustenance."
On another day, he first offered his food to the Saṃgha and intended to eat what remained himself.
Seeing a bhikṣu begging for alms with an empty bowl, he immediately gave his own portion to that person and remained without food for the rest of the day.
On the following day, she first offered food to the Saṃgha, and was about to eat herself when Upānanda came to beg for alms. Seeing the blue lotus, he thought to himself:
"Does this bhikṣuṇī offer her support only to the community of monks, or does she also have the universal intention to include individuals?"
"I should now put this to the test; let me go and seek food immediately.

With a heart of profound sincerity—lacking concern for herself and intent on saving others—the nun returned with her own portion and offered it to the Venerable One, while she herself continued to abstain from food as before.
On the third day, while wandering from door to door in the heat, his body became emaciated with hunger and he fainted upon the ground.
At that time, some non-Buddhist laypeople saw him and deliberated thus:

"We have heard that the Blue Lotus attains the fruit of liberation by being free from desire; how is it that we now see this son of the Śākyas, with such upright and handsome features, give rise to a mind of lustful passion and throw himself prostrate on the earth?"
At that time, the bhikṣus heard of this and, together with their reproaches, reported the matter to the Buddha. The Buddha said:
"I shall now establish a training rule for the bhikṣus, which should be recited as follows:
'If a bhikṣu, while on a village road, receives food with his own hand from a bhikṣuṇī who is not a relative and eats it.'"
That bhikṣu should return to the residence outside the village, go to where the other bhikṣus are, and address each of them individually, saying:
"Venerable sirs!
I have committed an offense that requires confession, which ought not to have been done; I now confess it before you."
"This is called the 'Teaching in Response' (paṭipucchāvinaya).
As for "if again a bhikṣu," this refers to Upānanda; the remaining meanings, up to "one who is not a relative," are as explained above.
"Bhikṣuṇī" refers to one who is within this Dharma.
"On the village road" means while on the way.
"With her own hand" means receiving it personally.
"Food" refers to the two types of fivefold food consisting of things that are chewed and eaten.
Furthermore, "food" refers to that which is swallowed and enters the throat.
"This bhikṣu" refers to a person who has committed an offense.
"A dwelling outside the village" refers to the location of a monastery.
"Going to where the bhikṣus are" refers to those within the monastery.
"Announcing individually" means speaking to each person separately.
Regarding "I have committed an evil dharma": this refers to the proclamation of having spoken words that constitute unwholesome dharmas which ought not to have been done.

In this context, "one who commits an offense" refers to a bhikṣu who, toward a nun who is not a relative, perceives her as such—or harbors doubt regarding it—takes with his own hand five kinds of masticable foods or five kinds of chewable foods from within a village street and swallows them; in all such cases, he incurs an offense of confession (*pratideśanīya*).
If one is a relative nun but perceives her as a non-relative, or has doubt regarding it, one incurs an *dukkaṭa* (offense of wrong-doing).
There is no offense in the cases explained at length above. 2.

The Training Rule on Receiving Food Directed by a Bhikṣuṇī. The second training rule on receiving food directed by a bhikṣuṇī. The Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, as it was a year of famine, alms were difficult to obtain; the six bhikṣus, suffering from hunger, went to the place where the twelve bhikṣuṇīs resided.
When the latter saw them, they invited them to take a light meal, but the six bhikṣus did not accept, saying:
"Sisters!..."
"When you invite me and the great assembly for a formal meal, you should direct the donor to provide us with abundant and excellent food; we shall then eat it."
At that time, a donor invited the Buddha and the Saṃgha to his residence for a meal. The bhikṣus went, but the World-Honored One did not go, because he was establishing a precept.

While the assembly of monks was eating, the nun Thullanandā said to the donor, "This venerable Nanda is a son of the Śākyas who has renounced the world to become a monk; he is well-versed in the Tripiṭaka and is a great Dharma-master. You should give him much excellent food."
The other five monks all likewise offered their praise.
Consequently, the donor gave many times more to those six individuals, causing the rest of the bhikṣus to go without food for many days.
At that time, the donor, knowing that this was contrary to the Dharma and lacked impartiality, began to revile and scold him.
The person who had received the food reported these matters in detail to the Buddha. The Buddha said:
"I have established a training rule (*śikṣāpada*), which should be recited as follows:..."
"If, moreover, a number of bhikṣus are eating at the home of a layperson, and there is a bhikṣuṇī who directs them, saying, 'This bhikṣu should be given much fine food and drink.'"
The bhikṣus should say to that bhikṣuṇī:
"Sister, please wait for a short while until the bhikṣus have finished eating."
If not a single person speaks these words, those bhikṣus should return to their residence outside the village and go to where the other bhikṣus are, addressing each one individually:
"Venerable sirs!..."
"I have committed an offense that requires confession; this was not what should have been done, and I now confess it before you.
This is called the "Dharma of Confession.
As for "a multitude of bhikṣus," this refers to two or three persons or more.
"Households of laypeople" refers to families of the four castes and so forth.
"Food" refers to food received through an invitation.
"Nun" refers to Pūtanā Nandā.
"Directing" refers to assigning tasks.
"This bhikṣu should be given abundant and excellent food and drink" means giving him food in excessive measure.
"The various bhikṣus" refers to those who utter words of reproach and prohibition.
"If there is not even one person" means that even at the minimum limit, all incur the fundamental offense.
"One should return to the residence outside the village, etc. refers to the method for confessing the offense, which is explained in detail as previously stated.

Regarding the offense herein: if a bhikṣu is eating on the upper floor while there is also food being served on the middle floor, and a bhikṣuṇī on the upper floor is directing the distribution of that food, that bhikṣu—or even a single person—should issue a reprimand to stop her.
If no one rebukes her, the bhikṣus commit the offense of speaking in the presence of another.
Among them, the bhikṣu on the lower floor should ask the bhikṣu on the upper floor:
"Has any bhikṣuṇī been rebuked?"
If one eats without being asked, one incurs an *dukkaṭa* (offense of wrong-doing) in all such cases.
If a bhikṣu is eating on the ground floor while another is eating in the gateway pavilion, if a bhikṣuṇī there gives instructions, one should reprimand her as previously described;
if one does not ask [for permission], one incurs the full offense.
Regarding the person under the porch, one should inquire as with those on the middle platform;

failure to inquire constitutes a *duṣkṛta* offense. Furthermore, if a bhikṣu is exiting the porch and another bhikṣu arrives from outside, upon hearing the sound of instructions, he should ask the one exiting:
"Has anyone rebuked a bhikṣuṇī?"
If she eats without being asked, she incurs an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*).
It should be understood in this way: if she eats at multiple locations within a single donor’s household, the nun incurs the full offense (*pācittiya*) for every location she was directed to.
All other cases constitute minor offenses; whether they are of higher or lower gravity should be understood according to the specific circumstances.
If the donor provides food for the Saṃgha on account of this nun, the bhikṣu commits no offense even if the nun directs him.

Or, although one has given instructions, if there is no discrimination in one's intention; or if one sees that someone is unable to eat and thus causes the giver to provide it—none of these constitute an offense.
Furthermore, those who are without offense are as explained in detail above.
The Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya, Volume Forty-nine.

Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Yijing by Imperial Decree. 3.
The Training Rule on Receiving Food from a Family. The third training rule concerning receiving food from a family. At that time, the Blessed One was staying in the city of Vaiśālī.

In this city there was an elder named Siṃha who had previously served non-Buddhist teachers; because he went to the Buddha’s presence to listen to and receive the Dharma, he attained the first fruit of the path.

Seeing that agricultural pursuits are fraught with many faults, he abandoned them all; he conceived deep faith in the Triple Gem, his disposition became pure and virtuous, and he constantly delighted in giving. Through his generosity toward the Triple Gem, he eventually reached the point of poverty.
At that time, Śāriputra and Mahāmaudgalyāyana came from another region to this dwelling place.
Then the householder Siṃha invited them both, requesting that they come for a meal the following day.
When the various brahmins and householders saw this, they gave rise to contempt and spoke thus:

"When the householder Siṃha followed the non-Buddhist teachers, his family estate was immense; but after he placed his faith in the bhikṣus, he suddenly fell into poverty, with clothes that do not cover his body and food that does not suffice for his mouth. Therefore, one knows that the sons of Śākya are no place of refuge."
Having heard these words, Śāriputra and Mahāmaudgalyāyana went to inform the Buddha.
The Buddha said: "O bhikṣus!

You should perform the formal procedure of a *jñapti-dvitīya-karman* for that householder Siṃha, designating him as a *śaikṣa-kuṭumbika*; you should likewise perform it for others who are in similar circumstances."
As is customary when assembling the Saṃgha, one person should perform the formal motion (*jñapti-karman*) as follows:
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!

This householder Siṃha possesses profound faith and a pure, virtuous intention; he bestows whatever he has in total generosity, never harboring avarice toward the Triple Gem, and he also provides for all who seek help. Consequently, his provisions of food and clothing have been completely exhausted."

If it is the proper time for the Saṃgha and they grant their consent, let the Saṃgha permit this: the Saṃgha now grants the *śikṣādattaka-karman* (the formal act of the householder-in-training) to the householder Siṃha.
This is the motion (*jñapti*).
The formal ritual (*karmavācanā*) should be performed according to the announcement (*jñapti*).

If a bhikṣu knows that the Saṃgha has already performed the ritual for a "family under discipline" (*śaikṣakulakarma*), he should not go there to receive food, drink, seats, or bedding, nor should he preach the Dharma for them.
At that time, although the two elders had previously accepted the invitation, they did not go to the meal because they knew it was the community’s formal practice. The Buddha said:
"If one who has accepted an invitation goes to eat, there is no offense."
The two men then went to accept the invitation. When the group of six saw them depart, they spoke thus:
"When he first realized the Truths, he also constantly invited us; it is now fitting that we go to receive his food and drink."
Having arrived there, the food and drink were insufficient; they consumed their entire allotted portions until nothing remained, and the children began to weep.
The laypeople censured them with disdain, and the bhikṣus rebuked them in disgust, saying:
"How can a bhikṣu, knowing that this is a family under formal observance, still go to that house to receive two sets of five kinds of food?"
The Blessed One, on this account, spoke at length until he established the training rule, which should be recited as follows:

"If a bhikṣu, knowing that a family of noble disciples has been granted the *śikṣādattaka-karman* by the Saṃgha, should go to that household without having previously received an invitation and take for himself with his own hand *khādanīya* or *bhojanīya* food."
That bhikṣu should return to the residence outside the village, go to where the other bhikṣus are, and address each of them individually, saying:
"Venerable sirs!
I have committed an offense that requires confession—a wrongful act that should not have been done—and I now confess it before you."
"This is called the 'Teaching in Response.
Thus the Blessed One established the training rule. At that time, the wife of the householder Siṃha said to her husband:
'For what reason has the Noble One not been seen for so long? "
Siṃha replied, "The Saṃgha knows that my family is impoverished; they performed a formal act (karmavācanā) and prohibited me from coming.
His wife said:
"If this is the case, the Saṃgha has performed the *pātrāvakarṣaṇa* (the ritual of overturning the alms-bowl) against my household; how then can my meritorious karma arise?
At that time, the elder went to inform the Buddha of these matters.
The Buddha said, "From this day forward, O Bhikṣus, when you go to the house of Siṃha to use seats and couches, and when you preach the Dharma for him, there is no offense."
When the bhikṣus went to that house, they entered with empty bowls and left with empty bowls; seeing this, his wife was filled with sorrow and dejection, her face bearing an expression of grief.
Then the bhikṣus reported the matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"A bhikṣu should not enter with an empty bowl.
Having received the Buddha's instruction, the bhikṣus went begging for food in their bowls and brought it into the house.
While the bhikṣus were eating, some young boys and girls desired the leftovers; when the bhikṣus did not give them any, the children began to weep.
They reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said, "You should give it to them."
The bhikṣus gave them whole cakes and fruits; having received them, the man and woman immediately took them outside.
When the various non-Buddhists saw this, they asked, "Where did you obtain these excellent cakes and fruits?"
He replied,
"Noble one, give it to me.
The outsider said:
"The lion takes his portion and gives it to the jackal; they pour from one vessel into another, providing for one another.
When the bhikṣus heard this, they informed the Buddha. The Buddha said:
"One should not give whole cakes or fruits; they should be broken into pieces before being given."
A member of the household brought some leaves to a bhikṣu to serve as a mat for his alms bowl, but the bhikṣu would not accept them. The Buddha said, "You should accept them.
At that time, the Licchavis of Vaiśālī, seeing that the wealth and provisions of the elder’s family were exhausted, sent laborers to assist him with the plowing and cultivation of the fields.

The lands formerly abandoned had long remained fallow, yet their soil was exceptionally fertile; with little expense, they yielded several times the harvest, and before long, food and clothing became so abundant that they surpassed those of former times by manyfold.

At that time, the elder, seeing that his household was flourishing and prosperous, yearned for a field of merit. He went to the Buddha’s dwelling and requested the lifting of the *karmavācanā* (formal act of suspension). The Buddha granted his permission.
The Buddha instructed the elder, saying:

"You should enter the monastery and report the matter in full to the *sthavira* (elder), requesting him to strike the gong to assemble the community. Before the *sthavira*, you shall prostrate toward the assembly, squat with palms joined, and make this formal announcement (*jñapti*):"
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!
My teacher Siṃha has conceived deep faith toward the Triple Gem; his intention is pure and wholesome, and he always delights in giving.

Because of his giving to the Triple Gem, he has fallen into poverty. Therefore, out of compassion for me, may the Saṃgha perform the formal ritual (karmavācanā) so that the noble assembly does not enter my home."
"Now my wealth and provisions have become abundant once more; however, my preceptor Siṃha first obtained the various dharmas. I now beg the great assembly for the lifting of the *karma*.
I pray that you will grant me the lifting of the *karmavācanā* out of compassion!"
Thus it is said three times.
Having made this announcement (*jñapti*), he pays homage to the assembly and departs.

At that time, the great assembly should appoint one person to perform the *jñapti-caturtha-karman* (the formal act consisting of one motion and three proclamations) corresponding to the matter at hand, and thus resolve the case.
Once this understanding has been established, the community of bhikṣus may proceed as they did before; whatever offerings they receive will not constitute an offense.
"If there is another bhikṣu" refers to the group of six; the rest is as explained above.
"Scholars" refers to those who have attained the realization of the truths through faith in the Triple Gem.
"Families" refers to the four castes.
"The Sangha" refers to the disciples of the World-Honored One.

Regarding the *karmavācanā*: this refers to the formal procedure consisting of one motion and one proclamation (*jñapti-dvitīya-karman*). If one goes to such a household to receive food without having previously accepted an invitation, one incurs an offense.

In this context, the transgression occurs when one receives two sets of five kinds of food in such a place; at the moment of chewing and swallowing, one incurs an offense identical to that described previously.
The method for repentance is as explained above.
If one attains the method of liberation, there is no offense regarding food.
Furthermore, those cases where there is no offense are as extensively described previously.

4. The Training Rule on Receiving Food Outside the Aranya Residence. This fourth training rule concerning receiving food outside the aranya residence was established when the Buddha was staying at the Nyagrodha Park in the city of Kapilavastu for the summer retreat.

At that time, the Śākyas, knowing that the bhikṣus had completed their earlier retreat (pūrvavārṣika), all went together to the Buddha’s dwelling on the fourteenth day of the eighth month. Having prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, they addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!...”
"Tomorrow the noble assembly will conclude the summer retreat; we shall bring food to your dwelling. We pray that the Buddha and the Sangha will graciously accept it out of compassion.
The World-Honored One remained silent.

At that time, the Śākya sons, knowing that the Buddha had accepted [the invitation], prostrated before him and withdrew. Then, on the following day, they filled carts with excellent food and drink and set out, sending various female attendants to follow them.
When they had reached the halfway point, a band of robbers came to plunder them. The leader of the robbers issued an order, saying:
"Do not seize that daughter of the Śākyas.
Disregarding his words, they stripped her of her clothes; with her body exposed, she felt ashamed and entered the grass to hide herself.
At that time, the six bhikṣus, wondering why the food was arriving so late, said to one another, "We should go out for alms;
it is not fitting to remain here for long.
As they were traveling along the road, they saw various vehicles laden with food and drink, and they immediately called out loudly:
"Who is here? At that time, the Śākya women from within the thicket called out to him from afar:
"We have been plundered by bandits and are naked and without clothes; take whatever food and drink you find as you please."
The group of six replied,
"Why do you not come out?
She answered:
"I am currently naked; how can we see one another?
She replied, "I have observed all the limbs and members of your body many times as if they were my own kin; why do you feel shame?"
"You should come out quickly and give us food and drink.
The women then came out with their bodies exposed and gave them the food; at that time, the group of six monks ate their fill and departed.

The Śākyas followed after them and, seeing that the women had been robbed, all scattered in pursuit to search for the bandits. They seized them and brought them back, intending to inflict punishment upon them, whereupon the women said:
"The bandit leader had no intention of robbing me.
Thereupon, the men released him.
At that time, the bandit leader entreated the Śākyamuni, saying:

"You all possess the flow of compassion and grace that reaches everywhere; how could you bear to kill such ignorant beings? We pray that you will release them so that their fragile lives may be preserved.
At that time, the sons of Śākya released them all and allowed them to depart, subsequently taking food and drink to the monastery to provide for the bhikṣus to eat.
The Śākya women did not give good food to the group of six monks;
when the Śākya sons asked, "For what reason do you serve the food unequally?
they replied:
"All of these have finished eating. He asked,
"Who should be given first?"
She replied,
"I gave it. The man,
finding this strange, questioned her further, and the woman answered him fully.
Upon hearing this, the Śākyas felt extreme contempt and disdain.
Then the Śākyas said to the bhikṣus:
"O Noble Ones!..."
"Why do you not have someone inform [the travelers] at the dangerous pass that we are prepared for them, so they may avoid being robbed?
The bhikṣus reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:

"At dangerous forest locations, one should appoint a bhikṣu who is accomplished in five qualities to act as a guard: he must be free from attachment, aversion, fear, and delusion, and he must know the road well."
First, one should inquire whether they are capable and exhort them with the details of the task.

If they say they are capable, they should be dispatched by means of a *jñapti-dvitīya-karman* (a formal motion followed by one proclamation). One person should then perform the *jñapti-karman* (the formal motion) in accordance with the specific task to be carried out.
The Buddha addressed the bhikṣus:
"I shall now explain the rules of conduct for a bhikṣu who is on guard duty.
A bhikṣu on guard duty must thoroughly inspect the area within half a yojana on all four sides of the monastery."
If there is a place of danger, one should emit smoke, or hang banners and flags, or spread tree leaves across the road, or write characters to inform others.
If there is no danger, one should hang white banners.
If one does not follow this rule of conduct, one incurs a *dukkaṭa* offense.
If the guardian is hungry and requires food, he may eat rice as he pleases during the morning meal; if a companion is required, one should provide him with one.

At that time, the bhikṣus heard that those six groups of monks had caused naked women to give them food and drink in a dangerous and terrifying forest outside the monastery. They were filled with mutual shame and reported the matter in detail to the Buddha. The Buddha said:
“To speak at length, [the Buddha] established a training rule for the bhikṣus, which should be recited as follows:

‘If a bhikṣu dwells in a forest hermitage in a place of fear and danger, and if there is no one previously stationed there to observe for risks and difficulties, yet he accepts food outside his dwelling and eats it, that bhikṣu must return to the residence and go before the other bhikṣus, addressing each of them individually, saying:’”
"Venerable One!
I have committed an offense that requires confession; it was improper for me to do so, and I now confess it before you.
This is called the "Dharma of Confession."
"Furthermore, 'if a bhikṣu' refers to the group of six [monks].
The meaning of 'araṇya' (wilderness) is as explained in the section on the *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* rules.
'Without observation' means that no person has been appointed to guard it."
"Outside the residence" means being outside the monastery.
Regarding the "two sets of five" [offenses], they are also as explained above.
As for the offense herein: if a bhikṣu is in a place of danger or fear where there is no guardian, and he perceives it as such or suspects it to be so, he incurs the full offense.
The next two phrases constitute minor offenses, while the final two involve no offense.
If there is a guardian at a dangerous location, there is no offense when eating there.
Furthermore, those cases involving no offense are as explained extensively above.
7. Numerous Rules of Training. Regarding the numerous rules of training: The Buddha was staying at Vārāṇasī, in the Deer Park at Ṛṣipatana.
At that time, although the five bhikṣus had gone forth, they still wore the dress of laypeople; their deportment and appearance were not at all dignified.
At that time, the World-Honored One had this thought:
"How did the Buddhas of the past instruct the assembly of śrāvakas regarding the wearing of robes?
Then, the devas addressed the Buddha, saying:
"It is like the garments worn by the gods of the Śuddhāvāsa heavens.
The Blessed One, observing with his divine eye that the matter was no different from what the gods had said, addressed the bhikṣus:
"From this day forward, you should wear the nivāsana robes in a neat and rounded manner, just like the gods of the Śuddhāvāsa heavens."
At that time, the six bhikṣus wore their robes too high; when the brahmins and others of pure faith saw that they were not properly adjusted, they gave rise to derision and spoke thus:
"These bhikṣus wear their robes improperly, just like shameless people."
When the bhikṣus heard this, they informed the Buddha.
The Buddha said, "One should not wear one's robes too high; you should train yourselves accordingly.
When the group of six heard this, they wore their robes too low. The laypeople again criticized and disparaged them, so the Buddha said:
"One should not wear the robes too low, like a newly married woman; this is how one should train.
At other times, they let the front of the robe hang down long, like the trunk of an elephant, which caused the laypeople to criticize and find it offensive. The Buddha said:
"One should not let the front hang down."
At times, the fine pleats at the waist were criticized by the laity; the Buddha said:
"One should not wear the robe like a palm leaf; this is how you should train."
At times, they would gather one corner of their robe and tuck it behind their waist like the head of a snake; the laypeople criticized and disparaged this, so the Buddha said:
"One should not tuck the robe behind the waist like the head of a snake; this is how you should train."
At another time, he grasped the upper corner [of his robe] and tucked it into his waist like a ball of beans. The Buddha said:
"One should not wear the robe like a ball of beans; you should train yourself thus."
Thus the Blessed One established this training rule for the bhikṣus, which should be recited as follows:
"One should train oneself to wear the lower robe neatly;
one should train oneself not to wear it too high, not too low, not like an elephant’s trunk, not like a snake’s hood, not like a *tāla* leaf, and not in the shape of a bean ball."
The Buddha said:
"One should train oneself to wear the three robes in a neat and orderly manner.
At that time, the six bhikṣus wore their robes too high; when faithful brahmins and others saw them were not properly adjusted, they began to mock them, saying these words:
"These bhikṣus wear their robes in such a disarray that they resemble those who have no sense of shame.
When the bhikṣus heard this, they informed the Buddha. The Buddha said:
"One should not wear the three robes too high; you should train yourselves accordingly."
When the group of six monks heard this, they wore their three robes too low; the laypeople criticized and disparaged them. The Buddha said:
"One should not wear the three robes too low like a newly married woman; you should train yourselves accordingly."
Or, some wore the upper robe with one corner hanging down in front like an elephant’s trunk; the laypeople criticized and disparaged this, as described at length above.
Thus, the Blessed One established this training rule for the bhikṣus, which should be recited as follows:
“One should train oneself to wear the three robes in a neat and orderly manner.”

One should train oneself thus: when entering the house of a layperson, one should not go too high nor too low; one should properly arrange the upper robe and properly cover the body; one should speak little and not look upward.
The Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove.
At that time, the six bhikṣus of the group entered the homes of laypeople with their heads covered.
When some brahmins of pure faith saw them with their heads thus covered, they spoke as follows:
"This is like a shameless person or a newlywed bride.
When the bhikṣus heard this, they informed the Buddha. The Buddha said:
"One should not enter the homes of laypeople with one's head covered; you should train yourselves thus."

The group of six bhikṣus entered the houses of laypeople with their robes tucked up on one side; consequently, the Buddha said, "One should train not to enter the houses of laypeople with the robe tucked up on one side.

The group of six bhikṣus entered the houses of laypeople with their robes tucked up on both sides; consequently, the Buddha said, "One should train not to enter the houses of laypeople with the robe tucked up on both sides."
The group of six bhikṣus entered the homes of laypeople with their hands on their hips; consequently, the Buddha said: "One should train not to enter the homes of laypeople with hands on the hips.

The group of six bhikṣus entered the homes of laypeople while slapping their shoulders against one another; consequently, the Buddha said: "One should train not to enter the homes of laypeople while slapping shoulders."
When the bhikṣus had heard this, they informed the Buddha. The Buddha said:
"To speak at length, up until the point where I establish a training rule for the bhikṣus, it should be stated as follows:

'One should train oneself not to enter the houses of laypeople with the head covered, nor with the robe tucked up on one side, nor with the robe tucked up on both sides, nor with hands on the hips, nor by slapping the shoulders.'"
The Buddha was staying at Jetavana.

At that time, the group of six bhikṣus entered the homes of laypeople while walking in a crouching posture. When the brahmins and others of pure faith saw them walking in this manner, they spoke thus:
"They are people as shameless as those who have no modesty."
When the bhikṣus heard this, they informed the Buddha.
The Buddha said, “One should not enter the houses of laypeople while walking on tiptoe; you should train yourselves accordingly.

This continued until a bhikṣu entered the house of a layperson walking on his toes. Thereupon the Buddha said, “One should not enter the houses of laypeople walking on one’s toes; you should train yourselves accordingly.”
A bhikṣu entered the house of a layperson while hopping; consequently, the Buddha said: "One should train oneself not to enter the house of a layperson while hopping.
A bhikṣu entered the house of a layperson while stamping his feet; consequently, the Buddha said: "One should train oneself not to enter the house of a layperson while stamping one's feet."
When a bhikṣu entered the house of a layperson with his body tensed, the Buddha said:
“To speak at length, [the Buddha] established a training rule for the bhikṣus, which should be recited as follows:
‘One should train oneself not to enter the house of a layperson sitting while squatting, nor walking on tiptoes, nor hopping, nor stamping the feet, nor with the body tensed.’”
The Buddha was staying at Jetavana.
At that time, the group of six bhikṣus swayed their bodies as they entered the homes of laypeople. When the brahmins and others of pure faith saw them swaying, they spoke these words:
"They are people of equal shamelessness."
When the bhikṣus had heard this, they informed the Buddha. The Buddha said:
"One should not sway the body when entering the home of a layperson; you should train yourselves accordingly.
When a bhikṣu entered the home of a layperson with his arms dangling, the Buddha said:
"One should not enter the house of a layperson with arms swinging; this is how one should train.
When a bhikṣu entered the house of a layperson shaking his head, the Buddha said:
"One should not enter the house of a layperson shaking one's head; this is how one should train."
When bhikṣus entered the homes of laypeople jostling shoulder-to-shoulder, the Buddha said:
"One should not enter the homes of laypeople jostling shoulder-to-shoulder; this is how you should train.
When bhikṣus entered the homes of laypeople holding hands, the Buddha said:
"One should not enter the homes of laypeople holding hands; this is how you should train.
The Buddha said:
"To speak at length, up until the point where he established the training rule for the bhikṣus, it should be stated as follows:"
"One should train oneself thus: when entering the house of a layperson, one shall not sway the body, nor dangle the arms, nor shake the head, nor shove with the shoulders, nor join hands.
This was spoken by the Buddha while he was at Jetavana.
At that time, the six bhikṣus were in the house of a layperson; when others had not yet invited them to sit, they sat down of their own accord.
When the brahmins and others of pure faith saw them sitting down on their own initiative, they spoke these words:
"They are as shameless as those who have no sense of modesty."
When the bhikṣus had heard this, they informed the Buddha. The Buddha said:
"To speak at length, up until the point where I establish a training rule for the bhikṣus, it should be stated thus:
'In the home of a layperson, one should not sit down abruptly when not invited to do so; this is how you should train.'"
The Buddha was staying at the Jeta Grove in Śrāvastī.
At that time, the six bhikṣus of the group sat down abruptly in the house of a layperson without first inspecting it properly.
When the pure-faithed Brahmins and others saw them sit down abruptly in a layperson's house without careful observation, they remarked,
"They are as shameless as those who have no sense of decorum.
When the bhikṣus heard this, they informed the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"Having explained at length, up to the point of establishing the training rule for the bhikṣus, it should be stated as follows:
'One should train oneself not to sit in the house of a layperson without having observed it well.'"

At that time, after twelve years had passed, the World-Honored One arrived at the city of Kapilavastu. On the first day, he took his meal within the royal palace; on the second day, he accepted offerings within his own palace. When the Buddha and the assembly were eating, Lady Gopī personally served the food with her own hands.
At that time, the Venerable Udāyin failed to restrain his body, causing Lady Gopī to find his conduct improper.

On another occasion, he went alone into the palace; the lady had him sit on a dilapidated bed, and as he sat down with full force, the bed broke and he fell to the ground, leading to public ridicule and shame. [The details] are related at length until the Buddha said:
"When a bhikṣu sits in a layperson's home, he should not sit with his body relaxed; he should sit with careful observation. This is how you should train."

Or they sit with their feet crossed in a layperson’s house; or they sit with their inner and outer ankles overlapping; or they draw their feet up tightly, or stretch them out long; or they sit with their bodies exposed.
The laity criticized and complained about this. The Buddha said:
"It should not be so. A training rule must be established:

When in the house of a layperson, one should train oneself not to cross one's legs, not to cross the inner ankles, not to cross the outer ankles, not to draw the feet up too tightly, not to stretch the feet out too far, and not to expose the body."
The Buddha was staying at Jiangzhushan.

At that time, a donor invited the Buddha and the Saṃgha to his residence for a meal. The person serving the food was not careful in his attentiveness and dropped a fine ball of rice; the bhikṣu did not guard his bowl with respect, and consequently, it was broken many times.
The Buddha said:
"One should train oneself to receive food with reverence.
This was when the Buddha was at Mount Jiangzhu.

At that time, the six bhikṣus entered the house of the householder Bodhi to beg for alms. When the householder gave them food, they accepted a full bowl of rice and then further accepted soup; the bowl consequently overflowed, and the excess spilled out, staining the ground and giving rise to public derision.
He reported the matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"I shall establish a training rule (śikṣāpada). It should be stated as follows:

'One must not receive rice in a bowl so full that it overflows when soup or vegetables are added; one should leave space around the rim of the bowl, measuring the width of a finger, and receive food with deliberate care. This is how you should train.'"
Some monks extended their bowls in advance before food had even arrived, manifesting the appearance of greedy beggars and thereby giving rise to derision and shame.
When this matter was reported to the Buddha, the Buddha said:
"I shall establish a training rule (śikṣāpada). It should be stated as follows:"
"One should train oneself: 'Do not extend the bowl in advance before the food has arrived.
One should train oneself: 'Do not place the bowl atop the food.
Furthermore, when eating, one should not manifest signs of arrogance, such as those of young children or courtesans. Thus spoke the Buddha.
"One should not eat with such arrogance; one should eat with reverence; thus one should train.
Furthermore, regarding those who, while eating, take morsels that are either too small or too large, like a poor beggar, the Buddha said:
"One should not do so. One should train to eat with morsels that are neither too small nor too large, but in a rounded and orderly manner."
The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī.
At that time, a donor invited the Buddha and the Saṃgha to his residence for a meal.
On this occasion, the bhikṣu Upānanda sat in immediate proximity to an elderly bhikṣu (mahallaka).
At that time, the mahallaka opened his mouth wide and looked upward; then Upānanda took a clod of earth and hurled it from afar into his mouth, saying, "Eat this for now."
The Buddha said:
"One should not open one's mouth in anticipation in this manner.
One should train oneself: 'If food has not yet arrived, I shall not open my mouth to wait for it.'"
The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī.
At that time, a donor invited the Buddha and the Saṃgha to his house for a meal.
Then the six bhikṣus of the group of six spoke while chewing their food, which caused the laypeople to criticize and disparage them.
"The śramaṇas, sons of the Śākyas, have no sense of shame or modesty; they are no different from the laity.
Thus, people together gave rise to reproach and censure.
They reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"One should not speak with food in one's mouth; this is how one should train.

Furthermore, when visiting the home of a donor, if one sees that the soup and vegetables are scant and fears they will not suffice, one might first ask for some soup and cover it with rice, hoping to receive more. Laypeople then criticize and find this offensive.
The Buddha said: "One should not act in this way. One must not cover soup or vegetables with rice, nor cover rice with soup or vegetables in the hope of obtaining more; this is how one should train."

At that time, there was a donor who invited the bhikṣus for a meal. If the food was excessively sweet, the group of six would immediately click their tongues and tell one another that the food was very sour.
Or, if the food was excessively sour, the group of six would immediately smack their lips and tell one another that the food was very sweet.
Once, a donor invited the bhikṣus for a meal, but the food was too hot.
The group of six immediately blew on it and signaled one another, saying, "The food is very cold," and only after blowing on it to make it appear hot did they eat.
Once, when a donor invited the bhikṣus for a meal, the food was excessively cold; the group of six immediately blew upon it and signaled one another, saying, "The food is very hot;
one must blow on it before eating."
"All of these are inverted explanations of the matter, and thus they distress the donors.
The Buddha said,
"You should not do so."
The training rule to be observed:

"One should train oneself not to make a clicking sound with the tongue while eating, not to make smacking sounds while eating, not to eat by blowing air onto the food, and not to eat by puffing air onto the food."

On another occasion, when the group of six monks was receiving an invitation for a meal, they scattered the food with their hands like chickens or birds; some spoke ill of the food and disparaged one another; others stuffed their cheeks with food and nibbled it out bit by bit; others took half-bites, leaving the other half behind; and others stuck out their tongues to lick their lips and mouths.
The Buddha said: "A training rule should be established:

'One shall not scatter food with the hand, shall not disparage the food, shall not stuff the cheeks with food, shall not take half-bites, and shall not stick out the tongue; this is how one should train.'"
The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī.

At that time, there was a donor who had previously taken refuge in the naked ascetics (nirgranthas), but having recently developed faith and reverence, he took refuge in the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha. He then invited the Buddha and the monks to his house for a meal.
At that time, the donor was serving various foods, including balls of parched grain, thin cakes, and radishes.
Then the group of six monks, wishing to mock the donor, fashioned a stūpa out of the balls of parched grain, placed a radish on top, and covered it with a thin cake.
They then said to one another, "This is the stūpa of Pūraṇa Kāśyapa, the naked ascetic from the miserable realms."
As they gradually began to eat it, the radish toppled over, whereupon they said to one another, "This was a stūpa built by a naked ascetic; now it has collapsed."
When the donor saw this, his heart of reverence subsided.
The Buddha said:
"A training rule (śikṣāpada) should be established:..."
"One should train oneself not to eat in the manner of a *stūpa*.

At one time, when the group of six monks accepted an invitation to a meal, they had some choice food remaining on their hands; they then repeatedly licked their hands with their tongues, and did the same with their alms bowls.
At times he would shake his hand or even shake his alms-bowl; that is to say, he would sprinkle water from the bowl onto others to soil their robes, out of envy for the fine garments they wore.
The Buddha said:
"All such things as these should not be done; you should train yourselves accordingly.
At that time, there was a donor who provided a meal for the assembly of monks, and [the Buddha] addressed him, saying:
"Noble ones!
There is much fine food; do not accept so much parched grain.
The group of six did not believe him and accepted a great deal of parched grain. Later, seeing the fine food, they wished to discard the parched grain.
Seated nearby was a certain mahallaka bhikṣu who was looking around in all directions.
At that moment, the group of six took balls of parched grain and placed them into his bowl until it was overflowing, leaving him no time to receive any more.
The Buddha said:
"One should always look at one's bowl while eating; this is how you should train.
At that time, there was a bhikṣu whose bowl was full during a meal, and the group of six monks watched him from the side and together showed contempt, saying:
"This mahallaka is capable of devouring [everything]," [someone said].
The Buddha said:
"One should train oneself not to look into the bowl of a fellow practitioner with a mind of contempt."
The group of six bhikṣus held the pure water flask with soiled hands, causing flies to swarm and gather around it, thereby inviting reproach and disgrace.
The Buddha said:
"One should train oneself not to hold the pure water flask with dirty hands."

The group of six bhikṣus were at Gaṅgāpura Hill, where they ate atop the high pavilion of the householder Bodhi; they discarded the water used for washing their bowls onto the fine ground, which caused the donor to feel resentment.
The Buddha said:
"A training rule should be established:
One should train oneself not to discard the water used for rinsing the bowl in the house of a layperson, unless one has asked the host."
The setting was in Śrāvastī. At that time, there was a Brahmin whose young son had fallen ill. A lay follower (*upāsaka*) who was a friend of his came and told him:
"If your child is ill, you should go to the Jeta Grove and beg for water from the bowls of the bhikṣus; have him wash and bathe with it, and he will surely recover."
At that time, the brahmin went to seek water and saw Upānanda begging for bowl-water.
Upānanda then placed the leftover rice and gruel inside the bowl-water and handed it to him. Seeing the mixture of water, the brahmin conceived a sense of revulsion and spoke these words:
"My son would rather die; who could use such vile and foul things to bathe?"
He reported the matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said: "One should not offer such foul water to others.

If someone comes to beg for bowl-water, one should wash the bowl clean, place pure water within it, and recite the *Ariṣa-gāthā* mantra three times before giving it to that person. Whether they wash with it or drink it, it can eliminate ten thousand ailments. The *Ariṣa-gāthā* refers to verses spoken by the Buddha that appear within the Holy Teachings; when recited, they possess great power. Any instances elsewhere where one is instructed to recite a *gāthā* are all of this same category."

For instance, when bathing or drinking water at a pond, river, or well; when resting briefly under a tree to seek coolness before departing; when staying in a guesthouse or entering a shrine hall to tread upon a maṇḍala or step on the shadow of a Buddha stūpa; when one’s own shadow obscures the image of the Honored One; when the great assembly disperses; when entering a city or village; when performing prostrations to the Honored One’s form at dawn or dusk; after every meal; or when sweeping and cleaning a stūpa or temple—such instances are indeed numerous. In all these cases, one must recite a gāthā and perform the practice to obtain merit. If one intentionally neglects or shows contempt for these, one incurs the offense of *duṣkṛta* (misdeed).
However, because this was not previously practiced by the monastic community of the East River, I have included it here in my commentary so that you may know it as part of the sacred teachings.
Regarding those verses found therein, there is a stanza that says:
"The pleasures of the five desires of the world, Or even the pleasures of the various heavens;..."
Compared to the bliss of the exhaustion of craving, it does not equal even one-thousandth part.
Because accumulation gives rise to suffering, and from suffering, accumulation arises again;
by means of the Noble Eightfold Path, one can transcend and reach the sublime state of Nirvana.
"Whoever practices giving will certainly obtain its benefit;
if one gives for the sake of happiness, they will surely attain peace and joy in the future.
Thus spoke the Buddha.
"One should train oneself: 'One must not place leftover food into the water inside the bowl.
At that time, there was a bhikṣu who placed his bowl on the ground without a cushion or stand beneath it; this led to public reproach and caused the bowl to deteriorate quickly.
The Buddha said: "A training rule should be established: [as follows...]"
"One should train oneself: 'One must not place the bowl on the bare ground without a mat.
At that time, a bhikṣu was washing his bowl while standing; he lost his grip, and the bowl fell to the ground and broke.
The Buddha said: 'One should train oneself: "One must not wash the bowl while standing."'"
At that time, there was a bhikṣu who placed his bowl on the edge of a dangerous precipice. The Buddha said:
"One should not do so; one should train oneself not to place a bowl on the edge of a dangerous precipice."
The river’s current was swift, so he scooped up water against the flow with his bowl, which subsequently broke it. The Buddha said:
“You should not do this; you must not scoop water against the current. You should train yourself thus.”
The group of six bhikṣus stood while their interlocutors sat, preaching the Dharma to them.
At that time, there were brahmins and householders who had faith and reverence for the Triple Gem, who rebuked and stopped the bhikṣus, saying:

"The Great Teacher, the World-Honored One, diligently practiced austerities over immeasurable kalpas, sacrificing his head, eyes, marrow, brain, kingdom, city, wife, and children, in order to seek and attain this Dharma."
"How is it that you, out of a spirit of negligence, preach the Dharma while others are seated and you yourself are standing?
The Buddha said, "You should not do so;
one should train oneself thus: 'When another is seated and I am standing, I shall not preach the Dharma.'"
At that time, there was a sick person who was unable to stand for long while listening to the Dharma. The Buddha said:

"If such a sick person is sitting or lying down—whether on high or low ground, on a path or a non-path, or in a carriage; or if they are wearing boots, covering their head, wearing a crown, flower garlands, or necklaces; or if they are holding a parasol, a sword, or a staff; or if they are clad in armor and the like."
If the listener is ill, there is no offense in preaching the Dharma to them regardless of one's own posture. To establish this training rule, it should be stated as follows:
"One should train oneself not to preach the Dharma while standing to someone who is seated, except in cases of illness."
"One should train oneself: unless the person is ill, one shall not preach the Dharma to someone who is lying down while one is sitting.
One should train oneself: unless the person is ill, one shall not preach the Dharma to someone who is on a high seat while one is on a low seat."
"One should train oneself: 'If another person is walking in front and I am walking behind, I shall not preach the Dharma to them, except in the case of illness.
One should train oneself: 'If another person is on the path and I am off the path, I shall not preach the Dharma to them, except in the case of illness.'"

"One should train oneself: except in the case of illness, one must not preach the Dharma to those who have their heads covered, those who have tucked up one side of their robe, those who have tucked up both sides of their robe, those who have their hands on their hips, or those who are slapping their shoulders."
"One should train oneself: except in cases of illness, one shall not preach the Dharma to those riding elephants, nor to those riding horses, nor to those in palanquins, nor to those in carriages."
"One should train oneself: 'I shall not preach the Dharma to those wearing wooden clogs, boots, shoes, or sandals, except when they are ill.

One should train oneself: 'I shall not preach the Dharma to those wearing hats or crowns, nor to those with their hair tied in a topknot like a Buddha’s usnīṣa, nor to those with their heads wrapped, nor to those wearing flower garlands, except when they are ill.'"
"One should train oneself thus: 'I shall not preach the Dharma to one who holds a sunshade, except in the case of illness.
This occurred at Kapilavastu, when Upānanda stood while defecating or urinating.
When the laypeople saw this, they spoke with reproach and disdain, saying:
"Your teacher, the World-Honored One, always maintains a sense of shame; how can you all feel no shame or embarrassment to stand and discharge impurity just like common worldly folk?"
The Buddha said:
"One should not do so; one must not stand while defecating or urinating.
Except in cases of illness, this is how one should train."

At that time, Upānanda saw some green grass and asked for it to use; when the owner refused to give it to him, he took laxatives and, using an impure bowl, sprinkled the contents upon the grass at night, thereby ruining its utility.
Upānanda went to his house and, seeing him distressed, asked the reason for his sorrow. He answered in full.
Upānanda said, "It was I who treated you;
it was not because you failed to offer grass."
Because of this, people began to revile him. The Buddha said:
"You should not do so. One must not void excrement, urine, mucus, or saliva upon green grass, except in cases of illness; you should train yourself in this."

At that time, Upānanda took his own old garment and had a washerman wash it; when the man refused to wash it, Upānanda gave rise to a mind of anger and intentionally discharged impurity into the water where he was washing clothes.
At that time, he inadvertently touched the water with his hand and soiled it; he then began to revile [the Buddha].
The Buddha said:
"You should not do so. One must not defecate, urinate, spit, or expectorate in the water, except when ill; this is how you should train."
The Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.

At that time, a donor in the city invited the Buddha and the Saṃgha to his house for a meal, while the monastery guard remained to protect the temple. Upānanda, having been invited by him for food, wished to play a trick on him and did not return quickly.
Having departed from the city and reached the Jetavana Grove, he measured the distance between them by pacing the ground; how much ground was there?
At that time, the monastery attendant marveled at his lateness and, fearing that the time for the meal would pass, climbed a tall tree to gaze out for his return.
At that time, some laypeople saw this and mocked him, saying, "The śramaṇa son of the Śākyas has climbed a tall tree; he is no different from a worldly person.
The Buddha said:
"One must not do so; one shall not climb a tree higher than the height of a person.
At that time, there was a bhikṣu who, because he had tied a dyeing rope [to his waist], did not dare to ascend a tree.
Furthermore, when the danger of tigers and wolves approached, he still did not dare to ascend, and as a result, he was killed. The Buddha said:
"One shall not climb a tree higher than a person's height, except in cases of emergency; this is how one should train.
The rules for training (śaikṣa-dharma) are concluded. 8.
The Seven Methods for Settling Disputes (saṃthaṇā-dharma). A summary verse (uddāna) says:
In the presence [of the accused], and through recollection; through being of sound mind, and through confessing the offense;
by the majority vote, and by one’s own admission; by the "covering over with grass"—these are the means for resolving communal disputes.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
“There are seven methods for settling disputes that should be practiced and studied.
One should apply the *vinaya* of presence; one should apply the *vinaya* of presence.
One should apply the *vinaya* of recollection; one should apply the *vinaya* of recollection.”
To one who deserves the *amūḍha-vinaya*, the *amūḍha-vinaya* should be granted;
to one who deserves the *tatsvabhāva-aiṣīya-vinaya*, the *tatsvabhāva-aiṣīya-vinaya* should be granted.
If the *yadbhūyaḥkṛta-vinaya* should be granted, the *yadbhūyaḥkṛta-vinaya* shall be granted.
If the *pratijñā-kṛta-vinaya* should be granted, the *pratijñā-kṛta-vinaya* shall be granted.
“The *tṛṇastāraka* (covering with grass) vinaya should be granted; indeed, the *tṛṇastāraka* vinaya shall be granted.
If any dispute arises, it should be extinguished in accordance with the Dharma and the Vinaya, following the seven methods taught by the Great Teacher.”
"Patience is the highest among forms of diligence; it can lead to the state of Nirvana.
One who causes distress to others while claiming to have left the household life is not called a śramaṇa."
This is the precept scripture spoken by the Tathāgata Vipaśyin, the Truly Enlightened One:
“As one with clear vision avoids dangerous paths and can reach a place of safety,
so too does the wise person within the realm of sentient beings remain far removed from all evils.”
"This is the precept scripture spoken by the Tathāgata Śikhin, the Samyaksaṃbuddha:
'Neither reviling nor harming, one should well protect this precept scripture;
knowing moderation in food and drink, one should use humble bedding.'"
"Diligently cultivate superior concentration; this is the teaching of all Buddhas.
Thus spoke the Tathāgata Viśvabhū, the Perfectly Awakened One, regarding this precept scripture.
"Just as a bee gathers from a flower, Without harming its color or fragrance,
But taking only its nectar to depart— So should a bhikṣu enter a village.
This is the precept scripture spoken by the Tathāgata, the Samyaksaṃbuddha Krakucchanda.
"Do not oppose others; do not look at what they have done or left undone.
But examine your own conduct alone, whether it is right or wrong.
This is the precept scripture spoken by the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha Kanakamuni.
"Do not be attached to a concentrated mind; diligently cultivate the state of tranquility.
One who is able to save themselves has no sorrow, and should always ensure that mindfulness is not lost.
If a person can practice giving, their merit will increase and enmity will naturally cease."
"By practicing good, one eliminates all evils; when delusion is exhausted, one reaches Nirvāṇa.
This is the precept scripture spoken by the Tathāgata, the Samyaksaṃbuddha Kāśyapa.
“Commit no evil in any way; cultivate all that is good;
thoroughly discipline your own mind—this is the teaching of all Buddhas.
To guard the body is excellent; to guard speech is also excellent.”
To guard the mind is excellent; to guard it completely is most excellent.
A bhikṣu who guards all [the sense faculties] can liberate himself from all suffering;
he should well-guard his verbal speech and also well-guard his mind.
"Not committing any evil with the body, Always purifying the three types of action—
This is how one can follow The path traveled by the Great Sage.
These were the words of the Precepts Sūtra spoken by the Tathāgata Śākyamuni, the Samyaksaṃbuddha.
Vipaśyin, Śikhin, Viśvabhū, Krakucchanda,
Kanakamuni, Kāśyapa, and the Honored One Śākyamuni—
such are the Gods among Gods, the unsurpassed Tamer of Men.
The seven Buddhas were all heroic and powerful, capable of protecting the world;
possessing great renown, they all proclaimed this Sūtra of Precepts.
All Buddhas and their disciples together revere and honor the precepts.
By revering the Sūtra on the Precepts, one attains the unsurpassed fruit.
You should seek liberation and diligently practice the Buddha's teaching;
subdue the army of birth and death, as an elephant destroys a thatched hut.
In this Dharma and Vinaya, by always practicing heedfulness, one can exhaust the ocean of afflictions and reach the end of suffering.
For this purpose the Prātimokṣa Sūtra was spoken; together, let us perform the Poṣadha ceremony.
We should all together revere the precepts, As the yak loves its tail.
I have now recited the Sūtra of Precepts; The Saṃgha has completed the Poṣadha ceremony.
May the merit and blessings benefit all sentient beings, And may they all together attain the Way of the Buddha.
The Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya, Fascicle Fifty.
